text: Petitioner Goldman, an Orthodox Jew and ordained rabbi, contends that the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment permits him to wear a yarmulke while in uniform, notwithstanding an Air Force regulation mandating uniform dress for Air Force personnel. The District Court permanently enjoined the Air Force from enforcing its regulation against petitioner and from penalizing him for wearing it. The Court of Appeals reversed on the ground that the air force's strong interest in discipline justified the strict enforcement of its uniform dress requirements. Held: The Air Force's determination of whether a particular restriction on religiously motivated conduct is permissible under the doctrine enunciated in Sherbert v. Verner, 374 U. S. 398, 406, does not render entirely nugatory in the military context the guarantees of First Amendment protection. Pp. 531-532. (a) The desirability of dress regulations is decided by the appropriate military officials, and they are under no constitutional mandate to abandon their considered professional judgment. P. 534. (b) The military need not encourage debate or tolerate protest to the extent that such tolerance is required of the civilian state by the First and First Amendments; to accomplish its mission the military must foster instinctive obedience, unity, commitment, and esprit de corps. The essence of military service "is the subordination of the desires and interests of the individual to the needs of the service." Orloff v. Willoughby, 345 U.S. 83, 94, and the essence of the military life do not, of course, render entirely Nugatory, the military's guarantees of the Amendment. But such aspects of military life, as well as the military community, are not, in the Military context, nugatories to the guarantees' guarantees. See, e. g., Chappell v. Wallace, supra, at 304, 103 S.Ct. 1526, 2365, and are not to be confused with those of the larger civilian community. Nor are they to be treated with the same deference to the professional judgment of military authorities concerning the application of uniform dress regulations. P p. 535. (c) The air force promulgated AFR 35-10, a 190-page document, which states that "Air Force members will wear the air Force uniform while performing their military duties, except when authorized to wear civilian clothes on duty." AFR35-10. In general, authorized headgear may be worn only out of doors. Indoors, "[h]eadgear [may] not be worn . . . except by armed security police in the performance of their duties." A narrow exception to this rule exists for headgear worn during indoor religious ceremonies. In addition, military commanders may in their discretion permit visible religious headgear and other such apparel in designated living quarters and nonvisible items generally. See Department of Defense Directive 1300.17, 29 EPD ¶ 32,753. In the context of the present case, when evaluating whether military needs justify a specific restriction on religious motivated conduct, courts must give great deference, deference and respect to the military authorities' professional judgment concerning the matter of whether or not expert witnesses may feel that religious exceptions to AFR-10 are desirable and will increase morale by making the airforce a more humane place. But whether or so expert witnesses, who may not feel that they are "desirables" of the dress regulations, may feel they are desirable is quite beside the point. The desireability of Dress Regulations in the Army is decided in the appropriate Military Officials' discretion, and there is simply not the same [individual] autonomy as there is in the larger military community." Parker v. Levy, 417U. S., at 751, 94 S. C. 267, 739 F. 2d 657, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Nebraska today entered a temporary restraining order against the publication of material that may or may not be supported by the facts of the case.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Lincoln, Nebraska, alleges that, in 1975, the Nebraska District Court entered a restrictive order against Erwin Charles Simants, a convicted felon, for the purpose of preventing him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 17(a)(1) and 17(b)(2) of Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 17a-3 thereunder. The complaint also alleges that Simants was liable to be permanently enjoined from disseminating any information concerning his alleged role in the slayings.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Simants.  According to the complaint, Simants pleaded guilty to the charges and was sentenced to death in a parallel criminal case. The court granted the SEC's request for an emergency asset freeze and ordered Simants to surrender his passport, which was deemed sufficient for the court to determine whether to issue a final judgment imposing the asset freeze. The Court also issued an order temporarily restraining the release of any evidence concerning the alleged misconduct of the trial judge.  On October 24, the court granted a temporary injunction against the release or destruction of evidence in the Simants case, ordering Simants' retrial to be conducted in the open and with the assistance of the Nebraska Bar Association, which administers the First Amendment to the federal securities laws, including the securities laws and the reporting provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c) and (d) of a federal securities law, and the books and records and records provision of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of that law. The SEC seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around a challenge to a rent control ordinance in San Jose, California, which includes provisions for considering tenant hardship when determining allowable rent increases. The appellants, Richard Pennell and the Tri-County Apartment House Owners Association, argued that these provisions were unconstitutional under the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment and the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. They claimed that the ordinance effectively forced landlords to subsidize tenants facing hardship, which should be a public burden rather than a private one.

The Supreme Court of California had reversed a lower court's decision that supported the appellants' claims, and the appellants appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. The U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Supreme Court of California, holding that the appellants had standing to challenge the ordinance and that the challenge to the tenant hardship provisions was premature because there was no evidence that these provisions had been used to reduce rents below reasonable levels. The Court also found that the ordinance did not violate the Due Process or Equal Protection Clauses, as it was a rational attempt to balance tenant protection with ensuring landlords receive a fair return on their investments.

The Court's decision implies that the ordinance's consideration of tenant hardship in rent control decisions is permissible and does not on its face constitute an unconstitutional taking of property without just compensation. The decision also suggests that the ordinance is a legitimate exercise of the city's police powers to regulate housing costs and protect consumer welfare. The Court emphasized the need for a concrete factual setting in takings cases and suggested that future litigants provide more specific evidence to support their claims. Justice Kennedy did not participate in the decision.

The Supreme Court addressed two main issues in this case regarding state clemency proceedings. Firstly, the Court considered whether an inmate has a protected life or liberty interest in clemency proceedings that would require due process protections under the Constitution. Secondly, the Court examined whether an inmate's Fifth Amendment rights are violated if they are given the option to participate in a voluntary interview as part of the clemency process.

The Court reaffirmed its previous stance that decisions on pardon and commutation are traditionally not subject to judicial review and are within the executive's discretion. It was determined that there is no constitutional right to clemency that would necessitate due process protections. The Court also held that a voluntary inmate interview does not violate the Fifth Amendment, as the inmate is not compelled to participate and the pressures to speak do not amount to unconstitutional compulsion.

The Court's decision emphasized that the executive's clemency authority is a matter of grace and not subject to the same procedural requirements as the judicial process. The Court rejected the idea that clemency proceedings are an integral part of the judicial system for adjudicating guilt or innocence. It concluded that the procedures in Ohio's clemency process, including the voluntary interview without counsel or immunity, do not violate the Constitution.

The implications of this decision are that inmates do not have a constitutional right to due process in clemency proceedings and that the executive branch retains broad discretion in these matters without being constrained by judicially mandated procedures. Additionally, the decision clarifies that an inmate's choice to participate in a clemency interview, even if it may affect their legal strategy, does not infringe upon their Fifth Amendment rights. The judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant in a civil action brought by the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Alabama.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Birmingham, Alabama, alleges that Alabama violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The complaint also alleges that, in violation of Section 13(b)(4), Alabama unlawfully imposed a sales and use tax on certain non-property taxes, including on motor and water carriers, and that the state could not impose a 4% property tax on those same taxes. The SEC also alleged that Alabama failed to consider the scope of the exemption provision when it entered the final judgment, which permanently enjoins the defendants from violating the federal securities laws and orders them to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount of their property taxes.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney’s Office for New York announced criminal charges against the defendants.  According to the SEC, the defendants agreed to settle the case by agreeing to the entry of judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating these provisions.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, Alabama agreed to a judgment permanently enjoining it from future violations of Sections 13(a), 13(c), and 13(d) of The Exchange Act and Rules 12b-20, 13a-1, and 13d-1 thereunder, and to pay civil penalties equal to their respective property taxes in the same jurisdiction. The settlement is subject to court approval. The court will determine whether to impose a permanent injunction, whether to issue an order appointing a receiver, and how to proceed with the litigation.  On August 2, 2019, the Honorable Judge William G. Donnelly of the Upland Division of Justice granted the SEC's motion for a temporary restraining order, ordering a preliminary injunction, and ordering the defendants to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest in the amounts to be determined by the court upon motion of the SEC.  A hearing for the defendants is scheduled for September 5, 2019.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 5, 2017.

The question presented is the validity of an injunction issued on behalf of a statewide class that requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to adjudicate all future disputed disability claims under Title II of the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C. § 401 et seq., according to judicially established deadlines and to pay interim benefits in all cases of noncompliance with those deadlines.  According to the SEC's order, filed on June 14, 1979, the District Court certified a nationwide class consisting of:  "All present and future Vermont residents seeking to secure Social Security disability benefits who, following an initial determination by the defendant that no disability exists, experience an unreasonable delay in the scheduling of and/or issuance of decisions in reconsiderations and fair hearings."&#160Vz;    The SEC alleges that the class was formed by Leon Day in November 1978 after his disability benefits were terminated and he suffered substantial delays in obtaining a reconsideration of that determination and securing a hearing before an administrative law judge.&#16&#17Vz&#20Vz

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a Chicago-based company for violating the anti-fraud provisions of the federal labor laws.  The court also entered a remedial order against the company, which was subject to court approval.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, John Surak, the company's president, told employees that he had known about the employees' illegal presence in the country for several months prior to the election, and that the company would receive a minimum of six months' backpay. The complaint further alleged that Surak told the employees that the employer would be required to check into the status of their Mexican employees "solely because the employees supported the union" and "with full knowledge that the employees in question had no papers or work permits."  The complaint also alleges that the employee's letter to the employer was the sole cause of the employee being taken into custody.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Surak consented to the court's order, which permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provision of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $150,000.  In a separate administrative proceeding, the court also issued a temporary restraining order preventing the company from issuing or selling any security documents related to the alleged violations of the Exchange Act.  On May 1, 1977, the Court of Appeals granted certiorari to the company and ordered it to comply with the Commission's order.   The SEC's investigation was conducted in the Office of Inspector General's Analysis and Detection Center, and the litigation will be led by Mr. and Ms. Bica. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the states in a related case.  The court held that the federal government has the right to regulate interstate commerce.  According to the court's order, the federal authorities can no more deny the power to regulate commerce because a State is involved.  For example, the court found that Santa Cruz Fruit Packing Co. was not subject to the federal regulation of out-of-state commodities, and that a state university that imported scientific apparatus from abroad could be made to pay import duties imposed pursuant to the power over foreign commerce. The court also ruled that the state could not impose duties on imported scientific equipment.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the company.   The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in California, charges the state with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal securities laws and orders them to pay civil penalties in amounts to be determined by the court upon motion of the court.

After respondent Pacific Gas & Electric Corporation (PG&E) filed a chapter 11 bankruptcy petition, petitioner Travelers Insurance Company (Travelers) submitted a proof of claim for attorney’s fees incurred in defending against a claim made by another company. The Bankruptcy Code allows a debtor’s creditors to submit proofs of claims for payment, 11 U. S. C. §101(5)(A), and the Bankruptcy Court must allow a claim unless it is unenforceable under §502(b)(1), which disallows any claim that is “unenforceable against the debtor and property of the debtor, under any agreement or applicable law for a reason other than because such claim is contingent or unmatured.” The Bankruptcy Court concluded that Travelers’ claim was unenforceable under §502(b)(1) because it was “unenforceable” under state law. Rejecting Travelers’ argument that the Bankruptcy Code’s silence meant that the claim was enforceable, the Ninth Circuit relied instead on its own rule, known as the Fobian rule, which holds that attorney fees are not recoverable in bankruptcy for litigating issues “peculiar to federal bankruptcy law.” 167 Fed. Appx. 593, 594. The court explained that, because the fees here were incurred litigating issues that were “governed entirely by federal bankruptcy law,” Travelers’ claim necessarily failed. Held: The Bankruptcy Code does not categorically disallow a contractual claim for attorney’s fees incurred while litigating issues of federal bankruptcy law. Pp. 4−10. (a) The Fobian rule is inconsistent with the Bankruptcy Code’s plain text and the settled principle that “creditors’ entitlements in bankruptcy arise in the first instance from the underlying substantive law governing the debtor’s obligations, subject to any qualifying or contrary provisions of the Bankruptcy Code.” Raleigh v. Illinois Dept. of Revenue, 530 U.S. 15, 20. The Court of Appeals did not conclude that Travelers’ claim was unenforceable under §502(b)(1) as a matter of applicable nonbankruptcy law, nor did it conclude that the claim was rendered unenforceable by any provision of the Bankruptcy Code. Rather, the court rejected the claim based solely on the Fobian rule. That rule finds no support in the Bankruptcy Code, either in §502 or elsewhere. Its absence of textual support is fatal. Moreover, the absence of an analogous provision excluding the category of fees covered by the Fobian rule suggests that the Code does not categorically disallow them. Where Congress intends to provide exceptions to Bankruptcy Code provisions, it does so clearly and expressly. Here, the Code says nothing about unsecured claims for contractual attorney’s fees incurred while litigating issues of bankruptcy law. On the contrary, the broad, permissive scope of §502(b)(1) necessitates that the Fobian rule cannot stand. Pp. 4−7. (b) PG&E raises two alternative arguments that purportedly demonstrate that the Bankruptcy Code categorically bars unsecured claims for contractual attorney’s fees. First, it argues that §506(b) categorically disallows such claims and that Travelers’ claim falls within that bar since it is unsecured. Second, it argues that the structure and purpose of the Bankruptcy Code, examined against the backdrop of pre-Bankruptcy Code bankruptcy law, confirms that Congress did not intend to allow unsecured creditors to recover attorney’s fees. These arguments were not raised below, and thus the lower courts never had occasion to address them. They are therefore not properly before this Court. Pp. 7−9. Vacated and remanded. Alito, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Stevens, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Scalia, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, J., joined.

Under the Federal Lands Highways Program, 23 U. S. C. § 204, the Federal Government finances road construction and improvement projects on federal public roads, including Indian reservation roads. Various federal agencies oversee the planning of particular projects and the allocation of funding to them. The Commissioner of Indian Affairs has the responsibility to "plan, survey, design and construct" Indian reservation roadways. The Bureau's contract with Blaze Construction Co., Inc. (Blaze) is incorporated under the laws of the Blackfeet Tribe of Montana and is owned by a member of that Tribe. Blaze protested the assessment and prevailed at the end of administrative proceedings, but the Arizona Tax Court granted summary judgment in the Department's favor. The Arizona Court of Appeals reversed, holding that federal law pre-empted the application of Arizona's transaction privilege tax to Blaze. Held: 1. A State generally may impose a nondiscriminatory tax upon a private company's proceeds from contracts with the Federal government. United States v. New Mexico, 455 U.S. 720, distinguished. Pp. 521-532. (a) The Indian preemption doctrine would apply when Tribes choose to take a more direct and active role in administering the federal funds, regardless of whether the contracted-for activity takes place on Indian reservations. P. 522. (b) The Tribes on whose reservations Blaze's work was performed have not exercised this option, and the Government has retained contracting responsibility. Applying those principles, the District Court upheld each of the taxes at issue in that case because the legal incidence of the tax fell on a nontribal entity engaged in a transaction with tribes or tribal members. The New Mexico Supreme Court applied the balancing test in Cotton Petroleum Corp. v. Arizona Tax Comm'n, 448 US. 160, 165 166, and reached the exact opposite conclusion from the Arizona Supreme Court, which held that a congressional intent to preempt Arizona's tax could be inferred from federal laws regulating the welfare of Indians. In a similar case, the New Mexico State Supreme Court issued a tax deficiency assessment against Blaze for its failure to pay the Arizona transaction privilege taxes on the proceeds from its contracts. The court below held that, although the tax cannot be applied to activities taking place on the Indian reservations, it could be applied in a case such as this one where a State seeks to tax a transaction between the federal Government and its non-Indian private contractor. Because the Tribes in this case have not assumed this responsibility, this Court has no occasion to consider whether the Indian Preemption doctrine applies to Tribes' actions when they choose to do so. The need to avoid litigation and to ensure efficient tax administration counsels in favor of a bright-line standard for taxation of federal contracts regardless of where the contracting-for activities takes place is not sufficient to foreclose the clear rule established by this case in New Mexico. Moreover, as we recognized, the "political process is "uniquely adapted to accommodating" the interests implicated by state taxation of Federal contractors. 455 U., at 737 (emphasis added); Accord, Washington v. United S. 536, 546 (1983). Whether to exempt Blaze from Arizona's transactions privilege tax is not our decision to make; that deci- sion rests, instead, with the State of Arizona and with Congress, and it is therefore remanded to the Arizona court of appeals.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed a lower court's decision that the Federal Trade Commission had the authority to remove a state-court action brought against Philip Morris for violating the federal officer removal statute. The court held that the FTC's detailed supervision of Philip Morris' cigarette testing process did not make it an "officer" of the federal government, as the lower court had concluded. The Eighth Circuit held that Philip Morris was "acting under" the federal law, and therefore the FTC had the power to remove the case. The Supreme Court agreed, holding that the lower-court ruling was wrong. The high court also held that it would not have allowed the removal of a case brought against the FTC by a private defense contractor. The justices noted that the Supreme Court's earlier decision in a similar case involving the FTC did not apply to the current case. In a separate decision, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled that a federal court could not remove a case against the Federal Bureau of Investigation for violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.

The U.S. Department of Transportation's Federal Railroad Safety Act of 1970 ("FRA") authorized the agency to issue regulations that mandate blood and urine tests of railroad employees involved in certain train accidents. The FRA also authorized railroads to administer the tests to employees who violate certain safety rules. The agency's regulations, which went into effect in 1985, prohibit employees from using or possessing alcohol or any controlled substance while under the influence of, or impaired by, alcohol, while having a blood alcohol concentration of .04 or more. The regulations do not restrict a railroad's authority to impose an absolute prohibition on the presence of alcohol. They do not "restrict the authority of a railroad to impose a prohibition" on the use or possession of controlled substances. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia ruled in favor of the railroad, finding that the regulations did not violate the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law.

In this Supreme Court case, five retired beneficiaries of a defined benefit plan filed a class action lawsuit against their former employer, Hughes Aircraft Company, and the associated retirement plan. They argued that Hughes violated the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) by amending the plan to introduce an early retirement program and a noncontributory benefit structure. The Ninth Circuit Court had previously ruled that these amendments might be prohibited under ERISA, but the Supreme Court reversed this decision.

The Supreme Court's reasoning was based on the distinction between defined contribution plans and defined benefit plans. In a defined contribution plan, individual accounts are funded by employee and employer contributions, and benefits are based on the account balance. In contrast, a defined benefit plan, like the one at Hughes, provides a fixed periodic payment upon retirement and is funded by a general pool of assets. The employer bears the investment risk and must cover any underfunding, but can also reduce contributions if the plan is overfunded.

The Court found that the plaintiffs, as participants in a defined benefit plan, had no vested interest in the plan's surplus. Their rights were limited to a defined level of benefits, and they were not entitled to share in the surplus, even if it resulted from the growth of their contributions. Therefore, Hughes did not violate ERISA's vesting requirements by using surplus assets to fund the noncontributory structure, as the rights of existing plan participants were not affected.

Additionally, the Court held that the anti-inurement provision of ERISA, which prevents plan assets from benefiting the employer, was not violated. The assets were used to pay pension benefits to plan participants, and Hughes maintained its obligation to ensure the plan was adequately funded.

The Court also addressed the fiduciary duty claims, stating that ERISA's fiduciary provisions do not apply to the act of amending a plan. Following the precedent set in Lockheed Corp. v. Spink, the Court reiterated that employers acting as plan sponsors are not considered fiduciaries when they amend a plan. Therefore, Hughes' amendments to the plan did not breach any fiduciary duties under ERISA.

Lastly, the Court rejected the argument that the amendments effectively terminated the plan, noting that ERISA specifies the exclusive means by which a plan can be terminated, and none of those conditions were met.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's decision, finding that Hughes Aircraft Company did not violate ERISA when it amended its defined benefit plan to introduce an early retirement program and a noncontributory benefit structure. The plaintiffs' claims regarding vested benefits, anti-inurement, fiduciary duties, and plan termination were all dismissed.

The text appears to contain a legal document related to a court case regarding a New York state law that prohibits the sale of certain types of literature to minors. The law defines "obscene" material as anything that is "patently offensive to prevailing standards in the adult community," and specifically mentions "sexual conduct." The law also specifies that a seller can be convicted of a crime if they knowingly sell such material to a minor. The document discusses various cases related to this law, including a case in which a man named Sampson was accused of selling "girlie" magazines to minors.

Under both the Louisiana Constitution and Code of Criminal Procedure, criminal cases in which the punishment is necessarily at hard labor are tried to a jury of 12, and the vote of nine jurors is sufficient to return either a guilty or not guilty verdict. Appellant was tried on May 14, 1968, by a 12-man jury and was convicted by a nine-to-three virdict. His due process and equal protection challenges to the Louisiana constitutional and statutory provisions were rejected by the Louisiana courts, 255 La. 314, 230 So. 2d 825, and he appealed here. Held: 1. In order to give substance to the reasonable-doubt standard, which the State, by virtue of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, must satisfy in criminal cases, the Louisiana statute must be construed to require a unanimous-jury verdict in all criminal cases. Pp. 531-532. 2. The verdicts rendered by nine out of 12 jurors are not automatically invalidated by the disagreement of the dissenting three. P. 532. 3. The Louisiana statute serves a rational purpose and is not subject to constitutional challenge. In view of the mere fact that three jurors voted to acquit, appellant does not in itself demonstrate that, had the nine jurors of the majority attended further to reason and the evidence, all or one of them would have developed a reasonable doubt about guilt. In appellant's case, nine jurors rather than five or 12 were required for a verdict, and there is no evidence that, if the verdict in this case had been unanimous, the evidence would have been insufficient to support it. The fact that the verdict was unanimous does not demonstrate that appellant was convicted on a lower standard of proof, since the State satisfied its burden of proving guilt beyond any reasonable doubt and his conviction is therefore infirm. P p. 533. 4. In light of the fact that appellant's nighttime arrest without a warrant was unlawful in the absence of a valid excuse for failing to obtain a warrant and, further, that his subsequent lineup identification was a forbidden fruit of the claimed invasion of his Fourth Amendment rights, the jury verdict was not invalidated, and appellant was not deprived of due process of law. Pt. 534-535. 5. The State's failure to treat less serious crimes as being more serious than those committed with lesser crimes does not constitute a proof of guilt, since no evidence could properly be characterized as the fruit of an illegal entry and arrest and the trial judge might not have reached the same conclusion as the jury, see Takahashi v. Woods, 392 U. S. 631, and even though appellate judges are closely divided on the issue whether there was sufficient evidnece to support a conviction, the verdicts are regularly sustained even though the evidence was such that the jury would have justified in having such a doubt, and that guilt cannot be said to have been proved beyond areasonable doubt when one or more of a jury's members at the conclusion of deliberation still possess such a doubtful doubt. Neither argument is persuasive, since it raises the question of whether the State's burden of proof is sufficiently heavy to prove guilt beyond a substantial doubt, or whether the defendant's guilt is sufficiently severe to constitute a substantial burden of guilt to be proved by the jury. Pts. 535-536. 6. The jury verdicts finding guilty beyond a reasonable- doubt are sustained, even though it is easier to convince nine of the 12 jurors than to convince all of five, and are simply challenging the judgment of the Louisiana Legislature. Pps. 536-542. 7. The question whether the jury unanimity was sufficient to support the conviction of appellant is not raised separately from the question whether he was convicted of capital and five-man crimes, since, as to the crimes triable by a fiveman jury, if appellant's position is that it is more difficult to convince 9 of 12 than to persuade all of the nine, he is simply challenging that body's judgment. Pn. 542-543. 8. The state's decision to allow less-than-unanimous verdicts in certain criminal cases is not based on a rational reason, and it is not required by the Equal Protection Clause to show that, when minority jurors express sincere doubts about guilt, their fellow jurors will nevertheless ignore them and vote to convict even if deliberation has not been exhausted and minority jurors have grounds for acquittal which, if pursued, might persuade members of the minority to acquite,

In the Supreme Court case involving BP America Production Co., the Court addressed whether the 6-year statute of limitations for government contract actions, as outlined in 28 U.S.C. §2415(a), applies to administrative payment orders issued by the Department of the Interior’s Minerals Management Service (MMS) for assessing royalty underpayments on oil and gas leases. The Court held that this statute of limitations does not apply to these administrative payment orders.

The case arose from the MMS directing lessees to calculate royalties based on the value of treated gas rather than the value at the well, resulting in MMS ordering Amoco (now BP America Production Co.) to pay additional royalties for a period dating back several years. Amoco appealed, arguing that the payment order was partly barred by the 6-year statute of limitations. The Assistant Secretary of the Interior denied the appeal, and the case eventually reached the Supreme Court.

The Court's reasoning focused on the statutory text, which uses terms like "action" and "complaint" that are typically associated with judicial, not administrative, proceedings. The Court found that the language of §2415(a) clearly applies to the initiation of court actions and not to administrative proceedings. The Court also noted that when Congress intends to subject the government to a statute of limitations, it does so explicitly, and the text of §2415(a) does not indicate an intent to apply this to administrative proceedings.

The Court rejected arguments that its interpretation would render certain subsections of the statute superfluous, explaining that these subsections were added later and addressed specific concerns unrelated to the broader application of the statute of limitations to administrative actions.

The Court acknowledged that while its interpretation might lead to some peculiarities in the statutory scheme, such as MMS being able to issue payment orders beyond the time lessees are required to keep records, this does not outweigh the clear meaning of the statutory text. The Court also pointed out that Congress has the power to enact specific statutes of limitations for specific administrative actions, as it did prospectively for oil and gas lease claims on non-Indian land.

Ultimately, the Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, holding that the 6-year statute of limitations in §2415(a) applies only to court actions and not to the administrative proceedings at issue in this case. The Chief Justice and Justice Breyer did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

In the case of Bush v. Gore, the U.S. Supreme Court faced the issue of whether the recount procedures ordered by the Florida Supreme Court in the aftermath of the 2000 presidential election were constitutional. The Florida Supreme Court had mandated a manual recount of undervotes (ballots where the machine did not detect a vote for president) in certain counties and included partial recount results in the certified vote totals.

The U.S. Supreme Court, in a per curiam decision, found that the recount procedures violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment due to the lack of uniform standards across different counties for determining what constituted a legal vote. This lack of standards led to arbitrary and disparate treatment of voters, as different counties, and even recount teams within counties, could assess voter intent differently when examining ballots.

The Court also noted that the recount process ordered by the Florida Supreme Court did not provide sufficient procedural safeguards to ensure fair and equal treatment of all ballots and voters. The Court was concerned that the recount included partial results and that the process for counting overvotes (ballots with more than one vote for president) was not addressed, potentially leading to further unequal treatment.

Given the December 12 deadline for resolving electoral disputes to ensure Florida's electors could participate fully in the federal electoral process, as required by federal law (3 U.S.C. § 5), the Court concluded that there was insufficient time to establish and implement appropriate recount procedures that would meet constitutional standards.

As a result, the U.S. Supreme Court reversed the Florida Supreme Court's decision ordering the recount and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with their opinion. The decision effectively ended the recount process and allowed the previously certified results, which showed George W. Bush as the winner of Florida's electoral votes, to stand.

The Court's ruling was controversial, with dissenting opinions arguing for alternative remedies. However, the majority held that any further recount efforts would be unconstitutional due to the lack of uniform standards and the time constraints imposed by the federal deadline for resolving electoral disputes.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of the defendant in a criminal case involving drug trafficking charges. The ruling reversed a lower court's decision to revoke the defendant's bond and reinstate the charges against him. The Supreme Court held that the defendant had a constitutional right to notice of the charges against him and an opportunity to appear before a neutral magistrate, and that these rights were violated when the defendant was arrested and charged without notice or opportunity to appear. The Court also held that the defendant's right to due process was violated when the magistrate refused to hear his motion for release on bond.

Respondent, an enrolled member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians, married a member of a different tribe and lived with his wife and children on the Spirit Lake Reservation, also located in North Dakota. The Spirit Lake Tribe subsequently prosecuted Lara for "violence to a policeman." After Lara's tribal conviction, the Federal Government charged him with the federal crime of assaulting a federal officer. Lara pleaded guilty and, in respect to that crime, served 90 days in jail. The Federal Magistrate Judge accepted the Government's argument and rejected Lara's double jeopardy claim. The en banc Court of Appeals, by a vote of 7 to 4, reached a different conclusion, holding that the Tribal Court, in prosecuting Lara, was exercising a federal prosecutorial power; hence the "dual sovereignty" doctrine does not apply; and the Double Jeopardy Clause bars the second, federal, prosecution. Held: Congress has the constitutional power to relax restrictions that the political branches have, over time, placed on the exercise of a tribe's inherent legal authority to prosecute nonmember Indians. Pp. 5-11. (a) The Constitution authorizes Congress to permit tribes, as an exercise of their inherent tribal authority, to prosecuteNonmember Indians for misdemeanors. The Constitution's "plenary" grants of power authorize Congress to enact legislation that both restricts and relaxes those restrictions on tribal sovereign authority. P. 5. (b) Congress' authority to regulate virtually every aspect of the tribes, including the right of an indigent defendant to counsel, is not an unusual legislative objective. The political branches, drawing upon analogous constitutional authority, have made adjustments to the autonomous status of other such dependent entities-sometimes making far more radical adjustments than those at issue here. Moreover, Congress' legislative authority would rest in part, not upon "affirmative grants of the Constitution," but upon the Constitution's adoption of preconstitutional powers necessarily inherent in any Federal Government, namely, powers that this Court has described as "necessary concomitants of nationality." United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp., 299 U. S. 304, 315-322. The power to bring federal prosecutions, which is part of the putative delegated power, is manifestly and quintessentially executive power, and the power to enforce such prosecutions is also inherent in the tribal sovereignty that the United States has recognized. Duro v. Reina, 495 U.S. 676, distinguished. In Duro, supra, the Court held that the Indian Civil Rights Act of 1968 (ICRA) preserved the tribes' "powers of self-government" to "recogniz[e] and affir[m]" the existence of "inherent power . . . to exercise criminal jurisdiction over all Indians." 25 U. C. § 1301(2). The Court also held that Congress did not possess the constitutional authority to enact a statute that modifies tribal power by "recognizing and affirm[ing]" the Tribes' "Inherent" authority to charge nonmember Indian Indians. Dore, supra. P p. 590. (c) The fact that Congress can authorize the States to exercise-as their own-inherent powers that the Constitution has otherwise placed off limits, see, e. g., Prudential Ins. Co. v. Benjamin, 328 U. s. 408, 437-438, does not mean that Congress cannot also relax restrictions on an ancient inherent tribal power. The Act's legislative history confirms that Congress' intent to restore to the tribes an inherent sovereign power to prosecute Indians is not a delegation of federal power, but rather an elaboration by the political branch of the fine details of the tribe's dependent position, which strips the tribes of any power to exercisecriminal jurisdiction over those outside their own memberships. Thus, Congress has enacted a new statute, relaxing restrictions on the tribal sovereign's inherent prosecutorial authority, and that fact makes all the difference in this case. The District Court's decision in Duro is reversed, and this case involves no interference with the power or authority of any State. The Eighth Circuit and Ninth Circuit have reached different conclusions about the new statute. The Court has only two options: Either the "Duro fix" changed the result, or it did nothing at all. The "duality" doctrine of dual sovereignty does not bar the subsequent federal prosecution. The double jeopardy Clause does not prohibit the Government from proceeding with the present prosecution for a discrete federal offense. The conclusion here is consistent with this Court's earlier cases, which have distinguished between "tribal power [that] is necessary to protect tribal self-determination or to control internal relations" and tribal power as it relates to the external world. The Government seeks to subject a citizen to the criminal jurisdiction of a third entity to be tried for conduct occurring wholly within the territorial borders of the Nation and one of the States. This is unprecedented. There is a historical exception for Indian tribes, but only to the limited extent that a member consents to

While serving in the Navy, respondent Derefeso pleaded guilty to several offenses arising out of a fraudulent scheme involving bribes paid to members of a Marine Corps unit. His convictions were upheld on appeal to the Navy-Marine Corps Court of Criminal Appeals (NMCCA), which ruled that it lacked jurisdiction to entertain a subsequent petition for a writ of coram nobis seeking to vacate the convictions on the ground that they resulted from ineffective-assistance-of-counsel violative of the Sixth Amendment. The NMCCA reasoned that although it had jurisdiction to issue extraordinary writs under the All Writs Act, 28 U. S. C. §1651(a), it lacked jurisdiction to do so here because the writ was not needed to correct a procedural defect, but instead involved a substantive right. The NMCCA’s ruling was later reversed by the Court of Appeal for the Armed Forces (CAAF), which concluded that the NMCCA erred in finding that it lacked jurisdiction to issue the writ. The CAAF remanded the case to the NMCCA for determination of the merits of the writ petition. Held: Article I military courts have jurisdiction to entertain coram nobis petitions to consider allegations that an earlier judgment of conviction was flawed in a fundamental respect. Pp. 4−12. (a) Subject-matter jurisdiction determines whether a court has authority to entertain a particular kind of case or controversy. Here, the CAAF’s jurisdiction to review the NMCCA’s judgment rested on the All Writs Act, which gives federal courts “power to issue all writs necessary or proper in aid of their respective jurisdictions.” 28 U.S.C. §1651(a). Although military courts, like Article III tribunals, are empowered to issue extraordinary writs under the All Writs Act, that authority does not determine the anterior question whether military courts have jurisdiction to entertain a petition for coram nobis. Such a petition is properly viewed as a belated extension of the original proceeding during which the error allegedly occurred. Thus, to issue respondent a writ of coram nobis on remand, the NMCCA must have had statutory subject-matter jurisdiction over respondent’s original judgment of conviction. Pp. 4−7. (b) The NMCCA has jurisdiction to entertain respondent’s request for a writ of coram nobis. Article 66 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) provides that the NMCCA may sit to review court-martial cases. Because respondent’s request for coram nobis is simply a further “step in [his] criminal” appeal, Morgan v. United States, 346 U.S. 502, 505, n. 4, the NMCCA’s jurisdiction to issue the writ derives from the earlier jurisdiction it exercised to hear and determine the validity of the conviction on direct review. The textual authority under the UCMJ to “ ‘revie[w] court-martial cases’ ” provided the NMCCA with jurisdiction to hear an appeal of respondent’s judgment of conviction. Moreover, the NMCCA’s exercise of its jurisdiction is limited to reviewing the findings and sentence as approved by the convening authority, but that limitation does not bar respondent’s request for a writ of coram nobis. An alleged error in the original judgment predicated on ineffective-assistant-of-counsel challenges the validity of a conviction, so respondent’s Sixth Amendment claim is “with respect to” the special-court-martial’s “findings of guilty,” U. S. C. §866(c). Pp. 7−10. (c) The Government errs in arguing that Article 76 of the UCMJ, which codifies the common-law rule that respects the finality of judgments, affirmatively prohibits the type of collateral review sought by respondent. The finality rule does not jurisdictionally bar the NMCCA from examining its earlier judgment, nor does it trump each and every competing consideration. The result reached here is of central importance for military courts. The military justice system relies upon courts that must take all appropriate means, consistent with their statutory jurisdiction, to ensure the neutrality and integrity of their judgments. Under the premises and statutes relied upon here, the jurisdiction and the responsibility of military courts to reexamine judgments in rare cases where a fundamental flaw is alleged and other judicial processes for correction are unavailable are consistent with the powers Congress has granted those courts under Article I and with the system Congress has designed. Pp. 10−12. 66 M. J. 119, affirmed and remanded. Roberts, C. J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The Supreme Court addressed the constitutionality of a $145 million punitive damages award against State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company, where compensatory damages were $1 million. The case arose from a car accident caused by Curtis Campbell, whose insurance company, State Farm, refused to settle claims within policy limits, leading to a jury verdict exceeding those limits. State Farm initially refused to cover the excess liability and did not post a bond for Campbell to appeal. The Campbells later sued State Farm for bad faith, fraud, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.

The Court held that the punitive damages award was excessive and violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court applied three guideposts from BMW of North America, Inc. v. Gore to determine the reasonableness of punitive damages: (1) the reprehensibility of the defendant's conduct, (2) the disparity between actual harm to the plaintiff and the punitive award, and (3) the difference between the punitive damages awarded and civil penalties authorized or imposed in comparable cases.

The Court found that State Farm's conduct was reprehensible but that the punitive damages award was grossly excessive in relation to the Campbells' harm. The Court criticized the use of evidence from dissimilar out-of-state conduct and emphasized that punitive damages should relate to the plaintiff's harm. The Court also noted that the ratio of punitive to compensatory damages was unconstitutionally high, suggesting that single-digit ratios are more likely to comply with due process.

The Court reversed the Utah Supreme Court's decision to reinstate the $145 million award and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The Court's decision implies that while states have discretion in awarding punitive damages, there are constitutional limits to ensure awards are reasonable, proportionate, and not arbitrary.

Dissenting opinions by Justices Scalia, Thomas, and Ginsburg argued against the Court's involvement in punitive damages, a matter traditionally left to the states, and questioned the Court's authority to impose substantive due process limits on such awards.

Petitioners, operators of several cable television systems in Oklahoma, filed this suit in Federal District Court, alleging that Oklahoma's advertising ban violated the Commerce and Supremacy Clauses, the First and Fourteenth Amendments, and the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court found that petitioners regularly carried out-of-state signals containing wine advertisements, that they were prohibited by federal law from altering or modifying these signals, and that "no feasible way" existed for petitioners to delete the wine advertisements. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that, while the wine commercials at issue were protected by the First Amendment, the state ban was a valid restriction on commercial speech. Held: The Oklahoma advertising ban as applied here is pre-empted by the Federal Communications Commission's (FCC), which has unambiguously expressed its intent to pre-pre-empt any state or local regulation of this entire array of signals carried by cable TV systems. Pp. 5-11. (a) The FCC's authority to regulate the signals carried in cable systems is not precluded from pre-emption by the Twenty-first Amendment. P. 5. (b) When a State has not attempted directly to regulate a particular area of interstate communication by wire or radio by virtue of § 2(a) of the Communications Act of 1934, 47 U. S. C. § 152(a), and that this comprehensive authority included power to regulate cable communications systems, it is clear that the State's interest is not of the same stature as the goals identified by both Congress and the FCC of facilitating and encouraging the importation of distant broadcast signals. Moreover, when this limited interest is measured against the significant interference with the federal objective of ensuring widespread availability of diverse cable services throughout the United States, the balance between state and federal power tips decisively in favor of the federal law, and enforcement of the state statute is barred by thesupremacy Clause. Thus, if the FCC has resolved to preempt an area of cable television regulation and if this determination "represents a reasonable accommodation of conflicting policies" that are within the agency's domain, the regulation may prevail, notwithstanding that its requirements directly conflict with express federal policies, and all conflicting state regulations have been precluded. The judgment of the Court is reversed, and it is remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in a civil injunctive action brought by a former employee of Chevron Oil Co., who was injured while working on an artificial island drilling rig owned and operated by the petitioner.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New Orleans, Texas, Gaines Ted Huson suffered a back injury while drilling on the artificial island rig. The complaint alleges that the rigidity of the Louisiana statute of limitations prevented him from obtaining a day in court to recover his injured body.  The complaint further alleges that Rodrigue's injury occurred more than three years before the announcement of our judgment in Rodrigue, and that he instituted the present action more than one year before the date of his injury.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New Orleans today announced that it had obtained a judgment that permanently enjoins Rodrigue from future violations of the federal securities laws, including the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Huson consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the federal statutes of limitations, ordering him to disgorge his ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and appointing a receiver to oversee the receiver's operations.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Karpel and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The litigation will be led by David A. Schiff. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 924(e)(2)(B) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Orlando, Florida, alleges that Curtis Johnson, a Florida resident, violated the federal securities laws by repeatedly touching or making unwanted physical contact with certain victims, such as police officers.  According to the complaint, Johnson was convicted of battery in 2003, a felony that, like those in Florida, requires the use of "force" to cause a serious potential risk of physical injury to another person.  Johnson was sentenced to 15 years and 5 months in prison.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Florida today announced criminal charges against Johnson.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, Johnson consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of Sections 924 and 924, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of 15 years, 5 months, and a $75,000 civil penalty.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the Commission's Order, Johnson agreed to a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and an officer-and-director bar, and to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years.  He also agreed to be enjoined from associating with any person who has been convicted of a "violent felony" with a felony, including a felony conviction for battery under the Armed Career Criminal Act of 1940.   The Commission's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted in the Office of the United States District Judge in Orlando. Â The SEC's litigation will be led by Scott Frost and supervised by Jennifer Chun Barry.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the logging companies in this case involving the Northern Spotted Owl. The court found that the Northwest Timber Compromise, which was passed by Congress in 1990, allowed for selective cutting of old growth trees in the Pacific Northwest while protecting the habitat of the Northern Spotted Owl. The compromise included provisions for timber sales, forestry practices, and protections for wildlife habitats. The court rejected arguments that the compromise violated the Endangered Species Act or other environmental laws.

As a disabled prisoner in a Georgia prison, petitioner Goodman filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the State and various prison officials, claiming, inter alia, that they had deprived him of his right to equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment by failing to provide adequate medical care and other necessary services. His complaint contained numerous allegations about the conditions of his confinement, including allegations that he was confined for 23 to 24 hours each day in a small cell where he could not turn his wheelchair around, that he was denied access to toilets and showers without help, and that he was denied physical therapy and medical treatment. The District Court ultimately dismissed his claims for failure to comply with the formalities required by the Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1982, 42 U. S. C. §1993e(d), and later entered summary judgment for the defendants, ruling that their conduct was protected by state sovereign immunity. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, concluding that the District Court correctly found that Goodman’s Fourteenth Amendment claims were barred by sovereign immunity. However, the court remanded the case to allow Goodman to amend his complaint to develop three specific Eighth Amendment claims relating to his conditions of confinement. Although the court did not address the sufficiency of Goodman’s allegations under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA), it affirmed the District Court’s holding that his Title II claims for money damages against the State were barred by sovereign immunity. Held: Title II of the ADA validly abrogates state sovereign immunity with respect to the claims at issue here. Pp. 4–8. (a) Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment gives Congress the power to “enforc[e] … the provisions” of the Amendment by creating private causes of action against the States for actual violations of those provisions. Fitzpatrick v. Bitzer, 427 U.S. 445, 456. That power includes the power to abrogate state sovereign immunity by authorizing private suits for damages against the States. See ibid.; Ex parte Virginia, 100 U.S. 339, 346. Thus, insofar as Title II creates a private cause of action for damages against the States for conduct that actually violates the Fourteenth Amendment, Title II validly abrogates state sovereign immunity. Here, the Eleventh Circuit erred in dismissing those of Goodman’s Title II claims that were based on unconstitutional conduct. Pp. 4–6. (b) Because the Eleventh Circuit did not address the issue, it is unclear to what extent the conduct underlying Goodman’s constitutional claims also violated Title II. And although the court ordered that the suit be remanded to the District Court to permit Goodman to amend his complaint, it instructed him to revise his factual allegations to exclude his “frivolous” claims—some of which are quite far afield from actual constitutional violations or even from Title II violations. It is therefore unclear whether Goodman’s amended complaint will assert Title II claims premised on conduct that does not independently violate the Fourteenth Amendment. Once his complaint is amended, the lower courts will be best situated to determine in the first instance, on a claim-by-claim basis, (1) which aspects of the State’s alleged conduct violated Title II; (2) to what extent such misconduct also violated the Fourteenth Amendment; and (3) insofar as such misconduct violated Title II but did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment, whether Congress’s purported abrogation of sovereign immunity as to that class of conduct is nevertheless valid. Pp. 6–8. 384 F.3d 1248, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. O’Connor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The Supreme Court addressed whether the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over an appeal in a case where the original complaint did not allege a federal patent law claim, but the defendant's answer included a patent-law counterclaim. The case involved Vornado Air Circulation Systems, Inc., which sued The Holmes Group, Inc., alleging trade dress infringement. Holmes sought a declaratory judgment that it did not infringe Vornado's trade dress and an injunction against Vornado's accusations. Vornado counterclaimed for patent infringement.

The District Court ruled in favor of Holmes, granting the declaratory judgment and injunction, and stayed proceedings on the patent counterclaim. Vornado appealed to the Federal Circuit, which vacated the District Court's judgment. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to determine the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court held that the Federal Circuit erred in asserting jurisdiction over the appeal because the well-pleaded-complaint rule dictates that federal appellate jurisdiction is determined by the plaintiff's complaint, not the defendant's counterclaim. The Court emphasized that the plaintiff is the "master of the complaint" and can choose to avoid federal claims to keep the case in state court. Allowing a counterclaim to establish jurisdiction would undermine the plaintiff's choice of forum and expand the class of removable cases, contrary to the respect for state governments.

The Court also rejected the argument that the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction should be interpreted differently to promote uniformity in patent law, stating that the statute's language must be understood as it is written. The Court vacated the Federal Circuit's judgment and remanded the case with instructions to transfer it to the Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit.

Justice Stevens concurred in part and in the judgment, emphasizing that the jurisdiction of the court of appeals is not fixed until the notice of appeal is filed and that the plaintiff's choice of forum includes the appellate court. He agreed that the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction should be limited to cases where the patent claim is in the plaintiff's original complaint or an amended pleading.

Implications of the Decision: The Supreme Court's decision clarifies that the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction is limited to cases where the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint includes a federal patent law claim. This ruling preserves the plaintiff's control over the choice of forum and maintains the well-pleaded-complaint rule as the standard for determining federal appellate jurisdiction. It also ensures that other circuits will continue to contribute to the development of patent law, potentially identifying issues for the Supreme Court's review.

This case concerns a dispute over the legality of renting apartments to transients in a building financed by a government loan guaranteed by the Federal Housing Administration (FHA). The plaintiff, a South Carolina corporation, received FHA insurance for an apartment complex and began constructing it. However, during the construction process, the corporation decided to rent some of the apartments to transients rather than to veterans as originally intended. The defendant, the FHA, argued that the corporation violated the terms of the loan agreement and the regulations governing the program. The case went through several rounds of litigation, including appeals to the Supreme Court. Ultimately, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the defendant, holding that the corporation could not rent apartments to transients unless it complied with specific requirements set forth in the loan agreement and regulations.

When a police officer makes a traffic stop, the driver of the car is seized within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. A person is seized by the police and thus entitled to challenge the government’s action under the Amendment when the officer, “ ‘by means of physical force or show of authority,’ ” terminates or restrains his freedom of movement, Florida v. Bostick, 501 U. S. 429, 434. An “unintended person … [may be] the object of the detention,” so long as the detention is “willful” and not merely the consequence of “an unknowing act.” Brower v. Inyo, 489 U.S. 593, 597. A police officer may make a seizure by showing authority and without the use of the physical force, but there is no seizure without actual submission; otherwise, there is at most an attempted seizure. The State concedes that the police had no adequate justification to pull the car over, see n. 2, but argues that the passenger was not seized and thus cannot claim that the evidence was tainted by an unconstitutional stop. The California Supreme Court reversed, holding that the traffic stop was unlawful because Simeroth was its exclusive target, id., at 1118, 136 P. 3d, at 851, that a passenger cannot submit to an officer “through means intentionally applied” to the point that no one in the car was free to depart without police permission. The Court of Appeal reversed. Held: A person, seized by police and entitled to challenges under the Fourth amendment to the action of the government, when “by means [by means] intentionally applied … ” is the “intent [that] has been conveyed to [the person confronted],” Id., at 575, n. 7, and the criterion of willful restriction on freedomof movement is no invitation to look to subjective intent when determining who is seized. Pp. 4–8. (a) A person who is not seized as well as a passenger is seized when the police do not show an unambiguous intent to restrain or when an individual’S submission to a show of governmental authority takes the form of passive acquiescence, there needs to be some test for telling when a seizure occurs in response to authority, and when it does not. A traffic stop necessarily curtails the travel a passenger has chosen just as much as it halts the driver, diverting both from the stream of traffic to the side of the road and the police activity that normally amounts to intrusion on “privacy and personal security” does not normally (and did not here) distinguish between passenger and driver. United States v. Martinez-Fuerte, supra, at 627. An officer who orders one particular car to pull over acts with an implicit claim of right based on fault of some sort, and a sensible person would not expect a police police officer to allow people to come and go freely from the physical focal point of an investigation into faulty behavior or wrongdoing. If the likely wrongdoing is not the driving, the passenger will reasonably feel subject to suspicion owing to close association; but even when the wrongdoing is only bad driving, he will expect to be subject to some scrutiny, and his attempt to leave the scene would be so obviously likely to prompt an objection from the officer that no passenger would feel free to leave in the first place. The test is not what a reasonable passenger would have understood but what a passenger would want to leave. P. 4. 8 Cal. Rptr. 3–882, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the United States Department of Justice in a case that was investigated by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) improperly classified day planners as "diaries" under the "other" HTSUS subheading. The complaint further alleges that, in reality, day planners were not diaries because they had no space for "relatively extensive notations about events, observations, feelings, or thoughts" in the statute.  According to the complaint, the SEC's final judgment, which permanently enjoins the agency from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the agency to provide notice-and-comment procedures only when it deems it necessary to do so.  In a parallel action, the United Kingdom's Attorney General's Office today announced criminal charges against the agency.  The U.K.'s Office of International Affairs today announced that it filed a civil injunctive action, seeking a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an accounting of the amount of money owed to the agency, as well as an order appointing a receiver to oversee the agency's compliance with the federal securities laws.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan today entered a final judgment in favor of a company that has been charged with violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Portland, Oregon, alleges that, in the late 1970's, a company named Qualitex Co. Inc. ("Qualitex") and its new competitor, TrafFix Devices, Inc., sold sign stands with a design that looked like MDI's.  According to the complaint, the company claimed trade dress protection based on the dual-spring design, and that the design was functional because it was "essential to the use or purpose of the product."  The complaint further alleges that the company failed to show a genuine issue of functionality in its claims of trade dress, and failed to demonstrate that it could not prevail in any event because the design is not functional.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Oregon today announced criminal charges against the company.   The court also issued a temporary restraining order and an order freezing the assets of the company and ordering the company to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest of $1,038, and a civil penalty of $100,000. Â The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by Michael J. Basinger and supervised by Marc J. Ricchiute. The litigation will be led by Jennifer C. Barry. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Internal Revenue Service, the Department of Justice, and the Federal Trade Commission.

Respondent, a teacher in the state college system of Texas, was elected president of the Texas Junior College Teachers Association. He left his teaching duties on several occasions to testify before committees of the State Legislature, and he became involved in public disagreements with the college's Board of Regents. In particular, he aligned himself with a group advocating the elevation of the college to four-year status. And, on one occasion, a newspaper advertisement appeared over his name that was highly critical of the College administration. The Regents refused to provide him an opportunity for a hearing to challenge the basis of the nonrenewal. The District Court granted summary judgment for the petitioners, holding that the non-renewation of his contract would violate the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of procedural due process if the respondent could show that he had an "expectancy" of re-employment. The Court of Appeals reversed the District Court's judgment. Held: 1. The respondent's lack of a contractual or tenure right to reemployment, taken alone, defeats his claim that the Nonrenewing of his Contract violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 542-543. (a) The fact that the decision not to rehire him was based on his public criticism of the colleges' policies and thus infringed his right to freedom of speech does not defeat his claim of a "property" interest in continued employment at the college. P. 543. 2. The failure to allow the respondent an opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his claim in light of "the policies and practices of the institution" does not violate the constitutional guarantee of due process protection, since the decision did not in fact involve his protected free speech. Pickering v. Board of Education, 391 U. S. 563, 568, and the Board of regents v. Roth, 408 U.S. 564, which held that the Constitution does not require a hearing before a nontenured teacher's contract, unless he can show that it somehow deprived him of an interest in "liberty" or that he has a property interest in continuing employment, despite the lack of tenure or a formal contract, and thus amounting to a showing of a loss of property, do raise a genuine issue as to respondent's interest in the college, though irrelevant to his free speech claim, and may not be entirely dispositive. Moreover, the mere showing that he was not rehired in one particular job, without more, did not amount to a show of loss of liberty. Nor did it amount to the showing of property. Nor was it a showing that the student with his long period of service at this particular State College had no less of a 'property' interest in future employment than a formally tenured teacher at other colleges, and had no more a procedural right to a statement of reasons and a hearing-before college officials upon their decision to retain him. Thus, the respondent has yet to show that his non-tenure "right" was, in fact, made in retaliation for his exercise of the constitutional right of free speech, since he has not made a showing on either point to justify summary judgment in his favor, and since the actual reason for the Regents' decision was "in total dispute" in the pleadings, the court remanded the case for a full hearing on this contested issue of fact. Id. at 942-943. Certiorari granted; 430 F. 2d 939, affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has ruled that the federal government's annual registration tax on all civil aircraft that fly in the navigable airspace of the United States does not violate the implied immunity of a state government from federal taxation. The court held that the tax is constitutional because it is intended to fund a comprehensive program to expand and improve the national airport and airway system. The federal government has spent significant amounts of federal funds to develop and strengthen an integrated national airsystem since the passage of the Air Commerce Act of 1959 and to make civil air transportation safe and practical. The revenue from the registration tax is used to fund the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, which was established in 1970 to provide funding for aviation that would "generally match and grow with the demand" for use of the airways. The Revenue Act also provides for a tax on aircraft owned by State and National Governments. The tax is applied to aircraft that are used exclusively for police functions. The Court held that this provision of the Revenue Act does not apply to aircraft owned and operated by the State.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi today entered a final judgment in favor of Mississippi State Tax Commission v. James B. Beam Distilling Co., a Mississippi-based distillery charged with violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, Regulation 25 of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) requires out-of-state distillers and suppliers to pay a markup of 17% to 20% on liquor sold to the military on purchases of tangible personal property, including purchases by national banks for their own use.  The SEC alleges that, in 1966, Mississippi passed a federal sales and use tax on liquor to the federal government, and the SEC charged the distillery with violating Section 105(a) of the SEC.  In its judgment, the court held that the markup was an "unconstitutional" tax upon federal instrumentalities, and that the SEC had the right to determine whether the markup should be treated as a sales tax upon those instrumentalities.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the SEC has agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins Mississippi State from violating the federal sales tax, imposes an injunction against its enforcement, and provides for a refund of the sums paid under protest.  On May 17, 2020, the U. S. District Judge for the southern District of New York entered a judgment against Mississippi State, ordering the SEC to determine the amount of the markup that it would impose upon the distiller and the purchaser, and imposing a civil penalty of $10,000.   In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Mississippi today announced criminal charges against the distilling company and its owner. Â The SEC's Office of Investor Education and Advocacy has issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the background of anyone selling or offering them an investment using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in a civil injunctive action against a group of booksellers charged with displaying for sale paper-covered obscene booklets incontestably found to be obscene.  According to the court's order, filed on September 10, 1954, the New York City Commission on the Protection of the Free and the Press issued an order suspending the sale and distribution of the booklets.  The Commission's order temporarily halted the sale of the books and ordered the bookseller to surrender to the sheriff for destruction of any copies in their possession.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against the defendants.  As alleged in the complaint, the Commission found that the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 22(a) of the federal securities laws.
