Without admitting or denying the Commission's findings, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the charged provisions, and orders them to pay a civil penalty of $500, which is twice the amount of their previous civil penalties.  On November 2, 2019, a federal district court in New York entered an order temporarily restraining the defendants from selling or distributing any obscene books, and ordering them to surrender their books and records to the authorities.  It also ordered the defendants to surrender all copies of the allegedly obscene books they had been selling.   The Court's order also temporarily suspended the sales of the offending books to the public, pending the outcome of a court-ordered injunction. Â The Commission's investigation was conducted by Paul A. Freund and supervised by Marc Blau of the SEC's New York Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Gregory A. Kasper. The Commission appreciates the assistance of the U.N. Office of the Inspector General, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Internal Revenue Service, the Department of Justice, the FBI, and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of a city's decision to allow a controversial Christian symbol to be placed on a public building. The court determined that the symbol was part of a larger artistic work and should be treated as a form of government speech, rather than being subject to the free speech clause.

Under Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U. S. 424, a prima facie violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, a seniority system "would seem to fall under the Griggs rationale" if it were not for § 703 (h), which provides that "notwithstanding any other provision of this subchapter, it shall not be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to apply different standards of compensation, or different terms, conditions, or privileges of employment pursuant to a bona fide seniority or merit system, . . . provided that such differences are not the result of an intention to discriminate because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin." The plain language of § 702 (h) makes no distinction between pre-Act and post-Act seniority systems. Respondent employees claim that the provision "provides a narrow exemption [from the ordinary discriminatory impact test] which was specifically designed to protect bona fide Seniority systems which were in existence before the effective date of [Title VII]." The Court of Appeals held that the section does not apply to seniority-system systems adopted after the Effective Date of the Act. Held: 1. Under § 704 (h)'s plain language, the plain language does not distinguish between seniority programs adopted before their effective date and those adopted after its effective date. Pp. 431-437. (a) Section 703(h) does not take the form of a saving clause or a grandfather clause designed to exclude existing practices from the operation of a new rule. P. 434. (b) The fact that a senior-ity system has a discriminatory impact is not alone sufficient to invalidate the system; actual intent to discriminate must be proved. See, e. g., Teamsters v. United States, 431 U.S. 324, 349. The mere fact that such a system has not been applied would not give rise to a cause of action. A discriminatory effect would arise only when the system is put into operation and the employer "applies" the system. Such application is not infirm under § 705(h), unless it is accompanied by proof of a discriminatory purpose. An adequate remedy for adopting a discriminatory juniority system would very likely include an injunction against the future application of the system and backpay awards for those harmed by its application. Such an injunction, however, would lie only if the requirement of §703 (H) that such application be intentionally discriminatory-were satisfied. P p. 437. 2. The plain-language provision of the statute does not make it illegal to adopt, and in practice to apply, juniority systems that fall within the class of systems protected by the provision. Consumer Product Safety Comm'n v. GTE Sylvania, Inc., 447 US. 102, 108, 100 S. C. § 2000e-(b), which the court below relied upon for its conclusion that post- Act seniority was not intended to be protected by § 707(h). Pp., 437-438. (c) The statutory history does not support the far-reaching limitation on the terms announced by the Court below and urged by respondents, regardless of how liberally they are construed, do not amount to a clearly expressed legislative intent contrary to the statute's plain language. The legislative history of Teamsters and Evans do not support this limitation on § 706 (h). Moreover, the history of the legislative history cited by respondents indicates that the proposed distinction between application and adoption on its face makes little sense, since it would require reading § 73(h as though it were followed by the words "adopted prior to the Effective date of this section." Teamsters, supra, makes no such limitation, and there is no such distinction. The history of § 701 (b), 78 Stat. 253, as amended, also shows that the statute was not designed, intended or used to discriminate even though it may have discriminatory impact on minorities. The record does not reveal that the bill would destroy existing seniority rights, and it is not inconclusive that a claim that a juniority scheme has a " discriminatory impact" must be accompanied by a proof of that discriminatory purpose, since the statute contains no such restriction. Moreover, for the purpose of construing § 709(h)-the proposed distinction-does not make little sense. The proposed distinction makes littlesense. The adoption of seniority which has not yet been applied does not give the rise to an action. Nor does it amount to any clearly expressed congressional intent. The absence of the usual legislative materials supports the farreaching limitation. The statute's legislative history also does not show that the legislature's intent was to protect postAct seniorities systems from attack even though they were not adopted with discriminatory intent, and such application is infirm even if it was accompanied by the discriminatory purpose of the seniority scheme. P, 438. 634 F. 2d 744, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed a lower court's decision to suppress evidence obtained as a result of law enforcement officials' entry into an area immediately surrounding a barn on a Texas ranch property. The lower court had previously found that the area surrounding the barn was within the curtilage of the ranch house. The appeals court held that the lower court should have suppressed the evidence because the agents entered the area without a warrant. The court concluded that the search warrant had been issued based on information obtained during the officers' unlawful warrantless entry onto respondent's ranch property and, therefore, all evidence seized should have been suppressed. We conclude that the barn and the area around it lay outside the curtilsage and accordingly reverse the judgment of the lower courts.

The Supreme Court reviewed cases involving the First Unitarian Church of Los Angeles and the Valley Unitarian-Universalist Church, Inc., which were denied property-tax exemptions by the Los Angeles assessor. The exemptions were denied because the churches refused to sign an oath stating they did not advocate the overthrow of the government by force or other unlawful means, as required by the California Constitution and state law.

The churches challenged the requirement, arguing that it violated the Federal Constitution. The Superior Court and the Supreme Court of California had previously upheld the validity of the oath requirement, but the churches appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court did not address the churches' arguments regarding religious freedom and the separation of church and state under the Fourteenth Amendment because it found a more fundamental issue with the cases. Drawing on the reasoning from Speiser v. Randall, the Court held that the procedures enforcing the oath requirement violated due process because they improperly placed the burden of proof on the taxpayer.

As a result, the Supreme Court reversed the judgments of the lower courts and remanded the cases for further proceedings consistent with their opinion. This decision implies that the state cannot deny tax exemptions based on an oath that places the burden of proof on the organizations or individuals seeking the exemption. Justice Burton concurred with the result, and the Chief Justice did not participate in the decision.

The Supreme Court case involves Local 100, a building trades union, which sought to organize mechanical subcontractors by picketing general contractors, including Connell Construction Co., to compel them to subcontract only to firms with a union agreement. Connell signed an agreement under protest and later challenged it as an illegal restraint on competition under federal (Sherman Act) and state antitrust laws. The union claimed immunity from antitrust statutes and argued that federal labor regulation preempts state law.

The District Court and the Court of Appeals had previously ruled in favor of the union, exempting the subcontracting agreement from federal antitrust laws and preempting state antitrust laws. However, the Supreme Court reversed the decision on federal antitrust immunity and affirmed the ruling on state law preemption.

The Supreme Court reasoned that while labor unions have certain exemptions from antitrust laws to promote collective bargaining, these exemptions do not extend to agreements that directly restrain competition in business markets. The Court found that the agreement between Local 100 and Connell indiscriminately excluded nonunion subcontractors, potentially curtailing competition based on efficiency, which is not a goal of federal labor policy and is protected by antitrust laws.

The Court also determined that the construction-industry proviso to § 8(e) of the National Labor Relations Act does not authorize the type of agreement obtained by Local 100, as it was not limited to a particular jobsite or related to collective bargaining. The Court concluded that the agreement could be the basis of a federal antitrust suit due to its potential to restrain competition in ways not related to the elimination of competition over wages and working conditions.

On the issue of state antitrust law, the Court held that federal law preempts state remedies that interfere with federal labor policy, as state antitrust laws may represent a different balance between labor and antitrust policies and could conflict with federal labor goals.

The case was remanded for consideration of whether the agreement between Local 100 and Connell violated the Sherman Act.

In 1972, the Governor of New York signed into law several amendments to the State's Education and Tax Laws. The first five sections of these amendments established three distinct financial aid programs for nonpublic elementary and secondary schools. Almost immediately after the signing of these measures a complaint was filed in the District Court challenging each of the three forms of aid as violative of the Establishment Clause. Motions to intervene were granted to a group of parents with children enrolled in nonpublic schools and to the Majority Leader and President pro tem of the New York State Senate. By consent of the parties, a three-judge court was convened pursuant to 28 U. S. C. § 2281 and 2283, and the case was decided without an evidentiary hearing. Because the questions before the court were resolved on the basis of the pleadings, that court's decision turned on the constitutionality of each provision on its face. The District Court, finding the provisions severable, enjoined permanently any further implementation of §§ 1 and 2 but declared the remainder of the law independently enforceable. Held: 1. New York's "maintenance and repair" grants to nonpublic school children are not violative, since they are designed to provide a form of tax relief to those who fail to qualify for tuition reimbursement. Pp. 531-532. (a) The New York statute does not provide a statistical guarantee of separation by limiting grants to 50% of the amount expended for comparable services in the public schools. P. 533. (b) The fact that aid is disbursed to parents rather than to the schools is only one of many factors to be considered, and it is equally well established that not every law that confers an "indirect," "remote," or "incidental" benefit upon religious institutions is, for that reason alone, constitutionally invalid. Everson v. Board of Education, 330 U.S. 1, and Tilton v. Richardson, supra, distinguished. The statute itself allows, as a ceiling, grants satisfying the entire "amount of expenditures for maintenance and repair of such school" providing only that it is neither more than $30 or $40 per pupil nor more than 50% the comparable public school expenditures, and that the "legislature . . . finds and determines that similar modications . . ." should also be provided to parents for tuition paid to non-public schools on behalf of their dependents. The state officials also argue that the expenditures for "Maintenance and Repair" are similar to other financial expenditures approved by this Court, but that they are not identical to those approved by the Court in Everson. The State Supreme Court, relying on findings in a similar case recently decided by the same court, adopted a profile of sectarian schools similar to the one suggested in the plaintiffs' complaint. The court held that the statute itself allowed grants satisfying that it was neither more nor less than 50%, but that the State claims no right to distribute religious literature, and no restrictions are imposed on the use of the funds by the reimbursed parents. Held, however, that the state officials have appealed so much of the Court's decision as invalidates the first and second portions of the 1972 law as invalid, since their effect, inevitably, is to subsidize and advance the religious mission of sectarian schoolchildren. The Court noted probable jurisdiction over each appeal and ordered the cases consolidated for oral argument, and ordered that the cases be consolidated. Cf. Appellee v. Senate, supra. P p. 534. (c) The state's tuition reimbursement program also fails the "effect" test. By reimbursing parents for a portion of their tuition bill, the State seeks to relieve their financial burdens sufficiently to assure that they continue to have the option to send their children to religion-oriented schools. And while the other purposes for that aid-to perpetuate a pluralistic educational environment and to protect the fiscal integrity of overburdened public schools-are certainly unexceptionable, the effect of the aid is unmistakably to provide desired financial support for nonreligious, sectarian institutions. In the absence of an effective means of guaranteeing that state aid derived from public funds will be used exclusively for secular, neutral, and nonideological purposes, it is clear from our cases that direct aid in whatever form is invalid. Pc. 535-537. (d) The State's tuition grants here are subject to no such restrictions. There has been no endeavor "to guarantee the separation between secular and religious educational functions and to ensure the State financial aid supports only the former." Lemon v. Kurtzman, supra; Lemon v Kurtzman. supra, and, third, must avoid excessive government entanglement with religion, e.g., Walz v. Tax Comm'n, supra

The Supreme Court reversed a lower court's decision regarding the search and seizure of materials from a bookstore, finding that the actions violated the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments. The case involved an investigator who purchased films from a bookstore, deemed them obscene, and obtained a warrant to search the store and seize similar materials. The warrant was executed with the participation of a Town Justice, who viewed and seized additional films and magazines, determining their obscenity on the spot.

The Court found that the warrant was too broad and lacked specificity, essentially functioning as a general warrant, which the Fourth Amendment prohibits. The search was not limited to the items specified in the warrant but expanded based on the Town Justice's discretion during the search. The Court emphasized that a neutral and detached judicial officer should issue warrants, but in this case, the Town Justice acted as part of the law enforcement team, compromising his neutrality.

The Court rejected the state's argument that the Town Justice's presence provided an immediate adversary hearing on the issue of obscenity, noting that the Justice's actions did not reflect the required neutrality. The Court also dismissed the state's new theory that the bookstore had no expectation of privacy due to its public nature, stating that inviting the public does not equate to consenting to unconstitutional searches and seizures.

The Court concluded that the search and seizure were unconstitutional and reversed the lower court's judgment, remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The decision underscores the importance of adhering to constitutional protections against unreasonable searches and seizures, even in cases involving allegedly obscene materials.

A private corporation sued in a Louisiana state court to establish its title to certain mineral rights under land owned by the United States. Respondents, lessees of the land, defended on the grounds that the suit was against the United States, which had not consented to be sued, that the United States was an indispensable party, and that the suit was essentially a suit against the United States. After finding that a cause of action had been stated, the state trial court overruled the exceptions. Meanwhile, the United States brought suit in a federal district court to quiet title to the mineral rights and to enjoin the state court proceedings. The United States claimed that irreparable injury in the form of loss of royalties would result from any temporary, wrongful dispossession of its lessees by the state court proceedings and that permanent loss of wells currently producing oil would probably result from any temporary cessation of production. The United States based its claim of ownership on a provision in a deed from the predecessor in title of the United States that the reservation of mineral rights would expire on April 1, 1945, subject to certain conditions not material here. The United States claimed that the federal court had exclusive jurisdiction to determine the title of the United States to the mineral rights. Held: 1. Section 2283 of Title 28 U. S. C. does not apply to stays sought by the United States because different answers to the question whether it applies to such stays will put different aspects on other issues in the case. Pp. 440-442. 2. Since the United States was not a party to the state court suit, the title of the United States could be tried only in the federal court action, and an injunction against prosecution of the state court proceedings should issue to protect the jurisdiction of the federal court pending determination of the ownership of the property. Pp. 442-444. 3. The United States should be permitted to choose the forum in this case, even though the state litigation has the elements of an action characterized as quasi in rem. Pp. 444-445. 4. Where questions of constitutionality are involved, federal courts do not decide questions of constitutionality on the basis of preliminary guesses regarding local law. P. 445. 5. Questions involving the application of a state statute to the facts of this case should be interpreted by the Louisiana Supreme Court. Pp. 445-446. 224 F. 2d 381, modified and affirmed.

The Supreme Court was tasked with determining whether a "freedom-of-choice" plan adopted by the New Kent County School Board in Virginia was an adequate method for desegregating public schools, as mandated by the landmark Brown v. Board of Education decisions (Brown I and Brown II). The plan allowed students to choose which public school to attend, but after three years of implementation, it had not resulted in significant desegregation; the majority of black students still attended the historically black school, and no white students had chosen to attend it.

The Court found that the "freedom-of-choice" plan was insufficient. The opinion, referencing Brown II, emphasized that school boards have an affirmative duty to eliminate racially discriminatory systems and that mere access to formerly segregated schools does not fulfill this duty. The Court stated that the plan placed the burden of desegregation on students and their parents, rather than on the school board as required.

The Court held that the school board must develop a new plan that promises to effectively and promptly transition to a nonracial school system. The Court suggested that other methods, such as zoning, might be more effective in achieving desegregation. The judgment of the Court of Appeals was vacated, and the case was remanded to the District Court for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The implication of this decision was that school boards could not rely on "freedom-of-choice" plans if they did not result in actual desegregation. Instead, they were required to take proactive steps to dismantle segregation and create truly integrated schools. This decision reinforced the principle that the responsibility for desegregation lies with the school authorities and that plans must be judged by their effectiveness in eliminating segregated schooling.

Appellants, attorneys licensed to practice law in the State of Arizona, are members of the Arizona Bar. Appellants' practice and clinical concept could not survive unless the availability of legal services at low cost was advertised and in particular, fees were advertised. They sought review in the Arizona Supreme Court, arguing, among other things, that the disciplinary rule violated §§ 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act because of its tendency to interfere with the free flow of commercial information. The court allowed the parties to develop a record on which such a challenge could be based, and recommended that each of the appellants be suspended from the practice of law for not less than six months. Upon further review by the Board of Governors of the State Bar, pursuant to the Supreme Court's Rule 36, the Board recommended only a one-week suspension for each appellant, the weeks to run consecutively. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The disciplinary rule is not violative of the First Amendment, made applicable to the State through the Fourteenth. Pp. 488-478. (a) The disciplinary rules reflect a clear articulation of the state's policy with regard to professional behavior. Moreover, the rules are subject to pointed re-examination by the policymaker the State Supreme Court in enforcement proceedings. P. 489. (b) Appellant attorneys may not be subjected to blanket suppression, and that the advertisement at issue is protected, because the State has imposed and enforces a disciplinary rule that restricts advertising by attorneys. The State Bar is the real party in interest; it adopted the rules, and it is the ultimate trier of fact and law in enforcing the rules. The rule serves to inhibit commercial information and to keep the public in ignorance. The regulation of the activities of the bar is at the core of its power to protect the public, and the bar's role is to assure that the populace is sufficiently informed as to enable it to place advertising in its proper perspective. Appellee acts as the agent of the court under its continuous supervision. The policymaker is also the ultimate body wielding the State's power over law, see, e. g., NLRB v. Gissel Packing Co., 395 U. S. 254, and, thus, the restraint is "compelled by direction of the States acting as a sovereign." P. 589. 2. The prohibition of advertising by lawyers is not an unmitigated source of harm to the administration of justice. It may offer great benefits. Although the public lacks sophistication concerning legal services, misstatements that might be overlooked or deemed unimportant in other advertising may be found quite inappropriate in legal advertising. In this day, we do not belittle the person who earns his living by the strength of his arm or the force of his mind. Since the belief that lawyers are somehow "above" trade has become an anachronism, the historical foundation for the advertising restraint has crumbled. The bar will have a special role to play in assuring that advertising flows both freely and cleanly in the enforcement process, and this Court is not persuaded that any of the proffered justifications rise to the level of an acceptable reason for the suppression of all advertising by the attorneys. See Virginia Pharmacy Board v. Virginia Consumer Council, 425 U.S. 748, and its Disciplinary Rule 2-101(B). Although advertising may increase the use of the judicial machinery, it must not be withdrawn from protection merely because it proposed a mundane commercial transaction. Even though the speaker's interest is largely economic, the Court has protected such speech in certain contexts. In fact, the court has permitted attacks on overly broad statutes without requiring that the person making the attack demonstrate that in fact his specific conduct was protected. See Olsen v. Smith, 195 US. 332, 344-345, and other cases of misconduct at the bar. The fact that the consumer is unable to determine in advance just what services he needs and to assist in weeding out those few who abuse their trust does not justify the prohibition. The ban on advertising is justified by the problems of enforcement if any other course is taken, and is also justified by concerns that strict requirements for truthfulness will undesirably inhibit spontaneity. The alternative the prohibition serves only to restrict the information that flows to consumers. Finally, the argument that advertising will diminish the attorney's reputation in the community is open to question. The argument that the public is not sophisticated enough to realize the limitations of advertising and that it is better kept in ignorance than trusted with correct but incomplete information may justify restraints on in-person solicitation. The justification for the application of overbreadth analysis reflects the conclusion that the possible harm to society from allowing unprotected speech to go unpunished is outweighed by the possibility that protected speech will be muted. The record of the public's interest in the legal services industry is not a barrier to entry into the market for such services, and thus the ban in this case serves to perpetuate the market position of established attorneys. The Supreme Court of the United States reviewed a case involving Ludenia Howard, who was charged with violating the Federal Black Bass Act by transporting fish across Florida's state lines in a manner contrary to Florida state law. The District Court had previously quashed the charge, ruling that the regulations set by the Florida Game and Fresh Water Fish Commission did not constitute "law" under the Black Bass Act. The Supreme Court was tasked with determining whether the Commission's regulations, which were enforceable by state statute as misdemeanors, could be considered "law" within the meaning of the Federal Act.

The Supreme Court noted that it had previously recognized orders from state administrative agencies as state law in other contexts. The Court distinguished the present case from United States v. Eaton, which dealt with regulations that did not have the same statutory backing as the ones in question. The Court emphasized that the Florida Legislature had clearly intended for violations of Commission regulations to be treated as violations of state law.

The Court also addressed the argument that the Commission's rules were too changeable to be considered "law," but found no evidence that the rule in question lacked permanence or procedural legitimacy. The Court highlighted the structured process for rule promulgation and public accessibility to the rules, suggesting a level of stability and formality.

The opinion recognized that many states prefer to regulate wildlife conservation through commissions and that Congress intended the Black Bass Act to support state enforcement efforts for the protection of game fish. The legislative history of the 1947 amendment to the Act supported this interpretation.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court held that the term "law of the State" in the Federal Black Bass Act was broad enough to include the type of regulation employed by Florida through its Game Commission. The Court reversed the District Court's decision and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

Respondent was subsequently indicted for the robbery, and the State trial court granted respondent's motion to suppress the evidence that had been seized. The Arizona Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. A warrantless seizure by police of an item that comes within plain view during their lawful search of a private area may be reasonable under the Fourth Amendment. Coolidge v. New Hampshire, 403 U. S. 443. Pp. 534-535. (a) A search is a search, even if it happens to disclose nothing but the bottom of a turntable. The mere recording of the serial numbers did not constitute a seizure. To say otherwise would be to cut the "plain view" doctrine loose from its theoretical and practical moorings. The theory of that doctrine consists of extending to nonpublic places such as the home, where searches and seizures without a warrant are presumptively presumptuous. P. 535. (b) The search of objects in plain view that occurred here could be sustained on lesser grounds. A dwelling-place search, no less than a dwellingplace seizure, requires probable cause, and there is no reason in theory or practicality why application of the doctrine would supplant that requirement. The same considerations preclude the State from holding that, even though probable cause would have been necessary for a seizure, the search of object in plain sight that occurred in this case could not have sustained a seizure of the equipment. The search here was valid if the plain view doctrine would have sustained the seizure. The State's claim that the mere recording did not "meaningfully interfere" with respondent's possessory interest in either the equipment or the equipment was stolen is rejected, since the search was a "cursory inspection" rather than a "full-blown search," and could therefore be justified by reasonable suspicion instead of probable cause. The fact that the equipment came lawfully within the officer's plain view does not mean that the search uncovered nothing of any great personal value to respondent-serial numbers rather than (what might conceivably have been hidden behind or under the equipment) letters or photographs, and no special operational necessities are relied on here, but rather the mere fact that items in question were lawfully within his plain view. That alone cannot supplant the requirement of probable. Moreover, the fact that it exposed to view concealed portions of the apartment or its contents, did produce a new invasion of respondent's privacy unjustified by the exigent circumstance that validated the entry. The state's contention that the officers' action directed to the stereo equipment was unrelated to the justification for their entry into respondent's apartment, it was ipso facto unreasonable. That lack of relationship always exists with regard to action validated under the doctrine; where action is taken for the purpose justifying the entry, invocation of the plain-view doctrine is superfluous. Mincey v. Arizona, supra, was addressing only the scope of the primary search itself, and was not overruling by implication the many cases acknowledging that theplain view doctrine can legitimate action beyond that scope. The court below should have admitted the evidence thus obtained under the "good faith" exception to the exclusionary rule. That was not the question on which certiorari was granted, and it declines to consider it.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota today entered final judgments in favor of Minnesota's tax deduction for education expenses incurred by parents sending their children to parochial schools.  According to the court's order, filed on May 2, 2018, Minnesota's exemption from the federal tax deduction was not sufficient to satisfy the court-ordered injunction.  The court also found that the exemption violated the antifraud provisions of Section 290.09 of the Minnesota tax law.  In its judgment, the court found that Minnesota violated the Establishment Clause when it provided a tax deduction to parents of children attending public schools, and that, contrary to the federal law, the exemption does not apply to religious education.  For example, the Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit held that, in its order imposing the exemption, Minnesota had violated the federal anti-fraud provision of the federal income tax law, and the exemption is subject to court approval.  Without admitting or denying the Court's findings, Minnesota consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins the state from violating the exemption provisions, and orders the state to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $500 per dependent, $700 per dependent in grades K through 12, and $700 for grades 7 through 12. The final judgment also orders the Minnesota Department of Revenue to comply with the court order.   The Court's order also prohibits Minnesota from imposing a penny-per-child tax deduction on parents or children attending private schools.

Title 42 U. S. C. § 1983 provides that "[e]very ...person...who, under color of any statute or ...under any agreement ... contracted .. , shall be liable to the same party.. . for the deprivation of any rights secured by the Constitution and laws." Petitioner Sheriff Moore, acting as the sole hiring agent for respondent county, hired respondent Burns, despite Burns' criminal record, which included convictions for misdemeanors such as driving under the influence and reckless driving. While working as a reserve deputy, Burns struck respondent with his fists during a domestic disturbance, causing her permanent facial injuries. Respondent filed suit against the county under § 1983, alleging that the county was liable for the injuries because Sheriff Moore's hiring decision was constitutionally flawed. The Federal District Court submitted the case to the jury, which returned a verdict for respondent. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that the jury could have found that Sheriff Moore's hiring decision reflected indifference to the public's welfare. Held: The county is not liable for Sheriff Moore's isolated decision to hire Burns without adequate screening, because respondent has not demonstrated that his decision reflected a conscious disregard for a high risk that Burns would use excessive force in violation of respondent's federally protected right. Pp. 10-18. (a) Before accepting a § 1983 claim resting on a single decision, not itself representing a violation of federal law and not directing such a violation, a plaintiff must demonstrate that the decision was taken with "deliberate indifference" as to its known or obvious consequences. This requires a showing that the decision was made with conscious disregard for the consequences of the decision. Moreover, the decision must be capable of producing the plaintiff's injury. Thus, the risk from a particular glaring omission in a training regimen is not "obvious" in the abstract; rather, it depends upon the background of the applicant. Here, the evidence was insufficient to support a finding that Sheriff Moore disregarded a known or obvious risk of injury. Even assuming that proof of a single instance of inadequate screening could ever trigger municipal liability, the evidence was inadequate to support a finding that Sheriff Moore disregarded a known or obvious risk of injury. To be sure, Burns' record revealed a strong propensity for violence. However, the primary charges on which respondent relies arise from a single incident on a college campus where Burns was a student. Unless Sheriff Moore would necessarily have rejected Burns' application because Burns' use of excessive force would have been a plainly obvious consequence of the hiring decision, Sheriff Moore's inadequate scrutiny of Burns' record cannot constitute "deliberate indifference" to respondent's federally protected right. Pp. 10-18. (b) Cases involving constitutional injuries allegedly traceable to an ill-considered hiring decision pose the greatest risk that a municipality will be held liable for an injury that it did not cause. Where a court fails to adhere to rigorous requirements of culpability and causation, municipal liability collapses into respondeat superior liability. As recognized in Monell v. New York City, 436 U. S. 692, Congress did not intend municipalities to be held liable unless deliberate action attributable to the municipality directly caused a deprivation of federal rights. A failure to apply stringent culpability and causation requirements raises serious federalism concerns, in that it risks constitutionalizing particular hiring requirements that States have themselves elected not to impose. Pp. 18-19. 67 F. 3d 1179, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit recently ruled that an interstate rail carrier can challenge Alabama's sales and use tax on the basis that its main competitors are exempt from those taxes. The court held that the Railroad Revitalization and Regulatory Reform Act of 1976 (11501(c)) bars states and localities from engaging in four forms of discriminatory taxes on rail carriers. The Court's decision was based on an earlier ruling by the same court in Norfolk Southern R. Co. v. Alabama Dept. of Revenue, 550 F. 3d 1306, which held that a railroad could not challenge a generally applicable property tax, but it could challenge a sales tax exemption for certain non-railroad property. We conclude that the court's earlier decision was wrong and that the ruling is consistent with the 4–R Act's intent. The case is now being appealed to the United States Supreme Court.

Respondent Tahoe Regional Planning Agency, which regulates land use in the Lake Tahoe basin, determined that respondent's property is ineligible for development but entitled to receive certain allegedly valuable "Transferable Development Rights" (TDRs). Respondent appealed the denial to the agency's governing board, which denied relief. Pursuant to the Regional Plan, respondent adopted a new Regional Plan providing for an "Individual Parcel Evaluation System" (IPES) to rate the suitability of vacant residential parcels for building and other modification. The agency's 1987 plan does not provide for the variances and exceptions of conventional land use schemes, but addresses the potential sharpness of its restrictions by granting property owners TDRs that may be sold to owners of parcels eligible for construction, id., §§20.3.C, 34.0 to 34.3, and the agency introduced an affidavit from a real estate appraiser, whose opinion was that the Residential Development Right that respondent already has and the three more to which she is entitled, have a market value between $1,500 and $2,500 each; that her Land Coverage Rights can be sold for $6 to $12 per square foot; and that her lot would sell for $7,125 to $16,750. With limited exceptions not relevant here, the agency permits no "additional land coverage or other permanent land disturbance" on such a parcel. Respondent denied relief, and respondent brought suit for compensation under Rev. Stat. §1979, 42 U. S. C. §1983, alleging that in denying her the right to construct a house on her lot, the Agency's restrictions deprived her of "all reasonable and economically viable use" of her property, and so amounted to a taking of the property without just compensation in violation of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Ninth Circuit affirmed. Held: 1. The claim is ripe for judicial review under prudential ripeness principles. Pp. 5-11. (a) The agency argues (for the first time, before this Court) that the claim is unripe under the "fitness for review" requirement of Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner, 387 U.S. 136, because no "values attributable to respondent's [tDRs] are known," and that the agency may validly bar her land development just as all agree it has actually done, as opposed to the issue of whether just compensation has been afforded for such a taking. The only discretionary step left to an agency in either situation is enforcement, not determining applicability. P. 5. (b) Where the regulatory regime offers the possibility of a variance from its facial requirements, a landowner must go beyond submitting a plan for development and actually seek such a variance to ripen his claim. There is no "final decision" for the agency to make: action on a possible application by Suitum to transfer the TDR to her land, as well as a potential application by respondent to obtain a new Residential Allocation or to offer them for sale. This is not, however, the type of final decision required by Williamson County precedents, which addressed the virtual impossibility of determining what development will be permitted on a particular lot of land when its use is subject to the decision of a regulatory body invested with great discretion, which it has not yet even been asked to exercise. The Supreme Court opinion addresses the constitutionality of the structure of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB), which was created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 in response to major accounting scandals. The PCAOB is a regulatory body that oversees the audits of public companies, and its members are appointed by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and can only be removed for cause.

The Court held that the PCAOB's structure, which includes multiple layers of protection from removal for its members, violates the separation of powers principle embedded in the U.S. Constitution. Specifically, the Court found that the President must have the ability to hold executive officers accountable by removing them if necessary, and that the PCAOB's structure impeded this executive power by insulating its members from removal by the President.

The Court determined that the PCAOB members are "inferior officers" and that their appointment by the SEC is constitutionally permissible. However, the Court struck down the for-cause removal protections as they apply to PCAOB members, making them removable at will by the SEC, which is itself subject to presidential oversight.

The Court's decision did not invalidate the entire Sarbanes-Oxley Act or the existence of the PCAOB but rather focused on the specific removal protections that were deemed unconstitutional. The Court concluded that the unconstitutional provisions could be severed from the rest of the statute, allowing the PCAOB to continue functioning with its members now subject to at-will removal by the SEC.

The implications of the decision are that while independent agencies and regulatory bodies can exist within the federal government, their structures must allow for executive oversight and accountability to the President, consistent with the separation of powers doctrine. The ruling reaffirms the President's authority to oversee and, if necessary, remove executive officers to ensure the faithful execution of the laws.

After information about Richard Hallock’s credit card was stolen and used to pay the subscription fee for a child pornography Web site, agents of the United States Customs Service, investigating the Web site traced the payment to Richard Hallocks’ card and got a warrant to search his residence. With that authority, they seized the Hallock computer equipment, software, and disk drives. No criminal charges were ever brought, but the Government‘s actions produced a different disaster. When the computer equipment was returned, several of the disk drives were damaged, all of the stored data (including trade secrets and account files) were lost, and the Hallocks were forced out of business. In July 2002, Susan Hallock and her company brought an action under the Federal Tort Claims Act, invoking the waiver of sovereign immunity, 28 U. S. C. §1346, and alleging negligence by the customs agents in executing the search. The merits of the claim were never addressed, for the District Court granted the Government a motion to dismiss, holding that the agents’ activities occurred in the course of detaining goods and thus fell within an exception to the Act’d waiver. Hallock v. United States, 253 F. Supp. 2d 361, vacated for want of appellate jurisdiction on the part of the Court of Appeals. Held: The collateral order doctrine, identified with Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp., 337 U.S. 541, is “best understood not as an exception” to the “final decision” rule laid down by Congress in §1291, but as a ‘practical construction’ of it.” Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct, Inc., 511 U. . S. 863, 867 (internal quotation marks omitted). Pp. 6–16. (a) The collateral-order doctrine is ‘stringent,’ Digital Equipment, 511, at 868, and unless they are kept so, the underlying doctrine will overpower the substantial finality interests §1292 is meant to further: judicial efficiency, for example, and “sensible policy ‘of avoiding[ing] the harassment and cost of a succession of separate appeals from the various rulings to which a litigation may give rise.’ ” Firestone Tire & Rubber Co.v. Risjord, 449 U. N. 368, 374. The collateral–order doctrine functions in much the same way, with both rules depending on a prior judgment as a condition precedent and neither reflecting a policy that a defendant should be scot free of any liability. The concern behind both rules is a different one, of avoiding duplicative litigation, “multiple suits on identical entitlements or obligations between the same parties,” and the concern behind “the concern behind” both rules. The Court has not mentioned applying the collateral-Order doctrine recently without emphasizing its modest scope. See, e.g., Digital Equipment. 511U. S., at 867. The judgment bar at issue in this case has no claim to greater importance than the typical defense of claim preclusion; and the Court holds true to form in deciding what Digital Equipment implied, that an order rejecting the defense of judgment bar under §2676 cries for no immediate appeal of right as a collateral order. But the cases are different. Qualified immunity is not the law simply to save trouble for the Government and its employees; it is recognized because the burden of trial is unjustified in the face of a colorable claim that the law on point was not clear when the official took action, and, the action was reasonable in light of the law as it was. The nub of qualified immunity is the need to induce officials to show reasonable initiative when the relevant law is not “clearly established, ” Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.

Respondents filed an action under 23 U. S. C. § 409, which protects information "compiled or collected" in connection with certain federal highway safety programs from being discovered or admitted in certain federal or state trials. While the appeal in the PDA action was pending, respondents served petitioner with interrogatories seeking information regarding accidents that had occurred at the 168/B intersection. Respondents successfully sought an order to compel, and petitioner moved for discretionary appellate review of the trial judge's interlocutory order. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The decision below did not result in a final judgment for purposes of § 409. Pp. 531-532. (a) The 1995 amendment to § 409 does not protect information compiled or collected for purposes unrelated to § 152, as held by the agencies that collected or collected that information. P. 534. (b) In light of its conclusion that § 409 exceeded Congress' power under the Constitution, and, therefore, was not binding on the States, the court held § 409 protected only information originally created for § 152 purposes. But, rather than determining whether the documents or data at issue in this case would be protected under § 409 under its reading, the Court vacated the lower court's judgment and remanded the case for the lower courts to consider the record in the first instance, and the case is remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion. P p. 535. (c) Respondents contend that the decision below does not constitute a "final judgment" with respect to the tort action, since the Washington Supreme Court resolved only a discovery dispute; it did not determine the final outcome of the litigation. Nor do any of the exceptions outlined in Cox Broadcasting Corp. v. Cohn, supra, apply to the Tort action. The District Court's conclusion, however, is that the 1995 amendment was a proper exercise of Congress' powers under the Spending, Commerce, and Necessary and Proper Clauses of Article I of the United States Constitution, since § 409 was not an "integral part" of the regulation of the federal-aid highway system and, thus, could not be upheld under Hodel v. Indiana, 452 U.S. 314 (1981). The PDA case falls squarely under the first Cox exception because the court's ruling on the federal privilege issue is "conclusive" and "the outcome of further proceedings preordained." Cox Broadcasting Co., supra, at 479. Accordingly, the four documents at issue before the State Supreme Court remained unprotected under §§ 409 and continued to be subject to disclosure under the Public Disclosure Act (PDA), and the District Court dismissed the writ of certiorari with respect thereto. The judgment of the Washington Court is reversed, and this case is dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware today entered a final judgment against a Wilmington, Delaware restaurant that refused to serve an African-American restaurant owner because he is a "second-class citizen."  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against Eagle Coffee Shoppe, Inc., a restaurant located within an off-street automobile parking building in Wilmington.  According to the court's order unsealed today, the restaurant's lease with the Wilmington Parking Authority was for 20 years and renewable for another 10 years. The court found that Eagle violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordered Eagle to pay a $220,000 civil penalty.  The Court also issued an order suspending the restaurant from serving as an "attorney" under the federal, state, and municipal securities laws.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Delaware today announced criminal charges against Eagle.   The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Wilmington, charges Eagle with violations of the federal securities laws and seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Eagle has consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the federal and state securities laws, orders it to pay civil penalties, and imposes a penny stock bar against Eagle, and orders the restaurant to pay an annual rent of $28,700. The order also prohibits Eagle from associating with any entity that does not already have an exemption from state securities law, including the Delaware Department of Commerce, and from participating in the issuance of any municipal bond.  It also prohibits the purchase, purchase, or sale of any automobile or building that is not subject to state jurisdiction, from making any investment in a public building, including a restaurant, other than for the purpose of providing for the convenience of the public and thereby relieving the parking crisis that threatens the welfare of the community.

The Supreme Court of the United States decided the case of Schnaekloth v. Bustamonte in 1971. The case concerned a warrantless search conducted by local police after a suspect was arrested outside of his home. The search revealed evidence that was later used to prosecute the suspect for theft. The main legal issue in the case was whether the government can conduct a warrantless search of a suspect's home with the consent of a third party, such as a roommate.

The Court held that a warrantless search conducted with the consent of a third party is constitutional under the Fourth Amendment. The Court cited previous decisions, including Frazier v. Cupp and Coolidge v. New Hampshire, which established that a consent search is fundamentally different in nature from a waiver of a trial right. The Court also noted that the Constitution does not require that the consent of the defendant must be obtained in order for a search to be valid. Instead, the Court recognized that "the concept of 'common authority'" allows for a search to be conducted with the consent of a third party who possesses that authority.

Overall, the Schnaekloth v. Bustamonte decision establishes that a warrantless search conducted with the consent of a third party is constitutional under the Fourth Amendment.

Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA or Act) prohibits certain employers, including the States, from "discriminat[ing] against a qualified individual with a disability because of the disability of such individual in regard to job application procedures, the hiring, advancement, or discharge of employees, employee compensation, job training, and other terms, conditions, and privileges of employment." Title I also prohibits employers from "utilizing standards, criteria, or methods of administration ... that have the effect of discrimination on the basis of disability." 12112(b)(3)(A). Respondent Milton Ash worked as a security officer for the Alabama Department of Youth Services (Department), where Ash informed the Department that he suffered from chronic asthma and that his doctor recommended he avoid carbon monoxide and cigarette smoke, and requested that the Department modify his duties to minimize his exposure to these substances. Ultimately, the Department granted none of the requested relief. Shortly after Ash filed a discrimination claim with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, he noticed that his performance evaluations were lower than those he had received on previous occasions. He then filed separate lawsuits in the District Court, both seeking money damages under the ADA. Petitioners moved for summary judgment, claiming that the ADA exceeds Congress' authority to abrogate the State's Eleventh Amendment immunity. The Court of Appeals agreed, and the Eleventh Circuit reversed. Held: 1. The ADA does not so broadly enlarge congressional authority by subjecting the States to suits in federal court for money damages. Pp. 5-11. (a) The Eleventh and Fifteenth Amendments do not extend to suits by citizens against their own States. P. 5. (b) Congress may not, of course, base its abrogation of the States' Eleventh amendment immunity upon the powers enumerated in Article I. Nor can it compel States to act on the ground that they embody the misconceived or malicious perceptions of some of their citizens. The legislative record of the ADA, however, simply fails to show that Congress did in fact identify a pattern of irrational state discrimination in employment against the disabled. Nor is there any evidence that Congress, acting pursuant to a power granted to it by the Constitution, can compel States' actions to act. Nor does the fact that there is a new awareness, a new consciousness, and a new commitment to better treatment of those disadvantaged by mental or physical impairments do not establish that an absence of state statutory correctives was a constitutional violation. The Act's constitutional shortcomings are apparent when the Act is compared to Congress' efforts in the Voting Rights Act of 1965 to respond to a serious pattern of constitutional violations. See, e.g., Kimel v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U. S. 432. The failure of a State to revise policies now seen as incorrect under a new understanding of proper policy does not always constitute the purposeful and intentional action required to make out a violation of the Equal Protection Clause. Moreover, the burden is on the challenging party to negative "any reasonably conceivable state of facts that could provide a rational basis for the classification." Moreover, even if it were to be determined that each incident upon fuller examination showed unconstitutional action on the part of the State, these incidents taken together fall far short of even suggesting the pattern of unconstitutional discrimination on which 5 legislation must be based. See City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507, 530-531. The District Court's judgment is reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California today entered a final judgment in favor of a proposed amendment to the federal securities laws that requires the issuance of search warrants.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in San Francisco, California, alleges that, in 1971, the Palo Alto Police Department and Santa Clara County Sheriff's Department issued search warrants to search the offices of the Stanford University Hospital.  According to the complaint, the warrants were issued on the basis of "just, probable and reasonable cause" and "reasonable cause" to believe that the person or things to be searched would be implicated in the crime being investigated.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the search warrants were not required where there is probable cause to believe a person or entity is involved in an act of criminal conduct.  For example, a search warrant issued for a private home for all books, records, and other materials related to the Communist Party could not be issued without a warrant.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.   The court also issued a temporary restraining order halting the search of the offices and prohibiting the officers from destroying any evidence or evidence that may be located on the property of the third party involved in the search. The Supreme Court was tasked with determining whether federal bankruptcy law prevents an unsecured creditor from recovering attorney's fees that were agreed upon in a contract before bankruptcy and incurred during post-bankruptcy litigation. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals had previously ruled that such fees are not recoverable when the litigation involves issues specific to federal bankruptcy law, even if they would be enforceable under non-bankruptcy law.

The Supreme Court vacated and remanded the Ninth Circuit's decision, stating that this categorical prohibition, known as the Fobian rule, has no basis in the Bankruptcy Code. The Court explained that under the American Rule, the prevailing party in litigation typically cannot collect attorney's fees from the loser unless a statute or contract specifically allows it. The Court noted that the Bankruptcy Code allows claims for attorney's fees if they are enforceable under applicable non-bankruptcy law, except where the Code provides otherwise.

The Court found that the Fobian rule, which disallows claims for attorney's fees incurred in litigating bankruptcy law issues, is not supported by the text of the Bankruptcy Code. The Court emphasized that claims enforceable under state law are generally presumed to be allowed in bankruptcy unless expressly disallowed by the Code.

The Court declined to consider alternative arguments presented by PG&E that were not raised in the lower courts or in opposition to certiorari, including the argument that Section 506(b) of the Bankruptcy Code categorically disallows unsecured claims for contractual attorney's fees.

The Supreme Court concluded that the Ninth Circuit erred in disallowing the claim for attorney's fees based solely on the fact that the fees were incurred in litigation involving bankruptcy law. The case was sent back to the lower courts for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

Case Name: Fisher v. University of Texas System
Case Number: 11-964
Issue: Does the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment permit the University of Texas System to use race as a factor in its college admissions process?
Decision Date: June 26, 2013
Opinion Author: Chief Justice John Roberts
Summary: The Supreme Court ruled in Fisher v. University of Texas System that the use of race as a factor in college admissions is constitutional under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court held that the University of Texas System's use of race in its admissions process was narrowly tailored to achieve a compelling state interest in promoting diversity and avoiding racial stagnation in higher education. The Court also rejected the plaintiff's argument that the use of race resulted in a denial of equal protection to white applicants.

In this Supreme Court case, the central issue was whether a defendant's conviction should be overturned if it was potentially influenced by a co-defendant's confession that implicated the defendant, even though the jury was instructed to disregard that confession when determining the defendant's guilt.

The petitioner and a co-defendant, Evans, were convicted of armed postal robbery. During the trial, Evans' confession, which implicated the petitioner, was presented as evidence. Although the confession was admissible against Evans, it was considered inadmissible hearsay against the petitioner. The jury was instructed to ignore Evans' confession when deciding the petitioner's guilt. The Court of Appeals upheld the petitioner's conviction based on the belief that the jury could follow the judge's instructions, as established in the precedent set by Delli Paoli v. United States.

However, the Supreme Court decided to overrule Delli Paoli, concluding that the risk of the jury considering the inadmissible confession was too great and that such an event would violate the petitioner's Sixth Amendment right to confront witnesses. The Court noted that since Delli Paoli, its decisions had moved away from the belief that juries could always follow instructions to disregard inadmissible evidence. The Court cited cases like Pointer v. Texas and Douglas v. Alabama, which emphasized the importance of the right to cross-examination as part of the Confrontation Clause.

The Court also referenced Jackson v. Denno, which questioned the jury's ability to disregard involuntary confessions, and amendments to Rule 14 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which aimed to prevent prejudice in joint trials. The Court acknowledged that while juries are expected to follow instructions, there are situations where the risk of them not doing so is too high, particularly when the evidence is as incriminating as a co-defendant's confession.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the petitioner's conviction, stating that the admission of Evans' confession in the joint trial violated the petitioner's right to cross-examination. The Court held that limiting instructions were not an adequate substitute for this constitutional right. Justice Black concurred with the result, aligning with his dissent in Delli Paoli, and Justice Marshall did not participate in the decision.

Title X of the Family Planning Services Program Act authorizes the Secretary of Health and Human Services to award grants to states to establish and operate Title X projects, which are operated exclusively for the purpose of promoting family planning. The regulations governing the projects contain various restrictions on the subsidization of abortion-related speech, including prohibitions on counseling or referring a client to an abortion facility, discussing abortion with a client, or distributing literature describing abortion as a method of family planning. Petitioners brought suit in the District Court, claiming that the regulations violate, inter alia, the First and Fifth Amendments. The court entered summary judgment for respondents, rejecting petitioners' claims. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The regulations do not violate the First Amendment. Pp. 10-18. (a) The regulations do not impermissibly discriminate against abortion-related speech. Although the regulations prohibit the use of federal funds to discuss abortion with a client, they do not prohibit the use of nonfederal funds to discuss abortion. Since the regulations do not affect the amount of money that a Title X project receives, they do not violate the Establishment Clause. And although the regulations prohibit the use of federal funds to distribute literature describing abortion as a method of family planning, they do not prohibit the use of nonfederal funds to distribute such material. Thus, the regulations do not violate the Free Speech Clause. Pp. 10-13. (b) The regulations do not violate the Due Process Clause by forcing a Title X project to abandon its existing practice of providing abortion counseling and referral. There is nothing in the regulations that requires a doctor to represent as his own any opinion that he does not in fact hold. Nor is the doctor-patient relationship established by the Title X program sufficiently all-embracngso as to justify an expectation on the part of the patient of comprehensive medical advice. The program does not provide post-conception medical care, and therefore a doctor's silence with regard to abortion cannot reasonably be thought to mislead a client into thinking that the doctor does not consider abortion an appropriate option for her. The doctor is always free to make clear that advice regarding abortion is simply beyond the scope of the program. Pp. 13-15. (c) The regulations do not violate the Equal Protection Clause by treating abortion differently from other forms of medical treatment. The Government has no constitutional duty to subsidize an activity merely because the activity is constitutionally protected and may validly choose to fund childbirth over abortion and "implement that judgment by the allocation of public funds" for medical services relating to childbirth but not to those relating to abortion. Webster v. Doe, ante, at 492, 496. The Government has no affirmative duty to commit any resources to facilitate abortions, and its decision to fund childbirth but not abortion places no governmental obstacle in the path of a woman who chooses to terminate her pregnancy, but rather, by means of unequal subsidization of abortion and other medical services, encourages alternative activity deemed in the public interest. McRae v. Califano, 448 U. S. 146, 315. Pp. 15-18. 2. The regulations do not violate the Fifth Amendment. Pp. 18-20. (a) The regulations do not impermissibly burden a woman's Fifth Amendment right to choose whether to terminate her pregnancy. The Government has no constitutional duty to subsidize an activity merely because the activity is constitutionally protected and may validly choose to fund childbirth over abortion and "implement that judgment by the allocation of public funds" for medical services relating to childbirth but not to those relating to abortion. Webster v. Doe, ante, at 492, 496. The Government has no affirmative duty to commit any resources to facilitating abortions, and its decision to fund childbirth but not abortion places no governmental obstacle in the path of a woman who chooses to terminate her pregnancy, but rather, by means of unequal subsidization of abortion and other medical services, encourages alternative activity deemed in the public interest. McRae v. Califano, supra, at 315. Pp. 18-19. (b) The regulations do not violate a woman's Fifth Amendment right to medical self-determination and to make informed medical decisions free of government-imposed harm. Even if the regulations impermissibly infringe on the doctor/patient relationship and deprived a Title X client of information concerning abortion as a method of family planning, the Constitution does not require that the Government distort the scope of its mandated program in order to provide that information. Pp. 19-20. 909 F. 2d 149, affirmed.

In the case before the Supreme Court, Alexandre Mirzayance challenged his conviction on the grounds of ineffective assistance of counsel, arguing that his attorney's recommendation to withdraw his insanity defense constituted poor legal representation. The California courts had previously rejected this claim, and the issue before the Supreme Court was whether this decision was an unreasonable application of federal law as established by the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that the California court's decision was not contrary to or an unreasonable application of clearly established federal law. The Court applied the standard from Strickland v. Washington, which requires a defendant to show both deficient performance by counsel and prejudice resulting from that deficiency. The Court found that Mirzayance failed to establish either.

The Court noted that the jury had already rejected medical testimony about Mirzayance's mental state during the guilt phase of the trial, making it unlikely that they would accept similar evidence during the insanity phase. Additionally, Mirzayance's parents, who were expected to provide emotional testimony, expressed a strong disinclination to testify. The Court found that counsel's decision to withdraw the insanity plea was a strategic choice made after careful consideration and was within the range of reasonable professional assistance.

The Supreme Court also addressed the standard of review under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA), emphasizing that a state court's decision must be given deference unless it is an unreasonable application of federal law as determined by the Supreme Court. The Court criticized the lower courts for applying an improper "nothing to lose" standard, which is not recognized by the Supreme Court.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case with instructions to deny the habeas corpus petition, finding that Mirzayance did not receive ineffective assistance of counsel under the Strickland standard.

Petitioner was convicted in a state court of violating two ordinances of the General Code of the City of Birmingham, Ala.: (1) § 1142, making it "unlawful . ..for any person to stand or loiter upon any street or sidewalk ...after having been requested by any police officer to move on," and (2) § 1231, making it a crime for any person "to refuse or fail to comply with any lawful order, signal or direction" of a police officer. Both ordinances were construed by the Alabama Court of Appeals to require a showing of blocking free passage of pedestrians. Held: 1. Since the trial court below did not follow the narrowed construction of § 1142 adopted by the Alabama Court of Appeals subsequent to petitioner's trial, petitioner's conviction under that ordinance cannot stand. Pp. 148-151. 2. Petitioner's conviction under § 1231 contravened the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment since he was not in, on, or around any vehicle at the time he was directed to move on or at the time he was arrested. Pp. 151-152. Reversed and remanded.

Respondent Snyder sued petitioner Westboro Baptist Church and its members for intentional infliction of emotional distress, alleging that they picketed outside his son’s funeral without permission and shouted slogans like “God Damned America” and “There Are No Heroes Here, Only Cowards!” After a jury awarded him damages, the Fourth Circuit reversed, ruling that the judgment attached tort liability to constitutionally protected speech. Held: 1. The First Amendment shields Westboro from liability for its picketing. Pp. 4−11. (a) Under Maryland law, Snyder suffered emotional distress because of the content and viewpoint of the message conveyed by Westboro’s picketing, not because of any interference with the funeral itself. Thus, the picketing was not merely upsetting or offensive, but was entitled to “special protection” under the First Amendment. Pp. 4−7. (b) This Court has recognized that the First Amendment bars a jury from imposing liability on the basis of the jurors’ tastes or views. Outrageousness is a highly malleable standard with an inherently subjective quality that risks making the jury an instrument for suppressing vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasant expression. Pp. 7−9. (c) Even assuming that Westboro’s speech is entitled to First Amendment protection generally, the church is not immune from liability for intrusion upon seclusion because Snyder was a member of a captive audience at his son’s funeral. Most circumstances do not permit the government to decide which types of otherwise protected speech are sufficiently offensive to require protection for the unwilling listener or viewer. Here, Westboro stayed far enough away from the funeral to prevent Snyder from seeing anything except the tops of the signs. Moreover, there is no indication that the picketing interfered with the funeral itself. Expanding the captive audience doctrine to the circumstances presented here would be inconsistent with the First Amendment’s core purpose of protecting public debate. Pp. 9−11. 2. Since the First Amendment bars Snyder from recovery for intentional infliction of emotional distress or intrusion upon seclusion, he cannot recover for civil conspiracy based on those torts either. P. 11. 580 F. 3d 207, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Souter, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

After a fire destroyed his pleasure yacht and damaged several neighboring vessels and the marina on which the yacht was docked, petitioner Sisson filed a petition in Federal District Court to limit his liability to $800, the salvage value of the yacht after the fire. The court dismissed the petition for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, holding that 28 U. S. C. § 1333(1), which grants federal district courts jurisdiction over "[a]ny civil case of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction," did not confer federal jurisdiction over the action. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that neither § 1333(1) nor the Limited Liability Act-which limits the liability of an owner of a vessel for any damage done "without the privity or knowledge of such owner" to the value of the vessel and its freight-conferred jurisdiction. 

Held: Section 1333(1) confers federal jurisdiction over Sisson's limitation of liability suit. Pp. 269-274.
	 (a) The jurisdictional inquiry does not turn on the actual effects on maritime commerce of the fire on Sisson's vessel, but rather on the general features of the type of incident involved to determine whether such an incident is likely to disrupt commercial activity. Here, the general features-a fire on a vessel docked at a marina on navigable waters-plainly satisfy the requirement of potential disruption to commercial maritime activity. Executive Jet Aviation, Inc. v. Cleveland, 409 U. S. 249; Foremost Ins. Co. v. Richardson, 457 U. S. 668. Pp. 269-271.
	 (b) The party seeking to invoke maritime jurisdiction must show a substantial relationship between the activity giving rise to the incident and traditional maritime activity. The relevant "activity" is defined not by the particular circumstances of the incident, but by the general conduct from which the incident arose. Here, the relevant activity was the storage and maintenance of a vessel at a marina on navigable waters. That activity has a substantial relationship to traditional maritime activity, since docking a vessel at a marina on a navigable waterway is a common, if not indispensable, maritime activity. Pp. 271-274. 867 F. 2d 341, reversed and remanded.
