Given the nature of the intrusion and the law enforcement interest at stake, this brief seizure of the premises was permissible. Pp. 6-8. (c) This Court's case law supports the conclusion that the restriction was lawful. Various cases have upheld temporary restraints where needed to preserve evidence until police can obtain a warrant in a reasonable period of time. Nor are the countervailing arguments persuasive. McArthur has waived his contention that the police proceeded without probable cause. Even assuming that the porch where McArthur stood was part of his home, the differences between porches and other parts of homes are insignificant from the Fourth Amendment's perspective. Also unpersuasive is McArthur's reliance on Welsh v. Wisconsin, 466 U. S. 740, wherein this Court held that police could not enter a home without a warrant in order to prevent the loss of evidence of the "nonjailable" traffic offense of driving while intoxicated. Here, the evidence at issue was of crimes that were "jailable," not "nonjailable," and the restriction at issue is less serious than police entry into the home itself in order to make a warrantless arrest or conduct a search. Pp. 8-10. Reversed and remanded.

Section 137 of the Illinois Corporation Tax Act makes it illegal for a corporation to engage in certain activities relating to a tender offer for its shares unless the offer complies with various requirements contained in the section. Petitioner, a Delaware corporation with its principal offices in Connecticut, made a tender offer for the common stock of respondent, an Illinois corporation whose principal executive office is in Illinois. When petitioner failed to comply with the Illinois Act, respondent brought suit in Illinois state court to enjoin the tender offer. The trial court granted the injunction, and the Illinois Appellate Court affirmed. The Illinois Supreme Court denied leave to appeal. Subsequently, petitioner sued in Federal District Court challenging the constitutionality of the Illinois Act. The District Court dismissed the complaint, but the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Illinois Act contravened the Commerce Clause of the Federal Constitution. Held: The Illinois Act is invalid under the Commerce Clause. Pp. 508-518. (a) By directly regulating and preventing, unless its terms are satisfied, interstate tender offers which in turn would generate interstate transactions, the Illinois Act directly regulates and prevents interstate commerce in violation of the Commerce Clause. Moreover, the burden the Act imposes on interstate commerce is excessive in light of the local interests the Act purports to further. Because the Act purports to regulate directly and to interdict interstate commerce, including commerce wholly outside the State, it must be held invalid. Pp. 510-514. (b) Even when a state statute regulates interstate commerce indirectly, the burden imposed on that commerce must not be excessive in relation to the local interests served by the statute. Here, the asserted local interests of protecting resident security holders and regulating the internal affairs of companies incorporated under Illinois law are insufficient to outweigh the burdens the Illinois Act imposes on interstate commerce. Pp. 514-518. Affirmed.

In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether a plaintiff bringing a lawsuit under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) needed to show that he was replaced by someone outside the age group protected by the ADEA in order to establish a prima facie case. The Court found that the fact that the plaintiff was replaced by someone significantly younger than him was sufficient to establish a prima facie case of age discrimination. The Court also clarified that the ADEA prohibits discrimination on the basis of age and not class membership, meaning that the fact that the plaintiff was replaced by someone outside the protected class was not enough to establish a prima facie case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit recently ruled that the bankruptcy court had no jurisdiction to hear a will dispute involving a deceased Texas businessman's son. The court held that the Bankruptcy Court had no authority to hear the will dispute because it was a matter that would be decided by a probate court in Texas. The bankruptcy court's decision was based on a longstanding legal doctrine that the federal courts have no jurisdiction over probate matters. The Court's ruling is the latest in a long line of court decisions that have limited federal courts' ability to hear will disputes. The Supreme Court recently ruled in favor of a bankruptcy trustee in a similar bankruptcy case that a bankruptcy court could not hear a dispute over a deceased man's will. In that case, the bankruptcy judge dismissed the bankruptcy trustee's claims against his father's deceased son, E. Pierce Marshall, who was the ultimate beneficiary of J. Howard Marshall II's estate plan. Pierce filed a proof of claim in the bankruptcy proceeding, alleging that Vickie Marshall had defamed him by making false statements to members of the press that Pierce had engaged in forgery, fraud, and overreaching to gain control of his father’s assets. Vickie filed a countersuit, claiming that she had been defamed by Pierce's actions. Pierce also filed a claim in bankruptcy court alleging that he had violated the terms of the will. The Bankruptcy Court dismissed his claims against Vickie, and the bankruptcy trial court concluded that Vickie had no standing to file the countersuit. The appeals were denied. The Appeals Court held that Vickie's motion for a preliminary injunction was not supported by the facts of the case, and that the trial court had jurisdiction to decide the case. The trial court also found that Pierce violated the Bankruptcy Code by failing to provide a copy of the final judgment, which was not required by the bankruptcy code. The Appeal Court concluded that the case should be dismissed. The full court will rule on the appeal on the issue of the bankruptcy.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against New York State Conference of Blue Cross & Blue Shield Plans v. Travelers Ins. Co., a self-insured, multiemployer welfare benefit plan.  The court's order, which entered a temporary restraining order against the defendants, permanently enjoins New York from imposing a gross receipts tax on the income of medical centers operated by ERISA funds.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, the Health Facility Assessment (HFA) is a state law that imposes a 0.6 percent tax on gross receipts for medical services provided at hospitals, residential health care facilities, and diagnostic and treatment centers. The complaint alleges that the HFA is a pre-empted provision of ERISA, and that the Fund and its plan beneficiaries are entitled to a tax on those services.  In addition, the complaint alleged that, as a result of the imposition of HFA, the Fund would have had to decide whether to cover a more limited range of services for its beneficiaries, or perhaps to charge plan members higher fees.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit today issued a final order permanently enjoining the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering the defendants to pay disgorgement of $7,066 plus prejudgment interest of $1,177,670, and a civil penalty of $100,000.   The defendants agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry of judgments that permanently enjoin them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and order them to pay a civil monetary penalty in the amount of $150,000, a $50,000 civil penalty, and to be barred from serving as officers or directors of any state-funded health care program. Â The court also granted the defendants' request for a partial injunction against future ERISA pre-emption, which is subject to court approval.

In 2004, Washington State voters approved Initiative 872 (I-872), which altered the state's primary election system. Under I-872, candidates could indicate their party preference on the ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two vote-getters for each office would advance to the general election, regardless of party preference. This system replaced the previous "blanket primary" system, which the Supreme Court had struck down in California Democratic Party v. Jones (2000) for violating political parties' First Amendment rights.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals found I-872 to be unconstitutional, arguing that it imposed an unconstitutional burden on political parties' associational rights. The Supreme Court, however, reversed this decision, holding that I-872 does not impose a severe burden on political parties' rights because it does not actually nominate party candidates. The Court emphasized that the law does not refer to candidates as party nominees and that parties are free to nominate their candidates through other means.

The Supreme Court rejected the argument that voters would be confused by the party-preference designations on the ballot, stating that this was speculative and that there was no evidence to support the claim of widespread voter confusion. The Court suggested that the state could implement measures, such as disclaimers or educational materials, to clarify the meaning of party preference on the ballot.

Since the Court determined that I-872 does not severely burden associational rights, the state did not need to demonstrate a compelling interest to justify the law. The Court found that the state's interest in providing voters with relevant information about candidates was sufficient to uphold I-872.

The Supreme Court concluded that I-872 is facially constitutional and allowed the law to be implemented, reversing the judgment of the Court of Appeals. The decision implies that states have some leeway in designing primary election systems, as long as they do not severely burden the associational rights of political parties and do not lead to voter confusion about party endorsements.

Pawtucket, Rhode Island, erects a Christmas display in a park owned by a nonprofit organization and located in the heart of the shopping district. The display is essentially like those to be found in hundreds of towns or cities across the Nation-often on public grounds-during the Christmas season. Each year, in cooperation with the downtown retail merchants' association, the City of Pawtucket erects the display as part of its observance of the Christmas holiday season. In 1973, when the present creche was acquired, it cost the City $1365; it now is valued at $200. The erection and dismantling of the creche costs the City about $20 per year. No money has been expended on its maintenance for the past 10 years. Respondents, residents and individual members of the Rhode Island affiliate of the American Civil Liberties Union, and the affiliate itself, brought this action in the Federal District Court, challenging the City's inclusion in the display. The District Court held that the City has tried to endorse and promulgate religious beliefs, and that the display has the real and substantial effect of affiliating the City with the Christian beliefs that it represents. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The City has not violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. Pp. 488-481. (a) The Establishment Clause is not barred by the First and Fourteenth Amendments. P. 489. (b) The fact that the city has not impermissibly advanced religion and that it includes the Creche does not create excessive entanglement between religion and government does not mean that the Clause is barred by any single test or criterion in this sensitive area of the country. In fact, it has been alert to the constitutionally expressed opposition to the establishment of religion since at least 1789, and it has scrutinized challenged legislation or official conduct to determine whether, in reality, it establishes a religion or religious faith, or tends to do so. See, e. g., Larkin v. Grendel's Den, supra, and McCollum v. Board of Education, 333 U. S. 203, 211. The case is distinguished from Larkin by the fact that it was a Congress whose constitutional decisions have always been regarded as the greatest weight in the interpretation of that fundamental instrument, Myers v. United States, 272 U.S. 52, 174-175, and which includes a creche in this case does not violate the Clause's Establishment Clause. In any event, apart from this litigation, there is no evidence of political friction or divisiveness over the display in the 40-year history of PawTucket's Christmas celebration. The evidence of accommodation of all faiths and all forms of religious expression, and hostility toward none, would inevitably lead to its invalidation under the Clause, and a litigant cannot, by the very act of commencing a lawsuit, create the appearance and effect merely happens to coincide or harmonize with the tenets of some . . . religions." See McGowan v. Maryland, 366 U. s. 420. Nor does the Clause require complete separation of church and state; it affirmatively mandates accommodation, not merely tolerance, of all religions, and forbids hostility toward any. The Clause's primary effect is to confer a substantial and impermissible benefit on religion in general and on the Christian faith in particular, and to depict the origins of that holiday long recognized as a National Holiday. The State, like the Congresses and Presidents, has principally taken note of a significant historical religious event long celebrated in the Western World. The creche's display depicts the historical origins of this traditional event long recognized by the three constitutional branches of government. The tangible material it contributes is de minimis, and there is nothing here, of course, to indicate that such hostility would bring us into "war with our national tradition as embodied in the First First Amendment's guaranty of the free exercise of religion." P. 589. 2. The city has a secular purpose for including the crechet, that the statute or activity was motivated wholly by religious considerations, and includes the display, which is sponsored by the City to celebrate the Holiday and to portray the origins. The public display, at the very time people are taking note of the season with Christmas hymns and carols in public schools and other public places, and while the Congress and Legislatures open sessions with prayers by paid chaplains, would be a stilted overreaction contrary to our history and to our holdings. The Supreme Court of the United States has reversed a lower court's decision in a capital punishment case involving a man accused of murder. The Court found that the lower court committed clear error in overruling a Batson objection made by the defendant, arguing that the prosecution used peremptory strikes against two African American jurors in violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court held that the prosecution's justifications for striking the jurors were insufficient and likely pretextual, and that the trial judge failed to properly evaluate the prosecution's explanations. The Court remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its decision.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the deputy prosecuting attorney in a civil lawsuit brought against her by a man who claimed that she violated his constitutional rights by filing false charges against him. The plaintiff argued that the prosecutor knowingly submitted false information in order to obtain an arrest warrant, and therefore should be held liable for damages. However, the Supreme Court held that the prosecutor was immune from liability under Section 1983 of the Civil Rights Act of 1871, which provides a damages remedy for anyone whose constitutional or statutory rights have been violated by a government official. The Court reasoned that the prosecutor's actions were taken within the scope of her duties as a public official and were therefore protected by absolute immunity.

When respondent was convicted of multiple counts of sexual battery and soliciting prostitution, he was ordered to participate in the State’s Sexually Violent Persons Program (SVPP), which includes a requirement that participants acknowledge their “responsibility” for their past sexual misconduct. Refusing to participate, respondent was stripped of his Medium Security Unit (MSU) status, which he had earned after seven years of good behavior, and was told that he would be transferred to Maximum Security Unit (MaxSec) status, which is reserved for the most serious offenders. He was also warned that he would be unable to regain MSU status during the remainder of his sentence. Respondent sued, claiming that the SVPP requirements violated his Fifth Amendment privilege against selfincrimination. The District Court agreed, concluding that the threats of transfer to MaxSec and loss of MSU status were sufficiently coercive to constitute compulsion. However, the Tenth Circuit vacated, holding that the consequences were not sufficiently coercive to meet the standards of United States v. LeValle, 490 U. S. 343, and United States v. Diniardo, 505 U. S. 863. Held: The consequences of respondent’s invocation of his Fifth Amendment privilege are sufficiently coercive to constitute compulsion. Pp. 31–39. (a) The plurality errs in attempting to balance the consequences of respondent’s invocation of his Fifth Amendment privilege against the SVPP’s legitimate therapeutic purposes. The fact that the SVPP serves legitimate therapeutic purposes does not justify reduced constitutional protection for those ordered to participate. Available alternatives—such as granting participants use immunity—allow the State to achieve the same objectives without impinging on inmates’ privilege. The plurality’s concern that requiring immunity will undermine the SVPP’s therapeutic goals is unfounded. Use immunity does not preclude prosecution; it merely prevents the State from using an inmate’s own words, and the fruits thereof, against him in a subsequent prosecution. Alternatively, the State could continue to pursue its rehabilitative goals without violating participants’ Fifth Amendment rights by offering inmates a voluntary program. Pp. 31–39. 242 F. 3d 1152, affirmed.

Petitioner eBay operates a popular Internet Web site that allows private sellers to list goods they wish to sell, either through an auction or at a fixed price. Petitioner Half.com, now a wholly owned subsidiary of eBay, operates a similar Web site. Respondent MercExchange, L. L. C., holds a number of patents, including a business method patent for an electronic market designed to facilitate the sale of goods between private individuals by establishing a central authority to promote trust among participants. A jury found that the patent was valid, that eBay had infringed that patent, and that an award of damages was appropriate. Following the jury verdict, the District Court denied the District’s motion for permanent injunctive relief. The Court of Appeals reversed, applying its “general rule that courts will issue permanent injunctions against patent infringement absent exceptional circumstances.” 401 F. 3d 1323, 1339. This Court has consistently rejected invitations to replace traditional equitable considerations with a rule that an injunction automatically follows a determination that a copyright has been infringed. See, e.g., New York Times Co. v. Tasini, 533 U. S. 483, 505, and Dun v. Lumbermen’S Credit Assn., 209 U.S. 20, 23–24, respectively. Neither the District court nor the Federal Circuit fairly applied these traditional equitable principles in deciding respondent’d motion for a permanent injunction. Although the Court recited the traditional four-factor test, 275 F. Supp. 2d, at 711, it appeared to adopt certain expansive principles suggesting that injunal relief could not issue in a broad swath of cases. Most notably, it concluded that a “plaintiff”s willingness to license its patents” and “its lack of commercial activity in practicing the patents,” would be sufficient to establish that patent holder would not suffer irreparable harm if an injunction did not issue. The District Court then denied the motion, holding that injunctions should be denied only in the “unusual” case, under “exceptional circumstances” or “ ‘in rare instances . . . to protect the public interest.’ ” Id., at 1338–1339. Held: Neither court below correctly applied the traditional Four-factor framework that governs the award of injuni relief. Pp. 5–7. (a) Respondent eBay Inc. and Half.Com, Inc., argue that this traditional test applies to disputes arising under the Patent Act. The decision to grant or deny permanent injuctive relief is an act of equitable discretion by the district court, reviewable on appeal for abuse of discretion. But the creation of a right is distinct from the provision of remedies for violations of that Act, which is “loyalty” to the same purpose as equity. To the extent that the district Court adopted such a categorical rule, then, its analysis cannot be squared with the principles of equity adopted by Congress. Cf. Roche Products v. Bolar Pharmaceutical Co., 733 F. 2-d 858, 865 (CAFed 1984), which rejected the contention that a court of equity has no jurisdiction to grant injunty relief to a patent holder who has unreasonably declined to use the patent. To be sure, the patent Act also declares that “patents shall have the attributes of personal property” §261, including the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, or selling the invention, §154(a)(1). According to the Court, this statutory right to exclusion alone justifies its general rule in favor of permanent injUNctive relief, but the creation-of-a-right is separate from the remedy for violations that Congress intended. Cf., e. g., Romero-Barcelo, 456 U., S. 531, 542. And, as in this Court, the decision whether to grant, deny, or deny injunctions “may” issue “in accordance with equity” is an exercise of the discretion of the district courts, not the court below, which may exercise its discretion in determining whether the facts of a situation require it to issue an injunction. P. 7. (b) The decision whether not to grant and deny injunctions to a prevailing plaintiff must be based on the principles that equity applies, not on the traditional equitable principle that an injunctions automatically follow a determination of a copyright infringement. The same principle applies with equal force to disputes between patent owners and patent holders, and, like the Copyright Act, is consistent with the principle of equity. The Copyright Act provides that courts “shall” grant injunctions on “such terms as it may deem reasonable to prevent or restrain infringement” 17 U. C. §502(a). And as in our decision today, this Court has repeatedly rejected invitations by traditional inequity considerations with regard to a rule requiring an injunction’ automatically follows

The Supreme Court ruled that CSX Transportation, Inc. (CSX), an interstate rail carrier, can challenge Alabama's sales and use taxes under the Railroad Revitalization and Regulatory Reform Act of 1976 (4-R Act). The 4-R Act aims to prevent state and local governments from imposing discriminatory taxes on rail carriers. CSX argued that Alabama's tax scheme is discriminatory because it taxes rail carriers for diesel fuel purchases while exempting their competitors in the transportation industry, such as interstate motor and water carriers.

The Court's decision focused on the interpretation of the 4-R Act, particularly Section 11501(b)(4), which prohibits states from imposing any tax that discriminates against a rail carrier. The Court concluded that an excise tax, like Alabama's sales and use tax, falls under the category of "another tax" mentioned in the statute. The Court also determined that tax exemptions for certain entities could constitute discrimination if no reasonable distinction justifies the different treatment.

The Court rejected Alabama's argument that the statute should be read to only prohibit discrimination against rail carriers compared to local businesses, noting that the Act's language does not make such a distinction. The Court also disagreed with the Eleventh Circuit's previous decision that relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in Department of Revenue of Ore. v. ACF Industries, Inc., which held that a railroad could not challenge a generally applicable property tax based on exemptions for non-railroad property. The Court clarified that the reasoning in ACF Industries was based on the structure of the 4-R Act concerning property taxes and did not apply to non-property taxes like sales and use taxes.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Eleventh Circuit and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The Court's decision allows CSX to proceed with its challenge to Alabama's tax scheme, but it did not address whether CSX would ultimately prevail in proving that the taxes are discriminatory. The implications of the decision are that rail carriers may challenge state tax schemes that exempt their competitors, potentially leading to changes in how states tax different transportation entities.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled that a fiduciary may not sue a beneficiary under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) for reimbursement of medical expenses paid by a plan when the beneficiary has recovered for its injuries from a third party. The court held that the District Court's order requiring the couple to set aside $74,869.37 in an investment account was not equitable. The Fourth Circuit also found that the Sereboffs had violated the terms of the plan's "Acts of Third Parties" provision, which requires the plan to pay a portion of a third-party's medical expenses when a beneficiary has not received the full damages claimed in a lawsuit. The Court concluded that the district court's decision was not consistent with the law's requirements for equitable relief. The 4th Circuit held that, in this case, Mid Atlantic Medical Services, Inc., the plan administrator, had not shown that the "act or omission" of another person or party caused the beneficiary to be injured. The decision also found, however, that the law requires that Mid Atlantic be compensated for the full amount of the medical expenses it paid on the beneficiary's behalf, even if the third party has not yet recovered. The appeals. The Supreme Court agreed, holding that the lower court had erred in denying Mid Atlantic's motion for a judgment of summary judgment, and that the trial court had properly entered a judgment in Mid Atlantic’s favor. The Appeals Court held that there was no reason to conclude that the court was wrong in its decision. The case is now remanded for further consideration.

After appellant had conducted a peaceful march through the streets of Baton Rouge, Louisiana, during which he sang patriotic songs and delivered a brief speech, he stood on a sidewalk adjacent to the courthouse and led a meeting consisting mainly of singing and prayer. During the meeting, the sidewalk was blocked by the throng of participants. When the police requested appellant to remove the blocking, he refused. Under a Louisiana statute making it a misdemeanor to obstruct the free use of a public sidewalk, appellant was convicted. His conviction was upheld by the Louisiana Supreme Court. Held: 1. The conviction for disturbing the peace can not stand, since the statute as authoritatively interpreted by the Louisiana Supreme Court is unconstitutionally vague in its overly broad scope. Pp. 468-474. 2. The conviction for obstructing the public sidewalk can not stand, since the practice of the authorities in granting or denying permission for peaceful parades and meetings is an unwarranted abridgment of appellant's freedom of speech and assembly secured to him by the First Amendment, as applied to the States by the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 474-480. 244 La. 1089, 156 So. 2d 445, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Halliburton Co. and its former CEO in a securities fraud action.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that Halliburto made numerous misrepresentations designed to inflate its stock price, in violation of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, the defendants later made a number of corrective disclosures that caused its stock to drop and, consequently, investors to lose money.  In addition, the court found that, in order to qualify for class certification, a defendant must prove that the misrepresentation caused the stock price to fall and resulted in the losses.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, Halliburco consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating these provisions and orders him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $10,000. Â Halliburton also agreed to pay a $1,500 civil penalty and to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years.Â The settlement is subject to court approval.   The court's order, which was entered on consent, requires the SEC to show that it has satisfied the general requirements of the federal securities laws for class actions, including that the SEC is required to prove loss causation, i.e., that the corrected truth of the former falsehoods actually caused the company's stock to fall, resulted in a subsequent loss, and is sufficient to justify the imposition of a class action order.  It also requires the court to determine whether a defendant is liable for the alleged loss, whether the company is liable, and whether it is liable to be required to show loss causation at the class certification stage.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 597 F. 3d 330 (January 24, 2011).  The Court also granted the SEC’s request for a temporary restraining order against further violations of the securities laws.  On May 24, 2012, the Court of Appeals issued an order granting the SEC an emergency asset freeze and ordering a preliminary injunction against future violations of these provisions.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses whether a company that is heavily regulated by a federal agency can be considered to be "acting under" a federal officer, and thus eligible to remove a state-court action to federal court under the federal officer removal statute, 28 U.S.C. §1442(a)(1). The case in question involves a lawsuit filed by Lisa Watson and Loretta Lawson against Philip Morris Companies in Arkansas state court, alleging deceptive business practices related to the marketing of "light" cigarettes.

Philip Morris sought to remove the case to federal court, arguing that their actions were taken "under" the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), a federal agency, due to the FTC's detailed supervision of cigarette testing. Both the District Court and the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the removal.

The Supreme Court, however, reversed this decision. The Court held that simply complying with federal regulations does not constitute "acting under" a federal officer. The Court emphasized that the statute's language, historical context, and purpose do not support such an expansive interpretation. The Court noted that the original intent of the statute was to protect federal officers from interference by state courts, not to shield private companies from state litigation merely because they are regulated by federal law.

The Court also rejected Philip Morris's argument that it was "acting under" the FTC because the FTC had delegated the responsibility of cigarette testing to the industry. The Court found no evidence of a formal delegation of legal authority from the FTC to Philip Morris or any other special relationship that would allow for removal under the statute.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court determined that Philip Morris's compliance with FTC regulations did not make it a federal actor for the purposes of the federal officer removal statute. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion. This decision implies that heavily regulated companies cannot use federal regulation alone as a basis for removing state court actions to federal court.

After giving chase, Police Officer Pertoso tackled respondent Hodari, handcuffed him, and radioed for assistance. During the search incident to his arrest, the police discovered crack cocaine on Hodari's person. He was charged with possessing the drug and moving to suppress the evidence relating thereto. The trial court denied the motion, and Hodari was convicted. On appeal, the California Court of Appeal reversed, ruling that Hodari had been "seized" when he saw Pertoso running toward him, that this seizure was unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment, and that the evidence of the cocaine had to be suppressed as the fruit of that illegal seizure. Held: Assuming that Pertoso's pursuit constituted a "show of authority" enjoining Hodari to halt, since Hodari did not comply with that injunction he was not seized until he was tackled. Thus, the cocaine abandoned while he was running was not the fruit of a seizure, and his motion to exclude evidence of it was properly denied. Pp. 120-124. (a) Although the term "seizure" traditionally included taking physical possession of property, for most purposes at common law it connoted not merely grasping, or applying physical force to, the animate or inanimate object in question, but actually bringing it within physical control. However, to constitute an arrest -the quintessential "seizure of the person" under the Fourth Amendment-the mere grasping or application of physical force with lawful authority, whether or not it succeeded in subduing the arrestee, was sufficient. Pp. 120-121. (b) With respect to a show of authority as with respect to application of physical force, a seizure does not occur even though the subject does not yield. The language of the Fourth Amendment cannot support Hodari's contention that Pertoso's pursuit qualified as a "show of authority" calling upon Hodari to halt. Moreover, it is undesirable to stretch the Fourth Amendment beyond its words and beyond the meaning of arrest, as Hodari urges. Compliance with police orders to stop should be encouraged, and only a few of those orders will be without adequate basis. Unlawful orders will not be deterred by sanctioning through the exclusionary rule those of them that are not obeyed. Pp. 121-122. (c) Even assuming that Pertoso's pursuit constituted a "show of authority" enjoining Hodari to halt, since Hodari did not comply with that injunction he was not seized until he was tackled. The cocaine abandoned while he was running was thus not the fruit of a seizure, and his motion to exclude evidence of it was properly denied. Pp. 123-124. 22 Cal. App. 4th 1150, 27 Cal. Rptr. 2d 18, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Connecticut upheld a lower court's ruling that a federal law prohibiting the use of federal funds for religious purposes at colleges and universities is constitutional. The law, the Higher Education Facilities Act of 1963, provides for a 20-year limitation on the religious use of the facilities constructed with federal funds. The appeals court found that the law does not prohibit the free exercise of religion in violation of the First Amendment. The court concluded that the limitation of federal interest in the facilities would be unconstitutional as a gift of taxpayers' funds and that in other respects the federal act violates the Establishment Clause. The case was brought by Elliot Richardson, the former Secretary of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, and his wife, Eleanor Taft . The appellants alleged that Richardson violated the law by failing to comply with the conditions of the law, and that their religious affiliations did not interfere with their secular educational functions. The Appeals Court agreed with the lower court, and the case was remanded for further proceedings.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit is considering whether a 1974 Minnesota law requiring a private employer to pay pensions to its employees violates the Constitution's Contract Clause. The law requires private employers with 100 or more employees to pay pension benefits to employees who have worked at least 10 years. In a case that arose out of a similar 1974 law, the Minnesota Supreme Court ruled that the law violated the Constitution because it requires the employer to provide pension benefits only to the extent of the employee's service with the company. The Court found that the employer's obligation to pay the pension benefits did not extend to the employees who were discharged after the company had closed its Minnesota office. The court found that, under the law's terms, the company was free to terminate the plan and distribute the trust assets at any time and for any reason. The high court concluded that the Act violated the Contract Clause because it required the company to provide the pension benefit only to those employees who had worked at the company and to those who were eligible for retirement. The appeals court agreed with the lower court's finding that the provision of the law did not apply to the discharged employees. The case is now being heard by the appeals court, which will determine whether the law is constitutional. The 8th Justice will rule on the issue of whether it is impermissibly unconstitutional.

Pier injuries to longshoremen occurring on piers permanently affixed to shore are compensable under the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act of 1927 (Act), which provides that "the admiralty and maritime jurisdiction of the United States shall extend to and include all cases of damage or injury, to person or property, caused by a vessel on navigable water, not-withstanding that such damage ... be done or consummated on land." Held: 1. The Act does not extend coverage to those injured on the seaward side of the pier even though the pier, like a bridge, extends over navigable waters. Pp. 479-481. (a) The language of the Act is to the contrary and the background of the statute leaves little doubt that Congress' concern in providing compensation was a narrower one. P. 478. (b) Since long before the Act was passed, it has been settled law that structures such as wharves and piers are extensions of the land. Parker v. Motor Boat Sales, 314 U. S. 244, 249, and Calbeck v. Travelers Insurance Co., 370 U.S. 114, approved recovery for injuries occurring on a pier by pier-based equipment. Calbeck made it clear that Congress intended to exercise its full jurisdiction seaward of the Jensen line and to cover all injuries on navigation waters, whether or not state compensation was also available in particular situations. The proviso to § 3(a) conditioning coverage on the unavailability of state remedies was not meant to deny federal relief where the injury occurred on the landward side, but removed uncertainties as to the Act's coverage of injuries on land traditionally within the ambit of state compensation acts, and the invitation to move that line landward must be addressed to Congress, not to this Court, since the Act has no bearing whatsoever on their right to a compensation remedy under the Act, and even contruing the Extension Act to amend the Act would not effect this result, since long-shoremen injured on pier by the pier would still remain outside the Act. P p. 477. (c) The extension Act was not aimed at broader coverage: coverage of the "status" of the longshoreman employed in performing a maritime contract. Nor was it intended to extend coverage only beyond the pier where the States could not reach. Nor is the extension Act to be limited to injuries occurring in loading or unloading a ship, since a pier injury is not covered unless it occurs on the ship or between the wharf and the ship so as to bring them within the maritime jurisdiction, and a pier injuries are not maritime torts if caused by vessels on the pier. P, 477 F. 2d 900, reversed.

The Supreme Court was tasked with determining whether federal criminal statutes that subject individuals to prosecution based on their status as Indians violate the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The case involved respondents, who are enrolled members of the Coeur d'Alene Tribe, and were federally indicted for crimes committed on the Coeur d'Alene Indian Reservation. They were convicted under the Major Crimes Act, which applies federal law to certain crimes committed by Indians on reservations.

The respondents argued that their convictions under federal law, which includes a felony-murder provision not present in Idaho state law, constituted racial discrimination since a non-Indian committing the same crime would be prosecuted under state law without the felony-murder rule. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals agreed, finding that the disparity violated the equal protection requirements implicit in the Fifth Amendment.

The Supreme Court reversed this decision, stating that federal legislation concerning Indian tribes is not based on impermissible racial classifications but on the unique status of Indians as members of quasi-sovereign tribal entities. The Court cited previous cases, such as Morton v. Mancari and Fisher v. District Court, to support the view that legislation affecting Indian tribes is a matter of political and not racial regulation.

The Court concluded that the federal criminal statutes in question do not violate equal protection principles because they apply the same legal standards to all persons within federal jurisdiction, regardless of race. The disparity between federal and state law was deemed irrelevant since Congress has the constitutional authority to prescribe a criminal code for Indian country. The Court held that the federal government's treatment of the respondents was evenhanded and did not involve impermissible racial classifications, thus upholding the convictions.

The judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

After respondent was arrested outside a house owned by one Marshall and occupied by respondent, Mrs. Marshall, and others, officers entered the house pursuant to the consent of Mrs. Marshall, who was wearing a robe and cradling her infant child, and after finding the east bedroom, which she said was jointly occupied by respondent and herself, they found $4,995 in a diaper bag in the only closet in the room. Respondent was subsequently tried and convicted of embezzlement. He moved to suppress the evidence so seized, claiming lack of probable cause for the arrest and illegal entry of the house, and that the consent of Mrs. Marshall to the search was invalid since she was not the owner of the house. The District Court agreed and suppressed the evidence. On appeal, the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The consent of one who possesses common authority over premises or effects is valid as against the absent, nonconsenting person with whom that authority is shared. Pp. 408-410. 2. The District Court erred in excluding from evidence at the suppression hearings, as inadmissible hearsay, the out-of-court statements of respondent himself that he and Mrs. Marshall were husband and wife, and the statements of Mrs. Marshall to the officers regarding her and respondent's joint occupancy and use of the east bedroom. Such statements were admissible for whatever inferences the trial judge could reasonably draw concerning joint occupancy of the east bedroom. And while the same rules of evidence governing criminal jury trials are not generally thought to govern hearings before a judge to determine evidentiary questions, nonetheless, in the circumstances present here, the trial judge should not have excluded Mrs. Marshall's statements. If there is remaining doubt about the matter, it should be dispelled by the considerations that cohabitation out of wedlock would not seem to be a relationship that one would falsely confess, that Mrs. Marshall's statements were against her penal interest, and that she was a witness for respondent at the suppression hearings and thus available for crossexamination. Pp. 410-414. 476 F. 2d 1083, reversed and remanded.

Police officers knocked on the door of petitioner Randolph’s home and asked to speak with him. His wife, Janet, opened the door and allowed the officers to enter. While speaking with her, the officers observed a small amount of white powdery substance near the coffee table. Believing that the substance was cocaine, Officer Mattingly asked Janet if she knew anything about it. She replied that she did not, but that her husband did. Officer Mattingly then spoke with Scott Randolph, who confirmed that he owned the substance and agreed to surrender it. The officers then left the home. Later that day, a detective called Janet and asked her to accompany him to the precinct for questioning. She declined, stating that she wanted to talk to her lawyer first. Meanwhile, the detectives obtained a search warrant based on the officers’ observations and testimony. Upon executing the warrant, they discovered additional quantities of cocaine throughout the home. Both Randolphs were subsequently charged with felony possession of cocaine. At trial, the State conceded that the initial entry was illegal, but argued that the subsequent search was proper under the doctrine of Plain View. The jury acquitted both defendants. The State Supreme Court affirmed, rejecting the defense’s argument that the search violated the Fourth Amendment. Held: Because a physically present inhabitant’s express refusal of consent to a police search is dispositive as to him, regardless of the consent of a fellow occupant, the search here was unconstitutional. Pp. 4–11. (a) The Fourth Amendment’s text indicates that the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the totality of the circumstances surrounding the search, including the degree of justification for the search and the extent to which the search interferes with the individual’s privacy interests. The amended Exclusionary Rule reflects this approach, making the exclusion of illegally seized evidence depend on the totality of the circumstances. Under this framework, the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the balance between the Government’s interest in enforcing laws against drug offenders and the individual’s privacy interests. Pp. 4–5. (b) The reasoning of United States v. Martinez-Villarreal, 498 U.S. 282, supports the conclusion that a physically present inhabitant’s express refusal of consent to a police search is dispositive as to him, regardless of the consent of a fellow occupant. The plurality’s analysis in Matlock v. United States, 415 U.S. 164, rested on mutual use of the property by persons generally having joint access or control for most purposes, so that it was reasonable to recognize that any of the co-inhabitants has the right to permit the inspection in his own right. However, the Court did not purport to address the question whether customary social understanding accords the consenting tenant authority powerful enough to prevail over the co-tenant’s objection. Here, the State does not argue that Janet gave any indication to the police of a need for protection inside the house that might have justified entry into the portion of the premises where the officers found the powdery substance. Nor does the State claim that the entry and search should be upheld under the rubric of exigent circumstances, owing to some apprehension by the officers that Scott would destroy evidence of drug use before any warrant could be obtained. Pp. 5–7. (c) The rule that a physically present inhabitant’s express refusal of consent to a police search is dispositive as to him comports with the principles governing the reasonableness of warrantless searches. First, the rule is consistent with the idea that the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the totality of the circumstances surrounding the search, including the degree of justification for the search and the extent to which the search interferes with the individual’s privacy interests. Second, the rule is consistent with the notion that the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the balance between the Government’s interest in enforcing laws against drug offenders and the individual’s privacy interests. Third, the rule is consistent with the idea that the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the degree of justification for the search. Fourth, the rule is consistent with the notion that the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the extent to which the search interferes with the individual’s privacy interests. Fifth, the rule is consistent with the idea that the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the degree of justification for the search. Sixth, the rule is consistent with the notion that the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the extent to which the search interferes with the individual’s privacy interests. Finally, the rule is consistent with the idea that the reasonableness of a warrantless search depends on the degree of justification for the search. Pp. 7–9. (d) The rule announced here is not inconsistent with the rule that a co-tenant’s consent to a warrantless search is binding on the other co-tenants. Nothing in the record justifies the search on grounds independent of Janet’s consent. The State does not argue that she gave any indication to the police of a need for protection inside the house that might have justified entry into the portion of the premises where the officers found the powdery substance. Nor does the State claim that the entry and search should be upheld under the rubric of exigent circumstances, owing to some apprehension by the officers that Scott would destroy evidence of drug use before any warrant could be obtained. Pp. 9–10. 270 Ga. 618, 786 S.E. 2d 50, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Roberts, C. J., and Souter, J., joined.

The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals, allowing the acquisition of banks across state lines within New England by bank holding companies based in the region. The acquisitions were challenged on the grounds that they were not authorized by the Bank Holding Company Act (BHCA) and violated the Commerce Clause and Compact Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

The BHCA requires Federal Reserve Board approval for bank holding companies to acquire banks in other states, and the Douglas Amendment to the BHCA allows such acquisitions only if the state where the bank is located specifically authorizes it. Some New England states enacted statutes permitting regional interstate bank acquisitions, which led to the contested acquisitions.

The Supreme Court found that the regional statutes from Massachusetts and Connecticut were consistent with the Douglas Amendment, which allows states to authorize interstate bank acquisitions to varying degrees. The Court also determined that the statutes did not violate the Commerce Clause because Congress had authorized such state actions through the BHCA and the Douglas Amendment.

Regarding the Compact Clause, the Court was skeptical that the statutes constituted a compact but noted that even if they did, they would not violate the Compact Clause because they did not infringe on federal supremacy or the political power of other states.

Lastly, the Court addressed the Equal Protection Clause, which was not initially argued but was later brought up by the petitioners. The Court held that the statutes were rationally related to the legitimate state interest of maintaining a banking system responsive to local needs and did not violate the Equal Protection Clause.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court upheld the state statutes permitting regional interstate bank acquisitions and affirmed the Federal Reserve Board's approval of the contested acquisitions. Justice Powell did not participate in the decision.

In the case of Wiggins v. California, the Supreme Court addressed the role of standby counsel in a trial where the defendant has chosen to represent himself, exercising his Sixth Amendment right as recognized in Faretta v. California. Carl Edwin Wiggins, after having his initial conviction overturned due to a defective indictment, was retried, convicted, and sentenced to life imprisonment. He challenged the participation of standby counsel in his second trial, arguing that it infringed upon his right to self-representation.

The Court acknowledged that a pro se defendant (one who represents himself) must be allowed to control his defense, make motions, question witnesses, and address the court and jury. The Court found that Wiggins was given these rights. His complaints were not about restrictions on his participation but about the alleged intrusive involvement of standby counsel.

The Court held that while a pro se defendant has the right to present his case without interference, this does not mean standby counsel must be completely silent. The Court outlined two limitations on standby counsel's participation: (1) the defendant must maintain actual control over his case, and (2) standby counsel's involvement should not undermine the jury's perception that the defendant is representing himself.

The Court determined that Wiggins had a fair chance to present his case and that conflicts between him and standby counsel were resolved in his favor. The Court also noted that a pro se defendant could waive his rights by inviting or agreeing to counsel's participation, which Wiggins did on several occasions.

The Court concluded that while standby counsel's participation was not ideal, it did not infringe upon Wiggins' Faretta rights. Wiggins maintained control over his defense, and his appearance as a self-representing defendant was not significantly compromised. Therefore, the Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had held that Wiggins' Sixth Amendment right was violated by standby counsel's unsolicited participation.

Implications of the decision include clarification that standby counsel can assist a pro se defendant, especially outside the jury's presence or with the defendant's consent, and that the defendant's control over his case and appearance of self-representation before the jury are the primary considerations in determining whether the defendant's rights have been respected.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Northern District of Indiana ruled that a federal prisoner's motion for postconviction relief under the federal court's one-year time limitation was granted. The court held that the time limitation for filing a petition for a writ of certiorari expired when the defendant's time for seeking review expired. The Court held that, for the purpose of starting the clock on the limitation period, a judgment of conviction becomes final when the time expires for contesting the appellate court' s affirmation of the conviction. The Seventh Circuit's decision in this case was consistent with the majority of other courts of appeals, which have held that a judgment becomes final upon the issuance of the court of appeals' mandate. The Supreme Court's recent decision in Gendron v. United States, 536 F. 3d 672, 674 (CA7 1998) ("Gendron"), provided guidance on the issue of when a federal prison's final judgment is final. In this case, the Court held, however, that it is not necessary to issue a final judgment to grant a motion for a postconviction review. In a separate opinion, the Supreme Court ruled that there is no need for the Court to issue final judgment in a case where the defendant has not yet filed a petition. The Second Circuit held that "a federal prison sentence is not final" when the prison sentence has been served. The Fourth Circuit agreed, holding that the Seventh Circuit was right to deny the motion. The Eighth Circuit agreed with the Second Circuit, and the Court granted the motion for review.

The Supreme Court reviewed several provisions of Pennsylvania's 1982 Abortion Control Act, which had been challenged as unconstitutional. The provisions in question related to informed consent, printed information, postviability abortions, and reporting requirements. The United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit had previously ruled these provisions unconstitutional.

The Supreme Court held that it did not have appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1254(2) because the judgment of the Court of Appeals was not final and the case was remanded for further development of the facts. However, the Court treated the jurisdictional statement as a petition for certiorari, granted the writ, and proceeded to the merits of the case.

The Court reaffirmed the principles established in Roe v. Wade and subsequent cases, emphasizing the constitutional dimensions of a woman's right to decide whether to end her pregnancy. The Court found that the Pennsylvania Act's provisions were not designed to protect maternal health or potential life but rather to deter women from obtaining abortions.

Specifically, the Court found that the Act's requirements for informed consent and printed information were designed to influence a woman's decision and were not medically necessary, thus violating her privacy and autonomy. The reporting requirements were deemed excessive and posed a risk of public exposure and harassment, which could deter women from exercising their constitutional rights. The provisions regarding postviability abortions were invalidated because they required a trade-off between the woman's health and fetal survival, which the Court found unacceptable.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, holding that the challenged provisions of Pennsylvania's 1982 Abortion Control Act were facially invalid and unconstitutional.

In Totten v. United States, the Supreme Court held that a civil lawsuit brought by a former Union soldier against the United States for damages arising from injuries sustained during the Civil War could not go forward because the soldier had previously waived his right to sue in exchange for receiving a pension. The Court relied on the principle of public policy, which holds that courts will not hear cases that threaten to expose confidential government information or jeopardize national security interests.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a Florida-based adult offender who was sentenced to life without parole for a nonhomicide crime.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Orlando, Florida, alleges that Terrance Jamar Graham violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, Graham was the only juvenile offender in the United States to be sentenced to the death without parole.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida today announced criminal charges against Graham arising from a similar case in which Graham was convicted of a similar criminal conduct.  Graham pleaded guilty to one count of capital punishment in a separate criminal case, and the court found that he was not eligible for the death penalty at the time he was sentenced.  As alleged in the complaint:  Graham was a victim of a home invasion robbery in which one of his accomplices, Meigo Bailey, stole a few golf clubs from a family member, and then used the stolen club to commit a second and third felony.  Bailey, Bailey, and Lawrence were also convicted of the same criminal conduct, and Bailey and Lawrence are charged with the same counts.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Graham consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the federal securities laws, imposes a mandatory minimum of five years of supervised release, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.  He also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company and to be prohibited from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any security deposit in the name of any company or entity that requires it to provide security deposit for the security deposit.  On May 14, 2010, the court granted a temporary restraining order against Graham and ordered him to surrender his passport and return to Florida.  A hearing on June 24, 2010 was scheduled for 7:30 p.m. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Florida Department of Corrections.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio today entered a final judgment against two former school board members who were charged with violating the due process provisions of the federal securities laws.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against two other school boards, ordering them to comply with the mandatory termination provisions of their maternity leave rules.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in the Eastern District of Virginia, Jo Carol LaFleur and Ann Elizabeth Nelson, both junior high school teachers employed by the Board of Education of Chesterfield County, Virginia, were charged by the school boards with breaching the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and with aiding and abetting violations of Section 17(a)(1) and 17(b)(2)(A) of Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 17a-3 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the school board and school boards have consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating the above-mentioned provisions, and from imposing any additional monetary penalty.  In addition, the court has ordered the district court to issue an order appointing a receiver for the receiver of the receiver, ordering the receiver to provide a copy of the final judgment to the receiver.

In the case of Alfred Dunhill of London, Inc. v. The Republic of Cuba, the Supreme Court addressed whether the refusal by Cuban government-appointed interventors to return funds mistakenly paid by Dunhill for cigars constituted an "act of state," which would preclude a U.S. court from rendering a judgment against the respondents.

The background of the case involves the 1960 Cuban government confiscation of five cigar companies, after which the interventors continued to sell cigars, including to U.S. importers. Disputes arose over payments for cigars shipped before and after the intervention. The U.S. importers, including Dunhill, paid the interventors for pre-intervention shipments under the mistaken belief that they were entitled to the funds. The former owners of the cigar companies claimed these payments, and the importers sought to recover the mistaken payments.

The District Court ruled that the interventors were entitled to collect for post-intervention shipments but not for pre-intervention accounts, which belonged to the former owners. The importers were allowed to set off their mistaken payments against amounts due for post-intervention purchases. The Court of Appeals, however, held that the obligation to repay had a situs in Cuba and was repudiated by the interventors in a manner that constituted an act of state, thus barring Dunhill from an affirmative judgment for the excess amount it was owed.

The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, concluding that the refusal to repay did not constitute an act of state. The Court reasoned that the interventors did not demonstrate sovereign authority to repudiate debts and that their refusal to repay was merely a continuation of their original position, not a new act of state. The Court also distinguished between the public acts of a sovereign and its private, commercial acts, stating that the act of state doctrine should not extend to the latter.

The Court was influenced by the U.S. government's shift to a "restrictive theory" of sovereign immunity, which does not grant immunity for commercial acts. The Court held that the repudiation of a commercial obligation by a foreign sovereign should not be considered an act of state, as this would conflict with the policy underlying the restrictive theory of sovereign immunity and could potentially harm international trade and the rule of law.

In summary, the Supreme Court ruled that the refusal by Cuban interventors to return mistaken payments did not qualify as an act of state, and thus, the importers, including Dunhill, were entitled to recover these payments. The decision reinforces the distinction between sovereign acts and commercial activities of a foreign state, with the latter being subject to judicial scrutiny in U.S. courts.

Petitioner was indicted for violating the federal narcotics laws. He retained a lawyer, pleaded not guilty, and was released on bail. While he was free on bail, a federal agent succeeded by surreptitious means in listening to incriminating statements made by petitioner. Evidence of these statements was introduced against petitioner at his trial over his objection. He was convicted, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. 

Held: Petitioner was denied the basic protections of the Sixth Amendment when there was used against him at his trial evidence of his own incriminating words, which federal agents had deliberately elicited from him after he had been indicted and in the absence of his counsel. Pp. 341-345. 307 F. 2d 67, reversed.

A jury found petitioner guilty on three counts of carjacking, as well as several other offenses related to stealing cars. The District Judge instructed the jury that the Government was required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the taking of a motor vehicle was committed with the intent "to cause death or serious bodily harm to the person from whom the car was taken." After explaining that merely using a gun to frighten a victim was not sufficient to prove such intent, he added the following statement over the defendant's objection: "In some cases, intent is conditional. That is, a de- fendant may intend to engage in certain conduct only if a certain event occurs. If you believe from the evidence that the intention of the defendants was only in the alternative that is, if the defendants, acting for and with the others, then and if that specific intent was formed in the minds of the defendant and the shooting of the said Bell with intent to kill was only prevented by the happening of the alternative. If the defendant had at least attempted to seriously harm or kill the driver if that action had been necessary to complete the taking, then the requirement of the law as to the specific intent is met." Held: 1. The intent requirement of §2119 is satisfied when the Government proves that at the moment the defendant demanded or took control over the driver's automobile the defendant possessed the intent to seriously injure the driver even if necessary to steal the car. Pp. 5-11. (a) A commonsense reading of the statute counsels that Congress intended to criminalize a broader scope of conduct than attempts to assault or kill in the course of automobile robberies. P. 5. (b) The statute's mens rea component thus modifies the act of "tak[ing]" the motor vehicle. It directs the factfinder's attention to the defendant defendant's state of mind at the precise moment he demanded or takes control of the car "by force and violence or by intimidation." If he has the proscribed state of Mind at that moment, the statute's scienter element is satisfied. Moreover, petitioner's reading would improperly transform the statute into one that focuses on attempting to harm a person in the car's course of the robbery of a vehicle. Pc. 5, 664 665, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California today entered a final judgment against a California-based corporation for violating the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in California, alleges that, from at least 2007 through at least 2010, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) failed to provide sufficient evidence to determine whether a corporation was a citizen of the United States when, in fact, it was not.  According to the complaint, the SEC also failed to show that a corporation's "principal place of business" was located in a state where it did most of its business activities, and that its "major administrative operations" were located in New Jersey, not in California.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the SEC failed to adequately assess the role of the corporation in determining whether it had a sufficient number of employees to carry out its business operations.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering the defendants to pay disgorgement of $1,078 in prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $100,000.  On May 24, 2011, the Court granted the SEC’s request for a temporary restraining order against the defendants, freezing the defendants’ assets, and issuing an order appointing a receiver to oversee the receivership of certain of the defendants. The court also issued an order temporarily suspending the defendants from appearing before the SEC as an impartial arbiter in the case.  To learn more about diversity jurisdiction, see Litigation Release No. 595, 599 (1936).

Case Name: United States v. Brown Shoe Co.
Case Number: 347 U.S. 420
Year Decided: 1958
Decision Date: June 23, 1958
Supreme Court Justices: Earl Warren, Charles Evans Hughes, William O. Douglas, John Marshall Harlan II, Harold Burton, Thomas Clark McReynolds, Robert Jackson
Issue: Whether the merger of two large shoe manufacturing companies, Brown Shoe Co. and Kinney Shoe Corp., violated Section 7 of the Clayton Antitrust Act.
Background Information:
* Brown Shoe Co. and Kinney Shoe Corp. were two of the largest shoe manufacturers in the United States.
* The two companies merged in 1955, forming the Brown-Kinney Shoe Group.
* The merger was challenged by the government, which claimed that it would reduce competition in the shoe industry.
Legal Analysis:
* The Supreme Court held that the merger of Brown Shoe Co. and Kinney Shoe Corp. violated Section 7 of the Clayton Antitrust Act.
* The Court found that the merger created a "lessening of competition," as it reduced the number of independent shoe manufacturers in the industry.
* The Court also found that the merger allowed the newly formed Brown-Kinney Shoe Group to increase its bargaining power vis-à-vis retailers and wholesalers.
Impact:
* The decision in United States v. Brown Shoe Co. helped solidify the concept of "lessening of competition" as a key element of antitrust law.
* The decision also highlighted the importance of preserving competition in industries, especially those with high barriers to entry.

Respondent filed a complaint in Federal District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, alleging that her son, who was injured while performing sandblasting work aboard the USNS Maj. Stephen W. Pless in the employ of Tidewater Temps, Inc., a subcontractor for petitioner Norfolk Shipbuilding & Drydock Corporation, sustained injuries on April 8, 1997, that caused his death one day later. Because the vessel was berthed in the navigable waters of the United States when Garris was injured, respondent invoked federal admiralty jurisdiction, U. S. Const., Art. III, 2, cl. 1, and prayed for damages under general maritime law. She also asserted claims under the Virginia wrongful death statute. The District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a federal claim, for the categorical reason that "no cause of action exists, under General maritime law, for death of a nonseaman in state territorial waters resulting from negligence." The Court of Appeals denied petitioner's suggestion for rehearing en banc, with two judges dissenting. Held: The maritime cause of actions that Moragne established for unseaworthiness is equally available for negligence. Pp. 531-531. (a) The common-law duties of care have not been adopted and retained, but have been adjusted to fit their maritime context, see, e.g., Kermarec v. Compagnie Generale Transatlantique, 358 U.S. 625, 630-632, and a century ago the maritime law exchanged the common law's rule of contributory negligence for one of comparative negligence. To the extent the amendment to 905(b) reflects any policy relevant here, it is in expressly ratifying longshore and harbor workers' claims against the vessel for negligence, see id., at 259-260. The LHWCA therefore does not preclude this negligence action for wrongful death. P. 532. (b) Even beyond the express pre-emptive reach of federal maritime statutes, however, Congress's occupation of this field is not yet so extensive as to preclude us from recognizing what is already logically compelled by Moragne's precedents. The choice-of-law anomaly occasioned by providing a federal remedy for injury but not death is no less strange when the duty is negligence than when it is seaworthiness. Of two victims injured at the same instant in the same location by the same negligence, only one would be covered by federal law, provided only that the other died of his injuries. The Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act (LHWCA), 44 Stat. 1424, as amended, provides nonseamage maritime workers such as respondent's son, see 902(3) (defining covered employees), with no-fault workers' compensation claims (against their employer, 904(b)) and negligence claims, against the employer's negligence law, and that death caused by breach of that duty is also compensable, Moragne v. States Marine Lines, Inc. at 409. The provision of the Act does not prevent respondent's negligence action, but it does not preempt respondent's action. Moreover, the Longshore-and-Harbor Workers' compensation Act (LBWCA) creates wrongful-death actions only by the personal representatives of people killed "beyond a marine league from the shore of any State," 46 U. C. App. 761. Respondent's son was not covered by the Jones Act, and this Court has held that the Act bears no implication for actions brought by nonseamen. The Jones Act is not intended to preclude the availability of a remedy for wrongful deaths under general Maritime law in situations not covered, but that does not resolve the issue here: whether requiring such an accommodation by refusing to recognize the federal remedy is preferable as a matter of maritime policy. Nor does requiring such a accommodation by refusal to recognize a federal statute is preferable, since Congress has acknowledged that they contain a further prudential effect. The fact that, even though the Act has not been enacted and retained unmodified by admalty, it was designed to preserve the maritime rights of third parties and preserve the rights of the third party in the maritime context. The "tensions and discrepancies" in our precedent arising from the necessity to accommodate state remedial statutes to exclusively maritime substantive concepts"-which ultimately drove this Court in Moragne to abandon The Harrisburg, see 398 U-S. 375, 594-were no less pronounced with maritime negligence than with unseaworthyiness. Nor is there any rational basis for denying respondent the recovery recognized by her son for the death of her son. Finally, there is no rational basis in the Maritime Law Department's interpretation of the law to preclude a wrongful-dying action for negligence-which, in fact, is not limited to any particular maritime duty, but to the purpose of preserving the maritime interests of the maritime community, see. e. g., Dooley v.
