Section 514(a) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) provides that no provision of ERISA shall apply to any employer plan if it conflicts with any state law relating to any plan. Respondent trustees of a self-insured, multiemployer welfare benefit plan (Fund) own and operate three medical centers that provide medical, dental, and other health care benefits primarily to longshoremen, retirees, and their dependents. Two of these centers are located in New York and are licensed there as "diagnostic and treatment centers," subject to a 0.6 percent gross receipts tax imposed by the Health Facility Assessment (HFA). During the period from January through November of 1991, respondents paid HFA assessments totaling $7,066 based on the two New York centers' patient care income of $1,177,670. They then stopped making the payments and sued petitioners, the New York officials responsible for collecting the taxes, seeking injunctive relief and a refund of the tax paid in 1991. Alleging that the HFA is a state law that "relates to" the Fund within the meaning of § 514(a) and is therefore pre-empted as applied to hospitals run by ERISA plans, respondents sought to enjoin future assessments and to recover the tax paid in 1991. The Federal District Court denied relief, holding that the HFA was not pre-empted because it was a "tax of general application" that did not interfere with the calculation of benefits or the determination of an employee's eligibility for benefits. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, reasoning that the HFA related to the Fund because it reduced the amount of Fund assets that would otherwise be available to provide plan members with benefits, and could cause the Fund to limit its benefits, or to charge plan members higher fees. On remand after this Court decided New York State Conference of Blue Cross & Blue Shield Plans v. Travelers Insurance Co., 514 U. S. 645, the Court of Appeals reinstated its original judgment, finding that the HFA depleted the Fund's assets directly and thus had an immediate impact on the Fund's operations, while the statute involved in Travelers had only an indirect economic influence on the decisions of ERISA plan administrators. Held: New York may collect its tax. Pp. 10-14. (a) When the Court of Appeals initially found the HFA pre-empted as applied to Fund-operated hospitals, that court relied substantially on an expansive and literal interpretation of the word "relate to" in § 514(a). In reconsidering the case on remand, however, the court failed to give proper weight to Travelers' rejection of a strictly literal reading of § 514(a)'s text. That section's history shows that the State includes the regulation of matters of health and safety within its traditional police powers. Since most hospitals are not owned or operated by ERISA funds, the Fund bears the substantial burden of overcoming the presumption that Congress does not intend to supplant state law when it arranges to provide medical benefits for its plan beneficiaries by operating hospitals itself. There is nothing in the HFA's operation that convinces this Court that it is the type of state law that Congress intended ERISA to supersede. Cf. Travelers, 514 U. S., at 668. Pp. 10-13. (b) Because the HFA is a tax on hospitals, most of which are not owned or operated by ERISA funds, it is one of "myriad state laws" of general applicability that impose some burdens on the administration of ERISA plans but nevertheless do not relate to them within the meaning of § 514(a). Even though the tax in circumstances like these might be said to be "indirect," its impact on the Fund's decisionmaking would be in all relevant respects identical to the "direct" impact felt here. Any state tax, or other law, that increases the cost of providing benefits to covered employees will have some effect on the administration of ERISA plans, but that simply cannot mean that every state law with such an effect is pre-empted by the federal statute. Pp. 13-14. 74 F. 3d 28, reversed.

Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 provides for a statutory proceeding for the determination of rights and duties arising thereunder, §§ 204-207, and courts should, therefore, ordinarily refrain from exercising their jurisdiction in such cases. Held: 1. The Act authorizes only preventive relief; that there has been no threat of enforcement against the appellees and that they have alleged no irreparable injury. Pp. 521-522. 2. The provision of the Act that all persons shall be entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the goods and services of any place of public accommodation without discrimination or segregation on the ground of race, color, religion, or national origin; and § 201(b)(2) and (c) place any "restaurant .. .. principally engaged in selling food for consumption on the premises" under the Act "if . . . it serves or offers to serve interstate travelers or a substantial portion of the food which it serves * . . has moved in commerce." Heart of Atlanta Motel v. United States, 379 U. S. 241, distinguished. P. 522. 233 F. Supp. 815, reversed.

Title: NAACP v. Alabama
Year: 1961
Decision: Reversed and Remanded
Issue: Whether the lower court erred in issuing a permanent injunction against the NAACP from operating in Alabama?
Summary: The Supreme Court holds that the lower court erred in issuing a permanent injunction against the NAACP from operating in Alabama. The Court finds that the injunction was based on vague and ambiguous language in the state constitution and that the NAACP's activities were protected by the First Amendment. The Court remands the case back to the lower court for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

During petitioner Blueford’s capital murder trial, the jury sent the court a note indicating that it was hopelessly deadlocked. The court issued an Allen instruction, emphasizing the importance of reaching a verdict, and sent the jurors back to the jury room. They deliberated for a half hour longer before returning a note saying that they were deadlocked. The court then gave another Allen instruction and sent the jurors back to the jury room. Upon receiving a third note from the jury reporting that it was deadlocked, the court gave another Allen instruction and sent the jurors back to the jury room. Finally, the jury returned a note stating that it was unable to reach a verdict. The court declared a mistrial and discharged the jury. Subsequently seeking to retry Blueford, the State filed a motion to dismiss the capital and first-degree murder charges on double jeopardy grounds, citing the foreperson’s report that the jury had voted unanimously against guilt on those offenses. The trial court denied the motion, and the State Supreme Court affirmed on interlocutory appeal. Held: Because the jury did not acquit Blueford of any offense, the Double Jeopardy Clause does not stand in the way of a second trial on the same offenses. Pp. 3−8. (a) Blueford contends that the foreperson’s report means that he cannot be tried again on charges of capital and first-degree murder. His primary submission is that he cannot be retried for those offenses because the jury actually acquitted him of those offenses. Although no formal judgment of acquittal was entered, Blueford maintains that an acquittal is a matter of substance, not form, and that a jury’s announcement constitutes an acquittal if it “ ‘actually represents a resolution …of some or all of the factual elements of the offense charged.’ ” United States v. Martin Linen Supply Co., 430 U.S. 564, 571. Here, Blueford claims, the foreperson’s announcement of the jury’s unanimous votes on capital and first-degree murder represented just that: a resolution of some or all of the elements of those offenses in Blueford’s favor. Held: The foreperson’s report was not a final resolution of anything. When the foreperson told the court how the jury had voted on each offense, the jury’s deliberations had not yet concluded. The facts that the jury’s deliberations continued after the report deprived that report of the finality necessary to constitute an acquittal on the murder offenses. Even assuming that the instructions required a unanimous vote before the jury could consider a lesser offense, nothing in the instructions prohibited the jury from reconsidering such a vote. The instructions said simply, “If you have a reasonable doubt of the defendant’s guilt on the charge of [the greater offense], you will [then] consider the charge of [the lesser offense].” The jurors were never told that once they had a reasonable doubt, they could not rethink the issue. The jury was free to reconsider a greater offense, even after considering a lesser one. Thus, it was possible for Blueford’s jury to revisit the offenses of capital and first-degree murder, notwithstanding its earlier votes. Pp. 3−6. (b) Blueford also maintains that even if the jury did not acquit him of capital and first-degree murder, a second trial on those offenses would nonetheless violate the Double Jeopardy Clause, because the trial court’s declaration of a mistrial was improper. Blueford acknowledges that a trial can be discontinued without barring a subsequent one for the same offense when “particular circumstances manifest a necessity” to declare a mistrial. Wade v. Hunter, 336 U.S. 684, 690. He also acknowledges that the trial court’s reason for declaring a mistrial here—that the jury was unable to reach a verdict—has long been considered the classic basis establishing such a necessity. Blueford therefore accepts that a second trial on manslaughter and negligent homicide would pose no double jeopardy problem. He contends, however, that there was no necessity for a mistrial on capital and first-degree murder, given the foreperson’s report that the jury had voted unanimously against guilt on those charges. However, this Court has never required a trial court, before declaring a mistrial because of a hung jury, to consider any particular means of breaking the impasse—let alone to consider giving the jury new options for a verdict. See Renico v. Lett, 559 U. S. ___, ___. As permitted under Arkansas law, the jury’s options in this case were limited to two: either convict on one of the offenses, or acquit on all. The instructions explained those options in plain terms, and the verdict forms likewise contemplated no other outcome. There were separate forms to convict on each of the possible offenses, but there was only one form to acquit, and it was to acquit on all of them. When the foreperson disclosed the jury’s votes on capital- and first-degree murder, the trial court did not abuse its discretion by refusing to add another option—that of acquitting on some offenses but not others. That, however, is precisely the relief Blueford seeks—relief the Double Jeopardy Clause does not afford him. Pp. 6−8. 2011 Ark. 8, 708 S. W. 3d 1, affirmed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Sotomayor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

The Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) governs the enforcement of arbitration agreements in the United States. Under the FAA, a written arbitration agreement is "valid, irrevocable, and enforceable" unless it can be shown to be "void or unenforceable." 9 U.S.C. § 2. The FAA's purpose is to promote efficient resolution of commercial disputes through arbitration, rather than lengthy and expensive legal battles.

The FAA sets forth several provisions that apply to arbitration agreements. These include:

* Parties to an arbitration agreement must be able to prove that the agreement was entered into voluntarily and with knowledge of the risks associated with arbitration.
* Evidence introduced during an arbitration proceeding is generally limited to evidence that was available at the time of the arbitration.
* The burden of proof in an arbitration proceeding is lower than in a court proceeding.
* The decision of an arbitrator is final and binding, except in rare circumstances such as fraud or coercion.

Arbitration agreements can be used in various types of disputes, including business disputes, consumer disputes, and labor disputes. However, the scope of an arbitration agreement depends on the specific language of the agreement and the type of dispute being resolved.

Petitioner Gall voluntarily withdrew from a methamphetamine conspiracy after deciding, on his own initiative, to change his life. His subsequent conviction resulted in a sentence of probation, which the Eighth Circuit vacated and remanded for resentencing, concluding that the sentence was unreasonable under the abuse-of-discretion standard set forth in United States v. Booker, 543 U.S. 220. Held: Because the Eighth Circuit failed to accord the District Court’s decision the requisite deference, its ruling is reversed. Pp. 4−12. (a) Under Booker, the abuse-of-discretion standard governs appellate review of all sentences imposed in light of the Guidelines. That standard calls for a determination whether the sentence is reasonable, i.e., whether the district judge abused his discretion in determining that the relevant factors under 18 U.S.C. §3553(a) justified a particular sentence and justified a substantial deviation from the Guidelines range. Pp. 4−5. (b) Here, the District Court committed no procedural error. Its commitment to the Guidelines was correct, and it conducted a thorough analysis of the relevant factors. Nor did the Government call the Court’s attention to a comparable defendant who received a more severe sentence. Thus, the only question for the Eighth Circuit was whether the sentence was reasonable. Pp. 5−6. (c) The Eighth Circuit gave virtually no deference to the District Court’s decision that the §3553(a) factors justified a significant variance in this case. Instead, it engaged in an analysis that more closely resembled de novo review of the facts presented and determined that, in its view, the degree of variance was not warranted. To the extent that the Guidelines were once mandatory, the “range of choice dictated by the facts of the case” is significantly broadened. However, the Guidelines are only one of the factors to consider when imposing sentence, and §3553(a)(3) directs the judge to consider sentences other than imprisonment. Furthermore, the Government did not argue below, and has not argued here, that a sentence of probation could never be imposed for a crime identical to Gall’s. Indeed, it acknowledged that probation could be permissible if the record contained different—but in the Court’s view, no more compelling—mitigating evidence. The District Court quite reasonably attached great weight to Gall’s self-motivated rehabilitation, which was undertaken not at the direction of, or under supervision by, any court, but on his own initiative. This also lends strong support to the conclusion that imprisonment was not necessary to deter Gall from engaging in future criminal conduct or to protect the public from his future criminal acts. The Eighth Circuit clearly disagreed with the District Judge’s conclusion that consideration of the §3553(a) factors justified a sentence of probation; it believed that the circumstances presented here were insufficient to sustain such a marked deviation from the Guidelines range. But it is not for the Eighth Circuit to decide de novo whether the justification for a variance is sufficient or the sentence reasonable. On abuse-of-discretion review, the Eighth Circuit should have given due deference to the District Court’s reasoned and reasonable decision that the §3553(a) factors, on the whole, justified the sentence. Pp. 6−12. Reversed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

Appellant, a lawyer practicing in Columbia, S. C., was associated with the "Carolina Community Law Firm" and was an officer of and cooperating lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). She was paid a retainer as a legal consultant for the South Carolina Council on Human Relations (Council), a nonprofit organization with offices in Columbia. After receiving appellant's letter, dated August 30, 19736-the centerpiece of this litigation-Williams visited Dr. Pierce to discuss the progress of her third child who was ill. At the doctor's office, she encountered his lawyer and at the latter's request signed a release of liability in her favor. At appellant's request, she showed the doctor and his lawyer a copy of the letter and announced her intention not to sue. There was no further communication between appellant and Williams. Appellant filed a jurisdictional statement and this appeal was docketed on October 3, 1977, sub nom. Held: 1. The activities of the NAACP, its affiliates and legal staff shown on this record are modes of expression and association protected by the First and Fourteenth Amendments which Virginia may not prohibit, under its power to regulate the legal profession, as improper solicitation of legal business violative of [state law] and the Canons of Professional Ethics. NAACP v. Button, 371 U. S. 415, distinguished. Pp. 5-7. (a) The activities in this case are not modes of expressive and associational conduct protected by § 2-103(D)(5) of the SC Constitution, which requires the State to regulate "the practice of professions within their boundaries," Button, supra, at 437, and the "interest of the States in regulating lawyers is especially great since lawyers are essential to the primary governmental function of administering justice, and have historically been "officers of the courts." Goldfarb v. Virginia State Bar, 421 U.S. 773, 792. The discipline administered to appellant was premised solely on the possibility of financial benefit to the organization, rather than any possibility of pecuniary gain to herself, her associates, or the lawyers representing the plaintiffs in the Walker v. Pierce litigation. As Button indicates, and as appellant offered to prove at the disciplinary hearing, the efficacy of litigation as a means of advancing the cause of civil liberties often depends on the ability to make legal assistance available to suitable litigants. Although a showing of potential danger may suffice in the former context, appellant may not be disciplined unless her activity in fact involved the type of misconduct at which South Carolina's broad prohibition is said to be directed. The record does not support appellee's contention that undue influence, overreaching, misrepresentation, or invasion of privacy actually occurred in the case. Appellee contends, however, that the disciplinary action is part of a regulatory program aimed at the prevention of undue influence and overreaching of personal political beliefs and to advance the civil-liberties objectives of the ACLU. The question presented here is whether, in light of the values protected by this Amendment, these differences materially affect the scope of state regulation of the conduct of lawyers. See Ohralik v. Ohio State Bar Assn. 447, 98 S.Ct. 1912, 56 L.Ed. 2d 444. The approach adopted today in Ohrik, 436 U. s. 446, that that the State may proscribe in-person solicitation for pecunniary gain under circumstances likely to result in adverse consequences, cannot be applied to appellant's activity on behalf of petitioner. The State must demonstrate "a subordinating interest which is compelling," Bates v. City of Little Rock, 361 US. 516, 524, and that the means employed in furtherance of that interest are "closely drawn to avoid unnecessary abridgment of associational freedoms." Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.

The Supreme Court reviewed the case involving maritime unions picketing against foreign-flag carriers, which employ foreign crewmen at lower wages than American seamen. The picketing took place in Mobile, Alabama, against the Aqua Glory, a Liberian-registered ship, and resulted in local longshoremen refusing to cross the picket lines.

The unions contended that the case was distinct from a previous case (Windward Shipping v. American Radio Assn.) on the preemption issue and that their First and Fourteenth Amendment rights were infringed by the temporary injunction upheld by the Alabama court. They argued that their activities were arguably prohibited under the secondary boycott provision of the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), and thus, the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) should have exclusive jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court disagreed, stating that the picketing activities did not meet the jurisdictional requirements of the NLRA, as they did not affect commerce within the meaning of the Act. The Court found that the picketing's impact on the maritime operations of foreign ships was not limited to American ports and that the response of American workers was part of the mechanism affecting those operations. Therefore, the activities were not in or affecting commerce, and the Alabama courts had jurisdiction to apply their own law to the dispute.

Regarding the First and Fourteenth Amendment claims, the Court referred to previous rulings that recognized a state's ability to balance the interests of pickets in disseminating their message against competing state policy interests. The Court found that Alabama's interference with the picketing was within the permissible scope, as the state policy against 'wrongful interference' was analogous to the federal policy against secondary boycotts. The Court concluded that the evidence supported the Alabama court's decision that the picketing had a prohibited purpose, and thus, the injunction did not violate the unions' constitutional rights.

In summary, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Supreme Court of Alabama, holding that the state courts had jurisdiction over the dispute and that the injunction against the picketing did not violate the unions' First and Fourteenth Amendment rights.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in a civil action brought by the Department of Veterans Affairs against David Henderson, who served in the military during the Korean War.  The court found that the 120-day deadline for filing a notice of appeal with the VA was not a jurisdictional requirement.  In its judgment, the court held that, as a matter of law, the VA had a statutory duty to assist veterans in developing evidence that supported their claims. The court also held that a 90-day filing window was not sufficient to determine the jurisdiction of a court of appeals, and that the deadline was not reasonable.  According to the court's order, Henderson was denied benefits because he failed to file a claim within 120 days of the deadline.  Without admitting or denying the court’s findings, Henderson has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering him to pay a $1,000 civil penalty. The judgment also ordered that he be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company and ordered to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.   The settlement is subject to court approval.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 561 U. S.C. (2010).

Section 9 (h) of the National Labor Relations Act, as amended, provides that the Board shall make no investigation nor issue any complaint on behalf of a union unless there is on file with the Board a non-Communist oath of each officer of the union and of each of its officers of any national or international labor organization of which it is an affiliate or constituent unit. Section 35 A of the Criminal Code applies a criminal sanction to false affidavits filed under § 9. The Board, in accord with its practice, refused to allow that issue to be litigated in the unfair labor practice proceeding. A hearing was held before an examiner who found, among other things, that the § 9(h) affidavit filed by Travis in August 1949 was false and that the union membership knew it was false, yet continued to re-elect him as an officer, and ordered that he be accorded no further benefits under the Act until it had complied. The District Court denied a preliminary injunction. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the criminal sanction was the exclusive remedy for filing the false affidavit. Held: 1. The criminal sanction of perjury was not exclusive to the filing of a false affidavit, since its power to act on union charges is conditioned on filing of the necessary affidavits. Pp. 531-532. (a) The fact that a union's officers are not members or affiliates of the Communist Party or any other proscribed themselves of Communist leaders does not deprive the union of its right to the benefits of the Act, even where its members were aware of the falsity of the affidavit. P. 533. (b) The Board is under a duty to determine whether a filing has been made by each person specified in § 9, since it has a duty under that provision to determine not only whether the affidavit has been filed but also whether it filed is true or false, and for that position reliance is placed on general statements in cases like National Labor Board v. Indiana and Michigan Electric Co., 318 U. S. 9, 18-19, which the Board has implied power to protect its process from abuse, and the Board's power under § 35 A to determine the validity of a complaint against a union is conditioned upon filing of such affidavits, and it cannot find an additional sanction which in practical effect would run against the union, not their guilty officers. That was the original position of the Board, and that was its original position, and is the correct one. Certiorari granted.

After concluding that electronic media coverage of judicial proceedings contributed to wider public acceptance and understanding of judicial decisions, the Florida Supreme Court promulgated a revised version of its Canon 3A (7)-which prohibits photographic and broadcast coverage of courtroom proceedings--permitting such coverage in accordance with specified standards. Under the revised Canon, the presiding judge retains complete discretion to exclude coverage of certain witnesses and to forbid coverage whenever satisfaction is expressed that coverage might adversely affect the defendant's right to a fair trial. While the revised Canon contains no express language purportedly making it applicable to appellant police officers' trial for crimes committed while on duty, the Florida Supreme Court held that the revised Canon was controlling since the officers were defendants in a criminal action rather than being mere spectators. Held: As long as the revised Canon remains within the bounds prescribed by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, it is constitutionally permissible for the Florida Supreme Court to apply it to appellants' trial even though the Canon itself makes no explicit mention of the rights of persons merely observing the trial. Pp. 108-113. (a) Since the revised Canon was promulgated pursuant to the Florida Supreme Court's supervisory authority over the Florida courts, this Court has no supervisory jurisdiction over the Canon; hence, in reviewing the Florida Supreme Court's application of the Canon here, this Court will evaluate the state-court judgment solely in relation to the Federal Constitution. Pp. 108-109. (b) Although the revised Canon contains no express language purportedly making it applicable to nonparticipants in the trial, nevertheless, so long as the Canon remains within the bounds prescribed by the Due Process Clause, it is constitutionally permissible for the Florida Supreme Court to apply it to appellants' trial. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the revised Canon was promulgated pursuant to the Florida Supreme Court's supervisory authority over the Florida courts, and not upon any constitutional imperative. Moreover, the revised Canon comports with the principle that the First and Sixth Amendments do not mandate entry of the electronic media into judicial proceedings. See Nixon v. Warner Communications, Inc., 435 U. S. 589, 610. Pp. 109-113. 381 So. 2d 117, affirmed.

After petitioner Fox sued respondent Vice, the Mayor of Ville Platte, Louisiana, in state court, Vice counterclaimed that Fox had threatened to kill him and his family members. Vice later filed a federal diversity action based on the same alleged threats, adding allegations that Fox had interfered with his voting rights. The Federal District Court entered judgment for Fox on the federal claims, dismissing the state-law claims. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the federal claims were not frivolous, but affirming the District Court’s conclusion that the state-law claims were. The court awarded Fox attorney’s fees for the time his attorneys devoted to the federal claims, rejecting Vice’s argument that the fees should be limited to the time spent on the frivolous claims. Held: A defendant may recover reasonable attorney’s fees incurred because of, but only because of, a frivolous claim. Pp. 4–11. (a) Under 42 U. S. C. §1988, a defendant may recover reasonable attorney’s fees incurred because of, but only because of, a frivolous claim. Fees may be shifted to recompense a defendant (as to recompense a plaintiff) not all-or-nothing: A defendant need not show that every claim in a complaint is frivolous to qualify for fees. Instead, the question is one of allocation: In a lawsuit involving a mix of frivolous and non-frivolous claims, what work may the defendant receive fees for? Vice argues that the trial court should have awarded fees for work that is “fairly attributable” to the frivolous portion of the lawsuit. But that standard is in truth no standard at all. The very question under consideration is: What fees may be fairly attributed to frivolous claims under §1988? To answer “those that are fairly attributable to frivolous claims” is just to restate this question. And that non-response response would leave to each and every trial court not only the implementation, but also the invention, of the applicable legal standard. Trial courts would not appreciate that lack of guidance, and such an empty and amorphous test would not ensure that all fee awards to defendants comport with Congress’s purpose in enacting §1988. That purpose is to relieve defendants of the burdens associated with fending off frivolous litigation. Thus, the basic American Rule operates. A standard allowing more expansive fee-shifting would furnish windfalls to some defendants, making them better off because they were subject to a suit including frivolous claims. Two defendants facing identical non-frivolous allegations could face different results under the more expansive standard, since the chance assertion of a frivolous claim could relieve one defendant of the incremental costs of that claim and the costs that he, like the other defendant, would have had to pay in its absence. Section 1988 provides no warrant for that peculiar result. At the same time, the “but-for” standard required here may in some cases allow compensation to a defendant for attorney work relating to both frivolous and non-frivolous claims. However, the dispositive question is not whether attorney costs at all relate to a non-frivolous claim, but whether the costs would have been incurred in the absence of the frivolous allegation. Answering that question will usually track the other, but when they diverge, it is the latter that matters. Pp. 4–9. (b) The District Court’s analysis fails to take proper account of the overlap between the frivolous and non-frivolous claims. Its decision to award full attorney’s fees to Vice failed to apply the but-for standard. Rather than ask whether Vice would have incurred part or most of his fees even if Fox had asserted only the non-frivolous state-law claims, the court suggested that the close relationship between the federal and state-law claims supported Vice’s request to recover all of his attorney’s fees. That reasoning stands the appropriate analysis on its head. It cannot be squared with the congressional policy of sparing defendants from the costs of frivolous litigation. The Ninth Circuit’s standard—that a defendant should receive fees for “work which can be distinctly traced to a plaintiff’s frivolous claims”—is inconsistent with this Court’s opinion. While the court correctly identified the key question, it did not engage the crucial question of whether Vice’s attorneys would have performed the same work to defend against the state-law claims. Pp. 9–11. 594 F. 3d 417, vacated and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

Under Chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code (Code), a debtor may obtain a discharge of certain government-sponsored student loan debts only if failure to discharge that debt would impose an “undue hardship” on the debtor and his dependents. The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure require bankruptcy courts to make this determination in an adversary proceeding, see Rule 7001(6), which the party seeking the determination must initiate by serving a summons and complaint on his adversary, see Rules 7003, 7004, 7008. Respondent Espinosa obtained four federally guaranteed student loans for a total principal amount of $13,250, but he filed a bankruptcy petition under Chapter 13. That Chapter permits individual debtors to develop a plan to repay all or a portion of their debts over a period of time specified in the plan, see §1328(a)(8). In 1992, Espinoosa filed a Chapter 13 bankruptcy petition, which required that the plan be effective upon confirmation, see §§1324, 1325, and will result in a discharge if the debtor completes the payments the plan requires. Espinos’ plan listed his student loan debt as his only specific indebtedness. The plan proposed to repay only the principal on that debt, stating that the remainder—the accrued interest—would be discharged once Espinoso repaid the principal. In May 1993, the Chapter 13 trustee mailed United a form notice stating that “[t]he amount of [his]responsibility may be paid.” The plan also noted the deadlines for filing a proof of claim or an objection to the plan. United received this notice and, in response, filed a proof-of claim for $17,832.15, an amount representing both the principal and the accrued interest on Espinaosa’s student loans. In response, United filed a notice of its plan and filed a statement of claim. In March 2004, the bankruptcy court confirmed the plan without holding a hearing or making a finding of undue hardship. In June 2005, the trustee received notice of the plan and sent it to petitioner United Student Aid Funds, Inc. (United), the creditor to whom Espinoos owed the student loan. United filed suit in Federal District Court, seeking to set aside as void the order confirming the plan as void because the order was issued in violation of Rule 60(b)(4). The District Court reversed. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the confirmation order was void because it was issued without service of the bankruptcy Rules. Held: 1. A failure to find undue hardship in accordance with §523(a) is on par with the jurisdictional and notice failings that define void judgments that qualify for relief under Rule 60 (b) (4). Section 1325(a), which provides that a bankruptcy court “shall confirm a plan” if the plan “complies with the provisions of” Chapter 13 and with “other applicable provisions of this title,” does not limit bankruptcy courts’ jurisdiction over student loans, but instead imposes a “ ‘self-executing’ limitation on the effect of a discharge order” that renders the order legally unenforceable, and thus void, if it is not satisfied. The error United alleges falls in neither category. Pp. 5–7. (a) Section 1326(a)-8 (which provides that bankruptcy courts have the discretion, but not the obligation, to raise on their own initiative certain nonjurisdictional barriers to suit. See, e.g., Nemaizer v. Baker, 793 F. 2d 58, 65 (CA2 1986); see Johnson v. Home State Bank, 501 U. S. 78, 87; Reed Elsevier, Inc., v. Muchnick, ante, at 12–13. This case presents no occasion to engage in such an inquiry or to define the precise circumstances in which a jurisdictional error will render a judgment void because United does not argue that the Court is jurisdictional. See Hood, 541 U.S. 440, 450, 450. Nor does the provision impose requirements that, if violated, would result in denial of due process. Moreover, §1325(b) requires a court to make a certain finding before confirming the discharge of a student loan, even if the creditor fails to object, or to appear in the proceeding at all. The “does not discharge” language in §523 (a), however, is inapplicable to this case. The phrase “‘[a] discharge under section 727 . . . or 1328(b)] does not discharge an individual debtor from any debt,’ ” applies only in the rare instance where a debtor has completed the repayments required by a confirmed plan, and is presumptively dischargeable “unless” the creditor requests a hearing to determine the dischargeability of that debt. See id., at 1202–1205. This is not what the Court

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit has remanded the case of Morris A. Kent, Jr., who came under the authority of the Juvenile Court of the District Of Columbia in 1959 when he was 14 years old. Kent was apprehended as a result of several housebreakings and an attempted purse snatching. He was placed on probation, in the custody of his mother, who had been separated from her husband since Kent was two years old, and was still on probation when an intruder entered a woman's apartment in 1961 and took her wallet and raped her. The police found Kent's fingerprints in the apartment and matched them to those of Kent. The court entered an order waiving jurisdiction of Kent and ordered that he be 'held for trial' for the alleged offenses under the regular procedure of the D.C. District Court. Kent appealed, claiming that the court had violated his right to a fair trial and had violated the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law. The appeals court found that Kent had not complied with the court's orders, and ordered the case to be returned to the trial court for further proceedings. The trial court granted the appeal, and the appeals court ruled that Kent was not entitled to a hearing on the issue of whether he should be held for trial. The case has now been remanded back to the District Court for further consideration.

The Supreme Court ruled in a 5-4 decision that federal courts cannot review a state court's application of a constitutionally narrowed aggravating circumstance in a death penalty case. The Court held that the "rational factfinder" standard established in Jackson v. Virginia should be used instead of a de novo review. The Court also emphasized that the decision of a state court regarding an aggravating circumstance is subject to review only for arbitrariness or capriciousness.

Title: Massachusetts v. Department of Transportation
Year: 1978
Decision Date: March 22, 1978
Judge: Burger
Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether the federal government could collect an excise tax on gasoline sales in Massachusetts. The court ruled that the tax was constitutional under the Interstate Commerce Clause of the US Constitution. The court held that the tax was not discriminatory towards Massachusetts residents, as it applied equally to all drivers regardless of their residence, and that the tax was rationally related to the regulation of interstate commerce.

After the Florida Division of Elections reported that Governor George W. Bush had won the November 7, 2000, presidential election by more than 1,700 votes, the Florida Election Code required automatic machine recounts in four counties where Vice President Al Gore had requested them. In an action brought by Volusia County and joined by the Palm Beach County Canvassing Board, Gore, and the Florida Democratic Party, the trial court ruled that the 7-day deadline for submitting late returns was mandatory, but that the secretary of state could consider extending the deadline based on the reasons offered by each county. She ultimately decided not to extend the deadlines. When the Democratic Party and Gore appealed, the intermediate appellate court certified the matter to the State Supreme Court, which sua sponte enjoined the secretary and the Elections Canvassing Commission from certifying the election result until further order. Relying partly on the right to vote set forth in the Florida Constitution, the court imposed a deadline of November 26 for returning ballot counts and directed the secretary to accept manual counts submitted prior to that date. Held: Because of the uncertainty as to the precise grounds for the State Supreme Court's decision, this Court will not now review the federal questions raised by petitioner. Although this Court generally defers to a state court's interpretation of a state statute, see, e. g., Rice v. Santa Fe, 466 U. S. 420, 426, in the case of a law enacted by a state legislature applicable not only to elections to state office, but also to the selection of Presidential electors, the legislature is not acting solely under the authority given it by the people of the State, but by virtue of a direct grant of authority under Art. II, § 1, cl. 2, of the Federal Constitution. Thus, the legislature is not subject to the limitations placed on state constitutional authorities by the State Constitution. Moreover, since 3 U. S. C. § 5 provides that, if a state legislature has provided for final determination of contests or controversies by a law made prior to election day, that determination shall be conclusive if made at least six days prior to the time of meeting of the electors, a legislative wish to take advantage of the safe harbor created by § 5 would counsel against any construction of the state election code that Congress might deem to be a change in the law. Vacated and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida denied a motion for a mistrial on the ground that the jury had been exposed to news accounts about a prior felony conviction and certain facts about the crime with which he was charged. The trial judge denied the motion, relying on the jurors' assurances that they could maintain impartiality in spite of the news articles. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the lower court's decision. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate decision, ruled that the trial judge had erred in denying a motion to dismiss the jury because the jury was not informed of the prior felony convictions. The high court held that it was not a matter of constitutional compulsion for the jury to be informed of prior convictions. In this case, the jury learned of the felony convictions and the facts of the crime from news reports. The court found that petitioner had not been denied due process. We therefore affirm the district court decision.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the conviction of Albert Roviaro for violating the Narcotic Drugs Import and Export Act. Roviaro was charged with selling heroin to an undercover individual known as "John Doe" and with the illegal transportation of narcotics. Before trial, Roviaro requested the identity of John Doe, which the government refused to disclose, claiming the informer's privilege.

The District Court allowed the government to withhold Doe's identity, and Roviaro was convicted. The Court of Appeals upheld the conviction, but the Supreme Court granted certiorari to address the issue of nondisclosure of the informer's identity.

The Supreme Court acknowledged the government's privilege to protect the identity of informants to encourage citizens to report crimes. However, the Court also recognized that this privilege has limits, especially when fairness requires disclosure for the accused's defense or for a fair trial.

The Court determined that the informer's identity was highly relevant to Roviaro's defense, particularly since Doe was a key participant in the alleged crime and the only other person present during the transaction. The Court reasoned that Doe's testimony could have been crucial in establishing whether Roviaro knew he was transporting heroin or if there was entrapment.

The Supreme Court concluded that the trial court made a reversible error by allowing the government to withhold Doe's identity, as it prevented Roviaro from accessing a material witness and potentially undermined his defense. The Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case to the District Court for further proceedings consistent with the opinion.

Justices BLACK and WHITTAKER did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana today entered a final judgment in favor of the United States in a civil injunctive action brought by a private party seeking to have its claim of title to the mineral rights in Louisiana.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New Orleans, Louisiana, the U. S. Attorney's Office for Louisiana announced criminal charges against the defendant.  The SEC alleges that the defendant, a Louisiana resident, filed an emergency action in the federal district court for the eastern district of Louisiana on December 21, 1938, alleging that the reservation of mineral rights would expire on April 1, 1945, subject to certain conditions not material to this case.  In its judgment, the court found that the defendants had violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and that the federal court had jurisdiction over the matter.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint, the defendant consented to the entry of a final judgement that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.   The court also granted the defendant's motion for a preliminary injunction, which is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by Michael J. Mascianica and Eric R. Werner of the Boston Regional Office, with the assistance of the Office of International Affairs' Office of Advocacy and Public Finance.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed a lower court's decision to exclude testimony by five former Sprint employees who alleged that their supervisors had discriminated against them because of their age. The court found that the lower court improperly applied a per se rule that excluded testimony from employees who were not similarly situated to the plaintiff, Ellen Mendelsohn. The Court concluded that the Federal Rules of Evidence required admission of the testimony, and remanded the case with instructions to admit the challenged testimony. The lower court previously ruled that the testimony was not relevant to the central issue in the case: whether Sprint's then-head of the Business Development Strategy Group, Paul Reddick, had terminated Mendel's employment as a result of her age. Sprint argued that Reddick was the decision-maker in any adverse employment action, and that it was irrelevant to the issue of whether he had terminated her because of her Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) status. The appeals court found, however, that the district court had improperly excluded the testimony of employees who had not worked under Reddick in the chain of command, which included James Fee, Fee's direct manager, and Paul Blessing, Reddick's supervisor and head of the BDS Group. The Appeals Court found that these employees did not report hearing any undue discrimination by Reddick or Blessing, nor did any of the proffered witnesses report hearing discriminatory remarks by either of them. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Reddick and Blessing, and sent the case back for a new trial.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a California-based company that claimed to recover attorney’s fees from the Department of Transportation.  According to the SEC’s complaint, Richlin Security Service Co. was engaged by the former Immigration and Naturalization Service to provide guard services for detainees at Los Angeles International Airport. The complaint alleges that the former agency misclassified the paralegal fees it paid to its attorney.  The complaint further alleges that Richlin was not entitled to recover his fees at market rates, and that he had not submitted any evidence to support his claim.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney for the Central District of California today announced criminal charges against Richlin.  On June 30, 2005, the court issued an order permanently enjoining Richlin from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering him to pay $45,141.10 for 523.8 hours of work on its contract claim and $6,760 for 68.2 hours of attorney-and-agent work on the application itself.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the SEC &rsqua;s order also ordered Richlin to pay a civil penalty of $125 per hour.   The court also issued a temporary restraining order halting the issuance of the order, ordering the payment of the civil penalty to be determined by the court at a later date.  A parallel action was instituted against the company, which was charged with recovering attorney fees under the federal securities laws.  This action was handled by Scott A. Thompson, Jr. of the Boston Regional Office, under the supervision of Joseph G. Sansone, and supervised by Eric R. Werner.

The Supreme Court reversed the conviction of Arthur Andersen LLP, Enron's auditor, for document destruction under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1512(b)(2)(A) and (B), which criminalize knowingly using intimidation or physical force, threatening, or corruptly persuading another person to withhold or alter documents for use in an official proceeding. The Court found that the jury instructions did not properly define what constitutes "corrupt persuasion" under the law.

The Court emphasized the need for restraint in interpreting the reach of federal criminal statutes to ensure fair warning of the law's requirements. Persuasion is not inherently wrongful, and the term "corruptly" implies a consciousness of wrongdoing. The Court stated that only those aware of their wrongdoing can be said to "knowingly corruptly persuade."

The jury instructions were problematic because they suggested that even if Andersen believed its actions were lawful, it could still be found guilty. The instructions also broadened the definition of "corruptly" to include any act that impeded the government's fact-finding ability, regardless of corrupt intent.

Furthermore, the instructions did not require a connection between the persuasion to destroy documents and a specific official proceeding. The Court held that there must be a "nexus" between the obstructive act and the proceeding, and a person must have a particular proceeding in mind where the documents might be material.

The Supreme Court concluded that the flawed jury instructions warranted reversal of the conviction and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

Plaintiff brought this action in 1954 seeking injunctive relief and damages against the City of Los Angeles and four private corporations for violations of §§ 1 and 2 of the Clayton Act arising out of a boycott of Iranian oil resulting from the nationalization of the oil fields of Iran in 1951. After the entry of default judgments against the private corporations, the City of Los Angeles settled with plaintiff for $1 million. Later, the City sued the United States in federal district court for refund of the settlement money, claiming that the settlement was void under the Fifth Amendment because the City had been coerced by the threat of loss of federal funds. The United States intervened in the suit and prevailed. The City appealed to the Court of Claims, which reversed and remanded the case to the District Court. The District Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. The Court of Claims reversed and remanded, and the District Court again dismissed the appeal. The Court of Claims reversed and remanded, and the District Court again dismissed the appeal. Ultimately the Court of Claims sustained the City's constitutional claim and awarded the City a refund of the settlement money. Held: 1. Summary judgment was properly granted to the City of Los Angeles. Pp. 138-146. (a) The Court of Claims erred in allowing recovery based on the City's constitutional claim, since the City had waived that claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 138-140. (b) The Court of Claims erred in sustaining the City's constitutional claim, since the City had waived that claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 140-141. (c) The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 141-142. (d) The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 142-143. (e) The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 143-144. (f) The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 144-145. (g) The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 145-146. 2. The Court of Claims erred in sustaining the City's constitutional claim, since the City had waived that claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 140-141. 3. The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 141-142. 4. The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 142-143. 5. The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 143-144. 6. The Court of Claims erred in reversing the dismissal of the City's appeal to the District Court, since the City had waived its constitutional claim by settling with plaintiff. Pp. 144-145. 159 Ct. Cl. 108, 315 F. 2d 558, affirmed.

In the case of Reverend Mr. B. Elton Cox, a civil rights leader who was arrested and charged with several offenses during a demonstration in Louisiana, the Supreme Court reviewed his convictions for disturbing the peace and obstructing public passages. Cox had been acquitted of criminal conspiracy but convicted of the other charges, which included picketing before a courthouse. The Louisiana Supreme Court had affirmed all three convictions.

The facts of the case involved a peaceful civil rights demonstration by students protesting racial segregation and the arrest of their peers. Cox took over the leadership of the demonstration when other leaders were arrested. The demonstration was orderly, with participants marching to the courthouse, singing hymns, and listening to speeches. However, the authorities deemed the demonstration a disturbance of the peace and used tear gas to disperse the crowd. Cox was arrested the following day.

The Supreme Court found that Cox's conviction for disturbing the peace was unconstitutional. The Court held that the Louisiana statute under which he was convicted was overly broad and vague, potentially punishing peaceful expression of unpopular views. The Court emphasized that free speech and assembly are fundamental rights, and the state cannot punish individuals for engaging in peaceful demonstrations. The Court also noted that the fear of violence from the demonstration was unfounded, as the students were not violent and the police had ample control over the situation.

Regarding the conviction for obstructing public passages, the Court found that the Louisiana statute, as applied, infringed upon Cox's constitutional rights. The statute allowed local officials to permit or prohibit demonstrations at their discretion, without clear standards. This selective enforcement was equivalent to censorship and violated the principles of free speech, assembly, and equal protection under the law.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Louisiana Supreme Court, concluding that Cox's convictions for disturbing the peace and obstructing public passages could not stand as they violated his First and Fourteenth Amendment rights.

The Supreme Court ruled that banks for cooperatives are not exempt from state income taxation. The court based its decision on the fact that Congress has not explicitly granted them immunity from state taxation, despite providing such immunity to other institutions within the Farm Credit System like farm credit banks and federal land bank associations.

Petitioner Virginia newspaper published an article based on information contained in a transcript of a tape recording of a meeting of petitioner Virginia Judicial Inquiry and Review Commission (JIRC), which was conducting an investigation of certain judicial proceedings. The article stated that the JIRC was considering whether to recommend that a state judge be removed from office for sexual misconduct with minors, and quoted extensively from the tape recording, which included testimony given by two women who claimed to have been victims of the judge's improper behavior. After the article was published, petitioner Virginia Attorney General obtained a criminal summons charging petitioner newspaper and its publisher with violating Va. Code Ann. § 18.2-186, which makes it a crime for any person to communicate to another person any information relating to the business of a judicial tribunal except as permitted by law. Section 18.2-186 provides exceptions for communications made during the course of a judicial proceeding, or pursuant to a court order, or in compliance with rules governing the practice of lawyers. The trial court upheld the validity of the statute and convicted petitioner newspaper and its publisher of violating it. The Virginia Supreme Court affirmed, concluding that the statute was applicable to the circumstances of this case and that the convictions were supported by the evidence. Held: 1. There is no absolute categorical exemption from the requirements of the First Amendment for truthful communication of information pertaining to ongoing judicial proceedings. Cf. Cox Broadcasting Corp. v. Cincinnati, post, p. 427. Pp. 413-414. 2. The Virginia statute infringes the First Amendment rights of petitioner newspaper and its publisher. Pp. 414-420. (a) The Virginia statute is invalid because it applies to truthful communication of information pertaining to ongoing judicial proceedings regardless of whether the recipient has a legitimate interest in receiving the information. Pp. 414-416. (b) The Virginia statute is invalid because it is too vague to permit fair enforcement. Pp. 416-417. (c) The Virginia statute is invalid because it conflicts with the First Amendment rights of recipients of truthful information pertaining to ongoing judicial proceedings. Pp. 417-419. (d) The Virginia statute is invalid because it is not narrowly tailored to meet the compelling state interest in protecting the confidentiality of judicial proceedings. Pp. 419-420. 3. Since the Virginia statute is void, petitioner newspaper and its publisher cannot be convicted of violating it. P. 420. 217 Va. 699, 233 S. E. 2d 118, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California granted a preliminary injunction against a timber salvage sale in the Sequoia National Forest. The Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed the lower court's decision, finding that Earth Island, a group of environmental organizations, had no standing to challenge the regulations. Earth Island's challenge to the regulations was based on the fact that the Forest Service did not provide notice in a form consistent with the Appeals Reform Act of 1992 and did not make an appeal process available to the public. The appeals court found that the District Court's earlier decision to grant a nationwide injunction against the regulations did not preclude Earth Island from challenging the regulations in the absence of a live dispute over a concrete application of those regulations. The court also found that Earth island's challenges to other regulations were not at issue in the Burnt Ridge Project, which Earth Island had successfully challenged. The 9th circuit held that the district court had not adequately addressed the issue of whether there was a need for a national injunction. The Appeals Court concluded that the parties had not shown that there would be a significant impact on the environment if Earth Island were granted relief. The 8th Circuit agreed, and the appeals court ruled that the federal district court should have granted relief to Earth Island. The full appeals court will review the case.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Arizona today ruled that Jeffrey Landrigan, a convicted felon in Oklahoma, was not entitled to an evidentiary hearing because he failed to present any mitigating evidence.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed on January 31, 1995, Landrigan was convicted of second-degree murder in 1982 and was subsequently sentenced to a prison term of 30 years.  The SEC alleges that Landrigan made a false statement to the Arizona state court that he had worked in a legitimate job to provide for his family, and that he did not want his counsel to present mitigating evidence at sentencing.  Landrigan also allegedly told the court that his counsel should have investigated the “biological component” of his violent behavior by interviewing his biological father and other relatives.  As alleged in the complaint, however, this was not reasonable because Landrigan had a history of drug and alcohol abuse and had been a bad father.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for Arizona today announced criminal charges against Landrigan.  On June 19, 1996, the court granted Landrigan a temporary restraining order and barred him from appearing before the SEC as a trial judge.  Without admitting or denying the SEC’s findings, the defendants agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders Landrigan to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest and a civil penalty of $1,000.   The court also ordered Landrigan not to participate in the development of a sentencing hearing for a prior criminal conviction. Â The SEC also issued an order suspending Landrigan from appearing as an attorney and ordering him to provide evidence to the court.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a worker's claim under the Federal Employers' Liability Act (FELA) for negligently causing emotional distress by exposure to asbestos. The court found that the worker did not "offer sufficient evidence" to allow a jury to find that he suffered a real emotional injury. The Second Circuit held that, in any event, the worker suffered no "physical impact" that would permit recovery under the FELA. The Court also held that Buckley did not show that he was entitled to recover for the costs of medical monitoring. We conclude that Buckley cannot recover unless, and until, he manifests symptoms of a disease. We also consider a related claim for medical monitoring costs, and we hold, for reasons set out below, that the respondent in this case has not shown that he is legally entitled to recovery those costs.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has rejected a challenge to the constitutionality of the Copyright Term Extension Act of 1998 (CTEA), which extended the duration of copyrights by 20 years. The CTEA is a content-neutral regulation of speech that fails inspection under the heightened judicial scrutiny appropriate for such regulations, the court found. The court also rejected the challengers' argument that the CTEA violated the First Amendment's right to free speech. The Copyright and Patent Clause of the Constitution, Art. I,  8, provides that "Congress shall have Power ... by securing [to Authors] for limited Times ... the exclusive Right to their .<n>writings."

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit affirmed a lower court's summary judgment in favor of Gerald D., the father of a child born to Carole D. who had an adulterous affair with Gerald's husband, Michael H., and who has always claimed Victoria D. as his daughter. The court also rejected Michael's and Victoria's due process and equal protection claims against Gerald and Michael, and against the wishes of the mother to a putative father who has been prevented by California law from establishing his paternity. The Court of Appeal concluded that the  621 presumption does not infringe upon any constitutional right to a child to maintain a relationship with her natural father. In a separate opinion, the court found that Michael had failed to meet his burden of proving that his claimed "liberty" interest is one so deeply embedded within society's traditions as to be a fundamental right, and that his request for a hearing to determine his paternity was not supported by the facts of the case. The appeals court also found that Victoria was entitled to continued visitation with Michael, despite the fact that the court denied her motion for visitation pending appeal under  4601, which provides that a court may, in its discretion, grant "reasonable visitation rights" to any person having an interest in the child's welfare. The trial court concluded that there were no triable issues of fact as to paternity, and Gerald was granted summary judgment on the ground that he was not the father. The Appeals Court concluded that Victoria had established her right to continue visitation with both Michael and Gerald. The decision is affirmed.

In the course of an attempted robbery in Union County, South Carolina, then-18-year-old Wesley Aaron Shafer, Jr., shot and killed a convenience store cashier. A grand jury indicted Shafer on charges of murder, attempted armed robbery, and criminal conspiracy. Prior to trial, the prosecutor notified Shafer that the State would seek the death penalty for the murder. The defense presented evidence of Shafer's abusive childhood and mental problems. Near the completion of the sentence, the jury found Shafer guilty on all three charges. In the initial (guilt phase) proceeding, the trial judge instructed the jury that, under the governing state law, he would not be eligible for parole in the event that the jury sentences him to life imprisonment without possibility of parole. After the prosecution's closing argument, and out of the presence of the jury, Shafer renewed his plea for a life without parole charge. The prosecutor further informed Shafer of the State's "prior bad acts," as well as his "propensity for [future] violence and unlawful conduct." The judge denied both requests and imposed the death sentence. Shafer appealed his death sentence to the South Carolina Supreme Court, which acknowledged that "[w]hen the State places the defendant's future dangerousness at issue and the only available alternative sentence to be imposed, due process entitles the defendant to inform the jury he is parole ineligible." Without considering whether the prosecutor's evidentiary submissions or closing argument in fact placed Shafer at issue, the court held Simmons generally inapplicable to South Carolina's "new sentencing scheme." The court held that, if the jury fails to agree unanimously on the existence of a statutory aggravating circumstance, it shall not make a sentencing recommendation. Held: 1. The trial court's refusal to give Shafer a life sentence under the new sentencing scheme does not render the sentence in question in Simmons "inapplicatable under the [State's] new sentencing" scheme. Simmons is not inappapplable under the "New sentencing scheme," 340 S. C. 298, 531 S. E. 2d 524, 528. Pp. 4-8. (a) The trial judge's failure to argue that the state's current sentencing scheme is not present here is not ripe for the resolution of the issue of whether the trial court properly held Simmons inappliable to the current sentencing regime. Simmons, supra, at 8-9, was held to be inappherent to the State Supreme Court's decision in Simmons, which held that "life imprisonment means until death of the offender," and that "the sentence you send to me by way of a recommendation will in fact be the sentence that the court imposes on the defendant." See, e. g., at 3-4, 5. The South Carolina Court of Appeals, in order to rule broadly that Simmons no longer governs capital sentencing in the State, apparently assumed, arguendo, that future dangerness had been shown at the sentencing proceeding. The court's instructions to the jury did nothing to ensure that the jurors were not misled and may well have been taken to mean "that parole was available but that it was not available." See Simmons, 512 U. S., at 161. The jury's comprehension was hardly aided by the court's final instruction: "Parole eligibility or ineligibility is not for your consideration." After the jury returned a sentence of death, the judge denied the defense counsel's request for permission to read the statute's text to the jurors. The State's Supreme Court did not home in on the question whether the prosecutors or defense counsel had placed the defendant at issue. The case is therefore remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.

After the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA), which substantially amended the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), a federal court may not “enjoin” the removal of an alien subject to a final removal order, “unless the alien shows by clear and convincing evidence that the entry or execution of such order is prohibited as a matter of law,” 8 U. S. C. §1252(f)(2), but does hold a ruling in abeyance to allow an appellate court the time necessary to review it. A stay does not make time stand still while it considers the legality of a removal order. The traditional stay factors governing stays of removal are the same as those governing injunctions. See, e.g., 8 U., S. §1158 (barring review of certain removal orders and exercises of executive discretion); § 1252(b)(3)(C) (establishing strict filing and briefing deadlines for review proceedings); and §1251(a)(9) (consolidating challenges into petition for review). Three changes effected by IIRIRA are of particular importance to this case. First, Congress repealed the presumption of an automatic stay, and replaced it with the following: “Service of the petition on the officer or employee does not stay the removal [of an alien] pending the court’s decision on the petition, unless the court orders otherwise.” (1) In general “Regardless of the nature of the action or claim or of the identity of the party or parties bringing the action, no court (other than the Supreme Court) shall have jurisdiction or authority to enjoin or restrain the operation of the provisions of part IV of this subchapter, as amended by [iiRIRA], other than with respect to the application of such provisions to an individual alien against whom proceedings under such part have been initiated. ” (2) Because courts were no longer prohibited from proceeding with review once an alien departed, see Dada v. Mukasey, 554 U.S. 1, ___ (2008) (slip op., at 19–20), a reviewing court must bring considered judgment to bear on the matter before it, but that cannot always be done quickly enough to afford relief to the party aggrieved by the order under review. This conclusion is reinforced by the fact that when Congress wanted to refer to a stay pending adjudication of a petition for a review, it used the word “stay” to refer exclusively to stays, so that a failure to include stays in subsection (f)2) would render the provision superfluous. The fact that the issuance of a stay is left to the court's discretion “does not mean that no legal standard governs that discretion…” Virginia Petroleum Jobbers Assn. v. Federal Power Comm’n, 259 F. 2d 921, 925 (per curiam). The interest in prompt execution of removal orders is heightened by the circumstances as well-if, for example, the alien is particularly dangerous, or has substantially prolonged his stay by abusing the processes provided to him. See ibid. (4) The ability to grant interim relief is accordingly not simply “[a]n historic procedure for preserving rights during the pendency of an appeal,’ ” id., at 15, but also a means of ensuring that appellate courts can responsibly fulfill their role in the judicial process. The whole idea is to hold the matter under review, because the appellate court lacks sufficient time to decide the merits. Pp. 6–8. 528 F. 3d 330, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eastern District of Michigan has ruled that Michigan's prison visitation regulations violate the First, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendments. The case involves the state's policy of limiting noncontact visits between inmates and their family members. The court ruled in favor of the prisoners, finding that the regulations violate their constitutional right of association. The Court also found that the policy limits the ability of the warden to determine whether an inmate is a security risk. The ruling is the latest in a series of decisions that have found that prison visitation restrictions violate the Constitution's guarantees of due process and the right to a private and family life. The Supreme Court has held that the Constitution does not guarantee the right of a person to visit his or her family member in prison. The high court has also held that a person's right to visit a relative in prison is not guaranteed by the Constitution.

The U.S. Supreme Court today ruled that the Orleans Parish District Attorney's Office cannot be held liable for failing to disclose evidence that should have been turned over to the defense under Brady v. Maryland. The case involves a 1985 attempted armed robbery conviction that resulted in the death of Raymond T. Liuzza, Jr. in New Orleans, Louisiana. In a 1999 trial, the jury found John Thompson guilty of the attempted robbery, and he was sentenced to death. A few weeks later, Thompson chose not to testify in his own defense in his later trial for murder. Because of that conviction, Thompson spent 18 years in prison, including 14 years on death row. One month before Thompson's scheduled execution, his private investigator discovered the undisclosed evidence from his armed robbery trial. The reviewing court determined that the evidence was exculpatory, and both of Thompson’s convictions were vacated. Thompson then sued the district attorney for damages under Rev. Stat. 1979, 42 U. S.C. C.1983. The jury awarded Thompson $14 million, and the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed by an evenly divided en banc court. We granted certiorari to decide whether a district attorney’s office may be held liability under 1983 for failure to train based on a single Brady violation. We hold that it cannot.

Eligible prevailing parties seeking fees and other expenses under the Equal Access to Justice Act of 1989 (EAJA) may receive “reasonable attorney or agent fees … at prevailing market rates.” 5 U. S. C. §504(b)(1)(A). After petitioner Richlin received an unfavorable ruling from the Social Security Administration, it applied for fees and other expenses under EAJA. Its request included paralegal fees, which it argued were recoverable under the statute’s definition of “reasonable attorney or agent fees.” The Merit Systems Protection Board disagreed, holding that EAJA capped paralegal and attorney’s fees at the same rate. The Federal Circuit affirmed. Held: A prevailing party that satisfies EAJA’s other requirements may recover its paralegal fees from the Government at prevailing market rates. Pp. 4–12. (a) An examination of EAJA’s text reveals that the statute does not clearly distinguish between attorney and paralegal fees. Rather, the statute uses the general term “reasonable attorney or agent fees” to describe what may be recovered. While the statute mentions “reasonable attorney fees” in the first instance, it does not suggest that the term excludes fees for paralegals. Nor does the statute indicate that the term applies only to fees for attorneys practicing law. The statute’s structure supports this conclusion. Paragraph (1)(A) specifies that “reasonable attorney or agent fees” shall be awarded “for services rendered in connection with a proceeding to determine whether or not social security benefits are due.” The words “services rendered” show that the statute covers fees for services beyond the rendering of legal advice. Thus, the statute likely extends to fees for paralegals, who often perform tasks outside the realm of legal advice. Furthermore, paragraph (1)(A) states that fees shall be awarded “to the extent that justice so requires.” This provision reinforces the idea that the statute covers fees for services beyond the rendering of legal advice. Pp. 4–6. (b) Traditional tools of statutory construction and considerations of stare decisis compel the conclusion that paralegal fees are recoverable as attorney’s fees at their “prevailing market rates.” 5 U. S. C. §504(b)(1)(A). There is no need for recourse to the canon of construction requiring strict construction of waivers of sovereign immunity. The Government erroneously claims that the canon displaces the other traditional tools of statutory construction. Here, the Government’s policy rationale for recovery at attorney cost founders on the text of the statute, which shows that Congress was untroubled by the very distortion the Government seeks to prevent. The Government also failed to offer a satisfactory explanation for how a law firm’s cost should be limited to salary. Market practice provides by far the more transparent basis for calculating a prevailing party’s recovery under EAJA. Pp. 6–12. 340 F. 3d 1368, reversed and remanded. Stevens, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, JJ., joined.
