Scalia, J., joined except as to Part III–A, and Thomas, J., joined except as to Parts II–B and III.

Petitioner Rothgery, who has never been convicted of a felony, was indicted by a Texas grand jury for unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon, resulting in rearrest the next day, and an order increasing bail to $15,000. When he could not post it, he was put in jail and remained there for three weeks. On January 23, 2003, six months after the article 15.17 hearing, Rothgery was finally assigned a lawyer, who promptly obtained a bail reduction (so Rothgery could get out of jail), and assembled the paperwork confirming that Rothgery had never been a felony. Counsel relayed this information to the district attorney, who in turn filed a motion to dismiss the indictment, which was granted. Rothgery then brought this 42 U. S. C. §1983 action against respondent Gillespie County, alleging that he had been arrested as a felon. The District Court denied Rothgery’s motion to rearrest, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The Sixth Amendment right to counsel guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment applies at the first appearance before a judicial officer at which a defendant is told of the formal accusation against him and restrictions are imposed on his liberty. Pp. 5–11. (a) The right to have counsel in “all criminal prosecutions” is limited by its terms: “it does not attach until a prosecution is commenced.” United States v. Gouveia, 467 U.S. 180, 188. The rule is not “mere formalism,” but a recognition of the point at which “the government has committed itself to prosecute” and the accused “finds himself faced with the prosecutorial forces of organized society, and immersed in the intricacies of substantive and procedural criminal law” Kirby, supra, at 689. The Rule is “offense specific, ” McNeil v. Wisconsin, 501 U. . S. 171, 175, and is the basis of the Fifth Amendment right of the “accused” to assistance of counsel, see, e.g., Kirk v. State, 199 S. W. 3d 467, 476–477. It is not mere formalism. It depends not on whether a first appearance has begun adversary judicial proceedings, but on whether the prosecutor had a hand in starting it. And that is just as true when the proceeding comes before the indictment (in the case of the initial arraignment on a formal complaint) as when it comes after it (at an indictment on an indictment). This standard is wrong. The cases have defined critical stages as proceedings between an individual and agents of the State (whether “formal or informal, in court or out” see United Statesv. Wade, 388 U. s. 218, 226 (1967)) that amount to “trial-like confrontations” at which counsel would help the accused in coping with legal problems or … meeting his adversary. See also Massiah v. United States, 377 U.s. 201 (1964). The conclusion was driven by the same considerations the Court had endorsed in Brewer v. Williams, 430 U. States 387, 398–399, and that there was no basis for “depart[ing] from our traditional interpretation of Sixth Amendment rights to counsel in order to provide additional protections for [the inmates],” ibid. The Court also held that the right has been violated and whether Rothgery has suffered cognizable harm are separate questions from when the right attaches, the sole question before us. This Court has held that attachment of the right also requires that a public prosecutor (as distinct from a police officer) be aware of that initial proceeding or involved in its conduct. See Grano, Rhode Island v. Innis: A Need to Reconsider the Constitutional Premises Underlying the Law of Confessions, 17 Am. Crim. L. Rev. 1, 31, and Rule of Criminal Procedure 28 (9th ed. 1999) (emphasis deleted). To the extent these States have been denying appointed counsel on the heels of the first-appearance hearing, they are a distinct minority. The Fifth Circuit, in its judgment, vacated, and remanded.

In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that a class action lawsuit brought under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 cannot include individual claims for monetary relief. The Court found that such claims would "predominate" over the class's request for injunctive or declaratory relief, which is the primary purpose of a class action. The Court also found that allowing individual claims for monetary relief would conflict with the principle of equality under the law, as it would give different outcomes to different groups of people based on their individual characteristics.

After investigating respondent Greenwood's suspected involvement in narcotics trafficking, two police officers conducted a surveillance of the exterior of his home. During the course of the surveillance, one officer noticed that the garbage cans near the roadside were being emptied into the street by someone leaving the premises. Subsequently, after obtaining a warrant, the officers picked up some of the garbage and examined it. Evidence of illicit drug use was found, leading to Greenwood's arrest and conviction. The California trial court refused to suppress the evidence, finding that the warrantless search was justified under California Penal Code Ann. § 1524(h)(1)-which authorizes warrantless searches where there is probable cause to believe that a crime has occurred and the place to be searched is open to the general public-and that the evidence was admissible under California Evidence Code Ann. § 352, which provides that evidence is admissible if it tends logically to prove the fact in question and if its probativeness is undetermined by the existence of other evidence. The California Court of Appeal affirmed, concluding that the warrantless search was valid under state law. Held: 1. Society will not accept as reasonable respondents' claim to an expectation of privacy in trash left for collection in an area accessible to the public. Having deposited their garbage in an area particularly suited for public inspection and, in a manner of speaking, public consumption, for the express purpose of having strangers take it, respondents could have had no reasonable expectation of privacy in the inculpatory items that they discarded. Furthermore, the police cannot reasonably be expected to avert their eyes from evidence of criminal activity that could have been observed by any member of the public. Thus, what a person knowsingly exposes to the public, even in his own home or office, is not a subject of Fourth Amendment protection. See, e. g., Smith v. Maryland, 442 U. S. 735. This conclusion is reinforced by the unanimous rejection of similar claims by the Federal Courts of Appeals. Pp. 108-111. 2. Whether or not a search is reasonable within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment does not depend upon the law of the particular State in which the search occurs. Here, society as a whole possesses no understanding that certain areas deserve the most scrupulous protection from government invasions. Pp. 111-112. 3. Nor does the California constitutional amendment eliminating the exclusionary rule for evidence seized in violation of state but not federal law violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment simply because the State recognizes a state-law right to be free from warrantless searches of garbage. Under the Due Process Clause, the States may balance the benefits of excluding relevant evidence of criminal activity against the costs when the police conduct at issue does not violate federal law. Pp. 112-114. 182 Cal. App. 3d 105, 286 Cal. Rptr. 798, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eastern District of Kentucky ruled that a bankruptcy trustee's effort to set aside preferential transfers by a bankrupt college to state agencies is barred by sovereign immunity. The court held that the Bankruptcy Code does not authorize the Bankruptcy Court's jurisdiction over the preferential transfers. The Supreme Court held in a similar case in 2004 that Congress has the power to abrogate state sovereign immunity in bankruptcy proceedings. The Court of Appeal for the Sixth Circuit agreed with the lower court's decision. The case involves a case involving a Virginia college that did business with Wallace's Bookstores, Inc., before it filed a petition for relief under chapter 11 of the bankruptcy code. The college was bankrupt and the liquidating trustee was seeking to avoid and recover alleged preferential transfers to each of the petitioners made by the debtor when it was insolvent. The bankruptcy trustee filed a motion to dismiss the petition on the basis of sovereign immunity, but the bankruptcy court denied the motion. The Bankruptcy Court held that it had jurisdiction because the bankruptcy law provides for the bankruptcy courts to determine the dischargeability of a debt. The appeals court agreed that the bankruptcy trustee had failed to show that he had the authority to do so under the Bankruptcy Act of 1940. The Appeals Court ruled that, without abrogating the Bankruptcy Clause, the bankruptcy bankruptcy court had jurisdiction to determine whether the transfer of funds to the state agencies was in the best interests of the state. The courts held that, in this case, the Bankruptcy Law provides for a bankruptcy court to determine a debtor's dischargeability based on the facts and circumstances of the case. The appellate court agreed, however, that it was not necessary to authorize bankruptcy court jurisdiction over these matters.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin granted a motion by a bank robbery suspect to suppress evidence seized from a home in which he had been living. The court ruled that the search of the home was valid under the Fourth Amendment because the suspect was arrested in the yard and the homeowner's daughter, Gayle Graff, was present at the time of the search. The Court also ruled that there was insufficient evidence to prove that Mrs. Graff's actual authority to consent to the search was binding on the defendant. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a similar case, ruled that a search of a home without a warrant and without probable cause can be valid if there is a reasonable belief that the person being searched consents to it. The high court held that there is no reason to conclude that a person's consent to a search is not binding on him or her. The case is being appealed. The United States is seeking to have the case dismissed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eastern District of Michigan ruled that the State of Michigan's tax treatment of federal retirement benefits violated the federal Public Salary Tax Act of 1939,  111, which protects federal employees' immunity from state taxation. The court found that the state's interest in "attracting and retaining qualified employees" was a "legitimate state objective" that was achieved by a retirement plan offering "economic inducements"<n>The court also found that, under the terms of the tax law, the State's use of the term "employee" was not a sufficient basis to justify the tax treatment. The Court concluded that the law does not apply to federal employees who are not currently employed by the federal government. In a second opinion, the court ruled that there was no reason to conclude that the tax was discriminatory against federal employees. The case is now before the United States Supreme Court.

Petitioner Ortiz, a convicted felony offender, sued respondents—Jordan, a case manager, and Bright, an investigator—under 42 U. S. C. §1983, alleging that they deprived her of her right to reasonable protection from violence while in custody in violation of the Eighth Amendment. Both defendants moved for summary judgment, claiming qualified immunity. The District Court denied the motions, and the case proceeded to trial, resulting in a jury award of damages. Neither defendant appealed the District Court’s denial of summary judgment. Instead, they requested judgment as a matter of law at the end of each side’s evidence, but also failed to renew their requests for judgment as a matter of law under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50(b). The Sixth Circuit reversed, holding that the denial of summary judgment constituted error. Held: An order denying summary judgment does not qualify as a “final decision” subject to immediate appeal. This conclusion comports with the general rule that summary judgments are “by their terms . . . interlocutory.” Liberty Mut. Ins. Co. v. Wetzel, 424 U.S. 737, 744. And there is a limited exception to that categorization where a qualified immunity plea raises a “purely legal issue,” e.g., the determination of “what law was ‘clearly established’ ” at the time the defendant acted. Johnson v. Jones, 515 U.S. 304, 313. But absent a timely Rule 50(b) motion, an appellate court lacks power to review the sufficiency of the evidence after trial. See, e. g., Unitherm Food Systems, Inc. v. Swift-Eckrich, Inc., 546 U.S. 394, 405. Here, the qualified immunity defenses asserted by Jordan and Bright do not present neat abstract issues of law. Rather, disputed facts relevant to resolving those defenses include whether Jordan knew of the identity of the assailant and of Ortiz’s fear of a further assault, and whether Bright placed and retained Ortiz in solitary confinement as a retaliatory measure or as a control needed to safeguard the investigation. Thus, to the extent that the officials urge Ortiz has not met her burden of proof, they were, by their own account, obliged to raise that sufficiency-of-the-evidence issue by postverdict motion for judgment as a matter of law under Rule 50(b). They did not do so. The Sixth Circuit had no warrant to upset the jury’s decision on the officials’ liability. Pp. 4−7. 316 Fed. Appx. 449, reversed and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits an employer from requiring a high school education or passing of a standardized general intelligence test as a condition of employment in or transfer to jobs when (a) neither standard is shown to be significantly related to successful job performance, (b) both requirements operate to disqualify Negroes at a substantially higher rate than white applicants, and (c) the jobs formerly had been filled only by white employees as part of a longstanding practice of giving preference to whites. Held: 1. The EEOC's construction of § 703 (h) to require that employment tests be job related comports with congressional intent. Pp. 531-532. 2. Title VII does not require that any person be hired simply because he was formerly the subject of discrimination, or because he is a member of a minority group. P. 532. 3. In the circumstances of this case, neither the high school completion requirement nor the general intelligence tests are shown to bear a demonstrable relationship to successful performance of the jobs for which it was used, and the evidence shows that employees who have not completed high school or taken the tests have continued to perform satisfactorily and make progress in the departments for which the high-school and test criteria are now used, the promotion record of present employees who would not be able to meet the new criteria thus suggests the possibility that the requirements may not be needed even for the limited purpose of preserving the avowed policy of advancement within the Company, and in the context of the case, it is unnecessary to reach the question whether testing requirements that take into account capability for the next succeeding position or related future promotion might be utilized upon a showing that such long-range requirements fulfill a genuine business need. In this case the Company has made no such showing.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia today entered a final judgment against a Virginia-based pharmaceutical company and its owner in a civil injunctive action.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia, on May 24, 2018, the Virginia State Board of Pharmacy issued an order suspending the sale of unregistered securities in the form of "commercial advertisements" in violation of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also issued a temporary restraining order, temporarily suspending the sales of any unregistered stock in the company, and ordering the company to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the pharmacist.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by John R. Rymas and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Virginia Department of Health and Human Services.

The Supreme Court held that for the purposes of the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA), the "maximum term of imprisonment" for a prior state drug offense is determined by the maximum sentence applicable at the time the defendant was convicted of that offense, not by the maximum sentence under current state law. 

The case involved Clifton Terelle McNeill, who argued that his prior state drug trafficking convictions should not be considered "serious drug offenses" under ACCA because the maximum sentences for those crimes had been reduced after his convictions. The Court rejected this argument, stating that ACCA requires looking at the law in effect at the time of the prior conviction to determine if it qualifies as a "serious drug offense."

The Court reasoned that ACCA is concerned with convictions that have already occurred, and the statute's language indicates that the maximum sentence "prescribed by law" refers to the law at the time of the conviction. The Court also noted that consulting current state law could lead to absurd results, such as prior convictions effectively disappearing for ACCA purposes if the state law changed.

The Court affirmed the lower court's decision to apply ACCA's sentencing enhancement to McNeill, who had two violent felony convictions and at least one serious drug offense conviction based on the laws in effect at the time of his state convictions. The Court's decision ensures that ACCA's applicability is determined by the legal context at the time of the prior offense, providing clarity and consistency in its application.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled that the United States Olympic Committee (USOC) had the right to use the word "Olympic" in its advertising and promotion of the 1982 San Francisco Gay Olympic Games. The SFAA had been told by the California Department of Corporations that the word Olympic could not appear in a corporate title. The court found that the USOC's interpretation of the Act raised serious First Amendment issues. The appeals court agreed with the lower court's finding that the Act did not violate the SFAA's First Amendment rights. The Court of appeals ruled that, in the absence of a First Amendment defense, the Act does not provide for the protection of the Olympic symbol. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the U.N.

A longstanding civil rights law provides that “[a]ll citizens of the United States shall have the same right, in every State and Territory, as is enjoyed by white citizens thereof to inherit, purchase, lease, sell, hold, and convey real and personal property,” §1982. Respondent, a white man, had rented his house to T. R. Freeman, Jr., a black man, and assigned Freeman a membership share in a corporation, which permitted the owner to use a private park that the corporation controlled. Because of Freeman’s race, the corporation, Little Hunting Park, Inc., refused to approve the share assignment, and when Sullivan protested, the association expelled him and took away his membership shares. The Court upheld Sullivan v., 396 U. S. 229, which was similar to §1981 except that it focused, not upon rights to make and enforce contracts, but rights related to the ownership of property. In doing so, the Court of Appeals rejected CBOCS’ argument that §1981 did not encompass a retaliation claim. Held: 1. The question before us is whether §1981 encompasses retaliation claims. See, e. g., Runyon v. McCrary, 427 U.S. 160, 173. Pp. 5–11. (a) The Court has long construed §§1981 and 1982 similarly, and its precedents have long construed §1981 similarly. See Runyon, supra, at 173. In 1991, Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1991, §101, 105 Stat. 1071, with the design to supersede §1981. Insofar as is relevant here, §1981 traces its origin to §1 of the Civil Act of 1866, 14 Stat. 27. See General Building Contractors Assn., Inc. v. Pennsylvania, 439–384. And, like §1981, §1982 represents an immediately post-Civil War legislative effort to guarantee the then newly freed slaves the same legal rights that other citizens enjoy. See §1981 represents an immediate post-civil war legislative effort “to guarantee” the then-newly freed slaves’ “same legal rights.” See §1982, supra. Like §1981 and its sister statute, Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, §1962, §1980, §1978, the text’ing language does not expressly refer to the claim of an individual (black or white) who suffers retaliation because he has tried to help a different individual, suffering direct racial discrimination, secure his §1981 rights. Nor is it obvious how §1981 to avoid employment-related overlap without eviscerating Title VII or its “necessary” procedural and administrative requirements. See Jones v. Donnelley & Sons Co., 541 U. . S. 369, 383. Moreover, the 1991 amendments’ history indicates that Congress intended to restore that interpretation. See Sullivan, supra at 173–174. P. 174. (b) The language of §1981 does not specifically refer to an individual who suffered retaliation because of his efforts to help the different individual secure his §§1981 rights, but rather to the “right . . . to inherit” and “enforce” contracts, which the Court has recognized the sister statutes’ common language, origin, and purposes. And it is not surprising that following Sullivan, federal appeals courts concluded, on the basis of Sullivan or its reasoning, that § 1981 encompassed retaliation claims, since the same kind of Title VII/§1981 “overlap” exists in respect to employment direct discrimination. Yet Congress explicitly created the overlap in the respect to direct employment discrimination. Nor was it obvious that §1980 to avoid that overlap without using the ‘ ‘necessary’ language. See id., at 93, n. 78 (emphasis added). Moreover, since §1981 differs from §1981 only in that it refers, not to “the ‘right’ to make’ and ‘enforce contracts,’” 42 S. C. §1981(a), but to the right “of white citizens to inherit and buy, lease and sell real andpersonal property” (§1982), §1982 has been interpreted to eliminate retaliation claims that the courts had previously recognized under § 1981. And in any case, it has long evinced a general intent to accord parallel or overlapping remedies against discrimination. See Great American Fed. Sav. & Loan Assn. v., Novotny, 442 U.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Alaska today announced criminal charges against two Native American communities for their alleged role in the illegal operation of fish traps.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in June, alleges that Alaska Secretary of the Interior John E. "Jay" B. Brennan improperly obtained a temporary restraining order to halt the illegal use of the fish traps at Kake and Angoon, Alaska's two largest Indian communities.  According to the complaint, in 1948 and 1950, the United States entered into agreements with Alaska to permit the construction and operation of a fish trap at both of these sites.  As alleged in the complaint:  In 1949, the Secretary of State issued an order requiring Alaska to recognize the right of Native American tribes to fish on its reservations.  In 1950, when Alaska became a state, it granted the right to fish with traps to the tribe.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants agreed to the entry of a final judgment permanently enjoining them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount of their disgorgement plus prejudgment interest in the matter.   The settlement is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by David Starr Jordan and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson.Â  The litigation will be led by Mr. Jordan and Ms. Graham.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (Commission) charged petitioner with violating and aiding and abetting violations of § 17 (a) of the Securities Act of 1933 (1933 Act) and Rule 10b-5 promulgated under that section of the 1934 Act. The Commission alleged that petitioner had violated and aided and abetted violations of three provisions of the 1933 Act, § 10 (b) of that section, and Rule 9b-1 promulgated in that section. The complaint alleged that the Commission violated and abated violations of §§ 17 (b), § 10(b), and Rule 12b-2, and that, under all the facts and circumstances of this case, the Commission was entitled to injunctive relief. Held: The Commission is required to establish scienter-an intent on the defendant to deceive, manipulate, or defraud5-as an element of a Commission enforcement action to enjoin violations of these provisions. Pp. 623-624. 605 F. 2d 612, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Supreme Court has upheld a life sentence without parole for a California man convicted of stealing three golf clubs worth $399 each. The Court found that the sentence did not violate the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishments. The three-strikes law requires that a person convicted of two or more serious or violent felonies receive an indeterminate life imprisonment term. In this case, the trial court found that, as required by the law, petitioner Ewing had been convicted previously of four serious or violence felonies. The trial court refused to exercise its discretion to reduce the conviction to a misdemeanor, or to dismiss the allegations of some or all of his prior relevant convictio. The State Court of Appeal reasoned that enhanced sentences under the three strikes law served the State's legitimate goal of deterring and incapacitating repeat offenders.

Petitioner, who has been deaf since birth, asked respondent school district to provide a sign-language interpreter to accompany him to classes at a Roman Catholic high school in Arizona pursuant to the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), 20 U. S. C. § 1400 et seq., and its Arizona counterpart, Ariz. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 15-253(B). The District Court denied petitioners' request for a preliminary injunction, finding that the provision of an interpreter at Salpointe would likely offend the Establishment Clause. The court thereafter granted respondent summary judgment, on the ground that "[t]he interpreter would act as a conduit for the religious inculcation of James-thereby, promoting James' religious development at government expense." The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that the IDEA and the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment do not bar such relief. Held: 1. The Establishment Clause does not bar petitioners from providing the requested interpreter. Pp. 5-7. (a) The IDEA creates a neutral government program dispensing aid not to schools but to individual handicapped children. If a handicapped child chooses to enroll in a sectarian school, the school district does not need to provide him with an interpreter there in order to facilitate his education. The service at issue in this case is part of a general government program that distributes benefits neutrally to any child qualifying as "handicapped" under the IdEA, without regard to the "sectarian-nonsectarian, or public-nonpublic nature of the institution benefited." Witters, supra, at 487, and Ball, 473 U.S. 373, distinguished. The program in Meek, a statute that, inter alia, provided "massive aid" to private schools-more than 75% of which were church related-through a direct loan of teaching material and equipment, included maps, charts, and tape recorders, and the program also authorized state-paid personnel to furnish "auxiliary services"-which included remedial and accelerated instruction and guidance counseling-on the premises of religious schools. Respondent did not urge any statutory grounds for affirmance upon the court of Appeals, and thus the court decided only the federal constitutional claims raised by petitioners. In the District Court, too, the parties chose to litigate the case on the Federal constitutional issues alone. The order granting respondent judgment addressed only First Amendment questions. App. to Pet. for Cert. A-35, reversed.

In the case of Arturo Recuenco, the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Supreme Court of Washington, which had vacated Recuenco's sentence due to a violation of the Sixth Amendment as interpreted in Blakely v. Washington. Recuenco had been convicted of second-degree assault with a deadly weapon and received a 3-year sentence enhancement for using a firearm, a decision made by the trial court rather than the jury. The Washington court had ruled that such a Blakely error could never be harmless and thus required automatic reversal of the sentence.

The U.S. Supreme Court disagreed, stating that most constitutional errors are subject to harmless-error analysis, meaning they do not automatically invalidate a conviction. The Court reasoned that the failure to submit a sentencing factor to the jury is not a "structural error" that would always lead to reversal. Instead, the Court held that such an error could be considered harmless if it did not fundamentally affect the trial's fairness or the determination of guilt or innocence.

The Supreme Court concluded that the nature of the error in Recuenco's case was similar to the error in Neder v. United States, where the failure to submit an element of the offense to the jury was subject to harmless-error analysis. The Court found no constitutional significance in the distinction between an "element" of an offense and a "sentencing factor," as both must be treated the same under the Sixth Amendment.

The Supreme Court's decision means that Recuenco's case will be remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion, and it establishes that Blakely errors can be subject to harmless-error analysis rather than mandating automatic reversal of a sentence.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Kelly O'Gilvie and two of his children in connection with a $10 million civil injunctive action brought by the United States District Court for the Northern District of California.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that, in November 2018, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. Schleier of the U.N. District Court in Manhattan issued an order imposing a temporary restraining order, freezing the assets of the defendants, and ordering the disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and other relief.  According to the complaint, the court found that punitive damages were not included in gross income and that the amount of any damages received was not subject to the court's jurisdiction.  In addition, the complaint alleges that Kelly and his children received the net proceeds of a jury award of $1,525,000 actual damages and $10,000 punitive damages.  As alleged, however, the jury award did not apply to all of the damages received, and the children were not entitled to a refund.    The court's order, which was issued on November 5, 2018, permanently enjoins the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount they received.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants have consented to the entry of a final judgment permanently enjoining them from future violations of the federal securities laws, ordering them to pay civil penalties equal to their alleged profits, and imposing a $1.5 million civil penalty against each of them. Â The settlement is subject to court approval.

The U.S. Department of the Interior's Minerals Management Service (MMS) has issued administrative payment orders for the purpose of assessing royalty underpayments on oil and gas leases. The MMS is authorized by Congress to audit those payments to determine whether a royalty has been overpaid or underpaid. In the event that an audit suggests an underpayment, it is MMS’ practice to send the lessee a letter inquiring about the perceived deficiency. If, after reviewing the lessee’s response, MMS concludes that the lessee owes additional royalties, MMS issues an order requiring payment of the amount due. Failure to comply with such an order carries a stiff penalty: "Any person who ... knowingly or willfully fails to make any royalty payment by the date as specified by [an] order ... shall be liable for a penalty of up to $10,000 per violation for each day such violation continues." 30 U. S.C. 1719(c)(1). The parties agree that this provision applies both to judicial actions ("demand[s] arising on or after September 1, 1996") and to MMS' administrative payment order ("demand(s)"). The court finds that the statute of limitations does not apply to these orders. The court also finds that there is no reason to believe that the order is subject to the provisions of the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982 (FOGRMA) or the Federal Energy Regulatory Authority Act of 1988 (FERA)

The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Louisiana Supreme Court, upholding the constitutionality of Louisiana's non-unanimous jury verdicts in certain criminal cases. The appellant, Johnson, was convicted by a 9-to-3 jury verdict for a crime punishable by hard labor. He challenged the verdict, arguing that the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment require unanimous jury verdicts to uphold the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

The Court noted that it has never held jury unanimity to be a requirement of due process and that previous cases have allowed for non-unanimous verdicts. The Court rejected the appellant's two-part argument that (1) a non-unanimous verdict cannot reflect a true belief in guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and (2) the dissenting votes of three jurors indicate that guilt was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

The Court reasoned that a substantial majority of the jury being convinced of guilt is not equivalent to a failure of proof by the State, and that the disagreement of a minority does not automatically invalidate the majority's verdict. The Court also found no evidence that majority jurors ignore the reasonable doubts of their colleagues or act irresponsibly.

Regarding the Equal Protection claim, the Court concluded that Louisiana's statutory scheme, which varies the number of jurors required for a verdict based on the seriousness of the crime, serves a rational purpose and is not unconstitutional. The Court stated that the State may treat capital offenders differently without violating the rights of those charged with lesser crimes.

Lastly, the Court dismissed the appellant's Fourth Amendment claim, stating that no evidence obtained as a result of the allegedly unlawful arrest was used at trial. The lineup identification, which occurred after Johnson was brought before a magistrate, was not tainted by the initial arrest.

In summary, the Supreme Court held that non-unanimous jury verdicts in Louisiana for crimes punishable by hard labor do not violate the Due Process or Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, and that the appellant's conviction by a 9-to-3 jury verdict was constitutionally valid.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in a case brought by the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that the Commission violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The complaint also alleges that, contrary to the Commission’s findings, the Commission failed to consider whether the contracts were just and reasonable when it entered into them. The SEC also alleged that the contracts did not meet the requirements for market-based pricing, and that, as a result of market manipulation, many of the contracts in question were not performing as they should have been. In addition, the complaint alleges that certain contracts were subject to market manipulation because they did not comply with the obligations of the federal securities laws.  In its judgment, the court found that, in exercising its broad discretion, FERC could not impose a price-based price-ratio bar on certain contracts. The court also ruled that, under the proposed rule, the amount of the price bar would be determined by the market, not by the price of the contract.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the SEC has agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins the Commission from violating the above-mentioned provisions, and orders the Commission to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The settlement is subject to court approval. The case is being handled by John Rymas, Eric Werner, and Glenn S. Gordon of the Boston Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Mr. Werner and Ms. Gordon.

In Faretta v. California, 422 U. S. 806, this Court recognized a defendant's Sixth Amendment right to conduct his own defense, provided only that he knowingly and intelligently forgoes his right to counsel and that he is able and willing to abide by rules of procedure and courtroom protocol. Faretta also held that a trial court may appoint "standby counsel" to assist the pro se defendant in his defense. Before the first trial, Wiggins filed a request for appointed counsel, stating that he wished to rescind his waiver of counsel, but simultaneously appointed two attorneys to act as standby counsel. Shortly thereafter, counsel asked Wiggins how they should conduct themselves at trial, and Wiggins expressly requested that they bring appropriate objections directly to the attention of the court, without first consulting him. After the trial, newly appointed counsel discovered that the original indictment was defective, and a new trial was granted. Wiggins then moved the trial court to order preparation of a transcript and announced ready for trial. The trial began later that day, and shortly thereafter Wiggins alone conducted the defense's voir dire of prospective jurors and made the opening statement for the defense to the jury. Wiggins filed numerous pro se motions in the course of the trial. He cross-examined the prosecution's witnesses freely, and requested that counsel not be allowed to assist or interrupt, but a short while after Wiggins interrupted his own cross-examination of a witness to confer with him. When the trial reconvened in the afternoon, Wiggins agreed to proceed in Samples' absence. After Samples returned, Wiggins objected to counsel's presence, but objected even to the court's insistence that counsel remain available for consultation. He also objected to the trial judge's suggestion that Graham would make Wiggins' opening statement to the jurors. Wiggins again objected to Samples's participation in the trial and, after the trial concluded, he filed a habeas corpus petition. The District Court denied Wiggins' request for a rehearing. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Faretta was based on the long-standing recognition of a right of self-representation in federal and most state courts, and on the language, structure, and spirit of the Sixth Amendment. Held: 1. The right to appear pro se exists to affirm the dignity and autonomy of the accused and to allow the presentation of what may, at least occasionally, be the accused's best possible defense. Both of these objectives can be achieved without categorically silencing standby counsel's participation. Pp. 479-481. 2. The purpose of Faretta, which permits the accused "to have the Assistance of Counsel for his defense," implies a right in the defendant to conduct himself pro se, with assistance at what, after all, is his, not counsel's trial. Both Faretta and its citation of the Dougherty case indicate that no absolute bar is appropriate or was intended. The specific rights to make his voice heard that Wiggins was plainly accorded form the core of a defendant’s right to participate, see supra, at p. 174-175. The defendants’ appearance in the status of one conducting his own defence is important in a criminal trial, since the right to speak for oneself entails more than the opportunity to add one's voice to a cacophony of others. As Wiggins contends, the objectives underlying the right-to proceed pro se may be undermined by unsolicited and excessively intrusive participation by standby counsel, particularly when standby counsel assists the prose defendant in overcoming routine procedural or evidentiary obstacles to the completion of some specific task, such as introducing evidence or objecting to testimony, that the defendant has clearly shown he wishes to complete. Moreover, participation in standby counsel without the defendant's consent should not be permitted to destroy the jury's perception that Wiggins is representing himself. P. 478. 681 F. 2d, reversed and remanded.

Respondents, teachers suing on behalf of all teachers in a Wisconsin school district and the collective-bargaining agent for the district's teachers, brought suit in state court, alleging, among other things, that the notice and hearing provided them by the School Board were inadequate to comply with due process requirements. The trial court granted the Board's motion for summary judgment on the due process claim, holding that the teachers, although on strike, were still employees of the Board under Wisconsin law and that they retained a property interest in their positions under this Court's decisions in Perry v. Sindermann, 408 U. S. 593, and Board of Regents v. Roth. The court concluded that the only question before the Board on April 1 and 2 was whether the teachers were on strike in violation of state law, and that no evidence in mitigation was relevant. Held: The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment did not guarantee respondents that the decision to terminate their employment would be made or reviewed by a body other than the school board. Pp. 479-481. (a) The Board's prior role as negotiator does not disqualify it to decide that the public interest in maintaining uninterrupted classroom work required that teachers striking in violation state law be discharged. Morrissey v. Brewer, ante, p. 491. (b) A showing that the Board was "involved" in the events preceding this decision, in light of the important interest in leaving with the Board the power given by the state legislature, is not enough to overcome the presumption of honesty and integrity in policymakers with decisionmaking power. Cf. Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35, 485, and Kingsley Pictures Corp. v. Regents, 360 U S. 684, 688, distinguished. P. 478. (c) The Court is bound to accept the interpretation of Wisconsin law by the highest court of the State, and this Court is, of course, bound, to accept that interpretation by that highest court. The due process Clause does not preclude the Board from making a "reasonable" decision on this issue, the Wisconsin Supreme Court held and respondents argue, because its members are biased in some fashion that the Due Process guarantees prohibit. The Court's judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded.

In the case of William James Rummel, the Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the lower courts, upholding Rummel's life sentence under Texas' recidivist statute. Rummel had been sentenced to life imprisonment after his third felony conviction, arguing that the life sentence was "grossly disproportionate" to his non-violent property crimes and thus violated the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments' prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment.

The Court noted that Rummel did not challenge the constitutionality of Texas' recidivist statute in general, nor did he dispute the classification of his offenses as felonies. Instead, his challenge focused on the severity of the life sentence for his third felony.

The Court reiterated that the Eighth Amendment prohibits sentences that are grossly disproportionate to the crime but also recognized that the death penalty is unique and that its precedents in capital cases are of limited assistance in non-capital cases. The Court found that successful challenges to the proportionality of non-capital sentences have been rare and that the Weems case, which did find a sentence disproportionate, involved unique and extreme facts that did not apply to Rummel's case.

The Court emphasized the state's interest in dealing more harshly with repeat offenders who have demonstrated an inability to conform to societal norms. It also pointed out that Rummel had been given multiple opportunities to reform, which he did not take. The Court acknowledged that while Rummel's life sentence might seem severe, it was within the legislative prerogative, and the judiciary should not substitute its judgment for that of the legislature.

The Court also considered Rummel's argument about a "nationwide trend" toward lighter sentences but found that the evidence did not support a conclusion that Texas' statute was grossly out of line with other states. It noted the complexity of comparing recidivist statutes across jurisdictions and the role of prosecutorial discretion and parole in the application of such statutes.

Ultimately, the Court concluded that Texas was entitled to make its own judgments regarding criminal punishment and that the life sentence imposed on Rummel did not violate the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, maintaining Rummel's life sentence.

Under the Tax Reform Act of 1986, the Internal Revenue Code gave property and casualty insurance companies a full deduction for loss reserves as "losses incurred" in each taxable year. Under the 1986 Act, increases in loss reserves that constitute "reserve strengthening" do not qualify for a certain one-time tax benefit. Section 1023 (e)(3)(A) of the 1986 Code gave insurers a "fresh start" allowance for future loss payments without adjusting for the "time value of money"-the fact that "[a] dollar today is worth more than a dollar tomorrow," D. Herwitz & M. Barrett, Accounting for Lawyers 221, distinguished. Under § 1023, any net additions to reserves (with two exceptions not here at issue, §1.846-3(c)(3) and (c)(4) are "reserves strengthening" under the regulation. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue determined that Atlantic, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986, made net additions of reserves-"reserve strengthen"-during 1986, reducing the "freshstart" entitlement by an amount that resulted in a tax deficiency of $519,987. The Tax Court disagreed, holding that Atlantic had not strengthened its reserves. The Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the Treasury regulation's definition of "Reserve strengthening'' to include any net addition to reserves is based on a permissible construction of the statute. Held: 1. The Treasury regulation represents a reasonable interpretation of the term, and neither prior legislation nor industry use establishes the plain meaning Atlantic ascribes to the term. Pp. 521-532. (a) The term is certainly broad enough to embrace all increases in (all "strengthening of") the amount of the reserve, for whatever reason and from whatever source. Atlantic contends that this interpretation is unreasonable because, in theory, it produces absurd results, as the following example supposedly illustrates: Assume that in 1985 a PC insurer had four case reserves of $500 each (total reserves) of $2,000. If two cases settled in 1986 for $750 each ($1,500 total), the remaining loss reserve would be $1,000, and the Commissioner would have been required to recognize as income the difference between undiscounted and discounted year-end 1986 loss reserves. Atlantic's first expert, before "constructing'' a definition, expressly acknowledged that the term is "not a well-defined PC insurance or actuarial term of art to be found in PC actuarial, accounting, or insurance regulatory literature." Id., at 60. On this point she was in agreement with the Commissioner's experts: "In the property-casualty industry the term "reserved strengthening" has various meanings, rather than a single universal meaning," id., at 124. If the expert reports establish anything, it is that "reserving strengthening" does not have an established meaning in the PC insurance industry. Because the requirement that PC insurers discount 1986 reserves changed the "method of accounting" for computing taxable income, PC insurers, absent another transitional rule, would have had to recognize that Atlantic "did not strengthen reserves." To avoid this consequence, §1023(e) (3)(B) afforded PC insurers an exclusion from taxable income of the difference-in 1986 and 1987 loss reserves, even though reserves did not increase. The greater the 1986 reserves, the greater the exclusion. The commissioner's contention that under the stipulation in this case the increase in the reserve would "reduced to zero" by an offsetting adjustment when the payment is made, and that adjustments in the IBNR reserve (reserve for claims "incurred but not reported) may result from payments in excess of prior reserve amounts, offsetting changes in other reserves. Respondent 36-39. The court, as well as the agency, must give effect to the unambiguously expressed intent of Congress. Chevron U. S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837, 842-843, 113 L. Ed. 2d 694, affirmed.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia today announced criminal charges against David Lee Moore for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia, Moore was arrested on February 20, 2003, for driving on a suspended license. The complaint alleges that Moore, who was a resident of Portsmouth, Va., was stopped by two officers, one of whom was a state trooper, and one of the officers. The officers determined that Moore was in violation of state law, and arrested him for the felony of possession of cocaine with the intent to distribute it. Moore was subsequently sentenced to a five-year prison term and ordered to pay a $2,500 civil penalty. Moore has agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws. The final judgment, which is subject to court approval, orders Moore to comply with the court's order. The SEC's investigation was conducted by David Houghton and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The litigation will be led by T.J.Annunziata and Graham Loomis.  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Virginia Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Virginia State Police.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Dow Chemical Co.'s (Dow) motion for summary judgment in a civil injunctive action brought by the District Court against the company.  The SEC's order, which entered final judgments against Dow on May 24, 2018, finds that Dow violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and that the company violated the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia, Dow's claims of search and seizure were based on the false assertion that Dow had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the open fields of a manufacturing plant.  Dow's complaint alleges that, contrary to Dow's representations, Dow did not engage in any unlawful aerial photography of the plant complex.  Instead, Dow alleges that it intentionally surrounded the plant area with buildings and other enclosures to conceal its equipment from aerial views.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Dow.  On May 25, 2019, the court entered a judgment that permanently enjoins Dow from future violations of the securities laws, orders the company to pay a civil penalty of $1,000, and orders Dow to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest of $2,500.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Dow consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining it from violating the charged provisions of the federal laws, ordering it to comply with the court's orders, and imposing a $10,000 civil penalty against Dow, ordering Dow to disgorge $1.5 million in ill-advised profits, and ordering Dow's payment of a $20,000 penalty in the amount of $100,000.  Additionally, Dow has agreed to a settlement that is subject to court approval.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina today entered a final judgment in favor of the apple industry in its ongoing litigation against the Washington State Department of Agriculture ("DDA").  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Charlotte, North Carolina, alleges that the DDA violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") by requiring all closed containers of apples shipped into or sold in the state to display either the applicable USDA grade or none at all. The DDA's complaint also alleges that North Carolina's DDA imposed a mandatory inspection and grading system on Washington apple growers and dealers. The complaint further alleges that, in 1974, the Washington DDA issued an order requiring all open containers of Washington apples to be inspected under the same USDA grade. The federal district court's order, which entered final judgments in the case, permanently enjoins North Carolina from violating the federal securities laws.  The court also granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an accounting of the losses.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for North Carolina announced criminal charges against North Carolina apple growers, dealers, and others.  According to the complaint, the SEC seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  On May 2, 2019, the Honorable Judge Robert E. Currid of the U.N. District court for the District of Columbia entered a judgment against the DAD, ordering the SEC to pay $10,000 in civil penalties, and imposing a $20,000 bar.  Without admitting or denying the Commission's allegations, Currid has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations of the charged federal statutes, ordering him to pay a $25,000 civil penalty, and ordering the issuance of an order permanently restraining him from further violations. The settlement is subject to court approval.

The National Childhood Vaccine Injury Compensation Fund (VCIF) was established in 1986 to compensate individuals who suffer severe side effects from vaccinations. The VCIF is funded primarily through taxes imposed on vaccine manufacturers and distributors. The purpose of the VCIF is to ensure that individuals who suffer severe side effects from vaccinations are fairly compensated, and to encourage continued participation in the vaccine program.

Petitioners were convicted of selling crack cocaine and sentenced under the Federal Sentencing Guidelines, which were based on the 1986 Antidrug Abuse Prevention and Control Act (Antidrug Act). After the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 reduced the Antidrug Act’s 100-to-1 mandatory minimum to an 18-to-1 minimum, the United States Sentencing Commission (Commission) adopted new Guidelines incorporating the new minimum. When petitioners were sentenced, the new Guidelines had not yet taken effect, but the Commission had announced plans to adopt them shortly. The District Courts rejected petitioners’ requests to apply the new Guidelines, holding that the Antidrug Act’s 100-to-1 minimum controlled. The Eleventh Circuit reversed, ruling that the new Guidelines governed. Held: The Fair Sentencing Act’s new, lower mandatory minimums apply to the post-Act sentencing of pre-Act offenders. Pp. 4–17. (a) An 18 U. S. C. §109 savings statute allows a new statute to supersede a previous one without regard to the former’s penal consequences. Here, the savings statute suggests that Congress intended the Fair Sentencing Act to replace the Antidrug Act’s 100-to-1 minimum with the new 18-to-1 minimum. Pp. 4–6. (b) The Commission’s duty to apply the applicable Guidelines, see 18 U. S. C. §3553(a)(4)(A)(ii), combined with the ordinary practice of applying new penalties to defendants not yet sentenced, while withholding that change from defendants already sentenced, supports the conclusion that the Fair Sentencing Act’s new, lower minimums apply to the post-Act sentencing of pre-Act offenders. Pp. 6–10. (c) There is no merit to the argument that the savings statute embodies exceptions permitting the old 100-to-1 minimums to apply to pre-Act offenders sentenced after August 3, 2010, when the Fair Sentencing Act took effect. Pp. 10–13. (d) If the Fair Sentencing Act’s new minimums apply to all of those sentenced after August 3, 2010, it is possible to foresee a smoothly transitioning process. On the other hand, it is difficult to foresee such a transition if the new Act’s application is keyed to a later date, thereby leaving the courts unable to take the new Act fully into account, particularly when that circumstance might create additional disparities and uncertainties that courts and the Commission may be helpless to correct. Pp. 13–14. (e) The Fair Sentencing Act’s new minimums apply to those who committed an offense prior to August 3, 2010, and were sentenced after August 3 but before November 1, 2010. Pp. 14–15. Vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses whether the respondents, collectively referred to as "Earth Island," a group of environmental organizations, have standing to challenge U.S. Forest Service regulations that exempt certain small fire-rehabilitation and timber-salvage projects from the standard notice, comment, and appeal process. The regulations in question allow projects under a certain size to proceed without an environmental impact statement (EIS) or environmental assessment (EA), thus excluding them from the usual public participation procedures.

The Court's analysis focuses on the constitutional requirement that federal courts can only hear actual "Cases" and "Controversies," which means plaintiffs must demonstrate a concrete and particularized injury that is actual or imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical. The injury must be traceable to the challenged action and likely to be redressed by a favorable court decision.

In this case, Earth Island initially had standing to challenge the regulations through a member who had concrete plans to visit the Burnt Ridge site, which was subject to a timber sale exempted from the notice and comment process. However, after the specific dispute over the Burnt Ridge Project was settled, the Court found that Earth Island no longer had a live dispute or imminent injury to confer standing.

The Court rejected the argument that Earth Island had procedural standing simply because they were denied the ability to comment on Forest Service actions. The Court emphasized that procedural rights must protect some concrete interest, and without a specific and imminent injury related to the regulations, Earth Island could not claim procedural injury.

The Court also dismissed the notion that organizational standing could be based on a statistical probability that some members might be affected by the regulations. The Court insisted on specific allegations showing that at least one identified member had suffered or would suffer harm.

The Supreme Court reversed the part of the Court of Appeals' judgment that upheld the District Court's invalidation of the regulations and the nationwide injunction against their application. The Court affirmed the dismissal of the challenge to the remaining regulations, which was not appealed.

The implications of the decision are that environmental organizations must demonstrate a concrete and particularized injury to have standing to challenge government regulations, and cannot rely on generalized harm or the mere possibility that members might be affected in the future. The decision reinforces the requirement for plaintiffs to show actual or imminent harm to their specific interests to engage the power of judicial review.

Title 15 U. S. C. § 2(b) makes it an unfair trade practice for any seller to engage in price discrimination tending to lessen competition unless the seller charges the lowest price received from any competitor except where the seller shows that "(1) the prices are substantially equalized by the action of the seller, and (2) the prices are substantially equalized by the action of the seller, not as a result of any special, exclusive, or preferential advantage accorded by the seller to any one or more of the producers or dealers involved." Respondent manufacturer brought this antitrust action against appellant wholesaler, claiming that appellant engaged in price discrimination in violation of § 2(b) by selling its products in Indiana at prices lower than those charged by another wholesaler in Kentucky. The District Court entered judgment for appellee after concluding that appellant had not satisfied the meeting-competition defense provided by § 2(b). The Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that the defense was unavailable since appellant had set prices statewide rather than on a customer-by-customer basis, and that the defense placed too much emphasis on individual competitive situations rather than on a general system of competition. Held: 1. Whether appellant satisfied the meeting-competition defense is a question of fact to be decided by the trier of fact. To satisfy the defense, appellant must show the existence of facts that would lead a reasonable and prudent person to believe that its lower price would meet the equally low price of a competitor, and must also demonstrate that its lower price was a good-faith response to a competitor's lower price. Pp. 108-115. (a) The defense is not rendered unavailable by the fact that appellant set prices statewide rather than on a customer-by-customer basis. It is clear that Congress did not intend to bar territorial price differences that are in fact responses to competitive conditions. Pp. 110-113. (b) While a seller may have good reasons to believe that a competitor or competitors are charging lower prices throughout a particular region, a customer-by-customer requirement might make meaningful price competition unrealistically expensive for smaller firms such as appellant. Pp. 113-115. 2. Because the District Court and the Court of Appeals did not decide whether appellant had shown facts that would have led a reasonable and prudent person to conclude that its lower price would meet the equally low price of its competitors in Kentucky during the period at issue in this suit, and because the Court of Appeals did not apply the proper standards to the question whether appellant's decision to set a single statewide price in Kentucky was a good-faith, well-tailored response to the competitive circumstances prevailing there, the case is remanded for further proceedings. P. 115. 654 F. 2d 1220, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed a lower court's conviction of an Algerian national for carrying an explosive during the commission of a felony. The court found that the word "explosive" in the federal statute used to describe the conduct was not a sufficient basis for a finding that the defendant was guilty of the felony. In a separate decision, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled that the lower court misapplied the law when it allowed the defendant to use the term "firearm" to describe his intent to carry the explosives. The high court held that the law does not require the government to establish a relationship between the explosive carried and the underlying felony.

Petitioners were tried and convicted in an Illinois State Court for conspiring to injure the property of a telephonen company in violation of a state statute. They were also tried and convicted in a Federal District Court for conspiring to destroy certain "coaxial repeaters" and related equipment owned by the United States and used in interstate communications, in violation of a federal statute. Held: Their convictions in the Federal Court did not violate the Double Jeopardy Clause of the Fifth Amendment, since the prior state conviction did not bar the federal prosecution. Pp. 38-46. (a) Since the Federal Constitution permits states to define and prosecute crimes based on acts which might also violate federal law, the States' primary responsibility for defining and prosecuting crimes includes the right to prosecute crimes involving acts which might also involve federal interests. Pp. 40-41. (b) Unless the Federal Government can assure that there will be no state prosecutions for particular acts that also constitute federal offenses, the efficiency of federal law enforcement must suffer if the Double Jeopardy Clause prevents successive state and federal prosecutions. Pp. 41-42. (c) The prior state conviction did not bar the instant federal prosecution, since the Double Jeopardy Clause does not apply when those prosecutions, as in this case, are under statutes which require different evidence for a conviction and which protect different interests. Pp. 42-43. (d) Successive federal prosecutions of the same person based on the same acts are prohibited by the Double Jeopardy Clause even though brought under federal statutes requiring different evidence and protecting different federal interests. Pp. 43-46. 247 F. 2d 401, affirmed.

Respondent State of New York, pursuant to § 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, changed its 1972 reapportionment plan for Kings County, which contained 35% nonwhites, to reflect the 1966 apportionment figures, which showed 35% nonwhites, but also to create 65% nonwhite majorities in approximately 30% of the senate and assembly districts. Petitioners, who are members of the Assembly, brought this action challenging the constitutionality of the 1974 plan. They claimed that the plan deprived them of their right to represent constituencies composed largely of white persons, contrary to the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, and that the plan constituted racial gerrymandering in violation of the Fifteenth Amendment. The Federal District Court dismissed the complaint, finding that the plan complied with the Voting Rights Act. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Neither the Fourteenth nor the Fifteenth Amendment requires that racial criteria may never be used in districting and apportionment, or that they may be used, if at all, only as a specific remedy for past unconstitutional apportionments. Nor does the permissibility of racial criteria depend on whether the State has done more than the Attorney General was authorized to require it to do under the "nonretrogression" principle of Beer v. United States, 425 U. S. 358, 370-371, i. e., whether the 1974 plan increased the number of nonwhite voting districts above the level existing in 1966. Pp. 50-55. 2. Even apart from the "nonretrogression" principle, the 1974 plan did not violate the Fourteenth or Fifteenth Amendment. Pp. 55-60. (a) Since the plan left white majorities in approximately 70% of the assembly and senate districts, which had a countywide population that was 65% white, even if voting in the county occurred strictly according to race, whites would not be underrepresented relative to their share of the population. And since the individual voter in the district with a nonwhite majority has no constitutional complaint merely because his candidate has lost out at the polls and his district is represented by a person for whom he did not vote, some candidate, along with his supporters, always loses. Pp. 56-58. (b) While it does not follow that the State is powerless to minimize the consequences of racial discrimination by voters when it is regularly practiced at the polls, nonetheless, New York was well within the rule that courts have no constitutional warrant to invalidate a state plan, otherwise within tolerable population limits, because it seeks to recognize and accommodate the political strength of racial groups. Pp. 58-60. Affirmed.

In the case before the Supreme Court, a group of petitioners, including Oregon irrigation districts and ranch operators, challenged a Biological Opinion issued by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The Biological Opinion concerned the operation of the Klamath Irrigation Project and its impact on two endangered species of fish. The petitioners, who have competing interests in the water from the project, sought judicial review of the Biological Opinion, claiming it would reduce their water supply and was not based on sound scientific evidence.

The main legal questions were whether the petitioners had the standing to bring the case under the citizen-suit provision of the ESA and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and whether their claims were reviewable by the courts.

The Supreme Court held that the petitioners did have standing to challenge the Biological Opinion under the ESA's citizen-suit provision. The Court reasoned that the provision's language, "any person may commence a civil suit," is broad and intended to encourage enforcement by private individuals. The Court also found that the petitioners' interests were within the "zone of interests" protected by the ESA because one of the Act's objectives is to avoid unnecessary economic dislocation due to erroneous implementation.

However, the Court determined that only the petitioners' claim regarding the designation of critical habitat under Section 1533 of the ESA was reviewable under the ESA's citizen-suit provision. Their other claims, alleging violations of Section 1536 of the ESA, were not reviewable under this provision because it only allows suits against the Secretary for failing to perform nondiscretionary duties under Section 1533.

The Court also concluded that the petitioners' claims under Section 1536 could be reviewed under the APA. The Biological Opinion was considered "final agency action" because it had legal consequences, such as authorizing the Bureau of Reclamation to take the endangered species if certain conditions were met.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had affirmed the District Court's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The decision implies that individuals with economic interests affected by environmental regulations can have standing to challenge government actions under the ESA and the APA, and that the courts can review such challenges.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit held that New York's tax on medical center gross receipts is not pre-empted by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) because it does not "interfere with the calculation of benefits or the determination of an employee's eligibility for benefits"<n>The court held that the HFA "depletes the Fund's assets directly, and thus has an immediate impact on the operations of an ERISA plan's." The court also held that it "relates to" the Fund within the meaning of 514(a) of the Act, and is therefore preempted as applied to hospitals run by ERISA plans. The court concluded that HFA was not empted because it was a "tax of general application'' that did not interfere with the calculations of benefits, or determine employee eligibility. The Second Circuit's decision is the latest in a series of decisions that have held that certain laws of general applications are pre-emphasised by the Act. The Court held that, in this case, New York may collect its tax on the income of medical centers operated by ERISA funds.

The Navy deploys its forces in “strike groups,” which are groups of surface ships, submarines, and aircraft centered around either an aircraft carrier or an amphibious assault ship. Seamless coordination among strike-group assets is critical. Before deploying a strike group, the Navy requires extensive integrated training in analysis and prioritization of threats, execution of military missions, and maintenance of force protection. The Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 (MMPA), 86 Stat. 1027, generally prohibits any individual from “taking” a marine mammal, defined as harassing, hunting, capturing, or killing it. Antisubmarine warfare is currently the Pacific Fleet’s top war-fighting priority, and the Navy has long used “mid-frequency active” sonar, which transmits sound waves at frequencies between 1 kHz and 10 kHz, to detect and track enemy submarines. In light of the threat posed by enemy submarines, all strike groups must demonstrate proficiency in antisubmarine Warfare. The Navy conducts regular training exercises under realistic conditions to ensure that sonar operators are thoroughly skilled in its use in a variety of situations, including, among other things, conducting realistic training exercises to ensure the combat effectiveness of strike groups. In order to comply with the requirements of the MMPA and the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), the Navy must prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS) for “every . . . major Federal actio[n] significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.” 42 U. S. C. §4332(2)(C) (2000 ed.). An agency is not required to prepare a full EIS if it determines—based on a shorter environmental assessment (EA)—that the proposed action will not have a significant impact on the environment. Thus, when the Government conducts an activity, “NEPA itself does not mandate particular results” Robertson v. Methow Valley Citizens Council, 490 U.S. 332, 350. Instead, NEPA imposes only procedural requirements to “ensur[e] that the agency, in reaching its decision, will have available, and will carefully consider, detailed information concerning significant environmental impacts. ” Id., at 696–697. The District Court and the Ninth Circuit concluded that plaintiffs have shown a likelihood of success on the merits, because the Navy reasonably concluded that “emergency circumstances” justified alternative arrangements to NEPA compliance. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that plaintiffs had established a “near certainty” of irreparable injury. Held: 1. A plaintiff seeking a preliminary injunction must establish that he is likely to succeed on his merits, that he will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of preliminary relief, that the balance of equities tips in his favor, and that an injunction is in the public interest. See Munaf v. Geren, 553 U. . S. __, __. Pp. 6–8. (a) The Navy has many remedial tools at its disposal, including declaratory relief or an injunction tailored to the preparation of an EIS rather than the Navy’S training in the interim. See, e.g., Steffel v. Thompson, 415 U.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered final judgments in a case brought by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) against three state-level bank holding companies for violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Boston, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire, the two states with the highest bar on interstate bank acquisitions, the Douglas Amendment, were among the states that passed laws in 1956 and 1977 that prohibited the issuance of federal securities.  The complaint alleges that the Douglas amendment, which was filed on the same day as the Connecticut and Connecticut amendments, violated the securities registration provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In addition, the complaint alleged that the Massachusetts and Connecticut statutes, by prohibiting the acquisitions of local banks by out-of-state holding companies, did not permit the acquisition of national banks.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the charged provisions, ordering them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and ordering the defendants to pay civil penalties of $10,000 and $20,000, respectively.  Finally, the court granted the defendants' requests for a temporary restraining order and an asset freeze, which will be instituted at a later date.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Basinger and supervised by Scott A. Kasper. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Massachusetts Department of Banking, and the Connecticut Department of Insurance.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Mexican citizen who was convicted of a classic identity theft.  The court's order, which was entered in a parallel criminal case, finds that the federal securities laws do not require a defendant to show that he or she has the necessary knowledge to commit a classic theft. The court also found that, contrary to the federal statutes, the defendant did not have the requisite knowledge to know that the documents on which he stole were real.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, the federal law requires that a person who knowingly transfers, possesses, or uses a means of identification of another person or a false identification document to be subject to imprisonment. The complaint alleges that, in doing so, a defendant may be able to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the papers on the forged documents belonged to another person.  In a parallel case, the U. S.
