Respondent State of Alabama filed a complaint for paternity and child support against petitioner J.E.B., the mother of a minor child. The matter was called for trial and jury selection began. After the trial court excused three jurors for cause, only 10 of the remaining 33 jurors were male. Petitioner objected to the State's peremptory challenges on the ground that they were exercised against male jurors solely on the basis of gender, in violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The jury found petitioner to be the father of the child and the court entered an order directing him to pay child support. On post-judgment motion, the court reaffirmed its ruling that Batson does not extend to gender-based challenges. The Alabama Court of Civil Appeals affirmed, relying on Alabama precedent, see, e. g., Murphy v. State, 596 So. 2d 42, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit granted certiorari and remanded the case of Gary Cone, a Vietnam War veteran sentenced to death for killing two people in Tennessee. The court ruled that Cone's right to a fair trial was violated when the State of Tennessee withheld evidence that would have bolstered his defense and bolstered his case in mitigation of the death penalty. The Court ruled that the lower courts failed to adequately consider whether the suppressed evidence was material to the question of whether Cone committed murder with the requisite mental state. The lower courts also failed to consider whether that same evidence would have altered at least one juror's assessment of the appropriate penalty for Cone. The Supreme Court ruled in a similar case in 1961 that the State violated Cones' right to due process when it suppressed evidence favorable to the defense. In that case, the Court held that when a State suppresses evidence that is material to guilt or to punishment, the State violates the defendant's rights. In this case, Cone argues that the state violated his right to Due Process by suppressing witness statements and police reports that would've corroborated his trial defense. The State's position was that Cone killed two people while suffering from acute amphetamine psychosis, a disorder caused by drug addiction. The state discredited that defense, alleging that Cone’s drug addiction was "baloney." The State denied Cone a hearing on the ground that his Brady claim had been "previously determined"

After extensive hearings, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) promulgated a standard establishing maximum permissible exposures to cotton dust in the textile industry. Subsequently, OSHA promulgated a standard implementing the textile industry portion of the cotton dust standard. Both standards rely heavily on the use of respirators to protect employees from exposure to cotton dust. Under the latter standard, an employer who gives an employee unable to wear a respirator the opportunity to transfer to another position, if available, where the dust level meets the standard's permissible exposure limit (PEL) must guarantee that the employee suffers no loss of wages or other employment rights or benefits. The Court of Appeals upheld the cotton dust standard and the implementing standard, holding that OSHA had authority to require employers to guarantee employees' wage and employment benefits following the transfer. Held: 1. Whether or not OSHA's cost estimate supporting the cotton dust standard was excessive, the Court of Appeals did not err in concluding that the estimate was "economically feasible" for the textile industry. Pp. 508-514. (a) Where the Act requires that the Secretary promulgate toxic material and harmful physical agent standards "on the basis of the best available evidence," 29 U. S. C. § 655 (b) (5), and where OSHA could not obtain the more detailed information needed to further precision its estimate, the agency acted reasonably in adopting the estimate. Pp. 508-511. (b) Whether or not in the first instance the Court of Appeals would find the Secretary's conclusions supported by substantial evidence, the Court of Appeals did not err in concluding that the agency reasonably evaluated the cost estimates before it, considered criticisms of each, and selected suitable estimates of compliance costs. Pp. 511-514. 2. OSHA exceeded its authority under the Act when it issued the wage guarantee regulation. Pp. 514-518. (a) Whatever methods the Act authorizes OSHA to apply, such methods must be justified on the basis of their relation to safety or health. Here, the wage guarantee provision is not justifiable on the ground that it minimizes any adverse economic impact on the employee by virtue of the inability to wear a respirator. Rather, the provision is an approach designed to contribute to increased health protection. Pp. 514-516. (b) Post hoc rationalizations of the agency or the parties to this litigation cannot serve as a sufficient predicate for agency action. P. 516. 3. Measurement of the validity of the Secretary's actions against the Act's requirements compels reversal of the Court of Appeals' approval of the wage guarantee provision. Pp. 518-519. 199 U. S. App. D. C. 79, 617 F. 2d 659, affirmed in part, vacated in part, and remanded.

Title: United States v. Doe (1972)

Summary:
United States v. Doe (1972) is a landmark Supreme Court case that established the doctrine of qualified immunity for government officials. The case involved a lawsuit brought against several government officials, including a police chief, for allegedly using excessive force during an arrest. The Supreme Court ruled that the officials were entitled to qualified immunity because their actions were based on a good faith interpretation of the law at the time, and that the plaintiff failed to show that the officials knew or should have known that their actions were unconstitutional. The decision set a high standard for proving that government officials acted maliciously or with reckless indifference to the rights of citizens, and it remains an influential precedent in the field of civil rights law.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Puerto Rico ruled that a political party's power to fill an interim vacancy in the Puerto Rico Legislature does not violate the United States Constitution. The court held that the parties' right to select candidates for the by-election was not violated by the provisions of Article 5 of the Puerto Rican Constitution, which provides that "the political party of the Senator or Representative causing the vacancy" may select a candidate to fill the vacancy. The Supreme Court also held that, in the event that the party fails to designate a replacement within 60 days after the vacancy occurs, that candidate is "automatically elected to fill" the vacancy, rendering a by- election unnecessary. The Court of Appeals, however, held that there was no basis for the lower court's finding that the provision violated the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment. The high court also found that the legislature's role as a check on the governor's authority to appoint legislators was not a sufficient basis for its decision. The justices concluded that the "legislative mandate" provided for by Article 5 was sufficient for the legislature to fill a legislative vacancy.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit granted a new trial for a man convicted of armed robbery in Louisiana. The trial was conducted by a 12-man jury, with three of the jurors voting to acquit the defendant. The jury was directed to return a guilty or not guilty verdict. The defendant, who was convicted by a nine-to-three vote, argued that the jury had not been able to reach a unanimous verdict. He also argued that he was denied his right to a fair trial under the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause. The court agreed with the district court's decision that there was no merit to his claim. The 5th Court agreed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings.

In this case, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Mandatory Minimum Penalties Act of 1996, which increased the penalties for certain types of drug trafficking offenses. The Court ruled that the Act did not violate the Eighth Amendment's prohibition of cruel and unusual punishment, despite evidence suggesting that the increase in penalties led to longer prison sentences for nonviolent drug offenders. The Court also held that the Act did not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, as it applied equally to all citizens regardless of race or socioeconomic status.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington today entered a final judgment against the United States and the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., John and Jane Doe, were formerly citizens of a foreign country that at the time was considered to be an enemy of the US, and John Doe was a high-ranking diplomat for the country.  The complaint alleges that the CIA designated them with "PL-110" status and began providing financial assistance and personal security to the widows of three civilians who died in the crash of a military B-29 aircraft.  As alleged in the complaint, however, the Totten bar prohibits the CIA from enforcing the terms of its agreements with the government.  In its judgment, the court found that Totten violated the procedural and substantive due process rights of the defendants by failing to bar them from violating the federal securities laws.  Without admitting or denying the allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal laws, and orders them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against them from serving as officers or directors of a public agency.    The SEC's investigation was conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by Eric R. Werner and Kurt L. Gottschall of the Boston Regional Office.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Southern District of Mississippi has reversed a lower court's decision that denied a tax refund to two Mississippi-based farmers who were required to pay interest on a loan to their regional bank. The lower court had found that the farmers' interest on the loan was not deductible as a capital asset as defined by  1221 of the Internal Revenue Code and that their purchase of the bank's stock was not part of their contract to pay for the use of borrowed money. The court held that the lower court misapplied the tax provisions of the Farm Credit Act of 1933, which provides that members may borrow money from their regional banks, and that the interest paid by the farmers on the loans is deductible as interest. The Court held that there was no evidence that the loan to the New Orleans Bank was part of the taxpayers' contract with the bank to pay the interest on their loans. The taxpayers filed a tax return for the years in question claiming a tax deduction for each $100 purchase of stock required by the loan statute. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed the deductions, and the taxpayers paid the assessed deficiencies. The District Court found for the taxpayers and the U.N. District Court for the southern district of Mississippi ruled against them. The appeals court ruled against the taxpayers. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate decision, ruled that the appeals court had erred in its decision. The case is now before the Court again.

In the case before the Supreme Court, Melvin Smith was charged with three offenses related to a shooting incident. During his trial, the judge granted Smith's motion for acquittal on the firearm possession charge due to insufficient evidence that the gun had a barrel less than 16 inches in length. However, before the trial concluded, the judge reversed her decision and allowed the firearm charge to go to the jury after the prosecutor presented a Massachusetts precedent. Smith was ultimately convicted on all counts.

Smith appealed, arguing that the Double Jeopardy Clause prevented the judge from reconsidering the acquittal. The Massachusetts Appeals Court affirmed the conviction, stating that the Double Jeopardy Clause was not violated because the judge's initial ruling was not final and could be reconsidered.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to address whether the Double Jeopardy Clause forbids a judge from reconsidering an acquittal. The Court held that the Double Jeopardy Clause does indeed protect against reexamination of a court-decreed acquittal, just as it does for an acquittal by jury verdict. The Court found that the judge's initial ruling was an acquittal because it resolved a factual element of the offense charged, and that the acquittal should have been treated as final once the defense had presented its case.

The Court concluded that the Double Jeopardy Clause barred the judge from reconsidering the acquittal, as there was no established Massachusetts rule or case law at the time of the trial that allowed for such reconsideration of a midtrial acquittal. Therefore, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Massachusetts Appeals Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

In dissent, Justice Ginsburg, joined by three other justices, argued that the Double Jeopardy Clause does not prevent states from allowing trial judges to reconsider midtrial acquittals and that the defendant suffered no prejudice from the trial court's error. The dissent would have upheld the conviction, emphasizing that the trial was a single, continuous proceeding and that the defendant had a full opportunity to present his defense.

The Supreme Court addressed the question of whether the federal crime of carjacking requires the government to prove that the defendant had an unconditional intent to kill or harm, or if it is sufficient to prove an intent to kill or harm if necessary to carry out the carjacking. The Court concluded that Congress intended to criminalize the broader scope of conduct, which includes threats of violence to coerce compliance, rather than only cases where the defendant has an unconditional intent to use violence.

The petitioner was convicted of carjacking and other related offenses. During the carjackings, the petitioner and an accomplice threatened victims with a gun, stating they would shoot if the victims did not comply. The District Judge instructed the jury that the government must prove the defendant intended to cause death or serious bodily harm if the victims refused to surrender their cars. The petitioner argued that this instruction was inconsistent with the statute, but the District Judge and the Court of Appeals affirmed the conviction.

The Supreme Court began its analysis by examining the language of the statute, its placement, and purpose within the statutory scheme. The Court determined that the intent to cause harm must be considered at the moment the defendant demands or takes control of the car. The Court rejected the petitioner's argument that the statute only covers cases where the offender intends to harm or kill the driver regardless of the driver's compliance.

The Court reasoned that the statute's broader purpose is to deter a type of criminal activity of national concern, and this purpose is better served by including both conditional and unconditional intent to harm. The Court also noted that Congress was likely aware of legal precedent and scholarship recognizing that specific intent can be conditional.

The Court concluded that the government must prove that at the moment the defendant demanded or took control of the car, the defendant had the intent to seriously harm or kill the driver if necessary to steal the car. The judgment of the Court of Appeals was affirmed, and the broader interpretation of the carjacking statute was upheld.

Appellant was prosecuted under two informations, each in two counts, which charged that he personally sold a 16-year-old boy two "girlie" magazines in violation of § 484-h of the New York Penal Law, McKinney's Consol.Laws, c. 40. He was found guilty on both counts. The judge found (1) that the magazines contained pictures depicting female "nudity" in a manner defined in subsection 1 (b), that was "the showing of [her] buttocks with less than a full opaque covering, or the showing of the female breast with more than a fully opaque covering of any portion thereof below the top of the nipple," and (2) that they were "harmful to minors" in that they had, within the meaning of subsection 1(f) "that quality of nudity . . . (which) predominantly appeals to the prurient, shameful or morbid interest of minors, and (ii) is patently offensive to prevailing standards in the adult community as a whole with respect to what is suitable material for minors." He held that both sales to appellant constituted the violation under § 48 4-h, insofar as that material is not obscene for persons 17 years of age or older, and therefore the conviction was affirmed without opinion by the Appellate Term, Second Department, of the Supreme Court. Held: 1. The New York statute does not bar the appellant from stocking the magazines and selling them to persons 17-18. Pp. 531-532. (a) The constitutional requirement of scienter, in the sense of knowledge of the contents of material, rests on the necessity "to avoid the hazard of self-censorship of constitutionally protected material and to compensate for the ambiguities inherent in the definition of obscenity," Mishkin v. United States, 354 U. S. 476, 485. The three-pronged test of subsection (f) for judgment the obscamenity of material sold to minors under 17 is a variable from the formulation for determining "clear and present danger" in its application to protected speech. Mishkin, supra, at 166, distinguished. P. 532. 2. It is not constitutionally impermissible for New York to accord minors under 18 a more restricted right than that assured to adults to judge and determine for themselves what sex material they may read or see. Roth v. States, ante, p. 534. (b) It is altogether fitting and proper for a state to include in a statute designed to regulate the sale of pornography to children special standards, broader than those embodied in legislation aimed at controlling dissemination of such material to adults. Roth, supra.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the issue was whether attempted burglary, as defined by Florida law, qualifies as a "violent felony" under the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA), which mandates a 15-year minimum sentence for felons convicted of unlawful firearm possession if they have three prior convictions for violent felonies or serious drug offenses.

The petitioner, Alphonso James, had pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm as a convicted felon and had three prior convictions, including one for attempted burglary in Florida. He argued that this conviction should not count as a "violent felony" under ACCA.

The Supreme Court held that attempted burglary under Florida law does qualify as a "violent felony" under ACCA's residual provision, which includes crimes that involve conduct presenting a serious potential risk of physical injury to another. The Court reasoned that the language of the statute does not exclude attempt offenses from qualifying as ACCA predicates when they involve such conduct. The Court also rejected the argument that the residual provision should only extend to completed offenses, noting that the enumerated offenses in the provision (burglary, arson, extortion, and use of explosives) create significant risks of bodily injury or confrontation.

The Court applied a "categorical approach," looking only at the statutory definition of the offense and not the specific facts of the case. Under Florida law, attempted burglary requires an "overt act directed toward entering or remaining in a structure or conveyance," which the Court found presents a risk of violent confrontation similar to that of completed burglary.

The Court also addressed the inclusion of "curtilage" (the land immediately surrounding a dwelling) in Florida's burglary statute, which differs from the generic definition of burglary. However, the Court found that the risk posed by attempted entry into curtilage is comparable to that posed by attempted entry into a structure, thus qualifying under ACCA's residual provision.

Lastly, the Court dismissed the petitioner's argument that the Sixth Amendment was violated by judicial fact-finding regarding the risk presented by attempted burglary, stating that the Court's analysis was based on statutory interpretation, not fact-finding, and therefore raised no Sixth Amendment issue.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, ruling that attempted burglary, as defined by Florida law, is a "violent felony" under the ACCA, and thus subject to the 15-year mandatory minimum sentence for the petitioner's firearm possession conviction.

The Supreme Court of the United States reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, which had affirmed the District Court's ruling that Chatham County, Georgia, was protected by sovereign immunity in a suit filed by Northern Insurance Company of New York. The insurance company sought damages for an alleged tort committed by County employees that resulted in damage to a boat when a county-operated drawbridge malfunctioned.

The legal question before the Supreme Court was whether a political entity like Chatham County, which is not considered an "arm of the State" for Eleventh Amendment purposes, could assert sovereign immunity in an admiralty suit. The Supreme Court concluded that only States and arms of the State have immunity from suits authorized by federal law, and it has consistently refused to extend sovereign immunity to counties or municipalities, even when they exercise a "slice of state power."

The County had argued for a "residual" immunity that would allow for a broader test to determine if an entity is acting as an arm of the State and thus entitled to immunity. However, the Supreme Court found that the term "residual" referred to the States' sovereignty that survived the Constitution, not to an expanded immunity for counties.

Furthermore, the County's alternative argument for a distinct sovereign immunity against in personam admiralty suits was rejected by the Supreme Court. The Court held that sovereign immunity in admiralty is governed by the same principles as in other sovereign immunity cases, and that historical cases, such as Workman v. New York City, established that cities and by extension counties do not enjoy sovereign immunity from admiralty suits.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court determined that Chatham County could not claim immunity based on its status as a county or under an expanded arm-of-the-State test. Since the County was not acting as an arm of the State when operating the drawbridge, it was not entitled to immunity from Northern Insurance Company's suit. The judgment of the Court of Appeals was therefore reversed, allowing the suit to proceed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Keith Bowles, a convicted felon who was executed on April 26, 2007, without any Member of this Court having even seen his appeal.  According to the court's order, Bowles failed to file a timely notice of appeal in accordance with the statutory time limits for filing an appeal pursuant to Rule 4(a)(6) and (c) thereunder.  The court found that Bowles violated the jurisdictional provisions of the federal securities laws, and that the Court of Appeals lacked jurisdiction to consider Bowles’s appeal. The court also ruled that the timely filing of an appeal was not jurisdictional.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Bowles. The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Jackson, Mississippi, charges Bowles with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty. Bowles has agreed to settle the SEC's charges by consenting to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the federal statutes, and orders him to pay a $10,000 civil penalty and a $20,000 officer and director bar. The settlement is subject to court approval.  On May 2, 2019, the court granted Bowles a temporary restraining order and ordered Bowles to comply with the court order. On June 2, 2020, the Court issued an order suspending Bowles from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney. On July 17, 2020 the court issued a judgment ordering the SEC to conduct an investigation into Bowles' alleged role in the alleged scheme. The case was supervised by Kelly L. Gibson, Chief of the SEC Enforcement Division's Cyber Unit. The litigation will be led by William K. Suter.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the First Amendment does not provide absolute immunity from liability for libel. The Court held that the "right to petition the Government for a redress of grievances" does not extend to the right to express opinions in letters to the President of the United States. The case involves a libel action brought by a North Carolina man against President Reagan for allegedly libelous and damaging statements in letters he sent to him. The complaint alleges that the letters falsely accused respondent of violating the civil rights of various individuals while a Superior Court Judge, "fraud and conspiracy to commit fraud," "extortion or blackmail," and "violations of professional ethics." The complaint further alleges that respondent's letters had their intended effect: respondent was not appointed United States Attorney, his reputation and career as an attorney were injured, and he "suffered humiliation, embarrassment, anxiety and mental anguish"

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled in favor of a ship's owner in a dispute over an unpaid bill for bunker fuel. The case raises the question whether admiralty jurisdiction extends to claims arising from agency contracts. In Minturn v. Maynard, the Court held that an agent who had advanced funds for repairs and supplies necessary for a vessel could not bring a claim in admiralty against the vessel's owners. We now consider whether Minturn should be overruled.

After petitioner, who was wearing a jacket emblazoned "F---K" ("F--k"), was arrested for violation of a California statute making it a crime to maliciously disturb the peace by any offensive conduct, he was found guilty after trial in a county municipal court. His motion to quash the information charging him with violating the statute was denied. On appeal, the intermediate appellate court affirmed, holding that the term "offensive conduct," as used in the statute, included behavior tending to create a clear and present danger of violence. Held: Petitioner's conviction violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments since the statute, as applied to him, constitutes an impermissible restriction on freedom of speech. Pp. 10-18. Reversed.

Title: Nuclear Waste Disposal Moratorium Under California Law

Case Name: Sierra Club v. County of San Diego

Year: 1983

Issue: Whether a county can adopt a moratorium on nuclear waste disposal under California law?

Background:

* The Atomic Energy Act of 1954 establishes the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to regulate the nuclear industry in the US.
* The NRC licenses nuclear power plants and oversees the transportation and disposal of nuclear waste.
* In 1976, the California Legislature passes AB 2712, which creates a moratorium on nuclear waste disposal in the state.
* The City of San Diego adopts Ordinance 2851, which extends the moratorium to include the city's boundaries.

Legal Issues:

* Does the NRC have exclusive authority over nuclear waste disposal in the US?
* Is the moratorium under California law preempted by federal law?
* Can a county adopt a moratorium on nuclear waste disposal under California law?

Analysis:

* The NRC has exclusive authority over nuclear waste disposal in the US, and therefore, the moratorium under California law is preempted by federal law.
* However, the NRC's authority is limited to the regulation of nuclear safety, and it does not extend to the economic or environmental impacts of nuclear waste disposal.
* Since the moratorium is not based on safety concerns, it is not preempted by federal law.
* The California Constitution grants counties home rule authority, allowing them to regulate land use and environmental issues within their borders.
* The ordinance extending the moratorium to include the city's boundaries is within the county's home rule authority and is not preempted by federal law.

Conclusion:

* The NRC has exclusive authority over nuclear waste disposal in the US, but this authority is limited to nuclear safety regulation.
* Counties in California have home rule authority and can adopt moratoriums on nuclear waste disposal based on economic or environmental concerns, as long as they do not conflict with federal law.

This Court will review the application of a specific consequence clause to a later class by identifying the principal consequential effects of that clause along with provisions whose applications help determine coverage or invocation. –RBH Illinois Bell Tel. Co. v. Public Util. Dist.No. 3 of Cook County, 662 F. 3d 853, 862 (7th Cir., ‘New Generation Enron Case Law Is Created’, January 2011, cited in Judge Posner’s list, DOJ Says Feds Shore Up Cause of Greatest Loss Since Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac Collapsed , Bloomberg News Businessweek, February 3, 2011. The decision below sent, May 19, 2010, reviewed in lower case only but referred in oral argument to §707(b)(2)(D).

While serving a sentence in a Michigan jail, Randall Fields was escorted by a corrections officer to a conference room where two sheriff’s deputies questioned him about allegations that, before he came to prison, he had engaged in sexual conduct with a 12-year-old boy. At the beginning of the interview, Fields was told that he was free to leave and return to his cell, but that he could leave whenever he wanted. At no time was Fields given Miranda warnings or advised that he did not have to speak with the deputies. The State of Michigan charged Fields with criminal sexual conduct. Respondent moved to suppress his confession, but the trial court denied his motion. Over the renewed objection of defense counsel, one of the interviewing deputies testified at trial about Fields’ admissions. On direct appeal, the Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed, rejecting Fields contention that his statements should have been suppressed because he was subjected to custodial interrogation without a Miranda warning. The court ruled that Fields had not been in custody for pur- poses of Miranda during the interview and that no Miranda warnings were required. The Michigan Supreme Court denied discretionary review. The Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding that the Miranda rule provides a permissible basis for federal habeas corpus relief under the relevant provision of the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA), 28 U. S. C. §2254(d)(1). Held: The record in Mathis, an inmate in a state prison, was not taken into custody for purposes of Miranda when he was questioned about events that occurred outside the prison walls. Because Fields was isolated from the general prison population and interrogated about conduct occurring in the outside world, the court found that the state court had violated clearly established federal law as determined by Mathis. 617 F. 3d, at 823. Pp. 5–11. (a) The record reveals that a prisoner is not in custody when he is removed from the prison population for purposes “custody,” Shatzer v. McCarty, 468 U.S. 420, 437–438. The record also reveals that the questioning of a prisoner in Miranda custody is always custodial when the prisoner is placed in custody, since such detention does not “sufficiently impair [the detained person’] free exercise of his privilege against self-incrimination to require that he be warned of his constiutional rights.” Williams v. Taylor, 529 US. 362, 412. The three elements of that rule—(1) imprisonment, (2) questioning in private, and (3) questioning about events in theoutside world—are not necessarily enough to create a custodial situation for Miranda purposes. See, e.g., Berkemer, supra, at ___–___ (slip op., at 13–16). In determining whether a person is in custody in this sense, the initial step is to ascertain whether, in light of the objective cir- cumstances of the interrogation, a “reasonable person [would] have felt he or she was not at liberty to terminate the interrogation and leave” Thompson v. Keohane, 516 U.

Petitioner was convicted in a state court of robbery and sentenced to imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years. At his trial, which resulted in a general verdict of guilty, the State relied primarily on a written confession which petitioner claimed was obtained by means of coercion and duress. On appeal, the State Supreme Court sustained the conviction, rejecting petitioner's contention that the confession was involuntary and therefore inadmissible. Held: The judgment is vacated and the cause is remanded for further proceedings. Pp. 44-56. (a) From the record in this case, it appears that petitioner's written confession was obtained in an atmosphere of substantial coercion and inducement created by statements and actions of state authorities. Pp. 48-52. (b) The fact that the trial judge or the jury may have reached a different result does not prevent this Court from independently examining the record and holding that the boundaries of due process were exceeded. Pp. 52-54. (c) Even assuming that the jury's verdict was correct, the error committed by the lower court in failing to instruct the jury on the requirements of due process renders the conviction invalid. Pp. 54-55. (d) The fact that there was substantial independent evidence tending to show petitioner's guilt does not render irrelevant the question whether the confession was obtained by coercion and duress. P. 55. 58 Wash. 2d 481, 364 P. 2d 102, judgment vacated and cause remanded.

Summary:
In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that a plaintiff bringing a disparate treatment claim under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that age was the "but-for" cause of the employer's adverse action. The court rejected the idea that the burden of proof shifts to the employer to show that they would have taken the same action regardless of age, even when a plaintiff presents some evidence that age was a motivating factor in the decision. The court also noted that the ADEA does not contain any language indicating that the burden of proof shifts in mixed motives cases, unlike Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.

The Supreme Court reversed a decision by the Court of Appeals that had upheld a preliminary injunction imposing restrictions on the U.S. Navy's use of mid-frequency active (MFA) sonar during training exercises off the coast of Southern California. The plaintiffs, including environmental groups and individuals, argued that the Navy's sonar training harmed marine mammals and that the Navy should have prepared an environmental impact statement (EIS) before commencing the exercises. The Court of Appeals acknowledged that there was no evidence of harm to marine mammals but still upheld the injunction.

The Supreme Court's opinion, delivered by the majority, emphasized the importance of the Navy's training exercises for national security and the need for realistic conditions to effectively prepare for potential submarine threats. The Court noted that the Navy had been conducting similar training exercises for 40 years without documented harm to marine mammals and had already implemented mitigation measures to minimize potential impacts.

The Court found that the lower courts had applied an incorrect standard for irreparable harm, requiring only a "possibility" of such harm rather than a likelihood, and had not properly considered the public interest in national defense. The Supreme Court held that the balance of equities and public interest strongly favored the Navy, given the importance of training for national security and the speculative nature of the alleged environmental harm.

The Court also criticized the lower courts for not giving due deference to the Navy's professional judgment regarding the impact of the injunction on training effectiveness. The Supreme Court concluded that the preliminary injunction, particularly the 2,200-yard shutdown zone for sonar use and the power-down requirement during certain conditions, unduly burdened the Navy's ability to conduct realistic training exercises.

The Supreme Court vacated the preliminary injunction to the extent challenged by the Navy, stating that the public interest in effective military training outweighed the plaintiffs' interests in marine mammals. The Court did not address the underlying merits of the plaintiffs' claims but indicated that a permanent injunction along the same lines as the preliminary injunction would be an abuse of discretion. The opinion suggests that other remedies, such as declaratory relief or an injunction tailored to the preparation of an EIS, might be more appropriate without jeopardizing national security.

Respondent Robbins owns and operates the High Island Ranch, a commercial guest resort in Hot Springs County, Wyoming, which is a patchwork of mostly contiguous land parcels intermingled with tracts belonging to other private owners, the State of Wyoming, and the National Government. In response to persistent requests by environmentalists and outdoor enthusiasts, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) tried to induce Robbins to grant an easement for public use over South Fork Owl Creek Road, which runs through the ranch and serves as a main route to the upper Rock Creek area. Robbins refused from fear that the public would disrupt his guests’ activities, but shortly after agreeing to sell the property to Robbins, he signed a nonexclusive deed of easement giving the United States the right to use and maintain the road along a stretch of land administered by the Bureau. Robbins declined to seek administrative review, however, in part because Bureau officials told him that the process would be lengthy and that his permit would be suspended until the IBLA reached a decision. The Board upheld the fine, but rejected Robbins’s claim that the Bureau was trying to “blackmail” him into providing the easement. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that Robbins inadequately pleaded damages under RICO and that the APA and the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) were effective alternative remedies that precluded Bivens relief. Held: Robbins has neither a private action for damages of the sort recognized here, nor a claim against the officials in their individual capacities under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO), 18 U. S. C. §§1961–1968 (2000 ed. and Supp. IV). Pp. 5–18. (a) Robbins‘ claim that he was harassed and intimidated by Bureau officials is not supported by the fact that he is a landowner and has no claim for damages. Nor does he face up to the real problem when he says that requiring proof of a wrongful intent to extort would shield well-intentioned Government employees from liability. The fact that Robbins has an administrative, and ultimately a judicial, process for vindicating virtually all of his complaints is not a fair summary of the body of allegations before him, according to which defendants’ improper exercise of their “regulatory powers” is essential to the claim. P. 5. (b) Robbins has no intuitively meritorious case for recognizing a new constitutional cause of action, but neither does it plainly answer no to the question whether he should have it. The question whether any alternative, existing process for protecting the interest amounts to a convincing reason for the Judicial Branch to refrain from providing a new and freestanding remedy in damages is a subject of judgment: “Congress is in a far better position than a court to evaluate the impact of a new species of litigation” against those who act on the publics behalf. See, e.g., Evans, 504 U.S. 669, at 264. But even in the absence of an alternative, the federal courts must make the kind of remedial determination that is appropriate for a common-law tribunal, paying particular heed to any special factors counselling hesitation before authorizing a new kind of federal litigation. And this case arises on interlocutory appeal from denial of respondents’ motion for summary judgment. Robbins describes the wrong here as retaliation for standing on his right as a property owner to keep the Government out (by refusing a free replacement for the right-of-way it had lost), and the mention of retaliation brings with it a tailwind of support from our longstanding recognition that the Government may not retaliate for exercising First Amendment speech rights, see Rankin v. McPherson, 483 U .S. 378 (1987), or certain others of constitutional rank, see, e., Lefkowitz v. Turley, 414 U. . . 70 (1973) (Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination); United States v. Jackson, 390 U . S. 570 (1968) (Sixth Amendment right to trial by jury). But even if a finding that an act for the benefit of the Government alone can be unconstitutional retaliation, there is no reason to enquire further into the merits of his claim or the asserted defense of qualified immunity. The claim against Robbins fails to fit the prior retaliation cases, which turn on an allegation of impermissible purpose and motivation; an employee who spoke out on matters of public concern and then was fired, for example, would need to prove that the conduct at issue was constitutionally protected, and that it was a substantial or motivating factor in the termination. And final agency action, as in canceling permits, was open to administrative and judicial review, as the Court realized, 433 F. 3d 772, reversed and remanded.

Respondent sued petitioner for damages under § 4 of the Clayton Act, claiming that petitioner's acquisition of respondent, a retail shoe merchant, violated § 7 of the Act. Petitioner challenged the constitutionality of § 7, claiming that it conflicted with the Fifth Amendment. After hearing evidence and arguments, the District Court concluded that § 7 was constitutional and that the merger violated § 7. Held: 1. Sections 1 and 7 of the Clayton Act are constitutional. Pp. 138-141. 2. Under § 7 of the Clayton Act, the merger violated the Act. Pp. 141-150. (a) Vertical aspects. Pp. 141-146. (b) Horizontal aspects. Pp. 146-150. 250 F. Supp. 455, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Massachusetts today entered a final judgment against a Massachusetts man who was convicted of violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order and ordered the release of a copy of the final judgment.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Boston, Massachusetts, Robert B. Baird, a registered physician, gave away a vaginal foam at the close of his lecture on contraception to a group of students at Boston University.  As alleged in the complaint, Baird was not himself a single person denied access to contraceptives, but rather an association of two individuals who had been convicted as accessories to the crime of using contraceptives.  In addition, the complaint alleges that Baird was neither a doctor nor a druggist, and neither he nor his wife were registered to sell or distribute contraceptives, and that he was not a member of any religious organization.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the SEC, Baird consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of five years, and bars him from serving as an officer or director of a public health organization for five years.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Massachusetts Attorney General's Office, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Massachusetts Department of Justice.

In this landmark case, the Supreme Court ruled that the Civil Rights Act of 1964 applies to private businesses that engage in interstate commerce, even if they are not physically located across state lines. The Court based its decision on the idea that modern transportation and communication technologies allow businesses to participate in interstate commerce, and that the effects of discrimination in one location can ripple through the entire economy. The Court specifically cited examples of how discrimination in restaurants affected the travel plans of African Americans, leading to decreased tourism and lost revenue for businesses along the route.

In the case of Bernadine Suitum versus the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency, the Supreme Court addressed whether Suitum's claim for compensation was ripe for adjudication. Suitum owned land near Lake Tahoe that the Agency determined could not be developed due to environmental protections but granted her Transferable Development Rights (TDRs), which could be sold to other property owners. Suitum claimed that the Agency's restrictions amounted to a regulatory taking of her property without just compensation, violating the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.

The central question before the Court was not whether the TDRs constituted just compensation or whether a taking had occurred, but whether Suitum's claim was ripe for review despite her not attempting to sell the TDRs she was entitled to. The Court held that her claim was indeed ripe.

The Court's reasoning was based on the following points:

1. The Agency had made a final decision that Suitum's land could not be developed, leaving no discretion over her right to use her land. Therefore, no further agency action was required to determine the application of regulations to her property, satisfying the demand for finality in ripeness doctrine.

2. The lower courts had erred in requiring Suitum to attempt to transfer her TDRs before her claim could be considered ripe. The Court clarified that the type of "final decision" required by precedent did not apply to the transfer of TDRs, as Suitum's entitlement to them was not in question, and no discretionary agency action was needed for her to obtain or offer them for sale.

3. The Court rejected the argument that Suitum's claim was not ripe because the value of the TDRs was unknown. It stated that the valuation of TDRs was a factual issue about market prices, which could be determined without an actual sale, and that the agency's concern over low valuation estimates was a risk inherent in regulatory innovation.

4. The Court distinguished this case from Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner, noting that Suitum was not challenging the validity of the regulations but seeking compensation for their consequences. The ripeness doctrine did not prevent her from proceeding with her claim.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, finding that Suitum's claim for compensation was ripe for judicial review.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Nevada today entered a final judgment in favor of a California-based company seeking to acquire land in the Lake Tahoe basin.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, alleges that the agency improperly granted the company's request for an asset freeze and other emergency relief.  According to the complaint, the agency's decision to grant the company the right to acquire and sell its land in violation of the federal securities laws was based on the fact that the company had not yet received a final decision on whether to apply for a permit to build on its property.  In addition, the complaint alleges that Suitum's claim was not ripe for adjudication because the agency had not received any final decisions on the application of the regulations.  As a result, the company was unable to acquire or sell the land.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Suitum has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining her from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering the company to pay a civil penalty of $1,000,000.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

The Supreme Court case in question dealt with the constitutionality of a Texas statute that required minors to be residents of a school district to attend public free schools without paying tuition. Roberto Morales, a U.S. citizen living with his sister in McAllen, Texas, was denied tuition-free admission to local schools because he was not living with a parent, guardian, or person with lawful control under a court order, and his primary purpose for residing in the district was to attend school.

The plaintiffs, including Morales's sister, argued that the Texas Education Code's section 21.031(d) violated the Constitution, specifically the Equal Protection Clause, the Due Process Clause, and the Privileges and Immunities Clause. They sought a declaration that the statute was unconstitutional, an injunction against its enforcement, restitution for tuition payments, and other legal costs.

The District Court ruled in favor of the defendants, finding that the state had a legitimate interest in preserving the quality of its educational system and the rights of bona fide residents to attend state schools on a preferred tuition basis. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed this decision.

The Supreme Court also affirmed the lower courts' decisions, distinguishing between durational residence requirements (which have been invalidated in the past) and bona fide residence requirements. The Court recognized that states have a legitimate interest in ensuring that services provided for residents are enjoyed only by residents and that local control over schools is essential for the quality of education.

The Court determined that section 21.031(d) is a bona fide residence requirement, as it allows children to attend school without paying tuition if they have a genuine intention to remain in the district indefinitely. The statute was found to be more generous than traditional residence criteria, extending benefits to many children who could be classified as nonresidents.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court held that the Texas statute was a constitutional bona fide residence requirement, and the judgment of the Court of Appeals was affirmed. This decision implies that states can impose residence requirements for tuition-free education, provided they are bona fide and not solely based on the duration of residence.

The Virginian Pilot, a Landmark newspaper, published an article which accurately reported on a pending inquiry by the Virginia Judicial Inquiry and Review Commission and identified the state judge whose conduct was being investigated. The article reported that "[n]o formal complaint has been filed by the commission against [the judge], indicating either that the five-man panel found insufficient cause for action or that the case is still under review." A month later, on November 5, a grand jury indicted Landmark for violating Va.Code § 2.1-37.13 (1973) by "unlawfully divulg[ing] the identification of a Judge of a Court not of record, which said Judge was the subject of an investigation and hearing" by the Commission. The newspaper's only witness testified that he decided to print the information about the Commission proceedings because he felt that the subject was a matter of public importance which should be brought to the attention of the Pilot's readers. The only reporter, witness, or representative of Landmark had been subpoenaed by or had appeared before the Commission in connection with the proceedings described in the article. Landmark was convicted and fined. The Virginia Supreme Court affirmed. Held: 1. The First Amendment permits the criminal punishment of third persons who are strangers to the inquiry, including the news media, for divulging or publishing truthful information regarding confidential proceedings of the Judicial Inquiry & Review Commission. Pp. 699-703. (a) The publication Virginia seeks to punish under its statute lies near the core of the First Amendment, and the Commonwealth's interests advanced by the imposition of criminal sanctions are insufficient to justify the actual and potential encroachments on freedom of speech and of the press which follow therefrom. See, e. g., Mills v. Alabama, 384 U. S. 214, 218. The confidentiality requirement can be said to facilitate the work of the commissions in several practical respects. When removal or retirement is justified by the charges, judges are more likely to resign voluntarily or retire without the necessity of a formal proceeding if the publicity that would accompany such a proceeding can thereby be avoided. Although it is assumed that judges will ignore the public clamor or media reports and editorials in reaching their decisions and by tradition will not respond to public commentary, the law gives "[j]udges as persons, or courts as institutions . . . no greater immunity from criticism than other persons or institutions." Bridges v. California, 314 U.S. 252, 289, and that a "solidity of evidence" Pennekamp v. Florida, supra, at 347, is necessary to make the requisite showing of imminence. P. 602. (b) The fact that the Commission's functioning is also claimed to be impeded by premature disclosure of the complainant, witnesses, and judge under investigation does not justify the subsequent punishment of speech at issue here, even on the assumption that criminal sanctions do in fact enhance the guarantee of confidentiality. In addition to advancing these general interests, the confidentiality of the proceedings allows the judge to be made aware of minor complaints which may appropriately be called to his attention without public notice. See New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, ante, at 270-271, and in the more common situation, where the alleged misconduct is not of the magnitude to warrant removal or even censure but rather served those interests in public scrutiny and discussion of governmental affairs which the First First Amendment was adopted to protect. The Commission's operations, no less than the operation of the judicial system itself, is a subject of public interest, necessarily engaging attention of news media. The commission's operations are matters of utmost public concern. The operations of the courts and the judicial conduct of judges, like that of all other public officials, are important public concern, and this Court is not concerned with the possible applicability of the statute to one who secures the information by illegal means and thereafter divulges it. Nor is there any constitutional challenge to a State's power to keep the Commission’s proceedings confidential or to punish participants for breach of this mandate. The Commissioner of the Commission has consistently rejected the argument that such commentary constituted a clear and present danger to the administration of justice, see Wood v. Georgia, 370 US. 375, 393-394, and is not a common characteristic of the state plans; indeed, only Virginia and Hawaii appear to provide criminal sanctions for disclosure. Nor has the Commission provided sufficient reason for disregarding these well-established principles in rejecting Landmark's claim that the "clear-and-present danger test" was the appropriate constitutional benchmark in rejecting it. The Court concluded that the clear-and present danger test was appropriate because it identified three functions served by the requirement of confidentiality in Commission proceedings: (1) protection of a judge's reputation from the adverse publicity which might flow from frivolous complaints, (2) maintenance of confidence in the judiciary by preventing the premature disclosure, and protection of complainants and witnesses from possible recrimination by prohibiting disclosure until the validity of the complaint. The judgment of the Supreme Court of Virginia is reversed

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit reversed a lower court's decision denying a motion for a new trial based on the prosecution's peremptory jury challenges based on race. The trial court dismissed the motion, and the Louisiana Supreme Court upheld the conviction. The lower court also dismissed Snyder's appeal based on a Batson objection. The court found that Snyder was competent to stand trial, and that the trial court had not violated the Batson rule. We conclude that the lower court committed clear error in its decision denying Snyder a retrial based on his Batson objections. The 5th Justices agreed with the majority that Snyder should be granted a new sentencing hearing. The case is remanded for further consideration.

Respondent petitioner Bond was convicted of using poison to kill her former lover. At trial, the District Court refused to suppress evidence seized during the investigation, rejecting her argument that the evidence was obtained in violation of 18 U. S. C. §229, which prohibits the knowing use of certain chemicals without a peaceful intent. The court found that the evidence was admissible under the exception created by United States v. Leon, 468 U. S. 897, 903, allowing admission of physical evidence seized after Miranda warnings have been given if the defendant voluntarily consented to the search. The First Circuit vacated the conviction, finding that the Fourth Amendment required suppression of the evidence. Rejecting Bond’s argument that the Fourth Amendment was made inoperative by the Supremacy Clause, the court reasoned that the Fourth Amendment was self-executing and that the Supremacy Clause rendered the relevant portion of the Chemical Weapons Convention Implementation Act of 1998 (Act) ineffective. Because the Act authorized the seizure of evidence without probable cause, the court ruled, it could not be reconciled with the Fourth Amendment. Held: A person seeking to challenge the validity of a federal statute on the ground that it exceeds the scope of Congress’ enumerated powers under Article I, §8, need not make a separate showing that the statute impermissibly burdens state sovereignty. Pp. 4–12. (a) The Court begins with the proposition that the Constitution grants Congress enumerated powers and reserves to the States all powers not delegated. Thus, the question whether a federal statute exceeds Congress’ enumerated powers is essentially a question of federalism. The Court will assume, for the sake of simplicity, that the Act falls within Congress’ enumerated powers. Nonetheless, the Act’s effect on the relationship between the Nation and the States raises important issues of federalism. Pp. 4–5. (b) The Court addresses three related questions: (1) Does the Court’s precedent require that a litigant raising a federalism challenge must also allege that the challenged legislation impermissibly burdens state sovereignty? (2) Is the Court bound by the reasoning of Tennessee Electric Co. v. Tennessee Valley Authority, 306 U. S. 118, 143–144, to hold that a party generally must assert his own legal rights and interests, and cannot rest his claim to relief on the legal rights or interests of third parties? (3) Can a litigant challenging a federal statute on the ground that it exceeds Congress’ enumerated powers properly assert that the statute impermissibly burdens state sovereignty? Pp. 5–12. (c) The answer to Question (1) is no. Although the Court’s precedent requires that a litigant asserting a federalism challenge must satisfy Article III’s standing requirements, the Court finds no basis in precedent or principle to deny Bond’s standing to raise her claims. The ultimate issue of the Act’s validity turns in part on whether the law can be deemed “necessary and proper for carrying into execution” the President’s Article II, §2 Treaty Power. This Court expresses no view on the merits of that argument. Instead, the Court remands for consideration of that issue. Pp. 12–13. 599 F. 3d 10, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Appeals for the Eastern District of Virginia granted certiorari in the case of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) and the NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund (Defense Fund) v. the Virginia State Conference of NAACP Branches (the Virginia Conference) on the constitutionality of Virginia's ban against the improper solicitation of any legal or professional business. The Virginia Conference's policy is to finance only cases in which the assisted litigant retains an NAACP staff lawyer to represent him, and the staff member may not accept, from the Conference or the staff lawyers, any other compensation for his services in an NAACP-assisted case. The litigation centers on the question of whether the Commonwealth's prohibition against the NAACP's solicitation of legal services is unconstitutional. The Commonwealth had previously held that the prohibition was not in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Supreme Court held that it was. The case is now before us for reargument. We conclude that the Virginia Court's decision in favor of the Commonwealth was correct.

The Supreme Court ruled in Geier v. American Honda Motor Co. that a federal regulation prohibiting automobile manufacturers from installing lap belts in rear seats does not preempt a state tort suit seeking damages against a manufacturer for injuries sustained due to the use of a lap belt in a rear seat. The Court based its ruling on the idea that the regulation allows manufacturers to choose between different kinds of seat belts, and that this choice is an important regulatory objective. The Court also looked at the history and contemporary explanations of the regulation, as well as the government's position on the issue, to support its decision.

In the case of United States v. Matlock, the Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether a warrantless entry and search by law enforcement officers is valid when based on the consent of a third party who the officers reasonably believe has authority over the premises, even if that belief is mistaken.

The case involved Edward Rodriguez, who was arrested in his apartment for possession of illegal drugs after the police entered with the consent of Gail Fischer, who claimed to have common authority over the apartment. However, it was later determined that Fischer did not have such authority as she was not a current resident, did not contribute to rent, and had limited access to the apartment.

The Illinois courts ruled that the search was invalid because Fischer did not have the authority to consent, and the police's belief that she did was not sufficient to justify the warrantless entry.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the lower courts, stating that the Fourth Amendment requires that government searches be reasonable, not necessarily correct. The Court held that if law enforcement officers have a reasonable belief that a person has the authority to consent to a search, even if that belief is mistaken, the search does not violate the Fourth Amendment.

The Court distinguished between the rights to a fair trial and the rights against unreasonable searches and seizures, emphasizing that the Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches, not against all searches without the actual consent of the property owner.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Illinois Appellate Court and remanded the case for further proceedings to determine whether the officers' belief in Fischer's authority was reasonable under the circumstances. The implication of this decision is that the validity of a search can be based on the reasonable perceptions of law enforcement officers, rather than solely on the actual authority of the consenting party.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington granted summary judgment in the case of Joshua Davey, a Christian college student who was denied a scholarship because he was pursuing a degree in "devotional theology" at a private Christian college. The court found that Davey's exclusion from the scholarship did not violate the First Amendment right to free speech. The legislature established the Promise Scholarship Program to assist gifted students with college expenses. The program is funded through the State's general fund. To be eligible for the scholarship, a student must graduate from a Washington public or private high school and either graduate in the top 15% of his graduating class, or attain on the first attempt a cumulative score of 1,200 or better. The student's family income must be less than 135% of the state's median. Once the student enrolls at an eligible institution, the institution must certify that the student is enrolled at least half time and that he is not pursuing a "degree in devotional theology" to receive the scholarship. Northwest College, a private, Christian college affiliated with the Assemblies of the denomination, is an "eligible institution" under the Promise Program. Davey was denied the scholarship because the college did not certify that he was not pursuing such a degree, and he refused to sign the scholarship form in writing that he could not use the scholarship funds to pay for tuition or other educational expenses. Davey then brought an action under the federal law that enjoins the State from refusing to award funds to students who are pursuing "degrees in devotional nature or designed to induce religious faith"

The Supreme Court opinion addresses whether a federal regulation, specifically Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208 (1989 version), preempts a state tort suit that could potentially limit auto manufacturers' choice in the type of seatbelts installed on rear inner seats of passenger vehicles. The regulation allows manufacturers to choose between installing simple lap belts or lap-and-shoulder belts on these seats.

The case arose from a 2002 accident involving a Mazda minivan where Thanh Williamson, who was wearing a lap belt in a rear aisle seat, died. Her family filed a tort suit in California against Mazda, claiming the company should have installed lap-and-shoulder belts, which might have saved her life. The California courts dismissed the claim, citing preemption by federal regulation, drawing parallels to the Supreme Court's decision in Geier v. American Honda Motor Co.

The Supreme Court, however, concluded that the federal regulation does not preempt the state tort suit. The Court reasoned that, unlike in Geier, providing manufacturers with a choice between types of seatbelts for rear inner seats was not a significant objective of the federal regulation. The Court found that the Department of Transportation (DOT) had not intended to preclude state tort suits through its regulation, and that the agency's primary concern was cost-effectiveness rather than maintaining manufacturer choice. The Court also noted that the Solicitor General confirmed that the DOT did not intend for the regulation to preempt state tort suits.

The Court's decision implies that the federal regulation sets a minimum safety standard, and state tort law can potentially impose stricter requirements. The Court reversed the judgment of the California Court of Appeal, allowing the state tort suit to proceed, and thus affirmed the role of state tort law in supplementing federal safety standards. Justice Kagan did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

After respondent Dow Chemical Company refused to permit Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) personnel to make site inspections of its industrial plant pursuant to §§ 114(a)(1) and (2) of the Clean Air Act, EPA obtained aerial photographs of the plant from a third party who flew an airplane equipped with a highresolution aerial camera. The photographs depicted the exterior of the plant, including many of its buildings and their contents, and were taken from altitudes ranging from 1,000 to 12,000 feet. Dow filed suit in Federal District Court, claiming that the photographs invaded its privacy interests and thus violated the Fourth Amendment. The court agreed, ruling that although Dow had a subjective expectation of privacy in certain areas from ground-level intrusion, it had no reasonable expectation of privacy from aerial surveillance since it had taken no steps to prevent such surveillance. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that the photographs were taken in violation of Dow's Fourth Amendment rights regardless of whether they were taken with or without permission. Held: 1. The photographs were not taken in violation of Dow's Fourth Amendment rights. Pp. 30-35. (a) Regardless of whether the photographs were taken with or without permission, they were not taken in violation of Dow's Fourth Amendment rights. Pp. 30-32. (b) The photographs were not taken in violation of Dow's Fourth Amendment rights because they were taken from navigable airspace. Under § 114(a)(2), EPA has a "right of entry to, upon, or through any premises"; and it is not suggested in the statute that the powers conferred by this section are meant to be exclusive. Thus, the use of aerial observation and photography is within EPA's statutory authority. Pp. 32-33. (c) Naked-eye aerial observation from an altitude of 1,000 feet of a backyard within the curtilage of a home does not constitute a search under the Fourth Amendment. Californiav . Ciraolo, ante, p. 207. Pp. 33-34. (d) Taking aerial photographs of an industrial plant complex from navigable airspace is not a search prohibited by the Fourth Amendment. Such photographs are not so revealing of intimate details as to raise constitutional concerns. They merely give EPA more detailed information than naked-eye views, but remain limited to an outline of the facility's buildings and equipment. The mere fact that human vision is enhanced somewhat, at least to the extent here, does not give rise to constitutional problems. Pp. 34-35. 2. Even if the photographs were taken in violation of Dow's Fourth Amendment rights, the photographs themselves should not be returned to Dow, since they were properly seized incident to arrests made during the flight of the plane that took the photographs. Pp. 35-36. 749 F. 2d 305, vacated and remanded.

In this Supreme Court case, the issue at hand was whether the State of Michigan's tax scheme, which exempted state and local government retirees from state income tax while taxing federal government retirees, violated federal law. The appellant, Paul S. Davis, a retired federal employee, argued that this scheme discriminated against federal retirees in violation of 4 U.S.C. § 111, which prohibits discriminatory state taxation against federal employees.

The Michigan Court of Appeals had previously rejected Davis's claim, stating that § 111 only applied to current federal employees, not retirees, and that the state's tax treatment was justified by its interest in attracting and retaining qualified employees.

The Supreme Court, however, disagreed with the lower court's interpretation. The Court held that the plain language of § 111 includes retirement benefits as deferred compensation for past service, and therefore, the statute applies to federal retirees. The Court also found that the nondiscrimination clause in § 111 must include retirement benefits, as they are a form of compensation for services rendered to the federal government.

The Court further explained that § 111 was enacted as part of the Public Salary Tax Act of 1939, which aimed to impose federal income tax on state and local government employees while ensuring that federal employees would not remain immune from state taxation. The Act preserved immunity from discriminatory state taxes, paralleling the constitutional doctrine of intergovernmental tax immunity.

The Supreme Court concluded that Michigan's tax scheme was discriminatory and violated principles of intergovernmental tax immunity. The Court determined that the state's justifications for the discrimination did not demonstrate significant differences between the two classes of retirees that would justify the disparate treatment.

As a result, the Court ruled that Davis was entitled to a refund for the taxes paid under the invalid tax scheme and remanded the case for further proceedings to determine the appropriate prospective relief. The Court suggested that the Michigan courts were in the best position to decide how to comply with the mandate of equal treatment, whether by extending the tax exemption to federal retirees or by eliminating the exemption for state and local government retirees.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Ohio today entered a final judgment against Ohio Attorney General Patrick J. McCluskey in a related case.  The court issued a temporary restraining order and issued an order temporarily freezing the assets of the Ohio Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Ohio Secretary of State's Office.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Columbus, Ohio on April 27, 1988, Margaret McIntyre distributed leaflets to persons attending a public meeting at the Blendon Middle School in Westerville, Ohio. The complaint alleges that the leaflets violated the antifraud provisions of Section 3599.09(A) of the federal securities laws.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Ms. McIntyre.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Ohio secretary of state's office and the Department of State Attorney General's Office have issued anÂ orderÂ toÂ instituate the issuance ofÂ aÂ noticeÂ ofÂ anÂ advisoryÂ requirementÂ thatÂ all materials containing suchÂ materialÂ are subject toÂ exchangeÂ registration requirements.Â The SEC's order, which was entered by the Ohio Court of Common Pleas, orders Ohio to comply with the requirements of the First Amendment, including that the amount of any civil penalty be determined by the court at a later date.
