This case involves a Title VII lawsuit brought by a group of African American firefighters in Chicago, Illinois against the city's fire department. The plaintiffs allege that the department's practice of only hiring firefighters who scored at least 89 on a standardized exam violates Title VII's prohibition of disparate impact. They argue that this practice has resulted in a significant disparate impact on African American firefighters, who historically have lower average scores on the exam compared to white firefighters. The case raises several important issues regarding the interpretation and enforcement of Title VII's disparate impact provisions.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed a lower court's summary judgment in favor of a company that claimed it had used the term "microcolor" in marketing and selling its product for more than 20 years. The court found that the company had acted fairly and in good faith in its use of the term, which is a word or two, singular or plural, and which is often used to describe a product or service. The lower court held that the term was not likely to confuse consumers about the origin of the goods or services affected. The appeals court held, however, that the lower court had not adequately addressed the issue of whether the use was likely to cause confusion. We conclude that there is no doubt that KP Permanent Make-Up, Inc.'s use of "micro color" in its advertising and in its product sales was fair and reasonable. We hold that the district court did not have to consider the likelihood of confusion when it entered summary judgment for KP on Lasting's trademark infringement claim. We also hold that KP has no obligation to show that its use is likely not to cause consumer confusion.

The Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949, as amended, authorizes the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare (HEW) to assume responsibility for disposing of surplus real property "for school, classroom, or other educational use." Subject to the disapproval of the Administrator of General Services, the Secretary may sell or lease the property to nonprofit, tax-exempt educational institutions for consideration that takes into account "any benefit which has accrued or may accrue to the United States" from the transferee's use of the property. The Secretary has provided for the computation of a "public benefit allowance," which discounts the transfer price of property "on the basis of benefits to [the United States from the use of such property for educational purposes." 34 CFR § 12.9(a) (1980). The Court of Appeals found that respondents lacked standing to challenge the conveyance under Flast v. Cohen, 392 U. S. 83, since that case extended standing to taxpayers qua taxpayers only to challenge congressional exercises of the power to tax and spend conferred by Art. I, § 8, and this conveyance was authorized by legislation enacted under the authority of the Property Clause of Art. IV, § 3, cl. 2. Held: 1. Respondents' standing to contest the transfer was barred by this Court's decisions in Schlesinger v. Reservists Committee to Stop the War and United States v. Richardson, 418 U.S. 166. Pp. 619-621. (a) The Art. III requirement of actual or threatened injury is not merely a troublesome hurdle to be overcome if possible so as to reach the "merits" of a lawsuit which a party desires to have adjudicated; it is a part of the basic charter promulgated by the Framers of the Constitution at Philadelphia in 1787, a charter which created a general government, provided for interaction between that government and the governments of the several States, and was later amended to either enhance or limit its authority with respect to both States and individuals. Thus, the power of the federal courts to adjudicate claims of constitutional violation by other branches of government where the claimant has not suffered cognizable injury. P. 622. (b) The "case or controversy" aspect of standing is unsatisfied "where a taxpayer seeks to employ a federal court as a forum in which to air his generalized grievances about the conduct of government." Flast, supra, at 487. Although respondents claim that the Constitution has been violated, they claim nothing else. They fail to identify any personal injury suffered by them as a consequence of the alleged constitutional error, other than the psychological consequence presumably produced by observation of conduct with which one disagrees. The Establishment Clause, on which plaintiffs' complaint rested,operates as a specific constitutional limitation upon the exercise by Congress of the taxing and spending power, and is not a permissible substitute for the showing of injury itself. The existence of injured parties who might not wish to bring suit becomes irrelevant, since respondents have established standing by virtue of an "injury in fact" to their shared individuated right to a government that "shall make no law respecting the establishment of religion." P. 630. (c) Respondents fail the first prong of the test for taxpayer standing. Their claim is deficient in two respects. First, the source of their complaint is not an action, but a decision by HEW to transfer a parcel of federal property. Second, and perhaps redundantly, the property transfer about which respondents complain was not an exercise of authority conferred by the Taxing and Spending Clause, the Court has refrained from adjudicating "abstract questions of wide public significance" which amount to "generalized grievances," pervasively shared and most appropriately addressed in the representative branches. The Court has required that the plaintiff's complaint fall within "the zone of interests to be protected or regulated by the statute or constitutional guarantee in question." Association of Data Processing Service Orgs. v. Camp, 397 US. 150, 153. The court found it unnecessary to determine whether this "arguable" proposition was correct, since it judged the mere allegation of a legal right sufficient to confer standing, even though the plaintiff contributes to the public coffers as a taxpayer. The "mere recital" of those claims "demonstrates that the Government has violated the Establishment Clause," id., at 499-500, and it is decisive of any claim of taxpayer standing under the Flast exception. The fact that respondents have alleged something more than "the generalized interest of all citizens in constitutional governance" does not mean that they have alleged an injury of any kind, economic or otherwise, sufficient to warrant standing under Art. II, even if they have not claimed cognizable standing. Moreover, the fact that the plaintiffs in those cases plainly asserted a "personal constitutional right" to a Government that does not establish religion does not necessarily mean that the Court itself has abandoned the right to assert its own legal rights and to reveal their discoveries in federal court. The Supreme Court ruled that a DUI conviction in Florida does not constitute a "crime of violence" under 18 U.S. Code § 16, and therefore does not make the defendant an "aggravated felon" subject to deportation. The court determined that the use of physical force against another person is necessary for a crime to be considered a "crime of violence", and that the DUI offense in question did not meet this standard.

The Promise Scholarship Program provides a scholarship, renewable for one year, to eligible students for postsecondary education expenses. To be eligible for the scholarship, a student must graduate from a Washington public or private high school and either graduate in the top 15% of his graduating class, or attain on the first attempt a cumulative score of 1,200 or better on the Scholastic Assessment Test I or a 27 or better score on the American College Test. A student must meet academic, income, and enrollment requirements, and must enroll "at least half time in an eligible postsecondary institution in the state of Washington," and may not pursue a degree in devotional theology. The institution, rather than the State, determines whether the student's major is devotional. The scholarship funds are sent to the institution for distribution to the student to pay for tuition or other educational expenses. Respondent, who was awarded a Promise Scholarship, chose to attend Northwest College, a private, Christian college affiliated with the Assemblies of God denomination, and is an eligible institution under the Promise Scholarship program. The Promise Scholarship is funded through the State's general fund, and their amount varies each year depending on the annual appropriation, which is evenly prorated among the eligible students. After the District Court denied Davey's request for a preliminary injunction, the parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment. The parties filed a summary judgment for the State. The District Court rejected the constitutional claims and granted summary judgment in favor of respondent. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the State had singled out religion for unfavorable treatment and thus under the decision in Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. Hialeah, 508 U. S. 520, the exclusion of theology majors must be narrowly tailored to achieve a compelling state interest. Held: The denial of funding for vocational religious instruction alone is inherently constitutionally suspect. The State's interest in not funding the pursuit of devotional degrees is substantial, not evidence of hostility toward religion. The question before us, however, is whether Washington, pursuant to its own constitution, which has been authoritatively interpreted as prohibiting even indirectly funding religious instruction that will prepare students for the ministry, is permitted by the Establishment Clause but not required by the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment. Pp. 5-11. 299 F. 3d 748, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama today entered a final judgment in favor of the SEC's motion for a temporary restraining order against Syngenta Crop Protection, Inc. (then known as Ciba-Geigy Corp.) asserting various tort claims related to petitioners' manufacture and sale of a chlordimeform-based insecticide.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Iberville Parish, Louisiana, alleges that the SEC obtained an emergency court order to remove the Henson action from state court jurisdiction.  According to the complaint, the court's order required that defendants show cause and effect in order for the action to be removed from the court.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Alabama announced criminal charges against Henson.  As alleged in the SEC complaint, Henson's action violated the antifraud provisions of Section 1441 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the court order, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the federal securities laws, orders them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and requires them to provide a civil penalty equal to the amount of their profits.  Henson also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years, and ordered to pay a penalty of $100,000.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

In the case concerning David H. Baral, the Supreme Court was tasked with determining when two types of tax remittances are considered "paid" under Internal Revenue Code §6511(b)(2)(A), which sets a limit on the amount of tax credit or refund a taxpayer can receive. The two remittances in question were estimated income tax paid by Baral and withholding tax paid by his employer for the 1988 tax year.

Baral filed his tax return late and claimed a credit for overpayment, which the IRS denied based on the look-back period defined by §6511(b)(2)(A). This period determines the timeframe within which tax payments are considered for credit or refund purposes. The IRS and lower courts concluded that both types of remittances were "paid" on the due date of the tax return (April 15, 1989), which fell outside the look-back period that started on February 1, 1990.

Baral argued that taxes cannot be considered "paid" until the tax liability is assessed, which in his case occurred when he filed his return or when the IRS formally assessed the liability. However, the Supreme Court disagreed, affirming the lower courts' decisions. The Court held that §§6513(b)(1) and (2) clearly define the "paid" date for withholding and estimated income tax as the due date of the tax return. Therefore, Baral's remittances were indeed "paid" on April 15, 1989, and since no payments were made within the look-back period, the IRS correctly denied the credit.

The Court rejected Baral's interpretation that withholding and estimated taxes are separate from income tax, clarifying that they are methods of collecting income tax, not standalone taxes. The Court also noted that accepting Baral's argument would disadvantage taxpayers who file timely returns, as it would delay the accrual of interest on overpayments until the IRS's assessment.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment that Baral was not entitled to the claimed credit because the remittances were made before the look-back period, and the IRS's denial of the credit was in accordance with the law.

The Supreme Court addressed whether an arbitration agreement between an employer and an employee can prevent the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) from seeking specific judicial remedies for the employee in a discrimination case under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The case involved Eric Baker, who was fired from Waffle House after suffering a seizure, and who had previously agreed to arbitrate any employment disputes.

The EEOC filed a lawsuit seeking remedies such as backpay, reinstatement, and damages on Baker's behalf, despite his arbitration agreement. The employer argued that the arbitration agreement should limit the EEOC's ability to pursue these remedies in court. The Court of Appeals had ruled that while the EEOC could seek broad injunctive relief, it could not seek victim-specific relief like backpay or damages due to the arbitration agreement.

The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision. It held that the EEOC has independent statutory authority to enforce the ADA and seek relief in court, regardless of any arbitration agreement between the employer and employee. The Court emphasized that the EEOC is not a party to the arbitration agreement and that its role is to enforce federal law and protect public interest, not just the interests of the individual employee.

The Court also clarified that the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) does not restrict a non-party's choice of a judicial forum and that arbitration agreements cannot bind non-parties like the EEOC. The Court concluded that the EEOC can seek all forms of relief authorized by the ADA, including victim-specific relief, in federal court.

The decision has implications for the enforceability of arbitration agreements in employment discrimination cases, affirming the EEOC's ability to pursue a range of remedies in court, even when an employee has agreed to arbitrate disputes. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that the Fifth Amendment's protection against self-incrimination includes the right to remain silent during questioning by law enforcement officers. The Court held that any statement made by a suspect during custodial interrogation, regardless of how voluntary it may seem, cannot be used as evidence against them in a criminal trial unless it was obtained through Miranda warnings. The ruling was based on the belief that individuals are vulnerable and susceptible to pressure and manipulation while in custody, and thus their statements must be carefully scrutinized before they can be used as reliable evidence.

This case involves a dispute between a father and a local school district over the placement of the father's child in a special education program. The father claims that the district violated his rights under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 by refusing to provide the child with accommodations needed for her disability. The district counters that the child's condition is not covered by the laws cited and that the proposed accommodations would be too expensive and disruptive to the educational environment.

The Supreme Court holds that the district cannot deny the child accommodations solely because they would be expensive or disruptive. The Court notes that Section 504 prohibits discrimination against individuals with disabilities in all programs and activities receiving federal funds, including schools. The Court also recognizes that the Americans with Disabilities Act extends protections to students with disabilities in elementary, secondary, and postsecondary institutions.

The Court remands the case back to the lower court to determine whether the child qualifies for accommodations under Section 504 and the Americans with Disabilities Act and to develop an Individualized Education Program (IEP) outlining the specific accommodations needed.

This is a loyalty oath case concerning the constitutionality of Section 29-3812 of the Indiana Code, which requires political parties to swear that they will not advocate the overthrow of local, state, or national governments by force or violence before being allowed to appear on the ballot. The case involved the Communist Party of Indiana, which sought to be placed on the ballot for the 1972 presidential election. The party submitted an affidavit stating that it did not advocate the overthrow of government by force or violence, but the Election Board rejected the application. The party then sued in federal court, challenging the constitutionality of Section 29-3812 and seeking an injunction to be placed on the ballot.

After petitioner benefited from its own self-funded employee welfare benefit plan when it recovered damages from respondent in a state-court action involving a car accident, respondent sued petitioner in Federal District Court seeking a declaration that Pennsylvania's Antisubrogation Law barred petitioner from recovering from respondent. The District Court entered summary judgment for respondent, ruling that the Antisubrogation Law fell within the savings clause of the Insurance Claims Preemption Provision of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), which provides that "[e]xcept as provided in [the deemer clause] ... , nothing in this subchapter shall be construed to exempt or relieve any person from any law of any State which regulates insurance," 29 U. S. C. § 1144(b)(2)(A), and that the deemer clause exempts employee benefit plans from state laws that "regulate insurance," § 1144(b)(2)(B). The Court of Appeals agreed, concluding that the deemer clause means that a state antisubrogation law like Pennsylvania's cannot be applied to prevent a self-funded plan from recovering from a third party who caused injury to the plan participant. Held: ERISA pre-empts the application of Pennsylvania's Antisubrogation Law to petitioner's self-funded employee welfare benefit plan. Pp. 58-68. (a) Because the preemption clause applies to state laws specifically designed to affect employee benefit plans, it would be incompatible with ERISA's legislative history to interpret the preemption clause to apply only to state laws dealing with the subject matters covered by ERISA. Instead, the preemption clause's broad language indicates that its pre-emptive scope is as broad as its language. Shaw v. Delta Air Lines, Inc., 463 U. S. 79, 98. Pp. 58-61. (b) Pennsylvania's Antisubrogation Law has a "reference" to benefit plans governed by ERISA, since it includes within its coverage any program, group contract, or other arrangement for payment of benefits, including benefits payable by a hospital plan corporation or a professional health services corporation. Its terms also have a "connection" to ERISA benefit plans, since they refer to benefits payable by any program, group contract, or other arrangement. And the Antisubrogation Law prohibits plans from being structured in a manner requiring reimbursement in the event of recovery from a third party, thus frustrating plan administrators' continuing obligation to calculate uniform benefit levels nationwide. Since the Pennsylvania law falls within ERISA's insurance saving clause, which provides, "[e]xcept as provided in [the deemer clause], nothing in this subchapter shall be construed to exempt or relieve any person from any law of any State which regulates insurance," § 1144(b)(2)(A), it is not pre-empted unless the deemer clause excludes it from the reach of the saving clause. Pp. 61-63. (c) Read consistently with ERISA's language, the deemer clause exempts self-funded ERISA plans from state laws that "regulate insurance" within the meaning of the saving clause. By forbidding States to deem employee benefit plans "to be an insurance company or other insurer... or to be engaged in the business of insurance," the deemer clause relieves them from state laws "purporting to regulate insurance." As a result, self-funded ERISA plans are exempt from state regulation insofar as that regulation "relate[s] to" the plans. State laws directed toward the plans are pre-empted because they relate to an employee benefit plan but are not "saved" because they don't regulate insurance. State laws that directly regulate insurance are "saved" but don't reach self-funded employee benefit plans because the plans may not be deemed to be insurance companies, other insurers, or engaged in the business of insurance for purposes of such state laws. On the other hand, employee benefit plans that are insured are subject to indirect state insurance regulation. An insurance company that insures a plan remains an insurer for purposes of state laws "purporting to regulate insurance" after application of the deemer clause. The insurance company is therefore not relieved from state insurance regulation. The ERISA plan is consequently bound by state insurance regulations insofar as they apply to the plan's insurer. Pp. 63-67. (d) Interpretation of the deemer clause as exempting employee benefit plans from only those state regulations that encroach upon core ERISA concerns or that apply to insurance as a business would be fraught with administrative difficulties, necessitating definition of core ERISA concerns and of what constitutes business activity. Such an interpretation would undermine Congress' desire to avoid endless litigation over the validity of state action and instead lead to employee benefit plans' expenditure of funds in such litigation. Pp. 67-68. 859 F. 2d 1150, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Alabama has upheld the conviction of a man sentenced to death for the attempted rape of the daughter of Selma's mayor. The court granted certiorari to determine whether the requirements of due process under the Fourteenth Amendment had been satisfied in these aspects of petitioner's conviction. The trial judge denied his request to testify about the manner in which the confessions were obtained without subjecting himself to unlimited cross-examination as to the facts of the crime charged. The jury also indicted him by a method that systematically discriminated against members of his race. The Supreme Court ruled that the trial judge's denial of his request for a preliminary hearing was not sufficient to prevent the jury from finding him guilty of the charges against him. The justices also ruled that there was insufficient evidence to support the jury's finding that petitioner had committed the crime.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against a former federal employee for his role in an employment discrimination case.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, alleges that, in 1972, the federal government issued a civil injunctive relief (CDA) against Michael Gibson.  According to the complaint, Gibson was falsely told that he was entitled to a jury trial in respect to compensatory damages when, in fact, he was not entitled to one at all.  Gibson's complaint also alleges that the CDA expressly prohibits the EEOC from imposing a "prejudgmental injunction" on a complaint brought by a complaining party.  In addition, the complaint alleges that Gibson did not "put the agency on notice" that he sought compensation.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, Gibson's claims were based on false claims that he had been hired by a company that did not have a right to trial by jury.   The complaint further alleges that in 1972 Congress authorized a federal employee to file a complaint in court, but prohibited the agency to challenge an adverse EEOC decision in court.  Without admitting or denying Gibson's allegations, the Commission has agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins the Commission from violating the federal employee-employee registration provisions of Section 717(a) of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and orders Gibson to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000.  Additionally, Gibson has consented to a bar prohibiting him from associating with any third party in an action brought under the federal employment law, and to the appointment of a receiver to determine whether to issue a civil monetary penalty.  On November 12, 1992, the Honorable Judge William G. Donnelly of the U. S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted the Commission's request for a preliminary injunction.  Donnelly agreed to a permanent injunction against future violations of the civil injunctions, ordered Gibson to comply with the court's order, and ordered him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties in a parallel action.  He also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Gibson and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Summary:

Marco DeFunis, Jr. applied to the University of Washington Law School in 1971 and was denied admission. He sued the school, claiming the admissions process discriminated against him based on race, violating the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The trial court ruled in his favor, and he was admitted to the law school. The Washington Supreme Court later reversed this decision, but DeFunis remained in school due to a stay pending the final disposition by the U.S. Supreme Court.

When the U.S. Supreme Court considered the case, DeFunis was in his final term of law school. The Court had to decide whether the case was moot, meaning it no longer presented an active controversy for the Court to resolve. The Constitution limits federal courts to deciding cases that affect the rights of the litigants involved, and a case or controversy must exist for the Court to exercise its judicial power.

The respondents (the law school) assured the Court that DeFunis would be allowed to complete his studies and graduate regardless of the Court's decision. Since DeFunis did not file the suit as a class action and only sought his own admission, the Court found that there was no longer a concrete controversy to resolve. The Court also noted that the issue was not "capable of repetition, yet evading review," as DeFunis would not reapply to the law school, and future similar cases could reach the Court more quickly.

Therefore, the Supreme Court concluded that it could not consider the substantive constitutional issues because the case was moot. The Court vacated the judgment of the Washington Supreme Court and remanded the case for appropriate proceedings, indicating that the lower court should dismiss the case as moot.

Title 42 U. S. C. § 1983 provides a remedy for deprivations of rights secured by the Constitution and laws of the United States when that deprivation takes place "under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage, of any State or Territory." In 1977, petitioner, a lessee-operator of a truckstop in Virginia, was indebted to his supplier, Edmondson Oil Co., Inc., which sued on the debt in Virginia state court. Ancillary to that action and pursuant to state law, petitioner sought prejudgment attachment of certain of his property, although it was left in his possession. Pursuant to the statute, a hearing on the propriety of the attachment and levy was later conducted. Thirty-four days after the levy, a state trial judge ordered the attachment dismissed because petitioner had failed to establish the statutory grounds for attachment alleged in the petition. Petitioner subsequently brought this action under 42 US. C.' § 1983, alleging that in attaching his property respondents had acted jointly with the State to deprive him of property without due process of law. The lower courts construed the complaint as alleging a due process violation both from a misuse of the Virginia procedure and from the statutory procedure itself. He sought compensatory and punitive damages for specified financial loss allegedly caused by the improvident attachment. The District Court held that the alleged actions of respondents did not constitute state action as required by the Fourteenth Amendment and that the complaint therefore did not state a claim upon which relief could be granted under § 1983. The Court of Appeals rejected the District Court's reliance on Flagg Brothers Inc. v. Brooks, 436 U.S. 149, in finding that the requisite state action was missing in this case. Held: 1. The state-action and under-color-of-state-law requirements are not identical. Pp. 636-637. (a) The two concepts cannot be so easily disentangled. Whether they are identical or not, the state action and the under- color of-state law requirements are obviously related. P. 638. (b) Respondents' joint participation with state officials in the seizure of disputed property is sufficient to characterize that party as a "state actor" for purposes of the Amendment, and this Court has consistently held that constitutional requirements of due process apply to garnishment and prejudgment attachments whenever officers of the State act jointly with a creditor in securing the property in dispute. Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp., 395 U. s. 337, distinguished. The two principles are not the same. They collapse into each other when the claim of a constitutional deprivation is directed against a party whose official character is such as to lend the State's weight to his decisions. See, e. g., the "public function" test, see Terry v. Adams, 345 U S. 461, and Marsh v. Alabama, 326 U S 501, respectively. The "state compulsion" test does not describe conduct that can be attributed to the State, but the procedural scheme created by the statute obviously is the product of state action. This is subject to constitutional restraints and properly may be addressed in a § 1983 action, if the second element of the stateaction requirement is met as well. In support of this proposition, the Court cited the part of United States v. Price, 383 U . S. 345, that "[m]isuse of power, possessed by virtue of state law and made possible only because the wrongdoer is clothed with with with it," and in that case, a "joint action test," Flagg Bros. 436 U S., at 157. Although it is not clear whether petitioner is referring to the state-created procedure or the misuse of that procedure by respondents, this Court agrees with the lower courts that the better reading of the complaint is that petitioner challenges the state statute as procedurally defective under the Fourth Amendment. Although private misuse of a state statute does not refer to the action of a private party subject to scrutiny under its provisions, it is clear that the statutory requirement of action "under Color of State law" and the "state action" requirement are identical. Moreover, the fact that respondents invoked the statute without the grounds to do so could not be ascribed to any governmental decision; those governmental decisions that did affect Moose Lodge were unconnected with its discriminatory policies. P p. 637. 2. Resolution of this issue is essential to the proper disposition of the case. Resolution was essential to that line of cases, beginning with Sniads v.Family Finance Corp. and North Georgia Finishing, Inc., ante, n. 2d 185, in which the Court considered constitutional due process requirements in the context of garnishment actions and prejudgments attachments, and where the Court resolved it, in any case, in favor of the view that petitioner was attacking the constitutionality of the statute as well as its misapplication. In this case, resolution of this ambiguity was not necessary to their disposition of this case: both resolved the question in any

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of a federal prosecution of two individuals for the same criminal conduct.  According to the court's order, the defendants were solicited by a union official in Chicago, Illinois, to dynamite facilities of the telephone company located in the States of Mississippi, Tennessee, and Louisiana. The four men met in Chicago where Shelby gave the petitioners and McLeod the plans of the facilities to be dynamited and instructed them as to the method to be used. The court found that the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also found that, based on the same conduct, each of the defendants was liable to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb in violation of the federal criminal laws.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the defendants.   The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Jackson, Mississippi, charges the defendants with violating the federal securities laws and seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the four defendants consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from future violations of the securities laws, and order them to pay civil penalties in the amount of $1,000, $2,500, or $3,500. Â The court also issued an order suspending the defendants from appearing before the SEC as an attorney or practicing before the Commission on the Securities and Exchange Commission.Â In a parallel administrative proceeding, the U. S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Illinois today announced parallel criminal prosecutions against the same individuals.  This action is the latest in a series of actions by the SEC to raise the issue of whether to impose a federal criminal penalty against the individual charged.  Among other things, the SEC previously charged two individuals in connection with the same federal criminal conduct for which they had been convicted in separate criminal proceedings.  On May 2, 2018, the Court issued a temporary restraining order against the two individuals and ordered them to return their allegedly forged criminal convictions to the Court for further determination by the court upon motion of the SEC.

While still under arrest for murder, petitioner was questioned by police officers without benefit of counsel. Though he had twice requested to see his lawyer, the police denied his request and he was never given Miranda warnings. During the interrogation, petitioner made a statement which was introduced into evidence at his trial and which helped lead to his conviction. His motion to exclude the statement was denied. Held: Where, as here, the investigation is no longer a general inquiry into an unsolved crime but has begun to focus on a particular suspect, the suspect has been taken into police custody, the police carry out a process of interrogations that lends itself to eliciting incriminating statements, the suspect has requested and been denied an opportunity to consult with his lawyer, and the police have not effectively warned him of his absolute constitutional right to remain silent, the accused has been denied "The Assistance of Counsel," in violation of the Sixth Amendment as made applicable to the States by the Fourteenth Amendment, and no statement elicited by the police during the interrogation may be used against him at a criminal trial. Pp. 208-217. 28 Ill. 2d 41, 190 N. E. 2d 825, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Arizona today entered a final judgment in favor of the Arizona Bar Association in a civil injunctive action.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Phoenix, Arizona, alleges that Arizona bar attorneys violated the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws by placing advertisements in the Arizona Republic, a daily newspaper of general circulation in the Phoenix metropolitan area.  According to the complaint, the Arizona bar association and its attorney, John R. Bates, raised the issue of whether to prohibit advertising in the form of a "legal clinic" in order to encourage the entry of attorneys into the market for legal services.  Bates and O'Steen agreed, without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, that the bar association violated Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and that Bates violated Section 15(a) of Exchange Act Rule 15b2-1 thereunder.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Bates.   The court's order, which entered final judgment on the matter, permanently enjoins the bar from imposing any additional restrictions on advertising, including a prohibition on the sale of securities, and orders the bar to pay a civil penalty of $150,000, $75,000 in disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a $50,000 civil penalty.  On the other hand, the court granted the bar's request for a temporary restraining order against Bates and the attorney association, and issued an order suspending Bates from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney in the future.  It also prohibits Bates from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in violation of Section 10 of the Exchange Act and orders him to pay $150 to settle the case.

Title 17 of the United States Code gives creators of “original” works exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, display, perform, and digitally transmit copies of their creations for a limited time. After the Copyright Office recommended that Congress extend the length of copyright protection to match that afforded by the Berne Convention, Congress enacted the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act of 1998 (Act), which increased the maximum copyright term for works authored by living human beings from 70 years to 95 years. It also gave creators of previously published works a new 20-year term of protection. Petitioners filed suit challenging the Act’s constitutionality, claiming that it violates the First Amendment by allowing copyright holders to control the use of their works indefinitely and that it exceeds Congress’ Article I powers under the Copyright Clause. The District Court dismissed the complaint, holding that the Act did not violate the First Amendment and that it fell within Congress’ enumerated powers. The DCA affirmed. Held: 1. The Act comports with the requirements of the Copyright Clause. Pp. 205–211. (a) The Act is a rational exercise of Congress’ power under the Copyright Clause. Its passage was motivated by factors such as the desire to bring domestic copyright protection in line with that available in Europe and to provide greater incentives for American and other authors to create and disseminate their work in the United States. These considerations reflect judgments of a kind Congress typically makes, judgments that this Court cannot dismiss as outside the Legislature’s domain. Pp. 205–207. (b) Petitioners’ claims that the Act is an impermissible exercise of Congress’ power under the Copyright Clause are unconvincing. Their claim that the Act creates perpetual copyrights is refuted by the absence of any evidence that Congress intended to overcome the “limited Times” constraint imposed by the Copyright Clause. Moreover, petitioners’ reliance on Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Tel. Serv. Co., 499 U. S. 340, to support their argument that the Act’s extension of existing copyrights overlooks the requirement of “originality,” is misplaced. Feist addressed the core question of copyrightability, i. e., the “creative spark” a work must have to be eligible for copyright protection at all, whereas the Act deals with the duration of copyright protection. More forcibly, petitioners’ contention that the Act’s extension of existing copyrights does not “promote the Progress of Science” as contemplated by the Copyright Clause’s preambulatory language is also unavailing. Although the Clause contains the phrase “to promote the Progress of Science,” it is generally for Congress, not the courts, to decide how best to pursue the Clause’s objectives. Here, Congress’ consistent practice of placing existing copyright holders in parity with future holders overwhelmingly supports the conclusion that the Act promotes the Clause’s objectives. Finally, petitioners’ assertion that the Clause imposes a quid pro quo requiring Congress to grant copyright protection only in exchange for a writing is untenable. Given the consistent placement of existing copyright holders in parity with future holders, the author of a work created in the past would reasonably understand that she received a copyright not only for the time in place when protection was gained, but also for any renewal or extension legislated during that time. Pp. 207–211. 239 F. 3d 373, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit held that the Establishment Clause of the First and Fourteenth Amendments was not offended by Minnesota's tax deduction for expenses incurred in sending children to private schools. The court held that this question was reserved in Committee for Public Education v. Nyquist, 413 U. S. 756, 93 S.Ct. 2955, 37 L.Ed.2d 948 (1973), and because of a conflict between that decision and that of the Court of Appeal for the First Circuit in Rhode Island Federation of Teachers v. Norberg, 630 F.1d 855 (CA1 1980), we granted certiorari. The petitioners, certain Minnesota taxpayers, claimed that  290.09(22) violated the Constitution's First Amendment protection against government assistance to religious institutions. The district court granted respondent's motion for summary judgment, holding that the statute was "neutral on its face and in its application and does not have a primary effect of either advancing or inhibiting religion"

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of the Hortonville School District in a case involving the firing of teachers who refused to end a strike despite being ordered to do so by the district. The Court held that the decision to terminate the teachers' employment was within the legal authority of the School Board and that the Board acted reasonably in carrying out its responsibilities. The Court also emphasized the importance of allowing the Board to maintain control over school district affairs and to strike a balance between the rights of workers and the needs of the community.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit held that a state may not exercise quasi in rem jurisdiction over a defendant who has no contact with the state in which the action is filed. The court held that the state's interest in protecting its residents and providing them with a forum in which to litigate their claims justified the exercise of quasi inrem jurisdiction. The Court held, however, that there was no reason to conclude that the State's interests in protecting the residents of the state outweighed those of the defendant. The 8th Court held that, in the absence of a finding of liability, the court of appeals should have granted the parties' motion to dismiss the action for lack of jurisdiction.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed a lower court's denial of a writ of habeas corpus for a North Carolina man convicted of second-degree murder. The court found that the man's plea of guilty to a reduced charge was not a violation of his constitutional rights because he had not waived his right to a trial by pleading guilty to the lesser charge. The lower court had denied Alford's motion for a writ on the basis that his attorney had advised him that he could not plead guilty to capital charges without the death penalty if he chose to go to trial. The appeals court held that Alford had waived his rights, and that the lower court was correct to deny his motion. The Supreme Court ruled in a similar case in 2014 that the trial court had erred in denying Alford a new trial because he was not entitled to a hearing on his motion to dismiss the murder charge. Alford was sentenced to 30 years in prison, the maximum penalty for second- degree murder. In a separate appeal, Alford claimed that he had been denied effective assistance of counsel prior to pleading guilty. The 4th Circuit found that his plea was voluntary and waived all defenses and nonjurisdictional defects in any prior stage of the proceedings. A federal district court denied his motion, and the appeals court reversed. The high court ruled that a trial court should have granted a new hearing. The Court also ruled that the district court was wrong to deny Alford his motion for post-conviction relief. The case is now before the Supreme Court.
