A grand jury in New York investigating possible violations of Part II of the Interstate Commerce Act issued a subpoena directing petitioner to appear and testify as to "all and everything which you may know in regard to an alleged violation of Sections 309, 322 Title 49, United States Code." Petitioner refused to answer the questions, and the grand jury then returned to the courtroom to request the aid and assistance of the District Court. The District Court, by adjudging petitioner in criminal contempt without following the procedural requirements of Rule 42 (b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, deprived him of due process of law. Held: 1. The judgment of 15 months' imprisonment was an abuse of the Court of Appeals' discretion. Pp. 531-532. (a) A witness who testifies before a grand jury investigating offenses under the Motor Carrier Act is accorded no statutory immunity from prosecution based upon his testimony. Even if some immunity is conferred, it is not coextensive with the constitutional privilege against self-incrimination. Brown v. Walker, 161 U. S. 591, distinguished. P. 532. 2. A grand jury is clothed with great independence in many areas, but it remains an appendage of the court, powerless to perform its investigative function without the court's aid, because powerless itself to compel the testimony of witnesses. It is the process which summons the witness to attend and give testimony, and it is the court which must compel a witness to testify if, after appearing, he refuses to do so. The fact that petitioner first disobeyed the order in his grand jury room, he was guilty of no contempt. He was entitled to persist in his refusal until the court ordered him to answer, and unless, therefore, it was to be frustrated in its investigative purpose, the grand-jury had to do exactly what it did-turn to the court for help. If the court had ruled that the privilege of selfincrimination had been properly invoked, that would have been the end of the matter. Even after an adverse ruling upon his claim of privilege, the petitioner was still guilty ofno contempt. It was incumbent upon the court unequivocally to order the petitioner to answer. Cf. Wong Gim Ying v. United States, 98 U.S. App. D. C. 23, 231 F. 2d 776. The court did so. In any event, the contempt proceeding could unquestionably and quite properly have been initiated, since the disobedience of the order did not take place in the actual presence of a court, and thus could be made known to the Court only by the taking of evidence, the proceeding would have be conducted upon notice and hearing in conformity with Rule 42(b). P. 530. 247 F.2d 332, affirmed.

Petitioners, who were found guilty of committing felonies, by less-than-unanimous jury verdicts, which are permitted under Oregon law in noncapital cases, claim that their convictions, upheld on appeal, contravene their right to trial by jury under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. Held: The judgment is affirmed. Pp. 410-414. 369 Ore. 380, 462 P. 2d 691, affirmed.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around a claim of sexual harassment under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Mechelle Vinson, the respondent, alleged that she was subjected to sexual harassment by her supervisor, Sidney Taylor, at Meritor Savings Bank, the petitioner. Vinson claimed that Taylor's advances were unwelcome and created a hostile work environment, which is a form of discrimination based on sex.

The District Court initially denied Vinson's claim, stating that if there was a sexual relationship between Vinson and Taylor, it was voluntary and unrelated to her employment or advancement. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed this decision, recognizing two types of sexual harassment under Title VII: quid pro quo (where employment benefits are conditioned on sexual favors) and hostile work environment (which may not affect economic benefits but creates an offensive working environment).

The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision but on different grounds. The Supreme Court held that Title VII's language is not limited to economic discrimination and that a hostile or abusive work environment due to sexual harassment is actionable under Title VII. The Court rejected the notion that a sexual relationship's "voluntariness" negates a sexual harassment claim, emphasizing that the key issue is whether the advances were unwelcome.

Regarding employer liability, the Supreme Court disagreed with the Court of Appeals' position that employers are strictly liable for harassment by supervisors, regardless of the employer's knowledge or consent. The Supreme Court stated that agency principles should guide employer liability under Title VII, meaning that an employer is not automatically liable for a supervisor's harassment. However, the mere existence of a grievance procedure and a policy against discrimination does not necessarily protect an employer from liability, especially if the procedures are not effective in encouraging victims to report harassment.

The Supreme Court remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, clarifying that a hostile work environment claim is valid under Title VII and that the District Court's findings were insufficient to dismiss Vinson's claim. The Court also noted that evidence of a complainant's sexually provocative speech or dress may be relevant to determining whether sexual advances were unwelcome, but there is no absolute rule against its admissibility.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against AT&T Inc., a telecommunications company, for violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that AT&&T violated Section 5(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 5b-5 thereunder, and that the Commission violated Section 17(a)(1) and (3) of Exchange Act Rule 17a-3 thereunder. The complaint further alleges that, in violation of Section 5 of the Exchange Act and Rule 17b2-1, AT&t violated Section 206(1) of its Code of Conduct by failing to comply with the Commission’s requirements.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the company.  According to the SEC, the Commission issued a memorandum to executive departments and agencies explaining that it had determined that the scope of the exemption was insufficient to determine whether it was appropriate to issue an order imposing a civil injunctive action.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Commission's memorandum to the court, AT &T agreed to a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the exemption, and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $500,000. The SEC also agreed to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and to pay civil penalties of $50,000 and $20,000, respectively. The Commission also agreed not to impose an officer-and-director bar.  On May 9, 2018, the Honorable Judge William R. Donnelly of the U District Court in New Jersey issued a temporary restraining order, ordering the Commission to conduct an examination of the Commission’s complaint, which was filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, ordering a hearing on May 10, 2018 on the SEC's motion for a preliminary injunction, ordering an accounting of the amount of money spent on the investigation, and ordering an injunction against further violations of Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 ("Advisers Act").  The Commission's investigation was conducted by W. David Pyszka and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The litigation will be led by Timothy J. Basinger. The case is being supervised by Sanjay Wadhwa.

When respondent Powell arrived at the Tampa Police Department station for booking, officers read him a consent form stating that he had “the right to talk to a lawyer before answering any of [their] questions” and “the right to use any of [his] rights at any time [he] want[ed] during th[e] interview.” Powell acknowledged receipt of the form, signed it, and admitted to having a concealed pistol. Later, the officers arrested him for carrying a concealed weapon despite knowing that he had a permit to carry such weapons. Before trial, the State filed a motion to suppress Powell’s statements, arguing that the officers’ Miranda warnings were insufficient because they did not mention the right to have an attorney present during the interrogation. The trial court agreed, finding that the warnings were too vague and confusing. However, the intermediate appellate court reversed, reasoning that the warnings met Miranda’s requirements. Ultimately, the Florida Supreme Court affirmed, agreeing that the warnings were adequate. Held: Because the warnings contained in the consent form complied with Miranda’s right-to-counsel requirement, the State Supreme Court erred in invalidating them. Pp. 4–10. (a) Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436, established certain procedural safeguards that require police to advise criminal suspects of their rights under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments before commencing custodial interrogation. Intending to ensure that individuals receive notice of their right to consult with a lawyer and to have the lawyer with them during interrogation, Miranda prescribed three warnings: (1) “you have the right to remain silent,” (2) “anything you say can be used against you in a court of law,” and (3) “you have the right to the presence of an attorney.” Id., at 471. Here, the fourth warning—the only one at issue—was the only one that addressed the concerns raised by Miranda. Pp. 4–5. (b) Reviewing courts examining whether police officers adequately conveyed the four Miranda warnings need not consider the words used, but only determine whether the warnings reasonably conveyed the suspect’s rights as required by Miranda. Duckworth v. Egan, 492 U.S. 195, 203. Pp. 5–6. (c) The Tampa officers did not omit any information Miranda required them to impart. They informed Powell that he had “the right to talk to a lawyer before answering any of [their] questions” and “the right to use any of [his] rights at any time [he] want[ed] during th[e] interview.” These statements combined to communicate that Powell could consult with a lawyer before answering any particular question and could exercise that right while the interrogation was underway. Thus, the warnings reasonably conveyed Powell’s right to have an attorney present, not only at the start of interrogation, but at all times. Pp. 6–8. (d) Contrary to Powell’s suggestion, the fact that many jurisdictions expressly advise suspects of the right to have counsel present both before and during interrogation does not render the warnings here inadequate. Law enforcement agencies have little incentive to adopt ambiguous warnings, since doing so increases the likelihood that a court will suppress the suspect’s statement on the ground that the advice was inadequate. Pp. 8–9. 998 So. 2d 531, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C.J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

In the case under review, the respondent was convicted of rape in a Tennessee court in 1965, with part of the evidence being the victim's station-house identification of the respondent. The conviction was affirmed by the Tennessee Supreme Court and later by the U.S. Supreme Court, which was equally divided on the case. The respondent then filed a federal habeas corpus action, challenging the identification procedure as violating due process. The District Court agreed, and the Court of Appeals affirmed this decision. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to address two issues: whether an affirmance by an equally divided Court bars subsequent habeas corpus consideration, and whether the identification procedure violated due process.

The Supreme Court held that an affirmance by an equally divided Court does not constitute an "actual adjudication" that would bar subsequent habeas corpus review. The Court reasoned that such an affirmance merely indicates that the lower court's judgment stands due to the absence of a majority position in the Supreme Court, and does not resolve the legal issues presented.

On the due process claim, the Court reviewed the identification procedure and applied the "totality of the circumstances" test to determine whether the identification was reliable despite the suggestiveness of the procedure. The Court considered factors such as the victim's opportunity to view the assailant, the degree of attention, the accuracy of the prior description, the witness's level of certainty, and the time between the crime and the confrontation. The Court found that the victim had a significant opportunity to observe the assailant, provided a detailed description, and maintained a high level of certainty about her identification. Additionally, the victim had not misidentified anyone in previous lineups or photo arrays, which supported her reliability.

The Supreme Court concluded that there was no substantial likelihood of misidentification and that the identification evidence was properly admitted at trial. Therefore, the Court affirmed the conviction in part, reversed the District Court's decision regarding the due process claim, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. Justice Marshall did not participate in the decision.

In the case before the Supreme Court, respondent Afton Callahan brought an action under 42 U.S.C. §1983 against state law enforcement officers for conducting a warrantless search of his house incident to his arrest for selling methamphetamine. The Court of Appeals had denied the officers qualified immunity, following the two-step procedure from Saucier v. Katz, which requires courts to first determine if a constitutional right was violated and then if the right was clearly established.

The Supreme Court was asked to review whether the Saucier procedure should be mandatory. The Court decided that the Saucier procedure should not be considered an inflexible requirement. Instead, courts should have the discretion to decide which part of the qualified immunity analysis to address first based on the specifics of each case.

The Court concluded that the officers were entitled to qualified immunity because, at the time of the search, the law was not clearly established that their conduct was unconstitutional. The "consent-once-removed" doctrine, which allows warrantless entry by officers when consent has been given to an undercover officer or informant who has observed contraband, had been accepted by several lower courts, although the Tenth Circuit had not yet ruled on it. Since the officers could have reasonably believed their conduct was lawful based on existing case law, they should not be subject to personal liability.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, granting the officers qualified immunity and emphasizing that qualified immunity protects officials from litigation unless they violate clearly established rights. The decision allows for more flexibility in lower courts when deciding qualified immunity claims and aims to prevent unnecessary litigation of constitutional questions that do not affect the case outcome.

Title: Recoverability of Paralegal Fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court holds that a prevailing party may recover paralegal fees from the government at "prevailing market rates" under the Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA). The Court rejects the government's argument that paralegal fees should be capped at "cost only," finding that such a restriction would distort litigant incentives and disproportionately burden defendants. The Court also notes that the EAJA's purpose of ensuring access to justice for all parties aligns with allowing for the recovery of paralegal fees at market rates.

Petitioner Gray was indicted in Harrison County, Miss., on a capital charge for the stabbing death of Ronald Wojcik while engaged in the commission of the felony of kidnapping. The trial judge began the jury selection process by assembling the entire venire in the courtroom. When the prosecutor acknowledged that he would accept the full panel as it stood, the voir dire shifted to the defense and petitioner's attorney followed the same procedure. After the prosecutor's examination of the venire members, he asked each venire member whether he or she had any conscientious scruples against capital punishment and whether he could vote to impose a death sentence. Whenever a prospective juror revealed any such scruple or expressed any degree of uncertainty in the ability to cast such a vote, the prosecutor moved to have the panel member excused for cause. In eight instances, however, the court denied the motion. The jury convicted Gray of capital murder and sentenced him to death. The Mississippi Supreme Court reversed, holding that Gray's death sentence was invalid because the exclusion of Bounds violated his right to a fair and impartial jury and was inconsistent with Witherspoon v. Illinois, 391 U. S. 510. Held: The judgment of the Supreme Court of Mississippi, insofar as it imposes the death sentence, is reversed, and the case is remanded to that court for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion. Davis v. Georgia, 429 U.S. 122, distinguished. Pp. 531-532. 472 So. 2d 409, reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court of the United States decided the case of Watson v. Fort Worth Bank and Trust in 1987. The case concerned a dispute over the constitutionality of affirmative action policies in public schools. The Court held that while affirmative action policies may be constitutionally permissible in limited circumstances, they must be carefully tailored to avoid creating a "quota system" that denies equal educational opportunities to students based on their race. The Court emphasized the importance of ensuring that every student receives an education that is free from discrimination and prejudice, regardless of their race or background.

Title: Takings and Due Process

Summary:
This case involves a dispute over a real estate development project in Tennessee. The city refused to approve the project based on environmental concerns, and the developer sued the city for a takings claim under the Fifth Amendment. The Supreme Court holds that the case is not yet ripe for decision because the city has not yet issued a final decision on the project.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida today entered a final judgment against a Florida man who was charged with attempted burglary in violation of the antifraud provisions of Section 924(e)(2)(B) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Orlando, Florida, Alphonso James, a convicted felon who was sentenced to 15 years in prison for attempted burglary, agreed to a 15-year mandatory minimum term. James also agreed to be barred from participating in any type of organized criminal activity, including burglary, arson, extortion, and other criminal activity.  The SEC alleges that James failed to adequately assess the risk posed by an attempt to break into a building or residence.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for Florida today announced criminal charges against James for his role in the attempted burglary.  On May 2, 2018, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against James, charging him with violating Section 923(e) ofÂ BÂ of the Securities Act of 1933, and ordering him to pay a $1,000 civil penalty.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, James consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, orders him to disgorge his ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and requires him to return his allegedly stolen property to the owner of the property.   The court also ordered James to comply with the entry-of-an-offender bar, which requires a court to determine whether a defendant is a serious risk of physical injury or death to another person.  James agreed to settle the case by consenting to a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations of Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and imposing a $500,000 penalty. The court granted the SEC’s request for a temporary restraining order against James and a preliminary injunction against further violations of Sections 924 and 924 of the securities laws.  It also ordered him to comply to a court order requiring him to provide a copy of the final judgment to the court.

Title: Voting Rights Act - Bailout Provisions

Summary:
In this case, the Supreme Court considers the eligibility of a political subdivision to seek bailout from the preclearance requirements of the Voting Rights Act. The Court holds that all political subdivisions, not only those described in §14(c)(2), are eligible to file a bailout suit. The Court finds that the language "political subdivision" in §4(a) refers to any entity that meets the definition of a political subdivision under state law, regardless of whether it registers voters or conducts its own elections. The Court also notes that the bailout provision serves a dual purpose: it allows jurisdictions to seek relief from the burden of preclearance while simultaneously providing a mechanism for challenging discriminatory voting practices.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia today entered final judgments against Virginia residents who have agreed to settle charges that they violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of its Investment Advisers Act of 1940.  The Court also entered judgments in favor of Virginia residents in two other cases in which it found that the right to vote in state elections violated the federal securities laws.  In Brown v. Board of Education, filed in federal district court in Alexandria, Virginia, the Court found that, contrary to the First Amendment, the right of a citizen to participate in state legislative representation is contingent upon the payment of a tax or fee.  According to the Court's order, however, that neither homesite nor occupation "affords a permissible basis for distinguishing between qualified voters within the State."  The court also ruled that, as a condition of obtaining a ballot, a citizen may not demand from all an equal poll tax for a driver's license, but must pay the fee if the citizen, otherwise qualified to vote, has $1.50 in his pocket or nothing at all, pays the fee or fails to pay it.

The boycott of white merchants in Claiborne County, Miss., that gave rise to this litigation had such a character that it included elements of criminality and elements of majesty. Evidence that fear of reprisals caused some black citizens to withhold their patronage from respondents' businesses convinced the Mississippi Supreme Court that the boycott was unlawful and that each of the petitioners was liable for all of its economic consequences. The chancellor issued an opinion and decree finding that the defendants were liable for the tort of malicious interference with the plaintiffs' businesses, which did not necessarily require the presence of a conspiracy. The court justified imposing full liability on the defendants on the ground that they had diverted black patronage from the white merchants to black merchants and to other merchants located out of the county and thus had unreasonably limited competition between black and white merchants that had traditionally existed. Held: 1. Petitioners' activities are entitled to the protection of the First Amendment. Pp. 563-564. (a) Civil liability may not be imposed merely because an individual belonged to a group, some members of which committed acts of violence, but it is necessary to establish that specific parties agreed to use unlawful means, that carefully identify the impact of such unlawful conduct, and that recognize the importance of avoiding the imposition of punishment for constitutionally protected activity. P. 567. (b) The presence of protected activity does not end the relevant constitutional inquiry. Governmental regulation that has an incidental effect on First Amendment freedoms may be justified in certain narrowly defined instances. See United States v. O'Brien, 391 U. S. 367, and Scales v. United States, 367 U.S. 449, distinguished. The right of the States to regulate economic activity could not justify a complete prohibition against a nonviolent, politically motivated boycott designed to force governmental and economic change and to effectuate rights guaranteed by the Constitution itself. Such a characterization must be supported by findings that adequately disclose the evidentiary basis for concluding that the group itself possessed unlawful goals and that the individual held a specific intent to further those illegal aims. The burden of demonstrating that it colored the entire collective effort, however, is not satisfied by evidence that violence occurred or even that violence contributed to the success of the boycott. A massive and prolonged effort to change the social, political, and economic structure of a local environment cannot be characterized as a violent conspiracy simply by reference to the ephemeral consequences of relatively few violent acts, such as the one in 1966. Moreover, there is no suggestion that the NAACP, MAP or the individual defendants were in competition with the white businesses or that they arose from parochial economic interests. The evidence in the record suggests the contrary. The Chancellor's findings do not suggest that any illegal conduct was authorized, ratified, or even discussed at any of the meetings, and there is nothing in the measure of damages to indicate that state power was exerted to compensate for anything more than the direct consequences of the violent conduct. The judgment against petitioners is reversed and the case is remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed a lower court's ruling that a school district's drug-testing policy violated the Fourth Amendment. The court held that the district did not show that there was a "identifiable drug abuse problem" among a sufficient number of students subject to the testing. The lower court had found that the policy did not address a "proven problem" of drug use among students participating in competitive extracurricular activities. The appeals court concluded that the "probable cause" standard was not sufficient to determine that the testing violated the Constitution's right to be secure in his persons, houses, papers, and effects. The Appeals Court held that, because the district failed to demonstrate a drug-abuse problem among those subject to testing, the policy was unconstitutional. The Supreme Court agreed with the lower court, and the appeals court reversed, holding that the District's policy is constitutional. The Court held, however, that there is no reasonable basis for the district to justify the testing policy. The high court held, for example, that it would be unconstitutional to require a student to submit to random drug testing while participating in an extracurricular activity. In a related case, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled in favor of the school district in a similar test case.

Based on information furnished by an informant, police officers learned that respondent, who had recently served a term of imprisonment for marijuana possession, would be arriving at a certain airport. When respondent appeared, the officers saw him enter a taxi and later followed the taxi to a motel room where respondent was staying. There, the officers arrested respondent and another person and seized a green suitcase belonging to respondent. Subsequent to receiving a report from the informant indicating that respondent possessed marihuana, the officers opened the suitcase and found marihuana. Respondent was convicted of possessing marihuana with intent to distribute it, and the Arkansas Supreme Court affirmed, holding that although the officers had probable cause to make the initial arrest, they lacked probable cause to open the suitcase without first obtaining a search warrant. Held: Under the circumstances of this case, the warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment applied to the opening of the suitcase, and hence the officers erred in doing so without first obtaining a search warrant. Pp. 449-456. (a) The warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment ordinarily requires that conclusions concerning probable cause and the scope of a search be drawn by a neutral and detached magistrate. However, there are some exceptions to the warrant requirement where it is shown that the societal costs of obtaining a warrant, such as danger to law officers or the risk of loss or destruction of evidence, outweigh the reasons for prior recourse to a neutral magistrate. Each exception to the warrant requirement, however, impinges to some extent on the protective purpose of the Fourth Amendment, and the burden is on those seeking the exemption to show the need for it. Pp. 449-451. (b) The warrant requirement does not apply to automobiles stopped on highways because of the inherent mobility of automobiles and the configuration, use, and regulation of automobiles, which often dilutes the reasonable expectation of privacy existing with respect to differently situated property. Pp. 451-452. (c) Nor does the warrant requirement apply to luggage taken from an automobile lawfully stopped on the highway simply because it was located in an automobile lawfully stopped by the police. Since once the police have seized a suitcase, as they did here, the extent of its mobility is in no way affected by the place from which it was taken, there is no greater need for warrantless searches of luggage taken from automobiles than of luggage taken from other places. Similarly, a suitcase taken from an automobile stopped on the highway is not necessarily attended by any lesser expectation of privacy than is associated with luggage taken from other locations. Pp. 452-455. 289 Ark. 10, 686 S. W. 2d 10, affirmed.

After appellant employees filed separate charges with the Minnesota Department of Human Rights (MDHR) alleging age discrimination against respondent University of Minnesota (University), the MDHR dismissed the charges and notified appellants that they had 45 days in which to file civil suits in state district court. On August 30, 1996, appellants sued the University in federal district court, alleging age discrimination under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1974 (ADEA) and the Minnesota Human Rights Act (MHRA). The federal district court dismissed the action for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. While the federal action was pending, appellants brought this action in state district court, again alleging age discrimination under the MHRA. The state district court dismissed the action, holding that the federal court never had "original" jurisdiction over the MHRA claim because the Eleventh Amendment bars suits in federal court against a state by citizens of that or another state. The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals stayed appellants' challenge to the federal district court's decision pending resolution of the Eleventh Amendment issue in another case. Twenty days after the federal district court dismissed the action, the state district court allowed the University to move to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds. Ultimately, the state district court ruled that the MHRA claim was not tolled under 28 U. S. C. § 1367(d), which provides that "[t]he period of limitations for any claim . . .shall be tolled while the claim is pending and for a period of 30 days after it is dismissed ...unless State law provides for a longer tolling period." Held: 1. Because the University's assertion of an Eleventh Amendment defense did not vitiate or destroy the federal district court's underlying original jurisdiction over appellants' ADEA claim or its mandatory, supplemental jurisdiction over appellants' MHRA claim, the 45-day limitations period for asserting appellants' MHRA claim was tolled during the pendency of the federal district court action. Section 1367(d)'s plain language allows tolling of any claim dismissed by a federal district court, whether dismissed on Eleventh Amendment grounds or at the discretion of the federal district court under § 1367(c). Morever, although Eleventh Amendment immunity can be waived and a federal court has discretion to raise it sua sponte, the amendment does not necessarily destroy a federal district court's underlying jurisdiction. See Wis. Dep't of Corr.v .Schacht, 118 S. Ct. 2047, 2052-53. Nor does § 1367(d) require a supplemental state law claim to be dismissed for a reason under § 1367(c) in order for that claim to be tolled. To the contrary, § 1367(d) expressly states that the tolling periods applies to "any" claim asserted under subsection (a), which discusses original and supplemental jurisdiction. And the plain language of § 1367(d) allows tolling of any claim dismissed by a federal district court, whether dismissed on Eleventh Amendment grounds or at the discretion of the federal district court under § 1367(c). Finally, although Pennhurst State Schp. v. Halderman, 465 U. S. 89, discussed a federal district court's "pendent" jurisdiction over state law claims and requires a federal court, once an Eleventh Amendment immunity defense is raised, to examine each claim in a case to see if the court's jurisdiction over that claim is barred by the Eleventh Amendment, it must be read in conjunction with § 1367 and with recent cases discussing the Eleventh Amendment, such as Schacht. Pp. 31-35. 2. Even if appellants are not entitled to relief under § 1367, their claims were equitably tolled during the pendency of the federal district court action. There is little or no evidence that the University would be prejudiced if appellants' claims were equitably tolled. With respect to appellants' conduct, the lack of clarity and clear precedent on the issues involved justifies equitable tolling. Here, given the lack of clarity in this area, appellants' decision to file suit only in federal district court was legally sound and not based on their attorney's incorrect interpretation of the law. Pp. 35-36. Reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota yesterday issued an order granting the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order and an asset freeze against Michael J. Greenlaw, a member of a Chicago-area gang that, for years, controlled the sale of crack cocaine in a southside Minneapolis neighborhood.  The SEC's order, which was issued yesterday, orders Greenlaw to pay a total of $622,000 in restitution and a $75,000 civil penalty.  According to the SEC, Greenlaw was convicted of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordered to pay restitution in amounts to be determined by the court at a later date.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Greenlaw.  Greenlaw pleaded guilty in a parallel criminal action and was sentenced to prison for 442 months.  On June 13, 2008, the court issued a final judgment that permanently enjoins Greenlaw from future violations of the federal securities laws.  Without admitting or denying the SEC’s allegations, the Court of Appeals agreed to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining the defendants from violating the charged provisions of the securities laws, ordering the defendants to pay disgorgement of their ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and imposing a civil penalty of up to 15 years.  It also ordered the defendants pay a $25,000 penalty.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit granted certiorari in the case of Sandra Lockett, an Ohio woman sentenced to death for the murder of a pawnshop owner. Lockett was charged with aggravated murder and aggravated robbery for her role in a robbery that resulted in the death of the pawn shop owner. The trial judge sentenced Lockett to death based largely on the testimony of a co-defendant, Al Parker, who agreed to testify against Lockett in exchange for the dismissal of the murder charge and the specifications to the aggravated robbery charge. The court concluded that Lockett's sentence was not "appropriate" for the circumstances of the crime and that the jury should have been allowed to consider the mitigating circumstances of her life, including her prior criminal record. The Court also concluded that the trial judge did not have the authority to impose the death penalty because Lockett did not testify against her co-conspirators. In a separate appeal, the Ohio Supreme Court agreed with the lower court's finding that Locket's sentencing was not disproportionate to the crime. The high court held that the sentencing judge had not properly instructed the jury on the sentencing guidelines. The appeals court also found that the prosecution had not proved Lockett acted with "reckless disregard for the life of the victim"

Respondent filed a complaint in Federal District Court against petitioners the United States Department of the Interior and the Director of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), an agency within the Department. The complaint alleged that petitioners had violated the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (FLPMA) by failing to "develop, maintain, and, when appropriate, revise land use plans which provide by tracts or areas for the use of the public lands," 43 U. S. C. § 1712(a) (1982 ed.). The complaint also alleged that the BLM had violated § 10 (a) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which provides that "a person suffering legal wrong because of agency action, or adversely affected or aggrieved by agency action within the meaning of a relevant statute, is entitled to judicial review thereof." The District Court granted respondent's motion for a preliminary injunction prohibiting petitioners from "[m]odifying, terminating or altering any withdrawal, classification, or other designation governing the protection of lands in the public domain that was in effect on January 1, 1981," and from "[t]aking any action inconsistent" with any such withdrawal. The Court of Appeals affirmed both orders. Held: 1. The affidavits, which were filed by petitioners, did not raise a genuine issue of fact as to whether an "agency action" taken by petitioner caused respondent to be "adversely affected" or "agrieved" within the Meaning of the APA. Pp. 5-11. (a). (b) Respondent does not contend that either the FLPMA or NEPA provides a private right of action for violations of its provisions. Rather, respondent claims a right to review under § 10(a). P. 5. (c) The provision of Rule 56 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure provides that, when, and to the extent that, a specific "final agency action" has an actual or immediately threatened effect, a District Court must resolve any factual issues of controversy in favor of the non-moving party, and the motion must be denied. P. 6. (d) The "land withdrawal review program" (which as far as we know is not derived from any authoritative text) does not refer to a single BLM order or regulation, or even to a completed universe of particular BLM orders and regulations. It is simply the name by which petitioners have occasionally referred to the continuing (and thus constantly changing) operations of the BLM in reviewing withdrawal revocation applications and the classifications of public lands and developing land uses plans as required by § 1701(a)(7) (1981 ed.). P. 7. 2. Respondent cannot seek wholesale improvement of this program by court decree, rather than in the offices of the Department or the halls of Congress, where programmatic improvements are normally made. The court must also decide whether respondent may seek § 702 review of petitioners' actions in its own right rather than derivatively through its members, since whatever "adverse effect," or "aggrievement" is established by the affidavits was "within the meaning" of § 702 if any of its members do, and it is no more an identifiable "agency" as that term is defined in § 551, than a "weapons procurement program" or a "drug interdiction program" of the Drug Enforcement Administration, which is not an identifiable action or event, but rather a generic action or action that is protected by the statutory provision whose violation forms the legal basis for his complaint. The proposition that it was compelled to receive them-that it was an abuse of discretion to reject them-cannot be accepted, since it is a world apart from "assuming" that general averments embrace the "specific facts" needed to sustain the complaint, and since the provision was obviously enacted to protect the parties to the proceedings and not those of the reporters, that company would not be affected by § 702's requirements if any member of the NLPMA's members do not do so, and because the "agency actions" in question are sufficiently related to the purposes of respondent association that respondent meets the requirements of § 704. The case-by-case approach that this requires is understandably frustrating to an organization such as respondent, which has as its objective across-the-board protection of our Nation's wildlife and the streams and forests that support it. But this is the traditional, and remains the normal, mode of operation of the courts. Except where Congress explicitly provides for our correction of the administrative process at a higher level of generality, we intervene in the administration of the laws only when the statute in question uses those terms (or terms like them)—as some pre-APA statutes in fact did when conferring rights of judicial review. The U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona yesterday ordered the school district to conduct a strip search in violation of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Phoenix, Arizona, alleges that the assistant principal of Safford Middle School, Kerry Wilson, conducted a school strip search on October 8, 2003, in which he asked Savana Redding to remove her bra and underpants from her room and show him a day planner that she had lent to her friend, Marissa Glines.  According to the complaint, Savana replied that she did not know anything about the pills, but that a few days before she lent them to another student, Jordan Romero, who had been at a party at Savana’s house where alcohol and cigarettes were served.  Wilson also allegedly told Savana that he had received a report that she was giving these pills to fellow students.  He also told her that one of the students had asked him to search her backpack, finding nothing.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Wilson, Romero, and Schwallier.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Wilson has consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $1,000,000.   The court also ordered Wilson to remove his jacket, socks, and shoes from his possession, and to search Savana's backpack.  On the same day, Wilson conducted a group strip search of a fifth grade student for a drug, without any reasonable suspicion that the drugs were hidden in her underwear.  As alleged in the SEC complaint, the strip search was unreasonable because it required reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing before a search could be conducted.  Finally, the complaint alleges that Wilson violated the Fourth Amendment by conducting a search at the direction of a school official, without reasonable suspicion or reasonable reason, of finding evidence of wrongdoing in the person or place to be searched.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 533 U. S.  (2001).

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of the Trump Administration in a challenge brought by several individuals and organizations arguing that the President's travel ban targeting predominantly Muslim countries exceeded his constitutional authority. The majority opinion, written by Justice John Roberts, affirmed the lower federal court decisions upholding the ban and found that the President's actions fell within the scope of his authority under Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. The Court also rejected arguments that the ban discriminates against Muslims based on their faith, noting that the ban targets specific countries rather than individual adherents of Islam. However, the Court did caution that the ban should be reviewed regularly to ensure that it remains constitutional and does not become overbroad or arbitrary.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against defendant Tony DeVore, Jr., who was convicted in a civil injunctive action on April 16, 1988, of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a judgment that permanently enjoins DeVore from future violations of the federal securities laws and orders him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois today announced criminal charges against DeVore.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Chicago, in April 1988, DeVore was awakened by a scream from the babysitter's bedroom. The complaint alleges that petitioner had put his hand over her mouth, choked her, threatened to whip her if she screamed and had "put his mouth on her front part."  The complaint also alleges that, in response to questioning, S.G. allegedly stated that petitioner "touched her in the wrong places."  In addition, the complaint further alleges that the defendant had "used his tongue on her private parts" in the course of receiving medical care.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the charged provisions, ordering him to disgorge his ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interests, and imposing civil penalties of up to $100,000.  DeVore also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company and to pay a civil penalty of $150,000, and to be prohibited from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in connection with the issuance of any security deposit or other security deposit in the name of the company or the security deposit of the individual or entity for which he or she consented.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael Meinzen, Cheryl Reents, Cheryl Wright, and Terry Lewis of the Chicago Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Illinois Attorney General's Office in this matter.

Petitioner Doe filed for benefits under the Black Lung Benefits Act with the Department of Labor, alleging repeated violations of the Act and seeking certification of a class of "all claimants for [Black Lung Benefits] since the passage of the Privacy Act." The Government conceded that following this practice led to disclosing Doe's Social Security number beyond the limits set by the Act, and the parties then filed cross-motions for summary judgment. The District Court denied class certification and entered judgment against all individual plaintiffs except Doe, finding that their submissions had raised no issues of cognizable harm. As to Doe, the court accepted his uncontroverted evidence of distress on learning of the improper disclosure, granted summary judgment, and awarded $1,000 in statutory damages under 5 U. S. C. § 552a(g)(4). A divided panel of the Fourth Circuit affirmed in part but reversed on Doe's claim, holding the United States entitled to summary judgment across the board. The Fourth Circuit treated the statutory minimum as available only to plaintiffs who suffered actual damages because of the agency's violation, and then found that Doe had not raised a triable issue of fact about actual damages, having submitted no corroboration for his claim of emotional distress, such as evidence of physical symptoms, medical treatment, loss of income, or impact on his behavior. In fact, the only indication of emotional affliction was Doe's conclusory allegations that he was "torn . . . all to pieces'" and "greatly concerned and worried" because of his disclosure of his Social Security numbers and its potentially "devastating" consequences. The court accepted Doe's uncontrovertible evidence of relief on learning that the violation had been intentional or willful, and granted him damages under the Act. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that some actual damages must be proven before a plaintiff may receive the minimum statutory award. Held: 1. The "entitle[ment] to recovery" necessary to qualify for the minimum minimum is not shown merely by an intentional and willful violation, but has proved no "actual damages" as a third liability-determining element. Pp. 5-11. (a) The statute does not authorize injunctive relief when suit is maintained under § 5 52a (g)(1)(C) or (D). Injunctive relief, and attendant counsel fees and costs, are available in two categories: suits to amend a record and suits for access to a record. But for cases like Doe's, only monetary relief is available, and Doe's manner of reading the statute simply pays no attention to the statute's language and to the fact that it does not speak of liability (and consequent entitlement to recovery) in a freestanding, unqualified way, but in a limited way, by reference to enumerated damages. The statute also does not require proof of intent or willfulness in addition to adverse effect, and if the specific state of mind must be proved additionally, it is equally consistent with logic to require someactual damages as well. Nor is it too strong to say that Doe does ignore statutory language. When Doe reads the statute to mean that the Government shall be liable to any adversely affected subject of an intentional or wilful violation, without more, he treats willful action as the last fact necessary to make the Government "liable," and he is thus able to describe anyone to whom it is liable as entitled to the $1000 guarantee. See, e. g., Johnson v. Department of Housing and Urban Development, 713 F. 2d 422, 424-435; Fitzpatrick v. IRS, 665 F.2d 327, 330-331. The Government's contention that the statute is not likely to produce "massive recoveries" against the Government is at odds with the interpretation prevailing in the Federal Circuits, which hold that tort recovery requires not only wrongful act plus causation reaching to the plaintiff, but proof of some harm for which damages can reasonably be assessed. The fact that the phrase "adverse effect" does not include the critical limiting phrase "shall be liable" is a "necessary" element of the statute. Moreover, Doe's reading of the phrase does not make it clear that it is not meant to provide a complete cause of action, since it is in tension with more than the text, and it is inconsistent with logic that requires some actual damage as well as with the statutory requirement that the plaintiff be entitled to recovery. The text is too far different from the language of the privacy Act to serve as any sound basis for analogy; it does include the crucial limiting "entitled to recovery," and it turns the phrase's phrase "willful, arbitrary, or capricious" into a "miscellaneous" element. The courts have disallowed the runaway liability that might ensue were they to count every single wrongful disclosure as a discrete basis for a $1k000 award, and this objection is open to the objection that no purpose is served by conditioning the guarantee on a person's being entitled to recover without actual damages. In the case of David Roth, an assistant professor at Wisconsin State University-Oshkosh, the Supreme Court held that Roth was not entitled to a statement of reasons or a hearing upon the university's decision not to rehire him for another academic year. Roth had completed a fixed one-year term and had no tenure rights or statutory entitlement to continued employment.

The Court's reasoning was based on the Fourteenth Amendment's procedural due process protections, which only apply to deprivations of liberty or property interests. The Court determined that Roth's interest in re-employment did not constitute a property interest because his contract explicitly ended on a certain date without any provision for renewal. Additionally, there were no state laws or university policies that created an entitlement to re-employment.

Furthermore, the Court found that Roth's liberty was not at stake because the university did not make any charges against him that could damage his reputation or impose a stigma that would restrict his freedom to seek other employment opportunities.

The Court emphasized that constitutional due process rights are not concerned with the wisdom or appropriateness of a hearing or statement of reasons in employment decisions at public institutions, but rather with the interpretation of constitutional protections.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had affirmed the District Court's decision to grant summary judgment for Roth on procedural grounds. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. Justice Powell did not participate in the decision.

Petitioner Johnnie Corley was suspected of robbing a bank in Norristown, Pennsylvania. After federal agents learned that Corley had been subject to arrest on an unrelated local matter, some federal and state officers went together to execute the state warrant on September 17, 2003, and found him just as he was pulling out of a driveway in his car. Corley nearly ran over one officer, then jumped out of the car, pushed the officer down, and ran. The agents gave chase and caught and arrested him for assaulting a federal officer. The arrest occurred about 8 a.m. 500 F. 3d 210, 212. The District Court denied Corley’s motion to suppress his oral and written confessions under McNabb v. United States, 318 U. S. 332 (1943). The Court of Appeals affirmed, reasoning that McNabb-Mallory “generally render[s] inadmissible confessions made during periods of detention that violat[e] the prompt presentment requirement of Rule 5(a).” United States v. Alvarez-Sanchez, 511 U.S. 350, 354. The Third Circuit affirmed. Held: Under the rule, which provides that any confession “shall be admissible in evidence” in federal court “if it is voluntarily given,” §3501(a) “a confession made … by … a defendant therein, while such person was under arrest … ,” “[a]ny statement, admission, or confession made by an arrested person within three hours immediately following his arrest … . . . shall not be excluded from evidence in the courts of the District of Columbia solely because of delay in presentment.” Id., at 340. Pp. 5–7. (a) Section 3501(b) provides that in any criminal prosecution by the United States … , a confession made “by … a person who is a defendant” while “an arrest without a warrant [to] take the arrested person without unnecessary delay before the nearest available commissioner or before any other nearby officer empowered to commit persons charged with offenses against the laws … .” Fed. Rule Crim. Proc. 5 (a)(1)(A) (2007). The rule remains much the same today: “A person making an arrest within the country must take the defendant without unnecessary delays before a magistrate judge … if such confession is found by the trial judge to have been made voluntarily … and if that confession was made within six hours [of arrest]”; the six-hour time limit is extended when further delay is “reasonable considering the means of transportation and the distance to be traveled to the nearest [magistrate].” Russello v. U. States, 464 U. . S. 16, 23. The Government points to nothing in this history supporting its view that (c) created a bright-line rule for applying the presentment obligation, id., at 345, but this is simply not so. To begin with, Congress used both terms in (c), itself, and (b) with its bar to admitting even a voluntary confession if given during an unreasonable delay. And there is, in fact, every reason to believe that Congress used the distinct terms very deliberately. Subsection (a), which specifies two criteria that must be satisfied to prevent a confession from being “inadmissible solely because” of delay, is admissible, subject to the other Rules of Evidence, so long as it was “made voluntarily and … [2] within six hour [of] arrest” and if it was made voluntarily and “without unnecessary delay” as the Government claims, “the weight to be given [it] is left to the jury” Ibid. If the confession occurred before presentment and beyond six hours, however, the court must decide whether delaying that long was unreasonable or unnecessary under the McNabb–Mallories cases. If it was, the confession is to be suppressed. In this case, the Third Circuit did not apply this rule and in the exercise of supervisory authority, the Court held confessions inadmissible when obtained during unreasonable presentment delay. The case for applying McNabb and Rule 5, which were meant to eliminate McNabb, is vacate and remanded. The Fourth Circuit, in its opinion, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Southern District of Texas ruled that a Texas law requiring children to live in the state to attend public free schools is unconstitutional. The court held that the law does not require children to be residents of the state in order to be eligible for tuition-free admission. The ruling was based on the fact that Roberto Morales, who was born in 1969 in McAllen, Texas, and was living with his sister for the primary purpose of attending school, was not a resident of Texas at the time of his admission. Morales's sister, Oralia Martinez, and four other adult custodians of school-age children filed suit against the Texas Education Agency, the Texas Department of Education, and local school officials. The district court granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment, and the court ruled in favor of the defendants. The Supreme Court of the United States later ruled that the case should be remanded for further consideration. The Court held that, in this case, the lower court's ruling was not subject to judicial review. The case is now before the Court again.

On February 27, 1980, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia entered a final judgment against a former partner of a large Atlanta law firm for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint alleges that Elizabeth Anderson Hishon accepted a position as an associate with respondent, a large Georgia law firm established as a general partnership. According to the complaint, the firm had more than 50 partners and employed approximately 50 attorneys as associates. The complaint alleges, however, that the firm did not consider and rejected Hishone for admission to partnership as a result of her sex in violation of the federal securities laws. The SEC alleges that the partnership's refusal to consider and reject her for partnership violated the federal anti-discrimination provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a)(2) of The Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act").  The complaint also alleges that respondent failed to consider Hishaon for partnership when it considered and rejected her for admission in May 1978.  As alleged, the partnership again declined to invite her to become a partner.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendant.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins her from future violations of the securities laws, orders her to pay a civil penalty of $1,000, and orders the defendant to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest of $2,500, and to pay civil penalties of $100,000.   The settlement is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Conley and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson of the Atlanta Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Gregory A. Kasper.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that the denial of a deduction of the amount of the excise taxes added to his pump prices in the computation of his 'gross proceeds of the retail sales' of gasoline is unconstitutional. The court held that the application of the 5% sales tax to so much of the pump prices as reflects the amount the taxes, and the resulting denial of the deduction, are unconstitutional as violating the constitutional immunity of the United States and its property from taxation by the States. The Court held that, as a matter of law, the legal incidence of the taxes is not upon petitioner, but upon the purchaser-consumer. Therefore, the decision as to where the tax falls is not determined by the fact that the economic burden of either tax is traditionally passed on to the purchasers of the merchandise. The decision also held that there is no reason to conclude that the tax is not a tax on the purchaser. In a related matter, the court held in favor of the state of Mississippi's appeal of the lower court's decision granting the state's motion for summary judgment. The Fifth Circuit's ruling is the latest in a long line of court decisions that have found that the Constitution's guarantees of due process and the right to a fair trial do not apply to state and federal tax matters. The Supreme Court of Mississippi, in a separate opinion, ruled that there was no legal basis for the state to impose a sales tax on petitioner's gross proceeds of retail sales of gasoline, and that the state had not shown that the sales tax was necessary to collect the taxes. The 5th Circuit held that it would be unconstitutional for the court to impose such a tax upon the gross receipts of a person. The appeals court concluded that the issue of whether the tax was a state or federal tax is a matter for the courts to decide. The case will be decided by a three-judge panel.

The Supreme Court of the United States reviewed regulations imposed by the Michigan Department of Corrections (MDOC) that restricted prison visitation rights. The regulations limited the number of visitors an inmate could receive, required visitors to be on an approved list, and imposed special rules for minors and former prisoners. The regulations also prohibited visitation for inmates with multiple substance abuse violations, with the possibility of reinstatement after two years at the warden's discretion.

The case was brought by prisoners and their families, who argued that the restrictions violated the First, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendments. The District Court and the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals found in favor of the prisoners, but the Supreme Court reversed these decisions.

The Supreme Court held that the regulations did not infringe upon a constitutional right of association, as the very nature of imprisonment involves the loss of many freedoms enjoyed by the general population. The Court applied the rational basis test, as established in Turner v. Safley, to determine whether the regulations were reasonably related to legitimate penological interests. The Court found that the regulations were indeed rational, as they aimed to maintain order, prevent drug trafficking, and protect child visitors.

The Court also considered whether there were alternative means for inmates to exercise their rights, the impact of accommodating the right on prison resources and safety, and whether there were obvious alternatives to the regulations that would impose minimal costs. The Court concluded that the regulations met these criteria and thus did not violate the Constitution.

Regarding the Eighth Amendment claim, the Court found that the restrictions did not constitute cruel and unusual punishment, as they were a common disciplinary measure and did not create inhumane conditions or deprive inmates of basic necessities.

In summary, the Supreme Court ruled that the MDOC's visitation regulations were constitutional, as they were rationally related to legitimate penological interests and did not violate the prisoners' rights under the First, Eighth, or Fourteenth Amendments. The decision emphasized the deference given to prison administrators in managing prison facilities and maintaining security.

Petitioner, who had been indicted for first-degree murder, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder, which carries a maximum penalty of 30 years' imprisonment. At the time of the plea petitioner admitted that he had taken a gun and announced his intent to kill, but he denied having done so. He thus presented conflicting versions of the facts. The trial judge accepted the plea over objections of petitioner's counsel, who concededly advised petitioner that the plea would be to petitioner's advantage. Following the acceptance of the plea the judge imposed the maximum sentence. Petitioner subsequently filed a habeas corpus petition claiming that his guilty plea was obtained through coercion and that he was entitled to a trial. The Federal District Court granted the writ and directed that petitioner be released unless the State complied with certain conditions. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that the guilty plea violated due process requirements. It based its ruling on United States v. Jackson, 390 U. S. 570, which held that the use of the death penalty as punishment for rape violates the Eighth Amendment. Held: 1. The trial judge did not commit constitutional error in accepting petitioner's guilty plea. Pp. 308-315. (a) While most guilty pleas contain both a waiver of trial and an express admission of guilt, the latter element is not a constitutional requirement to the imposition of criminal penalties. An individual accused of crime may voluntarily, knowingly, and understandingly consent to the imposition of a prison sentence even if he is unwilling or unable to admit his participation in the acts constituting the crime. Pp. 311-313. (b) Viewed in light of the evidence against petitioner, which substantially negated his claim of innocence and which further provided a means by which the judge could test whether the plea was being intelligently entered, the validity of petitioner's guilty plea cannot be seriously questioned. Pp. 313-315. 2. This Court will not construe the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment as requiring that the States permit the acceptance of guilty pleas to crimes carrying less severe sentences than those involved in the underlying homicide. Pp. 315-316. 386 F. 2d 102, vacated and remanded.

Respondents, individuals who bought stock in Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc., on the public securities market between April 15, 1997, and February 24, 1998, brought this securities fraud class action against Dura and its managers and directors in Federal District Court, alleging that, before and during the purchase period, Dura (or its officials) made false statements concerning both Dura's drug profits and future Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of a new asthmatic spray device. Dura falsely claimed that its drug sales would prove profitable. The next day Dura announced that its shares lost almost half their value (falling from about $39 per share to about $21). The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the complaint adequately alleged "loss causation." Held: 1. The Ninth Circuit's holding that a plaintiff can satisfy the requirement that "the price on the date of purchase was inflated because of the misrepresentation" is wrong. Pp. 531-532. (a) In cases involving publicly traded securities and purchases or sales in public securities markets, the action's basic elements include: (1) a material misrepresentation (or omission), see Basic Inc. v. Levinson, 485 U. S. 224, 231-232 (1988); (2) scienter, i. e., a wrongful state of mind; and (3) a connection with the purchase or sale of a security, see Blue Chip Stamps v. Manor Drug Stores, 421 U.S. 723, 730, 744 (1975); (4) reliance, often referred to in cases involving private securities markets (fraud-on-the-market cases) as "transaction causation," see Basic, supra, at 248-249 (nonconclusively presuming that the price of a publicly traded share reflects a materially misrepresentation and that plaintiffs have relied upon that misrepresentation as long as they would not have bought the share in its absence); (5) economic loss, 15 U. C. § 78u-4(b)(4); and (6) loss causation, which would permit recovery where a misrepresentation leads to an inflated purchase price but nonetheless does not proximately cause any economic loss. But, even so, the "short and plain statement" must provide the defendant with "fair notice of what the plaintiff's claim is and the grounds upon which it rests." Conley v. Gibson, 355 U. . S. 41, 47. The complaint does not allege that the defendants' loss consisted of the "artificially inflated" purchase "prices." The complaint's failure to claim that Dura share price fell significantly after the truth became known suggests that the plaintiffs considered the allegation of purchase price inflation alone sufficient. Moreover, for reasons set forth in Part II-A, the complaint's complaint contains nothing that suggests otherwise. P. 533. (b) The complaint lacks support in precedent. Judicially implied private securities fraud actions resemble in many (but not all) respects common-law deceit and misrepresentation actions. See, e. g., the common law of deceit subjects a person who "fraudulently" makes a "misrepresentation" to liability "for pecuniary loss caused" to one who justifiably relies upon it. The common law has long insisted that plaintiff in such a case show not only that had he known the truth he would not act but also that he suffered actual economic loss; and the statute expressly imposes on plaintiffs "the burden of proving" that the defendant's misrepresentations "caused the loss for which the plaintiff seeks to recover." 15 U.' S. C.' § 78j(b) (4). And the statute's common law, which forbids, among other things, the making of any "untrue statement of a material fact" or the omission of any material fact "necessary in order to make the statements made . . . not misleading," is not meant to impose a great burden upon a plaintiff. Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N. A., 534 U. K. 506, distinguished. Nor are ordinary pleading rules designed to protect investors against the risk of loss, but to protect them against the potential loss of confidence in the marketplace by providing them with an adequate understanding of what is likely to play a role in the future price of the securities, and by providing the defendants with notice of the relevant economic loss and what the causal connection might be between that loss and the alleged misrepresentation concerning the "spray device." Cf. Conley, supra. The court's holding, however, is inconsistent with the law's "inflated purchase price" approach to proving causation and loss. It is insufficient to allege proximate causation, since the complaint fails to allege the traditional elements of causation, loss, and loss, which the Ninth Circuit contends are not necessary to show proximate cause or loss-related questions.
