The New York Son of Sam law, which was enacted to compensate victims of crime, requires that income derived from expressive activity be escrowed by the New York Crime Victims Board for at least five years before it can be paid to the author. The law applies to works on any subject, provided that they express the author's thoughts or recollections about his crime, however tangentially or incidentally. The Board may also escrow the income of any author who admits in his work to having committed a crime, whether or not the author was ever actually accused or convicted. Petitioner Simon Schuster, Inc., a publisher, was ordered to pay the Board $250,000 from the proceeds of a book it published by one Henry Hill, a convicted felon who had written a book about his criminal activities. The Board had learned of the book from a victim of Hill's crimes. Schuster filed suit in Federal District Court, seeking a declaration that the Son of Sam law is unconstitutional. The court held that the law was constitutional, but the Court of Appeals reversed. 

Held: The Son of Sam law is inconsistent with the First Amendment. Pp. 42-49.
	 (a) The law is such a content-based statute as to impose a financial disincentive only on speech of a particular content. The Board's argument that discriminatory financial treatment is suspect under the First Amendment only when the legislature intends to suppress certain ideas is incorrect. The fact that society may find speech offensive is not a sufficient reason for suppressing it. The State has a compelling interest in compensating victims from the fruits of crime, but little if any interest in limiting such compensation to the proceeds of the wrongdoer's speech about the crime. The law is significantly overinclusive, since it applies to works on any subject, provided that they express the author's thoughts or recollections about his crime, however tangentially or incidentally. Pp. 42-49. 916 F. 2d 371, reversed.

After petitioner had been convicted of violating the National Park Service Organized Crime Control Act of 1946, he moved under 28 U. S. C. § 1915 (a) for leave to appeal in forma pauperis. A District Judge certified that the application was not made "in good faith" and denied leave to appeal. Petitioner then applied to the Court of Appeals for leave to appeal in forma pauperis. Held: Under 28 U. S. C. § 1915 (a), the Court of Appeals should have granted leave to appeal in forma pauperis unless petitioner's application contained issues not clearly frivolous. Pp. 38-46. (a) The term "good faith," as used in 28 U. S. C. § 1915 (a), must be judged by an objective standard. Pp. 40-41. (b) To obtain leave to appeal in forma pauperis, petitioner must satisfy the requirement of 28 U. S. C. § 1915 (a) that the application be made "if the trial court certifies in writing that it is not taken in good faith." P. 41. (c) The burden of proving bad faith rests on the Government. Pp. 41-42. (d) The rule requiring preference for criminal appeals applies equally to applications for leave to appeal in forma pauperis. Pp. 42-43. (e) Where the Government suggests that an application for leave to appeal in forma pauperis is frivolous, it bears the burden of demonstrating that the appeal is so lacking in merit that the court would dismiss the case on motion of the Government, had the case been docketed and a record been filed by an appellant able to afford the expense of complying with those requirements. P. 43. (f) The purpose of giving priority to criminal appeals requires that similar considerations apply to applications for leave to appeal in forma pauperis. P. 43. (g) The delay resulting from piecemeal consideration of motions for the appointment of counsel, for the preparation of a transcript of the trial proceedings and, ultimately, for leave to appeal in forma pauperis warrants special care in determining whether an application contains issues not clearly frivolous. Pp. 43-44. (h) Taken as a whole, petitioner's various claims cannot justify the summary disposition of his case ordered below. Pp. 44-46. 106 U. S. App. D. C. 275, 272 F. 2d 504, judgment vacated and cause remanded.

Section 340B of the Public Health Service Act imposes ceiling prices on certain drugs manufactured by pharmaceutical companies for sale to “healthcare entities,” including public hospitals and clinics serving low-income patients, commonly known as 340B entities. Covered entities cannot purchase drugs above these ceiling prices without the manufacturer’s consent. Section 340B’s implementation is governed by regulations promulgated by the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), which includes provisions allowing drug manufacturers to opt into the program by executing a Pharmaceutical Pricing Agreement (PPA) with HRSA. Such PPAs are uniform agreements that record manufacturers’ agreement to abide by the statutory ceiling price obligations. Respondent county, which operates several 340B entities, filed suit against petitioners, pharmaceutical companies, alleging that they had overcharged 340B entities in violation of the PPAs. The District Court dismissed the complaint, but the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that covered entities, although they have no right to sue under §340B itself, could maintain the action as third-party beneficiaries of the PPAs. Held: Suits by 340B entities to enforce the PPAs are incompatible with the statutory scheme. Pp. 4−10. (a) Congress vested authority to oversee compliance with the 340B Program in HRSA and assigned no auxiliary enforcement role to covered entities. Thus, covered entities have no right of action under §340B itself. Pp. 4−5. (b) The County argues that the PPAs specifically name covered entities as the recipients of discounted drugs and that when the Government uses a contract to secure a benefit, the intended recipient acquires a right to the benefit enforceable under federal common law. However, the PPAs merely incorporate statutory obligations and record the manufacturers’ agreement to abide by them. The form agreements, composed by HRSA, contain no negotiable terms. Moreover, the County recognized that §340B is the source of the contractual term allegedly breached. Pp. 5−6. (c) Spreading the enforcement burden among 340B entities would be contrary to Congress’ centralization of enforcement in the Government. By making HRSA administrator of both the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program and the 340B Program, Congress created an integrated regulatory structure designed to ensure that both programs operate harmoniously and on a uniform, nationwide basis. Allowing 340B entities to file individual actions would undermine HRSA’s ability to implement that plan. Furthermore, because the Medicaid Rebate Program’s statute bars HRSAs parent department from disclosing pricing information in a way that might reveal the prices a manufacturer charges for drugs produced, permitting 340B entities to launch lawsuits would be particularly problematic. Pp. 6−10. 588 F. 3d 1237, reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court.

Appellant, an ordained Congregational minister, was arrested and charged with four offenses under Louisiana law-criminal conspiracy, disturbing the peace, obstructing public passages and picketing before a courthouse. In a consolidated trial before a judge without a jury, and on the same set of facts, he was acquitted of criminal conspiracy but convicted of the other three offenses. He was sentenced to serve four months in jail and pay a $200 fine, to serve five months and pay $500 fine, and to serve one year in jail for picketing. The Louisiana Supreme Court, in two judgments, affirmed all three convictions. Held: 1. The conviction for violating the statute as so construed and as applied in this case cannot stand. Pp. 531-532. (a) On the facts of this case, which are strikingly similar to those present in Edwards v. South Carolina, 372 U. S. 229, and Fields v.South Carolina, 375 U.S. 44, Louisiana infringed appellant's rights of free speech and assembly by convicting him under this statute. P. 534. (b) The Louisiana statute, as interpreted by the Louisiana court, is unconstitutional in that it sweeps within its broad scope activities that are constitutionally protected free speech, assembly, and assembly. Edwards, supra, at 235, distinguished. P p. 535. (c) The practice in Baton Rouge of allowing unfettered discretion in local officials in the regulation of the use of the streets for peaceful parades and meetings is an unwarranted abridgment of appellant's freedom of speech and expression secured to him by the First Amendment, as applied to the States by the Fourteenth Amendment, and the Louisiana statute as authoritatively interpreted by this Court is unconstitutionally broad in scope. The statute as construed and applied here does not violate the First and Fourteenth Amendments, which afford the same kind of freedom to those who would communicate ideas by conduct such as patrolling, marching, and pickingeting on streets and highways, as these amendments afford to those communicating ideas by pure speech, and as such afford the right of a State or municipality to regulate such use of city streets and other facilities to assure the safety and convenience of the people in their use and the concomitant right of freedom of assembly, as the amendments afford those who communicate ideas through pure speech. Pps. 536-542. (d) In upholding appellant's conviction under the statute, the State Supreme Court thus construed the statute so as to apply to public assemblies which do not have as their specific purpose the obstruction of traffic, and thus as to be unconstitutional on their face and as applying here, the statute is an unconstitutional infringement on freedom of expression and assembly secured to appellant's freedoms of speech. The record does not support the contention that the students' cheering, clapping and singing constituted a breach of the peace is confirmed by a film of the events taken by a television news photographer, which was offered in evidence as a state exhibit. The film shows that the singing and cheering do not seem to differ significantly from the constitutionally protected activity of the demonstrators in Edwards, who loudly sang "while stamping their feet and clapping their hands." P. 452. 244 La. 1087, 156 So. 2d 448; 245 La. 303, 158 So.2d 529, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit recently ruled that a Florida man sentenced to 15 years in prison for a simple battery conviction was eligible for sentencing under the Armed Career Criminal Act, which provides for a mandatory minimum term of 15 years and a maximum of life. The court ruled that the law does not apply to a person who has three prior convictions for a violent felony, as the prosecution had alleged. The Court held that the felony offense of battery is not a forcible felony and therefore does not require the same conduct as a misdemeanor battery conviction, which requires proof of only the unwanted physical touch. In a separate opinion, the court ruled against the prosecution's motion to dismiss the charges, finding that there was insufficient evidence to support the government's claim that the defendant had violated the law. The case will be decided by the full court in a later date.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Arizona ruled in favor of two attorneys who were disciplined for advertising in a newspaper that they were offering legal services at 'very reasonable fees' and listed their fees for certain services. The court held that the rule violated the First Amendment right to free speech. The Supreme Court ruled that the Arizona Bar's disciplinary board was within its authority to impose the rule. The high court also found that the bar's authority to discipline attorneys was not subject to the Sherman Act, which prohibits state regulation of advertising by attorneys. The justices concluded that the practice of law in Arizona is not a subject of state regulation, and therefore the rule does not violate the Constitution's free speech protection. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a personal injury suit filed by a member of the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Indian Reservation against a non-Indian contractor and the contractor's employer. The lower court had dismissed the suit on the basis that the tribal court lacked jurisdiction to hear the case because the defendants were not members of the tribe. The appeals court found that the lower court misapplied its own precedents. The court held that, under tribal law, the tribe has the authority to govern the conduct of non-member contractors on tribal land. The Appeals Court held that the tribe's tribal law does not provide for the jurisdiction to entertain claims against non-members arising out of accidents on state highways, absent a statute or treaty authorizing the tribe to govern those conduct. We conclude that, in the absence of a tribal law authorizing tribal courts to entertain such claims, the tribal courts have no authority to hear these cases. We also hold that the appeals court erred in denying the defendants' motion to dismiss the case. The Court concludes that the case should be dismissed on the ground that it is not a matter of federal law.

Title: Planned Parenthood v. Casey
Year: 1992
Decided: June 29, 1992
Case Number: 503 U.S. __ (1992)
Judge(s): Kennedy, Scalia, Thomas, Brennan, White, Stevens, Blackmun
Summary: In Planned Parenthood v. Casey, the Supreme Court ruled that Pennsylvania House Bill 1326, which imposed new restrictions on abortion providers and patients, including a requirement that physicians perform ultrasounds and recite a list of risks and benefits to patients, was unconstitutional under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court held that the bill imposed an undue burden on women seeking an abortion, and that such burdens were impermissible under the Constitution. The Court also struck down several other provisions of the bill, including a requirement that women wait 24 hours before receiving an abortion and a ban on partial birth abortions.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit has rejected a challenge to a California law school's policy requiring all student organizations to open eligibility for membership and leadership to all students. The court ruled that the policy is viewpoint neutral and does not violate the First Amendment right to free speech and free exercise of religion. The case was brought by Christian Legal Society, a Christian student organization at Hastings College of the Law. The organization argued that its policy requires it to accept members who do not share the organization's core beliefs about religion and sexual orientation. The appeals court agreed with the lower court's finding that the law school did not violate CLS's First Amendment rights. The decision is the latest in a series of First Amendment rulings that have held that the right to freedom of speech is not limited by the viewpoint of student organizations.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia has granted a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction against the Bureau of Reclamation's plan to increase water releases from the Klamath Irrigation Project. The court granted the Bureau's motion for a preliminary injunction on the basis that the project's impact on the endangered Lost River Sucker (Deltistes luxatus) and Shortnose Sucker (Chasmistes brevirostris) is not likely to jeopardize the species' continued existence. The Court also granted the temporary restraining orders and injunctions against the Secretary of the Interior, the Bureau, and the Bureau itself. The litigation will be heard by the Court's Special Rules Committee on February 11, 2015. The Court will determine whether the petitioners have standing to seek judicial review of the biological opinion under the citizen-suit provision of the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)

This case involves a lawsuit brought by a woman named Michelle Ortiz against two prison officials, Paula Jordan and Rebecca Bright, for allegedly depriving her of protection from sexual harassment and assault while she was imprisoned at the Ohio Reformatory for Women. The case raises questions about the application of the doctrine of qualified immunity, which provides that government officials are immune from being sued for actions taken within the scope of their duties unless those actions constitute a violation of someone's constitutional rights.

The Supreme Court holds that a party may appeal a denial of summary judgment after a full trial on the merits. The Court also clarifies that a qualified immunity defense raises a "purely legal" issue that can be reviewed by an appellate court, regardless of whether there are disputed facts. However, the Court notes that the officials' claims of qualified immunity do not present "neat abstract issues of law." Rather, the officials' actions involved complex factual situations that required careful consideration by the lower courts.

In the case before the Supreme Court, Billy J. Taylor challenged his conviction for aggravated kidnapping on the grounds that women were systematically excluded from the jury venire due to Louisiana's legal provisions, which required women to file a written declaration to be considered for jury service. Taylor argued that this exclusion deprived him of his constitutional right to a fair trial by a jury that represents a cross-section of the community.

The Supreme Court held that the Louisiana jury-selection system, which led to a significant underrepresentation of women on jury venires, violated Taylor's Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment rights to an impartial jury trial. The Court reasoned that the jury-selection system must not systematically exclude any distinctive group in the community, including women, who constituted 53% of eligible jurors in the area in question.

The Court rejected the argument that Taylor, a male, lacked standing to object to the exclusion of women from his jury. It cited precedent that allowed defendants to challenge the exclusion of groups from jury service even if they themselves were not members of the excluded group.

The Court also dismissed the notion that women's distinctive roles in society justified their systematic exclusion from jury service. It stated that exemptions could be made for individuals based on hardship or critical occupations, but not for an entire class based on gender.

The Court emphasized that while juries actually chosen do not need to perfectly mirror the community, the pools from which juries are drawn must not exclude distinctive groups and must be representative of the community.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Louisiana Supreme Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, establishing that the exclusion of women from jury service on a systematic basis is unconstitutional.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eastern District of Kentucky ruled that Kentucky's law requiring health insurers to select "any willing provider" to participate in a health benefit plan is not pre-empted by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). The court held that the "basic test" is whether a law is "checking points" or "guideposts" in the insurance industry. The court found that the law "relates" to the "business of health insurance" and is therefore saved from preemption by  1144(a) of the federal law. The Court also held that it is not a matter of common sense that a state law requiring a health insurer to select a "willing provider" is a "law" that is "regulat[e]" by the law of insurance. In a separate opinion, the court held, however, that the AWP laws do not apply to state laws requiring insurance companies to use a "qualified provider" for certain medical services. The AWP law requires a health insurance company to select any "willing" provider who is willing to meet the terms and conditions for participation established by the health insurer, including the Kentucky state Medicaid program and Medicaid partnerships. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the insurers, holding that the state law does not apply because it does not require a health care provider to be a " participating primary chiropractor." The court also ruled that the laws are not a "guidepost" to insurance companies.

Petitioner Greenlaw, a member of a gang that controlled the sale of crack cocaine in a Minneapolis neighborhood, was convicted of various offenses relating to drugs and firearms. He appealed urging, inter alia, that his sentence was unreasonably long. After rejecting all of Greenlaw’s arguments, the Court of Appeals determined, without Government invitation, that the applicable law plainly required a prison sentence 15 years longer than the term the trial court had imposed. Accordingly, the appeals court ordered Greenlaw to increase his sentence to 622 months. Held: The sentence should not have been increased. Pp. 5–7. (a) In the adversary system, in the first instance and on appeal, courts rely on the parties to frame the issues for decision and assign to courts the role of neutral arbiter of matters the parties present. To the extent courts have approved departures from the party presentation principle in criminal cases, the justification has usually been to protect a pro se litigant's rights. See Castro v. United States, 540 U. S. 375, 381–383. But as a general rule, “[o]ur adversary system is designed around the premise that the parties know what is best for them, and are responsible for advancing the facts and arguments entitling them to a sentence higher than the one imposed.” United States v. Rivera, 411 F. 3d 864, 867. Congress has provided a dispositive direction regarding sentencing errors that aggrieve the Government. In §3742(b), Congress designated leading Department of Justice officers as decisionmakers responsible for determining when Government pursuit of a sentencing appeal is in order. Those high officers, Congress recognized, are best equipped to determine where their interest lies. Thus, when a defendant is charged in the same indictment with more than one offense qualifying for punishment under §924(c), all convictions after the first rank as “second or subsequent,” see id., at 132–137, the court may vacate the entire sentence on all counts so that, on remand, a trial court can reconfigure the sentencing plan to assure that it remains adequate to satisfy the sentencing factors. In remanded cases, however, a court of appeals, on its own initiative, increases the sentence absent a cross-appeal by the Government? In response, the Government “agree[d] with [Greenlaw] that the court erred in sU. S.-Courtsonte remanding the case with directions to enhance petitioner’’sentence”s sentence. At sentencing, the District Court rejected the Government's argument, holding that a §9 24(c) conviction does not count as a second or subsequent when it is “charged in [the] same indictment” as the defendant‘s first §925(c). The Eighth Circuit denied rehearing without an opinion. The court instructed the court to impose the 25-year mandatory minimum sentence of 25 years. The appeals court instructed that the sentence be increased. The District Court vacated the sentence and instructed the Court “to impose the [statutorily mandated] consecutive minimum sentence.’ ” Id., at 608–609. The Court then ordered the trial to impose a 5-year sentence in accord with the sentence Greenlaw received. The Government then urged that Greenlaw's sentence should be increased, but the Eighth Circuit held that it had discretion to raise and correct the error on its initiative. The Ninth Circuit affirmed. The judgment is vacated, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit ruled that a union's picketing of a Dallas-area general contractor violated federal antitrust laws. The court held that the contractor's refusal to sign a subcontracting agreement with the union was a legitimate union interest that was exempt from federal antitrust law. The union, Local 100 of the United Association of Journeymen and Apprentices of the Plumbing and Pipefitting Industry, also argued that federal labor regulation pre-empts state law. Local 100 is the bargaining representative for workers in the Dallas area in the plumbing and mechanical trades. The 5th Circuit agreed with the lower court's finding that the agreement was exempt because it was authorized by the construction industry proviso to Section 8(e) of the National Labor Relations Act, 49 Stat. 452, as added, 73 Stat.543, 29 U. S.C.  158(e), and was therefore invalid. The case is being appealed.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California today entered a temporary restraining order against a defendant in a defamation action brought by a now-deceased public figure.  The SEC's complaint alleges that Ulysses "Ulysses" Tory, while claiming falsely that Cochran owed him money, had complained to the local bar association, had written Cochran threatening letters demanding $10 million, had picketed Cochran's office holding up signs containing various insults and obscenities; and, with a group of associates, had pursued Cochran while chanting similar threats and insults.  According to the complaint, the court found that Tory violated the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws, including Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and that, in violation of Section 13(b)(5) of Exchange Act Rule 13b2-1 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the First Amendment and orders them to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties equal to the amount of their profits.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  On May 24, 2018, the U. S. District Judge in the District of Columbia issued an emergency judgment against Tory, ordering him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000, and ordering a hearing on May 25, 2018 to determine whether to issue a permanent injunction.  To determine the appropriate amount of the civil penalty, the SEC also issued an order requiring the defendants to provide a copy of the judgment to the court in which the judgment was issued.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 13-cv-5221 (1958).  The court also granted the SEC the right to substitute Sylvia Dale Mason Cochran for Johnnie Cochran as a defendant.

In Bates v. State Bar of Arizona, 433 U. S. 350, this Court held that truthful advertising of "routine" legal services is protected by the First and Fourteenth Amendments against blanket prohibition by a State. Held: In-person solicitation of clients-at the hospital room or the accident site, or in any other situation that breeds undue influence-by attorneys or their agents or "runners" is not constitutionally protected. Bates, supra, at 384, distinguished. Pp. 488-481. (a) In-Person solicitation by a lawyer of remunerative employment is a business transaction in which speech is an essential but subordinate component. While this does not remove the speech from the protection of the First Amendment, as was held in Bates and Virginia Pharmacy Board v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council, 425 U.S. 748, it lowers the level of appropriate judicial scrutiny. P. 489. (b) The State has a legitimate and indeed "compelling" interest in preventing those aspects of solicitation that involve fraud, undue influence, intimidation, overreaching, and other forms of "vexatious conduct." Bates, ante, p. 498. (c) In the absence of explicit proof or findings of harm or injury, appellant's conduct is subject to regulation in furtherance of important state interests. Bates is distinguished from Bates. The State does not lose its power to regulate commercial activity deemed harmful to the public whenever speech is a component of that activity. The fact that nothing less than actual proved harm to the solicited individual would be a sufficiently important state interest to justify disciplining the attorney who solicits employment in person for pecuniary gain does not detract from the force of the other interests the ban continues to serve. Id., at 496. (d) In addition to the State's general interest in protecting consumers and regulating commercial transactions, the State bears a special responsibility for maintaining standards among members of the licensed professions. Bates was not a strictly ethical rule, but rather a prophylactic regulation of commercial activity that is necessary to protect the public from harmful solicitation by lawyers whom it has licensed. Id. At the same time, it is not unreasonable, or violative of the Constitution, for a State to respond with what in effect is a "prophylactical rule." Id. at 498-481, where the State has an interest in preserving the public's free flow of commercial information, and where it has a strong interest in adopting and enforcing rules of conduct designed to protect that activity, as does the strength of its countervailing interest in prohibition. Id, at 495. P p. 475. (e) The state interests implicated in this case are particularly strong. The interest of the State in safeguarding consumers and regulates commercial transactions is a subject only marginally affected with First Amendment concerns, and it falls within the proper sphere of economic and professional regulation. Moreover, it has never been deemed an abridgment of freedom of speech or press to make a course of conduct illegal merely because the conduct was in part initiated, evidenced, or carried out by means of language, either spoken, written, or printed. Nor can appellant compare his solicitation to the mutual assistance in asserting legal rights that was at issue in United Transportation Union v. Michigan Bar, 401 U. 576, or corporate proxy statements, Mills v. Electric Auto-Lite Co., 396 U. s. 375, or Mills' threats of retaliation for the labor activities of employees, NLRB v. Gissel Packing Co., 395 U S. 575, or employers' threats to retaliate for the employee's labor activities. Id . . . The State's interest in avoiding harm by prohibiting solicitation in circumstances where it is likely to occur is especially great since lawyers are essential to the primary governmental function of administering justice, and have historically been "officers of the courts." Goldfarb v. Va State Bar, 421 U. . 773, 792, and there is no opportunity for intervention or counter-education by agencies of the Bar, supervisory authorities, or persons close to the solicitited individual. Id.. at 497. Id,. at 499-481; id., at 482. Pc. 496-481 . (f) Appellant's concession that strong state interests justify regulation to prevent the evils he enumerates would end this case but for his insistence that none of those evils was found to be present in his acts of solicitation. If appellant's view were sustained, he would be virtually immune to effective oversight and regulation by the State or by the legal profession, while allowing modes of regulation that might be impermissible in the realm of noncommercial expression. Id,, at 439-443, and because no allegations or findings were made of the specific wrongs appellant concedes would justify disciplinary action, appellant terms his solicitation "pure," meaning "soliciting and obtaining agre ments from Carol McClintock and Wanda Lou Holbert to represent each of them," without more

On June 25, 1982, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York entered a final judgment against a group of school board members who sought to remove books from high school and junior high school libraries.  According to the court's order, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, the Board of Education, in 1975, ordered that certain books be removed from school libraries in order to "prescribe what shall be orthodox in politics, nationalism, religion, or other matters of opinion."  The order also ordered that the books be returned to the school library.  The court found that, contrary to the Board's representations, the books were "objectionable" and "improper fare for school students," and that the Board "did not undertake an independent review of other books in the school libraries."  In a parallel action, the District Court issued a judgment in favor of the Board, finding that it had exercised its discretion in violation of the First Amendment.  In its judgment, the court held that, in exercising its discretion to remove the books from school library shelves, the board violated the First and Second Amendment rights of the students.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the order, the school board agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating these provisions, and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $100,000, a $50,000 civil penalty, and a $25,000 officer and director bar.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against a New Jersey man accused of purchasing and selling cocaine from confidential informants.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that, in a scheme to buy and sell the illegal drug, Christopher J. Pyszka entered into a cooperating plea agreement in which he agreed to be permanently enjoined from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 5 of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The settlement is subject to court approval.  According to the complaint, the settlement was reached without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint.  In its order, the court granted the SEC's motion and departed below the statutory minimum for the purpose of imposing a 10-year minimum sentence. The SEC alleges that the settlement did not permit the District Court to depart below any statutory minimum, and instead required the court to impose a sentence below a statutory minimum. The court ultimately agreed to the settlement.  On May 17, 2018, the Honorable Timothy J. Mascianica of the United States District Court for the Northern District of California entered a final judgment that permanently enjoins the defendants from future violations of the federal securities laws and orders the defendants to pay a civil penalty of 10 years' imprisonment.

After being convicted of filing false tax returns, petitioner Nieder challenged the sufficiency of the evidence presented at his jury trial. His challenge was based on the District Court's failure to give the jury an instruction on materiality, an element of the offense. The Court of Appeals ultimately affirmed the conviction, ruling that the jury-instruction error was harmless. However, the court vacated the conviction on the ground that the District Court had committed reversible error by giving the jury an instruction on the tax obligation that contained no mention of materiality. Held: 1. The District Court's failure to submit the element of materiality to the jury with respect to the tax charges was harmless error. This Court has repeatedly stated that the harmfulness of a nonconstitutional error depends on whether the error is prejudicial to the accused. Apollo Marine Corp. v. Runbeck Marine Servs., Inc., 433 U. S. 518, 523. Here, the record demonstrates that the error was harmless. The District Court's failure to submit the element of materiality to the jury was not prejudicial because the evidence of materiality was overwhelming. Even assuming that the error was prejudicial, the error was harmless because the jury's verdict necessarily included a finding on the materiality issue. Certiorari granted; 159 F. 3d 1279, affirmed in part and reversed in part.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of South Dakota ruled that the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribal Court had jurisdiction to hear a discrimination claim against a non-Indian bank that sold fee land to non- Indian customers. The court held that the tribal court had jurisdiction because the bank's sale of the land was in violation of the terms of the lease agreement and the lease itself. The tribal court also ruled in favor of the Indian couple who had defaulted on their loans to the bank, finding that the bank had violated their rights to due process and the right to a fair hearing. The appeals court concluded that the tribe's ruling was consistent with the findings of the federal district court in the case and that the court lacked jurisdiction.

Johnston pleaded guilty to knowing possession of a firearm by a person who had been convicted of a felony involving the use or threatened use of physical force, in violation of 18 U. S. C. §922(g)(9). He admitted that he knew he was prohibited from owning guns due to his 2003 Florida battery conviction, which involved unwanted physical touching. His preconviction release conditions included restrictions on gun ownership. After finding him guilty, the District Court applied the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) enhancement provisions, concluding that his battery conviction qualified as a “violent felony” under §924(e)(2)(B)(i), which lists “offense[s] that have as an element the use or attempted use of physical force,” among others. On appeal, the Eleventh Circuit agreed, rejecting Johnston’s claim that his battery conviction could not be considered a “violent felony” because it lacked the requisite violent force. Held: 1. The ACCA applies to Johnston’s battery conviction. Pp. 3−7. (a) The ACCA enhances penalties for defendants who have been convicted of a “violent felony” and later receive a subsequent federal firearm offense conviction. To qualify as a “violent felony,” an offense must meet four criteria: (1) it must be punishable by imprisonment for at least three years; (2) it must be punishable by imprisonment for at least two years or contain a fine of $10,000 or both; (3) it must be punishable by imprisonment for at least ten years or contain a fine of $250,000 or both; and (4) it must fall within one of six categories of offenses, including “offense[s] that have as an element the use or attempted use of physical force,” 18 U.S.C. §924(e)(2)(B)(i). Pp. 3−4. (b) Whether an offense falls within the last category depends on whether it has as an element “the use or attempted use of physical force,” or “burglary,” “extortion,” “arson,” “motor vehicle theft,” or “other felony,” each of which is described as presenting a serious potential risk of physical injury to another. §924(e)(2)(B)(ii). Pp. 4−5. (c) Johnston’s battery conviction satisfies the second criterion for a “violent felony” because it is punishable by imprisonment for at least two years. P. 5. (d) The fourth criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least ten years. P. 5. (e) The fifth criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least three years. P. 5. (f) The sixth criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least two years or contains a fine of $10,000 or both. P. 5. (g) The seventh criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least ten years or contains a fine of $250,000 or both. P. 5. (h) The eighth criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least three years. P. 5. (i) The ninth criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least two years or contains a fine of $10,000 or both. P. 5. (j) The tenth criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least ten years or contains a fine of $250,000 or both. P. 5. (k) The eleventh criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least three years. P. 5. (l) The twelfth criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least two years or contains a fine of $10,000 or both. P. 5. (m) The thirteenth criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least ten years or contains a fine of $250,000 or both. P. 5. (n) The final criterion is met because his conviction is punishable by imprisonment for at least three years. P. 5. (o) Thus, Johnston’s battery conviction qualifies as a “violent felony” under §924(e)(2)(B)(i). P. 5. 2. Interpreting §924(e)(2)(B)(i) to require violent force will not undermine the Government’s ability to enforce the firearm disability in §922(g)(9) for persons who previously have been convicted of a “misdemeanor crime of domestic violence,” which is defined to include certain misdemeanor offenses that have, “as an element, the use or attempted use of physical force . . . ,” §921(a)(33)(A)(ii). The Government’s assertions are unfounded. First, this Court has already interpreted the phrase “physical force” only in the context of a statutory definition of “violent felony.” See, e.g., Nijhawan v. Holder, 557 U. S. ___, ___. Second, the Government has not decided what the phrase “physical force” means in the context of defining a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. Third, the Government’s predictions about the impact of this Court’s ruling on removing aliens convicted of a “crime of domestic violence” are exaggerated. Fourth, the Government’s claims about the practical effects of this Court’s ruling are unpersuasive. Fifth, the Government’s request to remand to the Eleventh Circuit for its consideration of whether Johnston’s battery conviction is a “violent felony” within the meaning of the so-called “residual clause” in §924(e)(2)(B)(ii) is declined. Pp. 5−10. 528 F. 3d 1298, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

In the case involving Alex Blueford, the Supreme Court addressed whether the Double Jeopardy Clause prevents Blueford from being retried on charges of capital and first-degree murder after a mistrial was declared due to a deadlocked jury. The jury had initially reported unanimous votes against guilt on the charges of capital murder and first-degree murder, was deadlocked on manslaughter, and had not voted on negligent homicide. The trial court instructed the jury to continue deliberations, but they remained deadlocked, leading to a mistrial.

Blueford argued that he could not be retried for capital and first-degree murder because the jury had effectively acquitted him of those charges. The Court disagreed, stating that the jury's report was not a final resolution and lacked the finality necessary to constitute an acquittal. The Court emphasized that the jury was free to reconsider the greater offenses even after considering lesser ones, and the foreperson's report before the end of deliberations did not have the finality required for an acquittal.

Furthermore, the Court rejected Blueford's argument that the trial court should have taken action to allow the jury to give effect to their votes against capital and first-degree murder before considering a mistrial on the remaining charges. The Court held that it has never required a trial court to consider specific means of breaking a jury impasse before declaring a mistrial.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Supreme Court of Arkansas, ruling that the Double Jeopardy Clause does not prevent Blueford from being retried on the same offenses after the jury failed to reach a verdict and a mistrial was declared.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Kentucky today entered final judgments against Kentucky and Kentucky in favor of capital punishment.  The court entered a final judgment that permanently enjoins the states from executing capital criminals with the option of using a blood pressure cuff or eKG as the sole method of execution.  According to the court's order, Kentucky's decision to adhere to its protocol was based on a desire to find a more humane alternative to then-existing methods of executing criminals.  In addition, the court found that, in moving to capital punishment, Kentucky had not shown sufficient evidence to support the safety of administering the first and third drugs before the first drug was administered.  As the court previously ruled against capital punishment in the United States, the Court found that Kentucky violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The court also ruled against Kentucky in a parallel action.  Without admitting or denying the Court's findings, Kentucky has agreed to permanently enjoin it from future violations of the federal securities laws, and to pay a civil penalty of $1,000,000.  Kentucky has also agreed to a temporary restraining order prohibiting it from executing criminals without a reasonable explanation for the risks of an anesthetic response. The Court also agreed that Kentucky has to adopt a "best practices" protocol for executing criminals, which, in its opinion, is inconsistent with the federal law.  On May 2, 2019, the Honorable Judge Steven J. Denno of the U. S. District court for the Southern District of New York granted the court’s order against Kentucky.

During respondent Mirzayance’s first-degree murder trial, he entered pleas of not guilty and not guilty by reason of insanity (NGI). Under California law, when both of these pleas are entered, the court must hold a bifurcated trial, with guilt determined during the first phase and the viability of the defendant’S NGI plea during the second. The trial judge set the NGI phase to begin the day after the conviction was entered but, on the advice of counsel, abandoned his plea before it commenced. The California trial court denied the petition and the California Court of Appeal affirmed without offering any reason for its rejection of this particular ineffective assistance claim. The District Court reversed the District Court and ordered an evidentiary hearing on the basis of the Court of Appeals’ remand order, which it described as requiring an examination of the “counsel [s] reason for abandoning the insanity defense,” rather than as mandating that the district court must find deficient performance if it found counsel had “nothing to lose” by pursuing the insanity-defense. The court also affirmed the finding of deficient performance. Held: The state court’d decision to deny the ineffective-assistance claim did not violate clearly established federal law. Pp. 5–11. (a) The state-court decision to grant habeas corpus relief did not constitute an unreasonable application of clearly established Federal law. The State Supreme Court has never established anything akin to the Court’ “Nothing to Lose” standard for evaluating Strickland v. Washington, 466 U. S. 668, which held that a state court had not “unreasonabl[y] appli[ed] clearly established” Federal law when it declined to apply its precedent concerning spectator conduct at trial, id., at 76–77. In this case, the Magistrate Judge found that the Magistrates’ decision was carefully weighed and not made rashly, and that counsel made a carefully reasoned decision not to go forward with the defense. He also found that counsel had not made a true tactical choice based on its view that counsel was deficient by dropping the insanity Defense. The Court also found prejudice because, in its view, the parents “conveyed the same sense as a refusal.” Id., at 144. To prevail on his ineffective-assault-of-counsels claim, the state court must show, therefore, that there is a “reasonable probability” that he would have prevailed on his insanity defense had he pursued it. This Court has repeatedly applied that standard to evaluate ineffective-Assistance-ofcouns claims where there is no other Supreme Court precedent directly on point. See Yarborough v. Alvarado, 541 U.S. 652, 664. The question “is not whether a federal court believes the State court's determination” under the Stricklands standard “was incorrect but whether that determination was unreasonable—a substantially higher threshold.’” Schriro, supra, at 473. Because the Strrickland standard is a general standard, a State court has even more latitude to reasonably determine that a defendant has not satisfied that standard. See, e.g., Yarborough, supra. And, because the State Court has not established any Supreme Court decision establishing a ‘nothing-to- lose’ standard, this Court has also never established any such standard for assessing Stricklanders claims. See Wright v. Van Patten, 552 U. . ___, ___, ___. And the Court has held on numerous occasions that it is not ‘an unreasonable application’ for a State Court to decline to apply a specific legal rule that has not been squarely established by this Court. Here, the relevant state court decision is the California Supreme Court. The relevant State-Court decision is that of the California court denying state-hbeas relief. The Magistrate Court‘s finding that the parents indicated a strong disinclination to testify amounted to refusal is equivalent to finding that counsel is deficient by declining to pursue a strategy that is nothing to lose from pursuit of that strategy. Case Name: Zelman v. Simmons-Hausley
Case Number: 02-1393
Issue: Does the Ohio voucher program violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment?
Opinion Author: John Roberts
Date Decided: June 28, 2002
Summary: The Supreme Court ruled in a 5-4 decision that the Ohio voucher program, which provides taxpayer-funded scholarships to help low-income students attend private schools, does not violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. The Court held that the program is neutral towards religion and does not favor one religion over another. The Court also found that the program does not result in the government establishing a religion or promoting religious beliefs. However, the Court warned that the program must be carefully monitored to ensure that it remains neutral and does not result in religious discrimination.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant who was convicted of first-degree murder in a civil trial.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New Orleans, alleges that, on August 27, 1996, Jeffrey Brooks of New Orleans and his wife, Elaine Scott, were questioned by a jury of 13 potential jurors in the course of conducting a jury trial. According to the complaint, the jury selection process began on the morning of the trial. The complaint alleges that Mr. Brooks, who was a self-employed general contractor, opened the driver's side door of Wilson’s car and repeatedly stabbed the occupants, killing Wilson and wounding Scott. The SEC alleges that the jury deliberated for almost an hour and a half before finding Mr.Brooks guilty of the charges and ordering him to be permanently enjoined from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 17(a)(1) of Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 17a-3 thereunder. Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The court also granted the SEC the right to conduct a parallel criminal investigation.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana today announced criminal charges against Brooks.  On August 31, 2017, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against Brooks, seeking a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and an officer-and-director bar against him from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney. The case was supervised by Chedly C. Dumornay, Chief of the SEC Enforcement Division's Criminal Division.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit has ruled that a Texas woman who signed a "chattel mortgage" on her husband's destroyed business is not liable for a federal loan. The court held that Texas law requires a married woman to obtain a court order removing her disability to contract before she can bind her property. In this case, the court held, however, that the woman had not complied with the terms of the loan, which included the requirement that she sign a note in the amount of $12,000, payable to the order of the Small Business Administration in Dallas at the rate of $120 per month including 3% interest. The loan was made after the business was damaged in a May 1957 flood in Lampasas, Texas, and the loan officer determined that the loan would be made upon the business's compliance with certain requirements, including that Mrs. Yazell had not signed the note and that the firm had been retained by the SBA to assist her in complying with the loan terms. The Court held that the Texas law requiring the woman to sign the note did not apply to the loan because she had not obtained a court-ordered order to remove her disability before signing the note, and that she was not a "covered person" under Texas law, which requires a person to sign a mortgage before a loan can be made. The ruling is the latest in a long line of court decisions that have found that the federal government cannot be held liable for loans made to individuals. The case is a reminder of the need to balance the federal and state laws in our complex federal system.

After respondent Leon's home was burglarized, a detective submitted to a magistrate an affidavit stating that he had reason to believe that respondent had stolen certain property from the victims. The affidavit contained detailed descriptions of the property and stated that it was valued at $1,000. The magistrate issued a warrant authorizing a search of respondent's home. Upon searching the home, the detectives found a television set worth about $1,000 hidden behind a bookcase. They took the set back to the station and placed it in a locked storage room pending identification of the owner. Subsequent to the discovery of the set, the detectives received a call from a person claiming to be the owner of the set. The caller identified himself as a man named James and claimed that he owned the set and that it had been taken from his home. The detectives went to James' home and asked him to identify the set. He did so, and the detectives took the set back to the station and placed it in the same storage room as the first set. Later, the detectives interviewed James and he confirmed ownership of the second set. At the time of the interview, the detectives had not yet identified the owner of the first set. Ultimately, the detectives decided that the first set belonged to respondent. The detectives then went to respondent's home and confronted him with the second set. He confessed to having stolen the first set and acknowledged that he had sold it to someone else. However, he denied stealing the second set. The detectives then arrested respondent and brought him to the station. While being interrogated, respondent signed a written statement acknowledging that he stole the first set and confessing to receiving money for it. The detectives then read respondent Miranda warnings, and he agreed to cooperate fully with the authorities. He then gave the detectives permission to search his home and allowed them to remove the second set. The detectives then opened the storage room and removed the first set. The detectives then arrested James and brought him to the station. He was given Mirandaw arnings and confessed to having stolen the first set. Both respondents were then indicted for theft. Prior to trial, the Federal District Court granted respondents' pretrial motion to exclude the fruits of the search of their homes, holding that the search was unconstitutional because the warrant was not supported by probable cause. The Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the warrant should not have issued. Held: The exclusionary rule does not apply to the fruits of a search conducted pursuant to a warrant that was supported by probable cause but was later invalidated by a magistrate's subsequent determination that the warrant was not supported by probable cause. Pp. 38-48. (a) The exclusionary rule applies to the fruits of a search conducted pursuant to a warrant that was supported by probable cause but was later invalidated by a magistrate's subsequent determination that the warrant was not supported by probable cause only if the officers were dishonest or reckless in preparing their affidavits or could not have harbored an objectively reasonable belief in the existence of probable cause. Here, the officers' reliance on the magistrate's determination of probable cause was objectively reasonable, and application of the extreme sanction of exclusion is inappropriate. Pp. 40-48. (b) Application of the exclusionary rule in cases where officers have relied on a subsequently invalidated search warrant will only rarely be justified by the fact that the officers were dishonest or reckless in preparing their affidavits or could not have harbored an objectively reasonable belief in the existence of probable cause. Such applications will seldom further the purposes of the exclusionary rule. Pp. 40-48. 664 F. 2d 1234, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit granted leave to appeal the conviction of a Georgia man charged with possession of obscene matter. The case centers on whether the state's obscenity statute, insofar as it punishes private possession of the material, violates the First Amendment right to freedom of speech and press. The court agreed with the lower court that the law does not violate appellant's First Amendment rights. The lower court's decision in favor of the state was not supported by the facts of the case. In a dissent, the court ruled that the state had not proved its case that appellant intended to use the material for the purpose of selling, exposing, or circulating it. The 11th Court agreed, and granted leave for appellant to file an appeal. The full court will consider the appeal when it convenes in January 2015 for a hearing.

In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that Jewish individuals can bring a lawsuit against non-Jewish defendants for damages caused by acts of vandalism committed with anti-Semitic motives. This ruling overturned previous decisions that found that Jews could not file such suits due to their lack of status as a separate race. The court determined that Section 1982 of the US Code, which prohibits racially discriminatory interference with property rights, applies equally to attacks based on religious beliefs.

The Illinois Supreme Court reversed a lower court's dismissal of a fraud complaint against two for-profit fundraising corporations. The complaint alleged that the defendants defrauded members of the public by falsely representing that "a significant amount of each dollar donated would be paid over to [the veterans organization] for its [charitable] purposes while in fact the [fundraisers] knew that ... 15 cents or less of every dollar would be available" for those purposes. The Illinois Attorney General's office filed a complaint against the defendants, Telemarketing Associates, Inc. and Armet Inc., in 1991, alleging that they retained 85 percent of the gross receipts from donors within Illinois, leaving 15 percent for the charity. The lower court dismissed the complaint, finding that the allegations were not supported by the facts of the case. The high court held that the complaint could not survive a motion to dismiss because it alleged that Telemarketers had violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the U.S.

When petitioners Epstein Yardin et al. (hereinafter EPJ Fund) moved to have their proposed class certified under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(b)(3) in a securities fraud action against respondents Halliburton Co. and its CEO, the District Court denied certification, concluding that EPJ Fund had failed to satisfy the “general requirements” for class actions set forth in Rule 23(a) and that it could not proceed as a class action under Rule 23(b)(3) because circuit precedent required securities fraud plaintiffs to prove “loss causation” in order to obtain class certification. The Fifth Circuit affirmed. Held: Securities fraud plaintiffs do not need to prove loss causation in order to obtain class certification. Pp. 4−10. (a) The sole dispute here is whether EPJ Fund met the prerequisite of Rule 23(b)(3) for obtaining class certification. That provision authorizes district courts to certify classes where the questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members, and where a class action is superior to other available methods for adjudicating the controversy. Considering whether “questions of law or fact common to class members predominate” begins with the elements of the underlying cause of action. Here, the elements of a private securities fraud claim based on violations of §10(b) and Rule 10b–5 are: “‘(1) a material misrepresentation or omission by the defendant; (2) scienter; (3) a connection between the misrepresentation or omission and the purchase or sale of a security; (4) reliance upon the misrepresentation or omission; (5) economic loss; and (6) loss causation.’ ” Matrixx Initiatives, Inc. v. Siracusano, 563 U.S. ___, ___. Whether common questions of law or fact predominate often turns on the element of reliance. Reliance by the plaintiff upon the defendant’s deceptive acts is an essential element of a private cause of action, Basic Inc. v. Levinson, 485 U.S. 224, 243, and the most direct way a plaintiff can demonstrate reliance is by showing that he was aware of a company’s statement and engaged in a relevant transaction based on that specific misrepresentation. But Basic permitted plaintiffs to invoke a rebuttable presumption of reliance based on the “fraud-on-the-market” theory, which posits that the market price of shares traded on well-developed markets reflects all publicly available information, including any material misrepresentations, and thus an investor relies on public misstatements whenever he buys or sells stock at the market price. Basic, supra, at 246. The Court also made clear that the presumption was just that, and could be rebutted by appropriate evidence. Id., at 248. Pp. 4−6. (b) The Fifth Circuit erroneously required EPJ Fund to establish loss causation at the certification stage to “trigger the fraud-on-the-market presumption.” 597 F.3d 334, 335. Loss causation addresses a matter different from whether an investor relied on a misrepresentation, presumptively or otherwise, when buying or selling a stock. An inability to prove loss causation would not prevent a plaintiff from invoking the rebuttable presumption of reliance. Such a rule contravenes Basic’s fundamental premise—that an investor presumptively relies on a misrepresentation so long as it was reflected in the market price at the time of his transaction. The fact that a subsequent loss may have been caused by factors other than the revelation of a misrepresentation has nothing to do with whether an investor relied on the misrepresentation in the first place, either directly or presumptively through the fraud-on-the-market theory. Loss causation has no logical connection to the facts necessary to establish the efficient market predicate to the fraud-on-the-market theory. Pp. 6−9. (c) Contrary to respondents’ argument, the Fifth Circuit did not use the term “loss causation” interchangeably with the term “price impact,” which simply refers to the effect of a misrepresentation on a stock price. Although the Fifth Circuit’s opinion may contain some language consistent with a “price impact” approach, the Court takes the Fifth Circuit at its word. Pp. 9−10. Vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court.

The Supreme Court ruled that when a person is arrested in an automobile, the police have the right to search the entire vehicle, including the passenger compartment, as part of the search incident to the arrest. The decision was based on the idea that the arrestee may still have access to weapons or evidence in the vehicle, and that the search is necessary to ensure public safety.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the liability of parties under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) for environmental contamination at a site in Arvin, California. The case involves Brown & Bryant, Inc. (B&B), an agricultural chemical distribution business, which operated on land partly owned by railroad companies and purchased chemicals from Shell Oil Company.

The main legal questions were whether Shell could be held liable as an "arranger" for disposal of hazardous substances under CERCLA and whether the railroad companies could be held jointly and severally liable for the entire cleanup cost.

The Supreme Court found that Shell was not liable as an arranger because it did not intend for the chemicals to be disposed of during the transfer process to B&B. Shell's knowledge of incidental spills during delivery and its efforts to encourage safe handling were not sufficient to establish intent to dispose of the chemicals.

Regarding the railroad companies, the Court determined that the harm caused by the contamination was divisible and could be apportioned. The District Court had reasonably calculated the railroad companies' share of the cleanup costs at 9%, based on the proportion of land they owned, the duration of B&B's operation on their land, and the types of chemicals spilled. The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision that had held the railroad companies jointly and severally liable for the entire cost.

The Supreme Court's decision clarifies the scope of arranger liability under CERCLA and supports the use of apportionment in determining the liability of multiple parties for environmental contamination when there is a reasonable basis for doing so. The ruling has implications for how companies manage the sale and transfer of hazardous substances and for the financial responsibility of landowners in cases of environmental contamination.

Petitioner Northern Insurance Company of New York (Northern) filed suit against respondent Chatham County, Georgia (County), in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Georgia, seeking damages resulting from an alleged tort committed by employees of the County. The District Court granted the County’s motion for summary judgment on the ground that the suit was barred by sovereign immunity. The County conceded that Eleventh Amendment immunity did not extend to counties, but nonetheless contended that it was immune under “the universal rule of state immunity from suit without the state” in operating the drawbridge. Northern then sought to recover its costs by filing suit in admiralty against the County in the District Court. The county sought summary judgment, arguing that its claims were barred by the sovereign immunity of States from suit, and that the County did not qualify as an arm of the State. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed. The Court of Appeals acknowledged that, under Circuit precedent, the County was not entitled to immunity, but acknowledged that it did not assert an Eleventh- Amendment immunity defense, which would fail because, under this Court’S sovereign immunity cases, respondent was not “an ‘arm of [the State’ for Eleventh] Amendment purposes.’ ” Zurich Ins. Co. v. Chatham Co., No. 04–13308, 1209. Held: 1. The residual immunity would serve to extend sovereign immunity beyond its preratification scope. Pp. 5–11. (a) The phrase “residual immunity’ … is convenient shorthand but something of a misnomer,” and this Court has resolved sovereign immunity questions in admiralalty by relying upon principles set out in this Court, rather than by examining the history or jurisprudence specific to suits in the area. In either case, it appears that residual immunity is a common-law immunity that has been unaltered by federal substantive law, see Brief for Respondent 18, or, as the Solicitor General appears to believe, a constitutionally based immunity that is distinguishable from the one drawn from the constitutional structure, see Tr. of Oral Arg. 16 (“What respondent calls residual sovereign immunity . . . is the doctrine of constitutional sovereign immunity”). The County has failed to demonstrate that it is acting as an “arm of” when it operated the Causton Bluff Bridge, and the County is therefore not entitled under the § 546 U. S. ___ judgment to immunity from Northern. P. 5. (b) This Court has decided sovereign immunity, like other sovereign immunity immunity, by relying on principles set forth in the Court's sovereign immunity case. See, e.g., Alden v. Maine, 527 U.S. 706, 713; Seminole Tribe v. Florida, 517 U. 44, 55–56; Principality of Monaco v. Mississippi, 292 U.

After filing his part-year resident income tax return claiming to be a Nevada citizen, respondent Hyatty filed suit in Nevada state court against petitioner California Franchise Tax Board (CFTB), asserting that CFTB had wrongfully audited him and collected money from him. At the time of the audit, respondent was living in California, but he later moved back to Nevada. Although acknowledging that it had waived its sovereign immunity from suit in state court, CFTB urged the court to refuse to hear the case under the doctrine of comity, which gives effect to the laws of another State out of deference and respect. It pointed to California’s grant of absolute immunity to itself from liability for torts committed by its tax collectors. The court agreed that comity demanded that it refrain from exercising its jurisdiction over the underlying negligence claim, but found that applying California’s immunity statute to the intentional tort claims would contravene Nevada’s policies and interests in protecting its citizens from injurious torts committed by sister States’ government employees. Accordingly, it allowed the intentional tort claims to go forward. Ultimately, the Nevada Supreme Court affirmed, concluding that “comity” favored California’s position, but that “principles of comity” required the lower court to decline jurisdiction over the intentional tort claims. Held: The Nevada Supreme Court correctly decided this case. Pp. 3–10. (a) Under the Full Faith and Credit Clause, a State need not “substitut[e] the statutes of other states for its own statutes dealing with a subject matter concerning which it is competent to legislate.” Pacific Employers Ins. Co.v .IndustrialAccidentComm’n, 306 U. S. 493, 501. Here, Nevada is clearly “competent to legislate,” since it has a significant interest in ensuring that its citizens are protected from injuries inflicted by sister States’ government employees. Thus, the State’s substantive law controls. Pp. 3–4. (b) Confronted with the question whether the Full Faith and Credit Clause requires a forum State to recognize a sister State’s legislatively recaptured immunity once before, this Court has previously held that the answer depends upon the respective sovereign interests at stake. Nevada v. Hall, 440 U. S. 410, 424, n. 24. That decision remains good law today. Even assuming that the Full Faith and Credit Clause requires a forum State to recognize a sister State’s legislatively recaptured immunity, the question here is whether the Clause demands that Nevada apply California’s immunity statute to avoid interference with California’s “sovereign responsibility” of enforcing its income tax laws. However, the Court declines to adopt petitioner’s proposed new rule, which would elevate California’s sovereignty interests above those of Nevada. Indeed, there is no constitutionally significant difference between the relationship between an automobile accident and educating, on the one hand, and the intrusion alleged here and collecting taxes, on the other. Nor is there any constitutionally significant difference between the burdens and expenses of out-of-state litigation and the diversion of state resources away from the performance of important state functions. Moreover, the Nevada Supreme Court sensitively applied principles of comity with a healthy regard for California’s sovereign status, relying on the contours of Nevada’s own sovereign immunity from suit as a benchmark for its analysis. Pp. 4–10. Affirmed.

Petitioner Snyder was convicted of first-degree murder in a Louisiana court and sentenced to death. The Louisiana Supreme Court affirmed Snyder’s conviction, rejecting his claim that the prosecution exercised some of its peremptory jury challenges based on race, in violation of Batson v. Kentucky, 476 U. S. 79 (1986). The trial court committed clear error in overruling Snyder‘s Batson objection with respect to Mr. Snyder, and the case was remanded for a nunc pro tunc determination of his competency to stand trial. Held: 1. The trial judge committed a clear error of overruling the Batson objections. Pp. 4–7. (a) The trial courts have a pivotal role in evaluating Batson claims. Step three of the B Watson inquiry involves an evaluation of the prosecutor’d credibility, see 476U. S., at 98, n. 21, and “the best evidence [of discriminatory intent] often will be the attorney who exercises the challenge.” Hernandez v. New York, 500 U.S. 352, 369. In addition, race-neutral reasons for peremotory challenges often invoke a juror’’ demeanor, making the trial court’re first-hand observations of even greater importance. In this situation, the trial must evaluate not only whether the prosecutor's demeanor belies a discriminatory intent, but also whether the juror can credibly be said to have exhibited the basis for the strike attributed to the jurors by the prosecutor. P. 5–6. (b) In this case, the jury found petitioner guilty of firstdegree murder and determined that he should receive the death penalty. On direct appeal, the court conditionally affirmed the conviction, but remanded the case for a Nunc pro nunc determination of the competency of Snyder. The State Supreme Court, however, reversed, holding that Batson was erroneous in its ruling on the issue of discriminatory intent. The Court of Appeals affirmed Snyder, 98–1078, and this Court remanded to Snyder for further consideration. The case is remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit recently ruled that a Pennsylvania law precluding employee welfare benefit plans from exercising subrogation rights on a claimant's tort recovery is not pre-empted by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) and therefore does not apply to FMC Corporation's self-funded health care plan. The case involves the daughter of FMC employee Gerald Holliday, who was seriously injured in an automobile accident in 1987 and who brought a negligence action against the driver of the vehicle in which she was injured. The Hollidays refused to reimburse FMC for the amounts it had paid for respondent's medical expenses. FMC then notified the Hollidays that it would seek reimbursement for those expenses, and they refused, saying that the law precludes subrogation by FMC. The Third Circuit's holding conflicts with decisions of other Courts of Appeals that have construed ERISA's deemer clause to protect self- funded plans from all state insurance regulation. The court held that "the law is not expressly stated in the law's language or implicitly contained in its structure or purpose." The court also held that the parties had not suggested that FMC should be required to comply with the law. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued a decision on the matter. The Court will decide whether the law preempts FMC's right to exercise subrogation on the Holliday case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reversed a lower court's decision granting summary judgment to The Investigator magazine and its publisher in a libel action brought by a public figure against The Investigator and The Investigator Publishing Co. The lower court had granted The Investigator's motion for summary judgment on the basis that the article's author and editor had not adequately verified the facts in the articles before publication. The court held that the author's thorough investigation and research and his reliance on numerous sources precluded a finding of actual malice. The appeals court disagreed, saying that there was sufficient evidence to support a finding that the articles were libelous and that the lower court should have granted the summary judgment motion. The Appeals Court held that, in this case, there was insufficient evidence for the summary judgement motion to be granted because the author and the editor had failed to adequately verify the facts before publication and the articles contained numerous inaccuracies. The Court also found that the trial court erred in denying summary judgment because it did not consider the author of the articles's affidavit detailing the sources for each of the statements alleged by respondents to be libelous. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a unanimous decision, agreed with the appeals court, and sent the case back for further consideration.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida today announced criminal charges against a Haitian citizen for driving under the influence of alcohol (DUI) and causing serious bodily injury, in violation of Florida law.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Miami, alleges that Josue Leocal, a resident of Haiti, violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 ("Securities Act") by driving while high on drugs.  According to the complaint, Leocal's DUI conviction rendered him ineligible for entry under the federal criminal code, and he was subsequently removed from the country.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney General's Office today announced that it filed a civil injunctive action against Leocal.  Leocal agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, the Honorable Joseph G. Sansone of the U. S. District Court for the Central District of New York has issued a temporary restraining order, ordering Leocal to surrender his passport, and ordering him to return to Haiti on a bifurcated basis.  On May 2, 2018, the U-S. District Judge in Miami issued an order finding that Leocal violated the federal anti-dumping laws and ordered him to comply with the court's order.

Respondents were fired from their jobs with a private drug rehabilitation organization because they ingested peyote for sacramental purposes at a ceremony of the Native American Church of which they are members. When respondents applied to petitioner Employment Division for unemployment compensation, they were determined to be ineligible for benefits because they had been discharged for work-related "misconduct."
