The Oregon Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the denial of benefits violated respondents' free exercise rights under the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment. The Oregon Supreme Court, however, reversed, concluding that the illegality of respondents' use was irrelevant to resolution of their constitutional claim. Held: 1. The free exercise Clause does not require that an individual's religious beliefs excuse him from compliance with an otherwise valid law prohibiting conduct that the State is free to regulate. Pp. 622-624. (a) The Free Exercise clause does not permit the State to deny unemployment benefits to persons dismissed from jobs because of such religiously inspired use. P. 623. (b) The First Amendment's protection of religious liberty does not preclude the State from excluding persons whose religious beliefs compelled them to refrain from work on other days, and thus permits the State's denial of unemployment benefits. The State's prohibition on the use of "controlled substance" as a drug is not prohibited by law, since the purpose of the provision under which respondents had been disqualified was not to enforce its criminal laws but to preserve the financial integrity of the compensation fund, and since that purpose was inadequate to justify the burden that disqualification imposed on respondents' religious practice. The fact that respondents' drug use was prohibited under Oregon law, and because that prohibition is constitutional, does not mean that the claim for a religious exemption must be evaluated under the balancing test set forth in Sherbert v. Verner, 374 U. S. 398, and Hobbie v. Unemployment Appeals Comm'n of Florida, 480 U.S. 136, is not a permissible reading of the text, since it must be applied across the board, to all actions thought to be religiously commanded. Moreover, if "compelling interest" really means what it says (and watering it down here would subvert its rigor in the other fields where it is applied), many laws will not meet the test. Nor is it possible to limit the impact of the test to the mere possession of religious convictions which contradict the relevant concerns of a political society, see, e.g., Palmore v. Sidoti, 466 U. s. 429, 432, or before the government may regulate the content of speech, see Sable Communications of California v. FCC, 492 U. States 115, 126. The Government's ability to enforce generally applicable prohibitions of socially harmful conduct, like its ability to carry out other aspects of public policy, "cannot depend on measuring the effects of a governmental action on a religious objector's spiritual development." Lyng v. Northwest Indian Cemetery Protective Assn., 485 US. 439, 108 S. C. 1425, 99 L. Ed. 2d 753, reversed.

An Illinois statute authorizes law enforcement officers to detain and search any person found on premises being searched pursuant to a search warrant, to protect themselves from attack or to prevent the disposal or concealment of anything described in the warrant. A police officer, acting on information received from an informer, obtained a search warrant authorizing the search of a tavern and the person of the bartender, whom the informer indicated would have heroin for sale. Upon entering the tavern, the officers announced their purpose and advised all those present that they were going to conduct a cursory search for weapons. One of the officers then patted down the pockets of the patrons, including respondent Ybarra, who was seated near the bar. During the first patdown, the officer felt something in Ybarra's pocket, removed it, and found some tinfoil packets containing heroin. Respondent was subsequently convicted of the unlawful possession of a controlled substance. Held: The searches of respondent and the seizure of what was in his pocket contravened the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 409-415. (a) Probable cause to search respondent was absent when the warrant was issued, and it remained absent when the police executed the warrant, since the officers knew nothing in particular about respondent, except that he was present, along with several other customers, in a public tavern at a time when the police had reason to believe that the bartender would have heroin for sale. Cf. Terry v. Ohio, 392 U. S. 1. Pp. 409-411. (b) The initial frisk of respondent was not supported by a reasonable belief that he was armed and presently dangerous, a belief which this Court has invariably held must form the predicate to a patdown of a person for weapons. Here, the officers neither recognized respondent as a person with a criminal history nor had any particular reason to believe that he might be inclined to assault them. Nor did respondent act in a manner that was threatening. Thus, the State is unable to articulate any specific fact that would have justified a police officer at the scene in even suspecting that respondent was armed and dangerous. Pp. 411-413. (c) The narrow scope of the Terry exception to the probable cause requirement does not permit a frisk for weapons on less than reasonable belief or suspicion directed at the person to be frisked, even though that person happens to be on premises where an authorized narcotics search is taking place. To hold otherwise would make the Terry exception virtually limitless. Pp. 413-414. (d) The Terry "reasonable belief or suspicion" standard cannot be applied to aid the evidence gathering function of the search warrant. While the State correctly points out that the ease with which the evidence of narcotics possession may be concealed or moved around from person to person creates an important governmental interest in effectively controlling traffic in dangerous, hard drugs, nevertheless, the long prevailing constitutional standard of probable cause embodies "'the best compromise that has been found for accommodating [the] often opposing interests" in safeguarding citizens from rash and unreasonable interference with privacy and in seeking to give fair leeway for enforcing the law in the community's protection.'" Pp. 414-415. 58 Ill. App. 3d 57, 373 N. E. 2d 1013, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of New York yesterday entered a final judgment in favor of the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Connecticut and the Federal Bureau of Investigation in connection with an international passenger's death.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, Dr. Abid Hanson and his wife, Rubina Husain, traveled with their children and another family from San Francisco to Athens and Cairo for a family vacation.  The complaint alleges that the flight attendant's refusal to reseat Dr. Hanson was unexpected and unusual in light of industry standards, Olympic policy, and the simple nature of the passenger's requested accommodation.  As alleged in the complaint, the airline's policies permitted smoking on international flights, but did not permit the airline to allow its passengers to smoke on flights.  In a parallel action, the U.N. Office of Health and Human Services today announced that it has issued an emergency alert warning passengers to be aware of the presence of cigarette smoke in the cabin of an international flight.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Hanson and Husain consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, civil penalties, and officer-and-director bars. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry.Â  The litigation will be led by Ms. Barry and Ms. Birkenheier.

Respondent, the Chicago Park District (Park District), is responsible for operating public parks and other public property in Chicago. Pursuant to its authority to establish by ordinance all needful rules and regulations for the government and protection of parks and property under its jurisdiction, 1505/7.02, the Park District adopted an ordinance requiring a person to obtain a permit in order to conduct a public assembly, parade, picnic, or other event involving more than fifty individuals, or engage in an activity such as creat[ing] or emitting any Amplified Sound. The ordinance provides that [a]pplications for permits shall be processed in order of receipt, C.5.a, and the park district must decide whether to grant or deny an application within 14 days unless, by written notice to the applicant, it extends the period an additional 14 days, C5.c. Applications can be denied on any of 13 specified grounds. The application for permit contains a material falsehood or misrepresentation; (1) the applicant is legally incompetent to contract or to sue and be sued; (2) the application has damaged Park District property on prior occasions and has not paid in full for such damage, or has other outstanding and unpaid debts; (3) an unsuccessful applicant has seven days to file a written appeal to the General Superintendent, who must act on the appeal within seven days, and a permit has been or will be granted to a prior applicant authorizing uses or activities which do not reasonably permit multiple occupancy of the particular park or part hereof; (4) the use or activity intended by the applicant would conflict with previously planned programs organized and conducted by the Park and previously scheduled for the same time and place, and (5) the proposed use would present an unreasonable danger to the health or safety of the applicant or other users of the park, of Park District Employees or of the public; (6) a fully executed prior application for a permit for the date and place has been received, and, where feasible, must propose measures to cure defects in the application. C. 5.e. When the basis for denial is prior receipt of a competing application, the permit must suggest alternative times or places. The Park District may also deny an applicant a permit if the application is not fully completed and executed; (7) when the application for the permit is incomplete or contains false or misrepresentations; when the applicant has damaged or damaged park District property and has paid for the damage; (8) when an application has been granted to an earlier applicant for a same time or place; or when the intended use would be an unreasonable risk to the Health or Safety of park users or Park District employees; or (9) when applicant has violated the terms of prior permits issued to or on behalf of applicant. Pp. 5-11. 227 F. 3d 921, affirmed.

The Supreme Court had to decide if Section 54(1) of the Michigan Campaign Finance Act, which prohibits corporations from using their general treasury funds for independent expenditures in state elections, was constitutional under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. The Michigan State Chamber of Commerce challenged the law, arguing it violated their rights to free speech and equal protection.

The Court held that the law is constitutional. It found that while the law does burden the Chamber's ability to express itself politically, this burden is justified by a compelling state interest: preventing corruption or the appearance of corruption in elections. The Court reasoned that corporations, due to their special legal and economic characteristics, can amass large amounts of wealth and potentially use this to gain an unfair advantage in the political process. The law is narrowly tailored to address this issue by allowing corporations to make political expenditures through segregated funds, which are made up of contributions specifically for political purposes.

The Court rejected the Chamber's argument that the law is overinclusive because it applies to all corporations, including those that do not have large treasuries. It also dismissed the Chamber's claim that the law is underinclusive because it does not regulate independent expenditures by labor unions and media corporations. The Court found that labor unions and media corporations are different from other corporations in ways that justify their exclusion from the law's restrictions.

Finally, the Court addressed the Chamber's Fourteenth Amendment claim, finding that the law's classifications are narrowly tailored to serve the compelling state interest of preventing corporate influence from distorting the political process. The exemption for media corporations was also upheld because of the unique role the press plays in democracy.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding the constitutionality of Section 54(1) of the Michigan Campaign Finance Act.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit reversed the conviction of a theater manager in Georgia for showing a porn film in a movie theater. The court held that the film, "Carnal Knowledge," was not obscene under the constitutional standards established by the Supreme Court of California in Miller v. California. The Court held that it was constitutionally permissible to permit juries to rely on the understanding of the community from which they came as to contemporary community standards, and the States have considerable latitude in framing statutes under this element of the Miller decision. The trial court instructed the jury on charges other than the distribution charge. The jury returned a general verdict of guilty on March 23, 1972, and the trial court's judgment of conviction was affirmed on July 2, 1973 by a divided court of the Georgia Supreme Court. Appellant then appealed to this Court, which noted probable jurisdiction. We conclude that Carnal Knowledge was not protected by the First and Fourteenth Amendments, and that the court should reverse the conviction. We also conclude that the jury was not instructed to apply the standards of a hypothetical statewide community. The case is remanded for further consideration.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit held that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (FERC's) system agreement with Entergy Louisiana, Inc., a subsidiary of Entergy Corporation, pre-empts an order that adjudges Entergy's cost allocation to its sister companies. The court held that, under the "filed rate doctrine," a FERC-approved cost allocation between affiliated energy companies may not be subjected to reevaluation in state rate-making proceedings. In Entergy v. Mississippi Power & Light Co. (1988), the Court held that "the rate doctrine does not apply to the allocation of costs between operating companies" and that the "cost allocation is critical to the setting of retail rates"

This case involves a doctor named Dr. John Doe who worked at a gastroenterology clinic called Clackamas Gastroenterology Associates, P.C. He filed a lawsuit against the clinic for retaliation after he complained about harassment based on his disability. The main legal issue in the case is whether Dr. Doe qualified as an employee under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990.

Under the ADA, an employee is defined as an individual employed by an employer. However, the ADA does not specify what constitutes an employee. Therefore, the court looked to common-law definitions of the master-servant relationship to determine whether Dr. Doe could be considered an employee.

The court found that Dr. Doe met the criteria for an employee under the ADA. Specifically, he performed services on behalf of the clinic, received payment for those services, and was subject to the clinic's policies and procedures. Additionally, the court found that the clinic exercised sufficient control over Dr. Doe's work to establish him as an employee.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs in these cases, holding that the statutes in question violated the Compensation Clause of the US Constitution. The Court held that the statutes constituted a reduction in the compensation of federal judges, rather than merely a delay in payment, and that such a reduction was impermissible under the Clause. The Court also rejected the defendants' arguments regarding the historical background of the Clause and the role of the Rule of Necessity in construing it.

Title: United States v. Virginia

Case Number: 526 U.S. __ (2000)

Issue: Does the Fourth Amendment’s Exclusionary Rule apply to statements made by a defendant in a pretrial identification procedure?

Background: In this case, a man named Terry Stoppelmaier was stopped by police for driving erratically. When the police questioned him, they showed him photographs of people who had robbed a convenience store nearby. Mr. Stoppelmaier immediately identified one of the men in the photograph as the thief, stating that he saw him committing the robbery. Later, at trial, Mr. Stoppelmaier testified that he had seen the man in the photograph walking towards the convenience store shortly before the robbery began. However, the man in the photograph was later proven to be innocent of the robbery.
Mr. Stoppelmaier appealed his conviction, arguing that his identification of the man in the photograph was tainted by an illegal search and seizure of the photograph. The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case.
Opinion: The Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment’s Exclusionary Rule applied to statements made by a defendant in a pretrial identification procedure. Specifically, the Court found that the photograph was seized illegally and that Mr. Stoppelmaier’s identification of the man in the photograph was tainted by the illegal seizure. The Court held that the exclusionary rule applied to the photograph and the identification, and that Mr. Stoppelmaier’s conviction must be vacated.
Conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment’s Exclusionary Rule applies to statements made by a defendant in a pretrial identification procedure if the evidence used to obtain the identification was obtained illegally.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia today announced criminal charges against a defendant who was sentenced to death for a series of high-level crimes.  According to the SEC's complaint, Daryl Renard Atkins was the victim of an abduction, armed robbery, and capital murder perpetrated by Atkins and William Jones.  The complaint alleges that Atkins and Jones violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 13(b)(2)(A) and (c) thereunder.  In addition, the complaint alleges, Atkins' prior felony convictions as well as the testimony of four victims of earlier robberies and assaults made it unlikely that he would ever be sentenced to the death penalty.  Atkins also allegedly had a full scale IQ of 59.5.  As alleged in the complaint, Atkins was not mentally retarded, but rather was of "average intelligence, at least," and had "average capacity to learn from experience, to engage in logical reasoning, to control impulses," and to "control their conduct based upon that information."  In a parallel action, the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Atkins that permanently enjoins him from violating the federal securities laws and orders him to pay a penalty equal to the amount of his ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the SEC, Atkins has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations of the securities laws, and from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in the future, including securities in exchange for a share of the proceeds of the sale of a security deposit, a penny stock, and a bar against him from serving as an officer or director of a public company.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by John Rymas and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Boston Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Petitioner Dames & Moore International, S. R. L., filed suit in the District Court against the Government of the United States, the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, and a number of Iranian banks, seeking to prevent enforcement of the Executive Orders and Treasury Department regulations implementing the Agreement with Iran. The District Court granted petitioner's motion and awarded petitioner the amount claimed under the contract plus interest, and the property of certain Iranian banks was then attached to secure any judgment that might be entered against them. The Court of Appeals upheld the President's authority to issue the executive orders and regulations challenged by petitioner. Held: 1. The President, by suspending the attachments and ordering the transfer of Iranian assets, did not violate Art. III of the Constitution. Pp. 594-595. (a) Although the IEEPA authorized the nullification of the attachments, it cannot be read to authorize the suspension of the claims. P. 598. (b) The fact and extent of the taking in this case is inconsequential because there must be at the time of taking "reasonable, certain and adequate provision for obtaining compensation," and the President can sustain his actions only by disabling the President from acting upon the subject. P p. 599. (c) The President's action in nullifying the attachments was taken pursuant to specific congressional authorization, and it is supported by the strongest of presumptions and the widest latitude of judicial interpretation. The fact that the President has provided such a forum means that the claimants are receiving something in return for suspension of their claims, namely, access to an international tribunal before which they may well recover something on their claims. Neither the purpose the statute was enacted to serve nor its plain language supports such a result. Moreover, Congress has not disapproved of the action taken here, since the Act does not supply the President with power to override judicial remedies, such as attachments and injunctions, or to extinguish "interests" in foreign assets held by United States citizens. Pc. 597-604. (d) The history of the Act indicates that Congress has acquiesced in the President to suspend claims, even as against foreign governmental entities, and that the Act was designed to remove one particular barrier to suit, namely sovereign immunity, and cannot be fairly read as prohibiting him from settling such claims in the Court of Claims under the Tucker Act, 28 U. S. C. § 1491 (1976 ed., Supp. III), in such an event. The Act's principal purpose was to codify contemporary concepts concerning the scope of sovereign immunity and withdraw from the President the authority to make binding determinations of the sovereign immunity to be accorded foreign states. The legislative history also demonstrates that Congress did not intend the Act to give the President such extensive power over the assets of a foreign state during times of national emergency, and this is particularly true as respects cases such as the one before us, involving responses to international crises the nature of which Congress can hardly have been expected to anticipate in any detail. Pct. 596-595. (e) The Act is not intended to deprive the President of power to settle claims, but to depoliticize these commercial lawsuits by taking them out of the arena of foreign affairs-where the Executive Branch is subject to the pressures of foreign states seeking to avoid liability through a grant of immunity-and by placing them within the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts. The Congress has accepted the authority of Congress to enter into executive agreements without obtaining the advice and consent of the Senate, and has simply effected a change in the substantive law governing the lawsuit. Pt. 595-595, 651 F. 2d 871, affirmed.

The U.S. Supreme Court will hear oral arguments on a challenge to a 1976 California law that limits the state's ability to regulate nuclear power. The case centers on whether the law's provisions regarding the storage of spent nuclear fuel are preempted by the federal Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and other federal laws. The nuclear waste issue has generated considerable public and political debate. The Supreme Court's consideration of the case could determine the future of nuclear power in the United States. The law was amended in 1976 to provide additional state regulation of new nuclear power plant construction. The California Energy Commission determined that there will be "adequate capacity" for storage before additional nuclear storage plants may be built. The Energy Commission's finding that there are "unpredictable" problems with nuclear core storage led it to impose a moratorium on new nuclear plants until a long-term solution is found. The Act also requires that each utility provide continuous, on-site storage of nuclear fuel rods "at the time" for the entire reactor. In the case before the Supreme Court, the counsel argues that this provision of the law is inconsistent with the provisions of the federal nuclear law. The counsel also argues that the Energy Commission did not have the authority to determine that there is a demonstrated technology or means for the disposal of high-level nuclear waste. The court will hear arguments on the issue of whether the laws conflict with the federal law.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky today entered a final judgment against a defendant in a civil action brought by the United States Bankruptcy Commission against him for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a judgment against the defendant in the civil action, ordering him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties equal to the amount of his ill-gotten gains.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against him.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Atlanta, Georgia, the defendants violated the federal securities laws by failing to comply with a court order requiring them to issue a writ of habeas corpus, which is required for bankruptcy proceedings.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the securities laws, imposes a civil penalty of $10,000, and bars them from participating in any bankruptcy proceeding. The judgment also orders the defendant to pay a $5,000 civil penalty, which the court finds to be excessive.  On the other hand, the court found that the defendants were not entitled to a penny-per-share of the amount owed to them by the debtor in the bankruptcy proceeding, and that the court had no jurisdiction to issue the writ. The SEC's investigation was conducted by Michael J. Haines and supervised by Marc Blau of the Atlanta Regional Office. The litigation will be led by John R. Rymas. The case is being supervised by Kelly L. Gibson. The court will consider the merits of the case.

In the Supreme Court case concerning Dethorne Graham, a diabetic who alleged excessive force by police during an investigatory stop, the Court held that claims of excessive force by law enforcement should be analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's "objective reasonableness" standard, rather than a substantive due process standard. The case arose from an incident where Graham experienced a diabetic episode and was mistakenly suspected of criminal activity by police, resulting in physical injuries.

The Court emphasized that the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable seizures, is the appropriate constitutional provision for evaluating excessive force claims in the context of arrests or stops. The Court rejected the use of a generic "excessive force" standard and the four-factor test previously applied by lower courts, which considered the need for force, the relationship between the need and the amount of force used, the extent of injury inflicted, and whether the force was applied in good faith or maliciously.

Instead, the Court stated that the reasonableness of the force used must be assessed from the perspective of a reasonable officer at the scene, taking into account the severity of the crime, whether the suspect poses an immediate threat, and whether the suspect is resisting arrest or attempting to flee. The Court clarified that an officer's subjective intent is not relevant to the Fourth Amendment reasonableness inquiry.

The Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had affirmed the District Court's directed verdict for the officers, and remanded the case for reconsideration under the correct Fourth Amendment standard. This decision has implications for how courts evaluate claims of excessive force, focusing on the objective reasonableness of the officers' actions rather than their subjective motivations.

Respondents, plaintiffs in a securities fraud class action, allege that petitioners, Matrixx Initiatives, Inc., and three of its executives, failed to disclose reports of a possible link between its leading product, a cold remedy, and loss of smell, rendering statements made by MatriXX misleading. Respondents also allege that MatRIxx had received, but did not disclose, about consumers who had lost their sense of smell (a condition called anosmia) after using Zicam Cold Remedy, a product marketed under the brand of the brand. Respondent alleges that the company violated §§10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and SEC Rule 10b–5 by making untrue statements of fact and failing to disclose material facts necessary to make the statements not misleading in an effort to maintain artificially high prices for the stock. The District Court granted respondents’ motion to dismiss, holding that respondents had failed to plead the elements of a material misstatement or omission and scienter. The Court of Appeals reversed. Held: Respondents have adequately pleaded scienter, and the judgment of the Ninth Circuit is affirmed. Pp. 5–11. (a) Respondents’ allegations that MatriX violated §10 (b) are not material information. The court’s standard requires courts to take into account “plausible opposing inferences,” Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd., 551 U. S. 308, 318, and that the standard applied by the Court is sufficient to establish scienter under §§10 (a), 15 U.S. C. §78u–4(b)(2)(A), and Rule 10 (b). The Court has implied a private cause of action from the text and purpose of §10’b. See, e.g., Tellabs’ v.Makor Issues& Rights, LTD.,551 U .S. 308. Matrix contends that respondents have adequately plead scienter because they have not alleged a “statistically significant correlation” between the use of the drug, a common cold remedy and loss-of-stereotype, and a loss in smell, and they have alleged facts “giving rise to a strong inference” that Matrix “acted with the required state of mind.” Stoneridge Investment Partners, LLC v. Scientific-Atlanta Inc., 552 U . S. 148, 157. The fact that a user of a drug has suffered an adverse event, standing alone, does not mean that the drug caused that event. The FDA similarly does not limit the evidence it considers for purposes of assessing causation and taking regulatory action to statistically significant data. In assessing the safety risk posed by a product, the FDA considers factors such as the strength of the association between the drug and the adverse effects; a temporal relationship between exposure and exposure; consistency across studies; biological plausibility; consideration of alternative explanations; specificity (i.e., whether the specific chemical is associated with the specific disease); and the dose-response relationship; and the clinical and pathological characteristics of the event. In order to determine when additional inquiry or action is necessary, companies can control what they have to disclose by controlling what they say to the market. This contextual inquiry may reveal in some cases that reasonable investors would have viewed reports of adverse events as material even though the reports did not provide statistically significant evidence of a causal link. See Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U. s. ___, ___. The question remains whether a reasonable investor would regard the nondisclosed information “as having significantly altered the ‘total mix’ of information made available.’ ” Id., at 231–232. Assuming the facts to be true, these were material facts that would “artificially exclud[e] from the definition of materiality information concerning merger discussions, which would otherwise be considered sig- nificant to the trading decision of a reasonable” investor. The SEC points out, “medical professionals and researchers do not limit data they consider to the results of randomized clinical trials or to statistical significant evidence.“” Ibid. Moreover, it bears emphasis that §10(a) and Rule10b-5 do not create an affirmative duty to disclose any and all information. Disclosure is required under these provisions only when necessary “to make . . . statements made, in the light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading”

Petitioner Brecht, who was serving time in a Georgia prison for felony theft when his sister and her husband, Molly and Roger Hartman, paid the restitution for petitioner's crime and assumed temporary custody of him, brought petitioner home with them to reside with them before entering a halfway house. The Hartmans told him that he was not to drink alcohol or engage in homosexual activities in their home, but that he would be required to do so only if he "suffered a substantial and injurious effect or influence in determining the jury's verdict." Petitioner then sought a writ of habeas corpus under 28 U. S. C. § 2254, but the District Court agreed that the State's use of petitioner's post-Miranda silence violated Doyle v. Ohio, 426 U.S. 610, and set aside the conviction. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Chapman harmless-error standard applies in determining whether the error "was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt." Held: Petitioner is not entitled to relief under the Chapman standard. Pp. 488-481. (a) The Chapman harmlesserror standard is better tailored to the nature and purpose of collateral review than the Chapman or the Kotteakos standard on habea. P. 489. (b) The State's improper use for impeachment purposes of petitioner’s post-miranda silence, see n. 2, supra, did not "substantially influence" the jury verdict. The State bears the burden of proving that an error passes muster under this standard. Moreover, the State bears no burden of determining whether petitioner is entitled to habeAS relief based on the State’d Doyle error. The fact that the state references to petitioner's silence after that point in time were infrequent, comprising less than two pages of the 900-page trial transcript in this case, and in view of the extensive and permissible reference to petitioner”s silence at any time before trial, crossed the Doyle line. The Chapman standard, which applies in reviewing Doyle error on federal cases, does not apply here. The statute permits federal courts to entertain petitions on behalf of a state prisoner only on the ground that he is in custody in violation of the Constitution or laws or treaties of the United States, and directs simply that the court "dispose of the matter as law and justice require," § 2243. However real these concerns, Doyle does not "overprotec[t] "[t]he error" them. The principle that collateral review is different from direct review resounds throughout our habas jurisprudence. See, e. g., Wright v. West, 505 U. s. 624, 637. Federalism, comity, and the constitutional obligation of state and federal courts all counsel against any presumption that a decision of this Court will "deter" lower federal or state courts from fully performing their sworn duty. However, this Court has never squarely addressed the issue, and have at most assumed the applicability of the Chapman and Kotteaks standards on the issue of Doyle error, see Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U. .S. 651, 670-671. The same principle applies to criminal cases on direct review of Doyle errors, Teague v. Connolly, 111 U. F. 2d 460, followed by the Federal Rule, which prohibits federal courts from entertaining a habebeas petition on behalf only on ground that petitioner is in prison "only on the grounds that he has been in violation" and directs, inter alia, that the error was "harmless." The principle also applies here. Although new rules always have retroactive application to criminal criminal cases based on Doyle error and are more likely to promote the considerations underlying our recent cases, it hardly seems logical to require federal courts in the identical approach on collateral review that Chapman requires state courts to engage in on direct-review. The issue here is whether, in light of the record as a whole, petitioner met its burden in proving beyond areasonable doubt that the shooting was intentional, and whether the state courts met its obligation to uphold the Constitution. The question whether the State violated its Article VI duty to protect another prophylactic rule from erosion or misuse is not addressed here, since it is rooted in fundamental fairness and due process concerns, and since there is no statute of limitations governing federal habeacas, the only laches recognized are those which affect the State to defend against the claims raised on such claims, and because retrials following the grant of relief ordinarily take place much later than retrials after reversal on direct. Reversing the conviction is unlikely to confuse matters for state courts, since this Court is free to address its applicability on this issue on the merits. See Edelman, supra.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Florida-based Piccadilly Cafeterias, Inc., a now-bankrupt cafeteria chain, for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Orlando, Florida on October 29, 2003, Piccadrilly, a former member of the National Cafeteria Association, filed an application for a stamp-tax exemption under Section 11 of the Bankruptcy Code, which requires a debtor to submit a plan of reorganization to the court for approval. The complaint alleges that, in reality, the plan of the reorganization did not exist at the time of the plan’s filing, and that the stamp tax exemption applied only to preconfirmation transfers. The SEC further alleges that Piccarrilly failed to mention that, as a result of this conduct, the stamps tax exemption was not applied to postconfirmation transfer transactions. The court also ruled that, contrary to the stated intent of the federalism canon, §1146(a) does not apply to transfers made before the date of a plan is confirmed under Chapter 11. Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Picrilly has consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the Federalism canon and orders him to pay disgorgement of $39,200, prejudgment interest of $2,038, and a civil penalty of $100,000. Picrilla has also agreed to pay a $75,000 civil penalty.  The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted in the Miami Regional Office by Michael J. Pyszka and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson of the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis. The litigation will be led by Jennifer C. Barry.

Petitioner's wife, who was riding in an 18-foot ski boat equipped with a 115-horsepower outboard motor manufactured by respondent Mercury Marine, died as a result of a boating accident on an inland lake that spans the Kentucky-Tennessee border. The trial court granted respondent's motion to dismiss, and the intermediate appellate court affirmed on the ground that the action was expressly pre-empted by the Federal Boat Safety Act of 1971, 46 U. S. C. § 4301-4311 (FBSA, 1971 Act, or Act), or by the Coast Guard's decision not to promulgate a regulation requiring propeller guards on motorboats. Respondent filed a nine-count complaint in an Illinois court seeking damages from Brunswick on state-law theories. Each count alleged that Brunswick had manufactured an unreasonably dangerous product because, among other things, the motor was not protected by a propeller guard. The State Supreme Court rejected the appellate court's express pre-emption rationale, but affirmed on implied preemption grounds. The court's decision added to a split of authority on this precise issue arising from lawsuits against, among a few others, this particular respondent and its corporate subsidiaries. Relying on the intervening decision in Geier v. American Honda Motor Co., 529 U.S. 861, this Court has no occasion to consider the merits of petitioner's claims, or even whether the claims are viable as a matter of Illinois law. Because the FBSA contains an express preemption clause, the concern with uniformity does not justify the displacement of state common-law remedies that compensate accident victims and their families and that serve the Act's more prominent objective, emphasized by its title, of promoting boating safety. The Act's saving clause buttresses this conclusion. It states that "[c]ompliance with this chapter or standards, regulations, or orders prescribed under this chapter does not relieve a person from liability at common law or under State law." § 4311(g). The phrase "a" before "law or regulation" implies a discreteness-which is embodied in statutes and regulations-that is not present in the common law. The terms "law" and "regulation" used together indicate that Congress preempted only positive enactments. If the phrase were read broadly so as to include a common law, it might also be interpreted to include regulations, which would render the express reference to "regulation," in the pre--emption clause superfluous. The Coast Guard has never taken the position that the litigation of state-common-law claims relating to an area not yet subject to federal regulation would conflict with "the accomplishment and execution of the full purposes and objectives of Congress." Hines v. Davidowitz, 312 U. . S. 52, 67. Nor is there a clear and manifest intent to sweep away state common law established by an unembellished statement in a House Report that the 1971 Act "preempts the field on boating standards or regulations." Geier, 529 U., at 881. Pp. 5-11. 197 Ill. 2d 112, 757 N. E. 2D 75, reversed and remanded.

Appellants, who engaged in such mining operations prior to the enactment of an ordinance regulating mining excavations within its limits, claim that the ordinance in effect prevents them from continuing their business and therefore takes their property without due process of law in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment. Held: 1. The ordinance completely prohibits a beneficial use to which the property has previously been devoted. Pp. 563-567. 2. The prohibition of further excavation below the water table is not a valid exercise of the town's police power. P. 567. 3. Since enforcement of these provisions was not sought in the present litigation, this Court under well-established principles will not at this time undertake to decide the constitutionality of the ordinance, and since the ordinance does not erect a constitutional barrier to all other regulation, it does not need to consider to what extent such issues would have come under the protective wing of due process. Id. 9 N. Y. 2d 101, 211 N. E.2d 562, affirmed.

The False Claims Act (FCA) imposes civil liability on any person who knowingly uses a “false record or statement to get a false or fraudulent claim paid or approved by the Government,” 31 U. S. C. §3729(a)(2). The Navy’s contract with the shipyards specified that every part of each destroyer be built in accordance with Navy baseline drawings and military standards. These requirements were incorporated into each of petitioners’ subcontracts. In addition, the contracts required that each delivered Gen-Set be accompanied by a certificate of conformance (COC) certifying that the unit was manufactured in accordance. The Navy paid shipyards an aggregate total of $1 billion for each new destroyer. All of the funds used to pay petitioners ultimately came from the Federal Treasury, which paid them over $100,000 for each destroyer. The shipyards subcontracted with petitioner General Tool Company (GTC), formerly a division of General Motors, to build 90 Gen-Sets to be used in over 50 destroyers. The Shipyards paid them approximately $3 million per Gen- Set; GTC was paid approximately $800,000 per GenSet; and SOFCO was paid over $200,000. Respondents did not introduce invoices for payment to the Navy. At the close of respondents’ case, petitioners moved for judgment as a matter of law pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50(a). The District Court granted them a motion for judgment, holding that, absent proof that false claims were presented to the Government or that Government money was used to make the false claim, the evidence was legally insufficient under the FCA. The Court of Appeals reversed the District Court in relevant part. Held: 1. A plaintiff asserting a claim under these provisions must show that a false statement resulted in the use of Government funds to pay a false and fraudulent claim. Pp. 4–622. (a) Section 3729(A)(2) requires proof that a defendant “knowingly makes, uses, or causes to be made or used, a false record or statements to get [a] false . . .” (a)(1) or that a person who “conspires to defraud” the Government by getting a false claim “paid or approved” is not the same as getting a true or fraudulent claims paid or paid by the government. P. 6–7. (b) The interpretation adopted by the Court is based on an incorrect interpretation of §§3729’a(2) and (3), and that is endorsed by the respondents and the Government. In the view of the Court, it is sufficient for a §37 29(a) (2) plaintiff to show that, in the absence of a presentment requirement in subsection (a), the defendant must make the “claim” “to get” such a claim. This interpretation “would have, in effect, substituted ‘anyone receiving federal financial assistance and supervision’ for the phrase ‘paid by Government funds.’ ” Barnhart v. Sigmon Coal Co., 534 U.S. 438, 452 (internal quotation marks omitted). The interpretation urged on respondents would in effect substitute “for the phrase” for “pay by Government.” Had Congress intended to include the presentment provision in § 3729 (a (2), it would have so provided. The interpretation that was adopted in Tanner v. United States, 483 U.

The Supreme Court considered whether the denial of unemployment benefits to a Jehovah's Witness, who quit his job due to a transfer to a department that produced military tank turrets, violated his First Amendment right to free exercise of religion. The petitioner, Thomas, argued that working on armaments was against his religious beliefs. The Indiana Employment Security Act disqualified him from receiving benefits because his termination was not considered to be for "good cause" related to his work.

The Indiana Court of Appeals reversed the denial of benefits, finding it burdened Thomas's religious rights. However, the Supreme Court of Indiana reinstated the denial, viewing Thomas's beliefs as more personal than religious and holding that even if his termination was for religious reasons, it did not constitute "good cause" under state law. They also argued that granting benefits for religious reasons, while denying them for other personal reasons, would violate the Establishment Clause.

The U.S. Supreme Court, referencing its decision in Sherbert v. Verner, stated that religious beliefs do not need to be logical or comprehensible to others to merit protection. The Court found that Thomas had indeed quit his job due to his religious convictions, and that the state could not compel him to choose between his religious beliefs and receiving unemployment benefits. The Court held that the state must show a compelling interest to justify burdening religious practice and that the interests presented by Indiana did not meet this standard.

The Court also rejected the argument that granting benefits to Thomas would violate the Establishment Clause, noting that extending benefits to individuals who terminate employment for religious reasons reflects governmental neutrality and does not foster the establishment of a religion.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Indiana court, ruling that Thomas was entitled to unemployment benefits, as denying them would place an unconstitutional burden on his free exercise of religion. Justice Blackmun concurred with the majority opinion but wrote separately regarding the Establishment Clause issue.

Section 751 (a) (2) of the Higher Education Facilities Act of 1964 (Act) bars the use of federal grants under the Act for "sectarian" instruction or religious worship. The Act further provides that the Government shall retain a lien on any facility built with federal money until repayment of the federal grant plus administrative costs, and that upon default the Government may sell the facility and apply the net proceeds toward satisfaction of the debt. The Act limits the liability of the Government to the present value of the federal grant. The Act expires ten years after the date of enactment. Appellants sued in a three-judge District Court challenging the constitutionality of the Act. The District Court found that the Act served the legitimate governmental purpose of increasing access to higher education and that it did not impermissibly favor religion. The court also found that the Act did not violate the Establishment Clause of the Constitution. Held: 1. The Act does not violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment except that part of § 754 (b) (2) providing a 20-year limitation on the religious use restrictions contained in § 751 (a) (2). Pp. 670-681. (a) The Act applies to churches and other religious organizations. Pp. 670-671. (b) The Act serves the legitimate governmental purpose of increasing access to higher education. Pp. 671-672. (c) The Act does not impermissibly favor religion. Pp. 672-673. (d) The Act does not violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. Pp. 673-681. 2. The Act does not violate the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment. P. 681. 316 F. Supp. 1023, vacated and remanded.

Jennifer Arbaugh filed suit in Federal District Court against respondent Y&H Restaurants, LLC, claiming violations of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Louisiana state law. Before entering into default judgment for Arbaugh, the District Court dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, ruling that it lacked authority to entertain the suit because Arbaugh had not satisfied the 15-employee threshold specified in 42 U. S. C. §2000e(b), which defines the term “employer” for purposes of Title VII. The Tenth Circuit affirmed, finding that the District Court correctly interpreted §2000e(b) as a jurisdictional bar. Held: The 15-employee threshold is an element of a plaintiff’s claim for relief, not a jurisdictional issue. Pp. 5–11. (a) Because it determines whether the court has power to hear a case, subject-matter jurisdiction cannot be forfeited or waived. And courts, including this Court, have an independent obligation to determine whether subject-matter jurisdiction exists, even in the absence of a challenge from any party. Here, nothing in the text of Title VII indicates that Congress intended courts, on their own motion, to ensure that the employee-numerosity requirement is met. Pp. 5–6. (b) When a federal court concludes that it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction, it must dismiss the complaint in its entirety. Consequently, the District Court dismissed, along with the Title VII claim, pendent state-law claims that were fully tried by a jury and determined on the merits. Had the court granted a motion to dismiss for failure to state a federal claim, it would retain discretion to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the pendent state-law claims. However, given the unfairness and waste of judicial resources entailed in tying the employee-numerosity requirement to subject-matter jurisdiction, it is better to leave the ball in Congress’ court. If Congress clearly states that a threshold limitation on a statute’s scope shall count as jurisdictional, courts and litigants will be duly instructed and will not be left to wrestle with the issue. But when Congress does not rank a statutory limitation on coverage as jurisdictional, courts should treat the restriction as nonjurisdictional in character. Applying that readily administrable bright line to this case, the Court holds that the threshold number of employees for application of Title VII is an element of a plaintiff’s claim for relief, not a jurisdictional issue. Pp. 6–11. 367 F. 3d 1251, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

The Supreme Court of the United States decided the case of Arizona v. Evans in 1992. The case involved a man named John Evans who was stopped by police while driving a car registered to someone else. During the stop, the police discovered that Evans had outstanding traffic tickets and a suspended driver's license. They also found drugs in the car. Evans was arrested and charged with drug possession.

Evans argued that the police had no legal authority to stop him and search his car. He claimed that the police had based their suspicion on racial profiling, and that the search of his car was therefore unconstitutional. However, the Supreme Court disagreed with Evans and upheld the legality of the stop and search.

The Court held that the police had a legitimate concern about road safety, and that stopping drivers suspected of having outstanding traffic tickets or suspended licenses was a common practice. The Court also found that the search of Evans' car was consistent with the principles of Terry v. Ohio, which allows police to pat down suspects and perform limited searches of their clothing and belongings during a brief detention.

Overall, the Supreme Court's decision in Arizona v. Evans reinforced the idea that police stops and searches are generally allowed under American law, as long as they are carried out in accordance with the rules and procedures laid out in the Constitution and other legal precedents.

Respondent Mitchell was convicted of aggravated battery after beating a white child. At his trial, the jury heard evidence that Mitchell had intended to hurt the child because of his race. He was sentenced to four years' imprisonment plus five years of extended supervision. After exhausting state appellate procedures, Mitchell challenged the validity of the penalty-enhancement provision that applied to his case. The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed, concluding that the provision violated the First Amendment by punishing offenders' bigoted beliefs. Held: The penalty-enhancement provision does not violate respondents First Amendment rights. Pp. 10-16. (a) Although the provision applies to both violent and nonviolent behavior, it enhances the maximum punishment for conduct motivated by a discriminatory point of view more severely than the same conduct engaged in for some other reason or for no reason at all. Because the only reason for the enhancement is the defendants discriminatory motive for selecting his victim, the provision violates the First Amendment by punishing offenders' bigoted beliefs. Traditionally, sentencing judges have considered a wide variety of factors in imposing sentence, see, e. g., Payne v. Tennessee, 501 U. S. 808, 814, including the defendant's motive for committing the offense, see, e. g., id., at 815. However, a defendant's abstract beliefs, however objectionable, may not be taken into consideration. See, e. g., Dawson v. Delaware, 503 U. S. 157, 164. Here, the State's primary responsibility for fixing criminal penalties lies with the legislature. Nothing in the record indicates that the State acted solely out of disagreement with offenders' beliefs or biases. Instead, the State's desire to address the social costs associated with bias-motivated crimes explains why it chose to single out such crimes for heightened punishment. Moreover, the State's concern that bias-motivated crimes are more likely to provoke retaliatory crimes, inflict distinct emotional harms on their victims, and incite community unrest provides an adequate explanation for its penalty-enhancement provision over and above mere disagreement with offenders' beliefs or biases. Pp. 10-14. (b) Nor is the provision unconstitutionally overbroad because of its alleged chilling effect on free speech. Any deterrent effect is highly attenuated and unlikely, since the sort of speech that might lead to enhanced sentences is typically unpopular and rarely involves minor misdemeanors. More importantly, the First Amendment does not prohibit the evidentiary use of speech to establish the elements of a crime or to prove motive or intent. See, e. g., Haupt v. United States, 330 U. S. 631, 642. Pp. 14-16. 169 Wis. 2d 15, 464 N. W. 2d 42, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Fourth Circuit today entered a final judgment against Clifton Terelle McNeill, a North Carolina man charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Charlotte, North Carolina, alleges that McNeill was caught with 3.1 grams of crack cocaine packaged for distribution and a .38-caliber revolver.  According to the complaint, McNeill pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 10 years in prison for a prior drug-trafficking conviction.  McNeill's sentencing was for a "serious drug offense" and McNeill had previously been convicted of a similar felony.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the District of North Carolina today announced criminal charges against McNeill.  On October 1, 1994, the court entered a judgment ordering the SEC to determine the minimum sentence for McNeill for a felony or a serious drug offense.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, which was filed in the United States Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit, the Court held that the SEC should determine the maximum sentence for a person who has a prior felony drug conviction and a 10-year minimum prison sentence, and that the court should consider whether a prior conviction qualifies for ACCA purposes at the time of the federal sentencing proceeding.

In the Supreme Court case concerning Kevin Dewayne Powell, the central issue was whether the Miranda warnings provided to Powell by Tampa law enforcement officers were adequate. The warnings informed Powell that he had the right to speak with a lawyer before answering questions and could exercise this right at any time during the interview. Powell argued that the warnings were insufficient because they did not explicitly state that he had the right to have a lawyer present during the interrogation.

The Florida Supreme Court agreed with Powell, finding that the warnings did not clearly inform him of his right to have an attorney present throughout the interrogation. However, the U.S. Supreme Court reversed this decision. The U.S. Supreme Court held that the warnings, when read in a commonsense manner, reasonably conveyed the right to have an attorney present during the entire interrogation process. The Court emphasized that while the warnings were not the most clearly formulated, they were comprehensive enough when given a practical interpretation.

The Court also addressed jurisdictional concerns, noting that the Florida Supreme Court's decision did not rest on an independent state ground separate from Miranda, thus allowing the U.S. Supreme Court to review the case.

The implications of the decision are that law enforcement warnings do not need to follow a precise formulation as long as they effectively communicate a suspect's rights as required by Miranda. The Court's decision underscores that the essence of the warnings, rather than their exact wording, is what matters in determining their adequacy. The ruling also suggests that law enforcement agencies have little incentive to deviate from established, clear Miranda warnings, as doing so could increase litigation risks. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the U.S. Supreme Court's opinion.

Section 484-h of the New York Penal Code makes it a crime "knowingly" to expose minors to harmful materials, defined as materials which, because of their appeal to minors, predominately engage the prurient, shameful or morbid interest of minors, are patently offensive to prevailing standards in the adult community as a whole with respect to what is suitable material for minors, and are utterly without redeeming social importance for minors. Appellant, operator of a luncheonette, was convicted of violating § 484-h by selling to a 15-year-old boy two girls' magazines containing photographs of women's breasts and genitalia. The trial court upheld the conviction, holding that the magazines were "harmful to minors," since they depicted "sexual conduct." On appeal the New York Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Obscene material need not be excluded from circulation to minors merely because it is obscene for adults. Pp. 308-310. 2. Subsections (f) and (g) of § 484-h are not unduly vague. Pp. 310-311. (a) The definition of "obscene" in subsection (f) is virtually identical to the definition set forth in Roth v. United States, 383 U. S. 413, and satisfies the requirements of due process. Pp. 310-311. (b) The proviso in subsection (g) allowing a seller to escape liability if he acted honestly in believing that the minor was above the age of consent is not unduly vague. Pp. 310-311. Affirmed.

Petitioner, a black applicant, sued respondents, the officers, faculty members, and members of the board of regents of the University of Washington, challenging the validity of the university's racial quota system whereby petitioner was denied admission to its law school. After being initially denied relief, petitioner obtained a temporary restraining order preventing enforcement of the quota system while the case was pending. Subsequently, however, the Washington Supreme Court upheld the quota system, and petitioner appealed to this Court. While this Court was considering petitioner's certiorari petition, the Washington Supreme Court's judgment became final, and petitioner entered his final term of law school. Respondents assured the Court that petitioner would be allowed to graduate despite the Washington Supreme Court's ruling, and petitioner registered for his final term. Held: Under Article III of the Constitution, since petitioner will complete his law school studies at the end of the term for which he has now registered regardless of any decision this Court might reach on the merits of this litigation, the Court cannot consider the substantive constitutional issues tendered by the parties, and hence the Court cannot properly address the question presented by this case. Certiorari dismissed; 82 Wash. 2d 11, 507 P. 2d 1169, vacated and remanded.

Title 28 U. S. C. §1332(c)(1) renders a corporation a citizen of the “State where it has its principal place of business.” Section 1332(c)(2) defines “principal place of business” as “the place where a corporation exercises control and direction of its affairs and of the management of its property.” Petitioner Hertz Corporation, headquartered in New Jersey, moved to dismiss respondents’ diversity action, claiming that it was improperly removed to federal court. The District Court dismissed the motion, ruling that Hertz was a resident alien for diversity purposes. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit disagreed, reasoning that Hertz was a citizen of California because its “nerve center” was there. Held: The “nerve center” of a corporation is its headquarters, provided that the headquarters is the actual center of direction, control, and coordination, i.e., the “nerve center,” and not simply an office where the corporation holds its board meetings. Pp. 6−16. (a) The statute’s language supports this reading. The word “place” is in the singular, meaning a place within a State, not the State itself. The word “principal” requires picking out the leading place. And the fact that the word “place” follows the words “State where” means that the “place” is a place within a State. By contrast, the application of a more general business activities test leads some courts, as in the present case, to look, not at a particular place within a State, but incorrectly at the State itself, measuring the total amount of business activities that the corporation conducts there and determining whether they are significantly larger than in the next-ranking State. Pp. 6−8. (b) Administrative simplicity is a major virtue in a jurisdictional statute. Complex jurisdictional tests complicate a case, eating up time and money as the parties litigate, not the merits of their claims, but which court is the right court to decide those claims. Complex tests produce appeals and reversals, encourage gamesmanship, and, again, diminish the likelihood that results and settlements will reflect a claim’s legal and factual merits. Judicial resources too are at stake. Courts have an independent obligation to determine whether subject-matter jurisdiction exists, even when no party challenges it. Simple jurisdictional rules also promote greater predictability. Predictability also benefits plaintiffs deciding whether to file suit in a state or federal court. A “nerve center” approach, which ordinarily equates that “center” with a corporation’s headquarters, is simple to apply comparatively speaking. The metaphor of a corporate “brain,” while not precise, suggests a single location. By contrast, a corporation’s general business activities more often lack a single principal place where they take place. There will be hard cases under the “nerve center” test, but accepting occasional counterintuitive results is the price the legal system must pay to avoid overly complex jurisdictional administration while producing the benefits that accompany a more uniform legal system. Pp. 8−12. (c) While the burden of persuasion for establishing diversity jurisdiction remains on the party asserting it, when challenged on allegations of jurisdictional facts, the parties must support their allegations by competent proof. P. 13. 297 Fed. Appx. 690, vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced that it has obtained a court order halting insider trading in securities of a publicly-traded company.  The SEC's complaint, filed in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleges that Raymond Dirks received nonpublic information from Ronald Secrist, a former officer of Equity Funding of America, who allegedly claimed that the assets of the company were vastly overstated as a result of fraudulent corporate practices.  According to the complaint, Dirks then shared the information with a number of investors, including five investment advisers who liquidated holdings of more than $16 million.  As the complaint alleges, the insider then told Dirks that he had to "ferret out and analyze" the information before trading on it and that he would either publicly disclose the information or refrain from trading.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the complaint charges Dirks with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 206(3)-8 thereunder.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Dirks.

Respondent, a manufacturer of patented fans and heaters, sued petitioner, The Holmes Group, Inc., claiming that petitioner's use of a "spiral grill design" in its fans infringed respondent's trade dress. The Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit found for Duracraft, holding that Vornado had no protectable trade-dress rights in the grill design. Several weeks later, petitioner filed this action against respondent in the District Court for the District of Kansas, seeking, inter alia, a declaratory judgment that its products did not infringe the trade dress and an injunction restraining respondent from accusing it of trade-dress infringement in promotional materials. Respondent's answer asserted a compulsory counterclaim alleging patent infringement. The District Court granted petitioner's counterclaim, but the court also stayed all proceedings related to the counterclaim. Held: The Federal Circuit has exclusive jurisdiction over an appeal from a final decision of a district court of the United States if the jurisdiction of that court was based, in whole or in part, on 28 U. S. C. § 1338 (a), which provides that "[t]he district courts shall have original jurisdiction of any civil action arising under any Act of Congress relating to patents ...." Thus, the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction is fixed with reference to that of the district court, and turns on whether the action arises under federal patent law. Pp. 5-11. (a) The exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of appeals for patent cases is not "fixed" until the notice of appeal is filed. Section 1338(a)(1) provides that "the answer as well as the complaint ... be consulted before a determination [is] made whether the case `ar[ises] under' federal law ...." Franchise Tax Bd. of Cal. v. Construction Laborers Vacation Trust for Southern Cal., 463 U.S. 1, 10-11, n. 9. It follows that a counterclaim-which appears as part of the defendant's answer, not as part-the plaintiff's complaint- cannot serve as the basis for "arising under" jurisdiction. By limiting the jurisdiction to cases in which district courts would have jurisdiction under §1338, Congress referred to a wellestablished body of law that requires courts to consider whether a patent-law claim appears on the face of the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint. Because petitioner's complaint did not include any claim based on patent law, this Court vacates the judgment and remand the case with instructions to transfer the case to the Court's Tenth Circuit. P. 5. (b) A correct interpretation of § 1295(a) (1) limits the exclusive jurisdiction to those cases where the patent claim is alleged in either the original complaint or an amended pleading filed by the plaintiff. A plaintiff who has a legitimate interest in litigating in a circuit whose precedents support its theory of the case might omit a patent claim in order to avoid review in the federal Circuit. In some cases that interest would be defeated by a rule that allowed a patent counterclaim to determine the appellate forum. But the interest in maintaining clarity and simplicity in rules governing appellate jurisdiction will be served by limiting the number of pleadings that will mandate review in Federal Circuit courts. See, e. g., Griggs v. Provident Consumer Discount Co., 459 U. s. 56, 58-59. The rule proposed by respondent, in contrast, would leave acceptance or rejection of a state forum to the master of the counter claim. Moreover, allowing responsive pleadings by the defendant to establish arising under jurisdiction would undermine the clarity and ease of administration of the wellpleaded-complaint doctrine, which serves as a "quick rule of thumb" for resolving jurisdictional conflicts. Finally, the interest of preserving the plaintiff’s choice of forums includes not only the court that will conduct the trial but the appellate court as well, but also the appellate courts as well. The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of the state of California in a case challenging the constitutionality of Section 1101.1 of the California Political Syndicalism Law, which makes membership in a communist organization illegal. The Court held that the section was not unconstitutionally vague and that the state had a compelling interest in preventing the spread of communism.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled that a police officer's recording of serial numbers on stolen stereo equipment violated the Fourth Amendment because it was unrelated to the search for the shooter, victims, and weapons that was the lawful objective of his entry into the apartment. The court ruled that the officer had not violated the "plain view" doctrine of the law by recording the serial numbers. The opinion's majority agreed, saying that the recording did not "meaningfully interfere" with respondent's possessory interest in either the equipment or the equipment, and therefore did not amount to a seizure. The majority also agreed with the lower court's finding that the search was justified, and that the entry of the search warrant was not an independent search. In a dissent, Justice White wrote that the court should not have allowed the recording to be used as evidence, since it was not related to the investigation of the shooter or the search. The dissent concluded that the record should be excluded as evidence because it did not provide any information that would have led a reasonable officer to conclude that the stereo equipment was stolen. The Court ruled that, in the absence of a warrant, the entry and search of the apartment was not a search, but a search unrelated to that exigency. The decision is the latest in a long line of court rulings that have held that a warrantless search of a private area may be justified in certain circumstances, including when there is less than probable cause to believe that the item in question is evidence of a crime or is contraband.

In 1974, respondent Reader's Digest Association, Inc., published a book entitled KGB, the Secret Work of Soviet Agents (KGB), which describes the Soviet Union's espionage organization and chronicles its activities since World War II. In a passage referring to disclosures by "royal commissions in Canada and Australia, and official investigations in Great Britain and the United States," the book contains the following statements relating to petitioner Ilya Wolston: "Among Soviet agents identified in the [United States] were Elizabeth T. Bentley, Edward Joseph Fitzgerald, William Ludwig Ullmann, William Walter Remington, Franklin Victor Reno, Judith Coplon, Harry Gold, David Greenglass, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, Morton Sobell, William Perl, Alfred Dean Slack, Jack Soble, and Ilyas Wolston, Alfred and Martha Stern.* " Petitioner was a public figure for the limited purpose of comment on his connection with, or involvement in, Soviet espionage in the 1940's and 1950's. The District Court granted respondents' motion for summary judgment, holding that petitioner was a "public figure" and that the First Amendment therefore precluded recovery unless petitioner proved that respondents had published a defamatory falsehood with "actual malice," New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U. S. 254, 280, in order to recover from respondents. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The First Amendment does not pre-empt petitioner's right to be classed as such a limited-purpose public figure. Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (hereinafter Time, Inc.' v. Firestone, 424 U.S. 323, 344-347), distinguished. Pp. 5-7. (a) The undisputed facts do not justify the conclusion that petitioner "voluntarily thrust" or "injected" himself into the forefront of the public controversy surrounding the investigation of Soviet espionage. The mere fact that these events attracted media attention also is not decisive on the question of public-figure status. P. 5. (b) There is no basis whatsoever for concluding that petitioner relinquished, to any degree, his interest in the protection of his own name. Time,Inc. v., Firestone. supra, supra, at 431. P p. 545. (c) The fact that petitioner voluntarily chose not to appear before the grand jury, knowing that his action might be attended by publicity, does not justify his decision to meet the standard of New York-Times Co.'s standard of public figures, which is a normative consideration that public figures are less deserving of protection than private persons because public figures have voluntarily exposed themselves to increased risk of injury from defamatories, and thus are more likely to be drawn into a public forum largely against their will in order, to attempt to obtain the only redress available to them or to defend themselves against actions brought by the State or by others. It appears little reason why these individuals should substantially forfeit that degree of protection which the law of defamation would otherwise afford them simply by virtue of their being drawn in a courtroom. The public interest in accurate reports of judicial proceedings is substantially protected by Cox Broadcasting Co. [v. Cohn], which is the largest public figure in the country, and it is clear that petitioner played only a minor role in whatever public controversy there may have been concerning the investigation. Moreover, his mere citation for contempt did attract media attention, but the simple fact that the events attracted attention also was not sufficient on the issue of public figure status. The simple fact of petitioner's failure to appear at the grand-jury subpoena and citation for the contempt determinative of the Public-figure issue is not sufficient to justify his failure to comply with the subpoena. The court must focus on the "nature and extent of an individual's participation in the particular controversy giving rise to the defamation." Ibid. Pc. 546-544. (d) Petitioner's failure not to respond to the subpoena was in no way calculated to draw attention to himself or to invite public comment or influence the public with respect to any issue, and he did not in any way seek to arouse public sentiment in his favor and against the investigation, nor did petitioner engage the attention in an attempt to influence the resolution of the issues involved.
