Title: Montana v. United States

Year: 2009

Summary: In Montana v. United States, the Supreme Court considered the constitutionality of a federal law prohibiting firearms in national parks. The Court held that the ban violated the Second Amendment's right to bear arms. The Court also discussed the historical background of gun rights in America and the limitations placed on those rights by various laws and regulations.

The Supreme Court addressed whether punitive damages awarded in a tort suit for personal injuries are excludable from gross income under Internal Revenue Code § 104(a)(2) as it was in 1988. The petitioners, the family of Betty O'Gilvie who died from toxic shock syndrome, received a jury award that included punitive damages and sought a tax refund on those damages, arguing they were not taxable under the statute.

The Court concluded that punitive damages are not received "on account of" personal injuries and therefore do not fall under the exclusion provided by § 104(a)(2), making them taxable. The Court reasoned that punitive damages are intended to punish the defendant for reprehensible conduct and to deter future occurrences, not to compensate the victim for injury or sickness.

The Court's decision was based on the interpretation of the phrase "on account of" to require a strong causal connection to personal injuries, which punitive damages do not satisfy. The Court also considered the historical context of the statutory provision, which was originally intended to codify the principle that restorations of capital were not income and thus not taxable. The provision aimed to make victims whole by excluding from taxation damages that compensate for loss, but not punitive damages which do not compensate for any loss.

The Court rejected the petitioners' arguments that the statute's language could be read to include punitive damages and that Congress's later amendment to the law suggested an earlier intent to exclude punitive damages from income. The Court found no strong reason to interpret the statute to extend beyond compensatory damages.

Additionally, the Court addressed procedural issues related to the timeliness of the Government's lawsuit to recover the refund erroneously made to the children and the Government's appeal in Kelly O'Gilvie's case, siding with the Government in both instances.

In summary, the Supreme Court held that punitive damages awarded in a tort suit for personal injuries are taxable and do not qualify for exclusion under § 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code as it was written in 1988. This decision clarifies the tax treatment of such damages and upholds the Government's interpretation of the statute.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit has ruled that a federal law requiring an arresting officer to bring a prisoner before a magistrate as soon as he reasonably could is not a violation of the Constitution's guarantees of due process and the right to a fair trial. The court held that the law was intended to prevent secret detention and serve to inform a suspect of the charges against him, and it was the law in nearly every American State and the National Government. The Court's decision is the latest in a series of rulings that have invalidated the law. In the first case, the Court held that a defendant's confession to a murder charge was inadmissible when he was not brought before a judge within the required period of time. The second case held that an officer's failure to bring the defendant before the magistrate after a period of unreasonable delay violated the rule. The third case held a confession inadmissible when it was obtained during the period of delay. The fourth case found that the rule was not intended to prohibit the use of evidence that would be used to convict the defendant of the crime. The Appeals Court held, however, that there was no reason to conclude that Congress intended the presentment rule to be a narrow one. In a dissent, Justice Anthony J. Scalia argued that the Appeals Court should have held that Congress had intended the rule to apply only to the arrest of persons charged with a crime.

Arizona provides tax credits for contributions to school tuition organizations, or STOs. STOs use these contributions to provide scholarships to students attending private schools, many of which are religious. Respondents, a group of Arizona taxpayers who challenge the STO tax credit as a violation of Establishment Clause principles under the First and Fourteenth Amendments, sought intervention from the Federal Judiciary. The District Court dismissed respondents’ suit as jurisdictionally barred by the Tax Injunction Act, 28 U. S. C. §1341. Reaching the merits, the Court of Appeals ruled that respondents had stated a claim that §43–1089 violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. Held: Respondents lacked standing to commence this action, and their suit must be dismissed for want of jurisdiction. Pp. 5–11. (a) The concept and operation of the separation of powers in the National Government have their principal foundation in Article III, the Constitution. Under that provision, the Federal Government is vested with the “Power” to resolve not questions and issues but “Cases” or “Controversies.” This language restricts the federal judicial power “to the traditional role of the Anglo-American courts.’” Summers v. Earth Island Institute, 555 U.S. 488, ___. The concept of the Establishment clause is reinforced by the doctrine that an individual who has paid taxes has a “continuing, legally cognizable interest in ensuring that those funds are not used by the Government in a way that violates the Constitution,” Hein v. Freedom From Religion Foundation, Inc., 551 U. . S. 587, 599. This precept has been referred to as the rule against taxpayer standing. The doctrinal basis for the rule was discussed in Frothingham v. Mellon, 262 U. s. 447 (1923). There, a taxpayer-plaintiff had alleged that certain federal expenditures were in excess of congressional authority. The plaintiff argued that she had standing to raise her claim because she had an interest in the Government Treasury and because the allegedly unconstitutional expenditure of Government funds would affect her personal tax liability. The Court rejected those arguments. But the fact that respondents are state taxpayers does not give them standing to challenge the subsidies that §§43–989 allegedly provide to religious STOs, and the taxpayer’s “interest in the moneys of the Treasury” was necessarily “shared with millions of others,’ ” Doremus v. Board of Ed. of Hawthorne, 342 U., S. 166, 188–189. It followed that the plaintiff did not give rise to a case or controversy subject to judicial resolution under Article III. The primary contention of respondents, however, is that, despite the general rule that taxpayers lack standing to object to expenditures alleged to be unconstitutional, their suit falls within the exception established by Flast v. Cohen, 392 U., at 434. That rule is incompatible with the suggestion that federal courts might wield an “unconditioned authority to determine the constitutionality of legislative or executive acts” Valley Forge Christian College v. Americans United for Separation of Church and State, Inc. 464, 471 (1982). For the federal courts to decide questions of law arising outside of cases and controversies would be inimical to the Constitution's democratic character. And the resulting conflict between the judicial and the political branches would not, “in the long run, be beneficial to either. ” United States v. Richardson, 418 U.

The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled that a municipal park ordinance requiring a permit before a large-scale event can be justified under the First Amendment right to free speech. The Chicago Park District's ordinance requires a permit in order to conduct a public assembly, parade, picnic, or other event involving more than fifty individuals, or engage in an activity such as creating or emitting any amplified sound. The Park District has granted some permits and denied others. Petitioners filed an action alleging that the ordinance is unconstitutional on its face. The district court granted summary judgment in favor of the Park District, and the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed. The Supreme Court ruled that the park district's permit provision does not violate the free-speech rights of the public. The court held that the permit provision provides for a reasonable process to determine whether a permit is valid. The high court ruled that there is no reason to conclude that a permit provision that requires a prior approval by a government official cannot be justified.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California granted summary judgment in favor of the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation's (CDC) motion to dismiss the complaint filed by B. Garrison Johnson, an African-American inmate in the custody of the CDC. The complaint alleged that, from 1987 to 1991, former CDC Director James Rowland instituted and enforced an unconstitutional policy of housing inmates according to race. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that Johnson had stated a claim for racial discrimination in violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court dismissed his complaint for failure to state a claim, holding that Johnson's allegations were not clear-cut and that his conduct was not clearly unconstitutional. The appeals court granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment on the basis that they were entitled to qualified immunity. The court held that the defendants had not proven that their conduct was unconstitutional, and that the complaint was not filed with sufficient detail to support a finding of fact. The parties moved for a final judgment that would conclude that the policy is not unconstitutional and that it does not violate the Constitution's guarantees of equal protection under the law and of the equal protection clause. The final judgment would determine the amount of damages that Johnson would be entitled to. The defendants have also asked the court to rule that they are not liable for any of the costs associated with the case.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada granted Domino's Pizza's motion to dismiss a breach-of-contract action brought by John McDonald, the sole shareholder and president of JWM Investments, Inc., a Nevada corporation organized under Nevada law. The court granted the motion, finding that McDonald was not a party to any contract with Domino’s. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, however, held that McDonald could bring suit under  1981 because he had not been prevented from entering into such a contractual relationship. The Supreme Court, in a separate decision, held in a similar case that a corporation could not be held liable for a breach of contract by a nonparty. The high court held that the parties had not established a common law basis for the common law claim. The Ninth Circuit's decision was consistent with the decision in Gomez v. Alexian Bros. Hospital of San Jose, 698 F. 2d 1019, 102022 (1983), in which the Court held that an individual could not sue a corporation for breach of a contract if the corporation was the sole party to the contract. The decision was the first time the Supreme Court had held that a person could sue a company for breach under the 1981 provision of the federal securities laws. In a separate ruling, the Court of Appeal for the 9th Circuit held that there was no basis for McDonald's complaint. We conclude that McDonald did not have a common-law basis for his complaint.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) in a civil deportation case.  The court's order, which is subject to court approval, permanently enjoins the INS from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the INS to comply with the entry of an exclusionary rule.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against a San Mateo, California man accused of illegally entering the country.  According to the SEC's complaint, Sandoval-Sanchez was arrested at the plant shortly before 8 a.m. on July 7, 1976. The complaint alleges that the INS officers conducted a routine search and seizure of evidence in the course of their arrest. The INS officers allegedly conducted a series of searches and seizures, including one that led to the discovery of a large amount of contraband. The SEC's order also prohibits the INS agents from conducting any search or seizure without a warrant, and prohibits the agents from recording or recording the conduct of the officers. In addition, the order prohibits the officers from conducting searches or seizures of any kind. The court also ordered the INS not to conduct any search, search, or seizure of any evidence. The order also requires the agents to provide a "record of arrest" to prove the officer's bona fide immigration status.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the INS and the BIA have agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry and entry of a permanent injunction against future violations of the federal immigration laws. The final judgment also orders the agency to pay a civil penalty of $100,000, which will be determined by the court upon motion of the SEC.  Separately, the Court of Appeals has issued an order appointing a temporary receiver to oversee the repatriation of illegal aliens.  On August 2, 2018, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. Snyder granted the SEC request for a temporary restraining order against further violations of federal immigration law.

A federal statute entitles indigent defendants to the appointment of counsel in capital cases, including habeas corpus proceedings. The statute contemplates that appointed counsel may be “replaced . . . upon motion of the defendant,” §3599(e), but it does not specify the standard that district courts should use in evaluating those motions. See People v. Clair, 2 Cal. 4th 629, 644–647, 828 P. 2d 705, 713–714. The District Court denied Clair’s motion to change counsel. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit instructed the FPD to address whether substitution of counsel was now warranted, and in October 2005, the court informed the court that “the attorney-client relationship ha[d] broken down to such an extent that sub-stitution of counsel [would be] appropriate.” The State did not comment or object, and the court provided Clair with a new lawyer going forward. Clair then asked the District Court to vacate the denial of his habas petition under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b), arguing that he should be allowed to explore the significance of the new physical evidence for his case. The court denied the motion. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, but the court of appeals reversed. Held: 1. The district court did not abuse its discretion in denying the motion to alter counsel. Pp. 5–11. (a) The “interests of justice” standard is applicable to cases in which an individual has a Sixth Amendment right. A statute need not draw the same lines as the Constitution, and neither §3006A nor §3799 does so in addressing the substitution of the counsel. Section 3599(a)(2), (e). But the statute fails to specify how a court should decide such a motion. See, e.g., United States v. Taylor, 487 U. S. 326, 336–337. The State contends that the substitution standard is appropriate only when the defendant has suffered an “actual or constructive denial” of counsel. That denial occurs, the State contends, in just three situations: when the lawyer lacks the qualifications necessary for appointment under the statute; when he has a “disabling conflict of interest”; or when he “total[ly] desert[ed]” the client. Clair also argues that the trial court has not considered (much less adopted) the standard in any context; neither has a federal court used it in any case. But most naturally read, §2254(i) prohibits a court from granting substantive habeaas relief on the basis of a lawyer‘s ineffectiveness in post-conviction proceedings, not from substituting counsel on that ground. See Tr. of Oral Arg. 45–46. Moreover, the standard comports with the myriad ways that §3500 seeks to promote effective representation for persons threatened with capital punishment. See id., at 15–16. The standard also takes account of, rather than ignores or opposes, the state’S interest in avoiding undue delay. The question here is whether the court abused its discretion, since Clair, not the State, got it right. Clair argues that substitution motions will become a mechanism to defer enforcement of a death sentence, contrary to historic restrictions on “abuse of the writ” and to the goals of the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA). The State also makes a more specific argument based on AEDPA, see Brief for Petitioner 26–29, but this argument, like the last, forgets that the State thinks substitution proper “only when ... counsel is completely denied”-which occurs when counsel lacks the requisite experience; “actively represents conflicting interests” or has “completely abandoned” a client. And that consideration conflicts with the State’’d pro-vision for substitution motions, which is based on the fact that the standard is new to the State. The second letter, however, added a new and significant charge of attorney error. Clair alleges that counsel had refused to investigate particular, newly located physical evidence, which Clair alleged might have shown that the police had suppressed Brady material, that his trial counsel had been ineffective in investigating the murder, or that he had not committed the offense. Clair counters that only its approach comport with “this Court's long-established jurisprudence” that habeasc prisoners, including capital prisoners, have no right to counsel under the Sixth Amendment. But here, the timing of the second letter precludes a holding that the Court abused the discretion. The fact that Clair added the new charge to the substitution motion does not mean that the court did so, although it did not make any inquiry into the new evidence. The case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over a patent-law counterclaim filed by a Kansas-based manufacturer of patented fans and heaters against a competitor. The court held that the lower court's declaratory judgment and injunction in favor of the competitor did not constitute a change in the law of trade dress. The high court held, however, that the court had jurisdiction over the counterclaim because the complaint did not allege a claim arising under federal patent law, but the counterclaim contained a patent law counterclaim. The Supreme Court's decision was based on the fact that the case involved a dispute over the design of a "spiral grill" in a fan and heater, and that the complaint was filed in the same manner as a patent suit filed by Vornado Air Circulation Systems, Inc. in 1992 against Duracraft Corp. The lower court found that Vornado had no protectable trade-dress rights in the spiral grill design. Vornado filed a complaint with the U.N. International Trade Commission against The Holmes Group Inc., claiming that the Holmes's sale of fans with a spiral grill infringed Vornado's patent and the same trade dress held unprotectable in Vornado I. The Holmes group filed a declaration and injunction action against Vornado, seeking a judgment that its products did not infringe the patent and an injunction restraining the Holmes group from selling fans with the same design. The district court granted the Holmes Group's motion for summary judgment in favor, and the court stayed all proceedings related to the counterclaim until the case could be heard on appeal. The Federal Circuit vacated the lower-court's judgment, and remanded for consideration of the issue of whether the Federal Court had jurisdiction. The Court held that it had jurisdiction because the case was not based on a patent claim, but on the counterclaim itself. The High Court held the lower courts did not have jurisdiction because Vornado was not alleging a patent infringement claim. The appeals court held the case did not establish that the counterclaim was a trade dress claim under federal law exception to the collateralestoppel effect of the rule. The case was remanded for further consideration.

Case Name: Donovan v. New York City Department of Parks and Recreation
Case Number: 82-1001
Decision Date: July 1, 1982
Judge(s): Burger, Powell, Stevens, Blackmun, White, Marshall, Brennan, O'Connor
Issue: Whether the placement of a nativity scene in Central Park during the Christmas season violates the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.
Holding: No, the placement of a nativity scene in Central Park during the Christmas season does not violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment because it constitutes a form of secular expression rather than an attempt to promote religion.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of plaintiffs who had suffered damage due to the negligent operation of a drawbridge owned and maintained by the defendants. The Court found that the defendants, despite being a local government agency, could not rely on sovereign immunity to avoid liability for their actions. The Court noted that the concept of "sovereign immunity" refers to the idea that states and their agencies are immune from civil liability for injuries caused by their acts, but that this immunity is derived from the historical fact that states possessed absolute sovereignty before the ratification of the Constitution. Since the Constitution limits the powers of the states, the Court held that only states and arms of the state possess immunity from civil liability, and that local governments are not considered arms of the state for purposes of determining immunity.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a Canadian citizen who was convicted of making a false statement to a United States customs official in violation of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, Benni Noris, who was originally from Algeria, attempted to enter the United States by car ferry at Port Angeles, Washington. The complaint alleges that after being questioned by a customs official, Noris agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to complete a customs declaration form and carry an explosive "during the commission of any felony which may be prosecuted in a court of the States." The SEC's order also prohibits Noris from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any security-related product or service, and prohibits him from associating with any third party. Noris has agreed to settle the case by consenting, without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, to a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and an officer-and-director bar. The court also granted certiorari to the remaining defendants in the case.  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

Respondent Stewart worked as a mechanic aboard the “Super Scoop,” a large dredge operated by petitioner Dutra Marine Contractors, LLC. One day, while working near the surface of the Charles River, he was struck by debris falling from the Super Scoop’s sister scow. After filing suit against Dutra under the Jones Act, 46 U. S. C. § 1320(a), he also invoked the Longshoremen’s Harbour Workers’ Compensation Act (LHWCA), 33 U. S. C. § 902 et seq., claiming entitlement to benefits as a covered employee. The District Court entered summary judgment for Dutra, ruling that the Super Scoop was not a “vessel” within the meaning of the LHWCA. On interim appeal, the First Circuit affirmed, adhering to its precedent holding that the Super Scoop was not a “vessel.” Held: The Super Scoop is a “vessel” within the meaning of the LHWCA. Pp. 1–12. (a) Prior to the passage of the Jones Act and the LHWCA in the 1920s, the term “vessel” was defined in Rev. Stat. §3 as “any kind of watercraft … used, or capable of being used, as a means of transportation on water.” That definition has been interpreted to include dredges. See, e. g., Norton v. Warner Co., 321 U. S. 565. Although the Court has occasionally implied a narrower definition of “vessel” in specific cases involving drydocks and similar structures, see, e. g., Cope v. Valette Dry Dock Co., 119 U. S. 625, those decisions were based on distinctions drawn by the general maritime law between watercraft temporarily stationed in a particular location and those permanently affixed to shore or resting on the ocean floor. Such distinctions make sense, as a ship and its crew do not move in and out of Jones Act coverage depending on whether the ship is at anchor, docked for loading or unloading, or berthed for minor repairs, whereas permanent fixtures do not become vessels merely because of the remote possibility that they may someday sail again. Moreover, applying §3’s broader definition brings within the purview of the Jones Act the sorts of watercraft considered vessels at the time Congress passed that Act. Pp. 1–6. (b) The Court of Appeals erred in holding that the Super Scoop is not a “vessel” because its primary purpose is not navigation or commerce and because it was not in actual transit at the time of Stewart’s injury. Section 3’s definition applies to watercraft that are “capable of being used” to transport people, freight, or cargo from place to place, regardless of their primary purpose or state of transit at a particular moment. Here, the Super Scoop was not only “capable of being used” to transport equipment and workers over water—it was doing just that. Nor was it inactive at the time of Stewart’s injury. The Court of Appeals’ snapshot test rejecting a “vessel” determination based solely on whether the watercraft was moving at the time of the accident is inconsistent with the Court’s reasoning in Chandris, Inc. v. Phillips Petroleum Co., 515 U. S. 30, 373–374, which indicated that the requirement that a vessel be “in navigation” is an element of the vessel status of a watercraft, relevant to whether the craft is “used, or capable of being used” for maritime transportation. Finally, the Court of Appeals’ approach is untenable because the LHWCA does not meaningfully define the term “vessel” as it appears in either §902(3)(G), which excludes seamen from the Act’s coverage, or §905(b), which imposes liability on vessel owners for negligence to longshoremen. Instead, 1 U. S. C. §3 defines the term “vessel” throughout the LHWCA. Pp. 6–12. 230 F. 3d 458, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

Petitioner Bullcoming was arrested on charges of driving while intoxicated (DWI). At trial, the prosecution did not call as a witness the analyst who signed the certification. Instead, the State called another analyst who was familiar with the laboratory’s testing procedures, but had neither participated in nor observed the test on Bullcoming’d blood sample. The New Mexico Supreme Court determined that, although the blood-alcohol analysis was “testimonial,” the Confrontation Clause did not require the certifying analyst’“in-court testimony.” Held: A forensic laboratory report stating that a suspect substance was cocaine ranked as testimonial for purposes of the Sixth Amendment’S Confrontations Clause does not meet the constitutional requirement. Pp. 5–11. (a) The Confrontated Clause permits the prosecution to introduce a forensic laboratory Report containing a testimonial certification, made in order to prove a fact at a criminal trial, through the in-court witness’in-bout testimony of an analyst who did not sign the certification or personally perform or observe the test reported in the certification, unless that analyst is unavailable at trial, and the accused had an opportunity, pretrial, to cross-examine that particular scientist. The question presented in Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts, 557 U. S. ___ (2010), is whether the Court of Appeals erred in holding that, absent stipulation, the Court may not introduce such a report without offering a live witness competent to testify to the truth of the statements made in the report. Held: surrogate testimony of that order does not comply with the requirement. MelendezDiaz, supra, at 8–9. The Sixth Amendment confers upon the accused “[i]n all criminal prosecutions, … the right … to be confronted with the witnesses against him” in a pathmarking 2004 decision, Crawford v. Washington, 547 U.S. 813, 826. If an out-of-court statement is testimonial in nature, it may not be introduced against the accused at trial unless the witness who made the statement is unavailable and has had a prior opportunity to confront that witness. This Court has overruled Ohio v. Roberts, 448 U. s. 56 (1980), which had interpreted Crawford to allow admission of absent witnesses’ testimonial statements based on a judicial determination of reliability. Crawford held that fidelity to that Clause permitted admission of “testimonial statements of witnesses absent from trial … only where the declarant is unavailable, and only where [the defendant has] had a . prior opportunity . . . cross-examination.’ ” id., at 7–8. The State in the instant case never asserted that the analyst was unavailable. The record showed only that Caylor certified to more than a machine-generated number. The trial court overruled the objection, id., and admitted the SLD report as a business record, at 44–46, 57. In any event, the comparative reliability of a analyst's testimonial report drawn from machine-produced data does not overcome the Sixth amendment bar. The comparative reliability, however, does not dispense with that Clause’n’t dispense, because the court believes that the rights can be disregarded so long as the trial is, on the whole, fair. See, e. g., Crawford, 541 U. . . at 62. If repre-sentation by substitute counsel does not satisfy the Fifth Amendment, neither does the opportunity to confronted a substitute witness. In short, when the State elected to introduce Caylor‘s certification, Caylor became a witness Bullcoming had the right to confront. This precedent cannot sensibly be read any other way. See Melendez Diaz, 556 U . S., at ___ (slip op., at 6). Melendez–Diaz left no room for that argument, the court concluded, a conclusion inescapable. Because the analysts who write reports that the prosecution introduces must be made available for confrontation even if they possess “the scientific acumen of Mme. Curie and the veracity of Mother Teresa. ” Melendez

This case involves a dispute between a private party and the United States government over the validity of a mineral reserve created by a state act. The private party claims that the mineral reserves belong to them, while the United States argues that the reserve expires after a certain date and that the private party is trying to take advantage of the situation. The case raises several legal issues, including the scope of federal court jurisdiction, the role of state courts in resolving conflicts with federal court decisions, and the appropriate standard for determining the validity of a state statutory provision. Ultimately, the Supreme Court holds that the United States is entitled to seek a preliminary injunction to halt the private party's efforts to assert ownership of the mineral reserves until the matter can be fully heard in federal court.

The Supreme Court was tasked with determining whether the National Bank for Cooperatives, a federally chartered instrumentality of the United States, is exempt from state income taxation. The Court concluded that it is not exempt.

The Court's reasoning is based on the interpretation of the Farm Credit Act and its amendments. Initially, banks for cooperatives were exempt from state income taxes only when the United States held stock in them. This exemption ceased once the government's investment was repaid. Subsequent amendments to the Farm Credit Act did not change this rule.

In 1985, amendments to the Act removed language that had become irrelevant because the United States no longer held stock in these banks. The Court found no indication that Congress intended to change the taxation status of banks for cooperatives with these amendments. The Court reasoned that it would be surprising for Congress to make a significant change to the taxation of banks for cooperatives without explicitly stating so.

Furthermore, the structure of the Farm Credit Act, which specifies the tax exemptions for different entities within the Farm Credit System, does not grant banks for cooperatives the same comprehensive tax immunity as other institutions like farm credit banks and federal land bank associations. The Court inferred from Congress's silence on the matter that banks for cooperatives are subject to state taxation.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Missouri Supreme Court, which had held that banks for cooperatives were exempt from state income taxation, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

At a school-sanctioned and school-supervised event, a high school principal saw some of her students unfurl a large banner conveying a message she reasonably regarded as promoting illegal drug use. Consistent with established school policy prohibiting such messages at school events, the principal directed the students to take down the banner. One student-among those who had brought the banner to the event-refused to do so. The principal confiscated the banner and told the student to report to her office, where she suspended him for 10 days. The school board upheld the suspension, but the Juneau School District Superintendent upheld it, limiting it to time served. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the principal’s actions were permissible because the banner was “speech or action that intrudes upon the work of the schools.” Held: The school officials did not violate the First Amendment by confiscating the pro-drug banner and suspending the student responsible for it. Pp. 5–11. (a) The First Amendment rights of students in public school are not automatically coextensive with those entrusted to their care from speech that can reasonably be regarded as encouraging illegal drugs use. See, e.g., Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School Dist., 393 U. S. 503, 506. The Second question is whether a principal may restrict student speech at a school event, when that speech is reasonably viewed as promoting illicit drug use, and whether that right was so clearly established that the school principal may be held liable for damages. This Court has no occasion to reach the second question. See generally 1 National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health, Monitoring the Future: National Survey Results on Drug Use, 1975–2005, Secondary School Students (2006). Tinker, supra, at 506). Here, the school board and school superintendent, acting during a “school-authorized activit[y],” and “proceed[ing] on the basis that the banner expressed a positive sentiment about marijuana use,” the court nonetheless found a violation of Frederick, who cannot “stand in the midst of his fellow students, during school events” because he thought that his speech gave rise to a risk of substantial disruption. See Kuhlmeier, 484 U.S., at 271. The District Court granted summary judgment for the school and Morse, ruling that they were entitled to qualified immunity and that they had not infringed Frederick, and that the student could sue the principal for damages, since the principal could not “disagree with the views he sought to express” at the time of his suspension. The Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that Frederick had a First Amendment right to wield his banner, and, if so, whether that “right was clearly established” that the Principal may be liable. Held: Frederick cannot be held responsible for damages because the school punished him without demonstrating that his constitutionally protected speech was political speech, and the principal should instead enjoy qualified immunity for her actions. The question thus becomes whether a Principal may, consistent with the First First Amendment, restrict student Speech at a School Event, when the speech that she reasonably regard as promoting drug use constitutes promotion of illegal drug abuse. This is not a case about political debate over the criminalization of drug use or possession. See Wood v. Strickland, 420U. S., 308, 314, n. 6. In Tinker, this Court made clear that ‘First Amendment rights, applied in light of the special characteristics of the school environment, are available to teachers and students.’ “First Amendment Rights” are not required schools to tolerate at school event student expression that contributes to those dangers. See also, the Government interest in stopping student drug abuse—reflected in the policies of Congress and myriad school boards, including JDHS—allow schools to restrict students’ expression that they reasonably regard to be promoting illegal drugs. Tinker warned that schools may not prohibit student speech because of “undifferentiated fear or apprehension of disturbance” or “a mere desire to avoid the controversy which might result from the expression. . . . The school setting requires some easing of the restrictions to which searches by public authorities are ordinarily subject.“ Guiles v. Marineau, 461 F. 3d 320, 328. The School Board and the Department of Education have the authority to determine “what manner of speech in the classroom or in school assembly is inappropriate. See Guiles, 536 U.

Title: Bell Atlantic Corporation v. Twombly

Summary: In Bell Atlantic Corporation v. Twombly, the Supreme Court ruled that plaintiffs must plead facts that give rise to a plausible inference of fraudulent activity in order to survive a motion to dismiss. The Court clarified that a complaint must contain allegations that are sufficiently detailed to enable defendants to mount a meaningful defense. The Court also distinguished between claims that involve simple errors and those that involve fraudulent activity.

Background: Bell Atlantic Corporation sued Verizon Communications Inc. for patent infringement. Verizon filed a counterclaim accusing Bell Atlantic of engaging in false advertising and unfair business practices. Bell Atlantic moved to dismiss the counterclaim, arguing that Verizon had failed to plead sufficient facts to establish fraudulent activity.

Decision: The Supreme Court held that plaintiffs must plead facts that give rise to a plausible inference of fraudulent activity in order to survive a motion to dismiss. The Court clarified that a complaint must contain allegations that are sufficiently detailed to enable defendants to mount a meaningful defense. The Court also distinguished between claims that involve simple errors and those that involve fraudulent activity. Specifically, the Court held that a claim involving fraudulent activity requires more than a bare legal theory of liability; it must be supported by specific allegations that create a strong inference of dishonesty.

Impact: The decision in Bell Atlantic Corporation v. Twombly has had a significant impact on the litigation landscape. Plaintiffs are now required to plead more specific and detailed allegations in order to avoid dismissal of their claims. This has led to a shift away from the "pleading inflation" of the late 1990s and early 2000s, where plaintiffs would file vague and boilerplate complaints in hopes of surviving a motion to dismiss.

Petitioner Wiggin's convictions for murder and rape were upheld by the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals despite his assertion that he was entitled to appear pro se rather than with standby counsel. The Federal District Court ultimately denied Wiggin's petition for a writ of habeas corpus, rejecting his claim that his Sixth Amendment right to self-representation had been violated by the unwanted participation of standby counsel in the trial. Held: Although a pro se defendant has a right to appear on stage at his trial, standby counsel need not be excluded altogether, especially when the participation is outside the jury's presence or is with the defendant's express or tacit consent. Pp. 48-58. (a) A defendant's Sixth Amendment rights are not violated when a trial judge appoints standby counsel-even over the defendant's objection-to relieve the judge of the need to explain and enforce basic rules of courtroom protocol or to assist the defendant in overcoming routine obstacles that stand in the way of the defendant's achieving his own clearly indicated goals. Participation by counsel to steer a defendant through the basic procedures of trial is permissible even in the unlikely event that it somewhat undermines the pro se defendant's appearance of control over his own defense. Pp. 52-55. (b) Here, although Wiggin's objections to the presence and participation of counsel were general, many instances of counsel's involvement were either approved by Wiggin or attendant to routine clerical or procedural matters, and hence did not infringe upon Wiggin's Faretta rights. Moreover, Wiggin unquestionably maintained actual control over the presentation of his own defense at all times, and appeared before the jury in the status of one defending himself. Pp. 55-58. 652 F. 2d 115, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment that permanently enjoins the trustees of employee benefit trust funds from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 302(c)(5) of the Labor Management Relations Act of 1947.  According to the court's order, in 1967, the United Mine Workers of America and Bituminous Coal Operators' Association (BOOA) established a fund to provide pension, health, and other benefits for certain coal miners and their dependents. The fund was established for the sole and exclusive benefit of the employees and their families.  In 1974, the union and BOOA agreed to restructure the fund and to increase the eligibility requirements for certain widows and widows of deceased miners.  The court also found that, in 1974, a provision of the collective-bargaining agreement that prohibited employer contributions to pension funds was arbitrary and capricious.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the court, the trustees agreed to a judgment permanently enjoining them from future violations of the federal securities laws and ordering them to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount of their disgorgement plus prejudgment interest, and ordering the trustees to pay civil penalties equal to any amount owed to the fund.    The settlement is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by John Rymas of the SEC's Chicago Regional Office and supervised by Marc Blau of the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis. The litigation will be led by Mr. Blau.

In a condemnation proceeding in a federal district court, the Government obtained a writ of possession pending final disposition of the cause. Later, the Government filed a contested proceeding in the local land office of the Department of the Interior to determine the validity of respondent's mining claims. Alleging that the land embraced within respondents' claims is nonmineral in character and that minerals have not been found within the limits of the claims in sufficient quantity to constitute a valid discovery, the Government sought to have the validity of the claims determined administratively. Respondents sued in a federal district court to enjoin the officers of the Department from proceeding with the administrative action. Held: The District Court erred in granting summary judgment for the Government, because the institution of the suit in the District Court was an appropriate way of obtaining immediate possession, it was not inconsistent with the administrative remedy for determining the validity of the mining claims, and the District Court should have held its hand until the issue of the validity of the claims has been resolved by the agency entrusted by Congress with the task. Pp. 44-50. 293 F. 2d 553, reversed.

Case Name: Rodriguez v. Wainwright
Case Number: 410 U.S. __ (1973)
Decided Date: June 26, 1973
Issue: Does the Equal Protection Clause prohibit the use of race as a criterion for awarding scholarships in publicly supported universities?
Holding: Yes, the use of race as a criterion for awarding scholarships in publicly supported universities violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

During the closing days of the 1982 Minnesota gubernatorial race, Dan Cohen, an active Republican associated with Wheelock Whitney's Independent-Republican gubernatorial campaign, approached reporters from the St. Paul Pioneer Press Dispatch (Pioneer Press) and the Minneapolis Star and Tribune (Star Tribune) and offered to provide documents relating to a candidate in the upcoming election. Both papers agreed to keep Cohen's identity anonymous and Cohen turned over copies of two public court records concerning Johnson, the Democratic-Farmer-Labor candidate for Lieutenant Governor. The first record indicated that Johnson had been charged in 1969 with three counts of unlawful assembly, and the second that she had been convicted in 1970 of petit theft. Both newspapers interviewed Johnson for her explanation and one reporter tracked down the person who had found the records for Cohen. As it turned out, the unlawful assembly charges arose out of Johnson's participation in a protest of an alleged failure to hire minority workers on municipal construction projects and the charges were eventually dismissed. Cohen was fired by his employer. The same day the stories appeared, Cohen sued respondents, the publishers of the Pioneer Press and Star Tribune, in Minnesota state court, alleging fraudulent misrepresentation and breach of contract. The trial court rejected respondents' argument that the First Amendment barred Cohen's lawsuit. A jury returned a verdict in Cohen's favor, awarding him $200,000 in compensatory damages and $500,000 punitive damages. The Minnesota Court of Appeals reversed the award of punitive damages after concluding that Cohen had failed to establish a fraud claim, the only claim which would support such an award. However, the court upheld the finding of liability and the compensatory damage award. A divided Minnesota Supreme Court reversed the damages award, concluding that a contract cause of action is inappropriate for these particular circumstances. The court then went on to address the question whether Cohen could establish a cause of actions under Minnesota law on a promissory estoppel theory. Held: 1. The First Amendment does not confer on the press a constitutional right to disregard promises that would otherwise be enforced under state law. Pp. 583-588. (a) The First and First Amendments do not confer upon the press on the ground that they are not subject to stricter scrutiny than would be applied to enforcement against other persons or organizations. P. 586. (b) The fact that the state supreme court actually considered and decided the question of whether Cohen was entitled to recover damages, under the state-law doctrine, for a newspaper's breach of a promise of confidentiality given to the plaintiff in exchange for information, does not preclude the press from recovering damages for a libel or defamation claim. Nor is Cohen attempting to use a "denial of confidentiality" cause to avoid the strict requirements for establishing a libel and defamation claim, as was the case in Hustler Magazine, Inc. v. Falwell, 485 U. S. 46. Similarly, the media must obey the National Labor Relations Act, Associated Press v. Delaware, 438 U.S. 154, 161-162, and must pay non-discriminatory taxes. The press, like others interested in publishing, may not publish copyrighted material without obeying the copyright laws. Thus, it may not be said that the press' obligation shared by all citizens to respond to a grand jury subpoena and answer questions relevant to a criminal investigation, even though the reporter might be required to reveal a confidential source. Thus this is not a case where news organizations will have legal incentives not to disclose confidential sources' identity even when that person's identity is itself newsworthy. Moreover, the fact that this Court rested its holding on federal law could not be made more clear than by its conclusion that "in this case enforcement of the promise ... would violate defendants' First Amendment rights." 457 N. W. 2d 199, reversed and remanded.

The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced that it has filed a settled civil action in the United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma against Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc., a research and brokerage firm that offers securities trading services to investors.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York on April 10, 2003, Merrill Lynch violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The complaint alleges that Merrill Lynch used its misinformed brokers to enhance the prices of its investment banking clients’ stocks, and that the clients and brokers both continued to hold their stocks long beyond the point when the truth was revealed.  In a parallel action, the U.S. Attorney General of New York announced that he would order Merrill Lynch to pay a civil penalty of $1.5 million.  Merrill Lynch agreed to settle the SEC’s action without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint.  Dabit also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company and to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest of $2.2 million, which is equal to the amount of his civil monetary penalty.  Without admitting the allegations of the complaint in the SEC’s Complaint, the court agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins Merrill Lynch from violating the federal securities laws, and orders it to pay civil penalties of $100,000 and $50,000, respectively, for each of those violations.   The settlement is subject to court approval. Mississippi statutes authorize the State Tax Commission to purchase intoxicating liquors from out-of-state distillers and to require the distillers to add a price markup to cover the cost of operation of the wholesale liquor business, yield a reasonable profit, and keep Mississippi's liquor prices competitive with those of neighboring States. The Commission promulgated a regulation that gave post exchanges, officers' clubs, ship's stores, and other nonappropriated fund activities operating on military installations within the State the option of purchasing alcoholic beverages directly from out-of-state distillers or from the Commission. The regulation requires that orders from distillers bear the usual price markup as charged by the Commission on its sales, which the distiller in turn must remit to the Commission or face a fine, imprisonment, or delisting, i. e., withdrawal of the privilege of distributing alcoholic beverages to the Commission for resale in Mississippi. The United States, which has exclusive jurisdiction over the two exclusively federal military installations in Mississippi, challenged the regulation as a violation of its immunity from state taxation. The District Court held that the regulation was not invalid under the Twenty-first Amendment, which prohibits the States from levying taxes on the importation of distilled spirits into territory over which the United States exercises exclusive jurisdiction. The court also held that the regulation was not invalid under the Buck Act, which bars the United States from asserting immunity from state sales and use taxes on the ground that "the Federal Government has exclusive jurisdiction over the area where the transaction occurred." The court concluded that the regulation was valid under the Buck Act because the markup was intended to rest upon instrumentalities of the United States, i. e., the nonappropriated fund activities, and not upon the out-of-state distillers. 

Held: 
1. The regulation is invalid under the Buck Act. Pp. 372-377.
	 (a) Viewing the markup as a sales tax, the legal incidence of that tax was intended to rest upon instrumentalities of the United States. Pp. 372-375.
	 (b) The Buck Act is of no assistance to the State Tax Commission in its attempt to enforce the regulation. Pp. 375-377. 
2. The regulation is also invalid under the Twenty-first Amendment. Pp. 377-378. 378 F. Supp. 561, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed a lower court's decision to grant a new trial to a man convicted of armed postal robbery based on a codefendant's confession to a postal inspector that he had committed the crime. The court held that the jury should not have been allowed to hear the confession because the jury was told that it had to be disregarded in determining the defendant's guilt or innocence. The Supreme Court held in a separate case that the confession could not be used as evidence because it violated the Sixth Amendment's right to cross-examine a witness. The appeals court agreed with the lower court, but the Supreme Court ruled that the Court should have granted a retrial. The lower court had granted a motion for a mistrial based on the jury's instructions to the jury. The Court granted the retrial, and the jury returned a guilty verdict against the defendant. The case is now before the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri. The trial judge has granted the prosecution's motion to dismiss the case. The prosecution has also requested that the court grant it a new hearing.

These two cases involve petitions challenging the constitutionality of a provision requiring individuals seeking an exemption on their property taxes for religious purposes to swear an oath denying any advocacy of violent overthrow of the government or support for a foreign government against the US. The petitions were filed after the Los Angeles Assessor denied them the exemption based on their refusal to take the required oath. The cases went through various courts before being heard at the Supreme Court. In both cases, the Supreme Court found that the enforcement of the oath placed too much burden on the individual taxpayer and therefore constituted a violation of due process under the Fourteenth Amendment. As such, the judgments were reversed and the cases remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

In this landmark decision, the US Supreme Court established the concept of "limited-purpose public figures" under the First Amendment's right to freedom of speech. The Court clarified that someone does not need to be a celebrity or famous nationwide to qualify as a public figure. Instead, a person can become a public figure based on their involvement in specific public controversies or issues. However, the Court also set forth strict criteria for determining whether someone qualifies as a limited-purpose public figure, including whether the person has actively sought out public attention and whether their actions have resulted in significant consequences beyond their immediate circumstances.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed a lower court's ruling that a defendant had no standing to challenge the validity of a federal law that prohibits possession or use of any chemical that can cause death, temporary incapacitation, or permanent harm to humans or animals. The court found that the defendant, Carol Anne Bond, had standing to raise the issue of whether Congress exceeded its constitutional authority by enacting the law. The law was enacted to comply with the Chemical Weapons Convention, which was ratified in 1997 and prohibits the use or possession of chemical weapons. The Third Circuit held that the law violated the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law, and that Bond's challenge to the law's validity was based on the fact that it violated the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of the right to a private life. The Second Circuit agreed with the lower court that Bond did not have standing, and the case was remanded for further consideration. The case is now being handled by the same counsel who successfully argued the case before the Supreme Court.

Section 2607 (b) of the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) prohibits giving and accepting “any portion, split, or percentage of any charge made or received for the rendering of a real estate settlement service . . . other than for services actually performed.” Title 2607(a) provides that “no person shall give and no person shall accept any fee, kickback, or thing of value pursuant to any agreement or understanding, oral or otherwise, that business incident to or a part of a [real estate] settlement service involving a federally related mortgage loan shall be referred to any person,” §2607(b). The policy statement also provides that a settlement service provider may not mark-up the cost of another provider’s services without providing additional settlement services; such payment must be for services that are actual, necessary and distinct. Moreover, in addition to facing liability when it collects a fee that is entirely unearned, a provider may also “be liable under [§2607[b] when it charges a fee ... that exceeds the reason-able value of goods, facilities, or services provided, ibid., on the theory that the excess over reasonable value constitutes a “portion” of the charge “other than for Services actually performed,’” §§2607. The last mentioned point, however, is manifestly in-consistent with the statute HUD purported to construe. When Congress enacted RESPA in 1974, it included a directive that HUD make a report to Congress within five years regarding the need for further legislation in the area. See §2612(a). Among the topics required to be included in the report were “recommendations on whether Federal regulation of the charges for real-estate settlement services in federal related mortgage transactions is necessary and desirable, and, if so, recommendations with regard to what reforms should be adopted. §2613(b)(2). The directive for recommendations regarding the desirability of price regulation would make no sense if Congress had already resolved the issue-if §260 7(b) already carried with it authority for HUD to proscribe the collection of unreasonably high fees for settlement services, i.e., to engage in price regulation. Petitioners contend that, by allegedly charging each of them an unearned fee, respondent “accept[s]” a portion of a $575 loan “processing fee” and a $5,100 “loan origination” fee. Respondent removed petitioners’ lawsuits to federal court, where the cases were consolidated. The District Court agreed; and the Court of Appeals affirmed. A divided panel of the Fifth Circuit affirmed. The parties vigorously dispute whether the position set forth in the 2001 policy statement should be accorded deference under the framework announced by this Court in Chevron U. S. A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984). The parties need not resolve that dispute—or address whether, if Chevron deference would otherwise apply, it is eliminated by the policy statements’ palpable overreach with respect to price controls. Pp. 5–7. 626 F. 3d 799, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a company that was mining sand and gravel on property within its limits.  The court entered a temporary restraining order against the company, Builders Sand and Gravel Corporation, on the basis of which the court found that the company violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(3) of Exchange Act Rule 206(4)-8 thereunder.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Central District of California today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Brooklyn, New York, the company and its principal, Builds Sand andGravel, were mining on a portion of the lot, a use to which the company had been put continuously since 1927. The complaint alleges that, before the end of the first year the excavation had reached the water table leaving a waterfilled crater which has been widened and deepened to the point that it is now a 20-acre lake with an average depth of 25 feet.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from future violations of the federal securities laws, ordering them to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $100,000, and ordering the company to pay a $75,000 civil penalty. The court also granted the company's request for an asset freeze and an injunction against further mining on the lot.

After respondent had been indicted for violating California's "Syllabus" provision making it a crime to advocate the violent overthrow of the Government, appellee, a professor of history, moved to enjoin the District Attorney from prosecuting respondent on the grounds that the statute infringed freedom of speech and assembly. Respondent contended that he faced no threat of prosecution other than that incidental to every criminal proceeding brought lawfully and in good faith. The District Court ruled that the statute was void on its face and enjoined its enforcement. Held: An injunction against the enforcement of a state criminal statute is available only if the complainant shows bad faith or harassment or some other unusual circumstance justifying equitable relief. Pp. 308-316. Reversed and remanded.

When petitioner was arrested for unlawfully possessing marihuana, the arresting policeman patrolled the immediate vicinity of the arrest looking for other contraband. Petitioner's jacket, which was located in the passenger compartment of the car in which he had been a passenger just before he was arrested, was unzipped and a small amount of cocaine was found. Subsequently, petitioner was convicted of criminal possession of a controlled substance. Held: Where the arrest was lawful, the constitutonally permissible scope of a search incident thereto includes the passenger compartment of the automobile in which the arrest occurred. Pp. 108-114. (a) Although the principle limiting a search incident to a lawful custodial arrest may be stated clearly enough, courts have discovered the principle difficult to apply in specific cases. Here, the difficulty lies in determining the proper scope of a search of the interior of an automobile incident to a lawful custodial arrest of its occupants. No straightforward rule has emerged from the litigation respecting this question. Pp. 108-111. (b) It follows from this Court's decision in Chimelv . California, 395 U. S. 752, that when a policeman has made a lawful custodial arrest of the occupant of an automobile, he may, as a contemporaneous incident of that arrest, search the passenger compartment of that automobile. Pp. 111-112. (c) Since the passenger compartment is within reach of the arrestee, so too will containers in it be within his reach. P. 112. (d) Containers in the passenger compartment may be searched whether they are open or closed, since the justification for the search is not that the arrestee has no privacy interest in the container, but that the lawful custodial arrest justifies the infringement of any privacy interest the arrestee may have. P. 112. (e) Neither United States v. Chadwick, 433 U. S. 1, nor Arkansas v. Sanders, 442 U. S. 753, involved an arguably valid search incident to a lawful custodial arrest. Pp. 112-113. 50 N. Y. 2d 447, 429 N. E. 2d 420, reversed.

1. The Federal Government, in its zealous pursuit of the balance due on a disaster loan made by the Small Business Administration, may obtain judgment against Ethel Mae Yazell of Lampasas, Texas, a married woman who, under Texas law, could not bind her separate property unless she had first obtained a court decree removing her disability to contract. The loan was made to enable Yazell to reopen the store after the flood. The stock of Yazell's Little Ages was ruined. Yazell signed a note in the amount of $12,000 payable to the order of SBA in Dallas at the rate of $120 per month including 3% interest. On the same day they executed a chattel mortgage on their stock of merchandise and their store fixtures. By express reference to Article 4000 of the Revised Civil Statutes of Texas, the mortgage exempted from its coverage retail sales made from the stock. After a careful, detailed but commendably prompt investigation, the head of the SBA's Disaster Loan Office wrote to Yazell on June 20, 1957, that authorization for a loan of $ 12,000 had been received, and Yazell was informed that the loan would be made upon his compliance with certain requirements. On that same day he signed a certificate in the name of a law firm which had been employed by SBA to assist Yazell in complying with the terms of the loan. The certificate was accompanied by a separate acknowledgment of the wife before a notarized acknowledgment of her husband's wife. The certificates were signed by Yazell and the Acting Regional Counsel certified that "all action has been taken deemed desirable." Thereafter, the funds were made available to the Yazell family. The Government was rebuffed by the trial and appellate courts. Held: 1. In the circumstances of this case, the state rule governs, and, accordingly, the Federal Government is entitled to collect regardless of the limits of its contract and regardless of any state laws, however local and peculiarly domestic they may be. Pp. 461-464. 2. The State rule should govern. P. 462. 334 F. 2d 454, affirmed.

The Indian Land Consolidation Act (ILCA) was enacted in 1983 to reduce fractionated ownership of allotted lands. Section 207 of the act prohibited the decent or devise of small fractional interests in allotments and required that such interests escheat to the tribe. However, in 1984, Congress amended Section 207 to provide that an interest is considered fractional if it constitutes 2% or less of the total acreage of the parcel and "is incapable of earning $100 in any one of the five years" after the decedent's death. Additionally, the amended section allowed devise of an otherwise escheatable interest to another owner of an undivided fractional interest in the same parcel. The amended section also gave tribes authority to override the provisions of Section 207 through the adoption of their own codes governing the disposition of fractional interests.

Title: Durational Residence Requirement for Voting

Issue: Whether the durational residence requirement for voting in Tennessee is constitutional?

Background:

* The plaintiff, Harold Blumstein, is a retired businessman who moved to Tennessee in January 1972.
* After registering to vote, he discovered that he was unable to cast a ballot in the primary election due to the durational residence requirement.
* The defendant, the Secretary of State of Tennessee, maintained that the requirement was necessary to ensure the integrity of the electoral process and to prevent voter fraud.

Analysis:

* The Court examines the history of voter fraud in Tennessee and finds that the problem is exaggerated.
* The Court notes that the durational residence requirement is not a narrowly tailored solution to the problem of voter fraud and that it is instead a blunt instrument that disproportionately affects new residents.
* The Court holds that the durational residence requirement is not a valid justification for limiting the right to vote based on a person's status as a new resident.

Decision:

* The Court reverses the lower court's ruling and declares the durational residence requirement for voting in Tennessee to be unconstitutional.

The U.S. District Court for the Second Circuit today entered a final judgment against a former prison guard for failing to exhaust prison grievance procedures before seeking judicial relief.  According to the court's order, on June 10, 1999, Ronald Nussle, an inmate in a Connecticut prison, brought directly to court, without filing an inmate grievance, a complaint charging that corrections officers singled him out for a severe beating, in violation of the Eighth Amendment's ban on "cruel and unusual punishments."  The court also found that, in 1997e(a), a federal law requiring prisoners to exhaust administrative remedies before commencing a civil rights action, a violation of Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 17a-3 thereunder.  In addition, the court found that defendants could evade the exhaustion requirement by filing separate, separate, and unrelated complaints.  The Court also ruled that defendants can apply for injunctive relief only when there is sufficient evidence to support their claims.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the federal securities laws, ordering them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and imposing a civil penalty of $250,000.  On May 9, 2001, the Court of Appeals issued a temporary restraining order halting the defendants from further violating the securities laws and ordering the release of the defendants.   The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Connecticut, charges the defendants with violating the antifraud provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) ofÂ the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 ("Advisers Act"), and seeks permanent injunctions against future violations of the securities law, a conduct-based injunction, and an officer-and-director bar against the defendants, as well as a civil injunction against the officers' use of excessive force, and seeks a permanent injunction from future violations.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Quicken Loans, Inc. ("Quicken"), a Texas-based settlement service provider, for charging unearned fees in connection with mortgage transactions.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York on July 21, 2011, Quicken violated the antifraud provisions of Section 2607 of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The complaint alleges that Quicken and his co-conspirator, John R. Kelly, violated Section2607 by charging them fees for which no services were provided, and by failing to give them a percentage of the total amount of the unearned fee.  In addition, as alleged in the complaint, the Quicken loan discount fee charged to the Freemans and Bennetts was in fact a "loan discount fee" that was not tied in any respect to a charge paid by a particular consumer.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, QUicken and Kelly consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the federal securities laws, ordering Quicken to pay a $575 loan processing fee, a $1,100 loan origination fee, and a $5,100 fee in the future, and ordering Kelly to disgorge her ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest and pay civil penalties.  Quicken also agreed to pay disgorgement of $2,965, which represents approximately $3,500 in prejudgment interests, and to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years.  Kelly agreed to settle the case by consenting to a judgment that permanently enjoins her from future violations of the federal anti-fraud provisions, and orders her to pay an amount equal to three times the amount of her penalty.   The SEC's investigation was conducted by John Rymas and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The litigation will be led by Mr. Werner and Ms. Kelly. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Respondent Texas Secretary of State (Secretary) signed into law SB 1151C, a bill that provided for the redistricting of Texas’ 32 congressional districts. The bill was introduced in February 2003, and hearings were conducted in March and April of that year. The bill passed the House of Representatives on May 22, 2003, and the Senate on June 10, 2003. Governor Rick Perry signed the bill into law on July 1, 2003. The bill was published in the Texas Register on August 1, 2003, and went into effect on November 1, 2003. Petitioners, residents of Texas, filed suit challenging the bill’s constitutionality. The District Court ultimately struck down the bill, concluding that it violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Held: 1. The bill does not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 4–10. (a) The bill does not violate the Equal Protection Clause because it does not reflect a racially conscious decisionmaking process. Rather, the bill represents a neutral, technocratic solution to the problem of racial bloc voting. The bill’s sponsors and supporters testified that they were concerned about the impact of racial bloc voting on the competitiveness of elections in Texas. They believed that the bill would help to reduce the influence of racial blocs and improve the chances of minorities being elected to Congress. Their testimony shows that they were seeking a neutral solution to the problem of racial bloc voting, not a racially conscious one. Moreover, the bill’s provisions are facially neutral. Its provisions do not target any particular racial group, but instead aim to reduce the influence of racial blocs regardless of the racial makeup of the blocs. Nor does the bill contain any provision that would permit the State to engage in racial balancing. Finally, the bill’s provisions are not susceptible to a racial classification analysis. The bill’s provisions are not intended to serve a racial purpose, and they do not have a disparate impact on racial groups. Pp. 4–7. (b) The bill does not violate the Equal Protection Clause because it does not reflect a racially conscious decisionmaking process. Rather, the bill represents a neutral, technocratic solution to the problem of racial bloc voting. The bill’s sponsors and supporters testified that they were concerned about the impact of racial bloc voting on the competitiveness of elections in Texas. They believed that the bill would help to reduce the influence of racial blocs and improve the chances of minorities being elected to Congress. Their testimony shows that they were seeking a neutral solution to the problem of racial bloc voting, not a racially conscious one. Moreover, the bill’s provisions are facially neutral. Its provisions do not target any particular racial group, but instead aim to reduce the influence of racial blocs regardless of the racial makeup of the blocs. Nor does the bill contain any provision that would permit the State to engage in racial balancing. Finally, the bill’s provisions are not susceptible to a racial classification analysis. The bill’s provisions are not intended to serve a racial purpose, and they do not have a disparate impact on racial groups. Pp. 4–7. 2. The bill does not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 7–10. 2. The bill does not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 7–10. 3. The bill does not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 7–10. 298 F. Supp. 2d 479, affirmed in part, reversed in part, and vacated in part, and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part, in which Souter, J., joined. Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which O’Connor, J., joined.
