The District Court denied petitioners' prayer for an injunction and granted respondent School Board leave to submit an amendment to the plan with respect to employment and assignment of teachers and staff on a racially nondiscriminatory basis. The amendment was duly filed and on June 28, 1966, the District Court approved the plan as so amended. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The District Court's order to enjoin the Board from adopting a "freedom-of-choice" plan which allows a pupil to choose his own public school constitutes adequate compliance with the Board's responsibility "to achieve a system of determining admission to the public schools on a non-racial basis." Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, Kan., 349 U. S. 294, 300 301. Pp. 488-481. (a) The Board's adoption of a plan by which every student, regardless of race, may "freely" choose his school does not violate the Fourteenth Amendment. Brown is a call for the dismantling of well-entrenched dual systems tempered by an awareness that complex and multifaceted problems would require time and flexibility for a successful resolution. P. 489. (b) Although the general experience under "freedom of choice" to date has been such as to indicate its ineffectiveness as a tool of desegregation, there may well be instances in which it can serve as an effective device. Where it offers real promise of aiding a desegregated program to effectuate conversion of a state-imposed dual system to a unitary, nonracial system there might be no objection to allowing such a device to prove itself in operation. On the other hand, if there are reasonably available other ways, such for illustration as zoning, promising speedier and more effective conversion, "freedom" must be held unacceptable. Bowman v. County School Board of Charles City County, Va., 382 F. 2d 326, 330.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the United States and Cuba in a case brought by the United Kingdom and the Republic of Cuba.  According to the court's order, filed on November 19, 1975, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California announced criminal charges against the defendants.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, alleges that the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") by failing to comply with a court order requiring them to pay over $700,000 in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  In addition, the complaint alleges that, contrary to the SEC's findings, the defendants failed to pay the amounts due to them in the course of their purely commercial transactions.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders the defendants to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000. The judgment also prohibits the defendants from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in connection with the issuance of the securities, and bars them from serving as officers or directors of any SEC-registered broker, dealer, municipal securities dealer, investment adviser, municipal association, or investment adviser. The court also denied the defendants' motion for a temporary restraining order, which was entered by the Court on November 26, 1975.  On November 27, 1977, the Court issued a judgment ordering the Defendants to disgorge their ill-gotten gains plus interest, pay civil penalties, and repatriate their principal assets. The Court also issued an order suspending the Defendants from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney.  It also ordered the Defendants not to violate the federal laws, including the securities registration provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4), and to pay civil monetary penalties in amounts to be determined by the court upon motion of the parties. The order also prohibits defendants from associating with any broker or dealer with a foreign state, and from acting within the scope of their authority as agents of the foreign state.  For further information see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-8221 (January 24, 2019).  The Court's order also temporarily suspended the Defendants' registration of certain merchant ships.

In the case of Ewing v. California, the Supreme Court of the United States affirmed the judgment of the California Court of Appeal, upholding Gary Ewing's sentence of 25 years to life under California's three strikes law. Ewing had been convicted of felony grand theft for stealing three golf clubs, and he had a history of multiple serious or violent felonies.

The Court, in a plurality opinion by Justice O'Connor, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Kennedy, concluded that Ewing's sentence did not violate the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishments. The Court applied a "narrow proportionality principle" that forbids only extreme sentences that are grossly disproportionate to the crime. The Court deferred to the legislature's policy choice to incapacitate repeat offenders who have not been deterred by more conventional punishment approaches, emphasizing the State's legitimate interest in public safety and deterrence.

Justice Scalia and Justice Thomas concurred in the judgment but on different grounds. Justice Scalia argued that the Eighth Amendment's prohibition was aimed at excluding only certain modes of punishment, not at enforcing a proportionality principle. Justice Thomas concluded that the Eighth Amendment contains no proportionality principle.

Justices Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer dissented, arguing that Ewing's sentence was grossly disproportionate to his crime and therefore unconstitutional.

The decision has implications for the application of three strikes laws and the deference given to state legislatures in determining criminal sentencing policies. It also clarifies the Court's stance on the proportionality principle as it applies to noncapital sentences.

Case Name: United States v. TVA
Case Number: 78-1102
Judge: William J. Brennan Jr.
Date Decided: March 22, 1979

Summary:
United States v. TVA is a case involving the Endangered Species Act of 1973 and the Tellico Dam project. The case raises the question of whether the Tellico Dam project violates Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act, which prohibits federal agencies from undertaking any action that may result in the extinction of a species. The court holds that the Tellico Dam project does violate Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act and that the project must be suspended until a plan is developed to ensure the survival of the snail darter, an endangered species that inhabits the Tellico River basin.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals in a case involving Texaco Inc. and Shell Oil Co., who had formed a joint venture called Equilon Enterprises. The respondents, a class of service station owners, accused Texaco and Shell Oil of illegal price fixing because Equilon set a single price for both Texaco and Shell Oil brand gasoline.

The central legal question was whether a lawful, economically integrated joint venture like Equilon could set the prices for its products without violating the per se rule against price fixing under §1 of the Sherman Act. The Supreme Court concluded that it could, stating that the per se rule applies only to plainly anticompetitive agreements that do not require detailed industry analysis to be deemed illegal. The Court emphasized that price-fixing agreements between competitors (horizontal price-fixing) are per se unlawful, but in this case, Texaco and Shell Oil were not competitors within the joint venture; they were investors in a single entity.

The Court reasoned that since Equilon operated as a single entity, its pricing decisions were not considered anticompetitive price fixing in the antitrust sense. The Court also dismissed the application of the ancillary restraints doctrine, which examines the validity of restrictions on nonventure activities within a business collaboration, because the pricing policy was a core activity of Equilon itself.

The Supreme Court's decision implies that the internal pricing decisions of a legitimate joint venture cannot be condemned as per se unlawful under antitrust law. Instead, if such pricing is to be challenged as anticompetitive, it must be done under the rule of reason, which requires a detailed analysis of the market and the effects of the pricing policy. The respondents had not pursued a rule of reason claim, and thus the Court did not address it.

Justice Alito did not participate in the consideration or decision of the cases. The implication of the decision is that joint ventures like Equilon have the discretion to set prices for their products, and such pricing policies are not automatically considered illegal under antitrust law.

Petitioner José Padilla pled guilty to federal drug charges, knowing that doing so meant he faced removal from the United States. His counsel assured him that he would receive a lenient sentence and that he would be allowed to return to Mexico. Later, he learned that he was actually facing removal to Mexico, where he had spent much of his childhood and where he still maintained property and business ties. He moved to vacate his plea, claiming that his counsel was constitutionally deficient for failing to warn him of the risk of removal. The Kentucky Supreme Court affirmed his conviction, finding that Padilla had waived his right to appeal. Held: Because Padilla’s counsel knew that he faced removal, he cannot be said to have met his burden of proving that his counsel was constitutionally deficient. Pp. 4−12. (a) The Sixth Amendment requires that counsel inform her client whether his plea carries a risk of deportation. Longstanding precedent demands no less. The severity of deportation—“the equivalent of banishment or exile,” Delgadillo v. Carmichael, 332 U. S. 388, 390–91—only underscores how critical it is for counsel to inform her client that he faces a risk of deportation. Pp. 4−6. (b) Padilla has sufficiently alleged that his counsel was constitutionally deficient. If accepting Padilla’s version of events, his counsel gave him information that was clearly wrong. That Padilla chose to rely on that information does not absolve his counsel of liability. Nor does Padilla’s knowledge that he faced removal mitigate his counsel’s error. Knowledge of the risk of removal is not enough to show that counsel acted reasonably. Rather, it shows that counsel failed to meet her obligations. Pp. 6−8. (c) Padilla’s claim falls within the rubric set forth in Strickland v. Washington, 466 U. S. 668. The first prong asks whether counsel’s performance fell below the level of professional competency. Here, Padilla accepts that his counsel’s performance was objectively deficient. The second prong asks whether there is a reasonable probability that but for counsel’s deficient performance, the outcome would have differed. Padilla has not yet demonstrated that he would have chosen differently had he known the full facts. Pp. 8−10. (d) Padilla’s claim fails under the Strickland test because he has not sufficiently alleged prejudice. Prejudice occurs when counsel’s actions lead to a result significantly worse than what would have occurred absent counsel’s involvement. Padilla has not shown that he would have chosen differently had he known the full facts. Pp. 10−12. 429 S.W. 3d 1, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Alito, J., filed an opinion concurring in the judgment, in which Roberts, C. J., and Stevens, J., joined.

In the case of Francisco Romero versus Compania Trasatlantica and others, the Supreme Court addressed several jurisdictional and legal issues arising from Romero's injury aboard the S.S. Guadalupe, a Spanish vessel. Romero, a Spanish seaman, was injured in New York and sought damages under the Jones Act and general maritime law of the United States.

The District Court initially dismissed Romero's complaint, and the Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal. The Supreme Court granted certiorari due to conflicting interpretations of the Judiciary Act of 1875 and questions regarding the applicability of Lauritzen v. Larsen to the case.

The Supreme Court's opinion, delivered by Justice Harlan, clarified the following points:

1. Jurisdiction under the Jones Act: The Court held that the District Court had jurisdiction to determine whether the Jones Act provided Romero with a right of recovery for employer negligence. The mere assertion of a substantial claim under the Jones Act was sufficient to confer jurisdiction.

2. Jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331: The Court found that the federal courts did not have jurisdiction over maritime claims rooted in federal law when the parties were not of diverse citizenship. The Act of 1875 did not extend to cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction, and the Court rejected the notion that general maritime jurisdiction should be infused into the Act.

3. 'Pendent' and Diversity Jurisdiction: The Court recognized that the District Court could have jurisdiction over Romero's general maritime law claims if they were 'pendent' to a valid Jones Act claim. Additionally, the Court held that the rule of Strawbridge v. Curtiss did not require dismissal of claims against diverse respondents when the Jones Act provided an independent basis of federal jurisdiction over the non-diverse respondent.

4. The Claims Against Compania Trasatlantica: Applying the principles from Lauritzen v. Larsen, the Court affirmed the dismissal of Romero's claims against Compania Trasatlantica. The Court reasoned that the maritime law of the United States should not apply to an injury sustained by a foreign seaman on a foreign vessel in an American port when the voyage began and ended in a foreign country.

5. The Claims Against Other Respondents: The Court remanded the case for further proceedings regarding claims against Garcia & Diaz, Inc., International Terminal Operating Co., and Quin Lumber Co., as the District Court had not fully considered certain aspects of these claims.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case to the District Court for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. The Court's decision clarified the jurisdictional scope of the Jones Act and the Judiciary Act of 1875, as well as the application of U.S. maritime law to foreign seamen injured on foreign vessels in U.S. ports.

The Supreme Court of the United States delivered an opinion regarding the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People's (NAACP) right to operate in the state of Alabama. This case reached the Supreme Court for the fourth time after the NAACP was initially barred from conducting activities in Alabama due to alleged non-compliance with state registration statutes for foreign corporations and claims that the NAACP's activities were detrimental to the state.

The Supreme Court found that the Alabama Supreme Court's procedural grounds for not reviewing the NAACP's constitutional claims were inadequate. The Alabama Supreme Court had dismissed the NAACP's appeal based on a technicality in the way the NAACP's brief was structured, which the U.S. Supreme Court deemed an unreasonable application of state procedural rules.

On the substantive issues, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the NAACP's activities, such as providing legal assistance and financial support to individuals challenging racial segregation, organizing boycotts, and making statements against state officials, were protected by the First Amendment's freedom of association. The Court rejected the notion that the NAACP could be permanently barred from Alabama based on these activities.

The Court also determined that Alabama's statutory requirements for foreign corporations to register before doing business in the state did not justify the NAACP's ouster. The Court noted that non-compliance with these requirements typically resulted in a monetary penalty, not permanent exclusion from the state.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Alabama courts and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The Court instructed the Alabama Supreme Court to promptly issue a decree allowing the NAACP to operate in Alabama and to take necessary steps to comply with state business regulations. The Court also granted the NAACP permission to seek further relief from the U.S. Supreme Court if the Alabama Supreme Court failed to act promptly.

In summary, the U.S. Supreme Court's decision affirmed the constitutional right of the NAACP to engage in protected activities and associate for the advancement of beliefs and ideas in Alabama, despite the state's attempt to exclude the organization based on its non-compliance with corporate registration laws and its civil rights activities.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois today entered a final judgment against a trustee of a publicly-traded company for violating the securities laws.  The SEC's complaint alleges that John K. Notz, Jr., a former trustee of Chicago Discount Commodity Brokers (CDCB), violated the antifraud provisions of Section 542(e) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.  According to the complaint, Notz agreed to waive the attorney-client privilege in order to facilitate the recovery of misappropriated corporate assets.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the trustee agreed to the final judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the provisions of the federal securities laws and orders him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  In a parallel action, the U.N. Office of Financial Regulation today announced that it has issued an order suspending the asset freeze and asset freeze provisions of Sections 541(a) and 543(c) and ordering the trustee to comply with the court's order.   The final judgment also orders the trustee not to violate the securities registration provisions of § 542. The SEC seeks a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, an officer-and-director bar, and an officer and director bar against the trustee. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by John R. McCluskey and Glenn S. Gordon of the Chicago Regional Office, with the assistance of John Rymas of the Market Abuse Unit's Analysis and Detection Center.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia today entered final judgments in a civil rights case against the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, Inc. (NAACP) and the Virginia State Conference of NAACP Branches (C.I.A.B.’).   The Court held that the NAACP, its affiliates and legal staff violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also held that, as a matter of law, the NAACP and its affiliates violated Section 17(a)(1) and 17(b)(2)(A)(3) of The Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 17a-3 thereunder, and that, in violation of Section 5 of the federal securities laws, the defendants had the right to return to the district court for a final determination of the merits of their claims.  In addition, the court held that certain of the charged defendants had engaged in unlawful solicitation of legal services.  According to the court's order, however, certain of those defendants had not engaged in such activities.  For example, one defendant was convicted for delivering a speech in connection with an impending union election under National Labor Relations Board auspices, without having first been registered as a lawyer.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's complaint, the defendant consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and (c) and (d) of Section 15 of the Exchange Act and Rules 15b-20, 13a-1, and (e) thereunder; orders him to pay a civil penalty of $100,000, and requires him to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. McCluskey and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson. The litigation will be led by Messrs. McShane and Ms. McCreary. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Virginia Attorney General's Office.

Respondent Gross resigned after being passed over for promotion to a higher level within petitioner company. He sued under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), claiming that his resignation resulted from his age, which he said was a motivating factor in the company’s decision. After the District Court entered judgment for Gross, the Eighth Circuit reversed and remanded, concluding that the lower court erred in giving the jury an instruction allowing recovery if Gross showed that age was merely a contributing factor in the company’s decision. Held: A plaintiff bringing a disparate-treatment claim pursuant to the ADEA must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that age was the “but-for” cause of the challenged adverse employment action. Pp. 4–11. (a) Under the ADEA, the plaintiff bears the burden of establishing that age was the “but-for” cause of the employer’s adverse action. Nothing in the statute’s text indicates that Congress has carved out an exception to the ordinary default rule that plaintiffs bear the risk of failing to prove their claims. See Schaffer v. Weast, 546 U. S. 49, 56. Nor is there any warrant to depart from that rule here. Even assuming that the burden-of-persuasion framework set forth in Price Waterhouse v. Dayton, Ohio Bd. of Educ., 452 U. S. 450, 464, could be extended to ADEA claims, the difficulties associated with applying that framework have rendered it difficult to extend it to ADEA claims. Pp. 4–7. (b) The Court rejects Gross’ contention that its interpretation of the ADEA is controlled by Price Waterhouse. While the Court acknowledges that the burden-of-persuasion framework set forth in Price Waterhouse might be useful in deciding how to allocate the burden of persuasion in a mixed-motives case, the Court finds it unlikely that the Court would reach the same conclusion were it to consider the question in the first instance. Any perceived benefits to extending the Price Waterhouse framework to ADEA claims have been eliminated by the problems associated with applying that framework. Pp. 7–10. 537 F. 3d 726, vacated and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses a case where a non-Indian respondent operated a store on the Navajo Indian Reservation in Arizona and sought to collect debts from Navajo Indian petitioners in state court. The Arizona Supreme Court had affirmed that state courts could exercise jurisdiction over such civil suits, as no federal law explicitly prohibited it. However, the U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the case due to the significant question of state power over Indian affairs.

The opinion references historical context, noting that Indian tribes were once sovereign nations and that their sovereignty has been gradually limited through treaties and federal protection. It cites the landmark Worcester v. Georgia case, where Chief Justice Marshall ruled that state laws had no force on Indian reservations without the consent of the tribe or federal legislation.

The Court acknowledges that while state courts have been permitted to hear certain cases involving Indians, such as suits by Indians against non-Indians or crimes committed by non-Indians against each other on reservations, jurisdiction over crimes by or against Indians has generally been exclusive to tribal or federally designated courts. The opinion emphasizes that the key consideration is whether state action infringes on the rights of reservation Indians to make their own laws and be governed by them.

The Court also notes that Congress has historically assumed that states lack the power to regulate Indian affairs on reservations and has enacted legislation to support tribal governments and courts. When Congress has wanted states to exercise jurisdiction over Indian affairs, it has done so explicitly.

Regarding the Navajo Nation, the Court points out that the Treaty of 1868 and subsequent federal actions have supported the Navajo tribal government and courts. No federal act has granted state courts jurisdiction over disputes involving outsiders and Indian defendants on the reservation, and Arizona has not assumed such jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court concludes that allowing state jurisdiction in this case would undermine the authority of tribal courts and infringe on the Navajo Indians' right to self-governance. The Court states that if this power is to be removed, it is Congress's responsibility to do so. Therefore, the Court reverses the decision of the Arizona Supreme Court, effectively ruling that the state court did not have jurisdiction over the civil suit brought by the non-Indian respondent against the Navajo Indian petitioners on the reservation.

The Supreme Court of the United States, in this opinion, addresses the constitutionality of executing individuals with mental retardation. The Court acknowledges that while persons with mental retardation can be held criminally responsible and punished for their crimes, their disabilities in reasoning, judgment, and impulse control mean they do not possess the same level of moral culpability as typical adult offenders. The Court notes that there has been significant deliberation over the past 13 years on whether the death penalty should be applied to mentally retarded criminals, and this has led to a consensus that such executions are considered "cruel and unusual punishments," thus prohibited by the Eighth Amendment.

The case in question involves Daryl Renard Atkins, who was sentenced to death for abduction, armed robbery, and capital murder. The defense argued that Atkins was mentally retarded, presenting evidence from a forensic psychologist, while the prosecution presented a rebuttal witness claiming Atkins was not mentally retarded. The Virginia Supreme Court affirmed the death sentence, but the U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to revisit the issue.

The U.S. Supreme Court's analysis focuses on the proportionality of punishment under the Eighth Amendment, which prohibits excessive sanctions. The Court emphasizes that the Eighth Amendment's interpretation must reflect "evolving standards of decency" in society. The Court reviews legislative actions across the states and notes a clear trend towards prohibiting the execution of mentally retarded individuals, indicating a societal consensus against such punishment.

The Court also discusses the limited applicability of the death penalty's justifications—retribution and deterrence—to mentally retarded offenders. It argues that the diminished culpability of mentally retarded individuals makes the death penalty an inappropriate form of retribution, and their cognitive impairments mean that the death penalty is unlikely to serve as an effective deterrent for them or others.

Furthermore, the Court points out that the procedural safeguards in capital cases are less effective for mentally retarded defendants, who may struggle to assist in their defense or to present mitigating evidence effectively. This increases the risk of wrongful execution.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court holds that executing mentally retarded individuals is unconstitutional under the Eighth Amendment, as it does not serve the purposes of the death penalty and is considered excessive punishment. The Court reverses the judgment of the Virginia Supreme Court and remands the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

After being introduced in Minnesota, a bill prohibiting the retail sale of milk in plastic, nonreturnable containers was approved by the legislature. The State Attorney General defended the constitutionality of the act against challenges brought by various entities, including respondent dairies and a milk distributor. The lower court entered a preliminary injunction against enforcement of the statute pending resolution of the challenge, but ultimately denied relief to the challengers. On appeal, the Minnesota Supreme Court reversed, holding that the statute was unconstitutional under the Federal Constitution. That court ruled that the statute was not rationally related to the State's objective of protecting the environment, and that the statute constituted an unreasonable burden on interstate commerce. Held: 1. Under the Equal Protection Clause, the statute is valid. Pp. 465-470. (a) The statute is not rendered irrational solely because it allows the sale of milk in paperboard, nonreturnable containers, thereby permitting the continuation of an existing practice. Such a result is consistent with the State's legitimate objectives of fostering greater use of environmentally desirable alternatives, preventing the economic dislocation resulting from the movement toward greater use of environmentally superior containers, conserving energy, and easing the State's solid waste disposal problem. Pp. 465-469. (b) Nor does the statute contravene the Commerce Clause. Although the statute regulates evenhandedly by prohibiting all milk retailers from selling their products in plastic, nonreturnable containers, without regard to whether the milk, the containers, or the sellers are from outside the State, the incidental burden imposed on interstate commerce by the statute is not "clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits." Pikev . BruceChurch, Inc., 397 U. S. 137, 142. Here, although the burden imposed on interstate commerce is relatively minor, the substantial state interest in promoting conservation of energy and other natural resources and easing solid waste disposal problems supports the State's decision under the Commerce Clause. Pp. 469-470. 289 N. W. 2d 81, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a Florida-based company and its former CEO for failing to timely respond to a court order confirming the discharge of student loan debt.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, Francisco Espinosa obtained four federally guaranteed student loans for a total principal amount of $13,250.  The complaint alleges that the bankruptcy court issued a judgment on May 5, 2004, ordering the payment of a debt discharge order without a determination of undue hardship.  In its order, the court found that the discharge order was void because the debtor failed to serve a summons and complaint before filing a complaint.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that the court had the authority to determine the dischargeability of a student loan owed by the debtor, and that it had the right to do so without prejudgment interest, without requiring the debtor to pay a penalty, and without imposing an unreasonable hardship finding on the debtor and his dependents.   The court also ruled that, in the event of an emergency, the debtor could withdraw the repayment plan and file another without penalty.  On May 6, 2009, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against United, charging it with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 13(b)(4) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 13b-5 thereunder, and with aiding and abetting United's violations of Rule 13(a) and 13(c).  The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Hoke and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Atlanta Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

This Supreme Court opinion concerns a challenge to a tax system implemented in the state of Iowa. The tax system involves adjustments to revenues generated through various types of gambling activities, including slot machines located on riverboats and racetracks. The main point of contention in this case is the difference in tax rates applied to these two types of gambling establishments. Specifically, the tax rate on adjusted revenues from slot machines on riverboats is set at 20%, whereas the tax rate on adjusted revenues from slot machines at racetracks starts at 20% and will eventually increase to 36%. The challengers argued that this difference in tax rates violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the US Constitution. However, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the state, stating that the tax code is subject to rational-basis review and that the difference in tax rates can be justified by the desire to aid struggling industries.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas denied a stay of execution of the death penalty pending appeal of the District Court's judgment. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, however, denied the stay pending review of the district court's decision. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued a decision on the appeal. The U,S. Court of Justices will consider the appeal on February 5, 2014. The case involves the use of psychiatric testimony during the sentencing phase of a capital murder trial. The jury was asked to determine whether the conduct causing death was "committed deliberately and with reasonable expectation that the death of the deceased or another would result"; and whether "there is a probability that the defendant would commit criminal acts of violence that would constitute a continuing threat to society." The jury answered both of the questions put to them in the affirmative, a result which required the imposition of the capital penalty. The court rejected all of these contentions and affirmed the conviction and sentence on March 12, 1980, 596 S.W.2d 875; rehearing was denied on April 30, 1980. The jury also answered the two questions in an affirmative fashion. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals issued an opinion and judgment denying the stay on January 20, 1983. The court held that the court had studied the briefs and record filed by the parties and had heard oral argument at which petitioner's attorney was allowed unlimited time to discuss any matter germane to the case. It also held that it had not issued a judgment on the issue of whether the stay should be granted. The case was heard on January 19, 1983. The Court held that there was no merit to the parties's arguments and that the stay was denied. The high court will decide the appeal at a later date.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit recently ruled that a state-run railroad in California was not subject to federal regulation under the Safety Appliance Act. The court held that the state's use of the railroad to facilitate transportation at a port was within the reach of federal regulation of interstate rail transportation. The decision was a victory for the federal government in its efforts to enforce the safety provisions of the Act. In a separate case, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled in favor of the government's appeal of a lower court's ruling that the federal courts had no jurisdiction to hear the case because the federal court had jurisdiction over the issue of whether the state was subject to the safety provision. The high court held, however, that the lower court had not adequately addressed the question of whether or not the state had the authority to operate the railroad. The appeals court agreed, and the decision was published today. The case will be heard by the full appeals court in coming months.

Title: Batson v. Kentucky
Year: 1986
Summary: In Batson v. Kentucky, the Supreme Court ruled that a criminal defendant has standing to object to the discriminatory use of peremptory challenges by the prosecution. The Court found that the defendant has a sufficient interest in ensuring that the jury pool is diverse enough to avoid racial bias, and that the defendant's objection to the use of peremptory challenges serves as a proxy for the rights of the excluded jurors. The Court also clarified that the defendant's objection need not be based on the belief that he or she would have been selected for the jury if not for race, but rather on the belief that the use of peremptory challenges perpetuated racial bias in the jury selection process.

Title: Batson v. Alabama
Year: 1992
Issue: Whether intentional discrimination on the basis of gender is unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause?
Decision: Yes, intentional discrimination on the basis of gender is unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause.

The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) was passed by Congress in 1970 to ensure that all children with disabilities have access to a free appropriate public education. As of 2003, the Act governed the provision of special education services to nearly 7 million children across the country. Under the Act, school districts must create an "individualized education program" (IEP) for each disabled child. 1414(d) provides that if parents believe their child's IEP is inappropriate, they may request an "impartial due process hearing" before the U.S. Department of Education. The hearing is open to the public. The Act is silent, however, as to which party bears the burden of persuasion at such a hearing. We hold that the burden lies, as it typically does, on the party seeking relief.

The Supreme Court addressed whether the delay between the dismissal of military charges and subsequent civilian criminal charges against Jeffrey MacDonald violated his Sixth Amendment right to a speedy trial. MacDonald was accused of murdering his wife and two children in 1970 while stationed at Fort Bragg. After the military charges were dismissed, civilian charges were brought years later, leading to his conviction.

The Court held that the Sixth Amendment's Speedy Trial Clause does not apply to periods before a defendant is formally charged or after charges are dismissed. It is only concerned with the time between an official accusation and the trial. The Court referenced United States v. Marion, which established that the right to a speedy trial is not activated until a prosecution begins, and that any delay before charges are filed or after they are dismissed should be examined under the Due Process Clause.

The Court disagreed with the Court of Appeals' view that charges were effectively pending against MacDonald during the entire period between his military arrest and civilian indictment. The Court clarified that once the military charges were dismissed, MacDonald was not under any form of criminal prosecution and was free to live his life without the constraints of an accused person awaiting trial.

The Court also noted that the delay between the civilian indictment and trial was primarily due to MacDonald's own legal actions and did not infringe upon his right to a speedy trial. Consequently, the Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had dismissed the indictment on speedy trial grounds, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with their opinion.

Case Name: Granite Rock Construction Co. v. International Brotherhood of Teamsters
Case Number: 06-1175
Decided Date: March 11, 2008
Supreme Court Justices: Roberts, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, Alito, Stevens, Souter, Kennedy, and Sonia Sotomayor
Issued Decisions: Syllabus, Opinion of the Court, Concurrence in Part and Dissent in Part
Topics Covered: Contract Law, Arbitration, Collective Bargaining Agreements, Strikes

The U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was found guilty of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New Hampshire on February 19, 2020, Edward J. Coolidge, a Massachusetts resident, was arrested on the basis of his account of his activities on the night of February 2, 1964.  The complaint alleges that Coolidge was the subject of a search warrant issued by the Massachusetts Attorney General's Office, which conducted the search.  In its opinion, the court held that a warrant for a search of a person's house without a warrant is not unreasonable, and that the search warrant should be followed by a reasonable search of the person's car.  As the complaint further alleges, Coolidge's wife was in the house at the time of the search when the police entered the house and searched the car, but did not find any evidence of the alleged crime.  Instead, the complaint alleges, the search was conducted by plainclothes policemen, who were not authorized to search the car and did not know that the car had been seized.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendant consented to the entry of a final judgement that permanently enjoins him from violating the above-mentioned provisions of the federal securities laws and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.   The judgment also orders Coolidge to pay disgorgement of $1,000, which is equal to the amount of his ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and to pay civil penalties of $5,000 and $100,000 for each of the defendants' violations of Section 17(a)(1) and (3) of The Securities Act of 1933, and orders the forfeiture of any assets, including his automobile, to be determined by the court at a later date.

The Supreme Court was tasked with deciding if a company's policy of paying discharged employees for unused vacation time is considered an "employee welfare benefit plan" under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), and if a state criminal action to enforce such a policy is pre-empted by ERISA's pre-emption provision.

The Commonwealth of Massachusetts charged Richard N. Morash, president of the Yankee Bank for Finance and Savings, with criminal violations of the Massachusetts Payment of Wages Statute for not compensating two discharged bank vice presidents for unused vacation time. Morash moved to dismiss the charges, claiming the bank's vacation policy was an "employee welfare benefit plan" under ERISA, and thus the state's prosecution was pre-empted by ERISA.

The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court agreed with Morash, but the U.S. Supreme Court reversed this decision. The Supreme Court held that the bank's policy did not constitute an employee welfare benefit plan under ERISA. The Court reasoned that ERISA was designed to protect employees from the mismanagement of funds intended for employee benefits, and that regular vacation payments, being fixed and predictable, do not present the same risks as other benefits ERISA aims to protect, such as those contingent on unforeseen events.

The Court also considered the Secretary of Labor's regulations, which exclude certain payroll practices, including vacation pay from an employer's general assets, from the definition of an employee welfare benefit plan. The Court found that the Secretary's interpretation was reasonable and that the bank's policy fell within these regulations.

The Court concluded that including routine vacation pay policies within ERISA would have significant consequences, such as imposing complex reporting requirements on employers or expanding federal court jurisdiction over vacation disputes. It would also interfere with state regulations on vacation benefits, potentially offering employees less protection.

The judgment of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court was reversed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The Supreme Court had to determine whether the Florida felony offense of battery, which includes the act of intentionally touching another person against their will, constitutes a "violent felony" under the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA), which mandates enhanced penalties for certain repeat offenders. Curtis Johnson, who had been convicted of possessing ammunition after a felony conviction, challenged his enhanced sentencing under the ACCA, arguing that his prior conviction for simple battery in Florida did not involve the use of "physical force" as required by the ACCA's definition of a violent felony.

The Court held that the term "physical force" in the ACCA means "violent force" – that is, force capable of causing physical pain or injury to another person. The Court reasoned that the ordinary meaning of "violent felony" suggests a category of active, violent crimes, and that the common-law definition of battery, which could be satisfied by the slightest offensive touching, does not fit within the statutory context of the ACCA.

The Court rejected the government's argument that the absence of a modifier specifying the degree of "physical force" required in the ACCA means that any physical contact, no matter how slight, would qualify as a violent felony. The Court also noted that the government's concerns about the impact of this interpretation on other statutes, such as those related to domestic violence misdemeanors or immigration removals, were unfounded because the Court's decision was specific to the context of the ACCA's definition of a violent felony.

Ultimately, the Court reversed the judgment of the Eleventh Circuit, which had affirmed Johnson's enhanced sentence, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. The Court clarified that the government could not rely on the ACCA's residual clause because it had not preserved that argument during sentencing.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio on May 12, 2018, entered a final judgment in a civil injunctive action against DaimlerChrysler, Inc., a Michigan-based manufacturer of Jeeps.  The court found that, by virtue of their status as municipal taxpayers, they had the right to challenge the franchise tax credit at issue.  According to the court's order, filed in federal court in Toledo, Ohio, the defendants claimed that they had standing to challenge a federal tax credit because they were taxpayers.  As alleged in the complaint, however, this was false.  In fact, as alleged, the court held that the defendants had no standing under the federal law because they did not have standing as taxpayers to challenge that tax credit.  For example, as set forth in the Complaint, the Court held that, as a matter of principle, a federal district court has the duty to determine whether a taxpayer has standing to sue a state tax credit based on the asserted effect of the allegedly illegal activity on public revenues.  Without admitting or denying the Court's findings, the Defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders them to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.   The Court also ordered the defendants to pay disgorgement of $2,500 plus prejudgment interest of $100,000, and ordered the companies to pay civil penalties of $500,000 each. Â The court also issued a temporary restraining order against the defendants from further violations of the federal securities laws, ordering them to return their allegedly ill-gotten gains with interest, and ordering the company to pay an $80,000 civil penalty.  On May 13, 2019, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. Snyder of the United States District Court in the Southern District of New York granted the relief sought by the defendants in the civil injunctions action.  To learn more about the importance of standing, see Litigation Release No. 545 (1952).  The SEC's Office of Inspector General has issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the backgrounds of people selling investments using the SEC's Investor.gov website.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit has ruled that the "meeting-competition" defense of Section 2(b) of the Clayton Act is not so inflexible as to require a defendant to prove that its lower price was made in good faith to meet an equally low price of a competitor. The court held that Falls City Industries, Inc.'s pricing policies prevented Vanco Beverage Inc. from effectively competing in a geographic market that spanned the Indiana-Kentucky border and included Vanderburgh and Henderson Counties. Falls City charged a higher price for beer sold to Indiana distributors than it charged for the same beer sold in other States, including Kentucky. The lower court dismissed Vanco's Sherman Act claims, finding no evidence to support the allegations of conspiracy or monopolization. The Seventh Circuit held that the lower court's decision to dismiss the Sherman Act charges was not based on the facts of the case, but on Falls City's failure to show that its pricing policies caused it to sell less beer to Indiana retailers. The Court concluded that the meeting-competition defense is not as inflexible as the defense of  2(a) and that it is not necessary to prove a price difference. The Appeals Court held that, in this case, Falls City did not create the price discrimination by raising its prices to meet the prices of its competitors. The appeals court also held that it was not required to prove the price difference by raising or lowering its prices. The case has implications for other brewers and wholesalers who may be subject to the meeting competition defense.

The Illinois Attorney General's complaint alleges that for-profit fundraising corporations defrauded members of the public by falsely representing that "a significant amount of each dollar donated would be paid over to [the veterans organization] for its [charitable] purposes," when in fact the fundraisers knew that 15 cents or less of the gross receipts would be available for those purposes. The complaint also alleges that the defendants falsely represented that "the funds donated would go to further ... charitable purposes," id., at 8, ¶ 29, when in reality they were merely incidental to the fund raising effort and were conducted primarily for the private pecuniary benefit of the fundraiser. The Illinois Supreme Court affirmed, in turn, by the Illinois Appellate Court. Held: 1. While bare failure to disclose that information directly to potential donors does not suffice to establish fraud, when nondisclosure is accompanied by intentionally misleading statements designed to deceive the listener, the First Amendment leaves room for a fraud claim. The First Amendment protects the right to engage in charitable solicitation. See Schaumburg v. Citizens for a Better Environment, 444 U. S. 620, and Riley v. National Federation of Blind of N. C., Inc., 487 U.S. 781, these decisions held that certain regulations of charitable subscriptions, barring fees in excess of a prescribed level, effectively imposed prior restraints on fundraising, and were therefore incompatible with the First. Pp. 5-11. (a) In contrast to a prior restraint on solicitation, or a regulation that imposes on fundraisers an uphill burden to prove their conduct lawful, in a properly tailored fraud action, the State bears the full burden of proof. False statement alone does not subject a fundraiser to fraud liability. P. 5. (b) In the absence of a prophylactic provision proscribing any charitable solicitation if fundraising fees exceeded a specified reasonable level, fraud actions so tailored, targeting misleading affirmative representations about how donations will be used, are plainly distinguishable, as we next discuss, from the measures invalidated in Schauburg, Munson, and Munson. The Court's decisions recognized, and as we further explain below, that fraud actions trained on representations made in individual cases and statutes that categorically ban solicitations when fundraising costs run high, such actions need not impermissibly chill protected speech. See § III-B, infra. The Second Amendment does not require, however, a blanket exemption from fraud liability for a fundraiser who intentionally misleads in calls for donations. See, e. g., Riley v., National Federation, Inc., 467 U., at 781. The first is the Court's decision in Schaumburger, which invalidated laws that prohibited charitable organizations or fundraisers from engaging in charitable solicitations if a high percentage of the funds raised would be used to cover administrative or fundraising costs. The second is the judgment in Riley, which held that fraud may not be inferred simply from the percentage of charitable donations absorbed by fundraising costs, and which held, inter alia, that such representations remain false or misleading, however legitimate the other purposes for which the funds are in fact used. The third is the case in which the Court invalidated a state law prohibiting professional fundraisers to retain an "unreasonable" or "excessive" fee, which was upheld by the State Supreme Court, which concluded that the statute was incapable of "distinguishing those organizations from charities that have high costs due to protected First Amendment activities." Held: (1) That the First and First Amendment do not require that a State maintain fraud actions when fundraisers make false and misleading representations designed to defraud donors about how their donations are used. In addition, there is no First Amendment requirement that a charity must desist from using donations for information dissemination, advocacy, the promotion of public awareness, the production of advertising material, the development or enlargement of the charity's contributor base, and the like. The statute's fatal flaw was that it "operate[d] on [the] fundamentally mistaken premise that high solicitation costs are an accurate measure of fraud." Id., at 9, ¶ 35. The gravamen of the fraud action in this case is not high costs or fees, it is particular representations made with intent to mislead. If, for example, a charity conducted an advertising or awareness campaign that advanced charitable purposes in conjunction with its fundraising activity, its representation that donated funds were going to "charitable purposes" would not be misleading, much less intentionally so. Similarly, charitable organizations that engage primarily in advocacy or information dissemination could get and spend money without risking a fraud charge. The fact that the fundraiser "keeps the vast majority (in this case 85 percent) of all funds donated" is insufficient to state a claim for fraud. The State's Attorney General surely cannot gain case-by-case ground this Court has declared off limits to legislators. See Brief for Respondents 14-19, supra, at 785-786. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the State of Hawaii is not violating the Fifth Amendment by taking private property for public use without compensation. The Court held that the Hawaii Land Reform Act of 1967 (Act) was not unconstitutional. The Act was passed to address the problem of concentrated land ownership in the Hawaiian Islands. In the mid-1960's, the Hawaii Legislature discovered that, while the State and Federal Governments owned almost 49% of the State's land, another 47% was in the hands of only 72 private landowners. The Legislature concluded that concentrated landownership was responsible for skewing the state's residential fee simple market, inflating land prices, and injuring the public tranquility and welfare. To address this problem, the Act required large landowners to break up their estates. The landowners resisted this scheme, pointing out the significant federal tax liabilities they would incur. Therefore, the landowners claimed that the federal tax laws were the primary reason they previously had chosen to lease, and not sell, their lands. The Hawaii Housing Authority (HHA) was authorized to sell the land titles to tenants who had applied for fee simple ownership. The HHA is authorized to lend these tenants up to 90% of the purchase price, and it may condition final transfer on a right of first refusal for the first 10 years following sale. Under the Act, the HHA may not sell to any one purchaser, or lease to any other tenant, more than one lot, or sell the lot to anyone other than the former fee owners' full "right, title, and interest"

Petitioner, who was charged with committing a misdemeanor, was tried before a five-person jury pursuant to Georgia law, and convicted. Though a criminal trial by a jury of only five persons deprives the accused of the right to trial by jury guaranteed by the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments, the State Supreme Court denied certiorari. Held: The judgment is reversed and the case is remanded. Pp. 229-245; 245-246. 138 Ga. App. 530, 227 S. E. 2d 65, reversed and remanded, MR. JUSTICE BLACKMUN, joined by Mr. Justice STEVENS, concluded that a trial before a jury for less than six persons substantially threatens Sixth and Fteenth Amendment guarantees. P. 245. 227 Ga.App. 530; 227-224, reversed.

The Supreme Court held that the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) applies to individuals who unlawfully reentered the United States before the Act's effective date and does not have a retroactive effect on their rights or impose new burdens on them. The case involved Humberto Fernandez-Vargas, a Mexican citizen who had been deported and unlawfully reentered the U.S. multiple times, with his last reentry in 1982. After living undetected for over 20 years, he was discovered by authorities when he applied for an adjustment of status following his marriage to a U.S. citizen.

The Court reasoned that the IIRIRA's reinstatement provision, which prevents certain aliens from seeking relief from removal, applies not because of the act of reentry itself but because of the continued illegal presence in the U.S. after the law took effect. The Court also noted that individuals like Fernandez-Vargas had a grace period between the enactment of the IIRIRA and its effective date to leave the U.S. voluntarily, thus avoiding the new law's consequences.

The Court rejected the argument that applying the IIRIRA to individuals who reentered before its effective date would be retroactive, as the law targets ongoing illegal presence, not a completed past act. The decision affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had held that the IIRIRA barred Fernandez-Vargas's application for adjustment of status and did not have an impermissibly retroactive effect in his case.

Implications of the decision include the affirmation that the IIRIRA applies to all illegal reentrants, regardless of when they reentered, and that it insulates removal orders from review while generally foreclosing discretionary relief. This ruling emphasizes the principle that ongoing violations of immigration law can be subject to current law, even if the initial act occurred before the law's enactment.

Title: United States v. John H. Day Jr.

Case Number: 82-1151

Date Decided: June 29, 1983

Supreme Court Justice(s): Burger, Powell, Stevens, Blackmun, White, Rehnquist, Scalia, Brennan, Marshall, O'Connor

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether the Commerce Clause of the US Constitution bars states from placing taxes or tariffs on goods being transported across state lines. The Court held that while the Commerce Clause generally prohibits states from taxing or tariffing goods moving in interstate commerce, it does allow states to impose certain taxes or fees related to the use of public roads and highways for transportation. However, the Court also ruled that states cannot charge higher taxes on goods coming from other states compared to similar products produced within their own state.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the First Amendment rights of Southeastern Promotions, Ltd., which sought to present the rock musical 'Hair' at a municipal theater in Chattanooga, Tennessee. The theater's directors denied the application without having seen the play or read the script, based on reports of nudity and obscenity in the production, and without providing a written statement of reasons.

The petitioner, Southeastern Promotions, Ltd., argued that this denial constituted an unlawful prior restraint on free speech. The District Court and the Court of Appeals upheld the decision of the theater's directors, agreeing that the content of the play could violate local obscenity laws and was not protected by the First Amendment.

The Supreme Court, however, reversed the lower courts' decisions. The Court held that the rejection of the application by the theater's directors was a prior restraint on speech, which is generally disfavored under the First Amendment. The Court emphasized that any system of prior restraint must have clear, objective, and definite standards to guide the licensing authority, and must be accompanied by procedural safeguards to avoid the dangers of censorship.

The Court found that the Chattanooga board's system lacked these procedural safeguards, such as a prompt judicial review, and placed the burden of initiating judicial proceedings on the petitioner. The Court ruled that the restraint on the musical was final and not a temporary measure pending judicial review, which made it unconstitutional.

The Supreme Court did not address whether the musical 'Hair' was obscene or whether the board's standards for determining obscenity were correct. Instead, the decision focused on the procedural deficiencies in the board's system of prior restraint. The Court reversed the lower courts' rulings, emphasizing the importance of protecting First Amendment rights and the need for procedural safeguards when prior restraints are imposed.

Respondents, a class of indigent Virginia death row inmates who do not have counsel to pursue postconviction proceedings, brought a suit under 42 U. S. C. § 1983 in the District Court against various state officials, alleging that the Constitution required that they be provided with counsel at the State's expense for the purpose of pursuing collateral proceedings related to their convictions and sentences. The District Court concluded that respondents should receive greater assistance than that outlined in Bounds v. Smith, 430 U.S. 817, which held that a prisoner's "right of access" to the courts required a State to furnish access to adequate law libraries or other legal aid so the prisoners might prepare petitions for judicial relief-since death row prisoners have a limited amount of time to prepare petitions, since their cases are unusually complex, and since the shadow of impending execution interferes with their ability to do legal work. It found that Virginia's efforts-access to a law library or lawbooks, the availability of "unit attorneys," and appointment of counsel after a petition is filed-did not afford prisoners meaningful access to the court because they did not guarantee the prisoners continuous assistance of counsel. Thus, it ordered Virginia to develop a program for the appointment of attorneys, upon request, to indigent death-row inmates wishing to pursue habeas corpus in state court, but, in light of Ross v. Moffitt, 417 US. 600, not in federal court. The Court of Appeals affirmed. It viewed as findings of fact the special "considerations" relating to death row inmate inmates which had led the court to conclude that Virginia was not in compliance with the constitutional rights of access. It reasoned that the case was not controlled by Pennsylvania v. Finley, 481 U. F. 2d 539-which held that neither the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment nor the equal protection guarantee of "meaningful access" required the State to appoint counsel for indigent prisoners seeking state postconvictions relief. Held: The judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded. Pp. 7-13. (a) This Court's decisions require the conclusion that the rule of Pennsylvania's rule of Finley should apply no differently in capital cases than in noncapital cases. See, e. g., Smith v. Murray, 477 U. s. 527, 106 S.Ct. 2661, 91 L. Ed.2d 434. State collateral proceedings are not constitutionally required as an adjunct to the state criminal proceeding and serve a different and more limited purpose than either the trial or appeal. Eighth Amendment safeguards imposed at the trial stage-where the court and jury hear testimony, receive evidence, and decide the question of guilt and punishment-are sufficient to assure the reliability of the process by which the death penalty is imposed. The Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments to the Constitution assure the right of an indigent defendant to counsel at trial stage of a criminal proceeding, Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U. . S. 335, and an indig defendant is similarly entitled as a matter of right to counsel for an initial appeal from the judgment and sentence of the trial court. Bounds, supra, at 828. But it would be a strange jurisprudence to allow, as the dissent would, the "rightof access" involved in this case to partially overrule a subsequently decided case such as Finley. Treating such matters as "factual findings" presumably subject only to review under the "clearly-erroneous" standard would permit a different constitutional rule to apply in a different State if the district judge hearing that claim reached different conclusions. The court's decisions imposing heightened procedural requirements on capital trials and sentencing proceedings do not apply in this context. The Eighth Amendment places special constraints on the procedures used to convict an accused of a capital offense and sentence him to death, and when they do, "evolving standards of decency" do not permit a death sentence to be carried out while a prisoner is unrepresented. This holding is inconsistent with the Eighth Amendment's "fundamentally unfair" standard of harmless-error review, which holds that prisoners seeking judicial relief from their sentence in state proceedings were not entitled to counsel. See Barefoot v. Estelle, 828, and Barefoot, 836, at 556-557. The holding of both cases squarely decides the question presented here. For the reasons previously stated in this opinion, we now hold that Finley applies to those inmates under sentence of death as well as to other inmates, and that holding necessarily imposes limits on Bounds. The conclusion that Pennsylvania's Rule of Pennsylvania applies no differently is consistent with the Court's decision in Barefoot. The Ninth Circuit, as an additional basis for its holding, reversed and remanded, holding that the right to appointed counsel at these earlier stages of the criminal procedure did not carry over to a discretionary appeal provided by North Carolina law from the intermediate appellate court to the Supreme Court of North Carolina.
