In the case of Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts, the Supreme Court addressed whether affidavits reporting the results of forensic analysis, which identified seized material as cocaine, were "testimonial" and thus subject to the defendant's right to confront the witnesses under the Sixth Amendment.

The Court held that the affidavits in question were indeed testimonial because they were equivalent to in-court testimony and were prepared for the purpose of proving a fact at trial. The analysts who prepared the affidavits were considered witnesses, and the defendant had the right to confront them at trial. The Court rejected various arguments suggesting that the analysts were not typical witnesses or that their work was neutral and reliable enough to be exempt from confrontation.

The Court emphasized that the Confrontation Clause is a procedural guarantee that requires evidence to be tested through cross-examination. It rejected the notion that the Clause could be disregarded for convenience or because other methods of verifying evidence might exist. The Court also noted that forensic evidence is not immune to manipulation or error, and confrontation serves as a means to ensure accurate analysis.

The Court clarified that not every person involved in the chain of custody or equipment maintenance must testify, and that documents created in the regular course of business may not be testimonial. However, when the prosecution introduces testimonial evidence, the defendant has the right to confront the individuals who created that evidence.

The Court dismissed concerns about the practical implications of its decision, noting that many states already comply with the Confrontation Clause without experiencing systemic disruptions. The Court also pointed out that defendants often stipulate to the nature of the substance in drug cases, reducing the need for analysts to testify.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Massachusetts court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, emphasizing the importance of adhering to the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause.

The Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA) requires the Secretary of the Interior to promulgate regulations listing those species of animals that are "threatened" or "endangered" under specified criteria, and to designate their "critical habitat." The ESA further requires each federal agency to "insure that any action authorized, funded, or carried out by such agency ... is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any endangered species or threatened species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of habitat of such species which is determined by the Secretary . . . to be critical.'' Section 1536(a)(2). If an agency determines that action it proposes to take may adversely affect a listed species, it must engage in formal consultation with the Fish and Wildlife Service, as delegate of the Secretary, after which the Service must provide the agency with a written statement (known as the "Incidental Take Statement") specifying the "impact of such incidental taking on the species," any "reasonable and prudent measures that the [Service] considers necessary or appropriate to minimize such impact," and setting forth "the terms and conditions ... that must be complied with by the Federal agency." The District Court dismissed the complaint for lack of jurisdiction, concluding that petitioners did not have standing because their "recreational, aesthetic, and commercial interests" do not fall within the zone of interests sought to be protected by the ESA or its implementing regulations. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that the ESA's citizen-suit provision does not authorize judicial review of the types of claims advanced by petitioners, and that judicial review is unavailable under the APA because the Biological Opinion does not constitute final agency action. Held: 1. The judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. Pp. 531-532. (a) Petitioners' claims are not subject to judicial review under §1540(g)(1)(A), which authorizes injunctive actions against any person "who is alleged to be in violation" of the ESA. P. 534. (b) The ESA does authorize review of petitioners' §1533 claim, but does not support their claims based upon the Secretary's alleged failure to comply with §1536(b). The "zone of interests" test, which requires that each agency "use the best scientific and commercial data available" to determine whether an action will "jeopardize" the continued operation of the Klamath Irrigation Project by the Bureau of Reclamation (Bureau), and that the Bureau "will abide by the restrictions imposed by [the] Biological Opinion," is similarly intended, at least in part, to prevent uneconomic (because erroneous) jeopardy determinations. The "best scientific andcommercial data" provision, which provides exemption from the Bureau's no-jeopardy mandate where there are no reasonable and prudent alternatives to the action and the benefits of the agency action clearly outweigh the benefits, is similarly designed to prevent "uneconomic jeopardy" determinations, and is intended to encourage enforcement by so-called "private attorneys general"-evidenced by its elimination of the usual amount-in-controversy and diversity-of-citizenship requirements, its provision for recovery of the costs of litigation (including even expert witness fees), and its reservation to the Government of a right of first refusal to pursue the action initially and a right to intervene later-is similarly intended to prevent such a mistake, since it does not conclusively determine the manner in which the petitioners will be allocated water. The Government's contention that the cause of action against the Secretary set forth in the ESA citizensuit provision is exclusive, supplanting those provided by the Act, is simply incompatible with the principle that discretion as to the substance of the ultimate decision does not confer discretion to ignore the required procedures of decisionmaking. The Secretary's conduct in implementing or enforcing the ESA is a means by which private parties may enforce the substantive provisions of theESA against regulated parties-both private entities and Government agencies-but is not an alternative avenue for judicial review. The Act's purpose is to avoid needless economic dislocation produced by agency officials zealously but unintelligently pursuing their environmental objectives, and it is obvious that the Secretary is keenly aware of the virtually determinative effect of its biological opinions. The fact that the "case'' or "controversies" provision expressly precludes review under the ESA does not alter the categorical requirement that, in arriving at his decision, he "tak[e] into consideration the economic impact, and any other relevant impact, of specifying any particular area as critical habitat." Pp 534-535. (c) The Government contends that the District Court erred in affirming the dismissal of petitioner's claims for lack-of jurisdiction, since petitioners allege a violation of §7, 16 U. S. C. §1534(b)(2), which requires a court to set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions found to be arbitrary, capricious,

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a personal injury suit filed by a worker injured while working on an artificial island drilling rig owned and operated by Chevron Oil Co. The Fifth Circuit held that the doctrine of laches should have been applied by the District Court. The court held that, in order to provide a remedy for wrongful death, the "gap" must be filled with the applicable body of state law under  1333(a)(2) of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. The Court held that Louisiana's time limitation on personal injury actions need not be applied with the substantive remedy. The 5th Circuit agreed, holding that the Lands Act requires that the state statute of limitations be applied to personal injury claims. The case is now back before the Fifth Court for further consideration.

Petitioners, who were found guilty of committing felonies, by less-than-unanimous jury verdicts, which are permitted under Oregon law in noncapital cases, claim that their convictions, upheld on appeal, contravene their right to trial by jury under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. Held: The judgment is affirmed. Pp. 410-414, 369-380. (a) Petitioners' argument that the Sixth Amendment requires jury unanimity in order to effectuate the reasonable-doubt standard otherwise mandated by due process requirements is without merit since that Amendment does not require proof beyond a reasonable doubt at all. P. 411-412. (b) The Sixth Amendment guarantee of a jury trial, made applicable to the States by the Fourteenth (Duncan v. Louisiana, 391 U. S. 145, 88 .s.Ct. 1444, 20 L.Ed.2d 491), does not necessarily require that the jury's vote be unanimous. The Amendment's essential purpose of "interpos(ing) between the accused and his accuser . . . the commonsense judgment of a group of laymen' representative of a cross section of the community, Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S. 78, 100, is served despite the absence of a unanimity requirement, Pp . 410-412-411. (c) Petitioner's argument that, as it was introduced by James Madison in the House of Representatives, the amendment provided for trial "by an impartial jury of freeholders of the vicinage, with the requisite of unanimity for conviction, of the right of challenge, and other accustomed requisites . . ." was without merit, since that amendment does not mandate proof beyond that reasonable doubt. Pps. 410—412-414. (d) Although on the basis of history and precedent the Sixth amendment, while requiring States to provide jury trials for serious crimes, does not incorporate all the elements of the jury trial within the meaning of the Fifth Amendment, the Due Process Clause of the Federal Constitution, as required by the Due process Clause, is not violative of due process, since the Amendment does require proof to be constitutionally required, and the usual safeguards exist to minimize the possibility of jury irresponsibility. And, as in Williams, this Court's inability to divine "the intent of the Framers" when they eliminated references to the "accustomed requisites" requires that in determining what is meant by a jury we must turn to other than purely historical considerations. Pn. 378-380, affirmed.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses a zoning ordinance in the Village of Belle Terre, which restricts land use to one-family dwellings and defines 'family' in a specific way that excludes groups of more than two unrelated individuals living together. The case arose when the Dickmans, who leased their house to six unrelated students, were served with a violation notice by the village. The students and the Dickmans challenged the ordinance as unconstitutional.

The District Court upheld the ordinance, but the Court of Appeals reversed the decision. The Supreme Court, however, reversed the Court of Appeals, upholding the ordinance. The Court's reasoning is based on the broad powers of local governments to regulate land use under the police power of the state. The Court found that the ordinance did not involve a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, such as voting or privacy, and therefore, the law only needed to be reasonable and not arbitrary, and to bear a rational relationship to a permissible state objective.

The Court acknowledged that while the ordinance might exclude some individuals who could be considered a 'family,' the drawing of such lines is a legislative function, not a judicial one. The Court also dismissed the argument that the ordinance was discriminatory against unmarried couples, noting that the ordinance's definition of 'family' includes two unmarried people living together.

The Court concluded that the goals of the ordinance—to maintain a quiet, family-oriented community with wide yards and restricted traffic—were legitimate and within the scope of the police power. The Court also addressed the issue of mootness, stating that zoning ordinances typically affect property values and that the impact on the lessor's property in this case was clear.

In summary, the Supreme Court upheld the Village of Belle Terre's zoning ordinance as a valid exercise of local government power to regulate land use for the purpose of preserving the character of a community, and it did not find the ordinance to be unconstitutional.

The U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina ruled in favor of the Federal Housing Administration, finding that the agency's policy against renting apartments to transients was not violated by a South Carolina corporation's actions. The court found that the corporation, Appellee, had provided the agency with a schedule of monthly rates for its different types of apartments, but did not provide a schedule for transients. It also found that an affiliate of appellee without knowledge furnished a number of apartments; and some were leased to a daily basis at rentals never submitted to nor approved by FHA, part of the rental going to the affiliate as 'furniture rental.' The court held that  513(a) of the National Housing Act, which prohibits the use of housing insured under the Act for transient or hotel purposes while such insurance on the mortgage remains outstanding, was unconstitutional. The Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit agreed with the lower court's finding, and sent the case back to the district court for further proceedings.

The Supreme Court was tasked with determining whether the Petition Clause of the First Amendment provides absolute immunity from libel charges for statements made in letters to the President of the United States. The case arose after the respondent initiated a libel lawsuit against the petitioner, who had written letters to President Reagan containing allegedly false and damaging statements about the respondent, which purportedly led to the respondent not being appointed as United States Attorney.

The petitioner claimed that the Petition Clause granted him absolute immunity from liability for libel. The District Court and the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals both rejected this claim, holding that the Petition Clause does not confer absolute immunity from libel.

The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' decisions. The Court acknowledged the historical significance of the right to petition the government, tracing its roots back to the English Bill of Rights and colonial America. However, the Court found no evidence that the Framers of the First Amendment intended for the Petition Clause to offer absolute protection against liability for libelous statements.

The Court referenced early state court cases and the Supreme Court's own precedent in White v. Nicholls, which allowed for libel actions if the statements were made with "express malice," defined as falsehoods made without probable cause. The Court also noted that other forms of petitioning, such as filing a lawsuit, do not enjoy absolute protection if they are baseless.

The Court concluded that the Petition Clause does not grant a special status within the First Amendment that would allow individuals to make libelous statements with impunity. The right to petition is important, but it does not supersede the rights of individuals to be protected from malicious falsehoods.

The Supreme Court held that under state common law, damages for libel can only be recovered if the petitioner acted with malice, which is consistent with the standard set by New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, stating that while the right to petition is protected, the right to commit libel without consequences is not. Justice Powell did not participate in the decision.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the United States in a case brought by the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed on December 21, 1964, the U. S. Department of Commerce amended its regulations to prohibit Webb-Pomerene associations from bidding on certain procurement contracts whenever procurement was limited to United States suppliers.  The SEC alleges that the amended regulations made it uneconomical for the association and its members to continue in operation, since a large proportion of AID-financed procurement is limited to American sources.  In a parallel action, on January 1, 1967, the Department of State Department issued an order requiring the association to cease and desist from participating in any new export association.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Association dissolved itself on December 28, 1967.  As alleged in the court's order, the dissolved association was not the only defendant in this case; the agency that administers the foreign aid program, the State Department agency in charge of the foreign assistance program, amended its rules in January 1967 to prohibit the association from bidding for certain "eligible" procurement contracts when the contracts were limited to U. States suppliers, and to pay for the purchase of certain "essential" goods.  AID's new regulation, which the court held was necessary to assure compliance with the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws, prohibited the Association from participating directly or indirectly in any foreign procurement program, and prohibited it from participating as a party in any joint export association without court approval and from continuing in effect any prices jointly agreed upon by the Association.   The court also denied the Association's request for a temporary restraining order, which was granted by the court on December 27, 1967 and by the Secretary of State's Office on January 2, 2016. Schiff and Mr. Werner, and the case is being supervised by Jennifer C. Barry.

When petitioner Johnnie Williams sued respondents Pierce Marshall and others in Texas state court for breaches of contract and fraud, the parties reached a settlement agreement that gave Pierce a life estate in a portion of the marital home and left the remainder to Williams. Later, when the Marshalls divorced, Pierce sold the house to petitioner Vickie Marshall, claiming that he owned the entire property. Subsequently, Vickie sued Pierce in federal court, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief. The District Court ultimately entered judgment for Vickie, ruling that Pierce had committed fraud and that the settlement agreement violated the Texas Family Code. On appeal, the Fifth Circuit reversed, concluding that the federal courts lacked jurisdiction over Vickie’s claim. The court noted that the Texas Probate Court had ruled that it had exclusive jurisdiction over all of Vickie’s claims against Pierce, and held that the federal courts’ failure to abide by that ruling constituted a violation of the probate exception to the domestic relations exception to federal jurisdiction. Held: 1. This Court need not decide whether the probate exception applies to Vickie’s claim since the Fifth Circuit erred in deciding that the federal courts lacked jurisdiction over that claim. Pp. 10–14. (a) The probate exception reserves to state probate courts the probate or annulment of a will and the administration of a decedent’s estate; it also precludes federal courts from attempting to dispose of property that is in the custody of a state probate court. However, it does not bar federal courts from adjudicating matters outside those confines and otherwise within federal jurisdiction. Here, Vickie’s claim does not involve the administration of an estate, the probate of a will, or any other purely probate matter. Rather, it alleges a widely recognized tort. Moreover, no sound policy considerations militate in favor of extending the probate exception to cover the case at hand. Pp. 10–12. (b) The Fifth Circuit erred in advancing an alternative ground for its conclusion that the federal courts lacked jurisdiction over Vickie’s claim. Contrary to the court’s suggestion, the Texas Probate Court’s ruling that it had exclusive jurisdiction over all of Vickie’s claims against Pierce did not bind the federal courts. Instead, the federal courts’ jurisdiction to entertain Vickie’s tortious interference claim is governed by federal law, which allows states to reserve to their probate courts the exclusive right to adjudicate a transitory tort. Since Texas cannot make its probate courts exclusively competent to entertain a claim of that genre, the federal courts properly asserted jurisdiction over Vickie’s counterclaim against Pierce. Pp. 12–14. 2. The Fifth Circuit did not address the question whether Vickie’s claim was “core” or whether Pierce’s arguments concerning claim and issue preclusion are meritorious. Those issues remain open for consideration on remand. P. 14. 392 F. 3d 1129, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia ruled that the Bankruptcy Act of 1978 (Act) is unconstitutional. The Act established a bankruptcy court in each judicial district as an adjunct to the district court for such district. The bankruptcy court judges are appointed for 14-year terms, subject to removal by the judicial council of the circuit in which they serve on grounds of incompetence, misconduct, neglect of duty, or disability. Their salaries are set by statute and are subject to adjustment. Northern Pipeline Construction Co. (Northern) filed a suit in the bankruptcy court against appellee Marathon Pipe Line Co. seeking damages for an alleged breach of contract and warranty, as well as for misrepresentation, coercion, and duress. Marathon sought dismissal of the suit on the ground that the Act unconstitutionally conferred judicial power upon judges who lacked life tenure and protection against salary diminution. The Bankruptcy Court denied the motion to dismiss, but on appeal the District Court granted the motion. The Court held that the grant of jurisdiction to bankruptcy courts cannot be sustained as an exercise of Congress' power to create adjuncts to Art. III courts. The court held that there is no persuasive reason in logic, history, or the Constitution, why bankruptcy courts lie beyond the reach of Art. II courts of the Territories or of the D.C.

The Supreme Court of the United States decided the case of United States v. Jeffrey Skilling on June 27, 2010. The case concerned a man named Jeffrey Skilling, who was the CEO of Enron Corporation, a multinational energy company that filed for bankruptcy in 2001. Skilling was charged with multiple counts of fraud related to Enron's financial reporting and was found guilty on 19 of those counts. However, the Supreme Court reversed his conviction on 11 of those counts and remanded the case back to the lower court for retrial.

The Supreme Court held that the Honest Services Fraud Act, which makes it illegal to engage in corrupt activities related to labor relations, did not apply to Skilling's conduct. The Court found that the Act was designed to protect workers from corrupt employers, and that Skilling's actions did not involve any corrupt activity related to labor relations. Additionally, the Court held that the Act was too broadly written and could potentially be applied to a wide range of conduct that was not intended to be punishable under the statute.

Petitioners are Xerox employees who left the company in the 1980’s, received lump-sum distributions of retirement benefits they had earned up to that point, and were later rehired. Petitioners are the plan itself and the Plan Administrator. The dispute giving rise to this case concerns how to account for respondents’ past distributions when calculating their current benefits-that is, how to avoid paying respondents the same benefits twice. The Plan Administrator initially interpreted the Plan to call for an approach that calculated the hypothetical growth that respondents past distributions would have experienced if the money had remained in Xerox’S investment funds, and reduced the present benefits accordingly. But unlike the phantom account method, the new approach did not calculate the present value of a past distribution based on events that occurred after the distribution was made. Instead, it used an interest rate that was fixed at the time of the distribution, thereby calculating the current value of the distributed distribution. The Second Circuit vacated and remanded. Held: A single honest mistake in plan interpretation justifies stripping the administrator of that deference for subsequent related interpretations of the plan. Firestone Tire & Rubber Co. v. Bruch, 489 U. S. 101. Pp. 5–11. (a) The Court of Appeals’ exception to Firestone deference is not required by principles of trust law. The District Court was entitled to reject a reasonable interpretation of the Plan offered by the Plan administrator, solely because the Court had overturned a previous interpretation by the Administrator. See 472 F. Supp. 2d 452, 456–458. This Court rejects this “one-strike-and-you’re-out” approach. As an initial matter, it has no basis in the Court‘s holding in Firestone, which set out a broad standard of deference without any suggestion that the standard was susceptible to ad hoc exceptions like the one adopted by the Second Circuit. The question whether a deferential standard of review was required in this case turns on whether a plan administrator was interpreting the same terms or deciding the “same issue” on remand. See, e.g., Miller v. Xerox Corp. Retirement Income Guarantee Plan, 464 F. 3d 871, 875–876. The interests in efficiency, predictability, and uniformity-and the manner in which they are promoted by deference to reasonable plan construction by administrators—do not suddenly disappear simply because a plan Administrator has made a single honest error. P. 5. (b) Respondents and the United States as amicus curiae do not question the deference of Plan Administrator to plan administrators, who have a duty to all beneficiaries to preserve limited plan assets, and the principles of ERISA-plus, of course, Firestone. See 554 U.S., at ___ (slip op., at 4, 6–7, 9–10). P. 6. (c) In determining the proper standard for reviewing ERISA plan administrators’ decisions, the courts must look to trust law, the terms of a plan at issue, and ERISA principles. The purpose of the ERISA system is to create a “careful balancing” between ensuring fair and prompt enforcement of rights under a plan and the encouragement of the creation of such plans.” Aetna Health Inc., v. Davila, 542 U. . . 200, 215. A leading treatise states that a court will strip a trustee of his discretion when there is reason to believe that he will not exercise that discretion fairly—for example, upon a showing that the trustee has already acted in bad faith: “If the trustee’�s failure to pay a reasonable amount [to the beneficiary of the trust] is due to a failure to exercise [the trustee] discretion honestly and fairly, the court ordinarily will not fix the amount but will instead direct the trustee to make reasonable provision for the beneficiary” (i. e., “On the other hand, if the trustee is not satisfied that he has abused his discretion in some manner,” Rush Prudential HMO, Inc. v Moran, 536 U . S. 355, 379, “the court has no authority to substitute its judgment for that of the trustees”—and the District Court should not have “act[ed] as a substitute trustee” because that would violate ERISA. In this Supreme Court opinion, the central issue is whether taxpayers in Toledo, Ohio, have the standing to challenge state and local tax benefits offered to DaimlerChrysler for expanding its Jeep operation in Toledo, on the grounds that these benefits violated the Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

The Court of Appeals had previously found that a state tax credit offered to DaimlerChrysler violated the Commerce Clause. However, before the Supreme Court could address the Commerce Clause question, it had to determine if the taxpayers had the standing to bring their complaint to federal court.

The Supreme Court concluded that the taxpayers did not have standing to challenge the tax benefits. The Court reasoned that the taxpayers' alleged injury, which was based on the tax breaks depleting state funds and increasing their tax burden, was too speculative and not concrete enough to establish standing. The Court also noted that it was uncertain whether tax breaks actually deplete the treasury since their purpose is to stimulate economic activity, which could increase government revenues.

The Court rejected the idea that state taxpayers could challenge state tax or spending decisions simply by being taxpayers. It also dismissed the plaintiffs' argument that an exception to the general prohibition on taxpayer standing should exist for Commerce Clause challenges, noting that the Commerce Clause does not provide the same specific limitation on government power as the Establishment Clause does in cases like Flast v. Cohen.

Additionally, the Court found that the plaintiffs could not claim municipal taxpayer standing to challenge the state franchise tax credit because their challenge was to state law, not municipal action. The Court also rejected the application of "supplemental jurisdiction" to allow standing for related claims, emphasizing that standing must be established for each individual claim.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals in part and remanded the cases for dismissal of the plaintiffs' challenge to the franchise tax credit, as the plaintiffs lacked the standing to bring the case to federal court. This decision implies that taxpayers cannot challenge state tax incentives in federal court based solely on their status as taxpayers, and it underscores the importance of concrete and particularized injury for establishing standing in federal court.

Respondent was indicted for three counts of mail fraud, which involved a burglar alarm company's insurance claims arising from thefts committed by employees whom respondent consented to hire despite being aware of the risk of liability. The indictment clearly set out the offense for which respondent was ultimately convicted. However, the trial proof focused on a single incident rather than the full scope of the scheme. The Court of Appeals vacated the conviction, concluding that the variance between the indictment and the trial proof compromised respondent's Fifth Amendment right to be tried only on offenses for which a grand jury has returned an indictment. Held: There was no compromise of respondent's Fifth Amendment rights. Pp. 108-117. (a) The Court of Appeals erred in reaching its conclusion contrary to the holdings of this Court in cases such as Salinger v. United States, 361 U. S. 212, and Ford v. United States, 273 U. S. 593, wherein variations between indictment and proof were deemed irrelevant and inconsequential. Pp. 108-111. (b) Stirone v. United States, 361 U. S. 212, distinguished. Pp. 111-112. (c) Ex parte Bain, 121 U. S. 1, is distinguishable on the grounds that the indictment in question there was defective insofar as it purported to include an offense that was not included in the indictment as originally drafted, whereas here the indictment clearly covered the offense for which respondent was convicted. Pp. 112-116. Reversed.

In United States v. New Mexico, the Supreme Court ruled that a state generally may impose a nondiscriminatory tax on a private company's proceeds from contracts with the federal government. However, the court clarified that this rule applies only if the federal government is not involved in the activity being taxed. In this case, the Bureau of Indian Affairs contracted with Blaze Construction Company to build, repair, and improve roads on various Indian reservations in Arizona. While Blaze is incorporated under the laws of the Blackfeet Tribe of Montana and is owned by a member of that Tribe, the company did not perform any work on the Blackfeet Reservation. Instead, Blaze worked on Indian reservations across multiple states. The Arizona Department of Revenue assessed Blaze a tax deficiency for failing to pay Arizona's transaction privilege tax on the proceeds from its contracts with the bureau. The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Arizona Court of Appeals, which had found that federal law preempted the application of Arizona's tax to Blaze.

In this Supreme Court case, the Court reviewed a Minnesota statute that required a 48-hour notice to both parents before a minor could obtain an abortion, with certain exceptions. The Court concluded that the requirement to notify both parents was not reasonably related to legitimate state interests and was therefore unconstitutional. However, a different majority of the Court found that the judicial bypass provision, which allowed minors to obtain a court order to proceed with an abortion without parental notification, was constitutional.

The Court's reasoning included the following points:

1. The parental notice statute was initially intended to foster parent-child relationships and provide counsel to minors facing the decision to terminate a pregnancy. However, the Court found that the two-parent notification requirement did not serve these purposes effectively, especially in cases where parents were divorced, separated, or otherwise not involved in the minor's upbringing.

2. The Court noted that the requirement for two-parent notification could have harmful effects on minors and their families, particularly in dysfunctional or abusive situations. It could also discourage minors from communicating with the parent they are close to if they are forced to also notify the other parent.

3. The Court recognized that the state has a legitimate interest in the welfare of minors and in supporting parental involvement in important decisions. However, this interest is sufficiently served by requiring notification of only one parent.

4. The Court found that the judicial bypass procedure provided a confidential and expedited process for minors to obtain an abortion without parental notification if they could demonstrate maturity or that it was in their best interest. This procedure was deemed to protect the rights of minors while still serving the state's interests.

5. The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had found the two-parent notification requirement unconstitutional but upheld the constitutionality of the judicial bypass provision.

The implications of the decision are that states cannot impose a blanket requirement for two-parent notification before a minor can obtain an abortion, as it infringes on the constitutional rights of the minor. However, states can provide a judicial bypass as an alternative means for minors to exercise their right to an abortion without parental notification.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against the University of Michigan Law School for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17(b) thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Jackson, Mississippi, alleges that the Law School violated the anti-discrimination provisions of the federal securities laws by failing to consider race as a factor in its admissions decisions.  According to the complaint, the law school's admissions policy, drafted in 1992, expressly requires that all applicants be members of a "critical mass" of underrepresented minority students.  In addition, the complaint alleges that, as a result of this policy, the school was not able to adequately consider the diversity contributions of its underrepresented student body.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's complaints, the university consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from future violations of the charged provisions, and orders it to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against the school from participating in the admissions process.  Finally, the court granted the university's request for a temporary restraining order and an order requiring it to comply with the court's order.  On May 10, 2018, the Honorable Kathleen M. Burns of the United States District Court in Jackson issued an order imposing a preliminary injunction against the university from violating the federal anti-racism provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4)-8 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 206(3)-8 thereunder, and ordered the university to pay a $10,000 civil penalty.   The court also ordered the college to provide an accounting of the college admissions that it had received in the wake of the admissions decision.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-01-2017.

Section 3001 (3) of the New York Education Law provides that no person shall be certified as a teacher in the public schools if he is not a citizen of the United States. Appellants, two British women who had lived in the United States for several years but remained citizens of Great Britain, challenged the validity of § 3001 (3) under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. A three-judge Federal District Court held that the section violates the Equal Protection Clause, conclusively finding that it was not narrowly tailored to advance the asserted state interests in promoting the educational goals of the public schools and in ensuring that the teachers impart patriotism and devotion to the Government. Held: As applied to appellants, § 3001 (3) does not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 44-52. (a) Although the decision in Oyama v. California, 332 U. S. 633, marked the beginning of the end of the doctrine that classifications based on alienage are inherently suspect and subject to strict judicial scrutiny, subsequent cases have established that some state functions are so bound up with the operation of the State as a governmental entity as to permit the exclusion from those functions of all persons who have not become part of the process of self-government. Here, the State has a legitimate interest in furthering the educational goals of the public schools and in ensuring that the teachers impart patriotism and devotion to the Government, and § 3001 (3)'s bar on aliens who have demonstrated their unwillingness to obtain United States citizenship rationally advances these interests. Pp. 44-49. (b) Under the "governmental function" principle recognized in Sugarman v. Douglass, 413 U. S. 634, and Foley v. Connelie, ante, p. 291, public school teachers come within the category of governmental functions for which a citizenship requirement may be justified without meeting the stringent standards of strict judicial scrutiny. Such functions include the police function, which involves the exercise of substantial discretionary powers and is closely tied to the core functions of government. Similarly, here, public education fulfils a most fundamental obligation of government to its constituency, and teachers play a critical part in developing students' attitudes toward government and understanding of the role of citizens in society. Moreover, although not just those responsible for teaching the courses most directly related to government, history, and civic duties should help fulfill the broader function of the public school system, nevertheless all teachers, regardless of their specialties, may be called upon to teach other subjects, including those expressly dedicated to political and social subjects, and certainly a State may regard them as having an obligation to promote civic virtues and understanding in their classes, regardless of the subject taught. Pp. 49-52. Reversed.

After petitioner AT&T acquired ownership of several corporations involved in the retail sale of high-speed Internet service, some of whose stockholders sued AT&T in Federal District Court, claiming that AT&T had used its market power to monopolize the retail broadband market in violation of §§1 and 2 of the Sherman Act. The District Court dismissed the complaint, finding that AT&T had no duty to deal with its rivals in the wholesale market, and that even if it did, its retail prices were not too low. The Ninth Circuit reversed, concluding that the complaint stated a cause of action despite the fact that the District Court had not reached the merits. Held: The price-squeeze claims set forth in the complaint are not cognizable under the Sherman Act. Pp. 4−12. (a) The price-squeeze claims are based on the premise that a firm with market power in the wholesale market can use that power to reduce the profits of its rivals in the retail market. These claims fall into three categories. First, some plaintiffs claimed that AT&T had failed to deal with its rivals in the wholesale market. However, the Court has consistently held that a firm with no antitrust duty to deal with its rivals has no duty to deal under the terms and conditions preferred by those rivals. Verizon Commcns., Inc. v. Trinko, Inc., 540 U.S. 398, 409–410. Thus, the complaint fails to state a claim upon which relief may be granted unless the plaintiffs can show that AT&T has a duty to deal with its rivals in the wholesale market. Second, some plaintiffs claimed that AT&T’s retail prices were too low. However, to prevail on a predatory pricing claim, a plaintiff must demonstrate that the prices complained of are below an appropriate measure of its rival’s costs and that there is a “dangerous probability” that the defendant will be able to recover its investment in below-cost prices. Brooke Group LLC v. Southwest Airlines Co., 509 U.S. 233, 222–224. Third, some plaintiffs claimed that AT&T’s retail prices were too low because it was squeezing the profits of its retail rivals. However, the Court declines to recognize such claims. Although the Court acknowledges that the term “price squeeze” appears in early antitrust literature, the Court finds that modern antitrust principles render the concept obsolete. Moreover, the Court notes that the plaintiffs have not shown that AT&T’s actions resulted in any independent competitive harm beyond the harm that would result from a duty-to-deal violation at the wholesale level or predatory pricing at the retail level. Pp. 4−9. (b) The Court rejects the suggestion that the price-squeeze claims are cognizable under the Sherman Act because they fit within the framework of existing antitrust theories. The Court agrees with the plaintiffs that the price-squeeze claims are similar to the claims raised in United States v. Aluminum Co. of America, 148 F. 2d 416, and United States v. Eastman Kodak Co., 273 F. 2d 532, but the Court disagrees that the price-squeeze claims are analogous to the claims raised in Brooke Group. Nor does the Court accept the plaintiffs’ suggestion that the price-squeeze claims are cognizable under the Clayton Act. Finally, the Court rejects the suggestion that the price-squeeze claims are cognizable under the Sherman Act because they reflect the way in which market forces operate. Instead, the Court believes that the price-squeeze claims represent an attempt to merge two distinct concepts—wholesale and retail price fixing—into a single category. Pp. 9−12. Reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C.J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed a lower court's judgment against Bryan County, Oklahoma, for violating the civil rights of a woman who was arrested by a county police officer in a May 1991 traffic stop. The lower court had dismissed the county's motion for judgment as a matter of law. The appeals court found in favor of the county on the basis of its "hiring policy" and "training policy"<n>The lower court found that the county was liable for Stacy Burns' alleged use of excessive force when he arrested respondent Jill Brown without probable cause. Burns had a record of driving infractions and had pleaded guilty to various driving-related and other misdemeanors, including assault and battery, resisting arrest, and public drunkenness. Burns was hired by Bryan County Sheriff B.J. Moore, the son of his nephew, and the jury found that he had violated respondent's civil rights by using excessive force. The jury also found that Bryan County had violated its own hiring policy by failing to adequately review Burns' background. The court held that the hiring policy was inadequate as to amount to deliberate action by the county, and that the jury's finding of liability against the county could not be squared with that finding. We conclude that, in enacting 1983, Congress did not intend to impose liability on a municipality unless deliberate action attributable to the municipality itself is the "moving force" behind the plaintiff's deprivation of federal rights.

Petitioner López, a former undocumented immigrant, was convicted of aiding and abetting a controlled substance violation based on his assisting a friend in obtaining cocaine. His state conviction was upgraded to a federal felony because it involved “illicit trafficking in a controlled substance,” 8 U. S. C. §1101(a)(43), which is defined as including “drug trafficking crime,” 18 U. S. C. §924(c)(2). Section 924(c)(2) lists three types of drug trafficking crimes: (1) possession of cocaine base, 21 U. S. C. §844(a); (2) recidivist possession, ibid.; and (3) possession of more than five grams of cocaine base, §844(a). Because none of these offenses is a felony under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), the Immigration and Nationality Act (IMA) deems them “misdemeanors punishable under the [CSA].” López argued that his state conviction could not be considered an “aggravated felony” because it did not involve a felony punishable under the CSA. The Immigration Judge disagreed, ruling that the state conviction qualified as an aggravated felony because it involved “illicit trafficking in a controlled substance.” On appeal, the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) affirmed, concluding that the state conviction was a felony punishable under the CSA. The Tenth Circuit affirmed, rejecting López’s argument that the state conviction could not be considered an aggravated felony unless it proscribed conduct punishable as a felony under the CSA. Held: A state offense constitutes a “felony punishable under the Controlled Substances Act” only if it proscribes conduct punishable as a felony under that federal law. Pp. 4−12. (a) The IMA defines an “aggravated felony” as including “illicit trafficking in a controlled substance,” which is defined as including “drug trafficking crime,” 18 U. S. C. §924(c)(2). The latter term is defined elsewhere in the IMA as referring to “any … felony punishable under the Controlled Substances Act,” §1101(a)(43)(F). The Government claims that this definition allows states to supplant federal classifications when it comes to deciding whether a state offense qualifies as an aggravated felony. However, the Government offers no evidence that Congress intended to give states greater authority to determine the nature of federal crimes than it gave to Congress itself. To the contrary, the IMA explicitly provides as a specific example of an “aggravated felony” the type of “drug trafficking crime” covered by §924(c)(2). Moreover, the Government fails to explain how its proposed construction of the statute squares with the fact that the IMA uses the term “felony punishable under the [CSA]” rather than “offense punishable under the [CSA]” or “conduct punishable under the [CSA].” Such phrasing indicates that Congress understood the concept of a “felony punishable under the [CSA]” to be distinct from mere conduct punishable under the CSA. The Government’s reading would also render the law of alien removal and the law of sentencing for illegal entry into the country dependent on varying state criminal classifications even when Congress has apparently pegged the immigration statutes to the classifications Congress itself chose. Nothing in the statute’s text suggests that Congress changed the meaning of “felony punishable under the [CSA]” when it took that phrase from Title 18 and incorporated it into Title 8’s definition of “aggravated felony.” Furthermore, the Government’s reading would render the law of alien removal and the law of sentencing for illegal entry into the country dependent on varying state criminal classifications even when Congress has apparently pegged the immigration statutes to the classifications Congress itself chose. Pp. 4−8. (b) The Government’s reading would lead to results that are implausible on common sense grounds. By the Government’s logic, a State could overrule its judgment about the consequences of federal offenses to which its immigration laws expressly refer. For instance, the IMA expressly exempts from deportation a single offense involving possession of 30 grams or less of marijuana, yet by the Government’s reasoning, if a State were to draw the misdemeanor-felony line at six grams plus, a person convicted in state court of possessing six grams would not be guilty of an aggravated felony on the Government’s reading. Similarly, possessing more than five grams of cocaine base is a felony under federal law, but if a State draws the misdemeanor-felony line at six grams plus, a person convicted in state court of possessing six grams would not be guilty of an aggravated felony on the Government’s reading. These results are implausible because they would allow States to supplant Congress’s own classifications when it comes to deciding whether a state offense qualifies as an aggravated felony. Pp. 8−10. (c) The Government’s reading is also inconsistent with the plain meaning of the relevant provisions. The IMA uses the term “felony punishable under the [CSA]” instead of “offense punishable under the [CSA]” or “conduct punishable under the [CSA].” Such phrasing indicates that Congress understood the concept of a “felony punishable under the [CSA]” to be distinct from mere conduct punishable under the CSA. The Government’s reading would thus create confusion by suggesting that a state offense can be a felony punishable under the CSA despite the fact that it involves conduct punishable as a misdemeanor under the CSA. Pp. 10−11. 417 F. 3d 1175, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Thomas, J., joined.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the legality of a search warrant issued against the Stanford Daily, a student newspaper at Stanford University, which was not suspected of criminal activity. The warrant was issued to obtain photographs of a violent clash between demonstrators and police, believed to be evidence of felonies. The District Court had previously ruled that the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments forbid the issuance of a search warrant for materials in possession of someone not suspected of a crime unless a subpoena would be impracticable. The Supreme Court reversed this decision.

The Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment allows for the issuance of valid warrants to search any property where there is probable cause to believe that evidence of a crime will be found, regardless of the owner or possessor's suspected complicity in the crime. The Court emphasized that the critical element in a reasonable search is not the owner's suspected criminality but the reasonable cause to believe that the specific items to be searched for are located on the property.

The Court also addressed concerns about First Amendment interests when the third party is a newspaper. It acknowledged the historical conflict between the Crown and the press but concluded that the Fourth Amendment's requirements, when applied with precision, provide sufficient protection against the asserted threats to press freedom. The Court found no constitutional barrier against warrants to search newspaper premises and declined to require subpoenas as a general rule or demand prior notice and hearing for the issuance of search warrants.

In summary, the Supreme Court concluded that the search warrant issued against the Stanford Daily was reasonable under the Fourth Amendment and did not violate the First Amendment. The Court's decision implies that search warrants can be issued to third parties not suspected of criminal activity if there is probable cause to believe that evidence of a crime is located on their property.

The United States Constitution grants every citizen the right to a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury of his peers. However, the Supreme Court has ruled that states may choose to limit the size of the jury in criminal cases. In this case, the Supreme Court holds that a reduction in the number of jurors from six to five in criminal trials violates the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Court finds that the reduction undermines the essential role of the jury in determining the truth and applying the sense of the community. The Court cites numerous studies showing that smaller juries are less reliable and less representative of the community. The Court also rejects Georgia's argument that the reduction is justified by savings in court time and money.

Petitioner was indicted with two others, Edwin Roberts and Joseph Freeman, for importing heroin into the United States from Thailand and the Philippine Islands and for conspiracy to import heroin in violation of 21 U. S. C. §§ 952(a), 962(a) and 963. The indictment also named six unindicted co-conspirators, including petitioner's wife. Prior to trial on this indictment, petitioner moved to sever his case from that of Roberts and Freeman, who assisted them in its distribution. The District Court ruled that petitioner could testify in support of the Government's case to any act she observed during the marriage and to any communication "made in the presence of a third person"; however, confidential communications between petitioner and his wife were held to be privileged and inadmissible. At trial, petitioner testified within the limits of the court's pretrial ruling; her testimony, as the Government concedes, constituted virtually its entire case against petitioner. In the Court of Appeals, petitioner's only claim of error was that the admission of the adverse testimony of his wife, over his objection, contravened this Court's teaching in Hawkins v. United States, supra, and therefore constituted reversible error. Held: 1. The existing rule should be modified so that the witness-spouse alone has a privilege to refuse to testify adversely; the witness may be neither compelled to testify nor foreclosed from testifying; and the modification-vesting the privilege in the "spouse"-furthers the important public interest in marital harmony without unduly burdening legitimate law enforcement needs. Pp. 5-7. (a) A rule of evidence permitting an accused to prevent adverse spousal testimony seems far more likely to frustrate justice than to foster family peace, and the trend in state law toward divesting the accused of the privilege to bar adverse testimony has special relevance because the laws of marriage and domestic relations are concerns traditionally reserved to the states. See Sosna v. Iowa, 419 U.S. 393, 404, 95 S.Ct. 553, 559, 42 L.Ed. 2d 532, and Scholarly criticism of the Hawkins rule has also continued unabated. P. 5. (b) The present justification for affording an accused such a privilege is unpersuasive. When one spouse is willing to testify against the other in a criminal proceeding-whatever the motivation-their relationship is almost certainly in disrepair; there is probably little in the way of marital harmony for the privilege. In these circumstances, a rule of Evidence that permits an accused's denial or exclusion of relevant evidence seems far less likely to be frustrate or to foster the marital relationship. See, e. g., Elkins, ante, p. 206, 234, and it hardly seems conducive to the preservation of the marital relation to place a wife in jeopardy solely by virtue of her husband's control over her testimony. Moreover, the contemporary justification that "reason and experience" no longer justify so sweeping a rule as that found acceptable by the Court in Hawkins. Accordingly, the existing rule, which is modified so as to permit an accused the privilege, is modified to include the witness's privilege. This modification is not limited to confidential communications; rather it permits the accused to exclude all adverse testimony. As Jeremy Bentham observed more than a century and a half ago, such privilege goes far beyond making "every man's house his castle," and permits a person to convert his house into a den of thieves. Similarly, the physician-patient privilege recognizes the human need to disclose to a spiritual counselor, in total and absolute confidence, what are believed to be flawed acts or thoughts and to receive priestly consolation and guidance in return. The lawyer-client privilege rests on the need for the advocate and counselor to know all that relates to the client's reasons for seeking representation if the professional mission is to be carried out, and also the physician must know all the a patient can articulate in order to identify and to treat disease; barriers to full disclosure would impair diagnosis and treatment. Finally, there is reason to believe that vesting the accused in the accused could actually undermine the marriage relationship, and that the Government is unlikely to offer a wife immunity and lenient treatment if it knows that her husband can prevent her from giving adverse testimony, but chooses not to abandon it. The Government's argument that the privilege can have the untoward effect of permitting one spouse to escape justice at the expense of the other, and its use in the absence of such an offer, hardly seems that the government is dissuaded from making such a offer, the privilege may have the effect of allowing one spouse's escape from justice at expense of one. The Hawkins rule is invoked, not to exclude private marital communications, but rather to exclude evidence of criminal acts and of communications made in the Presence of third persons. The long history of this privilege suggests that it ought not to be casually cast aside. During the 1982-1983 school year, respondents, while enrolled in the Journalism II course at Hazelwood East High School in Missouri, served as editors of Spectrum, the school newspaper. Prior to the May 13 issue of Spectrum being submitted to Principal Reynolds for approval, the Journalism II teacher for most of the school year, who had been present when the previous issue was prepared, had marked certain parts of the manuscripts as objectionable. When Reynolds saw the proofs of the May 13 issue, he ordered that the two pages containing the problematic articles be removed. Thereafter, respondents filed suit in Federal District Court, claiming that the removal of the articles violated their right to free speech under the First Amendment. The court disagreed, concluding that the articles were inappropriate and that the principal's decision to remove them was reasonable. The Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that since Spectrum was a public forum, the principal's censorship of the articles was invalid absent a showing of clear intent to create a public forum. Held: 1. Since the principal's decision to remove the articles was reasonable, no violation of the First Amendment occurred. Pp. 10-16. (a) Under the facts here, the evidence failed to show the "clear intent to create a public forum" required to establish a public forum. Here, school officials did not evince either "by policy or by practice," Perry Ed. Assn. v. Perkins Sch. Bd., 460 U. S. 47, 47, any intent to open the pages of Spectrum to "indiscriminate use" by its student reporters and editors, or by the student body generally. Rather, they reserved the forum for its intended purpose as a supervised learning experience for journalism students. This standard, rather than the rule announced in Tinker v. Wright, 393 U. S. 504, that a school can punish student expression that occurs on the school premises, governs this case. Pp. 10-14. (b) The First Amendment does not require a school to tolerate particular student speech. However, it does require a school to refrain from affirmatively promoting particular student speech unless doing so furthers the goals of the school program. Thus, educators are entitled to exercise greater control over student speech in school-sponsored expressive activities than they are over speech occurring on the school premises. So long as their actions are reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns, educators do not offend the First Amendment by exercising editorial control over the style and content of student speech in school-sponsored expressive activities. Pp. 14-16. 2. Given the particular circumstances of this case, the principal's decision to remove the articles was reasonable. Pp. 16-17. 795 F. 2d 1372, reversed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Westboro Baptist Church, affirming that their picketing at a soldier's funeral was protected by the First Amendment, despite the distress it caused the family. The church's signs, which included messages such as "God Hates the USA/Thank God for 9/11" and "Thank God for Dead Soldiers," were deemed to address matters of public concern and were displayed on public land in a peaceful, non-disruptive manner.

The Court distinguished between speech on matters of public concern, which receives high First Amendment protection, and speech on private matters, which does not. The Court found that the content, form, and context of Westboro's speech were related to issues of public interest, such as military policy and moral behavior, rather than being a personal attack on the deceased soldier or his family.

The Court also noted that the church complied with local laws and police instructions, picketing 1,000 feet away from the church where the funeral was held, and did not disrupt the service. The Court rejected the argument that the church's speech should be less protected because the funeral setting made the family a captive audience, stating that the picketing did not interfere with the funeral itself.

The Court's decision was narrow, emphasizing the specific facts of the case and the importance of protecting public debate, even when the speech is hurtful. The ruling set aside the jury verdict that had imposed tort liability on Westboro for intentional infliction of emotional distress, intrusion upon seclusion, and civil conspiracy. The judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, which had reversed the District Court's decision, was affirmed.

Title 8 U. S. C. §1324(a)(1) makes it a federal misdemeanor for an alien to enter or remain in the United States without authorization. Section 1324(b) establishes a civil enforcement scheme in which the Federal Government contracts with states to remove aliens who entered or remained in the Country illegally. After petitioner Arizona Governor signed Senate Bill 1070 into law, the Federal Government sued to block several of its provisions. Among others, §3 criminalized the knowing hiring of an unauthorized worker, §5(C) criminalized using false identification documents, and §6 gave state officers authority to arrest anyone they suspect is removable. Section 2(B) required state officers to make a “reasonable attempt … to determine the immigration status” of any person they stop, detain, or arrest on some other legitimate basis if “reasonable suspicion exists that the person is an alien and is unlawfully present in the United States.” The District Court enjoined §§3, 5(C), and 6, but allowed §2(B) to go forward. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the lower court’s ruling on §§3 and 5(C), but reversed on §6. Held: Sections 3, 5(C), and 6 are preempted. Pp. 4−15. (a) Section 3 is preempted because it seeks to accomplish the same goal as the federal scheme, i.e., to prevent unauthorized aliens from entering or remaining in the United States. That goal is accomplished by the federal scheme, and therefore cannot be pursued simultaneously by the States. See, e.g., Medellín v. Texas, 552 U. S. 491 ; New York v. Harris, 403 U. S. 672 . Pp. 4−6. (b) Section 5(C) is preempted because it conflicts with the federal scheme. The federal scheme regulates the employment of aliens, whereas §5(C) purports to regulate the employment of citizens and residents. Moreover, the federal scheme allows for the expulsion of aliens who have worked in the United States, whereas §5(C) does not permit expulsions. Such differences render §5(C) incompatible with the federal scheme. Pp. 6−8. (c) Section 6 is preempted because it conflicts with the federal scheme and because it is an obstacle to the full purposes and objectives of the federal scheme. The federal scheme puts in place a system in which state officers may not make warrantless arrests of aliens based on possible removability except in specific, limited circumstances. By nonetheless authorizing state and local officers to engage in these enforcement activities as a general matter, §6 creates an obstacle to the full purposes and objectives of the federal scheme. Pp. 8−12. (d) Section 2(B) is not preempted. While the provision could be read to avoid the concerns raised by the State’s opponents, the nature and timing of this case counsel caution in evaluating the validity of §2(B). Without the benefit of a definitive interpretation from the state courts, it would be inappropriate to assume that §2(B) will be construed in a way that creates a conflict with federal law. Pp. 12−15. 677 F. 3d 1134, affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Kagan, J., took no part in the consideration or decision of the case.
