The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit granted certiorari in the case of a North Carolina man convicted of the rape of his grandmother, Hattie Leath, a 66-year-old Negro widow. The court denied his motion to suppress evidence that was introduced in evidence at his trial. The jury found him guilty, but recommended a sentence of life imprisonment. The trial court imposed that sentence, and the Supreme Court of North Carolina affirmed the judgment. The petitioner argues that his constitutional right to an impartial jury was violated in this capital case when the prosecution was permitted to challenge for cause all prospective jurors who stated that they were opposed to capital punishment or had conscientious scruples against imposing the death penalty. He also contends that the .22-caliber rifle that was used in the commission of the crime was obtained by the State in a search and seizure violative of the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Supreme Court ruled that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in denying the motion. The Court also denied the petition for a new trial on the basis that the jury was not impartial. The 4th Justices conclude that the case should be remanded for further consideration. The case will be decided by Justices

The Supreme Court addressed whether AT&T violated the Pregnancy Discrimination Act (PDA) by paying pension benefits calculated under a rule that, prior to the PDA, gave less retirement credit for pregnancy leave than for other medical leave. The Court held that there was no violation, as the benefit calculation rule was part of a bona fide seniority system under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which protects it from challenge.

AT&T's pension and benefits system, dating back to 1914, was based on an employee's term of employment, with adjustments for leave time. Before the PDA, pregnancy leave was considered personal leave and credited less than disability leave. In 1977, AT&T changed this practice, but only partially, and did not retroactively adjust service credits for women affected by the previous policy. After the PDA was enacted in 1978, AT&T fully aligned its policy with the Act, but still did not retroactively adjust past credits.

Several female employees and the Communications Workers of America filed discrimination charges with the EEOC, which led to a lawsuit. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals found that AT&T's calculation of service credit excluding time spent on pregnancy leave violated Title VII. However, the Supreme Court reversed this decision, emphasizing the special treatment of seniority systems under Title VII and the stability they provide.

The Court reasoned that AT&T's pre-PDA differential treatment of pregnancy leave was lawful at the time, as established by the Court's decision in General Electric Co. v. Gilbert, and that the PDA did not retroactively apply to recharacterize past acts as illegal. The Court also rejected the argument that the recent amendment to Title VII, in response to Ledbetter v. Goodyear, affected the case, as AT&T's decision not to award service credit for pre-PDA pregnancy leave was not discriminatory at the time.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court found that AT&T's seniority system was bona fide and that the pension calculations based on past rules, which were legal at the time, did not constitute a current violation of Title VII. The decision underscores the importance of stability and predictability in seniority systems and the protection of such systems under Title VII, provided they are not based on an intention to discriminate.

The Tort Claims Act allows individuals to bring tort claims against the United States for injuries sustained as a result of the negligent acts of government employees acting within the scope of their employment. The Act requires that the individual file a notice of claim within two years of the incident and that the claim be accompanied by a deposit. Once the notice of claim is filed, the individual can pursue the claim in court.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Wyoming granted summary judgment in favor of the Bureau of Land Management, finding that the agency's officials had not violated the law when they demanded an easement from the owner of a commercial guest resort in Hot Springs County, Wyoming. The court held that the Bureau's actions were not sufficient to constitute a violation of the law, and that Frank Robbins's complaint against the Bureau and its officials for harassment and intimidation should be dismissed. The Court held that Robbins had not shown that the defendants' actions caused him to lose his right-of-way over the South Fork Owl Creek Road, which runs through his property and serves as a main route to the upper Rock Creek area. The complaint alleges that in response to persistent requests by environmentalists and outdoor enthusiasts, the Bureau tried to induce the ranch's previous owner, George Nelson, to grant an easement for public use over the road. Nelson signed a nonexclusive deed of easement giving the United States the right to use and maintain the road along a stretch of his property. According to the complaint, in the summer of 1994, after the Bureau’s inaction had cost it the easement, one of its employees, Joseph Vessels, telephoned Robbins and demanded the easement to replace Nelson’s. Robbins refused but indicated he would consider granting it in return for something. In a later meeting, Vessels allegedly told Robbins that ‘the Federal Government does not negotiate.’  Robbins did not file a trespass complaint in response.  The complaint also alleges that Robbins was harassed and intimidated by other Bureau employees, including Edward Parodi, who was told by his superiors to ‘investigate harder’ for possible trespasses and other permit violations by Robbins. Parodi also heard colleagues make disparaging remarks about Robbins, such as, 'the rich SOB from Alabama [who] got [the Ranch]'

1. A State violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment whenever it makes the affluence of the voter or payment of any fee an electoral standard. Pp. 566-567. 2. The right to vote in state elections is implicit, particularly by reason of the First Amendment and that it may not constitutionally be conditioned upon the payment of a tax or fee. P. 567. 3. In the context of obtaining a ballot, the requirement of fee paying causes an invidious discrimination (Skinner v. State of Oklahoma, 316 U. S. 535, 514, 62 S.Ct. 1110, 1113, 86 L. Ed. 2d 675). P. 540. 4. The Equal Protection of the Clause does not deprive a State of the right to dilute a citizen's vote on account of his economic status or other such factors by analogy, since the right of suffrage "is subject to the imposition of state standards which are not discriminatory and which do not contravene any restriction that Congress, acting pursuant to its constitutional powers, has imposed." Lassiter v. Northampton County Board of Elections, 360 U.S. 45, 51, 79 S. C. 990, reversed.

The Supreme Court reviewed a case involving Section 22-a of the New York Code of Criminal Procedure, which allows municipal authorities to seek an injunction and the destruction of obscene materials. The appellants were accused of selling obscene booklets titled "Nights of Horror" and did not challenge the statute's construction or the finding of obscenity but questioned the constitutionality of the statute's remedial scheme.

The Court held that New York has the constitutional authority to use the injunctive remedy provided by Section 22-a to address the sale of obscene materials. The Court reasoned that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment does not restrict a state to criminal prosecution alone in combating the dissemination of pornography. The Court found that the procedure under Section 22-a does not constitute an unconstitutional prior restraint on freedom of speech or press, as it provides for a prompt and fair trial to determine obscenity and does not restrain materials not yet found to be obscene.

The Court distinguished this case from Near v. Minnesota, which involved prior restraint on future publications based on past offenses, noting that Section 22-a only applies to materials already published and adjudged to be obscene. The Court affirmed the judgment of the New York Court of Appeals, upholding the constitutionality of Section 22-a and its application in this case.

After petitioner Ulysses Tory (with the help of petitioner Ruth Craft and others) had engaged in unlawful defamatory activity, the California Superior Court issued a permanent injunction prohibiting Tory, Craft, and their "agents" or "representatives" from "picketing," from "displaying signs, placards or other written or printed material," and from "orally uttering statements" about Johnnie Cochran, Jr., and about Cochran's law firm in "any public forum." The court concluded that Tory's claim that Cochran owed him money was without foundation, that Tory engaged in a continuous pattern of libelous and slanderous activity, and that Tory had used false and defamed speech to "coerce" Cochran into paying "amounts of money to which Tory was not entitled" as a "tribute" or a "premium" for "desisting" from this libelous activity. The State Court of Appeal affirmed. The California Court of Appeals affirmed. After oral argument, Cochran informed the Court of his recent death and suggested that we dismiss the case as moot. The Court denied that the case was moot. Held: 1. The case is not moot. Pp. 566-567. (a) Petitioners' basic claims, namely, (1) that the First Amendment forbids the issuance of a permanent injunctive injunction in a defamation case, at least when the plaintiff is a public figure, and (2) that, as written, the injunction (considered prior to Cochran’s death) was not properly tailored and consequently violated the First. P. 567. 2. Petitioners’ basic claims are much diminished, if they have not disappeared altogether, since picketing Cochran and his law offices while engaging in injunction-forbidden speech could no longer achieve the objectives that the trial court had in mind (i. e., coercing Cochran to pay a “tribute” for desisting in this activity), the grounds for the injunction are much reduced, if their have disappeared altogether. Moreover, the court has now lost its underlying rationale, which now amounts to an overly broad prior restraint upon speech, lacking plausible justification. See Carroll v. President and Comm'rs of Princess Anne, 393 U. S. 175, 183-184 (an "order" issued in "the area of First Amendment rights" must be "precis[e]" and narrowly "tailored" to achieve the "pin-pointed objective" of the "needs of the case"); Pittsburgh Press Co. v. Pittsburgh Comm'n on Human Relations, 413 U.S. 376, 390 (a prior restraint should not "swee[p]" any "more broadly than necessary"). As such, the Constitution forbids it. Thus, petitioner Cochran died, and the injunction, as a result of picketing and his activity, has now become overly broad. Petitioner Cochran was not a party to this case, but his widow has an interest in enforcing the injunction. The courts can resolve the matter and, given the new state of affairs, might very well adjudge the case moot or the injunction invalid on state-law grounds rather than the constitutional grounds the Court rushes to embrace. The more prudent course is to dismiss the writ as improvidently granted.

The Supreme Court had to decide if the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause prevented the government from allowing timber harvesting or road construction through a part of the Six Rivers National Forest in California, which is used for religious purposes by three American Indian tribes. The Court concluded that the Free Exercise Clause does not prohibit these actions.

The case involved a plan to complete a road (the G-O road) through the forest, which is sacred to the Yurok, Karok, and Tolowa Indians. Despite a study recommending against the road due to its potential damage to religious practices, the Forest Service decided to proceed, selecting a route that avoided archaeological sites and minimized impact on spiritual activities. The Forest Service also planned timber harvesting with protective zones around religious sites.

Respondents, including Indian organizations, nature groups, and the State of California, challenged the decisions, claiming violations of the Free Exercise Clause and other federal laws. The District Court issued an injunction against the road and timber plan, citing violations of the Free Exercise Clause and other statutes. The Ninth Circuit affirmed in part but was divided on the constitutional issue.

The Supreme Court noted that the lower courts did not clearly articulate the necessity for their constitutional holdings. The Court emphasized that courts should avoid constitutional questions if statutory claims provide sufficient relief. However, the Court decided to address the constitutional issue due to the likelihood that it was necessary for the lower courts' decisions and to avoid unnecessary judicial procedures.

The Court disagreed with the respondents' contention that the government's actions violated the Free Exercise Clause unless a compelling interest was demonstrated. The Court referenced Bowen v. Roy, which held that the Free Exercise Clause does not require the government to conduct its affairs according to individual religious beliefs. The Court stated that the government's actions in this case did not coerce individuals into violating their religious beliefs or penalize religious activity.

The Court rejected attempts to distinguish this case from Roy and other precedents, stating that the government's incidental effects on religious practices do not require a compelling justification. The Court also noted that the government had taken steps to minimize the impact on religious practices and that the American Indian Religious Freedom Act (AIRFA) did not create enforceable individual rights or a cause of action.

The Court reversed the lower court's decision that the First Amendment precluded the government's actions and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. Justice Kennedy did not participate in the decision.

Implications of the Decision:
The Supreme Court's decision clarifies that the Free Exercise Clause does not prevent the government from using public lands for purposes like road construction or timber harvesting, even if these actions have adverse effects on religious practices. The decision emphasizes the government's ability to manage its own affairs without being compelled to comply with individual religious beliefs, while also acknowledging the importance of government sensitivity to religious practices. The ruling also indicates that AIRFA does not provide a legal basis for challenging government land use decisions on religious grounds.

The Supreme Court dismissed an appeal regarding the constitutionality of a Texas statute on disturbing the peace because the lower court had not issued a specific injunctive order. The case originated when individuals protesting the Vietnam War were arrested under the Texas statute, but the charges were later dismissed as the incident occurred on a military base outside of state jurisdiction. The protesters sought federal relief, claiming the statute was unconstitutional. The three-judge District Court agreed with the protesters in principle but did not issue a clear injunction, instead suggesting the Texas legislature could revise the law.

The Supreme Court emphasized that its jurisdiction under the Three-Judge Court Act is narrow and that it can only review cases where a district court has issued a clear injunction or order denying one. Since the District Court's opinion was not followed by a specific injunctive order, the Supreme Court found it had no jurisdiction to hear the appeal. The Court highlighted the importance of clear and specific injunctions to prevent confusion and ensure that those affected understand the court's requirements. The absence of such an order meant that state officials were left uncertain about how to comply and unable to appeal the decision. The appeal was dismissed, and the Court noted the situation should serve as guidance for future cases involving the constitutionality of state laws.

After a child born in North Carolina was killed in a bus accident in another country, her parents sued petitioners—subsidiaries of a multistate corporation—in a North Carolina state court, alleging that the death resulted from a defectively designed tire. The court dismissed the complaint, holding that it lacked personal jurisdiction over petitioners because they were incorporated in Delaware and Luxembourg and had no place of business in North Carolina. The State Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the court properly exercised general jurisdiction over petitioners under International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310, because they had done business in North Carolina. It rejected petitioners’ argument that the court should have applied the more stringent standard governing specific jurisdiction, i.e., that the court must find that petitioners had “minimum contacts” with North Carolina. The court thought that petitioners satisfied the less demanding test because they had placed their tires in the “stream of commerce” flowing into North Carolina. Held: The North Carolina Court of Appeals erred in applying the general jurisdiction standard to determine whether the State could assert jurisdiction over petitioners. Pp. 4–11. (a) The Due Process Clause prohibits a State from exercising personal jurisdiction unless the defendant has “minimum contacts” with the State. International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310. The Clause allows a State to assert jurisdiction over a defendant who has “continuous and systematic” contacts with the State. Helicopteros, LLC v. Hallanmon, Inc., 466 U.S. 408. Here, the court mistakenly chose the latter standard. Pp. 4–5. (b) The court’s error can be traced back to its failure to distinguish between the case-specific and all-purpose (general) jurisdiction tests. While ties linking a defendant to a forum may bolster an affiliation germane to specific jurisdiction, see, e.g., World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson, 444 U.S. 218, 297, they do not warrant a determination that, based on those ties, the forum has general jurisdiction over a defendant. See, e.g., Stabilisierungsfonds Für Wein v. Kaiser Stuh Wine Distributors Pty. Ltd., 647 F. 2d 200, 203, n. 5. The court’s conclusion that petitioners were amenable to suit in North Carolina rested on the flawed premise that mere sales of their tires sporadically made in North Carolina through intermediaries constituted the requisite “continuous and systematic general business contacts.” Helicopteros, 466 U.S., at 416. Pp. 5–8. (c) Nor is there merit to respondents’ single enterprise theory, which would treat petitioners as part of a larger entity with sufficient ties to North Carolina to confer general jurisdiction upon them. Pp. 8–9. 199 N.C.App. 57, 681 S.E. 2d 388, reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C.J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

After being convicted of murder and sentenced to death, respondent Landrigan moved for postconviction relief, claiming that his counsel’s failure to investigate and present mitigating evidence violated his rights under Strickland v. Washington, 466 U.S. 668. The Arizona trial judge who had sentenced Landrigan presided on postconviction review and ruled that Landrigan had waived his right to present mitigating evidence. The Arizona Superior Court agreed, and the State Supreme Court affirmed. While Landrigan’s postconviction petition was pending, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) became effective, requiring federal courts to apply a deferential standard in determining whether to grant habeas relief. See, e.g., Woodford v. Garceau, 538 U. S. 202. Nonetheless, the Federal District Court ultimately denied Landrigan’s habeas petition, ruling that he could not meet the heightened burden of demonstrating prejudice under Strickland. The Ninth Circuit disagreed, believing that Landrigan might be entitled to federal habeas relief and that the District Court had abused its discretion in denying him an evidentiary hearing. Held: The District Court did not abuse its discretion in denying Landrigan an evidentiary hearing. Pp. 4−12. (a) Where the facts of a case can be resolved by reference to the state court record, an evidentiary hearing is not required. Such a principle accords with AEDPA’s purpose of reducing delays in the resolution of capital cases. Several reasons support the District Court’s determination that Landrigan could not overcome §224(d)(2)’s bar to granting federal habeas relief. First, the Arizona postconviction court reasonably determined that Landrigan had instructed his attorney not to bring any mitigation to the attention of the sentencing court. Second, even if Landrigan did not want any mitigating evidence presented, the Arizona courts’ determination that his claims were frivolous and meritless was not an unreasonable application of United States Supreme Court precedent. Nor was it objectively unreasonable for the Arizona court to conclude that a defendant who refused to allow the presentation of any mitigating evidence could not establish Strickland prejudice based on his counsel’s failure to investigate further possible mitigating evidence. Third, even assuming that an “informed and knowing” requirement existed in this case, Landrigan could not benefit from it, since he never presented this claim to the Arizona courts, failed to develop it properly before those courts, and appeared to understand the consequences of his actions. Fourth, the poor quality of Landrigan’s alleged mitigating evidence prevented him from establishing prejudice. All but the last sentence of his proposed mitigation evidence refers to information that his birth mother and ex-wife could have offered if Landrigan had allowed them to testify. Fifth, the Arizona postconviction court was well acquainted with Landrigan’s extremely violent past and saw firsthand his belligerent behavior. Pp. 4−9. (b) Assuming the truth of all the facts Landrigan sought to prove at the evidentiary hearing, he still could not be granted federal habeas relief because the state courts’ factual determination that he would not have allowed counsel to present any mitigating evidence at sentencing is not an unreasonable determination of the facts under §224(d)(2) and the mitigating evidence he seeks to introduce would not change the result. In such circumstances, a District Court has discretion to decline to grant an evidentiary hearing. Pp. 9−12. 441 F.3d 639, reversed and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

Title I of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 authorizes the Secretary of Education to distribute financial assistance to local educational institutions to meet the needs of educationally deprived children from low-income families. The proposed programs must meet the following statutory requirements: the children involved in the program must be educationalally deprived, § 3804(a), the children must reside in areas comprising a high concentration of low- income families, and the programs must supplement, not supplant, programs that would exist absent funding under Title I. With respect to the religious atmosphere of the parochial schools, the Court of Appeals held that "the picture that emerges is of a system in which religious considerations play a key role in the selection of students and teachers, and which has as its substantial purpose the inculcation of religious values." Held: The Establishment Clause of the First Amendment does not properly lie. Pp. 488-481. (a) In School District of Grand Rapids v. Ball, 473 U. S. 373, the court has held unconstitutional under the Establishment Clause two remedial and enhancement programs operated by the Grand Rapids Public School District, in which classes were provided to private school children at public expense in classrooms located in and leased from the local private schools. At best, the supervision in this case would assist in preventing the Title I program from being used, intentionally or unwittingly, to inculcate the religious beliefs of the surrounding school. But the supervisory system established by the City of New York inevitably results in the excessive entanglement of church and state, an Establishment Clause concern distinct from that addressed by the effects doctrine. Even where state aid to parochials does not have the primary effect of advancing religion, the provision of such aid may nonetheless violate the Establishment Establishment Clause owing to the nature of the interaction of church-and-state in the administration of that aid. The principle that the state should not become too closely entangled with the church in the aid of assistance is rooted in two concerns. When the state becomes enmeshed with a given denomination in matters of religious significance, the freedom of religious belief of those who are not adherents of that denomination suffers, even when the governmental purpose underlying the involvement is largely secular. Moreover, there is limited freedom of religion of the adherents of the denomination limited by the governmental intrusion into sacred matters. P. 489. 739 F. 2d 48, affirmed.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the University of Michigan Law School's admissions policy, which considers race as one of many factors in its efforts to achieve a diverse student body. The policy aims to admit students who can contribute to the learning of their peers and enrich the educational experience through a variety of backgrounds and perspectives. The Law School seeks to enroll a "critical mass" of underrepresented minority students to ensure they do not feel isolated and can make unique contributions to the character of the Law School.

Barbara Grutter, a white Michigan resident, applied to the Law School and was rejected despite having a 3.8 GPA and 161 LSAT score. She filed a lawsuit alleging that the Law School discriminated against her based on race, violating the Fourteenth Amendment, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and 42 U.S.C. § 1981. Grutter claimed that the Law School used race as a predominant factor, giving certain minority groups a significantly greater chance of admission than students from disfavored racial groups.

The District Court found the Law School's use of race in admissions decisions to be unlawful, but the Court of Appeals reversed this judgment. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve whether diversity is a compelling interest that can justify the narrowly tailored use of race in selecting applicants for admission to public universities.

The Supreme Court held that the Law School's interest in obtaining the educational benefits that flow from a diverse student body is a compelling state interest. The Court deferred to the Law School's judgment that diversity is essential to its educational mission, and that the policy of considering race as a "plus" factor in a flexible, individualized review of applicants is narrowly tailored to achieve this interest. The Court emphasized that the policy does not operate as a quota system and that race is not the defining feature of the application process.

The Court also noted that the Law School's race-conscious admissions program must be limited in time and subject to periodic reviews to determine if racial preferences are still necessary. The Court expected that in 25 years, the use of racial preferences would no longer be necessary to further the interest approved.

The decision concluded that the Law School's admissions policy is lawful under the Equal Protection Clause, and therefore, Grutter's statutory claims also fail. The judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit was affirmed.

Dissenting opinions argued that the Law School's policy was not narrowly tailored, amounted to racial balancing, and failed to meet the strict scrutiny standard required for racial classifications. Dissenters also criticized the majority for deferring to the Law School's judgment and for suggesting that racial discrimination in admissions would be acceptable for another 25 years.

In the case before the Supreme Court, a mother, on behalf of her daughter (referred to as S.G.), sued two government officials for conducting an interview with S.G. at her school without a warrant, parental consent, or exigent circumstances, alleging a violation of the Fourth Amendment. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the interview was unconstitutional but granted the officials qualified immunity, protecting them from monetary damages since the law was not clearly established at the time of the interview.

The officials sought Supreme Court review of the Ninth Circuit's constitutional ruling, despite having won on the immunity issue. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to address two questions: whether government officials can seek Supreme Court review when they have won on immunity grounds but lost on the constitutional question, and whether the Ninth Circuit was correct in its Fourth Amendment determination.

The Supreme Court concluded that it generally has the authority to review lower court constitutional rulings at the request of government officials granted immunity. However, the Court did not decide the Fourth Amendment question in this case because it became moot; S.G. had grown up and moved out of state, meaning she would no longer be subject to the interviewing practices in question.

The Court vacated the part of the Ninth Circuit's opinion that decided the Fourth Amendment issue, following the practice of vacating rulings that become moot to prevent them from having legal consequences. The Court emphasized that this decision was specific to the unique circumstances of the case and did not signal a change in the general practice for handling moot cases.

The implications of the decision are that while government officials can seek Supreme Court review of constitutional rulings even if they have won on immunity grounds, each case will be considered individually based on the Court's usual standards for granting certiorari. Additionally, the decision clarifies that mootness can prevent the Supreme Court from reviewing certain issues, leading to the vacating of lower court decisions that have become moot.

Respondent District 2, Marine Engineers Beneficial Association (MEBA), represented the licensed marine engineers in respondent District 2's fleet under a collective bargaining agreement terminating on July 15, 1962. The complaint and affidavits alleged that MEBA was picketing Hanna's vessels at the docks of the Great Northern Railway Company at Superior in the same manner as the 1962 picketing and with the same improper aim of forcing its representation on unwilling engineers; Hanna stated that workers of other employers were refusing to render service to the vessels and the docks where they berthed and against any other attempt of MEBA to impose representation on Hanna engineers. The Circuit Court dismissed the suit in July for lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter. In April 1964 the Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed the decision. Held: 1. The Act does not preempt the State's authority to quench the picketing said to have occurred in this case. Pp. 488-481. (a) In concluding that the Act is not preempted by § 8 (b) (4) (B) of the National Labor Relations Act, it does not retreat from Garmon. Rather, the terms and policies of that decision justify its extension to the present facts, an extension producing untoward results noted by the Wisconsin State Supreme Court itself. P. 489. 2. Neither the terms nor the policies of the decision justify the extension to present facts. Nor is there a case in which the presence of arguably prohibited activity may permit the Board to afford complete protection to the legitimate interests advanced by the State. Moreover, since Hanna as the primary employer is present at the picketed situs, the primary picketing proviso of § 8(b)(4)(B) severely inhibits the Board's use of that section to reach the volatile core of the conduct, the impact on secondary employers that follows from the mere presence of the pickets at a common situs. Thus, so far as the opportunity belongs to the Board wherever it and the State offer duplicate relief, it has limited application to this case's facts. Id. 23 Wis. 2d 433, reversed and remanded.

In 1887, Congress made it a federal offense "for any individual knowingly to possess a firearm at a place that the individual knows, or has reasonable cause to believe, is a school zone." 18 U. S. C. § 922(q)(1)(A) (1988 ed., Supp. V). The Act neither regulates a commercial activity nor contains a requirement that the possession be connected in any way to interstate commerce. Respondent, who was then a 12th-grade student, arrived at Edison High School in San Antonio, Texas, carrying a concealed .38 caliber handgun and five bullets. Acting upon an anonymous tip, school authorities confronted respondent, who admitted that he was carrying the weapon. He was arrested and charged under Texas law with firearm possession on school premises. The next day, the state charges were dismissed after federal agents charged respondent by complaint with violating the Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990. The District Court denied respondent's motion to dismiss his federal indictment on the ground that the Act exceeded Congress' power to legislate under the Commerce Clause. The Court of Appeals agreed and reversed, holding that, in light of what it characterized as insufficient congressional findings and legislative history, § 9 22(q), in the full reach of its terms, is invalid as beyond the power of Congress under the commerce clause. Held: The Act exceeds Congress' authority to regulate intrastate economic activity. Pp. 5-7. (a) The Act does not regulate interstate commerce, nor is it an attempt to prohibit interstate transportation of a commodity through the channels of commerce; nor can it be justified as a regulation by which Congress has sought to protect an instrumentality of interstate commerce or a thing in interstate commerce; but Congress has the power to regulate, without more, the "mere possession" of firearms. P. 5. (b) Where economic activity substantially affects interstate commerce and thus are beyond the powers of Congress, legislation regulating that activity will be sustained. Jones & Laughlin Steel, ante, at 150, and Wickard v. Filburn, 317 U.S. 111, distinguished. The Commerce Clause is not limited to those powers enumerated in the Constitution, and so long as those enumerated powers are interpreted as having judicially enforceable outer limits, congressional legislation under that Clause always will engender "legal uncertainty." P. 6. 2 F. 3d 1342, affirmed.

After petitioner was injured in an automobile accident, a doctor drew a small amount of blood from his arm and sent it to a laboratory for chemical analysis. The result showed a high percentage of alcohol in the blood, and petitioner was charged with driving an automobile while under the influence of intoxicating liquor. At his trial in a municipal court, the chemical analysis was admitted in evidence over his objections based on his privilege against self-incrimination, his right to counsel, and his right to be free of unreasonable searches and seizures. He was convicted and fined. Held: 1. Denial of petitioner's motion to suppress the introduction of the chemical analysis in evidence did not violate his privilege against self-incrimination. Pp. 38-44. (a) This decision follows the ruling in Breithaupt v. Abram, 352 U. S. 436. Pp. 38-40. (b) The privilege against self-incrimination is not available to prevent compelled submissions for physical evidence. Pp. 40-44. 2. Petitioner's right to counsel was not violated by compelling him to submit to the chemical analysis in spite of his having received legal advice that he could assert his privilege against self-incrimination. Pp. 44-45. 3. The chemical analysis was properly admitted in evidence, since it was not the product of an illegal search and seizure in violation of the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 45-50. (a) Assuming that the privilege against self-incrimination has been found not to bar compelled intrusions into the body for blood to be analyzed for alcohol, the Fourth Amendment's proper function is to constrain, not against all intrusions as such, but against intrusions which are not justified in the circumstances, or which are made in an improper manner. Pp. 45-46. (b) Under the facts of this case, the attempt to secure evidence of blood-alcohol content was an appropriate incident to petitioner's arrest. Pp. 46-48. (c) The test chosen to measure petitioner's blood-alcohol level was a reasonable one. P. 48. (d) The record shows that the test was performed in a reasonable manner. P. 49. Affirmed.

In Bruton v. United States (1966), the Supreme Court established a narrow exception to the general rule that a defendant is entitled to confront witnesses against him. Under this exception, a defendant is deprived of his constitutional right to confrontation when the facially incriminating confession of a non-testifying codefendant is introduced at their joint trial, regardless of whether the jury is instructed to consider the confession only against the codefendant. However, the Court clarified that this exception applies only when the codefendant's confession expressly implicates the defendant as an accomplice.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Washington today entered a final judgment against Joe Shapiro, an undercover agent for the Federal Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs, for his role in an illegal drug manufacturing enterprise.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Seattle on December 7, 1969, Shapiro was charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The complaint alleges that Shapiro provided an essential ingredient for the manufacture of methamphetamine in return for one-half of the drug produced.  As alleged in the complaint, Shapiro's involvement in the illicit manufacture of meth was so high that he was unable to obtain the drug.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Shapiro.  To learn more about entrapment, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-8221.

On June 28, 1971, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York entered a final judgment against a convicted felon who was later sentenced to prison for his role in an illicit liquor ring.  The court's order, which was entered on March 23, 2016, permanently enjoins the defendant from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 5b-5 thereunder, and orders him to produce a copy of the warrant.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York today announced criminal charges against the felon.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, on August 20, 1957, a federal agent with the Bureau of Investigation located an illicit stash of illicit whiskey in an abandoned house under Harris' control. The agent allegedly purchased the illicit whiskey from the house under his control and used the illicit liquor to make purchases of other illicit liquor. The complaint alleges that the informant had previously been arrested for a similar felony and was later charged with possession of a controlled substance.  As alleged in the complaint, the FBI obtained a search warrant based on the tip provided by the FBI. The FBI obtained the warrant on the basis of the tip, which the court found insufficient to establish probable cause. The court also issued a temporary restraining order, freezing the informant's assets, and ordering him to surrender his passport.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the court's judgment, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations of Sections 5(a) and 5(c) of the federal securities laws, and from participating in any future search or prosecution of any kind. The judgment also orders the defendant to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by James R. Spinelli and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson. The litigation will be led by Roosevelt H. Starr.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Texas has ruled that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act of 2000 (FIFRA) does not pre-empt a state law suit brought by 29 Texas peanut farmers against Dow Chemical Co. for using a weed killer in their fields. The farmers allege that in the 2000 growing season their crops were severely damaged by the application of Dow's newly marketed pesticide named "Strongarm" on their farms. According to the farmers, Dow knew, or should have known, that Strongarm would stunt the growth of peanuts in soils with pH levels of 7.0 or greater. The court held that because petitioners' fraud, warranty, and deceptive trade practices claims focused on oral statements made by Dow and its agents that did not differ from statements made on the product's label, success on those claims would give Dow a "strong incentive" to change its label. The Supreme Court of the United States, however, ruled in favor of Dow, holding that the federal law does not preempt state law claims. The high court's decision is consistent with the decisions of other courts, including that of the Federal District Court for the Western District of California, which found that the state law claim was not viable. The case is now before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals.

The Supreme Court addressed whether a federal court could block a congressional subpoena requesting bank records from an organization claiming First Amendment protection. The organization, United States Servicemen's Fund (USSF), argued that the subpoena was an unconstitutional abuse of legislative power aimed at exposing private beliefs and associations, thus infringing on First Amendment rights.

The Senate Subcommittee on Internal Security had issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into subversive activities, including potential foreign influence on organizations like USSF. The USSF claimed that revealing its financial supporters would harm its ability to operate and that the subpoena was intended to harass and deter its activities.

The District Court initially ruled against the USSF, stating that the legislative interest in the investigation outweighed the USSF's First Amendment claims. However, the Court of Appeals reversed this decision, holding that the subpoena would violate the USSF's First Amendment rights and that the courts could intervene since the subpoena targeted a third party (the bank) and not the USSF directly.

The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, emphasizing the protection afforded to congressional activities by the Speech or Debate Clause of the Constitution. The Court held that the issuance of the subpoena fell within the legitimate legislative sphere and that the Members of Congress and their aides were immune from judicial interference in this context.

The Court reasoned that the power to investigate through subpoenas is an essential part of the legislative process and that the motives behind the subpoena are not subject to judicial scrutiny. The Court also rejected the argument that the subpoena's purpose was to infringe on First Amendment rights, stating that the Speech or Debate Clause provides absolute protection for legislative acts within the legitimate legislative sphere.

The Supreme Court's decision underscores the broad protection granted to congressional activities under the Speech or Debate Clause and reaffirms the independence of the legislative process from judicial intervention. The case was remanded to the Court of Appeals with instructions to direct the District Court to dismiss the complaint against the Senate Subcommittee. Issues related to similar subpoenas issued by the House were remanded for further consideration in light of the opinion.

1. The "practice of pharmacy" is statutorily declared to be "a professional practice affecting the public health, safety and welfare," and to be subject to regulation and control in the public interest. The statute provides that a pharmacist licensed in Virginia is guilty of unprofessional conduct if he " publishes, advertises or promotes, directly or indirectly, in any manner whatsoever, any amountprice, fee, premium, discount, rebate or credit terms . . . for any drugs which may be dispensed only by prescription." Held: 1. Commercial speech, like other varieties of commercial speech, is protected by the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 531-532. 2. The advertising of prescription drug prices is not protected because it is "commercial speech." P. 532. 3. The State's protectiveness of its citizens rests in large measure on the advantages of their being kept in ignorance, and the free flow of commercial information is indispensable. P. 529. 373 F. Supp. 683, affirmed.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding the attorney-client privilege posthumously in a case involving handwritten notes taken by an attorney during a meeting with his client, who later committed suicide. The government sought these notes for a criminal investigation, but the Supreme Court held that the privilege protects confidential communications even after the client's death.

The Court of Appeals had suggested a balancing test to determine if the privilege should apply posthumously, particularly in criminal cases, but the Supreme Court rejected this approach. The Court emphasized the importance of the attorney-client privilege in promoting full and frank communication between attorneys and their clients, which serves the broader public interest in the observance of law and administration of justice.

The Court acknowledged that while there are exceptions to the privilege, such as the testamentary exception (which allows disclosure in disputes among a deceased client's heirs), these exceptions are consistent with the privilege's purposes and do not support the creation of a new posthumous exception in criminal cases.

The Supreme Court concluded that the Independent Counsel had not provided sufficient reason to depart from the long-standing common law rule that the attorney-client privilege survives the death of the client. The Court's decision reinforces the confidentiality of attorney-client communications, ensuring that clients can seek legal advice without fear that their communications may be disclosed after their death, even in the context of criminal investigations.

This document contains information regarding a legal case involving the constitutionality of section 954(d)(1) of the National Endowment for the Arts Act. The case involves a lawsuit brought by five artists who claimed that the section was being improperly interpreted and applied by the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) to deny them funding for their proposed projects. The court discusses the history of the section and the goals of the NEA, as well as the legal precedents related to the First and Fifth Amendments. The court concludes that the section is not facially unconstitutional and that the NEA's implementation of the section is not arbitrary or capricious.

The Supreme Court of the United States reversed the decision of the Supreme Court of California, which had asserted jurisdiction over Asahi Metal Industry Co., Ltd. (Asahi), a Japanese corporation, in a product liability indemnification action. The case involved a motorcycle accident in California, where a tire manufactured by Cheng Shin Rubber Industrial Co., Ltd. (Cheng Shin), a Taiwanese company, and containing a valve assembly made by Asahi, allegedly failed. After settling the initial lawsuit, Cheng Shin sought indemnification from Asahi.

The central legal question was whether Asahi's act of placing its product into the "stream of commerce" with the knowledge that it could end up in California constituted sufficient "minimum contacts" with the state to allow California to exercise jurisdiction without violating the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Supreme Court held that merely being aware that a product could end up in a particular state through the stream of commerce does not establish "minimum contacts." The Court emphasized that there must be an action by the defendant purposefully directed toward the forum state. Asahi had no direct business activities in California, such as offices, agents, advertising, or a direct distribution system. Therefore, the Court found that Asahi did not purposefully avail itself of the California market.

Furthermore, the Court considered the international context and the burden on Asahi, a foreign defendant, to defend itself in a California court. The Court also noted that the interests of the plaintiff (Cheng Shin) and the forum state (California) were minimal, as the indemnification claim was based on a transaction that took place in Taiwan, and the dispute was primarily about indemnification rather than California's safety standards.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court determined that asserting jurisdiction over Asahi in California would be unreasonable and unfair, and it reversed the judgment of the Supreme Court of California, remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

After respondents' applications for permits to hold rallies advocating the legalization of marijuana were denied by petitioner City of Chicago Department of Streets and Sanitation (Department), they brought suit in Federal District Court, claiming, among other things, that the Department's ordinance is unconstitutional on its face. The District Court granted summary judgment in the Departments favor, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed. Held: Because the ordinance is not subject to the procedural requirements set forth in Freedmanv . Maryland, 380 U. S. 51, it does not need to include a provision specifying a deadline for judicial review of a challenge to a permit denial. Nor is the ordinance deficient because it sets forth general grounds for denying a permit, rather than grounds on which the Department must deny a permit. Rather, the ordinance's permissive nature furthers, rather than constricts, free speech. Certiorarigranted; 227 F. 3d 921, affirmed.

The Supreme Court considered whether the California Department of Corrections' (CDC) unwritten policy of racially segregating prisoners in reception centers for up to 60 days should be subject to strict scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The CDC justified the policy as necessary to prevent violence caused by racial gangs within the prison system.

Garrison Johnson, an African-American inmate, challenged the policy, arguing that it violated his right to equal protection by assigning cellmates based on race. The District Court dismissed his complaint, but the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the decision, stating that Johnson had stated a claim for racial discrimination. On remand, the District Court granted summary judgment to the defendants, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed, applying a deferential standard of review from Turner v. Safley rather than strict scrutiny.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to decide the appropriate standard of review. The Court held that all racial classifications imposed by the government must be analyzed under strict scrutiny, which requires the government to prove that such classifications are narrowly tailored measures that further compelling governmental interests. The Court rejected the CDC's argument that the policy was "neutral" and therefore exempt from strict scrutiny, emphasizing that racial classifications receive close scrutiny even when they may be said to burden or benefit the races equally.

The Court also rejected the CDC's invitation to apply the deferential standard from Turner v. Safley, stating that the right not to be discriminated against based on race is not inconsistent with proper prison administration and that compliance with the Fourteenth Amendment's ban on racial discrimination bolsters the legitimacy of the entire criminal justice system.

The Court held that the Court of Appeals erred by not applying strict scrutiny to the CDC's policy and remanded the case for the lower court to apply the correct standard. The Court did not decide whether the CDC's policy violates the Equal Protection Clause, only that strict scrutiny is the proper standard of review.

Justice Thomas, joined by Justice Scalia, dissented, arguing that the deferential standard from Turner should apply because the Constitution demands less within prison walls and that prison officials are better positioned to make judgments about prison administration. He also suggested that even under strict scrutiny, the CDC's policy might be justified due to the compelling interest in maintaining order and security within prisons.

The Supreme Court held that a religious test for public office in Maryland, requiring individuals to declare their belief in God, violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the US Constitution. The Court found that the state constitutional provision setting up a religious test was self-executing and required declaration of belief in God as a qualification for office without need for implementing legislation. However, the Court also noted that the power and authority of the state of Maryland was being used to favor certain religious beliefs over others, which goes against the principle established by the First Amendment that "neither a state nor the Federal Government can constitutinally force a person to profess a belief or disbelief in any religion".

Title II of the Low Level Radioactive Waste Policy Act of 1980 requires participating States to establish a schedule for the phasing in of the implementation of the Act, and to ensure that the amount of low-level radioactive waste generated within the State during the phase-in period is not greater than the amount of waste that can be accommodated in the State's existing storage facilities plus the amount of waste that can be stored in facilities in other States. However, if a State fails to meet the above requirements, the Act allows the State to take title to the excess waste and to sell it to the highest bidder. The State may also seek to recover the costs of managing the waste from the owners of the waste. Participating States may choose to satisfy the Act's requirements by entering into contracts with private firms to store the waste, by establishing their own storage facilities, or by purchasing storage rights from other States. The Act also establishes a program for the sale of excess waste to States that have entered into regional compacts to facilitate the sharing of storage facilities. The Act applies to States that have entered into such compacts and to States that have not done so but that have committed themselves to meeting the Act's requirements. The Act contains a sunset provision that renders it inapplicable to States that have not participated in the Act's implementation after December 31, 1985. The Act was passed by Congress pursuant to its authority under the Commerce Clause of the Federal Constitution and the Spending Clause of Article X of the Constitution. The Act was challenged by petitioners, who claimed that it violated the Take Title Provision of the Act, the Guarantee Clause of Art. IV of the Constitution, and the Commerce Clause. The District Court ruled in petitioners' favor, concluding that the Take Title Provision exceeded Congress' authority under the Commerce Clause and the Spending Clause. The court refused to strike down the Guarantee Clause provision, ruling that it was not properly before the court, and struck down the Commerce Clause provision as conflicting with the Guarantee Clause provision. The Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's rulings except as to the Guarantee Clause provision, which it concluded was not properly before the court. Held: 1. The Take Title Provision exceeds Congress' authority under the Commerce Clause and the Spending Clause. Pp. 10-16. (a) Neither the Commerce Clause nor the Spending Clause empowers Congress to direct the States to provide for the disposal of the radioactive waste generated within their borders. Although the Act's objectives are laudable, the Constitution does not authorize Congress simply to direct the States to provide for the disposal of the waste generated within their borders. Whatever the outer limits of the States' reserved sovereignty may be, the Constitution leaves to the States a residuary and inviolable sovereignty, and the Federal Government may not compel the States to enact or administer a federal regulatory program. Pp. 10-12. (b) The Take Title Provision is not saved by the fact that it is merely an optional incentive designed to encourage the States to attain local or regional self-sufficiency in the disposal of low-level radioactive waste. The provision is not severable from the rest of the Act, and its invalidation causes frustration of Congress' overall intent. Pp. 12-16. 2. The Guarantee Clause does not provide a basis upon which a State or its subdivisions may sue to enjoin the enforcement of the Act. Even assuming that the Guarantee Clause provides a basis upon which a State or its subdivisions may sue to enjoin the enforcement of the Act, petitioners have not made out such a claim in this case. The twin threats posed by the Take Title Provision-that New York may miss out on a share of federal spending or that those generating radioactive waste within New York may lose out-of-state disposal outlets-do not pose any realistic risk of altering the form or the method of functioning of New York's government. Pp. 16-18. Affirmed in part, reversed in part.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Kentucky today entered a final judgment against Kentucky's Department of Education and Health Services (DOH) for unlawfully denying a pension benefit to a state employee who became disabled before he became eligible for normal retirement benefits.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Kentucky, the Department of Health and Human Services instituted a special pension plan for state and county employees who were deemed to be vulnerable to age-related "disparities" in pension benefits. The complaint alleges that Kentucky's pension plan, which is subject to the DoH, improperly discriminated against certain employees by failing to provide them with a sufficient retirement benefit when they became disabled.  The complaint further alleges that, in calculating the pension benefits, Kentucky's plan placed an older worker at a disadvantage because he became disabled after he reached the age of 55.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Kentucky has consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders Kentucky to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount of pension benefits that would have vested after 10 years of service.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Kentucky. The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by John Rymas of the Chicago Regional Office and supervised by Eric Werner of the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis. The litigation will be led by Mr. Werner and Ms. Werner.

Petitioner maritime unions conducted picketing designed to convey information to the public concerning the adverse effects on American seamen caused by employment of foreign sailors at lower wages. The picketing was located near the docks used by a foreign flag ship and resulted in the refusal of American stevedores to cross the picket line. The Alabama Supreme Court sustained an injunction against the picketing, concluding that the picketers' purpose was to wrongfully interfere with the stevedores' businesses and that the trial judge had not abused his discretion in issuing the injunction. Held: 1. The Alabama courts were competent to resolve the dispute between petitioners and respondents unless the resolution violated petitioners' rights under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 208-213. (a) Neither the farmer seeking to ship his soybeans, the stevedores who contracted to unload the cargo of the foreign flag ship, nor the longshoremen whom the stevedores employed to carry out this undertaking, were for these purposes engaged in or affecting commerce within the purview of the National Labor Relations Act. Pp. 208-210. (b) The Alabama courts were not pre-empted by the National Labor Relations Act from adjudicating the dispute between petitioners and respondents. Pp. 210-213. 2. The Alabama courts' action in enjoining the picketing did not violate petitioners' rights under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 213-216. 275 Ala. 45, 154 So. 2d 10, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana has issued an order requiring the Indiana State Election Board to place the Communist Party of Indiana and its candidates on the ballot for the 1972 general election.  The order also requires the party to submit an affidavit in keeping with the First and Fourteenth amendments of the federal securities laws.  According to the order, filed on September 28, 1972, the Court granted the party's request for an emergency declaration of the unconstitutionality of § 29-3812, and an injunction requiring the Party to place its nominees on the National Ballot only in the event that the Party urges others to do something, now or in the future, to incite or produce imminent lawless action.  Without admitting or denying the Court's order, the party has consented to the entry of an order that permanently enjoins the Board from violating the First, Fourteenth, and Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the party and its nominees to submit affidavits in accordance with those provisions.  In addition, the court granted the Party's request to withdraw its application for a place on the national ballot, which was subject to approval by the court, on the advice of the Attorney General of Indiana, to a 60-day period for an affidavit required under the federal law to be filed with the court.  On October 3, the Judge granted the parties' motion for emergency relief, including a temporary restraining order, and ordered the Party and nominees to comply with the order.   The court's order also temporarily halted the filing of an emergency action against the Party.
