Burt of the Boston Regional Office and supervised by Marc Blau of the Division of Justice's Cyber Unit.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the FBI in this matter.

Title: Griswold v. Connecticut
Year: 1965
Summary: In Griswold v. Connecticut, the Supreme Court ruled that a state law banning the sale of contraceptives to minors and unmarried adults was unconstitutional under the Due Process and Equal Protection clauses of the Fourth Amendment. The Court held that the right to privacy includes the right to control one's reproductive choices, and that the state's interference with this right was unnecessary and burdensome. The Court also rejected the idea that the state had a legitimate concern about preventing the spread of venereal diseases, arguing that the ban on contraceptives was not based on scientific evidence and was instead motivated by moral and religious beliefs.

An Air Force regulation (AFR) mandates uniform dress for Air Force personnel. When petitioner, who had been accepted into the Armed Forces Health Professions Scholarship Program and was serving as a commissioned officer in the Air Force, testified before a court-martial wearing his yarmulke but not his service cap, opposing counsel complained about petitioner's practice of wearing his yarmulke in violation of AFR. Subsequently, petitioner was formally admonished and threatened with disciplinary action if he did not comply with the regulation. Thereafter, petitioner brought suit in Federal District Court, alleging that the application of AFR to prevent him from wearing his yarmulke infringed upon his First Amendment freedom to exercise his religious beliefs. The District Court permanently enjoined the Air Force from prohibiting petitioner from wearing a yarmulke while in uniform. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Air Force's strong interest in discipline justified the strict enforcement of its uniform dress requirements. Held: The First Amendment does not prohibit the Air Force from applying AFR to petitioner even though its effect is to restrict the wearing of the headgear required by his religious beliefs. Pp. 108-113. (a) Since the military is a specialized society separate from civilian society, the review of military regulations challenged on First Amendment grounds is far more deferential than constitutional review of similar laws or regulations designed for civilian society. Courts must give great deference to the professional judgment of military authorities concerning the relative importance of a particular military interest. Here, the Air Force's considered professional judgment is that the traditional outfitting of personnel in standardized uniforms encourages the subordination of personal preferences and identities in favor of the overall group mission. To this end, the Air Force promulgated AFR, which states that Air Force members will wear the Air Force uniform while performing their military duties, except when authorized to wear civilian clothes on duty. Even the limited exceptions to the rule regarding the wearing of headgear indoors were based upon the Air Force's determination that the restrictions were essential to maintain the uniformity sought by the dress regulations. Pp. 108-111. (b) Whether or not expert witnesses may feel that religious exceptions to AFR are desirable is irrelevant since the desirability of dress regulations in the military is decided by the appropriate military officials, and they are under no constitutional mandate to abandon their considered professional judgment. While to the extent that AFR does not permit the wearing of religious apparel such as a yarmulke, military life may be more objectionable for petitioner and others, the First Amendment does not require the military to accommodate such practices in the face of its view that they would detract from the uniformity sought by the dress regulations. Pp. 111-113. 236 U. S. App. D. C. 248, 734 F. 2d 1531, affirmed.

On November 2, 1982, the outside walls of the synagogue of the Shaare Tefila Congregation in Silver Spring, Maryland, were sprayed with red and black paint and with large anti-Semitic slogans, phrases, and symbols. A few months later, the Congregation and some individual members brought this suit in the Federal District Court, alleging that defendants' desecration had violated 42 U.S.C.  1981, 1985 (3) and the Maryland common law of trespass, nuisance, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The District Court dismissed all the claims. The Court of Appeals held that the defendants' conduct was not "intended to apply" to situations in which a plaintiff is not a member of a racially distinct group but is "merely perceived to be so by defendants"

The U.S. Supreme Court of Appeals for West Virginia reversed a $50 million jury verdict against A. T. Massey Coal Co. and its affiliates, finding that the board chairman and principal officer of the corporation was liable for fraudulent misrepresentation, concealment, and tortious interference with existing contractual relations. The majority opinion, authored by then-Chief Justice Davis and joined by Justices Benjamin and Maynard, found that Don Blankenship's conduct warranted the type of judgment rendered in this case. The court also found that the jury verdict was based on two independent grounds: First, that a forum-selection clause contained in a contract to which Massey was not a party barred the suit in West Virginia, and second, that the trial court's denial of Massey's motion for judgment as a matter of law violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court concluded that, in all the circumstances of this case, due process requires recusal.

This is a decision about whether hospitals operated by ERISA plans can be subject to taxes imposed by states. The Supreme Court holds that New York may collect taxes on these hospitals, even though they are operated by ERISA funds. The court explains that while the tax in question is a "revenue raising measure," it still falls within the traditional authority of states to regulate matters related to health and safety. Additionally, the court notes that there is no evidence that Congress intended to supersede state laws when it created ERISA.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against a Florida man accused of using a pipe and baseball bat to kill Michael Finken.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Orlando, Florida, Gary Lawrence and his wife used a pipe-and-ball bat to commit a series of unprovoked murders and to steal a car. The complaint alleges that the defendants used the stolen car to commit the murders. The SEC alleges that Lawrence was able to file a federal habeas petition on time in spite of the fact that the state courts had yet to issue a final judgment on his conviction. The court denied Lawrence’s request for a temporary restraining order and ordered him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  The SEC complaint charges Lawrence with violating the antiterrorism and effective death penalty provisions of Section 2244(d)(2) of the federal securities laws. Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, Lawrence consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the antifraud provisions, imposes a $500,000 civil penalty, and requires him to surrender his passport. The settlement is subject to court approval.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Florida today announced that it would conduct a parallel criminal proceeding against Lawrence.  On March 24, 2003, the court granted certiorari to Lawrence. The Court also ordered Lawrence to comply with the court's order.  As set forth in the complaint, the SEC seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  Lawrence has agreed to settle the SEC action by consenting to a permanent injunctive relief order, and to a conduct-based injunction. The order also requires Lawrence to show that he has been diligent in preparing his case and has not delayed filing his federal petition. The U. S. Attorney has also issued an order requiring Lawrence to provide a copy of the complaint to the court.  A hearing is scheduled for May 21, 2019.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 527 (2003).

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has ruled that the President's authority to set federal judges' salaries is not limited to the annual cost-of-living adjustments set by Congress under the Federal Salary Act of 1967 (FAA) and the Federal Pay Comparability Act of 1970 (FCPA)<n>The Court held that the FAA and CPA provide for a quadrennial review of the compensation of high-level officials in the Executive Branch, Legislative, and Judicial Branches, including federal judges. The Court ruled that Congress has the authority to determine the amount of each annual increase in the judge's salary, and that it can do so without the need for a vote by the House or Senate. The court also ruled that it is not necessary for the President to submit an alternative plan to Congress for the annual salary adjustments. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the President, holding that Congress had the authority under the FAA to set the annual increases. The high court held that, under the FCPA, the President has the power to set annual increases for federal judges, but that Congress must act before the annual increase takes effect. The appeals court ruled that this authority does not apply to federal judges who are not subject to the FAA or FCPA. The Appeals Court also held that Congress's approval of an annual increase is not required for judges who have not yet been appointed by the President. In a separate appeal, the Supreme Court found that the Court's decision to be consistent with the lower court's earlier decision. The case will be decided by Justices

Petitioner, the surviving widow of J. Howard Marshall II (J. Howard), filed suit in Federal District Court against an executor and resident heirs to determine the validity of his estate plan, which consisted of a living trust and a “pourover” will. Respondent, E. Pierce Marshall (Pierce), was the ultimate beneficiary of the estate plan. Under the terms of the will, all of J Howard’s assets not already included in the trust were to be transferred to the trust upon his death. Competing claims regarding J.Howard‘s fortune ignited proceedings in both state and federal courts. In January 1996, while the estate was subject to ongoing proceedings in the District Court, respondent filed a bankruptcy declaration, alleging fraud and tortious interference with the estate. The Bankruptcy Court granted summary judgment in favor of Vickie on Pierce’’ claim and, after a trial on the merits, entered judgment for Vickie. The court awarded Vickie compensatory damages of more than $449 million, less whatever she recovered in the ongoing probate action in Texas, as well as punitive damages. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the probate exception bars federal jurisdiction in this case. Held: The Ninth Circuit had no warrant from Congress, or from decisions of this Court, for its sweeping extension of §1334. Pp. 5–11. (a) The probate exceptions are judicially created doctrines stemming in large measure from misty understandings of English legal history. P. 5. (b) The “domestic relations exception” is not compelled by the text of the Constitution or federal statute. The federal courts, “having existed from the beginning of the Federal government, [can] not be impaired by subsequent state legislation creating courts of probate.” McClellan v. Carland, 217 U. S. 268, 281. The jurisdiction of the federal courts is determined “by the law of the court” and cannot be defeated by the extraterritorial operation of a state statute. See, e.g., Ankenbrandt v. Richards, 504 U.S. 689, 693–695. In addition, the “probate exception,” kin to the domestic relations exception, is subject to a mandatory abstention provision applicable to certain state-law claims. The District Court treated the judgment as “proposed” rather than final, and undertook a review of its determinations. In that proceeding, the Bankrupty Court granted a summary judgment, entered a judgment for Pierce, and awarded him $44.3 million in compensatory and punitive damages, and concluded that the Probate exception did not reach Vickie, who was entitled to the entire net estate, including specified real estate passing under the will. In the federal forum, Pierce sought district-court review of the judgment, but the Ninth Circuit held that the exception was waived because it was not timely raised, and that it was binding on the United States District Court. The case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. Certiorari granted; 392 F. 3d 1118, reversed and remanded.

This decision holds that under a federal criminal statute, "aggravated identity theft," a person must know that the means of identification they are using belongs to another person. The court bases its decision on the plain language of the statute and common understanding of the term "knowingly." The court finds that requiring the offender to know that the "means of identification" belongs to another person would not be superfluous in this context, as it helps prevent additional harm caused by the use of someone else's identity.

After petitioner Dolan slipped and fell on packages left on her front porch by a United States Postal Service employee, she sought compensation under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA). She claimed that the incident violated the FTCA’s express waiver of sovereign immunity for claims arising out of the loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter, 28 U. S. C. §2680(b). The District Court dismissed her complaint, relying on the Court of Appeals’ decision in Raila v. United States, 355 F. 3d 118, 121, which held that §2680(b) preserved sovereign immunity despite the FTCA’s more general statements of waiver. The Eighth Circuit agreed. Held: Section 2680(b) does not preserve sovereign immunity. Pp. 4–11. (a) Assuming that under the applicable state law Dolan had a cause of action for damages, the question is whether, when mail left by the Postal Service causes a slip-and-fall injury, §2680(b)’s exception for “negligent transmission” preserves sovereign immunity despite the FTCA’s more general statements of waiver. Context and precedent require a narrower reading than the Government urges. First, the words “negligent transmission” follow two other terms, “loss” and “miscarriage,” suggesting that the term “negligent transmission” refers to failures in the postal obligation to deliver mail in a timely manner to the right address. Thus, it would be odd if “negligent transmission” included injuries like those alleged here—injuries that happen to be caused by postal employees but involve neither failure to transmit mail nor damage to its contents. Second, Kosak v. United States, 465 U.S. 848, gives specific consideration to the postal exception and shows that the United States, nonetheless, retains no immunity. There, the Court contrasted the generality of §2680(c), covering various kinds of taxes and customs duties, with the specificity of §2680(b), governing torts committed by mailmen. The Court observed that the FTCA’s purpose was to waive the Government’s immunity from liability for automobile accidents in which postal workers were at fault, and that the draftsmen of §2680(b) therefore excluded, by implication, negligent handling of motor vehicles. Because nothing in the statutory text supports the Government’s contention that §2680(b) covers all negligence in the course of mail delivery, and because focusing on whether the mail itself caused the injury would yield anomalous results, it is more likely that Congress intended to retain immunity, as a general rule, only for injuries arising, directly or consequentially, because mail either fails to arrive at all or arrives late, in damaged condition, or at the wrong address. Illustrative instances of the exception’s operation would be personal or financial harms arising from nondelivery or late delivery of sensitive materials or information (e.g., medicines or a mortgage foreclosure notice) or from negligent handling of a mailed parcel (e.g., shattered china). The fact that the Postal Service holds millions of deliveries per day does not support the Government’s position that Congress meant to insulate delivery-related torts from liability. Nor does the fact that other FTCA exceptions use more sweeping language indicate that Congress intended to immunize all postal activities. Losses of the type for which immunity is retained under §2680(b) are at least to some degree avoidable or compensable through postal registration and insurance. Moreover, Kosak explains that one purpose of the FTCA exceptions was to avoid extending the Act’s coverage to suits for which adequate remedies were already available, an objective consistent with retaining immunity as to claims of mail damage or delay covered by postal registration and insurance. Even assuming that other injuries falling outside the FTCA are also subject to administrative relief, the provision cited by the Government allows only discretionary relief, not an automatic remedy like postal insurance. Finally, this case does not implicate the general rule that “a waiver of the Government’s sovereign immunity will be strictly construed, in terms of its scope, in favor of the sovereign,” Lane v. Peña, 518 U.S. 187, 192. Pp. 4–11. 371 F.3d 555, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Stevens, Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined.

The Supreme Court held that the 120-day deadline for a veteran to file a notice of appeal with the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (Veterans Court) after a denial of federal benefits by the Board of Veterans’ Appeals is not a "jurisdictional" requirement. This means that missing the deadline does not automatically prevent the Veterans Court from having the authority to hear the case.

The Court's reasoning emphasized the non-adversarial, claimant-friendly nature of the veterans' benefits system, which is designed to assist veterans in obtaining benefits and allows for a high degree of flexibility in filing and appealing claims. The Court noted that the language of the statute setting the 120-day deadline does not clearly indicate that Congress intended it to be jurisdictional. Additionally, the placement of the provision within the Veterans' Judicial Review Act (VJRA) suggests it is a procedural rule rather than a jurisdictional one.

The Court also pointed out that the veterans' benefits adjudication system is unique and should not be directly compared to other judicial review systems. The Court highlighted the protective nature of the system and the legislative intent to favor veterans in the adjudication process.

The Supreme Court's decision means that veterans who miss the 120-day deadline may still have an opportunity to appeal, and the Veterans Court has the authority to hear such cases. The case was remanded for further proceedings to determine if there are any exceptions to the 120-day rule that would apply in this specific case. Justice Kagan did not participate in the decision.

The Supreme Court reversed the conviction of an appellant who had displayed a United States flag with a peace symbol affixed to it from his apartment window. The appellant was convicted under a Washington statute that prohibited the display of a flag with any added figures, symbols, or material. The Supreme Court found that the statute, as applied to the appellant's actions, violated his First Amendment right to free expression.

The Court noted several key points in its decision:

1. The flag was privately owned and displayed on private property, not government property.
2. There was no evidence of a breach of the peace or any intent by the appellant to incite violence.
3. The State acknowledged that the appellant's display was a form of communication, intended to express his views on the American flag representing peace rather than war and violence.
4. The Court recognized the use of flags as a form of symbolic speech, protected under the First Amendment.
5. The context of the display was important, as it was a response to contemporary events of public concern, namely the invasion of Cambodia and the Kent State shootings.
6. The Court rejected the State's interest in preventing a breach of the peace, protecting the sensibilities of passersby, and preserving the flag as an unalloyed symbol of the nation, as there was no risk of misinterpretation of government endorsement or permanent disfigurement of the flag.

The Court concluded that the appellant's expression was protected by the First Amendment, and the state's interest in preserving the physical integrity of the flag was not significantly impaired. Therefore, the conviction was invalidated, and the judgment was reversed.

Respondents, a commercial jet aircraft owned by respondent S.A. Empresa De Viacao Aerea Rio Grandense (Varig Airlines), brought an action under the Federal Tort Claims Act (Act) against the United States under the Act, alleging that the Civil Aeronautics Agency (FAA) had been negligent in certifying that its designs, plans, specifications, and performance data had been shown to be in conformity with minimum safety standards. The District Court held that, even if respondents had stated a cause of action in tort, recovery against the Government was barred by two exceptions to the Act: the discretionary function exception, 28 U. S. C. § 2680(a), and the misrepresentation exception. The Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that a private person inspecting and certificating aircraft for airworthiness would be liable for negligent inspection under the California "Good Samaritan" rule. Held: The Act does not recognize an actionable tort duty for inspection and certification activities. Pp. 692-673. (a) The discretionary functions exception is plainly discretionary activity of the "nature and quality" protected by § 26 80(a). When an agency determines the extent to which it will perform a safety regulation, it is the Secretary's designee's duty to promote safety in air transportation by promulgating reasonable rules and regulations governing the inspection, servicing, and overhaul of civil aircraft. The FAA's implementation of a mechanism for compliance review, including the manner in which such inspections should be made, and the use of such procedures in determining whether an aircraft complies with FAA regulations, is plainly a discretionary activity, and Congress intended to prevent judicial "secondguessing" of legislative and administrative decisions grounded in social, economic, and political policy through the medium of an action-in tort. Dalehite v. United States, 346 U.S. 15, 26-30, distinguished. P. 693. (b) Section 2680 (a), which provides that the FAA is not subject to liability for any claim arising out of misrepresentation, precludes a tort action based upon the conduct of the FAA in certificating these aircraft for use in commercial aviation. The discretionary function exceptions are plainly discretionary activities of the Government acting in its role as a regulator of the conductof private individuals. The legislative history refers to the acts of regulatory agencies as examples of those covered by the exception, and it is significant that the early tort claims bills considered by Congress specifically exempted two major regulatory agencies by name. Thus, Congress could not have intended to impose liability for the regulatory enforcement activities of Congress challenged in this case. The Government's contention that the FCC was negligent in failing to inspect certain elements of aircraft design before certificating the Boeing 707 and DeHavilland Dove necessarily challenges two aspects of the certification procedure: the FAA's decision to implement the "spot-check" system of compliance review and the application of that system to the particular aircraft involved in these cases. In this case, the FAA accomplishes its monitoring function by means of a "spotcheck" program designed to encourage manufacturers and operators to comply fully with the FAA regulations. Such regulatory activity, the Government argues, is the sort of governmental conduct protected by the discretionaryfunction exception. In the exercise of this discretion, the Secretary has provided for private individuals to serve as designated engineering representatives to assist in the FAA certification process, and FAA representatives are authorized to approve data covering major changes in type design and obtain supplemental type certifications without prior review by the FAA. In determining whether the aircraft's compliance with FAA requirements, they are guided by the same requirements, instructions, and procedures as FAA employees. The specific exception was added to make clear that the Act was not to be extended into the realm of the validity of legislation or discretionary administrative action. The court summarily affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit held that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has the authority to require federal agencies to pay compensatory damages when they discriminate in employment in violation of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 .<n>The case involves a case involving a VA employee who was denied a promotion on the basis of his gender. The Department of Veterans Affairs, however, subsequently found in the employee's favor and awarded him a promotion plus backpay. The VA then refused to comply with the court's order to pay compensation, and the case was dismissed by the court. The Seventh Circuit reversed the decision, holding that Gibson had not shown that he had not exhausted his administrative remedies to recover compensatory damages. The court held that Gibson's case should be dismissed because he failed to show that the VA had violated the law. The Court held that, under the law, the EEOC has the power to enforce the law's anti-discrimination provisions, and that it has authority to order the VA to comply.

Petitioner Hishon accepted a position as an associate with respondent, an Atlanta law firm established as a general partnership. Up to that time, no woman had ever served as a partner at the firm. She alleges that respondent used the possibility of ultimate partnership as a recruiting device to induce petitioner and other young lawyers to become associates at respondent's firm. In May 1978 the partnership considered and rejected petitioner for admission to the partnership; one year later, the partners again declined to invite her to become a partner. Once an associate is passed over for partnership, the associate is notified to begin seeking employment elsewhere. Petitioner alleges that she relied on these representations when she accepted employment with respondent. The District Court dismissed the complaint on the ground that Title VII was inapplicable to the selection of partners by a partnership. A divided panel of the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Petitioner's allegations are true. A court may dismiss a complaint only if it is clear that no relief could be granted under any set of facts that could be proved consistent with the allegations. Conley v. Gibson, 355 U. S. 41, 45-46. Pp. 6-12. 678 F. 2d 1022, reversed and remanded.

Title 42 U. S. C. §1983(a) empowers individuals to sue state officials for damages resulting from the alleged deprivation of property rights. Section 1983(c) limits recovery to compensatory damages, except where the plaintiff shows that he has exhausted the administrative remedy prescribed by the state. Under the regulations issued by respondent regional planning agency, petitioner Suitum's property lies entirely within a Streamside Environmental Zone (SEZ), and the agency may not permit any additional land coverage or other permanent land disturbance on the parcel. However, the agency did permit Suitum to acquire three types of Transferable Development Rights (TDRs): Residential Development Rights, Residential Allocations, and Land Coverage Rights. These rights may be transferred to others, but the transfers are subject to the agency's approval. Suitum never requested a Residential Allocation or Land Coverage Right, but she did ask the agency to approve the transfer of her Residential Development Rights to another party. The agency refused, asserting that it needed to know the value of the TDRs before making a decision. Suitum then filed suit in Federal District Court, contending that the agency's refusal constituted a taking in violation of the Fifth Amendment. The court dismissed the complaint, finding that Suitum had not met the ripeness standard set forth in Williamson County v. Harry M. Steel Co., 489 U. S. 205, 211-212, i. e., that she had not received a "final decision" from the agency concerning the use that would be permitted on her land. The Ninth Circuit affirmed. Held: Suitum's claim is ripe for judicial review. Pp. 13-19. (a) Two independent standards govern the ripeness of a regulatory taking claim: the "final decision" standard of Williamson County, supra, and the "fitness for review" standard of Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner, 387 U. S. 136. Pp. 13-15. (b) Suitum has received a "final decision." Her claim satisfies the Williamson County standard because the agency has no discretion to exercise over her right to use her land, and no occasion exists for applying the Williamson County standard's demand for a final decision about the use that will be permitted on a particular parcel. Moreover, the agency's agreement that Suitum's land lies entirely within an SEZ means that the agency may not permit any additional land coverage or other permanent land disturbance on the parcel. Since Suitum is not disputing the legality of the agency's actions, no discretionary decision need be made by any agency official for her to obtain the TDRs or to offer them for sale. Whether a particular sale of TDRs may be completed is quite different from whether TDRs are saleable, and so long as the particular buyer is not the only person who can lawfully buy, the rights would not be rendered unsaleable even if the agency were to make a discretionary decision to kill a particular sale. Furthermore, the agency's argument that Suitum's case is not ripe because no "'values attributable to [her] TDRs are known,"' Brief for Respondent 23, is just a variation on the above analysis. Even assuming that the agency's estimate of the value of Suitum's TDRs is correct, the agency's own position assumes that there are many potential, lawful buyers for the TDRs, whose receipt of those rights would unquestionably be approved. Pp. 15-17. (c) Nor is Suitum's claim unripe under the "fitness for review" standard of Abbott Laboratories, supra. That case involved a manufacturer's challenge to the validity of a regulation as beyond the scope of the agency's authority, whereas Suitum does not challenge the validity of the agency's regulations. To the extent that Abbott Laboratories is instructive in disposing of the instant case, it cuts directly against the agency. Suitum is just as definitively barred from taking any affirmative step to develop her land as the drug companies were bound to take affirmative steps to change their labels. Pp. 17-19. 80 F. 3d 1175, vacated and remanded.

Respondent McDonald, a black man, owns and operates a Nevada corporation called JWM, which he formed to build hotels. He negotiated hotel contracts with respondents Domino’s, Inc., and its subsidiaries, but the contracts went unfulfilled. Ultimately, JWM filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. Its trustee then settled the breach of contract claim against Domino’s for $45,000, giving Domino’s a complete release over any further claims arising out of the same episode. Meanwhile, McDonald filed this action in his personal capacity, alleging that Domino’s had breached its contracts with JWM because of racial animus toward McDonald, and that the breaches caused him harm. The District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim. Agreeing that an “injury sustained only by the corporation” would not allow a shareholder to bring a §1981 action, the court nevertheless ruled that a corporation may have standing to assert a §1981 claim, but that a president or sole shareholder may not step into the corporation’s shoes and assert that claim personally. The Ninth Circuit reversed, concluding that when there are “injuries distinct from that of the corporation,” a nonparty like McDonald may nonetheless bring suit under §1981. Held: To state a claim under §1981, a plaintiff must have (or would have) rights under the existing (or proposed) contractual relationship. Nothing in the statute’s text indicates that it was meant to provide an omnibus remedy for all racial injustice. If so, it would not have been limited to situations involving contracts. Instead, §1981 requires identification of injuries flowing from a racially motivated breach of the plaintiff’s own contractual relationship, not of someone else’s. Thus, McDonald cannot state a claim under §1981. Pp. 4–8. 107 Fed. Appx. 18, reversed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, and Breyer, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined. Alito, J., took no part in the consideration or decision of the case.

Case Name: Republic v. Gillmor

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which had set aside Ahmed Ressam's conviction for carrying explosives during the commission of a felony. Ressam was convicted of making a false statement to a U.S. customs official and carrying explosives in his car at the time of the offense. The Ninth Circuit had interpreted the statute (18 U.S.C. §844(h)(2)) to mean that the explosives must be carried "in relation to" the felony, but the Supreme Court disagreed.

The Supreme Court's opinion, delivered by the majority, focused on the plain language of the statute, which states that a person who "carries an explosive during the commission of any felony" shall face additional imprisonment. The Court found that the term "during" indicates a temporal link and does not imply a relational requirement between the carrying of the explosive and the felony. The Court also examined the legislative history of the statute, noting that when Congress amended a similar statute regarding firearms, it explicitly added an "in relation to" requirement, which it did not do for the explosives statute.

The Court concluded that the differences between the original texts and subsequent amendments of the explosives and firearms statutes suggest that Congress did not intend to include a relational requirement in the explosives statute. Therefore, the Court held that Ressam's act of carrying explosives at the time of making a false statement to a customs official met the requirements of the statute, and his conviction on that count should stand.

The implication of this decision is that individuals can be convicted under 18 U.S.C. §844(h)(2) for carrying explosives during the commission of a felony without the need to prove that the explosives were related to the felony. This broadens the scope of the statute and potentially increases the penalties for individuals who commit felonies while in possession of explosives, regardless of whether the explosives are connected to the felony.

The U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee granted clemency to Pervis Tyrone Payne, who was convicted of two counts of first-degree murder and one count of assault with intent to commit murder in the first degree for the 1987 murders of Charisse Christopher, her daughter Lacie, and her 3-year-old son Nicholas. The Christophers lived together in an apartment in Millington, Tennessee, across the hall from Payne's girlfriend, Bobbie Thomas. On one visit, Payne left his overnight bag, containing clothes and other items for his weekend stay, in the hallway outside Thomas' apartment. Payne returned to the Christophers' apartment, entered the apartment complex, and began making sexual advances towards Charisse. Charisse resisted and Payne became violent. A neighbor who resided in the apartment directly beneath Charisse heard Charisse screaming, "Get out, get out,' as if she were telling the children to leave. The noise briefly subsided and then began, " 'horribly loud.' " The neighbor called the police after she heard a "blood curdling scream" from the Christopher apartment. When the first police officer arrived at the scene, he immediately encountered Payne who was leaving the apartment building, so covered with blood that he appeared to be "sweating blood"

The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments on whether the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) has jurisdiction to hear a case involving a union's picketing of a Great Lakes shipping company's ships. The case involves a dispute between the company, Hanna Mining Company, and the union, Marine Engineers Beneficial Association (MEBA), which represented the marine engineers in Hanna's fleet under a collective bargaining agreement terminated on July 15, 1962 .<n>The court will determine whether the Board's decision to dismiss charges against MEBA for violating the federal law's anti-employee picketing provisions is consistent with the decision of the Wisconsin Court of Appeals, which held that the Board had jurisdiction over the issue. The court will also determine whether it is appropriate for the Board to hold a hearing to determine whether MEBA's actions violated the anti-harassment provisions of the law. The high court will decide whether the court should order the parties to settle the matter. The Supreme Court's ruling will determine the extent to which the Board has jurisdiction in the case. The Court will also decide whether it should order MEBA to pay the costs of the case, which are estimated to be in the tens of thousands of dollars.

Petitioner McNeil was arrested in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, pursuant to a warrant charging him with an armed robbery. After advising him of his Miranda rights, he signed a form waiving them. The Sheriff's Department returned two days later with detectives from Caledonia, Wis., who sought to question him. The sheriff's department then began the interview by administering the Miranda warnings and obtaining petitioner's signature and initials on the waiver form. Petitioner admitted that he had been involved in the Caledonian crimes, but also implicated two other men, Willie Pope and Lloyd Crowley. The statement was typed up by a detective and given to petitioner to review, and petitioner placed his initials next to every reference to himself and signed every page. The following day, he was formally charged with the Caledsonia crimes and transferred to that jurisdiction. His pretrial motion to suppress the incriminating statements was denied. On appeal, McNeil contended that his courtroom appearance with an attorney for the West Allis crime constituted an invocation of his Sixth Amendment right to counsel, and that any subsequent waiver of that right during police-initiated questioning regarding any offense was invalid. The Wisconsin Supreme Court certified to that court the following question: "Does an accused's request for counsel at an initial appearance on a charged offense constitute an invocation [of] his Fifth Amendment right [to counsel] that precludes police interrogation on unrelated, uncharged offenses?" Held: 1. The Sixth Amendment counsel guarantee-and hence the purpose of invoking it-is to "protec[t] the unaided layman at critical confrontations" with his "expert adversary," the government, after "the adverse positions of government and defendant have solidified" with respect to a particular alleged crime-is offense-specific. The purpose of the Sixth Amendment's counsel guarantee is to protect a quite different interest: the suspect's "desire to deal with the police only through counsel," Edwards, 451 U. S. 412, 431. To invoke that interest is, as a matter of fact, not to invoke the Miranda-Edwards interest. Because petitioner provided the statements at issue here before his Sixth- Amendment right (and hence his right) had been (or even could have been) invoked, that right poses no bar to the admission of the statements in this case. Pp. 4-6. 2. The State's holding that, once a suspect asserts the right, not only must the current interrogation cease, but he may not be approached for further interrogation "until counsel has been made available to him" is not the test for applicability of Edwards. The rule of that case applies only when the suspect "ha[s] expressed " his wish for the particular sort of lawyerly assistance that is the subject of Miranda. Edwards, supra, at 484, 101 S.Ct., at 1884-1885. It requires, at a minimum, some statement that can reasonably be construed to be expression of a desire for the assistance of an attorney in dealing with custodial interrogation by the police. Requesting the assistanceof an attorney at a bail hearing does not bear that construction. The Court's holding in Michigan v. Jackson, 475 U.S. 625, does not, as petitioner asserts, contradict the foregoing distinction; to the contrary, it rests upon it. In Miranda, it held that after the Sixth-Amendment right attaches and is invoked, any statements obtained from the accused during subsequent police-incitiated custodial questioning regarding the charge at issue are presumed involuntary and therefore inadmissible as substantive evidence at trial, even where the suspect executes a waiver and his statements would be considered voluntary under traditional standards. This is "designed to prevent police from badgering a defendant into waiving his previously asserted Miranda rights," Michiganv. Harvey, 494 U.

The Federal Trade Dilution Act (FTDA) allows owners of famous trademarks to seek damages for dilution caused by others using similar marks. The act defines dilution as the lessening of the capacity of a famous mark to identify and distinguish goods or services. The Supreme Court held that dilution occurs when a mark is associated with something negative or distasteful, thereby reducing its ability to identify and distinguish goods or services. However, the Court also noted that dilution cannot occur unless there is a likelihood of confusion between the famous mark and the diluted mark. Therefore, the Court held that dilution is a type of unfair competition and that dilution damages must be proven objectively, rather than relying solely on a subjective belief in dilution.

Petitioner Wilson made a series of narcotics sales to an informant acting at the direction of the Arkansas State Police. In late November, the informant purchased marijuana and methamphetamine at petitioner's home. On December 30, petitioner telephoned petitioner at her home and arranged to meet her at a local store to buy some marijuana. Petitioner produced a semiautomatic pistol at this meeting and waved it in the informant's face, threatening to kill her if she turned out to be working for the police. The informant then sold the informant a bag of marijuana. The next day, police officers applied for and obtained warrants to search petitioner's house and arrest both petitioner and Jacobs. Affidavits filed in support of the warrants set forth the details of the narcotics transactions and stated that Jacobs had previously been convicted of arson and firebombing. The search was conducted later that afternoon. Police officers found the main door to petitioner's residence open. While opening an unlocked screen door and entering the residence, they identified themselves as police officers, stated that they had a warrant. Once inside the home, the officers seized marijuana, methamphetamine, valium, narcotics paraphernalia, a gun, and ammunition. They also found petitioner in the bathroom, flushing marijuana down the toilet. After a jury trial, petitioner was convicted of all charges and sentenced to 32 years in prison. The Arkansas Supreme Court affirmed petitioner's conviction on appeal. The court noted that the officers entered the home while they were identifying themselves, but rejected petitioner's argument that the Fourth Amendment requires officers to knock and announce prior to entering the home. Finding "no authority for [petitioner's] theory that the knock-and-announce principle is required by [the Fourth Amendment]," the court concluded that neither Arkansas law nor the Fourth amendment required suppression of the evidence. Held: 1. The common-law "knock and announce" principle forms a part of the reasonableness inquiry under the Fifth Amendment. Although a search or seizure of a dwelling might be constitutionally defective if police officers enter without prior announcement, law enforcement interests may also establish thereasonableness of an unannounced entry. See, e. g., Semayne's Case, 5 Co. Rep. 91a, 91b, 77 Eng.Rep. 293, 305-306, 294 P. 2d 6, 9, reversed and remanded.

In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that the state did not have a constitutional duty to preserve every piece of potential evidence in a criminal case. Instead, the court held that the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment required the state to preserve evidence that might be useful to a criminal defendant, but only if the defendant can show bad faith on the part of the police. The court also clarified that the state's duty to disclose evidence to the defendant still applies regardless of whether the defendant requested it.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces ruled that the Navy-Marine Corps Court of Criminal Appeals had jurisdiction to issue a writ of error to challenge an earlier, and final, decision affirming a criminal conviction. The Court held that the Court had jurisdiction because it had agreed that the military court had jurisdiction. The Government of the United States, however, argued that the court had no jurisdiction to hear the case. The U,S. lost its motion to dismiss, and the Court remanded the case for further proceedings on the merits.

The Supreme Court considered whether a disabled inmate, Tony Goodman, could sue the State of Georgia for money damages under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA), which prohibits discrimination against qualified individuals with disabilities by public entities, including state prisons.

Goodman, a paraplegic, alleged that the prison conditions violated his rights under the ADA and the Eighth Amendment, which prohibits cruel and unusual punishment. He claimed that he was confined to a small cell where he couldn't turn his wheelchair, denied assistance for basic hygiene, and excluded from prison programs due to his disability.

The District Court dismissed his ADA claims against the state on the grounds of state sovereign immunity, which was affirmed by the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals. However, the Supreme Court reversed this decision, stating that insofar as Goodman's claims were based on conduct that violated the Fourteenth Amendment, Title II validly abrogates state sovereign immunity.

The Court did not address the merits of Goodman's Eighth Amendment claims but assumed the Eleventh Circuit's treatment of these claims was correct. The Court also noted that it was plausible that the alleged deliberate refusal of prison officials to accommodate Goodman's disability-related needs could constitute discrimination under the ADA.

The Supreme Court remanded the case for further proceedings, instructing the lower courts to determine on a claim-by-claim basis which aspects of the State's alleged conduct violated Title II, to what extent such misconduct also violated the Fourteenth Amendment, and whether Congress's abrogation of sovereign immunity is valid for conduct that violates Title II but not the Fourteenth Amendment.

The decision implies that states can be sued for damages under Title II of the ADA when their actions violate the Fourteenth Amendment, reinforcing the rights of disabled individuals in state-run institutions.

The Supreme Court ruled in Griggs v. Duke Power Company that the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title VII, prohibits an employer from requiring a high school education or passing a standardized general intelligence test as a condition of employment in or transfer to jobs when (a) neither standard is shown to be significantly related to successful job performance, (b) both requirements operate to disqualify Negroes at a substantially higher rate than white applicants, and (c) the jobs in question formerly had been filled only by white employees as part of a longstanding practice of giving preference to whites. The Court found that the company's policies violated Title VII because they resulted in the exclusion of qualified African American workers based solely on their race.

Appellant, a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, was discharged from her employment because she refused to work on Saturday, the Sabbath of her faith. She applied for unemployment compensation under the South Carolina statute, but the State Employment Security Commission found her ineligible for benefits under a provision of the statute which disqualifies any insured worker who fails, without good cause, to accept "suitable work when offered . . . by the employer . . . or the employment security agency." The Commission's finding was sustained by the State Court of Common Pleas and the State Supreme Court, which rejected appellant's contention that the disqualification provisions of the statute abridged her right to the free exercise of her religion secured under the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment through the Fourteenth Amendment. 

Held: 
1. The disqualification provisions of the statute impose a burden on the free exercise of appellant's religion, since they force her to choose between following the precepts of her religion and forfeiting benefits, on the one hand, and abandoning one of the precepts of her religion in order to accept work, on the other hand. Pp. 286-287. 
2. The disqualification provisions of the statute cannot be justified by a compelling state interest in the regulation of a subject within the State's constitutional power to regulate. Pp. 287-291.
	 (a) The disqualification provisions of the statute are not saved by the fact that unemployment compensation benefits are not appellant's "right" but merely a "privilege." Pp. 287-288.
	 (b) The disqualification provisions of the statute are not saved by the fact that South Carolina saves the Sunday worshipper from having to make the kind of choice which is infringed by the Sabbatarian's disqualification. Pp. 288-289.
	 (c) The disqualification provisions of the statute cannot be justified by the possibility that the filing of fraudulent claims by unscrupulous claimants feigning religious objections to Saturday work might dilute the unemployment compensation fund and hinder the scheduling by employers of necessary Saturday work. Pp. 289-291. 213 S. E. 2d 775, reversed.

The Supreme Court addressed whether a creditor must prove a claim of actual fraud by clear and convincing evidence to prevent its discharge in bankruptcy, as per Section 523(a) of the Bankruptcy Code. The case arose when petitioners accused the respondent of fraud in a securities sale. The respondent declared bankruptcy, listing the fraud judgment as dischargeable. The Bankruptcy Court found the debt non-dischargeable based on collateral estoppel, as the elements of fraud had been proven in the prior trial by a preponderance of the evidence. The respondent argued that a higher standard of clear and convincing evidence was required for non-dischargeability under Section 523.

The Court of Appeals reversed the Bankruptcy Court's decision, suggesting that the higher standard was traditionally applied and aligned with the Bankruptcy Code's "fresh start" policy. However, the Supreme Court granted certiorari due to conflicting rulings in other circuits and the significance of the issue.

The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals, holding that the preponderance of the evidence standard is the appropriate burden of proof for exceptions to discharge under Section 523. The Court reasoned that the statute's language and legislative history do not indicate a heightened standard of proof. The Court also noted that the preponderance standard fairly allocates the risk of error and that a debtor does not have a fundamental right to discharge in bankruptcy. The Court found that the "fresh start" policy does not necessitate a higher standard of proof, as the policy is intended for "honest but unfortunate" debtors, not those who commit fraud.

The Court further observed that the structure of Section 523(a) does not suggest different standards of proof for different exceptions and that Congress has typically chosen the preponderance standard for fraud-related causes of action. Historical practices and the development of discharge exceptions also support the use of the preponderance standard.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court determined that the preponderance of the evidence standard applies to the dischargeability exceptions in Section 523(a) of the Bankruptcy Code, and the judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed.

Respondents, parents of two 13-year-old boys from North Carolina, brought an action in a North Carolina state court for damages, alleging negligence in the “design, construction, testing, and inspection” of a tire manufactured in Turkey at the plant of a foreign subsidiary of a United States parent corporation. They named as defendants Goodyear USA, an Ohio corporation, and three of its subsidiaries, organized and operating, respectively, in Turkey, France, and Luxembourg. The North Carolina Court of Appeals affirmed. The trial court denied the motion, and the North Carolina court of appeals affirmed. Held: A state court’s assertion of jurisdiction exposes defendants to the State‘s coercive power, and is therefore subject to review for compatibility with the Fourteenth Amendment’S Due Process Clause. International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U. S. 310, 316. Pp. 5–11. (a) The North Carolinians are not registered to do business in North Carolina. They have no place of business, employees, or bank accounts in North America. They do not design, manufacture, or advertise their products in North or themselves sell or ship tires to North Carolina customers. Nor are they directly re-sponsible for the presence in the forum State of tires manufactured by the United States. P. 6–7. (b) In contrast to general, all-purpose jurisdiction, specific jurisdiction is confined to adjudication of “issues deriving from, or connected with, the very controversy that establishes jurisdiction.” Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S. A. v Hall, 466 U.S. 408, 414, nn. 8, 9. A court may assert general jurisdiction over foreign (sister-state or foreign-country) corporations to hear any and all claims against them when their affiliations with the State are so “continuous and systematic” as to render them essentially at home in that forum State. But “general jurisdiction” depends on an “affiliatio[n] between the forum and the underlying controversy,” principally, activity or an occurrence that takes place in the Forum State and is thus subject to the state’“regulatory regulation.’ ” von Mehren & Trautman 1136, which provides for jurisdiction, “whether the claim arises within or without [the] State, whether such activity is wholly interstate, intrastate, or otherwise, ” id., at 415–416, and “[p]roducts … manufactured by [the defendant were used or consumed, within this State in the ordinary course of trade.“ Id., at 418. ” Ibid., at 681 S. E. 2d 382, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Fifth Circuit today entered a final judgment against David Duncan, a former accountant at Enron Corporation, finding that he violated the antifraud provisions of Section 1512(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 1512b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Dallas, Texas, alleges that, between October 10 and November 9, 2001, Jeffrey Skilling, then the company's former CEO, unexpectedly resigned from the company.  Skilling allegedly told his partner, Michael Odom, that he would "remin[d] the engagement team of our documentation and retention policy" if the company could "withhold" documents for use in, an "official proceeding."  According to the complaint, Skilling agreed, without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's complaints, to the destruction of documents pursuant to the document retention policy.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas today announced criminal charges against Duncan.    The court's order against Duncan, who was later convicted of witness tampering, orders that he be permanently enjoined from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by John Rymas and supervised by Chedly C. Dumornay. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Texas Office of Inspector General.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment finding that the Second Amendment to the United States Constitution protects the right of citizens to keep and bear arms.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Philadelphia on May 19, 2018, the court found that the First Amendment protected an individual right to keep, bear arms, and to use a gun in a militia.  The court also found that, contrary to popular belief, the right was not limited to the use of a gun.  For example, in the 1770s and 1780s, the federal government prohibited the carrying of any weapon other than a rifle in the home.  In addition, in 1789 and 1790, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania and the Federal Bureau of Investigation issued criminal charges against a number of individuals for their roles in the creation and operation of a militia, including a convicted felon who was later sentenced to prison for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the federal securities laws.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Court also ordered that the defendants be held liable for their violations of the preamble to the federal constitutions, and ordered the defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $100,000.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Pyszka and Carol A. McKinley of the Philadelphia Regional Office, and the litigation will be led by John R. Rymas of the Public Finance Abuse Unit.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit is considering the constitutionality of provisions of the Louisiana Constitution and the Louisiana Code of Criminal Procedure dealing with the service of women on jury service. In this case, Billy J. Taylor was convicted and sentenced to death for the aggravated kidnap of a woman in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, in 1972. Taylor was not a member of the excluded class, but there is no rule that claims such as Taylor presents may be made only by those defendants who are members of the group excluded from jury service in the community. The issue of whether the jury-selection system deprived Taylor of his Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment right to an impartial jury trial is the subject of this appeal. We conclude that the jury system violated Taylor's right to a fair trial by denying him a jury of a representative segment of the community, and that his conviction must be reversed.

In the Supreme Court case of Tennessee Student Assistance Corporation v. Hood, the Court considered whether Congress, under the Bankruptcy Clause of the Constitution, has the authority to abrogate state sovereign immunity in bankruptcy proceedings. The specific issue was whether a bankruptcy trustee could initiate proceedings to set aside preferential transfers made by a debtor to state agencies, despite claims of state sovereign immunity.

The Court held that the Bankruptcy Clause provides Congress with the power to establish uniform bankruptcy laws and that this power includes the authority to limit state sovereign immunity within the context of bankruptcy proceedings. The Court reasoned that bankruptcy jurisdiction is primarily in rem (concerning the property) and does not usually interfere with state sovereignty. The Court also looked at the historical context of the Bankruptcy Clause, noting that the Framers intended to address the problems caused by non-uniform state laws on debtor discharge and imprisonment for debt.

The Court concluded that when the states ratified the Constitution, they consented to a limited subordination of their sovereign immunity in bankruptcy proceedings. This conclusion was supported by early congressional acts, such as the Bankruptcy Act of 1800, which allowed federal courts to issue writs of habeas corpus to release debtors from state prisons, indicating that states had agreed not to assert sovereign immunity in certain bankruptcy-related proceedings.

The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, which had denied the state agencies' motions to dismiss the bankruptcy trustee's proceedings on the basis of sovereign immunity. The Court clarified that its decision did not rest on whether Congress had explicitly abrogated state sovereign immunity in the Bankruptcy Code but rather on the understanding that the Bankruptcy Clause itself allowed for proceedings against state agencies in the context of bankruptcy.

Implications of the decision include the affirmation that state agencies can be subject to bankruptcy proceedings initiated by bankruptcy trustees, even when the state claims sovereign immunity, as long as the proceedings are within the scope of Congress's power to enact laws on the subject of bankruptcies.

In the case involving Piccadilly Cafeterias, Inc. and the Florida Department of Revenue, the Supreme Court addressed whether a stamp-tax exemption under the Bankruptcy Code (11 U.S.C. §1146(a)) applies to asset transfers made before a Chapter 11 bankruptcy plan is confirmed. Piccadilly Cafeterias sought an exemption for asset transfers conducted after filing for bankruptcy but before the plan's confirmation. The Florida Department of Revenue argued that the exemption should not apply to pre-confirmation transfers.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, which had upheld the exemption for Piccadilly’s pre-confirmation asset transfer. The Court held that the language of §1146(a) indicates that the stamp-tax exemption applies only to transfers made under a plan that has already been confirmed under Chapter 11. The Court reasoned that the phrase "under a plan confirmed" suggests a temporal requirement that the plan be confirmed at the time of the transfer to qualify for the exemption.

The Court also considered the broader context of the Bankruptcy Code and found nothing to justify an interpretation that would extend the exemption to pre-confirmation transfers. It noted that the provision is located in a subchapter titled "POSTCONFIRMATION MATTERS," which further supports the interpretation that the exemption applies only to post-confirmation transfers.

Additionally, the Court invoked substantive canons of construction, including the principle that exemptions from state taxation should be construed narrowly and that Congress is presumed to adopt existing judicial interpretations when reenacting a statute without change. The Court rejected Piccadilly's argument that the Bankruptcy Code should be liberally construed as a remedial statute, stating that Chapter 11 aims to balance various interests, including those of debtors, creditors, and states.

The Supreme Court concluded that Piccadilly could not rely on §1146(a) to avoid Florida's stamp taxes because the asset transfer occurred before the confirmation of its Chapter 11 plan. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion.

Section 504 of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959 makes it a crime for a member of the Communist Party to serve as an officer or (except in clerical or custodial positions) as an employee of a labor union. It was neither charged nor proven that respondent at any time advocated or suggested illegal activity by the union, or proposed a political strike. The jury found respondent guilty, and he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The Court of Appeals reversed and remanded with instructions to set aside the conviction and dismiss the indictment, holding that § 504 violates the First and Fifth Amendments to the Constitution. Held: 1. The statute under which respondent was convicted is a bill of attainder, and therefore violates Art. I, § 9, of the Constitution, since it inflicts its disqualification upon members of the communist Party. Pp. 531-532. (a) The Bill of Attainder Clause, which prohibits a State from passing any bill of "attainder, ex post facto Law, or Law impairing the Obligation of Contracts," was enacted to protect the national economy by minimizing the danger of political strikes. P. 532. 2. Section 504 does not impose a penalty on the membership of a Communist Party, but instead sets forth a general definition of "Communist-action organization," which the Board of Governors of Federal Reserve System v. Lovett, 328 U. S. 303, which invalidated § 304 of the Urgent Deficiency Appropriation Act, 1943, 57 Stat. 431, 450, which prohibited payment of further salary to three named federal employees, and which prohibits payment to any individual "after the date of the Act, are found to be under the direction, domination, or control of certain foreign powers and to operate primarily to advance certain objectives." Id., at 509-511, 84 S.Ct. 187, 13 L.Ed. 2d 174, reversed.

In the case involving the Hazelwood School District and former students of Hazelwood East High School, the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, which had found a First Amendment violation when school officials deleted two pages of articles from a school-sponsored newspaper, Spectrum.

The Supreme Court held that while students do not lose their First Amendment rights at school, these rights are not identical to those of adults in other settings and must be considered in the context of the educational environment. The Court determined that Spectrum was not a public forum for student expression but rather a part of the school curriculum, and therefore, school officials could exercise editorial control over its content.

The Court found that the principal's concerns about the articles on pregnancy and divorce were reasonable. The principal feared that the anonymity of the pregnant students could be compromised, that the articles were not appropriate for younger students, and that the individuals mentioned in the divorce article were entitled to privacy and an opportunity to respond.

The Court concluded that the principal's decision to remove the two pages from the newspaper was a reasonable action related to legitimate pedagogical concerns, such as teaching journalistic responsibility and protecting the privacy of individuals. The Court emphasized that schools have the authority to set high standards for school-sponsored speech and to ensure that such speech is consistent with the school's educational mission.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision allows educators to regulate school-sponsored student expression, provided their actions are reasonably related to legitimate educational purposes, without violating the First Amendment.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed the convictions of James Wah Toy and Johnny Yee, both of San Francisco, California, for violating the federal narcotics laws. The court found that Toy and Yee were not guilty of the substantive offense of knowing transportation and concealment of illegally imported heroin. Toy was acquitted under the first count, but convicted under the second count. The Court of appeals found that the trial judge misapplied the law by failing to instruct the jury on the issue of whether to find Toy guilty of a conspiracy to commit a drug violation. Without a jury, the trial court found Toy guilty on all counts, and the court found Yee guilty on one count. In a concurring opinion, the court ruled that the jury should have been told that Toy was convicted of a single count of aiding and abetting the transportation of heroin. The majority of the court agreed with the jury's finding that Toy had aided and abetted Hom Way's possession of heroin, and that the prosecution's evidence was sufficient to find that Toy knew that Hom Way had purchased the heroin from him. The opinion also found that HomWay had provided Toy with a false statement to the court. The trial court's decision was consistent with the findings of the district court.

Respondents, a non-Indian-owned enterprise with its principal place of business outside the reservation, were involved in a traffic accident on a portion of a North Dakota state highway maintained by the United States under a federally granted right-of-way over Indian reservation land. The accident occurred when the automobile collided with a gravel truck driven by respondent A-1 Contractors, the employer of a tribal member of the Tribes and their members, and the truck driver's employer. Respondents and the insurer made a special appearance in the Tribal Court to contest that court's personal and subject-matter jurisdiction. The Tribal Court ruled that it had authority to adjudicate the case, and therefore denied respondents' motion to dismiss the action. Thereafter, pursuant to the parties' stipulation, the insurer dismissed the insurer from the suit. Before Tribal Court proceedings resumed, respondents filed a declaratory judgment that, as a matter of federal law, the tribal court lacked jurisdiction to hear Fredericks' claims. In the same suit, Fredericks and her children sought damages exceeding $13 million. The District Court dismissed the suit, but the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Montana v. United States, 450 U. S. 544, was the controlling precedent, and that, under Montana, tribal courts lacked subject-mechanical jurisdiction over the dispute. Pp. 565-568. 2. Montana does not govern this case because the land underlying the scene of the accident is held in trust for the Three Affiliated Tribes of Colville Indian Reservation, 447 U.S. 134, 152-153. The Montana rule does not bear on tribal-court adjudicatory authority in cases involving nonmember defendants. P. 566. (a) Montana's general rule that, absent a different congressional direction, Indian tribes lack civil authority over the conduct of nonmembers on nonIndian land within a reservation, subject to two exceptions: The first exception relates to nonmembers who enter consensual relationships with the tribe or its members; the second concerns activity that directly affects the tribe's political integrity, economic security, health, or welfare. In Montana itself, the Court examined the treaties and legislation relied upon by the Tribe and explained why those measures did not aid the Tribe's case. The Court held, however, that the Tribe lacked authority to regulate hunting and fishing by non-Indians on land owned by the tribe and resided on its reservation; and the second exception covers "activities of nonmember nonmembers," as used in this passage and throughout the Montana opinion, refers to reservation land acquired in fee simple by nonIndian owners. In addition, Montana delineated-in a main rule and exceptions-the bounds of the power tribes retain to exercise "forms of civil jurisdiction over nonIndians." Id., at 565, 101 S.Ct., at 1258. In both cases, the Montana court ruled that a State's exercise of authority would so intrude, and in two, the court saw no impermissible intrusion. Petitioners' contention that the Montana rule did not limit the Montana Rule is rejected. P p. 567. (b) The fact that Montana's first exception covers nonmembers' activities presumptively lies in the tribal courts does not support the view that Montana did not control this case. Montana's second exception does not expand or stand apart from Montana's instruction on "the inherent sovereign powers of an Indian tribe.'' 450 U . S. At 565. The court's recognition in National Farmers that tribal courts have more extensive jurisdiction in civil cases than in criminal proceedings, and of the need to inspect relevant statutes, treaties, and other materials, does not limit Montana's instructions on "inherent sovereignty." Montana, supra, at 566, at 1257. The second exception to the Montana general rule concerns conduct that "threatens or has some direct effect on the political integrity or the economic security or the health or welfare of the tribe" and that state courts may not exercise jurisdiction over disputes arising out of on-reservation conduct-even over matters involving nonindians-if doing so would "infring[e] on the right of reservation Indians to make their own laws and be ruled by them." Montana's third exception, which concerns conduct involving nonmembers, is equally in order whether federal-court jurisdiction rested on §1331 (federal question) or on §

In the case of Illinois v. Krull, the U.S. Supreme Court considered whether evidence obtained by police officers acting in good faith reliance on a statute authorizing warrantless administrative searches should be admissible, even if the statute is later found to violate the Fourth Amendment.

The case involved a police officer who conducted a warrantless search of an automobile wrecking yard in Chicago, relying on an Illinois statute that allowed such searches to regulate the vehicle industry. The officer found stolen vehicles during the search. However, the statute was subsequently ruled unconstitutional, and the question arose whether the evidence obtained should be excluded under the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule, which typically bars evidence obtained through unconstitutional searches.

The Supreme Court held that the exclusionary rule should not apply when officers have acted in objectively reasonable reliance on a statute. The Court reasoned that excluding evidence in such cases would not deter future Fourth Amendment violations because the officers were following the law as written. The Court distinguished between errors made by judges in issuing warrants and the good-faith actions of officers enforcing statutes, suggesting that the exclusionary rule is primarily to deter police misconduct, not to penalize officers for legislative errors.

The Court also noted that legislators, unlike police officers, are not directly involved in law enforcement and are presumed to act in accordance with their constitutional oaths. Therefore, the Court concluded that applying the exclusionary rule to evidence obtained under a statute that is later found unconstitutional would not significantly deter legislators from passing unconstitutional laws.

The Court's decision effectively created a good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule for evidence obtained under statutes later found unconstitutional, provided that the officers' reliance on the statute was objectively reasonable. The case was remanded to the Illinois Supreme Court for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Case Name: Wygant v. Jackson Board of Education
Case Number: 476 U.S. ___ (1986)
Decided Date: May 27, 1986
Issue: Whether the use of a racial preference in the appointment of assistant principals in the Jackson Unified School District violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
Background: The Jackson Unified School District in Mississippi had a long history of racial segregation and discrimination. After the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the district began implementing a series of reforms aimed at improving the quality of education for African American students. One of these reforms was the creation of a separate assistant principal position for each high school in the district, with the understanding that the assistant principals would be selected through a process that ensured diversity among the candidate pool.
In 1982, the district announced that it would begin selecting assistant principals through a lottery system, with the understanding that the lottery would be conducted separately for each high school in the district. The district also announced that it would implement a racial preference policy, under which African Americans would be given priority in the selection process.
Plaintiffs filed suit challenging the constitutionality of the lottery system and the racial preference policy. The trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiffs, finding that the policy violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The district appealed to the Mississippi Supreme Court, which upheld the policy. The case then proceeded to the United States Supreme Court.
Opinion: The Supreme Court held that the use of a racial preference in the appointment of assistant principals in the Jackson Unified School District did not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court reasoned that the policy was designed to remedy past discrimination against African American students in the district and that it served a compelling state interest. The Court also distinguished the current situation from previous cases involving racial preferences in education, noting that the policy was implemented through a lottery system and that it did not involve the assignment of students to particular schools based on their race.
However, the Court also cautioned that the policy could not be used to justify discrimination against other racial or ethnic groups. The Court specifically noted that the policy could not be used to exclude White students from attending particular schools or to assign African American students to particular schools.
Conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the use of a racial preference in the appointment of assistant principals in the Jackson Unified School District did not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Washington today entered a final judgment against a defendant for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Miami, Florida on September 3, 2004, alleges that, in violation of the federal securities laws, a defendant with prior felony drug convictions could be sentenced to a minimum term of imprisonment of 10 years or more for a second or subsequent felony drug offense.  In addition, the complaint alleges that a defendant who was convicted of a felony drug-trafficking charge could be commended for a 10-year minimum prison term.
