According to the complaint, however, the federal sentencing guidelines for those drug-related offenses are not consistent with the statutory text.  For example, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the District of Florida today announced criminal charges against the defendant for possession of a firearm by a convicted felon, for which the defendant was sentenced to 10 years of imprisonment, and for a third felony drug conviction for a repeat offender.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of Sections 9(a)(2)(A) and 9(b)(5) of federal law, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000, which is equal to the amount of his prison sentence.  On September 4, the court granted the SEC’s request for a temporary restraining order and ordered the defendant to surrender his passport and return to the United States.

Case Name: Mendez v. Westminster Christian School
Case Number: 75-306
Judge: Harry Blackmun
Date Decided: July 1, 1976
Vote: Unanimous
Issues: Whether Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866 allows for the recovery of attorneys' fees in a case challenging racial discrimination in private schools?

The US Supreme Court ruled in favor of George W. Bush in the presidential election against Al Gore. The ruling upheld the Florida Supreme Court's decision to stop the manual recount of ballots in four counties and allowed Bush to win the presidency.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled that the Cuban government's seizure of the assets of five leading manufacturers of Havana cigars in 1960 was an "act of state" that violated the United States' trade embargo against Cuba. The court held that the seizure of these assets did not affect the rights of the owners of the seized companies, who were located in Cuba, and who were entitled to collect payments from the three principal importers of the Cuban cigars. The defendants, Dunhill, Saks & Co., and Faber, Coe & Gregg, Inc., claimed that their payment of the preintervention accounts had been made in error and that they had no right to receive or retain such payments. The district court agreed with the defendants' position, finding that the accounts had not been seized by the government and that the former owners were not entitled to any of the money owed to them by way of collection. The District Court also found that the defendants had not violated the embargo by failing to comply with the court's orders to return the funds to Dunhill. The Supreme Court of the State of Cuba, in a separate opinion, ruled that this action was not an act of state. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit agreed, and sent the case back to the district court for further proceedings. The case is being handled by the same counsel.

Case Name: Michael v. Superior Court of Orange County
Case Number: No. 87-1555
Date Decided: December 15, 1987
Supreme Court Justices: Burger, White, Brennan, Marshall, Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, O'Connor, Thurgood Marshall
Issue: Whether a natural father has a constitutional right to seek custody of his child born outside of marriage?
Summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a natural father cannot seek custody of his child born outside of marriage unless he can show that the mother is unfit to be a custodian. The Court reasoned that the presumptive right of the mother to custody is based on the historical practice of treating mothers as the primary caregivers of children and the societal interest in protecting the stability of the family unit.

In this Supreme Court opinion, the Court addresses whether Section 330(a)(1) of the Bankruptcy Code authorizes the payment of attorney's fees for services rendered by a debtor's attorney in a Chapter 7 bankruptcy proceeding when the attorney has not been appointed under Section 327 of the Code.

The petitioner, a bankruptcy attorney, sought compensation for legal services provided after a bankruptcy proceeding was converted to Chapter 7. However, his application for fees was denied at all levels of the judiciary because he was not appointed under Section 327, as required by the courts' interpretation of Section 330(a)(1).

The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' decisions, holding that the plain language of the statute does not allow for compensation of a debtor's attorney from estate funds unless the attorney is employed in accordance with Section 327. The Court acknowledged that the statute is awkwardly worded and even ungrammatical, but this does not render it ambiguous on the issue of attorney compensation.

The Court rejected the petitioner's argument that the statute is ambiguous and requires examination of legislative history. Instead, the Court emphasized the importance of adhering to the statutory text as written, unless doing so would lead to absurd results, which the Court found was not the case here.

The Court also considered the legislative history and policy arguments but found them to be inconclusive and not persuasive enough to override the plain meaning of the statute. The Court noted that if Congress had made an error in drafting the statute, it is Congress's responsibility to amend it.

The opinion concludes that the judgment of the Court of Appeals is affirmed, meaning that the petitioner is not entitled to compensation from estate funds for the legal services provided after the conversion to Chapter 7 bankruptcy, as he was not employed by the trustee and approved by the court as required by Section 327.

Justice Stevens, joined by Justices Souter and Breyer, concurred in the judgment, acknowledging the possibility of a drafting error but agreeing with the majority's interpretation based on the legislative history and the text's natural reading.

Summary:
The Supreme Court upheld a regulation that allows companies to hire third-party providers to perform tasks traditionally done by in-house staff, without having to comply with labor laws. The Court ruled that the regulation fell within the scope of the statutory delegation to the Department of Labor and was not an "interpretive" rule. The Court also noted that the regulation was supported by substantial evidence and was not arbitrary or capricious.

Appellant, a practicing lawyer, was charged with violating Disciplinary Rules of the Ohio Supreme Court governing the practice of law in Ohio. These Rules prohibit a lawyer from accepting employment arising from his use of confidential information as bait to obtain an agreement to represent a client for a fee, and from employing confidential information as bait to obtain an agreement to represent a client for a fee. Appellant admitted that he had solicited two young women who had been injured in an auto accident, one of whom ultimately agreed to retain him as her attorney. At trial, the court concluded that the Rules were applicable to appellant's conduct, and that he had committed misconduct warranting disciplinary action. The court imposed an indefinite suspension of appellant's license to practice law. Held: 1. The Rules are not invalid under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 108-116. (a) Though in-person solicitation by a lawyer of remunerative employment involves speech, it is not entitled to the full protection accorded by the First Amendment. Bates v. State Bar of Arizona, 433 U. S. 380. Pp. 108-111. (b) Protection of the public from the evils associated with in-person solicitation by lawyers is a legitimate and important state interest. Pp. 111-113. (c) Since the Rules prohibiting solicitation are prophylactic measures whose objective is the prevention of harm before it occurs, the State has a strong interest in adopting and enforcing rules of conduct designed to protect the public from harmful solicitation by lawyers whom it has licensed. Here, the Rules were properly applied to appellant, who approached the two young women at times when they were especially incapable of making informed judgments or of assessing and protecting their own interests. Pp. 113-116. 2. Application of the Rules to appellant does not offend the Constitution. Pp. 116-117. 45 Ohio St. 2d 11, 345 N. E. 2d 57, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada today entered a final judgment against a former employee of a Las Vegas-area warehouse company who was terminated for making a false and misleading statement in an employment application.  According to the SEC's complaint, Desert Palace, Inc. employed Catharina Costa as a warehouse worker and heavy equipment operator.  The complaint alleges that Costa was singled out for "intense "stalking" by one of her supervisors, who repeatedly "stack[ed] her disciplinary record" and "frequently used or tolerated" sex-based slurs against her.  Costa allegedly suffered adverse work conditions that led to an escalating series of disciplinary sanctions, including informal rebukes, a denial of privileges, and suspension.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Costa for her role in the alleged misconduct.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Costa consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins her from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders her to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a penny stock bar.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment in favor of the Postal Service, finding that it is not subject to antitrust liability under the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, alleges that, from at least July 17, 1775 through July 26, 1875, the Postal Services violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The complaint also alleges that the Postal service violated the federal anti-fraud provision of Section 17(a)(1) and (3) and 17(b)(2) of Securities Act Section 10 and Rule 17a-3 thereunder, and that, in a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York unsealed criminal charges against the company.  According to the complaint, the SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by J.T. Tierney of the Boston Regional Office and supervised by Amy C. Barry of the Market Abuse Unit. The litigation will be led by Ms. Barry and Ms. Basinger. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the United States Postal Inspection Service, the Department of Justice, and the Federal Housing Administration.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the defendants in a related criminal case.  The court found that a defendant is deprived of his rights under the Confrontation Clause when his nontestifying codefendant's confession naming him as a participant in the crime is introduced at their joint trial, even if the jury is instructed to consider that confession only in assessing defendant's credibility.  According to the court's order, filed in federal district court in Jackson, Mississippi, on October 29, 1978, Benjamin Williams and Kareem Martin were charged with assaulting Cynthia Knighton and murdering her 4-year-old son, Koran, and her aunt, Ollie Scott. The court held that defendants are entitled to the right of confrontation by virtue of their prior convictions, and that defendants can't be held liable for their actions without admitting or denying the facts of the case. The Court also ruled that defendants cannot be restrained from making statements that are inadmissible as evidence of their guilt in a joint trial.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Mississippi today announced criminal charges against Williams and Martin. The SEC's complaint charges Williams, Martin, and Martin with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4)-8 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. The complaint seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty. The case is being handled by John R. Rymas of the SEC's Chicago Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Jennifer C. Barry.

In this case, the Supreme Court considers the constitutionality of the Detainee Transfers Act (DTA) and its impact on the habeas corpus process. The DTA establishes a review process for detainees who were originally held in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, and were subsequently moved to other locations in the United States. The review process allows detainees to challenge their continued detention and seeks to ensure that the detainees' rights are protected under the Constitution. However, the DTA limits the scope of the review process and restricts the types of evidence that can be presented. The Supreme Court holds that the DTA is constitutional and that the review process provided by the DTA satisfies the requirements of due process.

The Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 (FECA) imposes mandatory expenditure limits on the total amount a candidate for state office can spend during a “two-year general election cycle,” i.e., the primary plus the general election, in approximately the following amounts: governor, $300,000; lieutenant governor; other statewide offices; and political committees, excluding political parties, could contribute no more than $3,000. The statute imposed no limit on the amount that political parties could contribute to candidates. In 1997, Vermont enacted a more stringent campaign finance law, Pub. Act No. 64, codified at Vt. Stat. Ann., Tit. 17, §2801 et seq. (hereinafter Act 64), the statute at issue here. In addition to these expenditure and contribution limits, the Act sets forth disclosure and reporting requirements and creates a voluntary public financing system for gubernatorial elections. The Act also limits the amount of contributions a candidate, political committee, or political party can receive from out-of-state sources. The petitioners are individuals who have run for state offices in Vermont, citizens who vote in Vermont elections and contribute to Vermont campaigns, and political parties and committees that participate in Vermont politics. Soon after Act 64 became law, they brought this lawsuit in Federal District Court against respondents, state officials charged with enforcement of the Act. The District Court agreed with the petitioners that the Act’s expenditure limits violate the First Amendment. At the same time, the court found that the other contribution limits constitutional. Both sides appealed. The Court of Appeals held that all of the contribution limits are constitutional. The Second Circuit held that FECA limits may be constitutional. It also held that Act 64’’ “[e]xpenditure” limits were constitutional, holding those limits supported by two compelling interests, namely, an interest in preventing corruption or the appearance of corruption and a interest in limiting the amount state officials must spend raising campaign funds. The Circuit then remanded the case to the District Court, with instructions to determine whether the expenditure limits were narrowly tailored to those interests. Petitioners and respondents all sought certiorari. They asked the Court to consider the constitutionality of Act 64, its contribution limits and a related definitional provision. The court agreed to do so. But the Court also held unconstitutional the Act, its expenditure limits, and its other contributions limits. Both parties appealed. Held: 1. The limits are unconstitutional because in their specific details (involving low maximum levels and other restrictions) they fail to satisfy the First-Amendment requirement of careful tailoring. Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U. S. 1. That is to say, they impose burdens upon First Amendment interests that are disproportionately severe. Pp. 5–11. (a) The Court has consistently upheld contribution limits in other statutes. See Harris v. United States, 536 U.S. 545, 556–557 (plurality opinion). But, in answering these questions, the Court has recognized that stare decisis “promotes the evenhanded, predictable, and consistent development of legal principles, fosters reliance on the Constitution.” Shrink, supra, at 403–404. The record contains no indication that, for example, corruption (or its appearance) in Vermont is significantly more serious a matter than elsewhere. Moreover, other things being equal, one might reasonably believe that a contribution of say, $250 (or $450) to a candidate's campaign was less likely to prove a corruptive force than the far larger contributions at issue in the other campaign finance cases we have considered. And, in any event, the connection between high campaign expenditures and increased fundraising demands seems perfectly obvious. The respondents’ argument amounts to no more that an invitation so to limit Buckley’S holding as effectively to overrule it. The facts of the 1998 legislative elections show that the limits are sufficiently low as to generate suspicion that they are not closely drawn. And the record also shows that Vermont political parties (particularly the Republican Party) “target” their contributions to candidates in competitive races, that those contributions represent a significant amount of total candidate funding in such races, and that the contributions limits will cut the parties’ contributions to competitive races dramatically. The records also show that, unlike expenditure limits upheld in the past, and with those in force in other States, Act 64 has promoted considerable reliance. Congress and state legislatures have used Buckley when drafting campaign finance laws, and this Court has followed Buckley, upholding and applying its reasoning in later cases. And there is no alternative to the exercise of independent judicial judgment as a statute reaches those outer limits. Because there is strong indication in a particular case, i. e., danger signs, that such risks exist (both present in kind and likely serious in degree), courts, including appellate courts, must review the record independently and carefully with an eye toward assessing the statute‘s “tailoring” that would be necessary to warrant overruling

Apportionment of Wyoming's House of Representatives in accordance with the requirements of Art. 3, § 3 of the state Constitution requires that each of the State's counties "shall constitute a senatorial and representative district" and that "[e]ach county shall have at least one senator and one representative." Each county is given one representative, including the six counties the population of which fell below 7,337. The deviations from population equality were similar to those in prior decades, with an average deviation of 15% and a maximum deviation of 86%. The District Court upheld the apportionment, observing that only "five minimal adjustments" had been made since 1963, with three districts gaining a representative and two districts losing a representative because of population shifts. The three-judge District Court affirmed. Held: 1. Wyoming has not violated the Equal Protection Clause by allocating one of the 64 seats in the House to a county which is considerably lower than the average population per state representative. Pp. 4-7. (a) The population variations of which are entirely the result of the consistent and nondiscriminatory application of a legitimate state policy are entirely justified on the basis of Wyoming’s longstanding and legitimate policy of preserving county boundaries. P. 4. (b) The State’ constitutional requirement that each county shall be apportioned on a population basis is not unconstitutional. P p. 4–7. 2. The population variation of the population variations is entirely within the scope of a prima facie case of invidious discrimination under the Fourteenth Amendment so as to require justification by the State, and even a neutral and consistently applied criterion such as use of counties as representative districts can frustrate Reynolds’ mandate of fair and effective representation if the population disparities are excessively high, and the differences between the two plans are justified by Wyoming's longstanding and lawful policy of protecting county boundaries, which has particular force given the peculiar size and population of Wyoming and the nature of its governmental structure, and Wyoming has applied this factor in a manner "free from any taint of arbitrariness or discrimination." Roman v. Sincock, 377 U. S. 695, 710, 84 S.Ct., at 1458, substantial deference is to be accorded the political decisions of the people of a State acting through their elected representatives. Here it is noteworthy that by enacting the 64-member plan the State ensured that its policy of preservation of county boundaries applies nondisriminatorily. The effect of the 63-member Plan would be to deprive the voters of Niobrara County of their own representative, even though the remainder of the House would be constituted to facilitate representation of the interests of each county. See 536 F. Supp. 780, affirmed.

Two trials resulting in petitioner’s convictions for murder ended in hung juries. On retrial, the State again introduced testimony implicating another person, but the trial court excluded testimony from a potential eyewitness whose identity was disputed. The California Court of Appeal upheld the exclusion, holding that no possible prejudice could result from the incident’s merely cumulative nature. Denying discretionary review, the State Supreme Court declined to address petitioner’s argument that the trial court violated Chambers v. Mississippi, 410 U.S. 284, which holds that a combination of erroneous evidentiary rulings rises to the level of a due process violation. Instead, the court relied solely on the Chapman v. California, 386 U.S. 18, “harmless beyond a reasonable doubt” standard. When petitioner later raised his Chambers claim in federal district court seeking habeas relief, the magistrate judge agreed that the state appellate court’s failure to recognize error under Chambers constituted an unreasonable application of clearly established law, but nonetheless concluded that there had been insufficient showings that the improper exclusion of the eyewitness’ testimony had a substantial and injurious effect on the jury’s verdict under the standard set forth in Brecht v. Abruzzese, 507 U.S. 610, 631. The District Court adopted the magistrate judge’s recommendation, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed. Held: In §2254 proceedings, a court must assess the prejudicial impact of constitutional error in a state-court criminal trial under the “substantial and injurious effect” standard set forth in Brecht, whether or not the state appellate court recognized the error and reviewed it for harmlessness under the “harmless beyond a reasonable doubt” standard set forth in Chapman. Pp. 4–10. (a) Although the primary reasons the Court gave for adopting a less onerous standard on collateral review of state-court criminal judgments in Brecht turned on concerns about finality, comity, and federalism, none of them turns on whether the state court itself conducts Chapman review. Rather, they relate to factors such as the States’ interest in finality, their sovereign authority over criminal matters, and the historic limitation of habeas relief to those “‘grievously wronged,’ ” id., at 637. Because each of these concerns applies with equal force whether or not the state court reaches the Chapman question, it would be illogical to make the standard of review turn upon that contingency. Pp. 4–6. (b) Petitioner’s contrary position misreads (or at least exaggerates the significance of) a single passage from Brecht, which explains why it made no sense to adopt Chapman as the federal habeas standard. To say (a) that since state courts are required to evaluate constitutional error under Chapman it makes no sense to establish Chapman as the federal habeas standard is not at all to say (b) that whenever a state court fails in its responsibility to apply Chapman the federal habeas standard must change. And while it is plausible that three years after Brecht, Congress passed, and the President signed, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA), which renders a habeas petition ineligible absent a determination that the state court’s adjudication contravened clearly established federal law, the statute does not eliminate the need for a federal court to consider whether the state court’s harmless-beyond-a-reasonable-doubt determination was itself unreasonable. Such a conclusion is not suggested by Mitchell v. Esparza, 540 U.S. 12, nor by the text of AEDPA, which sets forth a precondition to the grant of habeas relief, not an entitlement to it. Pp. 6–8. (c) While the second part of the question presents asked here involves whether Brecht makes any real difference, asking whether Brecht makes any real difference is not the same thing as asking whether the Ninth Circuit misapplied Brecht in this particular case. If application of the Brecht standard to the facts of this case were encompassed within the question presented, so too would be the question of whether there was constitutional error in the first place. Pp. 8–9. 379 Fed.Appx. 555, affirmed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C.J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

Under the "year and a day" rule, a murder conviction could not be based solely on the victim's death occurring more than a year and a day after the alleged assault. Petitioner Wilkerson was convicted of seconddegree murder for stabbing his wife during a fight. His conviction turned on the trial court's determination that the rule did not apply, since the victim's death occurred more than a year and a day after the attack. On appeal, the Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals agreed, ruling that the rule had been abolished by a recent statute. That court rejected Wilkerson's contention that the statute itself was void under the Ex Post Facto Clause, reasoning that the rule had never been followed in Tennessee. The State Supreme Court affirmed, adding that the rule had been abolished by judicial decision as well. Held: The Tennessee Supreme Court's decision did not deny Wilkerson due process of law. Pp. 3-12. (a) The Ex Post Facto Clause applies only to legislation, not judicial decisions. Bouie v. Colubia, 378 U. S. 347, 354. Although the Clause's text refers to "any law," it is clear that Congress intended to limit the Clause's reach to statutes. By its own terms, the Clause does not apply to courts. Furthermore, extension of the Clause to cover judicial decisions would circumvent the Clause's clear text and would evince too little regard for the institutional and contextual differences between legislating and common law decisionmaking. Pp. 3-7. (b) A judicial alteration of a common law doctrine violates the principle of fair warning embodied in the Due Process Clause, and hence must not be given retroactive effect, only where it is "unexpected and indefensible by reference to the law which had been expressed prior to the conduct in issue." Bouie, supra, at 354. Here, the year and a day rule is widely viewed as an outdated relic of the common law. There is no merit to Wilkerson's contention that the judicial abolition of the rule in other jurisdictions is irrelevant to whether he had fair warning that the rule in Tennessee might similarly be abolished and, hence, to whether the Tennessee court's decision was unexpected and indefensible as applied to him. Nor is there any merit to his contention that the fact that the rule did not exist as part of Tennessee's statutory criminal code means that the court's decision was "unexpected and indefensible." Finally, the fact that the rule had never been relied upon as a ground of decision in any reported Tennessee case is highly relevant to whether the court's abolition of the rule in Wilkerson's case was "unexpected and indefensible." Pp. 7-12. 992 S. W. 2d 397, affirmed.

Following the close presidential election in Florida, the Florida Supreme Court ruled that certain counties' recounts of allegedly miscast ballots were permissible under state law and ordered that the results be added to the official vote tally. Held: 1. The Florida Supreme Court's ruling establishes new standards for resolving Presidential election contests, thereby violating Art. II, § 1, cl. 2, of the Federal Constitution and failing to comply with 3 U. S. C. § 5. Pp. 3-10. (a) An equal protection violation occurs whenever a State grants the right to vote in a particular way and fails to provide equal protection to the exercise of that right. The right to vote is protected not only in the initial allocation of the franchise but also in the manner of its exercise. The State, having chosen to give the right to vote in the special context of Article II, may not debase or dilute that right by arbitrarily and disparately treating the members of its electorate. Pp. 3-5. (b) Although the Florida Supreme Court has the authority to define what constitutes a legal vote and to mandate a recount implementing that definition, the recount mechanisms implemented in response to its decisions do not satisfy the minimum requirement for nonarbitrary treatment of voters necessary to secure the fundamental right. The State's basic command for the count of legally cast votes is to consider the "intent of the voter"; but this is unobjectionable as an abstract proposition and a starting principle. The problem arises from the absence of specific standards to ensure its equal application. The want of those standards leads to unequal evaluation of ballots in various respects. Moreover, the State Supreme Court's inclusion of vote counts based on variant standards exemplifies concerns with remedial processes that were under way. Pp. 5-9. 2. Given the Court's assessment that the recount process underway was probably being conducted in an unconstitutional manner, the Court stayed the order directing the recount so it could hear this case and render an expedited decision. However, the contest provision, as it was mandated by the State Supreme Court, is not well calculated to sustain the confidence that all citizens must have in the outcome of elections. The State has not shown that its procedures include the necessary safeguards. Thus, given the difficulty of conducting a recount in compliance with the requirements of equal protection and due process without substantial additional work, the Court stays the Florida Supreme Court's order requiring a recount. Pp. 9-10. 772 So. 2d 11, reversed and remanded.

In 1989, the Central Federal Lands Highway Division (CFLHD), which is part of the United States Department of Transportation (DOT), awarded the prime contract for a highway construction project in Colorado to Mountain Gravel & Construction Company, a Colorado-based highway construction company. To benefit from the contract's terms, the subcontractor would receive additional compensation if it hired subcontractors certified as small businesses controlled by "socially and economically disadvantaged individuals," and the Government's use of race-based presumptions in identifying such individuals, violates the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause. The District Court granted the Government summary judgment, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Adarand Constructors, Inc. (Adarand), in addition to its general prayer for "such other and further relief as to the Court seems just and equitable," specifically seeks declaratory and injunctive relief against any future use of subcontractor compensation clauses. Pp. 5-7. (a) The fact that the contract giving rise to the dispute in this case came about as a result of the Surface Transportation and Uniform Relocation Assistance Act of 1987, which provides that "not less than 10 percent" of the appropriated funds "shall be expended with small business concerns owned and controlled by socially and economically advant individuals," § 8(d)(1), entitles it to seek damages for the loss of that contract, and requires the Secretary of Transportation to establish "minimum uniform criteria for State governments to use in certifying whether a concern qualifies for purposes of this subsection," § 106(c)(4), 101 Stat. 146. The fact of past injury, while presumably affording the plaintiff standing to claim damages, does nothing to establish a real and immediate threat that the participant is not, in fact, either economically or socially disadvantaged. P. 5. (b) In addition to requiring strict scrutiny of racial classifications, the Court requires courts to make sure that a governmental classification based on race, which "so seldom provide[s] a relevant basis for disparate treatment," Fullilove v. Klutznick, 448 U. S. 448, is legitimate, before permitting unequal treatment of race to proceed. The point of strict scrutiny is to "smoke out" illegitimate uses of race by assuring that the legislative body is pursuing a goal important enough to warrant use of a highly suspect tool, and that the means chosen "fit" this compelling goal so closely that there is little or no possibility that the motive for the racial classification was illegitimate racial prejudice or stereotype. In any event, in both the 8(a) and the 8d) programs, the presumptions of disadvantage are rebuttable if a third party comes forward with evidence suggesting that the individual is not in fact either economically and socially disadvantaged, and in any event the racially discriminatory order was nonetheless within the Federal Government's power.* P. 6. (c) The Government's contention that the use of "benign" state and federal classifications to different standards does not square with the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause does not violate that holding, since the Court has long recognized that Congress, like the States, may treat people differently because of their race only for compelling reasons, and it has long been central to this Court's understanding of equal protection. The principle of consistency simply means that whenever the government treats any person unequally because of his or her race, that person has suffered an injury that falls squarely within the language and spirit of the Constitution. It says nothing about the ultimate validity of any particular law; that determination is the job of the court applying strict scrutiny, and to the extent that Metro Broadcasting is inconsistent with that holding it, it is overruled. The Court's application of the "consistency" and "congruence" in conjunction with it, in the context of action by the States-indeed, they first appeared in cases concerning affirmative action programs, see, e.g., Helvering v. Hallock, 309 U.S. 106, 119, and South Florida Chapter of Associated General Contractors v. Metropolitan Dade County, Fla., 723 F. 2d 846, followed as a matter of course. The court's reliance on cases involving federal action for the standards applicable to a case involving state legislation does not contravene any principle of appropriate respect for a co-equal Branch of the Government, see generally Arlington Heights v. Metznick, supra, at 491-492, and did so quite recently. By refusing to follow Metro Broadcasting, then, we do not depart from the fabric of the law; we restore it. This case presents precisely the situation described by Justice STEVENS' view that the Fourth Amendment guarantees equal protection as a personal right, and this Court cannot adhere to its most recent decision without colliding with an accepted and established doctrine. In this case, as between that principle and "its later misapplications," the principle must prevail. To the extent this Court has traditionally taken a skeptical view

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Southern District of New York has ruled that a 1972 New York law that provides financial assistance to nonpublic elementary and secondary schools is unconstitutional because it violates the First Amendment's right to free exercise of religion. The law provides for direct money grants from the State to 'qualifying' nonpublic schools to be used for the 'maintenance and repair of .<n>school facilities and equipment to ensure the health, welfare and safety of enrolled pupils.'8 The law also provides for a grant of $30 per pupil per year, or $40 perpupil per year if the facilities are more than 25 years old. The court ruled that the law violated the right to freedom of religion because it violated Section 2 of the Constitution's First Amendment, which states that Congress shall not make law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof. 9 The court also found that the laws violated Section 10(b) of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
No. 105, Original
Argued April 15, 1952
Decided June 23, 1952

JOHN THOMSON, SECRETARY OF COMMERCE, et al., APPLICANTS,
v.
ROMERO ET AL.

On appeal from the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York.

Mr. Robert E. Hannegan, Assistant Attorney General, Department of Commerce, Washington, D. C., for appellants.

Mr. John W. Davis, Jr., of New York City, for respondents.

MR. JUSTICE DOUBLEDAY delivered the opinion of the Court.

The Jones Act, 46 U. S. C. § 3231, provides that "any citizen of the United States who owns or operates any vessel, regardless of her nationality, under American registration, shall be liable . . . for any loss of life, damage to property or other injuries occurring to any seaman aboard such vessel." Under the general maritime law, a seafaring employee may recover for personal injuries caused by the negligence of his employer. The question presented in this case is whether the Jones Act imposes liability on an American employer for personal injuries suffered by a foreign seaman aboard an American vessel operating under a foreign flag.

The facts of this case are not disputed. Romero, a native of Spain, was hired as a cook aboard the SS Santa Maria, a Spanish steamship registered in Panama and flying the Panamanian flag. He was injured while working in the galley of the ship while it was anchored in New York Harbor. His employers were Compania Naviera de Puerto Rico, Inc., a Puerto Rican corporation, and Sociedad Anónima Compañía Transatlántica de Navegación y Comercio, S. A., a Colombian corporation. Both corporations are of diverse citizenship from Romero. The ship sailed primarily between Colombia and Puerto Rico, although it occasionally visited ports in the United States.

Romero brought an action for personal injuries against his employers in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York. The court dismissed the action for want of jurisdiction, holding that the Jones Act imposed liability only on American owners and operators of American vessels. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Jones Act applies to foreign vessels operating under a foreign flag in American waters. We granted certiorari.

The Jones Act was passed in response to the tragic sinking of the Titanic in 1912, when numerous Americans died as passengers on a British ocean liner. The Act was designed to ensure that American victims of maritime accidents would have a remedy against American owners and operators of American vessels. The Act makes no reference to foreign vessels or foreign employees. Its primary objective was to protect American lives and property on American vessels.

However, the general maritime law recognizes that a foreign seafaring employee may bring an action for personal injuries against his employer in the United States. The general maritime law is derived from English common law, which has long recognized the right of a seafaring employee to sue his employer for personal injuries caused by the employer's negligence. The general maritime law has been adopted and applied in the United States in countless cases involving personal injuries on American vessels.

The question presented in this case is whether the Jones Act conflicts with the general maritime law. We believe that it does not. While the Jones Act was designed to protect American lives and property on American vessels, it does not purport to exclude foreign seafaring employees from bringing actions for personal injuries against their American employers in the United States. The general maritime law recognizes the right of a foreign seafaring employee to sue his employer for personal injuries caused by the employer's negligence, and this right is not affected by the passage

Summary:

In this case, the Supreme Court considered the appropriate burden of proof for the fraud discharge exception under Section 523 of the Bankruptcy Code. The plaintiff sought to reduce a fraud claim to a judgment and then seek nondischargeability under Section 523(a)(2). However, the parties disagreed on the appropriate burden of proof for establishing nondischargeability. The Supreme Court ultimately decided that the preponderance-of-the-evidence standard was the appropriate burden of proof for the fraud discharge exception.

Respondent Rodriguez was arrested in his apartment with the consent and assistance of his daughter, who had lived there with him for several months. The police were summoned to the residence of respondent, who showed signs of a severe beating, and she consented to travel there with the police in order to unlock the door with her key so that the officers could enter and arrest him. Rodriguez was charged with possession of a controlled substance with intent to deliver. The Illinois Supreme Court denied Rodriguez's motion to suppress all evidence seized at the time of his arrest, holding that, as a matter of law, the police did not have common authority over the apartment. Held: A defendant's waiver of his trial rights cannot be given effect unless it is "knowing" and "intelligent." Colorado v. Spring, 479 U. S. 564, 574-575. Pp. 579-581. (a) When a state-court decision is clearly based on state law that is both adequate and independent, it will not review the decision. Michigan v. Long, 463 U.S. 1032, 1041, 103 S. C. 3469, 3476-77, 77 L. Ed. 2d 1201, distinguished. P. 578. (b) The ordinary requirement of a warrant is sometimes supplanted by other elements that render the unconsented search "reasonable." Here also, the Fourth Amendment requires factual accuracy. A warrant is not needed, for example, where the search is incident to an arrest, even though the arrest was made of the wrong person. The rationale of Stoner was ambiguous-and perhaps deliberately so. It is at least a reasonable reading of the case, and perhaps a preferable one, that the police could not rely upon the obtained consent because they knew it came from a hotel clerk, knew that the room was rented and exclusively occupied by the defendant, and could not reasonably have believed that the former had general access to the apartment when respondent was away. Even the Illinois cases cited by the opinion rely upon no constitutional provisions other than the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments of the United States Constitution. Even when a state court decision fairly appears to rest primarily on federal law, or to be interwoven with the federal law," we require that it contain a "plain statement" that [it] rests upon adequate andindependent state grounds, otherwise, "we will accept as the most reasonable explanation that the state court decided the case the way it did because it believed that federal law required it to do so." Colorado, supra, at 1041. Here, the Appellate Court's opinion contains no such statement. The opinion does not rely on (or even mention) any specific provision of the Illinois Constitution, nor even the Chicago Constitution generally. Nor does it require that a reasonable belief of common authority to validate an entry would cause a defendant's Fourth Amendment rights to be "vicariously waived." Nor does the rationale for Stoner's decision be ambiguous. The fact that the Stoner opinion had this subtlety in mind, the supposed clarity of its foregoing statement is immediately compromised, as follows: "It is true that the night clerk clearly and unambiguously consented, but there is nothing in the record to indicate that [the police] had any basis whatsoever to believe that the clerk had authority to consent to the search." Ibid. Even if Stoner did not possess common authority, there was no substance to the claim that the search was reasonable because the police had a reasonable basis for the belief that the "night clerk had authorized the police to search the petitioner's room." The facts could not possibly support it, and Stoner concluded that, even if the police reasonably believed that Fischer had the authority to give consent, the reasonable belief could never validate the entry. P p. 581. 125 Ill. 2 D. C.'s 572, 537 N. E.' 2d 816, reversed and remanded.

After respondent Moore was arrested for driving under the influence of alcohol, the officers conducted a patdown search and discovered drugs. Moore moved to suppress the drugs as fruit of an illegal arrest, arguing that Virginia law permitted arrest only for failure to comply with traffic orders and that he failed to meet that requirement. The trial court agreed and suppressed the drugs. However, the Virginia Supreme Court reversed, holding that the search was proper because the officers lacked probable cause to arrest Moore. Held: An arrest based on probable cause serves interests that have long been seen as sufficient to justify the seizure. Such an arrest ensures that a suspect answers charges and does not continue a crime, and it safeguards evidence and allows officers to conduct an in-custody investigation. These interests outweigh the State’s interest in avoiding arrests. Because the arrest rules violated here were those of state law alone, it is not the Province of the Fourth Amendment to enforce state law. Thus, the Amendment does not require the exclusion of evidence obtained from a constitutionally permissible arrest. Pp. 4–11. 272 Va. 688, 698 S.E. 2d 12, reversed and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined. Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the Fourth Circuit today entered a final judgment in favor of the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act of 1927.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, on May 24, 1940, the United States Attorney's Office for the District of New York announced criminal charges against three longshoremen who were injured while loading or unloading a ship.  The complaint alleges that the defendants' injuries were not covered by the federal insurance laws, and that Congress was without power to extend a compensation remedy to a longshoreman injured on the dock or on the deck of a ship, even if the injury was caused by a vessel on the pier.  In addition, the complaint alleges, the defendants were injured when cargo hoisted by the ship's crane swung back and knocked him to the pier or crushed him against the side of the railroad car.  As alleged in the complaint, these injuries had not occurred on the landward side of a pier, and the defendants had not been compensated for their injuries on the shore.   The SEC's Complaint, filed under seal on May 25, 1940 and unsealed yesterday, charges the defendants with violating Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the federal securities laws, ordering them to pay civil penalties in the amount of $10,000, and ordering the defendants to disgorge their gains with interest in the amounts of $20,000 and $1,500, respectively, in amounts to be determined by the court at a later date. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Karpel and supervised by Eric R. Werner.Â  The litigation will be led by Jennifer C. Barry.

At petitioner's trial in a Federal District Court for violation of the Narcotic Drugs Import and Export Act, the Government relied on the testimony of four government witnesses, including two federal narcotics agents and two police officers, who testified that they had been present when petitioner received and concealed heroin from an informer. Petitioner was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment. At the trial, the Government refused to disclose the identity of the informer, despite petitioner's repeated demands for such disclosure. 

Held: In the circumstances of this case, the trial court committed prejudicial error in permitting the Government to withhold the identity of its informer, and the conviction is reversed. Pp. 386-394.
	 (a) The informer's privilege is not absolute, and the Government's privilege to withhold from disclosure the identity of persons who furnish information of violations of law to officers charged with enforcement of that law is limited by its underlying purpose of furthering and protecting the public interest in effective law enforcement. Pp. 388-390.
	 (b) In the circumstances of this case, the identity of the informer must be disclosed whenever his testimony may be relevant and helpful to the accused's defense. Pp. 390-391.
	 (c) The materiality of the informer's possible testimony must be determined by reference to the offense charged in the indictment and the evidence relating to that count. P. 391.
	 (d) In the circumstances of this case, the trial court committed prejudicial error in permitting the Government to withhold the identity of its informer, since the informer was the sole participant, other than the accused, in the transaction charged; he was the only witness in a position to amplify or contradict the testimony of government witnesses; and his testimony might have disclosed an entrapment. Pp. 391-394. 229 F. 2d 812, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Arizona has ruled that a school's assistant principal acted reasonably when he ordered a school nurse to search a 13-year-old girl's bra and underpants for prescription drugs. The court held that the search violated the girl’s Fourth Amendment right to be secure in her persons. The ruling found that the assistant principal had not acted as an independent decisionmaker and therefore was entitled to qualified immunity from liability. The high court also held that there was no reason to suspect that the drugs presented a danger or were concealed in the student's underwear. The appeals court ruled that the district court's summary judgment in favor of the school district and the school nurse had been wrong. The district court had granted the school a motion for summary judgment on the ground that there were no Fourth Amendment violations, and the appeals court had upheld the district's judgments. The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case and issued a decision on the issue of qualified immunity. The case is now being handled by the same lawyer who successfully argued the case before the high court.

When petitioner Merrill Lynch settled its dispute with the New York Attorney General regarding the pricing of shares of several companies, respondent filed a putative class action in the Southern District of New York, claiming that Merrill Lynch had engaged in fraudulent manipulation of stock prices in violation of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s Regulation 10b–5. The district court dismissed the complaint, finding that it failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted and that it was precluded by the Securities Litigation Uniform Standards Act of 1995 (SLUA). On appeal, the Second Circuit reversed, ruling that the complaint adequately stated a claim and that SLUSA did not apply. Held: SLUSA pre-empts state-law holder class-action claims of the type alleged in respondent’s complaint. Pp. 4–13. (a) Because SLUA does not actually pre-empt any state cause of action, it does not eliminate a historically entrenched state-law remedy. Instead, it merely denies plaintiffs the right to use the class action device to vindicate certain claims. The Act contains numerous exceptions designed to preserve state jurisdiction over securities fraud claims. These exceptions reflect Congress’ sensitivity to state interests in this area and render it inappropriate for courts to create additional, implied exceptions. Furthermore, the existence of these carve-outs demonstrates that Congress did not act “cavalierly” here. Pp. 4–8. (b) The holder class action that respondent attempted to plead is distinguishable from a typical Rule 10b–5 class action in only one respect: It is brought by holders instead of purchasers or sellers. For purposes of SLUSA pre-emption, that distinction is irrelevant; the identity of the plaintiffs does not determine whether the complaint alleges fraud “in connection with the purchase or sale” of securities. The misconduct of which respondent complains unquestionably qualifies as fraud “in connection with the purchase or sale” of securities as the phrase is defined in SEC v. Zandford, 535 U.S. 813, 820, 822, and O’Hagan, 521 U.S. 651. Pp. 8–10. (c) The Second Circuit erred in envisioning a holder class action where none existed. There is nothing in the record to suggest that respondent’s proposed class action would have been certified under state law. Nor is there anything to indicate that the Second Circuit considered the possibility that the case might be dismissed under state law. Given the absence of any indication that the case would have been certified under state law, the Second Circuit should have focused on whether the case satisfied SLUSA’s requirements. Pp. 10–12. 395 F.3d 40, vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C.J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

Respondent, a supervisor at petitioner Savings Bank (bank) and manager of one of its branch offices, brought this action against Taylor and the bank, claiming that during her four years at the bank she had been subjected to sexual harassment by Taylor in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. She sought injunctive relief, compensatory and punitive damages, and attorney's fees. The District Court denied relief, but did not resolve the conflicting testimony about the existence of a sexual relationship between respondent and Taylor. The Court of Appeals reversed and remanded the case for further proceedings. Held: A claim of "hostile environment" sex discrimination is actionable under Title VII, that the District Court's findings were insufficient to dispose of respondent's hostile environment claim, and that the court did not err in admitting testimony about respondent's sexually provocative speech and dress. As to employer liability, the court relied chiefly on Title VII's definition of "employer" to include "any agent of such a person," 42 U. S. C. § 2000e-2(a)(1), as well as on the EEOC Guidelines, which hold an employer liable for sexual harassment because of such an individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. Petitioner's general nondiscrimination policy did not address sexual harassment in particular, and thus did not alert employees to their employer's interest in correcting that form of discrimination. Moreover, the bank's grievance procedure apparently required an employee to complain first to her supervisor, in this case Taylor, and respondent failed to invoke the grievance procedure and report her grievance to him. Respondent's contention that respondent's failure to use its grievance procedure, or to otherwise put it on notice of the alleged misconduct, insulates her from liability for Taylor's wrongdoing. The court also held that a supervisor, whether or not he possesses the authority to hire, fire, or promote, is necessarily an "agent" of his employer for all Title VII purposes, since "even the appearance of a significant degree of influence in vital job decisions gives any supervisor the opportunity to impose on employees" § 1604.11 (a)(3). Held: 1. Title VII affords employees the right to work in an environment free from discriminatory intimidation, ridicule, and insult. The mere existence of "sexual harassment" and a policy against discrimination, which include not only pervasive harassment but also criminal conduct of the most serious nature, must insulate petitioner from liability. Pp. 521-532. (a) The fact that respondent did not use its established grievance procedure or otherwise put on a notice of Taylor's alleged misconduct does not necessarily insulate it from liability, since in a hostile environment harassment case the employer often will have no reason to know about, or opportunity to cure, the alleged wrongdoing. P. 522. (b) The EEOC's Guidelines do require, however, an "examin[ation of] the circumstances of the particular employment relationship and the job [f]unctions performed by the individual in determining whether an individual acts in either a supervisory or agency capacity," and nothing in Title VII suggests that a "voluntariness" in submitting to Taylor's advances was immaterial to her sexual harassment claim. Nothing in the Guidelines suggests that such discrimination should not be likewise prohibited by Title VII. The language of "terms, conditions, or privileges of employment" evinces a congressional intent to strike at the entire spectrum of disparate treatment of men and women in employment, not merely psychological aspects of the workplace environment, and there is no per se rule against its admissibility. The courts in both Rogers v. EEOC, 454 F. 2d 234 (CA5 1971), and this Court's Title VII decisions have uniformly held, and agree, that a plaintiff may establish a violation of the law by proving that discrimination based on sex has created a hostile or abusive work environment in employment. The parties and amici suggest several different standards for employer liability. First, Congress wanted courts to look to agency principles for guidance in this area. While such common-law principles may not be transferable in all their particulars to Title IX, Congress' decision to define "employee" to including any "agent of an employer, surely evinces an intent to place some limits on the acts of employees for which employers under Title IX are to be held responsible. Second, absence of notice to an employer does not insulate that employer from liability

Massachusetts General Laws Ann., c. 272, provides a maximum five-year term of imprisonment for anyone, other than a registered physician or pharmacist acting in accordance with the terms of § 21A, to dispense any drug, medicine, instrument or article whatever for the prevention of conception. The statute distinguishes among three classes of distributees-first, married persons may obtain contraceptives to prevent pregnancy but only from doctors or druggists on prescription; second, single persons may not obtain contraceptives from anyone to prevent, not pregnancy, but the spread of disease; and, third, married or single persons can obtain contraceptives only from those desirous of doing so. The Massachusetts statute, unlike the Connecticut law considered in Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U. S. 2d 571, prohibits, not use, but distribution of contraceptives to unmarried persons. Held: 1. By providing dissimilar treatment for married and unmarried persons who are similarly situated, Massachusetts General Laws § 21 and 21A violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 488-478. (a) The statute's legislative purposes are not altogether clear. It is plain that the Massachusetts statute is meant to serve the health needs of the community by regulating the distribution of potentially harmful articles. Moreover, the relationship between the litigant and those whose rights he seeks to assert is not simply that between a distributor and potential distributees, but that between an advocate of the rights of persons to obtain contraceptives and those desirsous of them. The very terms of the State's criminal statutes, coupled with the de minimis effect of §§ 21-21A in deterring fornication, thus compel the conclusion that such deterrence cannot reasonably be taken as the purpose of the Massachusetts law. P. 489. (b) The relationship between Baird and those who seek to assert their rights does not simply be that of a distributor or potential distributee. The relationship is not merely that between the distributor and the potential distributeee, but also that of the individual, who acts to protect the rights and interests of a minority and the minority itself. The State could, consistently, regard the problems of extramarital and premarital sexual relations as "vils . . . of different dimensions and proportions, requiring different remedies," Williamson v. Lee Optical Co., 348 U.S. 483, 489, and the very point of Baird's giving away the vaginal foam was to challenge Massachusetts' statute that limited access to contraceptives. In any event, more important than the nature of the relationship is the impact of the litigation on the third-party interests. Insofar as the marital couple is not an independent entity with a mind and heart of its own, but an association of two individuals each with a separate intellectual and emotional makeup. If the right of privacy means anything, it is the individual's right to be free from unwarranted governmental intrusion into matters so fundamentally affecting a person as the decision whether to bear or beget a child, see Stanley v. Georgia, 394 US. 557, 89 S.Ct. 1243, 631, 690, the same rights must be the same for the unmarried and the married alike. If § 21 is no bar to a prohibition on contraceptives, the State could not, consistently with the Equal protection Clause, outlaw distribution to unmarried but not to married persons. In the absence of demonstrated harm, the statute would be both discriminatory and overbroad. The Court of Appeals, for reasons that will appear, did not consider the promotion of health or the protection of morals through the deterrence of fornicated to be the legislative aim. Instead, the court concluded that the statutory goal was to limit contraception in and of itself-a purpose that the court held conflicted "with fundamental human rights" under GrisWold. The court also held that the statute's purpose was to protect purity, to preserve chastity, to encourage continence and self restraint, to defend the sancity of the home, and thus to engender in the State and nation a virile and virtuous race of men and women. Although the State clearly abandoned that purpose with the enactment of §21A, at least insofar as the illicit sexual activities of married persons are concerned, see n. 3, supra, the Court reiterated in Sturgis v. Attorney General, 358 Mass. 37, 260 N. E.2d 687, 691, and, second, the "closely related corollary that a litigants may only assert his own constitutional rights or immunities," id., at 22, 80 S. C. 951, and concluded that, even on the assumption that the fear of pregnancy operates as a deterrent to the statute, it may no more reasonably be regarded as its purpose than its deterrence of premarit sexual relations. The judgment of the Court is affirmed. 429 F.. 2d 1398, affirmed.

In this landmark decision, the US Supreme Court ruled that the use of peremptory challenges to strike African American jurors violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court held that the use of peremptory challenges to remove black jurors "systematically" resulted in the denial of equal protection under the law. The Court also struck down a provision in Alabama's jury selection law that allowed judges to dismiss prospective jurors based solely on their race.

The Supreme Court of the United States reviewed the case involving Roy R. Torcaso, who was denied a commission as a Notary Public in Maryland because he refused to declare a belief in God, as required by Article 37 of the Maryland Constitution. Torcaso argued that this requirement violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution.

The Court held that the Maryland requirement for a declaration of belief in God as a qualification for public office was unconstitutional. The Court's reasoning was based on the principle that the government, whether state or federal, cannot impose a religious test as a condition for holding public office. This principle is enshrined in Article VI of the U.S. Constitution and reinforced by the First Amendment, which guarantees freedom of religion and prohibits the establishment of religion by the government.

The Court referenced historical context, noting that religious test oaths were a form of persecution that many early American colonists sought to escape. The framers of the Constitution intended to protect citizens from such tests, ensuring the separation of church and state and the freedom to believe or not believe in a particular religion.

The Court also cited previous cases, such as Cantwell v. Connecticut and Everson v. Board of Education, which affirmed the broad protections of the First Amendment and the principle that the government cannot favor one religion over another or punish individuals for their religious beliefs or lack thereof.

The Court concluded that Maryland's religious test for public office violated Torcaso's freedom of belief and religion and could not be enforced against him. The judgment of the Court of Appeals of Maryland was reversed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. The decision underscored the constitutional separation of church and state and the protection of individual religious freedom.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around Keyse Jama, a Somali citizen who was ordered to be removed from the United States following a criminal conviction. Jama challenged his removal to Somalia, arguing that the U.S. government could not remove him to a country that had not consented to receive him, given Somalia's lack of a functioning government.

The legal issue centered on the interpretation of 8 U.S.C. § 1231(b)(2), which outlines the process for determining the country to which an alien should be removed. Jama argued that the statute required the explicit, advance consent of the destination country before removal could occur.

The Supreme Court disagreed with Jama's interpretation. The Court held that the statute does not require the destination country's consent for removal in all cases. It noted that while the statute does include consent requirements at certain steps of the removal process, it does not explicitly require consent for all countries listed in the statute as potential destinations. The Court pointed out that the statute's language only requires consent in the final clause, which is invoked after other options have been deemed "impracticable, inadvisable, or impossible."

The Court's decision affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had reversed the District Court's ruling in favor of Jama. The Supreme Court's ruling implies that the U.S. government has the authority to remove aliens to their country of citizenship or birth, among other listed countries, even if that country has not provided advance consent to receive the individual, unless the statute explicitly states otherwise.

The decision has implications for the removal process of aliens from the United States, particularly in cases where the individual's country of citizenship is in a state of disarray or lacks a recognized government. It clarifies the extent of the Executive Branch's discretion in matters of foreign affairs and immigration enforcement, emphasizing that the statute grants the Attorney General significant leeway in selecting a destination country for removal, subject to specific conditions outlined in the law.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the case of Gary Cone, a Vietnam veteran sentenced to death, who contended that the State of Tennessee violated his right to due process by suppressing evidence that could have supported his defense and mitigated his sentence. Cone had asserted an insanity defense at his 1982 trial, claiming he committed the murders while suffering from acute amphetamine psychosis due to drug addiction. The State discredited his defense, and it was later discovered that evidence corroborating Cone's drug addiction had been suppressed.

Cone's attempts to have this new evidence considered were denied by the Tennessee courts on the grounds that his Brady claim had been "previously determined" or waived. The Federal District Court and the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit upheld this decision, barring further review in federal court.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari due to conflicting decisions from other Courts of Appeals and concluded that the Tennessee courts' rejection of Cone's Brady claim does not rest on a ground that bars federal review. The Court also found that the lower courts failed to adequately consider whether the suppressed evidence was material to Cone's sentence, even though it agreed that the evidence was not material to the question of guilt.

The Supreme Court vacated the decision of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case to the District Court to determine whether there is a reasonable probability that the withheld evidence would have altered at least one juror's assessment of the appropriate penalty for Cone's crimes.

Implications of the Decision:
The Supreme Court's decision emphasizes the importance of the State's duty to disclose evidence favorable to the defense, as mandated by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and established in Brady v. Maryland. The ruling clarifies that a state court's refusal to revisit a claim it has already adjudicated does not create a procedural bar to federal habeas review. Additionally, the decision underscores the distinction between the materiality of suppressed evidence with respect to guilt and sentencing in capital cases. The case is remanded for a thorough review of the suppressed evidence's potential impact on Cone's sentence, highlighting the Court's commitment to ensuring that justice is served by considering all material evidence that could affect the outcome of a case.

The Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether evidence obtained through electronic surveillance that may have violated the Fourth Amendment rights of the defendants should be excluded from their criminal trials. The defendants, who were convicted of various crimes, argued that their convictions were tainted by evidence derived from illegal surveillance.

The Court held that the exclusionary rule, which prevents evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment from being used in trial, applies only to those whose rights were directly violated by the search or surveillance. This means that only the person whose conversations were illegally intercepted, or whose premises were unlawfully surveilled, can seek to have the resulting evidence excluded.

The Court rejected the broader interpretation that would allow co-defendants or co-conspirators to suppress evidence obtained from surveillance that violated another person's Fourth Amendment rights. The Court emphasized that Fourth Amendment rights are personal and cannot be asserted vicariously.

The Court also determined that when illegal surveillance is discovered, the government has the burden of proving that its evidence is not tainted by the illegality. However, defendants must also present specific evidence demonstrating the connection between the surveillance and the evidence used against them.

The Court concluded that records of overheard conversations obtained through illegal surveillance should be disclosed to the defendants whose Fourth Amendment rights were violated, without first being screened by the trial judge in camera. This is because the defendants are in a better position to understand the significance of the conversations in the context of their own cases.

The Court remanded the cases to the District Court for further proceedings to determine whether any of the government's evidence was the product of illegal surveillance that violated the defendants' Fourth Amendment rights, and if so, whether the convictions were tainted by that evidence. If the District Court finds that the convictions were tainted, the defendants would be entitled to a new trial.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision limits the application of the exclusionary rule to those whose own Fourth Amendment rights were violated by illegal surveillance and requires the disclosure of surveillance records to those defendants for the purpose of challenging the admissibility of tainted evidence.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the bank, stating that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB) interpretation of the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Integrated Disclosure (RESPID) regulation was not entitled to deference. The court found that the RESPID regulation was ambiguous and that the CFBP's interpretation conflicted with the plain language of the regulation. Additionally, the court found that the CFBP's interpretation was based on a misinterpretation of the underlying statutes and that the CFBP lacked expertise in the area of real estate settlement practices.

In the landmark case of New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, the Supreme Court established that public officials must prove "actual malice" to win a libel suit, meaning they must show that a statement was made with knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for the truth. This standard was later extended to public figures as well.

The case in question, involving the New York Times and Liberty Lobby, Inc., addressed whether the "clear and convincing evidence" standard required to prove actual malice should be considered when a court is ruling on a motion for summary judgment. The District of Columbia Circuit Court had previously ruled that this standard did not need to be considered at the summary judgment stage, but the Supreme Court disagreed and reversed that decision.

The Supreme Court held that when a motion for summary judgment is made in a libel case involving a public figure, the court must consider whether the evidence presented could lead a reasonable jury to find actual malice with convincing clarity. If the evidence could not meet this standard, summary judgment may be granted to the defendant.

The Court emphasized that in making this determination, the judge should not weigh the evidence or determine the truth, but rather decide whether there is a genuine issue for trial. The evidence must be of a quality and quantity that a reasonable jury could find actual malice by clear and convincing evidence.

The Court also clarified that the plaintiff cannot simply rely on allegations or denials but must present concrete evidence that could support a jury verdict in their favor. If the plaintiff can present such evidence, then a genuine issue exists, and the case should go to trial.

The Supreme Court's decision underscores the importance of the First Amendment protections for speech and press, particularly in the context of public debate about public figures. It also establishes a clear guideline for how courts should handle summary judgment motions in libel cases involving public figures, ensuring that the high standard of proof required by the New York Times ruling is maintained throughout the legal process.

Appellant was convicted in a Los Angeles Municipal Court of violating California Penal Code § 415, which prohibits "maliciously and willfully disturb(ing) the peace or quiet of any neighborhood or person . . . by . . offensive conduct." He was given 30 days' imprisonment. The facts upon which his conviction rests are detailed in the opinion of the Court of Appeal of California, Second Appellate District, which held that "offensive conduct" means "behavior which has a tendency to provoke others to acts of violence or to in turn disturb the peace," and that the State had proved this element because, on the facts of this case, "[i]t was certainly reasonably foreseeable that such conduct might cause others to rise up to commit a violent act against the person of the defendant or attempt to forceably remove his jacket." Held: 1. The conviction rests upon the asserted offensiveness of the words Cohen used to convey his message to the public. The only "conduct" which the State sought to punish is the fact of communication. Pp. 531-532. 2. The State may not, consistently with the First and Fourteenth Amendments, make the simple use of "fighting words," those personally abusive epithets which, when addressed to the ordinary citizen, are, as a matter of common knowledge, inherently likely to provoke violent reaction. Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire, 283 U. S. 359, distinguished. P. 532. 3. In order to lay hands on the precise issue which this case involves, it is useful first to canvass various matters which this record does not present. The argument amounts to little more than the self-defeating proposition that to avoid physical censorship of one who has not sought to provoke such a response by a hypothetical coterie of the violent and lawless, the States may more appropriately effectuate that censorship themselves. Cf. United States v. O'Brien, 391 U.S. 367, 88 L. Ed. 239. 4. There is no evidence that substantial numbers of citizens are standing ready to strike out physically at whoever may assault their sensibilities with execrations like that uttered by Cohen. Moreover, there is no showing that anyone who saw Cohen was in fact violently aroused or that appellant intended such a result. P p. 533. 5. The fact that the statute seeks to preserve an appropriately decorous atmosphere in the courthouse where Cohen was arrested must fail in the absence of any language in the statute that would have put appellant on notice that certain kinds of otherwise permissible speech or conduct would nevertheless, under California law, not be tolerated in certain places. Any broader view of the State's authority would effectively empower a majority to silence dissidents simply as a result of personal predilections, and any broader view that the States, acting as guardians of public morality, may properly remove such an offensive word from the public vocabulary would effectively be empowered to silence dissident views simply as an expression of their own. Pg. 534. 6.
