Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibits discrimination on the basis of sex in educational programs and activities. The Supreme Court has held that Title IX's private cause of action allows individuals to sue schools for intentional sex discrimination. In this case, the Court considers whether Title IX's private cause of action extends to retaliation claims. The Court finds that Title IX does not allow private retaliation actions. The Court explains that retaliation is not discrimination on the basis of sex, and that the statutory language does not suggest that retaliation is a form of sex discrimination. Additionally, the Court notes that Congress has not spoken clearly enough to establish a private cause of action for retaliation under Title IX.

In this case, the Supreme Court of California held that a juvenile's request to speak with his probation officer was equivalent to a request to remain silent under the Fourth Amendment. However, the Supreme Court of the United States disagreed with this decision and held that a request for a probation officer was not a per se invocation of the Fifth Amendment right to remain silent. Instead, the Court held that whether a juvenile's request for a probation officer was a valid exercise of his right to remain silent depended on the totality of the circumstances surrounding the interrogation.

Appellants, Negro citizens of Greene County, Alabama, brought this class action against officials charged with the administration of the State's juryselection laws: the county jury commissioners and their clerk, the local circuit court judge, and the Governor of Alabama. The complaint alleged that qualified Negroes were systematically excluded from Greene County grand and petit juries, that the Alabama statutes governing jury selection were unconstitutional on their face and as applied, and that the jury commission was a deliberately segregated governmental agency; (1) a permanent injunction forbidding the systematic exclusion of Negroes from the Greene County juries pursuant to the challenged statutes and requiring that all eligible Negroes be placed on the jury roll; and (3) an order vacating the appointments of the jury commissioners, and compelling the Governor to select new members without racial discrimination. The District Court found no barrier to such a suit. Held: 1. The jury-selection process as it actually operated in Greene County at the outset of this litigation departed from the statutory mandate in several respects. It has long been accepted that the statute directed that the commission be representative of the community in which it functions, particularly in an area such as Greene County where Negroes constitute a majority of the population. Pp. 4-6. (a) The fact that § 21 is invalid on its face does not mean that it is necessarily and under all circumstances invalid. P. 5. (b) The record demonstrates that, by leaving Alabama's jury officials at large in their selection of potential jurors, it provides them an opportunity to discriminate on the basis of race-an opportunity of which they have in fact taken advantage. The record also demonstrates a causal relation between the conceded absence of Negroe from the commission for at least the past decade and the systematic racial discrimination in the selection of prospective jurors established before the District Court, and does not support the contention that the Governor deliberately appointed a segregated jury commission in exercising the discretion conferred upon him by statute. P p. 6. (c) The jury commission is not in itself unfair; it was "capable of being carried out with no racial discrimination whatsoever." P. 7. (d) The statute's antecedents are of ancient vintage, and there is no suggestion that the law was originally adopted or subsequently carried forward for the purpose of fostering racial discrimination at the hands of the officials empowered to administer it, P. 8. (e) The state courts are not incompetent to fashion detailed and stringent injunctive relief that will remedy any discriminatory application of the statute at the officials' hands, and so long as § 21 remains the law, Negro Citizens throughout Alabama will be obliged to attack the juryselection process on a county-by-county basis, thereby imposing a heavy burden on already congested court dockets and delaying the day that Alabama will not be free of discriminatory jury selection. Pc. 8-9. (f) The judgment below is of the appellants to seek modification of § 21 as circumstances may require.

In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether a statement made during a recorded conversation between a prisoner and an insurance agent was voluntary and admissible as evidence in a criminal trial. The prisoner, Raymond Atchley, had shot and killed his wife and was subsequently tried for her murder. One of the witnesses called to testify at the trial was Ray Travers, an insurance agent who had spoken with the prisoner just two days after the crime. During their conversation, the prisoner provided details of the incident, including that he had intentionally killed his wife. The conversation was recorded without the prisoner's consent.

At the trial, the prosecution presented the recorded conversation as evidence, arguing that it showed the prisoner's guilt. However, the prisoner argued that his statement was involuntary and therefore inadmissible. The Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the prisoner's statement was voluntary and admissible as evidence.

To arrive at this decision, the Supreme Court looked at various factors related to the prisoner's statement, including whether he had been threatened or coerced, whether he had been denied legal representation, and whether he had been informed of his right to remain silent. The Court found that none of these factors supported a claim of involuntariness, and that the prisoner's statement was consistent with his overall behavior throughout the trial.

Case Name: United States v. Johnson
Case Number: 07-1055
Judge: Samuel A. Alito Jr.
Date Decided: June 25, 2008

Summary:
This case involves a challenge to the constitutionality of Section 3501(c) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act, which requires financial institutions to report information regarding accounts that have been closed due to fraudulent activity. The plaintiff, a credit union, alleged that Section 3501(c) violated their privacy interests protected by the Fourth Amendment. The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of Section 3501(c) based on the principle of "fair game" in investigations involving consumer fraud. The Court held that consumers who engage in fraudulent activities lose their privacy interest in their personal financial information, and that reporting such information to law enforcement agencies is a legitimate and necessary aspect of combatting consumer fraud.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of Hanna Corporation in a labor dispute involving the Marine Engineers' Benevolent Association (MEBA). The dispute began in 1962 when MEBA attempted to organize the company's maritime engineers into a union. When Hanna refused to recognize the union, MEBA engaged in picketing at various locations where Hanna's vessels docked. The picketing involved a variety of tactics, including leaflet distribution, speeches, and demonstrations.

The Supreme Court found that the picketing was primarily aimed at compelling Hanna to recognize the union and therefore constituted "secondary" picketing, which is prohibited under Section 8(b)(4)(B) of the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA). The Court concluded that the NLRA preempts state laws that seek to enforce secondary picketing, as it conflicts with the federal interest in maintaining industrial peace and stability.

However, the Court also recognized that the NLRA contains exceptions to preemption, including situations where the state seeks to protect public health and safety or prevent fraudulent practices. In this case, the Court determined that the state's actions were justified under these exceptions, as they were taken to ensure the safe operation of the vessels and protect consumers from unsafe goods.

Overall, the Supreme Court's decision in Hanna Corporation v. Marine Engineers' Benevolent Association clarified the limits of federal preemption in labor disputes and provided guidance for states seeking to balance federal and state interests in protecting worker rights and ensuring fair business practices.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia today announced criminal charges against a Norristown, Pennsylvania man accused of stealing a bank.  According to the SEC's complaint filed in federal court in Philadelphia, Johnnie Corley, a convicted felon, was subject to an unreasonable delay in obtaining a guilty plea in a federal criminal case.  The complaint alleges that, as a result of the alleged delay, Corley was unable to consent to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of Exchange Act Rule 206(3) of 1940.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the SEC alleges that Corley consented to entry of the final judgment permanently enjoining him from violating these provisions, and ordering him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000,000.  In a parallel action, the United States District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania today entered final judgments against Corley and the other defendants in a related criminal case against him, ordering the defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and imposing civil penalties of $10,000 each.   The SEC's investigation was conducted by John Rymas and supervised by Marc Blau of the Philadelphia Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

A Washington statute provides that the designation of a spouse as the beneficiary of a nonprobate asset is revoked automatically upon divorce. Petitioner Egelhoff was married to a Boeing employee who provided him with a life insurance policy and a pension plan. Both plans were governed by ERISA. In April 1994, the Egelhoffs divorced, and Mr.Egelhoff designated his wife as his wife's beneficiary under both. Respondents sued petitioner in Washington state court to recover the life insurance proceeds. The trial courts, concluding that both the policy and the pension plan "should be administered in accordance" with ERISA, granted summary judgment to petitioner in both cases. The Washington Court of Appeals consolidated the cases and reversed, holding that the Washington statute was not pre-empted by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). The State Supreme Court affirmed. Held: The Washington statute is pre-emption under traditional principles of conflict preemption. Pp. 578-604. 139 Wash. 2d 557, 989 P. 2D 80, reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court of the United States has ruled that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies only to the offense that has been officially charged, rather than to any other offenses that may be "very closely related factually" to the charged offense. This means that a defendant's statements regarding offenses for which they have not been charged are generally admissible in court, unless the defendant has explicitly invoked their right to counsel.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit held that a patent on a device that absorbs shock from plow shanks is invalid under the new test of obviousness set out in the Patent Act of 1952. The court held that the test is not based on the manner in which the invention was made, but rather on the level of innovation necessary to sustain patentability. The Court held that there was no new result in the patented combination and that the patent was, therefore, not valid. In a separate action, the U.N. District Court for the District of Columbia granted summary judgment in favor of Calmar, Inc., a manufacturer of a finger-operated sprayer with a 'hold-down' cap, and against Cook Chemical Co., which used the sprayer in the distribution of its products. The Second Circuit, however, held that Calmar's patent was valid, and that Cook Chemical's was invalid. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued a decision on the issue. The case is being closely watched by patent attorneys and others in the patent industry.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the issue was whether an annual registration tax imposed by Congress on all civil aircraft flying in U.S. airspace, as part of a program to fund federal aviation programs, was constitutional when applied to state-owned aircraft used exclusively for police functions.

The Court held that the tax did not violate the implied immunity of state governments from federal taxation. The Court reasoned that the tax was part of a comprehensive program designed to ensure that users of the national air system contribute to its costs. The program included increased federal spending on airport and airway development, as well as various taxes on civil aviation conceived as user fees. These fees were intended to make users bear a fair share of the costs and to prevent the air system's capacity from becoming insufficient due to competing budgetary demands.

The Court rejected the argument that the tax was unconstitutional because it was not directly related to the use of the airways, noting that the tax was only one part of a network of user charges and that it was the only tax imposed on state-owned noncommercial aircraft. The Court also pointed out that the tax was nondiscriminatory, as it applied to all civil aircraft, including those owned by the federal and state governments.

The Court's decision affirmed the lower courts' rulings and held that the tax was a valid user fee. It concluded that a state has no constitutional objection to a revenue measure that does not discriminate against state functions, is based on a fair approximation of use, and is not excessive in relation to the benefits provided. The decision implies that states can be required to contribute to the costs of federal programs from which they benefit, as long as the charges are reasonable and nondiscriminatory.

The U.S. District Court for the District of North Dakota today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant in a product liability action against Marley Co., Inc., a company that manufactured and sold a baseboard heater.  The court's order, which entered the final judgment on the merits of the case, permanently enjoins the defendant from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendant to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty equal to the amount of his or her penalty.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Weisgram.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court for the district court's jurisdiction, the defendant failed to adequately disclose to the trial judge that he or she had failed to meet their burden of proof on the issues of defect and causation.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of judgment as a matter of law on the basis of the evidence that was improperly admitted at trial, and the jury agreed to a new trial based on the findings of the trial court.   The final judgment against the defendant, which was entered on a joint and several basis with the court of appeals, reserves the right to determine whether a judgment for the defendant is warranted.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 522 (1940).  The SEC's Office of Investor Education and Advocacy has issued an Investor Alert on the dangers of misapplying or misleading information in jury trials.  Investors can quickly and easily check the background of anyone offering or offering them an investment using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

When respondent Pelterier worked for petitioner Savings Assn. of Oakland County, Michigan, he was dismissed for failing to meet performance standards. He sued petitioner and others in Federal District Court, alleging, among other things, that petitioner had acted with malicious intent in firing him in violation of his Fourteenth Amendment right to equal protection. The District Court entered summary judgment for petitioner, rejecting Peliterier's qualified-immunity defense. The Court of Appeals vacated the summary judgment and remanded for entry of judgment on the pleadings, holding that a defendant can take only one interlocutory appeal from a denial of qualified immunity. Subsequently, the District Court again entered summary judgment for petitioner, and the Court of Appeals again vacated and remanded, holding that the District Court erred in considering Peliterier's lost-employment claims because they were untimely. Finally, the District Court entered summary judgment for petitioner on Peliterier's lost-employment claims, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. An order rejecting the defense of qualified immunity at either the dismissal stage or the summary-judgment stage is a "final" judgment subject to immediate appeal. While Mitchell v. Garrison, 472 U. S. 598, did not expressly hold that a defendant could appeal from denial of a qualified-immunity defense more than once, it clearly contemplated that he could raise the defense at successive stages. Here, the Court of Appeals' "one-appeal" pronouncement rested upon the proposition that resolving the question of entitlement to qualified immunity should not require more than one judicially timed appeal. However, that proposition is not sound. One appeal on the immunity issue may not be enough, because the legally relevant factors bearing upon the Harlow question will be different on summary judgment than on an earlier motion to dismiss. More importantly, the availability of a second appeal affords an opportunity for abuse, but there is no reason to believe that abuse has often occurred. Successive pretrial assertions of immunity seem to be a rare occurrence. In any event, the question before this Court is whether there is jurisdiction over the appeal, as opposed to whether the appeal is frivolous, and that question must be determined by focusing upon the category of order appealed from, rather than upon the strength of the grounds for reversing the order. Pp. 836-840. 2. Rejecting the one-interlocutory-appeal rule does not dispose of this case. Respondent's arguments that no appeal is available where, even if the District Court's qualified-immunity ruling is reversed, the defendant will be required to endure discovery and trial on matters separate from the claims against which immunity was asserted, and that appeal of denial of the summary-judgment motion is not available because the denial rested on the ground that "[m]aterial issues of fact remain," are rejected. Pp. 840-842. 968 F. 2d 869, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a Virginia-based company and its affiliated collective bargaining agent for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 703(h) of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Richmond, Va. on April 8, 1964, American Tobacco Co. ("T&T") and its affiliate Local 182 (collective bargaining agent) Gibson, Inc. ("GGI") agreed to settle charges that the company violated the federal anti-discrimination provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) of The Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The settlement is subject to court approval.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Gibson.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by John R. Rymas and Eric R. Werner of the SEC Enforcement Division's Market Abuse Unit, with assistance from Robert A. Hannan of the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis. The litigation will be led by Mr. Werner and Ms. Werner.

After petitioner was convicted of obtaining $120.75 by false pretenses, a violation of Texas law, he was tried and convicted of the felony of obtaining $120.75 by false pretenses, and the jury found that he had previously been convicted of two other felonies. Thereafter, pursuant to Texas law, he was sentenced to life imprisonment. Subsequently, he brought suit in Federal District Court challenging the constitutionality of his life sentence, claiming that it was grossly disproportionate to the three felonies for which he was convicted. The District Court entered judgment for petitioner, but the Court of Appeals reversed. Held: The mandatory life sentence imposed upon petitioner does not constitute cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 409-420. (a) While the Eighth Amendment prohibits a sentence that is grossly disproportionate to the offense, the uniqueness of the death penalty renders it impossible to determine what constitutes gross disproportion in noncapital cases. Pp. 409-410. (b) An examination of the precise operation of the Texas recidivist statute reveals that the mandatory life sentence imposed upon petitioner resulted solely from the combination of three consecutive felonies, none of which was a violent felony, and that the statutory requirement that the sentence include the possibility of parole was satisfied by the fact that petitioner had served 12 years before becoming eligible for parole. Pp. 410-415. (c) Comparison of Texas' recidivist statute with those of other States indicates that Texas' statute is not unusually severe. Nor does the possibility of parole serve to distinguish Texas' statute from others. Pp. 415-418. (d) Texas is entitled to make its own judgment as to where the line dividing felony theft from petty larceny lies, subject only to those strictures of the Eighth Amendment that can be informed by objective factors. Pp. 418-420. 587 F. 2d 115, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois today entered a final judgment against a federal judge who was found to have violated the pre-judgment provision of the Compensation Clause of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia on January 31, 1979, Judge Gouverneur Morris, a former federal judge, was found liable for violations of the compensation provision of Section 5 of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934.  The SEC alleges that, in the three preceding years, the court issued an order requiring the appointment of an agent to determine the amount of a judge's salary increase.  As alleged in the complaint, the order did not require a judge to pay the 5.8% increase, but instead required him to do so at a later date.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Morris.  On February 7, 2020, the District Court entered a judgment that permanently enjoins the court from future violations of this provision, and orders the court to issue an order imposing a temporary restraining order, imposing a $75,000 civil penalty, and appointing a temporary judge.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Morris consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the provisions of the Commission on Executive, Legislative, and Judicial Salaries, and ordering him to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount he received as a result of his misconduct.  Judge Morris also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public agency.  A hearing on the matter is scheduled for September 24, 2020.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 549 (1939).  The Commission's complaint charges the court with violating the antifraud provisions of Sections 549(1) and 575(2) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties against him.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina ruled in favor of the Washington State Apple Advertising Commission's challenge to a North Carolina law that prohibits the display of Washington State apple grades on closed containers of apples shipped into the state. The court found that the law violated the First Amendment right to free speech and the Fourteenth Amendment's right to equal protection under the law. The Court also ruled that the Commission did not have standing to bring the action. The case is being appealed by the North Carolina Board of Agriculture, which has refused to comply with the court's ruling. The Board's appeal will be heard by the full court on October 2, 2014.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was convicted of double jeopardy for the purpose of enhancing the prison sentence for a previous felony conviction.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Baltimore, Maryland, alleges that Millard Fillmore Ball was indicted for the murder of one William T. Box in the Indian Territory. He was found guilty of both the larceny and burglary counts and sentenced to 10 years in prison.  According to the complaint, the court found that the defendant was entitled to a concurrent three-year prison sentence.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Maryland today announced criminal charges against Palko for the same felony.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, the defendants were not convicted of the same crimes, and the judge sentenced them to 5 years and 5 years, respectively.  Palkos' double jeopardy claim was rejected on the basis of the fact that he had been acquitted of both counts in a single indictment tried on the same day.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the Complaint or otherwise, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $100,000, which is equal to the amount of his prison time.   The complaint also seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties against the defendants.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, which had held that a copyright holder's failure to comply with the registration requirement of §411(a) of the Copyright Act deprived federal courts of jurisdiction to adjudicate copyright infringement claims. The Supreme Court clarified that the registration requirement is a precondition to filing a claim, not a jurisdictional restriction. This means that while copyright holders must generally register their works before suing for infringement, this requirement does not limit the power of federal courts to hear such cases.

The Court's reasoning was based on the distinction between jurisdictional conditions, which concern a court's power to hear a case, and claim-processing rules, which are procedural requirements. The Court found that §411(a) does not clearly state that its registration requirement is jurisdictional. It also noted that the requirement is separate from the jurisdiction-granting provisions and allows for certain exceptions.

The Court also addressed the historical treatment of §411(a), stating that while it has been treated as jurisdictional in the past, this alone is not decisive. The Court concluded that the registration requirement is more analogous to nonjurisdictional conditions considered in previous cases.

The Supreme Court's decision means that federal courts have the authority to adjudicate copyright infringement claims even if the works involved are unregistered, subject to certain exceptions. The Court did not address the merits of the settlement at issue in the case or whether the registration requirement is a mandatory precondition to suit that district courts may enforce on their own initiative. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. Justice Sotomayor did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

The Supreme Court reversed a decision by the Court of Appeals regarding a case involving alleged violations of Section 2 of the Sherman Act, which addresses monopolization, attempts to monopolize, and conspiracies to monopolize trade or commerce. The case involved BTR, Inc., and its subsidiaries, which owned the patent rights to a shock-absorbing polymer called sorbothane, and their interactions with regional distributors, including the respondents, Shirley and Larry McQuillan of Sorboturf Enterprises.

The McQuillans sued BTR and its subsidiaries, claiming they had been unfairly pushed out of the market for sorbothane products, leading to the failure of their business. The jury found the defendants guilty of monopolizing, attempting to monopolize, and/or conspiring to monopolize, and the District Court entered a judgment against them, which was affirmed by the Court of Appeals. The Court of Appeals held that the defendants had attempted to monopolize, even though the respondents did not prove that the defendants had a specific intent to monopolize a relevant market or that there was a dangerous probability of them achieving monopoly power.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the Court of Appeals, stating that to prove attempted monopolization, it is necessary to show not only predatory or anticompetitive conduct and a specific intent to monopolize but also a dangerous probability of achieving monopoly power in a relevant market. The Court emphasized that the Sherman Act is designed to protect the public from market failures, not to protect businesses from competition. The Court found that the instructions given to the jury and the Court of Appeals' affirmation were legally incorrect because they did not require proof of the relevant market or the likelihood of achieving monopoly power in that market.

The Supreme Court's decision means that for a party to be liable for attempted monopolization under Section 2 of the Sherman Act, there must be proof of a dangerous probability of monopolizing a specific market, in addition to the specific intent to do so. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The Supreme Court was tasked with interpreting the term "reserve strengthening" as it pertains to the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and its impact on property and casualty (PC) insurance companies. The Act required PC insurers to discount their loss reserves to present value when claiming them as a tax deduction. A transitional rule allowed insurers to exclude from taxable income the difference between undiscounted and discounted year-end 1986 loss reserves, known as a "fresh start." However, any "reserve strengthening" occurring in 1986 was not eligible for this exclusion.

The central issue was whether "reserve strengthening" referred only to increases in reserves due to changes in methods or assumptions, as argued by Atlantic Mutual Insurance Co., or if it encompassed any increase in reserves. The Supreme Court had to determine the validity of the Treasury Department's regulation, which defined "reserve strengthening" as any net addition to reserves, regardless of the reason for the increase.

The Court found that the term "reserve strengthening" did not have a plain meaning either in the PC insurance industry or in prior tax legislation. Therefore, the Court's task was to assess whether the Treasury's regulation was a reasonable interpretation of the term, not necessarily the best one.

The Court concluded that the Treasury's broad interpretation of "reserve strengthening" to include all increases in reserves was reasonable. The Court rejected Atlantic's argument that this interpretation could lead to absurd results, stating that such scenarios were unrealistic in the context of the insurance industry, which deals with a large number of cases where discrepancies tend to offset each other.

The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, upholding the Treasury regulation as a reasonable interpretation of "reserve strengthening." This decision meant that PC insurers could not exclude from taxable income any net additions to their loss reserves for the year 1986, regardless of the reasons for those increases.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Texaco and Shell Oil in a lawsuit filed by a group of service station owners who alleged that the companies colluded to fix gasoline prices. The Court held that it is not per se illegal under section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act for a lawfully integrated joint venture to set the prices at which it sells its products. The Court based its decision on the historical relationship between Texaco and Shell Oil, noting that they had previously competed with each other in the national and international oil and gasoline markets. However, in 1998, they formed a joint venture called Equilon Enterprises to consolidate their operations in the western United States and end competition between the two companies in the domestic refining and marketing of gasoline. The Court emphasized that Equilon's pricing policy amounted to little more than price setting by a single entity and not a pricing agreement between competing entities with respect to their competing products.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California today entered a final judgment against the United States Forest Service for failing to enforce the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The final judgment, which is subject to court approval, permanently enjoins the Forest Service from enforcing certain of its regulations for more significant land management decisions.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in the Western District of Texas, filed on February 27, 2009, and unsealed today, the court found that, in violation of the federal securities laws, defendants lacked standing to challenge certain of the regulations.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against one of the defendants, Ara Marderosian, who was charged with violating Section 15(b)(5)(A) and Rule 15(c).  The court also found that the defendants had no standing to respond to the court order, and that the court had no jurisdiction to determine whether to issue an order imposing a temporary restraining order or an order requiring the defendants to return to their homes or businesses.   The SEC also announced that it had obtained a court order temporarily restraining the defendants from violating the federal anti-fraud provisions.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining them from future violations of the charged provisions, and ordering them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.  On February 26, 2008, the Court granted a preliminary injunction against the defendants and ordered them to comply with the court orders.

After petitioners, subcontractors to the United States Navy, allegedly submitted false statements to obtain payment for work performed on ships constructed under Navy contracts, respondents filed suit in the District Court as qui tam relators under the False Claims Act (FCA), 31 U. S. C. §§3729 et seq. They claimed that petitioners had submitted false invoices to the Navy, which paid the shipyards, and that petitioners had issued false certificates of conformity stating that the work had been completed according to Navy standards. The District Court granted petitioners’ motion for judgment as a matter of law, rejecting respondents’ argument that they did not have to present evidence that a claim had been submitted to the Government because they showed that Government funds had been used to pay the invoices. The Sixth Circuit reversed in relevant part, recognizing that liability under §3729(a)(1) requires proof that a false claim was presented to the Government, but concluding that §§3729(a)(2) and (a)(3) do not. Held: 1. To satisfy §3729(a)(2), a plaintiff must demonstrate that the defendant made a false record or statement for the purpose of getting “a false or fraudulent claim paid or approved by the Government.” Pp. 4−7. (a) Interpreting §3729(a)(2) as requiring only that a false statement result in the use of Government funds to pay a false or fraudulent claim impermissibly deviates from the statute’s language. That provision imposes civil liability on any person who “knowingly makes, uses, or causes to be made or used, a false record or statement to get a false or fraudulent claim paid or approved by the Government.” Here, the defendant must make the false record or statement “to get” a false or fraudulent claim “paid or approved by the Government.” “To get” denotes purpose, and thus a person must have the purpose of getting a false or fraudulent claim “paid or approved by the Government” in order to be liable under §3729(a)(2). Moreover, getting a false or fraudulent claim “paid . . . by the Government” is not the same as getting a false or fraudulent claim paid using “government funds.” Under §3729(a)(2), a defendant must intend that the Government itself pay the claim. Eliminating this element of intent, as the Sixth Circuit did, expands the FCA far beyond its intended role of combatting fraud against the Government. Pp. 4−5. (b) The Government’s contrary position is unpersuasive. Its example involving paying bills with parental funds is uncustomary in statutory drafting, where precision is both important and expected. And the fact that a “claim” under §3729(c) may be made to a contractor, grantee, or other recipient of Government funds without being made directly to the Government does not alter the meaning of the phrase “by the Government” in §3729(a)(2). Under §3729(c), a request or demand may constitute a “claim” even if the request is not made directly to the Government, but under §3729(a)(2) it is still necessary for the defendant to intend that a claim be “paid … by the Government” and not by another entity. Thus, §3729(a)(2) does not require proof that a defendant’s false record or statement was submitted to the Government. Although §3729(a)(1) requires a plaintiff to prove that the defendant “present[ed]” a false or fraudulent claim to the Government, the inclusion of an express presentment requirement in subsection (a)(1), combined with the absence of anything similar in subsection (a)(2), suggests that Congress did not intend to include a presentment requirement in subsection (a)(2). What §3729(a)(2) demands is not proof that the defendant caused a false record or statement to be presented or submitted to the Government but that the defendant made a false record or statement for the purpose of getting “a false or fraudulent claim paid or approved by the Government.” Pp. 5−7. 2. To satisfy §3729(a)(3), a plaintiff must demonstrate that the alleged conspirators intended “to defraud the Government.” Where the conduct that the conspirators are alleged to have agreed upon involved the making of a false record or statement, it must be shown that the conspirators had the purpose of “getting” the false record or statement to bring about the Government’s payment of a false or fraudulent claim. It is not necessary to show that the conspirators intended the false record or statement to be presented directly to the Government, but it must be established that they agreed that the false record or statement would have a material effect on the Government’s decision to pay the false or fraudulent claim. Pp. 7−8. 471 F. 3d 616, vacated and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Kentucky today entered a final judgment against a Kentucky-based company and its owner in a case that raised the issue of trademark dilution.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Elizabethtown, Kentucky, alleges that, in 1998, Victor and Cathy Moseley spent over $55 million advertising Victoria's Secret's "Victor's Secret" brand in a store setting designed to look like a wom'n's bedroom. The complaint alleges that the mark was "distinctive and fanciful" and, in addition, that it was "arbitrary," fanciful, and therefore deserving of a high level of trademark protection.  According to the complaint, the Moseleys' use of their mark was likely to cause confusion and/or mistake among potential customers, and would inevitably cause the mark to dilute the value of the mark.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  On March 24, 2018, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. Mascianica of the Federal District Court in Jackson, Mississippi issued a temporary restraining order and ordered the defendants to comply with the court's order.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering them to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest of $2,038, which is equal to the amount of their profits.   The court also ordered the companies to pay civil penalties of $250,000 and $100,000, respectively, for violations of the anti-dilution provisions of Sections 5(a) and 5(c).  The defendants also agreed to pay a civil penalty of $150,000. Â The SEC's investigation was conducted by Michael J. Klieger and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry. The litigation will be led by B. Pattishall, D. Hilliard, & J. Welch.

After respondent Cone was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death in 1982, the Tennessee Supreme Court ultimately affirmed, ruling that the evidence supporting his insanity defense was insufficient to meet the burden of proving that he was mentally unable to commit the crimes. Subsequently, Cone sought postconviction relief, claiming that the prosecution had withheld evidence that would have bolstered his defense and rebutted the State’s efforts to cast doubt on his claimed drug addiction. The trial court dismissed the claim as previously determined, and the intermediate appellate court affirmed, stating that Cone had failed to rebut the presumption of waiver as to all claims raised in his second petition for postconviction relief that had not been previously determined. The State argues that the latter court effectively held that Cone waived his Brady claim. Held: 1. The State’s procedural rejection of Cone’s Brady claim does not bar federal habeas review of the claim’s merits. Pp. 4–10. (a) The State’s argument that Cone waived his Brady claim ignores the fact that the State’s highest court approved the trial court’s reasoning rather than expressly holding that Cone waived the claim. Had the State meant to rely on the waiver theory, it should have raised the issue in the postconviction proceedings. Even assuming that the State meant to rely on the waiver theory here, the State’s mistake is understandable given that the State’s highest court initially thought that Cone’s Brady claim had been previously determined. Pp. 4–7. (b) The State’s argument that the waiver theory controls regardless of whether the State meant to rely on it overlooks the fact that the State’s highest court’s decision was based on an approval of the trial court’s reasoning rather than on an unmentioned failure by Cone to adequately challenge the dismissal of his Brady claim on appeal. If anything, the State’s highest court’s decision supports Cone’s view that the State’s courts should have accepted his belated challenge to the dismissal of his Brady claim. Pp. 7–8. (c) Assuming that the State meant to rely on the waiver theory, the State’s mistake is understandable given that the State’s highest court initially thought that Cone’s Brady claim had been previously determined. Even assuming that the State meant to rely on the waiver theory here, the State’s mistake is understandable given that the State’s highest court initially thought that Cone’s Brady claim had been previously determined. Pp. 4–7. (d) The State’s argument that the waiver theory controls regardless of whether the State meant to rely on it overlooks the fact that the State’s highest court’s decision was based on an approval of the trial court’s reasoning rather than on an unmentioned failure by Cone to adequately challenge the dismissal of his Brady claim on appeal. If anything, the State’s highest court’s decision supports Cone’s view that the State’s courts should have accepted his belated challenge to the dismissal of his Brady claim. Pp. 7–8. 2. Whether there is a reasonable probability that, had the suppressed evidence been disclosed, the result of the proceeding would have been different is the standard to be applied by the District Court in evaluating the merits of Cone’s Brady claim on remand. Because neither the District Court nor the intermediate appellate court considered the merits of Cone’s claim with respect to the effect of the withheld evidence on his sentence, it is appropriate for the District Court, rather than this Court, to do so in the first instance. Pp. 10–11. 527 F. 3d 451, vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Kagan, J., joined.

Petitioner Cone, a Vietnam veteran sentenced to death, contends that the State of Tennessee violated his right to a fair trial by suppressing witness statements and police reports that would have corroborated his trial defense and bolstered his case in mitigation of the death penalty. At his trial in 1982, Cone asserted an insanity defense, contending that he had killed two people while suffering from acute amphetamine psychosis, a disorder caused by drug addiction. The State discredited that defense, alleging that Cone’s drug addiction was “baloney.” Ten years later, he learned that the state had suppressed evidence supporting his claim of drug addiction, including statements by witnesses who had seen Cone during and several days after the murders. Cone then filed a petition for postconviction relief, primarily raising claims that his trial counsel had been ineffective; the Tennessee courts denied the petition, concluding that all the claims raised in it had either been “previously determined” or “waived,” Cone v. State, 747 S. W. 2d 353. On application for habeas corpus pursuant to 28 U. S. C. §2254, the Federal District Court concluded that state courts’ disposition rested on an adequate and independent state ground that barred further review in federal court, and the Court of Appeals agreed. The Sixth Circuit affirmed. Held: 1. The Tennessee courts rejected Cone's Brady claim. Pp. 5–11. (a) The State’S rejection of Cone ’s Brady claim does not rest on a ground that bars federal review. The fact that the evidence suppressed at his trial may well have been material to the jury‘s assessment of the proper punishment in this case does not bar federal review of the Brady claim, since it provides strong evidence that the claim has already been given full consideration by the state courts and thus is ripe for federal adjudication. See, e.g., Tenn. Code Ann. §39–2–203(j)(8). The State is obliged to “prosecute with earnestness and vigor” it “is as much [its] duty to refrain from improper methods calculated to produce a wrongful conviction as it is to use every legitimate means to bring about a just one.’” Berger v. United States, 295 U.S. 78, 88. P. 5. (b) The evidence suppressed by the State is not material to a claim that is material to his guilt or punishment, and it is not defaulted. Nor is the evidence in its entirety material to that claim. The evidence in question is not “material” within the meaning of Brady when there is a reasonable probability that, had the evidence been disclosed, the result of the proceeding would have been different. See id., at 756. The suppressed evidence, viewed cumulatively, may have persuaded the jury that the defendant had a far more serious drug problem than the prosecution was prepared to acknowledge, and that his drug use played a mitigating, though not exculpating, role in the crimes he committed. Moreover, the suppressed evidence might also have rebutted the State suggestion that he manipulated his expert witnesses into falsely believing he was a drug addict when in fact he did not struggle with substance abuse. Neither the Tennessee Court nor the District Court fully considered whether the suppressed information might have persuaded one or more jurors that the drug use was sufficiently serious to justify a decision to imprison Cone for life rather than sentence him to death. Because the evidence was suppressed at the time Cone was convicted of murder, no Tennessee court has reached the merits of his Brady claim either because the claim was twice presented to the State courts or because it was waived, and thus not presented at all. See Brady v. Ohio, 473 U.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana today entered a final judgment in favor of the city of Indianapolis in a related civil injunctive action.  The court found that the city violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois today announced criminal charges against the city.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Indianapolis, Indiana, the city agreed to pay $9,278, $927, and $1,038, respectively, in a lump sum and over time in installment plans.  As alleged in the complaint, the City then failed to provide the investors with refunds at the same time that it forgave the outstanding project debts of other investors.  Without admitting or denying the allegations, the court also ruled that the City violated the federal securities laws and that it had a reasonable basis for distinguishing between those who had already paid their Barrett Law assessment and those who did not.  For example, the complaint alleges that, in light of the federal law, that a city could not just "cut . . . checks,” without taking funding from other programs or finding additional revenue, without imposing an unreasonable burden of collecting and paying out small amounts of money for years, and without imposing a "fundamental right" or "suspect" to the city’s allocation of taxes.   The SEC also found that, contrary to what the court had previously ruled, a city can’t just “cut” the estimated total cost of a project by simply adding it to the total number of lots it has, even if the lot would benefit less than would others.  Specifically, the SEC has found that a municipal tax exemption does not apply to certain types of property, and that, as a result of the Barrett Law exemption, an individual may not be entitled to a refund.  It also finds that, based upon the nature of the alleged violations of the Federal securities laws, a municipality may not have the reasonable basis to make a rational determination about whether or how to allocate its funds.  Further, the Court found that in 2005, the Indiana Department of Public Works adopted a new system, called the Septic Tank Elimination Program (STEP), which allowed the city to allocate millions of dollars in annualized refund payments in part through bonds, thereby lowering in-state and out-of-state government debt. The court also granted summary judgment against the City in 2011.

Title 13 U. S. C. § 141 authorizes the Secretary of Commerce to prescribe the "form and content" of the decennial census, and § 144 specifies that the census shall be taken "in such manner as [Congress] shall by Law direct." Section 141(a)(1) empowers the Secretary to delegate his responsibilities to officers and employees of the Census Bureau. In 1990, the Bureau successfully counted 98.4 percent of the population. The Secretary then had to decide whether to adjust the census using statistical data derived from the PostEnumerate Survey (PES), a pilot program that tested the feasibility of using statistical adjustment to improve the accuracy of the census. Based on three determinations, the Secretary decided not to adjust the census. First, he held that in light of the census' constitutional purpose of determining the apportionment of representatives among the States, its distributive accuracy was more important than its numerical accuracy. Second, he determined that the unadjusted census data would be considered the most distributively accurate absent a showing to the contrary. Third, after reviewing the PES results in light of extensive research and the advice of his advisors, the Secretary found that the PES-based adjustment would not improve distributive accuracy. Respondents, individuals who claimed that the census undercounted certain minority groups, sought injunctive relief, alleging that the Secretary's failure to adjust the census violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court dismissed the complaint, but the Ninth Circuit reversed, applying the "one person-one vote" standard of Wesberry v. Sandoval, 524 U. S. 978, and its progeny, which holds that a State conducting intrastate redistricting must make a good-faith effort to achieve population equality. Held: The Secretary's decision not to adjust the census was well within the constitutional bounds of discretion over the conduct of the census provided to the Federal Government. Pp. 10-18. (a) This Court's intrastate districting cases establish that the "one person-one vote" standard does not translate into a requirement that the Federal Government conduct a census that is as accurate as possible. The Secretary's decision was made pursuant to Congress' direct delegation of its broad authority over the census. Furthermore, the Constitution itself provides no real instruction on how to balance numerical and distributive accuracy. Montana v. United States Dist. Judge Walgren, ante, p. 403, distinguished. Pp. 10-13. (b) So long as the Secretary's conduct of the census is "consistent with the constitutional language and the constitutional goal of equal representation," Franklin v. G. D. R. R. Corp., 505 U. S. 804, 804, it is within the limits of the Constitution. The Secretary's decision need bear only a reasonable relationship to the accomplishment of an actual enumeration of the population, keeping in mind the constitutional purpose of the census. Pp. 13-14. (c) The Secretary's first determination-that in light of the census' constitutional purpose, its distributive accuracy was more important than its numerical accuracy-is well within the bounds of his constitutional discretion. To the extent that the potentially divisive and complex issues associated with apportionment can be narrowed by the adoption of both procedural and substantive rules that are consistently applied year after year, the public is well served. P. 14. (d) Nor is the Secretary's second determination-that the unadjusted census data would be considered the most distributively accurate absent a showing to the contrary-flawed. The Secretary reasonably recognized that a PES-based statistical adjustment would be a significant departure from the traditional method of conducting the census. Moreover, the PES adjustment would have been the first time in history that the States' apportionment would have been based upon counts in other States. Pp. 14-15. (e) The Secretary's third determination-that the available evidence tends to support the superior distributive accuracy of the actual enumeration-also is well within the bounds of his constitutional discretion. The mere fact that the Secretary's decision overruled the views of some of his subordinates is by itself of no moment in any judicial review of his decision. Pp. 15-16. (f) There is nothing in the record to suggest that the Secretary's fourth determination-that the PES adjustment would not improve distributive accuracy-was erroneous. Both the Director of the Census Bureau and the Assistant Secretary of Commerce favored adjustment, while the Administrator of the Economics and Statistics Administration opposed it. More importantly, even those who recommended in favor of adjustment recognized that their conclusion was not compelled by the evidence. Pp. 16-17. 13 F. 3d 1459, reversed.

In the case of Slochower v. Board of Higher Education of the City of New York, the Supreme Court addressed the constitutionality of Section 903 of the Charter of the City of New York, which mandated the termination of employment for any city employee who invoked the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination in response to questions about their official conduct.

Harry Slochower, an associate professor at Brooklyn College, was dismissed from his position after invoking the Fifth Amendment during a Senate Subcommittee hearing investigating subversive activities in education. Slochower had tenure and could only be dismissed for cause after due process, as per state law. However, the New York courts upheld his dismissal under Section 903, interpreting the invocation of the Fifth Amendment as equivalent to a resignation.

The Supreme Court, in its decision, emphasized the importance of the constitutional right against self-incrimination and condemned the practice of penalizing individuals for exercising this right. The Court found that Section 903, as applied to Slochower, violated due process because it automatically terminated employment without considering the context or justification for invoking the Fifth Amendment. The Court held that such a summary dismissal was arbitrary and lacked the necessary protection against arbitrary state action, which is a core aspect of due process.

The Court did not address the issue of whether Slochower's dismissal violated the Privileges or Immunities Clause, as it concluded that the due process violation was sufficient to reverse the judgment. The Court reversed the decision of the lower courts and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, stating that while Slochower did not have a constitutional right to his specific job, the state must follow due process in its employment decisions.

The implication of this decision is that public employees cannot be dismissed solely for invoking their constitutional rights, and that due process requires a fair and individualized assessment before termination of employment can occur.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of New York today entered a final judgment against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in favor of a temporary restraining order that temporarily enjoins certain noncommercial radio and television stations from violating the First Amendment.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that the Commission's order, which entered into force on May 5, 1967, imposed a temporary injunction prohibiting noncommercial stations from participating in the issuance, purchase, or promotion of any radio or television program.  According to the complaint, the order imposed by the Commission was designed to protect the interests of the public and to prevent the loss of federal funds for the stations' broadcast operations.  In its order, the Commission also imposed a partial restraining order on certain radio and TV stations, including Columbia Broadcasting System, Inc., which received $32 million from the Commission.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Commission’s complaint, Columbia and its affiliated stations have agreed to the entry of permanent injunctions, to be permanently enjoined from future violations of the federal securities laws, and to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and injunctive relief.

This case involves a dispute over the application of a stamp tax exemption under Section 1146(a) of the Bankruptcy Code. The parties disagree on whether the exemption applies to transfers made before or after a Chapter 11 plan is confirmed. The majority holds that the exemption applies only to transfers made after a plan is confirmed, based on the plain language of the statute and the historical development of the code. The dissent argues that the exemption applies to transfers made before confirmation, based on the legislative history and the practical realities of Chapter 11 reorganizations.

After respondents, enrolled Coeur d'Alene Indians, were indicted for various offenses allegedly committed by them while residing on the Coeur d'Alene Indian Reservation in Idaho, they were tried and convicted in Federal District Court. Their convictions were affirmed by the Court of Appeals, which rejected their contentions that their felony-murder convictions were invalid under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because of differences between federal and state law. Held: 1. Federal criminal statutes violative of due process cannot be justified on the ground that they apply differently to Indians than to others merely because of the fact that the crimes occurred on an Indian reservation. Pp. 48-51. (a) Legislation with respect to Indian tribes, although relating to Indians as such, is not based upon impermissible racial classifications. Cf. Morton v. Mancari, 417 U. S. 535; Fisher v. District Court, 424 U. S. 382. Pp. 48-50. (b) Here, where there is no dispute that respondents were subjected to the same body of law as any other person indicted under the Major Crimes Act, the challenged statutes do not otherwise violate equal protection. And since Congress has undoubted constitutional power to prescribe a criminal code applicable in Indian country, it is immaterial that the federal scheme differs from a state criminal code otherwise applicable within the State of Idaho. Pp. 50-51. 2. Reversed and remanded.

Title: Federal Law Preempts Maine's Tobacco Shipping Regulations

Summary: In this decision, the US Supreme Court ruled that federal law preempts certain provisions of Maine's tobacco shipping regulations. These provisions include requiring licensed retailers to use a specific delivery service and creating a "deemed to know" provision that holds carriers liable for failing to properly inspect packages. The Court found that these regulations have a significant impact on the pricing, routing, and services provided by motor carriers and therefore fall within the scope of federal preemption. The Court also noted that allowing states to regulate carrier services would create a patchwork of conflicting regulations, which is inconsistent with Congress' major legislative effort to leave such decisions to the competitive marketplace.

Respondent Minnesota State Fair Society, a public corporation created to promote and operate the Minnesota State Fair, promulgates a rule requiring all who wish to distribute and sell written materials or to solicit funds at the Fair to do so from a booth rented for those purposes. The rule applies equally to all who wish to distribute and sell materials or to solicit funds, regardless of whether they are commercial or charitable organizations. After being denied permission to distribute and sell literature and solicit funds at the Fair pursuant to the rule, respondent International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCN) brought suit challenging the rule's constitutionality. The Minnesota Supreme Court ultimately sustained the rule's validity, rejecting ISKCN's contention that the rule infringes freedom of speech guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. Held: The rule is a permissible limitation on the place and manner of communicating ideas, and thus satisfies the requirements of the First Amendment. Pp. 644-651. (a) Since the rule applies evenhandedly to all who wish to distribute and sell materials or to solicit funds, it qualifies as a valid time, place, and manner restriction. Moreover, the rule is not open to the kind of arbitrary application that has been condemned as inherently inconsistent with a valid time, place, and manner regulation. And the rule serves a significant governmental interest in controlling the movement of the crowd and in avoiding congestion on the fairgrounds, which is a temporary event attracting great numbers of visitors who come to the event for a short period to see and experience the host of exhibits and attractions at the Fair. Pp. 644-648. (b) While the State's interest in confining distribution, selling, and fund solicitation activities to fixed locations is sufficient to satisfy the requirement that a place or manner restriction must serve a substantial state interest, the State could avoid the threat to its interest posed by ISKCN by less restrictive means, such as penalizing disorder or disruption, limiting the number of solicitors, or putting more narrowly drawn restrictions on the location and movement of ISKCN's representatives. However, looked at in the light of the much larger number of distributors and solicitors that would be present on the fairgrounds if the Minnesota Supreme Court's judgment were affirmed, such alternatives would not deal adequately with the problems posed by the presence of multiple distributors and solicitors on the fairgrounds. Pp. 648-650. (c) The rule is sufficiently clear that alternative forums for the expression of respondents' protected speech exist despite the effects of the rule. It does not prevent ISKCN from practicing Sankirtan anywhere outside the fairgrounds, and it has not been shown to deny access within the forum in question. Thus, while the rule does not exclude ISKCN from the fairgrounds, nor does it deny that organization the right to conduct any desired activity at some point within the forum, its members may mingle with the crowd and orally propagate their views, and the organization may also arrange for a booth and distribute and sell literature and solicit funds from that location on the fairgrounds itself. Pp. 650-651. Reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit recently held that it is prohibited from recovering attorney's fees authorized by a prepetition contract and incurred in postpetition litigation. The court's decision was based on a rule previously adopted by that court, which held that such fees are categorically prohibited under the Bankruptcy Code. We vacate and remand because that rule finds no support in the bankruptcy code. We conclude that there is no legal basis for the Court's conclusion. The Court also notes that the Court of Appeal for the Second Circuit held that the Fobian rule is not consistent with the bankruptcy law. The Second Circuit's opinion, however, did find that there was a conflict among the courts regarding the validity of that rule. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate decision, held that a "prevailing party in a bankruptcy proceeding may be entitled to an award of attorney fees in accordance with applicable state law" and that the " prevailing litigant is ordinarily not entitled to collect a reasonable attorneys' fee from the loser"

The Supreme Court decided in Turner v. Commonwealth that a trial judge's refusal to ask prospective jurors about their racial attitudes during voir dire violates a defendant's constitutional right to a fair and impartial jury in a capital sentencing proceeding. The Court held that the risk of racial prejudice infecting a capital sentencing proceeding is especially high due to the complete finality of the death sentence and the broad discretion given to juries in making highly subjective judgments about the punishment a person deserves. The Court established a new rule requiring that a capital defendant accused of an interracial crime be informed of the race of the victim and questioned on the issue of racial bias.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit held that the Florida Supreme Court did not have the authority to impose a ban on television and radio coverage of criminal trials. The court held that, under Florida law, the trial judge had the power to determine whether or not the coverage violated the rules of the Florida Code of Judicial Conduct. The trial judge also had the discretion to determine if there was a reasonable likelihood that the coverage would be prejudicial to the public interest. The 4th Justice held that Florida's ruling violated the Constitution's guarantees of due process and the right to a fair trial. The justices held that there was no basis for the court's finding that the broadcast coverage of the trial violated the bar. The defendants, however, argued that the trial court had no authority to determine the coverage's content and that the court had exceeded its authority by imposing restrictions on the coverage. The appeals court concluded that the bar had not exceeded its power by imposing the restrictions. The case is now being heard by the appeals court and the justices will rule on the issue of whether there is a constitutional right to broadcast trials.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio has ruled that a financial institution can claim a tax-deductible loss when it exchanges its interests in a group of residential mortgage loans for another lender's interest in a different group of mortgage loans. The Court of Appeals for the Ohio District Court ruled that the loss was not "actually" sustained during the 1980 tax year for purposes of Section 165(a) of the Internal Revenue Code. The Tax Court previously ruled that Cottage Savings Association, a savings and loan association, was not entitled to a tax deduction for the losses. The Supreme Court agreed, and the Court of Justices agreed that the Tax Court's earlier decision was correct. We conclude that, in this case, the loss did give rise to realized losses, and that the tax deduction is permitted.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that an officer's seizure of a small rock containing crack cocaine was reasonable under the Fourth Amendment. The officer, Jerry Pertoso, was on patrol in an unmarked police car when he saw four or five youths fleeing from him. The officers gave chase, and one of the youths ran through an alley, while the other fled south. Pertoto followed them, and when he approached Hodari D., who was hiding in the alley, Hodari threw away the rock. The California Court of Appeal held that Hodari had been "seized" when he was tackled by PertoSo. The court denied Hodari's motion to suppress the evidence relating to the cocaine. The high court ruled that the evidence had to be suppressed as the fruit of the illegal seizure. The Supreme Court held that the officer had reasonable suspicion that the drugs were abandoned by Hodari and lawfully recovered by the police. Hodari also argued that the court should have allowed the officer to use the evidence of his arrest as evidence in his criminal case. The justices ruled that this argument was not supported by the facts of the case.

Petitioners, individuals and businesses whose products or services build on copyrighted works that have gone into the public domain, seek a determination that the Copyright Term Extension Act (CTEA) fails constitutional review under both the Copyright Clause's "limited Times" prescription and the First Amendment's free speech guarantee. The CTEA, as in all previous copyright term extensions, provides that "Congress shall have Power ... by securing [to Authors] for limited Times ... the exclusive Right to their . . . Writings." In 1998, in the measure here under inspection, Congress enlarged the duration of copyrights by 20 years. Held: 1. In prescribing that alignment, Congress acted within its authority and did not transgress constitutional limitations. Pp. 531-532. (a) The Copyright Clause empowers Congress to prescribe a "limited Tim[e]" for copyright protection and to secure the same level and duration of protection for all copyright holders, present and future. P. 533. (b) The CteA is not a content-neutral regulation of speech that fails heightened judicial review under the Clause. The fact that Congress has repeatedly acted on a mistaken interpretation of the Constitution does not qualify our duty to invalidate an unconstitutional practice when it is finally challenged in an appropriate case. The Clause's purpose is to promote the creation and publication of free works, and its purpose is not to promote, but to encourage, the creation of new works and to encourage the dissemination of those works in the United States. Thus, Congress' consistent historical practice of applying newly enacted copyright terms to future and existing copyrights reflects a judgment stated concisely by Representative Huntington at the time of the 1831 Act: "[J]ustice, policy, and equity alike forb[id]" that an "author who had sold his [work] a week ago, be placed in a worse situation than the author who should sell his work the day after the passing of [the] act." United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc., 334 U. S. 131, 158. Thus understood, a timespan appropriately "limited" as applied to future copyrights does not automatically cease to be "limited," when applied to current copyrights. Moreover, the overriding purpose of providing a reward for authors' creative activity is to motivate that activity and "to allow the public access to the products of their genius after the limited period of exclusive control has expired." Sony Corp. v. United States Olympic Comm., 483 U.S. 488, 492. The Court of Appeals affirmed, rejecting petitioners' contention that the statute exceeds Congress' power to extend copyright's term in a manner that puts existing, and future, copyrights in parity. The District Court also upheld the statute's terms, which are still limited, not perpetual, and therefore fit within Congress' discretion. P p. 534. (c) Petitioners' Copyright Clause arguments rely on several novel readings of the Clause, and the reasons why such extensions of the patent monopoly are unconstitutional per se. First, the Court has clearly identified the overriding interest in the "release to the public of the products [of] the author's] creative genius," United Statesv. Masonite Corp., 316 US. 265, 280, and, as with patents, there is no cause to suspect that a purpose to evade the quid pro quo prompted Congress to adopt the statute. Second, the Act promotes the useful arts by providing incentives to restore old movies. The interest in preserving perishable copies of old copyrighted films does not justify a wholesale extension of the copyright term, since such restoration and preservation will not even arguably promote any new works by authors or inventors, and any original expression in the restored and preserved movies will receive new copyright protection. Finally, Congress has routinely applied new definitions or adjustments of copyright term to both future works and existing works not yet in public domain. The reasons for extending such extensions do not raise the free speech concerns present when the government compels or burdens the communication of particular facts or ideas. The First Amendment securely protects the freedom to make— or decline to make-one's own speech; it bears less heavily when speakers assert the right to make other people's speeches. To the extent such assertions raise First Amendment concerns, copyright's built-in free speech safeguards are generally adequate to address them. The history of retroactive extensions of existing and expired copyrights and patents, though relevant, is not conclusive of the Court's reading of Article I, § 8, to provide essentially no limit on congressional action under the Constitution. Nor is there any merit to petitioner's contention that Congress' actions under the copyright Clause are judicially unreviewable. The Act's history shows that Congress, from the start, has routinely used new definitions and adjustments of the Copyright Act's terms to ensure that they appropriately pursue the Clause's purposes.
