Section 15-32.1-10(1)(h) of the North Dakota Century Code authorizes local school boards to levy a user fee for bus service, but excludes reorganized school districts from the definition of "nonreorganized school district" contained in § 15-32.1-10(1)(k). As a result, although a school district in a county containing fewer than 10,000 inhabitants may charge a user fee for bus service, a school district in a county containing 10,000 or more inhabitants may not do so. Appellants, whose daughter attends a school in a county containing fewer than 10,000 inhabitants, sued in a North Dakota state court to enjoin enforcement of the statute on the ground that it violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. They claimed that the statute discriminated against a suspect class consisting of lowincome families, and that it interfered with the fundamental right to education. The trial court entered judgment for appellants, but the State Supreme Court reversed, concluding that the statute did not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Held: The statute does not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 108-116. (a) There is no merit to appellants' contention that they are entitled to relief regardless of whether the statute is subjected to strict or heightened scrutiny. The statute does not deny access to the school bus solely because of the failure of appellants' parents to pay the user fee. Instead, it prevents appellants' daughter from obtaining bus service because her parents refuse to pay the fee. Moreover, the statute does not promote the creation and perpetuation of a subclass of illiterates within the State's borders. Contrast Plyler v. Illinois, 351 U. S. 12. While the statute does create a disparity among classes of citizens, it does not discriminate against a suspect class or infringe upon a fundamental right. Pp. 108-111. (b) Even assuming that the statute subjects the State to strict scrutiny, it nevertheless passes rational-basis review. The State's decision to allow local school boards the option of charging patrons a user fee for bus service is constitutionally permissible. Encouraging local districts to provide bus service is a legitimate state purpose, and such encouragement would be undermined by a rule requiring that general revenues be used to subsidize an optional service that will benefit a minority of the district's families. It is manifestly rational for the State to refrain from undermining its legitimate objective with such a rule. Pp. 111-112. (c) The statute does not discriminate against a suspect class and does not interfere with a fundamental right. Appellants have failed to meet their heavy burden of demonstrating that the statute is arbitrary and irrational. The fact that the statute applies only to nonreorganized districts is justified by the need to encourage reorganizations, thereby expanding the tax base and enhancing the effectiveness of the school system. The statute does not reflect any intent to discriminate against reorganized districts, nor does it conflict with any applicable state law. Pp. 112-116. 402 N. W. 2d 899, affirmed.

Section 504 of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002 (BCRA) requires television and radio broadcasters to retain for two years “a complete record” of requests to purchase broadcast time made by or on behalf of a legally qualified candidate for federal office, and to place the record in a “political file.” 47 U. S. C. § 315(e)(1). Similar requirements apply to requests made by or on behalf of a candidate for statewide office. Id., § 315(e)(2). The Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) regulations implement these requirements. Petitioners—four major networks and several smaller ones—filed suit challenging the constitutionality of § 504, claiming that it violates the First Amendment by forcing them to give away valuable airtime to candidates. Respondents—candidates and organizations supporting them—counterclaimed that petitioners had failed to comply with § 504. After the District Court entered judgment for respondents, the Third Circuit affirmed. Held: Section 504 is constitutional. Pp. 234–244. (a) The Court begins with the presumption that Congress acted within constitutional bounds. However, the presumption turns on whether Congress has offered a rational explanation for its actions. Here, Congress has done precisely that. Its stated purpose is to ensure that broadcasters treat fairly all candidates, regardless of wealth, and thus promote democratic competition. By requiring broadcasters to retain and make available for public inspection detailed records of requests to purchase broadcast time, Congress aims to prevent abuse of power by wealthy candidates and to enable voters to assess competing candidates’ merits. Moreover, Congress seeks to deter fraudulent conduct by ensuring that broadcasters retain records of requests to purchase broadcast time. Such goals are legitimate ends served by a permissible means. Pp. 234–236. (b) Petitioners contend that the statute is unconstitutional because it forces them to give away valuable airtime to candidates. Their argument rests on the assertions that the statute is ambiguous, that it is subject to multiple interpretations, and that it is therefore impossible to know whether it will compel them to donate airtime to candidates. None of these points carries weight. The statute is clear: It requires broadcasters to retain and make available for public inspection detailed records of requests to purchase broadcast time. There is nothing inherently ambiguous about that command. Nor is there anything inherently uncertain about the consequences of failing to comply with the statute. The statute expressly states that failure to comply will result in fines and revocation of licenses. Even assuming that the statute is ambiguous, petitioners have not shown that it is subject to multiple interpretations. The statute contains no terms that could reasonably be construed to mean something other than what it plainly means. Furthermore, the FCC’s regulations clarify the meaning of the statute. Those regulations specify exactly what constitutes a “complete record,” and they describe the manner in which broadcasters must retain and make available for public inspection the requested information. Finally, the statute is not unenforceable because it is impossible to know whether it will compel broadcasters to donate airtime to candidates. While it is true that the statute creates uncertainty about the consequences of failing to comply, it is also true that the statute gives broadcasters notice of what they must do to satisfy its requirements. Pp. 236–237. (c) Petitioners also contend that the statute is unconstitutional because it is being enforced in violation of due process principles. Specifically, they claim that the FCC’s regulations allow broadcasters to refuse to accept requests to purchase broadcast time made by candidates who are not wealthy enough to pay for the airtime. Petitioners offer no evidence that the FCC’s regulations are being enforced in violation of due process principles. Rather, they rely solely on the assertions of the FCC’s critics. The Court declines to base its decision on such bare allegations. Pp. 237–238. (d) Petitioners also contend that the statute is unconstitutional because it is being enforced in violation of equal protection principles. Specifically, they claim that the statute allows broadcasters to refuse to accept requests to purchase broadcast time made by candidates who belong to minority groups. Again, petitioners offer no evidence that the statute is being enforced in violation of equal protection principles. Instead, they rely solely on the assertions of the FCC’s critics. The Court declines to base its decision on such bare allegations. Pp. 238–239. (e) Petitioners also contend that the statute is unconstitutional because it is being enforced in violation of the First Amendment. Specifically, they claim that the statute forces broadcasters to give away valuable airtime to candidates, and that doing so violates the First Amendment. Petitioners’ argument is flawed on several levels. First, the statute does not force broadcasters to give away valuable airtime to candidates. Second, the statute is not being enforced in violation of the First Amendment. The statute is a valid exercise of Congress’s power to regulate the broadcast media. Congress has a compelling interest in preventing abuse of power by wealthy candidates and promoting democratic competition. The statute furthers that interest by ensuring that broadcasters retain records of requests to purchase broadcast time. The statute is narrowly tailored to achieve that end. It applies only to requests made by or on behalf of candidates for federal or statewide office, and it exempts requests made by news organizations. The statute is also consistent with the First Amendment because it leaves broadcasters free to decide whether to accept requests to purchase broadcast time. Finally, the statute is not being enforced in violation of the First Amendment because it is being enforced inconsistently across the country. The statute is being enforced uniformly throughout the Nation. Pp. 239–244. 336 F. 3d 103, reversed in part and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined, and in which Stevens, J., joined as to Parts I, II-A, and II-B. Stevens, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part, in which White, J., joined.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central question was whether a military contractor could be held liable under state tort law for injuries caused by a design defect in military equipment. The case arose from the death of a Marine helicopter copilot, David A. Boyle, who drowned after being unable to escape from a crashed CH-53D helicopter manufactured by Sikorsky, a division of United Technologies Corporation.

The petitioner, Boyle's father, argued that Sikorsky was liable under Virginia tort law for a defective design in the helicopter's escape system. The jury initially found in favor of the petitioner, but the Court of Appeals reversed the decision, applying the "military contractor defense" and directing that judgment be entered for Sikorsky.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the petitioner's contention that there is no federal law basis for shielding government contractors from liability for design defects in military equipment. The Court recognized that certain areas involving "uniquely federal interests" may require federal law to preempt state law, and that the procurement of military equipment by the federal government is such an area.

The Court outlined three conditions under which a military contractor cannot be held liable for design defects under state law: (1) the United States approved reasonably precise specifications; (2) the equipment conformed to those specifications; and (3) the supplier warned the United States about known dangers in the use of the equipment that were not known to the United States.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for clarification on whether the Court of Appeals had determined that no reasonable jury could find against the military contractor defense based on the evidence presented. If the Court of Appeals had made such a determination, its judgment would stand; otherwise, it would need to conduct a proper sufficiency inquiry.

The implications of this decision are that military contractors are shielded from liability for design defects in military equipment when they meet the specified conditions, which aligns with the federal interest in the discretionary function of military equipment procurement. This decision limits the application of state tort law in cases involving military equipment provided by contractors to the federal government.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Wisconsin has ruled that a former political science professor had no right to a hearing after he was told he would not be rehired for the next academic year. The court held that the Wisconsin State University-Oshkosh had violated David Roth's Fourteenth Amendment rights by failing to give him a reason for the decision not to rehire him for the 1969-1970 academic year, and that he had not shown that his right to due process had been violated. The decision was based on the fact that Roth had completed his one-year term and had no tenure rights to continued employment. The Court ruled that the University's failure to give Roth a reason and an opportunity to challenge the decision violated his rights to a statement of reasons and a hearing. The ruling is a significant victory for the free speech rights of teachers in higher education. The Supreme Court has previously held that teachers have the right to challenge their employers' decisions not to renew their contracts.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit held that a defendant's request for counsel at an initial appearance on a charged offense does not constitute an invocation of his right to counsel. The court held that the defendant was not charged with an offense that he had been formally charged with, and that his waiver of his Miranda rights was not sufficient to suppress the incriminating statements he made to police. The Court held that there was no need for the court to determine whether the waiver of Miranda rights violated the Sixth Amendment because the defendant had not been charged with the crime at the time the statements were made.

The District Court, adopting the report and recommendation of the Magistrate, found that, throughout Harris' time at Forklift Systems, Inc., Hardy often insulted her because of her gender and often made her the target of unwanted sexual innuendos. The court found that some of Hardy's comments "offended [Harris], and would offend the reasonable woman," id., at A-33, but that they were not "so severe as to be expected to seriously affect [Harris'] psychological well-being." The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The District Court erred in relying on whether the conduct "seriously affect[ed] plaintiff's psychological wellbeing" or led her to "suffe[r] injury." Such an inquiry may needlessly focus the factfinder's attention on concrete psychological harm, an element Title VII does not require. Certainly Title VII bars conduct that would seriously affect a reasonable person's psychological health-being, but the statute is not limited to such conduct. So long as the environment would reasonably be perceived, and is perceived, as hostile or abusive, Meritor Savings Bank, FSB v. Vinson, 477 U. S. 57, and the reference in that case to environments "so heavily polluted with discrimination as to destroy completely the emotional and psychological stability of minority group workers," merely present some especially egregious examples of harassment. They do not mark the boundary of what is actionable. Certiorari granted; 976 F. 2d 733, reversed and remanded.

Petitioner was convicted of burglary and larceny in a Maryland state court. His conviction of larceny was based partly on testimony admitted in the trial for both crimes, which testimony was inadmissible under state law in a trial for burglary alone. The Maryland Court of Special Appeals ruled on petitioner's double jeopardy challenge to the larceny count, but it ultimately affirmed the convictions. Held: 1. There is no jurisdictional bar to consideration of petitioner's larceny conviction, even though concurrent sentences were imposed. Pp. 108-112. 2. The double jeopardy prohibition of the Fifth Amendment, which is "fundamental to the American scheme of justice," Duncan v. Louisiana, ante, p. 145, represents a fundamental ideal in our constitutional heritage and should apply to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment. Palko v. Connecticut, 302 U. S. 319, overruled. Pp. 112-115. 3. Conditioning an appeal of one crime on a coerced surrender of a valid plea of former jeopardy on another crime exacts a forfeiture in plain conflict with the constitutional bar against double jeopardy. Green v. United States, 355 U. S. 184, 193-194. Here petitioner was acquitted of larceny in his first trial. Because he decided to appeal his burglary conviction, he is forced to suffer retrial on the larceny count as well. Pp. 115-116. 4. Petitioner's larceny conviction cannot stand once federal double jeopardy standards are applied. Pp. 116-117. 5. Whether petitioner's burglary conviction should also be set aside depends on whether there was any evidentiary error resulting from the introduction of inadmissible evidence in the joint trial. This question was not decided by the Maryland Court of Special Appeals, and it is not obvious on the face of the record that the burglary conviction was affected by the double jeopardy violation. Accordingly, the judgment below is vacated and the case is remanded for consideration of this question. Pp. 117-118. 1 Md. App. 649, 232 A. 2d 541, vacated and remanded.

In the case involving Barbara Dolan, who tripped and fell over mail left on her porch by the United States Postal Service, the Supreme Court held that her lawsuit could proceed, reversing the decisions of the lower courts. The central legal issue was whether the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) waived the federal government's sovereign immunity for Dolan's injury claim.

The FTCA generally waives the government's immunity from lawsuits for negligence by federal employees. However, there are exceptions to this waiver, one of which, found in 28 U.S.C. §2680(b), pertains to the "loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter." The lower courts had ruled that Dolan's claim was barred by this exception, interpreting "negligent transmission" to include the act of delivering mail that led to her injury.

The Supreme Court disagreed with this broad interpretation. It reasoned that the context of the statute and precedent required a narrower reading of "negligent transmission," limiting it to negligence causing mail to be lost, arrive late, in damaged condition, or at the wrong address. The Court cited the principle that words in a statute should be interpreted in the context of the surrounding text and the statute's purpose. It also referenced the case of Kosak v. United States, which indicated that the government does not retain immunity for all activities related to mail delivery, such as the negligent operation of postal vehicles.

The Court also noted that the types of losses for which immunity is retained under §2680(b) are generally avoidable or compensable through postal registration and insurance. It dismissed the government's concerns about frivolous claims, stating that ordinary legal protections against such litigation should suffice.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court found that Dolan's claims did not fall within the postal exception of the FTCA and that the general waiver of sovereign immunity applied. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion. Justice Alito did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

Under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 32(h), a federal district court must give the parties reasonable notice that it is considering imposing a sentence that varies from the applicable sentencing range prescribed by the United States Sentencing Guidelines. Petitioner Irriyarrays pleaded guilty to one count of making a threatening interstate communication, in violation of 18 U. S. C. §875(c). His presentence report (PSR) recommended a Guidelines sentencing range of 41 to 51 months of imprisonment, based on various enhancements. The PSR also listed several potential grounds for departure from the Guideline range, including the possibility that petitioner’s criminal history category might not adequately reflect his past criminal conduct or future likelihood of committing additional offenses. The Government made no objection to the PSR, but announced plans to introduce evidence at the sentencing hearing. Petitioner objected to the PSR’s recommendation of a Guidelines range and its rejection of an adjustment for acceptance of responsibility. Both sides introduced evidence at the hearing, including petitioner’s ex-wife’s description of incidents of domestic violence and threats she received from petitioner. Petitioner also testified, denying that he spoke to his cellmate about killing his ex-wife’s husband and expressing remorse over sending the threatening emails. The court ultimately rejected the PSR’s recommendations and imposed a 60-month sentence. When defense counsel raised the objection that the court failed to follow Rule 32(h), the court responded that it had complied with the Rule since it had given both petitioner and counsel an opportunity to comment on the appropriateness of the sentence. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, holding that Rule 32(h) did not apply because the above-guideline sentence imposed by the district court was a variance, not a departure. Held: Rule 32(h) does not apply to every sentence that is a variance from the Guidelines range. This Court’s decision in Burns v. United States, 501 U. S. 103, extended the notice requirements of Rule 32(i)(1)(C) to cover only those situations in which a defendant was being considered for a departure from the Guidelines range. See id., at 138–139. Since the Guidelines are now advisory, neither the Government nor the defendant may rely on the type of “expectancy” that gave rise to a special need for notice in Burns. Moreover, the due process concerns that motivated the Court to require notice in a world of mandatory Guidelines no longer provide a basis for extending the rule set forth in Burns either through an interpretation of Rule 32(h) itself or through Rule 32(i)(1)(C). And contrary to what the dissent suggests, post, p. 4, Rule 32(h) does not apply to §3553 variances by its terms. Such variances are governed by the specific provisions of §3553, which authorizes a district court to impose a sentence outside the Guidelines range if it finds that the applicable Guidelines range is too low or too high. See §§3553(a)(1), (b). There is no longer a limit comparable to the one at issue in Burns on the variances from Guidelines ranges that a district court may find justified under the sentencing factors set forth in §3553(a). Thus, adding a special notice requirement whenever a judge is contemplating a variance may create unnecessary delay. Even assuming that the judge had contemplated a variance before the sentencing hearing began, the record does not show that a statement announcing that possibility would have changed the parties’ presentations in any material way. Nor would such a statement change the outcome in most cases. Judges and counsel are able to ensure that all relevant matters relating to a sentencing decision have been considered before the final determination is made without resorting to the blanket notice requirement of Rule 32(h). Pp. 4–7. 458 F. 3d 1208, affirmed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit held that New York's 'stop-and-frisk' law violated the Fourth Amendment by allowing police officers to search a person's home without a warrant. The court held that the evidence seized under the law was properly admitted, on the ground that the searches which uncovered it were authorized by the law. The appeals of two men convicted of drug possession on the basis of the evidence were denied. The Second Circuit's decision is the latest in a long line of court rulings that have held that searches conducted under the 'stop and frisk' law are unconstitutional on their face and as construed and applied. The Supreme Court of the State of New York, in a separate decision, ruled that the law does not violate the Constitution's guarantees of due process and the right to a fair trial. The Court of Appeal for New York held that, in the absence of a warrant, the searches were not illegal. The Appeals Court held that there was no evidence that the search was conducted in a manner that violated the defendants' Fourth Amendment rights. In a separate appeal, the New York State Supreme Court ruled in favor of the defendants. The New York Court of Justices held that it was not necessary for the court to determine the issue of whether the searches violated the Constitution because the defendants were not subject to the search provisions of the Constitution. The high court held, however, that the defendants had a right to be questioned in a public place without the consent of the officer and that the officer's search of their home was not a search that violated their constitutional rights.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Texas' sodomy law, finding that it violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against Bowers, who was later convicted of similar conduct.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Dallas, Texas, Bowers violated the federal securities laws by failing to recognize that certain forms of sexual activity are "immoral and unacceptable."  The complaint alleges that, in violation of the federal law, Bower violated the right to a fair and just trial.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas today announced criminal charges against two individuals for their roles in the same-sex acts.  Bowers also was found liable for violations of Section 15(a)(1) and 17(b)(3) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act").  The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael H. Fried, Carol A. Hahn, and John R. Rymas of the Boston Regional Office, with the assistance of trial counsel Robert C. Hannan of the Division of Justice's Office. The litigation will be led by Jennifer C. Barry and supervised by Amy C. Welshhans.

This case involves a dispute between the Federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and Dow Chemical Company regarding the legality of aerial photography of Dow's industrial plant complex in Midland, Michigan. The EPA obtained aerial photographs of the plant using a commercial aerial mapping camera, while flying at altitudes ranging from 1,200 to 3,000 feet. The photographs captured images of the exterior of the building structures, including exposed manufacturing equipment, but did not reveal any sensitive or confidential information.

The main issues in this case include:

1. Does the EPA have the legal authority to obtain aerial photographs of Dow's industrial plant complex?
2. Is the act of obtaining aerial photographs a violation of Dow's privacy interests under the Fourth Amendment?
3. Are the aerial photographs considered a search under the Fourth Amendment?

The Court of Appeals ruled in favor of the EPA, stating that the photographs were legally obtained and did not violate Dow's privacy interests. They also determined that the photographs were not a search under the Fourth Amendment, as they did not involve a physical invasion of Dow's property.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Maryland has ruled that the Court of Appeal of the State of Maryland is immune from suit under the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (FMLA) because it is an entity of a sovereign State. The Court held that the State's use of the FMLA's self-care provision did not constitute a violation of the Act's provisions, which provide for up to 12 work weeks of unpaid leave per year for family-care related reasons, including the birth or adoption of a child, the care of a spouse with a serious health condition, or the employee's own health condition. The court held that Congress's intent to abrogate the immunity was clear, and that Congress could subject the State to suit for violations of subparagraph (C), 2612(a)(1). The decision is the latest in a series of court rulings that have held that states are immune from suits under the FMLA. The Supreme Court's decision in Toeller v. Wisconsin Dept. of Corrections, for example, found that the Wisconsin Department of Corrections violated the law by failing to grant an employee leave to care for his child. In Brockman v. Wyoming Department of Family Servs., the court found that Wyoming's family leave policies were not neutral and that the state's employees were entitled to family leave. In Laro v. New Hampshire, the Court found that there was no evidence that the New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services violated the family leave provisions. The high court's ruling will have a significant impact on the future enforcement of the Family Leave Act.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of South Carolina today entered a final judgment against Wesley Aaron Shafer, Jr., a convicted felon who was sentenced to life imprisonment without possibility of parole.  The SEC's complaint alleges that, in 1997, in the course of an attempted armed robbery in Union County, South Carolina, Shafer shot and killed a convenience store cashier.  According to the complaint, the trial judge instructed the jury to determine whether or not Shafer was eligible for parole in the event that the jury found him guilty on all three charges.  As alleged, the jury deliberated for nearly an hour before finding Shafer guilty.  In its final judgment, the court held that, based on the evidence presented to the jury, that Shafer would not be eligible to be sentenced to a life sentence.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the South Carolina Attorney General's Office today announced that it filed criminal charges against Shafer.  On January 8, 2001, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against the defendant, charging him with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and a penalty of life imprisonment.  Shafer has consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000, which includes disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest of $2,500, and to pay civil penalties of $3,500 and $1,100, respectively.  Additionally, the judgment requires the defendant to inform the jury of his future dangerousness, his past aggressive conduct, and his "propensity for [future] violence and unlawful conduct."

Respondent attempted to enter the United States by car ferry at Port Angeles, Washington. Hidden in the trunk of his rental car were explosives that he intended to detonate at the Los Angeles International Airport. After the ferry docked, respondent was questioned by a customs official, who instructed him to complete a customs declaration form; respondent did so, identifying himself on the form as a Canadian citizen (he is Algerian) named Benni Noris (his name is Ahmed Ressam). The official discovered explosives and related items in the car’s spare tire well. The Court of Appeals set aside his conviction on Count 9 because it read the word “during,” as used in §844(h)(2), to include a requirement that the explosive be carried “in relation to” the underlying felony. Because that construction of the statute conflicted with decisions of other Courts of Appeals, this Court granted certiorari. Held: 1. Congress did not intend to require the Government to establish a relationship between the explosive carried and the felony. Congress originally enacted the “Explosives Offenses Amendments” in Title XI of the Organized Crime Control Act of 1970, 84 Stat. 957. The provision was modeled after a portion of the Gun Control Act codified, as amended, at 18 U. S. C. §924(c) (2000 ed. and Supp. V). The provisions were initially identical, but Congress’ replacement of the words “unlawfully” with the phrase “and” without any similar replacement in the explosives statute, convinces Congress not intended to introduce a relational requirement into the explosives provision, but rather intended us to accept the more straightforward reading of §845(h). Since respondent was carrying explosives when he violated §1001, he was carrying them “while in possession of a firearm.” 18 U., S.-C. §911(c)(2) (1994 ed., Supp.V). The statute as presently written requires nothing further. Pp. 5–11. (a) The most natural reading of the relevant statutory text provides a sufficient basis for reversal. The “In relation to,’” language was not intended by Congress to create an element of the crime that did not previously exist, but was intended to make clear a condition already implicit in the statute. The legislative history reveals that because the amendment eliminated the requirement that a firearm be carried unlawfully, the ‘in relation’ language was added to allay explicitly the concern that a person could be prosecuted under §925(c). In 1984, Congress revised section 924(C) … .to include a provision that the ”during and in relation to . . .” “explosive during the commission of any felony which may be prosecuted in a court of [the] United States, “including a felony which provides for an enhanced punishment if committed by the use of a deadly or dangerous weapon or device shall, in addition to the punishment provided for such felony, be sentenced to imprisonment for 10 years”18 U.S. C., §911. The history of the Act further supports this conclusion. Congress enacted §6474(b), 102 Stat. 4379, which modified the text of the Explosives provision. Those amendments increased the penalties for violating the provision, §64 74(b)(2); they also deleted the word "unlawful” at 4380; and they also added the words "unwlawfully" after the word“during” and “after” after “During.“” denotes a temporal link; that is surely the most natural read of the word as used. Because respondent”s carrying of the explosives was contemporaneous with his violation of §1001-and because his carrying of them was “at the same time” that violation-Congress did not mean that Congress would not include a relational element into the firearms provision, and that Congress intended to accept that more straightforward read. Since respondent, who had been carrying explosives at the time of his violation, was carrying the explosives “when he violated” §1001 when he knowingly made false statements to a customs officer, and those statements violated §911, there is no need to consult dictionary definitions to arrive at the conclusion that respondent engaged in the precise conduct described in § 844(H)(2). Title: Brady v. Mississippi

Summary: In Brady v. Mississippi, the Supreme Court holds that the exclusion of evidence that would have helped the defense in a criminal trial violates the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court finds that the evidence was "brandy" - i.e., it was material to the truth of the matter in controversy and tended to affect the outcome of the trial. The Court also holds that the government's policy of withholding evidence from the defense is inherently unfair and violates the principles of justice. Finally, the Court holds that the government's practice of withholding evidence from the defense is a violation of the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

After finding that petitioner Tory, along with petitioner Craft and others, had engaged in unlawful defamatory conduct toward respondent Cochran, a California state court permanently enjoined them from doing so again. In affirming, the State Court of Appeal held that the injunction did not violate the First Amendment. Held: Because Cochran’s death made it unnecessary to address the merits of the case, the Court will not explore the issues raised by the petition for certiorari. However, since the injunction, as written, has lost its original purpose, the Constitution forbids it. Thus, the Court grants the motion to substitute Cochran’s widow as respondent, vacates the lower court’s judgment, and remands the case for proceedings consistent with this opinion. Certiorari granted; 75 Cal. Rptr. 2d 555, vacated and remanded.

This case concerns a dispute between the government and a defendant about whether a government motion asking the court to depart below the recommended sentencing range under the Federal Sentencing Guidelines also allows the court to depart below any statutory minimum sentence. The court held that the motion does not authorize a departure below a lower statutory minimum.

Petitioner Allied Structural Steel Co. (company), a corporation with its principal place of business in Illinois, maintained a general pension plan under § 401 of the Internal Revenue Code. Under the plan, an employee aged 65 or more could retire without satisfying any particular length-of-service requirement, but the size of his pension would reflect the length of his service with the company. Once an employee satisfied any one of these conditions, his pension right became vested in the sense that any subsequent termination of employment would not affect his right to receive a monthly pension when he reached 65. Those employees who quit or were discharged before age 65 without fulfilling one of the other three conditions did not acquire any pension rights. The company was required to make its contributions throughout the pre-1974 life of its plan as if employees' pension rights had vested after 10 years, instead of vesting in accord with the terms of the plan. The State notified the company that it owed a pension funding charge of approximately $185,000 under the provisions of the Private Pension Benefits Protection Act, which, as applied to the company, unconstitutionally impaired its contractual obligations to its employees under its pension agreement. The three-judge Federal District Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Act, and an appeal was brought to this Court under 28 U. S. C. § 1253. Held: 1. The Act does not violate the Contract Clause of the Constitution. Pp. 449-491. (a) The Contract Clause does not operate to obliterate the police power of the States. P. 451. (b) The contract Clause is not, however, the Draconian provision that its words might seem to imply. The interdiction of statutes impairing the obligation of contracts does not prevent the State from exercising such powers as are vested in it for the promotion of the common weal, or are necessary for the general good of the public, though contracts previously entered into between individuals may thereby be affected. The Clause is an exercise of the sovereign right of the Government to protect the lives, health, morals, comfort, and general welfare of the people, and is paramount to any rights under contracts between individuals. The presumption favoring "legislative judgment as to the necessity and reasonableness of a particular measure," United States Trust Co. v. Thomas, supra, simply cannot stand in this case, and the presumption favoring the "imperative judgment" as to a specific measure cannot stand, since the contract Clause's basic contours are brought into focus by several of this Court's 20th-century decisions, and it is not necessary to hold that the contract clause impaired the obligations of the company's employment contracts "without moderation or reason or in a spirit of oppression." P. 551. 2. The contract clause does not apply to the employer, and its narrow aim was leveled, not at every Minnesota employer, not even at any Minnesota employer who left the State, but only at those who had in the past been sufficiently enlightened as voluntarily to agree to establish pension plans for their employees. The statute nullifies express terms of a company's contractual obligations and imposes a completely unexpected liability in potentially disabling amounts. There is no showing in the record before this Court that this severe disruption of contractual expectations was necessary to meet an important general social problem, and there is no indication of legislative intent in this court's opinion. P p. 552. 454 F. Supp. 644, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri today entered a final judgment in favor of the school district and its principal in a case that was investigated by the SEC.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in St. Louis, Missouri, alleges that, in 1982, Robert E. Reynolds, the principal of Hazelwood East High School, and Howard Emerson, a teacher in the school's Journalism II course, violated their First Amendment rights by deleting two pages of Spectrum, a high school newspaper.  According to the complaint, Reynolds and Emerson agreed that the newspaper violated the First Amendment by failing to adequately protect the identities of the pregnant students at the school.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the school officials violated their duty to protect the safety of the students, parents, and members of the community by not allowing the newspaper to be distributed to the public.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Reynolds, Emerson, and Emerson consented to the entry of judgments that permanently restrains and enjoin them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders them to pay disgorgement of $4,668.50, plus prejudgment interest of $1,166.84, a portion of the journalism teacher's salary, and a civil injunctive penalty of $2,500.  Additionally, the court issued an order requiring the school to comply with the court's order to remove the articles from Spectrum.  On May 10, 2018, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. Burt of the U. S. District court for the District of Columbia entered a temporary restraining order against Reynolds and ordered him to return the articles to their original publication date.   The court also granted the school the right to publish the articles on its own without a court order, without requiring the student to sign a copy of the newspaper.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri dismissed a student's complaint alleging that her dismissal from the University of Missouri-Kansas City Medical School violated the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed, 538 F.2d 1317 (1976), and a petition for rehearing en banc was denied by a divided court. We granted certiorari to consider what procedures must be accorded to a student at a state educational institution whose dismissal may constitute a deprivation of "liberty" or "property" within the meaning of the 14th Amendment. The court concluded that respondent had been afforded all of the rights guaranteed her by the Constitution and dismissed her complaint. We reverse the decision of the lower court and grant the students' motion for a temporary restraining order and for a preliminary injunction. We conclude that respondent's dismissal deprived her of her right to a fair and just hearing. The lower court's decision was consistent with the decisions of the Coordinating Committee and the Dean of the School of Medicine. We also conclude that the dismissal violated the due process rights of the students. The Supreme Court of the U.N., in a separate decision, ruled that the "due process" provisions of the Fourteent Amendment do not apply in this case.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, stating that the tax on the use of ink and paper for newspapers in Minnesota violated the First Amendment. The Court found that the tax served no complementary function, as it did not eliminate the incentive to shop out-of-state, and it targeted an intermediate transaction rather than the ultimate retail sale. Additionally, the Court pointed out that the tax placed a heavier burden on the press compared to other businesses, which could potentially lead to censorship.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Northern District of Illinois has ruled that a municipal ordinance prohibiting the solicitation of contributions by charitable organizations that do not use at least 75 percent of their receipts for "charitable purposes" is unconstitutional. The ordinance, adopted by the Village of Schaumburg in 1974, prohibits soliciting contributions without a permit. Section 22-20(g) of the Village's Code requires that at least 75% of the proceeds of such solicitations will be used directly for the charitable purpose of the organization. The Village denied a permit to a charitable organization, Citizens for a Better Environment (CBE), because it could not demonstrate that 75% of its receipts would be used for charitable purposes as required by the Code. The complaint alleged that more than two-thirds of the funds collected by CBE in fiscal year 1975 were spent on salaries and employee health benefits. The article also alleged that the Illinois Attorney General's office had sued CBE in 1971 for failing to register its solicitors and for making false claims that CBE was working to "increase the size of the attorney general's staff and consequently their effectiveness in the fight against pollution"

The Supreme Court was presented with the question of whether Texas could constitutionally deny free public education to undocumented school-age children, a benefit it provided to U.S. citizens and legally admitted aliens, under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court found that undocumented children are "persons" under the jurisdiction of the states and thus are entitled to the protections of the Equal Protection Clause. The Court rejected the argument that undocumented status could justify a state's decision to deny children education.

The Court determined that education is not a right granted by the Constitution but is of great importance to the nation, both for the preservation of democratic institutions and for the well-being of the children themselves. Denying education to these children was seen as counterproductive to the nation's interests and an unreasonable burden on a vulnerable group that cannot control their legal status.

The Court examined the state's justifications for the law, including the preservation of resources, protection from an influx of illegal immigrants, and the improvement of educational quality. The Court found these justifications either unsupported by evidence or insufficient to warrant the denial of education.

The Court concluded that Texas had not shown that the exclusion of undocumented children from public schools furthered any substantial state interest and that the law violated the Equal Protection Clause. Therefore, the Court affirmed the lower court's decision, allowing undocumented children to receive free public education in Texas.

The Supreme Court reversed a lower court's decision that had suppressed statements made by Lloyd Perkins, the respondent, to an undercover agent while in jail. Perkins had been placed in a cell with an undercover agent, John Parisi, who was posing as a fellow inmate. During their interaction, Perkins made incriminating statements about a murder he was involved in, without receiving Miranda warnings.

The Court held that Miranda warnings are not required when a suspect is unaware that they are speaking to a law enforcement officer and gives a voluntary statement. The Court reasoned that the coercive atmosphere, which Miranda warnings are designed to protect against, is absent when a suspect believes they are speaking to a fellow inmate rather than a law enforcement officer. The Court emphasized that the Fifth Amendment protects against coercion, not against a suspect's misplaced trust in someone they believe to be a fellow prisoner.

The Court distinguished this case from others where suspects were aware they were speaking to government agents, noting that the lack of awareness of speaking to an agent means there is no coercion. The Court also clarified that their decision does not conflict with Sixth Amendment rights to counsel, as no charges had been filed against Perkins for the crime discussed with the undercover agent at the time of the conversation.

The Court concluded that the use of undercover agents is a legitimate law enforcement technique and that the interests protected by Miranda are not implicated when inmates make voluntary statements to undercover agents. Therefore, the statements made by Perkins were admissible in court, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed a lower court's ruling that found that the American College of Physicians had not violated the tax laws by selling advertising space in its journal The Annals of Internal Medicine. The court held that the lower court had focused too much on the commercial character of the advertising business and not enough on the actual contribution of the advertisements to the education of the journal's readers. The Second Circuit's decision is consistent with the decisions of the U.N. Tax Court, the Tax Policy Center, and the Tax Court for the District of Columbia, all of which have concluded that the advertising was not substantially related to the organization's tax-exempt purposes. The Court of Appeal for the Federal Circuit reversed, holding that the trial court had erred in concluding that the advertisements were not "substantially related" to respondent's educational purpose. The Appeals Court also held that there was no basis for the lower-court's finding that the ads were not related. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate opinion, ruled that the Appeals Court was correct to conclude that the higher court had not erred in finding that respondent had established the requisite substantial relation and its entitlement to exemption from taxation. The appeals court also ruled that it was not necessary to determine the source of the profits generated by the advertising to determine whether the organization is in compliance with the tax law. The high court concluded that "the tax law does not require the use of advertising space for educational purposes"

In this Supreme Court opinion, the Court addresses the application of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The case involves a disparate-impact claim, where employment practices that are neutral in form may be deemed discriminatory if they have an adverse impact on a protected group, without the need to show the employer's intent to discriminate.

The case concerns two companies operating salmon canneries in Alaska, which were accused of discriminatory hiring and promotion practices by a class of nonwhite cannery workers. The workers claimed that these practices led to racial stratification, with nonwhites predominantly in lower-paying cannery jobs and whites in higher-paying noncannery jobs. They also complained about segregated housing and dining facilities.

The District Court initially ruled in favor of the companies, finding no proof of disparate impact. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed this decision, stating that once a plaintiff shows disparate impact caused by specific employment practices, the burden shifts to the employer to prove the business necessity of those practices.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to address the proper application of the disparate-impact theory of liability. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's decision, emphasizing that the proper comparison for establishing a prima facie case of disparate impact is between the racial composition of the jobs in question and the racial composition of the qualified population in the relevant labor market. The Court found that the comparison between the racial composition of cannery and noncannery workers was flawed and did not establish a prima facie case of disparate impact.

The Court also clarified that plaintiffs must identify specific employment practices causing the disparity and demonstrate that each challenged practice has a significantly disparate impact on employment opportunities for different racial groups. The employer's burden is to produce evidence of a business justification for the challenged practice, but the burden of persuasion remains with the plaintiff.

If plaintiffs establish a prima facie case and the employer fails to justify the practice, plaintiffs can still prevail by showing that alternative practices with less racial impact would also serve the employer's legitimate interests. However, any alternatives must be equally effective and not impose undue burdens on the employer.

The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion, which requires a more precise analysis of the impact of specific employment practices and the reasons behind them.

Respondents, enrolled Coeur d'Alene Indians, broke into the home of Emma Johnson, an 81-year-old non-Indian, in Worley, Idaho, and robbed and killed her. Because the crimes were committed by enrolled Indians within the boundaries of the Indian Reservation, respondents were subject to federal jurisdiction under the Major Crimes Act, 18 U. S. C. § 1153. Respondents were indicted by a federal grand jury on charges of burglary, robbery, and murder. Respondent William Davison was convicted of second-degree murder only. They contended that their felony-murder convictions were unlawful as products of invidious racial discrimination, since the Federal Government was not required to establish premeditation and deliberation in respondents' federal prosecution. The Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that respondents were "put at a serious racially-based disadvantage" under Idaho law. Held: The federal criminal statutes enforced here are based neither in whole nor in part upon impermissible racial classifications. Pp. 523-524. (a) Since Congress has undoubted constitutional power to prescribe a criminal code applicable in Indian country, United States v. Kagama, 118 U.S. 375, it is of no consequence that the federal scheme differs from a state criminal code otherwise applicable within the boundary of the State of Idaho. P. 526. (b) The challenged statutes do not otherwise violate equal protection, since they are not based on impermissible classifications, and the federal Government treated respondents in the same manner as all other persons within federal jurisdiction, pursuant to a regulatory scheme that did not erect impermissible racially classifications; hence, no violation of the Due Process Clause infected respondents' convictions. P p. 527. (c) Federal criminal statutes violate the due process Clause of the Fifth Amendment by subjecting individuals to federal prosecution by virtue of their status as Indians, since federal legislation with respect to Indian tribes, although relating to Indians as such, is expressly provided for in the Constitution and supported by the ensuing history of Federal Government's relations with Indians. Morton v. Mancari, 417 N. Y. 535, 552, and Fisher v. Idaho, supra, at 553 n. 24, do not, in whole or in part, violate the equal protection requirements implicit in the Due process Clause. Neither of these cases involved preferences or disabilities directly promoting Indian interests in self-government, whereas in the present case, federal regulation of criminal conduct within Indian country implicating Indian interests is not viewed as legislation of a "racial" group consisting of "Indians" . . . and is not to be viewed in the light of tribal self-regulation, but with federal regulation that implicates Indian interests. Morton and Fisher point more broadly to the conclusion that federal regulation is not based upon impermissible classifications and is rooted in the unique status of Indians as "a separate people" with their own political institutions, and Federal regulation of Indian affairs is not, therefore, a "race" group that is governed by once-sovereign political institutions. Mascari and Fisher involved preferences directly promoting Indians' interests, whereas Fisher involved a preference or disability directly promoting them, whereas both involved preferences that directly promote Indian interests and are directly implicating their interests. Pm. 528-534. (d) Respondents' convictions were not subjected to federal criminal jurisdiction because they are of the same race but because they were enrolled members of the Coeur-Alene Tribe, which is subject to the same federal criminal code as any other individual, Indian or nonIndian, charged with first degree murder committed in a federal enclave, and they did not, and could not, contend otherwise with respondents' equal protection claim. The fact that the challenged statutes are based on the disparity between federal and Idaho law as the basis for respondents' claim of racial discrimination does not mean that they violated equal protection. The challenged laws do not violate equalprotection when their own body of law is evenhanded, regardless of the laws of States with respect thereto. The Federal Government treated the same respondents in this case pursuant to the regulatory scheme, and their convictions are reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts today entered a final judgment against David Paul O'Brien, Jr., a Massachusetts resident charged with defrauding a federal agency by destroying and mutilating his Selective Service certificate.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Boston on March 31, 1966, O'Brien made a false and misleading statement in a complaint filed in the United States District Court against him.  The complaint alleges that, in violation of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, that he intentionally caused the destruction or mutilation of certificates issued by the federal agency, and that he was liable for a civil penalty of not more than $10,000 or imprisonment of not less than 5 years.  In a parallel action, the U.N. Office of Inspector General today announced that it has issued an order suspending the destruction and destruction of certificates of the agency's registered personnel.  On March 29, 2015, the SEC filed an emergency action against O’Brien, charging him with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 5 of the Exchange Act.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, O”Brien consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, orders him to pay a $1,000 civil penalty, and bars him from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years.

Petitioner was convicted of the armed robbery of the treasurer of the San Jose Coin Club, which he had attended. The trial court refused to suppress the evidence found in petitioner's home and, after a jury trial, petitioner was found guilty and sentenced to prison. The California Court of Appeal affirmed. Held: The warrantless seizure of evidence of crime in plain view is prohibited by the Fourth Amendment if the discovery of the evidence was not inadvertent. Coolidge v. New Hampshire, 403 U. S. 443, distinguished. Pp. 531-532. (a) A search compromises the individual interest in privacy; a seizure deprives the owner of the right to security in person and property protected by the Amendment. The "plain-view" doctrine is applicable where a police officer is not searching for evidence against the accused, but nonetheless inadvertently comes across incriminating evidence while in "hot pursuit" of a fleeing suspect. It is, of course, an essential predicate to any valid warrantless "plain view" seizure of incriminating information that the officer did not violate in arriving at the place from which the evidence could be plainly viewed. There are, moreover, two additional conditions that must be satisfied to justify the warrantless search. First, not only must the item be in plain sight; its incriminating character must also be "immediately apparent." Second, the search was authorized by a valid warrant. The object of a warrantless automobile search is the object of an automobile search, and the officer must be lawfully located in a place where the object can be plainly seen, but he or she must also have a lawful right of access to the object itself. The absence of inadvertence was not essential to the Court's rejection of the State's "plainview" argument in Coolidge, which held that the police, in seizing two automobiles parked on the defendant's driveway in the course of arresting the defendant, violated the First Amendment in arriving there. The court relied on Coolidge's decision in North v. Superior Court, 8 Cal. 3d 301, 104 Cal. Rptr. 833, 502 P. 2d 1305, which noted that the discussion of the inadvertence limitation on the doctrine in Justice Stewart's opinion had been joined by only three other Members of this Court and therefore was not binding on it. The Court denied petitioner's request for review. Because the California courts' interpretation of the doctrine conflicts with the view of other courts, and because the unresolved issue is important, the Court granted certiorari, 493 U.S. 889, 110 S.Ct. 231, 107 L.Ed.2d 183, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida today entered a final judgment against a Florida man charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17(b) thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Tampa, Florida, alleges that, in 2004, Tampa Police Officer Kevin Dewayne Powell received a warning from the Florida State Attorney General that he had the right to consult with an attorney before answering any of the officers’ questions. The complaint further alleges that Powell knew he was prohibited from possessing a gun because he had previously been convicted of a felony, but he had nevertheless purchased and carried a handgun for his protection. The SEC alleges that the warning, which Powell read to Powell, did not adequately convey his right to the presence of an attorney during questioning. The court also found that Powell could consult with his lawyer only before he answered any questions at all.  According to the complaint, Powell signed the warning without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Florida today announced criminal charges against Powell arising from the same conduct alleged in the Florida case.  On May 9, 2009, the U. S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York announced that it had obtained a temporary restraining order against Powell, freezing his assets, and ordering an asset freeze and other emergency relief. On May 10, 2010, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against Powell. On June 2, 2011, the Florida Court of Appeals issued an order permanently enjoining Powell from future violations of the federal securities laws, ordering him to comply with the court order, and requiring him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar. The order also ordered Powell to pay a $10,000 civil penalty.  As part of the settlement, Powell consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 5(d), and orders him to provide a copy of the judgment to the court upon motion by the SEC. The judgment also orders Powell to provide an accounting of the amount of money he has already paid to the Florida Attorney General, and to provide for an officer and director of a public company. Powell agreed to the settlement without admitting to the SEC's findings. The settlement is subject to court approval.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Vermont ruled in 1979 that the Secretary of Health and Human Services had violated the terms of the Social Security Act of 1935 by failing to adjudicate future disputed disability claims under the Act. The court ordered the Secretary to pay benefits in all cases of noncompliance with the deadlines established by the court. The Court held that the court's order was not valid because the Secretary had not complied with the requirements of the order. The Supreme Court held in a separate case that the order was valid because it was issued on behalf of a class of individuals who had not yet been determined to be disabled. The high court held that there was no need for the court to issue an injunction because the class was not of the same type as the one issued in this case. The case was brought by Leon Day and Amedie Maurais, both of Vermont, who had been denied disability benefits. Day and Maurais sought declaratory and injunctive relief from delays in obtaining a reconsideration determination and in securing a hearing before an administrative law judge. Maurais intervened in the action after suffering similar delays. The District Court found that the delays were caused by the Secretary's failure to comply with the deadline established in the order, and ordered that the benefits be paid in the cases of those who had already been denied benefits. The Supreme Court held that the statute of limitations in 28 U.S. Code §2415(a) applies only to judicial actions and not to administrative proceedings involving royalty payments under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. The Court found that the word "action" in §2415(a) primarily refers to court proceedings, and that an MMS payment order in this case played an entirely different role. Additionally, the Court determined that an MMS letter or payment order cannot be considered a "complaint" within the meaning of §2415(a).

In the case of William Fiore v. Gregory White, Warden, et al., the Supreme Court of the United States addressed the issue of whether a state must apply a new interpretation of a criminal statute retroactively to cases on collateral review under the Federal Due Process Clause.

William Fiore was convicted in Pennsylvania for operating a hazardous waste facility without a permit, despite actually having one. The conviction was based on the argument that Fiore had deviated from the permit's terms. After Fiore's conviction became final, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court interpreted the statute in a related case (Commonwealth v. Scarpone), clarifying that deviation from permit terms did not equate to operating without a permit. Fiore's attempts to overturn his conviction based on this interpretation were unsuccessful in state court, leading him to seek federal habeas corpus relief.

The federal District Court granted the writ, but the Third Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the decision, believing that the Pennsylvania Supreme Court had announced a new rule of law that did not apply retroactively to Fiore's case. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to determine if Fiore's conviction violated the Due Process Clause.

Upon review, the U.S. Supreme Court certified a question to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court to clarify whether its interpretation in Scarpone represented a change in law or was the correct interpretation at the time Fiore's conviction became final. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court responded that Scarpone did not announce a new rule but merely clarified the statute's language, indicating that the interpretation was the correct one at the time of Fiore's conviction.

The U.S. Supreme Court concluded that Fiore's conviction and continued incarceration violated due process because the Commonwealth did not prove a basic element of the crime—operating without a permit—since Fiore did possess a permit. The Court held that convicting a person without proving all elements of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt is forbidden by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Third Circuit and remanded the case for proceedings consistent with its opinion, effectively determining that Fiore's conviction was unconstitutional and could not stand under the clarified interpretation of the statute.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed the lower court's judgment of acquittal in the case of Humberto Regalado Cuellar, who was charged with attempting to transport the proceeds of unlawful activity across the border. The court held that the evidence showed that petitioner concealed the money for the purpose of transporting it, but it did not show that he intended to conceal or disguise the nature, the source, or the ownership of the money. We agree with the Government that the statute does not require proof that the defendant attempted to "legitimize" tainted funds, but we agree with petitioner that the Government must demonstrate that he did more than merely hide the money during its transport.

The Supreme Court held that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has the legal authority to award compensatory damages in Federal Government employment discrimination cases. The majority opinion relied on the language, purposes, and history of the 1972 Title VII extension and the 1991 Compensatory Damages Act (CDA), as well as the EEOC's role in enforcing Title VII. The dissenting justices argued that the CDA limits the EEOC's authority to award compensatory damages and that the EEOC should not be allowed to interpret the CDA in a way that expands its powers beyond what Congress intended.

In the early morning of February 17, 1970, respondent's pregnant wife and his two daughters, aged 2 and 5, were brutally murdered in their home on the Fort Bragg, N.C., military reservation. At the time, respondent was a physician in the Army Medical Corps stationed at Fort Bragg. The Army formally charged MacDonald with the three murders on May 1, 1970. The Army dismissed the military charges on October 23, 1970. After hearing a total of 56 witnesses, the investigating officer submitted a report recommending that the charges and specifications against MacDonald be dismissed. The Commanding General dismissed MacDonald's request for an honorable discharge based on hardship. In June 1972, the Army forwarded a 13-volume report to the Justice Department recommending further investigation. In August 1974, the grand jury returned an indictment charging MacDonald with three murders. The court of appeals denied the motion to dismiss the indictment, but the Court of Appeals allowed an interlocutory appeal and reversed, holding that the delay between the June 1972 submission of the CID report to Justice and the August 1974 convening of the Grand Jury violated MacDonald’s constitutional right to a speedy trial. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari, and we reverse. The Supreme Court held that MacDonald was not entitled to a hearing on the motion because he had not been charged with a crime at the time of the indictment. The Court also held that the indictment violated his Sixth Amendment right to speedy trial because it was not filed within the required period of time.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia today entered a final judgment in favor of Richmond, Va., in a case that raised the specter of race-based discrimination in the construction industry.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Richmond, Virginia, on April 11, 1983, the city of Richmond issued a bid for a 30% minimum-salary-based contract to minority contractors.  The SEC alleges that the city's bid was based on the false premise that there was no history of prior discrimination, that there had been no prior discrimination in any industry, and that minority contractors were not disadvantaged by prior discrimination.  In fact, according to the complaint, Richmond's bid for the 30% set-aside was so low that it could not be justified by any reasonable basis.  As the complaint alleges, the majority of the court found that Richmond violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 13(b)(5) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act"), and Rule 13b2-1 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, the City of Richmond consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins the city from violating these provisions, and orders the city to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The settlement is subject to court approval.

The U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina granted the government's motion to increase Keith Lavon Burgess' minimum sentence from 10 years to 20 years for his prior conviction for possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of cocaine base in violation of the federal Controlled Substances Act of 1980 (841(b)(1)(A)) and 846(c) of the same law. The court ruled that the term "felony drug offense" is not used in the federal law to mean "any federal or State offense classified by applicable Federal or State law as a felony." The court also ruled that Burgess' prior conviction did not qualify as a "felon drug offense," even if state law classifies the offense as a misdemeanor. The Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed the lower court's decision, holding that the District Court's ruling was consistent with the "plain language or statutory scheme" that Congress intended to use. The Supreme Court, in a separate opinion, held that the "clear and simple" language of 802(a) alone controls the meaning of the term 'felony' as that term is used in 841 (b)(1). The high court held that "the plain and simple language" of the statutory scheme does not adequately convey the intent of Congress's intent to include state drug offenses "punishable by imprisonment for more than one year under any law of the United States or of a State or foreign country"

The text appears to contain a statement regarding a judicial decision related to a church property dispute in Georgia. The decision holds that a State is constitutionally entitled to adopt neutral principles of law as a means of adjudicating a church property dispute. The neutral-principles approach is considered to be completely secular in operation and flexible enough to accommodate different forms of religious organization and polity. However, the application of the neutral-principles method may require a civil court to examine certain religious documents and interpret them in purely secular terms.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico today entered a final judgment in favor of an arbitration case brought by Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc., a Puerto Rican corporation, against Mitsubishi Motors Corporation, a Swiss corporation, and its wholly-owned subsidiary.  According to the court's order, Soler agreed to settle the case without admitting or denying the allegations in its response to the complaint.  The court also ruled that the arbitration provisions of the federal securities laws, which govern interstate commerce and trade, require that a party bound by an agreement to arbitrate a dispute be able to show cause and effect in a court-ordered manner.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Soler for violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Soler also agreed to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  Without admitting or denied the SEC's findings, the court agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins Soler from violating these provisions and orders it to submit an arbitration application to the Court of Appeals for the Northern District of California, which is scheduled to hold a hearing on the matter on May 17, 2018.  On May 24, 2018, the U. S. District Judge for the Central District of Florida entered a judgment against the defendants, finding that Soler violated Section 10 of the Exchange Act, and ordering the parties to jointly and severally settle the charges.   The Court also ordered Soler to comply with the court order, which requires that it comply with, among other things, with the agreed-upon settlement provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) ofÂ the Securities Act of 1933, and that it reserves the right to determine the amount of disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties of up to $100,000, which will be determined by the court upon motion of the parties.

Title 2 U. S. C. § 441b requires corporations and labor unions to spend independently of each other during federal elections. After petitioner Michigan Campaign Finance Act became effective, respondent Michigan Chamber of Commerce challenged the constitutionality of the Act's restriction on corporate political expenditures. The Federal District Court dismissed the complaint, finding that the Act did not violate the First Amendment. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the Act violated the First Amendment as made applicable to states by the Fifteenth Amendment. Held: 1. Petitioner Act does not violate the First Amendment. Pp. 658-665. (a) Expressive conduct involving political expenditures is protected by the First Amendment. Buckleyv . Valeo, 424 U. S. 1, 14. Since the Act applies to corporations, it necessarily affects the speech of the Chamber, which is a for-profit corporation. Pp. 658-659. (b) Application of the Act to the Chamber does not violate the First Amendment. Pp. 659-665. (1) The Act's limitation on corporate political expenditures furthers the State's compelling interest in protecting the political process from being influenced unfairly by the enormous amount of money that corporations can accumulate with the aid of the special advantages granted to corporations by state law. Pp. 659-660. (2) The Act is narrowly tailored to accomplish its objective. Under the Act, corporations are free to spend money from their general treasuries on purely informational material, but are restricted from doing so on political advertising. Moreover, the Act allows corporations to make independent political expenditures from a separately designated fund, thereby ensuring that the speech is clearly attributable to the corporation and reducing the risk that the expenditures will be misattributed to others. Pp. 660-661. (3) The Act is not substantively overbroad since it applies to all corporations regardless of size. Even closely held corporations, which may not have accumulated significant wealth, nevertheless receive from the State the special benefits conferred by the corporate structure and present the potential for distorting the political process. Pp. 661-662. (4) Nor is the Act underinclusive because it does not apply to unincorporated labor unions. Labor unions differ from corporations in that union members who disagree with a union's political activities need not give up full membership to avoid supporting its political activities. Excluding unincorporated labor unions from the Act's scope is therefore justified by the crucial difference between unions and corporations. Pp. 662-665.
