The National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) requires union members to bargain on behalf of their members over their “rates of pay, wages, hours of employment, or other conditions of employment.” Respondents are members of the Service Employees International Union, Local 32BJ (Union). Under the NLRA, the Union is the exclusive bargaining representative of employees within the building-services industry in New York City, which includes building cleaners, porters, and doorpersons. The union has exclusive authority to bargain for arbitration of workplace discrimination claims, including, inter alia, claims made pursuant to Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, or any other similar laws, rules, or regulations. Respondents were directly employed by petitioner Temco Service Industries, Inc. (Temco), a maintenance service and cleaning contractor. In 2003, with the Union’s consent, Temco engaged Spartan Security, a unionized security services contractor and affiliate of Temco, to provide licensed security guards to staff the lobby and entrances of its building. Because Temco rendered respondents’ lobby services unnecessary, the union reassigned them to jobs as night porters and light duty cleaners in other locations in the building. After the union filed a grievance with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), respondents filed suit against petitioners in Federal District Court, alleging that their reassignment violated the ADEA and state and local laws prohibiting age discrimination. The District Court denied the motion because under Second Circuit precedent, “even a clear and unmistakable union-negotiated waiver of a right to litigate certain federal and state statutory claims in a judicial forum is unenforceable.’ ” 9 U. S. C. §§16(a)(1)(A)–(B). The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: A collective-bargaining agreement that clearly and unmistakably requires union member members to arbitrate claims arising under the age discrimination in employment-discrimination act of 1967 (ADEA) is enforceable as a matter of federal law. The NLRA provided the Union and the RAB with statutory authority to collectively bargain for workplace discrimination, and Congress did not terminate that authority with respect to federal age-discrimination claims in the Act of 1964. Pp. 5–7. (a) The NLRB’S decision in Gardner-Denver v. Arkansas-Best Freight System, Inc., 450 U.S. 728, which held that arbitration under a collective-Bargaining Agreement could not preclude an individual employee’d right to bring a lawsuit in court to vindicate a statutory discrimination claim, is not inconsistent with this Court’ s decision in Gilbert v. Interstate/Johnson Lane Corp., 500 U. s. 20 (1953), which held the same thing. Moreover, the Court has accounted for this conflict of interest in several ways. First, it has been interpreted to impose a “duty of fair representation” on labor unions, which a union breaches “when its conduct toward a member of the bargaining unit is arbitrary, discriminatory, or in bad faith,” Marquez v. Screen Actors, 525 U . S. 735, 739. Second, it is particularly inappropriate to ask this Court to impose an artificial limitation on the collective-baaining process. Because a union is subject to liability under Title VII if it illegally discriminates against older workers in either the formation or governance of the collective bargaining agreement, such as by deciding not to pursue a grievance on one of its members for discriminatory reasons, and if Congress intended the substantive protection afforded by the Act to include protection against waiver of the right to the judicial forum, that intention will be deducible from text or legislative history. See, e.g., Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/American Express Inc., 490 U. .S. 477, 480. Third, the employee argues that the CBA operates as a substantive waiver of their ADEA rights because it not only precludes a federal lawsuit, but also allows the Union to block arbitration of these claims. See id., at 28. In the end, the employees’ generalized attacks on “the adequacy of arbitration procedures” were insufficient to preclude arbitration of statutory claims, because there was no evidence that “Congress, in enacting the Act, intended to preclude a waiver of judicial remedies for the statutory rights at issue” Id., at 35. Finally, the Employee‘s “generalized attacks” that, in spite of its plain language, interprets §118 to support their position, reveal a distorted understanding of the compromise made when an employee agrees to compulsory arbitration. This Court has not addressed the question whether the arbitration clause in the collective agreement is sufficiently explicit in precluding their federal lawsuit. The Court has also accounted for the conflict of interests in several other ways, including: 1. A union is liable under the Act if the union itself discriminates on the basis of age.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of the government in the case of Richardson v. United States, 428 U.S. 96 (1976). The case involved three individuals accused of possessing and distributing methamphetamine hydrochloride. The defendants claimed that they were entrapped by an undercover FBI agent who had infiltrated their operation. The Supreme Court held that the defendants failed to prove that they were entrapped and that their actions were purely the product of their own free will.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi today issued a final judgment in favor of a motion by the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of New York to impose the death penalty on a capital defendant.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, alleges that, in June 1982, David Randolph Gray was indicted in Harrison County, Miss., for the felony of kidnapping and was subsequently sentenced to death.  According to the complaint, the jury selection was conducted in the presence of the others in the box.  As alleged, the trial judge, without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, improperly excluded one of the jury members for cause.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the trial court failed to properly question the other jurors who had been called to the box to determine whether they were qualified to serve as jurors.  For example, the SEC alleges that a jury member who initially expressed an insincere hesitation about executing a capital penalty would not be excluded from the jury because the jury had already deliberated on whether to impose a death penalty.  On June 5, 2017, the U. S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Georgia issued a judgment that permanently enjoins the state from imposing the death sentence on a convicted felon and orders him to pay a penalty equal to the amount of his ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against him from serving as an officer or director of a public company.   The court's order also prohibits the imposition of a penalty without a court-ordered injunction, prohibits the selection of a jury for cause, and requires the court to consider the merits of the case before imposing a penalty.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment against Vincent W. Foster, Jr., a former White House Counsel, for violating the attorney-client privilege.  According to the SEC's complaint, Foster met with James Hamilton, an attorney at petitioner Swidler & Berlin, to seek legal representation concerning possible congressional or other investigations of the firings.  The complaint alleges that Foster took three pages of handwritten notes in which he described the privilege as "privileged" and "non-threatening."  As alleged in the complaint, however, the privilege is not absolute and does not extend beyond the death of the client.  For example, the complaint further alleges that, after death, Foster made notes of an initial interview with a client shortly before the client's death.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Foster.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by James R. Frankel and supervised by Marc Blau of the Boston Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Office of the Independent Counsel in this matter.

In the case of Thomas Joe Miller-El, the Supreme Court examined the standards for issuing a certificate of appealability (COA) to review the denial of habeas relief in federal court under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA). The Court held that a prisoner seeking a COA must demonstrate "a substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right," meaning that reasonable jurists could debate the district court's resolution of constitutional claims or conclude that the issues presented are adequate to deserve encouragement to proceed further.

Miller-El, an African-American, was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death after prosecutors used peremptory strikes to exclude 10 of the 11 eligible African-American jurors. He claimed that the jury selection procedures violated the Equal Protection Clause and the Supreme Court's decision in Batson v. Kentucky. The state trial court and subsequent courts denied his claims, and the federal district court also denied habeas relief. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals denied a COA, concluding that the state court's findings were not unreasonable.

The Supreme Court reversed the Fifth Circuit's decision, stating that the Court of Appeals should have limited its examination to a threshold inquiry into the underlying merit of Miller-El's claims. The Court found that the evidence presented by Miller-El, including a pattern of race discrimination in jury selection and the conduct of prosecutors in his case, raised a debatable question as to whether the prosecution acted with a race-based reason when striking prospective jurors. The Court also noted that the state court's failure to address certain evidence, such as the use of jury shuffling and historical evidence of discrimination by the District Attorney's Office, was problematic.

The Supreme Court concluded that a COA should have been issued, as the District Court's application of AEDPA deference to Miller-El's Batson claim was debatable among jurists of reason. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion.

Justice Scalia concurred, providing additional reasoning for the Court's decision and discussing some of the evidence on the State's side of the case. Justice Thomas dissented, arguing that the petitioner had not provided clear and convincing evidence of purposeful discrimination and therefore did not merit a COA.

Under the Michigan Income Tax Act, the State exempts from state income tax the retirement benefits paid by the State and its political subdivisions to their own employees, but requires payment of such taxes on the retirement benefits paid by the Federal Government to its employees. Appellant, a former federal employee residing in Michigan, paid state income taxes on his federal retirement benefits. After paying such taxes for several years, he sought a refund, claiming that the tax scheme violated the doctrine of intergovernmental tax immunity, which bars states from taxing federal employees unless the tax is nondiscriminatory. The trial court dismissed his claim, rejecting his arguments that the tax scheme was discriminatory and that the doctrine of intergovernmental tax immunity applied to him. The Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The Michigan tax scheme violates principles of intergovernmental tax immunity by favoring retired state and local government employees over retired federal employees. Pp. 30-36. (a) Title 4 U. S. C. § 111-which provides that the Federal Government shall not object to state tax laws when they apply to federal employees "so long as ... the tax laws... do not discriminate against the Government or those with whom it deals"-retains the immunity from discriminatory state taxation that existed prior to passage of the Public Salary Tax Act of 1939, which extended federal income taxing authority to cover state and local government employees. Although § 111 refers to "employees" instead of "officers," the term "employee" embraces persons whose compensation is derived from the performance of services, and thus covers civil service retirees like appellant. Moreover, although § 111's nondiscrimination clause draws upon the constitutional doctrine of intergovernmental tax immunity, the retention of immunity in § 111 is coextensive with the prohibition against discriminatory taxes embodied in that doctrine. On its face, § 111 purports to be nothing more than a partial congressional consent to nondiscriminatory state taxation of federal employees. However, by negative implication, § 111 also constitutes an affirmative statutory grant of immunity from discriminatory state taxation in addition to, and coextensive with, the pre-existing protection afforded by the constitutional doctrine. Regardless of whether § 111 provides an independent basis for finding immunity or merely preserves the traditional constitutional prohibition against discriminatory taxes, the scope of the immunity granted or retained by the nondiscrimination clause is to be determined by reference to the constitutional doctrine. Pp. 30-33. (b) So long as the challenged tax does not interfere with the Federal Government's ability to perform its governmental functions, the constitutional doctrine of intergovernmental tax immunity has not been violated. Here, the fact that the challenged tax does not interfere with the Federal Government's ability to perform its governmental functions does not mean that private entities or individuals who are subjected to discriminatory taxation on account of their dealings with a sovereign cannot themselves receive the protection of the constitutional doctrine. Rather, the relevant inquiry is whether the inconsistent tax treatment is directly related to, and justified by, "significant differences between the two classes." Phillips Chemical Co. v. Dumas Ind. Sch. Dist., 361 U. S. 376, 383. Even assuming that the State's retirement benefits are significantly less municifient than those offered by the Federal Government, in terms of vesting requirements, rate of accrual, and computation of benefit amounts, this difference alone does not suffice to justify the type of blanket exemption at issue here. There are undoubtedly many individual instances in which the opposite holds true. To the extent that appellant has paid taxes pursuant to the invalid tax scheme, he is entitled to a refund. Pp. 33-36. 2. Whether the appropriate remedy for appellant's claim of discriminatory taxation is to extend the tax exemption to retired federal employees (or to all retired employees), or to eliminate the exemption for retired state and local government employees, is a question of state law within the special expertise of the Michigan courts. Pp. 36-37. Reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit granted certiorari in a case involving an alleged price-fixing conspiracy in the parcel tanker industry. The court ruled that the parties involved in the case agreed that when a contract is silent on an issue there's been no agreement that has been reached on that issue. The parties agreed that as a result of these judgments and orders, AnimalFeeds and petitioners must arbitrate their antitrust dispute. The Second Circuit previously held that the charterers' claims were not subject to arbitration under the applicable arbitration clause, but the Court ruled against them. The Court's decision is consistent with the decision in Green Tree Financial Corp. v. Bazzle, 539 F.3d 539, and with the ruling in Stolt-Nielsen S. A.A., 387 F. 3d 163, in which the Court found that the class arbitration provision of the Federal Arbitration Act does not apply when the parties' contracts are silent on the issue of class arbitration. In this case, the parties agreed to a panel of three arbitrators to determine whether the arbitration clause permits the arbitration to proceed on behalf of or against a class. The panel agreed that it would follow the rules of the American Arbitration Association's Supplementary Rules for Class Arbitrations (AAA). The Court ruled that there was no agreement on this issue, and that it was appropriate for the court to decide whether the parties had agreed to class arbitration in this case. The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case and issued its decision on the matter.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a series of insider trading suits filed under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (16(b)) against financial institutions that had underwritten various initial public offerings (IPOs) in the late 1990's and 2000 . The court held that the SEC's two-year period of limitations for filing insider trading claims under  16(a) of the Act had expired long before the alleged profits were realized, and that the parties had failed to comply with the requirements of the law. The appeals court concluded that, even if the SEC had found that the defendants had violated the law, the court of appeals had not found that there was a need to dismiss the claims. The Court held that, in this case, the SEC could not hold the defendants liable because it had not alleged that the alleged profit was realized within two years of the date of the defendants' alleged violations. The Appeals Court concluded that the Securities Act does not provide for an extended period of repose. The Supreme Court has previously held that an insider trading suit must be filed within the two years after the date the insider's transactions are disclosed in a Form 4 filing. We conclude that the Court of Appeal's decision in Whittaker v. Whittaker Corp., 639 F.2d 516 (1981), was wrong and that, as a result, the parties should be allowed to proceed with their claims. We also conclude that, under the circumstances, the defendants were not liable for the alleged violations of Section 16(b). The Court's ruling will not affect the parties' ability to recover their ill-gotten gains under the securities laws.

Section 1982 of Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits official and private racially discriminatory interference with property rights. In 1982, the outside walls of petitioners' synagogue were painted over with red and black paint and with large anti-Semitic slogans, phrases, and symbols. Thereafter, petitioners filed an action in Federal District Court, alleging that respondents' actions had violated, inter alia, 42 U. S. C. § 1982. Respondents moved to dismiss the complaint, claiming that since Jews are not a racially distinct group, there could be no violation of § 1982. The court agreed and dismissed the complaint. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Jewish congregations may assert a cause of action under § 1982 even though Jews do not constitute a separate race by today's standards. Although a charge of racial discrimination within the meaning of § 1982 cannot be made out simply by alleging that the defendant was motivated by racial animus, it also must be alleged that such animus was directed toward the kind of group that Congress intended to protect when it enacted the statute. Here, it appears that Jews and Arabs were among those groups considered to be distinct races and hence protected by § 1982 at the time the statute was adopted. Certiorari granted; 785 F. 2d 523, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was charged with violating the antifraud provisions of the Juvenile Court Act of 1940.  According to the court's order, Morris A. Kent, Jr., a 14-year-old who was placed on probation in 1959, was not entitled to counsel in connection with a waiver of jurisdiction.  The court found that the defendant had a history of criminal conduct, including housebreaking, robbery, and rape, and that he had been previously incarcerated for housebreaking and robbery.  In addition, the court ruled that the juvenile was entitled to access to the social records of his mother, who had been separated from her husband since he was two years old.  As alleged in the order, the defendant was also entitled to the right to a hearing on a "critically important" waiver.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Kent consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently restrains his jurisdiction over the child, and permanently enjoins him from violating the pre-judgment provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against him from serving as an officer or director of a public school.    The Court of Appeals also issued a temporary restraining order against Kent from further violations of the federal securities laws, including Section 17(a)(1) and (3) of Section 13(b)(2)(A) and Rule 13b2-1 thereunder.  It also ordered Kent to pay a $25,000 civil penalty.  On January 22, 1963, the District Court granted the request for a preliminary injunction against Kent and ordered him to comply with the order by consenting to the issuance of an order appointing a receiver to oversee the transfer of a defendant to a federal district court.  A hearing on January 24, 2013, was scheduled for 5:30 p.m.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts today entered a final judgment against a defendant and representative of a class of adult minors who sought to have an abortion without parental consent.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Boston, Massachusetts, on August 2, 1974, Massachusetts passed a law requiring a minor to obtain parental consent before an abortion can be performed on an adult.  The complaint alleges that, in violation of the federal law, the minor was unable to consent to an abortion because she lacked the experience, perspective, and judgment to make the informed and reasonable decision.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Massachusetts today announced criminal charges against two adult defendants in connection with the same case.  On July 4, the court issued an order enjoining the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 12(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 12b-5 thereunder, and ordering the defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and injunctive relief.

After petitioner Texas Department of Assessment and Collection of Taxes denied respondent Texas monthly sales tax exemptions for religious publications sold through its subscription service, respondent brought suit in Texas trial court seeking declaratory and injunctive relief. Respondent claimed that the tax exemption for religious publications violated the First Amendment, as made applicable to the States by the Fourteenth Amendment. The trial court ultimately agreed and issued an injunction. The Texas Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Texas' sales tax exemption for religious publications violates the First Amendment, as made applicable to the States by the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 10-20. (a) Even though the tax exemption applies to all religious publications, it nevertheless manifests a preference for religious publications over nonreligious ones, and hence violates the Establishment Clause absent a compelling state interest in promoting religion. Nothing in this Court's decisions under the Free Exercise Clause prevents the State from eliminating altogether its exemption for religious publications. While the State may have a compelling interest in avoiding violations of the Free Exercise Clause, it cannot claim persuasively that its tax exemption is compelled by that clause in even a single instance, let alone in every case. Pp. 10-14. (b) The State's interest in maintaining a uniform sales tax system is comparable to the Federal Government's interest in the uniform collection of social security taxes, and mandatory exemptions under the Free Exercise Clause are arguably as difficult to prove. No one has suggested that members of any of the major religions in the United States -the principal beneficiaries of Texas' tax exemption-could demonstrate an infringement of their free exercise rights sufficiently serious to override the State's countervailing interest in collecting its sales tax. Pp. 14-15. (c) The State's interest in maintaining a uniform sales tax system is not compromised by the fact that compliance with government regulations by religious organizations and the monitoring of their compliance by government agencies would themselves enmeshthe operations of church and state to some degree. Such compliance would generally not impede the evangelical activities of religious groups, and the "routine and factual inquiries" commonly associated with the enforcement of tax laws bear no resemblance to the kind of government surveillance the Establishment Clause was designed to preclude. Pp. 15-16. (d) To the extent that language in Murdock v. Pennsylvania, 319 U. S. 105, and Follett v. McCormick, 321 U. S. 573, is inconsistent with this Court's decision here, based on the evolution in this Court's thinking about the Religion Clauses over the past 45 years, this Court disavows such language. Pp. 16-19. Reversed and remanded.

Percolating through each of these provisions for relief are interests of the United States and problems of immunity, agency, and consent to suit. The constitutionality of applying the substantive requirements of the Act to the States is not, in our view, affected by the possibility that one or more of the remedies the Act provides might not be available when a State is the employer-defendant. Pp. 466-467. (a) In order to be covered by the Act, an employer hospital or school must in fact have "employees engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce, including employees handling, selling, or otherwise working on goods that have been moved in or produced for commerce by any person . . .." 29 U. S. C. § 203(i). Appellants' contention that hospitals and schools simply have no such employees misses the mark, and the District Court found it inappropriate to explore fully in a declaratory judgment proceeding. Held: 1. The District Court was correct in declining to decide, in the abstract and in general, whether schools and hospitals have employees engaged in the commerce or production of out-of-state commodities, and it will not carve up the commerce power to protect enterprises indistinguishable in their effect on commerce from private businesses, simply because those enterprises happen to be run by the States for the benefit of their citizens. P. 467. 2. The principle of United States v. State of California is controlling here. Appelants' argument that the statute involved was somewhat more directly and obviously a regulation of "commerce," and that the state activity involved there was less central to state sovereignty, misses the marks, and this Court has examined and will continue to examine federal statutes to determine whether there is a rational basis for regarding them as regulations of commerce among the States, but it will do not carve them up the Commerce power to regulate commerce from the private businesses that are run for the State's benefit of its citizens. Id. (b) That the exercise of that power, in whatever capacity, must be in subordination to the power of interstate commerce, which has been granted specifically to the national government, is necessarily diminished to the extent of the grants of power to the federal government in the Constitution. Id., 3. The State can no more deny the power if its exercise has been authorized by Congress than can an individual. Id, 4. The "separability" provision of the Safety Appliance Act does not preclude the State from being liable for any amount of unpaid overtime or overtime, but does preclude the States' liability for any unpaid overtime, overtime, or overtime. Id . (c) In light of that provision, id. (d) Parden v. Terminal R. of Alabama, 377 U.S. 184, which held that a state university that imported scientific apparatus from abroad could be made to pay import duties imposed by the power over foreign commerce, id., 4. In neither instance, however, did any showing have been made that warrants declaratories or injunctive relief. Id: (1) That no showing has been made, in either instance, warranting relief. Nor was there any showing of showing that warrants such relief, since no showing of such relief was made. Id.: (2) That there has been no showing warranting such relief in either case, and that no showing had been made in either of these cases, which the Court found inappropriate in a judgment proceeding, was not a showing of state immunity, which is almost impossible and most unnecessary to resolve in advance of particular facts, stated claims, and identified plaintiffs and defendants, and is reserved for appropriate future cases. Id; (3) That, while the Commerce Power of the States may be limited to the activities of the State, valid general regulations of Commerce do not cease to cease to be regulations of the commerce because a State-involved. Cf. Parden

The Supreme Court in this case addressed the definition of a discriminatorily "abusive work environment" under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The case involved Teresa Harris, who sued her employer, Forklift Systems, Inc., claiming that the company's president, Charles Hardy, created an abusive work environment through gender-based insults and sexual innuendos.

The District Court had previously ruled that while Hardy's conduct was offensive, it did not create an abusive environment because it did not seriously affect Harris's psychological well-being or interfere with her work performance. The Court of Appeals affirmed this decision.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a conflict among the Circuits regarding whether conduct must seriously affect an employee's psychological well-being to be actionable as "abusive work environment" harassment. The Court reaffirmed the standard set in Meritor Savings Bank, FSB v. Vinson, which does not require conduct to cause tangible psychological injury to be considered discriminatory. Instead, the conduct must be severe or pervasive enough to create an objectively hostile or abusive work environment, and the victim must subjectively perceive the environment as abusive.

The Court clarified that Title VII is violated when the workplace is permeated with discriminatory intimidation, ridicule, and insult that is sufficiently severe or pervasive to alter the conditions of the victim's employment and create an abusive working environment. The Court emphasized that Title VII aims to prevent a work environment that is abusive to employees because of their race, gender, religion, or national origin, regardless of whether it causes psychological harm.

The Supreme Court concluded that the District Court erred by focusing on whether the conduct seriously affected Harris's psychological well-being and whether she suffered injury. The Court stated that such an inquiry might distract from the real issue, which is whether the environment was hostile or abusive. The Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion, indicating that the lower court should consider the full context of the behavior, including its frequency, severity, and impact on work performance, without requiring evidence of psychological harm.

The Supreme Court addressed whether a negligent breach of a general maritime duty of care that results in death is actionable under general maritime law, as it is when it results in injury. The case arose from the death of Christopher Garris, who was injured while working aboard a vessel in navigable waters and later died from those injuries. His mother filed a complaint invoking federal admiralty jurisdiction and sought damages under general maritime law and the Virginia wrongful death statute.

The District Court initially dismissed the complaint, stating that under general maritime law, there was no cause of action for the death of a nonseaman in state territorial waters resulting from negligence. However, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed this decision, citing the Supreme Court's decision in Moragne v. States Marine Lines, Inc., which recognized a maritime cause of action for wrongful death resulting from a breach of maritime duties.

The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, finding no rational basis to distinguish between negligence and unseaworthiness regarding the duty to compensate for wrongful death. The Court noted that the maritime law had already adjusted common-law duties of care to fit the maritime context and had long recognized the tort of negligence.

The Court also examined relevant federal statutes, including the Jones Act, the Death on the High Seas Act (DOHSA), and the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act (LHWCA), and determined that none of these statutes precluded the respondent's negligence action. The Court concluded that the general maritime law must comply with statutory resolutions, but in this case, the statutes did not resolve the particular issue at hand.

In summary, the Supreme Court held that the maritime cause of action established in Moragne for unseaworthiness is equally available for negligence, and thus, a negligent breach of maritime duty that causes death is actionable under general maritime law. The judgment of the Court of Appeals was affirmed, allowing the respondent to seek recovery for the wrongful death of her son.

After respondent was denied appointment as a Federal prosecutor, he filed suit in a North Carolina state court against petitioner, charging that petitioner had violated the First Amendment's Petition Clause by writing two letters to President Reagan accusing respondent of misconduct while a judge and seeking his removal from judicial office. The trial court entered judgment for petitioner on the ground that the Petition Clause did not provide absolute immunity from liability for libel. The North Carolina Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The Petition Clause does not provide absolute immunity to a defendant charged with expressing libelous and damaging falsehoods in letters to the President. Pp. 10-14. (a) Although the right to petition is assured by the First Amendment, it does not follow that the Framers of the Amendment believed that the Petition Clause provided absolute immunity from damages for libel. Early libel cases in state courts provide no clear evidence of the nature of the right to petition as it existed at the time the First Amendment was adopted. Nor do the Court's decisions interpreting the Petition Clause in contexts other than defamation indicate that the right to petition is absolute. To accept petitioner's claim of absolute immunity would elevate the Petition Clause to special First Amendment status. However, the Petition Clause was inspired by the same ideals of liberty and democracy that gave us the freedoms to speak, publish, and assemble. There is no sound basis for granting greater constitutional protection to statements made in a petition to the President than other First Amendment expressions. Pp. 10-14. (b) Under state common law, damages may be recovered only if petitioner is shown to have acted with malice. The Petition Clause does not require the State to expand this privilege into an absolute one. P. 14. 737 F. 2d 427, affirmed.

In the Supreme Court case involving Barclays Bank PLC and Colgate-Palmolive Co., the Court addressed the constitutionality of California's method of taxing multinational corporations. The state used a "worldwide combined reporting" system to calculate corporate franchise taxes, which aggregated the income of all entities within a multinational enterprise and then applied a formula to determine the taxable income attributable to California operations.

Barclays and Colgate argued that this tax system unfairly burdened foreign-based multinationals, resulting in double taxation and interfering with the federal government's ability to regulate international commerce consistently. They claimed this violated the Commerce and Due Process Clauses of the U.S. Constitution.

The Supreme Court rejected these arguments, affirming the judgments of the California Court of Appeal. The Court held that the Constitution does not prevent California from applying its corporate franchise tax to Barclays and Colgate. The Court found that California's tax system met the requirements of having a substantial nexus with the state, being fairly apportioned, not discriminating against interstate or international commerce, and being related to the services provided by the state.

The Court also addressed the concern of multiple taxation and the federal government's ability to "speak with one voice" in international trade. It concluded that while multiple taxation might occur, it was not inevitable, and the alternative method of separate accounting would not necessarily reduce the risk. Furthermore, the Court noted that Congress had not enacted legislation to prohibit states from using worldwide combined reporting, indicating a lack of congressional intent to preempt such state practices.

The Court emphasized that it is Congress's role, not the judiciary's, to decide on the balance between tax uniformity and state autonomy in the context of international commerce. Therefore, the Court deferred to Congress to determine whether to regulate state taxation of multinational enterprises.

Implications of the decision include the affirmation of states' rights to use worldwide combined reporting for taxing multinational corporations and the recognition that Congress has the authority to regulate this area if it chooses to do so. The decision also underscores the principle that the judiciary does not oversee the government's foreign policy decisions, which are entrusted to the political branches.

Petitioner Northern Insurance Company of New York (Northern) filed suit against respondent Chatham County, Ga., in Federal District Court, seeking damages resulting from an alleged tort committed by County employees who had caused damage to Northern’s insured’s boat after the County’s drawbridge fell into the river. The District Court granted the County’s motion for summary judgment on the ground that the suit was barred by sovereign immunity. Reasoning that sovereign immunity applies to counties as well as states, the court relied on Browder County v. Wickman, 195 F. 2d 614, which held that sovereign immunity extends to counties exercising powers delegated from the State. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, acknowledging that the County did not assert an Eleventh Amendment immunity defense, which would fail because, under circuit precedent, the County did not qualify as an arm of the State. Nonetheless, the court concluded that the County could invoke a “residual” immunity that would protect it from suit. Held: An entity that does not qualify as an “arm of the State” for Eleventh Amendment purposes cannot nevertheless assert sovereign immunity as a defense to an admiralty suit. Pp. 3–7. (a) Only States and arms of the State possess immunity from suits authorized by federal law. See Alden v. Maine, 527 U.S. 706, 740. Although this Court’s cases have used the term “sovereign immunity,” they have done so imprecisely, since the Court recognizes that the immunity of States from suit “is a fundamental aspect of the sovereignty which the States enjoyed before the ratification of the Constitution, and which they retain today…except as altered by the plan of the Convention or certain constitutional Amendments.” Id., at 713. The Supreme Court ruled that the petitions for criminal trespass against five black men who entered a privately owned amusement park in Maryland were violative of the Fourth Amendment. The park, although advertised to the public, had a policy of excluding blacks. The men were arrested by a "deputy" sheriff working for the park, despite possessing valid transferrable tickets. The Court found that the actions of the "deputy" sheriff were state action, and therefore subject to the protections of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

Respondents, a producer association and its members, engaged in the sale of fertilizers to South Korea pursuant to arrangements entered into under the United States foreign aid program. They brought this civil antitrust proceeding claiming that their concerted activities violated § 1 of the Sherman Act. Section 2 of the Webb-Pomerene Act provides an "exemption" from the Sherman Act for acts "done in the course of export trade." After respondents had answered the complaint, petitioner Government agency promulgated a regulation making it economically impracticable for respondents to continue operating. Thereafter respondents dissolved themselves. Petitioner appealed directly to this Court under the Expediting Act. Held: 1. Though the dissolution of respondents makes this case technically moot, it does not render the case wholly moot. Pp. 108-109. 2. The transactions here involved are not "acts done in the course of export trade," within the meaning of § 2 of the Webb-Pomerene Act. Pp. 109-116. Reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court held that a conviction for conspiracy to commit money laundering, under 18 U.S.C. § 1956(h), does not require proof of an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy. The case involved petitioners who were part of an organization that fraudulently induced investors to give money with false promises of high returns. They were charged with money laundering conspiracy, but argued that the government needed to prove an overt act to secure a conviction.

The Court's decision was based on the interpretation of the statutory language of § 1956(h), which does not explicitly require an overt act for a conspiracy offense. This interpretation aligns with the Court's previous ruling in United States v. Shabani, which found that the drug conspiracy statute, 21 U.S.C. § 846, similarly does not require proof of an overt act. The Court reasoned that when Congress omits an overt act requirement from a conspiracy statute, it intends to adopt the common law definition of conspiracy, which does not require an overt act for liability.

The Court rejected the petitioners' argument that § 1956(h) merely increased penalties for money laundering conspiracies under the general conspiracy statute, 18 U.S.C. § 371, which does include an overt act requirement. The Court found that § 1956(h) establishes a separate offense and that Congress would have explicitly referenced § 371 if it intended to link the two statutes.

The Court also dismissed arguments based on legislative history and the structure of § 1956, stating that the plain text of the statute was clear and unambiguous. The Court noted that Congress is presumed to be aware of the legal precedent and knows how to include an overt act requirement when it wishes to do so.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the lower court's decision, upholding the petitioners' convictions for money laundering conspiracy without the need for the government to prove an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy.

The Supreme Court considered whether the use of incriminating statements made by the petitioner, obtained by a federal agent through a concealed radio transmitter, violated the petitioner's constitutional rights. The petitioner had been indicted for federal narcotics offenses and was released on bail when the statements were surreptitiously recorded during a conversation in a car.

The Court did not address the Fourth Amendment issue regarding unlawful search and seizure but focused on the petitioner's Sixth Amendment right to counsel. The Court referenced the Spano v. New York decision, which established that a confession obtained after indictment and without counsel present could not be used against a defendant. The Court emphasized that the right to counsel is crucial from the time of arraignment until the trial, as established in previous cases such as Powell v. Alabama.

The Court held that the petitioner's Sixth Amendment rights were violated when the incriminating statements were deliberately elicited by federal agents after indictment and without his lawyer present. The Court rejected the government's argument that continuing the investigation was justified, stating that while the investigation itself was proper, the use of the petitioner's statements as evidence was unconstitutional.

The Supreme Court reversed the lower court's decision, concluding that the petitioner's right to counsel was infringed upon, and the incriminating statements could not be used against him at trial. This decision underscored the importance of the right to counsel during the pre-trial phase and the protection against indirect and surreptitious interrogations by law enforcement.

The Supreme Court decided that federal jurisdiction exists over Everett Sisson's limitation of liability lawsuit brought in connection with a fire on his vessel. The Court found that Section 1333(1) of Title 28 United States Code grants federal district courts jurisdiction over "any civil case of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction". The Court held that the fire on Sisson's vessel caused a potential hazard to maritime commerce and that the storage and maintenance of a vessel at a marina on navigable waters is substantially related to traditional maritime activity.

Petitioner white supremacist group held a public rally in the town of Princess Anne, Maryland, during which it announced plans to resume the rally the next night. Respondents, officials of Princess Anne and Somerset County, then secured a restraining order from the Circuit Court of Somerset County, which was extended into a permanent injunction. That court relied on tape recordings of the previous night's rally. The Maryland Court of Appeals affirmed the 10-day order but reversed the 10-month order. While the controversy remained pending in the lower courts, petitioners attempted to conduct further rallies in the county, but respondents threatened arrest unless they complied with the injunction. Held: 1. The case is not rendered moot by the passage of time since petitioners have continued to engage in activities which the injunction restrains. Pp. 108-109. 2. The 10-day restraining order was improperly issued ex parte, without giving petitioners an opportunity to participate in the proceedings. Such an order contravenes the requirements of due process and the First Amendment. Pp. 109-114. 223 Md. 45, 320 A. 2d 45, reversed.

After being arrested by petitioner Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) officers outside a plant in Texas, respondents were brought to an INS office in Dallas, where they were fingerprinted and photographed. Subsequently, after having been advised of their right to seek judicial review of their removal, they were transported to a Federal District Court in Los Angeles, where they were informed that they faced deportation because they had remained in the United States longer than authorized. Each respondent then waived his right to a hearing and signed a document acknowledging that he had been removed from the United States. Later, respondents filed petitions for writs of habeas corpus in Federal District Courts in Los Angeles and Houston, claiming that their removal violated their due process rights under the Fifth Amendment. While the suits were pending, Congress amended the Immigration and Nationality Act to make it mandatory that deportees be provided with a hearing before they could be removed. Ultimately, the District Courts denied relief, holding that the statutory changes rendered respondents' claims moot. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that the amendments did not affect the merits of respondents' claims. Held: Evidence derived from peaceful arrests by INS officers need not be suppressed in an INS civil deportation hearing. Pp. 1040-1050. (a) Under the doctrine announced in United States v. Leon, 468 U. S. 897, evidence is admissible in a deportation hearing if it meets the standards prescribed by the Rules of Evidence applicable to civil trials. Here, the evidence was not suppressed because it was physically coercive, but because it was obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment. Pp. 1040-1041. (b) Because the body of a noncitizen is not suppressible as evidence in a deportation hearing, the exclusion of the incriminating documents in question did not prejudice respondents' due process rights. Pp. 1041-1042. (c) Nor did the exclusion of the documents violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Such exclusion did not deprive respondents of any interest in the outcome of the deportation proceedings, since they were afforded a full hearing on the merits of their removal. Pp. 1042-1043. (d) Application of the exclusionary rule in INS civil deportation proceedings would not provide significant, much less substantial, additional deterrence to Fourth Amendment violations by INS officers. Rather, the costs of applying the rule in such proceedings would be unusually high, since application of the rule would force the courts to release from custody persons who would then immediately resume their commission of a crime through their continuing, unlawful presence in this country. Pp. 1043-1050. 705 F. 2d 1068, reversed.

On June 10, 2002, the U.S. District Court for the District of Kansas entered a final judgment against a convicted sex offender for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Kansas City, alleges that Robert G. Lile, a convicted felon in the custody of the Kansas Department of Corrections, violated the mandatory minimum security provision of the federal securities laws.  According to the complaint, Lile agreed to participate in a program designed to rehabilitate convicted sex offenders.  Lile also agreed to be barred from participating in the program.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Lile.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's findings, Lefkowitz and his co-defendants agreed to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from future violations of the securities laws, and impose a penalty equal to the amount of their prison time.  As a result of the settlement, the SEC is seeking a permanent injunction, a return of all of the defendants' allegedly ill-gotten gains plus interest, and the return of their previously-convicted convictions.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant in a carjacking case.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, on May 5, 1994, a jury found defendant Morgan H. Bell liable for a series of carjackings, including one in which the defendant threatened to use a gun if the victim refused to surrender her car keys.  The SEC alleges that the jury was told that the defendant had an unconditional intent to harm or kill the victim, and that he would have used his gun if any of the drivers had given him a "hard time."  The complaint further alleges that Bell refused to comply with the jury's orders to surrender the car.  As alleged in the complaint, Bell was the only person who had ever attempted to commit such a crime, and the jury found him liable for the majority of the charges.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Mississippi today announced criminal charges against Bell.  On May 6, 2018, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against Bell, charging him with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil money penalties.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the SEC, Bell consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $75,000.  Bell agreed to settle the case by consenting to a permanent bar from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any automobile, and to a five-year officer-and-director bar.  He also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years.

This case involves a dispute over whether the common-law knock-and-announce principle applies to searches and seizures carried out by law enforcement officials. The defendant, a woman named Sarah Smith, allegedly possessed illegal drugs and weapons in her apartment. She had previously been involved in several incidents related to drug trafficking and had threatened one of the witnesses testifying against her.

In October 2018, a team of police officers arrived at Ms. Smith's apartment to execute a search warrant. Upon arrival, the officers noticed that the front door was slightly ajar. They called out to Ms. Smith and asked her to let them in. However, Ms. Smith did not answer, and the officers forced entry into the apartment. Inside, they discovered several bags containing illegal drugs and weapons hidden throughout the apartment.

Ms. Smith was subsequently arrested and charged with multiple crimes related to drug trafficking and weapons possession. She filed a motion challenging the legality of the search and seizure, arguing that the officers had violated her rights under the Fourth Amendment by failing to follow the knock-and-announce procedure. Her motion argued that the failure to announce their presence constituted a violation of her privacy and security interest in her home.

The trial judge denied Ms. Smith's motion, finding that the officers had acted reasonably in carrying out the search and seizure. He determined that the officers had followed standard operating procedures and had acted based on credible information provided by reliable sources. The judge also ruled that the knock-and-announce procedure was not applicable in this situation because the officers had reason to believe that announcing their presence would put them in danger.

On appeal, Ms. Smith challenged the denial of her motion, arguing that the trial judge had erred in applying the knock-and-announce doctrine too narrowly. She claimed that the doctrine should apply broadly to all searches and seizures, regardless of the specific circumstances surrounding the case. Ms. Smith also argued that the trial judge had relied on insufficient evidence to determine that the officers had acted reasonably in conducting the search and seizure.

The appeals court upheld the trial judge's ruling, finding that the officers had acted reasonably in carrying out the search and seizure. The court determined that the officers had had valid reasons for believing that announcing their presence would place them in danger, and that the knock-and-announce procedure was therefore not applicable in this situation. The court also found that the trial judge had properly evaluated the evidence presented by both parties and had reached a valid conclusion regarding the reasonableness of the search and seizure.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit held that a federal court cannot recharacterize a motion filed under the federal habeas corpus provision of 28 U. S.C.  2255 as the litigant's first motion under the law's "second or successive" restrictions. The court held that the court's failure to do so did not legally undermine its recharacterization of the 1994 motion as being his second habeas motion, and that the 1997 motion was indeed Castro's second motion. The Court held that it would have to apply the same restrictions to both motions if it had applied the same rules to the 1994 and 1997 motions. We conclude that the courts should not apply the restrictions to the current motions. The Supreme Court's decision in Palmer, a case involving a habeas motion filed in federal court in Florida, provides an example of the circumstances in which a court may apply the rules. The high court held in Palmer that the "second" and " successive" provisions of the law apply to the same motion. In this case, the court held, however, that it is not necessary to apply those provisions to the second motion to determine whether a motion is a second motion under 2255. In the case of Castro, we held that, under the circumstances, a recharacterized motion would not be subject to the restrictions. We also held that there was no need for the court to determine that it was the second of the two motions, since it would not have been subject to those restrictions if it applied to the first motion.

After respondent Savchuk, a Minnesota resident, suffered injuries in an automobile accident in Indiana where petitioner Rush, an Indiana resident, was allegedly liable, Savchuk brought an action against Rush in a Minnesota state court seeking damages. Since Rush had no contacts with Minnesota that would support in personam jurisdiction, Savchuk attempted to obtain quasi in rem jurisdiction by garnishing petitioner insurance company's obligation under the insurance policy to defend and indemnify Rush in connection with the suit. Petitioner does business in Minnesota. Held: A State may not exercise quasi in rem jurisdiction over an absent defendant by attaching the insurance company's obligation to defend and indemnify the defendant in connection with liability claims. Pp. 449-456. (a) While the mere presence of property in a State does not establish a sufficient relationship between the owner of the property and the State to support the exercise of jurisdiction over an unrelated cause of action, here the fact that Rush's insurer does business in Minnesota suggests no further contacts between Rush and the forum, and the record supplies no evidence of any. Nor are there significant contacts between the litigation and the forum. Pp. 450-452. (b) An alternative approach for finding minimum contacts in Seider type cases, approved by the Minnesota Supreme Court, is to treat the attachment procedure as the functional equivalent of a direct action against the insurer. But since the State's ability to exert its power over the "nominal defendant" is analytically prerequisite to the insurer's entry into the case as a garnishee, and assuming that the defendant has no real stake in the litigation is far from self-evident, attributing the insurer's forum contacts to the defendant would be unconstitutional. And while the parties' relationships with one another may be significant in evaluating their ties to the forum, the requirements of International Shoe, Inc. v. Washington, 326 U. S. 310, must be met as to each defendant over whom a state court exercises jurisdiction. Pp. 452-455. (c) By shifting the focus of the inquiry from the relationship among the defendant, the forum, and the litigation to that among the plaintiff, the forum, the insurer, and the litigation, the justification offered in support of Seider jurisdiction shares a common characteristic: They substitute the State's contacts with the plaintiff and its regulatory interests for its contacts with the defendant and the cause of action. Such an approach is forbidden by International Shoe and its progeny. Pp. 455-456. Reversed.

Section 608 of the National Housing Act provides for the issuance of federally guaranteed mortgages on properties designed primarily for residential use and containing not less than eight dwelling units. Under regulations prescribed by the Federal Housing Administration, the mortgaged property must be "designed principally for residential use," and the rent schedule must be based upon a maximum average rental fixed prior to the insurance of the mortgage and shall not thereafter be changed except upon approval by the Commissioner. An applicant for insurance submitted to the Administrator a schedule of monthly rates for various types of apartments, but he made no disclosure of any apartments intended for transients or any arrangements for their rentals. After obtaining insurance, the applicant furnished some apartments and rented them to transients. He also maintained a separate schedule of rates for transients, which was not approved by the Administrator. Held: The Act does not give mortgagors the right to rent to transients, and the Administrator's contemporary construction of the Act to exclude such rentals is controlling. Pp. 408-415. (a) The Act gives no express provision one way or the other regarding transient rentals, but the limitation seems fairly implied. Pp. 410-411. (b) The Administrator's construction of the Act is clearly expressed in instructions to field officers and in planning manuals issued by the Agency. Pp. 411-412. (c) Prior approval by the Administrator of all rental schedules was always required by the regulations, and the applicant never obtained nor sought approval of a schedule of rents for transients. P. 412. (d) Although the Administrator had power to grant such approval, it did so only in exceptional cases. P. 412. (e) The Administrator's construction of the Act is supported by the history of the Act and by the fact that Congress accepted it when it passed the 1954 amendment. Pp. 412-413. (f) Since the Act does not give mortgagors the right to rent to transients, the Administrator's construction of the Act is controlling, and the 1954 amendment is not invalid as applied to the applicant. Pp. 413-415. 154 F. Supp. 411, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit recently ruled that a mistrial in the case of a man charged with capital murder in the death of a one-year-old Arkansas boy can proceed. The court ruled that the jury could not reach a verdict on the charges of capital murder and first-degree murder because it was deadlocked on the lesser charges of manslaughter and negligent homicide. The jury could have found Alex Blueford guilty of all three charges, but could not have found him guilty of the more serious charge of murder. Without a verdict, the court ordered a retrial. The Court ruled that Blueford could be tried again for the same charges, and that the trial court had violated the Double Jeopardy Clause by failing to disclose the jury's vote on the charge of manslaughter. Blueford's lawyers argued that the prosecution's case against him was based on a "mountain of evidence"

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit recently ruled that the Chicago Police Department violated the rights of a man arrested in connection with the murder of his brother-in-law by failing to honor his request to consult with his lawyer during the course of an interrogation. The court held that the refusal constituted a denial of 'the Assistance of Counsel' in violation of the Sixth Amendment to the Constitution as 'made obligatory upon the States by the Fourtee th Amendment' and thereby renders inadmissible any incriminating statement elicited by the police during the interrogation. On January 19, 1960, petitioner's brother- in-law was fatally shot. In the early hours of the next morning, at 2:30 a.m., petitioner was arrested without a warrant and interrogated. The next day, Benedict DiGerlando, who was then in police custody and who was later indicted for the murder along with petitioner, told the police that petitioner had fired the fatal shots. The day after his arrest, petitioner and his sister, the widow of the deceased, were arrested and taken to police headquarters. En route to the police station, the police 'had handcuffed the defendant behind his back,' and 'one of the arresting officers told defendant that Di Gerlando had named him as the one who shot' the deceased. Petitioner testified, without contradiction, that the 'detective said they had us pretty well, up pretty tight, and we might as well admit to this crime' and that he replied, 'I am sorry but I would like to have advice from my lawyer.'

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a Minnesota law banning the retail sale of milk in plastic nonreturnable, nonrefillable containers violated the Equal Protection and Commerce Clauses of the Constitution. The law was passed in 1977 with the support of the state Pollution Control Agency, Department of Natural Resources, and Department of Agriculture, Consumer Services Division, and Energy Agency. Proponents of the legislation argued that it would promote resource conservation, ease solid waste disposal problems, and conserve energy. Opponents argued that the Act would merely increase costs of retail milk products and prolong the use of ecologically undesirable paperboard milk cartons. The court found that the discrimination against plastic nonre fillables was not rationally related to the Act's objectives. The high court held that the district court's decision to enjoin enforcement of the law was not supported by the full record and an independent review of documentary sources. The justices ruled that the "rational basis" for the law's purpose was to promote the state interests of encouraging the reuse and recycling of materials and reducing the amount and type of material entering the solid waste stream.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a California man who was convicted of orchestrating a series of false statements in the wake of his wife's death.  According to the SEC's complaint filed in federal court in Jackson, California, Ray Travers, a former insurance agent, made a false and misleading statement in a telephone conversation with a co-defendant in which Travers told him that his wife had been killed and that she had been shot in the head. Travers allegedly told Travers that he had lain in wait for her with a gun and had fired six bullets into her body at close range. The complaint alleges that Travers replied, without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint, that his version of the story had been recorded without the respondent's knowledge and that the respondent knew it would be a matter of record.  Travers also allegedly told the codefendant that he would be willing to have his next conversation with the respondent electronically recorded, and, since he planned to return to get additional information for the insurance company, he agreed to do so.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Travers.  The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by Michael J. Basinger and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the FBI, the California Department of Insurance, and the U. S. Attorney's Department of Justice.
