The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the timeliness of claims filed against the United States under the Tucker Act, specifically concerning property owners who participated in a federal program to develop affordable rental housing. These property owners, the petitioners, had agreements with the Farmers Home Administration (FmHA) that included a right to prepay their loans at any time, which would release them from the program's restrictions. However, Congress passed the Emergency Low Income Housing Preservation Act of 1987 (ELIHPA), which imposed permanent restraints on prepayment of FmHA loans.

The petitioners argued that ELIHPA breached their contracts and constituted a taking of property without just compensation, violating the Fifth Amendment. Their claims were dismissed by the Federal Circuit as time-barred under a six-year statute of limitations, as they filed suit over nine years after ELIHPA's enactment.

The Supreme Court reversed the Federal Circuit's judgment, holding that ELIHPA's enactment was a repudiation of the contracts, not an immediate breach. The Court reasoned that a breach would occur, and the six-year limitations period would commence, when a borrower attempted to prepay and the government dishonored its obligation to accept the tender.

The Court rejected the government's argument that the statute of limitations should start on the earliest possible date, emphasizing that the traditional principles of contract law apply to the government in the same way they apply to private parties. The Court also noted that forcing plaintiffs to sue soon after the government's repudiation would lead to unnecessary litigation and could be counterproductive for the government.

The Supreme Court concluded that the petitioners' claims would be timely if filed within six years of a wrongly rejected tender of prepayment. The judgments of the Federal Circuit were reversed, and the cases were remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, holding that the amended § 207 of the Indian Land Consolidation Act (ILCA) remains unconstitutional. The original provision aimed to address the problem of highly fractionated ownership of Indian land parcels by escheating small fractional interests to the tribe upon the owner's death, without compensation. This was intended to consolidate land ownership within tribes. However, in Hodel v. Irving (1987), the Court found the original § 207 to be a violation of the Fifth Amendment, as it constituted a taking of private property without just compensation.

Despite amendments to § 207 in 1984, which included a longer period to assess the income-generating capacity of the land, permission for devise of fractional interests to current owners of the same parcel, and authorization for tribes to develop their own codes for disposition of fractional interests, the Court found that these changes did not sufficiently address the constitutional issues identified in Irving. The amendments still resulted in a significant restriction on the right to direct the descent of property and did not prevent the taking of property without just compensation.

The Court emphasized that the ability to pass property to one's heirs is a fundamental aspect of property rights, and the amended § 207 continued to abrogate this right in an extraordinary manner. The provision's focus on income rather than the actual value of the land, and the limited class of individuals who could receive fractional interests by devise, did not mitigate the economic impact or the character of the governmental regulation sufficiently to make it constitutional.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the lower court's ruling that the amended § 207 of the ILCA is unconstitutional because it still represents a taking of private property without just compensation, in violation of the Fifth Amendment.

In 1974, California adopted the Warren-Alquist State Energy Resources Conservation and Development Act (Act), which requires that a utility seeking to build in California any electric power generating plant, including a nuclear power plant, must apply for certification to the state Energy Resources and Conservation Commission (Energy Commission). The Act was amended in 1976 to provide additional state regulation of new nuclear power plants. The Act also requires that nuclear reactors must be periodically refueled and the spent fuel removed. The general practice is to store the fuel in a water-filled pool at the reactor site. For many years, it was assumed that this fuel would be reprocessed; accordingly, the storage pools were designed as short-term holding facilities with limited storage capacities. As expectations for reprocessing remained unfulfilled, spent fuel accumulated in the pools, creating the risk that nuclear reactor reactors would have to be shutdown. In recent years, some 8,000 metric tons of spent nuclear fuel have already accumulated, and it is projected that by the year 2000 there will be some 72,000. The lack of a long-term disposal option increases the likelihood that the insufficiency of interim storage space for spent fuel will lead to reactor-shutdowns, rendering nuclear energy an unpredictable and uneconomical adventure. The granting of state authority in §§ 271 and 274 (k) of the Act, combined with recent federal enactments, demonstrated that Congress did not intend that nuclear power be developed "at all costs," but only that it proceed consistent with other priorities and subject to controls traditionally exercised by the states and expressly preserved by the federal statute. The Court of Appeals affirmed the District Court's ruling that the petitioners have standing to challenge the California statutes, and also agreed that the challenge to § 25524.2 is ripe for review. It concluded, however, that the challenges to the two statutes are ripe for adjudication, and that the two provisions are void because they are preempted by and in conflict with the Atomic Energy Act. Held: 1. The challenge to the waste disposal regulations in § 255 24. 2 is not ripe for judicial review. The basic rationale of the ripeness doctrine is to prevent the courts from entangling themselves in abstract disagreements over administrative policies and also to protect the agencies from judicial interference until an administrative decision has been formalized and its effects felt in a concrete way by the challenging parties. Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner, 387 U. S. 136, 148-149. Pp. 5-11. 2. The question of whether § 25525.2 (b) is ripe and classified is a more difficult proposition. The statute does not seek to regulate the construction or operation of a nuclear plant, but is adopted because "uncertainties in the nuclear fuel cycle make nuclear power an uneconomically and uncertain source of energy." Pp 5-7. (a) State safety regulation is not preempted only when it conflicts with federal law. Rather, the federal government has occupied the entire field of nuclear safety concerns, except the limited powers expressly ceded to the states. When the federal interest is so dominant that the federal system will be assumed to preclude enforcement of state laws on the same subject, the test of preemption is whether "the matter on which the state asserts the right to act is in any way regulated by the Federal Government." Rice v. Santa Fe Elevator Corp., 331 U.S. 218, 230. P. 7. 3. The fact that the Act is not designed to provide protection against radiation hazards, but was adopted because the NRC's regulations are aimed at insuring that plants are safe, not necessarily that they are economical, does not interfere with the objective of the federal regulation. Moreover, a state prohibition on nuclear construction for safety reasons would also be in the teeth of the atomic Energy Act's objective to insure that nuclear technology be safe enough for widespread development and use-and would be preempted for that reason, Pp 7-8. 489 F. 2d 699, affirmed and remanded.

While serving a prison sentence for murdering his ex-girlfriend, petitioner Wood became subject to the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996’s requirement that states provide a mechanism allowing prisoners to seek postconviction relief from death sentences on the ground that they were rendered invalid due to newly discovered evidence of their innocence. He filed a motion seeking such relief in Alabama state court, alleging, inter alia, that he was mentally illiterate and that his trial counsel had failed to investigate and present evidence of his mental illness. The state court ultimately denied the motion, ruling that the counsel’s actions were not constitutionally deficient. Wood then filed a habeas petition in Federal District Court, challenging the state court’s factual determination that his counsel acted competently. That court ruled in favor of Wood, holding that the state court’s determination was an unreasonable determination of the facts in light of the evidence presented in the state-court proceedings. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed. Held: Even assuming that the state court’s factual determination should be reviewed under §224(d)(2) and not under §224(e)(1), the state court’s finding that Wood’s counsel made a strategic decision not to pursue or present evidence of his mental deficiencies was not an unreasonable determination of the facts. Pp. 4–10. (a) Assuming that the state court’s factual determination should be reviewed under §224(d)(2), the evidence in the state-court record supports the state court’s conclusion. All of the evidence cited by Wood speaks not to whether counsel made a strategic decision, but rather to whether counsel’s judgment was reasonable. And most of the evidence Wood cites as potentially supporting the opposite conclusion does not suffice to demonstrate that the finding was unreasonable. Rather, it is not unreasonable to conclude that, after reviewing the Kirkland report, counsel made a strategic decision not to inquire further into the information contained in the report about Wood’s mental deficiencies and not to present to the jury such information as counsel already possessed about these deficiencies. Pp. 4–7. (b) Wood’s argument that the state court unreasonably applied Strickland in rejecting his ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claim on the merits is not fairly included within the questions presented here. Whether the state court reasonably determined that there was a strategic decision under §224(d)(2) is a different question from whether the strategic decision itself was a reasonable exercise of professional judgment under Strickland or whether the application of Strickland was reasonable under §224(d)(1). Both of the latter questions may be related to the one presented here, but they are not fairly included therein. Pp. 7–8. 542 F. 3d 1281, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Sotomayor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Stevens, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona today entered a final judgment against a defendant in a civil injunctive action brought by a group of school parents seeking to bar them from providing interpreters to their children.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Arizona, James Zobrest, who has been deaf since birth, asked a school district to provide a sign-language interpreter to accompany him to classes at a sectarian high school.  The complaint alleges that, under the IDEA, no funds traceable to the government ever find their way into sectarian schools' coffers.  As alleged, the school district provided the interpreter only as a result of numerous private choices of individual parents of school-age children, and that the interpreter would not be a "joint sponsor" of the school's activities.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the district agreed to the court's order, which permanently enjoins the defendant from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and Rule 206(3)-8 thereunder.  In its judgment, the court also ordered the defendant to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and ordered the district to pay civil penalties in the amount of $10,000.   The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by Michael J. Welshhans and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson of the Chicago Regional Office.

The Supreme Court of the United States recently ruled in favor of the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) in a case concerning the release of certain information regarding a school district's participation in a federally funded educational technology program called E-rate. The ruling upheld the FTC's determination that the information requested by a third party was not subject to release under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) due to potential harm to the privacy of students and teachers.

In reaching its decision, the Supreme Court considered the language of FOIA Exemption 7(C), which provides for the withholding of "information contained in or relating to investigatory materials gathered during a civil, criminal, administrative, or arbitrational proceeding." The Court determined that the information requested fell outside the scope of this exemption, as it was not specifically related to an ongoing investigation or proceeding.

Additionally, the Court examined the concept of "personal privacy" as it relates to FOIA Exemption 7(C). While recognizing that corporations may have privacy interests, the Court ultimately held that the term "personal privacy" in this context primarily refers to the privacy of natural persons rather than artificial entities like corporations.

Overall, the Supreme Court's decision serves as a reminder that the protections afforded by FOIA are designed to safeguard the privacy and confidentiality of individuals, rather than corporations or other organizations.

In this case, the Supreme Court will examine whether a state can exercise quasi in rem jurisdiction over a nonresident defendant by garnishing the obligation of an insurance company to defend and indemnify the defendant in a liability claim brought by a resident of the state. The court will apply the principles established in International Shoe Co. v. Washington (1945) and its progeny, which require that a state may exercise jurisdiction over an absent defendant only if the defendant has "certain minimum contacts with [the forum] such that the maintenance of the suit does not offend 'traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.'" The court will evaluate whether the obligations of an insurance company to defend and indemnify a nonresident insured under an automobile liability insurance policy are a garnishable res in the state where the incident giving rise to the action occurred, and whether the assertion of jurisdiction over the defendant complies with due process standards.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Romani Industries, Inc., a Pennsylvania-based company that defrauded a Cumbria County, Pennsylvania resident out of approximately $490,000.  The court's order, which was entered on January 25, 1985, requires that a federal tax claim be given preference over a judgment creditor's perfected lien on real property even though such a preference is not authorized by the Federal Tax Lien Act of 1966.  According to the order, Romani's lien was "perfected in the sense that there is nothing more to be said to be certain than the priority of the federal government's claims over certain other kinds of debts."  The order also requires that the judgment creditor acquire a valid liens on the real property before it is recorded in the county where the property is located.  In a parallel action, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Pennsylvania today held that the priority statute did not apply to federal claims against national banks because it did not permit the government to "be paid first" in the adjudication of federal tax debts.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court's opinion, Romiani's estate's administrator sought permission from the court to transfer the property to the judgment debtor.  Romani consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $5,000, which is equal to the amount owed in the default judgment.  Additionally, the court granted the estate's request for a temporary restraining order and an asset freeze, and ordered the transfer of the property.   The SEC's investigation was conducted by Michael J. Conrrad and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Philadelphia Regional Office. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) was ordered by the U.S. Supreme Court of Alabama in 1961 to produce various records, including membership lists, by the Attorney General of Alabama. The Court of Appeals agreed that the matter 'should be initially litigated in the courts of the State' and ordered the case to be transferred to the District Court for further proceedings. The District Court dismissed the action, and the Supreme Court again upheld the contempt judgment. The case was re-opened and the Court ruled that it should be heard on the merits of the matter. The Supreme Court held that the case should be dismissed because it was not the subject of a hearing on the issue of the validity of the restraining order. The Appeals Court agreed, however, that the issue should be decided by the State Supreme Court, and that the Court should order the parties to settle the matter in the State Court. The appeals court agreed with the lower court's decision, and sent the case back to the district court for a hearing. The lower court dismissed the case, citing the lack of jurisdiction to hear the case. The United States Supreme Court ruled in the Association's favor, and this case is the fourth time the Court has reviewed the matter of contempt of court. The decision is remanded to the Court of Appeal for further consideration.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Contract Disputes Act of 1978 (CDA) is not applicable to contracts between the National Park Service (NPS) and concessioners doing business in the national parks. The CDA provides that disputes arising out of certain Government contracts must be submitted to an agency's contracting officer. A government contractor dissatisfied with the contracting officer's decision may seek review either from the United States Court of Federal Claims or from an administrative board in the agency. The court concluded that the CDA is ambiguous on whether it applies to concession contracts and found NPS' interpretation of the Act reasonable. The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, found that the Act does not apply to contracts that are not service or procurement contracts. The Supreme Court held that the case is not yet ripe for judicial resolution.

In the case of Board of Education, Island Trees Union Free School District No. 26 et al. v. Steven A. Pico et al., the Supreme Court of the United States addressed whether a local school board's decision to remove certain books from high school and junior high school libraries violated the First Amendment rights of students.

The school board had ordered the removal of books they deemed "anti-American, anti-Christian, anti-Semitic, and just plain filthy." Students challenged this action, claiming it infringed upon their First Amendment rights. The District Court initially sided with the school board, but the Court of Appeals reversed the decision, leading to the Supreme Court review.

The Supreme Court held that the First Amendment does impose limitations on a school board's discretion to remove books from school libraries. While school boards have broad discretion in managing school affairs, this discretion must align with the First Amendment's principles. The Court emphasized that students do not lose their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at school and that these rights are particularly implicated by the removal of books from a school library.

The Court distinguished between the removal of books from libraries and the selection of curriculum or textbooks, noting that the case only concerned the former. The Court also clarified that its decision did not affect a school board's discretion to choose which new books to add to a library.

The Court concluded that school boards cannot remove books simply because they disagree with the ideas within them. To do so would be to prescribe orthodoxy, which is contrary to the First Amendment. However, the Court acknowledged that if the removal was based on educational suitability or the presence of pervasive vulgarity, it might be permissible.

The Court found that the evidence presented raised a genuine issue of material fact as to whether the school board's actions were motivated by a desire to suppress certain ideas rather than legitimate educational concerns. As such, the Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had reversed the District Court's summary judgment in favor of the school board and remanded the case for trial.

The decision underscored the importance of the First Amendment in the educational context and the need for school boards to exercise their discretion within constitutional bounds, particularly when it comes to the availability of ideas and information in school libraries.

On June 14, 1969, two Woodville, Mississippi police officers entered a bar and pool hall to execute a warrant for the arrest of a youth named C.C. Jackson. Jackson resisted and a hostile crowd of some 50 or 60 persons gathered. The officers' first attempt to handcuff Jackson was frustrated when 20 or 25 men in the crowd intervened and wrestled him free. Officer James Forman radioed for assistance and Aaron 'Sonny' Liberty removed his riot gun, a 12-gauge sawed-off shotgun, from the car. When the officers again attempted to make their arrest, the officers were attacked by the onlookers and during the commotion five or six pistol shots were fired. Officer Forman was looking in a different direction when the shooting began, but immediately saw that Liberty had been shot several times in the back. Before Liberty died, he turned around and fired both barrels of his riot weapon into an alley in the area from which the shots appeared to have come. The first shot was wild and high and scattered the crowd standing at the face of the alley. Liberty appeared, however, to take more deliberate aim before the second shot and hit one of the men in a crowd in the front of the head and neck as he ran down the alley, that man was Leon Chambers. Shortly after the shooting, three of Chambers' friends discovered that he was not yet dead. He was transported to the same hospital and later charged with Liberty's murder. Chambers was subsequently convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison without parole. The Mississippi Supreme Court affirmed his conviction, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed. Chambers's conviction. Chambers filed a petition for certiorari for a new trial. The 5th Court granted his request for a retrial, and Chambers was granted bail pending the outcome of the appeal. The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced that it has obtained an emergency court order halting a multi-million dollar securities offering fraud.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that Norman Schreiber and Donald Jacobson conducted a sales campaign in which they repeatedly made false and misleading statements in an effort to solicit orders for the purchase of Lawn-A-Mat Chemical & Equipment Corp.'s common stock.  According to the complaint, the two registered representatives made projections of substantial increases in the price of the common stock and optimistic statements concerning the company's financial condition.  As the complaint alleges, these projections and statements were without basis in fact, since Lawn-a-Mat was losing money during the relevant period.  In addition, the complaint further alleges that the two representatives told prospective investors that the car would be marketed within six weeks, and that the company had no plans to manufacture a new car and tractor.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders them to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty equal to the amount of their profits.  Additionally, the court issued a temporary restraining order against the defendants from further violations of these provisions.  On May 4, 2018, the SEC filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, alleging that the defendants violated Section 17:a(a)(1) and Rule 17(b)(5) and that they violated Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934.   The complaint also alleged that the SEC failed to adequately consider the role of scienter in determining whether to impose a civil injunctive relief.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17:17(a).

Appellee association, a group of American producers of fertilizer, and its members, were charged in a civil antitrust complaint with violations of § 1 of the Sherman Act. The Government sought injunctive relief against the association's members as well; they were to be prohibited from forming any new export associations without court approval and from continuing in effect any prices jointly agreed upon. Held: 1. The Act does not immunize appellees from antitrust liability by § 2 of the Webb-Pomerene Act, as "act(s) done in the course of export trade." Pp. 531-532. 2. Appellees were not the only defendant in this case, since the dissolved association was the only party. P. 532. 3. The fact that the amended Act did not apply to all contracts on which the former members of the association might bid does not completely remove the controversy, since it stretches neither the language nor the purpose of the Act to determine that such sales are not "exports" within the meaning of the "export trade" provision of the statute, and that the dissolution of the Association does not moot the case is untenable. Pp532-534. 4. The Court of Appeals erred in holding that the Act did immunize the association and that its activities were not "act[s] done" in the "course ofexport trade." Held: The Act is not applicable to transactions initiated, controlled, and financed by the American Government, just because a foreign government is the nominal "purchaser." United States v. Union Oil Co. of California, 377 U. S. 13, 84 S. C. 1051, 12 L. Ed. 2d 98, and thus the Act is no exception to the antitrust laws, which are not bound by formal conceptions of contract law, but are bound by the language, purpose, and legislative history of the law. P p. 534. 273 F. Supp. 263, reversed and remanded.

Respondents, a New York corporation engaged in the business of promoting and presenting theatrical productions for profit, applied for the use of a municipal theater for the showing of the musical "Hair." The theater's directors met, after a brief discussion, voted to reject the play. None of them had seen the play or read the script, but they understood from outside reports that the musical, as produced elsewhere, involved nudity and obscenity on stage. Although no conflicting engagement was scheduled for the Tivoli, respondents determined that the production would not be "in the best interest of the community." Respondents then filed an answer to the complaint. The District Court denied preliminary relief, concluding that petitioner had failed to show that it would be irreparably harmed pending a final judgment since scheduling was "purely a matter of financial loss or gain" and was compensable. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Respondents' action here is indistinguishable in its censoring effect from the official actions consistently identified as prior restraints in a long line of this Court's decisions. Pp. 531-532. (a) A system of prior restraint runs afoul of the First Amendment if it lacks certain safeguards: First, the burden of instituting judicial proceedings, and of proving that the material is unprotected, must rest on the censor, and any restraint prior to judicial review can be imposed only for a specified brief period and only for the purpose of preserving the status quo. Second, a prompt final judicial determination must be assured. P. 533. (b) The Board's decision might not have had the effect of total suppression of a musical in the community, but it was not implemented by the board under a system with appropriate and necessary procedural safeguards. P p. 534. (c) Respondents had the same powers of licensing and censorship exercised by postal officials in Blount v. City of Baxley, 355 U. S. 313, 322, and Lovell v. Griffin, 303 U.S. 444, 451-452, and if judicial review is made unduly onerous, by reason of delay or otherwise, the board's determination in practice may be final. Bantam Books, Inc. v. Sullivan, 372 U. s. 51, 58, and the Board's standard for resolving that question was correct, for the Board did not implement the standard under which respondents' action was based under. The standard, whatever it may have been, was implemented by a system that assures prompt judicial review with a minimal restriction of First Amendment rights necessary under the circumstances, and it was no mere temporary bar while necessary judicial proceedings were under way. The Board was not required to apply the standard below. 2. Respondent's action was no less a prior restraint because the public facilities under their control happened to be municipal theaters. The First Amendment's protection "includes complete and absolute freedom to exhibit, at least once, any and every kind of motion picture . . . even if this film contains the basest type of pornography, or incitement to riot, or forceful overthrow of orderly government . . .." Id., at 46-47, 81 S.Ct. 935, 938, 22 L. Ed. 2d 894, reversed.

In the case of Lance Raygor et al. vs. University of Minnesota, the appellants, Lance Raygor and James Goodchild, filed a lawsuit against their employer, the University of Minnesota, alleging age discrimination under the Minnesota Human Rights Act (MHRA). The University moved to dismiss the case, arguing that the 45-day statute of limitations for filing a state lawsuit had expired and was not tolled by the federal "Supplemental Jurisdiction" statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1367(d). The district court agreed with the University and dismissed the case.

The appellants had initially filed their lawsuit in federal district court, including claims under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) and the MHRA. However, the federal court dismissed the case on Eleventh Amendment grounds, which bars suits against a state by citizens in federal court. The appellants then filed in state court, but the University argued that the statute of limitations had not been tolled during the federal case.

The Court of Appeals reversed the district court's decision. The appellate court held that the assertion of an Eleventh Amendment defense by the University did not eliminate the federal district court's original jurisdiction over the federal question claims or its supplemental jurisdiction over the related state law claims. The court found that the statute of limitations for the MHRA claim was indeed tolled while the federal case was pending, as per 28 U.S.C. § 1367(d), which states that the limitations period for any claim is tolled while the claim is pending in federal court and for 30 days after its dismissal, unless state law provides a longer tolling period.

Additionally, the court considered whether the statute of limitations could be equitably tolled based on the specific circumstances of the case. The court concluded that there was no evidence of prejudice to the University and that the appellants' decision to file in federal court was legally sound given the unclear legal landscape at the time regarding Eleventh Amendment immunity for ADEA claims against states. Therefore, even if the appellants were not entitled to statutory tolling under 28 U.S.C. § 1367, their claims could be equitably tolled during the pendency of the federal action.

The decision implies that state law claims can be tolled while federal claims are pending, even if the federal court ultimately dismisses the case on Eleventh Amendment grounds. This allows plaintiffs to pursue their state law claims in state court without being barred by the statute of limitations due to the time spent in federal court.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit has ruled that Ohio's laws requiring the Socialist Labor Party to submit more than the required number of signatures to be placed on the ballot violate the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The court ruled that the laws violate the Constitution's guarantee of equal protection under the law. The Socialist Party's complaint alleges that it was denied a place on the 1968 ballot because it failed to submit the required signatures. The party also argues that it has not filed petitions with the total signatures required under new Ohio laws for ballot position. The case was heard by the same three-judge panel that ruled against the Independent Party. The Sixth Circuit's decision is being appealed by the Ohio Attorney General's Office and the Ohio Secretary of State's office.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas today entered a final judgment against a defendant who claimed that he was unfairly excluded from the jury selection process because of his race.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Dallas, Texas, on May 10, 1986, the Dallas County District Attorney's Office and Dallas County district attorneys conducted a series of "jury shuffle" trials to determine whether or not a defendant should be barred from serving on a jury.  The SEC alleges that the defendants used the tactic to induce African-American jurors to participate in the trials.  As alleged in the complaint, the defendants were so strongly opposed to the death penalty that they did not bother to check the backgrounds of the jurors.  In addition, the complaint alleges that defendants who were not challenged by the prosecution were disproportionately likely to be struck by a jury that included African-Americans.  For example, as alleged, one of the defendants had relatives with criminal histories and therefore "should have been struck by the jury."  The complaint further alleges that one of these defendants had been convicted of a felony and served time in prison.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $1,000.   The court also issued a temporary restraining order halting the defendants from making any further statements or making any judgments regarding the merits of the case.  Finally, the court issued an order suspending the defendants' right to reapply for the bar against them from appearing or practicing before the SEC as a juror. Barry.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the United States Attorney's Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Texas Department of Criminal Investigation.

In the case involving Hodari D., the Supreme Court addressed whether Hodari had been "seized" within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment at the time he discarded drugs while being pursued by police. The California Court of Appeal had previously ruled that Hodari was seized when he saw an officer running towards him, making the seizure unreasonable and the evidence of cocaine inadmissible. The Supreme Court, however, disagreed.

The Supreme Court clarified that a "seizure" involves either the application of physical force or submission to an officer's show of authority. In Hodari's case, since he did not submit to the officer's authority and was not physically touched by the officer when he discarded the drugs, he was not seized at that moment. The Court emphasized that a seizure is a single act, not a continuous fact, and that a show of authority without the suspect's submission does not constitute a seizure.

The Court also referenced the Mendenhall test, which states that a person is seized only if a reasonable person would believe they were not free to leave. However, the Court noted that this is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a seizure. The Court concluded that since Hodari did not comply with the officer's show of authority, he was not seized until he was physically tackled.

Therefore, the evidence of the cocaine Hodari discarded was not the result of an illegal seizure and should not have been excluded. The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the California Court of Appeal and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with their opinion. The implication of this decision is that evidence discarded by a suspect during a police pursuit, prior to physical apprehension or submission to authority, is admissible in court.

Respondent McDonald, a black man, is the sole shareholder and president of JWM Investments, Inc. (JWM), a corporation organized under Nevada law. He sued petitioners (collectively Domino’s) for violations of §1981, which protects the equal right of “[a]ll persons within the jurisdiction of the United States” to “make and enforce contracts” without respect to race. JWM filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, and the trustee for JWM‘s estate initiated an adversary proceeding against JWM for breach of contract. For whatever reason, the trustee chose not to assert a §1981 claim. McDonald then filed a motion to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim. The District Court granted the motion, noting that McDonald had broken its contracts with JWM because of racial animus toward McDonald, and that the breach had harmed McDonald personally by causing him to suffer monetary damages and damages for pain and suffering, emotional distress, mental anguish, and humiliation. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that a plaintiff who lacks any rights under an existing contractual relationship with the defendant, and who has not been prevented from entering into such a contractual relationship, may bring suit under §1981. Held: Any claim brought under § 1981, therefore, must initially identify an impaired “contractual relationship,” §1981(b), under which the plaintiff has rights. Pp. 5–11. (a) Any claim under §1980 must initially identified an impaired contract relationship, §1981 (b). Any claim that a third-party intended beneficiary of a contract may have rights is not barred by §1981 unless he has (or would have) rights under the existing (or proposed) contract that he wishes “to make and enforce.” Patterson v. McLean Credit Union, 491 U. S. 164, 176, and Goodman v. Lukens Steel Co., 482 U.S. 656, which subjected defendants to liability under §§1981 when, for racially-motivated reasons, they prevented individuals who “sought to enter into contractual relationships” from doing so, on account of race. It is just the statutory construction we have always rejected. McDonald points to several of our prior cases involving plaintiffs whose status as contracting parties was unclear. Because they nonetheless prevailed, McDonald reasons, contractual privity cannot be a sine qua non of a § 1981 claim. Absent the requirement that the plaintiff himself must have rights, § 1981 would become a strange remedial provision designed to fight race in all of its noxious forms, but only if the animus and the hurt it produced were somehow connected to somebody’S contract. McDonald resorts finally to policy arguments. Unless his reading of the statute prevails, he warns, many discriminatory acts will go unpunished. See, e.g., Runyon v. McCrary, 427 U. s. 160 (1976), which subjected plaintiffs to liability for racial discrimination when racial discrimination blocks the creation of a contractual contract, id., at 660–664, and §1981 for a union to decline to press black employees’ grievances under the governing collective-bargaining agreement. The fundamental point, however, is that an individual seeking to make or enforce a contract under which he has rights will have a claim under 42 U S. C. §1981 while one seeking to enforce one under which someone else has rights does not. Absent that requirement, the Court will not consider, much less decide, the privity question. McDonald also argues in his merits brief (for the first time) that the Court should affirm the judgment because Domino-s interfered with McDonald's own contracts. The court correctly recognized and applied these principles, the Ninth Circuit erred in reversing its judgment. The Ninth Circuit reversed.
What is the main argument being made in this case?

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of the federal government in a dispute over a loan made to a couple in Texas. The couple, Delbert and Ethel Mae Yazell, took out a loan from the Small Business Administration (SBA) to help repair damages caused by a flood to their business. However, when the couple defaulted on the loan, the SBA attempted to collect the remaining balance from Ethel Mae's separate property.

In this case, the Supreme Court considered the extent to which the federal government could override state law regarding the ability of a married woman to enter into a contract without her "disability" being removed. The Court ultimately determined that the federal government could not override state law in this instance because the loan was negotiated with full awareness of the limitations imposed by state law. Additionally, the Court found that the SBA's failure to inform the couple of the potential consequences of entering into the loan agreement constituted bad faith.

On the evening of September 29, 1983, a 10-year-old boy was abused sexually by respondent. When the boy arrived at a local hospital, a physician used a sexual assault kit to collect physical evidence of the abuse. The kit included various items designed to collect saliva, blood, hair, and seminal fluid samples. However, the physician did not examine these samples at any time. Instead, the police placed the kit in a secure refrigerator at the police station. Nine days later, the police showed the boy photographs of suspects and he picked out respondent. Respondent was not located by the police until four weeks later, when he was arrested. Thereafter, the police examined the sexual assault kit, including the clothing worn by the boy. They found one semen stain on the boy's underwear and another on the rear of his T-shirt. Although they attempted to extract blood group substances from the stains, they were unable to do so. Subsequently, the police criminologist tested the clothing for the presence of blood group substances, but was unable to detect any. Both the State's and respondent's experts testified at trial that, had the semen samples been properly preserved and analyzed, the results might have exonerated respondent. The jury found respondent guilty, but the Arizona Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the State had violated respondent's rights under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by failing to preserve the semen samples. Held: Unless a criminal defendant can show bad faith on the part of the police, failure to preserve potentially useful evidence does not constitute a denial of due process of law. Pp. 108-112. (a) Where the State complies with Brady v. Maryland, 373 U. S. 83, and United States v. Agurs, 427 U. S. 97, by disclosing relevant police reports to the defendant, providing the defendant's expert with lab reports and notes prepared by the police, and giving the defendant's expert access to the relevant physical evidence, the Due Process Clause renders irrelevant the good or bad faith of the State. Cf. California v. Trombetta, 467 U. S. 479. Pp. 108-110. (b) However, the Due Process Clause requires a different result when the State fails to preserve evidentiary material of which no more can be said than that it could have been subjected to tests, the results of which might have exonerated the defendant. Requiring a defendant to show bad faith on the part of the police both limits the extent of the police's obligation to preserve evidence to reasonable bounds and confines it to that class of cases where the interests of justice most clearly require it, i. e., those cases in which the police themselves by their conduct indicate that the evidence could form a basis for exonerating the defendant. Pp. 110-112. 153 Ariz. 50, 734 P. 2d 592, reversed and remanded.

Respondents Lopez-Mendoza and Elias Sandoval-Sanchez, both citizens of Mexico, were summoned to separate deportation proceedings in California and Washington, and both were ordered deported. They challenged the regularity of those proceedings on grounds related to the lawfulness of their respective arrests by officials of the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS). On administrative appeal the Board of Immigration Appeals affirmed the deportation orders. The Court of Appeals reversed the deportation order and remanded the order to the BIA to determine whether the Fourth Amendment had been violated in the course of their arrest. Held: 1. An admission of unlawful presence in this country made subsequent to an allegedly unlawful arrest must be excluded as evidence in a civil deportation proceeding. Pp. 563-564. (a) A deportation proceeding is a purely civil action to determine eligibility to remain in the country, not to punish an unlawful entry, but to put an end to a continuing violation of the immigration laws. A deportation hearing looks prospectively to the respondent's right to remain, even if it is conceded that an unlawful arrest, search, or interrogation occurred. The INS currently operates a deliberately simple deportation hearing system, streamlined to permit quick resolution of very large numbers of deportation actions, and it is against this backdrop that the costs of applying the exclusionary rule, like the benefits, must be measured at the margin. P. 564. 2. In the absence of Miranda warnings, the INS must prove only alienage, and that will sometimes be possible using evidence gathered independently of, or sufficiently attenuated from, the original arrest. The BIA for its part has required only "clear, unequivocal and convincing" evidence of respondent's deportability, not proof beyond a reasonable doubt. In many deportation cases, the burden then shifts to the INS to prove the time, place, and manner of his entry. The court's decision as to respondent Lopez-mendoza, No. A22 452 208 (INS, Dec. 21, 1977), was vacated and his case remanded to the court. The Ninth Circuit, sitting en banc, reversed SandovalSanchez' deportation order, and vacated his deportation order. It held that the exclusionarian rule need not be based on "reasonable, substantial, and probative evidence," 8 U. S. C. § 1252(b)(4). Held: (1) The INS's task is simplified in this regard by the civil nature of the deportation proceedings, and a decision of deportability need be based only on reasonable, substantial evidence of the deportability of the respondent, not the likely costs of excluding unlawfully seized evidence from a deportation proceeding, and the BIE for the part of the INS has required no proof of the citizenship of the person and identity of respondent unless his actions had given the agents reason to believe that he was an undocumented alien. The order of deportation is not based on a criminal prosecution, but on the "prime purpose" of the [exclusionary] rule, if not the sole one, "is to deter future unlawful police conduct." United States ex rel. Bilokumsky v. INS, 525 F. 2d 803, 808, and an opinion with respect to Part V, in which Justice BLACKMUN, Justice POWELL, and Justice REHNQUIST joined. The case is remanded.

Summary:
The Supreme Court of the United States has ruled that Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866 encompasses claims of retaliation. The ruling came in response to a petition challenging the constitutionality of a California state law requiring employers to provide paid sick leave to employees. The petition argued that the law conflicted with federal labor laws, specifically Section 1981, which guarantees equal rights under the law regardless of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The Court disagreed, stating that "Section 1981's language does not exclude from its coverage allegations of retaliation." The Court cited previous decisions, including Sullivan v. Little Hunting Club, Inc., which held that Section 1982, a companion statute to Section 1981, covers retaliation. The Court also noted that Congress has repeatedly expressed its intention to protect workers from retaliation, including through the inclusion of anti-retaliation provisions in various labor laws.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California today entered a final judgment against a former member of the Communist Party who was convicted of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 504 of the federal securities laws.  According to the court's order, filed on May 24, 1961, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced criminal charges against the defendant.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that, from at least 1961 through at least the present, the federal government imposed a temporary restraining order on certain individuals and groups who were likely to engage in "subversive" activities.  As alleged in the complaint, the restraining order imposed by the court did not apply to specific individuals, but rather to certain groups of people.  For example, the complaint alleges that the defendant at issue was a member of a group of individuals who had been disfranchised, and therefore could not participate in the activities of the party.  In addition, the court found that the defendants violated the anti-fascism provision of Section 9(h) of the Securities Act of 1933.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating the federal laws, order them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, impose civil penalties, and impose officer-and-director bar against each of them.   The court also ordered the defendant to pay a civil penalty of six months' imprisonment. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Boston Regional Office.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) undertook to prescribe just, reasonable, and equitable divisions of joint rates pursuant to § 15 (6) of the Interstate Commerce Act, as amended. The Commission found that existing divisions violated § 15(6) because they allocated to Northern lines a lesser share of the revenues from the joint rates than would be warranted by their share of expenditures made in providing the joint service. The Southern lines brought suit before a three-judge District Court to enjoin and to set aside the Commission's order. The District Court held that the order was not supported by substantial evidence and reasoned findings within the meaning of §§ 8 (b) 2 and 10 (e)3 of the Administrative Procedure Act and, as modified, remanded the case for further proceedings. Held: The Commission's findings are adequate. Pp. 531-532. (a) The use of "unsifted averages" of costs does not necessarily establish greater costs either in rate cases or in divisions cases, and the use of such "adjustment" of average territorial costs is not a usable and useful tool for cost determination, but that territorial average costs could not be used consistently with the statutory requirements for precise and relevant findings without any evidence relating the territorial average cost to North-South traffic. P. 532. 270 F. Supp. 695, affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit has ruled that the "maximum term of imprisonment" for a prior state drug-trafficking conviction is the maximum sentence applicable to a prior drug offense when he was convicted of it. The court held that Clifton Terelle McNeill's prior convictions for assault with a deadly weapon and robbery were for "violent felonies" and not for "serious drug offenses" as he claimed. McNeill was sentenced to 300 months in prison for selling crack cocaine and possession with intent to sell cocaine base. The district court determined that McNeill qualified for ACCA's sentencing enhancement because he had three prior state convictions for violent felonies or serious drug offenses. McNeill argued that none of his six state drug trafficking convictions were for drug offenses, but the district court found that he had committed those crimes between 1991 and 1994 and each carried a 10-year maximum sentence. The 4th Circuit held that the District Court's decision to reduce the maximum prison term to 38 months was based on the "long and unrelenting history of serious criminal conduct" and "near certain likelihood of recidivism"

The Richmond City Council adopted the Minority Business Utilization Plan (the Plan), which required prime contractors to whom the city awarded construction contracts to subcontract at least 30% of the dollar amount of the contract to one or more Minority Business Enterprises (MBE's), defined as businesses effectively controlled by "citizens of the United States who are Negroes, Spanish-speaking, Orientals, Indians, Eskimos, or Aleuts." There was no geographic limit to the Plan; an otherwise qualified MBE from anywhere in the United S. could avail itself of the 30% set-aside. The Plan expired on June 30, 1988, and was in effect for approximately five years. The District Court upheld the Plan in all respects, except for the fact that it did not apply to city contracts awarded to minority-owned prime contractors. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The Richmond Plan is not narrowly tailored to remedy prior discrimination, since it is not linked to identified discrimination in the Richmond construction industry. Pp. 4-8. (a) The fact that the city has not identified the need for remedial action in the awarding of its public construction contracts does not mean that, a fortiori, the States and their political subdivisions are free to decide that such remedies are appropriate. P. 4. (b) The city has at its disposal a whole array of race-neutral devices to increase the accessibility of city contracting opportunities to small entrepreneurs of all races. The mere recitation of a "benign" or legitimate purpose for a racial classification is entitled to little or no weight. The purpose of strict scrutiny is to "smoke out" illegitimate uses of race by assuring that the legislative body is pursuing a goal important enough to warrant use of a highly suspect tool. The test also ensures that the means chosen "fit" this compelling goal so closely that there is little or any possibility that the motive for the classification was illegitimate racial prejudice or stereotype. The factfinding process of legislative bodies is generally entitled to a presumption of regularity and deferential review by the judiciary. However, when a legislative body chooses to employ a suspect classification, it cannot rest upon a generalized assertion as to the classification's relevance to its goals. Moreover, a governmental actor cannot render race a legitimate proxy for a particular condition merely by declaring that the condition exists. See, e. g., Fullilove v. Jackson Board of Education, 476 U. S. 267, which held that a congressional program requiring that 10% of certain federal construction grants be awarded "to minority business enterprises" did not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The City and the District Court relied on five predicate "facts" in reaching its conclusion that there was an adequate basis for a 30% quota: (1) the ordinance declares itself to be remedial; (2) several proponents of the measure stated their views that there had been past discrimination in a particular industry; and (3) several members of the City Council stated that the plan was "designed to further remedial goals," and (4) several of the MBE's named in the commitment form were in fact minority owned. The 30% figure was "chosen arbitrarily" and was not tied to the number of minority subcontractors in Richmond or to any other relevant number. The court concluded that the 30%, figure was not closely tailored to accomplish a remedial purpose, and that, once the "remedial" conclusion is reached, it could be used to "justify" race-conscious classifications in the city's construction industry, and would serve to increase opportunities available to minority business without classifying individuals on the basis of race. The dissenting judge argued that the majority had "misconstrue[d] and misapplied[d]" the decision in Wygant v. Klutznick, 448 U.S. 448, which upheld the minority setaside in part and concluded that it was justified in part because the city had demonstrated a compelling interest in remedying past discrimination. The district court also relied on Congress' finding in connection with the set-aide approved in Fullilve that there has been nationwide discrimination in construction industry; (5) the city and the court relied on its experience under § 8(a) of the Small Business Act of 1953, which had extended aid to minority businesses; (6) there was no direct evidence of race discrimination on the part of the city in letting contracts or any evidence that the prime contractors had discriminated against minority contractors; (7) there is no evidence that MBE membership in local contractors' associations was extremely low; (8) the "evidence" relied upon by the city did little to define the scope of any injury to minority contractors in Richmond, and (9) the factors relied upon could justify a preference of any size or duration

The Supreme Court was asked to consider whether the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule should be modified to allow evidence obtained by police officers acting in reasonable reliance on a search warrant, later found to be unsupported by probable cause, to be used in prosecution. The exclusionary rule typically prevents the use of evidence gathered in violation of the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.

The case involved a police investigation in Burbank, California, where officers, based on information from an informant and their own surveillance, obtained a search warrant for several locations and vehicles. The searches yielded large quantities of drugs, and the respondents were indicted. However, the respondents filed motions to suppress the evidence, arguing the warrant was not supported by probable cause. The District Court agreed in part, and the Court of Appeals affirmed the decision, rejecting the government's suggestion to recognize a good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, concluding that the exclusionary rule can be modified without undermining its purpose. The Court reasoned that the rule is intended to deter police misconduct, not to punish the errors of judges who issue warrants. The Court also noted that there is no evidence that judges and magistrates are inclined to disregard the Fourth Amendment, and thus, excluding evidence based on their errors would not have a significant deterrent effect.

The Court held that evidence obtained by officers acting in objectively reasonable reliance on a search warrant should not be excluded, even if the warrant is later invalidated. However, the Court clarified that this good-faith exception does not apply if the issuing magistrate was misled by false information from the police, if the magistrate abandoned their judicial role, if the warrant was based on an affidavit so lacking in probable cause as to be unreasonable, or if the warrant was facially deficient.

The Court emphasized that the probable-cause standard and warrant requirements remain intact, and the good-faith exception should be easy to apply. The Court also stated that this exception would not prevent courts from reviewing the constitutionality of searches and seizures or from providing guidance on Fourth Amendment issues.

In applying these principles to the case at hand, the Court found that the officers' reliance on the warrant was objectively reasonable, as the warrant application was based on more than a "bare bones" affidavit and there was enough evidence to create a legitimate debate over the existence of probable cause. Therefore, the evidence should not have been excluded, and the Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted Lockheed Corporation's motion to dismiss a complaint alleging that it violated the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) by creating two early retirement programs. The complaint alleged that Lockheed violated the provisions of both laws by creating the programs, which required employees to release any employment-related claims they might have against Lockheed. The court concluded that the programs constituted a use of Lockheed's plan assets for the benefit of a party in interest, which is a prohibited transaction under the laws. The district court agreed, and the case was dismissed on appeal. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's decision, holding that the board's actions were not unlawful under the law. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued a decision on the matter.

Case Name: Waldron v. Cities Service Corporation
Case Number: 54-1055
Decision Date: June 1, 1965
Supreme Court of the United States
Justice Writing Opinion: Earl Warren
Opinion Title: Summary Judgment
Issue: Whether summary judgment was properly granted to respondents based on the lack of evidence of conspiracy?
Background Information:
Waldron sued Cities Service Corporation and others for violating Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act. The case involved a conspiracy to fix prices for Iranian oil. The parties reached a settlement in 1953, but Waldron alleged that Cities Service breached the settlement by refusing to buy oil from him. The case went through multiple appeals, with the Supreme Court ultimately deciding the case.
Legal Analysis:
Summary judgment is appropriate when the evidence presented establishes that there are no genuine issues of material fact. The Supreme Court found that Waldron had failed to establish a prima facie case of conspiracy, and that there was no evidence to support his allegations. Additionally, the Court found that Cities Service had not engaged in any wrongdoing related to the settlement.
Impact:
The decision established that summary judgment was appropriate in antitrust cases, and that a plaintiff must establish a prima facie case of conspiracy in order to survive a motion for summary judgment.

In this Supreme Court case, the primary issue was whether the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) applies to undocumented alien employees and whether an employer commits an unfair labor practice by reporting undocumented workers to immigration authorities in retaliation for union activities.

The Court determined that undocumented aliens are considered "employees" under the NLRA and are therefore entitled to its protections. The Court found that the employer, Sure-Tan, Inc., had violated the NLRA by reporting its undocumented workers to the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) as a retaliatory measure for their union activities, which led to their constructive discharge.

The Court of Appeals had enforced the National Labor Relations Board's (NLRB) order for the employer to cease such practices and to offer reinstatement and backpay to the affected employees. However, the Court of Appeals also modified the Board's order, requiring that reinstatement be contingent on the employees' legal presence in the U.S. and that the offers be written in Spanish and remain open for four years, with a minimum of six months' backpay.

The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment that the employer violated the NLRA but reversed the Court of Appeals' decision regarding the specific remedies. The Supreme Court held that the Court of Appeals had overstepped its authority by imposing a minimum backpay award and by detailing the language and terms of the reinstatement offers. The Court emphasized that the NLRB has broad discretion to devise remedies that effectuate the policies of the NLRA, and such remedies must be tailored to the actual, not speculative, consequences of unfair labor practices.

The case was remanded to the Court of Appeals with instructions to send it back to the NLRB to formulate an appropriate remedial order consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. The decision underscores the NLRA's applicability to undocumented workers and the limited scope of judicial review in modifying the NLRB's remedial orders.

In the case of Michael J. Greenlaw v. United States, the Supreme Court addressed whether a Court of Appeals can increase a defendant's sentence on its own initiative, without a cross-appeal from the government. Greenlaw had been convicted of drug and firearm offenses and sentenced to 442 months in prison. He appealed, arguing his sentence was too long, but the Court of Appeals, while rejecting his arguments, noticed a sentencing error and ordered the District Court to increase his sentence by 15 years, even though the government had not appealed for a longer sentence.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals, holding that without a government appeal or cross-appeal, the sentence should not have been increased. The Court emphasized the principle of party presentation in the adversarial system, where courts act as neutral arbiters based on the issues presented by the parties. The Court also noted that Congress has specified when the government may seek appellate review of a sentence and requires high-ranking officials within the Department of Justice to personally approve such appeals, indicating that appellate judges should not independently seek to correct sentencing errors not pursued by the government.

The Court rejected arguments that Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 52(b) or 28 U.S.C. §2106 allowed for the increase in sentence without a cross-appeal. It also dismissed a novel interpretation of 18 U.S.C. §3742, which governs appellate review of criminal sentences, as unpersuasive and inconsistent with the cross-appeal rule.

The decision clarifies that appellate courts cannot increase a defendant's sentence on their own accord without a cross-appeal from the government, reinforcing the importance of the cross-appeal rule and the principle of party presentation in the U.S. legal system. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central issues were whether the payment of benefits under an early retirement program that required participants to release employment-related claims was a prohibited transaction under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), and whether amendments to ERISA and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) applied retroactively to prohibit age-based discrimination in pension plans.

The respondent, Paul Spink, had been employed by the petitioner, Lockheed Corporation, and was excluded from the company's retirement plan due to his age at the time of hiring, a practice that was legal under ERISA at the time. After Congress passed amendments in 1986 that prohibited age-based exclusions, Lockheed amended its plan to comply, but did not credit employees for service years prior to the amendment. Lockheed later created early retirement programs that offered increased benefits but required participants to waive any employment-related claims. Spink declined to participate and sued Lockheed, alleging violations of ERISA's duty of care and prohibited transaction provisions, as well as claiming that the OBRA amendments required Lockheed to count his pre-1988 service years toward his pension benefits.

The District Court dismissed the complaint, but the Court of Appeals reversed in part, finding that the retirement programs were unlawful under ERISA and that the OBRA amendments applied retroactively. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and reversed the Court of Appeals' decision.

The Supreme Court held that:

1. Employers are not considered fiduciaries when they amend the terms of a pension plan. Therefore, Lockheed's establishment of the early retirement programs did not violate ERISA's fiduciary rules.

2. The payment of benefits under the terms of an amended plan, even if conditioned on the waiver of employment claims, does not constitute a prohibited transaction under ERISA. The Court found that obtaining waivers of employment-related claims could not be meaningfully distinguished from other legitimate objectives of a pension plan.

3. The OBRA amendments to ERISA and the ADEA, which prohibit age-based benefit accrual rules, apply prospectively and not retroactively. The Court pointed to the explicit language in Section 9204(a)(1) of OBRA, which states that the amendments apply only to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 1988, and only to employees with service in those plan years.

The Supreme Court's decision clarified that employers have the freedom to amend pension plans without being considered fiduciaries under ERISA, and that the payment of benefits in exchange for waivers of claims is not a prohibited transaction. Additionally, the Court confirmed that the OBRA amendments do not apply retroactively, thus employers are not liable for using age-based accrual rules in plan years before the effective date of the amendments. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

After respondent Senator, as Chairman of the Senate Select Committee Investigating the Presidential Campaign Activities of 1972, publicly released portions of the classified "Pentagon Papers" (a secret study prepared by the Department of Defense), the Federal Grand Jury for the District of Columbia began an investigation of possible violations of federal criminal statutes arising out of the leakage of the documents. Respondent aide, whose salary was paid by the Senator, refused to comply with a subpoena calling for production of documents pertaining to the leakage of the documents. The District Court upheld the subpoena, rejecting the aide's claims of privilege under the Speech or Debate Clause of Art. I, § 6, cl. 1, of the Constitution. The Court of Appeals, in affirming, fashioned a nonconstitutional testimonial privilege protecting the aide from any questioning by the grand jury concerning the matter of republication of the Pentagon Papers. Held: 1. The Speech or Debate Clause does not apply to the aide, who is not a Member of Congress, and hence is not immune from grand jury questioning concerning the manner in which the Senator obtained the documents. Pp. 108-116. (a) The Clause applies to the aide only insofar as the aide's services would be immune legislative conduct if performed by the Senator himself. Pp. 110-112. (b) Private publication by the Senator through the cooperation of a publishing company was not part and parcel of the legislative process, and the aide's arrangements with the publishing company were not protected by the Clause. Pp. 112-115. 2. The protective order entered by the Court of Appeals is not an appropriate regulation of the pending grand jury proceeding. Paragraph two of the order, which bars questioning the aide with respect to any act performed by him within the scope of his employment, overly restricts the scope of grand jury inquiry. The aide's immunity, testimonial or otherwise, extends only to legislative acts as to which the Senator himself would be immune, and the grand jury, if relevant to its investigation into the possible violations of the criminal law, may require from the aide answers to questions relating to his or the Senator's arrangements, if any, with respect to republication or with respect to third-party conduct under valid investigation by the grand jury, as long as the questions do not implicate legislative action of the Senator. There is no constitutional or other privilege that shields the aide, any more than any other witness, from grand jury questions relevant to tracing the source of obviously highly classified documents that came into the Senator's possession and are the basic subject matter of inquiry in this case, as long as no legislative act is implicated by the questions. Paragraph one of the order, alone, would afford ample protection for the privilege if it forbade questioning any witness, including the aide, concerning the Senator's conduct, the motives and purposes behind the Senator's conduct, communications between the Senator and his aides during the term of their employment and related to the meeting or any other legislative act of the Senator, and except as it proves relevant to investigating possible third-party crime, concerning any act, in itself not criminal, performed by the Senator, or by his aides in the course of their employment, in preparation for the subcommittee hearing. Pp. 116-117. 455 F. 2d 757, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Western District of Pennsylvania has upheld a lower court's ruling that the state's anti-mining laws are not unconstitutional. The court found that Pennsylvania's Bituminous Mine Subsidence and Land Conservation Act (Subsidence Act) and certain implementing regulations violate the Constitution's Takings Clause and Contracts Clause. The Subsidence Act prohibits mining that causes subsidence damage to three categories of structures that were in place on April 17, 1966: public buildings and noncommercial buildings generally used by the public; used for human habitation; and cemeteries. The Court found that the Act's restrictions on mining in the vicinity of certain structures and areas are designed to diminish subsidence and subsidence damage. The Act also requires mining companies to leave coal in place as a means of providing surface support to the structures protected by  4. Section 6 of the Act also authorizes the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources (DER) to revoke a mining permit if the removal of coal causes damage to a structure or area protected by the DER. The DER has applied a formula that generally requires 50% of the coal to be kept in place to provide surface support. The lower court had previously found that  6 violated the Constitution, but the Court found it to be clear that neither of these provisions is unconstitutional on its face. The Supreme Court's decision in Pennsylvania Coal v. Mahon, in 1922, held that the Pennsylvania legislature had gone beyond its constitutional powers when it enacted a statute prohibiting the mining of anthracite coal in a manner that would cause the subsidence of land on which certain structures were located.

Title 11 of the Bankruptcy Code grants debtors who file a petition under Chapter 11 a “property right to exclude from gross income derived from participation in any trade or business during the calendar year” any gain realized through the sale of substantially all of their assets, 11 U. S. C. §1146(a), except gains attributable to property acquired after the filing of the petition, §1146(b). During respondent Picadilly Tea Company’s Chapter 11 reorganization, it sold its tea business for cash, but the transaction took place before the company’s plan was confirmed by the Bankruptcy Court. Under Florida’s stamp tax system, a tax is due on every document conveying real property located in the State, including documents covering the sale of personal property. Petitioner Florida sued to collect the tax based on the conveyance of Picadilly’s assets. Concluding that §1146(a) barred recovery, the district court dismissed the suit. The Eleventh Circuit disagreed, ruling that §1146(a) applied only to transfers taking place after plan confirmation. Held: Section 1146(a) affords a stamp-tax exemption only to transfers made pursuant to a Chapter 11 plan that has been confirmed. Pp. 4−13. (a) Interpretation of §1146(a) begins with consideration of the most natural reading of the statutory text. The provision uses the conjunction “under a plan confirmed under chapter…11” to describe the type of plan covered by the exemption. This phrasing shows that Congress meant to protect only those transfers that take place after the debtor has obtained plan confirmation. Any other reading renders the provision redundant with the general exclusions found in §§1146(b) and (c). Moreover, using the conjunction creates confusion regarding how to calculate the timing of the transfer, particularly where the transfer involves multiple stages of paperwork. Read literally, the clause might seem to permit the deduction of the tax liability associated with a future step in the plan’s execution, such as obtaining court approval of the plan. Pp. 4−6. (b) Substantive canons support the most natural reading of the statutory text. First, the federalism canon—which holds that “‘comity demands that States be accorded substantial autonomy in determining the proper scope of their taxing power,’ ” Sierra Summit Ltd. v. California Bd. of Equalization, 490 U. S. 844, 851—requires a strict application of §1146(a). This canon prevents federal interference with the administration of a State’s taxation scheme, and the canon also discourages federal interference with the administration of a State’s tax collection program. Second, applying the canon here does not violate the doctrine that a remedial statute such as the Bankruptcy Code should be liberally construed. There is no indication that §1146(a) is designed to reduce costs to debtors, nor is there evidence that the statute embodies a special congressional purpose aimed at facilitating reorganizations. Instead, §1146(a) sets forth a simple, bright-line rule governing when a debtor may seek a tax exemption.
