Title: Falling Prices and Robust Competition

Summary:
This article discusses the legal issues surrounding falling prices and robust competition in antitrust law. It examines the history of antitrust laws related to price discrimination and how they have evolved over time. The article highlights several key cases that illustrate the application of antitrust laws to falling prices and robust competition, including the famous case of FMC Corporation v. Holley Carburetor Company. The article concludes by discussing the implications of these cases for businesses operating in today's global economy.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Central District of California ruled that a search warrant issued by a magistrate judge in 1981 was not valid because it was not supported by probable cause. The court held that the search warrant was based on a confidential informant's report that two persons were selling large quantities of cocaine and methaqualone from their Burbank, California residence. The informant also reported that he had witnessed a sale of drugs by "Patsy" at the residence approximately five months earlier and had observed at that time a shoebox containing a large amount of cash that belonged to Patsy. The affidavit was insufficient to establish probable cause, however, and the court granted the defendants' motions to suppress the evidence seized pursuant to the warrant. The Court ruled that the magistrate judge's finding that the warrant was valid was not sufficient to support the magistrate's conclusion that the evidence was not of sufficient value to support a finding of probable cause against the defendants. The opinion concluded that the court should not have barred the use of the evidence obtained by officers acting in reasonable reliance on the warrant in the prosecution's case in chief. In a separate opinion, the court ruled that there was no need to modify the Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule because the court had found that it did not apply in this case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit held that Alabama's failure to comply with the provisions of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA) is barred by the Eleventh Amendment. The ADA prohibits certain employers, including the States, from "discriminat[ing] against a qualified individual with a disability because of the disability of such individual in regard to job application procedures, the hiring, advancement, or discharge of employees, employee compensation, job training, and other terms, conditions, and privileges of employment." 12112(a), 12111(2), (5), (7). The Act also prohibits employers from "utilizing standards, criteria, or methods of administration" that have the effect of discrimination on the basis of disability. The District Court granted the State's motion for summary judgment, finding that the State had not violated the ADA's provisions. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the lower court's decision, holding that the ADA does not extend to the State. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate opinion, held that the Eleventh amendment does not bar the State from recovering money damages under the ADA. The Court held that, under the circumstances, the State was not liable for the monetary damages sought by the state employees. The court held that it would have to show that the state's violations of the ADA would have resulted in "an undue hardship on the operation of the [employer's] business"

In this case, the Supreme Court reviewed a decision by the Florida Supreme Court regarding the certification of presidential electors in the 2000 election. The Florida Supreme Court had decided that the Secretary of State could not include certain late-filed ballot returns in the statewide certification, based on a 7-day deadline for submission of returns. However, the Supreme Court found that the Florida Constitution allowed for more flexibility in determining the qualifications of electors, and that the Secretary of State should consider each individual ballot and determine whether it meets the requirements for inclusion in the certification. Ultimately, the Supreme Court remanded the case back to the Florida Supreme Court for further proceedings.

The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) policy for deciding when resident aliens may apply to the Attorney General for relief from deportation under a now-repealed provision of the immigration laws governs both the exclusion of aliens from admission to this country and the deportation of aliens previously admitted. Before 1996, the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) authorized the AttorneyGeneral to admit certain excludable aliens, but §212(c) did not apply when an alien was being deported. In accord with this decision, the BIA adopted a policy of allowing aliens in deportation proceedings to apply for discretionary relief. The Immigration Judge ordered petitioner Judulang’s deportation, and the Immigration Judge affirmed. Responding to this apparent anomaly, Attorney General Jackson determined that L- could receive a waiver: L-, Jackson said, “should be permitted to make the same appeal to discretion that he could have made if denied admission” when returning from his recent trip. The BIA then considered whether L-could apply for §212 (c) relief, and it held that he did not do so because the “crime of violence” deportation ground is not comparable to any exclusion ground, including the one for crimes involving moral turpitude. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: When an administrative agency sets policy, it must provide a reasoned explanation for its action. Pp. 5–11. (a) When an agency’S policy is based on a reasoned decision, it is not to substitute its judgment for that of the agency. P. 5. (b) When a BIA is deciding whether to exclude an alien, applying §212’c is an easy matter. The Board first checks the statutory ground that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has identified as the basis for exclusion; the Board may note, for example, that DHS has charged the alien with previously committing a “crimes involving moral” involving “illicit trafficking in a controlled substance,” see 8 U. S. C. §1182(a)(2)(A)(i)(I), while another—sometimes overlapping and sometimes divergent—list specifies what kinds of crime render an alien deportable from the country, see §1227(a). An additional, historic difference between exclusion and deportation cases involved the ability of the AG to grant an alien discretionary relief based on such factors as “the seriousness of the offense, evidence of either rehabilitation or recidivism, the duration of the alien's residence, the impact of deportation on the family, the number of citizens in the family and the character of any service in the Armed Forces.” St. Cyr, 533 U.S. 289, 326. But when the Board is deciding when a resident alien may apply for relief under a deportation order, applying §§212(C) becomes a tricky business. Because an alien must be able to seek such relief in an exclusion proceeding, he must be willing to make that showing. The fact that §212[c] is “phrased in terms of waiving statutorily specified grounds of exclusion” is as extraneous to the merits of the case as a coin flip would be. And, contrary to this argument, it does not justify denying relief in deportation cases to a subset of that group. Because it is a single-level exception to the comparable-grounds rule, it cannot be justified by text or practice or cost considerations, and because it is an irrelevant comparison between statutory provisions to govern a matter of the utmost importance-whether lawful resident aliens with longstanding ties to the country may stay here—the BIA must do so in some rational way. The question arises: How is the Bureau to determine when a deportable alien should receive §212

Section 4401 of Title 26 imposes on those engaged in the business of accepting wagers an excise tax of 10% on the gross amount of all wagers they accept, including the value of chances purchased in lotteries conducted for profit. Parimutuel wagering enterprises, coin-operated devices, and state-conducted sweepstakes are expressly excluded from taxation. Section 4411 imposes in addition an occupational tax of $50 annually, both upon those subject to taxation under § 4401 and upon those who receive wagers on their behalf. The taxes are supplemented by ancillary provisions calculated to assure their collection. Section 6107 requires the principal internal revenue offices to maintain for public inspection a listing of all who have paid the occupational tax, and to provide certified copies of the listing upon request to any state or local prosecuting officer. The statutory obligations to register and to pay the occupational taxes are essentially inseparable elements of a single registration procedure. In addition, registrants are obliged to post the revenue stamps which denote payment of the tax "conspicuously" in their principal places of business, or, if they lack such places, to keep the stamps on their persons and to exhibit them upon demand to any Treasury officer. Petitioner, a wholesaler of fruit and produce, was convicted of willful failure to file an income tax return, despite his contention that the return would have obliged him to admit violations of the National Prohibition Act. He was nonetheless convicted, and his conviction was affirmed. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The privilege against self-incrimination may not appropriately be asserted by those who have defended a failure to comply with their requirements with a proper assertion of the privilege. Pp. 542-543. 2. The "required records" doctrine, Shapiro v. United States, 335 U. S. 1, distinguished. P. 543. 3. In the circumstances here, petitioner's failure to assert the constitutional privilege to Treasury officials at the moment the tax payments were due irretrievably abandoned his constitutional protection. The central standard for the privilege's application has been whether the claimant is confronted by substantial and "real" and not merely frifling or imaginary, hazards of incrimination. Rogers, The Albertson Case: Conflict Between the Privilege Against Self-Incrimination and the Government's Need for Information, 1966 Sup.Ct. Rev. 103, 159; and McKay, The Privilege against Selfincrimination, 1967 Sup. Ct.Rev. 193, 214-217. The Constitution has entrusted to Congress, and not to this Court, the task of striking an appropriate balance among such values. The Government's demand for information may not be met by the imposition of use-restrictions whould directly preclude effectuation of a significant element of Congress' purposes in adopting the wagers taxes, but would necessarily oblige state prosecuting authorities to establish in each case that their evidence was untainted by any connection with information obtained as a consequence of the taxes; and the federal requirements would thus be protected, only at the cost of hampering, perhaps seriously, enforcement of state prohibitions against gambling. Such restrictions would be unnecessary for present purposes to pursue in detail the competing demands of the federal treasury and of state gambling prohibitions; and it would be entirely inappropriate in the circumstances for the Court to impose such restrictions. Id., at 33. P p. 544. 159 F. 2d 890, reversed.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Padilla v. California that a person's right to effective assistance of counsel includes the right to receive information about the immigration consequences of a guilty plea. The Court found that the government cannot punish someone for committing a crime while simultaneously denying them access to information about the immigration consequences of that punishment. The Court also noted that the government's interest in maintaining the integrity of the criminal justice system does not justify denying people access to information about immigration consequences.

Case Name: Syngenta AG v. Knowles
Case Number: No. 09-1071
Issue: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts a lawsuit brought by farmers against seed corn producer Syngenta AG for patent infringement.
Background: Syngenta produces genetically modified seeds for various crops, including corn. One of its patented varieties, MIR 162, is resistant to a fungal disease called white rot. Farmers in Iowa purchased MIR 162 seeds from Syngenta and planted them on their land. Later, they discovered that their fields were contaminated with MIR 162 seeds, which they claimed resulted in reduced yields and increased costs. The farmers sued Syngenta for patent infringement, arguing that Syngenta had failed to protect its intellectual property rights by selling seeds to farmers outside of authorized channels.
Syngenta moved to dismiss the lawsuit, claiming that FIFRA preempted the farmers' claims. FIFRA establishes a framework for the regulation of agricultural chemicals, including genetic modification technologies. Syngenta argued that the farmers' lawsuit involved issues related to the cultivation and marketing of genetically modified crops, which fell within the purview of FIFRA. The district court agreed with Syngenta and dismissed the lawsuit.
Legal Analysis: The Supreme Court began by examining the text of FIFRA to determine whether it preempted the farmers' claims. The Court looked at the language of FIFRA, as well as its legislative history and purpose, to determine whether the farmers' lawsuit involved matters that were within the scope of FIFRA's regulation.
The Court ultimately ruled that FIFRA did not preempt the farmers' claims. The Court found that the farmers' lawsuit involved issues related to the ownership and protection of intellectual property rights, which were not within the scope of FIFRA's regulation. The Court also noted that FIFRA's purpose was to establish a regulatory framework for the safe and effective use of agricultural chemicals, not to protect intellectual property rights.
Conclusion: The Supreme Court held that FIFRA did not preempt the farmers' claims for patent infringement. The Court found that the farmers' lawsuit involved issues related to the ownership and protection of intellectual property rights, which were not within the scope of FIFRA's regulation.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California today entered a temporary restraining order against the Navy's use of active sonar during training exercises.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Los Angeles, alleges that the Navy violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Rule 17(b) thereunder, and that the court improperly restrained the Navy from using MFA sonar in training exercises that were conducted under the SEC's supervision.  According to the complaint, the court's order temporarily halted the Navy’s planned training exercises, which were scheduled to be conducted in the Southern California waters off the coast of southern California.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendants. The SEC also issued an emergency court order temporarily restraining the defendants from violating the federal securities laws and ordering the Navy to comply with the court order.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Defendants consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating these provisions, and orders them to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty. The court also granted the Navy and the District Court the right to apply for a preliminary injunction against further violations of the federal laws.

The Supreme Court addressed whether the Export Clause of the U.S. Constitution allows the federal government to impose a tax on goods that are in the process of being exported. The case in question involved International Business Machines Corporation (IBM), which insured its export shipments with foreign insurers. The IRS assessed a tax on the insurance premiums under Section 4371 of the Internal Revenue Code, and IBM challenged this tax as a violation of the Export Clause.

The Court's opinion, which Justice Stevens did not participate in, reaffirmed the decision in Thames & Mersey Marine Ins. Co. v. United States, which held that a federal tax on insurance policies covering export shipments was unconstitutional under the Export Clause. The government argued that this precedent should be overruled based on modern interpretations of the Commerce and Import-Export Clauses, suggesting that generally applicable, nondiscriminatory taxes should be allowed even on goods in export transit.

The Court disagreed with the government's position, emphasizing the textual differences between the Export Clause and the Import-Export Clause. The Court noted that the Export Clause explicitly prohibits any tax or duty on exports, while the Import-Export Clause prohibits states from imposing imposts or duties on imports or exports. The Court also highlighted that the historical context and purpose of the Export Clause were distinct from those of the Import-Export Clause.

The Court concluded that the Export Clause does not permit the imposition of a generally applicable, nondiscriminatory federal tax on goods in the process of being exported. The Court declined to overrule the precedent set by Thames & Mersey and affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which had ruled in favor of IBM.

Implications of the decision include the reaffirmation of the Export Clause's strict prohibition against federal taxation of goods in export transit and the protection of certain services and activities closely related to the export process from federal taxation. The ruling also underscores the importance of adhering to the text of the Constitution and the historical context in which its provisions were framed.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Michigan filed criminal charges against a Michigan dairy farm operator and his son in 1983 for holding two mentally retarded men in "involuntary servitude" on the farm. The defendants were charged with violating the federal law prohibiting conspiracy to interfere with an individual's Thirteenth Amendment right to be free from involuntary servitude. The court found that the defendants held the victims in "psychological hostage" conditions. The jury found the defendants guilty of conspiracy to injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate the two victims. The trial judge found that Ike and Margarethe Kozminski had "brainwashed" the victims into believing that they had no alternative but to work on the dairy farm, and that they were forced to work 17 hours a day, seven days a week, for no pay, in poor health, and in relative isolation from the rest of society. The federal court concluded that the evidence was sufficient to find that the Kozminskys violated the law, and the jury found them guilty of aiding and abetting the defendants' conspiracy. The case was appealed and the court ruled in favor of the defendants, finding that the jury was not allowed to consider the evidence that the victims were "psychological hostages" as the government had alleged. The appeals court ruled that the trial judge should have allowed the defendants to present evidence of their "contempt for the victims"

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit has ruled that the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) has failed to provide a reasoned explanation for its decision to deny a request for relief from deportation under a now-repealed provision of the immigration law. The court found that the BIA's decision was arbitrary and capricious, and that it violated the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment of the United States Constitution. The Court also found that, under the law, the Attorney General's discretion to grant relief under 212(c) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1940 was not limited to those who had previously been convicted of a criminal offense. The Second Circuit's ruling is the latest in a series of court decisions that have found that a person's right to a fair hearing under the 14th Amendment is not violated when the government seeks to deport him or her based on a prior criminal conviction. The case involves a man who was convicted of stealing from a grocery store and was later deported. The BIA denied his application for relief, saying that he had not previously been charged with a crime and that the law did not permit him to apply for relief under the provision. The 2nd Circuit ruled in favor of the man's appeal, and the court granted his motion for a preliminary injunction, and sent the case back to the Board for further proceedings. In a second appeal, the court ruled that there was no basis for the Board's denial of his application, and ordered the case to be sent back for further consideration. The Board'

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled that the Interstate Commerce Commission's division of freight rates for the Northern and Southern Railway lines was not justified by the amount of revenue allocated to the Northern lines. The District Court held that the Commission did not provide substantial evidence that the division was justified. The Court also held that there was no substantial evidence of the need for the division. The court remanded the case to the Commission for further proceedings. We conclude that the District Court's ruling was not supported by substantial evidence and reasoned findings within the meaning of  8(b)2 and 10(e)3 of the Administrative Procedure Act.

Petitioner St. Amant, a candidate for public office, read a series of questions which he had put to J. D. Albin, a member of a Teamsters Union local, and Albin's answers to those questions concerned the allegedly nefarious activities of E. G. Partin, Partin's president, and the alleged relationship between Partin and Partin. One of the questions concerned his efforts to prevent Partin from secreting union records; in this answer Albin referred to Herman A. Thompson, an East Baton Rouge Parish deputy sheriff and respondent here: "Now, we knew that this safe was gonna be moved that night, but imagine our predicament, knowing of Ed's connections with the Sheriff's office through Herman Thompson, who made recent visits to the Hall to see Ed, and knowing of money that had passed hands between Ed and Herman Thompson from Ed to Herman." The case was tried prior to the decision in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U. S. 254. The trial judge ruled in Thompson's favor and awarded $5,000 in damages. Thereafter, in the course of entertaining and denying a motion for a new trial, the Court considered the ruling in the Times, finding that rule no barrier to the judgment already entered. The Louisiana Court of Appeal reversed. In its view, there was sufficient evidence that St Amant recklessly disregarded whether the statements about Thompson were true or false. Held: 1. By no proper test of reckless disregard was St.Amant's broadcast a reckless publication about a public officer. Nothing referred to by the Louisiana courts indicates an awareness by St.Ambant of the probable falsity of Thompson's statement about Thompson. Failure to investigate does not in itself establish bad faith. Pp. 531-532. 2. The defendant in a defamation action brought by a public official cannot, however, automatically insure a favorable verdict by testifying that he published with a belief that the statements were true. The finder of fact must determine whether the publication was indeed made in good faith. Here, there is sufficient evidence to show that the defendant in fact entertained serious doubts as to the truth of his publication. P. 532. 250 La. 405, 196 So. 2d 255, reversed and remanded.

Under the Land Reform Act of 1967 (Act), tenants living on single-family residential lots within developmental tracts at least five acres in size are entitled to ask the Hawaii Housing Authority (HHA) to condemn the property on which they live. When 25 eligible tenants, or tenants on half the lots in the tract, whichever is less, file appropriate applications, the Act authorizes HHA to hold a public hearing to determine whether acquisition by the State of all or part of the tract will "effectuate the public purposes" of the Act. If HHA finds that these public purposes will be served, it is authorized to designate some or all of the condemned fees simple to existing lessees. Held: The Act does not violate the "public use" requirement of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 488-481. (a) The Act's goals are within the bounds of the State's police powers and the means the legislature had chosen to serve those goals were not arbitrary, capricious, or selected in bad faith. P. 489. (b) The mere fact that property taken outright by eminent domain is transferred in the first instance to private beneficiaries does not condemn that taking as having only a private purpose. The Act advances its purposes without a State's taking actual possession of the land, and it advances its purpose without the taking's purpose, and only its mechanics, that must pass scrutiny under the Public Use Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Moreover, the fact that a state legislature, and not the Congress, made the public use determination does not mean that judicial deference is less appropriate than that required by the Act, since the Act is not of an uncertain nature and has no reasonable limiting construction, and thus, Pullman abstention is unnecessary, since it is coterminous with the scope of a sovereign's police power, and the Act's approach to correcting the land oligopoly problem is an extremely narrow one, even when the eminent domain power is equated with the police power. The Court in Berman v. Parker, 348 U. S. 26, held that the power of eminent domain was rationally related to a conceivable public purpose and that, in such cases, courts must defer to its determination that the taking will serve a public use. The court concluded that the Act was simply a naked attempt on the part of Hawaii's legislature to take the private property of A and transfer it to B solely for B's private use and benefit. The majority of the Court of Appeals reversed, finding that the Hawaii Legislature's professed purposes were mere "statutory rationalizations." Held: Section 516-83(a)(12) of the Federal Constitution does not prohibit the State from taking, with just compensation, title in real property from lessors and transferring it to lesseees in order to reduce the concentration of ownership of fees simple in the State, since, where the exercise of the eminent-domain power is rationallyrelated to a possible public purpose, the Court has never held a compensated taking to be proscribed by the Public-Use Clause. P p. 490. (c) The fact that the State legislature and not Congress, and neither the legislature nor the courts, made public use determinations, did not render adjudication of the federal question unnecessary by their construction of the statute, and therefore, the statute is not "an extremely narrow" one. The "public-use" requirement is thus a cotermeous with that of the state courts. The State of Hawaii has never denied that the Constitution forbids even a compensated, compensated taking of property when executed for no reason other than to confer a private benefit on a particular private party. A purely private taking could not withstand the scrutiny of public use requirement; it would serve no legitimate purpose of government and would thus be void. But no purely private take is involved in these cases. The Hawaii Legislature enacted its Land ReformAct not to benefit a particular class of identifiable individuals but to attack certain perceived evils of concentrated property ownership in Hawaii-a legitimate public purpose. Use of the condemnation power to achieve this purpose is not irrational. Pc. 702 F. 2d 788, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit held that a federal district court erred in denying relief to a man whose property was seized by the state of Virginia in connection with an ex parte petition filed by his former supplier. The court held that the state had not violated the Fourteenth Amendment's right to due process by executing a writ of attachment under color of state law. The case involves the issue of whether the state's action was "state action" under the provisions of the U.N. Constitution's 14th Amendment Protection Act of Amendments,  1983 and the Virginia State Court Rules  8.01-533 and  8.10-3. The Court held that, in this case, the State's actions were not state action as required by the 14th amendment and that the complaint did not allege that the State had violated the due process provision of the Constitution. The Fourth Circuit also held that there was no basis for the complaint's allegations of a misuse of the Virginia state procedure and that it did not state a claim upon which relief could be granted under  1983.

The Supreme Court of the United States issued a landmark decision in Roe v. Wade in 1973, establishing a woman's constitutional right to choose to have an abortion. However, the decision did not provide complete guidance on how states should implement this right. Since then, numerous legal battles have ensued over the legality and accessibility of abortion, including the recent Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization decision in 2022, which overturned Roe v. Wade and ended federal protections for abortion rights.

In a habeas corpus proceeding challenging a Michigan conviction for first-degree murder and other offenses, the Supreme Court reviewed two constitutional errors identified by the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit. The first error involved a statement by the accused, Van Chester Thompkins, which the Court of Appeals believed was elicited in violation of Miranda v. Arizona. The second error was the failure of Thompkins's defense counsel to request a jury instruction regarding testimony from an accomplice, which was considered ineffective assistance of counsel under Strickland v. Washington.

The Supreme Court's opinion addressed the following key points:

1. Miranda Rights and Waiver:
   - Thompkins was given a Miranda warning, which he understood but did not explicitly acknowledge.
   - He remained largely silent during a three-hour interrogation but eventually made an incriminating statement.
   - The Court held that Thompkins did not unambiguously invoke his right to remain silent, and his eventual statement indicated a waiver of that right.
   - The Court rejected the argument that police must obtain an explicit waiver before questioning, citing North Carolina v. Butler, which allows for implied waiver.

2. Ineffective Assistance of Counsel:
   - The Court considered whether Thompkins's counsel was ineffective for not requesting a limiting instruction about the jury's consideration of an accomplice's trial outcome.
   - The Court determined that even if the counsel's performance was deficient, Thompkins could not show that the outcome of his trial would have been different with the instruction, given the other evidence against him.

Implications of the Decision:
   - The decision clarifies the standards for invoking and waiving Miranda rights, emphasizing that suspects must unambiguously invoke their right to remain silent to end questioning.
   - It confirms that an implied waiver of Miranda rights can be inferred from a suspect's conduct during interrogation.
   - The ruling underscores the burden on defendants to demonstrate both deficient performance and prejudice to succeed on an ineffective assistance of counsel claim.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case with instructions to deny the habeas petition, upholding Thompkins's conviction.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the NAACP, stating that Chapter 33 of the Virginia code, which defined "improper solicitation" to include "fomenting or stirring up litigation," was too broad and vague to be used to punish the NAACP for its activities. The Court found that the NAACP's activities, including providing legal advice and representation to African Americans, were protected by the First Amendment's guarantees of freedom of expression and association. The Court also noted that the Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals had erred in applying Chapter 33 to the NAACP's activities, as it had done so without sufficient evidence of wrongdoing.

The Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether an expired utility patent affects a claim of trade dress infringement. Marketing Displays, Inc. (MDI) sued TrafFix Devices, Inc. for trade dress infringement, among other things, after TrafFix sold sign stands with a dual-spring design similar to MDI's, which was previously patented but the patent had expired.

The District Court ruled against MDI on the trade dress claim, stating that the dual-spring design was functional and that MDI had not established secondary meaning (i.e., consumers did not associate the dual-spring design with MDI). The Court of Appeals reversed this decision, but the Supreme Court disagreed with the Court of Appeals.

The Supreme Court held that an expired utility patent is strong evidence that the features claimed are functional. Since the dual-spring design was the central advance in the expired patents and was essential to the operation of the sign stands, MDI could not claim trade dress protection for it. The Court emphasized that trade dress protection cannot be claimed for product features that are functional, as this would hinder competition.

The Court also clarified that the existence of alternative designs is not relevant when the feature in question is functional. The Court noted that trade dress protection is not intended to reward manufacturers for innovation (which is the purpose of patent law) or to protect investment in associating a feature with a manufacturer.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, reinforcing the principle that functional aspects of a product cannot be protected as trade dress once the utility patent has expired.

Petitioners, the Mayor and members of the Board of Commissioners of the District of Columbia, and the Federal Government, moved for summary judgment dismissing respondents' action challenging the validity of a test administered to persons seeking appointment as police recruits. The test resulted in the exclusion of a larger proportion of Negroes than of other racial groups. The District Court entered summary judgment for petitioners, concluding that the test met the requirements of the Fifth Amendment and that it was sufficiently related to the requirements of the police training program to justify its use. The Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that the test was inherently biased and that even assuming that it was properly related to the training program, the test results were not sufficiently correlated with the police officer's job performance to meet the requirements of the Fourth Amendment. Held: 1. Summary judgment for respondents based on the Fifth Amendment was improper. While the test was neutral on its face and rationally may be said to serve a purpose the Government is constitutionally empowered to pursue, nonetheless the test's substantially disproportionate racial impact, without regard to discriminatory purpose, cannot sustain a claim of racial discrimination violating the Equal Protection Clause absent some justification going substantially beyond what would be necessary to validate most other legislative classifications. Here, the test's disproportionate racial impact was negated by the affirmative efforts of the police department to recruit black officers, the changing racial composition of the recruit classes and of the force in general, and the relationship of the test to the training program. Pp. 308-316. 2. The Court of Appeals erred in requiring that the test results be closely correlated with the police officer's job performance. Training-program validation is sufficient to validate the test, and the District Court's conclusion that the test was sufficiently related to the requirements of the police training program was supported by a validation study, as well as by other evidence of record. Pp. 316-318. Reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment against a city-ordered zoning ordinance that prohibited two unmarried couples from acquiring real property in a given area.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the city's previous violations of the ordinance.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, the Belle Terre ordinance, which was promulgated in 1971, prohibits the purchase, sale, or purchase of any real property within four hundred (400) feet of the proposed building.  In addition, the court found that the city had violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206 and 206 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the city consented to the entry of an order that permanently enjoins the city from violating the federal securities laws, and orders the city to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a penny stock bar against the property owner.  Finally, the district court entered an order against Michael Truman, ordering the purchase of a house for the aged poor in a residential area, prohibiting the purchase or sale of any property in the area, and ordering the sale of the house to the purchaser. The court's order also ordered the purchase and sale of a second home for the poor, a condominium building for the elderly, and an apartment for the newly-settled elderly.  On May 2, 2018, the U.N. Office of Economic and Risk Analysis (OIEA) issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the background of anyone selling or offering them an investment using the free and simple search tool onÂ SEC.gov.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses a challenge to an Arizona tax credit program that benefits school tuition organizations (STOs), some of which provide scholarships to students attending private religious schools. The respondents, a group of Arizona taxpayers, argued that the tax credit violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, which prohibits the government from making any law "respecting an establishment of religion."

The central issue in the case was whether the respondents had the legal standing to sue. Standing is a constitutional requirement that ensures a plaintiff has a sufficient connection to and harm from the law or action challenged to support that party's participation in the case.

The Court's opinion, delivered by Justice Kennedy, concluded that the respondents did not have standing to challenge the tax credit program. The Court reasoned that the general rule against taxpayer standing prevents individuals from challenging government expenditures simply because they pay taxes. The Court acknowledged an exception to this rule from the case Flast v. Cohen (1968), which allows taxpayer standing in certain cases involving the Establishment Clause. However, the Court found that the respondents did not meet the criteria for this exception.

The Court distinguished between government expenditures and tax credits, noting that while both can have similar economic effects, they do not implicate taxpayers in the same way. The Court emphasized that tax credits involve private choices about private funds, not the extraction and spending of taxpayer money by the government. Therefore, any connection between the tax credit and the alleged establishment of religion was too tenuous to support standing.

The Court also addressed the requirements of causation and redressability, finding that any injury to the respondents was not directly traceable to the government's action and that an injunction against the tax credit would not necessarily redress their alleged injury.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, holding that the respondents lacked standing to challenge the Arizona STO tax credit program. The decision implies that challenges to similar tax credit programs on Establishment Clause grounds will face significant hurdles in demonstrating the necessary standing to proceed in federal court.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit granted certiorari to consider whether a North Carolina court erred in denying a motion to suppress evidence of a defendant's incriminating statements. The court held that the defendant, William Thomas Butler, had not waived his right to the assistance of counsel at the time the statements were made. The Court held that Butler was advised of his rights and that he effectively waived his rights. The trial court's denial of Butler's motion was consistent with the opinion of the United States Supreme Court in Miranda v. Arizona, which held that a person under custodial interrogation may not make a statement unless he waives his rights to the presence of a lawyer. The Supreme Court held in Miranda that "a valid waiver will not be presumed simply from the silence of a statement followed closely by a statement" and that a valid waiver "will not be recognized unless such waiver is 'specifically made' after the Miranda warnings have been given"

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Ohio today entered a final judgment against a lawyer who solicited clients in person for the purpose of obtaining a lawyer's services.  According to the court's order, filed on February 13, 1974, Carol McClintock and Wanda Lou Holbert of Montville, Ohio, solicited the services of a lawyer for the benefit of two young women who were injured and hospitalized.  The court found that the solicitation of legal services was not permissible under the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rules 10b-5(a) and (c) thereunder.  In addition, the Court found that in-person solicitation constitutes a violation of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Exchange Act.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in Bates, the court also ruled that the exemption is not sufficient to prevent future violations of the federal securities laws, and that the court has a duty to determine whether to impose a permanent injunction.   The Court's order also imposed a temporary restraining order and an officer-and-director bar against the lawyer, prohibiting him from soliciting clients through the internet, and ordering him to pay a $100,000 civil penalty.  On February 24, 2018, the Honorable Judge Robert E. Bentsen of the United States District Court in Ohio entered a judgment against the attorney for the Southern District of New York that permanently enjoins him from violating the above-mentioned provisions of the securities laws and orders him to comply with the bar's orders, including the issuance of an order suspending him from appearing or practicing before the court as a lawyer under the supervision of a judge. Â The court also issued an order requiring the lawyer to provide a copy of the SEC's complaint to the SEC, ordering the SEC to conduct an independent review of its books and records, and requiring the attorney to provide an account of his conduct.  Finally, the order requires that the lawyer provide an accounting of his or her compensation in a timely manner.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-8221 (1955).  The SEC's Office of Investor Education and Advocacy has issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the background of anyone selling or offering them an investment using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

The Supreme Court case in question deals with the interplay between federal and state authority in the regulation of nuclear energy, specifically regarding California's Warren-Alquist Act amendments that condition the construction of nuclear plants on the availability of adequate storage for nuclear waste. The main legal question is whether these state provisions are preempted by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954.

The Court determined that the challenge to California's long-term waste disposal regulation (Section 25524.2) was ripe for judicial review, as the issue was predominantly legal and postponing a decision would cause hardship to utilities. However, the challenge to the interim storage provision (Section 25524.1(b)) was not ripe for review, as it required case-by-case determinations by the state Energy Commission.

The Court's analysis focused on whether Congress intended to preempt state regulation in the area of nuclear safety and found that while the federal government regulates the safety aspects of nuclear power, states retain authority over economic decisions related to electricity generation. The Court accepted California's stated economic rationale for enacting Section 25524.2, which placed a moratorium on the certification of new nuclear plants until a federally approved disposal method for high-level nuclear waste was developed.

The Court rejected arguments that the California statute was preempted by federal law, including the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's (NRC) licensing authority and recent federal legislation addressing nuclear waste disposal. The Court also found that the state statute did not frustrate the federal goal of promoting nuclear power, as Congress had allowed states to make economic decisions that could affect the development of nuclear power.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, holding that California's statute was not preempted by federal law and that the state could regulate the construction of new nuclear plants based on economic considerations related to nuclear waste disposal.

Respondents, a private figure and a newspaper company, filed a defamation lawsuit in a Pennsylvania court against petitioners, a private figure and a newspaper company, alleging that respondents suffered damages as a result of the publication of several articles in petitioners' newspapers accusing respondents of using illegal means to secure contracts. Petitioners moved for summary judgment, claiming that the articles were privileged under Pennsylvania's "shield" law, which exempts members of the news media from being compelled to reveal their confidential sources. The motion was denied, and the case went to trial. At the end of the trial, the jury returned a verdict for respondents, finding that petitioners had failed to prove that the articles were true. However, the jury rejected respondents' request for $1 million in damages, finding that petitioners had proven that the articles were substantially true. On appeal, the Pennsylvania Superior Court entered judgment for respondents, rejecting petitioners' argument that the jury's rejection of the damages award constituted double jeopardy. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed, agreeing that the jury's rejection of the damages award constituted double jeopardy. Held: A private-figure plaintiff seeking damages for defamation must bear the burden of showing that the speech at issue is false. Pp. 770-777. (a) This Court's decisions establish that the common-law presumption that defamatory speech is false cannot stand when a plaintiff seeks damages against a media defendant for speech of public concern. When the plaintiff is a public figure or public official, the Constitution clearly requires the plaintiff to surmount a much higher barrier before recovering damages from a media defendant than is raised by the common law. When the plaintiff is a private figure, as here, the Constitution still supplants the common law, but the constitutional requirements are, in at least some of their range, less forbidding than when the plaintiff is a public figure or public official. And when the plaintiff is a private figure and the speech is of purely private concern, as in Dun & Bradstreet, Inc. v. Greenmoss Builders, Inc., 472 U. S. 749, the constitutional requirements do not necessarily force any changes in at least some of the features of the common-law landscape. Pp. 770-773. (b) Since the allocation of the burden of proof determines liability for some speech that is true and some that is false, but all of such speech is unknowably true or false, the Constitution requires that the plaintiff bear the burden of showing falsity, as well as fault, before recovering damages for defamation from a media defendant. Requiring the plaintiff to show falsity will insulate from liability some speech that is false, but unprovably so. Nonetheless, the Court's previous decisions on the restrictions that the First Amendment places upon the common law of defamation firmly support the conclusion here with respect to the allocation of the burden of proof. Moreover, since the plaintiff's burden in this case is weightier because of Pennsylvania's "shield" law, which allows employees of the media to refuse to divulge their sources, the Court does not address the question of the permissible reach of such laws. Pp. 773-777. 506 Pa. 105, 431 A. 2d 120, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit upheld the convictions of six former members of the International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers for violating the general conspiracy statute. The court held that the defendants were not guilty of the conspiracy charge because they did not commit the act of aiding and abetting the conspiracy. The defendants, however, were convicted of violating Section 9(h) of the National Labor Relations Act of 1933, which requires labor unions to file non-Communist affidavits to obtain the services of the Labor Board. According to the government's case, in 1949 the union and the Communist Party opposed compliance with the law, and the union's officers determined that petitioners' Communist Party affiliations were unaffected as did the Party's domination of the Union's affairs. As a result of these alleged fraudulent acts, the union obtained the Board's services, a privilege which it had obtained. The union subsequently, on several occasions, continued to use the services, and, in doing so, obtained the benefit of the law's provisions. The Court held that, in the light of these facts, the indictment properly charged the defendants with conspiracy to defraud the United States under 18 U. S.C.  371, and that the trial court erred in denying the defendants' motions for the production of grand jury testimony of prosecution witnesses. In a separate opinion, the Court of Appeal held that there was sufficient evidence to hold the defendants guilty on the conspiracy charges. The decision is consistent with the decisions of the U.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered final judgments in a civil injunctive action against the City of Columbus and two city officials for violating the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Columbus, Ohio, alleges that the federal government violated the antifraud provisions of Section 14501 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 145b-5 thereunder. The complaint also alleges that, in violation of the federal preemption rule, the city of Columbus failed to comply with certain pre-emption requirements, such as requiring tow truck operators to submit to city inspections, meet city standards for insurance and recordkeeping, and conform their vehicles to the city's detailed equipment requirements.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the city.  According to the SEC's Complaint, filed on May 24, 2018, the Court entered final judgment against the defendants, finding that the defendants violated the preemption provisions of Sections 14501(c)(2)(A) and (3) of the Exchange Act, and ordering the defendants to disgorge their ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, pay civil penalties, and pay disgorgement of $1,038,078, plus interest in the defendants' escrowed expenses.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating these provisions, ordering the destruction of any evidence, imposing a civil penalty, and imposing a penny stock bar against each of the defendants. The final judgments also order the city and the city officials to pay a penalty equal to the amount of their disgorgements, and require the city to pay for its own transportation expenses. The court also issued a temporary restraining order halting the issuance, purchase, offer, and offer of any emergency relief.  On May 26, 2019, the SEC filed a complaint in the United States District Court in the Eastern District of Michigan against the cities and towns of Ohio, Michigan, Kentucky, and Ohio. The SEC seeks a permanent injunction against future violations of the securities laws, an order appointing a receiver, and an officer-and-director bar against any future violations. The case was supervised by Kelly L. Gibson, Chief of the Market Abuse Unit. The litigation will be led by Mr. Gibson and Ms. Gibson.
