Respondent, who works as a pipefitter for a railroad, was exposed to a carcinogen (here, asbestos) but without symptoms of any disease. Since 1987, when he attended an "asbestos awareness" class, Buckley has feared that he would develop cancer-and with some cause, for his two expert witnesses testified that, even after taking account of his now-discarded 15-year habit of smoking up to a pack of cigarettes per day, the exposure created an added risk of death due to cancer, or to other asbestos-related diseases of either 1% to 5% (in the view of one of plaintiff's experts), or to 3% to 3%. Since 1989, he has received periodic medical checkups for cancer and asbestosis. So far, those check-ups have not revealed any evidence of cancer or any other asbestos related disease. After hearing Buckley's case, the District Court dismissed the action, finding that he did not "offer sufficient evidence to allow a jury to find that he suffered a real emotional injury" and that Buckley suffered no "physical impact" hence any emotional injury fell outside the limited set of circumstances in which, according to this Court, the FELA permits recovery. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Buckley could recover for the costs of medical monitoring because the statute permits recovery of all reasonably incurred extra medical monitoring costs whenever a "reasonable physician would prescribe . . . a monitoring regime different than the one that would have been prescribed in the absence of" a particular negligently caused exposure to a toxic substance. Held: 1. The Federal Employers' Liability Act (FELA), 35 Stat. 65, as amended, does not permit recovery for negligently inflicted emotional distress unless the distress falls within certain specific categories that amount to recovery-permitting exceptions. The law permits recovery for emotional distress where that distress accompanies a physical injury, see, e.g., Simmons v. Pacor, Inc., 543 Pa. 664, 678, 674 A. 2d 232, 239. Pp. 5-11. (a) The common law of torts does not allow recovery for such distress unless it satisfies the common law's "zone of danger" test-which, when present, permits a plaintiff seeking such damages to recover for accompanying emotional distress. Here, the relevant question concerns not simply recovery in an individual case, but the consequences and effects of a rule of law that would permit that recovery. And if the common-law court concludes that a legal rule permitting recovery here, from a tort law perspective, and despite benefits in some individual cases, would on balance cause more harm than good, and if we find that judgment reasonable, we cannot find that conclusion inconsistent with the FLEA's humanitarian purpose. P. 5. (b) The "humanitarian" nature of the F.ELA warrants a holding in Buckley's favor. The fact that, in addition to the fact that the particular, say cancer-related, costs at issue are the extra monitoring costs, over and above those otherwise recommended, their identification will sometimes pose special "difficulties" for judges and juries, since the relevant statistics themselves are controversial and uncertain (as is usually the case), and particularly since neither those exposed nor judges or juries are experts in statistics? The evaluation problem seems a serious one. And, along with uncertainty as to the amount of liability, could threaten both a "flood" of less important cases (potentially absorbing resources better left available to those more seriously harmed, see supra, at __) and the systemic harms that can accompany "unlimited and unpredictable liability" (say, for example, vast testing liability adversely affecting the allocation of scarce medical resources). The same characteristics further suggest what Gottshall called the problem of aflood of cases that, if not "trivial," are comparatively less important. In a world of limited resources, would a rule permitting immediate large-scale recoveries for widespread emotional distress caused by fear of future disease diminish the likelihood of recovery by those who later suffer from the disease? Cf. J. Weinstein, Individual Justice in Mass. Tort Litigation 10-11, 141, 114 S.Ct., at 2407-2408. The relevant question, however, is whether recovery in such a case would be sufficient to justify the recovery of medical costs damages in the form of a lump sum, see Stein v. Fibreboard Corp., 994 F.2d 253, 259, and, in particular, whether the distress is reasonable and genuine, rather than overstated-particularly when the relevant statistical themselves are uncertain and uncertain. And in part those difficulties can be reflected by uncertainty about just which tests are most usefully administered and when. Moreover, the risk that scientists will not always see a medical need to provide systematic scientific answers to the relevant legal question, namely whether an exposure calls for extra monitoring. Cf. Priest, The Current Insurance Crisis and Modern Tort Law, 96 Yale L.J. 1521, 1587,

The Supreme Court had to decide on the constitutionality and interpretation of § 318 of the Department of the Interior and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1990, also known as the Northwest Timber Compromise. This section was enacted in response to ongoing litigation regarding the harvesting of timber from old-growth forests in the Pacific Northwest, which environmentalists argued would harm the northern spotted owl, a threatened species. The timber industry, on the other hand, contended that restrictions on harvesting would harm the local economy.

The Compromise required the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to offer specified quantities of timber for sale while also expanding restrictions on harvesting in certain areas to protect the owl's habitat. It also established new environmental criteria for selecting harvesting sites and provided for limited, expedited judicial review of individual timber sales.

The controversy centered on subsection (b)(6)(A) of § 318, which stated that managing areas according to certain subsections was adequate consideration for meeting the statutory requirements that were the basis for the consolidated cases. Environmental groups argued that this subsection, by directing the outcome of pending cases, violated Article III of the Constitution. The District Courts upheld the subsection as a temporary modification of environmental laws, but the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed, finding it unconstitutional.

The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's decision, holding that subsection (b)(6)(A) did not direct specific results under old law but instead replaced the legal standards underlying the original challenges with new ones. The Court concluded that the subsection amended the law rather than directing particular findings of fact or applications of law. The Court also rejected the argument that the subsection could not modify substantive law because it was part of an appropriations measure, stating that Congress can amend substantive law in an appropriations statute if it does so clearly.

The Supreme Court's decision implies that Congress has the authority to enact laws that change the legal standards applicable to ongoing litigation, as long as the intent to modify the law is clear and express. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

Under petitioner AT&T’s longstanding seniority system, employees who left the company during a particular period while taking pregnancy leave were awarded fewer years of service credit toward retirement benefits than those who left during the same period while taking sick leave. When the Pregnancy Discrimination Act (PDA) became effective in 1979, the system changed to accord equal treatment to pregnancy and other temporary disabilities. Respondent Huluen, who worked for AT&T between 1969 and 1978, sued the company in Federal District Court, arguing that the pre-PDA system denied her equal protection under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The court dismissed the complaint, ruling that the pre-PDA system complied with the requirements of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The Ninth Circuit disagreed, concluding that the pre-PDA system violated Title VII because it excluded pregnancy leave from the calculation of seniority credits. Held: The pre-PDA system did not deny Huluen equal protection under the Due Process Clause. Pp. 3−12. (a) The pre-PDA system did not violate Title VII. Before the PDA, the Equal Protection Clause allowed states to limit benefits to disabled workers, including pregnant women, to avoid excessive costs associated with paying benefits to able-bodied individuals. General Electric Co. v. Gilbert, 429 U. S. 125, 144. However, the PDA invalidated such limitations, stating that “no woman shall be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity implemented pursuant to [Title VII], including participation in any benefit program under such program or activity, solely on the basis of such woman’s sex.” 42 U. S. C. §2000e(k). Thus, the pre-PDA system was inconsistent with the PDA. Moreover, the PDA expressly repealed the Equal Protection Clause limitation. See id., at 145. Pp. 3−4. (b) Nor did the pre-PDA system violate the Due Process Clause. The Due Process Clause requires that government actions imposing burdens on individuals be reasonably related to legitimate goals. Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U. S. 310, 335. Here, the pre-PDA system imposed no additional burden on pregnant women compared to other disabled workers. Indeed, the system was designed to reduce the cost of benefits to the company by eliminating the need to pay benefits to able-bodied pregnant women. The pre-PDA system thus satisfied the reasonableness test. Pp. 4−6. (c) The pre-PDA system did not violate the Due Process Clause because it did not deny Huluen equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Due Process Clause applies to the States only when the State fails to protect equal protection rights guaranteed by the Constitution. Vining v. Cook, 517 U. S. ___, ___. Huluen has not shown that the pre-PDA system denied her equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment. Rather, the pre-PDA system offered her the same opportunity to earn seniority credits as it did to other disabled workers. Even assuming that the pre-PDA system was facially discriminatory, the PDA rendered it constitutional. The PDA’s express repeal of the Equal Protection Clause limitation establishes that the pre-PDA system was constitutionally infirm. Pp. 6−8. (d) The pre-PDA system did not violate the Due Process Clause because it did not impair Huluen’s liberty interest in obtaining retirement benefits. Liberty interests are protected by the Due Process Clause when they are essential components of an individual’s identity or autonomy. Board of Regents of Univ. of Wis. v. Yoder, 406 U. S. 205, 242. Huluen has not demonstrated that the pre-PDA system interfered with her liberty interest in obtaining retirement benefits. Instead, the pre-PDA system created a fair opportunity for her to obtain such benefits. Pp. 8−9. (e) The pre-PDA system did not violate the Due Process Clause because it did not deprive Huluen of property without due process of law. Property interests are protected by the Due Process Clause when they are essential components of an individual’s identity or autonomy. Id., at 242. Huluen has not demonstrated that the pre-PDA system deprived her of a property interest in retirement benefits. Instead, the pre-PDA system created a fair opportunity for her to obtain such benefits. Pp. 9−10. (f) The pre-PDA system did not violate the Due Process Clause because it did not substantially affect Huluen’s life expectancy. Life expectancies are protected by the Due Process Clause when they are essential components of an individual’s identity or autonomy. Id., at 242. Huluen has not demonstrated that the pre-PDA system substantially affected her life expectancy. Instead, the pre-PDA system created a fair opportunity for her to achieve her expected lifespan. Pp. 10−11. (g) The pre-PDA system did not violate the Due Process Clause because it did not deprive Huluen of privacy interests. Privacy interests are protected by the Due Process Clause when they are essential components of an individual’s identity or autonomy. Id., at 242. Huluen has not demonstrated that the pre-PDA system deprived her of a privacy interest in retirement benefits. Instead, the pre-PDA system created a fair opportunity for her to obtain such benefits. Pp. 11−12. 498 Fed. Appx. 655, reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Stevens, Souter, and Breyer, JJ., joined.

Title: Windward Shipping Company, et al. v. Associated Marine Labor Unions, Local 1, et al.

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court considers whether the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) preempts a state court from issuing an injunction against a labor strike conducted by international marine labor unions. The Court holds that the NLRA does not preempt the state court's ability to hear the case, and that the injunction issued by the state court is constitutional.

Background: The case began in 1959 when several international marine labor unions organized a nationwide strike against American flagged ships owned by foreign governments. The goal of the strike was to protest the use of cheap foreign labor in the maritime industry. One of the strikes took place in Mobile Bay, Alabama, where the strikers blocked access to the bay and prevented American ships from entering or leaving.

Legal Issues: The main issues in the case include whether the NLRA preempts the state court's ability to hear the case, and whether the injunction issued by the state court is constitutional.

Decision: The Supreme Court holds that the NLRA does not preempt the state court's ability to hear the case, and that the injunction issued by the state court is constitutional. The Court finds that the strike falls outside the scope of the NLRA, as it is not related to collective bargaining or the enforcement of a collective agreement. Additionally, the Court notes that the strike poses a significant threat to the safety and security of the area, making it difficult for emergency medical personnel to reach patients and for firefighters to fight fires.

The U.S. Supreme Court reversed the Arizona Court of Appeals' decision that had overturned Larry Youngblood's conviction for child molestation, sexual assault, and kidnapping. The appellate court had found that the state's failure to preserve semen samples from the victim's body and clothing constituted a denial of due process, potentially exonerating Youngblood.

The Supreme Court, however, focused on the distinction between the state's failure to disclose material exculpatory evidence, which is always a due process violation regardless of the state's intent, and the state's failure to preserve evidentiary material that might be useful to the defense. The Court held that unless the defendant can show bad faith on the part of the police, the failure to preserve potentially useful evidence does not constitute a denial of due process.

In Youngblood's case, the police's failure to refrigerate the clothing and to perform certain tests on the semen samples was deemed at most negligent, not indicative of bad faith. The Court emphasized that the evidence was not concealed from Youngblood at trial, and his expert had access to it but chose not to perform any tests.

The Court also rejected the notion that the police have a constitutional duty to use specific investigatory tools or perform particular tests, such as the newer P-30 test mentioned by the appellate court.

The Supreme Court's decision implies that the state's duty to preserve evidence is limited and does not extend to all material that could potentially be of evidentiary significance. The ruling clarifies the standards for due process claims related to evidence preservation, emphasizing the importance of demonstrating bad faith by the police to succeed in such claims. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

Title: Alexander Mirzayance v. John Hickman

Summary: Alexander Mirzayance, a man convicted of first-degree murder in California, seeks release from prison due to alleged ineffective assistance of counsel during his trial. His attorneys withdrew the insanity defense after determining that there was little chance of success and that doing so might harm their clients' credibility. However, Mirzayange argues that his lawyers were deficient for abandoning the defense, despite there being "nothing to lose" from pursuing it. The Supreme Court disagrees, ruling that the lawyers' decision was not unreasonable and did not involve an unreasonable application of clearly established Federal law.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Michigan Campaign Finance Act, a federal law that prohibits corporations from making independent expenditures in connection with state elections.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia, alleges that the Michigan campaign finance law, Section 54(1), is substantially overinclusive, because it includes within its scope closely held corporations that do not possess vast reservoirs of capital.  According to the complaint, the complaint alleges that, absent application of the federal law, corporations can make independent political expenditures without violating the First and the Fourteenth Amendment.  For example, the SEC alleges that corporations can solicit contributions to their separate political fund only from members, officers or directors of members, and the spouses of any of these persons.  In addition, the court found that, under the federal laws, corporations are not permitted to make independent expenditures through separate segregated funds.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants have consented to the entry of judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the federal securities laws, ordering disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and imposing civil penalties against the defendants.

The Supreme Court held that a Massachusetts pricing order, which imposed an assessment on all fluid milk sold by dealers to Massachusetts retailers and then distributed the entire assessment to Massachusetts dairy farmers, unconstitutionally discriminated against interstate commerce. The order effectively taxed milk produced out of state while subsidizing Massachusetts dairy farmers, enabling them to compete with lower-cost producers from other states. This arrangement was found to violate the Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits economic protectionism and state regulations that unduly burden interstate commerce.

The Court rejected Massachusetts' arguments that the pricing order was not protectionist because it was funded by in-state consumers and dealers, and that the burden on interstate commerce was justified by the local benefit of preserving the dairy industry. The Court emphasized that the purpose and effect of the order were to divert market share to local producers, which necessarily injured out-of-state competitors and interfered with the national market.

The Court's decision reversed the judgment of the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, which had upheld the pricing order. The Supreme Court's ruling underscored the principle that states cannot use their regulatory powers to favor in-state economic interests over out-of-state competitors, and that measures that have the same effect as tariffs or customs duties are unconstitutional.

In the Supreme Court case under review, the central issue was whether state trial courts are constitutionally required to instruct juries on offenses that are not lesser included offenses of the charged crime under state law. The Court concluded that such instructions are not required and reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals.

The case involved a defendant in Nebraska who was convicted of felony murder and sentenced to death. The defendant had requested jury instructions on second-degree murder and manslaughter, arguing they were lesser included offenses of felony murder. The trial court refused, citing Nebraska Supreme Court precedent that these are not lesser included offenses of felony murder. The defendant was convicted, and the sentence was upheld on appeal.

The Court of Appeals had granted the defendant's petition for a writ of habeas corpus, finding a constitutional error in the trial court's refusal to give the requested instructions. They compared the situation to the Supreme Court's decision in Beck v. Alabama, which found unconstitutional a state statute that prohibited lesser included offense instructions in capital cases when such instructions were generally given in noncapital cases.

However, the Supreme Court distinguished the current case from Beck, noting that in Beck, the statute in question prohibited instructions on offenses that were recognized as lesser included offenses under state law, and this prohibition applied only in capital cases. In contrast, Nebraska law did not recognize second-degree murder and manslaughter as lesser included offenses of felony murder, and the trial court's refusal to give the instructions was consistent with longstanding state law applied in both capital and noncapital cases.

The Supreme Court emphasized that states are not required to provide jury instructions on "lesser related offenses" when no lesser included offense exists under state law. The Court also rejected the argument that its previous decisions in Tison v. Arizona and Enmund v. Florida required states to alter their definitions of felony murder to include a mens rea requirement with respect to the killing.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court held that the Court of Appeals erred in extending the rule from Beck to require instructions on offenses not recognized as lesser included offenses under state law. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment granting the defendant a conditional writ of habeas corpus, thereby upholding the original trial court's decision.

After respondent Castro, who acted pro se, filed a motion attacking his federal drug conviction, the District Court, although referring to the motion as a Rule 33 motion for a new trial, stated that it “twiced refer[red]” to it as a motion under 28 U. S. C. § 2255, which governs postconviction habeas petitions. When Castro appealed, he did not challenge the recharacterization. The Eleventh Circuit ruled on a motion based upon both Rule 33 and § 2255, affirming the District Court’s dismissal of Castro’s motion. Subsequently, after Castro again moved under § 2255, the District Court determined that the motion was his second § 2255 motion, rejecting his arguments that it was his first. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding that the 1994 court’s failure to issue the required warning did not render invalid its recharacterization. Held: A district court may not recharacterize a pro se litigant’s motion as a request for relief under § 2255—unless the court first warns the pro se litigant about the consequences of the recharacterization, thereby giving him an opportunity to contest the recharacterization, or to withdraw or amend the motion. Pp. 3–10. (a) Because Castro’s appeal concerned neither an “authorization … to file a second or successive application,” nor the denial of such an authorization, 28 U. S. C. § 2244(b)(3)(E) does not bar this Court’s review. Although the Eleventh Circuit suggested that its opinion fell within the scope of the jurisdictional provision, its language cannot be read as a statutorily relevant “denial.” Nor would doing so allow review where the lower court decision disfavored, but denied, the Government’s position, while closing the door to those seeking review without any clear indication that Congress intended to limit this Court’s jurisdiction. Pp. 3–5. (b) Numerous Circuits have recognized that, by recharacterizing as a first § 2255 motion a pro se litigant’s filing that did not previously bear that label, a court may make it significantly more difficult for that litigant to file another such motion. Thus, they have concluded that a district court may not recharacterize a pro se litigant’s motion as a request for relief under § 2255—unless the court first warns the pro se litigant about the consequences of the recharacterization, thereby giving him an opportunity to contest the recharacterization, or to withdraw or amend the motion. Here, the District Court that considered Castro’s 1994 motion failed to give Castro the requisite warnings. Since this Court’s “supervisory power” determinations normally apply, at least to the case in which the determination was made, Castro’s 1994 motion cannot be considered a first § 2255 motion, and his 1997 motion cannot be considered a “second or successive” motion—unless there is something special about Castro’s case. There is none. An unwarned recharacterization cannot count as a § 2255 motion for purposes of the “second or successive” provision, whether the unwarned pro se litigant takes an appeal. The law of the case doctrine cannot pose an insurmountable obstacle to this conclusion. Pp. 5–10. 290 F. 3d 1269, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York granted summary judgment in favor of The New York Times, Newsday, and Time, Inc., finding that the publishers had not violated the copyright of six freelance authors by placing their articles in a database without their consent. The freelance authors' complaint alleged that their copyrights had been infringed by the inclusion of their articles. The publishers, in response, relied on the privilege of reproduction and distribution accorded them by 201(c) of the Copyright Act. The court found that the databases did not violate the copyright because they did not reproduce and distribute the articles standing alone and not in context, not "as part of that particular collective work" to which the author contributed, "as a part of any revision" thereof, or "as an later collective work in the same series"

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Nevada granted certiorari to resolve whether the Nevada Supreme Court's refusal to extend full faith and credit to California's tax collection agency violated Article IV,  1, of the Constitution. The court held that the Nevada court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because it did not apply California law, which provides that "Neither a public entity nor a public employee is liable for an injury caused by an act or omission in the interpretation or application of any law relating to a tax." The court also held that Nevada's failure to apply the law did not violate Article IV.  1 because the court did not hold that the law violated the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law. We conclude that the court's decision does not violate the Constitution, and therefore affirm the judgment of the District Court.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Washington today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint alleges that, on November 22, 1997, Officer Joi Haner of the Washington State Patrol conducted a traffic stop on a disabled automobile. Haner stopped the car, activating his "wig-wag" headlights, which flash the left and right lights alternately, and obstructing a law-enforcement officer's view of the car. Haners allegedly told Haner that he had worked previously for the "State Patrol," but claimed instead to have worked in law enforcement in Texas and at a shipyard. Hanering allegedly claimed that his flashing headlights were part of a recently installed car-alarm system, and acted as though he was unable to trigger the system. The complaint further alleges that Haner followed Haner's instructions to remove respondent from the car and arrest him for the same conduct. The court also found that Hanering failed to disclose to the officers that he was recording his conversations with the officers. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit also ruled against Haner, finding that he lacked probable cause to arrest because he had made the arrest on the basis of his suspicions, and that Devenpeck had not abided the county's policy against stacking charges.  Haner agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The settlement is subject to court approval.  In a parallel administrative proceeding, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of New York today announced criminal charges against Hanering. The case was supervised by Kelly L. Gibson. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

A Massachusetts statute requires parental consent before an abortion can be performed on an unmarried woman under the age of 18. If one or both parents refuse such consent, however, the abortion may be obtained by order of a judge of the superior court "for good cause shown." In appellees' class action challenging the constitutionality of the statute, a three-judge District Court held it unconstitutional and enjoined its enforcement. Subsequently, this Court vacated the District Court's judgment and certified to the Supreme Judicial Court appropriate questions concerning the meaning of § 12S, pursuant to existing procedure in that State. Held: The judgment is affirmed. Pp. 633-651; 652-656. Rehearing Denied Oct. 1, 1979.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada today entered a final judgment in favor of JWM Investments, Inc., a Las Vegas-based corporation that has been charged with violating the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Las Vegas, JWM and its owner, Debbie Pear, entered into contracts under which JWM was to construct four restaurants in the Las Vegas area, which would be leased to Domino’s. The complaint alleges that, in violation of these contracts, the defendants failed to execute estoppel certificates for JWM required by the contracts to facilitate JWM’s bank financing.  The complaint further alleges that McDonald was the sole owner of the land JWM had acquired for the restaurants, and that he had to go to the Water District to prove that he was party to the contracts because the salesman was black.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against McDonald.   The SEC's Complaint against McDonald alleges that the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, JWP and McDonald consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the charged provisions of the federal laws, ordering JWM to pay a civil penalty of $45,000, and ordering Domino's to pay an $80,000 civil penalty.  JWM settled its charges in the same fashion, agreeing to settle its charges against it. The settlement is pending final approval by the court. Â The SEC's Office of Investor Education and Advocacy has issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the background of anyone selling or offering them an investment using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

Respondent, a practicing homosexual, was charged with violating the Georgia statute criminalizing sodomy by committing that act with another adult male in the bedroom of respondent's home. After a preliminary hearing, the District Attorney decided not to present the matter to the grand jury unless further evidence developed. Respondent then brought suit in Federal District Court challenging the constitutionality of the statute insofar as it criminalized consensual sodomy. The case was remanded for trial, at which, to prevail, the State would have to prove that the statute is supported by a compelling interest and is the most narrowly drawn means of achieving that end. The Attorney General's petition for certiorari questioning the holding that the sodomy statute violates the fundamental rights of homosexuals was denied. Held: 1. The judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed. Pp. 488-481. (a) Although the statute does not violate respondent's fundamental right to engage in homosexual sodomy, it does not qualify for recognition under the prevailing principles for construing the Fourteenth Amendment. Stanley v. Georgia, 394 U. S. 557, which this Court summarily affirmed, and Roe v. Wade, 410 U.S. 113, which held that the First Amendment prevents conviction for possessing and reading obscene material in the privacy of one's home is unsupportable. The privacy right pressed upon us here has no similar support in the text of the Constitution, and it is not qualified for recognition as one of the protections provided by the Due Process Clause. Nor is respondent's claim that the privacy right, which the Griswold line of cases found to be one of those protections, did not reach so far. P. 489. (b) Even if respondent's submission is limited to the voluntary sexual conduct between consenting adults, it would be difficult, except by fiat, to limit the claimed right to homosexual conduct while leaving exposed to prosecution adultery, incest, and other sexual crimes even though they are committed in the home. Moreover, respondent's contention that there must be a rational basis for the law and that there is none in this case other than the presumed belief of a majority of the electorate in Georgia that homosexuals sodomy is immoral and unacceptable, is said to be an inadequate rationale to support the law. The law, however, is constantly based on notions of morality, and if all laws representing essentially moral choices are to be invalidated under the due process Clause, the courts will be very busy indeed. Even respondent makes no such claim, but insists that majority sentiments about the morality of homosexuality should be declared inadequate. The Court does not agree, and are unpersuaded that sodomy laws of some 25 States should be validated on this basis. The issue presented is whether the Federal Constitution confers a fundamental right upon homosexuals to engagein sodomy and hence invalidates the laws of the many States that still make such conduct illegal and have done so for a very long time, and the case also calls for some judgment about the limits of the court's role in carrying out its constitutional mandate. Pc. 760 F. 2d 1202, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment in a case brought by the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York against a British citizen who was held at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, alleges that the U. S. Attorney’s Office for New York and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) issued false and misleading statements in connection with the issuance of a writ of habeas corpus.  According to the complaint, the court held that, in its view, the writ was an important tool to protect the rights of foreign citizens detained at Guantanamo.  For example, the complaint alleges that, at the time of the issuance, the Court held that the writ did not apply to citizens of any foreign country, and that the court had jurisdiction to issue the writ to any foreign citizen.  In addition, the SEC alleges that in the days leading up to the September 11, 2001 attacks, the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates had not issued the writ.  As alleged in the SEC complaint, however, the British government had no jurisdiction over Guantanamo Bay and no way to enforce the writ without the court finding that the British had the right to do so.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the complaint and in the court order, the government has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining it from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering it to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000,000.  Additionally, the judgment requires the court to determine whether to suspend the suspension of the writ for a period of five years.  On June 9, 2018, the Honorable William R. Rumsfeld of the New York District Court issued an order suspending the suspension for five years, ordering the release of all of the previously-convicted British citizens held in Guantanamo.

Title: Ripeness Doctrine Applies To Takings Claim Based On Transferable Development Rights

Summary:
This case involves a woman named Suitum who lives in a community governed by the Tahoe Regional Planning Authority (TRPA). Suitum wants to build a home on her property, but the TRPA has designated her property as part of a Streamside Environmental Zone (SEZ), which means that she cannot build anything on her property except for a single family residence. However, the TRPA allows property owners in the SEZ to transfer their "rights" to build something else on their property to someone else. These rights are called Transferable Development Rights (TDRs), and they come in three varieties: Residential Development Rights, Residential Allocations, and Land Coverage Rights.

Suitum has never built anything on her property, and she doesn't intend to build anything on it anytime soon. Nevertheless, she believes that the TDRs she owns are worth something, and she wants to sell them to someone else who can use them to build something on their own property. The TRPA, however, refuses to approve any transfers of TDRs, arguing that it hasn't yet decided how much development it will allow in the SEZ.

The case makes its way up to the Supreme Court, which ultimately rules that Suitum's takings claim is not ripe for judicial review. The Court explains that in order for a takings claim to be ripe, it must be supported by a "final decision" from the agency responsible for making the decision. In this case, the Court holds that the TRPA's decision not to approve any transfers of TDRs is not a final decision because it is subject to revision at any time. The Court also notes that the TRPA's policy of not allowing transfers of TDRs is designed to ensure that the rights are used efficiently and effectively, rather than sitting idle while the property owner waits for the perfect buyer to come along.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Arkansas ruled that police officers in Little Rock, Arkansas, did not have to obtain a warrant before searching a suitcase seized from an automobile. The court found that the officers had probable cause to believe that the suitcase contained marijuana. Without obtaining a warrant, the officers opened the suitcase and discovered 9.3 pounds of marihuana packaged in 10 plastic bags. The Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit reversed the lower court's finding that the search violated the defendant's Fourth Amendment rights. The Supreme Court ruled that the court should have granted a motion to suppress the evidence. The high court held that the trial court had erred in its finding that there was no need for a warrant because there was "nothing in this set of circumstances that would lend credence to an assertion of impracticality in obtaining a search warrant"

When petitioner airline denied respondents’ motion to change their assigned seats on a flight from Paris to Los Angeles, respondents’ son, who had severe asthma, became short of breath due to the heavy concentration of ambient cigarette smoke in the row where they sat. He received shots of epinephrine from a doctor accompanying them, but he died before landing. Respondents sued petitioner in California state court, claiming that the man’s death was caused by petitioner’s “failure” to reseat him. Petitioner removed the case to Federal District Court, which ruled for respondents. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit affirmed. Held: An airline employee’s refusal to reseat a passenger whose pre-existing medical condition was exacerbated by exposure to ambient smoke in the cabin constitutes an “accident” under Articles 17 and 18 of the Warsaw Convention. Pp. 3–10. (a) Under Article 17, an airline is strictly liable for damages arising out of the death or injury of a passenger caused by an “accident.” Neither party challenges Saks’ definition of the term “accident,” which holds that an “accident” is “an unexpected or unusual event or happening that is external to the passenger,” 470 U. S. 395, 405, 406, and that intentional conduct falls within the definition, id., at 405. This Court’s focus in Saks was on what causes can be considered accidents, and it stated that a plaintiff needs only to prove that “some link in the chain was an unusual or unexpected event external to the passenger,” ibid. Pp. 3–5. (b) Petitioner errs in arguing that the “accident” inquiry should focus on the “injury producing event,” i.e., the presence of ambient smoke in the cabin. That argument overlooks the reality that there are often multiple interrelated factual events that contribute to any given injury. Here, the exposure to smoke and the refusal to assist the passenger were happenings that both contributed to the passenger’s death. Nor is petitioner’s argument that the flight attendant’s failure to act cannot constitute an “accident” because only affirmative actions are “events or happenings” persuasive. Such a distinction would be relevant were this a tort law negligence case, but respondents do not advocate, and petitioner rejects, that a negligence regime applies under Article 17. Instead, the relevant inquiry is whether there is “an unexpected or unusual event or happening.” Saks, supra, at 405. Finally, petitioner’s contention that the Ninth Circuit improperly created a negligence-based “accident” standard under Article 17 by focusing on the flight crew’s negligence as the “accident” lacks merit. No party disputes the Ninth Circuit’s holding that the flight attendant’s conduct was “unexpected and unusual,” which is the operative language under Saks and the correct Article 17 analysis. Pp. 5–10. 316 F. 3d 829, affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Middle District of Tennessee ruled that the Supreme Court of the United States did not have jurisdiction to review a lower court's decision denying a habeas corpus appeal. The lower court held that a station-house identification procedure was so suggestive as to violate due process. The Supreme Court held that the lower court had not properly considered the issue of whether the identification procedure violated due process, and that the high court had actually adjudicated the case. The Court held, however, that it was not the Court's role to determine whether a state court had properly denied a state habeas appeal. In a separate appeal, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled in favor of the state, and the case was remanded for further consideration by the Court. The case was decided by a three-member panel of the Court, with Justices Anthony M. Scalia, Neil A. Kohn, and John G.

Petitioners, property owners who participated in a federal program to promote development of affordable rental housing in areas not traditionally served by conventional lenders, entered into a loan agreement with the Farmers Home Administration (FmHA) under §§ 515 and 521 "to provide rental housing and related facilities for eligible occupants ... in rural areas." App. to Pet. for Cert. A165. In the loan agreements, each petitioner certified that it was unable to obtain a comparable loan in the commercial market. The loan agreements contained various provisions designed to ensure that the projects were affordable for people with low incomes. Those provisions included restrictions as to eligible tenants, the rents petitioners could charge, and the rate of return petitionerers could realize, as well as requirements regarding the maintenance and financial operations of each project. The promissory notes executed by petitioners required payment of the principal on each mortgage in scheduled installments, plus interest. See id., at A176-A177. The notes also contained the words "first accrues," which convey Congress' intent to guard the sovereign against claims that might be deemed timely under statutes of limitations applicable to private parties. Petitioners' takings claims, filed over nine years post-ELIHPA's passage, were time barred for essentially the same reason. The Federal Circuit held petitioners' claims untimely, and their suits properly dismissed. Accepting for purposes of this decision that the loan contracts guaranteed the absolute prepayment right petitioners allege, the Court of Federal Claims reversed the Federal Circuit's judgment and remanded the Franconia and Grass Valley cases reviewed herein for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. Held: 1. The Government's construction of § 2501 qualified as a repudiation of the parties' bargain, not a present breach of the loan agreement. Pp. 5-7. (a) The "statement of intent not to perform" on which petitioners base their claim is an Act of Congress. P. 5. (b) The law of repudiation does not govern here, the Government ultimately contends, because the "statement" of intent "to allow" borrowers to prepay would be meaningless if the continuing duty was breached, and therefore the breach occurred immediately, totally, and definitively when the Government's repudiation took away the borrowers' unfettered right to prepays. P p. 5, 6. (c) The fact that the Government had an obligation under the agreements to continue to allow borrowers the "right" to "prepay their loans at any time" does not mean that it had a corresponding obligation to accept prepayments and execute the appropriate releases, since the Government has an obligation to keep its promise to allow such borrowers an "unfettered right." P. 6. 2. The "statutory period of accrual ... depends on whether the injured party chooses to treat the repudiation as a present violation of the Fifth Amendment," Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs, 498 U. S. 89, 95, and, if so, the statute of limitations begins to run, when a borrower tenders prepay and the Government then dishonors its obligations to accept the tender and release its control over use of the property that secured the loan. Thus, once it is understood that EL IHPA is most sensibly characterized as a " repudiation," the decisions below lose force. To recapitulate, "t]he time of accrueal depends ... on whether [the Government] chooses to ... treat [the repudiation] as a past breach." Mobil Oil Exploration & Producing Southeast, Inc. v. United States, 530 U.S. 604, 607. If that party "elects to place the repudiator in breach before the performance date, the accruals date of the cause of action is accelerated from [the] time of performance to the date of such election." Id., at 488-489. If petitioners enjoyed a "right to prepage" for limitations purposes on the date OF repudiation, the court reasoned, then the Government owed no future performance under the contracts. Id., supra, at 1364. The Court of Appeals erred in dismissing petitioners's takings theory on grounds of untimeliness, holding, inter alia, that the passage of ELI HPA qualified as repudiation. Were it so regarded, the suit would be timely if filed within six years of either the date performance fell due (the date petitioners tendered prepay) or the date on which petitioner elected to treat it as an present breach. If it was not, petitioner would find itself defending against highly speculative damages claims in a profusion of lawsuits, most of which would never have been brought under a less novel interpretation of §2501. Id. at 1363. The court's holding that takings relief was time barred hinged entirely on its conclusion that petitioners’ contract claims accrued upon passage of the ELI

The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) offers eligible students with disabilities a free appropriate public education. To implement the Act, states must establish Individualized Education Plans (IEPs) for individual students. An IEP contains, inter alia, an assessment of the student’s strengths and weaknesses, a statement of annual goals, and a plan for achieving those goals. If a parent believes that an IEP is inappropriate, the Act authorizes an “impartial due process hearing” administered by an administrative law judge (ALJ). The ALJ determines whether the IEP complies with the Act. If the ALJ finds that the IEP is defective, the ALJ orders corrective measures. If the ALJ finds that the IEP is inappropriate, the ALJ orders the student removed from the school system. Before initiating a due process hearing, the Act requires the parent to notify the school district of the intent to pursue a hearing and to provide the district with a copy of the IEP. During the hearing itself, both sides may call witnesses and submit exhibits. Either side may also retain experts to assist in making its presentation. Both sides must disclose evaluations and recommendations that they intend to rely upon. After the hearing, the ALJ issues a final decision. If the ALJ rules in the parent’s favor, the parent may recover reasonable attorneys’ fees. Here, petitioner Brian Schumacher, then five years old, had been receiving an IEP prepared by respondent Montgomery County Public Schools. His parents believed that the IEP was inadequate, and they filed a due process complaint. The ALJ found that the IEP complied with the Act, and the county circuit court affirmed. However, the Maryland Court of Special Appeals reversed, holding that the ALJ erred in applying the wrong legal standard. The State Supreme Court denied the county’s petition for review. Subsequently, the Federal District Court entered judgment for the Schumachers, finding that the ALJ applied the wrong legal standard. The Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that the burden of persuasion rested on the party seeking relief, and that since the Schumachers were seeking relief, they bore the burden of persuasion. Held: The burden of proof in an administrative hearing challenging an IEP is properly placed upon the party seeking relief. Pp. 4–11. (a) The plain language of the Act is silent on the allocation of the burden of persuasion. Ordinarily, the party bearing the burden of persuasion is the one seeking relief. There is no exception to this default rule unless Congress expressly indicates that it meant something else. Pp. 4–6. (b) Petitioners’ arguments to the contrary are unpersuasive. First, although the Act uses the word “due process,” the Court assumes, arguendo, that the Act incorporates constitutional due process doctrine. Nevertheless, outside the criminal law context, where special concerns attach, the locus of the burden of persuasion is normally not an issue of federal constitutional moment. Second, the fact that the Act borrowed from earlier decisions does not mean that Congress intended to adopt the ideas that it failed to write into the text of the Act. Third, assigning the burden of persuasion to school districts might encourage schools to spend more money on preparing IEPs and presenting their evidence. But the Act is silent about how marginal dollars should be allocated among litigation and administrative expenditures, litigation and educational services, and litigation and other activities. Furthermore, the Act relies heavily on the expertise of school districts to meet its goals. And the Act provides parents with extensive procedural protections. Those protections ensure that the school district bears no unique informational advantage. Pp. 6–10. (c) Because no state law or regulation puts the burden of persuasion always on the school district, this Court declines to decide whether States may do so. P. 11. 377 F. 3d 445, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of an antitrust suit against the U.N. Postal Service. The Second Circuit held that the Postal Service is not subject to liability under federal antitrust law for conduct undertaken at the command of Congress. The court held that it has a limited immunity from liability for conduct that it undertook at the direction of Congress, and that it is not liable for Flamingo Industries Ltd.'s alleged anticompetitive conduct. Flamingo Industries had been making mail sacks for the postal service, but then its contract was terminated. Flamingo and its owner and principal officer sued, alleging that the USPS had sought to suppress competition and create a monopoly in mail sack production. The lower court dismissed the complaint, concluding that the postal agency was not subject of liability under the federal antitrust laws. Flamingo's appeal was denied, and we reverse the lower court ruling. We conclude that Flamingo and the owner of the contract for mail sacks are not liable under the antitrust laws for the conduct of the USPS. The Postal Service's case will be heard by the U,S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

The Supreme Court of the United States reviewed whether the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) preempts Kentucky's "Any Willing Provider" (AWP) statutes. These statutes require health insurers in Kentucky to accept any provider willing to meet the terms and conditions of the health insurer, including for chiropractic services.

Health maintenance organizations (HMOs) and an association of HMOs (petitioners) challenged the AWP laws, arguing that they interfere with their ability to control costs and quality by creating exclusive provider networks. They contended that the AWP laws are preempted by ERISA, which generally preempts state laws relating to employee benefit plans but saves from preemption state laws that regulate insurance.

The District Court and the Sixth Circuit both concluded that the AWP laws regulate insurance and are thus saved from ERISA preemption. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to address this issue.

The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' decisions, holding that the Kentucky AWP statutes are not preempted by ERISA. The Court reasoned that for a state law to be saved from ERISA preemption, it must be specifically directed toward entities engaged in insurance and must substantially affect the risk pooling arrangement between the insurer and the insured.

The Court found that the AWP laws are directed specifically at the insurance industry and do not impose requirements on healthcare providers. The laws only apply when a health insurer or health benefit plan excludes a willing provider from its network. Additionally, the Court determined that the AWP laws substantially affect the risk pooling arrangement by expanding the number of providers from whom an insured may receive health services, thus altering the scope of permissible bargains between insurers and insureds.

The Supreme Court concluded that the AWP laws are state laws that regulate insurance and are therefore saved from preemption by ERISA. The judgment of the Sixth Circuit was affirmed, meaning that Kentucky's AWP statutes can remain in effect.

Title: Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act

Date: September 13, 2010

Author: John Roberts

Summary:
In this landmark ruling, the Supreme Court clarifies the scope of the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA), which requires certain individuals convicted of sex offenses to register with local authorities and notify neighbors of their presence. The Court holds that SORNA's definition of "sex offender" excludes individuals who were adjudicated delinquent based solely on child pornography charges, and that the Act's residency reporting requirements apply only to those who currently live in the United States. Additionally, the Court finds that SORNA's travel restrictions apply only to individuals who travel after the Act's enactment, and that the Act does not require individuals to disclose their internet activity or social media accounts.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the constitutionality of Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act, which requires certain jurisdictions to obtain federal preclearance before changing election laws. The plaintiff, a small utility district in Texas, challenged the requirement, arguing that it had never engaged in racial discrimination in voting and should be allowed to "bail out" from the preclearance obligations. The lower court denied the district's request, interpreting the Act to mean that only "political subdivisions" that register their own voters could seek bailout.

The Supreme Court reversed the lower court's decision, ruling that all political subdivisions, not just those that register voters, are eligible to seek bailout from the preclearance requirements. The Court avoided ruling on the constitutionality of Section 5 itself, emphasizing the principle of avoiding constitutional questions when possible. The Court noted the historic success of the Voting Rights Act in addressing racial discrimination in voting but also acknowledged that the current conditions may not justify the continued use of preclearance requirements. The Court highlighted the need for legislation to be justified by current needs and the principle of equal sovereignty among states.

The decision allows the utility district to seek bailout from the preclearance requirements and remands the case for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. The broader implications of the decision suggest that other jurisdictions may also seek relief from preclearance, and it raises questions about the future applicability and constitutionality of Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Bouie v. City of Columbia, 378 U.S. 347 (1964), that a judicial decision that applies a novel construction of a criminal statute to conduct that neither the statute nor any prior judicial decision has fairly disclosed to be within its scope violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court held that the Ex Post Facto Clause of the Constitution does not apply to courts, and that the principle of fair warning requires that a judicial decision not be retroactive in nature.

Title: United States v. Hughes Aircraft Corp.

Year: 1999

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) allows an employer to change the rules of a pension plan, even if the changes adversely affect some employees. The Court found that the amendments to the plan did not violate ERISA's anti-discrimination provisions, nor did they cause the plan to cease to exist. The Court also rejected arguments that the amendments were a sham transaction designed to hide illegal activity.

After respondent, a former student at petitioner private university’s School of Education, learned that petitioner faculty members were aware of incidents involving sexually violent behavior toward women committed by respondent during his time at the School, he filed suit in state court against petitioner and several of its employees, seeking damages for emotional distress caused by the release of his “education records” to third parties in violation of the Family Educational Records Privacy Act (FERPA). Under FERPA, the Secretary of Education may withdraw federal funds from an educational institution that has a policy or practice of permitting the release of education records. Petitioner argued that FERPA precluded respondent’s suit. The trial court agreed, holding that FERPA barred recovery under both state common law and 42 U. S. C. § 1983, which authorizes civil actions to enforce rights “secured by the Constitution and laws.” On appeal, the Washington Supreme Court reversed, reasoning that although FERPA does not itself grant a right to relief, its nondisclosure provisions convey a right to privacy that may be enforced under § 1983. Held: Because FERPA’s nondisclosure provisions contain no rights-creating language, they have an aggregate, not individual, focus, and they serve primarily to direct the Secretary of Education’s distribution of public funds to educational institutions, they create no rights enforceable under § 1983. Pp. 279–287. (a) Where Congress wishes to create new rights enforceable under § 1983, it must do so in clear and unambiguous terms—no less and no more than what is required for Congress to create new rights enforceable under an implied private right of action. Plaintiffs suing under § 1983 do not bear the burden of showing an intent to create a private remedy, since § 1983 generally supplies a remedy for the vindication of rights secured by federal statutes. One cannot go into court and claim a § 1983 violation, since § 1983 by itself does not protect anyone against anything. Rather, once a plaintiff shows that a statute confers an individual right, the right is presumptively enforceable under § 1983. However, the initial inquiry—determining whether a statute confers any right at all—is identical to the initial inquiry in an implied right of action case, the express purpose of which is to determine whether or not a statute “confers rights on a particular class of persons,” Californiav . SierraClub, 451 U.S. 287, 294. Courts applying a multifactor balancing test to pick and choose which federal requirements may be enforced by § 1983 and which may not are guided by nothing more than the notion that separation-of-powers considerations are more pronounced in the implied right of action context. Pp. 279–283. (b) Here, FERPA’s nondisclosure provisions fail to confer enforceable rights. First, they lack the sort of “rights-creating” language critical to showing the requisite congressional intent to create new rights. Second, they have an aggregate, not individual, focus, speaking only in terms of institutional policy and practice, not individual instances of disclosure. Third, they allow recipient institutions to avoid termination of funding so long as they “comply substantially” with FERPA’s requirements. Fourth, Congress expressly authorized the Secretary of Education to deal with FERPA violations and established a review board to investigate and adjudicate such violations. Fifth, Congress provided that none of the Secretary’s functions under FERPA shall be performed in regional offices. It is implausible to presume that the same Congress intended private suits to be brought before thousands of federal- and state-court judges, which could only result in the sort of “multiple interpretations” the Act explicitly sought to avoid. Pp. 283–287. 146 Wash. 2d 655, 38 P. 3d 1172, reversed and remanded. Stevens, J., dissented.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California today entered a final judgment in favor of the United States and the United Kingdom in an emergency action to suspend claims against Iran.  According to the court's order, on November 4, 1979, President Carter issued an executive order suspending the issuance, purchase, offer, and sale of assets in violation of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also issued a temporary restraining order halting the issuance of the order, freezing the assets of certain foreign entities, and ordering the transfer of assets.  In a parallel action, the U.K. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  As alleged in the complaint, the suspension order violated the federal securities laws and the pre-clearance provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a)(1) and (3), and (4) the reporting provisions of the Exchange Act.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's complaint, Carter consented to the entry of the final judgment, which permanently enjoins him from violating the above-mentioned provisions and orders him to pay disgorgement of $3,436,694.30 plus interest for a total of $1,078,871.30, and orders the forfeiture of any assets held by the defendants in the case.

A Jehovah's Witness who terminated his employment because his religious beliefs prevented him from participating in the production of war materials, the Indiana Review Board denied him unemployment compensation benefits by applying disqualifying provisions of the Indiana Employment Security Act. The Indiana Court of Appeals reversed, holding that, even assuming that Thomas quit for religious reasons, he would not be entitled to benefits: under Indiana law, a termination motivated by religion is not for "good cause" objectively related to the work. Held: 1. The denial of benefits to petitioner, who terminated because of religious beliefs, constituted a violation of his First Amendment right to free exercise of religion. Sherbert v. Verner, 374 U. S. 398, distinguished. Pp. 531-532. (a) The mere fact that petitioner's religious practice is burdened by a governmental program does not mean that an exemption accommodating his practice must be granted. The State may justify an inroad on religious liberty by showing that it is the least restrictive means of achieving some compelling state interest, but the burden is justified by the legitimate state interest in preserving the integrity of the insurance fund and maintaining a stable work force by encouraging workers not to leave their jobs for personal reasons. P. 533. (b) The State's determination of what is a "religious" belief or practice is more often than not a difficult and delicate task, as the division in the Indiana Supreme Court attests. However, the resolution of that question is not to turn upon a judicial perception of the particular belief and practice in question; religious beliefs need not be acceptable, logical, consistent, or comprehensible to others in order to merit First Amendment protection. Sherb v.Verner, ante, ante; Wis- consin v. Yoder, 406 U.S. 205, 215-216, and the judgment under review must be examined in light of prior decisions, particularly Sherbert, supra, at 403-404, and that the Indiana court held, such payment would violate the Establishment Clause of the Free Exercise Clause. Here, the burden upon religion here is only the indirect consequence of public welfare legislation that the State clearly has authority to enact, and there is no evidence in the record to indicate that the number of people who find themselves in the predicament of choosing between benefits and religious beliefs is large enough to create "widespread unemployment," or even to seriously affect unemployment-and no such claim was advanced by the Review Board. Similarly, although detailed inquiry by employers into applicants' religious beliefs may be undesirable, there is n n nt reason to believe that such inquiries will occur in Indiana, or that they have occurred in any of the states that extend benefits to people in the petitioner's position. Nor is there any reason to think that the numbers terminating employment for reasons of religious reasons will be so great as to motivate employers to make such inquiries. Neither of the interests advanced is sufficiently compelling to justify the burden on Thomas' religious liberty. Accordingly, Thomas is entitled to receive benefits unless, as respondents contend and the Indiana Court held, it would violate his religious liberty, and he is not entitled to be compensated for his termination for religious or nonreligious reasons. Certiorari granted; 391 N. E. 2d 751, reversed and remanded.

The Minnesota Agricultural Society (Society), a public corporation organized under the laws of Minnesota, operates a State Fair on a 125-acre state-owned tract located in St. Paul, Minn. The Fair is a major public event and attracts visitors from all over the country. Each year, the average total attendance for the Fair has been 1,320,000 persons. The average daily attendance on weekdays has been 115,000 and on Saturdays and Sundays 160,000. In 1977, respondents International Society for Krishna Consciousness, Inc. (ISKCON), an international religious society espousing the views of the Krishna religion, and Joseph Beca, head of the Minneapolis ISKCON temple, filed suit against numerous state officials seeking a declaration that Rule 6.05, both on its face and as applied, violated respondents' rights under the First Amendment, and seeking injunctive relief prohibiting enforcement of the Rule. The trial court entered temporary orders to govern the conduct of the parties during the 1977 Fair. When that event concluded and after a hearing, the trial court granted the state officials' motion for summary judgment, upholding the constitutionality of the rule. Relying on International Society's reasoning, the court found that the State's interest "in providing all fair goers and concessionaries with adequate and equal access to each other and in providing a minimum ofcongestion on the fairgrounds" was sufficient to sustain the Rule's limitations as applied to respondents. The court, however, provided that the Rule could not be applied to ISKcon and its members. The Minnesota Supreme Court reversed the State officials' summary judgment and granted summary judgment. Held: 1. A valid time, place, and manner regulation must also "serve a significant governmental interest." The First Amendment protects the right of every citizen to "reach the minds of willing listeners and to do so there must be opportunity to win their attention." Kovacs v. Cooper, 336 U. S. 77, 87, 69 S.Ct. 448, 453, 93 L.Ed. 2d 319, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit has upheld the Department of Health and Human Services's regulations that limit the ability of Title X fund recipients to engage in abortion-related activities. The regulations prohibit a project from referring a pregnant woman to an abortion provider or providing referral for abortion as a method of family planning. The project must also provide a list of available providers that promote the welfare of the mother and the unborn child. The court found that the regulations are consistent with the First and Fifth Amendments of the Constitution. The Court also found that they do not violate the anti-discrimination provisions of the federal law. The Supreme Court has not yet issued an opinion on the matter.

The Supreme Court addressed whether the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) has the authority to take administrative action against a union for filing a false non-Communist affidavit by an officer, as required by Section 9(h) of the National Labor Relations Act. The Court of Appeals had previously ruled that the only consequence for filing a false affidavit was the criminal penalty outlined in Section 35 A of the Criminal Code, not any alteration to the union's rights under the Act.

The Supreme Court agreed with the lower court, holding that the NLRB cannot strip a union of its compliance status based on a false affidavit and that the criminal penalty is the exclusive remedy. The Court reasoned that the statute only provides for a criminal sanction for making a false statement and does not imply any additional administrative penalties. The purpose of Section 9(h) is to deter Communist officers from filing affidavits and to encourage union members to elect non-Communist leaders who can file truthful affidavits, thereby allowing the union to benefit from the Act.

The Court emphasized that the NLRB's duty is limited to determining whether the necessary affidavits have been filed, not to investigate the truthfulness of those affidavits. This interpretation aligns with the legislative history of the Act, which was amended to prevent delays in representation proceedings that could result from the NLRB having to investigate the political affiliations of union officers.

The Court rejected policy arguments suggesting that allowing the NLRB to investigate the veracity of affidavits would provide greater incentive for unions to remove Communist leaders. The Court maintained that the statute's purpose is to protect unions and detect Communists, and it would be unfair to penalize a union if its members were deceived by an officer's false affidavit.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding that the filing of a false non-Communist affidavit by a union officer results only in criminal penalties against the individual officer, not administrative penalties against the union.

This case involves a dispute between two companies regarding ownership of certain designs used in their respective businesses. One company, Vornair Corporation, owns several patents for air conditioning systems designed for industrial applications. Another company, Duraflex Manufacturing Company, produces similar air conditioning units using a spiral grille design that Vornair believes violates its patents.

In 1992, Vornair filed a lawsuit against Duraflex in the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals, alleging that Duraflex's spiral grille design infringes on four of Vornair's patents. However, the suit was eventually settled out of court, and Vornair agreed to dismiss its claims without prejudice.

Later, in November 1999, Vornair filed a new lawsuit against Duraflex in the Eastern District of Missouri, alleging that Duraflex continues to manufacture and sell air conditioning units with the disputed spiral grille design. This time, Duraflex answered the complaint and filed a counterclaim against Vornair, alleging that Vornair's patents are invalid and that Duraflex has been manufacturing air conditioning units with the spiral grille design for years without infringement.

The parties reached a consent decree in February 2000, which provided for a stay of the proceedings while they engaged in settlement negotiations. During this time, both sides continued to file motions and appeals related to the case.

Eventually, the parties reached a settlement agreement, which was approved by the court in May 2000. Under the terms of the agreement, Duraflex paid $1 million to settle the case and agreed to stop selling air conditioning units with the disputed spiral grille design. Additionally, the parties agreed to jointly work together to develop a new spiral grille design that would comply with Vornair's patents.

C. §1804(b)(2)(F), petitioners Martha Fratta and Joseph Pace brought suit against respondents arguing that petitioners paid higher than usual loan origination fees and points than reasonably entitled based on comparatively low offered interest rates on their mortgage applications.
