The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida ruled in favor of the U.N. refugee agency in a case that challenges the government's forced repatriation of Haitians illegally entering the United States from Haiti. The court ruled that the government had violated the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 by sending the Haitians back to Haiti without first determining whether they qualify as refugees. The Court held that the Government's actions violated the Act's provisions against forced repatriation. The Government had previously agreed not to return Haitians to their point of origin without the consent of the Haitian government. The government had also agreed that it would not return any Haitians "whom the Government determines[d] to qualify for refugee status." The Court found that this agreement did not apply to actions taken by the Coast Guard on the high seas. The Coast Guard intercepted approximately 25,000 Haitians in the 1980s and 1990s and returned them to Haiti. In the ensuing decade, the Government had failed to establish and implement adequate procedures to protect Haitians who qualified for asylum. The Haitian Refugee Center, Inc., representing a class of interdicted Haitians, filed a complaint in the United State District Court in Florida alleging that the U,S. Government had not established and implemented adequate procedures. The District Court granted temporary relief that precluded any repatriations until February 4, 1992, when a reversal on appeal in the Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit dismissed the case, effectively ending the litigation. The Supreme Court ruled in the Haitian refugee center's favor in the same case. The case is being heard by Justices John G.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Philip Morris in a case challenging the constitutionality of a federal officer removal statute. The statute allows a party to remove a case from state court to federal court if the plaintiff's allegations "are directed" against the United States or any department or agency thereof." The Court held that the statute applied to private individuals "acting under" a federal officer or agency, but only if their actions involved a relationship of substantial direction and control by the federal government. The Court found that the relationship between Philip Morris and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) did not meet this standard because the FTC did not delegate legal authority to Philip Morris to undertake testing on its behalf.

A United States Senator read to a subcommittee from classified documents (the Pentagon Papers), which he then placed in the public record. The press reported that the Senator had arranged for private publication of the Papers. A grand jury investigating whether violations of federal law were implicated subpoenaed an aide to the Senator. The Senator, as an intervenor, moved to quash the subpoena, contending that it would violate the Speech or Debate Clause to compel the aide to testify. The District Court denied the motion but limited the questioning of the aide. The Court of Appeals affirmed the denial but modified the protective order, ruling that congressional aides and other persons may not be questioned regarding legislative acts and that, though the private publication was not constitutionally protected, a common-law privilege similar to the privilege of protecting executive officials from liability for libel, see Barr v. Matteo, 360 U. S. 564, barred questioning the aide concerning such publication. Held: 1. The Speech Or Debate Clause does not extend immunity to a Member of Congress but also to his aide, insofar as the aide's conduct would be a protected legislative act if performed by the Member himself. Pp. 622-627. (a) The Clause's language does not confer immunity on a Member from service of process as a defendant in civil matters, Long v. Ansell, 293 U.S. 76, or as a witness in a criminal case. The Clause foreclosed inquiry of both Senator and aide with respect to legislative acts, and the privilege as barring direct inquiry of the Senator or his aide but not of third parties, as to the sources of the senator's information used in performing legislative duties. P. 627. (b) Although the Clause itself mentions only "Senators and Representatives," it is sufficiently plain that the constitutional freedom from arrest does not exempt Members of Congress from the operation of the ordinary criminal laws, even though imprisonment may prevent or interfere with the performance of their duties as Members. Moreover, the Clause has not been extended beyond the legislative sphere. That Senators generally perform certain acts in their official capacity as Senators does not necessarily make all such acts legislative in nature. Nor does it immunize Senator or aide from testifying at trials or grand jury proceedings involving third-party crimes where the questions do not require testimony about or impugn a legislative act. Neither does it confer immunity upon a Senator's aide from participation in the activities of his or his aides in preparing for or implementing legislative acts. Neither do the Clause's provisions for the purpose of construing the privilege a Member and his aide are to be "treated as one," United States v. Doe, 332 F. Supp. 930, or, as the District Court put it, "only when necessary to prevent indirect impairment of such deliberations." P. 753. 2. The Act of Congress does not protect Members from liability or process in criminal cases, since they are not immune from prosecution by the Executive and accountability before a possibly hostile judiciary. The speech or debate clause does not in any way confer immunity to Members from prosecution for criminal conduct, and it does not immunize them from testifying before the grand jury about the arrangement between Senator Gravel and Beacon Press or about his own participation, if any, in the alleged transaction, so long as legislative acts of Senator are not impugned. Neither is it immune from inquiry by a grand jury into any act, in itself not criminal, performed by a Senator, or by his aide in the course of their employment, in preparation for or executing legislative acts or done without his knowledge or direction. Neither of these three cases adopted the simple proposition that immunity was unavailable to congressional or committee employees because they were not Representatives or Senators; rather, immunity was not unavailable because they engaged in illegal conduct that was not entitled to Speech and Debate Clause protection. Nor is there any constitutional or other privilege that shields a Member or aide, any more than any other witness, from testifying about the conduct of others in the normal course of a valid investigation by the grand-jury. Neither the Speech nor Debate Clause, which recognizes speech, voting, and other legislative acts as exempt from liability that might otherwise attach, extends immunity to Congress from prosecution even though the Senator himself would be immune. Neither, as a Senator nor aide, is it immunized against criminal conduct threatening the security of the person or property of others, whether performed at the direction of a Senator or by the aide on the Senator's behalf, or in execution of the legislative act or done with his knowledge and direction. Nor can the Clause be construed to immunize Members from testifying in any other place for any speech and debate in either House, as long as there might be circumstances in which the Senator is not implicated in the actual arrest. Neither would the Clause immunize Congress or aide to violate an otherwise valid criminal law in preparing and implementing legislative actions. Neither are there constitutional or any other privileges that would be exempt from grand jury questioning. Nor, as in Kilbourn v. Thompson, 103 U . S. 168, 204, or Powell v. McCormack

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of North Dakota ruled that the federal government had the authority to prosecute Billy Jo Lara, a member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians in north-central North Dakota, for assaulting a federal officer. The Spirit Lake Sioux Tribe, which Lara married and lived with on the Spirit Lake Reservation, issued an order excluding him from the reservation after several incidents of serious misconduct. Lara ignored the order; federal officers stopped him; and he struck one of the arresting officers. Lara pleaded guilty and, in respect to that crime, served 90 days in jail. After Lara's tribal conviction, the Federal Government charged Lara in the Federal District Court for the district of N.D. with the federal crime of assault on an officer. Lara argued that this action violated the "double jeopardy" clause of the Constitution, which prohibits the government from subjecting a person "for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb"

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California today entered a final judgment in favor of a federal court finding that the antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) does not apply to cases pending in federal court on April 24, 1996. Rather, the court found that the earlier version of § 2254 should apply throughout a habeas proceeding if the court that issued a preliminary look at the prospects for a successful execution of a defendant's claims was within the scope of the AEDPA provision. For example, the Court found that a defendant can receive the benefit of the pre-Advisatory Rule of Civil Procedure when he or she has filed an application for a writ of habeasa corpus. The Court also found that, in the case of Robert Garceau, a former state prisoner who was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, he was entitled to the same relief as a defendant who had already filed a petition for a temporary restraining order or a stay of execution prior to that date. Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court's judgment, however, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, orders him to pay a civil penalty of $100,000, and requires him to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years. The judgment also orders him not to participate in the issuance, purchase, offer, or offer of any securities in connection with the issuance of the SEC's order.  The court's order also prohibits the defendant from associating with any broker dealer or investment adviser.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Western District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendant. The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, alleges that the defendant violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. The complaint also alleges that, on May 12, 1995, the District Court issued a 45-day halt to the execution of defendant Travis Scott, who was awaiting trial on the same charges. Appellees, a Native American descended from the Abenaki Tribe, applied for and received benefits under the Aid to Families with Dependent Children program and the Food Stamp program. They refused to comply with the requirement that participants in these programs furnish their state welfare agencies with the Social Security numbers of the members of their household as a condition of receiving benefits. Appellees contended that obtaining a Social Security number for Little Bird of the Snow would violate their Native American religious beliefs. The Pennsylvania Department of Public Welfare terminated AFDC and medical benefits payable to appellees on the child's behalf and instituted proceedings to reduce the level of food stamps that appeles' household was receiving. The District Court concluded that the case was not moot, and the parties were enjoined until Little Bird's 16th birthday from denying them cash assistance, medical assistance, and food stamps "because of the [appellees'] refusal to provide a social security number for her." Held: 1. The federal and state defendants' request for injunctive relief, damages, and benefits should have been rejected. Pp. 5-11. (a) The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment does not compel the Government to accommodate a religiously based objection to the statutory requirements that an applicant seeking to receive certain welfare benefits and that the States use these numbers in administering the benefit programs. P. 5. (b) The requirement that applicants provide Social Security Number is facially neutral and applies to all applicants for the benefits involved. The First Amendment's guarantee that "Congress shall make no law . . . prohibiting the free exercise" of religion holds an important place in our scheme of ordered liberty, but the Court has steadfastly maintained that claims of religious conviction do not automatically entitle a person to fix unilaterally the conditions and terms of dealings with the Government. Not all burdens on religion are unconstitutional. See Reynolds v. United States, 98 U. S. 145, 8 Otto 145, 25 L. Ed. 2d 611, and United States v. Lee, 455 U.S. 252, distinguished. Nor is there any claim that there is any attempt by Congress to discriminate invidiously or any covert suppression of particular religious beliefs, since denial of such benefits by a uniformly applicable statute neutral on its face is of a wholly different, less intrusive nature than affirmative compulsion or prohibition, by threat of penal sanctions, for conduct that has religious implications. Moreover, legitimate interests are implicated in the need to avoid any appearance of favoring religious over nonreligious applicants, and legitimate reasons are implicated to avoid such appearance. Thus, a governmental burden on religious liberty is not insulated from review simply because it is indirect, Thomas v. Review Board of Indiana Employment Security Div., 450 U-S. 707, 717-718, and is relevant to the standard the government must meet to justify the burden of the Government's compliance with a condition that is binding on all other persons who seek the same benefits from the Government, and it is not appropriate to require the Government itself to conduct its own internal affairs in ways that comport with the religious beliefs of particular citizens. The general governmental interests involved here buttress this conclusion. Governments today grant a broad range of benefits; inescapably at the same time the administration of complex programs requires certain conditions and restrictions. Although in some situations a mechanism for individual consideration will be created, a policy decision by a government that it wishes to treat all applicants alike and that it does not wish to become involved in case-by-case inquiries into the genuineness of each religious objection to such condition or restrictions is entitled to substantial deference. Furthermore, legitimate interest are implicated, and they may not demand that the Government join in their chosen religious practices by refraining from using a number to identify their daughter. The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the District Court, which had found the Texas system of financing public education unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The case was brought by Mexican-American parents from the Edgewood Independent School District in San Antonio, Texas, who claimed that the state's reliance on local property taxes to fund schools resulted in significant disparities in educational funding and quality, particularly disadvantaging minority and poor students in districts with a low property tax base.

The Supreme Court acknowledged the importance of education but held that education is not a fundamental right explicitly or implicitly protected by the Constitution. Therefore, the Texas system did not require strict judicial scrutiny. The Court found that the Texas system, which combined state funding with local property taxes, was not so irrational as to be invidiously discriminatory. The system aimed to provide a minimum foundation of education while allowing for local control and participation.

The Court emphasized the principle of federalism and the traditional deference to state legislatures in matters of taxation and education policy. It cautioned against judicial interference in complex areas where the Court lacks specialized knowledge and where states have historically been allowed a wide latitude in making policy decisions.

The opinion suggested that while the Texas system was imperfect and could benefit from reform, such changes were the responsibility of state legislatures and the democratic process, not the judiciary. The Court expressed confidence that lawmakers and the public would continue to work towards improving the system of public education funding and quality.

The U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee today entered a final judgment against a Tennessee-based company for unlawfully taking its property in violation of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Memphis, Tennessee, on June 18, 1981, the Tennessee Secretary of State's Office issued an order requiring the company to submit a preliminary plat for a subdivision of its property.  The SEC alleges that the company failed to timely submit a final plat for the subdivision because it had not yet obtained a final decision regarding how to proceed with the application of the regulations.  In addition, the complaint alleges that, contrary to the Commission's finding, the company did not have a reasonable investment-backed expectation that the subdivision would be developed according to the proposed plat.  As alleged in the complaint, the defendants failed to apply for a "just compensation" for the taking of the property, and instead relied on the false testimony of an expert witness who testified that the project was not viable because the city had condemned part of the land for a parkway.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Defendants agreed to pay $350,000 in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty equal to the amount of their profits.  Defendants also agreed to be permanently enjoined from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and to pay civil penalties equal to their profits in the event of a default judgment by the court.

1. The "anti-evolution" statute which the State of Arkansas adopted in 1928 to prohibit the teaching in its public schools and universities of the theory that man evolved from other species of life was an unconstitutional and void restraint upon the freedom of speech guaranteed by the First Amendment. P. 542. 2. The challenged statute is vague and uncertain and therefore within the condemnation of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Id., at 225. 3. The State's undoubted right to prescribe the curriculum for public schools does not carry with it the right to prohibit, on pain of criminal penalty, the teaching of a scientific theory or doctrine where that prohibition is based upon reasons that violate the Constitution. Pp. 543-544. 4. Arkansas' law cannot be defended as an act of religious neutrality. The law selects from the body of knowledge a particular segment which it proscribes for the sole reason that it is deemed to conflict with a particular religious doctrine; that is, with the particular interpretation of the Book of Genesis by a particular group. Id. 545. 5. The statute is not unconstitutional because it "tends to hinder the quest for knowledge, restrict the freedom to learn, and restrain the freedom" to teach. Id, at 546. 6. The Act does not forbid mention of Darwin's theory, or forbid any or all of the infinite varieties of communication embraced within the term "teaching." Id. 7. It does not permit the State to require that teaching and learning must be tailored to the principles or prohibitions of any religious sect or dogma, and is contrary to the mandate of the First, and in violation of the Amendment's Fourteenth, Amendment to the Constitution, which forbids alike the preference of a religious doctrine or the prohibition of theory which is deemed antagonistic to a particular dogma. Id.. at 547. 8. In the present case, there can be no doubt that Arkansas has sought to prevent its teachers from teaching a theory which, it was thought, "denied" the divine creation of man, and that the statute is unconstitutional because, as an exercise of the State's power to specify the curriculum in public schools, it "does not tolerate laws that cast a pall of orthodoxy over the classroom," 385 U. S. 589, 603, and it did not address itself to the competing constitutional considerations. id., at 548. 9. The fact that the challenged statute does not discriminate between religion and nonreligion does not mean that the State may impose upon the teachers in its schools any conditions that it chooses, however restrictive they may be of constitutional guarantees. Keyishian v. Board of Regents, 385 U-S. 495, 684-685, 17 L. Ed. 2d 629, reversed.

Respondents, holders of liquor licenses issued by petitioner Director of the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control, an administrative agency vested by the California Constitution with primary authority for the licensing of the sale of alcoholic beverages and with the authority to suspend or revoke any such license if it determines that its continuation would be contrary to public welfare or morals, brought suit challenging the validity of regulations promulgated by petitioner department prohibiting specified types of "sexual" conduct in connection with the operation of licensed premises. Petitioner department had concluded after hearings that the sale of liquor by the drink and lewd or naked dancing and entertainment should not take place in bars and cocktail lounges for which it has licensing responsibility. The District Court held that the regulations conflicted with the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Held: On the basis of the evidence adduced at the hearings, petitioner department's conclusion that the sale of liquor by the drink and lewd or naked dancing and entertainment should not take place in bars and cocktail lounges for which it has licensing responsibility was not an irrational one, and given the added presumption in favor of the validity of the state regulation in this area that the Twenty-first Amendment requires, the regulations on their face do not violate the Federal Constitution. Pp. 108-114. Reversed.

Respondent was convicted in a North Carolina trial court of kidnaping, armed robbery, and felonious assault. Evidence at the trial showed that he and another man had robbed a service station and shot the station attendant while trying to escape. Incriminating statements made by respondent outside the presence of the jury shortly after his arrest by Federal Bureau of Investigation agents in New York City on the basis of a North Carolina fugitive warrant were admitted into evidence over objection based upon respondent's failure to waive his right to the presence of a lawyer before making the statements. On appeal, the North Carolina Supreme Court reversed the conviction, holding that the statements had been admitted in violation of the requirements of Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U. S. 436, because respondent had failed to waive in writing his right to have counsel present and there had not been a specific oral waiver. Held: An express statement of waiver of the right to remain silent or the right to counsel is not invariably necessary to support a finding that the defendant waived those rights. Pp. 44-48. (a) While an express statement can constitute a waiver, the Court did not hold that such an express statement is indispensable to a finding of waiver. Mere silence is not enough to show waiver, but the courts must presume that a defendant did not waive his rights, and the prosecution's burden is great. However, in at least some cases waiver can be clearly inferred from the actions and words of the person interrogated. Pp. 44-45. (b) The per se rule adopted by the North Carolina Supreme Court goes beyond the requirements of federal organic law. Every court that has considered the question has now reached the same conclusion as to the necessity of an express statement of waiver. Thus, the North Carolina Supreme Court has added to the mandates of the United States Constitution. Pp. 45-48. Vacated and remanded.

The Supreme Court of the United States holds that Texas' sales tax exemption for religious publications violates the First Amendment. The Court finds that the exemption is too narrow to serve a legitimate secular purpose and that it produces greater state entanglement with religion than the denial of an exemption. The Court concludes that the exemption manifests an endorsement of religion and that it cannot withstand Establishment Clause scrutiny.

The National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act of 1986 (NCVIA) established a no-fault compensation program designed to work faster and with greater ease than the civil tort system. The NCVIA provides compensation for medical, rehabilitation, counseling, special education, and vocational training expenses; diminished earning capacity; pain and suffering; and $250,000 for vaccine-related deaths. The Act requires claimants to seek relief through the compensation program before filing suit for more than $1,000. It also provides significant tort-liability protections for vaccine manufacturers, including immunity from liability for failure to warn if they have complied with all regulatory requirements, and for listed side effects that occur at times other than those specified in the Vaccine Injury Table. The Court of Appeals for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia has held that the Act does not preempt state law design-defect claims against vaccine manufacturers. The Supreme Court of the United States, however, has ruled that the NCVIA does not. The high court's decision is a significant victory for the public health benefit of vaccination.

The Supreme Court case in question dealt with whether a financial institution, specifically Cottage Savings Association, could claim tax-deductible losses after exchanging mortgage loan interests with other lenders. Cottage Savings had engaged in such an exchange to realize losses without affecting its economic position, as permitted by a regulatory directive known as "Memorandum R-49."

The Tax Court had allowed Cottage Savings to claim a deduction for the losses, but the Court of Appeals reversed this decision, arguing that the losses were not "actually" sustained during the tax year for purposes of 26 U.S.C. § 165(a). The Supreme Court granted certiorari due to the significance of the issue for the savings and loan industry and the conflicting opinions among the Circuits.

The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision. The Court held that tax liability is based on the realization of gains or losses, which occurs upon the "sale or other disposition of property." The Court agreed with the Commissioner of Internal Revenue that an exchange of property results in realization only if the properties exchanged are "materially different." However, the Court found that the Commissioner's interpretation of what constitutes "materially different" was too complex and subjective.

Instead, the Court determined that properties are materially different if they embody legally distinct entitlements. In this case, because the mortgage loans exchanged were secured by different homes and made to different obligors, they were considered legally distinct, and thus the exchange constituted a realization event for tax purposes.

The Court also addressed the issue of whether the losses were "sustained" under § 165(a) of the Internal Revenue Code. The Commissioner's defense that the losses lacked "economic substance" was deemed insufficient, as there was no indication that the transactions were not conducted at arm's length or that Cottage Savings retained control over the exchanged interests.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court ruled that Cottage Savings did realize and sustain losses through the exchange of mortgage participation interests, and therefore, the losses were tax-deductible. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion.

After petitioner Snyder was indicted for first-degree murder, the State filed charges seeking the death penalty. Following extensive voir dire, the trial court denied Snyder’s motion to compel the State to reveal the names of the jurors it planned to strike. The court then conducted voir dire, using random selection procedures to fill the jury box. Of eight African Americans on the venire, five were eventually struck. Three whites were ultimately chosen to sit on the jury, which returned a guilty verdict. The State Supreme Court reversed, holding that the State violated Snyder’s rights under Batson v. Kentucky, 497 U. S. 145, by striking two of the African American jurors. Held: The State Supreme Court erred in concluding that the State used peremptory strikes to exclude African Americans from the jury. Pp. 4–11. (a) To prevail on a Batson objection, a defendant must establish that the prosecution exercised its peremptory strikes with racially discriminatory intent. Miller-El v. Dretke, 545 U. S. ___, ___. The trial court’s rulings on the Batson objections are reviewed for manifest error. Id., at ___. Pp. 4–5. (b) The State Supreme Court correctly concluded that the trial court failed to properly apply the Batson framework. Its analysis focused solely on the racial makeup of the venire rather than on the individualized reasoning behind the strikes. However, the State Supreme Court erred in concluding that the State used peremptory strikes to exclude African Americans from the jury. Pp. 5–11. (1) The State Supreme Court identified four factors supporting its conclusion: (1) the racial composition of the venire; (2) the State’s failure to provide detailed reasons for the strikes; (3) the State’s failure to explain how the strikes related to the charges against Snyder; and (4) the State’s failure to address the impact of the strikes on the diversity of the jury pool. These factors are insufficient to support the State Supreme Court’s conclusion. First, the racial makeup of the venire is irrelevant to determining whether the State used peremptory strikes to exclude African Americans from the jury. Second, the State provided detailed reasons for the strikes. Third, the State’s failure to relate the strikes to the charges against Snyder is immaterial since the State’s theory of the case was not dependent on the charges. Fourth, the State’s failure to address the impact of the strikes on the jury pool is also immaterial since the State’s theory of the case was not dependent on the charges. Pp. 5–7. (2) The State Supreme Court incorrectly assumed that the State used peremptory strikes to exclude African Americans from the jury. While the State’s theory of the case was not dependent on the charges, the State’s theory was dependent on the facts underlying the charges. Specifically, the State argued that the victim’s injuries resulted from a violent confrontation, and that the State’s actions were justified because the victim threatened violence toward her children. The State Supreme Court ignored the relevance of these facts to the State’s argument that the strikes were proper. Had the State Supreme Court considered the facts underlying the charges, it would have realized that the State acted appropriately in striking the African American jurors. Pp. 7–11. Reversed and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California today entered a final judgment against the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Department of Justice in a related case.  The court's order, which entered the final judgment on June 6, 1980, permanently enjoins the Attorney General's Office from issuing an order requiring the registration of women in the armed forces.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Philadelphia, the court issued an order imposing a temporary restraining order on the registration and conscription of women as well as men in the Armed Forces.  In its order, the Court found that the registration provisions of the federal securities laws violated the First Amendment, and that the court was entitled to determine the appropriate level of deference to Congress in determining whether or how to proceed with the registration.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 596-826 (July 18, 1980).  The SEC's order also prohibits the issuance of any civil injunctive relief, including an order freezing the assets of any company or company that does not already have a registered representative, and orders the issuance and issuance of a cease-and-desist order.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint, the SEC has agreed to the entry of an order permanently enjoining it from future violations of the First and Second Amendments of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rules 10b-5, 13a-14, and 13b-20 thereunder, and to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,500,000.  On June 12, 2017, the Honorable Paul G. Sansone of the U.N. Court of Justice granted the court's request for an emergency asset freeze and ordered the SEC to conduct an examination of the merits of the proposed asset freeze.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of South Dakota ruled that an immigrant convicted of aiding and abetting another person's possession of cocaine is not eligible for cancellation of removal. The court held that the Controlled Substances Act does not apply to Jose Antonio Lopez's drug-trafficking conviction. Lopez was sentenced to five years in prison after pleading guilty to the drug charge in 1997. He was released from prison after 15 months and entered the United States as a legal permanent resident. The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) determined that his state conviction was an aggravated felony, which would disqualify him from cancellation. The BIA agreed with the BIA's decision, but the Court of Appeal for the Dakotas ruled that the State's conviction was not a felony and Lopez should be allowed to remain in the U. S.

After respondent Nation purchased untaxed motor fuel in Kansas, it resold the fuel through its casino gas station on its reservation in Kansas. When the Nation filed suit seeking to recover the taxes levied on the fuel purchase, the trial court entered judgment for petitioner Kansas. On appeal, the Tenth Circuit found that the Kansas motor fuel tax violated the Nation’s sovereignty, reasoning that the tax was subject to the interest-balancing test set forth in White Mountain Apache Tribe v. Bracker, 448 U.S. 136, 144–145. Held: The Kansas motor fuel tax is a nondiscriminatory tax imposed on an off-reservation transaction between non-Indians, and hence poses no affront to the Nation’s sovereignty. Pp. 4–12. (a) The Kansas motor fuel tax is a nondiscriminatory tax imposed on an off-reservation transaction between non-Indians. The tax is levied on the legal incidence of the distribution of motor fuel, which is the person who first receives the fuel. Here, that person is the distributor, who is a non-Indian. Because the distributor passes along the tax to the Nation, the tax is levied on the Nation’s off-reservation receipt of the fuel. The tax is not discriminatorily applied to the Nation, since Kansas offers no services to the several States or the Federal Government. To the extent that Kansas fuel retailers bear the tax, that burden falls equally upon all retailers within the State, regardless of whether those retailers are located on an Indian reservation. Pp. 4–7. (b) The Nation misreads Bracker to suggest that the interest-balancing test is always applicable whenever a State asserts its taxing authority outside of Indian Country. There is nothing in Bracker to indicate that the test is applicable to a tax imposed on non-Indians as a result of an off-reservation transaction. Rather, the test is designed to deal with situations in which a State asserts authority over the conduct of non-Indians on the reservation. Absent express federal law to the contrary, Indians going beyond the boundaries of the reservation have traditionally been held subject to nondiscriminatory state law otherwise applicable to all citizens of the State. See, e.g., Mescalero Apache Tribe v. Jones, 411 U. S. 145. If a State may apply a nondiscriminatory tax to Indians who have gone beyond the boundaries of the reservation, then it follows that it may apply a nondiscriminatory tax where, as here, the tax is imposed on non-Indians as a result of an off-reservation transaction. In these circumstances, the interest-balancing test is inapplicable. The Nation’s attempt to expand the application of the Bracker test is not supported by this Court’s cases. Nor is the Nation entitled to interest balancing by virtue of its claim that the Kansas motor fuel tax interferes with its own motor fuel tax. Even assuming that the Nation could properly label a portion of the station’s revenues as tax proceeds, it cannot invalidate the Kansas tax by complaining about a decrease in revenues resulting from the tax. The Nation merely seeks to increase its revenues by purchasing untaxed fuel. Its decision to impose a tax should have no effect on its net revenues from the operation of the station. Furthermore, the Nation’s argument that the Kansas motor fuel tax is impermissibly discriminatory is refuted by the fact that Kansas offers no services to the several States or the Federal Government. Pp. 7–10. 369 F. 3d 1178, reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Roberts, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

As part of a comprehensive program to recoup the costs of federal aviation programs from those who use the national airsystem, Congress in 1970 imposed an annual registration tax on all civil aircraft that fly in the navigable airspace of the United States. More importantly for present purposes, the Revenue Act adopted several measures to ensure that federal outlays that benefited the civil users of the airways would, to a substantial extent, be financed by taxing measures imposed on those civil users. The tax was designed to serve the congressional policy of having those who especially benefit from Government activity help bear the cost, and the financing provisions are intended to ensure, whatever the present scope of the constitutional principle of implied immunity of a state government from federal taxes, a user fee does not implicate the doctrine. Held: 1. A State enjoys no constitutional immunity from a nondiscriminatory revenue measure, like § 4491, which operates only to ensure each member of a class of special beneficiaries of a federal program pay a reasonable approximation of its fair share of the cost of the program to the National Government. Pp. 5-7. (a) The existence of the States implies some restriction on the national taxing power. The fact that the States have been in existence as independent sovereigns when the Constitution was adopted, and that the Constitution presupposes and guarantees the continued existence of these States as governmental bodies performing traditional sovereign functions, cannot be seriously contended with the values protected by the implied constitutional doctrine of state tax immunity. P. 5. (b) A State may not complain of the tax on the ground it is a flat annual fee and hence is not directly related to the degree of use of its airways, but rather is solely to protect the States from undue interference with their traditional governmental functions. The only advantage conceivably to be lost by denying the States such an immunity is that essential state functions might be obtained at a lesser cost because employees exempt from taxation might be willing to work for smaller salaries. The cost of essential state services is no more offensive to the constitutional structure than is the increase in costs of essential operations that results either from the fact that those who deal with the State may be required to pay nondiscrimination taxes on the money they receive or from a jury may award an eminent domain claimant an amount in excess of what would be "just compensation" in an ideal system of justice. The purpose of this implied constitutional restriction is not to give an advantage to the States by enabling them to engage employees at a lower charge than those paid by private entities, see Helvering v. Gerhardt, 304 U. S. 572, and are structured to produce revenues that will not exceed the total cost to the Federal Government of the benefits to be supplied, and there can be no substantial basis for a claim that the national Government will be using its taxing powers to control, unduly interfere with, or destroy a State's ability to perform essential services. The requirement that total revenues not exceed expenditures places a natural ceiling on the total amount that such charges may generate and the further requirement that the measure be reasonable and nondisriminatory precludes the adoption of a charge that will unduly burden state activities. See, e. g., Evansville-Vanderburgh Airport Authority v. Delta Airlines, Inc., 589-590. The State's claim of constitutional immunity is particularly insubstantial. First, there is no question but that the tax imposed by §4491 is nondiscinatory. It applies not only to private users of airways but also to civil aircraft operated by the United Sates, and it satisfies the requirement that it be a fair approximation of the costs that civil aircraft receive from the federal activities. Second, the tax satisfies the constitutional requirement that such "rough approximations of cost," while appropriate compensatory measures in other settings, should be closely calibrated to the amount of any taxpayer's actual use, and thus is not excessive in relation to the Government's costs. Finally, it is not unreasonable to be contended that federal exactions from the States of their fair share are not a sufficient basis for sustaining a claim of immunity. The Government may impose appropriate conditions on the use of federal property or privileges and may require that state instrumentalities comply with conditions that are reasonably related to federal interest in particular national projects or programs, see id., at 546-547, and where it is inconceivable that such a revenue measure could ever operate to preclude traditional state activities, the Tax is valid. Where the subject of tax is a natural and traditional source of federal revenue, it will no more preclude a State from performing traditional functions than it will prevent private entities from performing their missions. The Court has by no means abandoned its doubts concerning its ability to make particularized assessments of the impact of revenue measures on essential state operations, compare New York v. United States, supra, at 581, 66 S.Ct., at 313, and its exercise . . . does not curtail the business of the State government more than it does the like business of a citizen." 326 U.S., at

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a charge filed under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) by a former employee of Federal Express Corporation (FedEx) alleging that FedEx violated the ADEA. The lower court ruled that the employee had not filed her charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) at least 60 days before filing suit, as required by the law. The court held that the law does not define charge and that the EEOC's regulations do not provide a comprehensive definition of the term. The Second Circuit concluded that the lower court misapplied the law by failing to apply the law's requirements for timely filing of charges. The Court held that, under the law, a charge must be filed within 60 days of the date of the filing of the charge, and that there was no reason to believe that the filing was delayed by that time. In a related case, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled in favor of the EEOC, holding that the agency had the authority to issue regulations that provide a broad definition of charge. The ADEA provides for a two-year waiting period for a charge to be filed with the EEOC. In this case, however, the EEOC had not yet issued regulations that provided a statutory definition of a "charge"

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Alabama today issued a final judgment in a civil injunctive action against Jefferson County, Alabama.  The SEC's complaint alleges that, in 1991, Jefferson County filed a complaint in the Federal District Court in Birmingham, Alabama, alleging that the county's occupation tax violated the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.  According to the complaint, the complaint was filed in the form of a temporary restraining order, and the court granted the court's motion for summary judgment on the basis of a prior judgment that barred the county from enforcing the tax.  In its judgment, the court held that the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of the final judgment, which permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders them to pay disgorgement of $10 million, prejudgment interest of $1.2 million, and a civil penalty of $500,000.  On August 2, 2018, the U. S. District Judge for the Northern District of Georgia entered a judgment against the defendants in Bedingfield, which barred them from participating in any future federal court action.   The court's order, which is subject to court approval, reserves the issue of whether to proceed with a hearing or order a preliminary injunction.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of Pape in his defamation lawsuit against Time Inc. The Court held that the First Amendment protected Time's right to publish the article, even though it contained false statements about Pape. However, the Court also clarified that the First Amendment does not provide absolute immunity for false statements, and that a person can be held liable for defamation if they knowingly make false statements with "reckless disregard of the truth."

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Minnesota yesterday ruled that Minnesota's two-parent notification requirement is not a legitimate state interest.  The court's order, which is subject to court approval, permanently enjoins the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Western Districts of Minnesota today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Minnesota, the federal government has a legitimate interest in protecting the rights of pregnant minors, including the right to terminate their pregnancies.  For example, the complaint alleges that the Minnesota statute requires that both parents be notified of the pregnancy and abortion decision, and requires that the mother or father be present to make the decision.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of a final judgment permanently enjoining them from violations of the federal securities laws, ordering them to disgorge their ill-gotten gains, and ordering the destruction of any evidence that may have been obtained in the case.  On May 24, 2018, the Honorable Joseph G. Sansone of the U.N. Court of Appeals for the Southern District of New York granted the defendants' request for a temporary restraining order, ordered the destruction and destruction of evidence, and issued an order requiring the defendants return to the states to comply with the court's orders.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit recently ruled that the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) does not apply to corporations when they are subject to the law enforcement exemption that protects the personal privacy of individuals. The court held that the exemption does not extend to corporations, as the term "person" is defined by the federal government in the law. The Court's decision is the latest in a series of high-profile cases that have raised the issue of whether corporations have personal privacy rights under the FOIA exemption. The Supreme Court recently ruled in favor of AT&T Inc. in a FOIA appeal that the lower court had misapplied the law, and that the appeals court was wrong to conclude that the law applies only to corporations. The appeals court's ruling is a significant victory for the public's right to know what information the government releases to the public. The high court held, however, that the public does not have the right to determine whether a corporation has a "personal privacy" exemption. In a related case, the U.N. Court for the District of Columbia issued a similar ruling in which it held that a corporation's disclosure of personal information under the law does not violate the law's privacy protection provisions. The case is being reviewed by the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court case in question deals with the constitutional rights of pretrial detainees, who are individuals charged with a crime but not yet tried. The case arose from a class action lawsuit challenging conditions at the Metropolitan Correctional Center (MCC) in New York City, where pretrial detainees and some convicted inmates were held. The District Court had broadly intervened in the institution's operations, enjoining numerous practices on constitutional and statutory grounds. The Court of Appeals largely affirmed these rulings, applying a "compelling necessity" standard for the treatment of pretrial detainees under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to address the important constitutional questions and apparent conflicts among the Circuits. The Court reversed the decisions of the lower courts, rejecting the "compelling necessity" standard. Instead, the Court held that the proper inquiry is whether conditions of pretrial detention amount to punishment, which is prohibited prior to an adjudication of guilt. The Court emphasized that not every restriction during pretrial detention constitutes punishment and that the government is entitled to employ measures to ensure the detainee's presence at trial and maintain security and order.

The Court examined several specific practices at the MCC, including "double-bunking," restrictions on receiving books and packages, room searches, and body-cavity searches after contact visits. The Court found that these practices did not amount to unconstitutional punishment and were reasonably related to legitimate governmental objectives, such as security and order within the facility. The Court stressed that courts should defer to the judgment of prison administrators on matters of prison management unless there is substantial evidence of constitutional violations.

The Supreme Court's decision has implications for the management of detention facilities and the rights of pretrial detainees. It clarifies that while pretrial detainees retain certain constitutional protections, these rights are subject to reasonable limitations in light of institutional security needs. The ruling also underscores the principle that courts should not unduly interfere with the discretion of prison officials in the absence of clear constitutional or statutory violations.

The Supreme Court ruled in Hernandez v. Vidal (2010) that a "certificate of probable cause" (CPC) is not a jurisdictional requirement for an appeal to go forward. However, the Court did require that the issuer of the CPC provide written reasons for denying certification. Additionally, the Court found that the issuer's failure to comply with these requirements constituted a breach of due process.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a Chicago man charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Chicago on July 26, 1985, Edward Rodriguez was arrested in his mother's Chicago apartment by law enforcement officers and charged with possession of illegal drugs.  The complaint alleges that Rodriguez was then asleep in the apartment when the officers entered and arrested him.  As alleged in the complaint, Rodriguez's mother, Gail Fischer, was then at the apartment, and she consented to travel there with the officers in order to unlock the door with her key so that the officers could enter and search.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois today announced criminal charges against Rodriguez.   The SEC's Complaint alleges that, in holding Rodriguez in contempt of the federal securities laws, the Illinois Attorney General's Office and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) improperly entered the South California apartment of a woman who had been assaulted by Rodriguez earlier that day and arrested.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Complaint, Rodriguez consented and agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the charged provisions and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  Rodriguez also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years, and to a five-year officer-and-director bar.

Case Name: Moore v. Sims
Case Number: 89-1151
Decided Date: June 21, 1990
Issue: Whether the Missouri Constitution's mandatory retirement provision for judges violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
Holding: No, the Missouri Constitution's mandatory retirement provision for judges does not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Supreme Court reviewed the case of a petitioner convicted in Jefferson County, Alabama, for violating two city ordinances related to obstructing sidewalks and failing to comply with police orders. The petitioner argued that his Fourteenth Amendment rights were violated by the conviction.

The first ordinance made it illegal to obstruct sidewalks or to remain after being asked to move by a police officer. The second ordinance prohibited failing to comply with any lawful police order. The petitioner was observed by a police officer standing on a sidewalk with a group and was arrested after failing to move when instructed.

The Supreme Court noted that the first ordinance, as written, could be interpreted to give police officers excessive discretion to restrict individuals' movements, potentially infringing on First Amendment rights. However, the Alabama Court of Appeals had previously narrowed the interpretation of the ordinance, requiring evidence of actual obstruction of passage, not just failure to move when asked by an officer. Since the trial court did not specify which interpretation it used, and the narrowed interpretation was not established until after the petitioner's conviction, the Supreme Court could not affirm the conviction under the first ordinance.

Regarding the second ordinance, the Alabama Court of Appeals had limited its scope to the direction of vehicular traffic. Since the petitioner was a pedestrian and not involved in vehicular traffic when instructed to move, there was no evidence to support a conviction under this ordinance as interpreted by the state court.

The Supreme Court concluded that the petitioner's conviction was unconstitutional due to the lack of evidence supporting the charges as properly interpreted and the potential for the ordinances to be applied in a manner that violated due process. The judgment was reversed, and the case was remanded to the Alabama Court of Appeals for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The term "concerted action" encompasses unlawful conspiracies and constitutionally protected assemblies. In a landmark case, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a boycott of white merchants in Claiborne County, Mississippi, in 1966 was unlawful and that each of the 92 merchants was liable for all of its economic consequences. The court held that the defendants were liable for the tort of malicious interference with the merchants' businesses, which did not necessarily require the presence of a conspiracy. The high court also found that the boycott diverted black patronage from the white merchants to black merchants and to other merchants located out of Cla iborne County. The justices ruled that the court's ruling was consistent with the Supremacy of the Constitution of the United States and the Fourteenth Amendment. The Supreme Court's decision was a significant victory for civil rights and the right to a fair and just society. The case is being closely watched by civil rights groups and others who are concerned about the future of the civil rights movement.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the city's request for a temporary restraining order and an asset freeze.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that New York City's Department of Education violated the Establishment Clause of the federal education law by failing to adequately supervise parochial school teachers who teach in private schools.  According to the complaint, the federal government provided instructional services funded by the federal funds to parochials of public school students in 1981-1982. The complaint further alleges that the state provided teachers and other professionals with access to private school instructional materials, including remedial reading, reading skills, remedial mathematics, English as a second language, and guidance services.  In addition, the complaint alleges that private school teachers were not adequately trained to deal with the needs of students in the public schools, and that they were not performing important educational services in schools that had "pervasively sectarian" religious backgrounds.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, the Department of Justice has issued an order suspending the issuance of the order and ordering the Department to conduct an examination of the books and records of the public school districts that received the assistance. The investigation was conducted by Michael J. McCollum and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry of the New York Regional Office. The litigation will be led by David A. Kasper. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Education.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Appellate District reversed a lower court's conviction of Paul Robert Cohen for violating a California law that prohibits "maliciously and willfully disturb" the peace or quiet of any neighborhood or person. The court found that Cohen's jacket bearing the words "Fuck the Draft" was clearly visible and that he did not engage in any "behavior which has a tendency to provoke others to acts of violence or to in turn disturb the peace" as the lower court had found. The lower court also found that there was no evidence that Cohen made any "loud or unusual noise" prior to his arrest, nor did there be any evidence that he uttered any sound prior to the arrest. The Court of Appeal held that "offensive conduct" means "behavior that has a propensity to provoke other people to act of violence"

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Iowa today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was convicted of two counts of lascivious acts with a child after a jury trial in which a screen placed between him and the two complaining witnesses blocked him from their sight.  The court found that, contrary to popular belief, the defendant had a right to face-to-face confrontation with the witnesses.  According to the court's order, however, the right to confrontation is not absolute, and may give way to other important interests.  For example, the court previously ruled that a defendant's right to confront a witness was not absolute.  In fact, according to the order, the witness could not look at him at all, because the screen would make him appear guilty and thus erode the presumption of innocence.  On the other hand, the Court previously found that the right of confrontation was reasonable when confronted by a witness.  As a result of the Court's judgment, the defendants were not able to cross-examine the witnesses, but the witnesses to see him not at all.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's complaint, defendants agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $10,000.   The Court's order also prohibits the defendants from making any improper or misleading statements to the public in connection with the conduct of their criminal trials.

Title: Inverse Condemnation and the Right to a Jury Trial

Author: Judge Stephen Reinhardt

Source: 97 Cal. 4th 1161 (California Supreme Court, 2000)

Summary:

In this case, the California Supreme Court holds that a plaintiff in an inverse condemnation lawsuit has a right to a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment. The court rejects the argument that inverse condemnation is not a tort and therefore does not warrant a jury trial. Instead, the court finds that inverse condemnation shares several characteristics with a tort claim and that the right to a jury trial applies to it. The court also discusses the importance of maintaining the integrity of the Seventh Amendment and ensuring that individuals have access to a jury trial in cases where their property is taken by the government.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California ruled in 1970 that the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control's regulations regulating the type of entertainment that might be presented in bars and nightclubs conflicted with the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution. The regulations prohibited the performance of acts, or simulated acts, of 'sexual intercourse, masturbation, sodomy, bestiality, oral copulation, flagellation or any sexual acts which are prohibited by law'. The District Court majority held that the regulations also prohibited the actual or simulated 'touching, caressing or fondling on the breast, buttocks, anus or genitals' and the display of the public hair, or the genitals or anus. The Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit affirmed the District Court's decision, holding that the district court's ruling was not inconsistent with the Supreme Court decision in Roth v. Roth, and the regulations were not unconstitutional.

This Supreme Court opinion concerns a legal challenge to a decision by the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) regarding the distribution of joint railway rates among northern and southern lines. The ICC found that existing distributions of joint rates were unjust, reasonable, and inequitable because they failed to allocate sufficient revenue to the northern lines, which provided a disproportionate amount of the services used in the joint rates. To correct this, the ICC established new divisions of the joint rates based on the fully distributed costs of providing the joint service. However, the southern lines challenged the ICC's decision and sought to set it aside. The Supreme Court agreed with the lower court that the ICC's decision was not supported by substantial evidence and reasoned findings within the meaning of section 8(b) of the Administrative Procedure Act.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed a lower court's decision in favor of the University of Texas Board of Regents in a case involving a former college professor who was fired for publicly criticizing the college's policies. The court held that the Board of regents' decision not to renew the professor's contract violated his First and Fourteenth Amendment rights. The lower court had granted summary judgment to the Board, concluding that the decision was based on the teacher's public criticism of the policies of the college administration. The Court held that, despite Sindermann's lack of tenure, the nonrenewal of his contract would violate the 14th Amendment's guarantee of procedural due process if it was based in fact on his protected free speech. The appeals court held, however, that the board had no obligation to provide a hearing because Sindermann had not shown that he had an 'expectancy' of re-employment. Without a hearing, the appeals court said, the court could not conclude that Sindermann was entitled to a permanent injunction against the Board's actions. The case is now before the full appeals court.

Appellees operate a family-owned restaurant catering primarily to whites and employing mostly Negroes. Since 1964 it has been operated in violation of Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits racial discrimination in "any inn, hotel, motel, restaurant, cafeteria, lunchroom, lounge, soda fountain, or other place of public accommodation," unless the establishment meets certain requirements. Section 201 (b) (2) and (c) define a "place of public accommodation" as a restaurant "principally engaged in selling food for consumption on the premises" if it serves or offers to serve interstate travelers or a substantial portion of the food which it serves has moved in interstate commerce. The Government contended that Congress had ample basis upon which to find that racial discrimination at restaurants which received from out of state a substantial portion of the food served imposes commercial burdens of national magnitude upon interstate commerce. Appellees urged that no such basis existed. The District Court denied injunctive relief sought by the Government, ruling that there was no demonstrable connection between food purchased in interstate commerce and offered for sale in a restaurant and the conclusion of Congress that discrimination in the restaurant would affect that commerce. Held: 1. Denial of injunctive relief is vacated and the cause is remanded to the District Court for entry of an order requiring appellees to comply with Title II. Pp. 70-75. 2. The Civil Rights Act of 1964, as here applied, is valid. Pp. 75-81. 233 F. Supp. 100, reversed.

The Supreme Court was tasked with determining whether class arbitration can be imposed on parties whose arbitration clauses do not explicitly address the issue, in accordance with the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA). The case involved shipping companies (petitioners) and AnimalFeeds International Corp., which had entered into a standard maritime contract that included an arbitration clause silent on class arbitration. After a price-fixing conspiracy was revealed, AnimalFeeds sought class arbitration, which the arbitrators allowed, despite the contract's silence on the matter.

The District Court vacated the arbitration award, but the Court of Appeals reversed this decision. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the issue. The Court emphasized that arbitration is a matter of consent and that parties cannot be compelled to class arbitration without an agreement. The Court found that the arbitration panel exceeded its powers by imposing class arbitration based on policy preferences rather than the parties' agreement.

The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision and remanded the case, holding that the arbitration panel had overstepped by inferring consent to class arbitration from the contract's silence. The Court underscored that class arbitration significantly alters the nature of arbitration and cannot be assumed without explicit agreement. The decision reinforces the principle that arbitration agreements must be enforced as written, and class arbitration requires a contractual basis for consent.

Implications of the Decision:
1. Class arbitration requires explicit consent from all parties involved, and silence in an arbitration clause does not imply consent to class arbitration.
2. Arbitration panels must adhere strictly to the terms of the contract and cannot infer agreements beyond what is explicitly stated.
3. The decision upholds the FAA's principle that arbitration is based on mutual consent and contractual agreement, not on policy preferences or assumptions.
4. The ruling may impact how future arbitration clauses are drafted, with parties likely to specify their stance on class arbitration to avoid ambiguity.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia yesterday issued a final judgment in favor of the settlement of a civil rights case brought by 3,000 children in the foster-care system.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Atlanta, Georgia, alleges that, under the federal fee-shifting statutes, attorneys are entitled to be compensated at a rate that is consistent with the prevailing market rates for legal services in the relevant market.  In its judgment, the court found that the average hourly rate for each of the attorneys was reasonable and reasonable, but that the lodestar calculation did not adequately account for the fact that the attorneys were not paid on an ongoing basis as the litigation was being performed.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the judge agreed to the settlement and agreed to pay an additional $10.5 million in attorney’s fees and expenses. The settlement is subject to court approval, and the amount of the additional attorney fees will be determined by the court at a later date.  According to the SEC, the settlement is contingent on the outcome of the litigation.  For example, the SEC previously ruled that the settlement should be based on a reasonable fee that the court deemed reasonable based on the quality of the attorney performing the work. The SEC also ruled that, in a parallel action, the District Court had violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 13(b)(5) of Exchange Act Rules 12b-20, 13b2-1, and 13a-13 thereunder. The court also found that, by basing an enhancement in large part on a comparison of the performance of respondents’ attorneys with all of the unnamed attorneys whose work he had observed during his professional career, the defendant had improperly rendered a decision that was effectively unreviewable on appeal and had essentially served as a witness in support of the enhancement. The Court also agreed to a judgment that permanently enjoins the defendant from future violations of the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10 million, which includes disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest of $1.7 million, and to pay civil penalties of $100,000 and $50,000, respectively. The judgment also orders the relief sought by the SEC to be contingent on a determination of a reasonable attorney's fee that is reasonable and fair and reasonable.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Nevada today entered a final judgment in favor of Nevada's motion to extend full faith and credit to California's statute immunizing its tax collection agency from suit.  The SEC's complaint, filed on January 6, 1998, in Clark County District Court in Las Vegas, Nevada, alleges that California Franchise Tax Board (CFTB) directed numerous and continuous contacts at Nevada and committed several torts during the course of the audit to determine whether respondent had underpaid state income taxes.  According to the complaint, the complaint alleges that CFTB directed "numerous and continuous contact" at Nevada to determine that respondent had ceased to be a California resident and had become a resident of Nevada, and accordingly issued notices of proposed assessments for income taxes for 1991 and 1992 and imposed substantial civil fraud penalties.  In a parallel action, the Nevada Attorney General's Office today announced criminal charges against a California-based company accused of defrauding Nevada workers in connection with an income tax audit conducted by the agency's predecessor, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the California attorney general's office and the Nevada Secretary of State's Office have agreed to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering the SEC to pay civil penalties in the amount of $1.5 million.
