Barry.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Nevada Office of Inspector General, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the California Department of Insurance.

After a Marine Lance Corporal was killed in Iraq in the line of duty, the Westboro Baptist Church (collectively Westboro or the church) pickedeted on public land adjacent to public streets near the Maryland State House, the United States Naval Academy, and Matthew Snyder’s funeral. The picketers carried signs that were largely the same at all three locations. They stated, inter alia, that God hates and punishes America for its tolerance of homosexuality, particularly in the military. Snyder testified that he could see the tops of the picket signs as he drove to the funeral, but did not see what was written on the signs until later that night, while watching a news broadcast covering the event. The District Court remitted the punitive damages award to $2.1 million, but left the jury verdict otherwise intact. The Court of Appeals agreed. Held: The First Amendment shields the church members from tort liability for their speech in this case. Pp. 5–7. (a) To succeed on a claim for intentional infliction of emotional distress in Maryland, a plaintiff must demonstrate that the defendant intentionally or recklessly engaged in extreme and outrageous conduct that caused the plaintiff to suffer severe emotional distress. Such speech cannot be restricted simply because it is upsetting or arouses contempt. The fact that Westboro conducted its picketing adjacent to a public street does not insulate the speech from liability, but instead heightens concerns that what is at issue is an effort to communicate to the public the church‘s views on matters of public concern. That is why our precedents so clearly recognize the special significance of this traditional public forum. P. 5. (b) Whether the First Amendment prohibits holding Westboro liable for its speech here turns largely on whether that speech is of public or private concern, as determined by all the circumstances of the case. “ ‘[S]peech on ‘matters of public interest’ … is ‘at the heart of [the First Amendment’’ ’ ” Dun & Bradstreet, Inc. v. Greenmoss Builders, Inc., 472 U. S. 749, 758–759. The Free Speech Clause of the Constitution reflects “a profound national commitment to the principle that debate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open.” New York Times Co., v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254, 270. That principle requires that we shield Westboro from tort liabilities for its picketing in a case like this one. The “content” of the signs plainly relates to broad issues of interest to society at large, rather than matters of “purely private concern” and the “threat of liability” does not pose the risk of liability. The signs certainly convey Westboro's position on those issues, in a manner designed, unlike the private speech in the past. The speech is entitled to “special protection” under First Amendment protection, and where matters of purely private significance are at issue, First Amendment protections are often less rigorous. Hustler v. Bank of Boston v. Bellotti, 435U. S . 765, 776. On the facts before this Court, a jury is “unlikely to be neutral with respect to the content of the speech,” posing a real danger of becoming an instrument for the suppression of … “vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasan[t] ” expression. Bose Corp., 466 U. . S. 474, 480. Such a risk is unacceptable; “in public debate [we] must tolerate insulting, and even outrageous, speech in order to provide adequate ‘breathing space’ to the freedoms protected by the First.’ .” Connick v. Myers, 461 U.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a California police officer's seizure of a parole violator's vehicle during a traffic stop violated his Fourth Amendment rights. The court held that the officer had probable cause to believe that Bruce Brendlin was in possession of methamphetamine. The Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit agreed with the lower court's finding that the traffic stop was lawful. The Supreme Court's opinion, written by Justices Samuel Alito and Neil A. Cann, held that a warrantless search of the vehicle and its passenger's home was not a reasonable search under the Fourth Amendment. The justices ruled that the warrantless searches of the car and the passenger were not reasonable because the officers had no reasonable basis to suspect that the passenger was a drug dealer or a drug user. The high court ruled that, in this case, the search of a car and a passenger is not a legitimate law enforcement investigation. In a separate opinion, Justice Alito held that there was no probable cause that the search was unlawful. The opinion concluded that the officers' search was reasonable and that they did not search the car or the passenger because they had no reason to suspect they were being searched for drugs. Justices Alito, Cann ruled that this was not an issue of whether a passenger was seized, but whether the search violated his rights. In dissent, Justice Corrigan wrote that a passenger should not be seized even when the driver is the sole target of an investigation.

The US Supreme Court ruled in favor of AcroMed and its consultant, Petitioner, stating that the plaintiff's state-law fraud-on-the-FDA claims are implicitly preempted by federal law. The ruling came down in a 5-4 decision, with Justice Thomas writing for the majority. The case involved a dispute over the accuracy of information provided by AcroMed to the FDA regarding the use of its bone screw device in spinal surgery.

The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled that the Federal Aviation Administration is not liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act for the negligence of the FAA in issuing a type certificate to an aircraft that did not comply with fire protection standards. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that the FAA's failure to exercise its discretion in issuing the type certificate was not a violation of the Act's discretionary function exception, which exempts the United States from liability for any claim arising out of the agency's negligence. The Supreme Court held that, even if a private person inspecting and certificating aircraft for airworthiness would be liable for negligent inspection under the Good Samaritan rule, the U. S.C. should be judged by the same rule. In a separate case, the Supreme Court ruled that a federal court should not have granted the government's motion to dismiss a suit brought by the family of a passenger who died in an air taxi crash. The court ruled that, under the circumstances, the case should be dismissed and that the trial court should have granted summary judgment in favor of the government. The high court also ruled that it was not necessary for the court to determine whether there was a cause of action under the Act.

On February 18, 1975, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas entered a final judgment ordering the removal of five Texas justices of the peace and constables from office in Harris County, Tex.  The court's order, which was entered on March 18, 1974, permanently enjoins the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  In a parallel action, the Texas Attorney General's Office today announced that it had issued a temporary restraining order halting the implementation of the Texas redistricting plan.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Houston, Texas, the defendants sought to have the court order them to be removed from office before the expiration of their terms.  As alleged in the complaint, the court found that the Texas statute providing for the officers' removal from office at the time of the redistricting violated the federal securities laws and ordered them to resort to state court for relief.  Without admitting or denying the defendants' allegations, the Court also issued an order temporarily restraining the Defendants from further violations of the securities laws, ordering them to pay a civil penalty of $1,000, and ordering the officers to disgorge their ill-gotten gains with interest, pay civil penalties of $100,000 each, and pay a $50,000 civil penalty in the amount of $2,500.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by John R. Birkenheier and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter. The litigation will be led by Richard E. Moore. Â The SEC appreciates the assistance of the United States Attorney's Office for Texas and the Texas Secretary of State's Office.

Under the Mobile-Sierra doctrine, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) must presume that the rate set out in a freely negotiated wholesale-energy contract meets the “just and reasonable” requirement imposed by law. The presumption may be overcome only if FERC concludes that the contract seriously harms the public interest. See, e.g., Verizon Communications Inc. v. FCC, 535 U. S. 467, 479. In exercising its broad discretion, the Commission traditionally reviewed and set tariff rates under the "cost-of-service” method, which ensures that a regulated utility’s rates are just and reasonable. In enacting the Interstate Commerce Act (Act), the FPA requires regulated utilities to file compilations of their rate schedules, or “tariffs,” with the Commission, and to provide service to electricity purchasers on the terms and prices there set forth. Utilities wishing to change their tariffs must notify the Commission 60 days before the change is to go into effect. Under the Act, however, utilities must set rates with individual consumers through bilateral contracts. If FERC finds that a seller has reattained market power, it may revoke the authority prospectively. If the Commission finds that the seller has violated its Regional Transmission Organization (RTC) market rules, its tariff, or Commission orders, then the Commission may take appropriate remedial action, such as ordering refunds, requiring disgorgement of profits, and imposing civil penalties. The Ninth Circuit affirmed. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that rates set by contract (whether pursuant to a market-based tariff or not) are presumptively reasonable only where FERC has had an initial opportunity to review the contracts without applying the MobileSierra presumption. Held: 1. A “zone of reasonableness” test should be used to evaluate a contract rate solely for whether it violates a public interest or also for whether the contract results in an unfair rate of return. Pp. 5–11. (a) The Mobile-sierra presumption does not apply only to contracts that are “reasonable” when filed with FERC, but also applies where a purchaser, rather than a seller, asks FERC to modify a contract. P. 5. (b) The Commission has retained broad authority to specify whether FERC can review a contract solely for that question, but that standard remains the default rule. See United Gas Pipe Line Co.v. Memphis Light, Gas and Water Div., 358 U.S. 103, 110–113. But FERC must choose a method that entails an appropriate “balancing of the investor and the consumer interests.” FPC v. Sierra Pacific Power Co., 320 U. . S. 591, 603. The Commission traditionally reviews and set tariffs for the high-rate challenge of a purchaser (where, for example, the relevant question is not whether “other customers” [of the utility] would be excessively burdened, but whether any customers of the purchaser would be); and those three factors are in any event not the exclusive components of the Public Interest. In its decision below, the Ninth Circuit concluded that the contracts at issue did not contain “Memphis clause[s],” 471 F. 3d 1053, 1079–1090. The court also held that the Commission must promptly review the terms of contracts after their formation and must modify those that do not appear to be just-and-reasonable when evaluated without the Mobile Sierra presumption, but maintained that the authorization for market based rate authority qualified as that initial review. The judgment of the Court is affirmed, and the cases are remanded for proceedings consistent with this opinion. The Chief Justice and Justice Breyer took no part in the consideration or decision of these cases.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the issue revolved around the discharge of student loan debt in a Chapter 13 bankruptcy proceeding. The debtor, Francisco Espinosa, proposed a plan to repay only the principal of his student loan debt and discharge the accrued interest without initiating an adversary proceeding or demonstrating undue hardship, as required by the Bankruptcy Code and Rules. The creditor, United Student Aid Funds, Inc. (United), received notice of the plan but did not object or appeal the Bankruptcy Court's confirmation of the plan. Years later, United sought to have the confirmation order declared void, arguing that it was issued in violation of the Code and Rules and that its due process rights were violated due to the lack of a summons and complaint.

The Supreme Court held that the Bankruptcy Court's confirmation order was not void under Rule 60(b)(4) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. The Court reasoned that while the Bankruptcy Court made a legal error by not finding undue hardship before confirming the plan, the error did not amount to a jurisdictional defect or a due process violation. United had received actual notice of the plan and failed to object or appeal in a timely manner, thus forfeiting its right to challenge the confirmation order.

The Court also clarified that bankruptcy courts have the authority and obligation to ensure that a debtor's plan complies with the Code, including the requirement to determine undue hardship before discharging student loan debt. However, the Court of Appeals had erred in ruling that bankruptcy courts must confirm such plans unless the creditor objects. The Supreme Court emphasized that bankruptcy courts must make an independent determination of undue hardship before confirming a plan, regardless of whether the creditor objects.

The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit but clarified the proper procedure for discharging student loan debt in bankruptcy. The decision underscores the importance of procedural compliance in bankruptcy proceedings and the finality of judgments when parties fail to exercise their rights in a timely manner.

Petitioner Bond, a Pennsylvania resident, was indicted for violating a federal statute that prohibits knowing possession or use of any chemical that “can cause death, temporary incapacitation or permanent harm to humans or animals” where not intended for a “peaceful purpose.” §§229(a); 229F(1); (7); (8). The statute was en-acted as part of the Chemical Weapons Convention Implementation Act of 1998, which implements provisions of the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on their Destruction. Bond moved to dismiss the §229 charges, contending the statute was beyond Congress’ constitutional authority to enact. The District Court denied the motion, and Bond entered a conditional plea of guilty, reserving the right to appeal the ruling on the validity of the statute. In the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, Bond renewed her challenge to the statute, citing, among other authorities, the Tenth Amendment to the Constitution. The court of Appeals agreed, holding that because a State was not a party to the federal criminal proceeding, petitioner had no standing to challenge the statute as an infringement upon the powers reserved to the States. Held: The judgment of the Court is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. Pp. 5–7. (a) The Tenth Amendment does not bar a litigant from challenging a federal law in the absence of a State’s participation in the proceedings. The principle of separation of powers is not inconsistent with that of the Constitution, but rather with the principle of checks-and-balances. P. 6–8. (b) The question whether a plaintiff states a claim for relief “goes to the merits” in the typical case, not the justiciability of a dispute, id., at 92, and conflation of the two concepts can cause confusion. If the constitutional structure of our Government that protects individual liberty is compromised, individuals who suffer otherwise justiciable injury may object. Just as it is appropriate for an individual, in a proper case, to invoke separation-of-powers or checks andbalances constraints, so too may litigants challenge a law as enacted in contravention of constitutional principles of federalism. That claim need not depend on the vicarious assertion of a States’ and constitutional interests, even if a State's constitutional interests are also implicated. See New York v. United States, 505 U. S. 144, 181, or whether it has independent force of its own, the result here is the same. Here, Bond seeks to vindicate her own constitutional interests by asserting injury from governmental action taken in excess of the authority that federalism defines. Her rights in this regard do not belong to a State. The federal structure serves to grant and delimit the prerogatives and responsibilities of the States and the National Government vis-À-vis one another. The allocation of powers in our federal system preserves the integrity, dignity, and residual sovereignty of States. The Federal balance is, in part, an end in itself, to ensure that States function as political entities in their own right. But that is not its exclusive sphere of operation. Federalism has more than one dynamic. It is more than an exercise in setting the boundary between different institutions of government for their own integrity, and it is also a exercise in “state sovereignty,” New York, supra, at 156, and “State sovereignty is not just an end” (quoting United States v. Darby, 312 U.S. 100, 124). Federalism secures the freedom of the individual. It allows States to respond, through the enactment of positive law, to the initiative of those who seek a voice in shaping the destiny of their own times without having to rely solely upon the political processes that control a remote central power. Separation of-powers principles are intended to protect each branch of government from incursion by the others. By denying any one government complete jurisdiction over all the concerns of public life, federalism protects the individual from arbitrary power. When government acts in excess thereof, that liberty is at stake. States are not the sole intended beneficiaries. See, e.g., Spencer v. Kemna, 523 U.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Montana today entered a final judgment against Montana Fish and Game Commission v. Montana Outfitters Action Group, a Montana-based organization that seeks to preserve the elk and other game in Montana.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Montana, alleges that, in 1975, Montana passed a law requiring nonresidents of the State of Montana to purchase and maintain licenses to hunt elk.  According to the complaint, this law violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17(b) thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Montana consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins Montana from violating these provisions and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $150,000, a $25,000 civil penalty, and a $50,000 penalty.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Montana's three state residents.    The court's order, which is subject to court approval, reserves the issue of whether to impose civil penalties against Montana residents and prohibits the issuance of any such order. Â The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by John R. Rymas and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Montana Department of Natural Resources, and the Montana Office of the Secretary of State.

After the University of California, Hastings College of the Law (Hastings) denied petitioner Christian Legal Society of California (CLS) recognition as a student organization because it refused to comply with Hastings’ all-comers policy, which requires all student organizations to accept all students as members and leaders regardless of their viewpoint, CLS sued in Federal District Court, claiming that the policy violated its free speech and expressive-association rights. The District Court entered judgment for Hastings, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed. Held: 1. Because Hastings’ all-comers policy is viewpoint neutral, it survives intermediate scrutiny. Pp. 10–20. (a) Hastings’ policy falls within the broad category of viewpoint-neutral restrictions on speech that are acceptable under the First Amendment. See, e.g., Rosenberger v. Rector and Visitors of Univ. of Va., 515 U. S. 819, 829. Pp. 10–12. (b) Hastings’ policy is not rendered void by the fact that it applies to all student organizations, not just those espousing controversial views. While the policy might discourage some organizations from participating, it does not discriminate against them on the basis of their viewpoint. See, e.g., id., at 829. Moreover, the policy furthers Hastings’ goal of fostering the expression of diverse viewpoints. See, e. g., id., at 830. Pp. 12–15. (c) Hastings’ policy is not precluded by the Establishment Clause. The policy does not endorse religion, but instead promotes inclusiveness. See, e. g., Locke v. Davey, 526 U. S. 333, 341. Pp. 15–16. (d) Hastings’ policy does not violate the Free Speech Clause. See, e. g., Smith v. Hawaii, 468 U. S. 443, 450. Pp. 16–17. 2. Hastings’ all-comers policy is not selectively enforced. Pp. 17–20. (a) The policy is not selectively enforced because Hastings does not exempt religious groups from the policy. Rather, the policy applies to all student organizations. Pp. 17–18. (b) Nor is the policy selectively enforced because Hastings does not pick and choose which organizations must comply with the policy on the basis of viewpoint. Pp. 18–20. 561 F. 3d 1039, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Thomas, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Roberts, C. J., and Alito, J., joined.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against a New York City man accused of orchestrating a series of high-profile insider trading schemes.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that, from at least 1977 through the late 1990s, the New York State Attorney General's Office ("Securities and Exchange Commission") filed a civil injunctive action against convicted criminal David Berkowitz, who was later convicted of insider trading.  According to the complaint, Berkowitz agreed to settle the SEC's charges without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint and agreed to pay $27,958 in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  In a parallel action, the U.N. Office of Financial Regulation (OFI) today announced that it has issued an order suspending all payments to Berkowitz in the name of "public safety."  The OFI's complaint charges Berkowitz with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks permanent injunctions against future violations of the federal securities laws, disgorgements of ill-gotten gains, and civil money penalties.  Without admitting to any of these violations, the OFI has agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the above-mentioned provisions, and orders Berkowitz to disgorge his profits with interest, with the amount of any civil monetary penalty to be determined by the court at a later date.   The settlement is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Pyszka and supervised by Scott A. Kasper of the Boston Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the FBI.

In the case of Leon Chambers, the Supreme Court found that his trial for the murder of a police officer did not adhere to due process under the Fourteenth Amendment. Chambers was convicted by a Mississippi trial court and sentenced to life imprisonment, a decision upheld by the Mississippi Supreme Court.

The incident leading to the trial occurred when two officers attempted to arrest a youth, resulting in a confrontation with a crowd and the fatal shooting of Officer Liberty. Chambers was accused of the murder, but he maintained his innocence and claimed that another man, Gable McDonald, had confessed to the crime.

During the trial, Chambers faced significant obstacles in presenting his defense. The trial court applied Mississippi's rules of evidence strictly, preventing Chambers from fully cross-examining McDonald and from presenting testimony from witnesses who would support his defense by recounting McDonald's confessions to the crime. The Supreme Court held that these restrictions denied Chambers the right to a fair trial.

The Court emphasized the importance of the rights to confront and cross-examine witnesses and to call witnesses in one's own defense as essential to due process. The Court found that the Mississippi rules, as applied in this case, interfered with Chambers' ability to defend himself and that the exclusion of testimony that bore "persuasive assurances of trustworthiness" was contrary to the ends of justice.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Mississippi Supreme Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, underscoring that the decision did not establish new constitutional principles but rather applied established standards of due process to ensure a fair trial.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a Massachusetts bank's policy of paying its discharged employees for their unused vacation time was pre-empted by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 ("ERISA" or Act"). The high court held that the Act does not apply to the Massachusetts payment of wages statute, which requires an employer to pay a discharged employee his full wages, including holiday or vacation payments, on the date of discharge. The court found that under the plain language of the Act and its earlier decision in Nachman Guaranty Corp. v. Fort Halifax Packing Co., the Bank's vacation policy constituted an "employee welfare benefit plan" under the Act. The Court also held that, because the Bank did not maintain records relating to its employees' unused vacation, it was appropriate to treat the employer's promise to them as a "plan" and that the prosecution of the former bank president for failing to comply with the policy ran afoul of  514(a), which preempts "any and all State laws insofar as they relate to any employee benefit plan." The Court concluded that the Massachusetts statute related to the plan within the meaning of s. 149  148.1 and was not excluded from its coverage by the provision saving from preemption a "generally applicable criminal law"

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina today entered a final judgment in a civil injunctive action brought by Dethorne Graham, a diabetic, alleging that Charlotte, North Carolina, officers used excessive force in making an arrest, investigatory stop, or other "seizure" of a free person.  The court's order, which entered final judgment on the matter on May 9, 2018, requires that defendants prove that the force used against them is reasonable and reasonable.  For example, the court previously ruled that excessive force is permissible under the Fourth Amendment.  In a parallel action, on May 10, 2016, the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit entered final judgments in this matter that permanently enjoin the officers from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the officers to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $250,000.  On May 11, 2017, the Honorable Paul J. McCole granted the court's motion for a temporary restraining order against Graham and ordered him to return to his home to rest and recover from his injuries.  McCole also agreed to be enjoined from future securities law violations.

Title: United States v. Dennis et al.
Year: 1964
Decision Date: March 29, 1964
Case Number: 85 S.Ct. 1707
Judge: Warren E. Burger
Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court holds that the phrase "for the purpose of defrauding" in section 371 of the general conspiracy statute includes defrauding the government. The Court also rules that the trial court did not err in denying petitions for rehearing and clarifying its previous opinions regarding the scope of section 371.

A collective-bargaining agreement with the Indiana Education Employment Relations Board (EERB) provides that a school district, but no other union, would have access to the interschool mail system and teacher mailboxes in the Metropolitan School District of Perry Township, Ind. The school district's exclusive bargaining representative, Perry Education Association (PEA), was certified as the exclusive representative, as provided by Indiana law. PEA filed an election petition with the EERB, which was approved by the Board. The labor agreement noted that access rights were being accorded to PEA "acting as the representative of the teachers" and stipulated that these access rights shall not be granted to any other "school employee organization"-a term defined by state law to mean "any organization which has school employees as members and one of whose primary purposes is representing school employees in dealing with their employer." PEA and two of its members filed this action under 42 U. S. C. § 1983 (1976) against the school district and individual members of the Perry Township School Board. They sought injunctive and declaratory relief and damages. The district court entered judgment for the defendants. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that certain sections of the collective bargaining agreement entered into by the School District and PEA are constitutionally invalid; the Indiana statute authorizing such agreements is left untouched. Held: 1. The First Amendment, applicable to the states by virtue of the Fourteenth Amendment, is violated when a union that has been elected by public school teachers as their exclusive bargaining representatives is granted access to certain means of communication, while such access is denied to a rival union. Pp. 6-11. (a) The First and Fourteenth Amendments do not require a state statute to be held repugnant to the Constitution, treaties, or laws of the United States. P. 6. (b) In places which by long tradition or by government fiat have been devoted to assembly and debate, the rights of the state to limit expressive activity are sharply circumscribed. The right to make distinctions in access on the basis of subject matter and speaker identity is clearly found in the special responsibilities of a bargaining representative. The fact that other civilian speaker and entertainers had sometimes been invited to appear at Fort Dix did not convert the military base into a public forum, and Lehman v. Shaker Heights, 418 U.S. 298, a plurality of the Court concluded that a city transit system's rental of space in its vehicles for commercial advertising did not require it to accept partisan political advertising, and that a private non-school connected group may reasonably be considered a means of insuring labor-peace within the schools. Although a state is not required to indefinitely retain the open character of the facility, as long as it does so it is bound by the same standards as apply in a traditional public forum. Reasonable time, place, and manner regulations are permissible, and a content-based prohibition must be narrowly drawn to effectuate a compelling state interest. See, e. g., Lockwood v. Jefferson Area Teachers Ass'n v. Hohlt, IP 79-189-C, (appeal dismissed for want of jurisdiction and certiorari denied). P. 7. (c) The limited privileges PEA negotiated as the bargaining voice of the school teachers by misapplying the cases that have dealt with the right of free expression on streets, parks and other fora generally open for assembly and discussion. Virtually every other court to consider this type of exclusive access policy has upheld it as constitutional, see n. 6, supra, and today, so do we. The court's judgment is reversed.

The Supreme Court was tasked with determining whether the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) preempts a Pennsylvania state law that prohibits employee welfare benefit plans from seeking reimbursement from a claimant's tort recovery through subrogation rights. The case involved FMC Corporation's self-funded health care plan, which sought reimbursement for medical expenses from an employee's daughter who had settled a negligence claim related to an automobile accident.

The Court's analysis focused on the intent of Congress regarding preemption, examining the language and structure of ERISA. The Court identified three relevant provisions: the preemption clause, the saving clause, and the deemer clause. The preemption clause broadly supersedes state laws related to employee benefit plans, while the saving clause allows state laws that regulate insurance to remain in effect, except as limited by the deemer clause. The deemer clause ensures that self-funded ERISA plans are not considered insurance companies for the purposes of state insurance regulations.

The Court concluded that Pennsylvania's antisubrogation law "relates to" an employee benefit plan and is therefore preempted by ERISA. The law has both a "reference" to and a "connection" with ERISA benefit plans, and applying different state subrogation laws to plans would create inefficiencies and complicate the administration of nationwide plans.

The Court also determined that the deemer clause exempts self-funded ERISA plans from state laws that regulate insurance. This means that while insured plans may be subject to indirect state insurance regulation through their insurers, self-funded plans are not subject to direct state insurance regulation. The Court's interpretation respects the distinction Congress made between insured and uninsured plans and aligns with the intent to make pension plan regulation a federal concern.

The Court rejected narrower interpretations of the deemer clause that would limit its application to state insurance regulations that are pretexts for affecting core ERISA concerns or that apply only to the business of insurance. Such interpretations would lead to administrative difficulties and undermine Congress's desire to provide a uniform regulatory framework for employee benefit plans.

In summary, the Supreme Court held that ERISA preempts the application of Pennsylvania's antisubrogation law to FMC Corporation's self-funded health care plan, reversing the judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit and remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. Justice SOUTER did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

In this case, the defendant was convicted of possessing narcotics and challenged the constitutionality of the search and seizure of the evidence used against him. The court determined that the search and seizure were conducted in accordance with the Fourth Amendment and that there was probable cause for the arrest. As a result, the evidence was deemed admissible in court and the conviction was upheld.

Respondent, who had been arrested for first-degree murder, brought an affidavit to a neutral judge. The judge concluded that the affidavit established probable cause for an arrest warrant and a search warrant authorizing a search of her residence. The affidavit stated that the police wished to search for "a fifth bottle of amaretto liquor, 2 nickel bags of marijuana, a woman's jacket that has been described as black-grey (charcoal), possessions of Sandra D. Boulware, similar type wire and rope that match those on the body of Sandra, or in the above [T]hunderbird]. Blunt instrument that might have been used on the victim. Items that may have fingerprints of the victim." The judge then signed the affidavit, and the officer took the two documents and, accompanied by other officers, proceeded to Sheppard's residence, where the search was limited to the items listed in the affidavit and several incriminating pieces of evidence were discovered. Sheppard was then charged with murder. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court agreed, holding that the evidence obtained pursuant to the defective warrant should have been suppressed because this Court had not recognized a good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule. The Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that although the police conducted the search in a good faith belief, reasonably held, that the search they conducted was lawful and authorized by the warrant issued by the judge, the evidence had to be excluded. Held: The evidence in this case should be admitted. Pp. 524-525. 387 Mass. 488, 441 N. E. 2d 725, reversed and remanded.

Petitioner was convicted of capital murder in a Virginia state court of violating the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by failing to give adequate notice of the evidence the Commonwealth intended to use against him at the penalty phase of his trial. Petitioner then sought a writ of habeas corpus from the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. Having evidence that petitioner had announced before the killing that "he was going to get" McClelland for having fired his wife from her job as a saleswoman at the Murphy's Mart, and that he had told other witnesses after the killing, the prosecutor entered into a plea bargain with Tucker, who would testify at petitioner's trial about events leading up to the killing and would identify petitioner as the actual "trigger man." Petitioner's counsel moved that the trial court order the prosecution to disclose the evidence it planned to introduce, and the court dismissed the claim on the ground that it was procedurally barred. The Virginia Supreme Court affirmed and denied certiorari. The Court of Appeals dismissed petitioner's state petition for a writ, concluding that petitioner's notice-of-evidence claim was not compelled by existing precedent at the time his conviction became final, and thus could not be considered in federal habas corpus proceedings under Teague v. Lane, 489 U. S. 288. Held: The claim is procedurally defaulted and that it seeks retroactive application of a new rule of federal constitutional law. Pp. 6-8. (a) Petitioner is not entitled to relief on the basis of a claim, which was not raised in the state courts or in his federal habea petition, that the indictment procedure by which he was brought to trial violated equal protection. P. 6. (b) The fact that petitioner knew of the grounds of his Brady claim when he filed his first petition does not preclude review of his claim in any future state habbeas proceeding. The same principle applies to the claim of a defendant who was convicted with the aid of surprise testimony of an accomplice who was an undercover agent, and it is not enough to make a general appeal to a constitutional guarantee as broad as due process to present the "substance" of such a claim to a state court. In Anderson v. Harless, 459 U.S. 4, petitioner was granted relief for a jury instruction to obviate the requirement that the prosecutor prove all the elements of the crime beyond a reasonable doubt. The only manner in which petitioner had cited federal authority was by referring to a State-court decision in which "the defendant . . . asserted a broad federal due process right to jury instructions that properly explain state law," and that Tucker "sold" his testimony to the Commonwealth for less than a life sentence. The court thus concluded that the Sandstrom claim was never presented to, or considered by, the [state] courts, and dismissed the Claim on this basis. The rule in Teague therefore applies, and petitioner may not obtain habeAS relief on his notice-to-evidence claims. P p. 6-'8. Relying on cases like Gardner v. Florida, 430 U. s. 349 (1977), and Skipper v. South Carolina, 476 US. 1 (1986), petitioner argues that he should have been given "such notice" of the issues involved in the trial, but that the Commonwealth violated his due process rights under Brady by withholding evidence exculpating him from responsibility for the Sorrell murders. The District Court rejected petitioner's contention that the misrepresentation claim "was never argued before in any court," and the State Supreme Court concluded that petitioner, unlike Gardner, had no opportunity to even see the confidential information, let alone contest it. The State Court also dismissed the complaint on its basis, and this Court granted petitioner a stay of execution and denied his motion to dismiss the claim. The Fourth Circuit reversed the judgment of the Court, and remand the case for consideration of petitioner's claim in proceedings consistent with this opinion. The case is remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota today entered a final judgment in favor of the Minnesota State Fair, ordering the Minnesota Agricultural Society (MSFA) and its affiliated organizations to conduct sales, distribution, and fund solicitation activities at the fairgrounds.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Minnesota, alleges that the Minnesota Fair Rule 6.05, which was promulgated in 1977, violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and that the Rule was not sufficient to protect the interests of ISKCON and its members.  According to the complaint, the Rule is not necessary to the furtherance of the State's interest in crowd control, which could adequately be served by less intrusive means.

Respondent Manufacturing Distribuiors, Inc. (MDI), holds several utility patents covering temporary roadside warning signs featuring a dual-spring design. Its Windmaster line of sign stands includes a model whose frame contains two springs spaced apart vertically, each connected to opposite ends of the frame. Another firm, petitioner Trafix, produces a competing sign stand with two springs close together. After MDI sued Trafix for trademark infringement, the Federal District Court dismissed MDI's trade dress claim, concluding that the dual-spring design was functional and thus not entitled to trade dress protection. The Sixth Circuit reversed, noting that the lower court had taken too narrow a view of what constituted a functional design. Relying on Qualitex Co.v . Jacobsond Product Co., 514 U. S. 159, 165, the court interpreted the Lanham Act's requirement that a party asserting trade dress protection bear the burden of proving that the matter sought to be protected is not functional to mean that a necessary test for functionality is whether the particular product configuration is a competitive necessity. Because the dual-spring design provided a unique and useful mechanism to resist the force of the wind, the court concluded that MDI had not carried its burden of demonstrating that the design was functional. Held: The expiration of MDI's utility patents significantly weakened its ability to establish trade dress protection for the dual-spring design. Under the rule announced in Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. SamaraBrothers, Inc., 529 U. S. 205, 213, trade dress protection may not be claimed for product features that are functional. Since the dual-spring design is functional, it is unnecessary for competitors to explore alternative designs to hide the springs. Moreover, the dual-spring design is not an arbitrary flourish in MDI's product configuration; it is the reason the device works. Thus, the Lanham Act does not protect trade dress in a functional design simply because an investment has been made to encourage the public to associate a particular functional feature with a single manufacturer or seller. The Court of Appeals erred in viewing MDI as possessing the right to exclude competitors from using a design identical to MDI's and requiring those competitors to adopt a different design simply to avoid copying it. Pp. 44-50. 200 F. 3d 927, reversed and remanded.

This is a proceeding under Section 22-a of the New York Code of Criminal Procedure, which allows the chief executive or legal officer of a municipality to seek an injunction against the sale and distribution of certain types of literature. The case involves allegations that appellants displayed for sale and distributed fourteen booklets titled "Nights of Horror," which were found to be obscene by a judge. The judge granted an injunction ordering the appellants to stop selling and distributing the booklets and to surrender them to the sheriff for destruction. The appellants appealed the decision, arguing that the injunction amounted to prior censorship and was therefore a violation of their First Amendment rights.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit held that New York's law requiring local school authorities to lend textbooks free of charge to all students in grades seven through 12 is not in violation of the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the Constitution. The Court held that the law's purpose was to benefit all school children, regardless of the type of school they attended, and that only textbooks approved by public school authorities could be lent to parochial students. The court also held that it was not in conflict with the First Amendment because the law does not prohibit the free exercise of religion. The Second Circuit's decision is the latest in a long line of court rulings that have held that such laws violate the Constitution's free-exercise clause. The Supreme Court of the State of New York, in a separate decision, held that a law requiring the state to pay for the education of children attending private schools is not a violation of that clause.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a former high school biology teacher for violating the antifraud provisions of the federal education law.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Little Rock, Arkansas, alleges that Susan Epperson was confronted by a textbook that contained a chapter on the Darwinian Theory, which was deemed to conflict with the Biblical account.  According to the complaint, the teacher was confronted with the textbook, which contained a quote about the origin of man from the Bible, and was not permitted to teach the theory.  As the complaint further alleges, the teachers were told to use the new textbook for classroom instruction and presumably teach the statutorily condemned chapter; but to do so would be a criminal offense and subject her to dismissal from her position.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Central District of Illinois today announced criminal charges against Eppserson.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the South Carolina Supreme Court, which had upheld the denial of unemployment benefits to a Seventh-day Adventist who was fired for refusing to work on Saturdays, her Sabbath. The appellant claimed that the denial of benefits infringed upon her First Amendment right to the free exercise of religion.

The Court's opinion, delivered by Justice Brennan, emphasized that the government cannot regulate religious beliefs, compel affirmation of a repugnant belief, penalize or discriminate against individuals for their religious views, or use taxing power to inhibit religious views. However, the Court acknowledged that religiously motivated actions can be regulated if they pose a substantial threat to public safety, peace, or order.

The Court found that the appellant's refusal to work on Saturdays due to her religious beliefs did not pose such a threat and that the denial of unemployment benefits placed an unconstitutional burden on her free exercise of religion. The Court rejected the argument that benefits are a "privilege" and not a "right," stating that the denial of benefits based on religious grounds effectively penalizes the free exercise of constitutional liberties.

Furthermore, the Court noted that South Carolina law protected Sunday worshippers from being forced to work on their Sabbath, highlighting a discriminatory aspect of the law against those who observe a Sabbath on a different day.

The Court also considered whether a compelling state interest justified the infringement on the appellant's First Amendment right but found no such interest presented in the case. The Court stated that even if there were concerns about fraudulent claims or scheduling issues, the state would need to demonstrate that no alternative regulation could address these issues without infringing on First Amendment rights.

In conclusion, the Court held that South Carolina could not constitutionally apply its unemployment benefits eligibility provisions in a way that forced a worker to abandon their religious convictions regarding their day of rest. The decision reaffirmed the principle that no state may exclude individuals from public welfare benefits based on their faith or lack thereof. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around a property dispute following a schism within the Vineville Presbyterian Church in Macon, Georgia. The church, part of the hierarchical Presbyterian Church in the United States (PCUS), experienced a split where a majority of its members voted to leave the PCUS and join another denomination, while a minority wished to remain. The issue was which faction had the right to the church property.

The Court had to decide whether civil courts could use "neutral principles of law" to resolve the dispute without violating the First and Fourteenth Amendments, which would avoid entangling the courts in religious matters. The "neutral principles of law" approach involves examining deeds, corporate charters, and church constitutions without considering religious doctrines.

The Georgia courts had previously applied this neutral principles approach, awarding the property to the local church, which they identified with the majority faction. The Supreme Court of the United States agreed that the neutral principles approach is consistent with the Constitution, as it avoids religious entanglement and is secular in operation.

However, the Supreme Court found that the Georgia courts did not adequately explain how they determined that the majority faction represented the local church. The Court suggested that a presumptive rule of majority representation could be used, provided it does not involve religious doctrine and can be overridden by specific provisions in church documents.

The Supreme Court held that states can use neutral principles of law to adjudicate church property disputes, but it vacated the judgment of the Supreme Court of Georgia and remanded the case for further proceedings. The Georgia courts must clarify their reasoning and ensure that their approach does not require interpretation of religious doctrine or violate the First Amendment.

Petitioner Dolan pleaded guilty to a federal charge of assault resulting in serious bodily injury. He entered into a plea agreement that stated that restitution may be ordered by the Court. The presentence report, provided to the court by the end of May, noted that restitution was required. But, lacking precise information about hospital costs and lost wages, it did not recommend a restitution amount. On July 30, the District Court held Dolan’s sentencing hearing. The judge sentenced him to 21 months’ imprisonment along with 3 years of supervised release. The sentencing court nonetheless set a restitution hearing for February 4, 2008, about three months after the 90-day deadline expired. At the hearing, Dolan pointed out that the 90day deadline had passed. And he argued that the law no longer authorized the court to order restitution. The court disagreed and ordered restitution. Held: A sentencing court that misses the deadline nonetheless retains the power of order restitution-at least where, as here, the sentencing court made clear prior to the deadline’’ “jurisdictional” deadline that it would order restitution, leaving open (for more than 90 days) only the amount. Pp. 5–7. (a) The fact that a sentencing court misses the 90 day deadline, even through its own fault or that of the Government, does not deprive the court of the power to order the restitution. First, where a statute “does not specify a consequence for noncompliance with” its “timing provisions,” “federal courts will not in the ordinary course impose their own coercive sanction.” United States v. Cheal, 389 F. 3d 35 (CA1 2004). Second, to read the statute as depriving the sentencing judge of the “power to order” would harm those—the victims of crime—who likely bear no responsibility for the deadlines’ final determination. See, e.g., Corey v. United States, 375 U. S. 169, 174, 175. Third, the provision before us sets forth this third kind of limitation. The fact, even though it misses the statute's 90-days deadline does not “proportion[ately]” repair the harm caused the defendant through delay, particularly where the defendant “knew about restitution” including the likely amount, well before expiration of the 90 days’ time limit. Here, the statute seeks speed by creating a time-related directive that is legally enforceable but does not depri a judge or other public official of the authority to take the action to which the deadline applies if the deadline is missed. The statute also places primary weight upon, and emphasizes the importance of, imposing restitution upon those convicted of certain federal crimes. The text places primary- and emphasizes that, as in Montalvo-Murillo, supra, at 262, “[n]otwithstanding any other provision of law, when sentencing a defendant convicted of [a specified] offense … , the court shall order … that the defendant make restitution to the victim of the offense.�” §3664(a)(1)(A). The sentence imposes no time limit on the victim's subsequent discovery of losses. Consequently, a court might award restitution for those losses long after the original sentence was imposed and the 90–day time limit has expired. That fact, along with the Act’ main substantive objectives, is why we say that the Act's efforts to secure speedy determination of restitution is primarily designed to help victims of a crime secure prompt restitution rather than to provide defendants with certainty as to the amount of their liability. The “sole due process interest of the defendant being protected … is the right not to be sentenced on the basis of invalid premises or inaccurate information” (emphasis added). Moreover, the Act provides that a “sentence that imposes an order of restitution, such as the later restitution order here, ‘is a final judgment.’ . . . This Court has previously interpreted similar statutes similarly, including the Bail Reform Act of 1984, which states that a court “shall hold a hearing” to determine whether to grant bail to an arrested person and that “hearing shall be held immediately upon the person” and that a continuance of up to five days may also be granted. But the statute also provides that restitution shall be ordered in the full amount of each victims’ losses and “without consideration of the economic circumstances of each defendant.“ §3663A(a) (1) (emphasis deleted); Brock v. Pierce County, 476 U.S. 43, 63 (same), and Barnhart v. Peabody Coal Co., 537 U.

In Montana v. United States, 450 U. S. 544, the Court of Appeals held that, with limited exceptions, Indian tribes lack civil authority over the conduct of nonmembers on non-Indian fee land within a reservation. The question with which we are presented is whether this general rule applies to tribal attempts to tax nonmember activity occurring on non Indian fee land. Montana's "case-by-case approach" balanced the nonIndian fee status of the land with "the nature of the inherent sovereign powers the tribe is attempting to exercise, its interests, and the impact that the exercise of the tribe's powers has upon the nonmember interests involved." The court concluded that the status of nonmember nonmembers' nonmember fee land as "fee land or tribal land is simply one of the factors a court should consider" when determining whether civil jurisdiction exists, id., at 1258. Relying in part upon Merrion v. Jicarilla Apache Tribe, 455 U.S. 130 (1982), the court "complement[ed]" Montana's framework with a case-bycase approach that balanced the Non-Indian Fee Status of the Land with the nature of its inherent sovereign power to tax-whatever its derivation-reaches no further than tribal land. Respondents' argument that petitioner and its hotel guests have entered into a consensual relationship with the Navajo Nation justifying the hotel occupancy tax was rejected by both the Navajo Tax Commission and the Federal District Court, which upheld the tax. A divided panel of the Tenth Circuit affirmed, concluding that the nonmembers had not consented to the Tribe's adjudicatory authority by availing themselves of the benefit of tribal police protection while traveling within the reservation. Held: 1. The nonmember's nonmember status does not trigger tribal civil authority in another-it is not "in for a penny, in for a Pound." Pp. 5-7. (a) Montana's consensual relationship exception requires that the tax or regulation imposed by the Indian tribe have a nexus to the consensual relationship itself. The fact that nonmembers at the Cameron Trading Post have not subjected themselves to "tribal civil jurisdiction" through any agreements or dealings with the Tribe and that hunting and fishing on nonIndian fees land did not "imperil" the subsistence or welfare of the Tribe, does not render the hotel's regulations invalid. P. 7. (b) Because Congress has not authorized the Navajo Tribe's hotel occupancytax through treaty or statute, and because the incidence of the tax falls upon nonmembers in non-Indian fee land, it is incumbent upon the Tribe to establish the existence of one of Montana's exceptions. Pp 7-8. (c) The consensual relationship must stem from "commercial dealing, contracts, leases, or other arrangements," Montana, at 565. Although the legal incidence of petitioner's tax falls on nonmembers, the owner or operator of the hotel must collect and remit it to respondents, members of the Navajo Tribal Tax Commission. Respondent's hotel guests, who are nonmember guests, pay approximately $84,000 in taxes to respondents annually. The record reflects that the Arizona State Police and Navajo Tribal Emergency Medical Services Department patrol the portions of United States Highway 89 and Arizona Highway 64 traversing the reservation; that local Arizona Fire Departments and the Navajo Fire Department provide fire protection to the area; and that local fire Departments, Navajo Tribal Fire Department, and Navajo Volunteer Fire Department maintain fire protection in the area. Although we have no cause to doubt respondents' assertion that the Cameron Chapter possesses an "overwhelming Indian character," the judgment in Brendale turned on both the closed nature and the fact that its development would place the entire area "in jeopardy." Id., at 443 (internal quotation marks and citation omitted). Pp 8-10. (d) Because the tax is grounded in petitioner's relationship with its nonmember hotel guests and petitioner's status as an "Indian trader," respondents emphasize that petitioner employs almost 100 Navajo Indians; that petitioner derives business from tourists visiting the reservation, and that large amounts of tribal land surround petitioner's isolated property. The reservation is, like millions of acres throughout the United States throughout the U. States, nonIndianfee land. Petitioner cannot be said to have consentedto such a tax by virtue of its status as a "Indian Trader." P. 10. (e) The hotel's occupancy tax is warranted in light of the direct effects the Cameron trading Post has upon petitioner's hotel guest guests. The tax does not endanger the Navajo's political integrity, since the hotel guests' consensual relationship in one area thus does not invoke tribal civil jurisdiction in another, and it is therefore easily reconcilable with the Montana-Strate line of authority, which we deem to be controlling. The hotel tax is not invalid because it does not infringe on petitioner's right to self-government or to control internal relations, since a nonmember has consented not solely from an Indian tribe's power to exclude nonmembers from tribal land, but also from anIndian tribe

In this case, the United States Supreme Court considered the constitutionality of a zoning ordinance in the village of Belle Terre, New York. The ordinance defined a "family" as "one or more persons related by blood, adoption, or marriage, living and cooking together as a single housekeeping unit," and prohibited the renting of properties to anyone except families. The court found that the ordinance was constitutional under the police power of the state, stating that the line between what is legal and illegal in zoning matters is not always clear-cut and depends on various factors including the potential harm caused by the activity being regulated.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit has ruled that the death penalty is unconstitutional for Daryl Renard Atkins, who was sentenced to death for the 1996 abduction, armed robbery, and capital murder of Eric Nesbitt. The court's decision is the latest in a series of high-profile cases challenging the use of capital punishment for the most serious adult criminal conduct. Atkins' case is one of the most recent in which the court has reviewed the issue. In a landmark 1989 ruling, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled that executing mentally retarded defendants is impermissible. The 4th Court's majority opinion, however, agreed with the lower court that Atkins' death sentence was disproportionate to penalties imposed for similar crimes in Virginia. The majority of the Virginia Supreme Court rejected Atkins' argument that his sentence was not disproportionate because he was not "mentally retarded," but rather was of "average intelligence, at least," and diagnosable as having antisocial personality disorder. The Supreme Court of Virginia upheld the death sentence, and Atkins was re-sentenced to death. The Virginia Court of Justices ordered a new sentencing hearing. The trial court used a misleading verdict form, and an expert rebuttal witness, Dr. Stanton Samenow, determined that Atkins was not mentally retarding. The jury sentenced Atkins to death, and the trial court sentenced him to death again. Atkins appealed, claiming that he was denied a fair trial because he had not shown that he had a "diminished capacity" to understand the nature of the charges against him. Atkins was granted a re-sentencing hearing and the jury found him guilty of capital murder. The high court found Atkins guilty of murder, and sentenced him for the second time. The appeals were denied. The case has now been remanded for further consideration.
