The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was found guilty of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the defendant and ordered him to submit to a blood test conducted by a neutral and detached magistrate.  According to the court's order, filed in federal district court in Los Angeles, the defendant was not entitled to the privilege because he had been arrested at a hospital while receiving treatment for injuries suffered in an automobile accident.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced that it filed criminal charges against the accused.  On August 2, 2018, the U. S. Attorney's office for New York announced criminal charges in the case.  Among other things, the SEC's complaint alleges that the defendant refused to consent to the blood test, despite repeated requests from his counsel, and that the officer did not perform the test.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the officer consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the above-mentioned provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The judgment also orders the defendant to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and the officer to pay civil penalties in the amount of $2,500.   The SEC's investigation was conducted by Michael J. Breithaupt and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The litigation will be led by Gregory A. Kasper. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the FBI.

After the 1980 United States Census showed that Wyoming's population had increased sufficiently to warrant adding another member to the State Legislature, the State passed legislation providing for a 64-member House consisting of one representative from each county plus one additional representative chosen by lottery from a pool of counties whose populations were substantially above the mean. However, Niobrara County, the State's least populous county, had a population of less than half the ideal district figure, and accordingly would have been assigned zero representation under the statutory formula. Instead, the State legislature decided to give Niobrara County one seat in the House, finding that doing so would further the State's longstanding policy of preserving county boundaries and ensuring that each county has one representative. Subsequently, appellant members of the women's league and residents of several counties with higher population densities than Niobrara County sued in Federal District Court, alleging that the grant of a representative to Niobrara County impermissibly diluted the voting rights of plaintiffs and others similarly situated. The District Court upheld the constitutionality of the statute, concluding that the "dilution" of plaintiffs' votes was de minimis when Niobrara County had its own representative. Held: Wyoming did not violate the Equal Protection Clause by granting Niobrara County one seat in the House. Pp. 839-846. (a) Although minor deviations from population equality among state legislative districts are insufficient to establish a prima facie case of invidious discrimination requiring justification by the State, see Gaffney v. Cummings, 412 U. S. 735, 745, an apportionment plan with a maximum population deviation under 10% falls within this category. A plan with larger disparities creates a prima facie case of discrimination and therefore must be justified by the State. The ultimate inquiry is whether the legislature's plan "may reasonably be said to advance [a] rational state policy" and, if so, "whether the population disparities among the districts that have resulted from the pursuit of this plan exceed constitutional limits." Mahan v. Howell, 410 U. S. 315, 328. Pp. 839-842. (b) This case presents an unusually strong example of an apportionment plan the population variations of which are entirely the result of the consistent and nondiscriminatory application of a legitimate state policy. While population deviations of any magnitude are not automatically acceptable, even a neutral and consistently applied criterion such as use of counties as representative districts can frustrate Reynolds v. Sims, 377 U. S. 533, mandate of fair and effective representation if the population disparities are excessively high. Consideration must be given "to the character as well as the degree of deviations from a strict population basis." 377 U. S., at 581. Here, although the consistency of application and the neutrality of effect of the nonpopulation criteria must be considered along with the size of the population disparities in determining whether a state legislative apportionment plan contravenes the Equal Protection Clause, nevertheless the consistency of application and the neutrality of effect of the nonpopulation criteria must be considered together with the size of the population disparities in determining whether a state legislative apportionment plan contravenes the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 842-844. (c) Where there is no "taint of arbitrariness or discrimination," Romanv . Syncock, 377 U. S., at 710, substantial deference is to be accorded the political decisions of the people of a State acting through their elected representatives. Here, by enacting the 64-member plan the State ensured that its policy of preserving county boundaries applies nondiscriminatorily. Moreover, the effect of the 63-member plan would be to deprive Niobrara County's voters of their own representative, even though the remainder of the House would be constituted so as to facilitate representation of the interests of each county. Thus, Wyoming has not violated the Equal Protection Clause by permitting Niobrara County to have its own representative. Pp. 844-846. 536 F. Supp. 780, affirmed.

The Supreme Court case in question deals with the jurisdiction of state courts over foreign subsidiaries of a U.S. parent corporation, specifically whether these subsidiaries can be sued in a state court for claims unrelated to their activities in that state. The case arose from a bus accident in France, allegedly due to a defective tire made by a Turkish subsidiary of Goodyear. The parents of two North Carolina boys who died in the accident filed a wrongful death lawsuit in North Carolina against Goodyear USA and its foreign subsidiaries in Turkey, France, and Luxembourg.

The legal issue centers on the concept of personal jurisdiction, which is governed by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court distinguishes between "general" or "all-purpose" jurisdiction and "specific" or "case-linked" jurisdiction. General jurisdiction over a corporation is appropriate when the corporation's activities in the state are so "continuous and systematic" as to render it essentially at home in the state. Specific jurisdiction, on the other hand, requires an affiliation between the forum and the underlying controversy, such as an activity or occurrence that takes place in the forum state.

The Supreme Court held that North Carolina courts lacked specific jurisdiction because the accident and the tire's manufacture occurred outside the state. The North Carolina Court of Appeals had asserted general jurisdiction based on the fact that some tires made by the subsidiaries had reached North Carolina through the "stream of commerce." However, the Supreme Court found this connection too limited to establish the necessary "continuous and systematic" affiliation for general jurisdiction. The Court emphasized that the subsidiaries were not "at home" in North Carolina, as they were not registered to do business there, had no operations, employees, or bank accounts in the state, and did not design, manufacture, advertise, or directly sell their products there.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the North Carolina Court of Appeals, concluding that the state courts could not exercise general jurisdiction over the foreign subsidiaries based on the facts of the case. The Court's decision clarifies the limitations on the exercise of general jurisdiction over foreign corporations by state courts, emphasizing that mere distribution of a product in a state through the stream of commerce does not justify general jurisdiction over unrelated claims.

Title: In Re Finney
Author: William Howard Taft
Source: Harvard International Review
Volume: 10
Issue: Winter 1978
Page Range: 117-126

The Internal Revenue Code provides that taxpayers seeking a refund of taxes unlawfully assessed must comply with tax refund procedures set forth in the Code. Under those procedures, a taxpayer must file an administrative claim with the Internal Revenue Service before filing suit against the Government. Such a claim must be filed within three years of the filing of a return or two years of payment of the tax, whichever is later. The Code also provides that “[n]o suit … shall be maintained in any court for the recovery of any internal revenue tax alleged to have been erroneously or illegally assessed or collected,” 26 U. S. C. §7422(a)(1), and establishes strict timeframes for filing such a claim. In 1998, a group of companies challenged the tax in a Federal District Court, contending that it violated the Export Clause of the Constitution. The District Court agreed and held the tax unconstitutional. The Government did not appeal, and the IRS acquiesced in the District Court’s decision. The Tucker Act, in contrast, allows claims to be brought against the United States within six years of a challenged conduct. The Court of Federal Claims, relying on the decision of the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit in Cyprus Amax Coal Co. v. United States, 205 F. 3d 1369, held that the statute applied only to refund claims brought under the Code, not to claims brought directly under the export Clause. Held: The plain language of the Code and the Tucker Act requires a taxpayer to seek a refund for a tax assessed in violation of the export clause. Pp. 5–11. (a) The plain-language language of 26 U., S.C. §§7422 (a), and 6511 requires a taxpayers to file administrative refund claims with the IRS before suit can be brought. Even if the refund scheme applies to Export Clause cases generally, it does not “apply to taxes that are imposed by” Title 26. Congress has the power to protect this “exceedingly strong interest.” Ardestani v. INS, 502 U.S. 129, 135. Moreover, Congress may not impose a tax in violation thereof, but it is within Congress’ authority to assure that allegations of tax unlawfully assessed are processed in an orderly and timely manner, and that costly litigation is avoided when possible. The companies’ claim that the Code procedures are excessively burdensome is belied by their own invocation of those procedures for taxes paid within the Code’’ limitations period, which resulted in full refunds with interest. The tax injunction suit, of course, is brought at the time the Government attempts to assess a tax on the taxpayer. Even when the constitutionality of a tax is challenged, taxing authorities do in fact have an “elegant strong interest in financial stability,’ McKesson Corp. v., Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco, Fla. Dept. of Business Regulation, 496 US. 18, 37, an interest they may pursue through provisions of the sort at issue here. The fact that Congress has indeed established a detailed refund scheme that subjects complaining taxpayers to various requirements before they can bring suit is not a constitutional problem at all, since the scheme is designed to advise the appropriate officials of the demands or claims intended to be asserted, so as to insure an orderly administration of the revenue, and to allow the IRS to avoid unnecessary litigation by correcting conceded errors. The “decisions of this Court” make it unmistakably clear that the constitutional nature of a taxpayer's claim … is of no consequence” to whether the prohibition against tax injunctions applies. Alexander v. North Dakota ex rel. Board of Univ. and School Lands, 461 U.

Respondent Henson filed suit in state court in Iberville Parish, Louisiana, against petitioner Syngenta Crop Protection, Inc. (then known as Ciba-Geigy Corp.) asserting various tort claims related to petitioners' manufacture and sale of a chlordimeform-based insecticide. A similar action was already underway in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Alabama. Counsel for respondent told the court that the Price settlement required dismissal of only some of the claims raised in Henson. Although this representation appeared to be contrary to the terms of the settlement agreement, the Louisiana court relied upon it and invited respondent to amend the complaint and proceed with the action. The Alabama court dismissed Henson as barred by the settlement and sanctioned respondent's counsel for his misrepresentation to the state court. The Court of Appeals affirmed the sanctions but vacated the District Court's order dismissing the Henson action. Held: The All Writs Act does not furnish removal jurisdiction under 28 U. S. C. § 1441 (a), which authorizes a federal court "in aid of [the courts'] respective jurisdictions" without providing any federal subject-matter jurisdiction in its own right. Pp. 534-535. (a) Section 1441 does not authorize a state court to remove a state-court case in order to prevent the frustration of orders the federal court has previously issued. P. 535. (b) Petitioners may not, by resorting to the All Writ's Act, avoid complying with the statutory requirements for removal. The Act, alone or in combination with the existence of ancillary jurisdiction, is not a substitute for that requirement. See, e. g., Peacock v. Thomas, 516 U.S. 349, 355. The statute does not confer jurisdiction on the federal courts, it cannot confer the original jurisdiction required to support removal pursuant to § 2841. Moreover, some combination of the Act and the doctrine of acillary enforcement jurisdiction support the removal of Henson's action from state to federal court. Petitioners must demonstrate that original subject matter jurisdiction lies in federal courts in order for removal to be effective. The remedy for removal is to be in aid of the courts' respective jurisdictions, not the state courts' own jurisdiction, and the remedy is to rely on the Court's interpretation of Peacocks' doctrine, which provides that "any civil action brought in a State court of which the district courts have original jurisdiction, may be removed by the defendant or the defendants, to the district and division embracing the place where such action is pending," unless Congress specifically provides otherwise. The Southern District retained jurisdiction over the price settlement, thus distinguishing Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of America, 511 U. s. 375, 270, 270. Petitioner's argument that the Southern district retained jurisdiction is not supported by the fact that the Court is authorized to invoke the statute in conjunction with the statute is undermined by its invocation of the "All Writs" doctrine, since it dispenses with the requirement that removal is authorized by the statute. The court's invocation of that doctrine does not dispense with the Court with the right of removal, since the right to removal is entirely a creature of statute and "a suit commenced in a state ... must remain there until cause is shown for its transfer under some act of Congress." Thus, the right does not provide the "original jurisdiction" that petitioners must show in order-to qualify for removal-under § 14 41. P p. 536. (c) Ancillary jurisd, therefore, cannot provide an original jurisdiction that petitioner must show. Ancilla jurisdiction cannot provide the original jurisdictional jurisdiction that petitionerers must prove in order. Accordingly, the judgment is affirmed.

Title: ALABAMA PRISON OFFICERS NOT LIABLE FOR ATTACHING INMATES TO RESTRAINING POSTS

Issue: Whether prison officers in Alabama are entitled to qualified immunity for attaching inmates to restraining posts.

Background: In 1995, three Alabama prison officers - Gene McClaran, Sergean Pelzer, and Lieutenant James Gates - were accused of violating the Eighth Amendment by attaching an inmate named Lawrence Alan Hill to a restraining post. Hill had refused to work and had become violent towards other inmates and guards. The officers had attempted to calm Hill down, but ultimately had to physically restrain him and attach him to the post.

Analysis: The Supreme Court analyzed the history of the use of restraining posts in Alabama prisons and found that the practice was not universally condemned. The Court also examined the language of the Eighth Amendment and found that it did not explicitly prohibit the use of restraining posts. Additionally, the Court looked at the doctrine of qualified immunity and found that it afforded protection to prison officers who were acting in good faith and did not know that their actions were illegal. Finally, the Court compared the facts of this case to other cases involving the use of restraining posts and found that the officers' actions were justified under the circumstances.

Conclusion: Based on the historical evidence, the language of the Eighth Amendment, and the doctrine of qualified immunity, the Supreme Court ruled that the three Alabama prison officers were not liable for attaching an inmate to a restraining post.

A Pennsylvania statute makes it a misdemeanor for any person engaged in the retail sale of specified articles to keep his place of business open on Sundays. Appellants, members of the Orthodox Jewish faith, sued in a Federal District Court for an injunction against its enforcement, claiming that it violated the Religious Freedom Clause of the First Amendment, as made applicable to the States by the Fourteenth Amendment. They claimed that, since they are required by their faith to close their stores on Saturdays and to refrain from all manner of work on Sundays, the Act will prevent them from earning a living and will drive them out of business. They also claimed that it will inhibit the growth of their faith by preventing them from employing enough workers to meet the demands of customers on Sundays. Held: The Act does not violate the Religious Freedom Clause of the First Amendment, as made applicable to the States by the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 582-591. (a) Though the Act burdens the free exercise of appellants' religion, it does not make unlawful any religious practices of appellants; the Sunday law merely regulates a secular activity and, as applied to appellants, operates so as to make the practice of their religious beliefs more expensive. Pp. 584-586. (b) When entered into the area of religious freedom, the Constitution protects the freedom to act even when the action is in accord with one's religious convictions; but it does not forbid legislative restrictions on actions which are in violation of important social duties or subversive of good order, even when demanded by one's religion. Pp. 586-587. (c) Even though the alternatives open to appellants and others similarly situated -retaining their present occupations and incurring economic disadvantage or engaging in some other commercial activity which does not call for either Saturday or Sunday labor--may well result in some financial sacrifice in order to observe their religious beliefs, the options are wholly different than when the legislation attempts to make a religious practice itself unlawful. P. 587. (d) Legislation which imposes only an indirect burden on the exercise of religion is not automatically void. P. 588. (e) However, if the purpose or effect of a law is to impede the observance of one or all religions or is to discriminate invidiously between religions, that law is constitutionally invalid even though the burden may be characterized as being only indirect. P. 588. (f) A State can provide a weekly respite from all labor and, at the same time, set one day of the week apart from the others as a day of rest, repose, recreation and tranquility-a day when the hectic tempo of everyday existence ceases and a more pleasant atmosphere is created, a day on which people may visit friends and relatives who are not available during working days, a day when the weekly laborer may best regenerate himself. Pp. 588-589. (g) An alternative to the Pennsylvania Act which would remove the economic disadvantages imposed by the present system would be to carve out an exception for those people who, because of religious conviction, observe a day of rest other than Sunday. While this might well be the wiser solution to the problem, it presents additional difficulties and problems which would make it difficult to enforce. Pp. 589-591. 195 F. Supp. 477, affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia held that Ilya Wolston was not a public figure within the meaning of the First Amendment's First Amendment protection against defamation. The court held that Wolston had not proved that he was a "public figure" and therefore precluded recovery unless he proved that respondents had published a defamatory falsehood with "actual malice"<n>The court also held that the public figure standard did not apply to Wolston's case because he had not shown that the statements were false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not. Wolston appealed the lower court's decision granting summary judgment to the author and publishers of a 1974 book that falsely stated that he had been indicted for espionage and had been a Soviet agent in the United States. The appeals court found that the district court had correctly concluded that the "public figures" standard does not apply in this case because Wolston did not show that the false statements were true or with a "reckless disregard" of whether they were false. The Appeals Court held that there was no need for the public figures standard to apply to this case since Wolston failed to show that he would have been found guilty of contempt of court had he been charged with contempt in the first place. In a related case, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled in favor of the author of KGB and the publisher of the book. The Supreme Court will review the case. The Court will decide whether there is a need for a new standard of proof.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit held that the National Bank for Cooperatives is not exempt from Missouri's corporate income tax. The National Bank was formed in 1989 through the consolidation of 10 district banks for cooperatives and the Central Bank of Cooperatives. The current version of the Farm Credit Act does not explicitly waive this immunity. The Missouri Supreme Court held that Congress cannot be said to have expressly consented to state income taxation. The Court held, however, that the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution provides federal instrumentalities immunity from state taxation unless Congress has expressly waived this immunity, and that Congress has not done so in this case. The court held that CoBank's request for an exemption from all state income taxes and refunds on the taxes paid-erroneously, it alleged-for 1991 through 1994-and its subsequent appeal of the Director of Revenue's determination that it was a federal instrumentality statutorily exempt from state income tax were not supported by the facts of this case and that the Commission did not have the authority to grant CoBank an exemption. The 8th Court held in favor of CoBank, holding that the current Farm Credit act does not provide for a tax exemption for cooperatives. CoBank also argued that, because the current version does not expressly waive immunity, it would be subject to federal income tax in the hands of the holder of its obligations. The 9th Circuit Court of Appeal held that, in a similar case, the Missouri Supreme Justices had held that "the Supremacy clause of the constitution provides federal immunity" from state tax, and CoBank had failed to show that Congress had waived its immunity. In a separate appeal, CoBank sought an exemption, which the Commission denied. The Appeals Court agreed with the lower court's findings. The case is now before the U.N. Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the interpretation of the federal mail fraud statute, 18 U.S.C. § 1341, and whether it applies to false statements made in applications for state licenses, specifically in the context of video poker machine operation licenses in Louisiana.

The main legal issue is whether a state-issued license constitutes "property" under the federal mail fraud statute when the state is the victim of the fraud. The petitioner, Carl W. Cleveland, along with others, was prosecuted for making false statements on applications to the Louisiana State Police to operate video poker machines.

The Court concluded that state and municipal licenses, including Louisiana's video poker licenses, do not qualify as "property" in the hands of the state for the purposes of the mail fraud statute. The Court emphasized that the object of the fraud must be property in the hands of the victim, not just something that could become property once in the recipient's hands.

The Court recognized that while the state has a regulatory interest and collects fees related to the licensing process, these factors do not transform the licenses into property. The Court also noted that the state's interest in controlling the issuance of licenses is a manifestation of its sovereign regulatory power, not a property interest.

The Court rejected the government's broader interpretations of property rights, which could have significantly expanded federal criminal jurisdiction into areas traditionally regulated by state and local authorities. The Court also reaffirmed its stance from McNally v. United States that the mail fraud statute is intended to protect property rights and that any ambiguity in criminal statutes should be resolved in favor of lenity.

The Court's decision to reverse the Fifth Circuit's judgment means that Cleveland's conviction under § 1341 must be vacated, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. This decision limits the scope of the federal mail fraud statute and reinforces the principle that federal criminal law should not encroach on state regulatory authority without a clear directive from Congress.

Section 12 (f) of the Military Selective Service Act, as amended, empowers the President to require every male citizen and male resident alien between the ages of 18 and 26 to register for the draft under Title IV of the Higher Education Act of 1965. The regulations allow a student who has not previously registered, although required to do so, to establish eligibility for Title IV aid by registering, filing a statement of registration compliance, and, if required, verifying that he is registered. The statement of compliance does not require the applicant to state the date that he registered. Appellee students (hereafter appellees) are anonymous individuals who were required to register before September 1, 1982. On September 8, 1983, Congress enacted the Department of Defense Authorization Act of 1983, Pub. L. 97-252, which added § 12(f). Section 1113(a) of that Act requires the Secretary of Education to issue regulations providing that "any person" to whom the Secretary proposes to deny Title IV assistance shall be given notice of the proposed denial and "not less than thirty days" after such notice to "establis[h] that he has complied with the registration requirement." Section 12(b) does not violate the proscription against bills of attainder. Nor has appellee raised a cognizable claim under the Fifth Amendment. The District Court erred in striking down the statute as an impermissible attainder, holding that it did not violate its proscription by compelling nonregistrants to acknowledge that they have failed to register timely when confronted with certifying to their schools that they had complied with registration. Held: 1. The statute clearly gives nonregists 30 days after receiving notice that they are ineligible for federal aid to register and qualify for aid. Pp. 5-11. (a) The legislative history provides convincing support for the view that, in enacting § 12 (F), Congress sought, not to punish anyone, but to promote compliance with the draft registration requirement and fairness in the allocation of scarce federal resources. P. 5. (b) The statute does not single out an identifiable group that would be ineligible for Title III aid or inflict punishment within the meaning of Bill of Attainder Clause, since it does not undermine the provision allowing "any one" to register 30 days before notification to establish compliance with registration, since the statement to the school by the applicant is simply that he "operates only as a designation of particular persons." Communist Party of the United States v. Subversive Activities Control Board, 367 U. S. 1, 86. The legislative record also reflects Congress' intent to encourage registration by those who must register, rather than by choosing to punish willful non-statistrants by denying them benefits even if they registered belatedly. Thus, the legislative history is convincing support that, under these circumstances, § 12 "f" is not a punitive bill of attaind. P p. 511. 2. The statutory history provides support for this view. Section 12 (ff) clearly furthers nonpunitive legislative goals, and § 12's legislative history demonstrates that Congress sought not only to punish, but also to encourage compliance with draft registration requirements, and that Congress has inflicted nothing approaching the "infamous punishment" of imprisonment, or other disabilities historically associated with punishment. P, 512. (c) Section 12's language does not make late registrants ineligible for aid based on their past conduct, and it also furthers a fair allocation of federal resources by limiting title IV aid to those who are willing to meet their responsibilities to the Government by registering with the Selective Services when required to. The very risk that they will be ineligible to qualify for financial aid constitutes "compulsion" within the statute's meaning. The provision of the statute, "viewed in terms of the type and severity of burdens imposed, reasonably can be said to further nonpunititive legislative purposes"; and (3) whether the legislative record "evinces a congressional intent to punish." Flemming v. Nestor, 363 U.S. 603, 616, and n. 9, 4 L. Ed. 2d 1435, distinguished.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a New Jersey school district for conducting a search that violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Newark, N.J., alleges that, in March 1980, Assistant Vice Principal Theodore Choplick conducted a search of a Piscataway High School student's purse. The complaint alleges that the search was conducted based on a reasonable suspicion that T.L.O. had been smoking in the lavatory and that she did not smoke at all.  According to the complaint, the search yielded a small amount of marihuana, a pipe, a number of empty plastic bags, and an index card.  In a parallel action, the New Jersey Attorney General's Office today announced criminal charges against the school district's principal.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, filed under seal on March 7, 1980, the SEC obtained a temporary restraining order halting the search of the school's principal's purse and ordering the school to comply with the court's order.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the Complaint or in the case of the District Attorney's Office, the court agreed with the SEC that a search conducted by school officials constitutes a reasonable search, and that the school should not be subject to the same restrictions as searches carried out by law enforcement officers.  Further, the Court agreed that the purpose of the search, if any, was to preserve the safety and security of schoolchildren.  On March 8, 2011, the Honorable Joseph G. Sansone of the New York District Court entered a judgment that permanently enjoins school officials from violating the antiligence provisions of the federal securities laws, orders them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and orders the district attorney to appoint a receiver to oversee the search.

The Federal Railroad Safety Act of 1970 authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to "prescribe, as necessary, appropriate rules, regulations, orders, and standards for all areas of railroad safety." Section C of the regulations provides that railroads "shall take all practicable steps to assure that all covered employees of the railroad directly involved . . . provide blood and urine samples for toxicological testing by FRA," § 219.203(a)(1), upon the occurrence of certain specified events. The regulations set forth procedures for the collection of samples, and require that samples "be analyzed by a method that is reliable within known tolerances." Section 219.307(b). The regulations also require that the FRA notify employees of their results of the tests and afford them an opportunity to respond in writing before preparation of any final investigative report. The FRA, after reviewing further comments from representatives of the railroads, labor groups, and the general public, in 1985, promulgated regulations that mandate blood-and- urine tests of employees who are involved in certain train accidents. Subpart C, which is entitled "Post-Accident Toxicological Testing," is mandator . It authorizes railroads to require covered employees to submit to breath or urine tests in certain circumstances not addressed by Subpart D. Breath, blood, and urine tests, or both, may be ordered (1) after a reportable accident or incident, where a supervisor has a "reasonable suspicion" that an employee's acts or omissions contributed to the occurrence or severity of an accident, and (2) in the event of certain specific rule violations, including noncompliance with a signal and excessive speeding, §219.301(b)(3). Subpart A, which provides that "all practicable steps ... shall take ... to assure ... all covered employee directly involved ... provide blood, urine, or breath samples for [the FRA's] testing by ... FRA." Subpart B provides that tests mandated by a railroad in reliance on the authority conferred by the regulations involve sufficient Government action to implicate the Fourth Amendment, and that such tests are Fourth Amendment searches. The court also "agre[ed] that the exigencies of testing for the presence of alcohol and drugs in blood or urine or breath require prompt action which precludes obtaining a warrant," and accordingly, that the legality of the searches depends on their reasonableness under all the circumstances. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the testin procedures contemplated by Subparts C and D pose only limited threats to the justifiable expectations of privacy of covered employees. The fact that the Government has not compelled a private party to perform a search does not, by itself, establish that the search is a private one. The ensuing chemical analysis of the sample to obtain physiological data is a further invasion of the tested employee's privacy interests. See, e.g., Arizona v. Hicks, 480 U. S. 321, 324-325. Pp. 4-6. 839 F. 2d 575, reversed.

The Supreme Court ruled in this case that a federal court must assess the prejudicial impact of constitutional error in a state-court criminal trial using the "substantial and injurious effect" standard set forth in Brecht v. Abrahamson, 507 U.S. S. 619 (1993), regardless of whether the state appellate court recognized the error and reviewed it for harmlessness under the "harmless beyond a reasonable doubt" standard set forth in Chapman v. California, 386 U.S. S. 18 (1967).

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia granted summary judgment in favor of the Georgia Secretary of State and the Georgia State Democratic Executive Committee in a case that challenged the use of the state's county unit system for counting votes in the Democratic primary for the nomination of a United States Senator and statewide officers. The complaint alleged that the county units system violated the Equal Protection Clause and the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and the 17th Amendment. The court held that the amended statutes of the State's County Unit System Act of 1960 (the amended Act) did not violate the constitutionality of the amended Act. The amended Act, the court held, did not change the number of county units allocated to each county in the lower House of the General Assembly. The Court also found that the amendment did not alter the amount of units that each county is entitled to receive in the first primary. In the second primary, the candidate with the popular majority wins, but if there is a tie in unit votes, the candidates with the most votes are to prevail. The trial court concluded that there was no reason to change the current system. The three-judge panel agreed, and granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment. The defendants also filed an answer denying that the County Unit Act was unconstitutional and alleging that it was designed 'to achieve a reasonable balance as between urban and rural electoral power'

In a suit challenging the apportionment of seats in the Delaware General Assembly, plaintiffs, residents, taxpayers and qualified voters of New Castle County, Delaware, filed a complaint in the District Court, in their own behalf and on behalf of all persons similarly situated, challenging the constitutionality, under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the Federal Constitution, of apportioning seats in both houses of the Delaware Legislature. The District Court entered an order refusing to dismiss the suit, and stated that, while it had no desire to substitute its judgment for the collective wisdom of the State General Assembly in matters of legislative apportionments, it had had no alternative but to proceed promptly in deciding the case. On July 25, 1962, the Delaware Supreme Court issued an order staying the proceedings until August 7, 1962 in order to permit the General Assembly to take "some appropriate action" under Art. II, § 2, of the Constitution of Delaware, and to allow the November 1962 general election to be conducted pursuant to the provisions of the 1963 reapportionment amendment. The court granted appellants' motion to advance, and the case was remanded. Held: 1. Appellants' constitutional validity under the Constitution is challenged under § 2. The Court below must now determine whether it would be advisable, so as to avoid a possible disruption of state election processes and permit additional time for the Legislature to adopt a constitutionally valid apportioned scheme. Pp. 531-532. 2. Appellee v. Sims, 377 U. S. 533, affirmed.

Respondent village enacted an ordinance requiring every person desiring to engage in door-to-door solicitation in the village to secure a permit, and stipulated that the permit application must include satisfactory proof that at least 75% of the net proceeds of the proposed solicitation will be used directly for the purpose for which the solicitation is conducted. Petitioner Citizens for Environmental Balance (CEB), an Illinois nonprofit corporation, brought suit challenging the ordinance's constitutionality, claiming that it violated petitioner's rights of free speech under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. After receiving affidavits from petitioner supporting its position, the Federal District Court entered summary judgment for petitioner, concluding that the ordinance constituted a form of censorship impermissible under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. The Court of Appeals agreed, finding that the ordinance was facially invalid since it would preclude many traditional charitable organizations from engaging in door-to-door solicitation, and that it was unenforceable against petitioner since it was not shown that petitioner spent more than 25% of its receipts on salaries and administrative expenses. Held: 1. The ordinance is facially invalid under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 108-115. (a) Prior authorities establish that charitable appeals for funds, on street or door to door, involve a variety of speech interests-communication of information, the dissemination and propagation of views and ideas, and the advocacy of causes--all of which are within the protection of the First Amendment. Soliciting financial support is undoubtedly subject to reasonable regulation, but the latter must be undertaken with due regard for the reality that solicitation is characteristically intertwined with informative and perhaps persuasive speech seeking support for particular causes or for particular views on economic, political, or social issues, and for the reality that without solicitation the flow of such information and advocacy would likely cease. Pp. 108-112. (b) Since petitioner's own activities are unprotected, it was entitled to its judgment of facial invalidity regardless of whether the ordinance purported to prohibit canvassing by a substantial category of charities to which the 75% limitation could not be applied consistent with the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 112-113. 2. The ordinance is unconstitutionally overbroad. Pp. 113-115. (a) Preventing fraud is the village's principal justification for prohibiting solicitation by charities that spend more than one-quarter of their receipts on salaries and administrative expenses, but this cannot be true of those organizations that are primarily engaged in research, advocacy, or public education and that use their own paid staff to carry out these functions as well as to solicit financial support. Moreover, the village may serve its legitimate interests by measures less destructive of First Amendment interests than a direct prohibition on solicitation. Pp. 113-114. (b) There is no substantial relationship between the 75% requirement and the protection of public safety or of residential privacy. And the ordinance is not directed to the unique privacy interests of persons residing in their homes because it applies not only to door-to-door solicitation, but also to solicitation on "public streets and public ways." Pp. 114-115. 590 F. 2d 218, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment in favor of the defendants in a civil rights case brought by two Negro police officers who were charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, alleges that the Department of Justice improperly used a written personnel test to determine whether a certain number of black officers had been selected to serve as officers in the department.  According to the complaint, the test, which is designed to detect whether a person has acquired a particular level of verbal and/or written skill, was not sufficient to establish that a significant proportion of blacks failed the test.  In addition, the complaint alleges that a disproportionately high percentage of blacks fail the test and that the department had made substantial efforts to recruit them.  As a result, the defendants were not entitled to relief on the basis of any reasonable basis.  For example, the SEC's Complaint, filed on December 10, 2016, alleged that the District Court improperly used the written test as a basis for its decision to impose a temporary restraining order and order against the defendants.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the Complaint in the SEC, the Defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a penny stock bar.  On January 24, 2019, the Honorable Judge Robert E. Bentsen of the U. S. district court for the Southern District of New York granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment against them and ordered them to comply with the court's order.

After respondent was convicted of several counts of delivering cocaine base in violation of Washington law, the State Supreme Court reversed, concluding that the lower court erred in imposing consecutive sentences on the grounds that the drug trafficking offense involved was not a “serious” offense for purposes of the Armed Career Criminals Act (ACCA). The State Supreme Court relied on a Washington statute providing that a drug offense is “serious” if a maximum term of imprisonment of 10 years or more is prescribed by law for the offense. The State Supreme Court concluded that the maximum term of imprisonment for the drug offense at issue was 10 years. Held: The “maximum term of imprisonment … prescribed by law” for the state drug convictions at issue was the 10-year maximum set by the applicable recidivist provision. Pp. 4−12. (a) The ACCA defines a “serious drug offense” as an offense involving the manufacture, distribution, or possession of illegal drugs that carries a maximum term of imprisonment of 10 years or more. Here, the State Supreme Court identified the maximum term of imprisonment for the drug offense at issue as 10 years. That determination comports with the ordinary meaning of the phrase “maximum term of imprisonment … prescribed by law.” The phrase “maximum term of imprisonment” refers to the highest term of incarceration that a state law allows for the commission of a particular offense. And the phrase “prescribed by law” indicates that the maximum term of imprisonment is the term that a state law specifies. Both phrases are commonly used together in statutes setting forth maximum penalties. Moreover, the phrase “maximum term of imprisonment … prescribed by law” appears elsewhere in the ACCA, indicating that Congress intended the phrase to have the same meaning throughout the statute. Pp. 4−6. (b) Respondent attempts to limit the scope of the phrase “maximum term of imprisonment … prescribed by law” by arguing that the phrase applies only to the top sentence in a guidelines range. His argument fails. First, the top sentence in a guidelines range is generally not really the “maximum term… prescribed by law” for the “offense” because guidelines systems typically allow a sentencing judge to impose a sentence that exceeds the top of the guidelines range under appropriate circumstances. Second, the concept of the “maximum” term of imprisonment or sentence prescribed by law was used in many statutes that predate the enactment of the ACCA and the federal Sentencing Reform Act of 1984, and in all those statutes the concept necessarily referred to the maximum term prescribed by the relevant criminal statute, not the top of a sentencing guideline range. Pp. 6−10. (c) Respondent’s remaining arguments against the Court’s interpretation of the phrase “maximum term of imprisonment … prescribed by law” are unpersuasive. Pp. 10−11. 466 Fed. Appx. 658, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

After petitioners, who were appointed to the Missouri Supreme Court and intermediate appellate courts, lost their respective races for retention, they brought suit in Federal District Court alleging that the Missouri Constitution's mandatory retirement provision for judges violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court entered judgment for petitioners, concluding that the mandatory retirement provision constituted an invidious discrimination against judges who reach age 70. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that the provision did not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Held: 1. The Missouri Constitution's mandatory retirement provision does not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 108-114. (a) There is no merit to petitioners' argument that, even if they are not covered by the Americans with Disabilities Education Act of 1990 (ADEA), the mandatory retirement provision violates the Equal Protection Clause. Although the ADEA clearly excludes most important public officials, including judges, from its coverage, it is at least ambiguous whether Congress intended that appointed judges nonetheless be included. In the face of such ambiguity, this Court will not attribute to Congress an intent to intrude on state governmental functions regardless of whether Congress acted pursuant to its Commerce Clause powers or § 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 108-111. (b) The mandatory retirement provision passes constitutional muster under the rational basis test applicable where a classification burdens neither a suspect group nor a fundamental interest. The people of Missouri have a legitimate, indeed compelling, interest in maintaining a judiciary fully capable of performing the demanding tasks that judges must perform. Physical and mental capacity sometimes diminish with age, and voluntary retirement will not always suffice. Nor may impeachment serve acceptably the goal of a fully functioning judiciary. Similarly, the election process may be inadequate to remove judges whose performance is deficient. The mandatory retirement provision is also a rational explanation for the fact that state judges are subject to a mandatory retirement provision, whereas other state officials, whose performance is subject to greater public scrutiny and who are subject to more standard elections, are not. Finally, the distinction between judges and other state employees, in whom a deterioration in performance is more readily discernible and who are more easily removed, is also supported by the mandatory retirement provision. Pp. 111-114. 2. The people of Missouri have established a qualification for those who would be their judges. It is their prerogative as citizens of a sovereign State to do so. Neither the ADEA nor the Equal Protection Clause prohibits the choice they have made. P. 114. 909 F. 2d 1208, affirmed.

A New York Town Justice, acting on a police investigator's affidavit that "similar" films and printed matter portraying similar activities could be found on the premises of petitioner's bookstore, issued a warrant authorizing a search of the premises for such items. The warrant recited that the Town Justice had determined that the items to be seized were possessed in violation of the state obscenity laws, but it did not purport to particularly describe the items to be seized. The warrant also recited that the Town Justice would determine independently whether any other items at the premises were possessed in violation of the law and subject to seizure. The warrant was not completed until after the items had been seized, and the Town Justice did not list or describe the items seized. The items seized included 397 magazines, 431 reels of film, and various other items. Petitioner was convicted of violating the state obscenity laws, and the New York Appellate Term affirmed. 

Held: 
1. The warrant violated the Fourth Amendment. The warrant did not purport to particularly describe the items to be seized, and it left it entirely to the discretion of the officials conducting the search to decide what items were likely obscene and to accomplish their seizure. The Fourth Amendment does not permit such action, and nor does it countenance open-ended warrants, to be completed while a search is being conducted and items seized or after the seizure has been carried out. Pp. 329-330. 
2. The Town Justice's participation in the search did not ensure that no items would be seized absent probable cause to believe they were obscene, and it did not enable petitioner to enjoy an immediate adversary hearing on the issue. The Town Justice allowed himself to become a member, if not the leader, of the search party, which was essentially a police operation. Once in the store, he conducted a generalized search under authority of an invalid warrant, and he was not acting as a judicial officer but as an adjunct law enforcement officer. When he ordered an item seized because he believed it was obscene, he instructed the police officers to seize all "similar" items as well, leaving determination of what was "similar" to the officer's discretion. Indeed, he yielded to the State Police even the completion of the general provision of the warrant. Pp. 330-333. 
3. The Town Justice's participation in the search did not render petitioner's display of the items at issue to the public in areas of its store open to them a consent to wholesale searches and seizures that did not conform to Fourth Amendment guarantees. Pp. 333-334. 
4. There is no basis for the notion that because a retail store invites the public to enter, it consents to wholesale searches and seizures that do not conform to Fourth Amendment guarantees. P. 334. 
5. The suggestion that petitioner through its clerk consented to the sweeping search also comes too late. After the police investigator was placed under arrest and was aware of the presumed authority of the search warrant, his conduct complying with official requests cannot, on this record, be considered free and voluntary. Any "consent" given in the face of "colorably lawful coercion" cannot validate the illegal acts shown here. P. 334. 60 N. Y. 2d 410, 483 N. E. 2d 1112, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed a lower court's decision to dismiss a First Amendment challenge to a federal law that requires handlers of fresh mushrooms to pay a fee to the Mushroom Promotion, Research, and Consumer Information Act of 1990 (MPRIA) to fund advertising for the product. The Court held that the fee was not part of a more comprehensive program for agricultural marketing, thus dictating a different result than in Glickman v. Wileman Brothers & Elliott, Inc., 521 F.3d 221 (1999), which held that a similar law requiring producers of certain California tree fruit to pay for product advertising was constitutional. In this case, the Court found that the Mushroom Council's fee was a forced subsidy for generic advertising, which violated the First Amendment right to free speech. In a concurring opinion, Justice Thomas agreed with the Court, stating that the Court's earlier decision did not address the issue of whether the Council had the authority to impose the fee. The Supreme Court has not yet issued a decision on the matter. The case will be decided by Justices John G.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of New York's decision to deny certification to aliens who did not intend to renounce their foreign citizenship and swear allegiance to the United States. The Court held that the denial of certification was consistent with the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and did not violate the Due Process Clause. The Court reasoned that the right to hold public office carries with it significant responsibilities and that the ability to exercise those responsibilities effectively depends on the holder's commitment to the interests of the community. Therefore, the Court concluded that the State had a compelling interest in ensuring that public school teachers were committed to the welfare of the students and the community they served.

The Supreme Court addressed whether admiralty jurisdiction applies to claims arising from agency contracts, specifically in the context of a dispute over unpaid fuel bills for a vessel. The case involved Exxon Corporation, which had provided marine fuels to Waterman Steamship Corporation's vessels, including the vessel Green Harbour ex William Hooper, owned by Central Gulf Lines, Inc.

Exxon acted as an agent in procuring fuel from Arabian Marine Operating Co. and sought payment from Waterman, which had entered bankruptcy. Exxon claimed a maritime lien on the vessel under the Federal Maritime Lien Act. The District Court, following precedent from Minturn v. Maynard and the Second Circuit's interpretation, ruled it lacked admiralty jurisdiction over the claim, as agency contracts were traditionally excluded from such jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the conflict among circuits regarding the scope of the Minturn decision and to consider whether Minturn should be overruled. The Court concluded that the Minturn decision, which established a per se rule excluding agency contracts from admiralty jurisdiction, was no longer consistent with modern principles of admiralty law. The Court emphasized that the nature and subject matter of the contract should be the primary consideration for admiralty jurisdiction, not the status of the claimant or the form of the contract.

The Court overruled Minturn, stating that lower courts should assess whether the services performed under an agency contract are maritime in nature. Applying this reasoning, the Court found that admiralty jurisdiction did extend to Exxon's claim regarding the delivery of fuel in Jeddah, as the nature of the transaction was maritime.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, without expressing a view on whether Exxon is entitled to a maritime lien under the Federal Maritime Lien Act.

In this Supreme Court opinion, the central issue was whether individuals adversely affected by a federal agency's violation of the Privacy Act of 1974 must prove actual damages to qualify for a minimum statutory award of $1,000. The Court held that plaintiffs must indeed demonstrate actual damages to be eligible for the award.

The case involved petitioner Buck Doe, who filed for benefits under the Black Lung Benefits Act and had his Social Security number improperly disclosed by the Department of Labor, in violation of the Privacy Act. Doe and others sued the Department, seeking damages for the violation. The District Court awarded Doe $1,000 in statutory damages, but the Fourth Circuit reversed, requiring proof of actual damages.

The Supreme Court affirmed the Fourth Circuit's decision, emphasizing that the Privacy Act's text requires a plaintiff to show actual damages sustained due to the agency's intentional or willful violation to be "entitled to recovery." The Court reasoned that the statutory language, traditional tort principles, and the legislative history of the Privacy Act support the conclusion that presumed or general damages are not authorized without proof of actual harm.

The Court also addressed the argument that the requirement of actual damages undermines the purpose of the Privacy Act, which is to provide relief for adverse effects caused by violations. The Court found that the language of the Act, which allows for civil actions by those adversely affected, serves to establish standing to sue rather than to guarantee recovery without proof of actual damages.

The opinion concluded that the Privacy Act guarantees the $1,000 minimum only to plaintiffs who have suffered actual damages, and not merely for an adverse effect from an intentional or willful violation. Dissenting opinions argued that the Act should be interpreted to include anyone experiencing an adverse effect from such a violation, without the need to prove actual damages, to fulfill the Act's purpose of deterring violations and providing remedies.

Implications of the decision include a higher threshold for plaintiffs seeking statutory damages under the Privacy Act, as they must now provide evidence of actual harm to receive the minimum award. This may limit the number of successful claims against federal agencies for Privacy Act violations.

In the case of Karen Sutton and Kimberly Hinton v. United Air Lines, Inc., the Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals, which had dismissed the petitioners' claim under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA). The petitioners, twin sisters with severe myopia, argued that United Air Lines discriminated against them based on their disability when the airline refused to hire them as commercial airline pilots due to their uncorrected vision not meeting the company's minimum requirements.

The Supreme Court held that the determination of whether an individual is disabled under the ADA should consider any measures that mitigate the individual's impairment, such as eyeglasses or contact lenses. Since the petitioners' vision was corrected to 20/20 with such measures, they were not considered disabled under the ADA because they were not substantially limited in any major life activity.

Furthermore, the Court concluded that the petitioners did not adequately allege that United Air Lines "regarded" them as having a disability. The airline's requirement for uncorrected visual acuity did not suggest that it viewed the petitioners as substantially limited in the major life activity of working. The Court clarified that an inability to perform a single, specific job does not equate to a substantial limitation in the major life activity of working. The petitioners failed to show that they were regarded as unable to perform a broad class of jobs.

The implications of this decision are that individuals who can mitigate their impairments with corrective measures may not be considered disabled under the ADA, and that employers can have job requirements that disqualify individuals from specific positions without necessarily regarding them as disabled. This decision emphasizes an individualized assessment of disability and the consideration of mitigating measures in determining whether an individual is protected under the ADA.

In the case of John Thompson vs. Harry Connick (in his official capacity as the Orleans Parish District Attorney), the Supreme Court addressed whether a district attorney's office could be held liable under 42 U.S.C. §1983 for a single Brady violation due to failure to train prosecutors adequately. Brady v. Maryland requires prosecutors to disclose exculpatory evidence to the defense. Thompson, who was wrongfully convicted and spent 18 years in prison, sued the district attorney's office, claiming the nondisclosure of exculpatory evidence was due to inadequate training on Brady obligations.

The district attorney's office conceded a Brady violation occurred during Thompson's prosecution. Thompson was awarded $14 million in damages by a jury, and the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit affirmed the decision. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to decide on the liability of the district attorney's office for the failure to train based on a single violation.

The Supreme Court held that a district attorney's office cannot be held liable under §1983 for a failure to train based on a single Brady violation. The Court reasoned that a pattern of similar violations is typically necessary to demonstrate deliberate indifference, which is required to establish municipal liability. The Court found that the previous Brady violations by the district attorney's office were not similar to the violation in Thompson's case and therefore could not have put the district attorney on notice that specific training was necessary.

The Court also distinguished between the need for training in the hypothetical scenario posed in Canton v. Harris and the actual circumstances of Thompson's case. Lawyers, unlike police officers, are expected to have legal training and ethical obligations that equip them to handle Brady issues. The Court concluded that the lack of specific in-house training on Brady obligations did not amount to deliberate indifference.

Ultimately, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, ruling that the district attorney's office was not liable for the failure to train its prosecutors in this instance. The decision implies that for a district attorney's office to be held liable for failure to train under §1983, there must be evidence of a pattern of constitutional violations, not just a single incident.

The Supreme Court has reaffirmed its previous decision that the Navajo Nation's claim for compensation against the Federal Government for alleged breach of trust in connection with the approval of amendments to a coal lease fails. The Navajo Nation had argued that the Secretary of the Interior breached fiduciary duties by approving amendments to a coal lease under terms unfavorable to the Tribe, following ex parte contacts with the coal company.

The Court reiterated that the Federal Government cannot be sued without its consent, which is limitedly granted through statutes like the Indian Tucker Act. This Act allows for claims against the United States by Indian tribes based on laws, treaties, or executive orders, but does not create substantive rights itself. For a tribe to invoke jurisdiction under the Indian Tucker Act, it must identify a substantive source of law that establishes specific duties and allege that the Government failed to perform those duties. Additionally, the law must be interpreted as mandating compensation for damages sustained due to a breach of those duties.

The Court examined various statutes cited by the Navajo Nation, including the Indian Mineral Leasing Act of 1938 (IMLA), the Navajo-Hopi Rehabilitation Act of 1950, and the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (SMCRA). The Court found that none of these statutes provided a substantive source of law that established specific fiduciary duties related to the coal lease amendments, nor could they be fairly interpreted as mandating compensation by the Federal Government for the alleged breach of trust.

The Court concluded that the Navajo Nation's claim could not proceed because it could not identify a specific, applicable, trust-creating statute or regulation that the Government violated. As a result, the judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed, and the case was remanded with instructions to affirm the dismissal of the Tribe's complaint. The decision implies that the Navajo Nation has no further legal recourse against the Federal Government for this claim.

Respondent's pregnant wife and two daughters, aged 2 and 5, were brutally murdered in their home on the Fort Bragg, N. C., military reservation. The Army Criminal Investigation Division (CID) advised respondent that he was a suspect in the case and confined him to quarters. Respondent moved to dismiss the indictment, on the grounds that the delay in bringing him to trial violated his Sixth Amendment right to a speedy trial. The District Court denied the motion, but the Court of Appeals allowed an interlocutory appeal and reversed. Held: The delay between the submission of the CID report to the Justice Department and the August 1974 convening of the grand jury violated his rights under the Speedy Trial Clause of the Sixth Amendment. Pp. 531-532. (a) In addition to the period after indictment, the period between arrest and indictment must be considered in evaluating a Speedy trial Clause claim. Dillingham v. United States, 423 U. S. 64, 96 S.Ct. 303, 46 L.Ed. 2d 205. Although delay prior to arrest or indictment may give rise to a due process claim under the Fifth Amendment, see United States v. Lovasco, 431 U.S. 783, 788-789, and any undue delay after charges are dismissed, like any delay before charges are filed, must be scrutinized under the Due Process Clause and by statutes of limitations. P. 533. (b) The fact that respondent was not under arrest, not in custody, and not subject to any "criminal prosecution" was not sufficient to violate his rights, since the delay between dismissal of military charges and a subsequent indictment on civilian criminal charges did not violate his right under the First Amendment. In addition, the time between the civilian indictment and trial must be evaluated in evaluating an "speedy trial" claim, see, e. g., United Statesv. Marion, 404 U. s. 307, 313, or to a claim under any applicable statutes of limitation, no Sixth Amendment rights to trial arises until charges are pending. Similarly, the "Speedy Trial" Clause has no application after the Government, acting in good faith, formally drops charges. Any undue delay in the criminal prosecution and the continuing investigation after the Army charges have been dismissed must be examined under the due process Clause, not the Spey Trial Clause. P p. 534. (c) The facts in this case are not in issue; a jury heard and saw all the witnesses and saw the tangible evidence. The only point raised here by petitioner involves a legal issue under the Act of the Fifth and Sixth Amendments. The time between dismissal and indictment on military criminal charges is not limited to those persons who have been "accused" in the course of that prosecution, and, once the charges instituted by the Army were dismissed, respondent was legally and constitutionally in the same posture as though no charges had been made. During the intervening period, he was not in arrest and not in prison, and was free to go about his affairs, to practice his profession, and to continue with his life. During this period, there were undesirable consequences flowing from the initial accusation of the Army and the ongoing investigation after those charges were dismissed. In any event, there was no criminal prosecution pending on which MacDonald could have been tried until the grand juries returned the indictment on which he was tried and convicted. P, 535. (d) Respondent's constitutional right to the speedy trial was violated by the delay of his trial on the basis of the delay. The case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama ruled in favor of a restaurant in Birmingham, Alabama, in a case that challenged the constitutionality of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and its enforcement. The restaurant, Ollie's Barbecue, had refused to serve Negroes in its dining accommodations since its original opening in 1927, and since July 2, 1964, it had been operating in violation of the Act. The court found that a substantial portion of the food served in the restaurant had moved in interstate commerce, and that the restaurant would lose a substantial amount of business if it were required to serve them. The district court concluded that the Act could not be applied under the Fourteenth Amendment because it was conceded that the State of Alabama was not involved in the refusal of the restaurant to serveNegroes. The Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit, however, held that the district court's ruling was not inconsistent with the federal courts' prior decisions on the issue. The appeals court held that there was no reason to conclude that the District Court's decision was inconsistent with those decisions. The Appeals Court also held that it was not necessary to grant relief to the restaurant because it had not proven that it had violated the law. The case is now before us for further consideration. We conclude that, with the above caveat, the denial of discretionary declaratory relief is not required here.

Title: Gonzales v. United States

Summary: In Gonzales v. United States, the Supreme Court ruled that the Second Amendment allows individuals to possess handguns for self-defense outside their homes. The Court struck down a provision of the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act that required firearms purchasers to wait five days before taking delivery of their guns. Justice Scalia wrote the majority opinion, which was joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Alito, Thomas, and Kennedy. Justice Breyer dissented, while Justice Ginsburg concurred in part and dissented in part.

Petitioner was convicted in a Federal District Court of violating the Narcotic Drugs Import and Export Act by "knowingly receiving" heroin which he allegedly received from an informer named Doe. At the trial, the Government relied principally on the testimony of four government witnesses -two federal narcotics agents and two policemen-who had observed petitioner and Doe together in Doe's automobile and later in petitioner's automobile. One of the policemen had hidden himself in the trunk of Doe's automobile and had heard a conversation between petitioner and Doe. Another policeman had participated in the arrest of petitioner and Doe and had heard a similar conversation between them. A third policeman had participated in the arrest of petitioner and Doe and had heard a different conversation between them. And a fourth witness, a federal agent, had participated in the arrest of petitioner and Doe and had heard yet another conversation between them. All of these conversations occurred in the presence of Doe and concerned matters which were material to the issues in the case. Before trial, petitioner demanded the production of Doe, but the Government refused to produce him, claiming that he was an informer and that his identity was privileged. Held: Under the circumstances of this case, the trial court committed prejudicial error in permitting the Government to withhold the identity of its informer. Pp. 244-253. (a) No fixed rule with respect to disclosure of the identity of an informer can be justified. Balancing the public interest in protecting the flow of information against the individual's right to prepare his defense requires consideration of all the facts and circumstances of each case. Pp. 248-250. (b) Here, the materiality of Doe's possible testimony must be determined by reference to the offense charged in Count II and the evidence relating to that count. That count charged that petitioner "did then and there fraudulently and knowingly receive, conceal, buy and facilitate the transportation and concealment after importation of ...heroin, knowing the same to be imported into the United States contrary to law." This charge, when viewed in connection with the evidence introduced at the trial, is so closely related to Doe as to make his identity and testimony highly material. Pp. 250-252. (c) Since the Government's informer was the sole participant, other than the accused, in the transaction charged, and since he was the only witness in a position to amplify or contradict the testimony of government witnesses, the trial court committed prejudicial error in permitting the Government to withhold his identity. Pp. 252-253. 229 F. 2d 812, reversed and remanded.

("Advisers"), and Rules 206(3) and (4) thereunder.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-01-17 (1933). Case Name: Thomas Grimshaw vs. Virginia
Case Number: 95-10296
Decided Date: February 22, 1996
Judge: Justice John Paul Stevens
Issue: Whether the denial of Thomas Grimshaw’s request for a protective order preventing the introduction of certain evidence at his capital punishment trial constituted a violation of his Sixth Amendment right to due process?
Holding: Yes, the denial of Grimshaw’s request for a protective order constituted a violation of his Sixth Amendment right to due process. The Court remands the case to the lower courts for further proceedings.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Arizona has ruled that Arizona taxpayers who challenged a tax credit for contributions to school tuition organizations (STOs) did not have standing to do so because they were Arizona residents. The court found that the taxpayers did not show that they had standing to challenge the tax credit because they are taxpayers. The taxpayers alleged that 41–1089 allows STOs to use State income-tax revenues to pay tuition for students at religious schools, some of which "discriminate on the basis of religion in selecting students." The court ruled that the Arizona Supreme Court had rejected the taxpayers' claims on the merits, and that the case should be dismissed for want of jurisdiction. The Court found that, in the absence of a showing of standing, the taxpayers lacked standing to commence this action, and their suit must be dismissed. The Arizona Department of Revenue, which had previously dismissed the case, has now filed an emergency motion to dismiss the case. The case was brought by a group of Arizona residents who claimed that Arizona's tax credit violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the United States Constitution and the Arizona Constitution's Establishment Clause. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Arizona STOs, and the case is now being handled by a federal district court judge.

The Supreme Court of the United States decided the case of Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Haas, 559 U.S. __ (2010). The case involves a dispute between a group of American plaintiffs and several foreign companies over the quality of a tire that led to a fatal car accident in Argentina. The issue presented in the case is whether the foreign companies can be held liable for the death of the Argentinian driver under the principles of international civil procedure.

The majority opinion, written by Justice John Paul Stevens, holds that the foreign companies cannot be held liable for the death of the Argentinian driver under the principles of international civil procedure. According to the majority, the principle of comity, which recognizes the validity of foreign judgments and legal proceedings, precludes the imposition of liability on the foreign companies. The majority argues that the foreign companies' conduct in Argentina falls within the scope of their domestic law, and therefore, should not be judged according to the standards of another country's law.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor dissented from the majority opinion, arguing that the principle of comity should not prevent the imposition of liability on the foreign companies in this case. She believes that the death of the Argentinian driver resulted from the failure of the foreign companies to meet acceptable safety standards, and that these standards should be applied regardless of the location of the incident. Justice Sotomayor also notes that the foreign companies have significant economic interests in the United States, and therefore, should be held responsible for their actions in accordance with our nation's laws.

Respondent Nussle, an inmate in a Connecticut prison, brought a complaint charging that corrections officers singled him out for a severe beating, in violation of the Eighth Amendment's ban on "cruel and unusual punishments." The District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to exhaust administrative remedies. The Court of Appeals reversed the District Court's judgment, holding that "exhaustion of administrative remedies is not required for [prisoner] suits under 42 U. S. C. 1983." The Second Circuit held that 1997e(a)'s exhaustion requirement applies to all prisoners seeking redress for prison circumstances or occurrences. Held: 1. The exhaustion requirement does not apply to all inmate suits about prison conditions. Pp. 531-532. (a) The PLRA's text and context support the contention that prisoners alleging assaults by prison guards must meet the requirement before commencing a civil rights action. P. 533.
