(b) The phrase "prison conditions" in the exhaustion prescription is in large part discretionary; it could be ordered only if the State's prison grievance system met specified federal standards, and even then, only if, in the particular case, the court believed the requirement "appropriate and in the interests of justice." McCarthy v. Board of Regents of Fla., 457 U.S. 496, 150-151, and the Second Circuit found support for its position in pre-PLRA decisions in which this Court had "disaggreg[ed]" that Congress sought to curtail suits qualifying as "frivolous" because of their "subject matter," e.g., suits over "insufficient storage locker space," "a defective haircut," or "being served chunky peanut butter instead of the creamy variety." Ibid. The court's decision that the exhaustion requirement is not applicable to all prisoner suits is supported by the PLRA, which described the cases covered as "action[s] ... brought with respect to prison conditions" as amended, and that "no action shall be brought ... by a prisoner confined in any jail, prison, or other correctional facility until such administrative remedies as are available are exhausted." Certiorari granted; 224 F. 3d 446, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas today entered a final judgment against a Texas-based retired public school teacher for his alleged lack of a contractual or tenure right to re-employment.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Houston, Texas, Robert Sindermann was hired as a professor of Government and Social Science at Odessa Junior College in 1969. He was employed at the college for four successive years, under a series of one-year contracts. The complaint alleges that, despite his lack of tenure, the college's decision not to rehire him was based on his public criticism of the college administration and thus infringed his right to freedom of speech.  The complaint further alleges that the college did not provide him an opportunity to challenge the nonrenewal of his contract.  As alleged in the complaint, however, this was a "violation" of the First and Fourteenth Amendment of the federal securities laws.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the SEC, the respondent consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a penny stock bar against him.  In a parallel action, the Texas Attorney General's Office today announced criminal charges against the respondent.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Texas Department of Education and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Petitioner was indicted on two counts of violating the Narcotic Drugs Import and Export Act, as amended. The first count charged that he fraudulently and knowingly received, conceal, buy and facilitate the transportation and concealment after importation of heroin knowing the same to be imported into the United States contrary to law. The Government objected on the ground that John Doe was an informer and that his identity was privileged. Petitioner waived a jury and was tried by the District Court. The trial court denied petitioner's requests for disclosure of John Doe's identity. The Court of Appeals sustained the conviction, holding that the concurrent sentence was supported by the conviction on Count 2 and that the trial court had not abused its discretion in denying petitioner's request for disclosure. Held: 1. The conviction is sustained since the identity of the informer, in the circumstances of this case, had no real bearing on that charge and is therefore privileged. Scher v. United States, 305 U. S. 251, 254. Pp. 531-532. (a) The fact that petitioner was faced with the burden of explaining or justifying his alleged possession of the heroin emphasizea his vital need for access to any material witness. P. 533. (b) In the circumstances here present, the Government could not withhold his identity, his whereabouts, and whether he was alive or dead at the time of trial. The circumstances of the case demonstrate that petitioner's possible testimony was highly relevant and might have been helpful to the defense. So far as petitioner knew, he and John Doe were alone and unobserved during the crucial occurrence for which he was indicted. Unless petitioner waived his constitutional right not to take the stand in his own defense, he was his one material witness, and the fact that he was confronted with a police officer and a Chicago police officer who knew him by sight was not a substitute for an opportunity to examine the man who had been nearest to him and took part in the transaction. Thus, once the information of the officer had been disclosed to those who would have cause to resent the communication, the privilege is no longer applicable; and, in these situations, the Trial Court may require disclosure and, if the Government withholds the information, dismiss the action. Nor is the privilege limited by its underlying purpose, where the disclosure of the contents of a communication will not tend to reveal the person's identity, the contents are not privileged, and once the identity has been disclosed it is no more applicable. P p. 534. (c) A further limitation on the applicability of the privilege arises from the fundamental requirements of fairness. Where the disclosure is relevant and helpful in the defense of an accused, or is essential to a fair determination of a cause, a privilege must give way. In these situations the trial trial court may require disclosures and, under certain circumstances the Government dismisses the action; and where the legality of a search without a warrant is in issue and the communications of an informant are claimed to establish probable cause, it must disclose the person who provided the information to the Government. The only person, other than petitioner himself, who could controvert, emplain or amplify Bryson's report of this important conversation was John Doe. Contradiction or amplification might have borne upon petitioner's knowledge of the material contents of the package or might have tended to show an entrapment, and if the information was disclosed to others, it no longer applies to the individual who provided it to the government in the event of a crime charged, the possible defenses, possible significance of the informant's testimony, and other relevant factors. In such cases, the burden is on the accused, at a certain point, to go forward with his defense, and it is the accused rather than the Government to decide, since the accused is the one who is the material witness to the crime charged. In this case the materiality of the possible testimony, when viewed in connection with the evidence introduced at the trial, is so closely related to John Doe as to make his identity and testimony highly material, that it must be determined by reference to the offense charged and the evidence relating to that count, and that, therefore, the defendant's identity is highly material. The fact petitioner here was faced, at that point, with the burdens of explaining and justifying his claim of possession of heroin, emphasizeahis vital need to access any material witnesses. Otherwise the burden must be going forward with the defense, otherwise the burden will become unduly heavy. Pc. 535-542. 229 F. 2d 812, affirmed.

In the case of Jean Marc Nken v. Holder, the U.S. Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether a court of appeals can issue a stay of removal for an alien pending the outcome of an appeal under the traditional criteria for stays, or whether the more restrictive standard set by 8 U.S.C. §1252(f)(2) applies. Nken, a Cameroonian national, faced removal from the United States after his asylum claim and subsequent appeals were denied. He sought a stay of removal while his appeal was being considered, arguing that the traditional criteria for a stay should apply, rather than the stringent standard under §1252(f)(2), which requires clear and convincing evidence that the removal is prohibited by law.

The Supreme Court agreed with Nken, holding that the traditional criteria for issuing a stay, not the restrictive standard of §1252(f)(2), apply to stays of removal. The Court reasoned that the power to issue a stay is part of the inherent authority of appellate courts and is necessary to allow for responsible judicial review. The Court distinguished between injunctions, which direct a party's conduct, and stays, which suspend judicial proceedings or the enforceability of an order. The Court found that the language of §1252(f)(2) does not comfortably cover stays and that Congress did not intend to alter the traditional stay standard when it enacted the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA).

The Court clarified that the traditional criteria for a stay require the applicant to show (1) a strong likelihood of success on the merits, (2) that they will suffer irreparable injury without a stay, (3) that the stay will not substantially harm other parties, and (4) that the public interest supports granting a stay. The Court emphasized that removal alone does not constitute irreparable injury and that the public interest in prompt execution of removal orders must be considered.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for consideration of Nken's motion for a stay under the traditional criteria. The decision implies that appellate courts should continue to use their discretion in granting stays of removal based on the established four-factor test, rather than the more stringent standard previously applied by some courts under §1252(f)(2).

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a complaint filed by an inmate alleging that he was beaten by prison guards. The court found that the complaint, filed in federal district court, was filed before the three-year statute of limitations ran out on the 1983 claim. The Second Circuit held that the law's "exhaustion" provision applies only to "circumstances affecting everyone in the area" rather than "single or momentary matter[s] directed at particular individuals." The court also held that it is an exception "to the general rule of non-exhaustion in 1983 cases" because it is "not required for [prisoner] claims of assault or excessive force brought under 1983"<n>The Second Circuit's decision is consistent with the text and purpose of the Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (PLRA), which provides that "no action shall be brought with respect to prison conditions until such administrative remedies as are available are exhausted"

Section 802(13) defines the term “felony” to mean an offense involving specified drugs that is “punishable by imprisonment for more than one year under any law of the United States or of a State or foreign country,” 21 U. S. C. §841(b)(1)(A), and §802(44). The term is used in §802 (44) to mean “any Federal or State offense” classified by applicable federal or State law as a felony.” A prior drug offense does not rank as a misdemeanor unless it is (1) classified as felony under the law of a punishing jurisdiction, per §§802(13); and (2) punishable by more than a year’s imprisonment, per §802’44. Respondent Burgess pleaded guilty in the District Court for the District of South Carolina to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of cocaine base in violation of §§841 (a) and 846. The Government argued that the enhancement was mandatory because Congress defined “Felony drug offense’” as a term of art defined by § 802(44) without reference to the statute. The District Court rejected Burgess’ argument, but the Government moved for a downward departure based on his substantial assistance in another prosecution. The Fourth Circuit affirmed. Held: A state drug offense classified as a federal misdemeanor, but punishable by a more-than-one-year imprisonment, qualifies as a “ ‘felon drug offense,’ even if state law classifies the offense. Pp. 5–11. (a)(1) (emphasis added). (b) Section 802(4) provides that a drug crime classified by state law “[a] felony” “is punishable by imprisonment” under any federal or state law, but “possession of a firearm” is punishable “for more than two years under any [Federal or State] law … or … any [foreign] country” prohibiting or restricting conduct relating to certain types of drugs. Section 802’13 provides that “the term ‘[felone’ means an offense that is punishable by ... imprisonment ... .” and that term is defined exclusively by §802. “” Burgess argues here, as he did below, is defined only by §§802 (13) and (11) does not incorporate the definition of the term. The definition is coherent, complete, and by all signs exclusive. Accordingly, there is no ambiguity for the rule of lenity to resolve. The judgment of the Fourth Circuit is Affirmed.

A Massachusetts pricing order imposes an assessment on all fluid milk sold by dealers to Massachusetts retailers. About two-thirds of that milk is produced out of State. The entire assessment, however, is distributed to Massachusetts dairy farmers. Petitioners then filed an action in state court seeking an injunction against enforcement of the order on the ground that it violated the Commerce Clause of the Federal Constitution. The parties agreed to an expedited appellate procedure, and the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts affirmed. Held: 1. The pricing order is unconstitutional. Pp. 531-532. (a) The imposition of a differential burden on any part of the stream of commerce-from wholesaler to retailer to consumer-is invalid, because a burden placed at the expense of the producers is outweighed by the local benefit of saving the dairy industry from collapse. P. 533. (b) The order imposes no discriminatory burden on interstate commerce, because it is merely the combination of two independently lawful regulations. The Commerce Clause forbids economic protectionism-that is, regulatory measures designed to benefit in-state economic interests by burdening out-of-state competitors. The fact that the Massachusetts milk dealers who pay the order premiums are not competitors of the farmers who receive disbursements from the Dairy Equalization Fund does not immunize a discriminatory measure. New Energy Co. v. Limbach, 486 U. S. 269, 273-274, distinguished. The choice of constitutional means-nondiscriminatory tax and local subsidy-cannot guarantee the constitutionality of the program as a whole. The decision of the Massachusetts Department of Food and Agriculture to adopt regulations that discriminate against interstate commerce is also valid, because subsidies are constitutional exercises of state power, and because the order premium which provides money for the Fund is valid, since it is a nondiscriminatory. Therefore, state statutes that clearly discriminate against the interstate commerce are routinely struck down . . . unless the discrimination is demonstrably justified by a valid factor unrelated to economic protection. Newenergy Co. of Indiana v.Limbach,468 U.S. 263, 273, and other cases have eschewed formalism for a sensitive, case-by-case analysis of purposes and effects. See, e. g., Bacchus Imports, Ltd., v. Dias, 468 U., at 527, 527. The case is filled with state laws that aspire to reap some of the benefits of tariffs by other means. Baldwin v. G. A. F. Seelig, Inc., 294 U. s. 511, which involved a 20% excise tax on all liquor sales, coupled with an exemption for fruit wine manufactured in Hawaii and for okolehao, a brandy distilled from the root of a shrub indigenous to Hawaii. This effect was the motive behind the promulgation of the pricing order. The Massachusetts producers who deliver milk to dealers in that regulated market are participants in the same interstate milk market as the out- of-state producers who sell in the market and are guaranteed the same minimum blend price by the federal order. By granting a tax exemption for local products, Hawaii in effect created a protective tariff. Goods produced in Maine were taxed, but those produced in State were subject to no net tax. It is obvious that the result would have been the same if instead of exempting certain Hawaiian liquors from tax, Hawaii had rebated the amount of tax collected from the sale of those liquors. In addition, the Massachusetts order regulates a portion of a same interstate market in milk that is more broadly regulated by a federal milk marketing order which covers most of New England. The price of the milk is assessed only on Massachusetts sales and distributes it only to Massachusetts producers, and does not exclude either the assessments or the payments from the interstate market. By conjoining a tax and a subsidy, Massachusetts has created a program more dangerous to interstate commerce than either part alone. The Court's judgment is reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of a federal district court in Manhattan that permanently enjoins the Department of Education from enforcing federal law that prohibits the entry of aliens into the United States.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the District Court's order freezing the assets of the district court.  According to the SEC's order, filed on May 24, 2018, the Court entered final judgments in a related case against a former district court judge in which the Court held that the Department had violated the federal law prohibiting aliens from working as teachers.  In its order, the court also ordered the District Attorney's Office to conduct an investigation into the alleged violations of Section 3001(3) of the federal education law, and ordered the district attorney to conduct a parallel criminal investigation. The court's order freezes the assets and assets of any district court defendant and orders him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $10,000.   The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, charges teachers with violating the antifraud provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4), and seeks permanent injunctions, civil penalties, and injunctive relief. The case is being supervised by Joseph G. Sansone, Chief of the Division of Education's Public Finance Abuse Unit. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Respondent was stopped by petitioner police officer during a routine traffic patrol. After determining that respondent's driver's license had expired, petitioner arrested respondent for operating a motor vehicle without a valid license, a misdemeanor in the District of Columbia. Petitioner patted down respondent's jacket and found a packet of cigarettes. Upon opening the packet, petitioner found heroin capsules. Respondent was subsequently tried and convicted for the federal felony of possessing cocaine hydrochloride or any narcotic drug. The District of Columbia Court of Appeals vacated the conviction, ruling that the heroin had been illegally seized and that the search leading thereto was invalid under the Fourth Amendment. That court concluded that the only reason supporting the authority for a full search incident to lawful arrest was the possibility of discovery of evidence or fruits, and that since there could be no evidence or fruits in the case of an offense such as that with which respondent was charged, any protective search would have to be limited by the conditions laid down in Terry v. Ohio, 392 U. S. 1, for a search upon less than probable cause to arrest. Held: 1. The search of respondent's person and the seizure of the heroin were permissible under established Fourth Amendment law. Pp. 108-116. (a) The authority to search the person incident to a lawful custodial arrest, while based upon the need to disarm and to discover evidence, does not depend on what a court may later decide was the probability in a particular arrest situation that weapons or evidence would in fact be found upon the person of the suspect. A custodial arrest of a suspect based on probable cause is a reasonable intrusion under the Fourth Amendment; that intrusion being lawful, a search incident to the arrest requires no additional justification. Pp. 112-114. (b) The facts that petitioner did not indicate any subjective fear of respondent or that he did not himself suspect that respondent was armed are irrelevant to the question whether the search was permissible. Pp. 114-115. 2. The Court of Appeals erred in applying the Terry standard to determine whether the search was permissible. Pp. 115-116. 135 U. S. App. D. C.-207, 415 F. 2d 1197, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reverses a lower court's dismissal of a class action brought by two former University of Minnesota employees against the university for age discrimination in violation of the Minnesota Human Rights Act (MHRA) and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) of 1974 and 1974 respectively. The lower court dismissed the action on the basis that the MHRA's 45-day statute of limitations had lapsed and was not tolled by 28 U. S.C.  1367(d) (1994). The U's appeal has been stayed pending a decision by the United States Supreme Court in another case involving the issue of whether an ADEA claim against a state is barred by the Eleventh Amendment. The appeals court held that the lower court did not abuse its discretion by denying the University's motion to dismiss the action without prejudice. The court found that the University had not shown that it would be unable to prevail on the issues of material fact and that it had not proven that it was subject to MHRA or ADEA liability. The Court also found that there was no basis for the University to show that the appellants had been harmed by their employment. The Appeals Court concluded that the district court had not acted improperly in its dismissal of the action. The full appeals court will consider the matter at a later date.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit recently ruled that the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act of 1974 (RESPA) does not prohibit a single person from accepting a portion or split of a real estate settlement service charge that is not for services performed. The court held that the law does not apply to a person who shares a portion of a settlement-service charge with one or more other persons who did nothing to earn that portion of the charge. The Court's decision is the latest in a series of high-profile cases involving the use of 2607(b) in the settlement of real estate transactions. The case involves three married couples who obtained mortgage loans from Quicken Loans, Inc., and alleged that the company charged them fees for which no services were provided. The complaint alleged that they were charged loan discount fees of $980 and $1,100, respectively, but that Quicken did not give them lower interest rates in return. The Fifth Circuit held that because the alleged fees were not split with another party, the complaint is cognizable under  2607(d)(2) and the district court granted summary judgment in favor of Quicken, concluding that the alleged violations of the law were not of a significant nature and that the case should be dismissed. The Supreme Court agreed, and the case was remanded for further consideration.

After petitioner Baral failed to file his 1988 federal income tax return on time, he paid a penalty for late filing. When he subsequently filed the return, he also paid a penalty for failing to pay all of his 1988 tax liability. On the return, he claimed that he (and his employer on his behalf) had remitted $1,175 more with respect to the 1988 taxable year than he actually owed. Under Internal Revenue Code § 6511(a), he requested that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) apply this excess as a credit toward his outstanding tax obligations for the 1989 taxable year. However, the IRS denied the requested credit, concluding that the claim exceeded the ceiling imposed by § 6511(b)(2)(A)-which states that "the amount of the credit or refund shall not exceed the portion of the tax paid ... equal to 3 years plus the period of any extension of time for filing the return"-because Baral had filed his return on June 1, 1993, and had earlier received a 4-month extension from the initial due date. According to the IRS, Baral had paid no portion of the overpaid tax during the intervening period, and thus faced a ceiling of zero on any allowable refund or credit. Baral then brought suit in Federal District Court for a refund. The court upheld the IRS' denial of the requested credit, looking to § 6513(b)(1), which states that amounts of withheld from wages "shall be deemed to have been paid...on the 15th day of the fourth month following the close of his taxable year," and to § 6513(b)(2), which makes similar provision for amounts submitted as estimated income tax, and concluding that, under those sections, both of the remittances at issue were "paid" on April 15, 1989. Affirming, the Tenth Circuit agreed that the remittances were "paid" on April 15, 1989, but disagreed about why. Held: Both of the remittances at issue were "paid" on April 15, 1989, for purposes of § 6511(b)(2)(A), so that they precede the look-back period, which began on February 1, 1990. Pp. 4-8. (a) Sections 6513(b)(1) and (2) resolve when the remittance of withholding tax by Baral's employer was "paid": Since Baral is a calendar year taxpayer, the $4,104 withheld from his wages during the 1988 calendar year was "paid" on April 15, 1989. Section 6513(b)(2) determines when Baral's remittance of estimated income tax was "paid": Since the referenced § 6012 together with § 6072(a) require that a calendar year taxpayer like Baral file his income tax return on the April 15th following the close of the calendar year, the $1,100 remitted as an estimated income tax in respect of Baral's 1988 tax liability was likewise "paid" on April 15, 1989. And both of these statutorily defined payment dates apply "[f]or purposes of section 6511," the provision directly at issue in this case. Taking a more metaphysical tack, Baral argues that income tax is "paid" under § 6511(b)(2)(A) only when the income tax is assessed, i. e., when the IRS assessed the liability on June 1 or July 19, 1993. But the Code directly contradicts the notion that payment may not occur before assessment. See §§ 6151(a) and 6213(b)(4). Baral's argument finds no support in Rosenmanv . United States, 323 U. S. 658, where this Court applied § 6511's predecessor to a remittance of estimated estate tax. There, the remittance was not governed by a "deemed paid" provision akin to § 6513, and the Court had no occasion to consider the implications of such a provision for determining when a tax is "paid" under the predecessor to § 6511. Pp. 4-7. (b) Baral's position to the extent he submits that payment occurs only at the IRS' assessment would work to the detriment of taxpayers who timely file their returns and claim a refund or credit as compensation for an overpayment. If the IRS does not assess the taxpayer's liability immediately upon receiving the return, the Code allows for payment of interest to the taxpayer on overpayments once the return has been filed and the tax paid, 26 U. S. C. § 6611, but under Baral's view no interest could accrue during the time between the filing of the return and the IRS' assessment. Fortunately for the timely taxpayer, the Code definitively rejects Baral's position in this setting. Section 6611(d) explains that the date of payment is determined according to the provisions of § 6513, which clearly set a deemed date of payment for remittances of withholding and estimated income tax on the April 15 following the relevant taxable year. Pp. 7-8. 199 F. 3d 1255, affirmed.

The Vineville Presbyterian Church of Macon, Ga., was organized in 1904, and first incorporated in 1915. Pursuant to resolutions adopted by the congregation, the church repeatedly has borrowed money on the property, including from members of the congregation. In response to a schism within the church, the Augusta-Macon Presbytery appointed a commission to investigate the dispute and, if possible, to resolve it. The commission eventually issued a written ruling declaring that the minority faction constituted the true congregation of the Vineville church and withdrawing from the majority faction "all authority to exercise office derived from the [PCUS]." The majority took no part in the commission's inquiry, and did not appeal its ruling to a higher PCUS tribunal. The majority then brought this class action in state court, seeking declaratory and injunctive orders establishing their right to exclusive possession and use of the property as a member congregation. The trial court, purporting to apply Georgia's "neutral principles of law" approach to church property disputes, granted judgment for the majority. The Supreme Court of Georgia, holding that the trial court had correctly stated and applied Georgia law, and rejecting the minority's challenge based on the First and Fourteenth Amendments, affirmed the majority's claim. Held: 1. The judgment of the Supreme Court is vacated, and the case is remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion. Pp. 5-7. (a) The neutral-principles analysis of Presbyterian Church v. Eastern Heights Church, 225 Ga. 259, and Carnes v. Smith, 236 Ga. 30, 222 S. E. 2d 322, is consistent with the foregoing constitutional principles. P. 5. (b) Georgia law requires that civil courts defer to the resolution of issues of religious doctrine, practice, and polity by the highest court of a hierarchical church organization. This Court does not declare what the law of Georgia is. Since the grounds for respondents' decision that respondents represent the church remain unarticulated, the judgment is vacated and the cases are remanded to the higher court of the hierarchical church. P p. 6. 2. A State is constitutionally entitled to adopt a rule of compulsory deference to religious authority as a means of adjudicating a church property dispute, even where no issue of doctrinal controversy is involved. The First Amendment does not dictate that a State must follow a particular method of resolving church property property disputes. Nor does the First Amendment require the States to adopt the "neutral principle of law," defeasible upon a showing that the identity of the local church is to be determined by some other means, as in Presbyterian Church I, 393 U. S., at 449, or that the church property is held in trust for the general church and those who remain loyal to it. Nor is there any dispute in the present case about the extent to which the dispute has been resolved within that structure of government, or about the fact that a quorum was present, or whether the final vote has been made. The State may adopt any method of overcoming the majoritarian presumption, so long as the use of that method does not impair free-exercise rights or entangle the civil courts in matters of religious controversy. The Government of Georgia has adopted a presumptive rule of majority representation, defeasibly upon a show that the "local church is not to be established in some other way, or by providing that church property ... is held to trust for [the general church]." Presbyterian Church II, 394 U.S. 367, 368, and Serbian Orthodox Diocese, 426 U. K., at 426, have adopted such a rule, which would require civil courts to examine certain religious documents, such as a church constitution, for language of trust in favor of the General church. Such a determination would appear to require a civil court to pass on questions of religion, and to usurp the function of the commission appointed by the Presbybytery, which already has determined that petitioners represent the "true congregation" of the church. However, under Georgia law the process of identifying the faction that represents the "Vineville church" involves considerations of religion doctrine, polity, and practice. Moreover, the neutral rule is generally employed in the governance of religious societies, see Bouldin v. Alexander, 82 U. s 131, 15 Wall. 131, 21 L. Ed. 69, and can be overcome by providing, in the corporate charter or the constitution of thegeneral church, that, absent some indication to the contrary, a voluntary religious association is represented by a majority of its members. Such an approach is necessary in order to protect the free exercise rights "of those who have formed the association and submitted themselves to its authority." P. 7. (c) A State, constitutionally entitled, to adopt neutral principles of the law as a method of adjudication a churchproperty dispute, would have to adopt an "authoritative resolution of the dispute" method for resolving churchproperty disputes that did not draw the state courts into religious controversies.

Appellants were charged with displaying for sale paper-covered obscene booklets under the general title of "Nights of Horror." The complaint prayed that appellants be enjoined from further distribution of the booklets, that they be required to surrender to the sheriff for destruction all copies in their possession, and that the sheriff be commanded to seize and destroy those copies. The same day the judge, sitting in equity, found that the bookslets were clearly obscene, he enjoined their further distribution and ordered their destruction. Appellants consented to the granting of an injunction pendente lite and did not bring the matter to issue promptly, as was their right under subdivision 2 of the challenged section, which provides that the persons sought to enjoined "shall be entitled to a trial of the issues within one day after joinder of issue and a decision shall be rendered by the court within two days of the conclusion of the trial." Held: 1. The method devised by New York in § 22-a for determining whether a publication is obscene does not differ in essential procedural safeguards from that provided under many state statutes making the distribution of obscene publications a misdemeanor. Pp. 531-532. (a) The judicial angle of vision in testing the validity of a statute like § 22 is "the operation and effect of the statute in substance." P. 532. 2. The restraint upon appellants as merchants in obscenity was narrower than that imposed on Alberts. P. 555. (b) The restraint on appellants was narrower in its effective operation from the type of statute upheld in Albertt, and the restraint was to be closely confined so as to preclude what may fairly be deemed licensing or censorship, and it was a safeguard against frustration of the public interest in effectuating judicial condemnation of obscene matter. The duty of closer analysis and critical judgment in applying the thought behind the phrase has thus been authoritatively put by one who brings weighty learning to his support of constitutionally protected liberties: "What is needed," says Professor Freund, "is a pragmatic assessment of its operation in the particular circumstances. The generalization that prior restraint is particularly obnoxious in civil liberties cases must yield to more particularistic analysis." The Supreme Court and Civil Liberties, 4 Vand. L. Rev. 533, 539. (c) In the absence of any constitutional infirmity, the restraint upon the booksellers in the period before the law strikes is narrower than it was imposed on the defendant. P p. 534. (d) The Court of Appeals, in this case, did not assail the legislation insofar as it outlaws obscenities. P, 535. (e) Neither in the New York Court nor here, did appellants assail § 22's effective operation, since the limitation is the exception; it is closely confined to preclude anything that may fairly-be deemed licensing, censorship, or licensing. Nor is the restraint on the bookseller to dread that the offer for sale of a book may, without prior warning, subject him to a criminal prosecution with the hazard of imprisonment, the civil procedure assures him that such consequences cannot follow unless he ignores a court order specifically directed to him for a prompt and carefully circumscribed determination of the issue of obscensity. Until then, he may keep for sale only the particular booklets theretofore published and adjudged to be obscene, and thus the restraint is not to be held to be narrower than the in terrorem effect of § 1141 of New York's Penal Law, McKinney's Consol. Laws, c. 40, which, inter alia, provides for destruction of obscene matters following conviction for its dissemination. Nor are the consequences of a judicial condemnation under § 22 a more restrictive of freedom of expression than the result of conviction for a misdemeanor, since it is a brake on the temptation to exploit a filthy business offered by the limited hazards of piecemeal prosecutions, sale by sale, of a publication already condemned as obscene. The Court's judgment is affirmed.

The Supreme Court was presented with the question of whether the federal priority statute (31 U.S.C. §3713(a)) requires that a federal tax claim be prioritized over a judgment creditor's perfected lien on real property, despite the Federal Tax Lien Act of 1966 (26 U.S.C. §6321 et seq.) not authorizing such preference.

The case involved Romani Industries, Inc., which had a $400,000 judgment lien against Francis J. Romani, recorded before the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) filed tax liens amounting to approximately $490,000. When Romani died, his estate, consisting solely of real estate worth $53,001, was insufficient to cover both liens. The estate's administrator sought to transfer the property to Romani Industries, but the federal government opposed, citing the priority statute's command that its claim "shall be paid first."

The Pennsylvania courts ruled in favor of Romani Industries, finding an inconsistency between the priority statute and the Tax Lien Act of 1966. They concluded that the 1966 Act limited the operation of the priority statute regarding tax debts. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the conflict and consider the applicability of the priority statute.

The Supreme Court affirmed the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's judgment, holding that the priority statute does not give the federal government preference over secured creditors like Romani Industries with a perfected lien. The Court reasoned that the priority statute's text, history, and interpretation do not support the government's claim over antecedent perfected liens. The Court also noted that the Tax Lien Act of 1966, being the later and more specific statute, should govern the situation, as it reflects a detailed congressional judgment on the priority of federal tax liens and protects various secured interests.

The Court emphasized that the priority statute should not be interpreted to frustrate specific policies embodied in later federal statutes. It also pointed out that Congress' failure to amend the priority statute in 1966 and 1970 does not necessarily indicate an endorsement of the government's position. Instead, the Court suggested that the Tax Lien Act's detailed provisions and policy against secret liens should guide the harmonization of the two statutes.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court held that the federal priority statute does not authorize a preference for federal tax claims over a prior perfected judgment lien, affirming the lower court's decision to allow the transfer of property to Romani Industries.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit ruled that the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) exempts "bona fide executive, administrative, or professional" employees from overtime pay requirements. The court held that the Secretary of Labor's "salary-basis" test for determining an employee's exempt status reflects a permissible reading of the law as it applies to public-sector employees. The FLSA requires that an employee be paid on a salary basis, which in turn requires that his compensation not be subject to reduction because of variations in the "quality or quantity of the work performed"<n>The court found that the St. Louis Police Department's manual, which the department used to determine exempt status, did not address the issue of whether an employee should be paid for work that is not "quality" or "quantity" of work performed. The lower court found in favor of the department's position that the manual did not provide a clear exemption from the test. The appeals court agreed with the lower court's finding that the department did not have to pay overtime to petitioners who were not paid on the salary basis. The Court held that, under the circumstances, the department had not violated the FLSA's exemption provision for executive, Administrative, or Professional employees. In a separate opinion, the appeals court ruled against the department, holding that the exemption provision does not apply to employees who are terminated, demoted, or given restricted assignments. The case is now before the U.N. Supreme Court.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Georgia today entered a final judgment in favor of Chatham County, Georgia, against Northern Insurance Company of New York (Northern).  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Atlanta, Georgia on January 28, 2005, alleges that Chatham Co. and Northern violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The complaint also alleges that the County failed to adequately demonstrate that it was acting as an arm of the State when it operated the Causton Bluff Bridge.  According to the complaint, the County was not entitled to a distinct sovereign immunity defense under the federal securities laws, and instead relied upon principles set out in the SEC’s prior judgments.  In addition, the complaint alleges that, as a result of the collision, Mr. Ludwig and his wife incurred damages in excess of $130,000.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the Commission's judgment, Chatham agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins Northern from violating the federal law, and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $150,000, which is equal to the amount of its disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties to be determined by the court at a later date.  Northern has also agreed to be permanently enjoined from future violations of the federal anti-fraud provisions.  On January 31, 2018, the SEC filed a civil action in the United States District Court in Atlanta against Chatham, Georgia.   The Commission's action, which was filed in the District Court, is subject to court approval.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 565 (January 28, 2013).    In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the District of Florida today announced criminal charges against the County.

In this case, the Supreme Court considered a defamation lawsuit where the plaintiff sought a permanent injunction to prevent the defendants from making certain statements about him in the future. The court held that the injunction, as written, amounted to an overly broad prior restraint upon speech, lacking plausible justification, and therefore violated the First Amendment. The court also noted that since the original purpose of the injunction had been achieved, there were no remaining grounds for the injunction.

Title: Standing to Sue Under the Equal Protection Clause

Summary:

In this case, the Supreme Court considers whether a group of parents have standing to sue a school district under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The parents argue that the school district has failed to provide equal educational opportunities for students with learning disabilities. However, the Supreme Court holds that the parents do not have standing to bring this lawsuit.

Background:

The case began when a group of parents filed a class-action lawsuit against the school district, arguing that the district had failed to provide equal educational opportunities for students with learning disabilities. The parents claimed that the district had denied access to specialized instruction and accommodations needed by these students, leading to unequal treatment and discrimination.

However, the Supreme Court notes that the parents did not have children currently attending the school district. Instead, they were residents of the community who had previously sent their children to the district and were concerned about the quality of education offered to current students. Additionally, the parents had never attempted to obtain accommodations for their own children or participated in any formal complaints regarding the district's practices.

Analysis:

The Supreme Court uses the doctrine of standing to deny the parents' claim to bring the lawsuit. Standing refers to the legal capacity of a person or entity to participate in a lawsuit. The Court explains that standing requires three elements: (1) a connection to the subject matter of the lawsuit, (2) an injury that is concrete and particularized, and (3) a causal link between the injury and the defendants' actions.

First, the Court finds that the parents do not have a connection to the subject matter of the lawsuit. Specifically, the Court notes that the parents have never attended the school district and have no ongoing involvement in the education of current students. Therefore, they lack a personal stake in the outcome of the lawsuit.

Second, the Court determines that the parents' injuries are not concrete and particularized. The Court explains that while the parents may be concerned about the quality of education offered to current students, they have not experienced any harm or injury as a result of the district's actions. Furthermore, the Court notes that the parents' concerns are speculative and hypothetical, rather than concrete and particularized.

Finally, the Court concludes that there is no causal link between the parents' injuries and the defendants' actions. The Court explains that the parents' injuries are not caused by the district's failure to provide equal educational opportunities, but rather by their own perceived inadequacies in the education system. Therefore, the parents' injuries are not attributable to the district's actions.

Conclusion:

Based on these findings, the Supreme Court denies the parents' claim to stand in the lawsuit. The Court holds that the parents lack a connection to the subject matter of the lawsuit, their injuries are not concrete and particularized, and there is no causal link between their injuries and the defendants' actions.

On May 17, 1965, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia entered a final judgment against the school board for failing to comply with a federal court order requiring it to implement a "freedom-of-choice" plan for desegregating the school system.  The court's order, which was entered on March 17, 1966, finds that the school district violated the federal law by failing to adopt a plan that guaranteed that all Negro and White school children would be guaranteed equal protection of the federal and state laws.  According to the court order, the district court found that Brown I and Brown II, respectively, violated Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and that Brown II violated Section 13(b)(5) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") as well as Rule 13b2-1 thereunder.  In addition, the court found Brown II liable for violations of Section 15(a)(1) and (3) of Exchange Act Rule 13a-14.  Brown II was also liable for violating Section 13 of the Exchange Act for his role in the Exchange of Securities and Exchange Act violations.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court's opinion, Brown II consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the federal securities laws, ordering him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest and a civil penalty of $1,000.  He also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public school for five years, and to pay a $10,000 civil penalty.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Maryland granted certiorari in a case involving a group of white supremacists who held a rally in a town in Somerset County, Maryland, in 1966. The group, the National States Rights Party, held a public assembly or rally near the courthouse steps in the town of Princess Anne, the county seat of Somerset County. The group's speeches, amplified by a public address system so that they could be heard for several blocks, were aggressively and militantly racist. Their target was primarily Negroes and, secondarily, Jews. Their words were deliberately derogatory, insulting, and threatening language, scarcely disguised by protestations of peaceful purposes. The crowd listening to the speeches increased from about 50 at the beginning to about 150, of whom 25% were Negros. In the course of the proceedings it was announced that the rally would be resumed the following night, August 7.1. On that day, the respondents, Princess Anne and of Somerset county, applied for and obtained a restraining order from the Circuit Court for Somerset County that restrained petitioners for 10 days from holding rallies or meetings in the county 'which will tend to disturb and endanger the citizens of the County.'3 As a result, the rally scheduled for August 7 was not held. After the trial which took place 10 days later, an injunction was issued by the circuit court on August 31, in effect extending the restraint for 10 additional months. The court had before it, in addition to the testimony of witnesses, tape recordings made by the police of the August 6 rally. The Maryland Court of Appeal affirmed the 10-day order, but reversed the 10-month order on the ground that 'the period of time was unreasonable and that it was arbitrary to assume that a clear and present danger of civil disturbance and riot would persist for ten months.' Id.

In the Supreme Court case Taylor v. Crawford, the Court examined the constitutionality of Kentucky's lethal injection protocol under the Eighth Amendment, which prohibits cruel and unusual punishment. The Court affirmed the lower court's decision that Kentucky's procedure is consistent with the Eighth Amendment.

The main points of law and conclusions drawn include:

1. The Court determined that the Eighth Amendment requires a demonstration of a substantial risk of severe pain compared to known and available alternatives to succeed in an Eighth Amendment claim against a state's lethal injection protocol.

2. The Court found that the safeguards Kentucky has in place for administering the first drug, sodium thiopental, are adequate to ensure proper administration and to minimize the risk of pain.

3. The Court rejected the argument that additional measures, such as a blood pressure cuff or brain function monitoring, are necessary to avoid a substantial risk of suffering during execution.

4. The Court stated that an inmate cannot succeed on an Eighth Amendment claim by merely showing that the state could take one more step as a failsafe for other adequate measures.

5. The Court emphasized that the state has a legitimate interest in carrying out a sentence of death in a timely manner and that the additional measures proposed by the dissent would not serve a meaningful purpose.

6. The Court noted that reasonable people may disagree on the morality and efficacy of capital punishment, but the Court's role is not to reflect personal disapproval but to ensure compliance with the Constitution.

7. The Court acknowledged that society has moved towards more humane methods of execution over time, and the Eighth Amendment has accommodated this progress.

The implications of the decision are that states with lethal injection protocols substantially similar to Kentucky's are likely to be upheld as constitutional, and the Court has set a standard that requires a substantial and demonstrated risk of severe pain to challenge a state's execution method successfully. This decision may limit the ability of death row inmates to challenge lethal injection protocols on Eighth Amendment grounds.

In the case of Edelman v. Lynchburg College, the Supreme Court addressed the validity of an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) regulation that allows a complainant to verify a charge of employment discrimination after the filing deadline has passed. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 requires that a charge of discrimination be filed with the EEOC within a certain time frame and be verified under oath or affirmation.

The petitioner, Leonard Edelman, claimed he was denied tenure due to gender-based discrimination, as well as discrimination based on national origin and religion. He filed a letter with the EEOC but did not verify it under oath within the 300-day filing period. The EEOC later sent him a form to verify the charge, which he completed after the deadline. The College moved to dismiss the case, arguing that the lack of a verified charge within the filing period barred the lawsuit. The District Court and a divided panel of the Court of Appeals agreed, stating that the statute required verification within the limitations period.

The Supreme Court, however, reversed the lower courts' decisions. The Court found that the statute does not define "charge" as necessarily including verification at the time of filing. The Court held that the EEOC's regulation permitting verification to relate back to the original filing date is a reasonable interpretation of the statute. The Court reasoned that the verification requirement is meant to protect employers from frivolous claims, but it does not need to be met at the time of filing with the EEOC. The Court also noted that the practice of allowing later verification to relate back to an earlier filing is consistent with common law and that Congress had amended Title VII several times without rejecting the EEOC's approach.

The Court concluded that the EEOC's regulation is a valid interpretation of Title VII and reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, remanding the case for further proceedings. The opinion emphasized that Title VII is a remedial scheme intended to be accessible to laypersons, not just lawyers, and that the relation-back regulation ensures that individuals do not inadvertently forfeit their rights due to technicalities.

Justice Thomas concurred, emphasizing the EEOC's authority to issue procedural regulations. Justice O'Connor, joined by Justice Scalia, concurred in the judgment, stating that while she did not agree with the Court's interpretation of the statute, she would defer to the EEOC's reasonable interpretation under Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.

After the Planning and Zoning Commission of Shelby County, Tenn., denied approval of respondent's proposal to develop a subdivision, respondent brought an action in Federal District Court under 42 U. S. C. § 1983, claiming that the Commission's action violated the Just Compensation Clause of the Fifth Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court ultimately concluded that the Commission's action was not subject to liability under either clause, and accordingly dismissed the complaint. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Commission's action was subject to liability under both clauses. Held: Respondent's claim is premature, whether analyzed as a deprivation of property without due process under the Fourteenth Amendment or as a taking under the Just Compensation Clause of the Fifth Amendment. Pp. 639-648. (a) Whether a claim is ripe for adjudication under the Just Compensation Clause depends upon whether the governmental unit has finally determined whether it will permit the property owner to develop his property in accordance with his proposals. Here, the Commission's denial of approval does not conclusively determine whether respondent will be denied all reasonable beneficial use of his property, since the Commission's rejection of the preliminary plat does not prevent him from developing the subdivision according to his plat after obtaining the necessary variances. Moreover, respondent did not seek compensation through the procedures the State has provided for doing so. Pp. 639-643. (b) An action that goes so far as to destroy property rights is not a "taking" for which just compensation must be paid, but is an invalid exercise of the police power, violative of the Due Process Clause. To determine whether a regulation "goes too far," i. e., whether it destroys property rights, involves analyzing the effect the regulation had on the value of the property and investment-backed profit expectations. Such an analysis cannot be performed until a final decision is made as to how the regulation will be applied to the property. Since respondent failed to apply for variances from the regulations, no such decision had been made at the time respondent filed its § 1983 action. Pp. 643-648. 710 F. 2d 1271, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment in favor of the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New Mexico and the Department of Justice in connection with a related administrative proceeding.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New Mexico on September 29, 2014, the U. S. Attorney’s Office for New Mexico announced criminal charges against BP America Production Co., a New Mexico-based company that leases public-domain lands to private parties for the production of oil and gas.  The complaint alleges that, in 1966, the Secretary of the Interior issued an order requiring BP America to pay a royalty of 12.5 percent in amount or value of the production removed or sold from the lease.  As alleged in the complaint, this provision is not applicable to administrative proceedings.  In addition, the complaint further alleges that in 1996, Congress imposed a 6-year statute of limitations on certain non-Indian land, oil, and gas lease claims.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, BP America agreed to settle the matter by consenting to a settlement where it would pay a penalty of up to $10,000 a day, and the settlement was subject to court approval.  The complaint also seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 2415(a) (January 31, 2014).  The SEC &rsqua.gov website has a dedicated dedicated page for information about administrative proceedings, which includes an explanation for why it is important to check the background of anyone filing a complaint with the SEC.  Investors can also use the free and simple search tool onÂ Investor.gov to quickly identify whether there are any red flags of potential violations of the federal securities laws.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around whether a military appellate court, specifically the Navy-Marine Corps Court of Criminal Appeals (NMCCA), has the jurisdiction to consider a writ of error coram nobis to challenge a final decision affirming a criminal conviction. Jacob Denedo, a former Navy serviceman, sought this writ to overturn his conviction on the grounds of ineffective assistance of counsel, which he claimed led to his guilty plea and subsequent risk of deportation.

The NMCCA initially denied Denedo's petition for the writ, as did the United States Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces (CAAF), but the CAAF later remanded the case for further proceedings on the merits. The Government argued that military courts do not have the jurisdiction to entertain such petitions post-conviction.

The Supreme Court affirmed the CAAF's decision, holding that military courts do have the jurisdiction to consider coram nobis petitions. The Court reasoned that since the writ is a continuation of the original criminal proceeding, the NMCCA's jurisdiction over the original case extends to the consideration of the writ. The All Writs Act empowers federal courts to issue writs in aid of their jurisdiction, but it is not a source of jurisdiction itself. The Court clarified that while Article 76 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) emphasizes the finality of military court judgments, it does not preclude the NMCCA from examining its judgments in extraordinary circumstances where fundamental errors are alleged.

The Supreme Court's decision allows military courts to maintain the integrity of their judgments by providing relief in exceptional cases where there are claims of significant flaws in the original proceedings. However, the Court did not address the merits of Denedo's ineffective-assistance claim, leaving that to the NMCCA to determine on remand. The case was sent back to the NMCCA for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit ruled that the convictions of a civil rights activist in a 1961 protest in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, were unconstitutional on their face and as applied. The court held that the judge in the consolidated trial did not have jurisdiction to enter a verdict on the criminal conspiracy charge. The trial judge did have the authority to order a jury trial on the charges of disturbing the peace, obstructing public passages, and picketing before a courthouse. The appeals court found that the trial judge's decision to grant the jury trial was not a sufficient basis for the convictions. In a separate appeal, the 4th Circuit Court of Appeal agreed with the lower court's denial of appellant's request for a retrial. The 5th Court of appeals ruled that there was no basis for a finding that the charges against Mr. B. Elton Cox violated the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law. The case is remanded for further consideration.

After respondent Tribe obtained federal recognition in 1958, it entered into a lease with appellant Peabody Energy Corporation granting the corporation exclusive rights to mine coal on the Tribe’s reservation. When the lease expired in 1964, the Tribe attempted to obtain a higher royalty rate from the Secretary of the Interior. Instead, the Secretary approved a new lease with a lower rate. Subsequently, the Tribe filed suit in the Court of Federal Claims seeking damages for breach of trust, alleging that the Secretary acted improperly when he refused to raise the royalty rate. The court dismissed the suit, holding that the Tribe lacked standing to bring the suit. The Federal Circuit reversed, finding that the Tribe had standing to pursue its claim. The court reasoned that the Tribe could rely on a network of other statutes, treaties, and regulations to support its breach-of-trust claim. Ultimately, the court ruled that the Tribe prevailed on its claim because the Government had violated certain statutes and regulations. Held: The Tribe’s breach-of-trust claim fails because none of the sources of law identified by the Federal Circuit supports the claim. Pp. 8−14. (a) The Court of Federal Claims correctly dismissed the Tribe’s suit. Although the Tribe initially claimed that the Indian Tucker Act allowed it to seek damages for breach of trust, the Federal Circuit ultimately rejected that position, recognizing that the Tribe needed to find a different source of law to support its claim. The Tribe pointed to four potential sources of law: the Indian Mineral Leasing Act (IMLA), the Navajo-Hopi Rehabilitation Act of 1950, 25 U. S. C. §§635(a), 638, and the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, 30 U. S. C. §1201 et seq. However, the Tribe’s arguments fail because none of these sources of law provides any more sound a basis for its breach-of-trust claim than those analyzed in Navajo Nation v. United States, 537 U. S. 599. Pp. 8−12. (b) The Tribe’s argument that the IMLA does not apply because the lease was actually issued under the Navajo-Hopi Rehabilitation Act is flawed. Under the Rehabilitation Act, the Tribe could lease reservation lands only for up to 25-year terms, whereas the IMLA allows for indefinite terms. Moreover, the Tribe’s argument that the Secretary violated the Rehabilitation Act by failing to adhere to the Tribe’s wishes regarding the royalty rate ignores the fact that the Rehabilitation Act applies only to programs designed to improve the economic condition of the Navajo and Hopi peoples. Here, the lease was issued prior to the creation of such a program. Finally, the Tribe’s argument that the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 requires the Secretary to enforce whatever terms the Indians request with respect to coal leases is implausible given the fact that the lease was issued in 1964, many years before the date of enactment of the Surface Mining Act. Pp. 12−13. (c) The Federal Circuit erred in suggesting that the Government’s “comprehensive control” over coal on Indian land gives rise to fiduciary duties based on common-law trust principles. Such control alone is insufficient to establish a breach of trust. Rather, the analysis must begin with “specific rights-creating or duty-imposing statutory or regulatory prescriptions.” Navajo I, supra, at 506. Trust principles (including any such principles premised on “control”) could play a role in inferring that the trust obligation is enforceable by damages, but that must be the second step of the analysis, not the starting point. Pp. 13−14. 501 F. 3d 1330, reversed and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, Ginsburg, and Breyer, JJ., filed opinions concurring in the judgment.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Dallas-based construction contractor Connell Construction Co. and its affiliated companies in an antitrust case.  The court entered the final judgment in the case against Connell, finding that it violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering Connell to sign a contract that included a provision that prohibited the use of secondary-objective agreements in the construction industry.  Connell and Connell agreed to the contract without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, which was filed in federal district court in Dallas, that Connell violated Section 8(b)(4)(B) and Section 9(a)(1) and 10(l) and 13(c) of that federal securities laws, and that the contract with Connell was subject to the same exemption as the other contracts. The court also found that the subcontracting agreement was exempt from federal antitrust law because it was authorized by the federal government proviso that it was not a pre-condition for the operation of the antitrust laws.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  According to the SEC's complaint, the defendants agreed to settle the case by agreeing to the entry of judgments that permanently restrains trade within the meaning of the federal antitrust laws and requires them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and injunctive relief. The settlement is subject to court approval.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Dallas Regional Office, and the Texas Secretary of State's Office.

Respondent, an Air Force officer, was convicted of various crimes by general court-martial and sentenced to six years’ confinement. To avoid deportation, he decided to challenge his conviction once more, though at this point it had been final for eight years. In a petition for a writ of coram nobis filed with the Navy-Marine Corps Court of Criminal Appeals (NMCCA), respondent alleged that he informed his civilian attorney during plea negotiations that “his primary concern and objective” was to avoid deportation and that he was willing to “risk … going to jail” to avert separation from his family. The NMCCA affirmed. Respondent did not seek further review in the CAAF, and he was discharged from the Navy on May 30, 2000. In 2006, the Department of Homeland Security commenced removal proceedings against respondent based upon his special courtmartial conviction, which was final for 8 years. He sought extraordinary relief as authorized by the All Writs Act, 28 U. S. C. §1651(a), to enjoin the President from removing him from the rolls of the Armed Forces. The Government filed a motion to dismiss for want of jurisdiction, but the NMCCa summarily denied both the Government’s motion and respondent’d petition for coram- nobis. The CAAF denied relief, but respondent appealed on the ground that his sentence was unduly severe. The NAAF affirmed. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. An Article I military appellate court has jurisdiction to entertain a petition to challenge its earlier, and final, decision affirming a criminal conviction. Pp. 6–7. (a) The writ of §1259(4) does not confer subject-matter jurisdiction, since the statute authorizes “all writs necessary or appropriate in aid of their respective jurisdictions,” 10 U.S. C., §866(a). The authority to issue a writ is contingent on that court’re subjectmatter jurisdiction over the case or controversy, and assuming no constraints or limitations grounded in the Constitution are implicated, it is for Congress to determine whether the subject matter jurisdiction of federal courts. Bowles v. Russell, supra, at 536. The power of a court to issue any form of relief—extraordinary or otherwise—is contingent on its subject- matter jurisdiction. Assuming no constraints, limitations, and limitations grounded therein are implicated. P. 6. (b) The power to issue an extraordinary writ under §12 59(a) derives from the earlier jurisdiction it exercised to hear and determine the validity of the conviction on direct review, and, as the text of the Act recognizes, that authority is not a font of jurisdiction. See, e.g., Arthur Andersen LLP v. Carlisle, ante, at ___; FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., ante. at ___. The authority “to ‘revie[w’ court cases’ ” is sufficient to permit the court to entertain the petition for an appeal of the judgment of conviction. See Syngenta Crop Protection, Inc. v. Henson, 537 U.s. 28, 31. This rule applies with added force to Article I tribunals, which owe their existence to Congress’ authority to enact legislation pursuant to Art. I, §8 of the Constitution, and which have jurisdiction to issue extraordinary writs in extraordinary cases when it is shown that there were fundamental flaws in the proceedings leading to their issuance. The military appellate courts had jurisdiction to hear the petition, but they did not “ ‘grant relief ’” the petition. Because the CAG “granted relief” respondent, the text is satisfied here. Because a writ “may be regarded as ancillary to the prior suit, so that the relief asked may be granted by the court which made the decree in that suit … . The bill, though an original bill in the chancery sense of the word, is a continuation of the former suit, on the question of the jurisdiction of the [court]” §867(c). The CAG, however, had subject-maintaining jurisdiction to review the NMccA‘s denial of respondent, and the effect of the rule of judgment finality expressed in Article 76 of the UCMJ, “affirmatively prohibit[s] the type of collateral review sought by respondent.” Ibid. The court had jurisdiction over respondent, when exercising its jurisdiction, to hear his appeal, when he learned or should have learned of his counsel’as alleged deficiencies, but these limitations pose no obstacle to his requested review of the decision. The District of Columbia Court, in its opinion discussing the jurisdiction and authority of the NAAF, remanded to the NMCA so it could ascertain in the first instance “whether the merits of [respondent] petition can be resolved on the basis of the written submissions, or whether a factfinding

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Kansas today entered a final judgment in favor of a proposed amendment to the federal fuel tax that would have allowed Kansas to impose a tax on non-Indians purchasing fuel on the reservation.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Jackson County, Kansas, Kansas passed an interest-balancing test on the receipt of motor fuel from non-Indian distributors located off-reservation.  The complaint alleges that Kansas imposed a state fuel tax on the distributors based upon their receipt of the fuel.  As alleged in the complaint, the Kansas tax is not imposed on a tribe or tribal member, but rather on the distributor.  In fact, the complaint alleges, Kansas imposes the tax on a non-indian distributor based upon the tribe or tribe's receipt of that fuel, and the tax is imposed upon the distributor at the time of the distributor’s receipt.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, Kansas has agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders it to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount of the tax it has already paid to the tribe and to the extent that it is subject to the Bracker balancing test.

Petitioner Planned Parenthood of Central Missouri, a not-for-profit Missouri corporation which maintains a facility in Columbia, Mo., for the performance of abortions, brought this action on their own behalf and, purportedly, on behalf of the entire class consisting of their patients desiring the termination of pregnancy, all within the State. The District Court, largely by a divided vote, ruled that all except the first sentence of § 6 (1) withstood the attack on the ground, among others, that certain of its provisions deprived them and their patients of various constitutional rights: "the right to privacy in the physician-patient relationship"; the right to freedom of speech; the right of privacy of the competent minor mature enough to have become pregnant; and, inter alia, the "right to the protection of life and health of any fetus intended to be born and not aborted." Held: 1. The Act's definition of "viability" comports with Roe v. Wade, 410 U. S. 113, and is unconstitutional. Pp. 6-7. (a) Section 3 (2) of the Act imposes a special-consent provision, exercisable by a person other than the woman and her physician, as a prerequisite to a minor's termination of her pregnancy and does so without a sufficient justification for the restriction. P. 7. (b) The Act does not violate Roe and Doe, since § 3 (4) does not require the physician to exercise the prescribed skill, care, and diligence to preserve the life of the fetus, and the second sentence, even when read in conjunction with § 5 (proscribing the method of abortion known as saline amniocentesis "is deleterious to maternal health," and prohibiting that method after the first 12 weeks of pregnancy; and § 9 (1), as a condition for abortion contrary to the Act's provisions, does not impose an absolute, and possibly arbitrary, veto over the decision of the physician and his patient to terminate the patient's pregnancy, regardless of the reason for withholding the consent, and does not alter the duty imposed by the previous sentence or limit that duty to pregnancies that have reached the stage of viability. Id., at 1371. 2. The definition of viability in § 2 (2)'s language and context does not conflict with Roe. Roe, supra, at 164-165, which held that a requirement for consent by the father of a fetus, by the spouse, or by the parents, or a parent, of an unmarried minor, may be constitutionally imposed, and that § 3(4) imposes no additional burden on the physician because even prior to the passage of § 5 the physician would require parental consent before performing an abortion on a minor. P p. 7-8. (c) The fact that § 6(2) refers to a criminal penalty where the attending physician first certifies with reasonable medical certainty that the fetus is not viable, simply does not modify the duty that was imposed by § 3's previous sentence. Id. 392 F. Supp. 1371, reversed and remanded.

Appellees brought suit in District Court seeking declaratory and injunctive relief against enforcement of three New York statutes providing various kinds of financial aid to nonpublic elementary and secondary schools. Two of the statutes authorized direct "maintenance and repair" payments to nonpublic schools, virtually all of which are Roman Catholic schools in low-income areas, and the third provided for reimbursement to parents of tuition paid to nonpublic schools attended by their children. The District Court ruled that none of the statutes complied with the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. Held: 1. The "maintenance and repair" statute violates the Establishment Clause because its effect, inevitably, is to subsidize and advance the religious mission of sectarian schools. Pp. 108-115. (a) Since the statute makes no effort to limit the uses to which the state funds may be applied, it cannot be denied that this provision has a primary effect that advances religion in that it subsidizes directly the religious activities of sectarian elementary and secondary schools. Pp. 108-111. (b) That the statute limits the amount of the grants to 50% of the amounts spent for comparable services in the public schools does not save the statute from constitutional infirmities. Pp. 111-115. 2. The tuition reimbursement statute also violates the Establishment Clause for the same reasons that govern the "maintenance and repair" statute. Pp. 115-118. 3. The "elementary and secondary education opportunity" statute, which permits nonpublic schools to participate in state-administered tests for college entrance scholarships, does not violate the Establishment Clause. Pp. 118-120. 305 F. Supp. 1201, affirmed in part and reversed in part.

The Supreme Court of the United States reviewed a New York State law that required public school authorities to lend textbooks free of charge to all students in grades seven through 12, including those attending private and parochial schools. The central question was whether this statute violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, which prohibits the government from establishing a religion or favoring one religion over another, as applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court held that the New York law did not violate the Constitution.
