The Court's reasoning was based on the principle that the state can extend the benefits of state laws to all citizens regardless of their religious affiliation, as long as the purpose and primary effect of the law do not advance or inhibit religion. The Court found that the purpose of the law was secular—to further educational opportunities for all children—and that the primary effect did not advance nor inhibit religion. The textbooks provided were secular and approved by public school authorities, and no evidence suggested that religious books were being loaned.

The Court distinguished between the provision of textbooks and other forms of aid, noting that while books are integral to the teaching process, the state's interest in secular education justified the lending of textbooks to students in private schools, including religious ones. The Court also referenced previous cases that recognized the role of private schools in providing secular education and the state's interest in ensuring educational standards.

The Court dismissed the argument that all teaching in a sectarian school is religious or that secular and religious training are so intertwined that providing secular textbooks would amount to the teaching of religion. The Court found no evidence in the record to support this claim.

Additionally, the Court rejected the argument that the law violated the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, as there was no claim that the law coerced individuals in the practice of their religion.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the lower court, upholding the New York law as constitutional and not in conflict with the Establishment or Free Exercise Clauses of the First Amendment.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed a lower court's order requiring a bankruptcy trustee to waive a corporate debtor's attorney-client privilege with respect to communications that took place before the bankruptcy filing. The court found that the bankruptcy trustee had the power to waive that privilege, but that the trustee's waiver was not valid because he was "successor in interest of all assets, rights and privileges" of the bankruptcy debtor. The bankruptcy trustee, John K. Notz, Jr., filed a voluntary bankruptcy petition in 1980 on behalf of Chicago Discount Commodity Brokers, a discount commodity brokerage firm registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The Commission's complaint alleged that CDCB violated the Commodity Exchange Act of 1934 and the Securities Act of 1933. CDCB's former counsel, Gary Weintraub, was subpoenaed by the Commission to testify about alleged misappropriation of customer funds by CDCB officers and employees, and other fraudulent activities. The Court held that the Bankruptcy Court's earlier order requiring Notz to waive the attorney- client privilege was not

In the Supreme Court case involving Dwayne Giles, the central issue was whether Giles forfeited his Sixth Amendment right to confront a witness against him due to his own wrongful act that made the witness unavailable to testify. The witness in question was his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Avie, whom he was accused of murdering.

The trial court had allowed statements made by Avie to a police officer before her death to be admitted as evidence under California law, despite Giles' objection. These statements described a prior incident of domestic violence. Giles appealed his conviction, arguing that admitting these statements violated his right to confront the witness as outlined in the Sixth Amendment and as interpreted by the Supreme Court's decision in Crawford v. Washington.

The Supreme Court, referencing the historical context of the Confrontation Clause, determined that the exception to the confrontation right, known as "forfeiture by wrongdoing," applied only when the defendant's intentional act was designed to prevent the witness from testifying. The Court found no historical precedent for admitting unconfronted testimonial statements without evidence that the defendant intended to make the witness unavailable.

The Court vacated the judgment of the California Supreme Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. The implication of this decision is that defendants cannot be deprived of their confrontation rights unless it is shown that they intended to prevent a witness from testifying. This ruling upholds the strict interpretation of the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause and emphasizes the importance of a defendant's right to confront witnesses against them in a criminal trial.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas on January 24, 1983, entered a final judgment in favor of a temporary restraining order against the execution of a Texas man who was convicted of the capital murder of a police officer.  The court's final judgment, which permanently enjoins defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, orders defendants to submit to the court a written judgment that imposes a permanent injunction against future violations of the federal securities laws.  In its order, the court also ordered the defendants to provide testimony to the jury in response to hypothetical questions posed to them by psychiatrists who had not personally examined the defendant.  According to the Court's order, however, the psychiatrists were not competent to make predictions about the defendant's future dangerousness and should not be permitted to present their own side of the case.  As a result, the defendants were not permitted to testify at the sentencing hearing.  Instead, the Court of Criminal Appeals held that the defendants should be given an opportunity to make their own opinion on the merits of the defendants' case before it was decided whether to issue a stay of execution.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court's judgment, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations, ordering him to pay a penalty equal to the amount of his ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and requiring him to be permanently enjoined from future securities law violations.  To learn more about the Texas death penalty, see http://www.sec.gov/death-penalty.html  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Texas, charges the defendants with violating Sections 5(a), 5(c), and (3) ofÂ the Securities Act, and seeks permanent injunctions, civil penalties, and a penny stock bar against the defendants.  On January 26, 2018, the SEC issued its final judgment against the Defendants.  It also issued an order suspending the defendants from appearing or practicing before the SEC as part of a case-by-case review of the criminal justice system.

Respondent was tried along with two others in a Michigan state court for the murder of three individuals. One of the others gave a confession to the police shortly after his arrest, but the confession was redacted to eliminate all references to respondent. Although the confession was admitted into evidence over respondent's objections, the jury was instructed that it was not to be considered against respondent. Respondent was convicted, and the Michigan courts denied relief on her subsequent petition for a writ of habeas corpus. The Federal District Court likewise denied relief, but the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment, made applicable to the states by the Fourteenth Amendment, was violated by the admission of the confession with a proper limiting instruction. Held: Where a nontestifying codefendant's confession is redacted to eliminate not only the defendant's name, but any reference to his or her existence, the Confrontation Clause is not violated by the admission of the confession with a proper limiting instruction. Pp. 203-210. (a) Under ordinary circumstances, a witness whose testimony is introduced at a joint trial is not considered to be a witness "against" a defendant if the jury is instructed to consider that testimony only against a codefendant. However, where the necessity of linking the testimony with other evidence is involved, it is a less valid generalization that the jury will not likely obey the instruction to disregard the evidence. More specifically, evidence requiring linkage differs from evidence incriminating on its face in the practical effects which application of the Bruton exception to the general rule would produce. If limited to facially incriminating confessions, Bruton can be complied with by redaction-a possibility suggested in that opinion itself. But if extended to confessions incriminating by connection, not only is that not possible, but it is not even possible to predict the admissibility of a confession in advance of trial. Application of the "contextual implication" doctrine would require the trial judge to assess at the end of each trial whether, in light of all of the evidence, a nontestifying codefendant's confession has been so "powerfully incriminating" that a new, separate trial is required for the defendant. This obviously lends itself to manipulation by the defense -even without manipulation will result in numerous mistrials and appeals. And although a certain way of assuring compliance would be to try defendants separately whenever an incriminating statement of one of them is sought to be used, that is not as facile or as just a remedy as might seem. Both the efficiency and the fairness of the criminal justice system would be impaired by requiring, in all cases of joint crimes where incriminating statements exist, that prosecutors bring separate proceedings, presenting the same evidence again and again, requiring victims and witnesses to repeat the inconvenience (and sometimes trauma) of testifying, and randomly favoring the last-tried defendants who have the advantage of knowing the prosecution's case beforehand. Pp. 203-209. (b) Since the prosecutor in this case sought to undo the effect of the limiting instruction by urging the jury to use the confession in evaluating respondent's case, the question on remand is whether, in light of respondent's failure to object to the prosecutor's comments, the error can serve as the basis for granting a writ of habeas corpus. P. 210. 781 F. 2d 1201, reversed and remanded.

Petitioner was convicted of murder and armed robbery in a state court. Before trial, the trial court sustained his motion to exclude from evidence certain rifles and articles of clothing seized by police from petitioner's home on the night of the alleged crimes, holding that the seizure constituted a "search" and "seizure" violative of the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. The police had gone to petitioner's home pursuant to information received from petitioner's wife, whom they had previously interviewed, that petitioner had been seen carrying a rifle near the scene of the crime. Though the police had no warrant for the search, they had obtained consent to enter the home and had announced their purpose. Upon arrival, they asked petitioner's wife whether there were any guns in the house, and she led them to a room containing the rifles. Subsequently, the police asked her whether there were any guns that petitioner had been wearing on the night of the alleged crimes, and she produced the clothing. The rifles and clothing were taken to the police station and later used as exhibits at petitioner's trial. The New Hampshire Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's ruling sustaining the motion to exclude the evidence. Held: 1. The seizure of the rifles and clothing did not violate the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 508-517. (a) The seizure did not fall within the "plain view" exception to the warrant requirement. Pp. 510-515. (b) The seizure did not fall within the "incident to arrest" exception to the warrant requirement. Pp. 515-517. 2. Because of the possibility of a new trial, the efficient administration of justice counsels consideration of the question whether the seizure of the rifles and clothing violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 517-520. 106 N. H. -, 171 A. 2d 45, reversed and remanded.

An undercover government agent was placed in the cell of respondent, who was incarcerated on charges unrelated to the subject of the agent's investigation. While in the cell, the agent questioned respondent, who gave detailed accounts of several murders, including one that the agent sought to solve. Respondent claims that the statements should be inadmissible because he had not been given the warnings prescribed by Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U. S. 436, before making them. Held: Undercover law enforcement officers need not give Miranda warnings to incarcerated suspects before asking questions that may elicit an incriminating response. Such warnings are not required when the suspect is unaware that he is speaking to a law enforcement officer and gives a voluntary statement. Conversations between suspects and undercover agents do not implicate the concerns underlying Miranda. The essential ingredients of a "police-dominated atmosphere" and compulsion are not present when an incarcerated person speaks freely to someone whom he believes to be a fellow inmate. Coercion is determined from the suspect's perspective. Here, since respondent viewed the cellmate-agent as an equal and showed no hint of being intimidated by the atmosphere of the jail, there was no "interplay between police interrogation and police custody." See Kamisar, Brewer v. Williams, Massiah and Miranda: What is "Interrogation?" When Does It Matter? 67 Geo. L. J. 1, 63. Moreover, Miranda was not meant to protect suspects from boasting about their criminal activities in front of persons whom they believe to be their cellmates. Detention, whether or not for the crime in question, does not warrant a presumption that the use of an undercover agent to speak with an incarcerated suspect makes any confession thus obtained involuntary. Thus, the only difference between this case and Hoffa v. United States, 385 U. S. 293, is that the suspect here was incarcerated, but detention, whether or not for the crime in question, does not warrant such a presumption. Mathias v. United States, 391 U. S. 1, distinguished. Nor do the Sixth Amendment decisions in Massiah, supra; United States v. Henry, 447 U. S. 264; and Maine v. Moulton, 474 U. S. 159, apply. Certiorari granted; reversed and remanded.

Petitioner was arrested without a warrant and interrogated. He made no statement to the police and was released at 5 that afternoon pursuant to a state court writ of habeas corpus obtained by a lawyer who had been retained by petitioner. At the time of his arrest and denied an opportunity to consult with his lawyer, the investigation had ceased to be a general investigation of "an unsolved crime," Spano v. New York, 360 U. S. 315, 327, and petitioner was later indicted for the murder along with petitioner. Petitioner was convicted of murder. The Illinois Supreme Court held the statement inadmissible and reversed the conviction. Held: 1. Under the circumstances, the refusal by the police to honor petitioner's request to consult his lawyer during the course of an interrogation constitutes a denial of "the Assistance of Counsel" in violation of the Sixth Amendment to the Constitution as "made obligatory upon the States by the Fourtee th Amendment," Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335, 342, and thereby renders inadmissible in a state criminal trial any incriminating statement elicited by police during the interrogation. Massiah v. United States, ante, p. 201. Pp. 203-204. 2. The refusal by police to recognize petitioner's constitutional right to consult counsel during an interrogation was not constitutionally permissible. P. 204. 3. The right to counsel, under these circumstances, depends on the right of the accused to be advised by his lawyer of his privilege against self-incrimination, and the right to use counsel at the formal trial "would be a very hollow thing (if), for all practical purposes, the conviction is already assured by pretrial examination." Massiah, supra, at 204, distinguished. The fact that many confessions are obtained during this period points up its critical nature as a "stage when legal aid and advice" are surely needed, and it would exalt form over substance to make the "right to counsel" depend on the "stage to the accused in his need for legal advice." P. 206. 4. The "guiding hand of counsel" was essential to advise petitioner of his rights in this delicate situation, and he was a well-educated man who had studied criminal law while attending law school for a year. The question of whether the "trial is no longer a general inquiry into an unsolved crime but has begun to focus on a particular suspect, the suspect has been taken into police custody, the police carry out a process of interrogations that lends itself to eliciting incriminating tatements, and without informing him of his absolute right to remain silent in the face of this accusation, the accused has been denied advice from his lawyer and the police have not effectively warned him of the absolute constitutional right of remain silent, and his attorney has been refused permission to remain in the adjoining room while his own lawyer, seeking to speak with him, was kept from him by police. Respondent was convicted and the trial was held inadadmissible. The Supreme Court reversed.

Respondent Ceballos was employed as a deputy district attorney for the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office. During the period relevant to this case, he exercised certain supervisory responsibilities over other lawyers. In February 2000, a defense attorney contacted him about a pending criminal case. The attorney informed him that he had filed a motion to traverse, or challenge, the warrant, but he also wanted him to review the case. After examining the affidavit and visiting the location it described, he determined that the affidavit contained serious misrepresentations. He relayed his findings to his supervisors, petitioners Carol Najera and Frank Sundstedt, and followed up by preparing a disposition memorandum. On March 2, 2000, he submitted the memo to the District Attorney for his review. A few days later, he presented it to him for review. Based on his statements, a meeting was held to discuss the affidavit. The meeting allegedly became heated, with one lieutenant sharply criticizing Ceballoos for his handling of the case and other employees criticizing him. Despite his concerns, the trial court decided to proceed with the prosecution, pending disposition of the defense motion. The trial court held a hearing on the motion, but the court rejected the challenge to the warrant. The District Attorney filed a summary judgment, which was reversed by the Ninth Circuit. The court did not consider whether the speech was made by the speaker “as a citizen upon matters of public concern.” Rather, it relied on Circuit precedent rejecting the idea that “a public employee's speech is deprived of First Amendment protection whenever those views are expressed, to government workers or others, pursuant to an employment responsibility,” Pickering v. Myers, 461 U. S. 138, 142. Having concluded that the memo satisfied the public-concern requirement, the Court of Appeals proceeded to balance the speech against his supervisors’ interest in responding to it. Having found that the memorandum, which recited what he thought to be governmental misconduct, was incoherently a matter of public interest, the court held that the First Amendment protected a government employee from discipline based on speech made pursuant to his official duties. Held: The First Amendment does not prohibit managerial discipline based solely on an employee-“employee speech”. Pp. 5–7. (a) The First and Fourteenth Amendments protect a public employee’’ right, in certain circumstances, to speak as a citizen addressing matters of “public import.’ ” Connick v. Myers, 462 U.S. 138. The First, First, and Fourth Amendments protect public employees with certain rights, as well as obligations arising from any other applicable constitutional provisions and mandates of the criminal and civil laws, protect employees and provide checks on supervisors who would order unlawful or otherwise inappropriate actions. P. 6. (b) When public employees make statements pursuant to their official duties, the employees are not speaking as citizens for First Amendment purposes, and the Constitution does not insulate their communications from employer discipline. When a citizen enters government service, the citizen by necessity must accept certain limitations on his freedom. When, however, the employee is simply performing his or her job duties, there is no warrant for a similar degree of scrutiny. When an employee speaks pursuant to employment responsibilities, there are no relevant analogue to speech by citizens who are not government employees. When the employee speaks as a prosecutor fulfilling a responsibility to advise his supervisor about how best to proceed, the employer has the means at hand to avoid it. The proper inquiry is a practical one. Formal job descriptions often bear little resemblance to the duties an employee actually is expected to perform, and listing of a given task in an employee's written job description is neither necessary nor sufficient to demonstrate that conducting the task is within the scope of the employee‘s professional duties. Proper application of our precedents thus leads to the conclusion that the Constitution prohibits managerial discipline of an employee based on his expression made pursuant pursuant to official responsibilities. Because the memo falls into this category, his allegation of unconstitutional retaliation must fail. Two final points warrant mentioning. First, as indicated above, the parties in this case do not dispute that Ceballs’ disposition memo, which he wrote pursuant to the employment duties. See, e.g., Pickering, supra, at 568. Second, the fact that the document concerned the subject matter of his employment, but this, too, is nondispositive. The Government has broader discretion to restrict speech when it acts in its role as employer but the restrictions it imposes must be directed at speech that has some potential to affect the entity’S operations. The Constitution protects some expressions related to the speaker’ job. The same goes for writing a letter to a local newspaper or discussing politics with a co-worker, see Rankin v. McPherson, 483 U.

After concluding that the city of Richmond's 30% racial preference in the allocation of public construction contracts was valid under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, the District Court entered a permanent injunction against petitioners' suit challenging the plan. Petitioners contended that the plan was invalid because it rested on a mistaken belief that past societal discrimination alone could justify a racial preference. The District Court disagreed, ruling that the plan was valid because it was narrowly tailored to remedy past discrimination in the construction industry. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The plan is invalid because it fails to demonstrate a compelling interest in remedying past discrimination. Pp. 539-550. (a) None of the evidence presented by Richmond points to any identified discrimination in the Richmond construction industry. Although the District Court took judicial notice of the fact that the vast majority of "minority" persons in Richmond were black, it may well be that Richmond has never had an Aleut or Eskimo citizen. The random inclusion of racial groups that, as a practical matter, may never have suffered from discrimination in the construction industry in Richmond strongly impugns Richmond's claim of remedial motivation. Pp. 539-541. (b) Given the existence of an individualized procedure for considering bids and waivers on a case-by-case basis, the city's only interest in maintaining a quota system rather than investigating the need for remedial action in particular cases would seem to be simple administrative convenience. But the interest in avoiding the bureaucratic effort necessary to tailor remedial relief to those who truly have suffered the effects of prior discrimination cannot justify a rigid line drawn on the basis of a suspect classification. Here, the city has failed to ascertain how many minority enterprises are present in the local construction market or the level of their participation in city construction projects. The city points to no evidence that qualified minority contractors have been passed over for city contracts or subcontracts, either as a group or in any individual case. Pp. 541-548. Affirmed.

The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA or Act), as amended, provides that an employer is required to pay a discharged employee his full wages, including holiday or vacation payments, on the date of discharge. An employer's policy of paying its discharged employees for their unused vacation time constitutes an "employee welfare benefit plan" within the meaning of § 3 (1) of the Act, and is not excluded from its coverage by the provision saving from pre-emption a "generally applicable criminal law." ERISA § 514(b)(4). The Massachusetts statute, insofar as it applied to these complaints, had been pre-empted by ERISA. Respondent moved to dismiss the criminal complaints on the ground that the Bank's vacation policy constituted an employee Welfare Benefit Plan, and that the State's prosecution of him for failure to comply with the policy therefore ran afoul of § 5 14 (a) of ERISA, which pre-exists "any and all State laws insofar as they . . . relate to any employee benefit plan." The trial judge reported the preemption question to the Massachusetts Appeals Court for decision; the Supreme Judicial Court then transferred the case to its own initiative. For the purpose of answering the reported question, the parties stipulated that the bank had made oral or written agreements stemming from handbooks, manuals, memoranda, and practices to pay employees in lieu of unused vacation vacation time, and "such payments are made out of the bank's general assets" in lump sums upon termination of employment. The court held that the policy constituted the employee welfare benefits plan and was not excluded by the provisions saving from post-emption. Held: The policy here does not constitute an employee welfare benefit benefit plan. Pp. 522-527. 402 Mass. 287, 522 N. E. 2d 409, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a Connecticut man who was convicted of making a false and misleading statement in a federal criminal prosecution.  The court's order, entered by consent, permanently enjoins the defendant from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $500,000.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Connecticut today announced criminal charges against the defendant.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Hartford, Connecticut, the defendant refused to answer a series of questions related to his arrest and conviction, including whether he knew John Bergoti, the person who ran the pool-selling operation in which he had been arrested in 1959.  As alleged in the complaint, Bergoti consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations of Sections 5(a) and 5(c), and ordering him to be barred from participating in any federal criminal proceeding.  Bergoti also agreed to be permanently enjoined from violating Section 17(a)(1) of The Securities Act of 1933, Section 10 of the Exchange Act, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) ofÂ the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 206(3)-8 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the SEC, Bergotti consented, in a judgment entered by the court, to a permanent injunction against future violations, and to be subject to a conduct-based injunction.Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted in the Office of Inspector General and the Division of Justice's Cyber Unit, with the assistance of trial counsels in the Division's Office of Criminal Investigations.   The SEC's litigation will be led by Mr. Dolan, Ms. Rogers, and Mr. Wainwright.

Petitioner was indicted for violation of the federal narcotics laws and released on bail pending trial. A third party, acting pursuant to arrangements unknown to petitioner, furnished the Government with incriminating statements made by petitioner. These statements were introduced into evidence over petitioner's objections at his trial, resulting in his conviction. Held: Petitioner's conviction cannot be sustained, since the introduction of his own incriminating statements into evidence constituted a denial of his rights under the Sixth Amendment. Pp. 128-133. Reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant who was convicted in a series of high-profile criminal trials.  The court's order, which was entered yesterday, permanently enjoins the defendant from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against him from appearing or practicing before the court as a juror.  In addition, the court granted the defendant's motion for a temporary restraining order and ordered him to be barred from participating in any jury selection.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Miami, Fla., in August 1970, the defendant was indicted on two counts of murder in Broward County, Fla. and pleaded guilty to one count of attempted murder in the course of the trial. The jury deliberated for nearly two hours before finding that petitioner was competent to stand trial on the charges. The court also ruled that the jury selection process was not fundamentally fair, and that the defendants were not trying to avoid the death penalty.   The SEC's order also prohibits the defendants from making materially prejudgment statements to the jury, and prohibits the jury from making any prejudgment statement to the public. Â The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Florida Office of the Attorney General, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Miami Regional Office.

After respondents requested all communications between the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and AT&T regarding the latter’s participation in a government subsidy program, the FCC declined to release certain materials, claiming that doing so would constitute an unwarranted invasion of “personal privacy” prohibited by the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). The Fifth Circuit disagreed, holding that the FOIA’s exception covering law enforcement information that could cause an unwarranted invasion of “personal privacy” applied to corporations. Held: Corporations do not have “personal privacy” interests implicating the FOIA exception. Pp. 4−11. (a) There is no merit to AT&T’s argument that the word “personal” in the FOIA provision derives from the defined term “person,” rather than developing independently. While the two words share a common dictionary meaning, “personal” is not ordinarily linked to artificial entities such as corporations. Moreover, the Dictionary Act makes clear that “person” includes corporations in the legal context. However, the fact that “person” is commonly understood to include corporations in legal settings does not establish that “personal” carries a corresponding legal meaning outside of that context. Here, the FCC’s attempt to ascribe a corresponding legal meaning to “personal” falls far short of demonstrating that the term “personal privacy” in the FOIA provision necessarily excludes the privacy of corporations. Pp. 4−8. (b) The meaning of “personal privacy” in the FOIA provision is further clarified by the rest of the statute. Viewed in the context of pre-existing FOIA exceptions, the purpose and scope of the “personal privacy” provision become even more apparent. Of relevance here, the phrase “personal privacy” appears in both Exemption 6, which covers personnel and medical files and similar files whose disclosure would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, and Exemption 7(C), which covers law enforcement information that could cause an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy. By using the same phrase in both provisions, Congress indicated that the “personal privacy” phrase in Exemption 6 is pertinent in construing Exemption 7(C). Furthermore, the fact that Congress used language similar to that in Exemption 4, which pertains to trade secrets and confidential information obtained from a person, shows that it intended Exemption 7(C) to cover only information belonging to individuals. Thus, the Government’s longstanding interpretation of the “personal privacy” phrase in Exemption 7(C) as applying to individuals is consistent with the statute’s structure. Pp. 8−11. Reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

After respondents obtained federally insured mortgages from petitioners pursuant to the Housing Act of 1964, the Emergency Loan Insurance Corporation of America (FmHC) announced that it would not honor prepayment offers made under the terms of the mortgages. Respondents sued petitioners in the Court of Federal Claims, claiming that the FmHC’s policy amounted to a breach of contract and a taking of property without due process of law. The court dismissed the claims as untimely under 28 U. S. C. §2501, which requires that “every … claim” against the United States “shall be verified and filed … within six years after [the] claim first accrues.” It did so on the ground that the FmHC’s policy was a present breach of the mortgages’ prepayment clauses, which allowed borrowers to prepay their loans at any time. The Federal Circuit affirmed, ruling that the FmHC’s policy created a present breach of the prepayment clauses, and that the six-year statute of limitations began to run on the day ELIHPA was enacted. Held: The Federal Circuit erred in finding that the FmHC’s policy created a present breach of the prepayment clauses. Pp. 138–146. (a) The FmHC’s policy effectuated a repudiation of the prepayment clauses, not an immediate breach. Viewed in this light, ELIHPA effectuated a repudiation of the prepayment clauses, not an immediate breach. The Act conveyed an announcement by the Government that it would not perform as represented in the prepayment clauses if and when, at some point in the future, petitioners attempted to prepay their mortgages. Unless petitioners treated ELIHPA as a present breach by filing suit prior to the date indicated for performance, breach would occur when a borrower attempted to prepay, for only at that time would the Government’s responsive performance become due. Pp. 138–142. (b) The Government misconstrues §2501’s language—“first accrues”—as creating a special accrual rule for suits against the United States. Rather than presenting an unduly restrictive reading of the congressional waiver of sovereign immunity, the section’s plain meaning is best understood as requiring that the limitations period begin to run from the date of actual injury. Two practical considerations support this conclusion. First, assuming a claim could “first accrue” for limitations purposes on the date of repudiation, a party aggrieved by the Government’s renunciation of a contractual obligation anticipating future performance would be compelled by the looming limitations bar to forgo the usual option of awaiting the time performance is due before filing an action for breach. Second, putting prospective plaintiffs to the choice of either bringing suit soon after the Government’s repudiation or forever relinquishing their claims would surely proliferate litigation. There is also reason to doubt that the Government’s reading of §2501 would inure to the benefit of the United States. Faced with the prospect of forever forgoing such a claim, even a borrower that had not previously wished to prepay might well conclude that early exit from the FmHC program is the only safe course. Finally, the Government erroneously attacks as futile petitioners’ search for an exact parallel in contracts solely between private parties. An Act of Congress may constitute a repudiation of a contract to which the United States is a party. Congress may renounce the Government’s contractual duties without triggering an immediate breach because Congress may withdraw that repudiation if given the opportunity to do so. Pp. 142–146. Reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Lockheed Martin Corp. ("Lockheed") and its former CEO, Paul Spink, for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, Spink was employed by Lockheed Corporation from 1939 until 1950, when he left to work for one of Lockheed's competitors. As alleged in the complaint, when Lockheed and Spink implemented the amended pension plan, they violated the fiduciary duty provisions of the federal securities laws. The complaint alleges that Spink sought monetary, declaratory, and other relief, and that he then retired, without earning any extra benefits for doing so.  The SEC's final judgment, which is subject to court approval, permanently enjoins Lockheed from violating these provisions, and orders Spink to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount of his disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil monetary penalties.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Spink.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, the court agreed with Spink and the company that it had violated the duty of care and prohibited transaction provisions. The court also agreed to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining Lockheed from future violations of these provisions.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia today entered a final judgment in a case brought by the Commission on Judicial Inquiry and Review Commission against Joseph W. Dunn, Jr., the Managing Editor of the Virginian Pilot, for breaching the First Amendment.  According to the Commission's complaint, filed in federal court in Virginia on October 4, 1975, the Commission improperly disclosed the identity of a judge in a pending proceeding by the court.  The complaint alleges that at the time the Commission was conducting its investigation, the judge had not been subpoenaed by or appeared before the Commission in connection with the proceedings.  As alleged in the complaint, however, in the course of its investigation the Commission had not filed a formal complaint with the court with respect to the judge's conduct.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Dunn.  On November 5, a federal district court in Alexandria, Virginia, entered a judgment against Dunn, finding him liable for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Commission complaint, Dunn consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to comply with the SEC's requests for a temporary restraining order, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  Dunn also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public agency for five years, and to be prohibited from participating in any Commission proceeding or to the initial disclosure of confidential information.   The Commission's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by John R. Burt and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson and Kurt L. Gottschall of the Atlanta Regional Office.

Respondent Bayer Corporation (Bayer) removed respondent’s case from a federal district court in West Virginia on the basis of diversity jurisdiction. Petitioners Keith Smith and Shirley Sperlazza (Smith for short) filed state-law claims against Bayer, similar to those raised in McCollins’ suit, in the Circuit Court of Brooke County, West Virginia. Neither Smith nor McCollin knew about the other's suit. Applying Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23, the District Court declined to certify the proposed class of West Virginia Baycol purchasers. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The District Court exceeded its authority under the “relitigation exception” to the Anti-Injunction Act, 28 U. S. C. §2283, because ordinary rules of issue preclusion barred Smith from seeking certification of his proposed class. Because the issues before the two courts were not the same, and Smith was neither a party nor the ex-ceptional kind of nonparty who can be bound, the court erred in finding the certification issue precluded, and erred all the more in thinking an injunction appropriate. Pp. 5–7. (a) The Anti- Injunction’’ “same issue” requirement of preclusion law, which permits a federal court to enjoin a state proceeding only in rare cases, when necessary to “pro-tect or effectuate [the federal court’] judgments,” 28 U., S., §2282, is not met for two reasons. First, the issue presented in the state court was not identical to the one decided in the federal tribunal. Second, the parties in the two proceedings were sufficiently alike: Because Smith was an unnamed member of the class McCollains had proposed, and because their “interests were aligned, Smith was appropriately bound by the federal court's judgment.” Id., at 148. The court also held that the issue to be adjudicated in the State Court was “sufficiently identical” with the one the federal Court had decided to warrant preclusion, and that Smith was not bound by that judgment. In re Baycol Prods. Litigation, 593 F. 3d 716, the Eighth Circuit affirmed, holding that the order was appropriate to protect that judgment in the suit denying class certification. The Ninth Circuit also affirmed, concluding that the Court of appeals erred on both grounds when it granted the injunction, and now reverse. P. 7. (b) The order issued here implicates two circuit splits arising from application of the anti-injunction statute’re relitigation exemption. The first involves the requirement that a subsequent suit raise the same issue as a previous case. Chick Kam Choo v. Exxon Corp., 486 U.S. 140, 146, and the second concerns the scope of the rule that a court‘s judgment cannot bind nonparties. See, e.g., Taylor v. Sturgell, 553 U., at 901. In applying this exception, the Court has taken special care to avoid relying exclusively on the near-identity of the two Rules’ preclusion principles and instead applies a strict test barring class treatment when proof of each plaintiff is necessary. In In re Rezulin, 214 W. Va. 52, 585 S. E. 2d 52, this case involves the last of the three exceptions, which is de-signed to implement “well-recognized concepts” of claim and issue-preclusion. The provision authorizes an injunction to prevent state litigation of a claim or issue “that previously was presented to and decided by the Federal court” Ibid. But those exceptions, though designed for important purposes, “are narrow and are ‘not [to] be enlarged by loose statutory construction.’ . . .” id., at 297. Indeed, a person not a party to a class suit may receive certain benefits (such as the tolling of a limitations period) related to that proceeding. Cf. n. 1. The very ruling that Bayer argues ought to be given preclusive effect is that a class could not properly be certified. So Bayer wants to bind Smith as a member of a class action (because it is only as such that a nonparty in Smith’S situation can be binding) to a determination that there could not be a class class action. But if the judgment in this case can indeed bind Smith, it must do so under principles of non-party preclusion.
