The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia, alleges that the federal government violated the First and Second Amendment of the federal securities laws by failing to adequately protect the rights of women seeking an abortion.  According to the complaint, the federal funds that HHS provided for family planning services were not adequately protected by the federal law.  For example, the SEC's Complaint alleges that, in violation of Section 1008 of the Exchange Act, HHS violated the right to a fair and reasonable treatment of women who had abortions.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC Complaint, the HHS has consented to the entry of a Final Judgment that permanently enjoins HHS from violating these provisions and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $100,000.  In a parallel action, the U.N. Office of Inspector General today announced that it has issued an order imposing a temporary restraining order against HHS, imposing a $75,000 civil penalty, and imposing an officer-and-director bar on HHS.  HHS also has agreed to pay an $80,000 officer and director bar and to a $50,000 bar from serving as an attorney.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was found guilty of a charge of premeditated murder.  The court issued a temporary restraining order and issued an order temporarily suspending proceedings against the defendant.  According to the SEC's order, filed on May 14, 1968, the defendant was arrested at his home on January 20, 1968 and was arrested the next morning. The court found that, on the morning of his arrest, nine of 12 jurors were required to convict him. The SEC alleges that, because the defendant had a reasonable doubt about his guilt, he failed to follow instructions concerning the need for a jury to determine whether a defendant should be convicted by a jury of 12. The Court also ruled that, if the jury was unanimous, the jury could not have found him guilty.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana today announced criminal charges against the individual defendants.  On May 24, 2016, the U. S. Attorney's office for New Orleans announced criminal prosecutions against the defendants. The case was investigated by the Office of Inspector General's Criminal Investigations, which conducted an extensive examination of the case. The investigation was conducted by David A. Welshhans and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The litigation will be led by Mr. Werner and Ms. Werner under the supervision of C.J. Kerstetter.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the United Kingdom Financial Conduct Authority, the British Columbia Securities Commission, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Title: Immunity of Congressmen Under the Speech or Debate Clause

Summary:

The Supreme Court ruled in this case that Congressmen and their aides are immune from liability or questioning in connection with a subpoena seeking documents relating to their official activities, as long as those activities fall within the "legislative sphere" protected by the Speech or Debate Clause. The Court found that the subpoena in question was valid and that the plaintiffs did not have standing to bring the lawsuit. The Court also rejected arguments that the subpoena was being used to harass, chill, or punish the plaintiffs in the exercise of their First Amendment rights.

Title: Coolidge v. New Hampshire

Year: 1967

Issue: Whether the search and seizure of firearms and clothing from the residence of a suspect's wife constitutes a violation of the Fourth Amendment.

Background: John Coolidge was charged with robbery and murder. Before his trial, his wife allowed two police officers to search their home and take possession of several firearms and pieces of clothing. The trial court found the search and seizure constitutional, and the New Hampshire Supreme Judicial Court affirmed. The case was appealed to the US Supreme Court.

Decision: The US Supreme Court held that the search and seizure of firearms and clothing from the residence of a suspect's wife constituted a violation of the Fourth Amendment. The Court found that the search was not incident to a lawful arrest, and that the officers had no probable cause or exigent circumstances to justify the search. The Court also noted that the search was not consented to by the wife, and that the officers did not have a warrant. Therefore, the search and seizure were unreasonable and violated the Fourth Amendment.

In the case before the Supreme Court, petitioners Giglio, Livorsi, and Lawn, along with Roth, were convicted of evading and conspiring to evade federal income taxes for the year 1946, as well as other related charges. The petitioners appealed their convictions on several grounds, primarily arguing that their Fifth Amendment due process rights were violated during the trial process.

The petitioners contended that they were not given a proper hearing to determine if evidence obtained from them during a prior grand jury investigation was used to indict them, that the use of certain photostatic copies of checks as evidence violated their Fifth Amendment rights, and that they were denied the opportunity to examine and cross-examine witnesses to determine if evidence used at trial was derived from the prior grand jury investigation.

The Supreme Court found no merit in the petitioners' first contention, stating that the affidavits presented did not provide a foundation for the belief that the 1953 grand jury considered any materials from the 1952 grand jury. The Court also ruled that an indictment returned by a legally constituted and unbiased grand jury, if valid on its face, calls for a trial on the merits and satisfies the Fifth Amendment.

Regarding the second contention, the Court found that the petitioners' counsel had consciously and intentionally waived any objection to the receipt of the photostatic copies of checks in evidence, as they were used to support the defense's argument and were admitted without objection.

On the third contention, the Court concluded that the petitioners were given the opportunity to examine and cross-examine witnesses to show derivative use of evidence at the trial, and the trial court only sustained objections to questions attacking the procedural validity of the indictment.

Lastly, the Court found sufficient evidence to support the convictions of petitioners Lawn and Livorsi on the conspiracy count and other counts, and it was unnecessary to consider contentions on counts where sentences ran concurrently with affirmed counts.

The Supreme Court affirmed the judgments of conviction, rejecting the petitioners' arguments and upholding the trial court's decisions.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the case of David Randolph Gray, who was sentenced to death for a capital murder committed in Mississippi. The central issue is whether the exclusion of a potential juror, Mrs. H.C. Bounds, due to her views on the death penalty, violated Gray's right to a fair and impartial jury as established in Witherspoon v. Illinois and subsequent cases.

During jury selection, the prosecutor used peremptory challenges to remove several jurors who expressed reservations about the death penalty. When Bounds was questioned, she stated she could consider the death penalty in an appropriate case. The prosecutor, having used all peremptory challenges, requested an additional one or the reversal of a previous denial of a for-cause challenge. The trial judge ultimately excused Bounds for cause, despite her being qualified under the standards set by Witherspoon and related cases.

The Mississippi Supreme Court affirmed Gray's sentence, suggesting that the exclusion of Bounds corrected an earlier error where the trial court failed to dismiss other jurors for cause. However, the U.S. Supreme Court disagreed, stating that two wrongs do not make a right and that the exclusion of Bounds was a constitutional error that could not be considered harmless.

The U.S. Supreme Court held that the right to an impartial jury is so fundamental that any violation of the Witherspoon standard cannot be treated as harmless error. The Court emphasized that the composition of the jury as a whole could be affected by such an error, and it is impossible to know whether the prosecutor would have had an additional peremptory challenge to use if earlier motions had been granted.

The Court rejected the argument that a single technical error in excluding a juror could be considered harmless if the ultimate jury panel still fairly represented the community. The Court reaffirmed that a death sentence cannot stand if a juror who is qualified under Witherspoon is erroneously excluded for cause.

In conclusion, the U.S. Supreme Court reversed the death sentence imposed by the Mississippi Supreme Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, upholding the principle that a capital defendant has a constitutional right to a jury that is not predisposed towards a death verdict.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Oregon District Court, in a unanimous decision, affirmed the lower court's decision to uphold the convictions of Robert Apodaca, Henry Morgan Cooper, Jr., and James Arnold Madden, who were found guilty by less-than-unanimous jury verdicts in separate criminal cases. The court found that the defendants' claims that their convictions contravened their right to trial by jury under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments are without merit. The Court also found that there was no evidence that the jury members were racially biased against the defendants. The majority opinion, written by Justice Richard B. Sobol, concluded that the "ten of twelve" rule is not inconsistent with the due process requirement that a jury majority remain under the duty to consider the minority viewpoint in the course of deliberation. The decision was written by Mr. Justice White, joined by Chief Justice Richard Blackmun and Justice Rebecca Rehnquist. The opinion was published on May 22, 1972.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Delaware has ruled that the constitutional validity of the legislative apportionment of seats in the Delaware General Assembly has been established by the Supreme Court's recent decision in Baker v. Carr. The Court of Justice's decision was based on the testimony of political scientists who concluded that the legislature's current system of apportioning seats was unconstitutional. The Supreme Court held that the lower court's earlier ruling in Baker was not a sufficient basis for the Court to conclude that the current system is unconstitutional, and that the Court should order a new reapportionment of the General Assembly. The lower court held that, under the present system, New Castle County and the City of Wilmington were denied the right to cast votes for members of the Delaware Legislature that were of equal effect with that of every other citizen of the State of Delaware. The court concluded that, in the absence of a new system, the current legislature was dominated by legislators representing the two less populous counties and that it was impossible to amend the State Constitution or convene a constitutional convention for the purpose of reapportioning the State Assembly. In a separate decision, the Court ruled that, as a result of the earlier ruling, it was not necessary to hold a general election to determine the number of seats that would be apportioned to each of the state's General Assembly seats. The high court concluded, however, that the present legislature was not in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause because it did not provide for a reasonable classification of those voting for state legislators.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Service Employees International Union, Local 32BJ, against Temco Service Industries, Inc., a New York City-based building contractor, for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also found that, contrary to the Commission’s opinion, the arbitration provision in the Commission Act does not preclude arbitration of employment-discrimination claims.  For example, as set forth in its order, the Commission found that the Commission's finding was inconsistent with its prior opinion, which held that arbitration is not mandatory under the federal securities laws.  In addition, the Court found that arbitration does not require a waiver of the right to a judicial forum.  As set forth by the Commission, however, it does require arbitration of claims under the Exchange Act.  Specifically, the court ruled that, as a matter of law, a collective-bargaining agreement does not guarantee a right to arbitration, that an individual may not be entitled to that right, and that a party may not forgo the substantive rights afforded by the federal law, including, but not limited to, a contractual right. The Commission also ruled that arbitration could not preclude an individual from seeking relief from a court for a statutory claim.  According to the complaint, the Committee on Education, Science, and Advocacy (CIEA) has issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors toÂ check the background of anyone selling or offering them an investment using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

Appellants own a house in appellees' village, which they rented to various individuals. Six of these renters, including two unmarried males, occupied the premises when the village served appellees with an order requiring them to remedy alleged violations of the village's restrictive land-use ordinance, which defines "family," for zoning purposes, as "[o]r more than two [persons] ...living and cooking together as a single housekeeping unit, exclusive of household servants." After appellees filed suit challenging the ordinance's constitutionality, the village increased the rent to reflect the loss of the original tenants and acquisition of the new ones. Appellees then sought damages for the decrease in rental income resulting from the increase in rent. The District Court upheld the ordinance, holding it constitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court of Appeals reversed. Held: 1. Since the ordinance is not directed at transients, nor does it involve any fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, nor impose any disparate treatment on any group, nor discriminate against any individual based on his marital status, nor contravene any policy of racial equality, the ordinance satisfies the equal protection requirement of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 108-111. 2. In view of the ordinance's potential effect on the value of appellees' property, the question of the ordinance's constitutionality presents a controversy in the constitutional sense. Pp. 111-112. 476 F. 2d 806, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit reversed a lower court's order requiring the State of Virginia to provide counsel to death row inmates seeking postconviction relief. The court held that a prisoner's "right of access" to the courts requires a State to furnish access to adequate law libraries or other legal aid so the prisoners might prepare petitions for judicial relief, since their cases are unusually complex and since the shadow of impending execution interferes with their ability to do legal work. The lower court had found that Virginia's efforts did not afford prisoners meaningful access to the court because they did not guarantee the prisoners continuous assistance of counsel. The Court held that the case was not controlled by Pennsylvania v. Finley, which held that neither the Due Process Clause nor the equal protection guarantee of "meaningful access" required the State to appoint counsel for indigent prisoners seeking state collateral proceedings, since it did not address the rule enunciated in Bounds, and since Finley did not involve the death penalty. The appeals court found that there was no inconsistency between Bounds and Finley, and that the right of access at issue rests on a constitutional theory considered in the case. The case was remanded, and the court ruled that the State's scheme does not violate the Constitution.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 makes it unlawful “for an employer … to fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual, or otherwise to discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of such individual’s race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.” 42 U. S. C. §2000e–2(a)(1). To spare very small businesses from Title VII liability, Congress provided that “[t]he term ‘employer’ means a person engaged in an industry affecting commerce who has fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year, and any agent of such a person … .” §§2000e(b), which also prescribes the meaning, for Title VII purposes, of 12 other terms used in the Act. Title VII makes it “an unlawful employment practice” for an employer to fail to hire, refuse to discharge, or to discriminate on the basis of sex, and “employee” is defined as “any person engaged” in an “employment agency,” “labor organization,’” or “commerce,“ “eCommerce.’ ” (hereinafter “Employee). Title VII contains a separate jurisdictional provision that specifies, as a prerequisite to its application, the existence of a particular fact, i.e., 15 employees. The District Court dismissed the Title VII action for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The numerical threshold number of employees for application of Title VII is an element of a plaintiff’lls claim for relief, not a jurisdictional issue. Pp. 5–11. (a) Title VII‘s “subject matter jurisdiction, because it involves the district courts’ power to hear a case, can never be forfeited or waived” United States v. Cotton, 535 U.S. 625, 630, and it is not jurisdictional. P. 5. (b) The employee-numerosity requirement relates to the substantive adequacy of a Title VII claim, and therefore could not be raised defensively late in the lawsuit, since Y&H had failed to assert the objection prior to the close of trial on the merits. The other terms defined in Title VII are: “person, ‘employment agency’ (employee) and ‘commerce, ” ’ “industry affecting commerce” , “religion, “because of sex” . “demonstrates.“ §1332(a), authorizing suits by the Government to enjoin “pattern or practice discrimination.�” § 2000e–6(b). The Title VII statute also provides for “federal-question” jurisdiction, §1331, §12(h)(3), which authorizes suits by a Government agency to enfranchize “suspects” (other than labor organizations). The statute also specifies that a complaint “fail[s] to state a claim upon which relief can be granted … may be made in any pleading … or by motion for judgment on the pleadings, or at the trial on [the merits].” Cf. Kontrick v. Ryan, 540 U.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against the Federal Bureau of Investigation for its role in a fraud perpetrated by a private mortgage lender.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") by failing to provide timely relief to borrowers who had been denied the right to prepay their mortgages.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the FHFA has agreed to the entry of a permanent injunction against future violations of the federal securities laws, and to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000,000.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against the defendants.  On May 23, 1988, the date of enactment of ELIHPA, the court held that the federal government owed no future performance under the contracts.  According to the court's order, the defendants' claims were time barred for essentially the same reason.  For example, the complaint alleges that a borrower could not prepay his mortgage at any time and thereby gain release from federal restrictions on the use of a participating owner's property.  As a result, the federal court held the defendants untimely, and their suits properly dismissed.   The court also found that the defendants violated Section 5 of the FhFA, which provides for the right of a borrower to apply for a loan at a reasonable time.  Under the federal law, the borrower can't prepay before the date that the loan is due to be repaid, and the government has an obligation to determine when to accept the borrower's request for a repaying of the loan. Â The SEC's investigation was conducted by John R. Roehm and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry.   The litigation will be led by Mr. R. Barry and Ms. Burt of the New York office.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois dismissed a complaint alleging that two Chicago-area dairy distributors violated the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act. The complaint alleged that the two companies, Borden Dairy and Bowman Dairy, had engaged in price discrimination against independent stores that sold their dairy products. The District Court dismissed the charges, holding that there was no proof of the alleged Sherman Act violations and that no equitable relief was necessary because the companies were already restrained by a consent decree entered in a private antitrust case. The Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit reversed the lower court's decision, finding that the parties did not satisfy their burden of showing that their respective discriminatory pricing plans reflected only a 'due allowance' for cost differences. The appeals court held that the district court should have granted the parties' motion for a preliminary injunction. The lower court had previously granted the government's request for a permanent injunction against the defendants, but the appeals court found that the defendants had not shown that the injunction would be in the best interests of their customers. The court also found that Bowman's cost justification was based on a comparison of its average cost per $100 of sales to the chains in relation to the average cost of similar sales to each of the four groups of independents. The trial court had granted the Government's motion for an injunction against Bowman. The Appeals Court concluded that the trial court did not have jurisdiction to grant the injunction because the parties had agreed to the injunction in the consent decree.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia today entered a final judgment against Norfolk Shipbuilding & Drydock Corporation, a Virginia-based subcontractor for Mid-Atlantic Coatings, Inc., for violating the federal maritime duty of care.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Alexandria, Va., on April 8, 1997, Christopher Garris was performing sandblasting work aboard the USNS Maj. Stephen W. Pless in the employ of Tidewater Temps, Inc. when he was injured. The complaint alleges that Pless was liable for the loss of Garris' son, who was not a seaman, and that he was not liable under general maritime law for the death of his son.  The complaint further alleges that, in a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Virginia announced criminal charges against Pless.  In a parallel case, the U.N. Office of Justice for the Southern District of New York today announced parallel criminal charges.  On August 31, 2018, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action in federal district court in Virginia against Norfolk, charging Pless with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The SEC's Complaint charges Pless and Tidewater with violations of the federal securities laws and seeks disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, penalties, and permanent injunctions.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Complaint, Pless consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of The Maritime Act of 1940, and orders him to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000. The settlement is subject to court approval.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 531 (August 31, 1998).

The Supreme Court of the United States decided the case of Tasini v. New York Times Co. in 1997. The case involved a group of freelance writers who had sold their articles to various newspapers and magazines. Later, the articles were included in online databases operated by Lexis/Nexis and Micropaper. The writers argued that including their articles in the databases violated their exclusive rights under Section 201(c) of the Copyright Act of 1976. The Supreme Court agreed with the lower courts and found that the inclusion of the articles in the databases did not violate Section 201(c).

Under California's three strikes law, a defendant who is convicted of a felony and has previously been convicted of two or more serious or violent felonies must receive an indeterminate life imprisonment term. Such a defendant becomes eligible for parole on a date calculated by reference to a minimum term, which, in this case, is 25 years. While on parole, petitioner Ewing was convicted of felony grand theft for stealing three golf clubs, worth $399 apiece. As required by the three strikes statute, the prosecutor formally alleged, and the trial court found, that Ewing had been convicted previously of four serious orviolent felonies. In sentencing him to 25 years to life, the court refused to exercise its discretion to reduce the conviction to a misdemeanor- under a state law that permits certain offenses, known as "wobblers," to be classified as either misdemeanors or felonies- or to dismiss the allegations of some or all of his prior relevant convictio. The State Court of Appeal affirmed. Relying on Rummel v. Estelle, 445 U. S. 263, it rejected Ewing's claim that his sentence was grossly disproportionate under the Eighth Amendment and reasoned that enhanced sentences under the law served the State's legitimate goal of deterring and incapacitating repeat offenders. The California Supreme Court denied review. Held: The judgment is affirmed. Pp. 20-31. (a) The Eighth Amendment, which forbids cruel and unusual punishments, contains a "narrow proportionality principle" that "applies to noncapital sentences." Harmelin v. Michigan, 501 U.S. 957, 996-997. This Court has a longstanding tradition of deferring to state legislatures in making and implementing such important policy decisions. The Constitution does not mandate adoption of any one penological theory, and nothing in that Amendment prohibits California from choosing to incapacitate criminals who have already been convicted. However, recidivism has long been recognized as a legitimate basis for increased punishment and is a serious public safety concern in California and the Nation. Any criticism of the law is appropriately directed at the legislature, which is primarily responsible for making the policy choices underlying any criminal sentencing scheme. Thus, any criticism of this Court's policy choices must be weighed against the policy judgments that find expression in the legislature's choice of sanctions. Here, Ewing is not a recidivist, but rather a "wobbler" who has repeatedly engaged in serious and violent criminal behavior, and whose conduct has not been deterred by more conventional punishment approaches. The United States, bound by the federal Sentencing Guidelines, would impose upon him a 25-year sentence that, in any ordinary case, would not exceed 18 months in prison. The Court has long held that the Constitution directs judges to apply their best judgment in determining the proportionality of fines, see, e. g., United States v. Bajakajian, 524 U. . . 321, 334-336, and that recidivists who have engaged in far more serious conduct are disproportionately punished for their offense of conviction, conviction, and violent felony convictions. The proportionality test announced in Solem v. Helm, 463 U . S. 277 (1983), is incapable of judicial application but is generally a policy choice to be made by state legislatures, not federal courts. Moreover, some objective evidence suggests that many experienced judges would consider the sentence disproportionately harsh. The fact that the State of California has reserved, and still reserves, the Ewing-type prison time, i. e., at least 25 years without parole, for criminals convicted of crimes far worse than was Ewing’s is not determinative, since the State has reserved the sentence that it here imposes upon Ewing for nonrecidivist first-degree murderers, and it reserves the sentence for those who continue to commit crimes that are "grossly disproportionate" to the crime. The contrast between the sentences here and those in the two cases is particularly important because they provide proportionality review with objective content. The comparison places Ewing well within the twilight zone between Solem and Rummels, a zone where the argument for unconstitutionality is substantial, where the cases themselves cannot determine the constitutional outcome, and where Ewing himself, seriously ill when sentenced at age 38, will likely die in prison if he is sentenced to life imprisonment. This case demonstrates why a proportionality rule cannot be intelligently applied, and why Solem should not be given stare decisis effect. The Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause of the Eight Amendment contains no proportionality principles. See Harmelin, supra, at 276; Solem

Petitioner Payne was convicted of first-degree murder and one count of assault with intent to commit murder in the first degree. He was sentenced to death for each of the murders, and to 30 years in prison for the assault. The State Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and sentence. Held: The Eighth Amendment bars the admission of victim impact evidence during the penalty phase of a capital trial. Booth v. Maryland, 482 U. S. 496, and South Carolina v. Gathers, 490 U.S. 805, that the Eighth Amendment prohibits a capital sentencing jury from considering "victim impact" evidence relating to the personal characteristics of the victim and the emotional impact of the crimes on the victim's family. Pp. 531-532. (a) Where the State imposes the death penalty for a particular crime, it imposes special limitations upon that process. Booth, supra, at 507, n. 8, 107 S.Ct. 2529, distinguished. P. 532. 791 S. W. 2d 10, affirmed.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central question was whether Janus Capital Management LLC (JCM), an investment adviser to mutual funds, could be held liable for false statements included in the prospectuses of the mutual funds it advised. The specific legal provision at issue was Rule 10b–5, which prohibits making false statements in connection with the purchase or sale of securities.

The Court concluded that JCM could not be held liable because it did not "make" the statements in the prospectuses. The Court reasoned that the "maker" of a statement is the person or entity with ultimate authority over the statement, including its content and how it is communicated. In this case, the prospectuses were issued by Janus Investment Fund, a separate legal entity with its own board of trustees, which retained JCM for advisory services. Although JCM provided input, it did not have ultimate control over the prospectuses.

The Court emphasized the importance of maintaining a clear distinction between primary violators who can be pursued in private suits and secondary violators who cannot. It rejected broader interpretations of "make" that would undermine this distinction and potentially expand liability beyond what Congress has authorized.

The Court also rejected arguments that the close relationship between mutual funds and their investment advisers should influence the decision, stating that corporate formalities were observed and that any changes in liability should be addressed by Congress, not the courts.

The decision has implications for the scope of liability under Rule 10b–5, limiting it to those with ultimate authority over false statements and reinforcing the separation between primary and secondary violators in securities law. The ruling thereby narrows the potential for investment advisers to be held liable for false statements made by the mutual funds they advise, provided they do not have ultimate control over those statements.

The Supreme Court ruled in Eldred v. Ashcroft that the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act of 1998, which extended the term of copyright protection for works created before 1978, was unconstitutional. The Court held that the extension violated the First Amendment's protection of free speech and expression, as well as the separation of powers doctrine. The Court found that the extension gave too much power to copyright owners to suppress the public's access to creative works, and that it was an excessive burden on the public domain.

As part of the Federal Lands Highway Program, the Federal Government financed road construction and improvement projects on federal public roads, including Indian reservation roads. Over a several-year period, respondent Bureau of Indian Affairs contracted with appellant Blaze Construction Company, which is incorporated under the laws of the Blackfeet Tribe of Montana and is owned by a member of that Tribe, to build, repair, and improve roads on various Indian reservations in Arizona. At the end of the contracting period, the Arizona Department of Revenue assessed Blaze for failing to pay the State's transaction privilege tax on the proceeds from its contracts with the Bureau. That tax is levied on the gross receipts of companies doing business in the State. Blaze protested the assessment and prevailed at the end of administrative proceedings, but, on review, the Arizona Tax Court granted summary judgment in the Department's favor. The Arizona Court of Appeals reversed, holding that federal law pre-empted the application of the tax to Blaze. Held: A State generally may impose a nondiscriminatory tax upon a private company's proceeds from contracts with the Federal Government even if the federal contractor renders its services on an Indian reservation. United States v. New Mexico, 455 U. S. 720. Although the incidence of the tax falls on Blaze, not the Federal Government, Blaze argues that it should be exempted from the tax because the activity took place on an Indian reservation. However, interest balancing in this setting would only cloud the clear rule established by New Mexico. The need to avoid litigation and to ensure efficient tax administration counsels in favor of a bright-line standard for taxation of federal contracts, regardless of whether the contracted-for activity occurs on an Indian reservation. Moreover, since the Tribes on whose reservations Blaze worked have not assumed the responsibility of managing the federal funds and operating certain federal programs under the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, there is no need to depart from the New Mexico rule. Certiorari granted; 190 Ariz. 262, 947 P. 2d 836, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Massachusetts courts did not violate Luis Melendez-Diaz's Sixth Amendment right to be confronted with the witnesses against him when they admitted into evidence three certificates of analysis reporting the results of forensic analysis that showed that material seized by the police and connected to the defendant was cocaine. The certificates were sworn to before a notary public by analysts at the State Laboratory Institute of the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, as required under Massachusetts law, and were admitted pursuant to state law. The court held that the certificates were not subject to confrontation under the Sixth Amendment because they were "prima facie evidence of the composition, quality, and the net weight of the narcotic ... analyzed." The court also held that Melendez- Diaz had a prior opportunity to cross-examine the analysts. The Supreme Court's decision in Crawford v. Washington, 541 N. E. 2d 701, 827, 705, held that a witness's testimony against a defendant is thus inadmissible unless the witness appears at trial or, if the witness is unavailable, the defendant has a prior chance for cross-examination. The Court of Appeals agreed with the lower court's denial of Melendez's motion for a new trial. The high court ruled that Melendez' right to confront the witnesses was not violated by the admission of the certificates. The case is now before the United States Supreme Court.

After petitioner's husband died intestate, she received the proceeds of his life insurance policy and pension plan, even though a Washington statute provides that, upon dissolution of marriage, a provision relating to the payment or transfer of a decedent's interest in a nonprobate asset in favor of or granting an interest or power to the decedent's former spouse is revoked. She brought suit in state court seeking to recover the proceeds, arguing that she was entitled to them because the statute disqualified her as a beneficiary and left the proceeds without a qualified named beneficiary. Respondents, the couple's children by a previous marriage, sought the proceeds as their father's statutory heirs. The trial courts ruled that the insurance policy and pension plan should be administered according to the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), and granted summary judgment to petitioner. On appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the statute was not pre-empted by ERISA. Affirming, the State Supreme Court found that the statute did not refer to ERISA plans to an extent that required pre-emption; that it lacked a connection with an ERISA plan that would compel pre-emption; and that it did not conflict with any specific ERISA provision, including the antialienation provision. Held: The Washington statute is expressly pre-empted by ERISA. Pp. 12-17. (a) Under ERISA § 1144(a)-which declares that ERISA "shall supersede ... any...State laws ... relating to any ... employee benefit plan" covered by ERISA--this Court has observed repeatedly that the term "relate to" cannot be taken to mean anything beyond what is clearly encompassed by the statute's broad reach. However, the term "connect with" is used in describing the type of state law that Congress understood would survive ERISA's pre-emption provisions. Thus, to determine whether a state law has the forbidden connection, this Court looks both to ERISA's objectives as a guide to the scope of the state law that Congress understood would survive, as well as to the nature of the effect of the state law on ERISA plans. Here, the statute binds ERISA plan administrators to a particular choice of rules for determining beneficiary status, requiring them to pay benefits to the beneficiaries chosen by state law, rather than those identified in the plan documents. Such a requirement implicates an area of core ERISA concern, since it runs counter to ERISA's commands that a plan specify the basis on which payments are made to and from the plan, and that the fiduciary administer the plan in accordance with the plan documents. Moreover, the statute has a prohibited connection with ERISA plans because it interferes with nationally uniform plan administration. Since the statute requires administrators to identify the beneficiary specified by the plan documents, they must become familiar with state statutes so that they can determine whether the named beneficiary's status has been revoked by operation of law. And in this context, the burden is exacerbated by the choice-of-law problems that may confront an administrator when the employer is located in one State, the plan participant lives in another, and the participant's former spouse lives in a third. Even though the statute allows employers to opt out, it nevertheless dictates the choices facing ERISA plans with regard to matters of plan administration. Finally, while there is a presumption against pre-emption in areas of traditional state regulation such as family law, that presumption can be overcome where, as here, Congress has expressed its intent to pre-empt. Pp. 12-16. (b) The fact that the Washington statute involves both family law and probate law does not save it from pre-emption. Although there is a presumption against pre-emption in areas of traditional state regulation, that presumption can be overcome where, as here, Congress has expressed its intent to pre-empt. Pp. 16-17. 139 Wash. 2d 557, 989 P. 2d 80, reversed and remanded.

Section 1502(a) provides that Customs "shall, under rules and regulations prescribed by the Secretary [of the Treasury] ... fix the final classification and rate of duty applicable to ... merchandise" under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), 19 U. S. C. 1202. A ruling letter "represents the official position of the Customs Service with respect to the particular transaction or issue described therein and is binding on all Customs Service personnel in accordance with the provisions of this section until modified or revoked. In the absence of a change of practice or other modification or revocation which affects the principle of the ruling set forth in the ruling letter, that principle may be cited as authority in the disposition of transactions involving the same circumstances." Held: A tariff classification ruling is eligible to claim respect according to its persuasiveness under Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U.S. 134, which held that Customs regulations receive the deference described in Chevron U., S. A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U., 837 (1984). Pp. 542-543. (a) When Congress has "explicitly left a gap for an agency to fill, there is an express delegation of authority to the agency to elucidate a specific provision of the statute by regulation," Chevron, supra, at 843-844, and any ensuing regulation is binding in the courts unless procedurally defective, arbitrary or capricious in substance, or manifestly contrary to the statute. P. 543-544. (b) The authorization for classification rulings, and Customs's practice in making them, present a case far removed not only from notice-and-comment process, but from any other circumstances reasonably suggesting that Congress ever thought of classification rulings as deserving deference to it. This Court has identified a category of interpretive choices distinguished by an additional reason for judicial deference: judicial responses to administrative action must continue to differentiate between Chevron and the agency on a particular question, and that continued recognition of the agency's authority is necessary for just the reasons Justice Jackson gave when he gave when that case was decided. The approach has produced a spectrum of judicial responses, from great respect at one end, see, e.g., Aluminum Co. of America v. Central Lincoln Peoples' Util. Dist.,467 U. 380, 389-390 (1984), to near indifference at the other, see. e. g., Bowen v. Georgetown Univ. Hospital, 488 U. 204, 212-213. The agency's generally conferred authority and other statutory circumstances that Congress would expect the Agency to be able to speak with the force of law when it addresses ambiguity in the statute or fills a space in the enacted law, even one about which "Congress did not actually have an intent" as to a particular result. The fact that the tariff classification here was not a product of such formal process does not alone, therefore, bar the application of Chevron deference here. The congressional delegation to an agency is best treated like "interpretations contained in policy statements, agency manuals, and enforcement guidelines," Christensen v. Harris County, 529 U. .S. 576, 596-597, and the statute's direction to disseminate "information" necessary to "secure" uniformity seems to assume that a ruling may be precedent in later transactions, precedential value alone does not add up to Chevron entitlement; interpretive rules may sometimes function as precedents, see Strauss, The Rulemaking Continuum, 41 Duke L. J. 1463, 1472-1473, and they enjoy no Chevron status as a class. Nor is there any indication that a more potent delegation might have been understood as going to Headquarters even when Headquarters provides developed reasoning, as it did in this instance. Nor are there indications that the agency action (if reasonable) is "authoritative," post, at 17. Nor does the statute suggest any intent to create a Chevron patchwork of classification decisions that would naturally bind more than the parties to the ruling, once the goods classified are admitted into this country. Nor do the amendments to this statute make it appear that Congress intended such a broad range of statutory authority to produce only two varieties of administrative action, demanding either Chevron or none at all, but the breadth of the spectrum of possible agency action must be taken into account. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida today announced that it has issued a final judgment ordering the issuance of a temporary restraining order to halt an ongoing litigation action brought by the Florida Bar Association.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Miami, Florida, alleges that, in July 1977, the Florida State Court issued an order requiring the highest court of each state to promulgate standards and guidelines regulating radio, television, and other photographic coverage of court proceedings.  According to the complaint, defendants were charged with conspiracy to commit burglary, grand larceny, and possession of burglary tools. The complaint alleges that defendants were also charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The court issued its order requiring that all electronic media coverage of criminal proceedings be conducted by local rule and under the control of the trial judge.  In addition, the court ordered that the jury not to watch or read anything about the case in the media and suggested that jurors "avoid the local news and watch only the national news on television."  The court declined to give the order that the court issued.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of the final judgment, which permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar. The final judgment also prohibits the defendants from participating in any future litigation involving the subject matter of the court's order.  On May 17, 2020, the Honorable Gerald R. Mascianica of the Florida Court of Appeals issued a judgment enjoining the SEC from violating the charged provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4), and ordering the SEC to comply with the Commission's order by issuing an order permanently enjoining defendants from violating these provisions. The order also requires the court to appoint a receiver to record any testimony presented to the jury.  A hearing on May 24, 2020 is scheduled for 7:30 p.m. Eastern.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-5221.

In 1988, the Forest Service amended its regional guide to prohibit timber harvesting on certain designated areas within old-growth forests in Oregon and Washington known to contain the northern spotted owl. Respondent Seattle Audubon Society (joined by various environmental groups) and the Washington Contract Loggers Association filed separate lawsuits in Federal District Court, alleging violations of three federal statutes: the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA), which makes it unlawful to "kill" or "take" any "migratory bird," and the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), 83 Stat. 852, as amended, 42 U. S. C. § 4321 et seq. Subsection (g)(1) provided for limited, expedited judicial review of individual timber sales offered under § 318. The District Court consolidated the actions and preliminarily enjoined certain of the challenged harvesting pending appeal. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed. Held: 1. Section 318 of the Department of the Interior and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1990, does not repeal or amend the environmental laws underlying this litigation, but directs the court to reach a specific result and make certain factual findings under existing law, as long as it was a "possible" one. United States v. Klein, 80 U.S. (13 Wall.) 128, 20 L. Ed. 519 (1872), which it construed as prohibiting Congress from "direct[ing] . . . a particular decision in a case, without repealing or amending the law underlying the litigation." Pp. 6-8. 2. The first sentence of § 318 (b)(6)(A) "does not, by its plain language, repeal [or amend] [the environmental laws] or direct[ed]" any particular findings of fact or applications of law, old or new, to fact. The court then became obliged to impose that "saving interpretation," 914 F. 2d 1311, as the court held the provision unconstitutional under United Statesv. Klein. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that § 318 "could not" effect an implied modification of substantive law because it was embedded in an appropriations measure. P. 6. 3. The fact that subsection (b)6 (A) compelled changes in law, not findings or results under old law, did not mean that the provision did not modify the old provisions. Nor did the provision "direct" any particular finding of fact, applications, or findings under old laws. Nor was the provision directed to direct any particular new findings or applications under either the old or the new standards. Nor does the provision appear to have directed particular applications under the old and new standards, see, e. g., Pennsylvania v. Wheeling & Belmont Bridge Co., 421, 15 L.Ed. 435 (1856), which construed as permitting Congress to "amend or repeal any law, even for the purpose of ending pending litigation." The Court's reasoning contains several errors. First, although repeals by implication are especially disfavored in the appropriations context, Congress nonetheless may amend substantive law in appropriations statute, as far as it does so clearly. Second, because the provision incorporated by reference the harvesting prohibitions imposed by a BLM agreement not yet in existence when the Compromise was enacted, the intent to modify was not only clear, but express. Third, it emphasized the imperative tone of the provision, by which Congress "determine[d] and direct [ed]" that compliance with two new provisions would constitute compliance with five old ones. Finally, the fact that it explicitly made reference to pending cases in order to identify five statutory provisions served only to identify the five "statutory requirements that are the basis for" those cases-namely, pertinent provisions of MBTA, NEPA, NFMA, FLPMA and OCLA- served to serve only to define the five statutory requirements that the agencies could satisfy their MBTA obligations in either of two ways: by managing their lands so as not to violate the prohibitions of subsections (b3) and (b5). Finally, it did so by effectively modifiying the provisions at issue in those cases

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Minnesota ruled that a law that denies federal financial aid to students who fail to register for the draft under the Military Selective Service Act is a bill of attainder and a violation of the Fifth Amendment's right to privacy. The court held that the law is not a valid tool to determine whether a student is eligible for federal aid. The law requires students to register with the Selective Service and submit a statement of compliance to the Secretary of Education, which is required to verify their compliance with the draft registration law and regulations issued under it. In a 1983 case, the court ruled that this requirement violated the Fifth because it compelled the student to incriminate himself in violation of his Fifth Amendment right to remain silent. The appeals court agreed with the lower court's decision, and ruled that  12(f)(1) is a "Bill of Attainder" that "clearly singles out a group based on past conduct" and "legislatively determines the guilt of thisable group"

The Supreme Court addressed whether Congress could repeal or modify a statutory formula for annual cost-of-living increases in federal judges' compensation under the Compensation Clause of Article III, Section 1 of the U.S. Constitution. The Court also considered the timing of Congress's actions in relation to the effectiveness of such increases.

The Court's opinion, delivered by Justice Brennan, held that:

1. For Year 1, Congress's action to stop a cost-of-living increase after it had already taken effect was unconstitutional because it "diminished" the compensation of federal judges, violating the Compensation Clause.

2. For Year 2 and Year 3, Congress acted before the scheduled increases took effect, and thus it did not diminish judges' compensation. The Court ruled that Congress could rescind these planned increases without violating the Compensation Clause because the increases had not yet become part of the judges' compensation.

3. For Year 4, like Year 1, Congress acted after the increase had taken effect, and therefore the action was unconstitutional for the same reasons as in Year 1.

The Court's reasoning emphasized the importance of judicial independence and the historical context of the Compensation Clause, which aims to protect judges from undue influence and ensure a competent and independent judiciary. The Court also clarified that the Compensation Clause does not prevent Congress from adjusting judicial compensation before it becomes part of the judges' due and payable salary.

The Court remanded the cases for further proceedings to calculate the precise amounts owed to judges for the unconstitutional actions in Years 1 and 4. Justice Blackmun did not participate in the decision.

Implications of the decision include affirming the principle that judicial compensation cannot be reduced once it has become effective, thus protecting judicial independence, while also recognizing Congress's authority to adjust compensation before it becomes part of the judges' salary.

Respondents, employees of petitioner company, entered into a collective-bargaining agreement (CBA) that required them to arbitrate any statutory discrimination claims, including claims under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA). When respondents were laid off, they filed suit in Federal District Court, alleging that petitioners had discriminated against them on the basis of age in violation of the ADEA. They conceded that the CBA governed their employment relationship and that the arbitration requirement applied to their claims. However, they argued that the CBA was void under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) because it prevented them from filing charges with the National Labor Relations Authority (NLA) and from appealing adverse NLA rulings to the courts. The District Court disagreed, rejecting respondents’ argument that the CBA operated as a substantive waiver of their ADEA rights. On appeal, the Sixth Circuit affirmed, reasoning that the CBA was ambiguous about whether it applied to ADEA claims and that the parties’ conflicting views about how to resolve that ambiguity meant that the CBA was not enforceable. Held: A collective-bargaining agreement that clearly and unmistakably requires union members to arbitrate ADEA claims is enforceable as a matter of federal law. Pp. 3–19. (a) Although the Court’s early decisions in the area of arbitration of employment discrimination claims contained dictum suggesting that the decision to arbitrate such claims denies the full protection of the substantive guarantee against workplace discrimination, see, e.g., Alexander v. Gardner-Denver Co., 415 U. S. 36, 51, the voluntary decision to collectively bargain for arbitration does not deny the full protection of the ADEA’s substantive rights. Such a decision merely limits the procedural mechanism used to adjudicate those rights. See, e.g., Gilmer v. Utah Teachers Assns Health Care Plan, Ltd., 500 U. S. 31, 39. Pp. 3–10. (b) The Court’s modern arbitration jurisprudence supports this conclusion. The Court has repeatedly emphasized that the FAA’s goal of promoting efficient dispute resolution is best achieved when parties agree to arbitrate their disputes. See, e.g., Shearson/American Express Inc. v. McMahon, 482 U. S. 220, 229. By contrast, the traditional judicial process is slow, expensive, and uncertain. See, e.g., id., at 227. The Court has also stressed that the FAA’s goals are best served when parties agree to arbitrate their disputes before they become contentious. See, e.g., ibid. By contrast, the traditional judicial process typically occurs after the dispute has already developed into a controversy. See, e.g., id., at 227. Furthermore, the Court has consistently held that the FAA’s goals are best served when parties agree to arbitrate their disputes in accordance with the terms of their agreement. See, e.g., id., at 229. By contrast, the traditional judicial process usually results in a trial, which is not bound by the terms of the parties’ agreement. See, e.g., id., at 227. Pp. 10–16. (c) The Court’s modern arbitration jurisprudence also demonstrates that the FAA’s goals are best served when parties agree to arbitrate their disputes in accordance with the terms of their agreement. The Supreme Court reviewed whether Section 12(f) of the Military Selective Service Act, which denies federal financial aid to male students who fail to register for the draft, constitutes a bill of attainder or violates the Fifth Amendment by compelling self-incrimination.

The Court found that Section 12(f) does not meet the historical definition of a bill of attainder, as it does not legislatively determine guilt or inflict punishment without a judicial trial. The statute does not permanently bar non-registrants from receiving aid; they can become eligible by registering, even if late. The Court also determined that the statute serves non-punitive legislative purposes, such as encouraging draft registration and fair allocation of federal resources.

Regarding the Fifth Amendment, the Court held that individuals are not compelled to seek financial aid, and thus there is no compulsion to incriminate oneself. Even if someone registers late, the statement of compliance required for financial aid does not specify whether the registration was timely or late, so it does not require self-incrimination.

The Court reversed the District Court's decision, concluding that Section 12(f) does not constitute a bill of attainder and does not violate the Fifth Amendment rights of the individuals concerned. Justice Blackmun did not participate in the decision.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central issue was whether a plaintiff alleging securities fraud must show that the defendant's misrepresentation caused an actual economic loss, a concept known as "loss causation." The Ninth Circuit had previously ruled that a plaintiff could establish loss causation by simply demonstrating that the price of the security at the time of purchase was inflated due to the misrepresentation.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the Ninth Circuit's approach, stating that an inflated purchase price alone does not necessarily result in an economic loss at the time of the transaction, as the value of the security purchased equals the amount paid. The Court emphasized that a loss occurs only when the truth is revealed and the security's value decreases as a result. The Court also noted that many factors can influence a security's price over time, making it difficult to attribute a later loss directly to the initial misrepresentation.

The Court highlighted that securities fraud actions have common-law roots, which traditionally require a plaintiff to show actual economic loss caused by the defendant's misrepresentation. The Court found that the Ninth Circuit's approach was inconsistent with this requirement and with the objectives of securities law, which aim to protect investors from fraud-induced losses, not to provide a general insurance against market losses.

The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's decision, stating that the plaintiffs' complaint failed to adequately allege loss causation and economic loss. The complaint only suggested that the plaintiffs paid an inflated price for the securities but did not indicate how the misrepresentation caused a subsequent economic loss. The Court remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, emphasizing that plaintiffs must provide some indication of the loss and its causal connection to the misrepresentation in their complaints.

The implication of this decision is that plaintiffs in securities fraud cases must clearly allege and prove that the defendant's misrepresentation directly caused an actual economic loss, rather than relying solely on the fact that they purchased securities at an inflated price. This requirement aims to prevent frivolous lawsuits and ensure that securities fraud actions serve their intended purpose of compensating for fraud-induced economic harm.

The U.S. Supreme Court has granted certiorari in the case of two members of the Coeur d'Alene Indian tribe convicted of the 1974 murder of an 81-year-old non-Indian woman in Worley, Idaho. The case involves the issue of whether federal criminal statutes violate the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment by subjecting individuals to federal prosecution by virtue of their status as Indians. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit concluded that the defendants' felony-murder convictions were unlawful as products of invidious racial discrimination. The Supreme Court, however, found that the lower court's decision was correct. The high court held that "Indian tribes are unique aggregations possessing attributes of sovereignty over both their members and their territory" and that "the power of regulating their internal and social relations is not a separate person" from those of other tribes. The court also held that the federal statute does not require premeditation and deliberation to establish a felony murder charge. The justices agreed with the lower courts' conclusions that defendants were "put at a serious racially-based disadvantage" because they were not subject to the same federal prosecution as other non- Indians charged with the same crime. In a separate opinion, the Court of Justice found that defendants' convictions were not unlawful because they had not been subject to premeditation or deliberation in federal prosecution. The Justices also found that there was no basis for the Court's conclusion that defendants had been deprived of their right to a fair trial.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the application of the Batson v. Kentucky decision, which prohibits racial discrimination in jury selection through the use of peremptory challenges. The case in question involves a federal habeas corpus petition where the defendant, Collins, claimed that the prosecutor had used peremptory strikes in a racially discriminatory manner, violating the Batson ruling.

The opinion outlines the three-step process for evaluating claims of racial discrimination in jury selection: (1) the defendant must make a prima facie showing that a peremptory challenge has been exercised on the basis of race; (2) if shown, the prosecution must offer a race-neutral explanation for the strike; and (3) the court must then decide if the defendant has proven intentional racial discrimination.

The Supreme Court emphasizes that the burden of proving racial motivation remains with the defendant throughout this process. The opinion also clarifies the standard of review for federal habeas corpus cases under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act (AEDPA). The state court's factual findings are presumed correct, and the habeas petitioner must provide clear and convincing evidence to overcome this presumption.

In this case, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals had found that the state court unreasonably determined the facts when it accepted the prosecutor's race-neutral reasons for striking a juror based on her youth and demeanor. However, the Supreme Court disagreed with the Ninth Circuit's assessment, stating that the trial court's credibility determination was not unreasonable. The Supreme Court noted that the trial court was in a better position to make such determinations and that reasonable minds could differ on the prosecutor's credibility without necessarily overriding the trial court's findings.

The Supreme Court concluded that the Ninth Circuit erred in its application of AEDPA standards and reversed its judgment, remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. The decision underscores the deference federal courts must give to state court findings in habeas corpus reviews and the high threshold for proving purposeful racial discrimination in jury selection.

Under Pennsylvania law, an illegitimate child cannot sue his putative father for support until he files a suit to establish paternity within six years of the child's birth. Petitioner Clark, whose minor daughter was born out of wedlock, sued respondent Jeter in a Pennsylvania county court to establish paternity and to compel him to pay child support. When Jeter moved to dismiss the suit on the grounds that it was barred by the 6-year statute of limitations, the court ruled in his favor. The Pennsylvania Superior Court affirmed, holding that the statute was not unconstitutionally vague and that the trial court properly dismissed the suit. The court declined to rule on Clark's contention that the statute violated the Federal Constitution. Subsequently, the Pennsylvania Legislature amended the statute to give illegitimate children 18 years to file suit to establish paternity. After the Pennsylvania Supreme Court refused to hear her appeal, Clark sought rehearing in the Superior Court, arguing that the court had overlooked Pennsylvania cases applying similar statutes of limitations retroactively and indicating that the federal Child Support Enforcement Amendments required States to adopt retroactive 18-year statutes of limitations or their equivalents. However, the court again declined to rule on the constitutionality of the statute. Held: 1. Since Clark did not press or pass upon the lower courts the federal pre-emption argument that the Pennsylvania Legislature intended to comply with the new federal law, this Court will not decide that issue. Pp. 10-11. 2. The Pennsylvania statute violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Although six years does not necessarily provide a reasonable opportunity to assert a claim on behalf of an illegitimate child, the statute is not substantially related to Pennsylvania's interest in avoiding the litigation of stale or fraudulent claims. That interest is undermined by the fact that Pennsylvania permits the issue of paternity to be litigated more than six years after the birth of an illegitimate child in various types of suits, including suits to establish paternity where the father pays support. Moreover, Pennsylvania recently enacted an 18-year statute of limitations for paternity and support actions, thus concededly acknowledging that proof problems are not overwhelming. Pp. 11-15. Reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Supreme Court reversed the Iowa Supreme Court's decision that Iowa's differing tax rates on slot machine revenues from riverboats and racetracks violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Iowa Supreme Court had ruled that the tax rate differential (20% for riverboats and up to 36% for racetracks) was unconstitutional because it did not rationally serve the state's objective of aiding racetracks in economic distress.

The U.S. Supreme Court disagreed, applying a rational-basis review, which is a deferential standard used when a law does not involve fundamental rights or suspect classifications like race or gender. Under this review, the Court determined that the law is constitutional if there is a plausible policy reason for the classification, if the legislative facts could be considered true by the decision-maker, and if the relationship between the classification and its goal is not so weak as to be arbitrary or irrational.

The Court found that the Iowa law could rationally be seen as serving the general objective of helping racetracks by allowing them to operate slot machines, even though it also taxed their revenues. The Court noted that legislation often involves balancing multiple objectives and that the legislature has broad authority to decide how to distribute tax burdens.

The Court also found rational reasons for the tax rate differential, such as aiding the riverboat industry, promoting economic development in river communities, or preserving the history of riverboats. These reasons were sufficient to uphold the different tax rates.

The Court concluded that the differential tax rate does not violate the Equal Protection Clause and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with their opinion.

Respondents Shirley and Larry McQuillan, doing business as Sorboturf Enterprises, were regional distributors of sorbothane, a patented elastic polymer whose shock-absorbing characteristics make it useful in a variety of medical, athletic, and equestrian products. Petitioner Spectrum Sports, Inc. (Spectrum), a distributor, was at all relevant times owned by BTR, Inc., and its wholly owned subsidiaries manufacture the product in the United States and Britain. In 1981, Hamilton-Kent Manufacturing Co. (Hamilton-Kent) and Sorbothane (S.I.) decided to establish five regional distributorships for the product, including medical products and shoe inserts, in the Southwest, and Spectrum was selected as distributor for another region. In 1983, S.I. informed respondents that it wanted them to relinquish their athletic shoe distributorship as a condition for retaining the right to develop and distribute equestrale products. As of May 1982, the marketing manager of S. I. told respondents that they had to sell their athletic distributorship to keep their equestria distribution rights, and that if they did not come to agreement with him she would be "looking for work." In the fall of 1982, Spectrum was appointed as distributor, and in 1983, the distributor began marketing through a national distributor a horseshoe pad allegedly indistinguishable from the one designed by respondents. In August 1983, Spectrum thereupon became national distributor. In May 1982 it announced that it would no longer accept their orders. In July 1983, it informed respondents of the impending sale of their equipment, and they refused to sell and continued to distribute athletic shoe inserts. The jury awarded $1,743,000 in compensatory damages on each of the 11 alleged violations found to have occurred. The District Court also awarded nearly $1 million in attorneys' fees and denied motions for judgment notwithstanding the verdict and for a new trial. The Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment of the District Court, finding that the jury had properly instructed the jury on the Sherman Act claims and found that the evidence supported the liability verdicts as well as the damages awards on these claims. Held: 1. The trial instructions allowed the jury to infer specific intent and dangerous probability of success from the defendants' predatory conduct, without any proof of the relevant product and geographic market or of a realistic probability that the defendants could achieve monopoly power in that market. Swift & Co. v. United States, 196 U. S. 375, and its progeny. Pp. 7-11. (a) In order to determine whether there is a "danger probability of monopolization" of a relevant market, a plaintiff must prove (1) that the defendant has engaged in predatory or anticompetitive conduct with (2) a specific intent to monopolize and (3) a dangerous probability that he will monopolize that market, and the jury's verdict did not negate the possibility that the § 2 verdict rested on the attempted monopolization attempt alone. In this respect, the instructions misconstrued § 2, as did the Court's judgment. P. 11. (b) The instructions were inconsistent with the policy of § 2. The "any part" clause, however, applies only to charges of monopolizing as well and to attempts to monopolization, and it is beyond doubt that the former requires proof of market power in the relevant market and the defendant's economic power. Insofar as § 2 prohibits attempts to "monopolize" any appreciable segment of interstate sales of the product involved, this statute, like many others and like the common law in some cases, directs itself against that dangerous probability. Such conduct does not constitute an "unfair or predatory" conduct, but is merely an attempt to lessen or destroy competition, and therefore requires inquiry into the relevant products and geographic marketplace and defendant's economy power. The court's decisions since Swift and later Ninth Circuit decisions refining and applying it are inconsistent with § 2's policy. The Act directs itself not against conduct which is competitive, even severely so, but against conduct that unfairly tends to destroy competition itself. It does so not out of solicitude for private concerns but out of concern for the public interest. The purpose of the Act is not to protect businesses from the working of the market; it is to protect the public from the failure of competition. The law directs itself to protect competition, not only from conduct which unfairly tends, but also from conduct that threatens actual monopolization. The courts have been careful to avoid constructions of §2 which might chill competition, rather than foster it. See Areeda & Turner, supra, at ¶ 820, p. 312. The fact that § 2 does not explicitly forbid the use of the term "fair or competitive" does not necessarily mean that it does not violate § 2; it merely means that it is necessary to show that the charge is "fair and competitive."
