Police officers, with probable cause to believe that a man had hidden marijuana in his home, prevented that man from entering the home for about two hours while they obtained a search warrant. The officers, without probable cause, searched the trailer and, along with other officers, searched it. They found under the sofa a marijuana pipe, a box for marijuana (called a "one-hitter" box), and a small amount of marijuana. They then arrested the man. The trial court granted McArthur's suppression motion, and the Illinois Supreme Court denied the State's petition for leave to appeal. Held: The Fourth Amendment prohibits the kind of temporary seizure at issue. Pp. 531-532. (a) The restriction at issue was reasonable, and hence lawful, in light of the following circumstances. First, the police had probable cause that the man, if left free of any restraint, would destroy the evidence. They reasonably believed that McArthur, consequently suspecting an imminent search, would, if given the chance, get rid of the drugs fast. Second, they made reasonable efforts to reconcile their law enforcement needs with the demands of personal privacy. They did not search the trailer nor arrest McArthur before obtaining a warrant. They imposed a significantly less restrictive restraint, preventing McArthur only from entering his trailer unaccompanied. They left his home and his belongings intact-until a neutral Magistrate issued a warrant for entry of the home. Third, they imposed the restraint for a limited period of time, namely, two hours. The Court of Appeals affirmed, but held that the warrantless seizure was reasonable because, had the police acted lawfully throughout, they could have discovered and seized the drugs pursuant to the validly issued warrant. P. 532. 185 Ill. 2d 651, 720 N. E. 2nd 1101, reversed and remanded.
What is the main idea behind the article "The Unearned Fees Case"?

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Payton v. New York (1980) that the Fourth Amendment protects individuals from warrantless entry into their homes, even if the government has probable cause to believe that illegal activity is occurring inside. The Court held that the warrant requirement is essential to protecting privacy and security within the home, and that exceptions to the warrant requirement, such as hot pursuit and plain view, must be strictly construed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of New Mexico has ruled that a blood-alcohol test that was used to determine a driver's level of alcohol was not testimonial under the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause. In Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts, the Court held that a forensic laboratory report stating that a suspect substance was cocaine ranked as testimonial for purposes of the Constitution's Sixth Amendment. The New Mexico Supreme Court, however, held that, although the test was "testimonial," it did not require the certifying analyst's in-court testimony. The Court ruled that the prosecution did not have to offer a live witness competent to testify to the truth of the statements made in the report. We hold that surrogate testimony of that order does not meet the constitutional requirement. The accused's right is to be confronted with the analyst who made the certification, unless that analyst is unavailable at trial, and the accused had an opportunity, pretrial, to cross-examine that particular scientist.

Petitioner Wal-Mart operates four types of retail stores throughout the country: Discount Stores, Supercenters, Neighborhood Markets, and Sam’s Clubs. Those stores are divided into seven nationwide divisions, which in turn comprise 41 regions of 80 to 85 stores apiece. Each store has between 40 and 53 separate departments and 80 to 500 staff positions. As evidence that there were indeed “questions of law or fact common to the class,” §2000e–1(a)(2), respondents relied chiefly on three forms of proof: statistical evidence about pay and promotion disparities between men and women at the company, anecdotal reports of discrimination from about 120 of the women, anecdotal testimony of discrimination, and testimony of a sociologist, Dr. William Bielby, who conducted a “social framework analysis” of Wal-mart‘s “culture” and personnel practices, and concluded that the company was “vulnerable” to gender discrimination. Respondents moved the District Court to certify a plaintiff class consisting of “[a]ll women employed at any time since December 26, 1998, who have been or may be subjected to” Wal-MMart’ “pay and management track promotions policies and practices.” 222 F. R. D., at 141–142. The District Court granted respondents’ motion and certified their proposed class. With one limitation not relevant here, the Court of Appeals substantially affirmed the certification order. Held: The class action is an exception to the usual rule that litigation is conducted by and on behalf of the individual named parties only. Rule 23(a) ensures that the named plaintiffs are appropriate representatives of the class whose claims they wish to litigate. Pp. 5–7. (a) The Rule’’ four requirements—numerosity, commonality, typicality, and adequate representation—effectively “limit the class claims to those fairly encompassed by the named plaintiff ’s claims.’ . . .” General Telephone Co. of Southwest v. Falcon, 457 U. S. 147, 156. The Rule does not speak of ‘equitable’ remedies generally but of injunctions and declaratory judgments. P. 7. (b) The key to the (b)(2) class is “the indivisible nature of the injunctive or declarative remedy warranted—the notion that the conduct is such that it can be enjoined or declared unlawful only as to all the class members or as to none of them.“ Nagareda, Class Certification in the Age of Aggregate Proof, 84 N. Y. U. L. Rev. 97, 131–132. This is not to say that claims for individualized relief (like the backpay at issue here) do not satisfy the Rule. The key is that the Rule requires the plaintiff to demonstrate that the class has suffered a violation of the same pro-vision of law. Title VII, for example, can be violated in many ways-by intentional discrimination, or by hiring and promotion criteria that result in disparate impact, and by the use of these practices on the part of many different superiors in a single company. The mere claim by employees of that same company that they have suffered a Title VII injury, or even a disparate-impact Title VII claim, gives no cause to believe that all their claims can productively be litigated at once. The rule also forbids interpreting Rule 23 to “abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right” 28 U.S. C. §2072(b); see Ortiz v. United States, 527 U.

The Supreme Court reversed a decision by the Mississippi Supreme Court that held 92 petitioners liable for the economic consequences of a boycott against white merchants in Claiborne County, Mississippi. The boycott was initiated by black citizens after their demands for racial equality and integration were not satisfactorily addressed by local officials. The boycott included both nonviolent elements, such as speeches and lawful picketing, and some instances of violence.

The central issue was whether the state court's judgment was consistent with the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. The Supreme Court found that the nonviolent elements of the boycott were protected by the First Amendment, which covers freedom of speech, assembly, association, and petition. The Court emphasized that civil liability may not be imposed merely for association with a group, some of whose members may have participated in unlawful activities, unless it is established that the group had unlawful goals and the individual had a specific intent to further those illegal aims.

The Court held that the damages awarded by the Mississippi Supreme Court could not be justified solely based on the nonviolent elements of the boycott, as these were constitutionally protected activities. The Court also stated that only those losses directly caused by unlawful conduct, such as violence or threats of violence, could be recovered. The Court found that the Mississippi Supreme Court's findings were insufficient to demonstrate that all business losses were proximately caused by violence or threats of violence.

The Supreme Court's decision has significant implications for the constitutional protection of political expression and association. It clarifies that nonviolent advocacy and collective action, even if it results in economic impact, are protected under the First Amendment, and that liability for damages must be closely tied to direct and unlawful conduct.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Tennessee today entered a final judgment in favor of a Tennessee-based agricultural company that refused to pay mandatory assessments for product advertising.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Memphis, Tennessee, in 1990, the United States Department of Agriculture ("DOA") issued mandatory assessments on handlers of fresh mushrooms to fund advertising for the product. The DoA's complaint alleged that the DoA imposed the mandatory assessments because it did not meet the First Amendment requirements. The complaint also alleged that, contrary to the stated First Amendment principles, DoA required producers of certain types of mushrooms to pay for the assessments. DoA requires producers to pay a fee in support of a specific purpose, such as disciplining members of the bar or proposing ethical codes for the profession. The Commission's complaint alleges that DoA failed to meet these requirements and instead relied on the mandatory assessment requirements imposed by the Department of Justice.  The complaint further alleges that, in Glickman, the DoD imposed mandatory assessments based on a subjective evaluation of the value of the information presented by the subject matter of the offering, and did not require that producers of any particular type of mushroom be required to pay such a fee.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Commission's opinion, the Secretary of Agriculture and DoA have agreed to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin DoA from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and require DoA to comply with the mandatory disclosures provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) the Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 17a-1 thereunder. The Court has also agreed to order DoA not to violate the mandatory disclosure provisions of the federal securities laws.  DoA has agreed to be enjoined from violating these provisions. The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by John Rymas and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson of the Atlanta Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Mr. Gibson and Ms. Gibson.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit granted certiorari in a case involving the seizure of magazines, films, and other items from a so-called "adult" bookstore. The court held that the search warrant executed by a judge in a criminal case against the store's owner violated the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments. The warrant was issued after a state investigator purchased two reels of film from the store and concluded that the films violated New York's obscenity laws. The store clerk was arrested for selling the films to the investigator and the store was searched. The search was conducted in an area of the store where silent films were shown by coin-operated projectors. The clerk was the only employee present; he was free to continue working in the store to the extent the search permitted, and he was allowed to continue doing so. The trial court found that the warrant violated the Store Act of 1933 and the Store and Exchange Act of 1934, and that the store had violated the terms of the warrant. The Court held that there was probable cause to believe the films were obscene and ordered the seizure. The Second Circuit agreed, and the Court granted the Store's motion for a temporary restraining order and a preliminary injunction, and granted the Stores' motion for summary judgment. The Appeals Court ruled in favor of the Store, holding that the Store had violated its right to a fair trial, and holding that it was not subject to the warrant's terms.

The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the lower courts, upholding the Town of Hempstead's ordinance that regulates dredging and pit excavating within its limits. Appellants, who had been engaged in such operations, argued that the ordinance effectively prevented them from continuing their business and thus constituted a taking of their property without due process, in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court found that the ordinance was a valid exercise of the town's police power. It stated that while the ordinance prohibits a beneficial use of the property, this alone does not make it unconstitutional. The Court emphasized that legislation that prohibits the use of property to prevent harm to the health, safety, or morals of the community is not a taking that requires compensation.

The Court also noted that there is no clear formula to determine when regulation becomes a taking that necessitates compensation. In this case, there was no evidence to suggest that the prohibition of further mining would reduce the value of the property in question. The Court presumed the ordinance to be constitutional and found no indication that its prohibitory effect was sufficient to render it an unconstitutional taking.

The Court examined whether the prohibition of further excavation below the water table was a valid exercise of the town's police power. It considered the public interest, the reasonableness and necessity of the ordinance, and its potential oppressiveness. The Court found that the appellants did not meet their burden to prove the ordinance was unreasonable.

The Court also addressed the remaining unmined portion of the property, concluding that if the depth limitation was valid for the existing pit, it was also valid to prevent the creation of new pits. The Court dismissed the appellants' other contentions, including the argument that the ordinance undermined rights acquired in previous litigation and that it was unconstitutional for imposing affirmative duties.

In summary, the Supreme Court held that the ordinance was a reasonable exercise of the town's police power and did not constitute an unconstitutional taking of property. The decision affirms the town's ability to regulate land use for public safety reasons without compensating property owners, provided the regulation is reasonable and not overly oppressive.

Seven groups of Negro residents of Chicago sued in federal district court challenging the validity of several Illinois statutes and Chicago ordinances on the ground that they violate the Federal Constitution. Though none of the complainants had been arrested or charged under the statutes attacked, they claimed that Negroes were being intimidated in the exercise of their First Amendment rights through the wholesale use of the statutes to prosecute members of the Negro community and through the use of arrests without probable cause, coupled with the setting of exorbitant bail. A three-judge District Court upheld most of the challenged laws but struck down two sections of the Illinois "mob action" statute and one section of the Illinois "intimidation" statute as too broad. It permanently enjoined the officials from enforcing or prosecuting under the latter two statutory sections. Held: Since the complaint failed to allege any irreparable injury to any individual from threats or actual prosecutions under the "intimidation" statute or from any other conduct by state or local officials, the normal course of state criminal prosecutions may not be disrupted or blocked on the basis of charges that amount to little more than speculation about the future. Pp. 10-12. Reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio granted the State's motion for judgment on the pleadings, and the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part. Eugene Woodard was sentenced to death for aggravated murder committed in the course of a carjacking. The Ohio Adult Parole Authority conducted a clemency investigation into Woodard. When Woodard failed to obtain a stay of execution more than 45 days before his scheduled execution date, the Authority commenced its clemencies investigation. The Authority informed respondent that he could have a c-lemency interview on September 9, 1994, if he wished, and that his clemence hearing would be on September 16, 1994. Respondent did not request an interview. Instead, he objected to the short notice of the interview and requested assurances that counsel could attend and participate in the interview. When the Authority failed to respond to these requests, respondent filed suit in United States District Court on September 14, 1997, alleging under Rev. Stat. 1979, 42 U.N.C., 2 2, 3 4  The District Court granted the state's Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings. The Sixth Circuit held that under the "first strand" of due process analysis, Woodard had failed to establish a protected life or liberty interest. The Court held that there was no state-created life or Liberty interest. Woodard's appeal was denied. The Supreme Court of Ohio ruled that the case should be remanded for further consideration.

In this Supreme Court case, the issue was whether the University of Missouri at Kansas City could deny a religious student group, Cornerstone, the use of university facilities for religious worship and discussion, despite the university's general policy of allowing registered student groups to use its facilities. The university had previously allowed Cornerstone to use the facilities but later barred them based on a regulation against using university property for religious purposes.

The District Court upheld the university's decision, citing the Establishment Clause, which prohibits government support of religion. However, the Court of Appeals reversed this decision, finding that the university's regulation was a content-based discrimination against religious speech without a compelling justification.

The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision. The Court reasoned that by creating a forum open to student groups, the university could not exclude groups based on the content of their speech, including religious speech, without a compelling state interest. The Court applied the three-pronged test from Lemon v. Kurtzman, which assesses whether a governmental policy has a secular purpose, does not advance or inhibit religion, and does not excessively entangle the government with religion.

The Court found that an open forum policy at the university would have a secular purpose and would not result in excessive entanglement with religion. It also determined that any religious benefits from the policy would be incidental and would not constitute the primary advancement of religion. The Court noted that the forum was available to a wide range of groups, both religious and nonreligious, which indicated a secular effect.

The Court also addressed the university's argument that the Missouri Constitution required a stricter separation of church and state than the Federal Constitution. The Court did not rule on how the Missouri courts would interpret this but stated that the state's interest was not compelling enough to justify discrimination against religious speech.

The Supreme Court's decision emphasized that while the university could establish reasonable regulations on time, place, and manner, it could not enforce content-based exclusions of speech in a generally open forum. The Court's ruling supports the principle of content neutrality in state regulation of speech and upholds the rights of religious groups to access public university facilities on the same terms as other student groups.

In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether a federal court can dismiss a state prisoner's habeas corpus petition on the ground that it was filed too late, even if the state did not object to the timing of the petition. The Court held that a federal court has the authority to dismiss a habeas corpus petition on the ground of untimeliness, even if the state fails to object to the timing of the petition. However, the Court also held that a federal court cannot dismiss a habeas corpus petition on the ground of untimeliness if the state has waived the right to object to the timing of the petition.

Title IX provides that "[n]o person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity" covered by Title IX. Title IX prohibits a funding recipient from subjecting any person to "discrimination" "on the basis [of] sex," but Title IX does not provide a private right of action for retaliation. A funding recipient's deliberate indifference to a teacher's sexual harassment of a student, Gebser v. Lago Vista Independent School Dist., 524 U. S. 274, 290-291, or to sexual harassment by another student, Davis v. Monroe County Bd. of Ed., 526 U.S. 629, 642, may prevail. The District Court dismissed Jackson's Title IX claim on the ground that Title IX's private cause of action does not include claims of retaliation. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Title IX, which, subject to a list of narrow exceptions not at issue here, broadly prohibits the funding recipient to subject any person "to discrimination" on the "basis of sex." Title IX is a broadly written general prohibition on discrimination, followed by specific, narrow exceptions to that prohibition, and Title VII spells out in greater detail the conduct that constitutes discrimination in violation of that statute. Pp. 5-11. (a) Title IX provides a general prohibition against discrimination on the grounds of sex. Title VII's plain terms do not prohibit retaliation, and the statute's text does not encompass it. P. 5. (b) The statute's language does not expressly prohibit retaliation. It does not require that the victim of the retaliation must also be the subject of the discrimination that is the original complaint. Thus, Title IX clearly does not authorize private parties to invoke Title IX regulations to obtain redress for disparate-impact discrimination because Title VI itself prohibits only intentional discrimination. The same reasons militate equally against extending Title IX to retaliation claims, since Title IX was enacted as an exercise of Congress' powers under the Spending Clause, see, e. g., Franklin v. Gwinnett Co. v. Pinhas, 500 U. . . 322, 325, and because Congress did not list any specific discriminatory practices when it wrote the statute, its failure to mention one such practice does not tell us anything about whether it intended that practice to be covered. Moreover, Title VII does not explicitly prohibit retaliation because it does not mention retaliation, since the statute itself contains the necessary prohibition. P p. 511. 309 F. 3d 1333, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado today entered a final judgment against six individuals charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 9(h) of the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Denver, Colorado, alleges that, prior to June 1949, the International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers (IUPW) and its parent organization, the Communist Party of China (C.L.Ed.’), filed false affidavits in purported satisfaction of the requirements of Section 10(b) ofÂ The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The complaint alleges that the defendants, unable to secure the Board's services and facilities for the union, coldly and deliberately concocted a fraudulent scheme.  According to the complaint, some of the petitioners did in fact submit the affidavits and the union did thereafter use the Labor Board facilities made available to them.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against four of the defendants. The SEC alleges that these defendants violated Section 10 of the Exchange Act by filing false statements in violation of the charged provisions.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from future violations of the securities laws, ordering disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and ordering the defendants to pay civil penalties in the amount of $2,000 each. The settlement is subject to court approval.  On May 2, 2020, the Honorable Judge William J. Bufalino of the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit issued a temporary restraining order against the defendants from violating Section 10Â the Exchange Act, ordering the filing of false statements, and imposing a civil penalty of $3,500. The court also granted the defendants' motion for a preliminary injunction against further violations of Section 15(a) of Exchange Act Rules 10b2-1 and Rule 15a-2 thereunder, and ordered the defendants be barred from serving as officers or directors of any federal agency for five years and ordered to pay a $10,000 civil penalty.  A hearing on May 24, 2020 is scheduled for 7:30 p.m. Eastern.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-0117 (January 17, 2020).

This decision involves a challenge to the validity of a naturalization order issued to Peter Chaunt, who was born in Hungary but became a US citizen through a decree in 1940. The challenge was based on the claim that Chaunt had hidden certain information about himself, including past arrests and membership in the Communist Party, when applying for citizenship. The Supreme Court held that while complete responses to all relevant questions were necessary for determining eligibility for citizenship, the evidence against Chaunt was insufficient to prove that he had intentionally concealed or lied about his background. As a result, the Court overturned the denial of citizenship and sent the case back to the lower courts for consideration of the remaining issues.

Petitioner, an attorney, made notes of an initial interview with a client shortly before the client's death. The Government, represented by the Office of Independent Counsel, now seeks his notes for use in a criminal investigation. The notes are protected by the attorney-client privilege. The District Court, after examining the notes in camera, concluded they were protected from disclosure by both doctrines and denied enforcement of the subpoenas. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the privilege survived death. Held: 1. The attorney client privilege is one of the oldest recognized privileges for confidential communications. Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U. S. 383, 389. Pp. 588-599. (a) The privilege serves much broader purposes. Clients consult attorneys for a wide variety of reasons, including possible criminal liability. Many attorneys act as counselors on personal and family matters, where confidences about family members or financial problems must be revealed in order to assure sound legal advice. P. 589. (b) The Attorney-Client privilege extends beyond the death of the client, even in the criminal context, and there is no persuasive reason to depart from this accepted rule, particularly given the importance of the privilege to full and frank client communication. Glover v. Patten, 165 U.S. 394, 406-408, n. 11. (c) There is no reason to suppose as a general matter that grand jury testimony about confidential communications furthers a client's intent, see Glover, supra, at 462-464, 357 A. 2d 689, but other than these two decisions, cases addressing the privilege after death-most involving the testamentary exception-uniformly presume the privilege survives, even if they do not so hold. See, e. g., Cohen v. Jenkintown Cab Co., 238 Pa. Super. 456, 357-693. The exception to the privilege is a posthumous exception for communications whose relative importance to particular criminal litigation is substantial. The presumption that the attorney is being required to disclose only what the client could have been required to disclosure is at odds with the purpose of encouraging full and honest communication and of protecting the client. P p. 590. (d) The fact that the client may not know at the time he discloses information to his attorney whether it will later be relevant to a civil or a criminal matter, let alone if it will be of substantial importance to a particular criminal case, does not square with the caselaw's implicit acceptance of that privilege's survival and with the treatment of testamentary disclosure as an "exception" or an implied "waiver." And the premise of his analogy is incorrect, since cases consistently recognize that the rationale for the exemption is that it furthers the client’s intent and that a “no harm in one more exception” rationale could contribute to the general erosion of the privileged privilege, without reference to common law principles or "reason and experience.'' P. 540. 2. The privilege survives even during death. Although there is weighty reasons that counsel in favor of posthumously application may not depart from Rule 501's direction to look to "the principles of the common law as they may be interpreted by the courts of the United States in the light of reason and experience'' does not mandate that a rule, once established, should endure for all time, Funk v. U. States, 290 U. s. 371, 381, the Independent Counsel suggests that his proposed exception would have little to no effect on the client or his attorney's willingness to confide in his attorney. He reasons that only clients intending to perjure themselves will be chilled by a rule of disclosure after death, as opposed to truthful clients or those asserting their Fifth Amendment privilege. This is because for the latter group, communications disclosed by the lawyer after the client-s death purportedly will reveal only information that he himself would have revealed if alive. The Independent Counsel assumes, incorrectly, that the privileged is analogous to the Fifth Amendment's protection against self-incrimination. But as suggested above, the privilege serves many broader purposes, including advising clients on personal matters, including the need for professional advice, confidences that may not come close to any sort of admission of criminal wrongdoing, but nonetheless be matters which the client would not wish divulged. Moreover, it seems unreasonable to assume that disclosure of such communications vanishes altogether, since such confidences may come close in the course of the business, but nevertheless be matters that the clients would not want divulged, and the risk of disclosure may be minimal if confined to criminal cases, or, as the Court suggests, if it is limited to information of substantial interest to a specific criminal case. The independent counsel also argues that existing exceptions to the exemption make the impact of one additional exception marginal, but these exceptions do not demonstrate that the impact would be insignificant, and that there is little empirical evidence on this point. In 1985, appellant, the publisher of a general interest magazine that was not entitled to the exemption, paid under protest sales taxes on the price of its qualifying subscription sales and sued to recover those payments. The State Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the exemption satisfied the tripartite test of Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U. S. 602, 612-613, and declaring itself "without power to rewrite the statute to make religious periodicals subject to tax," the court struck down the tax as applied to nonreligious periodicals and ordered the State to refund the tax paid by appellant, plus interest. Held: The judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded. Pp. 7-8. 731 S. W. 2d 160, reversed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the respondent who was convicted of kidnapping, armed robbery, and felonious assault based on incriminating statements made outside the presence of a lawyer. The Court overturned the conviction because the North Carolina Supreme Court had erroneously interpreted the Miranda decision to require an explicit waiver before a statement can be used in evidence. The Court clarified that while an express statement of waiver is often strong proof of a valid waiver, it is not always necessary or sufficient to establish waiver. The Court emphasized that the determination of waiver depends on the particular facts and circumstances of the case, including the background, experience, and conduct of the accused.

The Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA) permits a prevailing party in a case brought by or against the Government to recover fees for paralegal services at the market rate for such services or only at their cost to the party’s attorney. In this case, petitioner Richlin Security Service Co. (Richlin) was engaged by the former Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) to provide guard services for detainees at Los Angeles International Airport. Through mutual mistake, the parties’ two contracts misclassified Richlin employees under the Service Contract Act of 1965, 41 U. S. C. §351 et seq. The Department of Labor discovered the misclassification and ordered Richlin to pay its employees back wages. Richlin responded by filing a claim with the Board of Contract Appeals (Board). The claim sought reformation of the two contracts in order to force them to make additional payments. The Board entered an award in its favor. In addition to its other fees and expenses, Richlin sought $45,141.10 for 523.8 hours of paralgal work on its contract claim and $6,760 for 68.2 hours of Paralegal service on its EAJA application itself. The board found that Richlin met §504(b)(1)(B) eligibility requirements, and that the Government‘s position had not been “substantially justified” within the meaning of §§504(a)(1), id., at 32a. It concluded, however, that it was not entitled to recover its paralegals fees at the rates (ranging from $50 per hour to $95 per hour) at which Richlin was billed by its law firm. The Federal Circuit denied rehearing, holding that EAJA limited recovery to “the cost to [the] firm rather than … the billed rate.” Held: 1. A prevailing party that satisfies EAJA requirements may recover its services at prevailing market rates. EAJA, like §1988, entitles certain parties to recover “reasonable attorney … fees,” which are defined as the reasonable expenses of expert witnesses, the reasonable cost of any study, analysis, engineering report, test, or project which is found by the agency to be necessary for the preparation of the party's case, and reasonable attorney or agent fees (the amount of fees awarded under this section shall be based upon prevailing market- rates for the kind and quality of the services furnished, except that (i) no expert witness shall be compensated at a rate in excess of the highest rate of compensation for expert witnesses paid by the Agency involved, and (ii) attorney or agents fees shall not be awarded in excessof $125 per hour unless the agency determines by regulation that an increase in the cost of living or a special factor, such as the limited availability of qualified attorneys or agents for the proceedings involved, justifies a higher fee. Pp. 5–11. (a) The legislative history is a wash in this case. The Government seeks shelter in a canon of construction. It contends that the term “attorney … fees” must be read narrowly in light of the statutory canon requiring strict construction of waivers of sovereign immunity. It is not persuaded by either the legislative history cited by the Government, nor the policy considerations actually counsel in favor of Richlin’S interpretation of the statute. Nor is it persuaded by the fact that a 1984 Senate Report accompanying the EAJA bill explicitly expressed congressional intent to limit recovery of paralegan fees to the “prevailing market rates” because, since EAJA expressly permits recovery (albeit at “cost”) for items other than attorney, agent, and expert witness fees, the Government sees no reason to give EAJA the broad construction that Jenkins gave §1988. Moreover, the report does not address the critical question whether EAJA limits recovery to attorney cost regardless of market practice, since the Government observes that the phrase “fees” did not include charges for law clerk and paraleegal services. The fact that paralesgal salaries respond to market forces no less than the fees that clients pay suggests to the Government that this case has more to do with determining whose expenditures get reimbursed (the attorney) than with determining how expenditures are calculated (at cost or at market). The Government also contends that, even if EAJA did limit recovery to the attorney cost, it would not follow that the cost should be measured from the perspective of the attorney rather than the litigant. The Report does not even address the question presented at all, and the Government has no difficulty concluding that the latter question is fairly included within the former question. P. 11. 472 F. 3d 1370, reversed and remanded.

A federal agent, acting under instructions from the Drug Enforcement Administration, infiltrated respondent's drug manufacturing operation and furnished him with a small amount of a chemical needed in the production of methamphetamine. Subsequently, respondent and others were arrested and tried for various crimes involving the manufacture and sale of methamphetamine. Though concededly "harboring a predisposition," respondent claimed entrapment as a defense. The trial court instructed the jury that entrapment occurs when a person is induced by improper outside pressure to engage in criminal behavior that he would not otherwise have done. The jury found respondent guilty, rejecting his entrapment defense. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that entrapment occurred even absent proof of corrupt influence by the Government, and that the defense of entrapment includes the concept of "intolerable government intrusiveness." Held: Entrapment is a relatively limited defense rooted in the notion that Congress could not have intended criminal punishment for a defendant who has committed all the elements of a proscribed offense but was induced to do so by the Government. Pp. 108-116. (a) To permit the defense of entrapment to expand to cover the situation involved here would require that any prosecution be barred absolutely because of the Government's involvement in criminal activity, a conclusion that goes too far in deterring undesirable official conduct. Cf. Sorrells v. United States, 287 U. S. 435; Sherman v. United States, 356 U. S. 384. Pp. 108-111. (b) Here, the Government's contribution of the chemical to the criminal enterprise was scarcely objectionable, and the record demonstrates that the chemical was readily obtainable. Pp. 111-112. (c) The defense of entrapment is not of a constitutional dimension, and Congress may define the defense as it sees fit. P. 113. (d) The defense of entrapment is not intended to give the judiciary a chancellor's foot veto over law enforcement practices of which it does not approve. Pp. 113-115. (e) The Court of Appeals erred in introducing an unmanageably subjective standard that is contrary to the holdings of this Court in Sorrells and Sherman. Those cases establish that entrapment is a relatively limited defense rooted in the notion that Congress could not have intended criminal punishment for a defendant who has committed all the elements of a proscribed offense but was induced to do so by the Government. Pp. 115-116. 459 F. 2d 667, reversed.

Petitioner Desert Palace, dba Caesar's Palace Hotel & Casino of Las Vegas, employed respondent as a warehouse worker and heavy equipment operator. The District Court dismissed the sexual harassment claim, but allowed the claim for sex discrimination to go to the jury. At trial, respondent presented evidence that (1) she was singled out for "intense "stalking" by one of her supervisors, (2) she received harsher discipline than men for the same conduct, (3) supervisors repeatedly "stack[ed" her disciplinary record and "frequently used or tolerated" sex-based slurs against her. Based on this evidence, the District Court instructed the jury that "[t]he plaintiff has the burden of proving . . . by a preponderance of the evidence that her sex was a motivating factor in any such work conditions imposed upon her," 42 U. S. C. § 2000e-2(m). The jury rendered a verdict for respondent, awarding backpay, compensatory damages, and injunctive relief. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the statute "imposes no special [evidentiary] requirement and does not reference `direct evidence." Held: A plaintiff must present direct evidence of discrimination in order to obtain a mixed-motive instruction under 42 US. C.'s Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended by the Act of 1991. Pp. 5-11. (a) The statute unambiguously states that a plaintiff need only "demonstrat[e]" that an employer used a forbidden consideration with respect to "any employment practice." On its face, the statute does not mention, much less require, that plaintiff make a heightened showing through direct evidence. Moreover, Congress explicitly defined the term "demonstration" in the 1991 Act, leaving little doubt that no special evidentiary showing is required. Title VII defines the term as to "mee[t] the burdens of production and persuasion," and if Congress intended the term to require that the "burdens of production" be met by direct evidence or some other heightened showing, it could have made that intent clear by including language to that effect in §§ 2000e(m), 253-254, 253. The use of the term "[demonstrates'" in other provisions of Title VII tends to show further that §2000e- 2(m) does not incorporate a direct evidence requirement. See, e. g., 43 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(2)(B) requires an employer to demonstrate that race, color, religion, sex, or national origin was the motivating factor for any employment practice, even though other factors also motivated the practice. Thus, the phrase "demonstrate" does not require direct evidence, since it is inconsistent with Title VII's text. The statute does, however, require that a disparate treatment plaintiff demonstrate that an illegitimate consideration played a substantial role in an adverse employment decision, and that a reasonable jury could have found that "absent further explanation, the employer's discriminatory motivation ...caused" the employment decision. P. 5. (b) The fact that no heightened showing was required under § 2000E-2 (m) is flawed, primarily because the third step of petitioner's argument is flawed. The court's precedents make clear that the starting point for this analysis is the statutory text, and where, as here, the words of the statute are unambiguous, the "judicial inquiry is complete," and that Congress has been unequivocal when imposing heightened proof requirements in other circumstances, including in Title 42. The phrase "Demonstrates" in some provisions of the Act tends to demonstrate further that an unlawful employment practice is established when the complaining party demonstrates that race or color or religion was a "substantial factor" in an employment practice. On the face of that provision, it would be logical to assume that the term would carry the same meaning as the word "demonstates" and that petitioner would agree that the defendant or the employer has any heightened standard to satisfy. But when pressed at oral argument about whether direct evidence is required before the partial affirmative defense can be invoked, petitioner did not "agree that . . ."

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit granted habeas relief to Robert Garceau, who was sentenced to death for the murder of his girlfriend and her 14-year-old son. The court held that the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) does not apply to cases pending as of the date AEDPA's effective date. In a similar case, the U.N. District Court for the Eastern District of California granted a stay of execution to Garceau. The State filed a motion to vacate the stay, in part because Garceau had failed to file a "specification of nonfrivolous issues" as required by local court rules. The District Court denied the State's motion and ordered that the habeas petition be filed within nine months. On August 1, 1995, the District Court appointed counsel and extended the stay for another 120 days. On July 2, 1996, Garceau filed a federal habeas application for relief. The district court concluded that the application was not subject to AEDPA. The Court of Appeal for the Central Dist. of California, however, reversed the district court's decision, and granted the defendant habeas relief for reasons that are not relevant to this case. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued an opinion on the issue. The case will be decided by the full Court.

The Indiana General Assembly initiated the process of reapportionment pursuant to the 1980 census. In early 1981, there were Republican majorities in both the House and the Senate, and the Governor was Republican. In November 1982, before the case went to trial, elections were held under the new districting plan. The results of the 1982 elections seemed "to support an argument that there is a built-in bias favoring the majority party, the Republicans," the District Court ruled. The District Court held that the new plan violated equal protection provisions of the Fourteenth Amendment. The district court held that there was no evidence that the Republican-controlled General Assembly intended to dilute the votes of Indiana Democrats. The court concluded that the General Assembly's intent was not to favor the Republican Party, but rather to ensure that Democrats would have a fair chance to win seats in future elections. The Supreme Court agreed with the district court's finding that the Reapportionment Plan violated the equal protection provision of the 14th Amendment, but the high court ruled that the lower court did not have jurisdiction to determine the issue of whether there was a political gerrymander. The Indiana Supreme Court reversed, and ruled that there had been no political gerrymandering. The high court also found that the trial court had erred in its finding that it had jurisdiction to decide the issue.

This case involves a man named Johnny Johnson who was accused of robbing a store. He was arrested at his home without a warrant and later identified a suspect during a lineup procedure. The prosecution argued that Johnson's conviction was based on sufficient evidence and did not rely on any illegally obtained information. The defense attorney argued that Johnson's arrest was unlawful and that the lineup identification was tainted by the illegal arrest. However, the Supreme Court found that no evidence obtained through the illegal arrest was used against Johnson at trial and that the lineup identification was conducted in a manner that distinguished it from the initial arrest. Therefore, the Supreme Court upheld Johnson's conviction.

Petitioner was convicted in Tennessee state court of second degree murder. The statute, which makes no mention of the year and a day rule, defines criminal homicide simply as "the unlawful killing of another person which may be first degree murder, seconddegree murder, voluntary manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide or vehicular homicide." The State Supreme Court of Tennessee abolished the rule as it had existed at common law in Tennessee and applied its decision to petitioner to uphold his conviction. The question before us is whether, in doing so, the court denied petitioner due process of law in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment. Held: 1. A judicial alteration of a common law doctrine of criminal law violates the principle of fair warning, and hence must not be given retroactive effect, only where it is "unexpected and indefensible by reference to the law which had been expressed prior to the conduct in issue." Bouie v. City of Columbia, 378 U. S. 349, 396. Pp. 5-7. (a) The term "law" in the Ex Post Facto Clause of the Federal Constitution prohibits the retroactive application of a judicial decision abolishing the common law "year and day rule," which provides that no defendant could be convicted of murder unless his victim had died by the defendant's act within a year and one day of the act. P. 5. (b) A court's "opportunity for discrimination," however, is more limited than [a] legislature's, in that [it] can only act in construing existing law in actual litigation." James v. United States, 366 U.S. 213, 247, n. 3. Moreover, "[g]iven the divergent pulls of flexibility and precedent in our case law system," incorporation of the Calder categories into due process limitations on judicial decisionmaking would place an unworkable and unacceptable restraint on normal judicial processes and would be incompatible with the resolution of uncertainty that marks any evolving legal system. This language, however, was dicta. The decision in Bouie was rooted firmly in well established notions of due process. See supra, at 5. Its rationale rested on core due process concepts of notice, foreseeability, and, in particular, the right to fair warning as those concepts bear on the constitutionality of attaching criminal penalties to what previously had been innocent conduct. And it also adequately respects the due process concern with fundamental fairness and protects against vindictive or arbitrary judicial lawmaking by safeguarding defendants against unjustified and unpredictable breaks with prior law. Pc. 6-9. (c) The fact that a vast number of jurisdictions have abolished a rule that has so clearly outlived its purpose is surely relevant to whether the abolition of the rule in a particular case can be said to be unexpected and indefricable by reference thereto as it then existed. The common law, in short, presupposes a measure of evolution that is incompatible with stringent application of ex post facto principles. It was on account of concerns such as these that Bouie restricted due process-based limitations on the retroactivity application of judicial interpretations of criminal statutes to those that are "unwexpected and ... indefensible" by reference the law that had been expressing prior to that conduct. Bouie, at 359-360. This case involves not the precise meaning of the words of a particular statute, but rather the continuing viability of acommon law rule. Common law courts frequently look to the decisions of other jurisdictions in determining whether to alter or modify a common-law rule in light of changed circumstances, increased knowledge, and general logic and experience. Due process, of course, does not require a person to apprise himself of common law of all 50 States in order to guarantee that his actions will not subject him to punishment in the light of a developing trend in the law's not yet made its way to his State. And due process is a necessary part of the judicial business in States in which the criminal law retains some of its common law elements. Strict application of such judicial acts in that context would unduly impair the incremental and reasoned development of precedent that is the foundation of the common- law system. And, in this case, the alleged impermissible judicial application of the Rule of Law involves not merely the interpretation of a statute but an act of common -law judging. The rule is generally believed to date back to the 13th century, when it served as a statute of limitations governing the time in which an individual might initiate a private action for murder known as an "appeal of death"; that by the 18th century the rule had been extended to a law governing public prosecutions for murder; that the primary and most frequently cited justification for the rule is that 13th-century medical science was incapable of establishing causation beyond a reasonable doubt when a great deal of time had elapsed between the injury to the victim and his death; and that, as practically every court recently to have considered the rule has noted, advances in medical and related science have so undermined the usefulness of theRule as to render it without question obsolete. Thus, incorporation

After respondent Evans filed suit alleging that petitioners Long Island Care Center, Inc., and its president, Mary O’Donnell, violated federal labor laws by failing to compensate her properly for companionship services provided to elderly patients, the Federal District Court entered judgment for Evans. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, rejecting Evans’ contention that the companion-ship services exception to the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) excluding from minimum wage and overtime protections employees providing “complimentary services” to persons who are “incapacitated” due to injury or illness, 29 U. S. C. §213(a)(15), applied to her. The court ruled that the companion-ship services exception was ambiguous, and that the Department of Labor’s (DOL) implementing regulation, 29 CFR §552.109(a), which excepts from the exemption companionship workers employed by “any person” regardless of whether that person belongs to the employee’s household, was invalid because it exceeded the bounds of the statutory delegation. Held: Section 552.109(a) is a valid exercise of the DOL’s authority to fill statutory “gaps.” Pp. 4−14. (a) An agency’s interpretation of its own regulations is “controlling” unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulations being interpreted. Auer v. Robbins, 519 U.S. 452, 461. Here, the DOL’s interpretation of the two conflicting regulations falls within the principle that an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations is controlling. Pp. 4−10. (1) Evans’ argument that the third-party regulation is an “interpretive” regulation, which may persuade a reviewing court but cannot bind it, cf. Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U. S. 134, 140, is without merit. Other considerations strongly suggest that the DOL intended the third-party regulation as a binding application of its rulemaking authority. The regulation directly governs the conduct of members of the public, affecting individual rights and obligations. The DOL used full public notice-and-comment procedures when promulgating the rule, which it need not do when producing an “interpretive” rule. According to the DOL’s advisory memo, the department has treated the third-party regulation like the others, i.e., as a legally binding exercise of its rulemaking authority. Moreover, the heading “Interpretations” could well refer to the fact that the section contains matters of detail, interpreting and applying the more general definitions of the preceding section. Pp. 4−7. (2) The DOL’s 1974 agency notice-and-comment procedure, leading to the promulgation of the third-party regulation, was not defective because notice was inadequate and the DOL’s explanation also inadequate. The Administrative Procedure Act requires an agency conducting notice-and-comment rulemaking to publish in its notice of proposed rulemaking either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved. The object is one of fair notice. The initial DOL proposal was simply a proposal, meaning that the department was considering the matter; after that consideration the department might choose to adopt the proposal or to withdraw it. As it turned out, the department withdrew the proposal for special treatment of employees of “covered enterprises” whose compensation was covered by the FLSA prior to 1974. The result was a determination that exempted all third-party-employed companionship workers from the Act. Such a possibility was reasonably foreseeable. Nor is there any significant legal problem with the DOL’s explanation for the change. Pp. 7−10. (b) Evans’ additional argument that the third-party regulation fails to comply with the FLSA’s requirement that the companion-ship services exception apply only to those who are paid by the household for whom they provide services is rejected. The FLSA’s language referring to “domestic service employees” is ambiguous, and the DOL’s resolution of that ambiguity is reasonable. Pp. 10−14. 462 F.3d 50−11, reversed and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky today entered a final judgment in favor of Kentucky's and Kentucky's insurance laws.  The SEC's complaint alleges that Kentucky and Kentucky insurance companies violated the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws, including the securities laws and the broker-dealer registration provisions of Section 1144(b)(2)(A) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, Kentucky's laws are not specifically directed toward the insurance industry. Rather, the complaint alleges, the state laws that govern insurance companies and their affiliated health-care providers do not apply to insurance companies. The complaint further alleges that, contrary to our view, Kentucky and its insurance companies are exempt from pre-emption because they do not directly or indirectly regulate insurance.  In addition, the SEC's Complaint against Kentucky's AWP laws, filed in the Eastern district of Kentucky, alleges that the state's laws do not adequately regulate insurance, and that Kentucky has failed to specifically direct its approach to insurance. Specifically, the complaints allege that Kentucky's policies do not permit insurers to discriminate against any willing provider, and they are not subject to the same regulatory scrutiny that the federal laws do.  For example, the Complaint charges Kentucky with failing to specifically control the conduct regulated by the state law, rather than the state-law itself. The SEC seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s Complaint, the Court granted a temporary restraining order, entered a preliminary injunction, and issued an order requiring Kentucky to comply with the federal law. The court also ordered Kentucky to provide an accounting of the amount of premium paid to certain insurance companies, and to pay a civil penalty of $100,000. The Court's order also requires Kentucky insurers to pay their janitors twice the minimum wage in order to participate in limited network contracts with insurers, and requires Kentucky-based insurance companies to provide independent review of whether their policies meet certain contractual requirements. Without providing any guidance to lower federal courts, the court's order requires Kentucky to consider whether certain insurance policies qualify as "business of insurance" under the federal insurance laws, and whether they are relevant to the type of risk pooling arrangements that insurers may offer. In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that a person who has already served 10 years in prison for a murder cannot argue that he is actually innocent and deserves to be released. The Court held that the legal concept of "actual innocence" is not recognized in the United States, and that a person must prove his innocence through a new trial, which is generally restricted to cases involving newly discovered evidence. The Court also rejected the idea that a person can rely on executive clemency to secure release, stating that clemency is reserved for exceptional cases where the legal system has failed to protect a person's rights.

In this case, the Supreme Court holds that the Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board's decision to renew a liquor license to a private club does not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The court finds that the impetus for the discriminatory behavior in question comes from the private entity rather than the state, and that the state has not "significantly involved" itself in the behavior. The court distinguishes this case from previous cases involving discriminatory treatment in public accommodations, citing the lack of evidence that the Pennsylvania laws and regulations governing the sale of liquor are intended to encourage discrimination.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended, makes it an unfair employment practice for an employer to discriminate against any individual with respect to hiring or the terms and condition of employment because of such individual's race, color, religion, sex, or national origin; or to limit, segregate, or classify his employees in ways that would adversely affect any employee because of the employee's racial or ethnic origin. Petitioners' "objective" employment practices (e.g., an English language requirement, alleged nepotism in hiring, failure to post noncannery openings, the rehire preference, etc.) were found to be subject to challenge under the disparate-impact theory, but these claims were rejected for failure of proof. Judgment was entered for petitioners. Held: 1. A facially neutral employment practice may be deemed violative of Title VII without evidence of the employer's subjective intent to discriminate that is required in a "disparate-treatment" case. Pp. 531-532. (a) In holding that respondents had made out a prima facie case of disparate impact, the Court of Appeals relied solely on respondents' statistics showing a high percentage of nonwhites in the cannery jobs and a low percentage of such workers in the non-cannery positions. Although statistical proof can alone make out a "ppfacie" case, any inquiry by the courts into whether the specific challenged employment practices of petitioners caused that disparity is pretermitted, as is any inquiry into the disparate impact that any employment practice has had was justified by business considerations. P. 533. (b) The Court's ruling that a comparison between the percentage of cannery workers who are nonwhite and that of the nonwhite workers' hiring process has a significantly disparate impact on nonwhite employees is not defensible, since the Court's theory would leave the employer little choice but to engage in a subjective quota system of employment selection, and thus would be unreasonably burdensome on Title VII plaintiffs. Moreover, if on remand the case reaches this point, and respondents cannot persuade the trier of fact on petitioners' business necessity defense, respondents may still be able to prevail. The only practicable option for many employers would be to adopt racial quotas, insuring that no portion of their work forces deviated in racial composition from the other portions thereof; this is a result that Congress expressly rejected in drafting Title VII. The fact that the statistical disparity relied on by the court did not suffice to make out such a case does not mean that any employer bears the burden of disproving an employer's assertion that the adverse employment action or practice was based solely on a legitimate neutral consideration, see Texas Dept. of Community Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U. S. 248, 256-258. Nor does the fact that respondents' reliance on the union to fill cannery positions does not stand alone-make out such an ironic result that the court of Appeals reached below. The Court also erred in erring with regard to the unskilled noncanner jobs, since racial imbalance in one segment of an employer’s work force does not, without more than the racial disparity between cannery and nonwhite jobs, establish a “ppFacie case” with respect thereto. P p. 534-535. (c) The court of appeals’ ruling is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was convicted of capital murder in 1985 for orchestrating a double-murder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia, alleges that Richard McClelland was the manager of a department store, Murphy's Mart, in Portsmouth, Virginia. The complaint alleges that, shortly after the Sorrell murders, the defendant pulled into the parking lot of the store and confronted McClellan and a store security guard inside. According to the complaint, the guard told McClello that he was going to get him for having fired his wife from her job as a saleswoman at the store, and that petitioner had told other witnesses after the killing that he would not be harmed by the crime. The SEC alleges that the guard replied that he had "knocked off" Sorrell.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Virginia today announced that it filed criminal charges against the defendant.  On January 5, 1996, the court granted the SEC's motion for a temporary restraining order and ordered a preliminary injunction against the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of Investment Advisers, LLC, and Rule 206(3) thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the SEC, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating these provisions, ordering them to pay disgorgement of $12,000 and $13,000, respectively, and ordering the defendants to pay prejudgment interest of $1,038, which is equal to the amount of their civil penalties. The court also granted the defendants the right to return to the country and issue a judgment imposing a permanent injunction against future violations of the federal securities laws, ordering a temporary injunction against further violations, ordering the destruction of evidence, and appointing a receiver for the victims of the alleged crime.  A hearing for the receiver was scheduled for December 14, 1995, and a hearing for January 17, 1996. The hearing was conducted in the private capacity of a federal district court.   The litigation will be led by John R. Kelly and supervised by Amy C. Barry.

Respondent Mitchell was convicted of aggravated battery on the ground that he intentionally selected his victim on account of the victim's race. The Wisconsin Supreme Court reversed, holding that the penalty-enhancement statute was unconstitutionally overbroad, and that the Wisconsin statute punishes only the "conduct" of intentional selection of a victim. Held: Mitchell's First Amendment rights were not violated by the application of the penalty enhancement provision in sentencing him. Pp. 531-532. (a) The Wisconsin statute does not punish bigoted thought, as the Supreme Court of Wisconsin said, but instead punishes the "because of" aspect of the defendant's selection, the reason the defendant selected the victim, the motive behind the selection, and the State's desire to redress perceived harms. P. 533. (b) The State's argument that the state statute is overbroad because of its "chilling effect" on free speech is not persuasive. The fact remains that the same criminal conduct may be more heavily punished if the victim is selected because of his race or other protected status than if no such motive obtained. Thus, the statute impermissibly chills free expression with respect to such matters by those concerned about the criminal justice system, see Roberts v. United States Jaycees, 468 U. S. 609, 628, and under R. A. V. v. St. Paul, 505 U.S. 576, 594, does not alter the result here, and Mitchell's case is remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.

The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit held that the criminal sanction for filing a false affidavit under the Act was the exclusive remedy for the filing of the false affidavit. The Supreme Court held that that decision conflicts with a decision in which the Court ruled in favor of the Board that the only remedy for filing false affidavits is the criminal penalty provided in Section 35 A of the Criminal Code. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Georgia yesterday entered a final judgment against the City of Macon, Georgia and the trustees of certain residuary beneficiaries of Senator Augustus O. Bacon's estate, finding that the city could not legally enforce racial segregation in the park.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Atlanta, Georgia, the city resigned as trustee of the park in 1911 and appointed new trustees in the future.  The complaint alleges that the new trustees violated the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  In a parallel action, the Georgia Secretary of State's Office today announced that it had obtained a court order to remove the city from acting as trustee under a private will.  As alleged in the complaint, this order was in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, the City consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the federal law, requires the city to pay a civil penalty, and requires the trustee to be permanently enjoined from participating in the management and operation of a public facility.  Additionally, the court granted the city's request for a temporary restraining order and appointed a temporary receiver over the park to facilitate the appointment of new trustees.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted in the Atlanta Regional Office and the Atlanta Office of Public Education. Seats in both houses of the Delaware Legislature were not apportioned substantially on a population basis. Held: Such failure violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 248-258. 215 F. Supp. 169, affirmed and remanded.

Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA or Act) provides that "no qualified individual with a disability shall, by reason of such disability, be excluded from participation in or be denied the benefits of the services, programs or activities of a public entity, or be subjected to discrimination by any such entity." Title II's enforcement provision incorporates by reference § 505 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which authorizes private citizens to bring suits for money damages. The Court of Appeals, sitting en banc, heard argument in a Title II suit brought by a hearing-impaired litigant who sought money damages for the State's failure to accommodate his disability in a child custody proceeding. Respondents, both of whom are paraplegics who use wheelchairs for mobility, claimed that they were denied access to, and the services of, the state court system. Respondent, a certified court reporter, alleged that she has not been able to gain access to a number of county courthouses, and, as a result, has lost both her work and an opportunity to participate in the judicial process. The State moved to dismiss the suit on the ground that it was barred by the Eleventh Amendment. The District Court denied the motion without opinion. The United States intervened to defend Title II of that Act, which prohibits discrimination against persons with disabilities in three major areas of public life: employment, which is covered by Title I of the statute; public services, program, and activities, which are the subject of Title II; and public accommodations, which, under Title III, are covered by § 12131(2). Title II, as it applies to the class of cases implicating the fundamental right of access to the courts, is valid § 5 legislation. To determine whether it has done so in any given case, the Court must resolve two predicate questions: first, whether Congress unequivocally expressed its intent to abrogate that immunity; and second, if it did, whether it acted pursuant to a valid grant of constitutional authority. The first question is easily answered in this case. The Act specifically provides: "A State shall not be immune under the eleventh amendment to the Constitution of the United States from an action in Federal or State court of competent jurisdiction for a violation of this chapter." 42 U. S. C. § 12132. Title II is a legitimate attempt to remedy or prevent actual constitutional violations by the States or an illegitimate attempt to rewrite the constitutional provisions it purports to enforce. This conclusion gains even more support when Title II identifies nothing in the legislative record that shows Congress was responding to widespread violations of the due process rights of disabled persons. Rather than limiting its discussion of constitutional violations to the due-process rights on which it ultimately relies, Title II sets out on a wide-ranging account of societal discrimination against the disabled. The statute is not limited to cases involving arguable due process violations, see, e. g., Faretta v. California, 422 U.S. 11, 31-32. Nor is it limited to occasions when the failure to modify results, or will likely result, in an actual due process violation, such as when the infringement was nonnegligent or uncompensated. Moreover, liability is triggered if an inaccessible building results in a disabled person being "subjected to discrimination" — a term that presumably encompasses any sort of inconvenience in accessing the facility, for whatever purpose. Pp. 5-7. (a) Title II does not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by issuing a still broader prohibition directed to the same end. Nor does Title II violate the Equal Protection Clause by requiring special accommodations for disabled persons in virtually every interaction they have with the State. P. 7. (b) The statute's scope of application is more difficult because it is not tailored to provide prophylactic protection of these rights; instead, it applies only to facilities that have a disparate impact on the disabled, and in no event is the entity required to undertake measures that would impose an undue financial or administrative burden, threaten historic preservation interests, or effect a fundamental alteration in the nature of the service. The record is also inconsistent with Garrett and the well-established principles it embodies.
