The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia granted clemency to a man sentenced to death for the 1985 murder of a store manager. The court granted the defense motion for a mistrial after the defense raised questions about the prosecution's evidence. The trial judge denied the motion, and the jury convicted petitioner on all counts. The prosecution had planned to use other evidence, including testimony from the detective who investigated the murders of Lisa and Shanta Sorrell, a mother and daughter who had been murdered five months before the murder of Richard McClelland. Petitioner's counsel moved that the trial court order the prosecution to disclose the evidence it planned to introduce in the penalty phase. The defense then filed a motion to have the evidence excluded from the trial because it violated the defendant's right to due process of law under the Fourteenth Amendment. The D.C. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit agreed with the defense, and granted the motion for mistrial on the grounds that petitioner had not shown that he was deprived of his right to a fair trial. The Court also denied the defense's motion to dismiss the charges against him. The case is remanded for further consideration.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit recently ruled that the Michigan Supreme Court erred in holding that only a State's "generic" registration fee is relevant to determining the fee that was "collected or charged as of November 15, 1991" under the Interstate Commerce Commission's ("ICC's") new registration system. The ICC's new system, called the Single State Registration System, was established to replace the old "bingo card" system. Prior to 1994, the ICC allowed States to charge interstate motor carriers annual registration fees of up to $10 per vehicle. As proof of registration, participating States would issue a stamp for each of the carrier's vehicles. The stamp was affixed on a "uniform identification cab car[d] carried in each vehicle, within the square bearing the name of the issuing State. Id., at617. The Court ruled in favor of the ICC, finding that the ICC' s new fee system was not subject to the "reciprocity" provisions of the Interstate Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991 ("ISTEA"). The Court also found that, under the new rules, the ICC had the power to require States to preserve pre-existing reciprocity agreements, and that the fee system would "be deemed to be a burden on interstate commerce"

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit granted a re-examination of a case involving the testimony of a co-conspirator's wife in a heroin distribution conspiracy. The court previously rejected the defense's motion to sever his case from that of two other co-defendants. The case involves a 1976 indictment alleging that Otis Trammel and his wife, Elizabeth Ann Trammel, were part of a conspiracy to import heroin into the United States from Thailand and the Philippine Islands. The indictment also named six unindicted accomplices, including Elizabeth Trammel. The trial court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss the indictment, and the trial court ruled that Elizabeth TramMel could testify in support of the government's case to any act she observed during the marriage and to any communication "made in the presence of a third person" in return for her testimony. The motion to cut the case was denied. The 9th Court granted the motion to re-examine the issue of whether an accused may invoke the spousal privilege against adverse spousal testimony so as to exclude the voluntary testimony of his wife. The Court concluded that Hawkins v. United States did not prohibit "the voluntary testimony" of a spouse who appears as an "un indicted co-convicted" under the grant of immunity from the Government in exchange for his testimony." 583 F.2d 1166, 1168 (CA10 1978). The Court further concluded that it was not a matter of law that a wife could be produced "either against or for her husband"

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California today entered a final judgment in a civil injunctive action against a California officer who conducted a traffic stop on a motorcyclist.  The court held that a driver is not seized as a constitutional matter when the officer, “by means of physical force or show of authority,” is acting as a reasonable person.  In its judgment, the court held, without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, that the officer violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The court also held that, as alleged, the officer had no reasonable suspicion to warrant the stop, and that the driver was not seized because the officer was not in control of the car at the time.  According to the court's order, however, this finding is inconsistent with the Fourth Amendment.  For example, the Court previously held that when an officer makes a stop, he or she must be the target of the officer’s show of force, not just the driver.  As set forth in the court order, the judge held that the officers did not have reasonable reason to detain the driver, and therefore could not have conducted the stop without reasonable suspicion of the passenger.  Further, the judgment held that there was no reasonable basis for the officer to conduct the stop because the driver had dropped out of parole supervision and asked Brendlin to surrender before the officer could arrest him.   The Court also ruled that, in a parallel action, the United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Brendlin.  On November 27, 2001, the California Court of Appeals issued a temporary restraining order halting the officer from conducting a search and seizure of a car.  It also issued an order suspending the officer-in-charge search of Brendlin's car, ordering him to remain inside the car, and imposing a $1,000 civil penalty. Â The court also issued a preliminary injunction against further violations of the federal securities laws, including Section 17(a)(1) and (3) the registration provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and (c) of The Securities and Exchange Commission's Rules of Practice, ordering Brendlin and Simeroth to comply with the order.  Separately, on November 29, 2011, a federal district court in California entered a judgment in favor of the officers in a related action against the driver of a vehicle who had been stopped by the same officer.

The Mobile-Sierra doctrine requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to presume that the rate set out in a freely negotiated wholesale-energy contract meets the "just and reasonable" requirement imposed by law. The presumption may be overcome only if FERC concludes that the contract seriously harms the public interest. These cases present two questions about the scope of the Mobile- Sierra doctrine. First, does the presumption apply only when FERC has had an initial opportunity to review a contract rate without the presumption? Second, does it impose as high a bar to challenges by purchasers of wholesale electricity as it does by sellers?

Section 513(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (Act) prohibits tax-exempt organizations from engaging in any "trade or business" that is not "substantially related" to the purposes for which they enjoy an exemption from federal taxation. Under § 513(c), the term "trade or business" includes "advertising activities ... conducted by or on behalf of" a tax-exempt organization. Petitioner American College of Physicians (College) publishes a monthly journal, Annals, which contains advertisements for pharmaceuticals and other items of interest to physicians. At the time of the events giving rise to this action, the College enjoyed tax-exempt status pursuant to § 501(c)(3) of the Act. The College's bylaws state that its primary purpose is to improve the maintenance of life and health by advancing knowledge of diseases and their causes, treatment, and prevention. Pursuant to its mission, the College publishes Annals, which contains articles and other editorial material relating to current advances in medicine. The College receives no compensation for the advertisements appearing in Annals, except for the cost of printing and mailing them. The College's advertising policy calls for screening advertisements to ensure that they relate directly to the practice of medicine and that they accurately represent the product advertised. However, the College makes no attempt to present the advertisements systematically or comprehensively. Instead, the College sells advertising space to interested parties on a hit-or-miss basis. Ultimately, the College decided to report the income generated by the advertisements as gross income subject to federal income tax. Subsequently, the College sought a refund of the taxes paid on the ground that the advertisements were not "substantially related" to the College's tax-exempt purposes. The Comptroller of the Treasury agreed, and the Court of International Trade entered judgment for the College. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the advertisements contributed significantly to the College's educational purposes and thus satisfied the requirements of §§ 513(a) and 513(c). Held: Advertising income is not automatically taxable simply because it is sold by a tax-exempt organization. Satisfaction of the three conditions precedent to taxation of such income -publication of the advertisements is a "trade or business"; the advertisements are "regularly carried on"; and the advertisements are "not substantially related" to the organization's tax-exempt purposes-must be made separately in each instance. Here, although the College's advertisements are a "trade or business" and are "regularly carried on," the advertisements do not contribute importantly to the College's educational purposes. Pp. 10-18. (a) There is nothing in the text of the Act to suggest that Congress intended to require the taxation of income from all commercial advertisements of all tax-exempt journals without a specific analysis of the circumstances. Nor is there anything in the Treasury Regulations to support the conclusion that the Treasury and Congress intended to establish a per se rule requiring the taxation of income from all commercial advertisements of all tax-exempt journals without a specific analysis of the circumstances. Pp. 10-15. (b) The Court of Appeals erred in focusing exclusively upon the information that is invariably conveyed by commercial advertising, and consequently failed to give effect to the governing statute and regulations. The proper focus is upon the manner in which the tax-exempt organization operates its business. Since the College did not use the advertising to provide its readers a comprehensive or systematic presentation of any aspect of the goods or services publicized, and since the College permitted only those companies willing to pay for advertising space to get it, the advertising in Annals does not contribute importantly to the College's educational purposes. Pp. 15-18. 743 F. 2d 1565, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Hawaii today entered a final judgment in favor of a proposed amendment to the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Hawaii on September 9, 1998, alleges that the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) improperly sought to conceal the existence of state-owned companies in violation of the federal securities laws.  According to the complaint, the SEC's proposed amendment would have allowed the SEC to determine whether a foreign state had the right to acquire a majority ownership interest in a company that, in turn, owned a subsidiary of a foreign company.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, however, the court has not ruled on whether the proposed amendment should apply to all foreign companies.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's office for New York today announced criminal charges against two Israeli companies for their roles in an alleged insider trading scheme that targeted farm workers in Costa Rica, Ecuador, Guatemala, and Panama.  As alleged, the complaint alleges that Israel was not entitled to a sovereign immunity bar under Section 1603(b)(2) of the Securities Act of 1933, and that Israel had no right to have its claim of sovereign immunity determined by the federal court.   The complaint also alleges that, at the time of the alleged trading scheme, Israel owned a majority of shares in two foreign companies, Bromine Co., Ltd. and Bromine Compounds, Ltd., which were not directly or indirectly owned by the foreign state.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-01-593, July 17, 2018. After appellant's arrest without a warrant during the early hours of the morning, he was taken to a police station and later advised of his right to counsel and the charges against him. Following advice of counsel, he participated in a lineup procedure involving several persons suspected of involvement in a shooting incident. One of the participants was subsequently indicted for murder and appellant was indicted for attempted murder. At his trial, which resulted in a conviction, the prosecution introduced testimony regarding the participant's confession and other incriminating evidence. Appellant did not object to the introduction of such evidence, claiming that it was improperly admitted as the product of an illegal search and seizure. Held: 1. Under the Louisiana constitution, which provides that in criminal cases the reasonable-doubt standard requires a unanimous jury verdict in all cases except those involving capital offenses, where nine jurors rather than 12 are necessary for a verdict, appellant was not deprived of due process of law since the State met its burden of proving guilt beyond any reasonable doubt. Pp. 108-113. 2. The Louisiana statutory scheme providing different standards for various classes of crimes is not violative of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 113-115. 3. Since no evidence that might properly be characterized as the fruit of an illegal entry and arrest was used against appellant at his trial, the use of the participant's confession and other incriminating evidence did not result in the admission of forbidden fruit. Pp. 115-116. 253 La. 101, 199 So. 2d 10, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Fifth Circuit today entered a final judgment against a former Orleans Parish district attorney for failing to train his prosecutors adequately about how to deal with Brady violations.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New Orleans, alleges that, in 1985, John Thompson was charged with the murder of Raymond T. Liuzza, Jr., a New Orleans resident.  According to the complaint, after learning about the Brady violations, Thompson decided not to cooperate with the district attorney’s office and instead to participate in his own defense.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney for the District of Louisiana today announced criminal charges against Thompson.  On May 20, 1999, the court granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order and ordered Thompson to pay $14 million in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, Thompson consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a $20,000 civil penalty and a $10,000 officer-and-director bar.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment against a former Metropolitan Police Department officer for his role in a search that resulted in the unlawful arrest of a suspect.  According to the court's order, on April 23, 1968, Officer Richard Jenks, a 15-year veteran of the Metropolitan Police department, observed a man driving a 1965 Cadillac driving recklessly through the streets of New York City.  The court found probable cause to arrest the man for possession and facilitation of concealment of heroin in violation of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In its judgment, the court held that the authority to search a person was based upon the need to detect and seize the substance of the person's drug use.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Court's judgment, Jenks consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty equal to the amount of his ill-gotten gains.  On May 9, 2020, the Court granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an officer-and-director bar against Jenks from participating in any search of a person's person for purposes of obtaining a warrant for his or her arrest.   The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Manhattan, charges Jenks with violating Section 17(a)(1) and (3) of The Securities Act of 1933, and seeks permanent injunctions, civil penalties, and penny stock bars against him.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 539 (1952).

After being fired by respondent employer for refusing to work certain scheduled hours because of sincerely held religious convictions adopted after beginning employment, appellant sought unemployment compensation benefits pursuant to Florida law. However, the Florida Department of Labor and Employment Security denied benefits, finding that appellant had been discharged for "misconduct connected with [her] work," and thus was disqualified therefrom. An administrative appeal was similarly denied. Subsequently, the Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal affirmed. Held: Florida's denial of unemployment compensation benefits to appellant violates the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, as applied to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 232-237. (a) Both Sherbert v. Verner, 374 U. S. 398, and Thomas v. Review Board of Indiana Employment Security Div., 450 U. S. 707, held that a State's denial of unemployment benefits unlawfully burdens an employee's right to free exercise of religion. Where the State conditions receipt of an important benefit upon conduct proscribed by a religious faith, or where it denies such a benefit because of conduct mandated by religious belief, thereby putting substantial pressure on an adherent to modify his behavior and to violate his beliefs, a burden upon religion exists. Such infringements must be subjected to strict scrutiny and can be justified only by proof by the State of a compelling interest. Cf. Bowen v. Roy, 476 U. S. 693, 707-708. Respondent commission does not seriously contest that its denial of benefits cannot withstand strict scrutiny, but instead urges that the justification should be determined under the less rigorous standard articulated in Chief Justice Burger's opinion in Bowen, supra, at 707-708. That standard has no basis in precedent and relegates a serious First Amendment value to the barest level of minimal scrutiny that the Equal Protection Clause already provides. Pp. 232-234. (b) There is no merit to respondent commission's suggestion that the instant case can be distinguished from Sherbert and Thomas on the asserted ground that, whereas the employees in those cases were deemed completely ineligible for benefits under the state unemployment schemes because they would not accept work that conflicted with their Sabbath, appellant faced only a limited disqualification from receiving benefits, and once this fixed term has been served, she will again be on an equal footing with all other workers if she avoids employment that conflicts with her religious beliefs. The immediate effects of ineligibility and disqualification are identical, and the disqualification penalty is substantial. Nor is there any merit to the suggested ground that appellant was the agent of change and is therefore responsible for the consequences of the conflict between her job and her religious beliefs. The timing of her adoption of religious beliefs is immaterial to the determination that her free exercise rights have been burdened; the salient inquiry under the Free Exercise Clause is the burden involved. Finally, there is no merit to the argument that the awarding of benefits to appellant would violate the Establishment Clause. The accommodation at issue here does not entangle the State in an unlawful fostering of religion. Pp. 234-237. 298 So. 2d 101, reversed.

Title: Regional Acquisitions of Local Banks by Out-of-State Bank Holding Companies

Issue: Do the Massachusetts and Connecticut statutes that limit the ability of out-of-state bank holding companies to acquire local banks within their respective states violate the Commerce Clause, the Compact Clause, or the Equal Protection Clause?

Background: The Bank Holding Company Act (BHCA) allows bank holding companies to engage in interstate banking activities. However, prior to the passage of the BHCA, interstate banking was largely restricted due to the McFadden Act. After the passage of the BHCA, Congress amended the act to include the Douglas Amendment, which allows states to lift the interstate banking ban if they wish to do so. The Massachusetts and Connecticut statutes in question limit the ability of out-of-state bank holding companies to acquire local banks within their respective states.

Analysis: The Supreme Court holds that the Massachusetts and Connecticut statutes are of the kind contemplated by the Douglas Amendment to lift its bar against interstate acquisitions. The Court finds that the regional limitations in the Massachusetts and Connecticut statutes burden commerce from without the region while permitting a free flow of commerce among the States within the region. The Court notes that Congress has explicitly authorized the Massachusetts and Connecticut statutes, and thus they are invulnerable to constitutional attack under the Commerce Clause. Additionally, the Court determines that the state statutes do not violate the Compact Clause or the Equal Protection Clause.

The Supreme Court of the United States reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding the Kansas motor fuel tax applied to non-Indian fuel distributors who deliver fuel to a gas station owned by the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation on their reservation. The Nation had argued that this tax was an impermissible violation of their sovereignty.

The Court's reasoning was based on the legal principle that the Bracker interest-balancing test, which considers the balance of state, federal, and tribal interests, only applies to activities conducted on the reservation by non-Indians. Since the tax in question was imposed on a transaction occurring off the reservation, the Bracker test was deemed inapplicable.

The Court found that the legal incidence of the tax fell on the non-Indian distributors when they first received the fuel off-reservation, and not on the subsequent on-reservation sale and delivery to the Nation. The Court also noted that the tax was a nondiscriminatory tax imposed on an off-reservation transaction between non-Indians and therefore did not infringe upon the Nation's sovereignty.

The Court rejected the Nation's argument that the tax was discriminatory because it exempted sales to other sovereigns, such as the federal government and other states, noting that Kansas provides services to the Nation's reservation that it does not provide to these other sovereigns.

The implications of the decision are that states may impose taxes on off-reservation transactions involving non-Indians, even if the products are ultimately used on a reservation, without violating tribal sovereignty. The decision clarifies the application of the Bracker interest-balancing test and reinforces the principle that state taxes that do not directly impose legal incidence on tribes or tribal members within Indian Country are generally permissible.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central issue was whether a plaintiff must present direct evidence of age discrimination to receive a mixed-motives jury instruction under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA). The petitioner, Jack Gross, had filed a lawsuit against his employer, FBL Financial Group, Inc., claiming that his reassignment to a lesser position was due to age discrimination. The District Court had instructed the jury that if Gross proved his age was a motivating factor in the demotion, the burden of proof would shift to FBL to show they would have demoted him regardless of age. The jury found in favor of Gross, but the decision was appealed.

The Supreme Court vacated the lower court's decision, holding that a mixed-motives jury instruction is never appropriate in an ADEA case. The Court determined that the ADEA requires a plaintiff to prove that age was the "but-for" cause of the employer's adverse action, meaning that the action would not have occurred if not for the individual's age. The Court emphasized that the burden of persuasion does not shift to the employer, even if the plaintiff has shown that age was one of the factors in the decision.

The Court's reasoning was based on the textual differences between the ADEA and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, noting that Congress had amended Title VII to explicitly allow for mixed-motives claims but did not make similar amendments to the ADEA. The Court concluded that the ADEA's language requires a plaintiff to prove age was the decisive factor in the employment decision, not just a contributing factor.

The implications of this decision are significant for age discrimination claims. Plaintiffs must now meet a higher standard of proof, showing that age was the sole reason for an adverse employment action, without the benefit of a burden-shifting framework that applies in certain Title VII claims. This ruling makes it more challenging for employees to succeed in age discrimination lawsuits under the ADEA.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Maryland granted certiorari in the case of a group of 12 Negro students who were convicted for their participation in a 'sit-in' protest at Hooper's restaurant in Baltimore, Maryland in 1960. The defendants, who were charged under the state's criminal trespass law, had their convictions overturned on appeal. The court ruled that the defendants' conduct in entering or crossing over the premises of the restaurant after being notified not to do so because of their race would not be a crime today. The law of Baltimore and of Maryland now vindicates their conduct and recognizes it as the exercise of a right, directi g the law's prohibition not at them but at the restaurant owner or manager who seeks to deny them service because of the race, creed, color, or national origin of any person. The appeals court held that the trial court should have granted a motion for a retrial. The trial court denied the motion, and the case was remanded to the lower court for further consideration. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued a decision on the issue.

Respondent was employed in the Business Development Strategy Group of petitioner Sprint/United Management Company (Sprint) from 1989 until 2002, when Sprint terminated her as a part of an ongoing companywide reduction in force. She sued Sprint under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), alleging disparate treatment based on her age. In support of her claim, she sought to introduce testimony by five other former Sprint employees who claimed that their supervisors had discriminated against them because of age. Sprint claimed that the testimony would be relevant only if it came from employees who were “similarly situated” to Mendelsohn in that they had the same supervisors. Sprint also argued that, under Rule 403, the probative value of the evidence would be substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice, confusion of the issues, misleading of the jury, and undue delay. The District Court granted the motion, excluding, in relevant part, evidence of “discrimination against employees not similarly situated to plaintiff.” App. to Pet. for Cert. 24a. The Court of Appeals, having concluded that the District Court improperly applied a per se rule, engaged in its own analysis of the relevant factors under Federal Rules of Evidence 401 and 403, and remanded with instructions to admit the challenged testimony. The parties focus their dispute on whether the Court correctly held that the evidence was relevant and not unduly prejudicial under the Rules. Because the evidence here is not of that dispositive character, it is improper for the court of appeals to presume that the lower court reached an incorrect legal conclusion. Rather, as explained below, the court should have allowed the district court to make these determinations in the first instance, explicitly and on the record. Pp. 6–8. 112 F. 3d, vacated and remand remanded.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the constitutionality of a New York Education Law that prohibits non-citizens from being certified as public school teachers unless they show an intention to apply for U.S. citizenship. The law was challenged by two resident aliens who were denied teaching certificates due to their refusal to seek citizenship, despite being eligible.

The District Court previously ruled that the law violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, as it discriminated against aliens. However, the Supreme Court reversed this decision.

The Supreme Court's reasoning acknowledged that while historically, the Court has struck down discriminatory practices against aliens in employment, it has also recognized that states have more leeway in excluding aliens from public employment. The Court noted that its more recent decisions have limited the activities from which states can exclude aliens, but it has not abandoned the principle that states can exclude non-citizens from certain government functions.

The Court determined that teaching in public schools is a governmental function, as teachers play a critical role in preparing students for citizenship and instilling democratic values. Because of this, the Court held that a citizenship requirement for public school teachers only needs to have a rational relationship to a legitimate state interest.

The Court concluded that New York's law is rationally related to the state's interest in the educational system, as it only bars those aliens who have chosen not to pursue U.S. citizenship. The law was seen as a way for the state to ensure that those teaching its young are willing to fully commit to the responsibilities and duties of U.S. citizenship. Therefore, the Supreme Court reversed the lower court's decision, upholding the New York law.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Alabama today entered a final judgment against the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) for failing to comply with a court order requiring it to register and perform other acts in order to do business within the State. The Supreme Court of the United States decided the case of Eligibility for Loan Redemption in the context of the Tucker Act, which allows private persons to bring civil actions against the United States for injuries sustained as a result of the government's activities. The case involves two separate groups of farmers who received loans from the Federal Mortgage Corporation for Housing and Rural Development (FMCHRD) to build homes in California and Colorado. These loans were intended to help low-income households purchase land and build homes in rural areas. However, the farmers eventually defaulted on their loans and sold their properties back to FMCHRD. They argued that they had the right to redeem their loans and receive refunds of the money they paid towards their loans.
The Supreme Court held that the farmers did indeed have the right to redeem their loans and receive refunds, but that the redemptions were subject to certain conditions. First, the farmers had to give written notice to FMCHRD of their desire to redeem their loans. Second, the farmers had to pay off any outstanding debts they owed to FMCHRD. Third, the farmers had to sign a document stating that they would not seek any further assistance from FMCHRD for five years. Finally, the farmers had to submit their applications to the local office of the USDA, where they would be processed and approved or denied based on certain criteria.
The Supreme Court also clarified that the Tucker Act applies to all types of government programs, regardless of whether they are funded directly by the federal government or indirectly through grants or subsidies. Additionally, the Court emphasized the importance of clear and unambiguous language in determining the scope of the Tucker Act.

Title: Wisconsin v. Illinois Department of Revenue Division of Tax Services

Case No.: 97-1175

Date Decided: June 23, 1998

Judges: Thomas J. Rehnquist, Chief Justice, Antonin Scalia, Associate Justice, Anthony M. Kennedy, Associate Justice, Sandra Day O'Connor, Associate Justice, Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Associate Justice, Stephen G. Breyer, Associate Justice

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment allowed the State of Illinois to retroactively apply changes to its personal property tax code to real estate transactions occurring before the effective date of the new rules. The Court held that the change was permissible, reasoning that the plaintiffs had notice of the pending legislation and had an opportunity to adjust their behavior accordingly. The Court further clarified that due process protections applied only to government actions taken after the effective date of the new rules, rather than to prospective changes in the law.

Respondents filed suit challenging the constitutionality of the Federal Railroad Administration's (FRA) regulations requiring covered employees to submit to blood, breath, and urine tests for the purpose of determining whether they had consumed alcohol or controlled substances prior to engaging in safety-sensitive tasks. Covered employees are those whose jobs involve critical safety responsibilities, such as switching trains, inspecting cars, and maintaining track signals. Under the regulations, blood tests are mandatory for employees who operate locomotives or switch engines, and voluntary for those who drive locomotives or switch cars. Blood tests are also mandatory for employees who handle hazardous materials, maintain track signals, or inspect cars. Breath tests are mandatory for employees who operate locomotives or switch engines, and voluntary for those who drive locomotives or switch cars. Urine tests are mandatory for employees who handle hazardous materials, maintain track signals, or inspect cars. The regulations specify that the tests must be conducted by qualified professionals, that the specimens must be handled properly, and that the results must be reported to the FRA. The regulations also contain provisions for confidentiality and for protecting the rights of employees. The Court of Appeals upheld the challenged regulations, rejecting respondents' claim that they violated the Fourth Amendment. Held: The alcohol and drug tests contemplated by the FRA regulations are reasonable within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Pp. 609-619. (a) The Government's compelling interests in preventing accidents caused by impaired employees and in ensuring the safety of the public outweigh privacy concerns. The Government's interest in testing without a showing of individualized suspicion is particularly compelling in the context of safety-sensitive tasks. Such testing helps to deter employees from using controlled substances or alcohol while on duty, increases the likelihood that employees will refrain from using such substances while subject to being called for duty, and enables the railroads to obtain invaluable information about the causes of major accidents and to take appropriate measures to safeguard the public. Moreover, the testing procedures contemplated by the regulations effectuate the Government's goals of preventing accidents and ensuring public safety. Pp. 609-615. (b) On the present record, the toxicological testing contemplated by the regulations is not an undue infringement on the justifiable expectations of privacy of covered employees. The testing procedures are not excessively intrusive, since they are minimally disruptive to employees' daily routines and are conducted in a medically acceptable setting. Furthermore, the expectations of privacy of covered employees are diminished by reason of their participation in an industry that is regulated pervasively to ensure safety, a goal dependent, in substantial part, on the health and fitness of covered employees. Pp. 615-617. (c) Since the testing procedures mandated or authorized by the regulations effectuate searches of the person, they must meet the Fourth Amendment's reasonableness requirement. In light of the limited discretion exercised by the railroad employers under the regulations, the surpassing safety interests served by toxicological tests in this context, and the diminished expectation of privacy that attaches to information pertaining to the fitness of covered employees, it is reasonable to conduct such tests in the absence of a warrant or reasonable suspicion that any particular employee may be impaired. Pp. 617-619. 839 F. 2d 583, reversed.

The Supreme Court of the United States issued a landmark ruling in the case of Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36 (2004), which set forth a new interpretation of the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment to the Constitution. Prior to Crawford, the Supreme Court had interpreted the clause to apply primarily to situations in which the accused's statements were obtained through physical force or coercion. However, in Crawford, the Court held that the clause applied equally to situations in which the accused's statements were obtained through psychological manipulation or trickery.

This change in interpretation was significant because it extended the protections of the Confrontation Clause to a wider range of situations. Previously, defendants who had made statements under duress or pressure were not entitled to have those statements excluded from evidence at trial. Now, defendants who have made statements under psychological manipulation or trickery are also protected by the Confrontation Clause.

One key aspect of the Crawford decision was the Court's recognition that psychological manipulation or trickery can be just as effective in obtaining a confession as physical force or coercion. The Court cited examples of cases in which defendants had been induced to confess through promises of leniency or protection, and held that these tactics amounted to "psychological manipulation" that fell within the purview of the Confrontation Clause.

Overall, the Crawford decision represents a major shift in the interpretation of the Confrontation Clause, and it has had a profound impact on the field of criminal justice. By extending the protections of the clause to a broader range of situations, the Court has helped ensure that defendants are not pressured into giving false or involuntary confessions, and that their rights are respected throughout the criminal justice system.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in favor of a group of doctors and clinics challenging the constitutionality of several provisions of Pennsylvania's 1982 Abortion Control Act. The act included restrictions on informed consent, mandatory waiting periods, and reporting requirements for physicians who perform abortions. The Court found that these provisions placed an undue burden on women seeking abortions and violated their constitutional right to privacy.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Utah today entered a final judgment against State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company, Inc., a Utah-based insurance company, in a civil action brought by the Campbells.  The court found that, contrary to the company's claims, State Farm violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act"), and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In its judgment, the court also ordered State Farm to pay a $145 million civil penalty.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Utah, the company failed to comply with the court's order to impose punitive damages.  As alleged in the complaint, however, this conduct was not a product of State Farm's conduct, and the amount of the punitive damages awarded by the court was not substantial enough to justify a punitive damages award.  Further, the complaint alleges that State Farm failed to disclose to the Campbell's insurance company that it had violated the federal securities laws, and that it was liable for the amount and severity of the damages awarded.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the securities laws and orders them to pay civil penalties equal to the amounts of their compensation.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

Respondent Jeffrey Landrigan was convicted of second-degree murder in 1982. At sentencing, his counsel attempted to present the testimony of Landrigan’s ex-wife and birth mother as mitigating evidence. But at Landrigan and his request, both women refused to testify. Respondent then filed a habeas application under §2254(e)(2), which determined that Landrigan could not make out a colorable claim of ineffective assistance of counsel and therefore was not entitled to an evidentiary hearing. After reviewing the state-court record and expanding the record to include additional evidence offered by the respondent, the District Court refused to grant the hearing. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit affirmed, but the full court granted rehearing en banc, holding that the district court abused its discretion in declining to grant Landrigan a hearing because he raised a “colorable claim” that his counsel’d performance fell below the standard required by Strickland v. Washington, 466 U. S. 668 (1984). The court also held that, even assuming the truth of all the facts Landrigan sought to prove, he could not demonstrate that he was prejudiced by any error his counsel may have made. Because Landrigan refused to present this claim to the Arizona courts, the court denied him an evidential hearing. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding, inter alia, that the Arizona postconviction court could not have found that the defendant could not establish prejudice based on his counsel's failure to present any mitigating evidence at sentencing. Held: Respondent Landrigan, due to his failure to investigate, could not show that he had been prejudiced. Pp. 5–7. (a) The District Court abused its prosecutorial discretion in refusing to grant a hearing on the ground that it could not prove that the state court had made a decision that was contrary to, or involved an unreasonable application of, clearly established Federal law. See, e.g., Rompilla v. Beard, 545 U.S. 374, 381. The record conclusively dispels that interpretation. First, Landrigan would have offered testimony that overlapped with the evidence Landrigan now wants to present. Second, he would have interrupted repeatedly when counsel tried to proffer anything that could have been considered mitigating. He even refused to allow his attorney to introduce that evidence at one point. This behavior confirms what is plain from the transcript of the colloquy: that Landigan would have undermined the presentation of any mitigating information that his attorney might have uncovered. On the record before this Court, the Arizona court’ed determination that the judge would have allowed his counsel to present no mitigating evidence was not an unreasonable determination of the facts under § 2254(d)(2) and the mitigating evidence he seeks to introduce would not have changed the result. In such circumstances, a District Court has discretion to deny a hearing. Because the Arizona state court reasonably determined that respondent “instructed his attorney not to bring any mitigation to the attention of the [sentencing] court,” App. to Pet. for Cert. F–4, it was not a abuse of discretion for the court to conclude that respondent could not overcome the state courts’ factual findings that established a hearing would be futile. The court erred in finding that respondent was entitled to a hearing, since the record clearly indicates that respondent informed his counsel that he did not wish to allow the presentation. Even assuming that an “informed and knowing” requirement exists in this case, the Court cannot benefit from it, for three reasons: First, the record shows that counsel planned to call Landrigan's birth mother to testify about her “drug us[e] during her pregnancy” id., at D–10, and the possible effects of such drug use, and second, that he interrupted repeatedly to try and proffer the evidence his attorney was about to introduce—that of his exwife, birth mother, and birth father. Finally, the fact that the sentencing court had much of the evidence before it in a manner that “amounts to an ‘unreasonable determination’ ’ ” Id., at F–5—a substantially higher threshold—is not objectively unreasonable for that Court to conclude, since a defendant who refuses to allow a presentation of such evidence could establish a prejudicial basis for his habeaas relief claim. The fact that respondent refused to offer any mitigatingevidence was not objectively reasonable for that court, for the record does not indicate that he could have known about the evidence he now want to explore, and it is not unreasonable for the Court to infer that a defendant refused to give counsel the opportunity to present such evidence. P. 6–8. 441 F. 3d 638, reversed and remanded.

Section 4491 of the Revenue Act of 1971 imposes an annual aircraft registration tax of $10 on civil aircraft weighing more than 5,000 pounds, except for aircraft registered before January 1, 1972, and aircraft operated by the United States. Appellants filed suit challenging the constitutionality of the tax on the grounds that it violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and the doctrine of state tax immunity. They claimed that the tax is not a fair approximation of the cost of the benefits civil aircraft receive from federal activities, and that it is excessive in relation to the cost of the Government benefits supplied. The District Court entered judgment for appellees, rejecting appellants' arguments. The court below noted that the tax is nondiscriminatory, applying equally to private users of the airways and to civil aircraft operated by the United States, and that the tax satisfies the requirements of the doctrine of state tax immunity. Held: 1. The doctrine of state tax immunity, which bars the Federal Government from taxing the States directly, exists to protect constitutionally valuable activity from the undue and possibly destructive interference that could result from certain taxing measures. Pp. 10-15. 2. Taxes that operate as user fees may constitutionally be applied to the States. Such taxes are permissible since they are closely related to the federal interest in recovering costs from those who benefit and since they effect no greater interference with state sovereignty than do the restrictions placed on the taxing power of government by the Commerce Clause and the right to travel. Pp. 15-18. 3. Even though the tax imposed by § 4491 is an annual flat fee, it is not inconsistent with the doctrine of state tax immunity. Whatever the present scope of the principle of state tax immunity, a State can have no constitutional objection to a revenue measure that satisfies the three-prong test of Evansvilla-Vanderburg Airport Authortiy v. Delta Airlines, Inc., 405 U. S. 707, namely, that the charges do not discriminate against state functions, are based on a fair approximation of use of the system, and are structured to produce revenues that will not exceed the total cost to the Federal Government of the benefits to be supplied. Here, the tax is nondiscriminatory, satisfies the requirement that it be a fair approximation of the cost of the benefits civil aircraft receive from federal activities, and is not excessive in relation to the cost of the Government benefits supplied. Pp. 18-21. Affirmed.

The Supreme Court ruled in Wilson v. Seiter (1991) that prison officials who intentionally mistreat prisoners can be sued for damages under Section 1983 of the Civil Rights Act. The Court held that the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishment includes conditions of confinement that are not explicitly mentioned in the text of the amendment. The Court also established that the term "deliberate indifference" refers to a state of mind where an official knows about a problem and actively chooses not to fix it, rather than being ignorant or passive.

The court's order, which was entered on April 9, 1978, permanently enjoins the officer from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Roger Belton.  According to the SEC's complaint filed in federal court in Manhattan, Belton was arrested for possession of marihuana and was subsequently indicted for criminal possession of a controlled substance.  Belton pleaded guilty to a lesser-charged felony and was later sentenced to a four-year prison term.  On April 19, 2018, the U. S. Attorney's Court for New York entered a judgment against Belton, finding him liable for a five-year felony and ordering him to disgorge his ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interests, pay a civil monetary penalty, and pay a $10,000 civil penalty to be determined by the court at a later date.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, the officer agreed to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations of the charged provisions of the federal securities laws.  He also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years, from participating in any officer-related search or prosecution of a person for a specified period of time, and to pay a penalty of $25,000. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Exxon Corporation in a dispute involving a marine fuel requirements contract with Waterman Steamship Corporation. The Court overruled the decision of the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, which had held that the contract was outside the scope of admiralty jurisdiction. The Court found that the contract fell within the purview of admiralty because it involved the provision of marine fuels to a vessel calling at port, regardless of whether the fuels were purchased locally or imported from another country.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eastern District of Virginia granted a new trial for Willie Lloyd Turner, Jr., a black man sentenced to death for the murder of a white storekeeper. The trial judge refused Turner's request to question prospective jurors about their racial attitudes. The jury that was empaneled, which consisted of eight whites and four blacks, convicted petitioner on all of the charges against him. The court held that "[t]he mere fact that a defendant is black and that a victim is white does not constitutionally constitutionally deprive [him] of a fair and impartial jury by refusing to ask this question." Id. at 523, 273 S.E. 2d 46, and Turner v. Commonwealth, 221 Va., 522, 273 E.2d 36, 42, and ruled that the trial judge's refusal to ask the question was reversible error. The Court concludes that Turner was not deprived of his right to a fair trial because the jury was not aware that the murder victim was white. The new trial will be held in Northampton County, Virginia, a rural county some 80 miles from the murder scene. The Supreme Court of Virginia ruled in favor of the Commonwealth in a separate appeal that Turner had not shown that his trial was tainted by racial prejudice. The appeals court concluded that the jury could have convicted Turner on the evidence without knowing the victim's race, and that Turner would have been sentenced to life in prison without parole if the jury had known that the victim was a white man. The high court ruled that there was no reason why the jury couldn't have been informed of the race of the victim. The appeal was denied on the basis of the jury's findings of guilty verdict. The case was remanded to the trial court for further consideration.

The Supreme Court of the United States upheld the conviction of a man who was charged with smuggling drugs into the country. The Court held that the government's use of wiretaps to gather evidence was constitutional under the Fourth Amendment, even though the tapping occurred outside the United States. The Court also held that the government's use of informants to obtain evidence was constitutional under the Fifth Amendment, even though the informants received money in exchange for their assistance.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit has ruled that the University of Missouri at Kansas City violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments by barring a registered student group from using its facilities for religious worship and discussion. The University's Board of Curators adopted a regulation in 1972 that prohibits the use of University buildings or grounds "for purposes of religious worship or religious teaching"<n>The University challenged the regulation in the Federal District Court for the Western District of Missouri. The District Court found that the regulation not only justified, but required, by the Establishment Clause of the Constitution. The Court held that the Court had not found a compelling justification for the regulation's exclusion of religious activity. The Eighth Circuit reversed, holding that the rule violated the Constitution's free-exercise and equal protection provisions. The Supreme Court agreed, and the Court ruled in favor of the University.

A split occurred among the members of a local Presbyterian Church (hereafter respondents) after a majority of the members decided to leave the Presbyterian Church, USA (hereafter appellants), and a minority wished to stay. When the former group left, the latter continued to meet and call itself the Vineville Presbyterian Church. Both groups claimed to be the true representatives of the local church. Ultimately, the Presbytery of the Presbyterian Church, USA, ruled that the majority group represented the "true congregation." Subsequently, the local church filed suit against the minority group in a Georgia state court, claiming that the local church owned the real estate comprising the church building and parsonage. The trial court entered judgment for the local church, finding that the local church was represented by the majority group and that the property belonged to the local church. The Georgia Supreme Court affirmed, viewing the case as merely an application of the neutral principles of law developed in Presbyterian Church v. Board of Trustees of Bladensburg College, 393 U. S. 440, and Carnes v. Local Council of Churches, 236 Ga. 30, 222 So. 2d 321, to settle church property disputes. Held: 1. Civil courts are constitutionally authorized to resolve church property disputes on the basis of neutral principles of law. While the First Amendment prohibits civil courts from resolving church property disputes on the basis of religious doctrine and practice, it does not dictate that a State must follow a particular method of resolving such disputes. Thus, a State may adopt any one of various approaches for settling such disputes so long as it involves no consideration of doctrinal matters. Neutral principles of law provide a completely secular method of settlement that is flexible enough to accommodate all forms of religious organization and polity. Pp. 598-602. 2. Whether the Georgia neutral principles analysis was constitutionally applied on the facts of this case depends on whether the Georgia courts adopted a presumptive rule of majority representation, defeasible upon a showing that the identity of the local church is to be determined by some other means. If such a presumptive rule exists, it would be consistent with both the neutral principles analysis and the First Amendment. However, since the Georgia courts did not articulate that they were adopting a presumptive rule of majority representation, and since there are some indications that under Georgia law the process of identifying the faction representing the local church involves considerations of religious doctrine and polity, the First Amendment might require the Georgia courts to give deference to the presbyterial commission's determination of the identity of the local church. Pp. 602-606. 243 Ga. 861, 254 S. E. 2d 855, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Third Circuit today entered a final judgment in favor of the estate of Albert F. Meyer, who died in September 1939.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Manhattan, alleges that Meyer's life insurance policy violated the antifraud provisions of Section 812(e)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1940.  According to the complaint, the policy obligated the insurer to pay a death benefit of $25,187.50, and that sum was to be paid in one sum to the wife, the daughter, or estate of the last survivor of the spouse.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, however, that the insurer's treatment of that sum on its books created a separate "property" or fund payable to her for her actuarial expectancy beyond the 240 months certain, and therefore it qualified for the marital deduction under the statute because it is payable, if at all, only to the widow and daughter, and no other person has any interest in it.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the policy made no provision for the creation of two separate properties, one a property sufficient to provide payments for the wife while she lived and any remainder to the daughter if she died, and another property that provided for the payment of a commuted value of those unpaid, without any special fund, in which event the unpaid ones must be paid to the widows' estate.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the SEC, Meyer's estate has consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the above-mentioned provisions of the federal estate tax laws, orders it to pay disgorgement of $17,956.41 plus prejudgment interest of $7,231.09, and orders the estate to pay civil penalties of $10,000 and $20,000, respectively, for amounts due her under the policy.  It also orders the wife and the daughter to return any remaining $1,000 owed to them by the estate or appointee, and to pay any civil penalty owed to the estate at the time the estate is due to the beneficiary.   The court also granted the estate's request for a temporary restraining order, which is subject to court approval.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Minnesota today entered a final judgment against Dan Cohen for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17b-5 thereunder, and ordering Cohen to pay $200,000 in disgorgement, $500, and a $100,000 civil penalty.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Minnesota, alleges that Cohen, then a member of Wheelock Whitney's Independent-Republican gubernatorial campaign, approached reporters from the St. Paul Pioneer Press Dispatch (Pioneer Press) and the Minneapolis Star and Tribune (Star Tribune) and offered to provide documents relating to a candidate in the upcoming election. Both newspapers interviewed Johnson for her explanation and one reporter tracked down the person who had found the records for Cohen. Cohen agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws. Cohen also agreed to pay a civil penalty of $500.  Cohen was fired by his employer the same day the stories appeared.  In a parallel action, the Minnesota Attorney General's Office today announced criminal charges against Cohen arising from the same conduct alleged in the complaint.  According to the SEC's order, Cohen has consented to a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(b)(2)(A) and (c) ofÂ the Securities Act of 1933. Cohen has agreed to a permanent injunction, to be barred from the securities industry, and to pay civil penalties in the amount of $250,000. The settlement is subject to court approval.  On May 2, 2019, the Honorable Amy C. Welshhans of the Minnesota Court of Appeals issued a temporary restraining order against Cohen and ordered him to comply with the court's order. The court also issued a preliminary injunction against Cohen, ordering him to disgorge his allegedly ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and imposing civil penalties of $200 to $500 per day.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint, Cohen consented and was sentenced to a five-year officer-and-director bar. The judgment also ordered him not to violate the federal reporting laws, including the reporting and dissemination provisions of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's ("FBI") books and records, and that he would pay a $200-million civil penalty, which would be the same as Cohen's $250 million civil monetary penalty. The order also prohibits Cohen from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in violation of federal law.

Respondents brought suit alleging that petitioner Navy’s use of mid-frequency active (MFA) sonar during training exercises in Southern California harbors violated the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) and related laws. The District Court enjoined the use of MFA sonar, but the Ninth Circuit reversed, ruling that the injunction would not unduly burden the Navy’s training exercises and that the Navy had adequately addressed the plaintiffs’ concerns. Held: The Ninth Circuit erred in vacating the injunction. Pp. 4–14. (a) To determine whether to grant a preliminary injunction, a plaintiff must prove that there is a likelihood of irreversible injury, that the plaintiff has suffered no prejudice, that the balancing of equities favors the plaintiff, and that the public interest weighs in the plaintiff’s favor. Munaf v. Smith, 553 U.S. ___, ___. Because the Ninth Circuit focused solely on whether the Navy had complied with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), it overlooked the latter three factors. Pp. 4–5. (b) With respect to the third factor, the Ninth Circuit erred in failing to recognize that the Navy’s training exercises are essential to national security. The Navy has conducted MFA sonar training in the interim for 40 years with no documented incident of harm to a marine mammal. Thus, the Navy’s need to conduct realistic training exercises far outweighs the plaintiffs’ ecological, scientific, and recreational interests in marine mammals. Pp. 5–8. (c) Regarding the fourth factor, the Ninth Circuit erred in focusing exclusively on the balance of equities. The Court agrees with the Ninth Circuit that the Navy’s training exercises would not be significantly affected by the requirement that it power down MFA sonar by 6 decibels during significant surface ducting conditions. However, the Ninth Circuit understated the burden that the 2,200-yard shutdown zone would impose on the Navy’s ability to conduct realistic training exercises. The record shows that the Navy has employed mitigation measures in the past, without sacrificing training objectives. Pp. 8–10. (d) The Ninth Circuit also erred in concluding that the Navy’s training exercises would not be significantly affected by the 2,200-yard shutdown zone. Such a conclusion ignores the fact that the Navy needs to conduct realistic training exercises to ensure that it is able to neutralize the threat posed by enemy submarines. Pp. 10–11. (e) Finally, the Ninth Circuit erred in focusing exclusively on the balance of equities. The Court disagrees with the Ninth Circuit’s suggestion that the modified conditions imposed by the stay order should remain in force until the Navy completes its environmental impact statement (EIS). Once the Court concludes that the preliminary injunction should be vacated, the stay order is no longer pertinent. Pp. 11–14. 518 F.3d 697, reversed and vacated. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined. Breyer, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part.

At respondent Richard Bryant’s trial, the court admitted statements that the victim, Anthony Covington, made to police officers who discovered him mortally wounded in a gas station parking lot. A jury convicted Bryant of, inter alia, second-degree murder. The State Supreme Court held that the circumstances of the interaction between the victim and the police objectively indicate that the “primary purpose” of the interrogation was to enable police assistance to meet an ongoing emergency. Held: The statements at Bryant were not testimonial statements. Davis v. Washington, 541 U. S. 36, and Davis, 547 U.S. 813, distinguished the facts of this case from those in Crawford v. W. S., at 829–832, and held that they were testimonial hearsay for purposes of the Confrontation Clause. Pp. 5–7. (a) The circumstances of this trial, as well as the circumstances in which the victim was confronted with the police, clearly indicate that, in order for testimonial evidence to be admissible, the Sixth Amendment “demands what the common law required: unavailability and a prior opportunity for cross-examination.” Davis, at 822. The fact that the trial court admitted the statements to the police and admitted the oral statements as excited utterances under state hearsay rules, does not bar their admission at Bryant. P. 6. (b) The record in this case was not developed to ascertain the ‘primary purpose of the questioning,’ Davis, supra. Davis and Hammon v. Indiana, supra, distinguished. The record was developed prior to Crawford and Davis’ decisions in Crawford, supra and Davis. The purpose of an interrogation is not to establish or prove past events potentially relevant to later criminal prosecution, but rather to establish the existence and magnitude of a continuing threat to the victims, themselves, and the public at large. The circumstances are fluid and somewhat confused: the officers arrived at different times; apparently each, upon arrival, asked the victim “what happened?”; and, contrary to the standard rules of hearsay, Bryant did not even define the extent of the emergency in that case. In addition, the police officers did not conduct a structured interrogation. The court noted that they did not “attemp[t] to produce an exhaustive classification of all conceivable statements,” id., at 157–158, and did not address their admissibility as dying declarations. The Michigan Supreme Court affirmed Bryant‘s conviction. Held : The record is not developed for the purpose of ascertaining whether the statements are testimonial or nontestimonial, and therefore did not violate the Clause. Davis is remanded.

In the case of Sereboff v. Mid Atlantic Medical Services, Inc., the Supreme Court addressed whether a fiduciary under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) could seek reimbursement from a beneficiary for medical expenses paid by the ERISA plan when the beneficiary has recovered damages from a third party.

The Sereboffs, beneficiaries of an ERISA-covered health plan, received medical expense payments from Mid Atlantic after an automobile accident. They later settled a tort action related to the accident but did not reimburse Mid Atlantic, which had asserted a lien on the settlement proceeds. Mid Atlantic sued the Sereboffs under ERISA §502(a)(3) to enforce the plan's "Acts of Third Parties" provision, which required reimbursement from third-party recoveries.

The Supreme Court held that Mid Atlantic's claim was for "equitable relief" under ERISA §502(a)(3)(B) because it sought to enforce an equitable lien on specifically identified funds within the Sereboffs' control—the settlement proceeds. The Court distinguished this case from previous rulings by noting that the funds were in the Sereboffs' possession, unlike in Great-West Life & Annuity Ins. Co. v. Knudson, where the funds were not in the defendant's possession.

The Court also rejected the Sereboffs' argument that equitable liens by agreement required strict tracing rules, noting that such rules did not apply to equitable liens established by agreement, as in the case at hand. The Court further dismissed the Sereboffs' contention that equitable defenses applicable to subrogation claims should limit Mid Atlantic's recovery, explaining that Mid Atlantic's claim was based on an equitable lien by agreement, not subrogation.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the lower court's decision, allowing Mid Atlantic to recover the medical expenses from the Sereboffs' settlement funds. The decision clarified the circumstances under which fiduciaries could seek reimbursement under ERISA and the nature of equitable relief available to enforce plan terms.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Mexican government in a related case.  The court granted the government's request for a temporary restraining order and other emergency relief.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Salt Lake City, Utah, on April 1, 1997, the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) issued an order suspending the entry of an illegal alien who had reentered the country before IIRIRA’s effective date. The order temporarily enjoins USCIS from violating the antifraud provisions of Section241(a)(5) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1940, and orders the repatriation of any person who has been removed from the country. The court also granted the U. S.CIS’ request for an emergency restraining order.  In a parallel action, the Mexican Attorney General announced criminal charges against Fernandez-Vargas, who was later convicted of the same felony and sentenced to 10 years in prison. The United States Attorney for the Central District of California today announced parallel criminal proceedings against Fernandez. The SEC also announced that it would conduct an expedited review of the USCIS case. The case is being handled by David J. St. Cyr, John R. Rymas, and Eric R. Werner of the SEC Enforcement Division.

As relevant here, 21 U.S.C. §841(b)(1)(A) requires a 10-year minimum sentence for a federal drug trafficking offense involving more than 500 grams of cocaine, and a 20-year minimum for a similar offense involving between 500 grams and 1 kilogram of cocaine. After petitioner Burgess pleaded guilty to a charge of possession with intent to distribute more than 500 grams of cocaine, the District Court imposed a 10-year sentence, rejecting his claim that the 20-year minimum applied because his previous conviction for possessing cocaine in amounts exceeding 500 grams was classified as a misdemeanor under South Carolina law. On appeal, the Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that the 20-year minimum applies to any subsequent offense involving more than 500 grams of cocaine, regardless of how the offense was classified under state law. Held: The 20-year minimum applies to a subsequent offense involving more than 500 grams of cocaine, even if the offense was classified as a misdemeanor under state law. Pp. 4–11. (a) The 20-year minimum applies to a subsequent offense involving more than 500 grams of cocaine, regardless of how the offense was classified under state law, because the plain language of §841(b)(1)(A) specifies that the 20-year minimum applies to a “felony drug offense.” And the controlling definition of “felony drug offense” is set forth in 21 U. S. C. §802(44): An offense is a “felony drug offense” if it is “an offense … punishable by imprisonment for more than one year … ,” i.e., if it involves more than 500 grams of cocaine. Because §802(44) uses the same phrase as §841(b)(1)(A), the latter provision cannot be interpreted independently of the former. To construe §841(b)(1)(A) apart from §802(44) would render §802(44) redundant, since it would allow the same offense to qualify for either the 10-year or the 20-year minimum depending on how it was classified under state law. Moreover, the legislative history shows that Congress meant to use §802(44) as the exclusive definition of “felony drug offense.” When Congress first used the term in 1988, it included it within §841(b)(1)(A) itself, covering “an offense that is a felony under any … Federal law … or … any law of a State” prohibiting or restricting conduct relating to certain types of drugs. However, in 1994, Congress amended the definition, placing it instead in a distinct §802 definition section. This alteration lends considerable support to the conclusion that §802(44) is the exclusive definition of “felony drug offense.” Pp. 4–8. (b) The rule of lenity does not come into play here, since Congress expressly defined the term “felony drug offense” in §802(44), which is coherent, complete, and by all signs exclusive. Pp. 8–9. 484 Fed. Appx. 277, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the issue of whether Congress has the constitutional authority to recognize and affirm the inherent power of an Indian tribe to prosecute nonmember Indians for criminal offenses. This authority was previously denied to tribes by the Supreme Court in Duro v. Reina (1990). The case at hand involves Billy Jo Lara, a nonmember Indian who was prosecuted by the Spirit Lake Tribe for violence against a policeman and subsequently charged by the Federal Government for the same conduct.

The Court's opinion, delivered by Justice Breyer, concludes that Congress does indeed have the constitutional power to relax restrictions previously placed on the exercise of a tribe's inherent legal authority. The Court reasons that Congress has broad general powers to legislate in respect to Indian tribes, as described as "plenary and exclusive," and identifies the Indian Commerce Clause and the Treaty Clause as sources of that power.

The Court also notes that Congress has historically made significant policy changes affecting tribal sovereignty, such as recognizing or terminating the existence of individual tribes, and that the Constitution does not explicitly limit Congress's authority to adjust tribal sovereignty. The Court further emphasizes that the change in question is a limited one, consistent with the tribes' status as "domestic dependent nations," and does not interfere with the power or authority of any State.

The Court rejects Lara's double jeopardy claim, which hinges on whether the tribal prosecution was an exercise of inherent tribal sovereignty or delegated federal authority. The Court finds that the statute in question intended to recognize the inherent power of tribes to prosecute nonmember Indians, not to delegate federal power. Therefore, the Spirit Lake Tribe's prosecution of Lara was an exercise of its own inherent authority, making the "dual sovereignty" doctrine applicable. As a result, the second federal prosecution does not violate the Double Jeopardy Clause.

The Court reverses the judgment of the Eighth Circuit, which had held that the Tribal Court was exercising federal prosecutorial power, and therefore the "dual sovereignty" doctrine did not apply, and the Double Jeopardy Clause barred the second prosecution.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision affirms that Congress has the constitutional authority to recognize and affirm the inherent power of Indian tribes to exercise criminal jurisdiction over all Indians, including nonmembers, and that such recognition does not violate the Double Jeopardy Clause when a nonmember Indian is subsequently prosecuted by the federal government for the same offense.

Respondent longshoremen were injured when cargo being loaded onto a ship swung back and crashed into them. They sought compensation under the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act of 1927 (Act), which covers "injury . .. upon the navigable waters" of the United States. Their claims were denied on the ground that the injuries had not occurred there. Held: Permanently affixed piers extending over navigable waters are not considered to be "navigable waters." Southern Pac. R. Co. v. Jensen, 244 U. S. 205. Pp. 108-115. 398 F. 2d 900, reversed.

On June 29, 1971, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York entered a temporary restraining order against a member of Congress who was subpoenaed to testify before a grand jury investigating the release of the Pentagon Papers.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that Mike Gravel, as Chairman of the Committee on Buildings and Grounds, improperly obtained a subpoena to compel an aide to testify about the alleged arrangement for private publication of the documents.  According to the complaint, Gravel's aide, Leonard S. Rodberg, assisted him with the subpoena.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York today announced criminal charges against Rodberg.  On June 30, 2016, the court granted the SEC's request for an emergency court order halting the subpoena and ordering the aide to appear and testify before the grand jury.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Rodberg consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against him from appearing or practicing before a federal grand jury as a witness in the course of his duties as a senator.
