The court's order also prohibits Gravel from participating in any conduct that constitutes a violation of the free and simple search and registration provisions of the federal securities laws, including the right to reapply after five years of service, and prohibits him from serving as an officer or director of a public company or association with a company that publishes or sells classified documents.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Western District of Texas granted certiorari in the case of William James Rummel, who was sentenced to life in prison under the state's "recidivist" statute for three prior felony convictions. Rummel's first conviction was for fraudulent use of a credit card to obtain $80 worth of goods or services; his second was for passing a forged check in the amount of $28.36, a crime punishable by imprisonment in a state penitentiary for not less than two or more than five years. He also was convicted of felony theft for obtaining $120.75 by false pretenses. The trial court imposed a life sentence on Rummel under Art. 63 of Texas's Penal Code, which provided that Rummel would be imprisoned for life if he had been convicted of three prior felonies. In 1976, Rummel filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus, arguing that life imprisonment was "grossly disproportionate" to the three felonies that formed the predicate for his sentence and that the sentence violated the ban on cruel and unusual punishments of the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments. We granted Rummel a rehearing, and the court found no unconstitutional disproportionality. The majority relied upon the Court's decision in Weems v. United States, which held that the life sentence could not be viewed as life imprisonment because he would be eligible for parole in approximately 12 years. The court also found that R Hummel's life sentence was not disproportionate to the crimes he had committed. The case was remanded to the lower court for further consideration. The Court concluded that there was no basis for the rehearing. The rehearing was not necessary because Rummel had failed to show that his sentence violated his right to a fair trial and that he had not shown that he was entitled to a hearing. The Supreme Court of the United States agreed.

Petitioners were indicted for conspiracy to defraud the Government by obtaining the services of the National Labor Relations Authority (NLRA) without paying fees therefor, in violation of 29 U. S. C. § 112. Four of petitioners were NLRAs, two were former NLRAs, and one was a union official. The indictment alleged that they had knowingly and wilfully caused the submission of false reports to the NLRA, claiming that they had complied with § 9 (h) of the National Labor Relations Act, which requires employers to furnish the names of employees who belong to the Communist Party or who "believe" in the overthrow of the Government by force or violence. The indictment further alleged that the NLRA had accepted the false reports and used them to grant the union permission to represent workers at a plant. The indictment contained a count charging petitioners with conspiracy to defraud the Government by obtaining the services of the NLRA without payment of fees, in violation of 29 U. S. C. § 112. The indictment also contained counts charging petitioners with substantive offenses arising out of the same transactions. After a hearing, the District Judge dismissed the indictment on the grounds that the indictment failed to state a charge against petitioners and that the indictment was defective in failing to allege that the conspiracy was intended to achieve a goal contrary to public policy. The Court of Appeals reversed the dismissal of the indictment and remanded the case for trial. During the trial, petitioners moved for production of grand jury testimony of four government witnesses. These motions were denied by the District Judge on the ground that no "particularized need" had been shown. The Court of Appeals affirmed the denials of the motions. Held: 1. The indictment adequately stated a charge of conspiracy to defraud the Government of a lawful function, in violation of 18 U. S. C. § 371. Pp. 871-875. 2. The trial court erred in denying petitioners' motions for production of grand jury testimony of the four government witnesses. Pp. 875-880. Reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a New York state trooper's search of a man's car during a traffic stop violated his Fourth Amendment rights. The court held that the officer had probable cause to search the car and had not violated the warrantless search rule. The justices also ruled that the search violated the search policy of the New York State Police, which requires officers to obtain a warrant before conducting a search of an individual's vehicle during a custodial arrest. The Court of Appeals had previously held that a search in the car's passenger compartment was not constitutionally permissible. The Supreme Court's ruling is the latest in a series of high-profile cases involving the search of vehicles during custodial arrests. The case is being closely watched by other state and federal courts, and the Supreme Court is expected to rule soon on the issue.

Petitioner Falls City Industries, Inc., sold beer to wholesalers throughout Indiana, Kentucky, and 11 other States. The two distributors did not compete for sales to the same retailers because Indiana law prohibited them from selling to out-of-state retailers. The District Court found that Falls City had discriminated in price against petitioner in violation of § 2 (a) of the Clayton Act, 38 Stat. 730, as amended by the Robinson-Patman Act, 15 U. S. C. § 13 (a), by charging Vanco a higher price than it charged Dawson Springs. The court concluded that, instead of reducing its prices to meet those of a competitor, Falls City's higher Indiana price was not set in good faith; instead, it was raised "for the sole reason that it followed the other brewers . . . for its profit." The Court of Appeals affirmed the finding of liability. Held: The "meeting-competition" defense is available only if the defendant sets its lower price on a customer-by-customer basis and creates the price discrimination by lowering rather than by raising prices. Pp. 5-11. (a)(1) The meetingcompetition defense requires the seller at least to show the existence of facts that would lead a reasonable and prudent person to believe that the granting of a lower price would in fact meet the equally low price of the competitor, and that the lower price must actually have been a good faith response to that competing low price. P. 5. (b) Section 2 (b)'s definition of competitive injury is not controlling; the statute places the burden of establishing the defense on Falls City, not Vanco. The facts in Staley's case are supported by direct evidence of diverted sales, and more than established the competitive injury required for a prima facie case under § 4 of the Federal Trade Commission Act. The "facts and circumstances" present here differ markedly from those present here. Although the District Court characterized the Indiana prices charged by Falls City and its competitors as "artificially high," there is no evidence that Falls city's lower prices in Kentucky were set as part of a plan to obtain artificially high profits in Indiana rather than in response to competitive conditions in Kentucky. Falls City did not adopt an illegal system of prices maintained by its competitors. The plain language of §2 (b), which permits a seller to retain a customer by realistically meeting the price offered to that customer, without necessarily changing the seller's price to his other customers, would not meet the standard of good faith. Moreover, if some of Vanco's injury was attributable to price discrimination, the seller is not required to show that the difference resulted from subtraction rather than addition. Thus, even had Falls City been able to prove that its prices throughout the country did not undercut those of its competitors, it also was not a good-faith response to the competitor's low price, and thus the defendant's low offer was not that good-feeling response. The fact that the price difference between the Indiana and Kentucky prices was not the result of a competitive price discrimination was not sufficient to establish that the seller was responsible to that extent, and the court's conclusion that the discrimination was a goodfaith effort to defend against competitors' low prices is a question for the trier of fact, not this Court. The Court's conclusion, however, is that the meeting-Competition defense was not misapplied in this case, since it requires that a seller, meeting in goodfaith a competitor's lower price to certain customers, to forgo the profits that otherwise would be available in sales to its remaining customers, and to demonstrate that his lower price was a "good faith" response to competition's low prices. In the absence of further findings, this inquiry is guided by the standard that the prudent businessman responding fairly to what he reasonably believes are the competitive necessities. P p. 5–7. 654 F. 2d 1224, vacated and remanded.

Case Name: Judulang v. Holder
Case Number: 10-1175
Judge: Justice Sonia Sotomayor
Date: June 27, 2011

Summary:
In Judulang v. Holder, the Supreme Court ruled that the Board of Immigration Appeals' (BIA) "comparable-grounds" policy for determining whether a lawful permanent resident alien is eligible for discretionary relief from deportation under Section 212(c) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) is arbitrary and capricious. The Court held that the BIA's policy fails to provide a rational basis for its determinations and creates inconsistent results across cases. The Court remanded the case back to the lower courts for further proceedings.

An Illinois statute authorizes law enforcement officers to detain and search any person found on premises being searched pursuant to a search warrant, to protect themselves from attack or to prevent the disposal or concealment of anything described in the warrant. A special agent of the Illinois Bureau of Investigation presented a "Complaint for Search Warrant" to a judge of an Illinois Circuit Court, reciting that the agent had spoken with an informant known to the police to be reliable and that the informant had used heroin in the past and knew that tin-foil packets are a common method of packaging heroin. The court denied the motion to suppress, finding that the search had been conducted under the authority of subsection (b) of the statute, to "prevent the disposal of [the] things particularly described in [the warrant]." The Illinois Appellate Court held that the Illinois statute was not unconstitutional "in its application to the facts" of this case. Held: 1. The searches of Ybarra and the seizure of what was in his pocket contravened the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 541-542. (a) The initial frisk of YBarra was simply not supported by a reasonable belief that he was armed and presently dangerous, a belief which this Court has invariably held must form the predicate to a patdown of a person for weapons. The "long-prevailing" constitutional standard of probable cause embodies the best compromise that has been found for accommodating the often opposing interests in "safeguarding" citizens from rash and unreasonable interferences with privacy" and in "seek[ing] to give fair leeway for enforcing the law in the community's protection." Sibron v. New York, 392 U. S. 40, 62-63, 20 L. Ed. 2d 917. P. 542. 2. Where the standard is probable cause, a search or seizure of the person must be supported by probable cause particularized with respect to that person. This requirement cannot be undercut or avoided by simply pointing to the fact that coincidentally there exists probable cause to search or seize another or to search the premises where the person may happen to be. The Fourth Amendment protects the "legitimate expectations of privacy" of persons, not places. See Rakas v. Illinois, 439 U.S. 128, 138-143, 148-149. Nothing in Terry can be understood to allow a generalized "cursory search for weapons" or indeed, any search whatever for anything but weapons. Nor can the "narrow scope" of the Terry exception permit a frisk for weapons on less than reasonable belief or suspicion directed at the person to be frisked, even though that person happens to be on premises where an authorized narcotics search is taking place. P p. 543-544. 3. The initial search yielded probable cause that Ybarbarra was carrying narcotics, and that probable cause constitutionally supported the second search, no warrant being required in light of the exigencies of the situation coupled with the ease with which he could have disposed of the illegal substance. The fact that the police possessed a warrant authorizing the search of the Aurora Tap Tavern does not, without more, give rise to probable cause for search that person, and the Fourth Amendment does not permit a search of such a person's mere propinquity to others independently suspected of criminal activity does not. without more. The Terry exception is not applicable to aid the evidence-gathering function of the search warrant. The statute's governing principle is basically the same, and it follows that principle today. The governing principle in both cases embodies the "best compromise" for accommodating "the often opposing" interests" in 'safeguard[ing]" citizens' privacy and in seeking to give "fair leeway" to enforce the law'in the community's protection. The Fourteenth Amendment's "longprevailing constitutional standard" embodies "the best compromise" in accommodating "both opposing interests," in "safeguarding ... citizens' interferences ... with privacy," and in the "seek ... to give ... fair leageway for enforcement the law ... in thecommunity's protection," and the Fourteenth is applicable to any search of persons who, at the commencement of a search, are on "compact" premises subject to a warrant, at least where the police have a "reasonable belief" that such persons "are connected with" drug trafficking and "may be concealing or carrying away the contraband." P. 444. 4. The first frisk yielded probable evidence to believe that the bar was frequented by persons illegally purchasing drugs. The second search yielded no warrant, and no warrant was required in the light of exigency and the ease of the Ybarran's disposal or disposal of anything. The third search, which was conducted in a one-room bar where it was obvious from the complaint . . . that heroin was being sold or dispensed, was constitutional because it had been "conducted in a place where it [was] obvious

In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that a state prisoner cannot seek federal habeas corpus relief on the grounds that evidence obtained in an unconstitutional search or seizure was introduced at his trial. The Court held that the contribution of the exclusionary rule, if any, to the effectuation of the Fourth Amendment is minimal, and the substantial societal costs of application of the rule persist with special force.

Section 411 (a) of the Copyright Act (Act) requires copyright holders to register their works before suing for copyright infringement. Section 411 (b) provides, inter alia and with certain exceptions, that “no civil action for infringement of the copyright in any United States work shall be instituted until preregistration or registration of the claim has been made in accordance with this title.” This provision is part of the Act’s remedial scheme. The Act establishes a condition—copyright registration—that plaintiffs ordinarily must satisfy before filing an infringement claim and invoking the Act. The class, however, included both authors who had registered their copyrighted works and authors who did not. Because of the growing size and complexity of the lawsuit, the District Court referred the parties to mediation. For more than three years, the freelance authors, the publishers (and their insurers), and the electronic databases (and insurers) negotiated. Finally, in March 2005, they reached a settlement agreement that the parties intended to achieve a global peace in the publishing industry. In re Literary Works in Electronic Databases Copyright Litigation, 509 F. 3d 116, the Court of Appeals held that a copyright holder’d failure to comply with §411 (a). The Court of Appeal overruled respondents’ objections to the settlement, concluding that §411(a) is more like the “nonjurisdictional employee-numerosity requirement in Arbaugh [v. Y & H Corp., 546 U. S. 500 (2006)]” than the jurisdictional statutory time limit in Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007). The court also overruled the respondents on procedural grounds. Held: The District Court lacked jurisdiction to certify a class of claims arising from the infringement of unregistered works. Pp. 5–11. (a)-Section 411(a), which provides that a federal court can determine “the issue of [the] issue of] registrability of copyright claim” even if the copyright owner does not appear in the infringement suit, is a precondition to filing a claim that does not restrict federal subject-matter jurisdiction over infringement claims involving unregistered copyrights. P. 6. (b). (c) Section 411(b) does not “clearly stat[e]” that the employee numerosity threshold on Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 “count[s] as jurisdictional,” §501(b). Nor does it show that Congress “rank[ed]’ ” that requirement. Bowles, supra, at 515–516. Nor does any other factor suggest that the numerosity requirement can be read to “speak in jurisdictional terms or refer in any way to the jurisdiction of the district courts.’” Arbaugh, supra. Nor is it dispositive that §412(a)-which provides that courts may adjudicate infringement claims in three circumstances: where the work is not a U. s. work, where the infringement claim concerns rights of attribution and integrity under §106A, or where the holder attempted to register the work and registration was refused, the applicant is entitled to institute a civil action if notice thereof, with a copy of the complaint, is served on the Register of Copyrights. This Court has sometimes mischaracterized claim-processing rules or elements of a cause of action as “ jurisdictional limitations, particularly when that characterization was not central to the case, and thus did not require close analysis. Here, that same analysis leads us to conclude that §§411(A)-which does not implicate federal courts’ jurisdiction by dismissing copyright infringement claims, is dispositive. The other factors discussed below demonstrate that § 411(A)’S registration requirement is more analogous to the nonjictional limitations on causes of action, Kontrick v. Ryan, 540 U., at 514–515. Moreover, the statute “conferring jurisdiction over objections to discharge” is a provision “separate” from §2000e–5(f)(3), which expressly state that they “shall not be construed to extend or limit the jurisdiction” of the courts, and specifically in statutes that predated the courts of appeals. See, e.g., §411

A husband purchased a life insurance policy providing for equal monthly payments to his wife during her lifetime and, if she survived him, to his daughter until the end of 240 months, when the remainder of the premiums became payable to the estate of the last survivor. Held: Under § 812 (e) (1) (B) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939, the portion of the proceeds of the policy payable to the wife did not qualify for the marital deduction. Pp. 2-8. (a) Whether a life insurance policy can create several "properties" or funds, either terminable or nonterminable or both, is not here decided, since the policy here involved constituted only one property and made only so much of its proceeds payable to the wife as she might live to receive in equal monthly installments, and made any guaranteed balance payable to the daughter. Pp. 4-5. (b) Since the proceeds of the policy were payable to the wife (or to her estate or appointees) alone and at all events in monthly installments to her for life, and if any obligation under the policy remained undischarged at her death it was payable to the daughter if living or, if not, to the estate of the last of them to die, the "interest passing to the surviving spouse . . . may terminate or fail," and a "person other than [the] surviving spouse ... may possess or enjoy [a] part of such property after such termination or failure of the interest so passing to the surviving spouse." Pp. 5-8. 275 F. 2d 83, affirmed.

On June 25, 1982, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed a lower court's summary judgment in favor of a New Jersey school board that ordered the removal of books from high school and junior high school libraries. The Board's decision was based on the recommendations of a committee of parents and school staff that it had appointed. The committee recommended that the school board remove "anti-American, anti-Christian," and "just plain filthy" books from the libraries. In its decision, the Board rejected the committee's recommendations and ordered that certain books be removed. The district court granted summary judgment to the Board in its favor. The appeals court found that the district court had erred in finding that the Board had violated the First Amendment by removing the books. The court also found that there was no need for a trial to determine the merits of the allegations of the complaint against the Board.

Appellant Slochower invoked the privilege against self-incrimination under the Fifth Amendment before an investigating committee of the United States Senate, and was summarily discharged from his position as associate professor at Brooklyn College, an institution maintained by the City of New York. He now claims that the charter provision as applied to him violates both the Due Process and Privileges and Immunities Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. Held: The summary dismissal of appellant violates due process of law. Pp. 531-532. (a) Appellant has a constitutional right to be an associate professor of German at Brooklyn, and the State has broad powers in the selection and discharge of its employees, and it may be that proper inquiry would show his continued employment to be inconsistent with a real interest of the State, but there has been no inquiry here. P. 532. Reversed and remanded.

Title: Fees Awarded to Defendants Under Section 1988 of Civil Rights Act

Summary: This case deals with the issue of whether a defendant can receive fees awarded under section 1988 of the Civil Rights Act for work done in defending against a frivolous claim. The Supreme Court held that a defendant may receive fees for work directly related to the frivolous claim, but not for work that would have been done regardless of the existence of the frivolous claim. The Court also clarified that a defendant's fees may include work done in responding to a false accusation, even if the accused person later pleaded guilty to a crime based on that accusation.

After respondent Teresa Harris, who is a woman, left her position as a manager at petitioner Forklift Systems, Inc., she filed suit in Federal District Court, alleging that petitioners' president, Charles Hardy, had engaged in conduct that created a discriminatorily abusive work environment for her because of her gender. She sought damages under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In holding that Hardys conduct did not create an abusive work environment, the District Court focused on whether the conduct "seriously affected" Harris' psychological well-being or caused her to suffer injury. It concluded that although some of Hardys comments "offended" Harris, they were not "so severe as to be expected to seriously affect" her psychological well-being, and that she was not "subjectively so offended that she suffered injury." Held: Whether an environment is "hostile" or "abusive" can be determined only by looking at all the circumstances, including the frequency of the discriminatory conduct; its severity; whether it is physically threatening or humiliating, or a mere offensive utterance; and whether it unreasonably interferes with an employee's work performance. No single factor is required. Pp. 10-12. Reversed and remanded.

Respondent Hastings College of the Law (Hastings or the Law School), an association of Christian lawyers and law students, charters student chapters at law schools throughout the country. The law school’s “Registered Student Organization” (RSO) program, which extends official recognition to student groups, offers students “opportunities to pursue academic and social interests outside of the classroom [to] further their education” and to help them “develo[p] leadership skills.” See Rosenberger v. Rector and Visitors of Univ. of Va., 515 U. S. 819; Widmar v. Vincent, 454 U.S. 263; and Healy v. James, 408 US. 169. In requiring CLS—in common with all other student organizations—to choose between welcoming all students and forgoing the benefits of official recognition, Hastings did not transgress constitutional limitations. The First Amendment shields CLS against state prohibition of its expressive activity, however exclusionary that activity may be. But CLS enjoys no constitutional right to state subvention of its selectivity. See, e.g., Rosenberger, supra, at 622. The Court of Appeals affirmed in part, holding that Hastings’ all-comers policy impairs its First Amendment rights to free speech, expressive association, and free exercise of religion by prompting it, on pain of relinquishing the advantages of recognition, to accept members who do not share its core beliefs about religion and sexual orientation. The court also rejected CLS’ Free Exercise Clause argument, noting that “[t]he Nondiscrimination Policy does not target or single out religious beliefs,” id., at 63a–64a; rather, the policy “is neutral and of general applicability” as it relates to the RSO program. And “the conditions on recognition are therefore viewpoint neutral and reasonable.’ ” Ibid. Held: 1. The District Court and the Ninth Circuit correctly held that Hastings did violate the First Amendment by requiring CLS to choose between accepting all comers or forgoing official recognition because of the groups’ viewpoints. The Ninth Circuit erred in holding that the parties stipulated that Hastings imposes an open membership rule on all student groups—all groups must accept only comers even if those individuals disagree with the group’S mission—and that Hastings, in common with other RSOs, should not restrict membership and leadership to individuals committed to the group's ideology. This Court has long recognized, “First Amendment rights” must be analyzed by the educational context in which it arises, and this Court has rigorously reviewed laws and regulations that constrain associational freedom. In the context of public accommodations, the Court has subjected restrictions on that freedom to close scrutiny; such restrictions are permitted only if they serve “compelling state interests” that are “unrelated to the suppression of ideas”—interests that cannot be advanced “through … significantly less restrictive [means].” Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Ed. Fund, Inc., 473 U. . .

The Town of Hempstead has enacted an ordinance regulating dredging and pit excavating on property within its limits. The appellants, who engaged in such operations prior to the enactment of the ordinance, claim that it in effect prevents them from continuing their business and therefore takes their property without due process of law in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment. The trial court held that the ordinance was a valid exercise of the town's police power. The Appellate Division affirmed, 9 N.Y.2d 941, 196 N. Y.S. 2d 577, and the New York Court of Appeals in a divided opinion affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania today entered a final judgment in favor of a Pennsylvania law that requires states to adopt a six-year statute of limitations for paternity and child support actions.  According to the court's order, filed on September 22, 1983, Cherlyn Clark filed a support complaint in the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas on behalf of her minor daughter, Tiffany, who was born out of wedlock on June 11, 1973. The court found that the 6-year statutory limitation was not substantially related to Pennsylvania's interest in avoiding the litigation of stale or fraudulent claims.  The court also found that, under Pennsylvania law, a child must prove paternity before seeking support from his or her father, and that, in the alternative, a parent must show that the child was the father of the child.  In addition, the court found insufficient evidence to support a parent's action to establish paternity.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Clark consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins her from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders her to pay a civil penalty of $100,000.  Clark also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years, and to be prohibited from participating in the child support enforcement program.  On November 2, 2018, the U. S. District Judge for the Eastern District of New York granted Clark's motion for a temporary restraining order against further violations of the federal securities laws, ordered her to return to the district court for a hearing scheduled for October 30, 2018.  A hearing on the same matter is scheduled for Oct. 30, 2019.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-01221 (January 24, 2019).  The SEC's Office of Investor Education and Advocacy has issued an Investor Alert to encourage investors to check the backgrounds of people selling or offering them investments using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

The text appears to contain a legal document related to a habeas corpus case in the United States. Habeas corpus is a process by which individuals can challenge their detention in court. The document discusses the decision of a lower court to deny a habeas corpus petition and the subsequent appeal to a higher court. The appeals court reviews the evidence presented by both parties and determines whether the lower court's decision was proper.

On May 29, 1961, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled that a Pennsylvania law prohibiting the sale of certain goods on Sundays is unconstitutional because it violates the First Amendment right to free exercise of religion. The three-judge panel ruled that the law does not violate the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because it does not prohibit the religious exercise of the merchant's right to freedom of speech and expression. The court also ruled that it is not unconstitutional for the city of Philadelphia to enforce the law. The appeals court concluded that the city's enforcement of the law is not a violation of the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law, and that the trial court properly dismissed the complaint on the authority of the Orthodox Jewish merchants. The case was brought by Abraham Braunfeld, David Berger, and Theodore Mann, who are all merchants in Philadelphia who sell clothing and home furnishings. The defendants were Philadelphia City Police Commissioner Albert Brown and Chief of Police for the City of Philadelphia. In a concurring opinion, Justice WHITTAKER agreed with the court's decision, and ruled that Braunfeld's complaint was without merit.

The Government, pursuant to the Defense Production Act of 1950 (DPA), entered into a series of fixed-price production contracts with petitioners Hercules Incorporated (Hercules) and Wm. T. Thompson Company (Thompson), to manufacture and sell a specific phenoxy herbicide, code-named Agent Orange. The contracts also instructed the suppliers to mark the drums containing the herbicide with an orange band with "n]o further identification as to content." Petitioners fully complied. The Government then sued the Government in Federal District Court under tort theories of contribution and noncontractual indemnification. The Claims Court granted summary judgment against petitioners and dismissed both complaints. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that petitioners' claim of implied warranty of specifications failed because petitioners could not prove causation between the alleged breach and the damages. Held: 1. Petitioners are not entitled to recover their costs from the Government on the basis of the Government contractor defense. Pp. 563-567. 2. The Tucker Act confers upon the court jurisdiction to hear and determine, inter alia, claims against the United States founded upon any "express or implied" contract with the Government, 28 U. S. C. § 1491(a), and not to claims on contracts either express or implied in fact, and not on contracts implied in law. United States v. Spearin, 248 U.S. 132, 39 S.Ct. 59, 63 L.Ed. 166, distinguished. P. 567. 3. The fact that the Government compelled it to manufacture Agent Orange constitutes an implied-in-fact agreement by the Government to indemnify for losses to third parties does not give rise to an implied indemnity agreement. The contract must be read to include an implied agreement to protect the contractor and indemnify its losses. The circumstances surrounding the contracting are only relevant to the extent that they help us deduce what the parties to the contract agreed to in fact. Moreover, there is no reason to think that a contracting officer would not agree to the open-ended indemnification alleged here. The relevant statute, Executive Order, and regulations read very differently, and the relevant regulations were also either silent or much more ambiguous than they are today. The statute's language has always been nonspecific or ambiguous on the procedures required for indemnification, and, in many respects, the statute has always made no explicit reference to indemnification; and the fact that veterans who claimed physical injury from the use of Agent Orange could not recover against the Government considerably weakens petitioners's equitable appeal. The District Court's decision to grant summary judgment to petitioners is reversed. P p. 568. 24 F. 3d 188, affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit recently ruled that a Pennsylvania newspaper cannot be held liable for a series of articles published in the Philadelphia Inquirer that alleged that a state legislator had connections to organized crime and used those links to influence state government. The Inquirer's articles were published between May 1975 and May 1976, and the trial court concluded that the newspaper had the burden of proving the truth of the statements. The trial court instructed the jury that the defendants violated the First Amendment by failing to show that the statements were false. The court ruled that the Inquirer could not be liable for the articles' accuracy because it had not shown that the articles were true. The Court held that, at least where a newspaper publishes speech of public concern, a private figure who brings a suit for defamation cannot recover damages without also showing that the media defendant was at fault in publishing the statements at issue. In Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc., 418 U.N. 323, 325, 94 S.Ct. 2997, 3000, 41 L.Ed.2d 789 789, we held that the court cannot determine the proper accommodation between the law of defamation and the freedoms of speech and press protected by the First amendment. In this case, we hold that the lower court's ruling is not consistent with the Gertz ruling. The Third Circuit also held that there was no basis for the trial judge's conclusion that the newspapers violated the Constitution's "shield law"

Article 37 of the Declaration of Rights of the Maryland Constitution provides that "no religious test shall ever be required as a qualification for any office of profit or trust in this State, other than a declaration of belief in the existence of God." Held: 1. Neither a State nor the Federal Government can constitutionally force a person "to profess a belief or disbelief in any religion." Neither can constitutionally pass laws or impose requirements which aid all religions as against non-believers, and neither can aid those religions based on a belief in God as against those founded on religion. Pp. 463-464. 2. The Maryland religious test for public office is not self-executing and requires declaration of his belief. P. 464. 3. The state constitutional provision does not bar every person who refuses to declare a belief from holding a public "office of profit" in Maryland. Everson v. Board of Education, 330 U. S. 1, at pages 15 and 16, and Everson, at page 511, stated: "We follow the McCollum case." Everson also stated that, "In this case, the Court of Appeals erred in holding that the state religious test is not a threat to freedom of belief and religion, and that the State's requirement that he declare this belief violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the Constitution of the United States." P. 470. 4. The State's religious test, which was designed to and, if valid, does bar every "person who refuses" to declare his belief in "the existence of" God, is unconstitutionally invades the appellant's freedom of religion and therefore cannot be enforced against him. P p. 466. 5. The fact that the Maryland test does not violate the First Amendment does not mean that it cannot be applied to any person who does not believe in God, since it is not compelled by the Constitution to hold the office of public official. Pg. 467. 6. This Court's later holding and opinion in Zorach v. Clauson, 343 U.S. 306, had in part repudiated the statement in the Everson opinion quoted above and previously reaffirmed in McCollums. Held: (1) That the Court there intended to open up the way for government, state or federal, to restore the historically and constitutionally discredited policy of probing religious beliefs by test oaths or limiting public offices to persons who have, or perhaps more properly profess to have, a belief of some particular kind of religious concept, does not support the idea that the Court was seeking to establish in Maryland a colonial government free from the religious persecutions that had been brought about by the imposition of burdens and disabilities of various kinds upon varied beliefs depending largely upon what group happened to be politically strong enough to legislate in favor of its own beliefs. The effect of all this was the formal or practical "establishment" of particular religious faiths in most of the Colonies, with consequent burdens imposed on the free exercise of the faiths of nonfavored believers, and the State has staked the very existence of our country on the faith that complete separation between the state and religion is best for the state, best for religion. Cf. Zoracher v. Santa Fe University, 330 N. W. 2d 624, distinguished.

Section 523(a) of the Bankruptcy Code specifies various circumstances under which a debtor may be denied discharge of a debt. One such circumstance is where the debtor has engaged in conduct constituting an act of fraud, in which case § 523(a)(2) provides that "[i]f the acts ... are proven by a preponderance of the evidence, the debtor shall be presumed guilty of having engaged in such acts." After petitioner prevailed on his fraud claim against respondent in a Missouri state court, respondent sought protection from discharge under § 523(a)(2) in a subsequent bankruptcy proceeding. However, the Bankruptcy Court ruled that the state-court judgment did not meet the requirement of § 523(a)(2)'s preponderance-of-the-evidence test, since the state court had used a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard rather than the lower preponderance standard. On review, the Court of Appeals disagreed, ruling that the higher standard was more likely to further the Bankruptcy Code's "fresh start" policy. Held: The standard of proof for the dischargeability exceptions in § 523(a) is the ordinary preponderance-of-the-evidence standard. Pp. 108-116. (a) The language of § 523 does not prescribe the standard of proof for the discharge exceptions. Nor does the legislative history of § 523 or its predecessor, 11 U. S. C. § 35, indicate that Congress intended to require a special, heightened standard of proof. Moreover, requiring the creditor to establish by a preponderance of the evidence that his claim is not dischargeable reflects a fair balance between the competing interests of the victim of fraud and the perpetrator of fraud. Application of the ordinary preponderance standard to the fraud exception is not inappropriate simply because, at the time Congress enacted the current Bankruptcy Code, the majority of States required proof of fraud by clear and convincing evidence. Although Congress has chosen the preponderance standard when creating substantive causes of action for fraud, most notably in determining under § 727(a)(4) whether a debtor has committed a fraud on the bankruptcy court, the fact that most States required fraud claims to be proved by clear and convincing evidence would not support the conclusion that Congress intended to adopt the clear-and-convincing standard for the fraud discharge exception. Rather, it would be reasonable to conclude that Congress adopted the preponderance standard in light of the longstanding practice among courts of applying that standard in fraud cases. Pp. 108-114. (b) Application of the preponderance standard will permit exception from discharge of all fraud claims creditors have successfully reduced to judgment. That result accords with the historical development of the discharge exceptions. Under the 1898 Bankruptcy Act, judgments sounding in fraud were exempt from discharge; in the 1903 revisions, Congress substituted the term "liabilities" for "judgments," thereby expanding the scope of the fraud exceptions. Absent a clear indication from Congress of a change in policy, it would be inconsistent with this earlier expression of congressional intent to construe the exceptions to allow some debtors facing fraud judgments to have those judgments discharged. Pp. 114-115. 875 F. 2d 1179, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio ruled that the federal government's preemption of state and local regulation of motor carriers does not apply to the City of Columbus, Ohio's efforts to regulate the operation of tow trucks that pick up vehicles within the city limits. The court held that the preemption provision does not restrict the safety regulatory authority of a State with respect to motor vehicles. The Court held that Columbus's regulations, which require the operators to obtain city licenses, meet city standards for insurance and recordkeeping, and conform to city inspections, are not covered by the federal preemption. The case was brought by the Ohio Department of Transportation and the Ohio Attorney General's Office against the city and the tow truck operators. The litigation will be heard by Judge Paul J. Prendergast of the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals.

Case Name: United States vs. James Wah Toy & Wong Sun
Case Number: 371 U.S. 497 (1962)
Date Decided: June 27, 1962
Supreme Court Justices: Earl Warren, Hugo Black, Stanley Reed, Harold Burton, Felix Frankfurter, John Marshall Harlan II, Robert Jackson, Charles Evans Hughes, Thomas Clarkson Eldridge
Summary: In this landmark decision, the Supreme Court clarified the Miranda rights and established the standard for determining whether a confession is admissible in criminal trials. The Court held that a confession must be voluntary, made freely and without undue pressure or coercion, and must be supported by corroborating evidence. Additionally, the Court emphasized the importance of protecting individual liberties and ensuring that defendants receive fair treatment throughout the legal process.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia entered a consent decree in a class action brought on behalf of 3,000 children in the Georgia foster-care system. The consent decree resolved all pending issues other than the fees that respondents' attorneys were entitled to receive under 42 U. S.C. 1988. The district court entered a final judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, concluding that the amount of attorney's fees requested was not sufficient to induce lawyers of comparable skill, judgment, professional representation and experience to litigate this case. The court reduced the fee amount requested by respondents by 50% and increased it by 75%. The final judgment did not take into account the fact that class counsel were required to advance case expenses of $1.7 million over a three-year period with no on-going reimbursement, and that the court did not make a larger reduction in the number of hours for which respondents’ attorneys sought reimbursement. On appeal, the district court vacated the final judgment and remanded the case to the lower court for further proceedings. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued an opinion on the matter. The U

Respondent received an anonymous telephone tip that marijuana was growing in respondent's backyard. Police were unable to observe the contents of respondent's yard from ground level because of a 6-foot outer fence and a 10-foot inner fence completely enclosing the yard. Later that day, Officer Shutz secured a private plane and flew over respondent's house at an altitude of 1,000 feet, within navigable airspace; he was accompanied by Officer Rodriguez. Both officers were trained in marijuana identification. From the overflight, the officers readily identified marijuana plants 8 feet to 10 feet in height growing in a 15- by 25-foot plot in the yard; they photographed the area with a standard 35mm camera. Respondent pleaded guilty to cultivation of marijuana. After the trial court denied respondent's motion to suppress the evidence of the search, respondent pleaded guilty. The California Court of Appeal reversed, however, on the ground that the warrantless aerial observation which led to the issuance of the warrant violated the Fourth Amendment. Held: 1. The Fourth Amendment does not require the police traveling in the public airways at this altitude to obtain a warrant in order to observe what is visible to the naked eye. Pp. 516-517. (a) Respondent appears to challenge the authority of government to observe his activity from any vantage point or place if the viewing is motivated by a law enforcement purpose, and not the result of a casual, accidental observation. Katz v. United States, 466 U. S. 170, distinguished. P. 517. (b) The touchstone of Fourth Amendment analysis is not whether the individual chooses to conceal assertedly "private" activity, but instead "whether the government's intrusion infringes upon the personal and societal values protected by the Amendment." Oliver v. U.S. District Court, 407U.S., at 361, 88 S.Ct. 2556, 2561, 65 L.Ed. 2d 633, reversed.

In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether the denial of a theatre rental to a promotional company for a production of the musical "Hair" amounted to a violation of the First Amendment's right to freedom of speech. The Court found that the denial was indeed a violation of the First Amendment, as it was a form of prior restraint that was not supported by sufficient procedural safeguards. Specifically, the Court found that the denial was not accompanied by a prompt final judicial determination, and that the burden of initiating legal proceedings rested solely on the promotional company. As a result, the Court reversed the decision of the lower courts and remanded the case for further consideration.

After respondent Carr, a convicted child rapist, traveled from Alabama to Indiana, he was arrested for failing to register as a sex offender under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA), which requires registrants to notify local authorities of their presence and to submit photographs and personal identification information. 42 U. S. C. §16913(a). His conviction was ultimately vacated based on the intervening enactment of SORNA, which covers only those convicted of sex offenses after the statute’s July 2006 enactment. But while awaiting trial, Carr pled guilty to a charge of failing to register under SORNA. The Seventh Circuit reversed his conviction, concluding that §2250(a), which subjects to federal criminal liability any person who “receives a notice from an official that such person is required to register under [SORNA] and . . . thereafter travels in interstate or foreign commerce, or enters or leaves Indian country,” 42 U. S. C. §16913(b), extends to preenactment travel. Held: Section 2250(a) does not extend to preenactment travel. Pp. 4−12. (a) Interpreting §2250(a) to reach only postenactment travel is supported by the statutory text. The statute contains no ambiguity suggesting that it applies to preenactment travel. Rather, the statute’s focus on the timing of the “failure to register” element, §2250(a)(1), and the conspicuous placement of the “travels” element in the middle of the list of places where a registrant may go, §2250(a)(2)(B), indicate that the latter element pertains to postenactment travel. Moreover, the statute’s sequential structure shows that the “travels” element follows the “failure to register” element, indicating that the former element is dependent on the latter. And the statute’s legislative history demonstrates that Congress intended to limit §2250(a)’s scope to postenactment travel. Pp. 4−7. (b) Nor does the statute’s structure render §2250(a)’s temporal limitation unconstitutional. Although the Government argues that the statute’s purpose is to find missing sex offenders, taking account of SORNA’s overall structure reveals little reason to doubt that Congress intended §2250(a) to do exactly what it says: subject to federal prosecution sex offenders who elude SORNA’s registration requirements by traveling in interstate commerce. Pp. 7−10. (c) Contrary to the Government’s additional argument, §2250(a) does not constitute an exception to the general rule that a statute applying to conduct occurring after its enactment does not automatically apply to conduct occurring beforehand. Here, the statute’s temporal limitation is not rendered invalid by the fact that it addresses the consequences of failing to register, rather than the act of registration itself. Pp. 10−11. 551 F. 3d 578, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit granted certiorari to resolve the conflict between the circuits on the issue of whether a money laundering conspiracy conviction requires proof of an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy. The court previously held that the jury instructions approved by the district court did not require proof that a co-conspirator had committed an act that would be required to be charged under the anti-money laundering statute. The Court further held that, in the case of the defendants, the defendants were not charged with the commission of a conspiracy because they were not alleged to have committed any overt acts. The Supreme Court, in a separate opinion, held that there was no need for the jury to be told that it was not required to find that a defendant had committed a conspiracy to commit money laundering. The high court's decision is consistent with the decisions of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and the U.N. District Court of the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. The U,S. Supreme Court will review the case and make a final decision on the matter in due course.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant in a civil injunctive action brought by the Federal Bureau of Investigation against him.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the defendant.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Portland, Oregon, Alfred Smith and Galen Black were fired from their jobs with a private drug rehabilitation organization because they ingested peyote, a hallucinogen derived from the plant Lophophora williamsii Lemaire. The complaint alleges that Smith and Black violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and that Black violated Section 15(a) of Exchange Act Rule 15b2-3 thereunder. The court agreed with the complaint that the exemption was permissible because the alleged violations of the federal securities laws were not consistent with the First Amendment. In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Smith. The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by John R. Rymas of the Boston Regional Office and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Division of Justice's Office. The litigation will be led by Jennifer C. Barry.

After respondent had been elected to the Puerto Rico House of Representatives, he died before taking his seat. Under Puerto Rican law, the Governor, acting pursuant to certain articles of the Electoral Law of Puerto Rico, called for a "by-election" to fill the resulting vacancy. Respondents, ten qualified electors in the district who were not affiliated with respondent's political party, then brought suit challenging the validity of the by-election procedure. They alleged that the articles of the Electoral Law authorized only candidates and electors affiliated with respondent's party to participate in the by-election. The trial court granted relief, holding that the articles allowed only party-affiliated candidates to run in the by-election but that all qualified electors might vote. Rejecting respondents' contentions that the procedure violated the Federal Constitution, the Puerto Rican Supreme Court affirmed, noting that the Constitution does not expressly require a fixed method for filling vacancies in a state or commonwealth legislature, and holding that Puerto Rico's party appointment system served several compelling interests, including ensuring the stability and continuity of the legislative balance until the next general election, protecting the eletorial mandate of the previous election, and reducing interparty political campaigns to once every four years. Held: The mechanism adopted by the Puerto Rican Legislature for filling legislative vacancies is not foreclosed by the Federal Constitution. Pp. 40-46. (a) Although the fundamental protections of the United States Constitution extend to the inhabitants of Puerto Rico, the voting rights of Puerto Ricans are constitutionally protected to the same extent as those of all other American citizens. At the same time, Puerto Rico, like a state, is an autonomous political entity sovereign over matters not ruled by the Constitution. This Court accords weight to the Puerto Rican Supreme Court's assessment of the justification and need for particular provisions to fill vacancies caused by the death, resignation, or removal of a member of the legislature. Pp. 40-41. (b) There is no provision of the Federal Constitution expressly mandating the procedures that a state or the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico must follow in filling vacancies in its own legislature. While there is a right to vote for the members of a state or commonwealth legislature, even when a special election is required for this purpose, the Constitution does not confer the right of suffrage upon anyone and does not compel a fixed method of choosing state or local officials. When a state or Puerto Rico has provided that its representatives be elected, a citizen has a constitutionally protected right to participate in elections on an equal basis with other citizens in the jurisdiction. Here, however, the Puerto Rican statute does not restrict access to the electoral process or afford unequal treatment to different classes of voters or political parties. Rather, the interim appointment provision applies uniformly to all legislative vacancies, whenever they arise, and ensures that vacancies are filled promptly, without the necessity of the expense and inconvenience of a special election. The Constitution does not preclude this practical and widely accepted means of addressing an infrequent problem. Pp. 41-44. (c) That the interim appointment power is given to the political party with which the previous incumbent was affiliated does not render the appointment mechanism constitutionally defective. The Puerto Rican Legislature could reasonably conclude that appointment by the previous incumbent's political party would more fairly reflect the will of the voters than appointment by the Governor or some other elected official. And since Puerto Rico law authorized the Political Democratic Party to designate an interim replacement to fill respondent's seat, the Party was entitled to adopt its own procedures to select this replacement, and respondents' exclusion from the Party-sponsored election did not violate their rights of association or deprive them of equal protection of the laws. Pp. 44-46. 103 D. R. 105, 809 N. E. 2d 105, affirmed.

The Supreme Court reviewed a case involving the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) aerial photography of Dow Chemical Co.'s 2,000-acre plant without a warrant. The Court of Appeals had previously ruled that the EPA's actions were within its statutory authority and did not constitute a search under the Fourth Amendment.

The Supreme Court held that the EPA's use of aerial photography was within its statutory investigatory powers, as Congress had granted the agency broad authority to monitor and enforce environmental standards. The Court reasoned that explicit authorization for every investigatory technique was not necessary and that aerial observation was a commonly available method.

Regarding the Fourth Amendment, the Court determined that the aerial photography of Dow's plant did not constitute an unreasonable search. The Court distinguished between the protected privacy of a home's curtilage and the less protected "open fields" doctrine, which applies to areas outside the curtilage. The Court found that the outdoor areas of Dow's industrial complex, despite being secured at ground level, were more akin to open fields than to the curtilage of a home.

The Court also noted that while Dow had a reasonable expectation of privacy within its buildings, the expectation did not extend to the outdoor areas of the complex. The use of a standard aerial mapping camera, which enhanced the view but did not reveal intimate details, did not raise constitutional concerns. The Court suggested that more intrusive surveillance methods might require a warrant.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court held that the EPA's aerial photography of Dow's industrial complex from navigable airspace did not violate the Fourth Amendment, as it was not a search and was within the agency's statutory authority.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against the defendant for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, alleges that on December 14, 1961, 23 students from Southern University, a historically black college, were arrested in downtown Baton Rouge for participating in a civil rights demonstration.  According to the complaint, the defendants had been previously convicted of violating the federal securities laws and were sentenced to prison terms ranging from four months to five years.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  On January 24, 2017, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action and obtained a temporary restraining order, ordering the defendants to return to their respective locations, and ordering them to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest in the amounts of their respective monetary penalties.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) of The Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act"), and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $250,000.  He also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years, and to be prohibited from participating in any form of political or social activity that constitutes a breach of the free and fair use of the public square.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Massachusetts today entered a final judgment against Boston Police Officer Peter O'Malley in a parallel criminal case.  The court entered the final judgment on May 5, 2018, ordering the arrest of Osborne Sheppard, who was charged with first-degree murder.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Boston, Sheppard told the officers that he had last seen the victim on Tuesday night in order to give two men a ride home from a local gaming house. The complaint alleges that Sheppard did not return with the car until nearly 5 a.m. on Saturday morning, shortly before he borrowed an automobile to give the two men rides home. The court concluded that the search was lawful and authorized by a valid warrant issued by the judge, and that the officers should have examined the warrant to make sure that the necessary changes had been made.  In a parallel action, the Massachusetts Attorney General's Office today announced that it filed criminal charges against Sheppard. The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael O'Halloran, John Rymas, and Patrick McCluskey of the Boston Regional Office. The case has been supervised by Jennifer Chun Barry and Joseph G. Sansone. The litigation will be led by Ms. Barry.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Michigan today entered a final judgment against the defendants in a civil action brought by the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Illinois.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Jackson, Mississippi, alleges that the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Rule 17(b)(5) and (c) thereunder. The complaint also alleges that defendants were not required to submit written complaints to the court as required under the federal securities laws, and that defendants failed to adequately exhaust their administrative remedies before filing a complaint.  In addition, the complaint alleges that, as a result of the defendants’ misconduct, defendants were subject to a total exhaustion requirement.  According to the SEC’s complaint, the defendants were never named in the complaint, and defendants were simply told that they had exhausted all available administrative remedies.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, defendants agreed to be permanently enjoined from violating the federal registration provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and (d) the securities laws. The defendants also agreed to pay a civil penalty of $1,000, which is equal to the amount of their disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  Finally, the court found that defendants had failed to comply with the requirements of the federal complaint, which requires defendants to submit a written complaint before proceeding to court. The court also ruled that defendants could be barred from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any security deposit, without requiring the defendants to show cause and effect of any such security deposit. The SEC also ruled against defendants who failed to satisfy the requirements under Section 5(b).  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Missouri today announced criminal charges against two other defendants for their roles in the scheme of the scheme.  On December 19, 2018, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action in federal court against two defendants for violating the same conduct-based provisions of the securities law. The case was supervised by Kelly L. Gibson, Chief of the SEC Enforcement Division's Cyber Unit. The litigation will be led by Mr. Gibson and Ms. Gibson.

The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which upheld the United States Olympic Committee's (USOC) right to prohibit San Francisco Arts & Athletics, Inc. (SFAA) from using the word "Olympic" in the promotion of their "Gay Olympic Games." The Court found that the Amateur Sports Act of 1978 granted the USOC exclusive use of the word "Olympic" without requiring proof of confusion or the availability of trademark defenses under the Lanham Act.

The Court rejected SFAA's argument that the Act only granted the USOC a normal trademark, which would require proof of confusion and allow for defenses. The Court examined the legislative history and determined that Congress intended to give the USOC exclusive control over the word "Olympic," regardless of confusion.

The Court also addressed First Amendment concerns, stating that while words have expressive value, Congress can grant a limited property right in a word when it has acquired secondary meaning through an entity's efforts. The Court found that the USOC had given the word "Olympic" such value and that the restrictions of the Act were not broader than necessary to protect the USOC's interests and the government's interest in promoting the Olympic movement.

The Court concluded that the USOC's enforcement of its rights was not discriminatory in violation of the Fifth Amendment, as the USOC is not a governmental actor and its decisions are not governmental decisions. The Court held that the USOC's actions were not coerced or encouraged by the government, and thus, the USOC's enforcement of its exclusive rights did not constitute government action.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision affirmed the USOC's exclusive right to use the word "Olympic" and rejected the SFAA's statutory and constitutional challenges to this right.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida yesterday entered a final judgment against Costa Cruise Lines, N.V., LLC, a cruise ship company, for violating the antifraud provisions of Rule 15(c)(1)(C) of the federal securities laws.  The court also found that Costa Cruise failed to adequately disclose that it was not named as a defendant in its original complaint.  According to the court's order, Costa Cruise filed an amended complaint on February 21, 2007, alleging that it had failed to name Costa Cruise as a party in its answer, corporate disclosure statement, and motion for summary judgment, and that Krupski had delayed filing her amended complaint until after the statute of limitations had expired.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in Costa Cruise’s amended complaint, the court also ruled that the amended complaint was not sufficient to satisfy the requirements of the court.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney for Florida today announced that it filed a civil injunctive action, charging Costa Cruise with violations of the anti-fraud provisions.  Costa Cruise has agreed to settle the SEC action by consenting to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the charged provisions, orders it to pay a civil penalty of $75,000, and requires it to disgorge its ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest of $2,038, and orders the company to pay civil penalties of $100,000 and $50,000 in disgorgement and prejudgment interests, respectively.  On May 9, 2010, the U. S. District Judge for the southern district of Florida granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order and ordered Costa Cruise to comply with the court order.

After respondents' church was damaged by a wildfire caused by a firestorm resulting from a nearby mountain fire, petitioner county adopted an emergency ordinance restricting construction in the affected area. Respondents sued petitioner in California Superior Court, claiming that the ordinance violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The court dismissed the suit, finding that the ordinance was valid and that the church could be repaired once the restrictions expired. On appeal, the California Court of Appeal affirmed. Subsequently, the California Supreme Court held that the ordinance was void, and the Court of Appeal vacated its previous judgment. Meanwhile, respondents brought this action in Federal District Court, claiming that the ordinance violated the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment, as made applicable to the states by the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court entered summary judgment for petitioner, ruling that the ordinance did not take respondents' property for public use and that, even assuming that it did, the ordinance was saved by the fact that it was adopted pursuant to the county's police powers. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The Takings Clause applies to "temporary" regulatory takings. Although the typical taking occurs when the government acts to condemn property in the exercise of its power of eminent domain, the entire doctrine of inverse condemnation is predicated on the proposition that a taking may occur without such formal proceedings. Here, although the ordinance was not a permanent taking, it nonetheless resulted in a taking of all use of respondents' property for a considerable period of years. Pp. 10-13. 2. Since the ordinance was void, invalidation of the ordinance without payment of fair value for the use of the property during this period of time would be a constitutionally insufficient remedy. The Fifth Amendment's just compensation provision is designed to bar the Government from forcing some people alone to bear public burdens that, in all fairness and justice, should be borne by the public as a whole. Where the Government's activities have already worked a taking of all use of property, no subsequent action by the Government can relieve it of the duty to provide compensation for the period during which the taking was effective. Pp. 13-17. 765 F. 2d 1368, reversed and remanded.

On December 9, 2000, the U.S. Supreme Court of Florida granted an emergency application by George W. Bush and Richard Cheney, Republican candidates for the Presidency and Vice Presidency, to stay the order requiring manual recounts in Florida's four most populous counties. The emergency application was treated as a petition for a writ of certiorari and granted on December 9. On December 11, the Florida Supreme Court issued a decision on remand reinstating that date. The court held that the Circuit Court had been correct to reject Vice President Gore's challenge to the results certified in Nassau County and his challenge to Palm Beach County's determination that 3,300 ballots cast in that county were not, in the statutory phrase, "legal votes." The court also held that Gore had satisfied his burden of proof under 102.168 (3)(c) of the Florida contest provisions. The Florida Court of Appeals, however, held that he had not met that burden. The Court of Appeal, in a separate opinion, found that the Florida Secretary of State's Office had violated Florida law by failing to comply with the court's order. The Supreme Court held that, in this case, Gore had not shown that he was deprived of his right to a fair hearing. The high court concluded that the case should be decided by a jury, not by a single judge. The case is now before the Florida High Court, which will decide whether the emergency application should be granted.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan today entered a final judgment in a civil action brought by a former owner of a luxury pleasure yacht who died in a fire on his vessel.  The SEC's complaint alleges that, on September 24, 1985, Everett Sisson was the owner of the Ultorian, a 56-foot pleasure yacht that was docked at a marina on Lake Michigan, a navigable waterway. According to the complaint, Sisson and his company, Executive Jet Aviation, Inc., were engaged in commercial maritime activity when a jet aircraft struck a flock of sea gulls while taking off, lost power, and crashed into the marina. Sisson's company, Southport Fisheries, Inc. (now Executive Jet), filed a complaint in federal district court in Cleveland, Ohio, alleging that the Limited Liability Act of 1940 ("LLLA") conferred jurisdiction over commercial maritime actions. The complaint further alleges that Sisson failed to raise the issue before the court. The court ultimately ruled against Sisson.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against him.  On May 2, 2019, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. McCole granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an order appointing a receiver to oversee the investigation of the fire.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s Complaint, filed in federal court in Ohio, the Court granted the court's order and ordered Sisson to pay $275,000 in disgorgement and prejudgment interest, and ordered him to pay a civil penalty of $800, the amount of which will be determined by the court at a later date. The SEC also issued an order suspending Sisson from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney.  A hearing on the matter has been scheduled for May 24, 2019.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 1333(1).
