Petitioner Travelers Insurance Company issued policies insuring exports shipped abroad. Respondent Commissioner of Social Security assessed petitioner $1 million pursuant to § 4371 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, which authorizes the Secretary of the Treasury to collect from individuals who fail to pay estate taxes owed by decedents whose estates include specified types of assets, including "any property distributed ... in connection with the administration of an estate." The Commissioner claimed that petitioner owed estate taxes on the value of the export policies. Petitioner brought suit challenging the assessment, claiming that § 4371 violates the Export Clause of Article I of the Constitution, which prohibits Congress from laying any "Duty" on exports. The District Court dismissed the complaint, but the Fourth Circuit reversed, concluding that the Export Clause does not apply to nondiscriminatory taxes on exports. Held: The Export Clause does not permit assessment of nondiscriminatory federal taxes on goods in export transit. Pp. 4-14. (a) The Export Clause prohibits Congress from laying any "Tax" on exports, whereas the Import-Export Clause prevents the States from laying any "Imposts or Duties" on imports or exports. Both clauses were included in the Bill of Rights to address fears that the North would dominate trade with Great Britain and thereby gain undue influence over the new nation. However, unlike the Import-Export Clause, which was intended to protect federal supremacy in international commerce, to preserve federal revenue from import duties and imposts, and to prevent coastal States with ports from taking unfair advantage of inland States, the Export Clause serves none of those goals. Rather, it specifically prohibits Congress from regulating international commerce through export taxes, disallows any attempt to raise federal revenue from exports, and has no direct effect on the way the States treat imports and exports. Even assuming that Michelin Ultra Ltd. v. Wisconsin, 423 U. S. 203, and Washington Stevedoring Co. v. Seaman, 435 U. S. 788, govern this case's inquiry, the Government fails to demonstrate that the Export Clause allows Congress to impose a nondiscriminatory tax directly on goods in export transit. Neither Michel nor Washington Stevedoring permitted a State to impose a nontax on goods in transit. To the extent that the Government seeks to distinguish those cases, it has failed to meet its burden. Pp. 4-14. 199 F. 3d 1055, affirmed.

Title: United States v. Lockheed Martin Corp.

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether the Early Retirement Programs (ERPs) established by Lockheed Martin Corp. violated the Prohibited Transaction Exemption (PTE) under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA). The Court held that the PTE applied to the ERPs and that Lockheed Martin did not violate ERISA by offering the programs. The Court also ruled that the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) regulations requiring employers to offer safety training to workers did not conflict with the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA).

The Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether the inadvertent discovery of evidence is a necessary condition for the warrantless seizure of items in plain view under the Fourth Amendment. The case involved the petitioner's conviction for armed robbery, where during a warranted search for stolen property, police seized weapons and other items not listed in the warrant but in plain view.

The Court concluded that while inadvertence is common in "plain-view" seizures, it is not a required element. The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, and the "plain-view" doctrine is an exception to the requirement of a warrant. For a warrantless seizure to be valid, the officer must lawfully be in the position to view the item, the item's incriminating nature must be immediately apparent, and the officer must have lawful access to the item.

The Court found that the requirement for inadvertent discovery is not necessary to prevent general searches, as the scope of a search is already limited by the specificity of the warrant and the circumstances justifying a warrantless search. The Court emphasized that objective standards of conduct should guide law enforcement, rather than the subjective state of mind of the officer.

In this case, the Court determined that the items seized from the petitioner's home were discovered during a lawful search authorized by a valid warrant, and their incriminating nature was immediately apparent to the officer. Therefore, the seizure was justified under the "plain-view" doctrine, and the Court affirmed the judgment of the lower court, upholding the petitioner's conviction.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California granted a new trial to a man convicted of stabbing his 19-year-old cousin to death with a hunting knife and shooting her four times. The trial judge set the NGI phase to begin the day after the conviction was entered but, on the advice of counsel, Mirzayance abandoned his NGI plea before it commenced. He would have borne the burden of proving his insanity during the NG I phase to the same jury that had just convicted him of first-degree murder. The court denied his motion for new trial, and the California Court of Appeal affirmed the trial court's denial of his motion. In a second motion for a retrial, Mirzalyance claimed that his counsel's recommendation to withdraw his NG I plea constituted ineffective assistance of counsel under the Federal Bar Association's Rules of Professional Conduct and Rules of Evidence. The Court of Appeals granted his motion, but the trial judge denied it without an evidentiary hearing. Mirzayances then filed an application for federal habeas relief under 28 U. S.C. C. 2254, which the District Court later adopted. The Federal Court granted his request for a hearing on the issue of ineffective assistance. The District Court's decision to grant his motion was consistent with the Magistrate Judge's findings that the NGIs phase of the trial was not an appropriate venue for the defense of insanity, and that the jury had rejected the defense's medical evidence. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate decision, ruled that the trial trial court did not have the jurisdiction to grant a new hearing on this issue.

The Mineral Leasing Act of 1920 (MLA) authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to lease public-domain lands to private parties for the production of oil and gas. Under §1701(a) of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, MLA lessees are obligated to pay a royalty of at least “12.5 percent in amount or value of the production removed or sold from the lease.” §226(b)(1)(A). In 1982, Congress enacted the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1996 (FOGRSFA), which authorizes a “court, in issuing any final order in any action brought pursuant to subsection (a) … to award costs of litigation … to any party,” 42 U. S. C. §2000e–16(b). Under §2415(a), the Secretary is authorized to audit those payments to determine whether a royalty has been overpaid or underpaid. In the event that an audit suggests an underpayment, MMS will usually suspend the order’s effect after the lessee complies with applicable bonding or financial solvency requirements, §243.8. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The 6-year statute of limitations applies only to court actions and not to the administrative proceedings involved in this case. Pp. 5–7. (a), (b) The language of the Act does not apply to administrative payment orders. P. 5. (c) The statutory text does not support petitioners’ argument that the 6year statute is superfluous, since the text of §22(a)(1) betrays no intent to change this rule as it applies to administrative proceedings. Nor does the text suggest that Congress intended to impose a shorter statute of limitation for payment orders regarding pre-September 1, 1996 production. Pc. (d) Petitioner BP America Production Co. holds gas leases from the Federal Government for lands in New Mexico. Under these leases, royalties should be calculated based not on the value of gas at the well, but on the amount of the gas after it was treated to meet the quality requirements for introduction into pipeline pipelines. Under FOGRSFA, royalties are now prospectively subject to 7-year limitations except with respect to obligations arising out of leases of Indian land, oil, and gas leases. Under the Clean Water Act (CWA), MMS is responsible in the first instance for the accurate calculation and payment of royalties. Under that provision, an administrative offset that is the functional equivalent of a pretrial attachment is also unavailable. Petitioners argue that their broader interpretation of the statutory term “action” is supported by the reference to “every action for money damages” founded upon “any contract” and the occasional use of the term to describe certain administrative filings does not alter its primary meaning, which concerns the initiation of “a civil action” or “administrative enforcement actions”. But even if the distinction between administrative and judicial proceedings is put aside, an MMS payment order, standing alone, ordinarily refers to a judicial proceeding. Petitioner Atlantic Richfield Co., filed an appeal, first to the Director of MMS and then to the Interior Board of Land Appeals or to an Assistant Secretary. While filing an appeal does not generally stay the payment order (§218.50(c), the statute usually suspends the order, and the Court concluded that the canon had no application in that case because the relevant statute applied clearly and separately to the relevant terms. The court also concluded that administrative offsets are not covered by subsection (i) even if they are viewed as an adjunct of a court action. The District of Columbia Circuit affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California today entered a final judgment in favor of Miller, a former bank cashier who was convicted of mail fraud in violation of the federal securities laws.  According to the court's order, Miller was charged with mail fraud based on an indictment that alleged that he had defrauded his employer.  The court found that, contrary to what the indictment alleged, Miller had not engaged in a scheme to defraud his employer, and had instead simply lied to his insurer about the value of his loss.  As alleged in the complaint, the indictment also alleged that, prior to the burglary, Miller actually had possessed all the property that he later claimed was taken during the alleged burglary.  Miller's complaint, filed in federal district court in San Diego, California, alleges that, based on this finding, he was liable to be tried only on the basis of a finding that he "well knew and believed" the amount of his claimed loss was inflated for the purpose of fraudulently obtaining $150,000 from Aetna Insurance Company."  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Miller consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000,000.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Miller.  On May 24, 2018, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. Kerstetter of the U.N. Court of Appeals for the District of San Diego entered a judgment ordering Miller to be barred from appearing or practicing before the court as an attorney, and ordering Miller not to participate in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in connection with the alleged scheme.  Without further explanation, the court granted Miller's request for a temporary restraining order, a conduct-based injunction, and an officer-and-director bar against him from participating in any future solicitation of an offering of securities in the securities industry.

In the case of Hansberry v. Lee, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that it is a violation of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to bind individuals to a judgment from previous litigation in which they were not parties and were not adequately represented. This principle was applied to the case at hand, where Jason Richards and Fannie Hill, employees in Jefferson County, Alabama, challenged the validity of a county occupation tax. Their claims were initially dismissed due to the Tax Injunction Act, leading them to file a new action in state court.

The petitioners argued that the tax, which had numerous exemptions, violated the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment and the Alabama Constitution. The county moved for summary judgment, claiming the petitioners' claims were barred by a prior adjudication in a case called Bedingfield, where the tax was upheld. The trial court agreed regarding the state constitutional claims but not the federal ones. The Alabama Supreme Court, however, concluded that both federal and state claims were barred by the Bedingfield judgment.

The U.S. Supreme Court disagreed with the Alabama Supreme Court, stating that the petitioners were deprived of due process. The Court noted that the Bedingfield litigants did not represent the petitioners in any class action capacity, nor did they assume to represent the interests of county taxpayers like the petitioners. The Court emphasized that due process requires that individuals have the opportunity to present their case in court, and this was not provided to the petitioners in the Bedingfield litigation.

The Court also rejected the argument that the public nature of the tax issue allowed the petitioners to be bound by the Bedingfield judgment, stating that individuals have a protected property interest in their "chose in action" and cannot be deprived of their right to challenge a tax on constitutional grounds without due process.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Alabama Supreme Court, ruling that the petitioners must be allowed to challenge the occupation tax without being barred by the previous Bedingfield judgment. The case was remanded to the Alabama Supreme Court for further proceedings consistent with the U.S. Supreme Court's opinion.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of North Dakota is considering a challenge to a state law that allows some local school boards to charge fees for transporting students between their homes and the public schools. The case involves a school district in Dickinson, North Dakota, which began charging a fee for school bus service in the late 1970s. The Kadrmas family, who live about 16 miles from the school, had agreed each year to pay $97 for one child or $150 per year for two children to ride the school bus. In 1985, the family refused to pay the fee, and the family arranged to transport Sarita, their daughter, to school privately. Sarita's school bus stopped for the 1985 school year because the family had fallen behind on other bills. The family's annual income at the time of trial was at or near the officially defined poverty level. The court found that the law violated the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution. We conclude that the legislature did not intend to prohibit the charging of fees for school transport, and that the court's decision is consistent with the legislature's intent.

Petitioners Alderman and Alderisio, along with Ruby Kolod, now deceased, were convicted of conspiring to transmit murderous threats in interstate commerce, 18 U. S. C. §§ 371, 875(c), and of conspiring with the Government to violate the Fourth Amendment by causing Butenko to act as an agent of the Soviet Union without prior notification to the Secretary of State. The Court of Appeals affirmed all but Ivanov's conviction on the conspiracy count. Petitioners opposed the motion, and the matter was argued before the Court last Term. Following the first argument in Alderman (sub nom. Kolod v. United States), the petitions for certiorari of both petitioners were granted, limited to questions nearly identical to those involved in the reargument of the Alderman case. Held: 1. In order to qualify as a "person aggrieved by an unlawful search and seizure" one must have been a victim of a search or seizure, one against whom the search was directed, as distinguished from one who claims prejudice only through the use of evidence gathered as a consequence of an illegal search directed at someone else. Pp. 488-478. 2. The Fourth Amendment rights of a person's private conversations as well as his private premises are protected by the Fourth. P. 489. 3. The right to be secure in one's house against unauthorized intrusion is not limited to protection against a policeman viewing or seizing tangible property-'papers' and "effects." P. 589. 4. The rights of the owner of the premises are as clearly invaded when the police enter and install a listening device in his house as they are when the entry is made to undertake a warrantless search for tangible property; and the prosecution as surely employs the fruits of a illegal search of the home when it introduces tangible evidence belonging not to the homeowner, but to others. P p. 591. 384 F. 2d 554, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a challenge to a Georgia law that criminalized consensual sodomy. The court held that the law violated the Constitution's "fundamental right" to private and intimate association. The case involves the issue of whether the Constitution confers a fundamental right upon homosexuals to engage in such conduct. The Supreme Court has held that such conduct is not protected by the "right to privacy" clause of the Constitution. The Court's decision in this case is the latest in a long line of court rulings that have held that private associations between consenting adults in general and homosexuals in particular are beyond the reach of state regulation. In the case of Hardwick, the Court held that Hardwick's private association with another adult male in the bedroom of his home violated his right to a private life and that the Georgia law violated his constitutional rights. The Eleventh Circuit held that, because Hardwick was distinguishable and in any event had been undermined by later decisions, our summary affirmance in that case did not require affirmance of the District Court. The issue presented is whether the Federal Constitution gives homosexuals a right to engaged in consensual, consensual sexual activity. Hardwick argues that this is a private, intimate association that is beyond state regulation by reason of the Ninth Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Hardwick also argues that the statute placed him in imminent danger of arrest and that it violates the Constitution because it criminalizes consensual consensual homosexual activity. The High Court agreed with Hardwick, and reversed the lower court.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit reversed a lower court's decision to grant a preliminary injunction against the city of Chattanooga, Tennessee, barring a theater company from using a municipal facility for a performance of the musical "Hair"<n>The court held that the city's rejection of the application for the use of the Tivoli Theatre was a prior restraint under the First Amendment's protection of free speech. The court concluded that conduct in the production would violate city ordinances and state statutes making public nudity and obscene acts criminal offenses. The lower court agreed, and the jury found that the musical was obscene. The district court granted a temporary restraining order and a permanent injunction. The appeals court found that neither the district court nor the lower court had adequately addressed the issue of whether the musical's content violated the prohibition against obscene conduct. The majority of the appeals court agreed with the lower-court decision, holding that the action was indistinguishable from the actions taken by city officials to censor the musical and was not a violation of First Amendment free speech rights. The opinion concludes that "Hair's" content is not a sufficient basis for a finding that it is obscene." The court concludes that the decision to deny the request for the Tivoli's use was not an unlawful prior restraint.

The Supreme Court upheld the application of the Armed Career Criminal Act's (ACCAs) sentencing enhancement to a man named Clifton Terelle McNeill. McNeill was found guilty of unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon and possession with intent to distribute cocaine base in August 2008. The Court ruled that the "maximum term of imprisonment" for McNeill's prior state drug offense is the maximum sentence applicable to his offense when he was convicted of it.

Respondents, officials of Kentucky’s Department of Insurance, brought suit in Federal District Court seeking declaratory relief regarding the applicability of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) to Kentucky’s “Any Willing ProvidervWorking Together” (AWP) statutes. Under those statutes, no employer can exclude from its health benefit plan any qualified health care provider willing to meet the plan’s terms. The court ruled that while both AWP statutes related to employee benefit plans under ERISA’s definition of “plan,” each fell within ERISA’s exception for laws that “regulate insurance.” On appeal, the Sixth Circuit affirmed, finding that the AWP laws regulate insurance under the standard set forth in UNum Life Ins. Co. of Am. v. Ward, 526 U. S. 358—i. e., whether, from a commonsense view, the laws regulate insurance. Held: Neither of Kentucky’s AWP statutes is saved from pre-emption by ERISA’s savings clause. Pp. 4–11. (a) To determine whether a state law is saved from pre-emption, this Court must ascertain whether it is “specifically directed toward” the insurance industry. Pilot Life Ins. Co. v. Dedeaux, 481 U. S. 41, 50. Here, petitioners argue that Kentucky’s AWP laws are not specific to insurers because they apply to doctors who seek to form and maintain limited provider networks with HMOs. However, the AWP laws are not imposed on health-care providers, and they are transgressed only when a health insurer or a health benefit plan excludes from its network a doctor who meets the plan’s terms. Thus, the AWP laws are specifically directed toward the insurance industry. Nor does it follow from the fact that the AWP laws also regulate doctors that they cannot be saved from pre-emption. Even where a state law prevents insurers and providers alike from forming certain agreements, the law remains “specifically directed toward” the insurance industry unless it is incapable of being applied to insurers. Such is not the case here. Pp. 4–6. (b) Petitioners also claim that the AWP laws do not regulate insurers with respect to an insurance practice because, like the state laws in FMC Corp. v. Holliday, 498 U. S. 52, and Rush Prudential HMO, Inc. v. Moran, 536 U. S. 355, they focus on the relationship between insurers and third-party providers, not on the terms of insurance policies themselves. However, ERISA’s saving clause is not concerned with how to characterize conduct undertaken by private actors, but with how to characterize state laws in regard to what they “regulate.” It does not follow from Royal Drug Co. v. Thouless, Ltd., 440 U. S. 205, 210, that a law mandating certain insurer-provider relationships fails to “regulate insurance.” Whether or not an HMO’s contracts with providers constitutes “the business of insurance” under Royal Drug is irrelevant. Conditions on the right to engage in the business of insurance must also substantially affect the risk pooling arrangement between insurer and insured to be covered by ERISA’s saving clause. Kentucky’s AWP laws substantially affect the type of risk pooling arrangements that insurers may offer. They expand the number of providers from whom an insured may receive health services, thereby altering the scope of permissible bargains between insurers and insureds in a manner similar to the mandated-benefit laws upheld in MetropolitanLifeIns.Co.v.Massachusetts,471U.S.724,andtheindependentreviewprovisionapprovedindRushPrudential.No.longerrelianceonMcCarrafonguidesisnecessaryorthelawfuloraccuratelycharacterizetheconductregulatedbyastatelaw. Pp. 6–10. 337 F. Supp. 2d 675,affirmed. Scalia, J.,deliveredtheopinionfortheCourt,inwhichO’Connor,JUSTICESOUTER,THURSTON,GINSBURG,andALITO,JJ.,joined.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed, 275 F.2d 83, and granted the executors' petition for a refund of $7,231.09 in estate tax paid on a life insurance policy. The court held that the amount was not a separate property and therefore did not qualify for the marital deduction under  812(e)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939, and that the deceased's daughter was not entitled to receive the remainder of the policy's proceeds. In a separate action, the District Court for the District of Columbia granted the estate's motion for a judgment against the insurance company, concluding that the policy was a death benefit and the tax was paid on it. The appeals court ruled that the lower court's decision was wrong. The lower court had found that the insurance policy was in all material respects identical to the policy in question, and that there was no need for the court to determine whether the policy constituted a separate 'property' or fund. We conclude that the case is not a matter of law.

Respondents, two companies providing internet marketing services, filed suit in the District Court, claiming that Ohio statutory exemptions for local exchange telephone service providers violated the Commerce Clause and the Equal Protection Clause. They argued that those exemptions allowed competitors to treat them unfairly by charging less for similar services. The District Court dismissed the suit, relying on the Tax Injunction Act (TIA), which bars suits for declaratory or injunctive relief that would thwart state tax collection. The Sixth Circuit reversed, concluding that the TIA did not apply because respondents were not “outsiders” to the tax expenditures at issue. Held: The TIA applies here, and thus the District Court correctly dismissed the suit. Pp. 4–12. (a) The TIA was enacted to close two loopholes created by federal courts’ application of the comity doctrine, which prevents federal courts from exercising jurisdiction over suits involving state tax collections. The first loophole permitted federal courts to grant injunctive relief to states that failed to exhaust administrative remedies before filing suit. The second loophole allowed federal courts to grant injunctive relief to states that exhausted administrative remedies but failed to show that the state courts were incapable of giving effect to the federal court’s orders. Enactment of the TIA closed both loopholes by making clear that federal courts cannot grant injunctive relief unless the state courts are unable to afford relief. Pp. 4–6. (b) Application of the comity doctrine here is justified by the facts that respondents seek federal-court review of commercial matters over which Ohio enjoys wide regulatory latitude; their suit does not involve any fundamental right or classification that attracts heightened judicial scrutiny; and they are in fact seeking federal-court aid in an effort to improve their competitive positions. The individual circumstances may not compel forbearance on the part of federal district courts, but together they demand deference to the state adjudicative process. Pp. 6–12. 554 F. 3d 1087, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

Title: Cohen v. California
Year: 1971
Summary: Cohen v. California is a landmark United States Supreme Court case concerning freedom of speech. The case centers around a young man named Paul Cohen who was charged with "disturbing the peace" after wearing a t-shirt with the words "F--- the Draft" in a Los Angeles courthouse. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Cohen, stating that the government cannot punish someone for using "offensive language" merely because it is considered offensive. The Court found that the government's efforts to maintain public decency and order cannot be used to restrict constitutionally protected speech.

The Supreme Court ruled that the Illinois statute allowing law enforcement officers to detain and search individuals found on premises being searched pursuant to a search warrant, to protect themselves from attack or to prevent the disposal or concealment of anything described in the warrant, violates the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. The decision was based on the fact that the search was not supported by probable cause, and that the initial frisk of Ybarra was not supported by a reasonable belief that he was armed and presently dangerous.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri today issued an order requiring the Kansas City, Missouri, School District to file a civil injunctive action against the State of Missouri and surrounding school districts in order to fund the desegregation remedy.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Missouri on October 14, 1988, the court found that the District Court lacked the power to impose a tax increase on a public school district.  The complaint alleges that the Court of Appeals held that, under federal law, a district court has the right to determine whether a state-imposed limitation on the amount of a school district's property tax liability is sufficient to fund a desegregated school system.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia today announced criminal charges against the school district for its role in the alleged violations.  On October 19, 2018, the Court issued a final judgment ordering the district court to issue an order imposing a $88 million property tax increase, which it did not impose on the state, and ordering KCMSD to pay $20,140,472 in additional capital improvements.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the district Court agreed to the court's order imposing the additional $8 million tax increase and to the issuance of a final order imposing an injunction against further violations of the federal securities laws.  It also ordered the school board to pay a $52,858,301 civil penalty, which is equal to the civil penalty imposed by the court on the school districts.   The SEC's investigation was conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Chicago Regional Office. Â The SEC's litigation will be led by David A. Schiff.   The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Missouri Secretary of State's Office.

Title: Mendez v. Westminster School District
Year: 1946
Judge: Vinson
Summary: In this landmark case, the Supreme Court ruled that Mexican Americans living in California were entitled to attend integrated public schools. The Court struck down a series of laws passed by the state legislature that created separate schools for Mexican Americans, arguing that such segregation violated the Equal Protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court emphasized that the doctrine of "separate but equal" applied only to African Americans, and that Mexican Americans were entitled to receive the same educational opportunities as white students. The ruling paved the way for the integration of public schools across the nation and marked a major victory for civil rights advocates.

Petitioner was convicted of first degree murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. At his trial in a North Carolina court, where the death penalty was authorized by statute, the prosecution introduced into evidence a rifle allegedly used in committing the crime. The defense moved to exclude the weapon on the grounds that it had been seized illegally. The trial court overruled the objection and admitted the rifle in evidence. On appeal, the Supreme Court of North Carolina sustained the ruling admitting the rifle in evidence. Held: 1. There was no violation of petitioner's rights under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments by allowing the prosecution to challenge for cause all prospective jurors who stated that they were opposed to capital punishment or had conscientious scruples against imposing the death penalty. Pp. 208-209. 2. Admission of the rifle in evidence constituted constitutional error since the "consent" to the search was given only after the official conducting the search had asserted that he possessed a warrant. Pp. 209-212. Reversed and remanded.

After receiving an anonymous telephone call reporting that a young black man wearing a plaid shirt carried a gun, police officers responded to a designated bus stop and spotted respondent J. L., who matched the description given in the call. Without seeing a firearm or making any threats, J. L. was frisked and a gun was discovered. Charged with violating Florida statutes prohibiting the carryinq of a concealed firearm without a permit and possessing a firearm while underage, J. L. moved to suppress the gun as the fruit of an unlawful search. The trial court agreed, but the State Supreme Court reversed, holding that the search was invalid under the Fourth Amendment unless the tip providing the basis for the stop contained specific indicia of reliability. Held: An anonymous tip that a person carries a gun is not, without more, sufficient to justify a police officer's stop and frisk of that person. Pp. 24-29. (a) While there are situations in which an anonymous tip, suitably corroborated, exhibits sufficient indicia of reliability to provide reasonable suspicion to make an investigatory stop, cf. Alabama v. White, 496 U. S. 325, 327, the tip here lacked the moderate indicia of reliability present in White and essential to the Court's decision in that case. Here, the tip provided no predicitive information and therefore left the police without means to test the informant's knowledge or credibility. That the allegation about the gun turned out to be correct does not suggest that the officers, prior to the frisks, had a reasonable basis for suspecting J. L. of engaging in unlawful conduct: Reasonableness of official suspicion must be measured by what the officers knew before conducting the search. All the police had to go on was the bare report of an unknown, unaccountable informant who neither explained how he knew about the gun nor supplied any basis for believing he had inside information about J. L. Pp. 24-26. (b) Accurate descriptions of a subject's readily observable location and appearance are reliable in identifying the person meant to be accused, but they do not show that the tipster has knowledge of concealed criminal activity. The reasonable suspicion required here arises from the assertion of illegality, not just from the tendency to identify a determinate person. Pp. 26-27. (c) Modification of the Terry analysis to allow a "firearm exception"would rove too far. Such an exception would enable anyone seeking to harass another to set in motion an intrusive, embarrassing police search merely by placing an anonymous call falsely reporting the target's unlawful carriage of a gun. Moreover, several Circuits have held it per se foreseeable for drugcarriers to be carrying guns as well. If police officers may properly conduct Terry frisks on the basis of bare-boned tips about guns, it would also be reasonable to maintain that they should similarly have discretion to frisk based on bare-boned tips about narcotics. The Fourth Amendment is not so easily satisfied. Pp. 27-28. (d) Requiring an anonymous tip to bear standard indicia of reliability in order to justify a stop does not diminish a police officer's prerogative, in accordance with Terry, to conduct a protective search of a person who has already been legitimately stopped. However, an anonymous tip lacking such indicia of reliability does not justify a stop and frisk whenever and however it alleges the illegal possession of a firearm. Pp. 28-29. 727 So. 2d 204, affirmed.

The Supreme Court ruled in Hamm v. South Carolina and Lupper v. Arkansas that the Civil Rights Act of 1964 applies to sit-ins at lunch counters in retail stores. The Court found that the act covers both the McCrory and the Blass lunch counter operations and that petitions for sitting in these places could not be considered acts of trespass. The Court also found that the Civil Rights Act prohibits discrimination in places of public accommodation and that petitioners' conduct could not be the subject of trespass prosecutions, federal or state.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was convicted of violating the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that in April of that year, a member of the crew of the S. S. Santa Maria was arrested, promptly arraigned, and subsequently indicted for possession of narcotics aboard a United States vessel. The complaint alleges that a federal agent installed a Schmidt radio transmitter under the front seat of Colson's automobile, by means of which Murphy, equipped with an appropriate receiving device, could overhear from some distance away conversations carried on in the car. According to the complaint, Colson decided to cooperate with the government agents in their continuing investigation of the nacotics activities in which the petitioner, Colman, and others had allegedly been engaged. Colson and the petitioner allegedly held a lengthy conversation while sitting in Colson’s automobile, and the agent overheard the entire conversation. The defendants allegedly made several incriminating statements during the course of this conversation. At the trial, the jury convicted the petitioner and Colson of several related narcotics offenses, and he was subsequently sentenced to prison. The SEC alleges that the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 17(a)(1) of Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 17a-3 thereunder. Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the charged provisions, ordering them to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. The final judgments also order the defendants to pay civil penalties in the amount of $10,000 each. The court granted the defendants' requests for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an officer-and-director bar. The case was supervised by Joseph G. Sansone, Chief of the New York Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Gregory A. Kasper.

The Supreme Court addressed the patentability of inventions under the U.S. Constitution and the Patent Act of 1952, focusing on the requirement of non-obviousness in addition to novelty and utility. The Court examined several cases to determine the effect of the 1952 Act on patent validity and the tests required for patentability.

In Graham v. John Deere Co., the Court found a patent for a plow clamp invalid because the combination of old mechanical elements did not produce a new result and was obvious to someone skilled in the art. The Court affirmed the Eighth Circuit's judgment that the patent was invalid under § 103 of the Patent Act.

In Calmar, Inc. v. Cook Chemical Co. and Colgate-Palmolive Co. v. Cook Chemical Co., the Court reversed the Eighth Circuit's decision that upheld a patent on a finger-operated sprayer with a 'hold-down' cap. The Court concluded that the patent did not meet the non-obviousness requirement because the differences between the patented device and prior art were obvious to a person skilled in the art.

The Court emphasized that the constitutional grant of patent power is both a grant and a limitation, meant to promote advances in the "useful arts" and not to remove existing knowledge from the public domain. The Court also clarified that the 1952 Act intended to codify judicial precedents and did not change the general level of patentable invention.

The Court outlined the factual inquiries necessary under § 103: determining the scope and content of prior art, ascertaining differences between prior art and the claims at issue, and resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. Secondary considerations like commercial success and long-felt but unsolved needs could be relevant to the obviousness or nonobviousness of the subject matter.

The Court's decision reaffirmed the importance of the non-obviousness standard and clarified that the Patent Office and courts must strictly adhere to the 1952 Act as interpreted. The ruling aimed to bring uniformity and definiteness to patent validity determinations and to ensure that patents are granted only for genuine innovations that advance human knowledge.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit held that the common law "knock and announce" principle forms a part of the reasonableness inquiry under the Fourth Amendment. The court ruled that the officers who entered the home of Sharlene Wilson did not violate her right to a fair trial by failing to announce their presence and authority prior to entering her home. In a separate opinion, the court held that a warrantless search of Wilson's home violated her Fourth Amendment right to be secure in her home against unreasonable searches and seizures. We reverse and remand, holding that the lower court erred in denying her motion to suppress the evidence seized during the search. We conclude that the "knock-and-announce" principle is a reasonable basis for the search, and that the warrantless entry of the home violated petitioner's Fourth Amendment rights.

Title 18.1 of the Code of Virginia forbids the advertising of the prices of prescription drugs sold by pharmacists in the Commonwealth. Petitioner, a licensed pharmacist, brought this action challenging the constitutionality of the statute. The District Court held the statute invalid on its face as violating petitioner's rights of free speech under the First Amendment, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The statute is invalid on its face as violative of the First Amendment since it totally suppresses the dissemination of truthful information about entirely lawful activity, regardless of the possible effects on the pharmacists and their patrons. Pp. 408-419. (a) Commercial speech, like other varieties, is protected by the First Amendment. Pp. 410-413. (b) The advertising ban does not directly affect professional standards of pharmacists, but instead affects them only through the reaction it is assumed people will have to the free flow of drug price information. Pp. 413-416. (c) While certain types of commercial speech regulation are permissible, the statute here involved goes beyond the bounds of permissible regulation. Pp. 416-418. (d) The statute does not prohibit the advertising of prescription drug prices because the advertisements are false or misleading, nor does it prohibit the transactions proposed in the advertisements from being conducted illegally. P. 418. 508 F. 2d 115, affirmed.

This case involves a man named Robert Marrama who filed a Chapter 7 bankruptcy petition in Maine in 2003. Later, he attempted to convert his case to Chapter 13, but the bankruptcy court denied his motion due to concerns about his past behavior. The Supreme Court reviewed the case and upheld the lower court's decision, finding that Marrama had engaged in "prepetition bad-faith conduct" that undermined his eligibility for Chapter 13 relief. Specifically, the Court found that Marrama had failed to accurately report the ownership of a valuable piece of land in Maine, and had attempted to hide this fact from the bankruptcy court.

An assistant professor of German at Brooklyn College, an institution maintained by the City of New York, claimed his privilege against self-incrimination before a Federal Committee and refused to answer questions concerning his membership in the Communist Party during 1940 and 1941. Shortly thereafter, he was notified that he was suspended from his position "pursuant to the provisions of Section 903" of the Charter of the City of New York, which provides that whenever an employee of the City uses the privilege against self-incrimination to avoid answering a question relating to his official conduct, "his term or tenure of office or employment shall terminate and such office or employment shall be vacant." His suspension was automatically changed to discharge, and he was informed that he was barred from holding any future municipal employment. Held: The summary dismissal of the professor violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 552-559. (a) A person does not lose his constitutional right to government employment simply because he exercises his privilege against self-incrimination. Wieman v. Updegraff, 344 U. S. 183. Pp. 555-556. (b) The statutory procedure permitting summary dismissal of a city employee who invokes the Fifth Amendment is invalid, since it deprives the employee of his job without giving him any opportunity to defend himself against charges of misconduct. Pp. 556-559. 202 Misc. 915, 118 N. Y. S. 2d 487, reversed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the city of Baltimore, Maryland, in a lawsuit filed by a group of residents seeking to remove a Confederate statue from a park. The statue, known as the "Angels Landing" monument, features four angels standing guard around a Confederate soldier. The residents argued that the statue violated the First Amendment's prohibition on government endorsement of religion, as it appeared to promote Christianity and white supremacy. However, the Supreme Court found that the statue did not violate the First Amendment, stating that it was a work of art rather than religious speech and that the city had not taken any steps to endorse or promote the message conveyed by the statue.

In the case involving William Baird, the Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals to vacate Baird's conviction for giving away contraceptive foam after a lecture at Boston University. Baird was initially convicted under Massachusetts law, which allowed only registered physicians and pharmacists to provide contraceptives to married individuals with a prescription, while prohibiting the distribution of contraceptives to unmarried individuals entirely.

The Supreme Court held that the Massachusetts statute violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because it discriminated between married and unmarried individuals without a rational basis. The Court rejected the state's arguments that the law served to deter premarital sex or protect health, finding these justifications either unrelated to the statute's actual effects or not credible given the statute's design and existing health regulations.

The Court also addressed the issue of standing, concluding that Baird had the right to challenge the statute's validity on behalf of unmarried individuals who were denied access to contraceptives. This decision was based on the principle that the enforcement of the statute would significantly impact the ability of single persons to obtain contraceptives, and that Baird, as an advocate for their rights, was in a position to assert those rights.

Ultimately, the Court determined that the rights of individuals to access contraceptives must be the same for both married and unmarried persons. The Court referenced the precedent set in Griswold v. Connecticut, which recognized a right to privacy in marital relations, and extended this reasoning to affirm that individuals, regardless of marital status, have the right to be free from unwarranted government intrusion in decisions about bearing or begetting children.

The implications of this decision were significant, as it struck down a state law that discriminated against unmarried individuals in terms of contraceptive access, thereby reinforcing the right to privacy and equal protection under the law.

Title: Stanford v. Texas

Year: 1965

Summary: In this landmark case, the Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment requires that warrants be obtained before conducting searches and seizures, including those targeting newspapers. The Court emphasized the importance of protecting freedom of speech and press, stating that the press plays a vital role in ensuring transparency and accountability in government. However, the Court also recognized that the government has legitimate concerns regarding national security and maintaining order, and therefore, warrants may be obtained if there is probable cause and the search is narrowly tailored to meet those needs.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the government in a lawsuit against two dairy companies, Borden and Bowman Milk Company, who were accused of engaging in illegal price discrimination under Section 2 of the Sherman Antitrust Act and Section 2(a) of the Clayton Antitrust Act. The court found that the cost justifications provided by the companies were insufficient to justify the price disparities between independent and chain stores. Specifically, the court found that the cost justifications were based on arbitrary classifications and that the classes used were not homogenous enough to accurately reflect the cost savings associated with each type of customer. The court also found that the cost justifications were based on incorrect assumptions about the behavior of customers and the distribution of costs among them.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses a case involving allegations of illegal price discrimination by two major distributors of fluid milk products in metropolitan Chicago. The appellees (the milk distributors) were accused of violating the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act by offering different pricing plans to independent stores and grocery store chains, with the latter receiving substantially greater discounts.

The central legal issue was whether the price differences were justified by corresponding differences in the costs of serving the two types of customers. The appellees presented cost studies to support their pricing strategies, but the trial court's acceptance of these justifications was challenged.

The Supreme Court found that the appellees had not adequately demonstrated that their customer classifications for pricing purposes were sufficiently homogeneous to justify the price disparities. The Court noted that the cost factors considered did not necessarily align with the ownership type of the customer and that the appellees failed to prove that the cost savings were isolated within the favored class (chain stores). The Court also criticized the appellees for attributing certain costs to all independent stores without showing that these costs were actually incurred by each store.

The Court acknowledged that while class pricing based on average costs is a practical necessity and has been approved by the Federal Trade Commission, it cannot be justified if the classifications are arbitrary or not representative of the individual members. The Court emphasized that the burden of proof for cost justification lies with the appellees and that they had not met this burden.

As a result, the Supreme Court reversed the trial court's decision and remanded the case for further proceedings. The Court suggested that the trial court should reevaluate the sufficiency of the appellees' cost justifications based on the current facts and in light of the principles outlined in the opinion. The Court also indicated that it was unclear whether equitable relief, such as an injunction, was still appropriate given the age of the case and the possibility that the pricing practices may have changed.

Respondent National Wildlife Federation (NWF), a nonprofit organization with the mission of protecting wildlife and the streams and forests that support it, brought suit in Federal District Court under 5 U. S. C. § 702, which provides that any person suffering legal injury as a result of an "agency action" may seek judicial review thereof. NWF alleged that petitioners, the Secretary of the Interior and the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), had violated the Federal Land Management Policy Act (FLMPA) and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) by revoking certain land withdrawals and by failing to revise land use plans and to provide adequate environmental impact statements with respect to the "land withdrawal review program." The District Court granted summary judgment for petitioners, holding that NWF had not shown that it was "adversely affected or aggrieved" by the agency actions. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that NWF had shown that it was "adversely affected or aggrieved" by the agency actions and that the four additional affidavits submitted by NWF in response to the District Court's briefing order established its right to § 702 review of the agency actions. 

Held: 
1. The four affidavits submitted by NWF in response to the District Court's briefing order were insufficient to establish NWF's right to § 702 review of the agency actions. Pp. 122-127.
	 (a) The "land withdrawal review program" is not an "agency action" within the meaning of § 702, much less a "final agency action" within the meaning of § 704. Pp. 122-124.
	 (b) The District Court did not abuse its discretion in declining to admit the affidavits. The affidavits were untimely under both Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56, which requires affidavits in opposition to a summary judgment motion to be served prior to the day of the hearing, and Rule 6(d), which states more generally that opposing affidavits may be served not later than 1 day before the hearing, unless the court permits them to be served at some other time. The District Court would have had to regard the very filing of the late document as the "motion made" to file it; it would have had to interpret "cause shown" to mean merely "cause"; and it would have had to find as a substantive matter that there was indeed "cause" for the late filing, and that the failure to file on time was the result of "excusable neglect." Pp. 124-127. 
2. NWF cannot seek § 702 review of petitioners' actions in its own right, rather than derivatively through its members. Even assuming that the affidavit set forth "specific facts" adequate to show injury to NWF through the deprivation of information and that providing information to organizations such as NWF was one of the objectives of the statutes allegedly violated, so that NWF is "aggrieved within the meaning" of those statutes, the affidavit fails to identify any particular "agency action" that was the source of the injuries. Pp. 127-128. 278 U. S. App. D. C. 313, 878 F. 2d 423, reversed.

Respondents, retirees of a defined benefit plan subject to the terms of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), filed a class action against their former employer, Hughes Aircraft Company (Hughes), and the Non-Bargaining Retirement Plan (Plan), alleging that Hughes violated ERISA by amending the Plan to provide for an early retirement program and a noncontributory benefit structure. The District Court granted respondents' motion to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the 1991 amendment may have terminated the Plan and created two plans: one consisting of pre-existing members and the other consisting of new participants. Held: Respondents' vested-benefits and anti-inurement claims proceed on the erroneous assumption that they had an interest in the Plan's surplus, which was used exclusively to benefit Hughes. The Court of Appeals concluded that respondents had alleged six causes of action in their complaint. Specifically, respondents claimed that Hughes had violated the employer's prohibition against using employees' vested, nonforfeitable benefits to meet its obligations by depleting the surplus to fund the noncontributionory structure. Respondents also alleged that, even if they have no interest, the creation of the new contributory structure permitted Hughes to use assets from the surplus attributable to employer and employee contributions for its sole and exclusive benefit, in violation of ERISA § 1104(c)(1), which requires that residual assets in a terminated plan be distributed to its beneficiaries. The court also held that the Act of Amending a Pension Plan does not trigger ERISA's fiduciary provisions. Pp. 5-11. 105 F. 3d 1288, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California held that an air carrier was liable for a passenger's death or bodily injury caused by an "accident" that occurred in connection with an international flight. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit agreed, holding that the District Court's finding that a flight attendant's refusal to reseat a passenger was an accident constituted a "blatant disregard of industry standards and airline policies" and was not expected or usual. We conclude that this finding is consistent with the ruling in Air France v. Saks, which held that the term "accident," in the Warsaw Convention, refers to an "unexpected or unusual event or happening that is external to the passenger" and not to the "passenger's own internal reaction to the usual, normal, and expected operation of the aircraft"

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Indiana Court of Appeals erred in denying unemployment benefits to a Jehovah's Witness who terminated his employment because of his religious beliefs. The Court held that the lower court's decision to deny benefits violated the First Amendment right to free exercise of religion. The court held that Thomas' termination was not based upon a "good cause" as required by the Indiana unemployment compensation statute. The lower court found that Thomas terminated his job because his religious convictions prevented him from participating in the production of war materials. The Supreme Court of Indiana agreed, and ruled that Thomas was entitled to benefits.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Washington granted certiorari to review the case of Arturo Recuenco, who was convicted of assault in the second degree based on the jury's finding that he assaulted his wife "with a deadly weapon" and sentenced him to 39 months in prison. The trial court applied a 3-year firearm enhancement to his sentence based on its own factual findings, in violation of the court's decision in Blakely v. Washington, 542 U. S. 296 (2004). The court concluded that the trial court could not have subjected respondent to a firearm enhancement based only on the jurors' finding that respondent was armed with a "deadly weapon" under Blakely. The court also concluded that Blakely violations can never be harmless. The Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit agreed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings.

The Minnesota parental notice statute, which remains in effect as subdivision 1 of the Minors' Consent to Health Services Act, authorizes an "unemancipated minor" to give effective consent to an abortion by requiring that either her physician or an agent notify "the parent" personally or by certified mail at least 48 hours before the procedure is performed. If the pregnant minor can convince "any judge of a court of competent jurisdiction" that she is "mature and capable of giving informed consent to the proposed abortion," or that an abortion without notice to both parents would be in her best interests, notice to one parent is sufficient. Subdivision 6 of the statute authorizes a judicial bypass of the two-parent notice requirement if subdivision 2 is ever "temporarily or permanently" enjoined by judicial order. If a court enjoins the enforcement of subdivision 2, the same notice requirement shall be effective unless the pregnant woman obtains a court order permitting the abortion to proceed. The Court of Appeals upheld the constitutionality of subdivision 6. Held: A requirement that a minor wait 48 hours after notifying a single parent of her intention to get an abortion would reasonably further the legitimate state interest in ensuring that the minor's decision is knowing and intelligent. Under any analysis, the Minnesota statute cannot be sustained if the obstacles it imposes are not reasonably related to legitimate state interests. Pp. 6-8. (a) The requirement that both parents be notified, whether or not both wish to be notified or have assumed responsibility for the upbringing of the child, does not reasonably further any legitimate stateinterest. The fact that the statute unquestionably places obstacles in the pregnant child's path to anabortion does not justify the requirement that one parent be notified. P. 6. (b) The State has a strong and legitimate interest in providing a pregnant minor with the advice and support of a parent during the decisional period. A general rule requiring the minor to obtain the consent of one parent reasonably furthers that interest. An exception from the general rule is necessary to protect the minor from an arbitrary veto that is motivated by the separate concerns of the parent rather than the best interest of the minor. The state has no more interest in requiring all family members to talk with one another than it has in requiring certain of them to live together. See, e. g., Maher v. Roe, 432 U. S. 464, and the only other Minnesota statute that the State has identified which requires two parent consent is that authorizing a minor to change his name. The statute does not impose any period of delay once a court, acting in loco parentis, or the parents express their agreement that the child is mature or that the procedure would be "in her best interest." P. 7. (c) The state courts who have interpreted the statute in over 3,000 decisions implementing its bypass procedures have found no legislative intent to disfavor the decision to terminate a pregnancy. On the contrary, in all but a handful of cases they have approved such decisions, the statute has the burden of establishing its constitutionality. The usual justification for a parental consent or notification provision is that it supports a parent who is presumed to act in the minor’s best interest and thereby assures that her decision to terminating her pregnancy is knowing, intelligent, and deliberate. However, a state policy favoring childbirth over abortion is not in itself a sufficient justification for overriding the woman's decision or for placing "obstacles-absolute or otherwise" in the pregnancy's path. Moreover, considering her probable education, employment skills, financial resources, and emotional maturity, unwanted motherhood may be overcome by a minor acting with consent of both parents. The State does not rely primarily on the minor in defending this statute, since it argues that, in the ideal family, the minor should make her decision only after consultation with both parents who should naturally be concerned with the child's welfare, but such communication may not be decreed by the State. The focus on notifying the second parent distracted both the parent and minor from the decision's imminent abortion decision, and thereby avoided "much of what was objectionable in the statute successfully challenged in Danforth," id., at 645. P p. 759. 853 F. 2d 1452, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant who was convicted of a charge of mail fraud based on the jury’s finding that he assaulted his wife “with a deadly weapon.”  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the defendant and ordered him to pay a civil penalty of 39 months.  According to the SEC’s complaint, filed in federal district court in New Jersey, on September 18, 1999, Arturo Recuenco was charged with mail fraud, in violation of the federal securities laws, and for filing a false income tax return.  The SEC alleges that the jury did not find the defendant guilty of each of the charged offenses, and accordingly imposed a total sentence of 39.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Washington today announced criminal charges against him.  As alleged in the complaint, the jury found the defendant not guilty of all of the charges, and instead returned a guilty verdict only on the offense of assault in the second degree, as opposed to any other kind of "deadly weapon."  In addition, the court issued an order requiring the jury to determine whether a defendant was armed with a "firearm" when the jury had concluded, if given the opportunity, that the defendant had engaged in an assault with a “active weapon,” which is the equivalent of a directed verdict of guilt on an offense, and a "defective reasonable-doubt instruction" when presented to the jury.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint filed in the United States District Court, the Court of Appeals for the Western Districts of New Jersey yesterday entered a judgment that permanently enjoins the defendant from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendant to pay civil penalties of at least $10,000 each.  On August 2, 2018, the Honorable Judge William G. Hannan of the U District Court in New York granted the SEC and the District Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California the right to a preliminary injunction against future violations, including the issuance of a civil injunctive relief, a conduct-based injunction, and the imposition of a mandatory 3-year firearm enhancement.  Hannan also agreed to the appointment of an independent trial judge to determine the amount of a penalty that should be imposed upon the defendant.

Case Name: United States vs. William J. Steigerwald
Case Number: 377 U.S. __ (1964)
Decided Date: June 22, 1964
Issued By: United States Supreme Court
Subject Areas: Constitutional Law, Criminal Procedure
Keywords: Contempt Power, Immunity, Free Press, Right to Privacy, Self Incrimination

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Iowa reversed a lower court's ruling that found a tax difference between state and federal tax rates on slot machine adjusted revenues violated the Equal Protection Clause. The Iowa Supreme Court held that this difference in tax rates violated the Constitution's equal protection clause. The lower court held that there was no rational reason for the tax difference. The court found that the tax rate on riverboat slot machines was 20 percent, and that it would automatically rise over time to 36 percent. The higher tax rate did not alter the amount of tax revenue that was subject to the tax, and the lower court upheld the higher rate. The Supreme Court's decision was based on the language of both State and Federal equal protection laws. The Court found that this language does not distinguish between instate and out-of-state businesses. The majority concluded that the difference in state tax rates does not violate the equal protection Clause because the tax is not a tax on the basis of race, gender, or other factors.

In 2006, Congress enacted the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA) as part of the Adam Walsh Child Protection and Safety Act. Among its provisions, §2250 (a) provides that “Whoever is required to register under [SORna],” “travels in interstate or foreign commerce,” and “knowingly fails to register or update a registration.” 18 U. S. C. §922(g), which prohibits convicted felons from “possess[ing] in or affecting commerc[e] any firearm or ammunition” , “shall be subject to the Act but not someone who crossed state lines before the Act was passed,’ ” 551 F. 3d 582, 582. The Court of Appeals held that § 2250 “does not require that the defendant’s travel postdate the Act” United States v. Dixon, 551F.3d 578. Held: Section2250 does not apply to sex offenders whose interstate travel occurred prior to SORNA‘s effective date and, if so, whether the statute runs afoul of the Constitution’S prohibition on ex post facto laws. Pp. 6–8. (a)(2)(A) The statutory context strongly supports a forward-looking construction of “Travels.’” First, the word is followed by a series of other present-tense verbs-“enters or leaves, or resides in, Indian country” (Emphasis added). Second, the words are used in the present tense rather than in the past or present perfect (“traveled” or “has traveled”). Third, a statute that regulates a sex offender is not readily understood to encompass a person whose only travel occurred before the statute took effect. See, e.g., United Statesv. Wilson, 503 U.S. 329, 333. Fourth, the statute is triggered by a sex-offense conviction, which must be followed by interstate travel, and then a failure to register. Only the last of these events, the Government maintains, must occur after the statute has taken effect; the predicate conviction and the travel may both have predated the statute. Fifth, the statutory sequence begins when a person becomes subject to SorNA’d registration requirements. The person must then travel in interstate commerce and thereafter fail to register, and all of these actions, Carr avers, necessarily postdate SORN’t’. P. 6. 551

Petitioner county sheriff obtained a warrant from a magistrate to search the offices of respondent daily newspaper for evidence of crimes committed by certain students at Stanford University. Respondents filed suit in Federal District Court challenging the validity of the warrant and the subsequent search, claiming that the warrant violated the Fourth Amendment and that the search violated the First Amendment. The District Court agreed and enjoined the search. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The Fourth Amendment does not categorically prohibit the issuance of a warrant to search the premises of a newspaper for evidence of crime reasonably believed to be on the premises, and the search here involved comported with the Fourth Amendment. Pp. 108-118. (a) Whether the third-party occupant of the place to be searched is suspect or not, the State's interest in enforcing the criminal law and recovering the evidence remains the same; and it is the seeming innocence of the property owner that the District Court relied on to foreclose the warrant to search. If the third party knows that contraband or other illegal materials are on his property, he is sufficiently culpable to justify the issuance of a search warrant. Similarly, if his ethical stance is the determinant, whether or not he knows that the sought-after articles are secreted on his property and whether or not he knows that the articles are in fact the fruits, instruments, or evidence of crime, he will be so informed when the search warrant is served, and it is doubtful that he should then be permitted to object to the search, to withhold, if it is there, the evidence of crime reasonably believed to be possessed by him or secreted on his property, and to forbid the search and insist that the officers serve him with a subpoena duces teucum. Pp. 108-111. (b) Denial of the warrant and insistence on the subpoena instead when the custodian of the object of the search is not then suspected of crime, involves hazards to criminal investigation much more serious than the District Court believed. Forbidding the warrant and insisting on the subpoena instead when the custodian of the object of the search is not then suspected of crime, involves hazards to criminal investigation much more serious than the District Court believed. Pp. 111-112. (c) No more than the prior cases require that the owner of the place to be searched, if connected with the press, must be shown to be implicated in the offense being investigated. Pp. 112-115. (d) The warrant issued in this case authorized nothing of the type, scope, and intrusiveness that would actually interfere with the timely publication of a newspaper. Nor are there any indications that confidential sources will disappear and that the press will suppress news because of fears of warranted searches. Pp. 115-116. (e) Presumptively protected materials are not necessarily immune from seizure under warrant for use at a criminal trial. Not every such seizure, and not even most, will impose a prior restraint. P. 116. (f) If the evidence sought by warrant is sufficiently connected with the crime to satisfy the probable-cause requirement, it will very likely be sufficiently relevant to justify a subpoena and to withstand a motion to quash. P. 117. (g) The Fourth Amendment does not prevent or advise against legislative or executive efforts to establish nonconstitutional protections against possible abuses of the search warrant procedure, but the Amendment will not be reinterpreted to impose a general constitutional barrier against warrants to search newspaper premises, to require resort to subpoenas as a general rule, or to demand prior notice and hearing in connection with the issuance of search warrants. P. 118. 548 F. 2d 1195, reversed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the state in this case, finding that the petitioner had not been denied a fair trial despite the fact that several jurors had learned about the petitioner's previous criminal history and the details of the crime with which he was charged from news reports. The Court determined that the petitioner's trial was not fundamentally unfair and that the jurors' assurances of impartiality were sufficient to rebut any presumption of bias.
