Respondents were convicted of conspiring to violate 18 U. S. C. §§ 241 and 1584, which make it a crime to conspire to obstruct justice by engaging in behavior designed to influence the official conduct of government agencies, and to violate § 1584, which makes it a crime to knowingly and willfully hold another person in involuntary servitude. During respondents' trial, the District Court gave a jury instruction that included the elements of involuntary servitude under § 1584, namely, "(1) that the defendant knew or ought reasonably to have known that the victim was in involuntary servitude; (2) that the defendant knew or ought reasonably to have known that the victim was in involuntary servitude because of the victim's status as a boy or girl under the age of 18; and (3) that the defendant knew or ought reasonably to have known that the victim was in involuntary servitude because of the victim's race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, marital status, familial relationship, property ownership, occupation, or membership in a labor union." However, the instruction also permitted the jury to infer involuntary servitude if it found that the victim was induced by threats of economic loss or social ostracism to engage in sexual activity with the defendant. The Court of Appeals vacated the convictions, ruling that the instructions allowed the jury to convict respondents for conduct that did not involve the use or threatened use of physical or legal coercion, and that, accordingly, the convictions were void. Held: Absent change by Congress, for purposes of criminal prosecutions under §§ 241 and 1584, the term "involuntary servitude" necessarily means a condition of servitude in which the victim is forced to work for the defendant by the use or threat of physical restraint or physical injury, or by the use or threat of coercion through law or the legal process. Evidence of other means of coercion, or of poor working conditions, or of the victim's special vulnerabilities is relevant in determining whether the physical or legal coercion or threats thereof could plausibly have compelled the victim to serve. However, the jury must be instructed that compulsion of services by the use or threatened use of physical or legal coercion is a necessary incident of a condition of involuntary servitude. Because the District Court's instruction encompassed other means of coercion, the Court of Appeals correctly ruled that the convictions must be reversed and the case remanded for a new trial. However, since the record contains sufficient evidence of physical or legal coercion to enable a jury to convict respondents even under the stricter standard announced here, the Court of Appeals erred in determining that a judgment of acquittal was warranted. Pp. 958-966. 849 F. 2d 146, affirmed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled that the Federal Communications Commission properly interpreted the law when it found that the three major television networks violated the law by refusing to sell time to the Carter-Mondale Presidential Committee for a 30-minute program about President Carter's administration. The Commission's finding that the networks violated  312(a)(5) of the Communications Act of 1934 was based on the networks' failure to provide "reasonable access to ... the use of a broadcasting station" as required by the law. The Court held that the Commission properly concluded that the law created a new, affirmative right of access to the broadcast media for individual candidates for federal elective office, and the Commission had the authority to independently evaluate whether a campaign has begun for purposes of evaluating whether a candidate is qualified for office. The court held that, in this case, the Commission correctly concluded that there was no evidence that a candidate had begun a campaign, and that the statute did not require the networks to provide reasonable access to their stations for the purpose of selling time for political programs. The Supreme Court agreed to review the case because the Court found that "the Commission properly applied the law in this instance, and we conclude that it did not violate the law"

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Nevada held that the trial court did not have to hold a hearing to determine whether a defendant was competent to plead guilty or to waive his right to counsel. The court held that it did not need to hold the hearing because it had determined that respondent was not pleading guilty in response to threats or promises, that he understood the nature of the charges against him, and that he was aware of the rights he was giving up. The Court held that "the record clearly shows that [respondent's] competency to represent himself was determined by two psychiatrists both of whom declared [him] competent" and that the Due Process Clause requires the court to "enter a voluntary, knowing, and intelligent waiver of constitutional rights" before accepting a guilty plea. The Supreme Court of Nevada dismissed respondent's appeal, Moran v. Warden, 105 Nev. 1041, 810 P.2d 335 (1989), and we denied certiorari, 493 S.C.t. 207, 110 L.Ed. 2d 160 (1989). The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the "record in this case should have led [the trial court] to enter a good faith doubt about [respondents] competency" to make a voluntary waiver of his constitutional rights." The Court concluded that the court's error was "cured" by the postconviction hearing. The District Court denied the petition for post-conviction relief, but the Ninth Circuit held that a hearing should have been held to determine the defendant's competency. The Second District Court of Appeal granted a motion for a new trial. The trial court held a hearing on the issue of competency, and the court held again that it was not necessary. The Third District Court granted a new hearing. In a second hearing, the court found that respondent had been competent to stand trial and that his guilty pleas were "freely and voluntarily given"

Under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976 (Act), a “foreign state” may remove an action against it from a state court to a federal court. 28 U. S. C. § 1441(d). The Act’s defining clause—“ ‘foreign state’ includes … any agency or instrumentality of a foreign state,” § 1603(a)—also applies to corporations, § 1603(b). Thus, a corporation incorporated in Israel could remove from a state court an action against it based on allegedly tortious activity occurring outside Israel. However, the Act contains a proviso stating that a corporation shall not qualify as an instrumentality unless “more than half of the voting equity of the corporation is owned by a foreign state.” § 1603(b)(2). Because Israel has never owned more than 50 percent of the voting equity of the corporations at issue, the corporations were denied relief. Held: 1. Only direct ownership of a majority of shares by a foreign state satisfies the statutory requirement. Pp. 473–475. (a) The Act uses the word “shares” to speak of ownership in a corporation. Given the Act’s purpose of providing a foreign-state defendant in a legal action the right to have its claim of a sovereign immunity bar decided by the federal courts, § 1441(d), and of ensuring that the merits of unbarred claims against foreign states will be decided in the same manner as similar claims against private individuals, § 1606, it is likely that the Act’s authors chose “shares” to reflect the traditional concept of ownership in a corporation. Although the Act’s use of “shares” suggests that Congress meant to incorporate formal, technical American legal requirements, the Act had to be written for the contingency of ownership forms in other countries, or even in this country, that depart from conventional corporate structures. Therefore, the Act’s use of “shares” cannot mean to exclude from the scope of “other” any kind of mixed, say, debt/equity, ownership arrangement that might involve shares only in part. Nor does the Act’s use of “ownership” mean “only direct ownership,” ante, at 474. Such a reading would be contrary to the Act’s purpose of protecting foreign nations not only when they act directly in their own names but also when they act through separate legal entities, including corporations and other “organs,” § 1603(b). Pp. 473–475. (b) The Act’s proviso is not rendered ambiguous by the fact that the corporations at issue were subsidiaries of corporations that were themselves instruments of Israel. The proviso’s language clearly indicates that only direct ownership of a majority of shares by a foreign state satisfies the statutory requirement. Pp. 475–476. 2. The proviso is satisfied only if the foreign state owns a majority of the corporation’s shares directly. Here, Israel never owned more than 50 percent of the voting equity of the corporations at issue. Pp. 476–477. 277 F. Supp. 2d 1275, vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined. Breyer, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which O’Connor, J., joined.

Respondent, one of about 900 members of the Fallon Paiute-Shoshone Tribes of western Nevada, came under suspicion of having killed, off the reservation, a California bighorn sheep, a gross misdemeanor under Nevada law. A state game warden obtained from state court a search warrant "SUBJECT TO OBTAINING APPROVAL FROM THE FALLON TRIBAL COURT IN AND FOR THE FALON PAIUTE-SHOSHONE TRIBES." According to the issuing judge, this tribal-court authorization was necessary because "[t]his Court has no jurisdiction on the Fallon ... Indian Reservation." App. G to Pet. for Cert. 1. A search warrant was obtained from the tribal court, and the warden, accompanied by a tribal police officer, searched respondent's yard, uncovering only the head of a Rocky Mountain Bighorn, a different (and unprotected) species of sheep. Respondent, claiming that his sheep-heads had been damaged, and that the second search exceeded the bounds of the warrant, brought suit against the Tribal Judge, the tribal officers, the state wardens in their individual and official capacities, the State of Nevada in the Tribal Court in and for the Fallon Tribes. The District Court granted summary judgment to respondent on the issue of jurisdiction, and also held that the state officials would have to exhaust any claims of qualified immunity in the tribe court. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, concluding that the fact that respondent's home is located on tribe-owned land within the reservation is sufficient to support tribal jurisdiction over civil claims against nonmembers arising from their activities on that land. Held: 1. Tribal authority to regulate state officers in executing process related to the violation, off reservation, of state laws is not essential to tribal self-government or internal relations to "the right to make laws and be ruled by them." Montana v. United States, 450 U. S. 544, supra, at 445. The existence of tribal ownership is only one factor to consider in determining whether regulation of the activities of nonmembers is "necessary to protect tribal selfgovernment or to control internal relations" in either state or federal court, but not in tribal court. Pp. 5-11. (a) The existence and scope of tribal jurisdiction are not alone enough to support regulatory jurisdiction over nonmembers. P. 5. (b) The absence of tribal control has been virtually conclusive of the absence of Tribal civil jurisdiction; with one minor exception, this Court has never upheld under Montana the extension of tribal civil authority over nonmember on non-Indian land. And with regard to the jurisdiction at issue here that has not occurred, the Government's assertion that "[a]s a general matter, although state officials have jurisdiction to investigate and prosecute crimes on a reservation that exclusively involve non-Indians, . . . they do not have jurisdiction with respect to crimes involving Indian perpetrators or Indian victims," Brief for United States as Amicus Curiae 12-13, n. 7, is misleading. The term "other arrangements" in a passage from Montana referred to other "private consensual" arrangements so that it did not include the State officials' obtaining of tribal warrants in the present case. But the ownership status of land, in other words, is only a factor to be considered in determining if regulation of such activities may be "necessary" to protect the tribe's self-governance or tocontrol internal relations. Montana,450 U.S., at 564-565. When, however, state interests outside the reservation are implicated, States may regulate the activities even of tribe members on tribal land, as exemplified by our decision in Confederated Tribes, 526 U. s. 473, where the claims were not initially federal claims, but Navajo tort claims that the Price-Anderson Act provided "shall be deemed to be .. . action[s] arising under"42 U S. C. § 2210; there was little doubt that the tribe had jurisdiction over such tort claims, see Mescalero Apache Tribe v. Jones, 411 US. 145, 148-149. The Government's contention that tribal authority over state officers pursuing off-reservation violations of state law may be necessary to protect Tribal self-guaranteed immunity or control internal-relations is completely missing from tribal court jurisdiction. This is not to say that States may exert the same degree of regulatory authority within a reservation as they do without. To be sure, Indian tribes retain inherent sovereign power to exercise some forms of civil jurisdiction over their members on their reservations, even on nonIndian fee lands. And the existence of Tribal ownership is not alone sufficient to justify regulatory jurisdiction. P p. 5–7. (c) The fact that respondents' home and yard are on tribal-owned tribal land does not exclude all state regulatory authority on the reservation. The State's interest in execution of process is considerable, and even when it relates to Indian-fee lands, the tribe and tribe members are of course able to invoke the authority of the Federal

In this Supreme Court case, the central issue was whether a prisoner, who claims that their conditions of confinement are cruel and unusual punishment, must prove that prison officials had a culpable state of mind, and if so, what level of state of mind is required.

Pearly L. Wilson, the petitioner, is an inmate who sued prison officials under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging that various conditions of his confinement at the Hocking Correctional Facility violated the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments. His complaints included overcrowding, excessive noise, and inadequate facilities, among others. Both parties sought summary judgment, but the District Court ruled in favor of the prison officials, a decision which the Court of Appeals affirmed.

The Supreme Court's opinion, written by Justice Scalia, clarified that the Eighth Amendment's prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment does apply to conditions of imprisonment, not just the sentence itself. However, to establish a violation, a prisoner must show that prison officials were "deliberately indifferent" to their basic needs. This standard was first established in Estelle v. Gamble, which required a showing of deliberate indifference to serious medical needs.

The Court rejected the distinction between short-term and long-term or systemic conditions, stating that the intent requirement is derived from the Eighth Amendment itself. The Court also noted that the duration of a condition might make it easier to prove knowledge and intent, but it does not eliminate the requirement of intent.

The Court held that the same standard of "deliberate indifference" applies to claims about inadequate medical care and other conditions of confinement. The Court disagreed with the respondents' argument that a malice standard should apply to cases not involving physical injury, stating that the wantonness of conduct depends on the constraints facing the official, not the effect on the prisoner.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Sixth Circuit and remanded the case for reconsideration under the "deliberate indifference" standard, as the Court of Appeals may have applied an incorrect standard of "malicious and sadistic" intent, which is more appropriate for cases involving the use of force rather than conditions of confinement.

The decision implies that prison officials can be held liable for cruel and unusual punishment if they are deliberately indifferent to the basic needs of prisoners, and it sets a consistent standard for evaluating such claims.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reversed a lower court's denial of an injunction against eBay Inc. and Half.com, Inc. for violating a patent owned by a company that had previously tried to license its patent to other companies. The lower court had granted a motion for a permanent injunction on the basis of a jury verdict that the defendants had infringed a patent held by MercExchange, L.L.C., that was designed to facilitate the sale of goods between private individuals by establishing a central authority to promote trust among participants. The appeals court held that the lower court erred in denying the injunction because it did not consider the balance of hardships between MercExchange and eBay. The Supreme Court agreed, holding that the district court had erred in its decision. The court vacated the injunction and remanded the case for further proceedings.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of a man named Nathaniel McLeod, who sued the city of New York over injuries sustained when police officers shot him during a traffic stop. The Court held that the Fourth Amendment's protection against excessive force applies to individuals who are being arrested, regardless of whether they pose a threat to public safety. The Court also clarified that the use of deadly force by police officers must be justified based on a reasonable belief that the individual poses an immediate danger to themselves or others.

In the Supreme Court case Beal v. Doe, the Court ruled that Title XIX of the Social Security Act does not mandate states participating in the Medicaid program to fund nontherapeutic abortions. The case arose when two indigent women, unable to obtain a physician's certificate of medical necessity, challenged a Connecticut Welfare Department regulation that limited Medicaid benefits for first-trimester abortions to those deemed "medically necessary."

The District Court initially ruled that the Social Security Act required state funding of nontherapeutic abortions, but this was overturned on appeal. The Court of Appeals determined that the Act allowed, but did not require, such funding. Upon further review of the constitutional issues, a three-judge District Court invalidated the Connecticut regulation, arguing that it violated the Equal Protection Clause by excluding nontherapeutic abortions from a state welfare program that subsidized medical expenses related to pregnancy and childbirth.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the District Court's interpretation, stating that the Constitution does not obligate states to fund the medical expenses of indigent women, including pregnancy-related costs. The Court held that while states are subject to constitutional limitations when providing medical care, the Connecticut regulation did not discriminate against a suspect class nor impinge upon a fundamental right protected by the Constitution.

The Court clarified that the fundamental right recognized in Roe v. Wade protects a woman from undue interference with her decision to terminate her pregnancy, but it does not imply a limitation on a state's authority to favor childbirth over abortion through the allocation of public funds. The Connecticut regulation did not place any new obstacles in the way of a woman seeking an abortion; it simply did not subsidize the cost, leaving the woman to rely on private sources as before.

The Court concluded that the Connecticut regulation was rationally related to the state's legitimate interest in encouraging childbirth and did not constitute invidious discrimination. The Court also upheld the state's procedural requirements for obtaining a Medicaid-funded abortion, such as prior written request and authorization, as they were not unreasonable and did not impose an impermissible burden.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision in Beal v. Doe affirmed that the Constitution does not require states to fund nontherapeutic abortions and that states have broad discretion in how they allocate public funds, particularly when it comes to sensitive policy choices like abortion funding. The decision emphasized that such policy decisions are best resolved through the legislative process rather than judicial intervention.

Petitioners, 12 Negro students, were convicted in a Maryland state court of participating in a "sit-in" demonstration at Hooper's restaurant. The convictions were based on a record showing in summary that a group of 15 to 20 Negroes, including petitioners, went to the restaurant to engage in what their counsel describes as a protest because the restaurant would not serve Negroes. The "hostess," on orders of the president of the corporation owning the restaurant, told them, "solely on the basis of their color," that they would not be served. Petitioners did not leave when requested to by the hostess and the manager; instead they went to tables, took seats, and refused to leave, insisting that they be served; and they were arrested. The Maryland Court of Appeals affirmed the convictions. Held: 1. The judgment is vacated and the case is remanded so that the state court may consider the effect of the supervening change in state law. Pp. 531-532. (a) The constitutional right of all Americans, regardless of race or color, to be treated equally by all branches of government, is protected by the Fourteenth Amendment. P. 533. (b) The fact that a state saving clause or similar provision was involved in this case does not render the judgment "in accordance with the law at the time of final judgment." P. 540. (c) In the absence of such terms from the public accommodations laws, it is not possible to determine what is or what is not "state" action within the meaning of the Amendment, since the legislative abolition of the crime for which petitioners were convicted occurred after rather than before the decision of the Maryland court of appeals, and that the judgment is not yet final, for it is on direct review in this Court, and hence it is "appropriate to leave the determination of the question to the State court." Pp 540-531. (d) The question of whether the Maryland saving clause would be applicable to save these convictions is a question of interpretation and of legislative intent, and the question is whether the legislature acts before the affirmance of the conviction becomes final, since it is an aid merely; not an inexorable command, and thus it is appropriate to remand the case to that court, so that it may reconsider it in the light of the Supervening Change in State Law. P p 531. 2. The state law is not relevant to the question of the effect on the convictions of petitioners. The Act of March 29, 1963, as amended by the Maryland Supreme Court, which held that segregated restaurants, whose racial policies were enforced by a State, violated the Equal Protection Clause, would now reverse petitioners' convictions and order their indictments dismissed, and remanded the case for reconsideration in light of a state law that was repealed and re-enacted by the state legislature. The fact alone raises a substantial possibility that the saving clause might be narrowly construed to constitute an "express provision" by the legislature that it did intend its new enactment to apply to past as well as future conduct-that it did not intend its saving clause to be applied, in derogation of the common-law rule, so as to permit the continued prosecution and punishment of persons accused of a "crime" which the legislature has now declared to be a right under the Amendment. The question is not whether the state law was repealed, pending the appeal or writ of error from the court's decision, but whether the provision in the Act is inapplicable, because the decision must be in accordance with that Act's meaning and purpose, and because the question must be decided by the State Court at this critical hour. The case is ripe for decision, and petitioners are entitled to an answer to their complaint here and now.

In the case of Jill Brown versus Bryan County, the Supreme Court reversed a decision by the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit that held Bryan County liable for the actions of a county police officer, Stacy Burns, who used excessive force during an arrest. Brown claimed that the county was responsible for her injuries due to the sheriff's negligent hiring and training of Burns.

The Supreme Court emphasized that under 42 U.S.C. §1983, a municipality can only be held liable for a deprivation of rights if the municipality's deliberate action is the "moving force" behind the violation. The Court clarified that a single hiring decision by a municipal policymaker, such as a sheriff, does not automatically establish municipal liability unless the decision was made with "deliberate indifference" to the risk of constitutional violations and directly caused the injury.

The Court found that the evidence presented did not support a finding that the sheriff's hiring decision was made with deliberate indifference to the risk that Burns would use excessive force. The sheriff's failure to thoroughly review Burns' background, which included various misdemeanors, was not enough to demonstrate that the hiring decision was the direct cause of Brown's injuries.

The Court concluded that holding the county liable based on the sheriff's single hiring decision without stringent proof of fault and causation would effectively turn municipal liability into a form of respondeat superior, which is not the intent of §1983. The decision underscores the need for a clear connection between a municipality's action and the specific constitutional violation alleged.

The judgment of the Court of Appeals was vacated, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

In the case of Deck v. Missouri, the Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the Constitution forbids the routine use of visible shackles on a defendant during the penalty phase of a capital case, just as it does during the guilt phase, unless there is a specific and essential state interest, such as courtroom security, that justifies their use.

The case involved Carman Deck, who was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. During his sentencing, Deck was visibly shackled, and his counsel objected to this, arguing that it could prejudice the jury. The trial court overruled the objections, and the Missouri Supreme Court affirmed the sentence, stating there was no evidence that the jury was aware of the restraints and that there was a risk Deck might flee.

The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to review Deck's claim that his shackling violated the Federal Constitution. The Court's opinion, delivered by Justice Breyer, drew on historical legal principles, including the presumption of innocence, the right to counsel, and the dignity of judicial proceedings, to conclude that visible shackling during the penalty phase of a capital case is inherently prejudicial and violates due process unless justified by specific security needs related to the defendant on trial.

The Court reversed the judgment of the Missouri Supreme Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The decision emphasized the need for individualized determinations by trial courts regarding the use of restraints and the importance of maintaining the fairness and dignity of the judicial process.

Justice Thomas, joined by Justice Scalia, dissented, arguing that the decision defies common sense and overlooks the serious security issues facing courts. The dissent criticized the majority for extending a historical rule against shackling, which was based on the physical pain caused by old restraints, to modern restraints that do not cause such pain. The dissent also argued that there is no deeply rooted legal principle against shackling at sentencing and that the majority's decision imposes unnecessary restrictions on the ability of courts to ensure security.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Louisiana State Police against a defendant who was convicted of making false statements in an application for a state license for video poker.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New Orleans, alleges that Carl W. Cleveland, a New Orleans lawyer, assisted in preparing a video poker license application for Truck Stop Gaming, Ltd. (TSG). The complaint alleges that Cleveland violated the antifraud provisions of Section 1341 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The complaint further alleges that, contrary to the stated intent of the federal government, the video poker licensing scheme violated the "property" provision of Section1341.  According to the complaint, Cleveland and his law firm had loaned Alex and Maria all initial capital for the partnership and thereby committed the first offense even if the license was not "property."  The complaint also alleges that Ohio violated the registration provisions of Sections 13(a)(1) and 13(b)(3) of the Exchange Act and Rules 12b-20, 13a-1, and 13b2-3 thereunder, and that Ohio was liable as a defendant for violating the registration provision.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating the federal securities laws, and order them to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest in the amount of $10,000, and a civil penalty of $1,000.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Louisiana today announced criminal charges against Cleveland.  On May 24, 2018, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against Cleveland, charging him with violating Section 13(e) of The Exchange Act. The SEC is seeking a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and an officer-and-director bar against Cleveland from participating in any future penny stock offering.  To learn more about penny stock offerings, see Investor.gov.

After protracted administrative hearings and judicial proceedings, the Alabama Attorney General sued in a state court to expunge the name of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored Peoples (NAACP) from the state registry of foreign corporations, claiming that the NAACP had engaged in "illegal" activities in Alabama and had falsely accused state officials of engaging in such activities. He prayed for a permanent injunction against the NAACP and its agents operating in Alabama. The trial judge denied the prayer for a permanent injunction but ordered the NAACP to cease and desist from all activities in Alabama pending the outcome of the suit. The intermediate appellate court sustained the lower court's order. The Alabama Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the trial court's order was proper since the NAACP had committed numerous acts of misconduct in Alabama and had falsely accused state officials of engaging in such activities. All of the acts complained of by the Attorney General were either purely symbolic or political in nature and were not in themselves unconstitutional. They included attempts to pressure universities and athletic associations to abandon policies of racial segregation, encouraging Negroes to enroll in the University of Alabama, furnishing legal advice to Negroes seeking admission to the University, and organizing protests against racial discrimination in transportation facilities. Held: 1. The Alabama Supreme Court erred in sustaining the trial court's order, since the Act of May 19, 1940, c. 194, Title 10, §§ 192-194, of the Alabama Code of 1940, which sets forth the requirements for a foreign corporation to do business in Alabama, contains no provision for the permanent ouster of a foreign corporation which fails to comply with the statutory requirements. Pp. 408-410. 2. The allegations that the NAACP had encouraged and incited persons to commit crimes and had violated the peace in Alabama furnished no basis for the restrictions imposed on the NAACP. Pp. 410-412. 3. The allegations that the NAACP had made "false charges" against state officials furnished no basis for the restrictions imposed on the NAACP. Pp. 412-413. 4. The allegation that the NAACP had violated the temporary restraining order issued by the trial court in 1956 furnished no basis for the restrictions imposed on the NAACP. P. 413. 5. Since the case now comes to this Court for the first time, the Court prefers to remand the case to the Alabama Supreme Court for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. If the Alabama Supreme Court does not promptly enter a decree vacating the injunction and allowing the NAACP to operate in Alabama, the NAACP may apply to this Court for further appropriate relief. P. 414. Reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court was asked to determine if the Military Selective Service Act (MSSA), which requires only males to register for the draft, violates the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause. The Court recognized Congress's broad constitutional powers to raise and support armies and to regulate military affairs. It also acknowledged the deference traditionally given to Congress, especially in military matters.

The Court noted that the purpose of the MSSA is to facilitate conscription by creating a pool of individuals eligible for military service. The reactivation of the registration process was deemed necessary by President Carter in response to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, and Congress allocated funds for male registration but declined to include women.

The Court emphasized that judicial deference to legislative and executive judgments is particularly important in military affairs. It pointed out that Congress had explicitly considered and rejected the registration of women after extensive debate and hearings. The decision was based on the fact that women are not eligible for combat roles, and a draft would primarily require combat troops. Therefore, Congress concluded that women would not be needed in the event of a draft.

The Court rejected the argument that the MSSA should be invalidated because it discriminates based on gender. It stated that men and women are not similarly situated regarding the draft because of the combat restrictions on women. The Court found that Congress's decision to exclude women from registration was closely related to its goal of drafting combat troops and did not violate the Due Process Clause.

The Court reversed the District Court's decision, which had found the MSSA unconstitutional, and upheld the Act's male-only registration requirement.

Implications of the Decision:
The Supreme Court's decision means that the MSSA's male-only registration requirement remains constitutional and in effect. The ruling reinforces the principle that Congress has broad discretion in matters of military and national defense, and that the courts will generally defer to congressional judgment in these areas. The decision also clarifies that gender-based distinctions in military policy can be constitutional if they are closely related to legitimate military goals and reflect the different roles and opportunities available to men and women in the armed forces.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the government in this case involving a tax-exempt college's profits earned from commercial advertising in its medical journal. The court held that the advertising was not substantially related to the college's exempt purpose of advancing medical knowledge and improving patient care. The court looked to the manner in which the college conducted its advertising business, focusing on the hit-or-miss nature of the advertising and the fact that the college did not use the advertising to provide a comprehensive or systematic presentation of any aspect of the goods or services publicized.

The Supreme Court affirmed the conviction of the petitioner for concealing and transporting narcotics, upholding the use of evidence obtained from a search and seizure following his arrest. The petitioner had moved to suppress the evidence, arguing it was the result of an unlawful search and seizure, violating the Fourth Amendment. However, the Court found that the arresting officer had probable cause to arrest the petitioner without a warrant, making the subsequent search and seizure lawful as they were incident to a lawful arrest.

The Court rejected the petitioner's argument that the information provided to the arresting officer by an informant was hearsay and thus could not establish probable cause. The Court cited precedent that the requirements for proving guilt at trial differ from those needed to establish probable cause for an arrest or search. The Court emphasized that probable cause deals with practical, everyday considerations rather than technicalities, and that the information provided by the reliable informant, corroborated by the officer's observations, was sufficient to warrant a reasonable belief that the petitioner was committing a narcotics offense.

The Court concluded that the arresting officer had reasonable grounds to believe the petitioner had committed or was committing a violation of the narcotic laws, justifying the arrest without a warrant. Consequently, the motion to suppress was properly overruled, and the heroin seized was admissible evidence at the trial. The petitioner's conviction was therefore affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of a clerical worker who was barred by the federal government from participating in the creation, operation, or promotion of a medical practice.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Portland, Oregon, Clackamas Gastroenterology Associates, P. C., a medical clinic in Oregon, employed four physician-shareholders, Deborah Anne Wells, as bookkeepers from 1986 until 1997. The complaint alleges that the physicians were "more analogous to partners in a partnership than to shareholders in a general corporation" and therefore were not employees for purposes of the federal antidiscrimination laws.  The complaint further alleges that Wells was not a "mere" employee because she was not subject to the employer's control.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Wells consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins her from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders her to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and injunctive relief. The settlement is subject to court approval.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the District of Oregon today announced criminal charges against Wells. The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by Michael Darden and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter. The litigation will be led by Mr. Darden.

This text appears to contain a Supreme Court ruling in the United States. The case involves a bankruptcy proceeding for a commodities brokerage company called CDCB. The ruling discusses the concept of the attorney-client privilege, which protects confidential communication between a lawyer and a client. The ruling determines that the trustee of the bankruptcy estate has the power to waive the attorney-client privilege with respect to prebankruptcy communications.

The Supreme Court reversed the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit's decision that the pretrial detention provision of the Bail Reform Act of 1984 was unconstitutional. The Act allows federal courts to detain an arrestee pending trial if it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that no release conditions will ensure the safety of the community or any person.

The Court of Appeals had ruled that detaining individuals based on potential future dangerousness violated substantive due process. However, the Supreme Court disagreed, stating that the Act is a legitimate response to the problem of crimes committed by released individuals and includes sufficient procedural safeguards to protect the rights of the accused. These safeguards include the right to counsel, the ability to testify and present evidence, and the requirement for the judicial officer to provide written findings of fact and reasons for detention.

The Supreme Court also addressed the respondents' arguments that the Act violated the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause and the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Bail Clause. The Court found that the government's interest in community safety can outweigh an individual's liberty interest in certain circumstances, such as war, insurrection, or when dealing with dangerous individuals. The Court concluded that the Act's provisions for pretrial detention on the basis of future dangerousness are permissible under the Due Process Clause because they are regulatory, not punitive, and are narrowly tailored to address a specific problem.

Regarding the Eighth Amendment, the Court determined that the Excessive Bail Clause does not categorically prohibit the government from pursuing interests other than preventing flight. The Act's detention provisions were found not to be excessive in relation to the government's interest in preventing crime.

In summary, the Supreme Court held that the Bail Reform Act's pretrial detention provisions are constitutionally valid, as they represent a necessary, carefully limited exception to the norm of liberty, and are designed to protect the safety of the community and individuals. The judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed the conviction of Richard Russell for his role in the manufacture and sale of methamphetamine. The court ruled that Russell's sole defense was entrapment because an undercover agent supplied an essential chemical for manufacturing the methamphetamine which formed the basis of his conviction. Russell and two codefendants were charged in a five-count indictment returned against them in federal court in Washington state for unlawfully manufacturing and processing methamphetamine ('speed') and for unlawfully selling and delivering that drug in violation of the federal antidrug laws. Russell was sentenced to concurrent terms of two years in prison for each offense, the terms to be suspended on the condition that he spend six months in prison and be placed on probation for the following three years. In a dissenting opinion, the court concluded that as a matter of law 'a defense to a criminal charge may be founded upon an intolerable degree of governmental participation in the criminal enterprise'

The Tax Injunction Act (TIA or Act), 28 U. S. C. §1341, prohibits lower federal courts from restraining “the assessment, levy or collection of any tax under State law where a plain, speedy and efficient remedy may be had in the courts of such State.” More embracive than the TIA, the comity doctrine applies in state taxation cases. See Fair Assessment in Real Estate Assn., Inc. v. McNary, 454 U.S. 100 (1981). The Comity doctrine, which requires that a claim of the kind here presented proceed originally in state court, is applicable here. Respondents Commerce Energy, Inc., a California corporation, and Interstate Gas Supply, Inc. (Inter-LDC), an Ohio company, are IMs that market and sell natural gas to Ohio consumers. Alleging discriminatory taxation of IMs and their patrons in violation of the Commerce and Equal Protection Clauses, respondents sued Richard Levin, Tax Commissioner of Ohio (Commissioner), in Federal District Court. Invoking that court’s federal-question jurisdiction, respondents sought declaratory and injunctive relief. The District Court granted respondents’ motion to dismiss the complaint, but the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the TIE did not bar their suit. The Sixth Circuit rejected the District Court comity ruling. Held: Comity considerations preclude the exercise of lower federal-court adjudicatory authority over this controversy, given that an adequate state-court forum is available to hear and decide respondents' constitutional claims. Pp. 5–11. (a) The comity principle is a prudential doctrine. When economic legislation does not employ classifications subject to heightened scrutiny or impinge on fundamental rights, courts generally view constitutional challenges with the skepticism due respect for legislative choices demands. See, e.g., Hodel v. Indiana, 452 U. s. 314, 331–332. In enacting the Tax Injunctive Act, Congress recognized and gave sanction to the practice of equal protection and dormant Commerce Clause theory, and the Act precludes relief that would diminish state revenues, even if such relief is the remedy least disruptive of the state legislature’’ design. The Act also provides that “if the State voluntarily chooses to submit to a federal district court, … the ‘adequate legal remedy’ must be one cognizable in federal court,” Fair Assessment,454 U . S., at 129, n. 15. The Court has had no prior occasion to consider, under the comities doctrine, a taxpayer complaint about allegedly discriminatory state taxation framed as a request to increase a competitor’S tax burden. And “in taxation, even more than in other fields, legislatures possess the greatest freedom in classification” Madden v. Kentucky, ante, p. 83, 88. Of key importance, when unlawful discrimination infects tax classifications or other legislative prescriptions, the Constitution simply calls for equal treatment. How equality is accomplished—by extension or invalidation of the unequally distributed benefit or burden, or some other measure—is a matter on which the Constitution is silent. See Heckler v. Mathews, 498 U. . S. 439, 447–448, and n. 6. In this case, respondents, who are financially disinterested “third parties” who do not object to their own tax situation measured by the allegedly more favorable treatment accorded LDCs, did not seek such relief. Instead, they sought relief that could “requir[e] Ohio to collect taxes which its legislature has not seen fit to impose” id., at 93–94, 110–112. The relief the complaining party requests does not circumscribe this inquiry. The fact that respondents sought relief in Hibbs is most sensibly read to affirm that, just as the case was a poor fit, so it was a bad fit for comity, and nothing would be lost in the currency of comity or state autonomy by permitting the Hibbs suit to proceed in a federal forum. Moreover, the fact that the complaint was filed in a state court does not preclude state authorities from deciding the remedial effects of such a holding. The complaint was dismissed on comity grounds, and respondents sought to dismiss it on the ground that it would disrupt the flow of the complaint. The court did not reach the question whether the exemptions were indispensable parties. The Ninth Circuit reversed, concluding that Hibbs, supra, at 107. The Tenth Circuit also reversed, reasoning that the tIA does not bar respondents from pursuing constitutional challenges to tax benefits in a Federal forum, and that the State legislature may not be convened on the spot. The Fifth Circuit, however, held that the state remedy was “plain, adequate, and complete” and that it did not preclude a federal challenge by a third party who objected to a tax credit received by others, but in no way objected to her own liability under any revenue-raising tax provision.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Alabama declined to review a lower court's conviction of a man for violating two sections of Birmingham's General Code of the City of Birmingham, Alabama. The lower court found him guilty of two counts of violating  1142 and  1231 of the General Code. He was sentenced to 180 days in prison and ordered to pay a $100 fine and costs. The Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court judgment of conviction. The Supreme Court declined to hear the case. The case involves the issue of whether a person standing on a public sidewalk in the city of Birmingham can be charged with violating the city's laws against standing on the street or sidewalk after being asked to move on by a police officer. The court found that the city had not provided for government by clearly defined laws, but rather by the 'moment-to-moment opinions of a policeman on his beat'

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed and remanded the lower court's decision in favor of the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors and the County of Los Angeles in a dispute over a property tax exemption for religious organizations. The court held that the enforcement of the provisions of Art. XIII,  1 1/2 of the California Constitution, through proceedures which place the burden of proof and persuasion of the taxpayer is a violation of due process. The Court also held that, in the absence of a showing that the provisions violate the Constitution, the court of appeals should have granted a motion for summary judgment on the issue. In a related action, the U.N. Supreme Court of Justice ruled that the Constitution does not provide for the exaction of the oath required to qualify for a property-tax exemption.
