It also underscores the importance of distinguishing between jurisdictional issues and substantive elements of a claim, which can affect the handling of cases and the ability to raise certain defenses. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. Justice Alito did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central issue was the appropriate standard for awarding attorney's fees to a prevailing defendant in a copyright infringement action under 17 U.S.C. § 505. The petitioner, musician John Fogerty, sought attorney's fees after successfully defending against a copyright infringement lawsuit brought by respondent Fantasy, Inc. The lower courts had denied Fogerty's request for fees, applying the "dual standard" which required a prevailing defendant to show that the plaintiff's suit was frivolous or in bad faith.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the conflicting approaches among the Courts of Appeals regarding the award of attorney's fees under § 505. The Ninth Circuit had applied a "dual standard," treating prevailing plaintiffs and defendants differently, while other circuits, like the Third Circuit, favored an "evenhanded" approach without such a distinction.

The Court, in its opinion, rejected the "dual standard" and held that prevailing plaintiffs and defendants should be treated alike when it comes to the award of attorney's fees. The Court found that the language of § 505 does not suggest different treatment for prevailing parties based on their status as plaintiffs or defendants. The Court also noted that the legislative history of § 505 did not support a dual standard, and that the objectives of the Copyright Act were broader than simply encouraging the filing of meritorious copyright claims.

The Court concluded that attorney's fees should be awarded to prevailing parties at the court's discretion, without a presumption in favor of either plaintiffs or defendants. The Court emphasized that the decision to award fees should be based on equitable discretion, considering various factors but not bound by a rigid rule or formula.

The judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. Justice Thomas concurred in the judgment but criticized the inconsistency with the Court's statutory analysis in a previous case, Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC.

The implication of the decision is that both prevailing plaintiffs and defendants in copyright infringement cases have an equal opportunity to be awarded attorney's fees, and such awards are at the discretion of the courts, not automatic or subject to a dual standard.

During the early months of 1953, a number of housebreakings, some involving rape or attempted rape, were committed in the City of Selma, Alabama. During the first week of his incarceration, an intruder broke into the apartment of the daughter of the city's mayor, and she awoke to find a Negro man sitting on her with a knife at her throat. A struggle ensued which carried the woman and her assailant through the bedroom, hall, and living room, where she finally was able to seize the knife, at which point he fled. Held: 1. Admission into evidence of two confessions extracted from him under circumstances demonstrating that the statements were coerced or involuntary. Pp. 531-532. (a) Denial by the trial judge of petitioner's request to testify about the manner in which the confessions were obtained without subjecting himself to unlimited cross-examination as to the facts of the crime charged. P. 532. 2. Selection of the grand jury which indicted him by a method that systematically discriminated against members of his race. 263 Ala. 89, 81 So. 2d 303, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit reversed a lower court's decision to deport a Haitian national convicted of driving under the influence of alcohol (DUI) and causing serious bodily injury under Florida law. The court held that the term "crime of violence" under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) does not count as a crime of violence under the INA. The INA defines "aggravated felony" as "an offense that has a substantial risk that physical force against the person or property of another may be used in the course of the offense"<n>The INA's definition of a "crime" of violence includes "the use or threat of force against another" or "any other offense that is a felony or that involves the use of any other element or component of that offense"

Petitioner was convicted of violating 2 U. S. C. § 192 by refusing to answer questions of a Subcommittee of the Committee of Un-American Activities of the House of Representatives. The questions related to the extent of Communist infiltration in labor in the Chicago area. The Subcommittee had been appointed by the full Committee of Un-American Activities of the House of Representatives, and the full Committee had been created by the House of Representatives. The authorizing resolution of the full Committee was so broad that it could be read to cover any subject related to un-American activities. 

Held: The conviction is reversed, because the questions were not pertinent to the "question under inquiry" within the meaning of 2 U. S. C. § 192, and petitioner was not accorded a fair opportunity to determine whether he was within his rights in refusing to answer. Pp. 171-184.
	 (a) The Committee of Un-American Activities of the House of Representatives is not authorized to investigate un-American activities in the Chicago area, and its members are not authorized to ask questions about Communist infiltration in labor in the Chicago area. Pp. 174-177.
	 (b) The authorizing resolution of the full Committee is so broad that it could be read to cover any subject related to un-American activities. P. 177.
	 (c) The Chairman's response to petitioner's objection to the questions on the grounds of lack of pertinency was woefully inadequate to convey sufficient information as to the pertinency of the questions to the subject under inquiry. Pp. 177-184. 277 F. 2d 625, reversed.

Respondent was convicted of violating 26 U. S. C. § 5205 (a) (2) by possessing nontaxed liquor. An affidavit submitted to a magistrate in connection with a search warrant recited that the affiant had "received reliable information" from a "credible person," who related that he had observed respondent purchasing illicit liquor at his home over a period of several months and that others had done likewise. The affidavit further recited that the affiant had personally witnessed the consumption of illicit liquor at respondent's home and that he had learned from a local constable that illicit liquor had been concealed in respondent's home. The magistrate issued the warrant, which yielded incriminating evidence leading to respondent's conviction. The Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that the affidavit was insufficient to show probable cause for issuing the warrant. Held: 1. The affidavit contained an adequate factual basis for believing the informant, which, when combined with the affiant's knowledge of respondent's background, afforded a basis upon which a magistrate could reasonably issue a warrant. Pp. 588-592. 2. The fact that the informant was paid or promised a break did not render his out-of-court declarations inadmissible in the warrant proceeding. Pp. 592-594. Reversed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Domino's in a lawsuit brought by John McDonald, a Black man who owned a corporation called J WM Investments LLC. McDonald alleged that Domino's breached a contract with J WM and caused harm to him personally due to racial animosity. However, the court found that McDonald did not have rights under the contract and that his injuries were not distinct from those of J WM. Therefore, McDonald could not bring a claim under Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866.

The Supreme Court case in question deals with the constitutionality of various provisions of a Missouri statute regulating abortion, enacted after the landmark Roe v. Wade decision. The plaintiffs, including Planned Parenthood and individual physicians, challenged the statute on the grounds that it infringed upon constitutional rights, including the right to privacy, the right to practice medicine, and the right to due process.

The Court's opinion, delivered after reviewing the provisions of the Missouri Act and the lower court's rulings, can be summarized as follows:

1. Viability Definition: The Court upheld the Missouri statute's definition of "viability" as the stage when a fetus can survive indefinitely outside the womb with artificial support. The Court found this definition consistent with Roe v. Wade and not an unconstitutional expansion of the term.

2. Woman's Consent: The Court found that requiring a woman's written consent before an abortion is not unconstitutional, as it ensures that the decision is made with full knowledge and is not the result of coercion.

3. Spousal Consent: The Court struck down the provision requiring spousal consent for an abortion during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, stating that the State cannot delegate a veto power to the spouse that it does not possess itself.

4. Parental Consent: The Court also invalidated the requirement for parental consent for minors seeking an abortion during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, emphasizing that constitutional rights are not limited to adults and that the State cannot give a third party an absolute veto over the abortion decision.

5. Saline Amniocentesis: The Court ruled that the prohibition of saline amniocentesis after the first 12 weeks of pregnancy was unconstitutional because it was not reasonably related to maternal health and effectively limited the majority of second-trimester abortions.

6. Recordkeeping: The Court upheld the recordkeeping requirements for health facilities and physicians as permissible and not an undue burden on the abortion decision or the physician-patient relationship, provided they are not abused or overdone.

7. Standard of Care: The Court agreed with the lower court that the provision requiring the same standard of care for a fetus as for a fetus intended to be born was unconstitutionally overbroad, as it did not exclude pre-viability stages of pregnancy.

The Court's decision affirmed some parts of the lower court's judgment and reversed others, remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The ruling has implications for the regulation of abortion, reinforcing the principles established in Roe v. Wade while allowing for certain state regulations that do not infringe upon constitutional rights.

Title 10 U. S. C. §2403(a) prohibits the detention of any person “who is an alien unlawfully within any area of the world under the control of the United States.” The Detainee Treatment Act of 2005 added §2403(b), which bars the filing of a habeas corpus petition challenging the lawfulness of a detainee’s detention unless the detainee is physically present in the United States. Petitioners, aliens detained at the United States Navy Base at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, filed suits in Federal District Courts challenging the lawfulness of their detention. They alleged that they were being held pursuant to orders issued by the President under the Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq, which was promulgated in connection with Operation Enduring Freedom, a campaign launched in response to the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The District Courts entered judgments upholding the Government’s position that the detainees were covered by §2403(b) and thus could not invoke the writ. The Fourth Circuit affirmed. Held: 1. Section 2403(b) strips the federal district courts of jurisdiction to adjudicate the merits of the detainees’ claims. Pp. 4–10. (a) The plain meaning of §2403(b)’s text establishes that the section bars the filing of a habeas corpus petition unless the detainee is physically present in the United States. Although the section uses the conjunctive “is an alien unlawfully within any area of the world under the control of the United States,” the words “within any area of the world” indicate that the section applies only to aliens who are actually present in the United States. Moreover, the section’s use of the word “physically” reinforces this reading. The section’s phrasing is supported by its placement in the same sentence as the requirement that the alien be an unlawful inhabitant of a territory controlled by the United States. Pp. 4–6. (b) The Court rejects the Government’s argument that the section’s ambiguity requires deference to the Executive Branch’s construction. The Court notes that the Government’s position is inconsistent with the ordinary rules governing the relationship between the different Branches of Government. The Court finds nothing in the section’s text or history suggesting that the framers intended to give the Executive Branch exclusive authority to resolve disputes about the applicability of the section. Nor is there anything indicating that the framers meant to limit the role of the courts to determining whether the alien is an unlawful inhabitant of a territory controlled by the United States. Instead, the Court concludes that the section’s ambiguous language reflects a division of responsibility between the different Branches of Government. Pp. 6–9. (c) The Court rejects the Government’s alternative argument that the section’s ambiguity permits the Court to look beyond the section’s text to ascertain the intentions of the framers. Such an approach would render superfluous the Court’s normal methodology of interpreting statutory provisions according to their plain meaning. Pp. 9–10. 2. Neither the detainees’ status as aliens nor the site of their detention renders them ineligible for the writ of habeas corpus. Pp. 10–16. (a) Protection of the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus is central to the Constitution’s design. The Framers’ inherent distrust of governmental power was the driving force behind the Constitution’s allocation of powers among the separated Branches. By allocating powers among the Branches, the Constitution secures individual liberty. The Framers considered the writ a vital instrument for protecting individual liberty. The Framers’ concern about the writ’s vulnerability to executive and parliamentary encroachments led them to include the Suspension Clause in Article I, §9, cl. 2, which specifies that the writ’s privilege shall not be suspended “except when in Cases of Rebellion or Invasion the public Safety may require it.” The Clause protects the rights of the detained by a means consistent with the Constitution’s essential design. It ensures that, except during periods of formal suspension, the Judiciary will have a time-tested device, the writ, to maintain the delicate balance of governance that is itself the surest safeguard of liberty. The Clause protects the rights of the detained by affirming the duty and authority of the Judiciary to call the jailer to account. Pp. 10–14. (b) Founding era authorities do not establish that the common-law writ ran only to those territories over which the Crown was sovereign or that jurisdiction followed the King’s officers. Rather, the evidence suggests that the common-law courts entertained habeas petitions brought by enemy aliens detained in England. However, there are critical differences between the sites of the detainees here and the places to which the writ ran historically. Common-law courts granted habeas corpus relief to prisoners detained in the so-called “exempt jurisdictions,” like the Channel Islands, but these areas, while not in theory part of the realm, were nonetheless under the control of the Crown. Similarly, although common-law courts granted habeas corpus relief to prisoners detained in India, that country was a British colony. Unlike the Channel Islands and India, Guantánamo is not under the control of the United States. Pp. 14–16. 427 F. 3d 119, vacated and remanded. Roberts, C. J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined. Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

In 1959 a California jury found a man guilty of murdering his wife by firing six bullets into her body at close range. A key prosecution witness at the trial was Ray Travers, an insurance agent. Two days after the respondent's wife was killed, Travers visited the respondent in jail at the latter's request, and the two conversed regarding an insurance policy on the life of the decedent. During the course of this conversation the respondent told Travers his version of how his wife had been killed, admitting that he had lain in wait for her with a gun, but insisting that her shooting had been accidental. The accuracy of the recording and of Travers' testimony was not questioned. Indeed, when the respondent took the stand, the respondent gave substantially the same account of the circumstances of his wife's death as he had given to Travers. On appeal to the Supreme Court of California, the respondents contended that the second conversation with Travers was an involuntary confession, and that the record of the conversation and Travers' supporting testimony had, therefore, been wrongly admitted in evidence. The state appellate court unanimously rejected this contention and affirmed the conviction. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari and remanded the case for further consideration. The Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit agreed with the lower court that there was no merit in the defense contention that Travers' statements were involuntary under the criteria stated in Leyra v. Denno, and granted a new trial. The Supreme Court ruled that the trial court did not abuse its discretion by admitting the recording of the Travers' conversations with the respondent. The court also ruled that it was not necessary to determine whether the recording was of a type reasonably likely to procure an untrue statement.

Case Name: Zicam Cold Remedy Marketing and Sales Practices
Case Number: 09-cv-00001
Court: United States District Court for the Southern District of California
Judge: Judge Ronald S. Brundage
Date Filed: July 2, 2009
Date Ruled: March 1, 2011

Summary:
In Zicam Cold Remedy Marketing and Sales Practices, the United States District Court for the Southern District of California found that Matrixx Therapeutics, Inc. ("Matrixx") committed false advertising and securities fraud by promoting its over-the-counter cold medication, Zicam Cold Remedy, as effective in relieving upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) despite a lack of clinical evidence supporting its effectiveness. The court ordered Matrixx to pay $11 million in damages and banned the marketing and sale of Zicam Cold Remedy until it obtained FDA approval.

Background:
Matrixx acquired rights to Zicam Cold Remedy in 2007 and began promoting it as a cure for URTIs. However, the FDA had never approved Zicam Cold Remedy for URI treatment, and the agency had issued warnings about the dangers of using the product for off-label uses. Despite these concerns, Matrixx continued to promote Zicam Cold Remedy as an effective treatment for URTIs, claiming that it contained unique ingredients that made it superior to other cold medications.

Legal Analysis:
The court analyzed the legal issues surrounding false advertising and securities fraud under Sections 10(b) and Rule 10b–5 of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 (SEA) and the False Advertising Lanham Act. The court found that Matrixx's promotional activities constituted false advertising because they represented Zicam Cold Remedy as effective in treating URTIs, despite a lack of clinical evidence supporting its effectiveness. Additionally, the court determined that Matrixx's promotion of Zicam Cold Remedy amounted to securities fraud because the company made false representations about the product's benefits and risks, which influenced investors' investment decisions.

Impact:
The ruling in Zicam Cold Remedy Marketing and Sales Practices has important implications for pharmaceutical companies engaging in off-label marketing practices. The case highlights the risks associated with promoting products for uses that have not been approved by the FDA and underscores the importance of ensuring that marketing and advertising efforts accurately reflect the truth about a product's effectiveness and risks.

This case involved a challenge to a state scholarship program that provided funding for students attending eligible colleges and universities, except for those pursuing a degree in divotional theology. The plaintiff, a student who wished to pursue a degree in divotional theology, sued the state for violation of his rights under the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment. The lower courts held that the state's exclusion of divotional theology majors was necessary to prevent the establishment of religion and did not violate the plaintiff's rights. However, the Supreme Court reversed the lower courts' decisions and ruled that the state's exclusion of divotional theology majors was unconstitutional.

After respondents’ pesticide product harmed users, petitioners sued in Texas state court, claiming that the product was defectively designed and manufactured, failed to warn of potential harm, and committed fraud. The jury returned a $1 million verdict for petitioners, which the Fifth Circuit reversed, concluding that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) pre-empted the lawsuit. The court relied on §136v(b) of FIRFA, which bars States “from impos[ing] …any requirement…which is in addition to or different from” FIRFA’s requirements. The court ruled that petitioners’ claims fell outside FIRFA’s ambit because they sought relief for conduct—design and manufacturing defects—not covered by FIRFA. Held: 1. Section 136v(b) applies to petitioners’ claims. Pp. 443–454. (a) The term “impose[] …any requirement,” which begins §136v(b), refers to any state-law requirement that is not equivalent to a requirement under FIRFA. The Court’s “inductive method” of determining what constitutes a “requirement” is most persuasive. Induction entails identifying the essential features of a category and drawing conclusions about the boundaries of the category based on those features. Here, the essential features of a requirement include a mandatory nature, a causal connection to behavior, and a nexus to the actor’s status. Using this method, the Court identifies four categories of requirements: (i) those that are mandatory, (ii) those that are causal, (iii) those that are connected to the actor’s status, and (iv) those that are not equivalent to a requirement under FIRFA. Only the fourth category is relevant to this case. Pp. 443–446. (b) Common-law duties fall within the fourth category. The Court’s “plain meaning” approach to construing the term “requirement” leads to the conclusion that common-law duties are not equivalent to FIRFA requirements. The Court’s “analogical” approach, which looks to how courts have applied the term “requirement” in past cases, also points toward this conclusion. Furthermore, the Court’s “functional” approach, which considers the purpose behind the term “requirement,” shows that the term covers only those duties that are directly related to the actor’s ability to perform his obligations. Since common-law duties are not directly tied to the actor’s ability to fulfill his obligations, they fall outside the functional approach’s purview. Pp. 446–448. (c) The Court’s “presumptive” approach, which assumes that the term “requirement” includes everything except for those things that are excluded by the other approaches, is less reliable than the other methods. Nonetheless, applying this approach yields the same result as the other methods. Pp. 448–449. (d) The Court’s “hybrid” approach combines the analogical and functional methods. By considering the purpose behind the term “requirement,” the hybrid approach allows the Court to identify the core functions performed by the term. Then, by examining how courts have applied the term in past cases, the hybrid approach ensures that the Court’s construction is faithful to the term’s historical usage. Again, this approach yields the same result as the other methods. Pp. 449–450. 2. Whether §136v(b) pre-empts petitioners’ fraud and failure-to-warn claims depends on whether those claims involve requirements that are equivalent to FIRFA’s. Pp. 450–454. (a) The Court’s “inductive” approach reveals that the essential features of a requirement that is equivalent to a FIRFA requirement include a causal connection to behavior, a nexus to the actor’s status, and a mandatory nature. All of these features are present in petitioners’ fraud and failure-to-warn claims. Pp. 450–451. (b) The Court’s “analogical” approach indicates that courts have consistently identified the presence of a causal connection to behavior, a nexus to the actor’s status, and a mandatory nature as factors indicating that a requirement is equivalent to a FIRFA requirement. Pp. 451–452. (c) The Court’s “functional” approach demonstrates that the purpose behind the term “equivalent” is to cover only those duties that are directly related to the actor’s ability to perform his obligations. Since petitioners’ fraud and failure-to-warn claims are not directly tied to the actor’s ability to fulfill his obligations, they fall outside the functional approach’s purview. Pp. 452–453. (d) The Court’s “presumptive” approach presumes that the term “equivalent” does not include those things that are excluded by the other approaches. Applying this approach yields the same result as the other methods. Pp. 453–454. (e) The Court’s “hybrid” approach combines the analogical and functional methods. By considering the purpose behind the term “equivalent,” the hybrid approach allows the Court to identify the core functions performed by the term. Then, by examining how courts have applied the term in past cases, the hybrid approach ensures that the Court’s construction is faithful to the term’s historical usage. Once again, this approach yields the same result as the other methods. Pp. 454–455. 3. The Court remands the case to the lower court to determine whether Texas law mirrors the federal standards for liability-incurring statements. Pp. 455–456. 332 F. 3d 323, vacated and remanded. Stevens, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Alito, JJ., joined. Scalia, J., filed an opinion concurring in the judgment in part and dissenting in part. Roberts, C. J., took no part in the consideration or decision of the case.

The Supreme Court reversed a lower court's decision that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits employment discrimination based on sex, did not apply to partnership decisions within a law firm. The case involved Elizabeth Anderson Hishon, an associate at a large Atlanta law firm, who alleged that the firm discriminated against her by not offering her a partnership, despite earlier indications that satisfactory performance would lead to such an offer.

The Court held that at the litigation stage, Hishon's allegations must be accepted as true, and a complaint can only be dismissed if it is clear that no relief could be granted under any set of facts consistent with the allegations. The Court found that Hishon's claim that the firm's promise of partnership consideration was a term, condition, or privilege of her employment fell within the scope of Title VII. The Court reasoned that once an employment relationship is established, Title VII governs certain aspects of that relationship, including benefits that are part of an employment contract or even non-contractual benefits that are an integral part of the employment relationship.

The Court rejected the firm's arguments that partnership decisions are categorically exempt from Title VII scrutiny, that a change in status from employee to employer (as in becoming a partner) falls outside the statute, and that applying Title VII to partnership decisions would infringe on constitutional rights of expression or association.

The Supreme Court concluded that Hishon's complaint stated a claim under Title VII and that she was entitled to attempt to prove her allegations in court. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion.

After the Commodity Credit Corporation of Batavia, Ill. (CCCB), a commodities broker registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), was charged with violating the Commodity Exchange Act (Act) by using manipulative devices to corner the market in wheat futures contracts traded on the Minneapolis Grain Exchange, Inc., its president resigned and was replaced by appellee Notz. Shortly thereafter, the CFTC brought suit against CCB and Notz in Federal District Court, charging them with violating the Act. While the suit was pending, the District Court appointed a receiver to manage CCB's affairs, and Notz consented to the entry of a stipulation appointing a receiver and providing for the liquidation of CCB's business. However, the receiver was never appointed, since the District Court ultimately dismissed the charges against CCB and Notz. Nevertheless, while the suit was pending, the CFTC issued a ceaseanddesistorderagainstCCBforviolatingtheActbyusingmanipulativedevices.Afterward, the CFTC sued CCB again, and Notz was indicted for violating the Act. Before trial, the District Court entered an order granting the CFTC permission to examine CCB's records and compelling Notz to appear and testify at the examination. At the examination, Notz invoked the attorney-client privilege of CCB and declined to answer certain questions. The District Court then ruled that Notz had waived CCB's privilege by appearing and participating in the proceedings. Ultimately, the CFTC obtained a default judgment against CCB, and Notz was convicted of violating the Act. The Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that the District Court erred in finding that Notz had waived CCB's privilege. Held: The trustee of a corporation in bankruptcy has the power to waive the corporation's attorney-client privilege with respect to prebankruptcy communications. Pp. 348-356. (a) The attorney-client privilege is controlled, outside of bankruptcy, by a corporation's management, and the actor whose duties most closely resemble those of management should control the privilege in bankruptcy, absent policies underlying the bankruptcy laws that would require a different result. Pp. 348-351. (b) Vesting in the trustee control of the corporation's attorney-client privilege most closely comports with the allocation of the waiver power to management outside of bankruptcy without in any way obstructing the careful design of the Bankruptcy Code. Pp. 351-353. (c) Nor is it true that the trustee should not obtain control over the privilege because, unlike the management of a solvent corporation, the trustee's primary loyalty goes not to shareholders but to creditors, who elect him and who often will be the only beneficiaries of his efforts. The trustee's fiduciary duty runs to shareholders as well as to creditors, and the management of a debtor-in-possessioh would have to exercise control of the privilege consistently with its obligation to treat all parties, not merely the shareholders, fairly. Moreover, the result reached here has no bearing on the problem of individual bankruptcy, which is not addressed in this case. Pp. 353-355. (d) Giving the trustee control over the attorney-client privilege will not have an undesirable chilling effect on attorney-client communications, since corporate managers will be equally wary of speaking freely with corporate counsel if their communications might subsequently be disclosed due to bankruptcy. Nor does the result here discriminate against insolvent corporations, since corporations in bankruptcy are treated differently from solvent corporations. Finally, upholding trustee waivers does not create a disincentive for debtors to invoke the protections of bankruptcy and provide an incentive for creditors to file for involuntary bankruptcy. Pp. 355-356. 722 F. 2d 339, reversed.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central issue was whether the federal government could enforce a debt against Ethel Mae Yazell's separate property, despite Texas law at the time stating that a married woman could not bind her separate property without a court decree removing her disability to contract, which Mrs. Yazell had not obtained.

The Small Business Administration (SBA) had granted a disaster loan to the Yazells for their business, which was damaged in a flood. The loan was secured with a chattel mortgage and was negotiated with explicit reference to Texas law, including the coverture doctrine that limited a married woman's ability to contract.

The Supreme Court held that in this specific case, the state law of Texas should govern, affirming the decision of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. The Court reasoned that the SBA was aware of the Texas law of coverture and entered into the contract without any indication that the defense of coverture would not apply to Mrs. Yazell's separate property. The Court found no "federal interest" that justified overriding the Texas law, especially since the federal government had not indicated at the time of the contract that it intended to enforce the debt against Mrs. Yazell's separate property.

The Court emphasized the importance of respecting state interests, particularly in the realm of family and property law, and stated that federal courts should only override state laws when there is a clear and substantial national interest that cannot be served otherwise. The Court also noted that the coverture institution was outdated and had been repealed in Texas, but the decision did not rest on the merits of the coverture doctrine itself.

The Court concluded that the federal government could not collect on the negotiated debt in disregard of the state law limitations, in the absence of a federal statute, regulation, or contract provision indicating that state law would be disregarded. The decision was to maintain the effectiveness of state laws concerning the contractual positions of married women and to avoid disrupting the carefully evolved state arrangements designed to balance property rights between spouses.

The Supreme Court's decision affirmed the lower court's ruling, thereby preventing the federal government from collecting the remaining debt from Mrs. Yazell's separate property under the circumstances of this case.

In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that a group of citizens who were challenging a tax credit given to automobile manufacturers did not have standing to sue in federal court. The court held that the citizens' injuries were not concrete enough to qualify as "actual" injuries under the standing requirement of Article III of the US Constitution. Additionally, the court found that the citizens' complaints were not sufficient to constitute a "controversy," as required by Article III. Finally, the court concluded that the citizens' arguments were not based on a "live controversy" between the parties, as necessary for standing under Article III.

The Supreme Court held that an anonymous tip claiming a person is carrying a gun is not sufficient on its own to justify a stop and frisk by police. The case in question involved an anonymous call to Miami-Dade Police reporting a young black male wearing a plaid shirt at a bus stop was armed. Police responded, found the individual matching the description, and frisked him without observing any illegal conduct or threatening behavior. A gun was found on his person.

The Florida Supreme Court ruled the search invalid under the Fourth Amendment, emphasizing that anonymous tips are less reliable than those from known informants and require specific signs of reliability, such as accurate predictions of a person's movements, which were absent in this case.

The U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the Florida Supreme Court's decision, referencing the precedent set by Terry v. Ohio, which allows for a stop and frisk only when an officer observes unusual conduct that leads them to reasonably suspect criminal activity and that the person may be armed and dangerous. The Court noted that the anonymous tip in this case provided no predictive information to assess the informant's credibility or knowledge.

The Court rejected the argument for a "firearm exception" to the reliability requirement for anonymous tips, stating that such an exception could lead to abuse and unwarranted searches, and could not be confined to firearms without also extending to other allegations like drug possession.

The Court clarified that its decision does not affect the ability of police to conduct protective searches when there is a legitimate stop based on reasonable suspicion, nor does it address situations with an immediate threat to public safety, such as a bomb threat, or in areas with diminished expectations of privacy, like airports and schools.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed that an anonymous tip must have sufficient indicia of reliability to justify a stop and frisk, and in the absence of such reliability, the Fourth Amendment's protections against unreasonable searches and seizures are not satisfied.

The Supreme Court of the United States reversed the decision of the California Court of Appeal, which had held that a landowner could not recover damages for the period before a land-use regulation was determined to be a "taking" of property under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments. The case involved the First English Evangelical Lutheran Church, which owned land in California that was rendered unusable by an interim ordinance passed by Los Angeles County following a flood. The church claimed that the ordinance constituted a taking of its property without just compensation.

The Supreme Court concluded that if a regulation goes so far as to deny a landowner all use of their property, it constitutes a taking for which compensation is required, even if the regulation is later invalidated. The Court emphasized that the Just Compensation Clause of the Fifth Amendment is designed to ensure that the government pays for the use of private property when it effectively takes that property, even temporarily.

The Court rejected the California Supreme Court's reasoning in Agins v. Tiburon, which had limited remedies for regulatory takings to nonmonetary relief. The Supreme Court held that denying compensation for the period before a regulation is invalidated is inconsistent with the Fifth Amendment's requirement for just compensation.

The Supreme Court's decision means that landowners are entitled to compensation for the period during which a regulation denies them all use of their property, even if the regulation is eventually found to be unconstitutional. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

In this case, the Supreme Court determined whether a person was "seized" within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment when he saw an officer running toward him and threw away what appeared to be a small rock. The Court held that the individual was not seized, as there was no physical contact or attempt to apprehend him. Instead, the Court ruled that the encounter amounted to a "show of authority" calling upon the individual to halt, but that such a show of authority alone did not constitute a seizure unless accompanied by physical force or submission to the assertion of authority.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit granted a stay of removal for a Cameroonian asylum seeker who claimed he was persecuted in his home country for participating in protests against the Cameroon Government. The Court held that the stay was granted on the basis of a statutory provision that sharply restricts the circumstances under which a court may issue an injunction blocking the removal of an alien from this country. The Government argues that this provision applies to the granting of a stay by a court of appeals while it considers the legality of a removal order. The court agreed, and granted the Government's motion to vacate and remand for application of the traditional criteria of the stay. The decision is the latest in a series of cases involving the issue of injunctions granted by courts of appeal. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Government in a similar case in 2008 and the Court of Justices ruled in a separate case in 2012 that the injunctions are not subject to the statutory provision. The case is now being reviewed by the Court and the decision is expected to be issued soon.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the subcommittee and upheld the petitioner's conviction for refusing to answer a question about his Communist Party membership during a subcommittee hearing. The court found that the subcommittee had the authority to investigate Communist activities and that the petitioner's refusal to answer the question was relevant to the subject matter of the investigation. Additionally, the court found that the petitioner's First Amendment rights were not violated during the interrogation.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of North Dakota today entered a final judgment against a group of school district defendants who claimed that North Dakota's busing law violated the federal securities laws.  The court's order, which entered a temporary restraining order on April 6, 2019, permanently enjoins the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay a $97 per year user fee for bus service provided to students living as far away from school as Sarita Kadrmas does.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Fargo, North Dakota, the state's 1979 school district law prohibits school districts from charging a fee for school bus transportation.  In its order, the court found that the district had failed to show that its 1979 law violated federal and state equal protection laws, and ordered the district to impose a $100,000 fee on all of its students.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining them from future violations of the federal, state, and municipal securities laws, ordering them to disgorge their allegedly ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and ordering the District Attorney's Office to issue an order appointing a receiver for the receiver of the receiver.   The SEC's order also orders the district attorney's office to conduct an examination of the receivers' records to determine whether they are appropriate to issue a civil injunctive action. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted in the Chicago Regional Office by Michael J. Karpel and supervised by Scott A. Thompson. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Minnesota Department of Education, and the Federal Office of Education.

Iowa taxes adjusted revenues from slot machines on excursion riverboats at a maximum rate of 20 percent. Before 1989, Iowa permitted only one form of gambling-parimutuel betting at racetracks-the proceeds of which it taxed at a six percent rate. In 1989, it authorized other forms of gambling, including slot machines and other gambling games on riverboats, though it limited bets to $5 and losses to $200 per excursion. In 1994, Iowa enacted a law that, among other things, removed the riverboat gambling $5/$200 bet/loss limits, and authorized racetrack slot machines to operate slot machines, but did not alter the tax rate on riverboat slot machine adjusted revenues, thereby leaving the existing 20 percent rate in place. Respondents brought this lawsuit in state court challenging the 1994 legislation on the ground that the 20 percent/36 percent tax rate difference that it created violated the Federal Constitution's Equal Protection Clause, Amdt. 14, § 1. The Iowa Supreme Court disagreed and, by a 4-to-3 vote, reversed the District Court, holding that the "differential tax completely defeats the alleged purpose" of the statute, namely, that there could be no rational reason for the differential tax, and that the Equal protection Clause consequently forbids its imposition. The State Supreme Court held that this state-law holding bars review of the federal issue. Held: 1. Iowa's differential tax rate does not violate the Federal Equal Protection Act. Pp. 648-562. (a) There is "a plausible policy reason" for the classification, that the legislature "rationally may have . . . considered ... true" the related justifying "legislative facts," and the "relationship of the classification to its goal is not so attenuated as to render the distinction arbitrary or irrational." Nordlinger v. Hahn, 505 U. S. 1, 11-12. (b) The Iowa law, like most laws, might predominantly serve one general objective, say, helping the racetrackers, while containing subsidiary provisions that seek to achieve other desirable (perhaps even contrary) ends as well. The Constitution grants legislators, not courts, broad authority (within the bounds of rationality) to decide whom they wish to help with their tax laws and how much help those laws ought to provide. And the Constitution grants legislatures broad authority to decide who they want to help, and what they wish not to, with their taxes laws. Thus, in such circumstances, this Court shall consider a state-court decision as resting upon federal grounds sufficient to support this Court's jurisdiction. See Pennsylvania v. Muniz, 496 U.S. 582, 588, n. 4. Nor could the Iowa Court deny that the 1994 legislature's 1994 legislation, seen as a whole, can rationally be understood to do what that court says it seeks to do, which is to advance the Racetracks' economic interests. That difference, harmful to the rac racetracking, is helpful to the riverboats which, as respondents concede, were also harmed by the fact that the law provides less help than respondents might like. At least a rational legislator might so believe. Moreover, there is a plausible policy explanation for the legislature's classification, and the legislature has considered the related factors justifying the related reasons. The legislature's relationship to the classification is not too attenuated to render an inference that the reasons for the different tax rates was to help the Riverboat industry or the river communities. Nor is there any indication in Allegheny Pittsburgh Coal Co. v. Commission of Webster Cty., 488 U. . . 336 (1989), that the policies underlying an acquisition-value taxation scheme could conceivably have been the purpose for the unequal assessment. The facts do not "preclud[e]" an inference of a reason that the different taxes rates were to help riverboats or river communities, and no rational person, it believed, could claim the contrary. Nor can the Iowa State Court deny, however, that it might serve one specific objective, such as, helping riverboats from economic distress, while also containing subsidiary provision that seeks to achieve "other desirable" ends as also, thereby producing a law which balances objectives but still serves the general objective when seen as

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that an Ohio law that prohibits the distribution of anonymous campaign literature is a violation of the First Amendment right to freedom of speech. The high court held that the law does not violate the right to free speech because it provides for the identification of persons who distribute materials containing false statements. The case involves a 1988 case in which Margaret McIntyre distributed leaflets opposing a proposed school tax levy. The Ohio Elections Commission charged Mrs. McIntyre with violating  3599.09(A) of the Ohio Code. The Commission agreed and imposed a fine of $100. The Franklin County Court of Common Pleas reversed, and the Ohio Court of Appeals reinstated the fine. The Supreme Court's ruling was a victory for free speech and for the public's right to know the identity of those who distribute campaign literature.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit recently ruled that a Minnesota state law restricting the distribution of religious literature and soliciting donations at a state fair does not violate the First and Fourteenth Amendment rights of a religious organization. The court held that the law does not prohibit a religious group from distributing religious literature at the fair, but rather requires that the group conduct its sales, distribution, and solicitation operations from a booth rented from the Minnesota Agricultural Society. The Court held that this rule does not apply to the religious group International Society for Krishna Consciousness, Inc. (ISKCON), an international religious society espousing the views of the Krishna religion. ISKCON argued that the rule would suppress the practice of Sankirtan, one of its religious rituals, which enjoins its members to go into public places to distribute or sell religious literature, and to solicit donations for the support of the religion. The Minnesota Supreme Court reversed the lower court's ruling, holding that the Rule was not restrictive of ISK CON's First Amendment rights. The 8th Court ruled that the Court's decision is consistent with the decision in Evans v. Evans, 440 F.Supp. 414 (SD Ohio 1977), which found that the State's interest "in providing all fair goers and concessionaries with adequate and equal access to each other" was sufficient to sustain Rule 6.05's limitations as applied to respondents. The 9th Circuit held that, in light of that decision, the Court should have granted the State a writ of certiorari to determine whether the rule is a violation of the First Amendment right to freedom of speech. The 10th Circuit agreed, holding, however, that "the rule is not inconsistent with the Constitution's right to a free and open society" and that the Society's justifications for the rule were insufficient to justify its application. The Supreme Court held, however. The case is not without significant implications for other states and the courts of appeal.

Appellants contend that the Texas Legislature’s redistricting plan is an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander and that the redistricting statewide violates §2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, as amended, 42 U. S. C. §1973. The three-judge panel, consisting of Circuit Judge Higginbotham and District Judges Ward and Rosenthal, brought considerable experience and expertise to the instant case, based on their knowledge of Texas’ people, history, and geography. They were intimately familiar with the history and intricacies of the cases. Appellants also contend that, because the Texas population has shifted since the 2000 census, the 2003 redistricting, which relied on that census, created unlawful interdistrict population variances. The District Court held that an equal protection challenge to a political gerrymandering challenge presents a justiciable case or controversy, id., at 118–127, but there was disagreement over what substantive standard to apply. Held: Appellant appellants have established no legally impermissible use of political classifications. Pp. 5–11. (a) Appellate appellants’ contention that the new redistricting violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment is not supported by the facts of the case, since the District Court relied on the “ ‘neutral’ redistricting standards” when drawing Plan 1151C. Henderson v. Perry, 399 F. Supp. 2d 756, which provides that “[t]here is little question but that the single-minded purpose of the Texas legislature in enacting Plan 1374C was to gain partisan advantage” for the Republican majority over the Democratic minority, Session, supra, at 767. The recognition of nonracial communities of interest reflects the principle that a State may not “assum[e] from a group of voters’ race that they ‘think alike, share the same political interests, and will prefer the same candidates at the polls.’ ” Miller v. Johnson, 515 U.S. 900, 916–917. In the absence of any contested Democratic primary in the State, no obvious benchmark exists for deciding whether African-Americans could elect their candidate of choice. Moreover, the fact of mid-decade redistricting alone is no sure indication of unlawful political grymanders. The fact that the legislature acted to protect the incumbent congressman from the growing dissatisfaction of the cohesive and politically active Latino community in the district, and to bring the community into the full stream of political life of the county and State by encouraging their further registration, voting, and other political activities, does not resolve the issue of vote dilution. P. 5. (b) Appellee Perry et al. (1) The districting map resulting from the Balderas litigation is known as Plan 13 74C. It is the only area of the State where reasonably compact Latino opportunity districts can be drawn, and the Court has identified three threshold conditions for establishing a §2 violation: (1), the racial group is “sufficiently large and geographically compact to constitute a majority in a single-member district,” (quoting Rogers v. Lodge, 458 U. s. 613, 613), and (2) the majority “vot[es] sufficiently as a bloc to enable it . . . usually to defeat the minority” . (3) The composition of the district lines is important because the right to an undiluted vote does not belong to the minority as a group, but rather to “its individual members.” Shaw v. De Grandy, 512 U. . S. 997, and (4) there is no constitutional requirement of proportional representation, and thus the State cannot remedy the District 23 violation through the creation of a noncompact district. The Court also rejected a test proposed in Vieth v. Jubelirer, 543 U. States, Civ. Action No. 6:01CV158 (per curiam), which identifies factors typically relevant to §2, including: “the history of voting-related discrimination in [Texas], the extent to which voting in the elections of [the State or political subdivision] is racially polarized; (1] the extent that the State has used voting practices or procedures that tend to enhance the opportunity for discrimination against the minority group; (2] the political processes leading to nomination or election in [a] political subdivision are not equally open to participation; and (3] the party balance more congruent to statewide party power . . ..” Gingles, 478 U.

The Arizona Court of Appeals reversed the conviction of Larry Youngblood on the grounds that the State had failed to preserve semen samples from the victim's body and clothing. Youngblood was convicted of child molestation, sexual assault, and kidnaping. The court held that the "Due Process Clause" of the Fourteenth Amendment requires the State to preserve evidentiary material that might be useful to a criminal defendant. We granted certiorari to consider the extent to which the Due Process Clause requires the state to preserve such material.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia granted summary judgment in favor of the Federal Home Administration in a case that arose out of the Emergency Low Income Housing Preservation Act of 1987 (ELIHPA) and its subsequent enforcement. The Federal Circuit had held that petitioners' claims against the federal government for violating the terms of their low-interest mortgage loans had not been filed within six years of the date they "first accrue[d]" under the Tucker Act. We reverse the Federal Circuit's judgment, finding that petitioners had not filed their claims within the six-year limitations period. The Court also notes that the Federal District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri previously granted summary judgments in the case. We conclude that the emergency law did not constitute a present breach of the loan agreements. The case is now settled.

In the case before the Supreme Court, Morris A. Kent Jr., a juvenile, was subjected to a waiver of jurisdiction by the Juvenile Court, which allowed him to be tried as an adult in the District Court for serious offenses including rape and robbery. Kent's counsel argued that the waiver was invalid because it was made without a hearing, without findings by the Juvenile Court, without stated reasons for the waiver, and with denial of access to Kent's social service files.

The Supreme Court agreed that the waiver was invalid. It emphasized that the waiver of jurisdiction from the Juvenile Court to an adult court is a critically important decision that affects the rights of the juvenile. The Court held that due process requires a hearing before such a waiver, access to social records for the juvenile's counsel, and a statement of reasons for the decision to waive jurisdiction. The Court found that the Juvenile Court had not provided these procedural safeguards.

The Supreme Court vacated the lower courts' judgments and remanded the case to the District Court for a new hearing on the waiver. If the District Court finds the original waiver was inappropriate, Kent's conviction must be vacated. If the waiver is found to have been appropriate at the time it was made, the District Court may proceed with appropriate judgment.

The decision underscored the importance of procedural fairness and due process in the juvenile justice system, ensuring that juveniles are afforded the same legal protections and considerations as adults when being tried for serious offenses.

In the case involving the Perry Education Association (PEA) and the Perry Local Educators' Association (PLEA), the Supreme Court addressed whether the exclusive access granted to PEA to use the school district's internal mail system, while denying similar access to PLEA, violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

The Court found that the school mail system is not a public forum, and therefore, the school district is not required to grant access to all organizations. The Court distinguished between different types of government property, noting that traditional public forums like streets and parks have strong protections for free speech, while nonpublic forums can have more restricted access based on the property's intended purpose.

The Court concluded that the differential access provided to PEA was reasonable because it was consistent with the district's legitimate interest in preserving the mail system for its intended school-related use. PEA, as the exclusive bargaining representative, had certain responsibilities that justified its access to the mail system. PLEA, on the other hand, did not have official responsibilities that necessitated the same level of access.

The Court also addressed the argument that the access policy constituted content discrimination in violation of the Equal Protection Clause. It rejected this argument, stating that PLEA did not have a fundamental right to access the mail system, and the school district's policy only needed to rationally further a legitimate state purpose, which it did through the special responsibilities of an exclusive bargaining representative.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding the exclusive access policy as constitutional. The opinion clarified that not all government-owned properties are subject to the same free speech standards and that distinctions can be made based on the nature and purpose of the property.

In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that a conviction obtained in a state court based on eyewitness identification of a suspect in a lineup was constitutional, even though the lineup was "unnecessarily suggestive" within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. The Court held that the determination of whether a particular identification procedure is "unnecessarily suggestive" depends on the "totality of the circumstances," including the opportunity of the witness to view the suspect, the witness' ability to accurately describe the suspect, the level of certainty expressed by the witness, and the duration of time between the crime and the identification. The Court concluded that the identification in this case was reliable and therefore constitutional, despite the use of a lineup in the identification process.

1. The 1952 Patent Act of 1952 provides that when a combination produces an "old result in a cheaper and otherwise more advantageous way," it is patentable. Pp. 531-532. 2. The patent is invalid under § 103, since the differences between them and the pertinent prior art would have been obvious to a person reasonably skilled in that art. P. 532. 3. The patents in issue in these cases are clearly evident from the prior art as it stood at the time of the invention, and the differences are so inconsequential that the device as a whole would have had to be obvious at that time the invention was made to a "person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains." P. 529. 4. The Patent Act was intended to codify judicial precedents embracing the principle long ago announced by this Court in Hotchkiss v. Greenwood, 11 How. 248, 13 L. Ed. 683, and that, while the clear language of § 103 places emphasis on an inquiry into obviousness, the general level of innovation necessary to sustain patentability remains the same. P p. 533. 5. The claims in the patent in issue are clearly apparent from their prior art, since they are not meeting § 103's test of obviousness and the fact that they are based on a combination of old mechanical elements that were not disclosed in the original art. Held: 1. In the circumstances of this case, the patent must fall as not meeting the § 103 test, since, in addition to novelty and utility as articulated and defined in § 101 and § 102, the materiality of the patent is to depend upon the "non-obvious" nature of the subject matter sought to be patented to the person having ordinaryty in the pertinent art, and it is in this light that patent validity "requires reference to a standard written into the Constitution." Great A. & P. Tea Co. v. Supermarket Equipment Corp., 340 U. S. 147, and this Court has held that § 103 is both a grant of power and a limitation, since it may not overreach the restraints imposed by the stated constitutional purpose, and may not authorize the issuance of patents whose effects are to remove existent knowledge from the public domain, or to restrict free access to materials already available. See, e. g., Mast, Foos & Co.' v. Stover Mfg. Co., 177 U.S. 485, 20 S.Ct. 708, 44 L.Ed. 856, and, in the circumstances here, the emphasis on nonobviousness is one of inquiry, not quality; and, as such, comports with the constitutional strictures. Cf., Lohse U. P.'s Patent No. 2,627,798 (hereinafter called the "798 patent"), which provides that a patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in § 102 of this title, if the differences from the subjectmatter sought to-be patented and the prior Art are such that the subject-matter as to the relevant subject matter as to which it was made-is such that it is a prerequisite to patentability and validity. The fact that the shank is held in place by the spring rod which is hooked against the bottom of the hinge plate and a gasket, rather than a rib-rather than a washer or gasket-is not a significant feature in the Patent Act does not tip the scales of patentability, since such inquiries are not required to cover that which was previously by limitation eliminated from the patent, and they may also serve to guard against slipping into use of hindsight, Monroe Auto Equipment Co., v. Heckethorn Mfg., & Supply Co., 332 F. 2d 406, 412, and to resist the temptation to read into prior art the teachings of the inventor in issue. Cf. Littman v. Stewart-Warner Corp., 303 U. s. 545, and Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. of America v. United States, 320 U . S. 1, 60, where the Court called such an effort "an afterthought" and would not permit interrogation as to flexing in the accused devices. The Court of Appeals in Nos. 37 and 43 is reversed and remanded and cases remanded to the District Court for disposition not inconsistent with this opinion.

Title: Direct Entry of Judgment as Matter of Law Based on Erroneous Admission of Evidence

Subject Area: Federal Courts

Keywords: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50, Jurisdiction, Verdict, Damages, Expert Testimony, Evidentiary Error, Summary Judgment, Preemption, Due Process Clause

Summary:

Direct Entry of Judgment as Matter of Law Based on Erroneous Admission of Evidence

Introduction:

The United States Constitution guarantees citizens the right to a fair trial by jury. However, what happens when the jury renders a verdict that goes against the overwhelming evidence presented in court? Can the losing party seek relief through the judiciary system? Yes, according to the United States Supreme Court, the losing party can ask for a new trial or even a judgment as a matter of law.

Background Information:

The United States Supreme Court has long recognized the importance of ensuring that juries reach accurate and reliable verdicts. To achieve this goal, the Court established rules governing the conduct of trials and the admissibility of evidence. One such rule is Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50, which provides that a party may file a motion for judgment as a matter of law if there is no legally sufficient evidence to support the opposing party's claim or defense.

However, the application of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50 has been the source of much confusion and debate within the legal community. Some scholars believe that judges should automatically grant a motion for judgment as a matter of law whenever the evidence presented fails to establish a prima facie case. Others argue that judges should carefully consider each case on its merits and only grant a motion for judgment as a matter of law when the evidence is so weak that it amounts to a complete absence of factual support for the opposing party's claims.

Case Analysis:

In the recent case of Weisgram v. Marbury, the United States Supreme Court provided clarity on the proper application of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50. The case involved a dispute between two families over ownership of land in Texas. After several years of litigation, the case finally reached the Supreme Court, which affirmed the lower court's decision to grant judgment as a matter of law in favor of the defending family.

According to the Supreme Court, the decision to grant judgment as a matter of law depends on two factors: the strength of the evidence presented and the likelihood that the jury would have reached a different verdict if the evidence had been presented differently. In this case, the Supreme Court determined that the evidence presented by the plaintiff was so weak that it amounted to a complete absence of factual support for their claims. Furthermore, the Supreme Court noted that the jury was likely to have reached a different verdict if the evidence had been presented differently.

Conclusion:

The United States Supreme Court's decision in Weisgram v. Marbury provides valuable guidance for attorneys representing clients in civil disputes involving complex issues of evidence and fact. By establishing clear criteria for evaluating motions for judgment as a matter of law, the Supreme Court ensures that juries receive the benefit of the strongest possible evidence and that justice is served in all cases.

Under §16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, a corporation or security holder may bring suit against the officers, directors, and certain beneficial owners of a corporation who realize any profits from the purchase and sale, or sale and purchase, of the corporation’s securities within any 6-month period. “The statute imposes a form of strict liability” and requires insiders to disgorge these “short-swing” profits “even if they did not trade on inside information or in- tend to profit on the basis of such information.” Gollust v. Mendell, 501 U. S. 115, 122. Petitioners filed nearly identical actions under §16 (b) against financial institutions that had underwritten various initial public offerings (IPOs) in the late 1990s and 2000, including these petitioners. In 2007, respondent Simmonds filed 55 nearly identical action under §§16 (a) and the reporting requirements of §§16(a). Simmonds alleged that the underwriters and the insiders owned in excess of 10% of the outstanding stock during the relevant time period, which subjected them to both disgorgement of profits under § 16(b), and the disclosure requirements of §16. The latter required insiders to disclose any changes to their ownership interests on a document known as a Form 4, specified in the Securities and Exchange Commission regulations. Simmonds’ lawsuits were consolidated for pretrial purposes, and the District Court dismissed all of her complaints. The Court of Appeals reversed in relevant part. Held: 1. The 2-year period to file suit against a corporate insider is tolled until the filing of a statement. The Whittaker rule is best understood as applying legal-rather than equitable-tolling principles. Pp. 5–7. (a), 638 F. 2d 1072, vacated and remanded.

Mississippi imposes a 5% sales tax upon the "gross proceeds of the retail sales" of tangible personal property, including gasoline. Petitioner operates as a sole proprietorship from West Memphis, Ark. He owns and operates five gasoline service stations in Mississippi and also sells gasoline at four other stations in Arkansas on a consignment basis. He purchases his gasoline tax free from sources in Tennessee and Arkansas. He transports the gasoline to his Mississippi stations in his own trucks. He holds a Mississippi distributor's permit and is federally licensed because he is a "producer" within the meaning of the Internal Revenue Code as one who sells gasoline bought taxfree from other "producers." He adds to his pump prices the amount of a Mississippi gasoline excise tax, now nine cents per gallon, Miss.Code Ann. § 27-55-11 (Supp.1974), and a federal gasoline excisetax of four cents pergallon, 26 U. S. C. § 4081(a). The State computes his gross proceeds of retail sales "without any deduction for . . . taxes of any kind." Petitioner paid the sales taxes to that extent under protest, and used for a refund in Mississippi Chancery Court, Hinds County. After trial, the State dismissed petitioner's suit and entered judgment for respondent on the cross-claim. The Supreme Court affirmed. Held: The Mississippi Supreme Court properly concluded that the federal excise tax is imposed solely on petitioner and not upon the purchaser-consumer. Pp. 6-8. 288 So. 2d 868, affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Hawaii recently ruled that a Hawaii law limiting the rent that oil companies may charge to dealers who lease service stations owned by the companies is not a taking of private property under the Fifth Amendment. The law limits the amount of rent that an oil company may charge a lessee-dealer to 15 percent of the dealer's gross profits from gasoline sales plus 15 per cent of gross sales of products other than gasoline. The lower courts held that the rent cap effects an uncompensated taking of Chevron's property in violation of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments because it does not substantially advance Hawaii's asserted interest in controlling retail gasoline prices. The court found that the law does not "substantially advance any legitimate government interest"

In the case of David Paul O'Brien, who was convicted for burning his Selective Service registration certificate in protest against the Vietnam War, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of a 1965 amendment to the Universal Military Training and Service Act that made it a crime to knowingly destroy or mutilate such certificates.

The Court's reasoning was based on several key points:

1. The Act's Purpose: The Court recognized that the Selective Service certificates had multiple administrative functions beyond mere notification of registration or classification. These included facilitating communication between registrants and local boards, serving as proof of compliance with Selective Service obligations, and aiding in the detection of fraud.

2. Government Interest: The Court found that the government had a substantial interest in maintaining the integrity of the Selective Service system, which was essential for the efficient functioning and administration of the military draft.

3. Free Speech: While O'Brien argued that his act of burning the draft card was symbolic speech protected by the First Amendment, the Court held that the government could regulate conduct that combined speech and non-speech elements if it had an important interest unrelated to the suppression of free expression. The Court determined that the 1965 amendment met this standard because it targeted the non-communicative aspect of the conduct (the destruction of the certificate) and was not aimed at suppressing the communicative aspect (the anti-war protest).

4. Legislative Intent: The Court rejected the argument that the amendment was unconstitutional due to Congress's alleged intent to suppress free speech. It stated that the judiciary does not invalidate legislation based on speculative motives of lawmakers but focuses on the actual effect of the statute.

5. Narrow Scope: The Court concluded that the amendment was narrowly tailored to serve the government's interest, as it only criminalized the knowing destruction or mutilation of the certificates and did not prohibit other forms of protest or expression.

The Supreme Court's decision vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had found the 1965 amendment unconstitutional, and reinstated O'Brien's conviction and sentence by the District Court. The ruling clarified that while the government cannot suppress free speech, it can enact laws that incidentally limit speech if those laws serve a substantial government interest and are not broader than necessary.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the state of Mississippi in this case involving a dispute over a tax on liquor purchased by the US Navy from out-of-state distillers. The court found that the tax was not a violation of the US Constitution's commerce clause, as it was being used to raise revenue for the state and was not discriminating against interstate commerce. Additionally, the court found that the tax was not a violation of the Twenty-First Amendment, which ended Prohibition, as it was not aimed at punishing the consumption of alcohol.

In 2005, nearly 10 percent of all civil cases filed in federal courts nationwide were prisoner complaints challenging prison conditions or claiming civil rights violations. The Supreme Court of the United States recently ruled that the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals had exceeded its authority by adopting rules that require a prisoner to exhaust prison grievance procedures before filing a suit. The Court's decision was based on the Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (PLRA), which requires prisoners to exhaust their administrative remedies before filing suit against prison officials. The PLRA also requires that the prisoner identify each individual named in his complaint. The Sixth Circuit's rules require the prisoner to show that he has exhausted all of his administrative remedies. The court found that the rules conflict with the PLRA's requirements that the complaint be filed within 30 days of the date of the complaint's filing and that the court should dismiss the entire action if the prisoner fails to meet the exhaustion requirement. The justices ruled that these rules violated the proper limits on the court's authority under the Constitution and the Constitution's First Amendment protection against excessive judicial activism. The opinion concludes that the Supreme Court will not rule on the issue of whether the rules are required by PLRA. The case will be decided by the full court in a few months.

Respondent T.L.O., a 14-year-old high school freshman, discovered two girls smoking in a lavatory. Because smoking in the lavatory was a violation of a school rule, the teacher took the two girls to the Principal's office, where they met with Assistant Vice Principal Theodore Choplick. The teacher asked T.O. to come into his private office and demanded to see her purse. The search revealed a small amount of marihuana, a pipe, a number of empty plastic bags, a substantial quantity of money in one-dollar bills, an index card that appeared to be a list of students who owed the teacher money, and two letters implicated T. L.O.'s in marihua dealing. The court found that the search was a reasonable one, and that the evidence of drug use that he saw inside did not justify the extensive "rummaging" through T. O.'s papers and effects that followed. The Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court denied the motion to suppress. The New Jersey Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Appellate Division and ordered the suppression of the evidence found in the purse as well as her confession, which, she argued, was tainted by the allegedly unlawful search. Held: 1. The Fourth Amendment applies to searches conducted by school officials. Although the underlying command of the Fourth Amendment is always that searches and seizures be reasonable, what is reasonable depends on the context within which a search takes place. The determination of the standard of reasonableness governing any specific class of searches requires "balancing the need to search against the invasion which the search entails." Camara v. Municipal Court, 387 U. S. 528, at 532-537. Pp. 539-541. 2. A search of a student by a teacher or other school official will be "justified at its inception" when there are reasonable grounds for suspecting that it will turn up evidence that the student has violated or is violating either the law or the rules of the school. Such a search will be permissible in its scope when the measures adopted are reasonably related to the objectives of the search and not excessively intrusive in light of the age and sex of the student and the nature of the infraction. The standard will spare teachers and school administrators the necessity of schooling themselves in the niceties of probable cause and permit them to regulate their conduct according to the dictates of reason and common sense. P. 541. 3. The Court has held that the accommodation of the privacy interests of schoolchildren with the substantial need of teachers and administrators for freedom to maintain order in the schools does not require strict adherence to the requirement that searches be based on probable cause to believe that the subject of a search has violated the law, and they cannot claim the parents' immunity from the strictures of that Fourth Amendment. The requirement of reasonable suspicion is not a requirement of absolute certainty: "sufficient probability, not certainty, is the basis of any fact that is of consequence to the determination of an action more probable or less probable than it would be without the evidence."
