Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1, 7-8, and even firemen entering privately owned premises to battle a fire, see Michigan v. Tyler, 436 US. 499, 506, are all subject to the restraints imposed on subjective expectations of privacy that are unreasonable or otherwise "illegitimate," Camara, supra, at 463 A. 2d 621. The same standard will not unduly burden the efforts of school authorities to maintain an environment in which learning can take place nor authorize unrestrained intrusions upon the privacy of school children. The "reasonable grounds" standard applied by the State Supreme Court in its consideration of this question is not substantially different from the standard that was adopted today. The fact that the New Jersey court's application of that standard to strike down the search of T. o.'s purse reflects a somewhat crabbed notion that the purse was a substantial invasion of privacy does not necessarily mean that it was unreasonable in any respect. The relevance of the possession of cigarettes to the question whether she had been smoking and to the credibility of her denial that she smoked supplied the necessary "nexus" between the item searched for and its infraction under investigation. Moreover, even if a reasonable suspicion that T. had cigarettes in her purse would justify a search, it was not unreasonable to extend the search to a separate zippered compartment of the purse; and when a search of that compartment revealed an index and a letter containing a list that would be perfectly permissible if undertaken by an adult, the inference that the child was involved was substantial enough to justify Mr.'s search in examining the letters to determine whether they contained any further evidence. Finally, even assuming that a search might under some circumstances be reasonable in light the accusation made against T. l. o. that she did not smoke at all, the discovery of the rolling papers would both corroborate the report that she was smoking and undermine her defense to the charge of smoking.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Northern District of Ohio ruled that taxpayers in Toledo, Ohio did not have standing to sue the city of Toledo and the State of Ohio for tax breaks that they claimed increased their local and state tax burdens. The court held that the taxpayers had not shown that they had standing to press their complaint in federal court. The lower court had previously ruled that the tax breaks violated the Constitution's Commerce Clause. The Ohio legislature passed a law offering a tax credit against the state franchise tax for businesses that purchase new manufacturing machinery and equipment and install it at sites in the state. The taxpayers claimed that this tax credit violated the Commerce Clause, and they sued the city and the state, alleging that their tax burdens were increased. The district court agreed with the lower court, and the case was remanded to the state court for further proceedings. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the city, finding that the city's tax breaks did not violate the Constitution. The high court also found that the state's franchise tax credit was not a violation of the Constitution because the taxpayers did not show that they would be harmed by the tax break. After the Bank Holding Company Act (BHCA) became effective in 1956, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) issued regulations requiring interstate acquisitions of radio stations to be approved by the Attorney General of the affected State. In 1970, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) promulgated rules requiring advance notice of interstate acquisitions of voting stock in publicly traded companies. Both sets of regulations were challenged as exceeding the scope of the respective statutes. Ultimately, the District of Columbia Circuit struck down the FTC rules, finding that the FTC lacked jurisdiction to issue them. However, the court remanded the case to the FTC for consideration of the possibility that the regulations could be saved by incorporating the requirements of the BHCA. The FTC subsequently reinstituted the regulations, including the BHCA requirements, and again brought the case to the District of Columbia Circuit, which upheld the regulations. Held: The FTC's regulations are valid. Although the BHCA applies only to interstate acquisitions involving radio broadcasting facilities, the FTC properly incorporated the BHCA requirements into its regulations governing interstate acquisitions of voting stock in publicly traded companies. Such incorporation was proper since the BHCA clearly manifested congressional intent to include interstate acquisitions of voting stock in publicly traded companies within its coverage. Moreover, the FTC's interpretation of the BHCA comports with the statute's legislative history and is supported by the views expressed in the BHCA's implementing regulations. Thus, the FTC's regulations are entitled to deference under Chevron U S Ol. Ltd. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., ante, p. 803. 216 U. S. App. D. C.- -, 674 F. 2d 137, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of South Dakota today entered a final judgment in favor of the Longs in a civil injunctive action brought by the tribe against the bank.  The court found that the tribe had no jurisdiction over the sale of non-Indian fee land.  According to the court's order, the tribe consented to tribal court jurisdiction over its sale of fee land in violation of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Tribe agreed to settle the matter by consenting to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins the tribe from violating the federal securities laws and orders it to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $750,000.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the Long's.   The settlement is pending final approval by the court.

After petitioners eBay Inc. and Half.com, Inc., refused to pay royalties for licensing a patent held by respondent MercExchange, LLC, MercExchange sued both companies for patent infringement. A jury awarded damages, but the District Court denied MercExchange’s request for permanent injunctive relief. On appeal, the Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that courts generally issue permanent injunctions against patent infringement absent exceptional circumstances. Held: Traditional principles of equity—which provide that a plaintiff seeking a permanent injunction must show that he has suffered irreparable injury, that remedies available at law are inadequate to compensate for that injury, that, considering the balance of hardships between the plaintiff and defendant, a remedy in equity is warranted, and that the public interest would not be served by a permanent injunction—apply equally to disputes arising under the Patent Act. Permanent injunctive relief is authorized by the Act, which states that injunctions “may” issue “in accordance with the principles of equity.” 35 U. S. C. §283. That section does not indicate that Congress intended a departure from the longstanding traditions of equity practice. Nor can the right to exclude others from making, using, or selling an invention justify the lower court’s general rule. Rather, the creation of a right is distinct from the provision of remedies for violations of that right. Here, because neither court below correctly applied the traditional four-factor framework governing the award of injunctive relief, the judgment is vacated so that the District Court may apply that framework in the first instance. Certiorari granted; 401 F. 3d 1323, vacated and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Alito, and Roberts, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The Michigan Department of Corrections (MDOC) revised its prison visitation policies in 1995, promulgating the regulations here at issue. One aspect of the Department's approach was to limit the visitors a prisoner is eligible to receive, in order to decrease the total number of visitors. Under the regulations, an inmate may receive visits only from individuals placed on an approved visitor list, except that qualified members of the clergy and attorneys on official business may visit without being listed. Minors under the age of 18 may not be placed on the list unless they are the children, stepchildren, grandchildren, or siblings of the inmate. If an inmate's parental rights have been terminated, the child is not permitted to visit. A child authorized to visit must be accompanied by an adult who is an immediate family member of the child or of an inmate or who is the legal guardian of a child. An inmate may not place a former prisoner on the visitor list unless the former prisoner is a member of his immediate family and the warden has given prior approval. The restriction on visitation for inmates with two substance-abuse violations, a bar which may be removed after two years, serves the legitimate goal of deterring the use of drugs and alcohol within the prisons. Prison officials found it difficult to maintain order during visitation and to prevent smuggling or trafficking in drugs. Special problems were encountered with the increase in visits by children, who are at risk of seeing or hearing harmful conduct during visits and must be supervised with special care in prison visitation facilities. In addition, the restriction on visits by former inmates was a necessary and even necessary management technique to induce compliance with the rules of inmate behavior, especially for high-security prisoners who have few other privileges to lose. In this regard, prison officials have reasonably exercised their judgment as to the appropriate means of furthering penological goals, and that was the controlling rationale for their decision. Respondents are prisoners, their friends, and their family members. They brought this action under Rev. Stat. § 1979, 42 U. S. C. § 1983, alleging that the restrictions upon visitation violate the First, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendments. It was certified as a class action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23. The Court of Appeals affirmed the regulations as invalid. Held: 1. The regulations are not punishment within the meaning of the Eighth Amendment. Pp. 6-17. (a) The regulations bear a rational relation to MDOC's valid interests in maintaining internal security and protecting child visitors from exposure to sexual or other misconduct or from accidental injury. P. 6. (b) The regulation promotes internal security, perhaps the most legitimate penological goal, see, e. g., Pell, supra, at 128; O'Lone v. Estate of Shabazz, 482 U.S. 342, 350; and they enjoy the protections of due process, Wolff v. McDonnell, 418 US. 539; Haines v. Kerner, 404 U.

At the time petitioner provided the incriminating statements at issue, his Sixth Amendment right to counsel with respect to the charged offense had attached and had been invoked. However, that right is offense specific and cannot be invoked once for all future prosecutions. Therefore, it poses no bar to the admission of the statements in this case. Petitioner also claims that his statements were inadmissible because he had invoked his Fifth Amendment right to remain silent and his right to counsel under Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U. S. 436, and that any subsequent waiver of these rights during police-initiated questioning regarding any offense was invalid. Held: Petitioner's Sixth Amendment right to counsel and his Miranda-Edwards "Fifth Amendment" right to counsel are distinct interests that cannot be combined. As to the latter, the Edwards rule applies only when the suspect has expressed his wish for the particular sort of lawyerly assistance that is the subject of Miranda. A request for counsel at a bail hearing does not bear that construction. Moreover, the holding in Michigan v. Jackson, 475 U. S. 625, that, after the Sixth Amendment right to counsel attaches and is invoked, any statements obtained from the accused during subsequent police-initiated custodial questioning regarding the charge at issue (even if the accused purports to waive his rights) are inadmissible, rests upon the distinction between the Sixth Amendment and Miranda-Edwards rights. Even assuming that the assertion of the Sixth Amendment right to counsel implies an assertion of the Miranda-Edwards right, it would not be wise to exercise the expansive power to make such an assumption as a matter of sound policy. Such a rule would seriously impede effective law enforcement. Certiorari granted; 152 Wis. 2d 1, 446 N. W. 2d 42, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment ordering Mid Atlantic Medical Services, Inc. to pay $74,869.37 in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, Mid Atlantic agreed to settle a civil action brought by the Sereboffs, who were involved in an automobile accident in California.  The complaint alleges that Mid Atlantic sought a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to prevent the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Mid Atlantic also agreed to a lien on a portion of the settlement that it owed to a third party.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants agreed to pay a total of $75,000, which is equal to the amount Mid Atlantic paid to them.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against Mid Atlantic.  On May 24, 2018, the U. S. District Judge for the Northern District of California entered a judgment that permanently enjoins Mid Atlantic from violating these provisions, ordering it to disgorge its ill-gotten gains plus interest, pay civil penalties, and pay a civil penalty of $7,500, and appoint a receiver to oversee Mid Atlantic’s litigation.   The SEC also ordered Mid Atlantic to provide a copy of the judgment, which was entered by the court on May 25, 2018.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington granted summary judgment in favor of two salmon canneries, finding that the companies had not violated the anti-discrimination provisions of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Equal Employment Opportunity Act of 1974 by failing to show that their practices were "fair in form but discriminatory in practice"<n>The court also found that the defendants had not shown that they were liable for the disparate impact of their hiring practices. The court concluded that the parties had not established that they had violated the provisions of Section 10(b) of the Equal Protection Act of 1963. The court also concluded that there was no evidence that the employers had violated Section 15(a)(1) of the Fair Employment and Equal Pay Act of 1963, and that the employer's practices were not subject to the disparate-impact theory. The parties agreed that the court's findings of fact would be sufficient to determine that the employment practices of the two companies were fair in form and discriminatory. The companies also agreed that they did not have to show they violated Section 17(a), which provides for the protection of workers from discrimination based on their race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.

After petitioner companies reported to the Immigration and Naturalization Services (INS) that respondents, undocumented aliens employed by petitioners, had engaged in concerted activity prohibited by the National Labor Relations Act (Act), the INS took steps leading to the deportation of respondents. Thereafter, the National Labor Relations Board (Board) found that petitioners had committed an unfair labor practice by discouraging union organizing through their actions toward respondents, and ordered petitioners to cease and desist from such behavior and to take such affirmative action as would effectuate the Act's policies, including reinstating respondents with or without backpay. The Court of Appeals, while sustaining the Board's finding of an unfair labor practice, modified the Board's order by ordering petitioners to pay each respondent $6,000 in backpay for at least six months, and by requiring petitioners to draft the reinstatement offers in Spanish and to ensure verification of receipt. Held: 1. The Board's finding of an unfair labor practice is sustained. Pp. 10-13. (a) The Board's interpretation of the Act as embracing undocumented aliens is reasonable, and is not inconsistent with the Immigration and Nationality Act. Pp. 10-11. (b) An employer's use of undocumented aliens does not automatically render him immune from liability under the Act. P. 11. (c) Reporting undocumented aliens to the INS is not per se an unfair labor practice. P. 12. (d) The Board's finding that petitioners' reports led to the deportation of respondents is sufficient proof that petitioners acted intentionally to discourage union organizing. P. 12. 2. The Court of Appeals exceeded its limited authority under the Act by modifying the Board's order to provide that each respondent would receive backpay for at least six months on the ground that six months is a reasonable assumption as to the minimum time during which the respondents might reasonably have remained employed without fear of deportation, but for petitioners' unfair labor practice. Pp. 13-16. (a) The Court of Appeals' award of a minimum amount of backpay in the complete absence of record evidence as to the circumstances of the individual respondents constituted pure speculation and did not comport with the Act's general reparative policies. Pp. 13-15. (b) Compliance proceedings provide the appropriate forum where the Board and petitioners will be able to offer concrete evidence as to the amounts of backpay, if any, to which the respondents are individually entitled. P. 15. (c) Implementation of the Board's traditional remedies at the compliance proceedings must be conditioned upon the respondents' legal readmission to the United States. Pp. 15-16. 3. The Court of Appeals likewise exceeded its limited authority by modifying the Board's order so as to require petitioners to draft the reinstatement offers in Spanish and to ensure verification of receipt. Pp. 16-17. 4. The Court of Appeals had no justifiable basis for displacing the Board's discretionary judgment about the proper time period for acceptance of the reinstatement offers, and should have remanded the case to the Board to consider the alternative grounds on which the Court of Appeals believed the offers to have been deficient and to decide upon new forms for the reinstatement offers. P. 17. 672 F. 2d 599, reversed in part and remanded.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 provides that "[i]n any action or proceeding under this title ... aggravated by a discriminatory employment practice .. , the plaintiff shall recover . . . actual damages . . . not less than $100 . . . or punitive damages . . . not less than $500 . . . or such amount of liquidated damages as may be fixed by the court for the failure of the defendant to comply with a preliminary injunction or temporary restraining order obtained by the plaintiff." Respondent, a former employee of the Department of Agriculture, brought this action under Title VII against petitioners, current and former Department officials, alleging that he suffered discrimination in violation of Title VII. The District Court awarded respondent nominal damages, concluding that petitioners were not liable for damages because they enjoyed absolute immunity from liability for their actions. The Court of Appeals reversed, reasoning that petitioners were not entitled to absolute immunity because they were not members of the judiciary, and that they were instead entitled to only a qualified immunity. Held: 1. Persons subject to the restrictions and performing adjudicatory functions within a federal agency are entitled to absolute immunity from damages liability for their judicial acts. Pp. 489-495. (a) Adjudication within a federal administrative agency shares enough of the characteristics of the judicial process that those who participate in such adjudication should also be immune from suits for damages. Pp. 489-493. (b) Agency officials performing certain functions analogous to those of a prosecutor should be able to claim absolute immunity with respect to such acts. Pp. 493-495. 2. An agency attorney who arranges for the presentation of evidence on the record in the course of an adjudication is absolutely immune from suits based on the introduction of such evidence. P. 495. 535 F. 2d 688, vacated and remanded.

Minnesota, by a law originally enacted in 1955 and revised in 1976 and again in 1978, permits taxpayers to claim a deduction from gross income for certain expenses incurred in providing for the education of their children. The deduction is limited to actual expenses incurred for the "tuition, textbooks and transportation" of dependents attending elementary or secondary schools. A deduction may not exceed $500 per dependent in grades K through six and $700 per dependent, grades seven through twelve. Petitioners-certain Minnesota taxpayers-sued in Federal District Court claiming that § 290.09 (22) violated the Establishment Clause by providing financial assistance to sectarian institutions. The District Court granted respondents' motion for summary judgment, holding that the statute was neutral on its face and in its application and does not have a primary effect of either advancing or inhibiting religion. On appeal, the Court of Appeals affirmed, concluding that the Minnesota statute substantially benefited a "broad class of Minnesota citizens." Held: The Minnesota tax deduction for educational expenses satisfies the primary effect inquiry of the Establishment Clauses. Pp. 514-521. (a) The tax deduction is available only as a result of decisions of individual parents no "imprimatur of State approval," Widmar v. Vincent, 454 U. S. 263, and the "three-part" test laid down in the Lemon framework. P. 515. (b) The statute does not "excessively entangle" the state in religion. The only plausible source of the "comprehensive, discriminating, and continuing state surveillance" necessary to run afoul of this standard would lie in the fact that state officials must determine whether particular textbooks qualify for a deduction. In making this decision, state officials are required to disallow deductions taken from "instructional books and materials used in the teaching of religious tenets, doctrines or worship, the purpose of which is to inculcate such tenets." Madden v. Kentucky, 309 U.S. 83, 87, 60 S.Ct. 406, 407, 84 L.Ed. 2d 745. The general nature of the inquiry in this area has been guided, since the decision in Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U . S. 602, to the principle that a tax deduction fairly equalizes the tax burden of its citizens and encourages desirable expenditures for educational purposes is entitled to substantial deference. See, e. g., Wolman v. Walter, supra, at 782, n. 38. The same result follows in this case, where the tax deduction adopted by Minnesota is more similar to the type of tax deduction established by Nyquist, and where the statute is only one among many deductions-such as those for medical expenses, Minn. Stat. § 290 .09(10), charitable contributions, and charitable contributions. P p. 516-517. (c) The fact that the tax deductions are available for educational costs incurred by all parents, including those whose children attend public schools and those whose own children attend nonsectarian private schools or sectarian private schools, does not mean that they are exempt from § 290's "primary effect of advancing the sectarian aims of the nonpublic schools." Nor does the fact of the statute that, notwithstanding the facial neutrality of § 290, in application, the statute primarily benefits religious institutions, which are not readily subject to challenge under the Clause. Moreover, the deduction is not available for the educational expenses incurred by parents of children attending parochial schools, since, as here, the bulk of deductions taken under §290.09(22) will be claimed by parents' children in sectarian schools. The statute also provides no more than a helpful signpost in dealing with Establishment Clause challenges, since a plausible secular purpose for the state's program may be discerned from the statute's face. The statutory provision of a forum neutrally "open to a broad class of nonreligious as well as religious speakers" plainly serves this secular purpose of ensuring that the State's citizenry is well-educated. Nor does it encompass the sort of attenuated financial benefit, ultimately controlled by the private choices ofindividual parents, that eventually flows to parochials from the neutrality of a facially neutral law on annual reports reciting the extent to which various classes of private citizens claimed benefits under the law. See also Wolman, supra

A state university has established a policy whereby it permits various student groups to use its meeting rooms, subject to certain restrictions, including a regulation prohibiting the use of University buildings or grounds "for purposes of religious worship or religious teaching." When petitioner religious group, consisting entirely of students enrolled at the university, requested permission to continue using the meeting rooms, the university denied the request on the ground that the regulation precluded such use. Thereafter, eleven members of the group filed suit challenging the regulation as violative of their rights to free exercise of religion, equal protection, and freedom of speech under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. The Federal District Court upheld the regulation, finding it justified, inter alia, by the Establishment Clause of the Federal Constitution. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, viewing the regulation as a content-based discrimination against religious speech, for which it could find no compelling justification. Held: The university's exclusionary policy violates the fundamental principle that a state regulation of speech should be content-neutral, and the university is unable to justify this violation under applicable constitutional standards. Pp. 108-116. (a) Here, the university has discriminated against student groups and speakers based on their desire to use a generally open forum to engage in religious worship and discussion, which are forms of speech and association protected by the First Amendment. To justify discriminatory exclusion from a public forum based on the religious content of a group's intended speech, the university must demonstrate that its regulation is necessary to serve a compelling state interest and that it is narrowly drawn to achieve that end. Pp. 108-110. (b) The university's claim that it cannot offer its facilities to religious groups and speakers on the same terms available to other groups without violating the Establishment Clause of the Federal Constitution is not persuasive. Although the university has opened its facilities for use by student groups, the question is whether it can now exclude groups because of the content of their speech. Any religious benefits of an open forum at the university would be "incidental" within the meaning of this Court's cases, since the forum does not confer any imprimatur of state approval on religious sects or practices, and since the forum is available to a broad class of nonreligious as well as religious speakers. Thus, the advancement of religion would not be the forum's "primary effect." Moreover, although the university contends that the State of Missouri has gone further than the Federal Constitution in proscribing indirect state support for religion, it is unnecessary to determine how the Missouri courts would decide this issue, since the State's interest in achieving greater separation of church and State than is already ensured under the Establishment Clause of the Federal Constitution is not sufficiently compelling to justify content-based discrimination against respondent students' religious speech. Pp. 110-115. 635 F. 2d 1278, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant in contempt of court for failing to comply with a court order to hold him in contempt.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that the defendant violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, the defendant refused to answer the questions put to him by the grand jury, and instead refused to respond to the subpoena.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the defendant.  As alleged, the court had no choice but to impose criminal contempt proceedings against him at once, under the provisions of Rule 42(b)(5).  The complaint further alleges that when the defendant first refused to comply, he was guilty of no contempt, because he had no immunity from prosecution under the applicable federal law.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, the Defendant has consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, orders him to pay a civil penalty of 15 months' imprisonment, and imposes a five-year officer-and-director bar against him.   The judgment also orders the defendant to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest and a $1,000 civil penalty.

In the Farm Credit Act of 1933, 48 Stat. 257, as amended, 12 U. S. C. 2001 et seq., Congress created various lending institutions to meet the credit needs of farmers. Among these institutions were banks for cooperatives, one in each of 12 farm credit districts, and a Central Bank for Cooperatives. These banks were designed to make loans to cooperative associations engaged in marketing farm products, purchasing farm supplies, or furnishing farm services. The Farm Credit System includes banks for cooperative associations, production credit associations, farm credit banks, and federal land bank associations. The provision applicable to a bank for cooperativeatives, the institution at issue in this case, states: "Each bank for ... cooperatives and its obligations are instrumentalities of the United States and as such any and all notes, debentures, and other obligations issued by such bank shall be exempt, both as to principal and interest from all taxation (except surtaxes, estate, inheritance, and gift taxes) now or hereafter imposed by the States or any State, territorial, or local taxing authority, except that interest on such obligations shall be subject to Federal income taxation in the holder's hands." The Director of Revenue of Missouri denied the request. On appeal, the Administrative Hearing Commission upheld the Director's assessment of corporate income tax, because the National Bank for Cooperativeatives had not established that it was a federal instrumentality statutorily exempt from state taxation of its income. The Commission reasoned that Congress intended to confer upon banks for co-operatives the same immunity that was provided to farm-credit banks and federal-land bank associations, it would have done so expressly. For jurisdictional reasons, the commission did not decide CoBank's constitutional claim. The Missouri Supreme Court reversed the Commission's decision and held that banks are subject to state income taxation unless Congress has expressly waived this immunity. The New Mexico Court of Appeals and the Indiana Supreme Court have reached the opposite conclusion with respect to state taxation. Held: 1. The National Bank is not exempt from State income taxation under McCulloch v. Maryland, 4 Wheat. 316 (1819). Pp. 521-532. 2. The deletion of the two sentences within 2134 that, first, exempted a bank from state taxes and, second, limited that exemption to periods when the Governor held stock in the bank. This is not a radical-but entirely implicit-change in the taxation of banks' taxation with the 1985 amendment to 2134. The amendment was merely one of numerous "technical and conforming amendments" to the Farm credit Act, which Congress had expressly designated as "instrumentalities" of the States. P. 532. (a) The deletion eliminated the express statutory authorization for such taxation, and it would be surprising, indeed, if Congress had eliminated this important fact sub silentio. (b) The structure of the Act confirms that banks for the cooperatives are subject. With respect to each lending institution, the Act contains a taxation provision that specifically delineates the immunity from taxation enjoyed by that entity. For example, farm and land bank association receive the type of immunity that the Missouri Supreme Supreme Court held to be implied here for banks' capital, reserves, and surplus thereof, and the income derived therefrom, and that exemption provided herein shall not apply to any ... bank for cooper

After respondents were indicted on federal drug charges, they sought discovery on the grounds that the prosecutor had singled them out for prosecution because of their race. The District Court entered an order granting the requested relief, but the Government appealed. Ultimately, the Court of Appeals vacated the order, concluding that the Government had satisfied its burden of proving that it had not engaged in selective prosecution. Held: The Court of Appeals erred in reaching that conclusion. Pp. 12-21. (a) The Government satisfies its burden of proving that it has not engaged in selective prosecution if it shows that it did not fail to prosecute similarly situated individuals of other races. Although the Court of Appeals correctly identified the two essential components of a selective-prosecution claim-discriminatory effect and discriminatory intent-it erred in ruling that the Government need not show that it has failed to prosecute similarly situated individuals of other races. That showing is necessary to ensure that the Government has not abused its prosecutorial discretion. Pp. 12-16. (b) The Court of Appeals also erred in concluding that respondents had not shown a sufficient basis for establishing a discriminatory effect. Such a showing requires that respondents produce some evidence that similarly situated defendants of other races could have been prosecuted, but were not, and this requirement adequately balances the Government's interest in vigorous prosecution and the defendant's interest in avoiding selective prosecution. Here, however, respondents' "study" did not constitute "some evidence tending to show the existence of the essential elements of" a selective-prosecution claim. Their evidence in opposition to the Government's motion for reconsideration was irrelevant to an allegation of discrimination in decisions to prosecute. And their affidavits recounted hearsay and reported personal conclusions based on anecdotal evidence. Pp. 16-21. Reversed and remanded.

Petitioner Marrama filed a voluntary petition under Chapter 7, thereby creating an estate consisting of all his property “wherever located and by whomever held.” Petitioner Citizens Bank of Massachusetts (hereinafter Bank) is the trustee. In verified schedules attached to his petition, Marrama made a number of statements about his principal asset, a house in Maine, that were misleading or inaccurate. For instance, while he disclosed that he was the sole beneficiary of the trust that owned the property, he listed its value as zero. He also denied that he had transferred any property other than in the ordinary course of business during the year preceding the filing of his petition. Marrama later admitted that the purpose of the transfer was to protect the property from his creditors. After Marrama’s examination at the meeting of creditors, see 11 U. S. C. §341, the trustee advised Marrama that he intended to recover the Maine property as an asset of the estate. Thereafter, thereafter, the notice of conversion was treated as a motion to convert, to which both the trustee and the Bank filed objections. Relying primarily on Marrama, the Bankruptcy Court rejected his conversion request. On appeal from the panel, the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit also rejected the argument that §706(a) gives a Chapter 7 debtor an absolute right to convert to Chapter 13. Held: The Court correctly held that Marrama forfeited his right to proceed under Chapter 13 under the plain language of §706 (a) of the Code. Pp. 5–7. (a). (b) Section706(d) provides that a Chapter 13 proceeding may be either dismissed or converted to a Chapter 11 proceeding “for cause” and includes a nonexclusive list of 10 causes justifying that relief. The text of §§706(c) and (c) provides adequate authority for the denial of his motion. Since the sufficiency of the evidence of bad faith is not at issue, this Court may assume that the debtor did have more income available when he sought to convert than when he commenced the Chapter 7 case. In the former context, despite the absence of any statutory provision specifically addressing the issue, the bankruptcy court has unquestioned authority to dismiss a chapter 13 petition—as distinguished from converting the case to chapter 13—based upon a showing of “bad faith’ on the debtor.’ ” In re Marrama. 430 F. 3d 474, 479. While other Courts of Appeals and bankruptcy appellate panels have refused to recognize any exception to the conversion right created by §706’a, see n. 2, supra, the courts in this case concluded that the courts’ decision to dismiss the Chapter 13 case was not based on a procedural anomaly. P. 5. (1) The two provisions of the bankruptcy Code most relevant to this resolution are subsections (a), (d), and (e), which provide: “Only an individual with regular income that owes, on the date of the filing, unsecured debts of less than $250,000 and noncontingent, liquidated, secured debts at any time, if the case has not been converted under section 1112, 1208, or 1307 of this title. Any waiver of that right is unenforceable,” §105(a). The broad authority granted to bankruptcy judges to take any action that is necessary or appropriate “to prevent an abuse of process” described in §105 (a)(3) is surely adequate to authorize an immediate denial of a motion filed under §706 in lieu of a conversion order that merely postpones the allowance of equivalent relief and may provide a debtor with an opportunity to take action prejudicial to creditors. Moreover, as the Solicitor General has argued in his brief amicus curiae brief, even if §105 had not been enacted, the inherent power of every federal court to sanction “abusive litigation practices” might well provide an adequate justification for a prompt, rather than a delayed, ruling on an unmeritorious attempt to qualify as a debtor in Chapter 13, and §1307(c), which provides, in relevant part, that the court may convert a case under this chapter to a case “under this chapter, whichever is in the best interests of creditors and the debtor” if the debtor may be a debtor under such chapter. The provision also provides that, “Except as provided in subsection (e) of this section, on request of a party in interest or the United States trustee and after notice and a hearing, the court’ll convert a [case] under this Chapter to a [chapter] case under chapter 7 of this Title, or may dismiss a (case) under that title, whichever . . . is the best interest of the debtor, and may issue any order, process, or judgment that is appropriate to carry out the provisions of §105. In 1960, the Cuban Government confiscated the business and assets of five leading manufacturers of Havana cigars. The Cuban Government named "interventors" to take possession of and operate the business of the seized Cuban concerns. Interventors continued to ship cigars to foreign purchasers, including the United States importers. The former owners of the Cuban companies, most of whom had fled to the States, brought various actions against the three American importers for trademark infringement and for the purchase price of any cigars that had been shipped to importers from the seized plants and that bore United States trademarks claimed by the former owners to be their property. Following the conclusion of the related litigation in F. Palicio y Compania, S.A. v. Brush, ante, p. 527, the District Court held that the Cuban interventors were entitled to recover the sums due them from the importers by way of set-off against the amounts due from them for postintervention purchases. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the obligation to repay had a situs in Cuba and had been repudiated in the course of litigation by conduct that was sufficiently official to be deemed an act of state. Held: 1. The mere refusal of the interventor to repay funds followed by a failure to prove that interventORS were not acting within the scope of their authority as agents of the Cuba government satisfied respondents' burden of establishing their act of State defense. Menendez v. Faver, Coe & Gregg, Inc., 345 F. 2d 527 (SDNY 1972), and in closely related litigatn, F.Palicio yCompania, supra, pp. 526-527 (CA2), which held that it was required to give full legal effect to the 1960 confiscation of the five cigar companies insofar as it purported to take the property of Cuban nationals located within Cuba. Pp. 529-529. (a) The mere assertion of sovereignty as a defense to a claim arising out of purely commercial acts by a foreign sovereign is no more effective if given the label "Act of State" than if it is given a label "sovereign immunity." Underhill v. Hernandez, 168 U. S. 250, this Court has on two occasions expressed to courts in this country its views concerning acts of state adjudications. First, in the Sabbatino case, the Executive Branch declined to make a determination under the Hickenlooper Amendment that application of the Act of State doctrine is required in this case by the foreign policy interests. Second, in that case, a party claimed to have had the authority to exercise sovereign power, but the only authority shown is commercial authority. In both cases, the parties were denied the right to return the money. P. 529. (b) In the event that the Court reaches the question whether the Sabbataino holding should be reconsidered, the Court should not so act as to embarrass the executive arm in its conduct of foreign affairs, since it is unlikely to touch very sharply on "national nerves," since the courts are less likely to allow a plea of sovereign immunity where the executive has declined to do so, and since there is no basis for assuming that the master of the Gul Djemal possessed such authority. Moreover, the fact that subjecting foreign governments to the rule of law in their commercial dealings presents a much smaller risk of affronting their sovereignty than would an attempt to pass on the legality of their governmental acts, and that such adjudications are consistent with international law on sovereign immunity, does not mean that the courts should not anticipate embarrassment to the conduct of the Foreign Policy of the United S. A.

Case Name: Johnson v. Railway Clerk's Association
Case Number: 06-1176
Decided Date: June 25, 2007
Supreme Court Justices: Roberts, Scalia, Thomas, Kennedy, Breyer, Alito, Sotomayor
Summary: The Supreme Court holds that a collective bargaining agreement that clearly and unmistakably requires union members to arbitrate age discrimination claims is enforceable as a matter of federal law. The Court finds that the ADEA does not contain any language or structure that would render arbitration unsuitable for resolving age discrimination claims. The Court also rejects the notion that the ADEA contains a "right" to a judicial forum that cannot be waived. Instead, the Court views the ADEA as providing a procedural framework for addressing age discrimination claims, which can be modified through collective bargaining agreements.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment in favor of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in a related case.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New England, alleges that, in 2006, the Commission improperly concluded that a contract rate was unjust and unreasonable.  According to the complaint, the contract rate is a precondition to changing a rate, not an authorization to do so in violation of a lawful contract.  For example, the complaint alleges that the Commission had suggested that, when a contract is challenged by a non-contracting party, a new contract rate should be filed with the Commission.  In its order approving the settlement, the court held that the Mobile-Sierra presumption applies only to contracts that meet the just and reasonable standard.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, FERC has agreed to the settlement. The settlement is subject to court approval, and the court will determine the amount of disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties to be determined by the court upon motion of the SEC. The SEC also agreed to a judgment that permanently enjoins the Commission from future violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the Commission to pay a civil penalty of $100,000. The court also granted the Commission the right to appoint a receiver to oversee the receiver. Respondents, who resided in New York, purchased a new Audi automobile from petitioner Volkswagen of America, Inc. (Volkswagen) in Massena, N. Y., in 1976. As they passed through Oklahoma, another car struck their Audi in the rear, causing a fire which severely burned the Robinsons and their two children. Respondents brought a products-liability action in Oklahoma state court, claiming that their injuries resulted from defective design and placement of the Audi's gas tank and fuel system. The District Court denied their motion for reconsideration, holding that personal jurisdiction over petitioners was authorized by Oklahoma's "longarm" statute Okla. Stat., Tit. 12, § 1701.03(a)(4) (1971). The Oklahoma Supreme Court denied the writ. Held: 1. The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment limits the power of a state court to render a valid personal judgment against a nonresident defendant when the defendant's only connection with Oklahoma is the fact that an automobile sold in Oklahoma to New York residents became involved in an accident in Oklahoma. Pp. 5-11. (a) The fact that petitioners have no "contacts, ties, or relations" with the State of Oklahoma does not preclude the exercise of in personam jurisdiction over them. P. 5. (b) The protection against inconvenient litigation is typically described in terms of "reasonableness" or "fairness." The concept of minimum contacts, in turn, can be seen to perform two related, but distinguishable functions. It protects the defendant against the burdens of litigating in a distant or inconvenient forum, and it acts to ensure that the States through their courts, do not reach out beyond the limits imposed on them by their status as coequal sovereigns in a federal system. In addition, the protection of inconvenient litigation, by ensuring the orderly administration of the laws, gives a degree of predictability to the legal system that allows potential defendants to structure their primary conduct with some minimum assurance as to where that conduct will and will not render them liable to suit. In the absence of affiliating circumstances that are a necessary predicate to any exercise of state-court jurisdiction, petitioners carry on no activity whatsoever in Oklahoma, close no sales and perform no services there. They avail themselves of none of the privileges and benefits of Oklahoma law. They solicit no business there either through salespersons or through dealers, and they do not seek to exercise a power of appointment in a child-support action over the former husband who had remained in Oklahoma with the wife. The court's rationale was contained in the following paragraph, 585 P. 2d 351, at 354: "In the case before us, the product being sold and distributed by the petitioners is by its very design and purpose so mobile that petitioner can foresee its possible use in Oklahoma." P. 6. (c) The Due process Clause does not contemplate that a state may make binding a judgment in person against an individual or corporate defendant with which the state has no contacts, ties or relations." International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U. S. 319, 319, at 319. It is a mistake to assume that this trend heralds the eventual demise of all restrictions on the personal jurisdiction of state courts, since those restrictions are more than a guarantee of immunity from inconvenient or distant litigation, and are a consequence of territorial limitations on power of the respective States. The due Process Clause, in its role as an instrument of interstate federalism, may sometimes act to divest a State of its power to render an invalid judgment. Hanson v. Denckla, 357 U.S. 235, 250-251, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a California-based manufacturer of seatbelts for passenger vehicles.  The SEC's complaint alleges that, in 2002, a California court found that the Department of Transportation (DOT) improperly required manufacturers to install lap-and-shoulder belts on seats next to a vehicle’s doors or frames.  According to the complaint, the SEC also found that, because many car occupants did not “buckle up,” they would be more likely to use those belts when riding in the rear.  In addition, the complaint alleged that the federal government had rejected an "all airbag” rule that required car seat belts on rear aisle seats.  As alleged in the SEC complaint, however, the federal regulation did not pre-empt the state tort suit.  Instead, it provided manufacturers with a choice of whether to install a lap or a lap belt, without admitting or denying the SEC's findings.  For example, in Geier v. American Honda Motor Co., 518 U. S. 470, 502–503 (1941), the SEC found that manufacturer choice was an important means for achieving its basic objectives.  Specifically, the court held that, by requiring manufacturers to provide lap and shoulder belts, a federal safety standard does not preclude a manufacturer from violating the pre-emption provisions of the federal law, and that manufacturers should not be liable for failure to install such a safety standard.  Further, the Court found that a separate, earlier version of the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208 (FMVSS 208) did not preempt a state tort action that sought to hold an auto manufacturer liable for failing to install any kind of passive restraint, namely, airbags.   The court also ruled that a later version of FMVSS 206 (1984) precluded the imposition of a federal "minimum standard" for rear seat belts, but did not rule out the possibility that it could impose a "pre-emptive injunction" on manufacturers who did not comply with the federal requirements.  On the same day that the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against General Motors Corp., the SEC issued an order imposing a temporary restraining order against the company, which it deemed to be violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering the company to pay a civil penalty of $1,000,000. In 1990, faced with the choice of either curtailing its Medicaid program or generating additional revenue to reduce the program deficit, the New York General Assembly enacted the Health Facility Assessment (HFA). The HFA imposes a tax on gross receipts for patient services at hospitals, residential health care facilities, and diagnostic and treatment centers. The assessments become a part of the State's general revenues. Respondents are the trustees of the NYSA-ILA Medical and Clinical Services Fund (the Fund), which administers a self-insured, multiemployer welfare benefit plan. The Fund owns and operates three medical centers-two in New York and one in New Jersey-that provide medical, dental and other health care benefits primarily to longshore workers, retirees, and their dependents. The New York centers are licensed by the State as "diagnostic and treatment Centers," App. 80, and are subject to a 0.6 percent tax on the income of medical centers operated by ERISA funds. Respondent hospitals paid HFA assessments totaling $7,066 based on the two New York hospitals' patient care income of $1,177,670. At that time, they discontinued the payments and brought this action against appropriate state officials to enjoin future assessments and to obtain a refund of the tax paid in 1991. The complaint alleged that the HFA is a state law that "relates to'' the Fund within the meaning of §514 (a) of ERISA, and is therefore pre-empted as applied to hospitals run by the Fund. The District Court denied relief. It concluded that HFA was not preempted because it was a "tax of general application" that did not "interfere with the calculation of benefits or the determination of an employee's eligibility for benefits" and thus had only an incidental impact on benefit plans. The Court of Appeals reversed. It distinguished cases in which the text could not be read to "extend to the furthest stretch of its indeterminacy, [or] for all practical purposes preemption would never run its course, for "[r]eally, universally, relations stop nowhere," H. James, Roderick Hudson xli (New York ed., World's Classics 1980). Held: 1. Any state tax, or other law, that increases the cost of providing benefits to covered employees will have some effect on the administration of the ERISA plans, but that simply cannot mean that every state law with such an effect is pre-emption by the federal statute. Hillsborough County v. Automated Medical Laboratories, Inc., 471 U. S. 707, 715. Pp. 521-522. 2. In order to evaluate whether the normal presumption against preemption has been overcome in a particular case, we "must go beyond the unhelpful text and the frustrating difficulty of defining its key term, and look instead to the objectives of [the ERISA statute as a guide to the scope of the state law' that Congress understood would survive.'' Id., at 656, 115 S. C. 1671, 131 L. Ed. 2d 695, reversed.

In the case of Bush v. Palm Beach County Canvassing Board, the U.S. Supreme Court reviewed a decision by the Florida Supreme Court regarding the 2000 presidential election recount. The central issues were whether the Florida Supreme Court's decision violated the Due Process Clause or federal statute 3 U.S.C. § 5, and whether it infringed upon the state legislature's authority under Article II, Section 1, Clause 2 of the U.S. Constitution.

The Florida Supreme Court had extended the deadline for recounting ballots and directed the Secretary of State to accept manual counts submitted before the new deadline. This decision arose from discrepancies in machine and manual recounts and conflicts within Florida's election laws.

The U.S. Supreme Court noted that while it generally defers to state courts on state law interpretation, the state legislature's role in selecting presidential electors is also governed by the U.S. Constitution. The Court referenced 3 U.S.C. § 5, which provides a "safe harbor" for states to have their elector selections be conclusive if determined by laws enacted before election day and resolved at least six days before the electors meet.

The Supreme Court found the Florida Supreme Court's decision to be unclear, particularly regarding the extent to which the Florida Constitution limits the legislature's power and the consideration given to 3 U.S.C. § 5. Consequently, the U.S. Supreme Court vacated the Florida Supreme Court's decision and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, seeking clarification on these points.

The implication of this decision was that the Florida Supreme Court needed to reconsider its ruling in light of the federal constitutional and statutory provisions, ensuring that any changes to the election procedures complied with the legislature's authority and the established federal "safe harbor" provisions.
