Respondents sued in a Federal District Court to condemn certain property needed for the construction of the Trinity River Dam and Reservoir in California, to obtain immediate possession of it, and to secure title to it, the complaint asking that the United States be allowed to reserve authority to have the validity of mining claims determined in administrative proceedings before the Bureau of Land Management of the Department of the Interior. The District Court allowed the States a writ of possession; but no other issues in the action have been determined. The Court of Appeals reversed. Held: 1. The institution of the suit in the District Court was an appropriate way of obtaining immediate possession, that it was not inconsistent with the administrative remedy for determining the validity, and that the court acted properly in holding its hand until the issue of the claims has been resolved by the agency entrusted by Congress with the task. Pp. 542-543. 2. The United States, which holds legal title to public lands, plainly can prescribe the procedure by which claims against the public domain may be perfected. P. 543. 3. A mining claim on public lands is a possessory interest in land that is "mineral in character" and as respects which discovery "within the limits of the claim" has been made. Cameron v. United States. 252 U. S. 450, 456, and United States v. Logomarcini, 60 L. D. 371, 373, distinguished. 4. A claim on a public land is not an unpatented claim, but is valid against the United S. if there has been a discovery of mineral within the limits, if the lands are still mineral, and if other statutory requirements have been met. P p. 544. 293 F. 2d 553, reversed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the petitioner in this case, holding that the use of evidence of the petitioner's own incriminating statements at his trial violated his rights under the Federal Constitution. Specifically, the Court found that the petitioner's Fifth and Sixth Amendment rights were violated by the use in evidence against him of incriminating statements which government agents had deliberately elicited from him after he had been indicted and in the absence of his retained counsel. The Court further held that the petitioner was denied the basic protections of the Sixth Amendment guarantee when there was used against him at his trial evidence of his own incriminating words, which federal agents had deliberately elicited from him after he had been indicted and in the absence of his counsel.

Respondents include three doctors and four medical clinics (two of which are part of larger hospital complexes) in and around Rochester and Buffalo in upstate New York. These health care providers perform abortions and other medical services at their facilities. The complaint alleged that defendants had consistently engaged in illegal blockades and other illegal conduct at facilities in the Western District of New York where abortions were performed. The District Court issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) to stop the blockades, and the complaint also sought a permanent injunction and damages. The court held that the injunction was grounded not only on the §1985(3) claim, but two state-law claims, and that the same conduct that infringed this class of women's constitutional rights under §1985 (3). The court also held that "those women denied unimpeded access to [the clinics] cannot be compensated merely by money damages," and that injunctive relief alone can assure women unimpeed access by way of public streets and sidewalks. Held: The injunction is not content based, even though it was directed only at abortion protesters, because it was only abortion protesters who had done the acts which were being enjoined. Pp. 4-7. (a) The injunction's provisions are clearly crafted to remedy the violations. P. 4. (b) The First Amendment does not require that a court impose a "speech-restrictive" injunction (or TRO) without first trying a "non-speech restriction" or "cease and desist" injunction, as the trial court did in Madsen v. Women's Health Center, Inc., 512 U. S. 753, which also involved the effect of an injunction on the expressive activities of antiabortion protesters. Madsen, supra, held that, because the injunction is based on a number of governmental interests, including protecting a woman's freedom to seek pregnancy-related services, ensuring public safety and order, promoting the free flow of traffic on streets and sidewalk, protecting property rights, and protecting the medical privacy of patients whose psychological and physical well-being were threatened as they were held "captive" by medical circumstance. The combination of these interests was "quite sufficient to justify an appropriately tailored injunction" to protect unimpeding access to the clinic by wayof public streets, sidewalks, and driveways, and, in addition, the fixed buffer zone was a necessary restriction on defendants' demonstrations. The Court of Appeals then heard the case en banc, and affirmed the District Court by a divided vote. P p. 5. 67 F. 3d 377, affirmed in part and reversed in part.

The Low-Level Radioactive Waste Policy Amendments Act of 1985 provides three types of incentives to encourage States to provide for the disposal of low-level radioactive waste generated within their borders. The first type of incentive involves denial of access to disposal sites. States that fail to meet the July 1986 deadline may be charged twice the ordinary surcharge for the remainder of 1986 and may be denied access thereafter. The second type involves denying access to waste generated in States that do not meet federal deadlines. The Secretary of Energy collects a portion of the surcharge and places the money in an escrow account held by the Secretary. The rest of the account is to be paid out to those States or compacts able to dispose of all low level radioactive waste in their borders by January 1, 1993. Each State that has not met the 1993 deadline must either take title or forfeit to the waste generators the incentive payments it has received. The District Court dismissed the complaint, concluding that the Act is inconsistent with the Tenth and Eleventh Amendments to the Constitution, with the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment, and with the Guarantee Clause of Article IV of the Constitution. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The Act does not violate the Tenth Amendment. Pp. 531-532. (a) Where Congress has the authority to require the States to regulate, the departure from the constitutional plan cannot be ratified by the "consent" of state officials. Where Congress exceeds its authority relative to the States, it simply does not give Congress the power to require them to regulate. Where federal regulation of private activity is within the scope of the Commerce Clause, the Federal Government has authority to offer States the choice of regulating that activity according to federal standards or having state law pre-empted by federal regulation. The Supremacy Clause gives Congress the ability to exercise that power through the mechanism of mandating state regulation. Here, Congress has placed conditions-the achievement of the milestones-on the receipt of federal funds. The Act permits a State to choose first between regulating pursuant to federal standard and losing the right to a share of the Secretary's escrow, and then to choose third between regulating under federal standards and progressively losing access to the disposal sites in other States. If a State does not wish to submit a proposed permanent program that complies with the Act and implementing regulations, the full regulatory burden will be borne by the Government. P. 532. 942 F. 2d 114, affirmed.

Section 2 of the Sherman Act makes it unlawful to “monopolize, or attempt to monopolize,” or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolise any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations. Simply possessing monopoly power and charging monopoly prices does not violate §2; rather, the statute targets “the willful acquisition or maintenance of that power as distinguished from growth or development as a consequence of a superior product, business acumen, or historic accident.” United States v. Grinnell Corp., 384 U. S. 563, 570–571. As a general rule, businesses are free to choose the parties with whom they will deal, as well as the prices, terms, and conditions of that dealing. But there are rare instances in which a dominant firm may incur antitrust liability for purely unilateral conduct. See, e. g., United Statesv. Colgate & Co., 250 U.S. 300, 307. To the extent a monopolist violates one of these doctrines, the plaintiffs have a remedy under existing antitrust law. See Covad Communications Co. v. Bell Atlantic Co., 398 F. 3d 666, 673–674. The complaint at issue does not contain allegations meeting those requirements. Rather, it alleges that the defendants (upstream monopolists) abused their power in the wholesale market to prevent rival firms from competing effectively in the retail market. The District Court held that AT&T had no such antitrust duty to deal with its rivals at all, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. A price-squeeze claim may not be brought under §2 when the defendant has no antitrust obligation under the antitrust laws. Pp. 5–7. (a) A price squeeze should be presumed if the upstream monopolist could not have made a profit by selling at its retail rates if it purchased inputs at its own wholesale rates. Trinko, supra, at 222–224. The nub of the complaint is identical-the plaintiffs alleged that they abused their monopoly power to prevent rivals from competition at the wholesale and retail levels. The court held that the plaintiffs’ original complaint stated a potentially valid claim under § 2 of §2. But the reasoning applies with equal force to price-Squeeze claims. To that extent, there is no basis for imposing antitrust liability simply because a vertically integrated firm’s wholesale price happens to be greater than or equal to its retail price. If the wholesale price does not satisfy the requirements of Brooke Group, then a firm is certainly not required to price both of these services in a manner that preserves its rivals’ profit margins. See Town of Concord v. Boston Edison Co., 915 F. 2d 17, 25 (CA1 1990). The problem, however, is that amici have not identified any independent competitive harm caused by price squeezes above and beyond the harm that would result from a duty-to-deal violation at wholesale or predatory pricing at the retail level. See United States-v. Aluminum Co. of America, 148 F.2d 416 (Alcoa), at 225–224, and there are also limited circumstances in which an antitrust duty may be imposed if the retail pricing does not meet the requirements. See Aspen Skiing Co., v. Aspen Highlands Skiing Corp., 472 U.K. 585, 608–611. In the absence of a decision from this Court on the merits, the case will remain a live dispute appropriate for decision. Cf. Friends of Earth, Inc. v., Laidlaw Environmental Services (TOC), Inc., 528 U. . . . 189, 189. The case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Georgia today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was convicted of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Atlanta, Georgia, alleges that Art Garfunkel, who was the manager of the theater where the film was being shown, was convicted in March 1972 of the same charge and sentenced to 12 months' probation.  According to the complaint, the film "Carnal Knowledge" is not obscene under the First and Fourteenth Amendments because it is not part of the "community standards" set forth in Miller. The complaint further alleges that the film's subject matter is, in a broader sense, "hard core" pornography. The film is about two college men, roommates and lifelong friends forever preoccupied with their sex lives. Both are first met as virgins. Both men are in their thirties, pursuing successful careers in New York, when they meet in a movie theater. As alleged in the complaint: "The movie is about hard core sexual conduct for its own sake, and for the ensuing commercial gain." The movie is a classic example of how the First Amendment does not protect the commercial exhibition of 'hard core' pornography." The complaint alleges that, in the movie, Nicholson has been running through an average of a dozen women a year but has never managed to meet the right one, the one with the full bosom, the good legs, the properly rounded bottom, during these scenes. The movie also features a scene in which Nicholson falls in love with the lovely Susan (Candice Bergen) and unknowingly shares her with her college buddy. The jury, having seen the film and heard testimony, returned a general verdict of guilty on March 23, 1972.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal obscenity laws, requires him to pay a civil penalty of $750, and orders him to be barred from appearing or practicing before the SEC as a public figure. The court also ordered him to comply with the entry-of-the-judgment order.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Georgia today announced criminal charges against Appellant. The SEC is continuing its investigation into the matter. The case is being handled by Jennifer C. McKinley, John R. Rymas, and Amy C. Welshhans of the Atlanta office.

Respondents, a class of interstate motor carriers whose vehicles travel billions of miles on Pennsylvania's highways every year, brought separate actions in the Commonwealth Court challenging the constitutionality of two taxes imposed on interstate truckers for the privilege of using a State's highway system. In each case, appellants argued that the entire economic burden of each tax fell on out-of-state vehicles because the 1980 statute "deemed" the marker fee for Pennsylvania vehicles to be a part of the registration fee, and the 1982 legislation granted Pennsylvania vehicles a reduction in registration fees that neatly offset the newly imposed axle tax. The State Supreme Court upheld the taxes, interpreting them as facially neutral and in accord with a line of decisions in the pre-Spector era approving flat taxes on the operation of trucks and truck tractors. The Commonwealth Court overruled defendants' exceptions to the trial judge's order. Held: 1. The flat taxes do not discriminate against interstate commerce. Pp. 479-481. (a) The fact that the marker and axle taxes are wholly unlike those imposed by the other taxes does not mean that the flat taxes are discriminatory. P. 478. (b) The way in which a tax levied on participants in interstate commerce is measured and assessed bears directly on whether it implicates central Commerce Clause values. The method of assessing the markers and axle tax on Pennsylvania-based vehicles and on other vehicles establishes that the State is not treating the two types of vehicles with an even hand. The distinction between the State's registration fees and fuel taxes is also dispositive in Spector Motor Service, Inc. v. O'Connor, 340 U. S. 602, which held that a flat tax on interstate commerce causes no impermissible interference with interstate commerce because every State respects the registration of every other State, and is not a tax on sales or use. Moreover, even if the statute had not explicitly provided that Pennsylvania-registered vehicles are regarded as having paid a marker fee, the simultaneous increase in the registration fees when the $25 marker fee was enacted made itapparent that the fee does not work any discrimination against interstate Commerce in practical operation. The distinctions between the state's fees and the fees are distinguishable in two ways. First, the amount of Pennsylvania's marker and the axle taxes owed by a trucker does not vary directly with miles traveled or with some other proxy for value obtained from the State. Second, the amounts of the reductions in all classes were a multiple of the $36 per axle which is used as the measure for the axle tax; whether the shipment crossed a state border was irrelevant to the magnitude of the tax burden imposed by Montana. The third, the method of determining the fees' effect on the number of miles traveled in Pennsylvania and in other States, does not show that the state is imposing an undue burden on the interstate commerce that it does not impose on its own residents who also engage in commerce among States. Although out of-state and in-state carriers obtain a privilege to use Pennsylvania's roads when considered alongside the high price that Pennsylvania's truck-trucks pay, imposition of the flat tax for a privilege that is several times more valuable to a local business than to its out ofstate competitors is unquestionably discriminatory and thus offends the Commerce Clause. The fourth, and most important, distinction between a state's registration fee and fuel tax is not dispositive because it exerts an inexorable hydraulic pressure on interstate businesses to ply their trade within the State that enacted the measure rather than "among the several States." P. 579. (c) A State's imposition of an unapportioned flat tax, unlike the neutral user fee in Evansville-Vanderburgh Airport Authority District v. Delta Airlines, Inc., 405 U.S. 707, can no longer suffice to uphold flat taxes with the blatantly discriminatory consequences associated with the marker-fee and axle-tax. The cases in support of the State’s authority to impose flat taxes, while lending support to appellees’ argument, cannot be upheld flat taxes. The Commerce Clause does not require the States to avoid flat taxes when they are the only practicable means of collecting revenues from users and the use of a more finely gradated user-fee schedule would pose genuine administrative burdens. See, e. g., id., at 457, 509 A. 2d 838, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit has ruled that the Department of Labor's admission of daily and seasonal commuters as 'lawfully admitted for permanent residence' is consistent with the meaning of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1961 and other provisions of the law. The court held that the admission of commuters is not in violation of the Act's numerical limitations. The Court also found that the use of the term 'green card' in the entry of these workers is not inconsistent with the terms of the act and other federal immigration laws. The ruling is a significant victory for the agricultural industry, which has long complained about the lack of employment opportunities for workers in the United States.

Respondent CoBank ACB, the successor to all rights and obligations of the National Bank for Cooperatives, which had been formed in 1989 through the consolidation of 10 district banks for cooperatives and the Central Bank for Cooperatives, filed Missouri corporate income tax returns for the years 1991 through 1994 and paid the taxes shown on those returns. In 1996, CoBank filed amended returns on behalf of the National Bank for Cooperatives, requesting an exemption from all state income taxes and refunds on the taxes erroneously paid. Asserting that the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution accords federal instrumentalities immunity from state taxation unless Congress has expressly waived this immunity, CoBank claimed that, because the current version of the Farm Credit Act does not expressly waive this immunity, banks for cooperatives are exempt from Missouri's corporate income tax. The Director of Revenue denied the request. On appeal, the Administrative Hearing Commission upheld the denial, reasoning that Congress did not provide expressly that banks for cooperatives, in contrast to farm credit banks and federal land bank associations, would have immunity from state income taxation. The Missouri Supreme Court reversed, holding that banks for cooperatives are exempt from state income taxation because the Supremacy Clause provides federal instrumentalities immunity from state taxation unless Congress has expressly waived this immunity and because the current version of the Farm Credit Act is silent as to such institutions' immunity from state taxation. Held: The National Bank for Cooperatives is not exempt from state income taxation. Pp. 24-29. (a) An instrumentality is entitled to implied tax immunity only when it is "so closely connected to the Government that the two cannot realistically be viewed as separate entities," United States v. New Mexico, 455 U. S. 720, 735. Here, Congress has provided that banks for cooperatives are subject to state taxation. While nothing in the statute indicates a repeal of the previous express approval of state taxation, the structure of the Farm Credit Act indicates by negative implication that banks for cooperatives are not entitled to immunity. Pp. 24-26. (b) The structure of the Farm Credit Act confirms that banks for cooperatives are subject to state taxation. Each lending institution in the system receives the type of immunity from state taxation that the Missouri Supreme Court held to be implied here for banks for cooperatives. But, unlike banks for cooperatives, farm credit banks and federal land bank associations received the more comprehensive exemption from taxation that Congress had provided elsewhere in the Act. Thus, in light of the structure of the Farm Credit Act-and the explicit grants of immunity to other institutions within the system-Congress' silence with respect to banks for cooperatives indicates that they are subject to state taxation. Pp. 26-29. Reversed and remanded.

Title: Taylor v. Louisiana
Year: 1976
Decision: The Supreme Court ruled that the exclusion of women from jury service in Louisiana violates the Sixth Amendment's right to a fair trial.
Summary: The case involves a man named Taylor who was charged with kidnapping and attempted murder. He requested a jury trial, but the court refused to seat any women on the jury. Taylor argued that this violated his right to a fair trial under the Sixth Amendment, which guarantees the right to a jury trial. The Supreme Court agreed, ruling that the exclusion of women from jury service in Louisiana violates the Sixth Amendment's right to a fair trial. The Court found that women make up approximately half of the eligible voting population in Louisiana and that their exclusion from jury service undermines the principle of a fair cross-section of the community.

In the Supreme Court case under review, the central issue was whether the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment is violated when a redacted confession of a nontestifying codefendant, which omits direct references to the defendant, is introduced at a joint trial and later linked to the defendant by other evidence. This question arises from the precedent set in Bruton v. United States, which established that a defendant's rights are violated when a codefendant's confession naming them is admitted at trial without the opportunity for cross-examination, even if the jury is instructed to consider the confession only against the codefendant.

The case involved Clarissa Marsh, who was convicted of felony murder and assault based on her codefendant's redacted confession and other trial evidence. The confession was admitted with a jury instruction not to use it against Marsh, but the prosecutor later referenced it in relation to Marsh's involvement. The Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed her conviction, applying an "evidentiary linkage" approach to determine that the confession, when considered with other evidence, was incriminating to Marsh and violated her Confrontation Clause rights.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the Sixth Circuit's approach, emphasizing the distinction between a confession that is directly incriminating on its face and one that becomes incriminating only when linked with other evidence. The Court held that the Confrontation Clause is not violated by the admission of a redacted confession with a proper limiting instruction, as long as the confession does not directly implicate the defendant. The Court reasoned that juries are generally presumed to follow instructions, and the risk of them not doing so with inferential incrimination is not as great as with direct incrimination.

The Court also highlighted the practical implications of requiring separate trials or excluding confessions entirely, which would undermine the efficiency and fairness of the criminal justice system. The Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings, instructing the lower court to consider whether the prosecutor's comments, unobjected to by the defense, could serve as the basis for granting a writ of habeas corpus.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision clarified that the Confrontation Clause does not require separate trials or the exclusion of all codefendant confessions, as long as they are properly redacted and accompanied by instructions that prevent the jury from using the confession against the defendant. The decision balances the rights of the defendant with the practical needs of the criminal justice system.

Petitioner was arrested in Spokane, Wash., for robbery and taken to a police station, where he was questioned by officers without benefit of counsel, without being advised of his rights, and without being allowed to call his wife. He was not permitted to make a phone call until he had acceded to demands that he give and sign a written statement. He was held incommunicado for some five or seven days after signing the statement, during which time he was not advised of his rights or warned that his answers might be used against him. He was then allowed to call his wife. The written confession was admitted in evidence at his trial, which resulted in his conviction. 

Held: The admission of the written confession violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, and the conviction is reversed. Pp. 304-316.
	 (a) The record discloses that the written confession was obtained in an atmosphere of substantial coercion and inducement created by statements and actions of state authorities. Pp. 308-312.
	 (b) The fact that the trial judge or the jury may have reached a different result on the issue of voluntariness of the confession does not foreclose this Court's independent determination that the confession was coerced. Pp. 312-315.
	 (c) The fact that the jury was instructed, in effect, not to consider as relevant on the issue of voluntariness of the confession the fact that a defendant is not reminded that he is under arrest, that he is not cautioned that he may remain silent, that he is not warned that his answers may be used against him, or that he is not advised that he is entitled to counsel, is another reason for refusing to consider the present inquiry foreclosed by the verdict of the jury to which the issue of voluntariness of the confession was submitted. Pp. 315-316. 56 Wash. 2d 527, 354 P. 2d 100, reversed and remanded.

Without admitting or denying the allegations in Brecht's complaint, the court also ordered Brecht to pay a $1,000 civil penalty, which he will pay in the amount of $100,000. Office of Justice's Office of Inspector General issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the background of anyone selling or offering them investments in an investment in a real estate development project.  Investors can also check the backgrounds of people selling investments by using the SEC's investor.gov website to quickly identify whether they are registered professionals.

To address pressing issues related to the large number of aliens within its borders who do not have a lawful right to be in the United States, the State of Arizona enacted a statute called the Support Our Law Enforcement and Safe Neighborhoods Act (S. B. 1070), which makes it a misdemeanor for an unauthorized alien to seek or engage in work in the State; this provision is referred to as §5(C). Section 2(B) provides that officers who conduct a stop, detention, or arrest must in some circumstances make efforts to verify the person’s immi- gration status with the Federal Government. Section 3 makes failure to comply with federal alien-registration requirements a state misdemeanor. Section 5 authorizes officers to arrest without a warrant a person “the officer has probable cause to believe . . . has committed any public offense that makes the person removable from the United . ...” §13–3883(A)(5). Section 5(C) provides, inter alia, that officers “may not consider race, color or national origin except to the extent permitted by the United [and] Ari- zona Constitution[s],” §§13–2928(C), and that “a person who accepts unlawful employment is not eligible to have his status adjusted to that of a lawful permanent resident.” See §1301–1306. Failure to do so is a federal misdemeanor. See §1304(e), 1306(a). Section 6 authorizes States to deny noncitizens a range of public benefits, §1622; and it imposes sanctions on employers who hire unauthorized workers, §1324a. As a con sequence, the Court of Appeals concluded that §§3 and 5 (C) were likely preempted. Held: The United States had established a likelihood of success on its preemption claims. Pp. 5–7. (a) Section 3 is preempted by federal law. The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled. Immigration policy can affect trade, investment, tourism, and diplomatic relations for the entire Nation, as well as the perceptions and expectations of aliens in this country who seek the full protection of its laws. See, e.g., Chamber of Commerce of United States of America v. Whiting, 563 U. S. ___, ___. State law must also give way to federal law in at least two other circumstances. First, the States are precluded from regulating conduct in a field that Congress, acting within its proper authority, has determined must be regulated by its exclusive governance. See Gade v. National Solid Wastes Management Assn., 505 U.S. 88, 115. The intent to displace state law altogether can be inferred from a framework of regulation “so pervasive that Congress left no room for the States to supplement it” or where there is a “federal interest . . .. so dominant that the federal system will be assumed to preclude enforcement of state laws on the same subject,” Rice v. Santa Fe Elevator Corp., 331 US. 304, 318. Second, state laws are preempted when they conflict with federal law, see, e-g., Chambers v. American Honda Motor Co., 529 U. s. 861, 869–872. The Federal Government has made a deliberate choice not to impose crim- inal penalties on aliens who seek, or engagein, unauthorized employment. See Hines v. Davidowitz, 312 U. .S. 52, 64 (West Supp. 2011). Congress has made clear that no formal agreement or special training needs need be in place for state officers to “communicate with the [Federal Government] regarding the immigration status of any individual, including reporting knowledge that a particular alien is not lawfully present in [the] United States” and that any information employees submit to indicate their work status may not be used for purposes other than prosecution under specified federal criminal statutes for fraud, perjury, and related conduct. There are significant complexities involved in enforcing federal immigration law, including the determination whether a person is removable, and Congress has obligated ICE to respond to any request made by state officials for verification of a person's citizenship or im- migration status. Congress has also made clear, however, that if the police stop someone based on nothing more than possible removability, the usual predicate for an arrest is absent. The Texas School Finance System is a dual approach to the financing of public education, relying on mutual participation by the local school districts and the State. As early as 1883, the state constitution was amended to provide for the creation of local school district empowered to levy ad valorem taxes with the consent of local taxpayers for the "erection . . . of school buildings" and for the maintenance of public free schools. The Permanent School Fund, which received income from the Permanent Fund, was thereafter endowed with millions of acres of public land set aside to assure a continued source of income for school support. Prior to 1939, the Available School Fund contributed money to every school district at a rate of $17.50 per school-age child. Although the amount was increased several times in the late 1800's and first half of this century, the disadvantaged class was composed only of persons who were totally unable to pay the demanded sum. The District Court rendered its judgment in a per curiam opinion holding the Texas system unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Held: 1. The Texas system of school financing does not operate to the disadvantage of some suspect class or impinges upon a fundamental right explicitly or implicitly protected by the Constitution, thereby requiring strict judicial scrutiny. Pp. 531-532. (a) To the extent that the Texas school finance system results in unequal expenditures between children who happen to reside in different districts, it cannot be said that such disparities are the product of a system that is so irrational as to be invidiously discriminatory. P. 533. (b) Appellees' argument that the system discriminates against a large, diverse, and amorphous class, unified only by the common factor of residence in districts that happen to have less taxable wealth than other districts, is unpersuasive. The system of alleged discrimination and the class it defines have none of the traditional indicia of suspectness: the class is not saddled with such disabilities, or subjected to such a history of purposeful unequal treatment, or relegated to a position of political powerlessness as to command extraordinary protection from the majoritarian political process is not alone a sufficient basis for striking down the entire system. McGinnis v. Royster, 410 U. S. 263, 270. Nor must the Texas scheme be examined to determine whether it rationally furthers some legitimate, articulated state purpose and therefore does not constitute an invidious discrimination in violation of the equal protection Clause. The question whether equal protection is denied to persons with relatively less money on whom designated fines impose heavier burdens, and whether the State's system impermissibly interferes with the exercise of a "fundamental" right, must be decided by the legislature and from the democractic pressures of those who elect them, and accordingly the prior decisions of this Court require the application of the strict standard of judicial review.

Appellant dairy companies defended against charges of price discrimination brought by the United States under § 2 (a) of the Clayton Act, claiming that the price differential between "chains" and "independents," who purchased from them, resulted from due allowances for cost differences. They supported this claim by offering evidence of cost savings accruing to them from serving the "chains." Held: Their evidence was insufficient to meet the requirement of § 2 (a) that the price differential be justified by a showing of actual cost differences resulting from the differing methods or quantities in which the commodities are sold or delivered. Pp. 440-447. (a) Price differentials can not be justified on the basis of arbitrary classifications or even classifications which are representative of a numerical majority of the individual members. Pp. 444-445. (b) Classifications submitted by the appellees were not sufficiently homogenous to warrant the joinder of the purchasers thereunder for cost allocation purposes. Pp. 445-447. (c) Whether the appellees' cost justifications can be sufficiently unscrambled to remove any taint that this Court finds in them and still show a cost gap sufficient to justify the price disparity between the "chains" and any independent, is a question which should be decided on remand after evaluation of the mass of underlying statistical data not considered by the trial court and now tied together by untried theories. P. 447. Reversed and cause remanded.

Petitioner, a merchant seaman, was indicted for violating the federal narcotics laws. While he was free on bail, a federal agent succeeded by surreptitious means in listening to incriminating statements made by him. Evidence of these statements was introduced against petitioner at his trial over his objection. He was convicted, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The prosecution's use at the trial of evidence of the petitioner's own incriminating statement deprived him of any right secured to him under the Federal Constitution. Pp. 561-564. 2. The use of the evidence against petitioner of incriminating incriminating words which government agents had deliberately elicited from him after he had been indicted and in the absence of his retained counsel. P. 564. 3. In Spano v. New York, 360 U. S. 315, this Court held that petitioner was denied the basic protections of the Sixth Amendment when there was used against him at trial evidence of his own incriminates statements which he had overheard under the circumstances disclosed by this record, and that all evidence which Murphy thereby obtained was, under the rule of Weeks v. United States, 232 U.S. 383, inadmissible against petitioner. P p. 567. 307 F. 2d 1030, reversed.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Arizona announced today that it filed a civil injunctive action against Arizona for unlawfully detaining an illegal alien.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Phoenix, Arizona, alleges that Arizona violated the federal immigration laws by failing to impose a pre-emption provision on certain aliens who sought or engaged in unauthorized work.  According to the complaint, Arizona violated Section 5(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1940, which requires federal authorities to determine whether an alien is removable from the United States. The complaint further alleges that the federal authorities failed to enforce the preemption provision, and that Arizona failed to implement it.  In a parallel action, the U.N. Office of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security today announced that it has issued an order requiring Arizona to comply with the pre-emptive provisions of the federal law.  Arizona has agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins Arizona from violating these provisions, and orders Arizona to pay a civil penalty of $2,500. The settlement is subject to court approval.  On June 21, 2011, the court granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order and an asset freeze against Arizona, which is pending final approval by the court. The court also granted the court's motion for a preliminary injunction against further violations of Section 5 of the immigration law, and ordered Arizona to cooperate with the federal government in determining whether to issue a preemption order.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit held that a pricing order imposed by the Massachusetts Department of Food and Agriculture on milk dealers in the state does not discriminate against interstate commerce. The court held that the order was designed to aid only Massachusetts dairy farmers. The order requires every dealer in Massachusetts to make a monthly "premium payment" into the "Massachusetts Dairy Equalization Fund." The fund is distributed each month to each of the state's dairy farmers, who receive a share of the total amount of the dealer's Class I6 sales in Massachusetts. The Court held that "the order is not designed to discriminate on its face, is even in its application, and only incidentally discriminates interstate commerce"

The U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona today entered final judgments against Arizona-based defendant Jimmie Wayne Jeffers and his girlfriend, Penelope Cheney, in a civil injunctive action brought by the Arizona Department of Justice.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Phoenix, Arizona, alleges that Jeffers violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act"), and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Jeffers consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.  In a parallel action, the Arizona Attorney General's Office today announced criminal charges against Jeffers.  According to the SEC's order, Jeffers pleaded guilty to a felony count of first-degree murder and was sentenced to 10 years in prison.  As part of the settlement, the court agreed to the imposition of a permanent injunction, which prohibits Jeffers from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in the United States, including securities in exchange for a share of the proceeds of the sale of a security deposit, and to a five-year officer-and-director bar.

After petitioner's son died while piloting a helicopter manufactured by respondent, petitioner filed a diversity action in Federal District Court, alleging that respondent was liable for the death under state tort law because the helicopter's escape hatch was defectively designed. Respondent counterclaimed that it was immune from liability under the "government contractor defense," which bars recovery against a contractor whose design complied with the Government's reasonably precise specifications. At trial, the District Court instructed the jury that the defense applied if the Government approved reasonably precise specifications, the equipment conformed to those specifications, and the supplier warned the Government about the dangers in the use of the equipment that were known to the supplier but not to the Government. However, the court declined to give the instruction requested by respondent that the defense barred liability if the contractor did not participate, or participated only minimally, in the design of the defective equipment, or if the contractor timely warned the Government of the risks of the design and notified it of alternative designs reasonably known by it, and the Government, although forewarned, clearly authorized the contractor to proceed with the dangerous design. The jury returned a verdict for petitioner, and the District Court entered judgment for him. The Court of Appeals reversed, finding that the record showed that respondent had satisfied the requirements of the government contractor defense. Held: 1. State law which holds Government contractors liable for design defects in military equipment does in some circumstances present a "significant conflict" with federal policy and must be displaced. Such law presents a conflict when (1) the United States approved reasonably precise specifications; (2) the equipment conformed to those specifications; and (3) the supplier warned the United States about the dangers in the use of the equipment that were known to the supplier but not to the United States. These conditions assure that the suit is within the area where the policy of the "discretionary function" would be frustrated -that is, they assure that the design feature in question was considered by a Government officer, and not merely by the contractor itself. They also ensure that the displacement of state tort law would not create some incentive for the manufacturer to withhold knowledge of risks, since conveying that knowledge might disrupt the contract but withholding it would produce no liability. Pp. 40-45. 2. Whether the Court of Appeals conducted a factual evaluation of whether the Government contractor defense was inapplicable, or simply assessed whether the defense had been established, is uncertain from the Court of Appeals' opinion. Accordingly, the case is remanded for clarification of this point. Pp. 45-46. Vacated and remanded.

The Civil Rights Attorney's Fees Awards Act of 1976, as amended by 42 U. S. C. § 1983, authorizes the Virginia Court to promulgate rules and regulations "organizing and governing the association known as the Virginia State Bar, composed of the attorneys-at-law of this State, to act as an administrative agency of the Court for the purpose of investigating and reporting . . . violation[s]" of the State Bar Code. The Virginia Court and its chief justice, acting under this authority, issued a rule to show cause against the charged attorney, the prosecution of the case by the commonwealth attorney, and the hearing of a case by a judge issuing the rule together with two other judges designated by the Chief Justice of the Virginia Supreme Court. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Appellees properly prevailed in their § 1983 action, and appellees were entitled under § 1983 to receive and gather nonfee information and information concerning initial consultation fees. Pp. 523-524. 2. The Civil Rights attorney's fees Awards Act, which provides that the Court may award attorneys' fees for failure to correct a challenged judicial act, does not bar prospective relief. P. 524. 470 F. Supp. 506, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reversed a lower court's decision that limited recovery of attorney's fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act of 1976 (EAJA) to the cost of the party's attorney. The lower court held that the EAJA does not allow recovery of fees at the market rate for paralegal services. The court held, however, that the law does allow recovery at the rate of $35 per hour to the law firm of the prevailing party in a case brought by or against the Government. Richlin Security Service Co., a California-based security company, filed an EAJA-related claim with the Department of Transportation's Board of Contract Appeals. The Board entered an award in favor of Richlin, and Richlin filed an application with the Board for reimbursement of its attorney’s fees, expenses, and costs pursuant to EAJA. The board granted Richlin's application in part, but the court of appeals held that it was not entitled to recover its paralegal fees at that rate. The appeals court reversed, holding that the lower court was wrong to conclude that the Board's award was not justified by the Government's position. The Court also held that Richlin had not shown that it would have prevailed had it not filed its application. The case is now before the United States Supreme Court.

Respondents, individuals who applied for and received an Aspire Visa credit card marketed by petitioner CompuCredit Corporation and issued by Columbus Bank and Trust, now a division of petitioner Synovus Bank, agreed to be bound by a provision of the Credit Repair Organizations Act (CROA) that “Any claim, dispute or controversy (whether in contract, tort, or otherwise) at any time arising from or relating to your Account, any transferred balances or this Agreement (collectively, ‘Claims’), upon the election of you or us, will be resolved by binding arbitration . . .” App. 62. The District Court denied the defendants’ motion to compel arbitration of the claims, concluding that Congress intended claims under the CROA to be non-arbitrable. A panel of the Ninth Circuit affirmed. Held: The CROA precludes enforcement of an arbitration agreement in a lawsuit alleging violations of that Act. Pp. 615 F. 3d 1204, reversed and remanded.

Under AEDPA, a federal habeas court must find the state-court conclusion “an unreasonable determination of the facts in light of the evidence presented in the State court proceeding.” 28 U. S. C. §2254(e)(1). The credibility findings a trial court makes in a Batson inquiry are reviewed for clear error. Hernandez v. New York, 500 U.S. 352, 364–366 (plurality opinion) (holding that evaluation of a prosecutor’s credibility “lies ‘peculiarly within a trial judge’’ ”). Under AEDpa, however, the state court decision was not an unreasonable determination. Because the California Court of Appeal accepted the trial court credibility finding, the Court of Appeals majority drew this conclusion based on three considerations: first, the prosecutor‘s erroneous statement concerning another prospective African-American juror’d age; second, her improper attempt to use gender as a basis for exclusion; and third, the majority’vibe skepticism toward the prosecutor ’s explanation that she struck Juror 16 in part because of her youth and lack of ties to the community. The panel majority found no error in the trials or rulings in the first two steps of the inquiry, and it disagreed with its conclusions on the third step, holding that it was unreasonable to accept the prosecutor's explanation that juror 16 was excused on account of her age and her demeanor. Held: The Ninth Circuit erred, for the trial-court determination was not unreasonable. Pp. 5–7. 365 F. 3d, 679; 28 U S. S.-C. § 2254(d)(1), reversed and remanded.

In this landmark case, the US Supreme Court ruled that a confession obtained by physical abuse, known as "third degree" torture, is inadmissible in criminal trials as it violates the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court held that the use of force to extract a confession goes beyond mere psychological pressure and rises to the level of physical brutality that shocks the conscience. The Court emphasized that the Constitution prohibits cruel and unusual punishment, and that using physical violence to obtain a confession falls squarely within this category. The ruling set important standards for the treatment of defendants and established a higher threshold for the use of coercive tactics in law enforcement.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the constitutionality of admitting victim impact evidence during the penalty phase of a capital trial. The case involves Pervis Tyrone Payne, who was convicted of two counts of first-degree murder and one count of assault with intent to commit murder in the first degree, and sentenced to death.

The Court revisits its previous decisions in Booth v. Maryland and South Carolina v. Gathers, which held that the Eighth Amendment prohibits the admission of victim impact evidence during capital sentencing. The Court now overrules these decisions, stating that such evidence can be relevant to the jury's determination of a defendant's moral culpability and blameworthiness.

The Court reasons that the harm caused by the defendant is a legitimate concern in criminal law, both for defining offenses and determining appropriate punishment. It argues that sentencing authorities have traditionally considered the harm done by the defendant, and that victim impact evidence is simply another form of informing the sentencing authority about the specific harm caused by the crime.

The Court acknowledges the principle of stare decisis but notes that it is not an inexorable command, especially in constitutional cases where legislative correction is practically impossible. It points out that Booth and Gathers were decided by narrow margins and have been difficult to apply consistently.

The Court concludes that victim impact evidence does not create an impermissible risk of arbitrary imposition of the death penalty and can serve legitimate purposes in the sentencing phase. It holds that if a state chooses to allow such evidence, the Eighth Amendment does not bar it. The Court affirms the judgment of the Supreme Court of Tennessee, upholding Payne's death sentence.

Implications of the decision include that states are now permitted to introduce evidence about the victim and the impact of the murder on the victim's family during the sentencing phase of capital trials. This decision allows juries to consider the full extent of the harm caused by the defendant when determining whether to impose the death penalty.

In the case of Michigan v. Bryant, the U.S. Supreme Court addressed whether statements made by a dying victim to police officers could be admitted at trial without violating the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment. The victim, Anthony Covington, had identified his shooter, "Rick," to police officers before dying of his wounds. The Michigan Supreme Court had previously ruled that Covington's statements were testimonial hearsay and thus inadmissible, leading to the reversal of Richard Bryant's conviction for second-degree murder.

The U.S. Supreme Court, however, disagreed with the Michigan Supreme Court's assessment. The Court held that the primary purpose of the interaction between Covington and the police was to address an ongoing emergency, not to establish facts for a future prosecution. Therefore, Covington's statements were deemed non-testimonial, and their admission at Bryant's trial did not violate the Confrontation Clause.

The Court's decision emphasized an objective analysis of the circumstances surrounding the interaction, including the nature of the emergency, the type of weapon used, and the formality of the encounter. The Court noted that the police were responding to an emergency without knowing the shooter's location or motive, and the victim was in a dire medical state, which influenced the nature of his statements.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Michigan Supreme Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The decision clarified the application of the Confrontation Clause to statements made during ongoing emergencies and the factors that courts should consider in determining the primary purpose of an interrogation.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Montana granted summary judgment in favor of the ATF agent who conducted a search of the home of a Montana family without a warrant. The court found that the search violated the Fourth Amendment because the agent failed to describe the "persons or things to be seized" in his application for a warrant to search the home. The ATF officer, Jeff Groh, had been a Special Agent for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms since 1989 and had served as the agent in charge of the field office in Butte-Silver Bow County since 2002. The court concluded that Groh was entitled to qualified immunity under the provisions of the federal law that provide for the protection of law enforcement officers who conduct searches without the need for a search warrant. Without a warrant, the court concluded, the search could not have been conducted without the assistance of the officer who signed it. The appeals court held that the warrant's failure to identify the items that petitioner intended to seize was a mere "typographical error" that amounted to a violation of the law, and that the officer had not violated the law by failing to provide a specific description of the items he intended to search. The Appeals Court concluded that, in light of the Magistrate Judge's finding that probable cause existed for the search, the warrant should be granted. The Court also concluded that the officers' conduct did not violate the law because the search was conducted in a manner that was reasonable and without the use of a warrant and that there was no evidence that the items were concealed on the ranch. The case is now before the Appeals Court.

In the case of Alford, the Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether a guilty plea can be considered voluntary and constitutionally valid when the defendant maintains their innocence but pleads guilty to avoid a harsher sentence, such as the death penalty. Alford had been indicted for first-degree murder but entered a guilty plea to second-degree murder, despite claiming innocence, because he faced the possibility of the death penalty if convicted of the higher charge.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had found Alford's plea involuntary due to the fear of the death penalty. The Supreme Court held that a plea of guilty is not compelled and unconstitutional merely because it was entered to avoid the possibility of a death sentence. The Court emphasized that the validity of a guilty plea is determined by whether it represents a voluntary and intelligent choice among the alternatives available to the defendant.

The Court noted that while a guilty plea typically includes an admission of guilt, the Constitution does not require such an admission for the imposition of a criminal penalty. The Court found that Alford's plea was entered voluntarily, with full awareness of the consequences, and with competent legal counsel advising that it was in his best interest given the strong evidence against him.

The Supreme Court concluded that the trial judge did not commit constitutional error in accepting Alford's guilty plea, even though he professed innocence, because the plea was made intelligently and voluntarily as a strategic choice to limit the potential penalty. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the constitutionality of a Texas statute criminalizing intimate sexual conduct between same-sex adults. The case arose after two men were arrested in a private residence for engaging in consensual homosexual acts. They were charged under the Texas "Homosexual Conduct" law, which they challenged as violating the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court's analysis focused on whether the Texas statute infringed upon the liberty of adults to engage in private consensual conduct as protected by the Due Process Clause. The Court also considered whether to overturn its previous decision in Bowers v. Hardwick, which upheld a similar statute criminalizing sodomy.

The Court concluded that the Texas statute was unconstitutional. It held that the liberty protected by the Constitution allows adults to engage in private, consensual sexual conduct without government intervention. The Court found that the statute did not serve any legitimate state interest that could justify its intrusion into the personal and private lives of individuals. The Court overruled Bowers v. Hardwick, stating that it was not correct when decided and is not correct today.

The Court's decision emphasized that the state should not intrude upon the personal and private lives of individuals, particularly in the area of sexual conduct, unless there is a compelling state interest. The ruling effectively invalidated similar laws in other states and marked a significant shift in the legal recognition of the rights of homosexual individuals.

The opinion also addressed the Equal Protection argument, suggesting that while the statute applied equally to all persons, it effectively discriminated against homosexuals as a class by criminalizing conduct closely associated with being homosexual.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision recognized a broader scope of liberty under the Due Process Clause, which includes the right of adults to engage in consensual intimate conduct without unwarranted government intrusion. The ruling struck down the Texas statute and overruled Bowers, acknowledging that societal views on morality and personal relationships evolve over time and that the Constitution protects personal decisions relating to intimate conduct.

The Supreme Court case in question dealt with the enforceability of a provision in a collective-bargaining agreement that required union members to arbitrate claims under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA). The Second Circuit Court of Appeals had previously ruled that such arbitration provisions were unenforceable based on the Supreme Court's decision in Alexander v. Gardner-Denver Co. However, the Supreme Court disagreed with the Second Circuit and reversed its judgment.

The Supreme Court's reasoning was based on the following points:

1. The National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) allows unions to be the exclusive bargaining representatives for employees, with the authority to negotiate over wages, hours, and other conditions of employment, which can include arbitration agreements.

2. The collective-bargaining agreement in question clearly required arbitration of employment discrimination claims, including those under the ADEA.

3. The Court found that the ADEA does not preclude arbitration of claims brought under the statute, as established in the Court's decision in Gilmer v. Interstate/Johnson Lane Corp.

4. The Court clarified that an agreement to arbitrate statutory discrimination claims is not a waiver of the substantive rights afforded by the ADEA; it is merely a waiver of the right to seek relief from a court in the first instance.

5. The Court addressed concerns about the arbitration process and the competence of arbitrators, stating that these concerns are outdated and that arbitration is a valid alternative dispute resolution method that does not undermine the remedial and deterrent functions of the ADEA.

6. The Court also addressed the potential conflict of interest between a union and its members, noting that the NLRA imposes a duty of fair representation on unions, and that other remedies are available if a union fails to represent its members' interests adequately.

7. The Court did not consider certain contract-based arguments that were not raised in the lower courts, as well as the question of whether the collective-bargaining agreement allowed the union to block arbitration of ADEA claims, as these issues were not properly before the Court.

The Supreme Court concluded that a collective-bargaining agreement that clearly and unmistakably requires union members to arbitrate ADEA claims is enforceable as a matter of federal law. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Implications of the Decision:
The Supreme Court's decision has significant implications for labor law and the enforceability of arbitration agreements within collective-bargaining agreements. It affirms that unions can negotiate arbitration clauses that cover statutory discrimination claims, including those under the ADEA, and that such clauses are enforceable. This decision reinforces the validity of arbitration as an alternative to litigation for resolving employment disputes and upholds the principle of freedom of contract in the collective-bargaining process.

Case Name: Randolph County Board of Commissioners v. City of Franklin
Case Number: 17-1001
Judge: Justice Thomas
Date Decided: July 12, 2018

Summary:
Justice Thomas delivered the majority opinion in Randolph County Board of Commissioners v. City of Franklin, a case concerning North Carolina's "sanctuary city" law. The law prohibits cities from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement agencies, and it allows residents to sue cities for damages resulting from illegal immigrants. The plaintiffs in this case sued the City of Franklin for allowing illegal immigrants to reside in the city and causing property damage. The trial court dismissed the suit, ruling that the sanctuary city law conflicted with federal law. On appeal, the North Carolina Supreme Court ruled that the sanctuary city law was constitutional and allowed the suit to proceed. However, the Supreme Court also clarified that the law did not create liability for cities for property damage caused by illegal immigrants. Instead, the law provides a cause of action for residents to sue cities directly for damages. Justice Thomas concurred with the majority opinion, but he disagreed with the Supreme Court's interpretation of the law regarding liability for property damage. He believed that the language of the law clearly indicated that cities could be liable for property damage caused by illegal immigrants.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a former federal judge for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, alleges that Arthur N. Economou and Co., Inc., a former executive director of the Department of Agriculture, violated the anti-fraud provision of the federal securities laws by issuing a press release that contained false and misleading information about the nature of a civil disturbance.  According to the complaint, the press release, which was issued without the proper warning or warning required by the federal law, constituted an egregious violation of the First Amendment.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Economou consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the charged provisions and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against Economou for his role in a related administrative proceeding.   The court also issued a temporary restraining order halting the issuance of the press releases. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by John R. Rymas and supervised by Eric R. Werner.Â  The litigation will be led by Gregory A. Kasper.

The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDA) separates medical devices into three categories: Class I devices are those that present no unreasonable risk of illness or injury and therefore require only general manufacturing controls; Class II devices require more stringent controls; and Class III devices require the applicant to demonstrate a "reasonable assurance" that the device is both "safe ... [and] effective under the conditions of use prescribed, recommended, or suggested in the proposed labeling thereof." 360c(a)(1)(c)(ii)(II). In order to avoid the potentially monopolistic consequences of this predicate-device exception, the MDA allows other manufacturers to distribute (also pending completion of the predicate device's PMA review) devices that are shown to be "substantially equivalent" to a predicate device. The FDA's review requires an average of 1,200 hours for each submission, and the very subject matter of petitioner's statements were a critical element in their case. The District Court dismissed the "fraud-on-the-FDA" claims, first on the ground that they were expressly pre-empted by the FDA, and then, after our decision in Medtronic, on the grounds that these claims amounted to an improper assertion of a private right of action under the FDA. A divided panel of the Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that plaintiffs' fraud claims were neither expressly nor impliedly preempted. Held: 1. The MDA empowers the FDA to enforce its statutory and regulatory objectives. Pp. 521-522. (a) The relationship between a federal agency and the entity it regulates is inherently federal in character because the relationship originates from, is governed by, and terminates according to federal law. To the extent respondent posits that anything other than our ordinary pre-emption principles apply under these circumstances, that contention must fail in light of the conclusion last Term in Geier v. American Honda Motor Co., 529 U. S. 861 (2000), that neither an express preemption provision nor a saving clause "bar[s] the ordinary working of conflict preemption principles." Id., at 869. P. 522. 2. Respondent's claims are not expressly precluded by the FDA, and they do not and cannot stand for the proposition that any violation of the FDCA will support a state-law claim. The FDA has at its disposal a variety of enforcement options that allow it to make a measured response to suspected fraud upon the Agency. Moreover, this flexibility is a critical component of the statutory framework under which the FDA pursues difficult (and often competing) objectives. For example, with respect to Class III and Class IV devices, the FDA simultaneously maintains the exhaustive PMA and the more limited 510(k) processes in order to ensure both that medical devices are reasonably safe and effective and that, if the device qualifies under the 510 (k) exception, it is on the market within a relatively short period of time. Similarly, "off-label" usage of medical devices (use of a device for some other purpose than that for which it has been approved) is an accepted and necessary corollary of the FDA's mission to police fraud consistently with the Agency's judgment and objectives. Thus, complying with the agency's detailed regulatory regime in the shadow of 50 States' tort regimes will dramatically increase the burdens facing potential applicants-burdens not contemplated by traditional state tort law which had predated the federal enactments in questions, but which are now in the hands of the agency itself. For the reasons stated above, this sort of litigation would exert an extraneous pull on the scheme established by Congress, and it is therefore pre-pre-empting by that scheme. Id. 159 F. 3d 817, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit held that the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) did not have jurisdiction to order a leather processing company to pay back pay to five undocumented workers who were fired for supporting a union. The court held that, because the employees were fired in retaliation for their union activity, the Board had no authority to order the employer to pay them back. The Court held that "the employees' subsequent deportation was the proximate result of the discriminatorily motivated action by [petitioners] and constitutes a constructive discharge"

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit has ruled that an Alaska high school principal violated the First Amendment rights of a student who unfurled a banner promoting the use of illegal drugs at a school-sanctioned event. The student, Joseph Frederick, was suspended for 10 days by the principal for refusing to take down the banner. The court ruled that the principal's actions violated Frederick's right to freedom of speech and that the student could sue the school for damages. The ruling is the latest in a series of high-profile First Amendment cases that have found that the right to free speech is not guaranteed in public schools. In a similar case, the court held that the rights of adults in other settings are not automatically coextensive with those of students in public school. The case is being appealed by the school district.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit reversed a lower court's decision granting summary judgment to officers who conducted a warrantless search of a Utah man's home to arrest him for the sale of methamphetamine to an undercover informant. The court held that the officers' conduct violated respondent's Fourth Amendment rights and that the unconstitutionality of their conduct was clearly established. The lower court had granted the officers summary judgment on the basis that they could reasonably have believed that the consent-once-removed doctrine authorized their conduct. The appeals court found that the lower court misapplied the "consent once-removed" doctrine because the officers had not established that they violated the Fourth Amendment by entering the home without a warrant. In a separate opinion, the appeals court concluded that the warrantless arrest and search were supported by exigent circumstances, but that the inevitable discovery doctrine justified introduction of the fruits of the search. The 10th circuit held that this doctrine applies when an undercover officer enters a home at the express invitation of someone with authority to consent, establishes probable cause to consent and is not a pre-existing law enforcement policy. The majority concluded that "the consent once removed" doctrine does not apply in this case because it was not clearly established at the time that the conduct was unconstitutional. We conclude that petitioners are entitled to qualified immunity on the ground that their conduct did not violate their rights.

Two men were indicted together for armed robbery. One gave a detailed oral confession to police officers, which was later introduced in evidence over his objection. He was convicted after a joint trial. His codefendant, whose alibi was corroborated by independent evidence, was exonerated. On appeal the codefendant moved to suppress the confession, claiming that it was inadmissible hearsay. The trial court ruled that the confession was admissible, but instructed the jury to disregard it in determining the guilt or innocence of the codefendant. The appellate court upheld the conviction. Held: Introduction of the codefendant's confession, though accompanied by instructions to disregard it, violated the nonconfessor's right of confrontation guaranteed by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 387-395. 380 F. 2d 1074, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit recently ruled that a securities fraud class action against Halliburton Co. and one of its executives could proceed as a class action under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The Second Circuit held that the district court's decision not to certify the class was based on a lack of loss causation. The Court held that, in the absence of such a finding, the class would be entitled to relief under the provisions of the federal securities laws. The court concluded that the class could be certified under Rule 23(b)(3), which provides that a court must find that the questions of law or fact common to class members predominate over any questions affecting only individual members, and that class action is superior to other available methods for fairly and efficiently adjudicating the claims. The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case and ruled that the lower court had erred in denying the class certification request. The First Circuit agreed, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari and remanded the case for further consideration.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed the 10-year sentence imposed on a convicted drug dealer for his role in a conspiracy to distribute more than five kilograms of cocaine. The Third Circuit held that the district court had no authority to depart below the statutory minimum sentence. The court's decision was based on a government motion to depart from the sentencing range set by the Sentencing Guidelines. The government did not object to the departure, but the court held that it did not have the authority to do so. The Second Circuit also held that, based on the government's letter to the court, the District Court had no power to depart. The Supreme Court held in a separate opinion that the lower court had not violated the law by imposing a sentence that was below the minimum. The Court of Appeal for the Second Circuit agreed, and the Court of Justice agreed with the majority.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit is considering whether the use of a pre-trial recording in the case of Todd A. Brecht, convicted of first-degree murder in the shooting death of Roger Hartman, violated his right to a fair trial under the Constitution's due process clause. The standard for determining whether a conviction must be set aside because of a federal constitutional error is whether the error "was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt"<n>In this case, the court is deciding whether the "harmless error" standard applies in determining whether the prosecution's use for impeachment purposes of petitioner's post-Miranda silence violated the due process provision of the Constitution. We conclude that the standard does not apply, and that petitioner is not entitled to habeas relief.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado today entered a final judgment in favor of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission ("EEC") in a related case.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Denver, Colorado, alleges that, in 1992, the Department of Health and Human Services ("DOH") issued an order requiring that certain individuals with disabilities be evaluated in their uncorrected state.  According to the complaint, the DOE's order required that individuals with severe myopia be evaluated as having "substantially limited" in one or more major life activities, including driving a vehicle, watching television or shopping in public stores, and performing certain basic tasks.  In addition, the order requires that the person with a severe impairment be able to perform certain basic activities without impairments, including, without limitation, using corrective eyeglasses and contact lenses.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the DOE order, the agency has agreed to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining it from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering it to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and injunctive relief.  Additionally, the court has ordered the DOE to provide an accounting of the number of people with disabilities who have been permanently disabled by the federal government, including those with disabilities, and to pay a civil penalty of $100,000.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 12102(2)(A).  The Office of Inspector General's Office has issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the background of anyone selling or offering them an investment in a business using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

Respondents brought suit challenging the constitutionality of a rent control ordinance adopted by the City of San Jose, California. Among other things, respondents claimed that the ordinance's tenant hardship provisions violated the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment and the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. After the trial court sustained the challenge, the California Supreme Court reversed. Held: 1. The record in this case leaves much to be desired in terms of specificity for purposes of determining appellants' standing to challenge the ordinance. However, since the record suggests that the tenant hardship provisions are unlikely to be invoked in practice, it is premature to consider appellants' Takings Claim. Moreover, appellants' facial challenge to the ordinance under the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment is rejected. Pp. 108-114. 2. The ordinance's tenant hardship provisions are designed to serve the legitimate purpose of protecting tenants, and it is rational for the ordinance to treat certain landlords differently on the basis of whether or not they have hardship tenants. Pp. 114-115. Affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a federal criminal charge against a Maine man for violating a state law prohibiting the importation of live golden shiners, a species of minnow commonly used as live bait in sport fishing.
