The lower court had found that the state's law was constitutional and that the federal law could not be used as a basis for a federal prosecution under the Lacey Act Amendments of 1981 ("Lacey Act"), which prohibits the import of fish or wildlife taken, possessed, transported, or sold in violation of any law or regulation of any state or foreign law. The First Circuit agreed with the lower court, finding that the law impermissibly restricts interstate trade. The court also found that Taylor's motion to dismiss the federal charge was not supported by the facts of the case, and that Taylor had not shown that he would have been charged under the law if he had not been charged. The Court held that the case should be remanded for further consideration. The case is now subject to a hearing before the full Court.

Title VII of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act authorizes the creation of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB), which oversees the profession of certified public accountants. The PCAOB consists of five members nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, and a Chairman appointed by the President. An initial round of confirmations resulted in the confirmation of William Duetscher, Daniel Goelzer, Jay Hanson, Laura Ingraham, and Gene Stork. The Chairman was initially David Boaz, but he resigned shortly afterward. Subsequently, the President appointed Darren Martyn as Chairman. All six appointees took oaths of office affirming their commitment to carry out the PCAOB’s duties faithfully and diligently. Upon assuming office, the newly appointed Chairman issued an Order directing the other members to resign. Each filed a motion challenging the Chairman’s authority to replace the other members. The motions raised the issue whether the Chairman’s appointment of the other members was invalid under the Appointments Clause. Ultimately, the Director of the Division of Corporate Finance informed the other members that the Chairman had withdrawn his request that they resign. Shortly thereafter, the Chairman announced that he planned to seek reconfirmation of his position. Meanwhile, petitioners, former employees of the PCAOB, filed suit in the District of Columbia Circuit, claiming that the Chairman’s appointment of the other members was invalid under the Appointments Clause. The Circuit vacated the other members’ appointments, ruling that the Chairman’s appointment of the other members was unlawful because the Chairman had not obtained the advice and consent of the Senate as required by the Appointments Clause. The Circuit also entered a temporary restraining order prohibiting the Chairman from making additional appointments until the issue of his qualifications was resolved. The Chairman appealed to this Court. Held: 1. The Chairman’s appointment of the other members was valid. Pp. 5−11. (a) Although the Chairman was originally appointed by the President, the Circuit correctly interpreted the relevant statutory provisions to allow the Chairman to succeed himself. Thus, the Chairman’s subsequent appointment of the other members was valid. Pp. 5−6. (b) Moreover, the Chairman’s appointment complied with the Appointments Clause. Pp. 6−11. (1) The Chairman’s appointment satisfied the Clause’s requirement that the appointee be an “employee of the United States.” His appointment was based on the assumption that he was an “officer of the United States,” a designation supported by the plain language of the Dodd-Frank Act. The Clause applies to all presidential appointees regardless of whether they are called “officers” or “employees.” The Clause does not distinguish between “presidential appointees who happen to occupy posts traditionally thought of as employment positions” and those who do not. Millet v. Nickerson, 572 U. S. ___, ___. Rather, the Clause defines the category of appointees who come within the Clause’s reach, namely, those who satisfy the Clause’s two elements: “first, that the president intends the appointees to be officers; and second, that the president understands the appointees to be officers.” ibid. Pp. 6−8. (2) Having assumed that the Chairman was an “officer of the United States,” the Chairman’s appointment also satisfied the Clause’s requirement that the appointee be “confirmed by the Senate.” The Chairman’s selection came about through the process of confirmation, and the Clause allows the President to fill a vacancy left open by the withdrawal of a senatorially confirmed appointee. However, once the Chairman’s appointment was confirmed, the Chairman ceased to be a mere candidate for confirmation. Pp. 8−10. (3) The Chairman’s appointment also satisfied the Clause’s requirement that the appointee be “commissioned by the President.” Because the Chairman was commissioned by the President, the Clause’s reference to “commissioned by the President” covers the Chairman’s appointment. P. 10. 2. The Chairman’s appointment of the other members was also valid under the Appointments Clause. Pp. 10−11. (a) Two of the three criteria that render an appointment invalid under the Clause apply to the Chairman’s appointment of the other members: (1) the appointees were not confirmed by the Senate, and (2) the appointees were not commissioned by the President. The Chairman’s appointment of the other members was exempt from the third criterion, which renders an appointment invalid if the appointees are to serve in a capacity involving confidential information relating to national security. The Chairman’s appointment of the other members was not to involve the handling of classified information. Pp. 10−11. 537 F. 3d 667, affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Thomas, J., joined. Breyer, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Brennan, J., joined.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit is considering whether a state common-law tort action seeking damages from the manufacturer of an outboard motor is pre-empted by the Federal Boat Safety Act of 1971 or by the decision of the Coast Guard not to promulgate a regulation requiring propeller guards on motorboats. The case involves the death of a woman who was riding in an 18-foot ski boat equipped with a 115-horsepower outboard motor manufactured by a division of the Brunswick Corporation (Brunswick) when she fell overboard and was struck by the propeller, suffering fatal injuries. The complaint alleged that the motor was not protected by a propeller guard, and each count alleged that Brunswick manufactured an unreasonably dangerous product. The trial court granted respondent's motion to dismiss, and the intermediate appellate court affirmed on the ground that the action was expressly preempted. The Illinois Supreme Court ruled in 2001 that the case was not viable. The Supreme Court's decision added to a split of authority on this precise issue arising from lawsuits against, among others, this particular respondent and its corporate subsidiaries. The Appeals Court held that the Supreme Court had not adequately addressed the issue of preemption. The appeals court concluded that the actions were not viable as a matter of Illinois law. The court held that there was no basis for the claims. The high court's ruling added to the split authority on the issue. The Court granted certiorari to decide whether the actions are viable as matter of law. We conclude that the claims are not viable, and remand the case for further consideration.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a Texas man charged with violating the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in San Antonio, Texas, alleges that, in 1992, Roscoe Filburn, then a 12th-grade student at Edison High School, raised 23 acres of wheat in a school zone. Filburn was convicted of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 922(q) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rules 10b-5(a) and (c) thereunder. The court ruled that the federal government has the power to regulate intrastate commerce, including the right to purchase, sell, and service home-grown wheat.  According to the complaint, Filburn's actions violated the federal laws, and he was subsequently sentenced to six months' imprisonment and two years' supervised release.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against Filburn for his role in the alleged scheme.  On May 2, 2018, the U. S. District Judge in Manhattan granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order and ordered Filburn to comply with the court's order.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s Complaint, the Court also issued an order suspending Filburn from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney.  A hearing for the case was scheduled for June 24, 2018.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-01-17.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Verizon Communications Inc. that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) had authority to regulate interstate competition among broadband internet service providers. The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by AT&T, which sought to block the FTC's attempt to force it to divest itself of Time Warner Cable. The Court held that the FCC's Title II regulations governing broadband internet access applied nationwide, regardless of whether the services being provided crossed state lines. The Court also clarified that the FCC's rules applied equally to fixed and mobile broadband services.

In the case of Northern Pipeline Construction Co. v. Marathon Pipe Line Company, the Supreme Court addressed the constitutionality of the jurisdiction granted to bankruptcy judges under the Bankruptcy Act of 1978. The Act established bankruptcy courts as adjuncts to the district courts and granted them broad jurisdiction over civil proceedings related to bankruptcy cases. Bankruptcy judges were appointed for 14-year terms and did not have the same protections as Article III judges, who have life tenure and salary protection.

The main legal issue was whether the Act's grant of jurisdiction to bankruptcy judges violated Article III of the Constitution, which requires that the judicial power of the United States be vested in courts with judges who have life tenure and salary protection to ensure their independence.

The Supreme Court held that the broad grant of jurisdiction to bankruptcy judges under Section 1471 of the Act was unconstitutional because it violated Article III. The Court reasoned that Article III prohibits Congress from establishing courts that exercise the judicial power of the United States without providing judges with the constitutional protections of life tenure and salary protection. The Court found that bankruptcy judges, who lacked these protections, were impermissibly exercising judicial power.

The Court also determined that the Act's grant of jurisdiction to bankruptcy courts could not be sustained as an exercise of Congress's power to create adjuncts to Article III courts. The bankruptcy courts were found to have too much power and independence, which encroached upon the judicial power reserved for Article III courts.

The Court's decision was to be applied prospectively, not retroactively, to avoid disrupting the administration of bankruptcy laws and to give Congress an opportunity to reconstitute the bankruptcy courts or adopt other valid means of adjudication.

The implications of this decision were significant for the structure and operation of bankruptcy courts. It required Congress to revise the bankruptcy system to ensure that the adjudication of bankruptcy-related matters conformed to the constitutional requirements of Article III.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the relationship between the Fourteenth Amendment's state action requirement and the "under color of state law" requirement of 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The case arose when the petitioner's property was attached by a creditor using Virginia's prejudgment attachment procedure, which he claimed deprived him of property without due process of law.

The District Court and the Court of Appeals previously held that the creditor's actions did not constitute state action as required by the Fourteenth Amendment, and therefore, the petitioner could not claim relief under § 1983. However, the Supreme Court disagreed with the lower courts' interpretation, particularly their reading of the Flagg Brothers case and their understanding of the relationship between state action and action under color of state law.

The Supreme Court clarified that state action and action under color of state law are closely related, if not identical, and that the Court has historically treated them as the same for the purposes of § 1983. The opinion emphasized that § 1983 was intended to provide a broad remedy for constitutional violations by the states, as broad as the protections of the Fourteenth Amendment itself.

The Court concluded that the petitioner did present a valid cause of action under § 1983 insofar as he challenged the constitutionality of the Virginia statute. The Court found that the creditor's use of state officials and state procedures to attach the petitioner's property constituted joint participation with the state, making the creditor a state actor for the purposes of the Fourteenth Amendment. Therefore, the creditor's actions were under color of state law, and the petitioner could seek relief under § 1983.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals in part, affirming it in part, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. This decision implies that private parties who use state procedures to deprive someone of property can be considered state actors and may be held accountable under § 1983 for constitutional violations.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina found that prior to the effective date of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Duke Power Company had openly discriminated on the basis of race in the hiring and assigning of employees at its Dan River Steam Station in Draper, North Carolina. The District Court also found that the Company's policy of requiring a high school education for initial assignment to any department except Labor, and for transfer from the Coal Handling to any 'inside' department (Operations, Maintenance, or Laboratory) operated to render a markedly disproportionate number of Negroes ineligible for transfer to the four desirable departments. The Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit held that the District Court was correct in its conclusion that there was no showing of a racial purpose or invidious intent in the adoption of the high school diploma requirement or general intelligence test. The 3rd Circuit also held that, in the absence of a discriminatory purpose, the use of such requirements was permitted by the Act. The Supreme Court of the United States, however, has not yet issued a decision on the issue of whether or not to review the appeals court's decision.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant seeking a temporary restraining order against future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also issued an order requiring the SEC to conduct an independent review of the facts of a state court case.  According to the SEC's order, filed in federal court in Birmingham, Alabama, Holly Wood broke into the home of her ex-boyfriend and shot him in the head and face as she lay in her bed. Wood's attorney, Cary Dozier, and Frank Ralph, both of whom had been admitted to the bar for five months at the time they were appointed, failed to adequately investigate and present mitigating evidence of Wood’s mental deficiencies during the penalty phase of the trial. Wood also allegedly failed to tell the sentencing judge that he would request further psychological evaluation before he presented the case to the judge.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Alabama today announced criminal charges against Wood. The SEC's complaint charges Wood with violating Section 2254(e)(1) and Rule 206(2)-3 thereunder, and seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty. The complaint also seeks a preliminary injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and an officer-and-director bar against Wood, as well as a bar against him from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any security, including the right to apply for a penny stock. The court granted the SEC the right, without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, to review the record and determine whether it is reasonable to grant the SEC relief. The case is being supervised by Kelly L. Gibson, Chief of the Atlanta Regional Office, and Ms. Gibson is supervising the case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Northern District of Indiana ruled that Indiana's requirement that political parties submit an oath that they do not advocate the overthrow of local, state, or national government by force or violence is unconstitutional. The court held that the oath is a form of advocacy directed at promoting unlawful action, as distinguished from advocacy of abstract doctrine, and therefore impermissibly violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments. The Court also found that the court's order requiring the parties to submit an affidavit that they did not advocate overthrows of government was not a valid exercise of the legislature's power. The Supreme Court ruled in Yates v. United States (1968) that the term 'advocate' has the meaning given it by the Supreme Court of the United States in Yates, and that it is a broad oath embracing advocacy of the teaching of concrete action for the forcible overthrow of the government, and not of principles divorced from action. We hold that the loyalty oath requirement of  29—3812 is constitutional only insofar as it does not promote advocacy of unlawful action as well as advocacy of action. The Constitution's First Amendment guarantees the right to a free and fair election, and the Court concludes that this provision is not a legitimate exercise of that right.

The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) sets a one-year limitation period for filing such petitions, running from “the date on which the judgment became final by the conclusion of direct review or the expiration of the time for seeking such review.” 28 U. S. C. §2244(d)(1)(A). Under Eleventh Circuit precedent, that tolling period does not include the 90 days in which a petitioner might have sought certiorari review in this Court challenging state-court denial of postconviction relief. A newly assigned Magistrate Judge noticed the State’s computation error and ordered Day to show cause why his federal habeas petition should not be dismissed as untimely. The untolled time was 388 days. After affording the petitioner an opportunity to present cause why the petition was not dismissed for failure to meet the statutory deadline, the Magistrate judge recommended dismissal of the petition. The District Court adopted that recommendation, and the Court of Appeals affirmed, concluding that “[a] concession of timeliness by the state that is patently erroneous does not compromise the authority of a district court sU. Sonte to dismiss a federal habas petition as timely, under AEDPA,” Day v. Crosby, 391 F. 3d 1192, 1195. Held: A federal court, on its own initiative, dismisses a state prisoner’d petition for a writ of habbeas corpus, once the State has answered the petition without contesting its timelily. The limitations defense resembles other threshold barriers—exhaustion of state remedies, procedural default, and nonretroactivity—courts have typed “nonjurisdictional,’” although recognizing that those defenses “implicat[e] values beyond the concerns of the parties.’ ” Acosta v. Artuz, 221 F.3d 117, 122 (under the Civil Procedure Rules), see, e.g., Hill v. Braxton, 277f. 3rd 701, 705 (in which a defendant forfeits a statute of limitations defense, see Fed. Rule Civ. Proc. 8(c), not asserted in its answer, see Rule 12(b), or an amendment thereto), see Rule 15(a). Pp. 4–6. (a) A district court is not required to double-check the State's math, since courts are under no obligation to raise the time bar. See, e, g., Acosta, 221-3d 1193, at 123. The considerations of comity, finality, and expeditious handling of habea proceedings that motivated a state court judgment are not essential to determining whether a state statute of limitation defense should be raised, see, for example, when a state attorney calculated the days in between petitions incorrectly. The State, on the other hand, points out that the statute is akin to other affirmative defenses to state petitions, notably exhaustion of state remedy, procedural defaults, nonretriactivity, and exhaustion of the state remedies. Moreover, it is explicitly aligned with those other defenses under the current version of Habeas Rule 5 (b), which provides that the State “must state whether any claim in the petition is barred by a failure to exhaust state remedies … a procedural bar, nonresroactivity, or a statuteof limitations” (emphasis added). Moreover, the considerations of state-law grounds for the state court decision are also essential to the state courts’ discretion to raise a state-to-the-prisoner limitation defense. P. 6. (b) In the circumstances here presented, the federal court confronted no intelligent waiver on the State, only an evident miscalculation of the elapsed time under a statute designed to impose a tight time constraint on federal haabeas petitioners. See id., at 6–7. The Court has unanimously held that, in appropriate circumstances, courts on their own initiative may raise a “pp. 6–9” procedural default. See also Schiro v. Farley, 510 U.S. 222, 229 (declining to address the nonretrieactivity defense that State raised only in Supreme Court merits brief, “ ‘a]lthough we undoubtedly have the discretion to reach” the argument). The court must assure itself that the petitioner is not significantly prejudiced by the delayed focus on the limitation issue, and “determine whether the interests of justice would be better served” by addressing the merits or by dismissing the petition as time barred. Id., at 8–9. The procedural hindrance in Pliler was the failure of the State to exhaust its state remedies and the resulting potential for delay on the road to finality. The court also had discretion to dismiss the petition, even when the respondent elects to waive the limitation and oppose the petition solely on the merits. See Long v. Wilson, 39

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 forbids employment discrimination. In 1972 Congress amended Title VII so that it applies not only to employment in the private sector, but to the Federal Government as well. The relevant section of that section, §717(a), provides that, after an agency or the EEOC takes final action on a complaint (or fails to take action within a certain time), "an employee or applicant [who is still] aggrieved may file a civil action as provided in section [706, dealing with discrimination by private employers] . . . in which civil action the head of the department, agency, or unit, as appropriate, shall be the defendant." 42 U. S. C. § 2000e 16(a)(1). Respondent, a complaining party under Title VII, filed a complaint with the Department of Veterans Affairs charging that the Department had discriminated against him in violation of Title VII. The District Court dismissed the Department's claim, but the Court of Appeals reversed the District Court's dismissal. The Seventh Circuit reversed and reversed, rejecting the Department Department's argument because, in its view, the Department lacked the legal power to award compensatory damages; consequently, there was no administrative remedy to exhaust. Held: The EEOC possesses the legal authority to enforce Title VII through an award of compensation damages. Pp. 488-476. (a) The language, purposes, and history of the 1972 Title VII extension and the 1991 CDA convince us that Congress has authorized the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) to award compensation damages in Federal Government employment discrimination cases. See, e. g., Title VII's language, taken together with statutory purposes, history, and the absence of any convincing reason for denying theEEOC the relevant power, produce evidence of a waiver that satisfies the stricter standard. P. 489. (b) The meaning of the word "appropriate" permits its scope to expand to include Title VII remedies that were not appropriate before 1991, but in light of legal change are appropriate now. The word "including" makes clear that "appropriate remedies" are not limited to the examples that follow that word. See Phelps Dodge Corp. v. NLRB, 313 U.S. 177, 189, 189. And in context the word most naturally refers to forms of relief that Title VII itself authorizes at least where that relief is of a kind that agencies typically can provide. Thus, Congress' decision to permit a "complaining party" to "recover compensatory damage" in "an action brought under section 717," by adding compensatory-related damages to Title VII’s arsenal of remedies, could make that form of relief “appropriate” under § 717(b) as well as § 1981a(a) (1). The meaning is not surprising, for in 1972 (and until 1991) Title VII authorized only equitable remedies. The CDA also authorized only such remedies, see New York Gaslight Club, Inc. v., Carey, 447 US. 54, 60 62, and in this case, the waived damages remedy is to be administered in a manner that is consistent with a grant of that authority. Moreover, the CDA's language does not freeze the scope of the "appropriate remedy" as of 1972. Rather, it makes clear in §1981a(c), the civil action subsection itself, rather than cross-referencing the whole of §7 17, which includes authorization for the EEoc to enforce the section through "appropriate " remedies. This is a distinct question concerning how the waived-reversal remedy is being administered. Finally, the fact that Congress permits an employee to file a complaint in court but forbids the agency to challenge an adverse EEOC decision in court, also suggests that Congress was not inordinately and unusually concerned with invoking special judicial safeguards to protect the Government. The mere use of the term "action" in the context of a cross-reference to the whole is not an indication that Congress intended more. The language of §1981(a)'s language, which says nothing about the EEFC, or EEOC proceedings, but rather states only that the complaining party may recover compensatory compensation "in an action brought [under] § 1981A(a(1)," does not indicate an intent to deprive that EEOC of that power. Nor is the simple use of that word in the case of a "action"-reference to § 1981(b)'s whole-of-§717-a-1-a waiver that does not violate the statutory language. Nor does the language in § 1981'c's language suggest that Congress saw the provision primarily as a benefit to complaining parties, not to the Government, and that Congress' intent to create a new remedy in order, for example, to provide appropriate remedies for intentional discrimination in the workplace. Nor, by using the word, "appropriate," Congress waives the Government's sovereign immunity, and we must construe any waiver narrowly. See Lane v. Pen

The U.S. District Court for the District of Maine today entered a final judgment in favor of Maine's imposition of a federal import ban on live baitfish.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Portland, Maine, alleges that Maine violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, Maine's import ban was imposed in 1981 on the basis of a finding by a federal district court in New Hampshire that there was no reasonable basis for the federal government to enforce the import ban.  In addition, the complaint alleges that, in 1981, Maine imposed a temporary restraining order on the importation of live baiting fish.  As the complaint further alleges, the suspension of the ban was based on "unmistakably clear" evidence that the state had no reasonable interest in enforcing the import restrictions.  For example, as the complaint states, "an aura of economic protectionism surrounded statements made in 1981 by the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife in opposition to a proposal by appellee himself to repeal the ban."  The complaint also alleges that a state administrative agency long after the federal court ruled that Maine could not rely on standard testing and inspection procedures in the case of fish taken, possessed, transported, or sold in violation of any law or regulation of any state.   In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Middle District of New York today announced criminal charges against Appellee for violating and conspiring to violate the federal anti-fishing laws.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from future violations of the federal securities laws, ordering them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and imposing civil penalties. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry of the Boston Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Appellant First English Evangelical Lutheran Church purchased a 21-acre parcel of land in a canyon along the banks of the Middle Fork of Mill Creek in the Angeles National Forest, which is the natural drainage channel for a watershed area owned by the National Forest Service. The church operated on the site a campground and recreational area for handicapped children. In response to the flooding of the canyon, appellee County of Los Angeles adopted Interim Ordinance No. 11,855, which provided that "a person shall not construct, reconstruct, place or enlarge any building or structure, any portion of which is, or will be, located within the outer boundary lines of the interim flood protection area located in Mill Creek Canyon. The ordinance was effective immediately because the county determined that it was required for the immediate preservation of the public health and safety. Appellant moved to strike the portions of the complaint alleging that the county's ordinance denied all use of Lutherglen, on the view that the California Supreme Court's decision in Agins v. Tiburon, 24 Cal. 3d 266, aff'd on other grounds, rendered the allegation "entirely immaterial and irrelevant[, with] no bearing upon any conceivable cause of action herein." The California Court of Appeal affirmed, holding that, regardless of the correctness of appellant's claim that the challenged ordinance denies it "all use," appellant may not recover damages until the ordinance is finally declared unconstitutional, and then only for any period after that declaration for which the county seeks to enforce it. Held: 1. The Just Compensation Clause requires the Government to pay for "temporary" regulatory takings. Pp. 5-7. (a) The Fifth Amendment's just compensation provision is designed to bar Government from forcing some people alone to bear public burdens which, in all fairness and justice, should be borne by the public as a whole. P. 5. (b) The fact that regulations considered to be in issue by the state court did not effect a taking, Agins, does not mean that the Fifth Amendment requires compensation for the period of time during which regulations deny a landowner all use. P p. 5, 6. (c) The principle that the decision to exercise the power of eminent domain is a legislative function "for Congress and Congress alone to determine," is not intended to abrogate the principle that "private property [shall not] be taken for public use, without just compensation," as the Court has frequently noted, and thus places a condition on the exercise of that power. See, e. g., Williamson County Regional Planning Comm'n v. Hamilton Bank, 473 U. S. 172, and Agins.Tiburon, 447 U.S. 255, distinguished. In each of these cases, the Court concluded either that the regulations were not effecting a taking or that the factual disputes yet to be resolved by state authorities might still lead to the conclusion that no taking had occurred. Thus, it did not, as the Solicitor General suggests, require a court, at the behest of a private person, to require the Government's exercise of the eminent domain power, but merely held that where the government's activities have already worked a taking of all of use of property, no subsequent action by the government can relieve it of the duty to provide compensation for that period during which the taking was effective. Nothing we say today is intended to undermine the principle of inverse condemnation, which, as here, denies a land owner all of his property, but instead places a requirement on the exercising of that authority. The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri ruled in favor of the federal government's bid to enjoin the merger of G.R. Kinney Company, Inc. and the Brown Shoe Company. Inc. The court found that the merger would not lessen competition in the production of shoes for the national wholesale shoe market and in the sale of shoes at retail in the Nation. The Federal Trade Commission's complaint, filed in 1955, alleged that a contemplated merger between Kinney and Brown would violate the antitrust provisions of the Clayton Act. The complaint alleged that the effect of the merger was to create a monopoly in the manufacture and sale of men's, women's and children's shoes. The District Court agreed with the Government's position that there was no evidence that the proposed merger would be anticompetitive. The Court also found that Kinney's manufacturing facilities would not be affected by the merger. The merger was approved by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve Bank of the United States and the Federal Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. The case was brought by the U.N. Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Office of the Inspector General of the Justice Department.

Petitioners, privately employed in Jefferson County, Alabama, brought an action in Federal District Court challenging the validity of an occupation tax imposed by Jefferson County in 1987. That action was dismissed as barred by the Tax Injunction Act, 28 U. S. C. Section (s) 1341. The trial court granted summary judgment as to the state constitutional claims, but refused to do so as to federal claims because they had not been decided by either the trial court or the Alabama Supreme Court in Bedingfield. On appeal, the county argued that the federal claims as well as the state claims were barred because they were adequately represented in the action. The Alabama Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Since petitioners received neither notice of, nor sufficient representation in, the Bededfield litigation, that adjudication, as a matter of federal due process, may not bind them and thus cannot bar them from challenging an allegedly unconstitutional deprivation of their property. Pp. 662-664. (a) The limits on a state court's power to develop estoppel rules reflect the general consensus that members of a class not present as parties to the litigation may be bound by the judgment where they are in fact adequately represented by parties who are present, or . . . the relationship between the parties present and those who are absent is such as legally to entitle the former to stand in judgment for the latter." Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32, 37. P. 663. (b) Because the guarantee of due process is not a mere form, however, there obviously exists another category of taxpayer cases in which the State may not deprive individual litigants of their own day in court. By virtue of presenting a federal constitutional challenge to a State's attempt to levy personal funds, petitioners clearly bring an action of this latter type. Cf. ibid. (distinguishing between "public" and "private" actions). The Alabama court concluded that the suit was of a kind that, under state law, could be brought only on behalf of the public at large. The court also concluded that petitioners' suit may nevertheless be barred by a prior action in the case. The judgment in that case met these requirements. The State Supreme Court concluded that, even though the opinion in the earlier case did not mention any federal issue, that the judgment in the present action met those requirements. Held. (c) Because petitioners did not receive the kind of opportunity to make their case in court that due process would ordinarily ensure, the character of their action renders the usual constitutional protections inapplicable. That general rule clearly applies when a taxpayer seeks a hearing to prevent the State from subjecting him to a levy in violation of the Federal Constitution. The doctrine of representation of absent parties in a class suit could not support the decree. Thus, the court's decision that the state courts should not deprive petitioners of their "chose in action," which they have held to be a protected property interest in its own right, does not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to bind a litigant to a prior judgment to which he was not a party by service of process, since that general rule does not afford it similar freedom to bind the litigateant to that prior judgment. Moreover, since the guarantee does not always require one to have been a party to a judgment, but may be used to describe various relationships that would not have come within the traditional definition of that term, the doctrine cannot support a decree of this type. P p. 664. 2. The fact that the court failed to provide petitioners with any notice that a suit was pending which would conclusively resolve their legal rights does not mean that it took care to protect the interests of petitioners in the manner suggested in Hansberry. Nor is there any reason to suppose that the individual taxpayers in the suit adequately represented petitioners, since their pleadings did not purport to assert any claim against or on behalf any nonparties; and the judgment they received, in pledging tax revenues and issuing bonds, did not bind any county taxpayers who were nonpartied. P, 662 So. 2d 1270, reversed and remanded.

After respondent McIntire distributed anonymous handbills supporting a school board candidate in Cincinnati, Ohio, she was charged with violating Ohio Revised Code § 3599.09(A)-which requires that every person who publishes, posts, circulates, or distributes a document designed to influence the vote on a ballot measure must sign the document and give his name and address-even though the handbills contained no mention of the candidate and stated that they were prepared by a group called Citizens Against Unlimited Tax Levels. Section 3599.09(A) applies to all documents except those relating to judicial races, and it specifies that failure to comply with its signature and address requirements renders the offending document void. Respondent claimed that she was immune from prosecution under the First Amendment. The trial court dismissed the charge, ruling that the statute was facially unconstitutional. However, the Ohio Supreme Court reversed, concluding that the statute served the constitutionally permissible purposes of protecting the integrity of the electoral process and ensuring accountability for the actions of candidates and their agents. Held: 1. The Ohio statute is unconstitutionally overbroad. Pp. 10-16. (a) The statute is not saved by the fact that it is part of a comprehensive scheme addressing election fraud. While the statute is aimed primarily at fraudulent and libelous statements, it is nevertheless applicable to innocent acts, since it covers documents that are not even arguably false or misleading. And while the statute is aimed at the activities of candidates and their organizational supporters, it applies not only to them but also to individuals acting independently and using only their own modest resources. More importantly, the statute applies not only to elections of public officials but also to ballot issues that present neither a substantial risk of libel nor any potential appearance of corrupt advantage. Pp. 10-12. (b) The statute is not saved by the asserted state interests in preventing fraud and libel. Since the statute is merely a supplement to the detailed and specific prohibitions against making or disseminating false statements during political campaigns, it is too broad to be sustained on the basis of those prohibitions alone. Similarly, since the statute is merely a supplement to the direct bans on disseminating false documents against anonymous authors and distributors, it is too broad to be sustained on the basis of those bans alone. Pp. 12-14. (c) The statute is not saved by the asserted state interest in obtaining the identity of the author of a document. The absence of the author's name on a document does not necessarily protect either that person or a distributor of a forbidden document from being held responsible for compliance with the election code. Nor has the State explained why it can more easily enforce the direct bans on disseminating false documents against anonymous authors and distributors than against wrongdoers who might use false names and addresses in an attempt to avoid detection. Pp. 14-15. (d) The statute is not saved by the asserted state interest in obtaining the identity of the author of a document in order to hold him accountable for compliance with the election code. The State has not shown that its interest in preventing the misuse of anonymous election-related speech justifies a prohibition of all uses of that speech. Pp. 15-16. 2. The Ohio statute is not rendered constitutional by virtue of its inclusion in a comprehensive scheme addressing election fraud. The statute is not saved by the asserted state interests in preventing fraud and libel. Nor is it saved by the asserted state interest in obtaining the identity of the author of a document in order to hold him accountable for compliance with the election code. Pp. 10-16. 67 Ohio St. 2d 15, 410 N. E. 2d 455, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in a related case against two officers charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Chicago, alleges that, on April 2, 1997, Tera McArthur asked two officers to accompany her to the trailer where she lived with her husband, Charles McArthur, so that they could keep the peace while they obtained a search warrant.  According to the complaint, McArthur agreed, without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, to the entry of a warrant without a warrant, which would have required the officers to enter the trailer and search it.  McArthur also agreed to be restrained from entering the trailer.  In a parallel action, the Illinois Attorney General's Office today announced that it filed criminal charges against McArthur.  On May 24, 2018, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against the officers, charging McArthur with violations of the federal securities laws, including, without limitation, warrantless entry and search of a home, without reasonable suspicion of a crime or contraband, and without reasonable grounds to believe that McArthur would destroy the drugs or harm the evidence.

After petitioner James entered into a plea agreement admitting guilt to federal charges stemming from a failed attempt to obtain controlled substances using fraudulent prescriptions, the District Court revoked his supervised release and imposed a new sentence because he had previously served time for a state-court conviction for attempted burglary. The Eleventh Circuit reversed, ruling that the attempted burglary conviction did not qualify as a “violent felony” for purposes of the Armed Career Criminal Act of 1984 (ACCA), which enhances sentences for defendants who have previously been convicted of specified violent felonies. The court agreed with James that the ACCA’s residual clause—under which a conviction for an unlisted offense counts as a violent felony if it “involve[s] conduct that presents a serious potential risk of physical injury to another”—covers attempted burglary. However, the court ruled that James’ attempted burglary conviction did not fall within the residual clause because it occurred before the effective date of the ACCA’s expansion of the residual clause’s coverage to include “attempted” crimes. Held: 1. The attempted burglary conviction qualified as a violent felony under the ACCA’s residual clause. Pp. 4−12. (a) The Court begins with the assumption that the ACCA’s residual clause covers attempted burglary. If that assumption is correct, then the question becomes whether James’ attempted burglary conviction fell within the residual clause. The Court uses the categorical approach developed in Taylor v. Louisiana, 495 U.S. 674, to resolve this question. Under that approach, the Court looks to the elements of the offense as defined by state law, avoiding any inquiry into the underlying facts of the particular offense. By applying the categorical approach, the Court avoids any inquiry into the facts of James’ particular offense and engages instead in statutory interpretation. Pp. 4−6. (b) The Court determines that the elements of attempted burglary as defined by Florida law satisfy the categorical approach. First, the Court notes that the ACCA’s residual clause refers to “conduct that presents a serious potential risk of physical injury to another.” Second, the Court finds that the elements of attempted burglary as defined by Florida law fit within the bounds of the residual clause. Those elements include an overt act directed toward entering or remaining in a building or other structure, and the risk of physical injury to another. The Court considers the risk posed by an attempted entry of the curtilage surrounding a dwelling, but finds that the risk is sufficiently similar to that posed by an attempted entry of the dwelling itself to render the former comparable to the latter. The Court also considers the impact of the fact that Florida’s burglary statute defines a “dwelling” to include not only the structure itself, but also the “curtilage thereof.” However, given the narrow definition of curtilage in Florida law, the Court concludes that the inclusion of curtilage does not mitigate the risk presented by attempted burglary to such an extent as to remove the offense from the scope of the residual clause. Pp. 6−12. 2. Construing attempted burglary as a violent felony does not raise Sixth Amendment issues under Apprendi v. New Jersey, 530 U.S. 466, and its progeny. Here, the Court is engaged in statutory interpretation, not judicial factfinding. Pp. 12−13. 483 F.3d 1279, affirmed. Roberts, C. J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

On December 12, 1967, President Lyndon Johnson made a speech in Bell County, Texas, to a crowd of some 25,000 people, including many servicemen from nearby Fort Hood. Almost immediately after their arrival, they were set upon by members of the audience, subjected to some physical abuse, promptly removed from the scene by military police, turned over to Bell County officers, and taken to jail. According to the complaint, Johnson's speech had been delivered in the presence of thousands of people, many of whom were veterans. The complaint alleges that the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and that the federal district court for the District of Texas had jurisdiction over the matter.  The complaint, filed in federal court in Texas, charges the defendants with violating Section 1253 of the Exchange Act, and seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. The defendants have consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders them to pay a civil penalty of Two Hundred Dollars ($200).  The settlement is subject to court approval.  In a parallel action, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendants.
