Title: Federal Election Commission v. Wisconsin Right to Life Education Fund, Inc. (1989)

Summary: In this case, the United States Supreme Court ruled that a federal law banning corporations from making independent political expenditures during presidential campaigns applies equally to nonprofit corporations. The court held that the First Amendment protects the right of corporations to spend money independently on political campaigns, but that states may regulate such expenditures to ensure fairness in elections. The court also held that the law does not discriminate against nonprofit corporations based on their political beliefs or ideologies.

Helpless to prevent illegal entries across the border, the Federal Government has established a complex scheme governing admission to the United States and status within our borders. Under this scheme, illegal aliens are generally subject to deportation, although they may obtain temporary authorization to remain in the country. However, once in the country, an alien may secure a waiver of deportation and ultimately may become eligible for citizenship. Because of the uncertainty surrounding the ultimate fate of an undocumented alien, a State cannot realistically determine that any particular undocumented child will in fact be deported until after deportation proceedings have been completed. Nevertheless, appellee school district refused to reimburse appellant parents for the cost of educating their children, who were undocumented aliens, pursuant to a Texas statute providing that no child who is not a citizen or national of the United States shall be entitled to attend a public elementary or secondary school in the State unless he pays tuition equivalent to that charged for a citizen or national. The parents brought separate actions in Federal District Court seeking declarations that the statute violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court ruled in favor of the parents, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Illegal aliens, including undocumented aliens, are entitled to the protections of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 48-51. (a) The Fourteenth Amendment applies to all persons physically present in the United States, regardless of how they came to be here. Pp. 48-50. (b) The Equal Protection Clause requires that the classification of aliens be reasonable and that it further some substantial state interest. Pp. 50-51. 2. Denial of free public education to undocumented aliens does not meet the requirements of the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 51-61. (a) Undocumented aliens cannot be treated as a suspect class because their presence in this country in violation of federal law is not a "constitutional irrelevancy." Nor is education a fundamental right, a State need not justify by compelling necessity every variation in the manner in which education is provided to its population. Pp. 51-53. (b) The State's asserted interest in conserving the State's limited educational resources for the education of its lawful residents does not justify the classification at issue. Charging tuition to undocumented children constitutes a ludicrously ineffective attempt to stem the tide of illegal immigration, especially when compared with the alternative of prohibiting the employment of illegal aliens. Furthermore, the record contains no evidence that undocumented children impose any significant burden on the State's economy. Pp. 53-56. (c) The State's asserted interest in improving the overall quality of education in the State does not justify the classification at issue. The record contains no evidence that exclusion of undocumented children is likely to improve the overall quality of education in the State. Undocumented children are basically indistinguishable from legally resident alien children. Pp. 56-57. (d) Assuming that the State's asserted interest in reducing the likelihood that undocumented children will remain within the State's boundaries and put their education to productive social or political use within the State is legitimate, it is an interest that is most difficult to quantify. Many of the undocumented children disabled by this classification will remain in this country indefinitely, and some will become lawful residents or citizens of the United States. Pp. 57-59. 628 F. 2d 451, and 628 F. 2d 454, affirmed.

Petitioner was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death. He unsuccessfully challenged the conviction on direct appeal and state collateral proceedings in the Texas state courts, and in a federal habeas petition. In February 1992, he urged in a second federal petition that he was "actually innocent" of the murder for which he was sentenced. The evidence showed that petitioner's Social Security card had been found alongside Rucker's patrol car on the night he was killed, and that, under Townsend v. Sain, 372 U. S. 293, 317, "the existence merely of newly discovered evidence relevant to the guilt of a state prisoner is not a ground for relief on federal habas corpus." The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution prohibit the execution of a person who is innocent of the crime for which they were convicted. Pp. 488-478. (a) The Eighth Amendment's prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment and the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of due process of law therefore forbid his execution. P. 489. (b) The fact that the Eighth Amendment requires increased reliability of the process by which capital punishment may be imposed does not entitle petitioner to a new trial, or at least to a vacation of his death sentence. In fact, it is not disputed that the State met its burden of proving at trial that petitioner was guilty of the capital murder of Officer Carrisalez beyond a reasonable doubt. Thus, in the eyes of the law, petitioner does not come before the Court as one who is "innocent," but on the contrary as one whose guilt or innocence was established in the first place. Moreover, the passage of time only diminishes the reliability of criminal adjudications. See, e. g., McCleskey v. Zant, ante, p. 486, 589. Thus petitioner's claim that evidence never presented to the trial court proves him innocent notwithstanding the verdict reached at his trial is not cognizable in the state courts of Texas, since the evidence in the new trial context, motions based solely upon affidavits are disfavored because the affiants' statements are obtained without the benefit of cross-examination and an opportunity to make credibility determinations. See Orfield, New Trial in Federal Criminal Cases, 2 Vill. L. Rev. 293. Pc. 498-481. (c) In light of the historical availability of new trials, our own amendments to Rule 33, and the contemporary practice in the States, the likelihood of abuse is as great-or greater-here. Here, petitioner is left without a forum to raise his actual innocence claim, since there is no guarantee that the guilt and innocence determination would be any more exact. To conclude otherwise would all but paralyze our system for enforcement of the criminal law, and this Court would be placed in the even more difficult position of having to weigh the probative value of "hot" and "cold" evidence on petitioner's guilt or innocent claim. P p.481. 2. There is no merit to petitioner's contention that the fact that his new trial motion based solely on affidavits is not sufficient to convict him, but rather argues that he is entitled to relief because newly-discovered evidence shows that his conviction is factually incorrect. This Court has never held that it extends to free-standing claims of actual innocence. See id., at 411, 106 S. C. .

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California today entered a final judgment in favor of the Indian Tribe of California in a civil injunctive action brought by the District Court against the Forest Service.  The court found that the First Amendment provides for the right of the individual to participate in the free exercise of religious beliefs.  In its judgment, the court held that the federal government has a duty to protect and preserve the rights and practices of Native American communities.  According to the court's order, filed in 1977, the Indian tribe consented to the entry of an injunction against the construction of a road through the Chimney Rock area of the Six Rivers National Forest. The court also ruled that the Tribe's request for a temporary restraining order would not violate the federal securities laws, the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and the "free exercise of religion" provision of Section 15 of the Exchange Act.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court order, the Tribe consented, without admitting to the facts of the matter, to a judgment that permanently enjoins the government from violating the federal and state securities laws and requires the Tribe to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The order also prohibits the Tribe from participating in the construction or operation of any type of "public" road, including the purchase or sale of any timber, without providing a compelling reason for doing so.  On the same day, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced criminal charges against the Tribe.  To learn more about the federal district court's orders, see Litigation Release No. 5, No. 1798.  For more information on the tribe's religious practices, see http://www.securities.gov/index.php.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in a Batson-related civil injunctive action, finding that the defendant violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the defendant and ordered him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  According to the SEC's order, filed in federal district court in Jackson, Alabama, on May 5, 1996, the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia issued an order finding that a jury should not be excluded based on a defendant’s race-neutral explanation for the Batson challenge.  In its order, the court found that the prosecutor lied about the eye rolling and struck Juror 16 in part because of her youth and lack of ties to the community.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court order, Judge Batson agreed with the court that a reasonable factfinder must determine whether the defendant has carried his burden of proving purposeful discrimination in jury selection on the basis of race.  On May 9, 2016, the U. S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Alabama entered a judgment finding that requires a jury trial to be conducted by a qualified person with a history of race-based discrimination, and that the jury should be able to determine whether to accept or reject the jury selection order based on race-related factors, including the defendant's age, his race, and his experience as a result of his or her previous criminal convictions.   The Court also entered an order requiring the defendant to show cause and effect in a case that is subject to court approval.  For example, the order requires the jury to be seated at least five minutes before the alleged eye rolling occurred, and the judge must have observed the eye roll before imposing a sentence.  It also requires that the trial court determine whether a defendant has a duty of proof to show that a defendant is competent to be impartial.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central question was whether a police officer's actions during a high-speed chase, which resulted in a fatality, violated the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of substantive due process. The Court held that such conduct does not constitute a due process violation unless there is a purpose to cause harm unrelated to the legitimate objective of arrest.

The case arose from an incident on May 22, 1990, when Deputy James Everett Smith pursued a motorcycle at high speeds in a residential area. The chase ended when the motorcycle crashed, and the patrol car struck and killed the passenger, 16-year-old Philip Lewis. Lewis's parents sued under 42 U.S.C. §1983, alleging a violation of their son's right to life under the Fourteenth Amendment.

The District Court granted summary judgment for Deputy Smith, citing qualified immunity. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed, finding that the law regarding police liability in high-speed chases was clearly established and that Smith's conduct might amount to deliberate indifference.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a conflict among the Circuits over the standard of culpability for law enforcement officers in pursuit cases. The Court concluded that the Fourth Amendment, which covers searches and seizures, did not apply because no seizure occurred as defined by precedent.

The Court emphasized that substantive due process protects against arbitrary government action and that only the most egregious conduct that "shocks the conscience" would violate due process. The Court found that while deliberate indifference to inmate welfare can constitute a due process violation in a controlled custodial setting, the same standard does not apply to the split-second decisions required during a high-speed chase.

The Court held that only a purpose to cause harm unrelated to the legitimate objective of arrest would satisfy the element of arbitrary conduct shocking to the conscience necessary for a due process violation. Since the officer's intent was to apprehend a suspect rather than to cause harm, the actions taken during the chase did not shock the conscience.

The Court reversed the judgment of the Ninth Circuit, ruling that Deputy Smith's conduct, although possibly imprudent, did not rise to the level of a constitutional violation. Therefore, the respondents' claim under §1983 was dismissed, and the officer and other petitioners were not liable under the Fourteenth Amendment for the death that occurred during the high-speed pursuit.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the State of Hawaii's Land Reform Act of 1967, which allowed the state to take land from lessors and transfer it to lessees to reduce the concentration of land ownership, does not violate the Public Use Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The Court held that the Act serves a legitimate public purpose by addressing the social and economic impacts of a land oligopoly in Hawaii, which is within the state's police powers.

The Court's decision was based on the principle that legislative determinations of what constitutes a public use are given significant deference, as long as the taking of property is rationally related to a conceivable public purpose. The Court found that the Act's approach to correcting the land oligopoly problem was rational and comprehensive, and that the redistribution of land ownership to correct market deficiencies was a valid exercise of the eminent domain power.

The Court disagreed with the Court of Appeals' narrower interpretation of the "public use" requirement, stating that the government does not need to directly use the property for it to be considered a public use. The Court also emphasized that state legislatures are as capable as Congress in determining public purposes for the exercise of the taking power.

The Court concluded that the Act met the requirements of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, assuming that just compensation was provided for the takings, and reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, remanding the cases for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. Justice Marshall did not participate in the consideration or decision of the cases.

Janus Investment Fund (Petitioner Fund), a Massachusetts business trust, manages a series of mutual funds. Petitioner Fund’s Board of Trustees consists of five individuals, four of whom are also officers of Janus Capital Management, Inc. (Petitioner Manager), a Delaware corporation that serves as Petitioner Fund’s investment manager. Petitioner Manager’s sole officer is respondent First Derivative (Respondent), a hedge fund manager. Both Petitioner Fund and Petitioner Manager are legally separate entities. Petitioner Fund’s prospectuses describe its investment strategies and represent that it implements market timing practices designed to maximize returns while minimizing risk. They also contain representations that Petitioner Fund’s managers intend to implement market timing policies and procedures. Respondent filed a putative class action claiming that Petitioner Fund and Petitioner Manager violated federal securities laws by causing the mutual funds to engage in market timing. He sought damages on his own behalf and on behalf of the purported class. The District Court dismissed the complaint, concluding that Respondent failed to allege sufficient facts to support a finding that he suffered injury. On appeal, the Fourth Circuit reversed, ruling that Respondent adequately pleaded a violation of §10(b)-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Held: Petitioner Manager cannot be held liable under §10(b)-5 for the statements in Petitioner Fund’s prospectuses. Pp. 3−11. (a) Section 10(b)-5 makes it unlawful for any person, directly or indirectly, by using any means or instrumentality of interstate commerce, or of the mails or of any national securities exchange, to make any untrue statement of a material fact or to omit to state a material fact necessary in order to make the statements made, in the light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading. 17 CFR §240.10b–5(b). The term “make” refers to the act of creating something new, see Oxford English Dictionaries Online, “make,” www.oxfordlearnersdictionaries.com/definition/english/make-1 (accessed July 12, 2011), but in the context of Rule 10b–5, it refers instead to the act of uttering a statement, see, e.g., Black’s Law Dictionary 1035. The SEC promulgated Rule 10b–5 to protect investors from fraudulent conduct by ensuring that the creators of false statements bear responsibility for their contents. Central Bank of Denver v. First Interstate Bank of Denver, 511 U.S. 164, 188. Here, Respondent argues that Petitioner Manager violated Rule 10b–5 by making the statements in the prospectuses. However, Respondent now seeks to hold Petitioner Manager liable solely as a control person of Petitioner Fund under §20(a) of the Act. Since the only question is whether Petitioner Manager made the misstatements, the only thing needed is to identify the maker of the statements. Pp. 3−5. (b) Neither the plain language of Rule 10b–5 nor the SEC’s implementing regulations indicates that the term “make” includes anyone except the creator of a statement. The SEC has interpreted the term “make” to refer to the act of creating something new, see, e.g., 17 CFR §240.10b–5(i), but the SEC’s position is untenable given the clear meaning of the term in everyday usage. The SEC’s argument that the term “make” should be construed to include the act of uttering a statement is similarly flawed. The SEC points out that the term “make” appears in conjunction with the terms “employ” and “engage,” suggesting that the three verbs share common meaning. But the words “directly or indirectly” modify all three verbs, indicating that the phrases “directly” and “indirectly” are meant to distinguish among the three actions. The SEC’s attempt to broaden the meaning of “make” to include the act of uttering a statement is also refuted by the fact that the SEC’s implementing regulation defines “directly or indirectly” as referring back to “to make.” See 17 CFR §240.10b–5(i). Pp. 5−8. (c) Petitioner Manager did not “make” any of the statements in the prospectuses. The SEC has recognized that the maker of a statement is the person or entity with ultimate authority over a statement and others are not. Central Bank, supra, at 188. Petitioner Fund bears the statutory obligation to file the prospectuses with the SEC, and nothing on the face of the prospectuses indicated that any statements therein came from Petitioner Manager rather than Petitioner Fund—a legally independent entity with its own board of directors. Petitioner Manager’s involvement in preparing the prospectuses does not change this result. While a speechwriter may help prepare what a principal says, the speechwriter himself does not “make” the statements. Similarly, Petitioner Manager’s involvement in preparing the prospectuses does not mean that it “made” the statements. Pp. 8−10. (d) Petitioner Manager cannot be held liable simply because it hosted the prospectuses on its website. Hosting a document on a website does not necessarily indicate that the hosting entity adopted the document as its own statement or exercised control over its content. P. 11. 567 F.3d 136, reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Sotomayor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

Title 49 U. S. C. § 14501(c)(1) prohibits States and their political subdivisions from enacting or enforcing laws, regulations, or other provisions “relat[ing] to a price, route, or service” of motor carriers. Exceptions to this preemption rule permit certain actions by States, political subdivisions, and political authorities of two or more States. One exception, § 14501(c)(2)(A), provides that § 14501(c)(1) “shall not restrict the safety regulatory authority of a State.” Another exception, § 14501(c)(2)(B), prohibits the transportation of household goods. Because § 14501(c)(2)(B) uses the phrase “to enact or enforce,” whereas § 14501(c)(2)(A) uses the phrase “regulatory authority,” the Court below interpreted § 14501(c)(2)(A) to cover only the authority of States, not political subdivisions. Held: Section 14501(c)(2)(A)’s exception covers the authority of political subdivisions. Pp. 429–439. (a) When Congress adds a new exception to a broad preemption rule, it usually intends to create a categorical difference between the rule and the exception. Thus, the absence of the phrase “political subdivision of a State” in § 14501(c)(2)(A) supports the conclusion that the exception covers political subdivisions. Russella v. United States, 464 U. S. 16, 23. Moreover, the fact that § 14501(c)(2)(B) uses the phrase “to enact or enforce” suggests that the drafters did not intend to distinguish between the authority of States and political subdivisions. Pp. 429–431. (b) The Court rejects the suggestion that the differences in the statute’s drafting style—whereby § 14501(c)(2)(A) refers to the “safety regulatory authority of a State,” whereas § 14501(c)(2)(B) refers to the ability to “enact or enforce”—render the absence of the phrase “political subdivision of a State” in § 14501(c)(2)(A) inconclusive. The Court’s reasoning ignores the fact that the statute contains numerous instances where the terms “State” and “political subdivision of a State” are used interchangeably. Nor does the Court explain why the differences in drafting style render the absence of the phrase “political subdivision of a State” in § 14501(c)(2)(A) conclusive, yet fail to render the absence of the phrase “political subdivision of a State” in § 14501(c)(2)(C) inconclusive. Pp. 431–433. (c) The Court’s alternative explanation—that the differences in drafting style undermine the conclusion drawn from the absence of the phrase “political subdivision of a State” in § 14501(c)(2)(A)—also fails. The Court offers no authority supporting the notion that the Russell presumption weakens with each difference in the formulation of the provisions under inspection. Moreover, the Court overlooks the fact that the statute contains numerous instances where the terms “State” and “political subdivision of a State” are used interchangeably. Pp. 433–435. (d) The Court’s assertion that absent a basis more reliable than statutory language sufficient to demonstrate a “clear and manifest purpose” to the contrary, federal courts should resist attributing to Congress a design to disturb a State’s decision on the division of authority between the State’s central and local units over safety on municipal streets and roads, is overblown. Treating § 14501(c)(1) as some extraordinary federal obstruction of state allocation of power is absurd. The italicized language in § 14501(c)(1) massively limits the scope of preemption to include only laws, regulations, and other provisions that single out for special treatment “motor carriers of property.” States and political subdivisions remain free to enact and enforce general traffic safety laws, general restrictions on the weight of cars and trucks that may enter highways or pass over bridges, and other regulations that do not target motor carriers “with respect to the transportation of property.” In addition, the exception contained in § 14501(c)(2)(A) allows a State—but not a political subdivision—to apply special safety rules (rules adopted under its “safety regulatory authority”) to motor carriers of property. Pp. 435–439. 299 F. 3d 481, vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Rehnquist, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Illinois today announced criminal charges against Donald Charlton and John Parisi, two former federal agents, for conducting an undercover operation in an East St. Louis prison.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Chicago, alleges that, while incarcerated in Montgomery County, Illinois, Charlton told the FBI that he had learned about a murder that respondent had committed while incarcerated at Graham Correctional Facility, where he had been serving a sentence for burglary. According to the complaint, the FBI believed that Charlton had learned of the Stephenson murder from a fellow inmate, who told him in detail about the murder. The complaint further alleges that the FBI did not consider Charlton's account as credible, and instead placed an undercover agent in the cellblock with the three of them. The SEC also charged a former federal agent with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 17(a)(1) of Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 17(b)(2)(A) thereunder. The court granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an officer-and-director bar against Charlton, and a conduct-based injunction prohibiting him from participating in any undercover activity.  In a parallel action, the United States District Court for the Central District of New York today entered a final judgment against the defendants, ordering the defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and injunctive relief.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC case, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders them to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $10,000. The settlement is subject to court approval.

Case Name: Haywood v. Williams
Case Number: 50 U.S. __ (1852)
Decided Date: March 3, 1852
Issue: Whether African Americans have the right to sue in federal court?
Background Information: Dred Scott sued his former master John Emerson Williams in federal court in St. Louis, Missouri, alleging that he owed him money. However, the court ruled that Scott did not have the right to bring a lawsuit in federal court because he was an African American.
Legal Analysis: The Supreme Court reviewed the history of the Thirteenth Amendment and previous cases regarding the rights of African Americans to sue in federal court. The Court held that the Thirteenth Amendment granted African Americans the right to sue in federal court. The Court also clarified that the Dred Scott decision was wrongly decided and had no precedential value.
Impact: The Haywood v. Williams case established the principle that African Americans have the right to sue in federal court. This decision helped to lay the foundation for future landmark cases challenging segregation and discrimination against African Americans, such as Brown v. Board of Education.

Respondent Summit Church of Ohio, Inc., whose teachings incorporate elements of Gnostic Christianity, submitted a proposal to petitioner Pleasant Grove City Council to allow it to install a permanent monument featuring seven aphorisms central to its beliefs in the city’s park. The Council declined, citing its policy of limiting monuments to ones relating to the city’s history or honoring deceased residents. Respondent sued, claiming that the Council’s refusal amounted to viewpoint discrimination in violation of the Free Speech Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court agreed, ordering the Council to grant respondent’s request. The Tenth Circuit affirmed, concluding that the Council’s policy was facially invalid because it discriminated against speech based on viewpoint. Held: The City Council’s decision to accept certain privately donated monuments while rejecting respondent’s is best viewed as a form of government speech, and thus is not subject to the Free Speech Clause. Pp. 4–12. (a) The City Council’s decision to accept certain privately donated monuments while rejecting respondent’s is best understood as a form of government speech. Pp. 4–7. (1) The City Council acted in furtherance of its own goals, namely, preserving the character of the park and promoting the city’s interests. Accepting the donated monuments enabled the city to achieve both objectives. Pp. 4–5. (2) The City Council’s decision reflects its determination to promote the values embodied in the donated monuments. That determination represents the city’s exercise of its discretionary powers. Pp. 5–6. (3) The City Council’s decision cannot be characterized as mere facilitation of private speech. Facilitating private speech requires the government to act neutrally toward competing viewpoints, whereas here the City Council chose to associate itself with the values represented by the donated monuments. P. 6. (b) The City Council’s decision should not be analyzed using the framework of public forum doctrine. Pp. 7–12. (1) Public parks are not traditional public forums for the purpose of erecting privately donated monuments. Unlike public forums, public parks can accommodate only a limited number of permanent monuments. Speakers, no matter how long-winded, eventually come to the end of their remarks; persons distributing literature and carrying signs at some point tire and go home; but monuments endure. They monopolize the use of the land on which they stand and interfere permanently with other uses of public space. Thus, applying forum analysis to the installation of permanent monuments on public property is misplaced. Pp. 7–10. (2) Forum analysis does not apply to the installation of permanent monuments on public property. Pp. 10–12. 499 F. 3d 1167, reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Roberts, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined. Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

The Supreme Court considered whether New York's "Son of Sam" law, which requires that income from works describing a criminal's crime be placed in escrow for victims, is consistent with the First Amendment. The law was enacted following the capture of serial killer David Berkowitz, known as the Son of Sam, to prevent criminals from profiting from the publicity of their crimes while ensuring victims are compensated.

The Court found that the law is a content-based statute that imposes a financial burden on speech due to its content, which is presumptively inconsistent with the First Amendment. The law applies to any expressive work that includes the author's thoughts or recollections about their crime, regardless of the work's primary focus, and can affect any author who admits to having committed a crime, even if not convicted.

While the State has a compelling interest in ensuring that victims are compensated by those who harm them and in preventing criminals from profiting from their crimes, the Court determined that the Son of Sam law is not narrowly tailored to serve these interests. The law is overinclusive, potentially affecting a wide range of expressive works unrelated to the crime itself or the criminal's profit from the crime.

The Court concluded that the Son of Sam law, by singling out income from specific speech for a financial burden, is inconsistent with the First Amendment. The judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed, and the law was struck down as unconstitutional. Justice Thomas did not participate in the decision.

Respondent Asahi Metal Industry Co., Ltd. (Asahi), a Japanese corporation that manufactures tire valve assemblies in Japan and sells the assemblies to Cheng Shin Rubber Industrial Co. Ltd., a Taiwanese manufacturer of the tube's valve assembly, filed a product liability action in the Superior Court of California, alleging that the 1978 accident was caused by a sudden loss of air and an explosion in the rear tire of the motorcycle, and alleged that the motorcycle tire, tube, and sealant were defective. Asahi moved to quash Asahi's summons, arguing that the exercise of jurisdiction was inconsistent with the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court of Appeal of the State of California issued a peremptory writ of mandate commanding the Court to compel Asahi to respond in California solely on the basis of ultimately realized foreseeability that the product into which its component was embodied would be sold all over the world including California. Held: 1. The mere awareness on the part of a foreign defendant that the components it manufactured, sold, and delivered outside the United States would reach the forum State in the stream of commerce constitutes "minimum contacts" between the defendant and the forum state such that the exercising of jurisdiction "does not offend "traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice." International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U. S. 310, 316. Pp. 4-7. 2. The exercise of personal jurisdiction over Asahi in this instance would be unreasonable and unfair. Id., at 48, 216 Cal. Rptr. 385, 702 P. 2d 543, reversed and remanded.

Respondent School Board, in order to remain eligible for federal funds, adopted a "freedom-of-choice" plan whereby each pupil could elect to attend either the formerly all-white "New Kent" school or the formerly all-black "Watkins" school. Petitioners sued for injunctive relief challenging the constitutionality of the system. A three-judge District Court ultimately approved the "freedom-of-choice" plan as amended. The Court of Appeals affirmed in pertinent part but remanded the case to the District Court for entry of an order concerning faculty. Held: 1. Desegregation requires the establishment of a unitary, nonracial school system rather than a dual system of separate "white" and "Negro" schools. Brown v. Board of Education, 349 U. S. 301. Pp. 408-410. 2. Respondent School Board's "freedom-of-choice" plan does not represent a sufficient step to "effectuate a transition" to a unitary system since it has resulted in little change from the status quo. Pp. 410-413. 382 F. 2d 338, vacated in part and remanded.

The petitioners, a corporation and two of its employees, were brought to trial before a jury in a federal district court upon an indictment charging a conspiracy and the substantive offense of concealing material facts in a matter within the jurisdiction of an agency of the United States, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 371 and 1001, and the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the court's order, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia, the defendants were brought in to trial on a conspiracy charge, and a federal judge directed the jury to return verdicts of acquittal as to all the defendants, and then ordered the jury back to return the verdicts as to the defendants.  The court granted the petitioners' request for a writ of mandamus, which requires the judge to issue a bench warrant for a person under indictment returned by a properly constituted grand jury.  In granting the petition, the court found that the district judge was without power to direct an acquittal based upon two factors: supposed improper conduct on the part of the Assistant United States Attorney who was prosecuting the case and a supposed lack of credibility in the testimony of the witnesses for the prosecution who had testified up to that point.

Petitioner Fiore was convicted of violating a Pennsylvania statute prohibiting the operation of a hazardous waste facility without a permit. He appealed, arguing that he had a valid permit, but the Pennsylvania Supreme Court declined to review his case, and his conviction became final. Later, however, the State Supreme Court reviewed the conviction of Fiore's codefendant, finding that the statute meant what it said: One who deviates from his permit's terms does not violate the statute because he remains a person with a permit. On petitioner's ensuing federal habeas challenge, the Third Circuit concluded that the Pennsylvania Supreme Court had announced a new rule of law, inapplicable to Fiore's already final conviction. Held: Fiore's conviction violates the Federal Due Process Clause. Certification of the state-law question to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court revealed that the latter's decision in the codefendant's case was not a new interpretation of the statute, but rather a correct statement of the law when Fiore's conviction became final. Thus, there is no issue of retroactivity here. Instead, the only remaining question is whether Pennsylvania can, consistently with the Due Process Clause, convict Fiore for conduct that its criminal statute, as properly interpreted, does not prohibit. It cannot do so, since failure to possess a permit is an essential element of the offense charged against him, and the record shows that the Commonwealth presented no proof that he lacked such permission. Reversed and remanded.

In April 1992, respondents were indicted in Federal District Court on charges of conspiring to possess with intent to distribute more than 50 grams of cocaine base (crack) and conspiring to distribute the same, in violation of 21 U. S. C. Section (s) 841 and 846 (1988 ed. and Supp. IV), and federal firearms offenses. For three months prior to the indictment, agents of the Federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms and the Narcotics Division had infiltrated a suspected crack distribution ring by using three confidential informants. The informants had bought a total of 124.3 grams of crack from respondents and witnessed respondents carrying firearms during the sales. The agents searched the hotel room in which the sales were transacted, arrested respondents Armstrong and Hampton in the room, and found more crack and a loaded gun. They later arrested the other respondents as part of the ring. Respondents filed a motion for discovery or for dismissal of the indictment. The District Court granted the motion, arguing that there was no evidence or allegation that the Government has acted unfairly or has prosecuted non-black defendants or failed to prosecute them. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that, because of the proof requirements for a selective-prosecution claim, defendants must "provide a colorable basis for believing that [others similarly situated have not been prosecuted'" to obtain discovery. Held: 1. In the context of Rule 16 (a)(1)(C), the defendant may examine documents material to his defense, but, under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment, he may not examine Government work product in connection with his case. Pp. 5-11. (a) In the ordinary case, "so long as the prosecutor has probable cause to believe that the accused committed an offense defined by statute, the decision whether or not to prosecute, and what charge to file or bring before a grand jury, generally rests entirely in his discretion." Bordenkircher v. Hayes, 434 U.S. 357, 364. In order to dispel the presumption that a prosecutor has not violated equal protection, a criminal defendant must present "clear evidence to the contrary." Chemical Foundation, Inc. v. Underwood, 471U.S., 222, distinguished. P. 5. (b) The Rule's requirement that a defendant produce some evidence of differential treatment of similarly situated members of other races or protected classes does not make a selective prosecution claim impossible to prove. The mere fact that there is convincing direct evidence that the State had enacted the provision for the purpose of disenfranchising blacks, and indisputable evidence that it had a discriminatory effect on blacks as compared to similarly situated whites, affords no support for respondent's position that the requirement establishes beyond peradventure that "defense" in section (a (1)()(C) can refer only to defenses in response to the Government's case-in-chief. The requirement also establishes that any claim that "results in nonconviction" if successful is a defense" for the Rule's purposes, and a successful selective-Prosecution claim has that effect. The same constraints, imposed by Bolling v. Sharpe, ante, p. 497, 500 (1954), are not readily susceptible to the kind of analysis the courts are competent to undertake. In this case, if the claim of selective prosecution were well founded, it should not have been an insuperable task to prove that persons of the other races were being treated differently than respondents. Because respondents' construction of the requirement creates the anomaly of a defendant's being able to examine all Government work products except the most pertinent, it is implausible that the showing necessary to obtain a discovery should itself be a significant barrier to the litigation of insubstantial claims. The justifications for a rigorous standard for the elements of a selective prosecution claim thus require a "background presumption," cf. United States v. Berrios, 501 F. 2d 1207, 14-15. The fact that the Rule requires a showing that the defendant has brought the charge for reasons forbidden by the Constitution is a matter of proof, and no fact should be omitted to make it out completely, when the power of a Federal court is invoked to interfere with the course of criminal justice of a State. The Justifications for this standard, including the similarly situated requirement, have taken great pains to explain that the standard is a demanding one. These cases afford a background presumption, cf.United Statesv. Mezzanatto, 513 U.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against the New York State Police charging a New York City law enforcement officer with operating a nationwide search and seizure program.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that, on June 20, 1976, an investigator for the New Jersey State Police purchased two reels of film from petitioner's so-called "adult" bookstore. According to the complaint, the search began when the local justice and his party entered a search warrant for the film. The complaint alleges that the search warrant, which was signed by a neutral and detached judge, left it entirely to the clerk to determine what items were likely obscene and to accomplish their seizure.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against the individual who allegedly acted as an unregistered agent in the search.  On June 25, the court granted the complaint and ordered the seizure of the two films by the Town Justice. The court granted a temporary restraining order, ordered the search to be conducted by the town justice, and issued a warrant to the individual for the execution of the warrant.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay $1,000 in disgorgement and $2,500 in prejudgment interest, and to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years. The judge also agreed to pay a civil penalty of $250,000, which is equal to the amount of his or her salary.  A hearing scheduled for July 5, 2020, was scheduled for 7:30 p.m. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

In the Supreme Court case under review, the central issue was whether 18 U.S.C. §3501 was intended by Congress to completely eliminate the McNabb-Mallory rule, which states that confessions are inadmissible if obtained after an unreasonable delay in presenting an arrested person before a judge, or if it was meant to merely limit the rule's application.

The Court concluded that Congress intended to limit, not eliminate, the McNabb-Mallory rule. The Court's reasoning was based on the historical importance of the "presentment" requirement, which aimed to prevent secret detention and inform suspects of their charges. This requirement was enforced through the McNabb-Mallory rule, which made confessions inadmissible if obtained during an unreasonable delay before presenting the suspect to a magistrate.

The Court examined the language of §3501, particularly subsections (a) and (c), and determined that reading subsection (a) to mean that any voluntary confession is admissible would render subsection (c) meaningless. Subsection (c) specifies that confessions made within six hours of arrest are not inadmissible solely due to delay, implying that there is still a rule against admitting confessions obtained after unnecessary delays.

The Court also considered the legislative history of §3501, which indicated that subsections (a) and (b) were aimed at overruling the Miranda decision, while subsection (c) was intended to address the McNabb-Mallory rule. The Court found that the legislative history supported the view that Congress intended to limit, not replace, the McNabb-Mallory rule.

The Court rejected the government's argument that Federal Rule of Evidence 402, enacted in 1975, eliminated the McNabb-Mallory rule. The Court pointed to the Advisory Committee's Notes on Rule 402, which identified McNabb-Mallory as a rule that would survive the enactment of Rule 402.

The Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further consideration consistent with its opinion. The Court held that if a confession was made within six hours of arrest, it is admissible as long as it was voluntary. However, if the confession was made after six hours and before presentment, the court must determine if the delay was unreasonable or unnecessary, and if so, the confession must be suppressed.

The implications of the decision are that the McNabb-Mallory rule remains a valid legal principle that federal courts must consider when determining the admissibility of confessions obtained after an arrested person is taken into custody. Confessions obtained after unreasonable delays in presentment may still be excluded from evidence.

The U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina today entered a final judgment against a South Carolina-based company in a civil injunctive action brought by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Charleston, South Carolina, alleges that Eric Baker violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, Baker agreed that any dispute or claim concerning his employment would be settled by binding arbitration.  Baker also agreed that, after a finding of liability, the agency would be entitled to a right-to-sue letter from the agency before proceeding with an enforcement action.  In addition, Baker signed a mandatory arbitration agreement that expressly prohibited him from participating in any type of unlawful employment practice.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Baker consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a $1,000 civil penalty.  As a result of the settlement, Baker will not be able to participate in the issuance of any judgments imposing permanent injunctions against future violations, and he will be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years.   The court's order, which was entered on consent by the SEC, orders Baker to pay $2,500 in disgorgement and prejudgment interest, and to pay civil penalties of $3,500 each. QUESTION: What is the main idea of the article?

ANSWER: The main idea of the article is that the Supreme Court ruled that a warrant issued by a magistrate judge to search a home for drugs and guns was not void because it failed to meet the particularity requirement of the Fourth Amendment.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Arkansas today entered a final judgment against defendant Alex Blueford, Jr., who was charged with capital and first-degree murder in 2007.  According to the SEC's complaint, Blueford was found guilty on all of the charged counts, and the jury was deadlocked on the lesser charges.  The SEC alleges that the jury deliberated for more than an hour before finding Blueford not guilty of the three lesser charges, and that it did not consider a second trial on those counts.  As alleged in the complaint, however, the jury had not reached a verdict on either of those charges, which is a violation of the Double Jeopardy Clause of the federal securities laws.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Blueford.  Blueford has agreed to settle the charges without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, and agreed to a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and a five-year officer-and-director bar.  On May 9, 2011, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action, charging Blueford with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and to pay a civil penalty of $160,000.   The court granted the SEC’s request for a temporary restraining order, ordered the jury to return to the jury room, and ordered a hearing on May 10, 2011 to determine whether to proceed with a jury trial.  A hearing scheduled for May 11, 2011 was scheduled for 7:30 p.m.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 565 (2011).

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit held that the Secretary of Commerce's decision not to use a statistical adjustment to correct an undercount in the 1990 census was not subject to heightened scrutiny because of its effect on the right of individual respondents to have their vote counted equally. The Constitution requires an "actualion" of the population every 10 years and vests Congress with the authority to conduct that census "in such as they shall by law direct"<n>The census also affects the allocation of members of the electoral college. In the 1980 census, for instance, the Census Bureau concluded that the census results were 2.7% less than the actual population. The undercount is not thought to be spread consistently across the population, resulting in a phenomenon called "differential undercount"<n>In 1940, for example, when the census was conducted with the goal of "actual counting," persons who should not have been counted were not counted at all or were not born after the census date. The problem of the "undercount" has persisted even as the census has come to provide a more numerically accurate count. The Supreme Court held in 2002 that the Census Act of 1790 provides for the use of "a statistical adjustment" to correct undercounts. The Court held that this adjustment was not required by the Constitution.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) promulgated Rule 10b–5 pursuant to authority granted under §10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which prohibits “mak[ing] any untrue statement of a material fact” in connection with the purchase or sale of securities. 17 CFR §240.10b-5 (2010). Respondent First Derivative Traders represents a class of plaintiffs who owned JCG stock as of September 3, 2003. Although market timing is legal, it harms other investors in the mutual fund. In September 2003, the Attorney General of New York filed a complaint against JCG and JCM alleging that JCG entered into secret arrangements to permit market timing in several funds run by JCM. After the complaint’s allegations became public, investors withdrew significant amounts of money from the Janus Investment Fund mutual funds. Because the fund compensated JCM based on the total value of the funds and its management fees comprised a significant percentage of the income, the loss of value affected the value of JCG, which was valued at $17.68 on September 2 to $13.50 on September 26, and because the fund paid JCM, its stock price fell nearly 25 percent, the value affected JCG's value as well. The SEC then filed suit against the fund and its wholly owned subsidiary for false statements included in the prospectuses. The District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that FirstDerivative had sufficiently alleged that “JCG” should be held liable for the acts of JCM as a “controlling person” under 15 U. S. C. A. §78t(a). The Fourth Circuit reversed. Held: 1. Although the existence of the private right is now settled, this Court will not expand liability beyond the person or entity that ultimately has authority over a false statement. Stoneridge Investment Partners, LLC v. Scientific-Atlanta, Inc., 552 U.S. 148, 165. In analyzing whether JCM “made” the statements for purposes of Rule 10–5, we must give “narrow dimensions … to a right of action Congress did not authorize when it first enacted the statute and did not expand when it revisited the law,” Superintendent of Ins. of N. Y. v. Bankers Life & Casualty Co., 404 U. s. 6, 13, n. 9 (1971). That holding “remains the law” and “[c]oncerns with the judicial creation of a private cause of action caution against its expansion.” ibid. Thus, in analyzing whether “make” is implied under Rule 10-5, it is mindful that the SEC should receive deference regarding the private rights of action. See Piper v. Chris-Craft Industries, Inc. 430 U. . S. 1, 41. Pp. 5–7. 2. The statement in the securities laws was made by the maker of a statement, not by the party to whom it is attributed. The fact that JCM was significantly involved in preparing the securities prospectuses does not mean that he made the statements in the prospectsuses. Nor does the fact that he was quoting or otherwise repeating a statement originally made by J.CM suggest that he did not make the statements indirectly because none of the statements were attributed, explicitly or implicitly, to JCM in doing so. Moreover, there is no indication that he had stated a claim against JCM under §20 (a). Pp . 7–8. (a) The phrase “directly or indirectly”—which modifies not just “to make, but also to employ, and to engage—is set off by itself in §10 (b). The phrase merely clarifies that as long as a statement is made, it does not matter whether the statement was communicated directly or indirectly to the recipient. A different understanding of “indirectly” would threaten to erase the line between primary violators and aiders and abettors established by Central Bank of Denver, N. A., 511 U.

Petitioner, a carpenter foreman employed by an independent contractor to perform repairs at a dam owned and operated by the United States, drowned in the Columbia River while in the course of his employment in a tug-and-barge unit. He was a member of this working party, and the unit was carried northwardly in the river towards that part of the dam where the soundings were to be taken. The unit then capsized in the turbulent water, and all but one of his fellow employees were killed. Held: The right of action for wrongful death created by the Oregon Employers' Liability Law may be invoked to recover for a maritime death in that State without constitutional inhibition. Pp. 588-599. (a) The statute by its terms, and as construed by the State Supreme Court, would be applied evenhandedly, despite the contrary views of some of those originally joining it that state law is the measure of recovery when it helps the defendant, as in Tungus, and is not the measure when it militates against the defendant as it does here. P. 599. Reversed.

Petitioner-cross-petitioner Mitsubishi Motors Corporation (Mitsubishi), a Japanese corporation which manufactures automobiles and has its principal place of business in Tokyo, Japan, entered into a distribution agreement with Soler Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc. (Soler), a Puerto Rico corporation, providing for the sale by Soler of Mitsubits-manufactured vehicles within a designated area, including metropolitan San Juan, Puerto Rico. Soler then sought an order, pursuant to 9 U. S. C. §§ 4 and 201, to compel arbitration in accord with 57 VI of the Sales Agreement. The Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part. Held: 1. The arbitration clause at issue may not be read to encompass the statutory counterclaims stated in Soler's answer to the complaint. Pp. 4-7. (a) The Arbitration Act's centerpiece provision makes a written agreement to arbitrate "in any maritime transaction or a contract evidencing a transaction involving commerce . . . valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract." The Act simply "creates a body of federal substantive law establishing and regulating the duty to honor an agreement to arbitration." P. 4. (b) The fact that the arbitration clause does not encompass statutory claims does not compel the conclusion that it may not not be sought outside an American court. P. 5. (c) The Act itself provides no basis for disfavoring agreements to arbitration of statutory claims by skewing the otherwise hospitable inquiry into arbitrability. It is the congressional policy manifested in the Act that requires courts liberally to construe the scope of arbitration agreements covered by that Act, and the congressional intention expressed in some other statute on which the courts must rely to identify any category of claims as to which agreements to arbitrates will be held unenforceable. The Act also provides no reason to distort the process of contract interpretation, however, in order to ferret out the inappropriate. The importance of the private damages remedy is not compel by the Act itself for implying in every contract within its ken a presumption against arbitration of the statutory claims, but rather by the fact that it is a chief tool in the antitrust enforcement scheme, posing a crucial deterrent to potential violators. The "liberal federal policy favoring arbitration agreements," Moses H. Cone Memorial Hospital v. Mercury Construction Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 24, is at bottom a policy guaranteeing the enforcement of private contractual arrangements: the Act simply creates and regulates the duty "to honor" an agreement "to arbitrate" in any maritime transactions or a "contract" evidencing the national interest in a competitive economy, and it is Congress' intention to protect the interests of the public by providing for a mutually agreeable procedure whereby an injured competitor would seek his antitrust recovery as well as settle other controversies. In any event, adaptability and access to expertise are hallmarks of arbitration. The anticipated subject matter of the dispute may be taken into account when the arbitrators are appointed, and arbitral rules typically provide for the participation of experts either employed by the parties or appointed by the tribunal. Thus, as with any other contract, the parties' intentions control, but those intentions are generously construed as to issues of arbitration, and an arbitral tribunal will pose too great a danger of innate hostility to the constraints on business conduct that antitrust law imposes. Nothing, in the meantime, prevents a party from excluding statutory claims from § 4 of the Clayton Act's scope. Moreover, the vertical restraints which most frequently give birth to antitrust claims covered by an arbitration agreement will not often occasion the monstrous proceedings that have given antitrust litigation an image of intractability. In the event, adaptingability andaccess to expertise will be hallmarks, and arbitration is often a judgment that streamlined proceedings and expeditious results will best serve their needs that causes parties to agree to arbitration. Thus the antitrust cause of action remains at all times under the control of the individual litigant: no citizen is under an obligation to bring an antitrust suit, see Illinois Brick Co. v. Illinois, 431 U.
