After learning that certain students were distributing prescription and over-the-counter drugs at Safford Middle School, Assistant Principal Wilson summoned Savanna Redding to his office and showed her a day planner belonging to another girl, Marissa Glines. She confessed to having borrowed the planner and producing the pills. Wilson then questioned Marissa about the pills, but did not ask her about the planner or try to determine whether Savanna might be hiding the pills. Later, Marissa was searched by respondent nurses Schwallier and Romero, revealing no additional pills. Suspicion of Wilson’s about Savanna’s involvement in pill distribution was enough to justify a search of her backpack and outer clothing. However, when the nurses subsequently removed Savanna’s clothes down to her underwear and directed her to expose her bra and the elastic band on her underpants, she refused. They claimed that they saw nothing, but Savanna felt embarrassed, frightened, and humiliated. The Ninth Circuit concluded that the strip search was unconstitutional under New Jersey v. T. L. O., 469 U. S. 325, and that the school district was liable for damages under Monell v. New York City Dept. of Social Services, 436 U. S. 658. Held: 1. The strip search was unreasonable and a violation of the Fourth Amendment. Pp. 4−10. (a) While the exact label for removing the underwear is not important, the fact of Savanna’s doing so necessarily exposed her breasts and pelvic area to some degree, and both subjective and reasonable societal expectations of personal privacy support treating such a search as categorically distinct, requiring distinct elements of justification on the part of school authorities for going beyond a search of outer clothing and belongings. Savanna’s subjective expectation of privacy against such a search is inherent in her account of it as embarrassing, frightening, and humiliating. The reasonableness of her expectation is indicated by the consistent experiences of others similarly searched, whose adolescent vulnerability intensifies the patent intrusiveness of the exposure. The indignity of the search does not outlaw it, but it does implicate the rule of reasonableness as stated in T. L. O.: “ ‘the search as actually conducted [be] reasonably related in scope to the circumstances which justified the interference in the first place.’ ” 469 U. S., at 341. Here, the content of the suspicion—that Savanna was involved in pill distribution—failed to match the degree of intrusion. Wilson knew beforehand that the pills were prescription-strength ibuprofen and over-the-counter naproxen, common pain relievers equivalent to two Advils, or one Aleve. He must have been aware of the nature and limited threat of the specific drugs he was searching for, and while just about anything can be taken in quantities that will do real harm, Wilson had no reason to suspect that large amounts of the drugs were being passed around, or that individual students were receiving great numbers of pills. Nor could he have suspected that Savanna was hiding common painkillers in her underwear. General background possibilities fall short; a reasonable search that extensive calls for suspicion that it will pay off. But nondangerous school contraband does not raise the specter of stashes in intimate places, and there is no evidence in the record of any general practice among Safford Middle School students of hiding that sort of thing in underwear. Neither Marissa nor Jordan Romero, the student who reported the initial incident, suggested to Wilson that Savanna was doing that, and the previous search of Marissa that Wilson ordered yielded nothing. Moreover, Wilson never even determined when Marissa had received the pills from Savanna, if it had been a few days before, that would weigh heavily against any reasonable conclusion that Savanna presently had the pills on her person, much less in her underwear. Pp. 4−8. (b) Even as to action less than an outrage, school officials can still be on notice that their conduct violates established law in novel factual circumstances. Thus, the intrusiveness of the strip search here cannot be seen as justifiably related to the circumstances. But realizing that the lower courts have reached differing conclusions regarding how the T. L. O. standard applies to such searches counsels doubt that the Court was sufficiently clear in the prior statement of law. Qualified immunity is warranted. Pp. 8−10. 2. The strip search was unreasonable and a violation of the Fourth Amendment, but petitioners Wilson, Romero, and Schwallier are nevertheless protected from liability through qualified immunity. The Court’s conclusions here do not resolve, however, the question of the liability of petitioner Safford Unified School District under Monell. The Ninth Circuit did not address that claim, which is remanded for consideration. P. 10. 531 F. 3d 1139, affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Roberts, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

Appellants Richard Pennell and the Tri-County Apartment House Owners Association sued in the Superior Court of Santa Clara County, California, seeking a declaration that the rent control ordinance, in particular the "tenant hardship" provisions, are "facially unconstitutional and therefore . . . illegal and void." Appellants' claim that the ordinance violates the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment, as made applicable to the States by the Fourteenth Amendment, is sustained. The Court of Appeal affirmed, but the California Supreme Court reversed. Held: Appellant appellants lack standing under either the test for individual standing, see, e. g., Valley Forge Christian College v. Americans United for Separation of Church & State, Inc., 454 U. S. 464, 472, or associational standing. Pp. 5-7. (a) Appellate appellants' contention that the tenant hardship provisions are a "forced subsidy imposed on the landlord" in violation of the Due Process Clause does not on its face violate the Equal Protection Clause. The standard for determining whether a state price-control regulation is constitutional under the Due process Clause is deferential; appellees need only show that the classification scheme embodied in the Ordinance is "rationally related to a legitimate state interest." New Orleans v. Dukes, 427 U.S. 297, 303. P. 5. (b) The Ordinance does not violate Art. III's requirement that "[a] plaintiff who challenges a statute must demonstrate a realistic danger of sustaining a direct injury as a result of the statute's operation or enforcement." Babbitt v. Farm Workers, 442 U. s. 289, 298. The fact that appellants have not identified any property that had allegedly been taken by the Act, nor had they sought administrative relief from the Act's restrictions on surface mining, does not render appellants ineligible for the right to a hearing officer to determine whether to allow an additional increase in rent over and above certain amounts that are deemed reasonable does not constitute a "taking" under the First Amendment. Appellees do not need to show that they have been or will be aggrieved by the determination of the hearing officer that a certain proposed rent increase is unreasonable on the ground of tenant hardship. Appelants do not allege that either Pennell or any member of the Association has "hardship tenants" who might trigger the Hearing Officer's hearing process, nor did they specifically allege that they had been or would be aggregrieved by a determination of a hearing-officer that a rent increase was unreasonable on that ground. The ordinance, which so carefully considers both the individual circumstances of the landlord and the tenant before determining whether to permit an additional rent increase, is a rational attempt to accommodate the conflicting interests of protecting tenants from burdensome rent increases while at the same time ensuring that landlords are guaranteed a fair return on their investment. The standards set out in § 5703.28(c)(7) are deferential, and appelleees need not show that, under the standard, the classification schemes embodied in §5703. 28(c) (7) is "rately related to the legitimate State interest." Appellee v. Virginia Surface Mining & Reclamation Assn., Inc., 452 U. . . 264, 294-295, distinguished. Appellees do not dispute that the ordinance's asserted purpose of "prevent[ing] excessive and unreasonable rent increases" caused by the "growing shortage of and increasing demand for housing in the City of San Jose," § 5701.2, is not a legitimate exercise of appellee's police powers. The ordinance distinguishes between landlords and tenants because doing so furthers the purpose of ensuring that individual tenants do not suffer "unreasonable" hardship; it would be inconsistent to state that hardship is a legitimate factor to be considered but then hold that appellees could not tailor the Ordinances so that only legitimate hardship cases are redressed. P p. 511. 42 Cal. App. 3d 365, 721 P. 2d 1111, affirmed.

The Supreme Court reviewed the case of United States District Judge Robert Aguilar, who was convicted of disclosing a wiretap and obstructing justice. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals initially affirmed one conviction and reversed the other, but later reversed both upon rehearing en banc. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to address two issues: whether false statements to potential grand jury witnesses are punishable under 18 U.S.C. § 1503 and whether disclosing an expired wiretap violates 18 U.S.C. § 2232(c).

The Supreme Court held that for a conviction under § 1503, there must be a "nexus" between the defendant's actions and a judicial proceeding. The defendant must have knowledge that their actions are likely to affect the proceeding, and the actions must have the "natural and probable effect" of interfering with justice. The Court found that Aguilar's false statements to FBI agents, who were not proven to be acting on behalf of a grand jury, did not meet this standard. Therefore, the Court affirmed the reversal of Aguilar's conviction under § 1503.

Regarding § 2232(c), the Court disagreed with the Ninth Circuit's interpretation that the statute only applies to disclosures of pending wiretaps. The Supreme Court clarified that the statute criminalizes disclosures made with the intent to obstruct an interception, regardless of whether the wiretap authorization was still in effect. The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's decision on this count, holding that Aguilar's disclosure of an expired wiretap could still violate § 2232(c).

The Supreme Court remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its decision, affirming the reversal of the obstruction of justice conviction under § 1503 and reversing the reversal of the conviction for disclosing a wiretap under § 2232(c).

Title: Nebraska v. Simants
Year: 1976
Decision: Reversed
Issue: Whether a prior restraint on publication of information related to a criminal trial is justified?
Summary: The Supreme Court holds that the barriers to prior restraint on publication remain high and the presumption against its use remains intact. The Court finds that the order entered in Nebraska v. Simants prohibiting reporting or commentary on judicial proceedings held in public is clearly invalid.

Petitioners are shipping companies that serve a large share of the world market for parcel tankers-seagoing vessels with compartments that are separately chartered to customers wishing to ship liquids in small quantities. One of those customers is AnimalFeeds International Corp., which supplies raw ingredients, such as fish oil, to animal-feed producers around the world. Petitioners served petitioners with a demand for class arbitration, designating New York City as the place of arbitration and seeking to represent a class of “[a]ll direct purchasers of parcel tanker transportation services globally for bulk liquid chemicals, edible oils, acids, and other specialty liquids from [petitioners] at any time during the period from August 1, 1998, to November 30, 2002.” The parties entered into a supplemental agreement providing for the question of class arbitration to be submitted to a panel of three arbitrators. The parties agreed that as a consequence of these judgments and orders, they must arbitrate their antitrust dispute. The District Court vacated the award, concluding that the arbitrators’ decision was made in “manifest disregard” of the law insofar as they failed to conduct a choice-of-law analysis. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the arbitration clause in the Green Tree Financial Corp. contracts was “silent regarding class-wide arbitration,” but the Second Circuit reversed. Held: The arbitration panel’s decision was simply to impose its own view of sound policy regarding class arbitration. Pp. 5–11. (a) The arbitrators had no authority applying a rule of federal maritime law requiring that contracts be interpreted in light of custom and usage, and the fact that the parties’ supplemental agreement expressly assigned this issue to the arbitration panel did not establish the standard to be applied by a decision maker in determining whether a contract may permissibly be interpreted to allow class arbitration does not render petitioners’ argument under §10(a)(4) “scarcely debatable” under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U. S. C. §1 et seq., which provides that a “written provision in any maritime transaction” calling for the arbitration of a controversy arising out of such transaction “shall be valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract.’” Major League Baseball Players Assn. v. Garvey, 532 U.S. 504, 509 (per curiam) (“It is only when [an] arbitrator strays from interpretation and application of the agreement and effectively ‘dispense[s] his own brand of industrial justice’ that his decision may be unenforceable””). This is because class-action arbitration changes the nature of arbitration to such a degree that it cannot be presumed the parties consented to it by simply agreeing to submit their disputes to an arbitrator. In bilateral arbitration, parties forgo the procedural rigor and appellate review of the courts in order to realize the benefits of private dispute resolution: lower costs, greater efficiency and speed, and an ability to choose expert adjudicators to resolve specialized disputes. See, e.g., Howsam v. Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc., 537 U.

In the case of Texas Monthly, Inc. v. Bullock, the Supreme Court of the United States decided on February 21, 1989, that a Texas statute exempting religious periodicals from sales and use taxes violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. The Court held that the exemption, which was not extended to nonreligious periodicals, constituted an endorsement of religion and lacked a secular legislative purpose.

The Court reasoned that while incidental benefits to religious groups do not necessarily violate the Establishment Clause, a subsidy directed exclusively to religious organizations without a secular objective is impermissible state sponsorship of religion. The Court rejected Texas's argument that the exemption was necessary to avoid violating the Free Exercise Clause, noting that there was no evidence that paying sales taxes on religious materials would infringe on religious beliefs or practices.

The Court also dismissed the notion that the Establishment Clause mandated the exemption, as it could lead to greater entanglement between the state and religion. The Court clarified that the exemption could be seen as an endorsement of religious belief, which is contrary to the principles of the Establishment Clause.

The Court's decision reversed the judgment of the Texas Court of Appeals, which had upheld the exemption, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. The Court's ruling emphasized the importance of maintaining a separation between church and state and ensuring that government actions do not favor one religion over another or religion in general.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against the Federal Bureau of Investigation ("FBU") in a related case.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, alleges that, in 1995, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Mississippi unsealed criminal charges against the agency.  According to the complaint, the SEC's findings were consistent with the agency's previous findings concerning the safety and effectiveness of tobacco products.  For example, the complaint alleges that the FDA had no jurisdiction to regulate cigarettes or smokeless tobacco, and that the agency had no authority to determine whether a product was "safe" or "dangerous."  The complaint further alleges that in addition to being a "drug," the FDA also had the authority to regulate "tobacco products" by requiring manufacturers to disclose on all packaging and in all print advertising "that cigarette smoking is highly addictive and may cause death from cancer, coronary heart disease, and other serious illnesses."  In addition, as alleged, the FDA's previous opinion that it lacked jurisdiction under the federal health law required it to regulate tobacco products was inconsistent with that of the FDA.  In its final judgment, the court held that the federal agency lacked jurisdiction over the issue of tobacco.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, however, the agency has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining it from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering the agency to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

In the Supreme Court case involving Roderick Jackson and the Birmingham Board of Education, the Court ruled that Title IX, which prohibits sex discrimination in federally funded education programs, also covers claims of retaliation against individuals who complain about sex discrimination. Jackson, a teacher and girls' basketball coach, alleged that after he complained about unequal treatment of the girls' team, the Board retaliated by giving him negative evaluations and removing him from his coaching position.

The District Court initially dismissed Jackson's complaint, stating that Title IX does not cover retaliation claims, and the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed this decision. However, the Supreme Court disagreed, holding that retaliation for complaining about sex discrimination is a form of intentional discrimination based on sex and is therefore prohibited under Title IX.

The Court's reasoning was that retaliation is an intentional act of differential treatment and is inherently connected to the nature of the complaint, which in this case was sex discrimination. The Court also noted that Congress, when enacting Title IX, was likely influenced by earlier decisions that recognized retaliation claims under other anti-discrimination laws.

The Court rejected the argument that Title IX does not cover retaliation because the statute does not explicitly mention it. The Court pointed out that it has previously interpreted Title IX broadly to include various forms of intentional sex discrimination, such as sexual harassment, even though these are not explicitly mentioned in the statute.

The Court also dismissed the Board's claim that it was not on notice that retaliation could lead to liability under Title IX, stating that the Board should have been aware of the broad interpretation of Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination, which includes retaliation.

The Supreme Court's decision has significant implications, as it ensures that individuals who report sex discrimination in educational settings are protected from retaliation, thereby supporting the enforcement of Title IX and the reporting of discrimination.

Justice Thomas, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist, Justice Scalia, and Justice Kennedy, dissented, arguing that retaliation is not the same as discrimination based on sex and that Congress did not unambiguously include retaliation claims within Title IX's scope. The dissenting opinion emphasized the need for clear congressional intent when imposing conditions on federal funding recipients and when implying causes of action from statutes.

On January 13, 1964, Pamela Mason, a 14-year-old girl, left her home in Manchester, New Hampshire, during a heavy snowstorm, apparently in response to a man's telephone call for a babysitter. Eight days later, after a thaw, her body was found by the site of a major north-south highway several miles away. The case created great alarm in the area, and the police immediately began a massive investigation. On January 28, having learned from a neighbor that the petitioner, Edward Coolidge, had been away from home on the evening of the girl's disappearance, the police went to his house to question him. They asked him, among other things, if he owned any guns, and he produced three, two shotguns and a rifle. They also asked whether he would take a lie-detector test concerning his account of his activities on the night of the disappearance. He agreed to do so on the following Sunday, his day off. The police later described his attitude on the occasion of this visit as fully 'cooperative'

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri today entered a final judgment against Delli Paoli, a St. Louis, Missouri man convicted of a federal felony armed postal robbery.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in St.Louis, Pa., Paoli was charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The complaint alleges that Paoli consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently restrains the jury's ability to determine the guilt or innocence of the defendant.  Paoli also agreed to be barred from cross-examination by a trial judge based on his inability to cross-examine the co-defendant in determining the latter's guilt.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Middle District of New York today announced criminal charges against Paoli.   The SEC's Complaint alleges that, in a joint trial, Paoli made two admissions to the jury: one in which he admitted he had an accomplice whom he would not name, in the course of two interrogations of Evans at the city jail, and another that he admitted to having had an "an accomplice" who he did not name.  Both of these admissions were inadmissible hearsay, and the jury was instructed not to disregard them.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Complaint, the jury found Paoli liable for a total of 17 felony counts, including one that he was convicted of in a separate criminal case.  As a result of the Commission's finding, Paolo was permanently barred from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in the securities industry, and was ordered to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar in the amount of $1,000,000.  He was also barred from serving as an officer and director of a public company, and from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney.  To learn more about jury selection, see Litigation Release No. 5, No. 206, No 1, and No. 207 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against AnimalFeeds International Corp., a microcap company that supplies raw ingredients, such as fish oil, to animal feed producers around the world.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that, in 2003, a federal district court in New York City issued an order suspending the suspension of a class-action arbitration award.  According to the complaint, the court found that the arbitration clause in the arbitration agreement was non-existent and that the parties had not reached an agreement on how to resolve their disputes.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the arbitrator had not consulted with the parties about the arbitration provisions of the arbitration agreements, and that, as a result of his inaction, the arbitration award was not subject to the court’s jurisdiction.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, which was filed in the United States District Court, the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia issued a temporary restraining order, freezing the assets of the defendants, and ordering the arbitration to be conducted by an independent arbitrator.   The court also issued a preliminary injunction, which prohibits the parties from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the parties to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000,000. Â The SEC's investigation was conducted by John Rymas and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter of the SEC's Chicago Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois dismissed a limitation of liability action brought by a yacht owner in connection with a fire that destroyed his vessel. The District Court held that the Limited Liability Act did not confer federal jurisdiction over the action. The Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit affirmed, holding that neither the Act nor the federal law conferred federal jurisdiction. The Supreme Court of the United States has since ruled that the limitations of liability provision does confer jurisdiction. We hold that it does, and reverse the lower court's dismissal of the petition for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

In this Supreme Court case, the Court addressed the balance between defamation law and First Amendment protections of speech and press. The case involved Maurice S. Hepps, the principal stockholder of General Programming, Inc., and the Philadelphia Inquirer, which published articles suggesting Hepps had ties to organized crime and influenced state government processes. Hepps sued for defamation.

The Court had to decide who bears the burden of proof regarding the falsity of the statements in a defamation case involving a private figure and speech of public concern. Historically, under common law, defamatory statements were presumed false, and the defendant had to prove their truth as a defense. However, the Court held that this common-law presumption is incompatible with the First Amendment when it comes to matters of public concern.

The Court referenced previous landmark cases, such as New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, which established that public officials must prove "actual malice" to win a defamation case, and Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc., which allowed states to set their own standards of liability for defamation involving private individuals, provided they do not impose liability without fault.

The Court concluded that requiring the media defendant to prove the truth of their statements would deter speech on public issues due to the fear of unjustified liability. To protect true speech on matters of public concern, the Court ruled that the plaintiff must bear the burden of proving that the statements are false, as well as showing fault, before recovering damages in a defamation suit against a media defendant.

The Court recognized that this decision might protect some false speech that cannot be proven false, but emphasized that the First Amendment requires some protection of falsehood to ensure the freedom of speech that matters. The Court reversed the judgment of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, which had placed the burden of proving truth on the defendant, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central issue was whether the police's refusal to allow the petitioner, Danny Escobedo, to consult with his lawyer during interrogation violated his Sixth Amendment right to counsel, as applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment. Escobedo had been arrested and interrogated in connection with a murder, during which he repeatedly requested to see his lawyer. His lawyer was also present at the police station but was denied access to Escobedo. The police did not inform Escobedo of his right to remain silent, and he eventually made incriminating statements.

The Supreme Court of Illinois initially reversed Escobedo's conviction, finding the statement inadmissible, but upon rehearing, affirmed the conviction. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to determine the admissibility of the statement.

The U.S. Supreme Court concluded that Escobedo's Sixth Amendment rights were violated. The Court reasoned that once the investigation focuses on a specific suspect who has been taken into custody, and the suspect has requested and been denied access to counsel, the suspect must be allowed to consult with a lawyer. The Court emphasized that the right to counsel is essential to ensure fairness in the criminal justice system and to prevent coerced confessions.

The Court distinguished this case from previous decisions, noting that Escobedo was not informed of his right to remain silent and was not an educated individual with knowledge of criminal law. The Court held that any statements obtained during the interrogation without the opportunity to consult with counsel could not be used against Escobedo at trial.

The decision underscored the importance of legal counsel during critical stages of the criminal process and reinforced the protection against self-incrimination. The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Illinois Supreme Court and remanded the case for proceedings consistent with its opinion. This decision had significant implications for police interrogation practices and the rights of the accused, establishing the precedent that access to counsel must be granted during pre-trial interrogations once formal judicial proceedings have been initiated.

Petitioner Harbison was sentenced to death by a Tennessee court in 1983. In 1997, after the state courts rejected challenges to his conviction and sentence, the Federal District Court appointed the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee to represent him in filing a petition for a writ of habeas corpus pursuant to 28 U. S. C. §2254. During the course of that representation, counsel developed substantial evidence relating both to his culpability and to the appropriateness of his sentence. Although the courts did not order relief, the evidence proved persuasive to one Circuit Judge. Shortly after his petition was denied, federal counsel moved to expand the authorized scope of her representation to include state clemency proceedings. In 2006, the Tennessee Supreme Court held that state law does not authorize the appointment of federal counsel. The District Court denied the motion, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Relying on Circuit precedent construing 18 U.S. C., §3599, which provides for federal counsel’s representation, the District Court granted the motion and the court of appeals affirmed. Held: A certificate of appealability (COA) is not required to appeal an order denying a request for federally appointed counsel pursuant to §2253(c)(1)(A). Section 3599 (e) provides that unless a circuit justice or judge issues a COA, an appeal may not be taken from “the final order in a habea corpus proceeding in which the detention complained of arises out of process issued by a State court.” This provision governs final orders that dispose of the merits of a habas corpus proceeding—a proceeding challenging the lawfulness of the petitioner’’ detention. See generally Slack v. McDaniel, 529 U. States 473, 484–485. An order that merely denies a motion to enlarge the authority of appointed counsel (or that denies motion for appointment of counsel), is not such an order and is therefore not subject to the COA requirement. Subsection (a)(1) is properly understood as describing federal defendants because the statute is primarily concerned with postconviction litigants, and all proceedings listed in this subsection should be understood to be federal. The absence of the word “federal” in this section is not dispositive, but the parties agree that provision concerns only federal defendants. Moreover, the Government’ repeated use of “available” supports this reading: Congress contemplated that not all catalogued proceedings would be available to any given client, and clemeency proceedings are simply not available to state petitioners because they are ineligible for federal clemperency. The Government contends that, fairly read, the statute as a whole is intended to furnish representation only in federal proceedings and that all proceedings in subsection (e), including clem-ency proceedings, should be interpreted to be “subsequent.’ ” Hain v. Mullin, 436 F. 3d 1168 (CA10 2006) (en banc). The Government argues that reading § 3599(e) to authorize federally funded counsel for state clients is clearly an appealable order under §1291, since it is the sequential organization of the statute and the term “Subsequent” that circumscribe counsels’ representation, not a strict division between federal and state proceedings. Pp. 5–7. 503 F.3d 566, reversed.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) regulates the content of radio and television broadcasts under Section 316 of the Communications Act of 1934. Under this section, the FCC has the authority to refuse to renew a broadcast license if the licensee engages in conduct that is deemed detrimental to the public interest, convenience, or necessity.

In this case, the FCC determined that the content of a radio show hosted by comedian George Carlin was detrimental to the public interest, convenience, or necessity. The show featured crude and offensive language, including multiple instances of the words "shit," "fuck," "cunt," "cock," "motherfucker," and "tit." The FCC found that the use of this language was not necessary to convey the comedian's message and that it was likely to offend a substantial portion of the viewing public.

Based on this finding, the FCC refused to renew the broadcast license of the radio station that carried the show. The decision was upheld by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court of the United States.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania ruled that Grove City College violated the federal law prohibiting sex discrimination in education by refusing to comply with the Department of Education's request to execute an "assurance" of compliance. The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed the lower court's decision, finding that the Department had acted properly in terminating federal financial assistance to Grove City and its students. The appeals court held that the lower-court's ruling violated Grove City's First Amendment rights. The lower court had concluded that the federal government furnishes "indirect or non-marked aid to an institution, it is apparent to us that the institution itself must be the 'program.' " 687 F.2d 684 (CA3 1982)

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Oregon today entered judgment in favor of the Oregon Department of Justice in a wrongful death case.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Portland, Oregon, alleges that George W. Graham was drowned in the Columbia River while in the course of his employment as a carpenter foreman for Larson Construction Company, an independent contractor which had undertaken to perform repairs at Bonneville Dam. That structure is owned and operated by the United States.  According to the complaint, Graham was a member of a working party that was requested to close two additional spillway gates near the point where the soundings were to be taken. The complaint alleges that Graham's death was proximately caused by the failure of operating personnel of the dam to close a sufficient number of those gates, staving a hole in the barge's hull.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, Graham died in the action, along with four others, and all but one of his fellow employees were killed. Investors canÂ check the backgroundÂ of anyone selling, offeringÂ investor.govÂ by using theÂ instant search toolÂ onÂ theÂ appÂ feature.gov to quickly identify whether they are registered professionals.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York has ruled that Janus Capital Management LLC (JCM), a mutual fund investment adviser, cannot be held liable in a private action for false statements included in its client mutual funds' prospectuses. The SEC's complaint alleges that JCM and Janus Capital Group, Inc. (JCG), a publicly traded company that created the Janus family of mutual funds, entered into secret arrangements to permit market timing in several funds run by JCM. According to the complaint, the prospectuses for several Janus mutual funds represented that the funds were not suitable for market timing and can be read to suggest JCM would implement policies to curb the practice. The complaint also alleges that the mutual fund's loss of value affected JCG's stock price, which caused the company's share price to fall nearly 25 percent. The court ruled that JCG and JCM did not make the false statements in the Janus mutual fund prospectuses because they did not provide investors with the information they needed to make an informed decision about the funds' investment strategy and operations. In a parallel action, the Securities and Exchange Commission has charged JCG with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and JCG has agreed to pay a total of $1 million in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Vermont today entered a final judgment in favor of a proposed amendment to the federal campaign finance law that imposes mandatory limits on contributions to candidates for state office.  The court found that the proposed amendment violated the antifraud provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) of the federal securities laws.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Middle District of New York today announced criminal charges against two individuals for violating the federal limits on campaign contributions.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, Act 64 imposes mandatory contribution limits on political parties to candidates. The complaint alleges that, in violation of Section 5(b), the federal contribution limits imposed by Act 64, the contribution limits are so low that they imperil the ability of candidates to raise money for their campaigns. The SEC also alleges that Act 64 is not closely-drawn to meet its objectives.  For example, the SEC alleges that certain of the contributions to campaigns that were coordinated with a political party violated the First Amendment, and that some of those contributions were improperly solicited by others.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the court has agreed to the entry of a final opinion that permanently enjoins the defendants from violating the anti-fraud provisions and orders them to pay a civil penalty of $100,000. The court also ordered the defendants to pay disgorgement of their ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and ordered the parties to pay civil penalties in the amount of $200,000 each.   The SEC's investigation was conducted by Michael J. Karpel and supervised by Marc Blau of the Boston Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Timothy J. Burt.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Minnesota yesterday entered a final judgment against Marshall Murphy, a Minnesota man who was convicted of a felony for making false statements to a probation officer.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Minnesota, Murphy, who was on probation at the time of his arrest, made a series of incriminating admissions during a routine telephone interview with a probation probation officer in September 1981.  The complaint alleges that, during the course of his probation, Murphy admitted to a rape and murder that occurred in 1974.  As alleged in the complaint, the probation officer told Murphy that he was required to be truthful with his probation officer and that he would not be required to answer questions that would incriminate him in a subsequent criminal prosecution.  In addition, the complaint alleges, Murphy was not required to provide any corroborating evidence to justify his nonparticipation in the probation program.  Murphy also allegedly failed to disclose that he had committed a false imprisonment charge and that his probation was conditional on his waiving the privilege.  Without admitting or denying the allegations, Murphy consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.  Additionally, the court granted Murphy a temporary restraining order, barring him from participating in any future criminal proceedings, and ordered him to comply with a court order requiring him to provide an accounting of his prior criminal history.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted in the Office of the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and the Division of Criminal Justice's Office of Inspector General's Office. Â The SEC's litigation will be led by Michael J. Kordel and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry.

After petitioners, parents of children in the county’s foster care program, sued respondents, the governor and others, alleging that they failed to provide constitutionally adequate educational opportunities, the Federal District Court entered a consent decree resolving the claims. Under the agreement, respondents would pay petitioners’ attorneys a fee equal to twice the amount of time spent on the case times the prevailing hourly rate for private sector attorneys. The District Court ultimately awarded petitioners nearly $4.5 million, finding that the hourly rate was eminently fair and reasonable and that the total fee was reasonable. Rejecting respondents’ argument that the fee was inflated by duplicative efforts and unnecessary delays, the court declined to reduce the fee. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed. Held: The District Court erred in enhancing the lodestar fee beyond the amount that would have been charged by a hypothetical attorney working in the same market. Pp. 4–12. (a) The lodestar method, which determines a reasonable attorney’s fee by multiplying the number of billable hours by the prevailing hourly rate, was never intended to be conclusive in every circumstance. Rather, there is a “strong presumption” that the lodestar figure is reasonable, but that presumption may be overcome in those rare circumstances in which the lodestar does not adequately take into account a factor that may properly be considered in determining a reasonable fee. Pp. 4–6. (b) Superior attorney performance is a relevant consideration in determining whether to enhance the lodestar. If the method used in determining the hourly rate employed in the lodestar calculation does not adequately measure the attorney’s true market value, as demonstrated in part during litigation, an enhancement may be appropriate. Similarly, if the attorney’s performance includes an extraordinary outlay of expenses and the litigation is exceptionally protracted, an enhancement may be appropriate, but the amount of the enhancement must be calculated using a method that is reasonable, objective, and capable of being reviewed on appeal. Moreover, if an attorney’s performance involves exceptional delay in the payment of fees, an enhancement may be appropriate, but the enhancement should be calculated by applying a method similar to that described above. Permitting the award of enhancements on the ground that departures from hourly billing are becoming more common is not appropriate. Neither respondents nor their amici have shown that permitting the award of enhancements on top of the lodestar figure corresponds to prevailing practice in the general run of cases. Pp. 6–10. (c) Here, the District Court did not provide proper justification for the large enhancement that it awarded. The court increased the lodestar award by 75%, but provided no explanation for this figure. Nor did the court calculate the amount of the enhancement that is attributable to the fact that respondents’ counsel had to make extraordinary outlays for expenses and had to wait for reimbursement. Furthermore, the court did not sufficiently link the delay factor to proof in the record that the delay here was outside the normal range expected by attorneys who rely on §1988 for the payment of their fees or quantify the disparity. Nor did the court provide a calculation of the cost to counsel of any extraordinary and unwarranted delay. And the court’s reliance on the contingency of the outcome contravenes this Court’s holding in Burton v. Dague, 505 U.S. 557. Finally, insofar as the District Court relied on a comparison of the performance of counsel in this case with the performance of counsel in unnamed prior cases, the court did not employ a methodology that permitted meaningful appellate review. Pp. 10–12. 532 F.3d 1203, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined. Breyer, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part.

Title: Immunization of Government Officials

Summary:
The Supreme Court holds that government officials who secure a favorable judgment on immunity grounds may obtain the Court's review of an adverse constitutional holding. The Court finds that the doctrine of sovereign immunity applies to the states and localities, and that Congress has waived immunity in certain instances where it is inconsistent with the Constitution. However, the Court also recognizes that the doctrine of qualified immunity provides a strong incentive for officers to respect individual rights, and that the doctrine should be interpreted broadly to encourage responsible policymaking. Finally, the Court suggests that the doctrine of qualified immunity may be extended to cover non-government actors who perform essential functions related to public health and safety.

The Commonwealth of Kentucky permits “hazardous position” workers to retire and to receive “disability retirement” benefits after either (1) working for 20 years; or (2) working 5 years and attaining the age of 55. The Plan sets forth two routes through which such employees can become eligible for what is called “normal retirement benefits.” The first makes an employee eligible for retirement after 20 years of service provided that the employee has attained 55. A hazardous position worker in the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Department, became eligible for normal retirement benefits after only 5 years. In calculating his benefits, Kentucky will add a certain number of (“imputed”) years to his actual years of work. The number of imputed years equals the number of years that the disabled employee would have had to continue working in order to become eligible, i. e., the years necessary to bring the employee up to 20 years service or to at least 5 years service when the employee would turn 55 (whichever number is lower). A dismissal based on pension status was not a dismissal “because . . . of age,” 507 U. S., at 610. The District Court, making all appropriate evidence-related assumptions, held that the EEOC could not establish age discrimination; and it granted summary judgment in the defendants’ favor. A panel of the Sixth Circuit affirmed. The Sixth Circuit then granted rehearing en banc, holding that the District Court did not violate the ADEA, and reversed and remanded for further proceedings. Kentucky sought certiorari. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The ADEA forbids an employer to “fail or refuse to hire or to discharge any individual or otherwise discriminate against any individual with respect to his compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of such individual”s age. Hazen Paper Co. v. Biggins, 492 U.S. 604, distinguished. Pp. 5–11. (a) Where an employer adopts a pension plan that includes age as a factor, and that employer treats employees differently based on their pension status, a plaintiff, to state a disparate treatment claim, must adduce sufficient evidence to show that the differential treatment was “actually motivated” by age, not pension status. The above factors convince the Court that the Plan does not, on its face, create treatment differences that are actually motivated by age. See, e. g., National Railroad Passenger Corporation v. Morgan, 536 U. . 101, 111, n. 6. The difficulty of finding a remedy that can both correct the disparity and achieve its legitimate objective—providing each disabled worker with a sufficient retirement benefit, namely, the normal retirement benefit that the worker would receive if he were pension eligible at the time of disability—further suggests that this objective and not age is actually motivated. See id., at 611–612. The fact that the plan does not rely on any of the sorts of stereotypical assumptions that the AdEA sought to eradicate does not help the Government here. Moreover, the fact that it does not rest on any stereotype about the work capacity of “older” or “younger” employees relative to older workers does not give the Government the necessary “power to persuade” us. P. 5. (b) The Plan at issue simply seeks to treat disabled employees as if they had worked until the point at which they would be eligible for a normal pension. The disparity turns upon pension eligibility and nothing more. The Act does not deference to a regulation of the same kind as the regulation of a regulation that is explicitly defined (in whole or in part) by age; and, as a matter of pure logic, age and pension status remain “analytically distinct” concepts. The rule that a statute or policy that facially discriminates based on age suffices to show disparate treatment is clear: Where a statute, such as a pension scheme, imposes age-related disparities in the provision of benefits are lawful only when they are justified in respect to cost savings. See Public Employees Retirement System of Ohio v. Betts, 49 2 U.

After respondent was convicted of multiple murders, the Nevada Supreme Court affirmed his death sentences for the Red Pearl Saloon murders, but reversed his sentence for the murder of his ex-wife and remanded for imposition of a life sentence without the possibility of parole. Respondent then sought postconviction relief in state court, which rejected his claim that he was mentally incompetent to represent himself. The Federal District Court subsequently denied his subsequent habeas petition, but the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that the state court's postconviction ruling was based on the incorrect "reasoned choice" standard rather than the correct "competency to stand trial" standard set forth in Dusky v. United States, 362 U. S. 402. According to the Ninth Circuit, the latter standard is insufficient for determining whether a defendant is competent to waive a constitutional right. Held: There is no heightened competency standard for pleading guilty or waiving the right to counsel. Pp. 10-15. (a) Although the Ninth Circuit correctly notes that the standard for competence to stand trial is whether the defendant has sufficient present ability to consult with his lawyer with a reasonable degree of rational understanding and has a rational as well as factual understanding of the proceedings against him, Westbrookv . Arizona, 384 U. S. 150, per curiam, cannot be used to establish a higher standard for pleading guilty or waiving the right to counsel. That decision simply holds that where a defendant seeks to waive his constitutional right to counsel, a determination that he is competent to stand trial is not enough; the waiver must also be intelligent and voluntary before it can be accepted. Pp. 10-12. (b) Since the decision to plead guilty involves making important decisions similar to those faced by a defendant who pleads not guilty, there is no basis for requiring a higher level of competence for those who choose to plead guilty. Nor is there any reason to believe that the decision to waive counsel requires an appreciably higher level of mental functioning than the decision to waive other constitutional rights. Moreover, the competence that is required of a defendant seeking to waive his right to counsel is the competence to waive the right, not the competence to represent himself. Finally, although a finding that a defendant is competent to stand trial is necessary before he may be permitted to plead guilty or waive his right to counsel, it is not all that is necessary. In addition, the waiver of his constitutional rights must be knowing and voluntary. Pp. 12-15. 972 F. 2d 263, reversed and remanded.

Respondent, who had run only a few paces farther, was arrested and charged with knowingly and intentionally possessing heroin, tablets containing codeine, and tablets containing diazapam. At a preliminary hearing, at which Officer Peltier was the only witness, respondent moved to dismiss the charges on the ground that he had been unlawfully seized during the police pursuit preceding his disposal of the packets. The presiding Magistrate ruled from the bench that a police "chase" like the one involved in this case implicated Fourth Amendment protections and could not be justified by the mere fact that the suspect ran at the sight of the police. Applying a clearly-erroneous standard to the Magistrate's ruling, the trial court upheld the dismissal order. The Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed, concluding that respondent's flight from the police was insufficient, by itself, to give rise to the particularized suspicion necessary to justify this kind of seizure. Held: Respondent was not unlawfully seized in the initial police pursuit, and the charges against him were improperly dismissed. Pp. 488-481. (a) The test is necessarily imprecise, because it is designed to assess the coercive effect of police conduct, taken as a whole, rather than to focus on particular details of that conduct in isolation. Moreover, what constitutes a restraint on liberty prompting a person to conclude that he is not free to "leave" will vary, not only with the particular police conduct at issue, but also with the setting in which the conduct occurs. United States v. Mendenhall, 446 U. S. 544, 554, 100 S.Ct. 1870, 1877, 64 L.Ed. 2d 497. Rather than adopting either rule proposed by the parties and determining that an investigatory pursuit is or is not necessarily a seizure under the Fourth Amendment, we adhere to our traditional contextual approach, and determine only that, in this particular case, the police conduct in question did not amount to a seizure. P. 489. (b) The police conduct involved here would not have communicated to the reasonable person an attempt to capture or otherwise intrude upon respondent's freedom of movement. P p. 490. (c) The record does not reflect that the police activated a siren or flashers; or that they commanded respondent to halt, or displayed any weapons; or operated the car in an aggressive manner to block respondent's course or otherwise control the direction or speed of his movement. Contrary to respondent's assertion that a chase necessarily communicates that detention is intended and imminent, this kindof police presence does not, standing alone, constitute a seizure, as long as the police did not succeed in apprehending the individual. P, 489-481, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Department held that a New York City man's conviction for burning an American flag violated his First Amendment right to free expression. The court held that the New York State Penal Law Section 1425, subd. 16, par. d, which prohibits the mutilation, deface, or trample upon any flag of the United States, is vague and imprecise because it does not clearly define the conduct which it forbids. The Court also held that it is unconstitutional to punish a person who publicly destroys or damages a flag as a means of protest. The Appellate Term, Second Department, affirmed the lower court's decision. The Supreme Court of the State of New York, in a separate opinion, held that there was insufficient evidence to support the criminal charges against appellant, and that the trial judge misapplied the law. The Second Department's opinion is consistent with that finding, and the Court held that, in light of all the circumstances, the conviction denied appellant rights of free expression protected by the First Amendment and assured against state infringement by the Fourteenth Amendment.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled in favor of the Bureau of Prisons in a class action brought on behalf of pretrial detainees at the Metropolitan Correctional Center ( MCC) in New York City. The District Court enjoined the MCC from violating the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment of the United States Constitution, which prohibits the government from imposing restrictions or privations that "inhere in the confinement itself or which are justified by compelling necessities of jail administration"<n>The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, however, largely affirmed the District Court's constitutional rulings and held that pretrial detainees may "be subjected to only those 'restrictions and privations' which ... [inhere] in their confinement itself ... or which ... are justifications by compelling realities of jail adminstration"

The Socialist Labor Party, an appellant in No. 544, has all the formal attributes of a regular party. It has conventions and a State Executive Committee as required by the Ohio law, and it was permitted to have a place on the ballot until 1948. Since then it has not filed petitions with the total signatures required under new Ohio laws for ballot position, and indeed it conceded it could not do so this year. The same three-judge panel heard the Party's suit and reached a similar result-write-in space was ordered but ballot position was denied. Held: 1. Ohio's claim that the political-question doctrine precludes judicial consideration of these cases requires very little discussion. Pp. 542-543. (a) The State has a well-established claim to inclusion in justiciable, as distinguished from "political," questions; and the relief the Court grants meets the practical needs of appellees in preparing and distributing the ballots. P. 545. (b) The fact that Ohio has already provided for them to be chosen by right to popular suffrage does not justify the very severe restrictions on voting and associational rights which Ohio has imposed. P p. 546. (c) The totality of the Ohio restrictive laws taken as a whole imposes a burden on voting rights which we hold is an invidious discrimination, in violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, and the State has no interest, "compelling" or not, in abridging those rights, because "the men who drafted our Bill of Rights did all the "balancing" that was to be done in this field." P. 555. (d) In determining whether or not a state law violates the equal protection Clause, the State must consider the facts and circumstances behind the law, the interests which the State claims to be protecting, and those who are disadvantaged by the classification. Pc. 547-548. (e) The state laws do not give the two old, established parties a decided advantage over any new parties struggling for existence and thus place substantially unequal burdens on both the right of individuals to associate for the advancement of political beliefs, and qualified voters, regardless of their political persuasion, to cast their votes effectively, but the State is left with broad powers to regulate voting, which may include laws relating to the qualification and functions of electors, and there is no such remote danger that the absence of such voices would be a symptom of grave illness in our society. P, 548. 290 F. Supp. 983, affirmed and modified.

Respondents in No. 72-777 are female public school teachers employed by the Board of Education of Cleveland, Ohio. Pursuant to a rule first adopted in 1952, the school board requires every pregnant teacher to take maternity leave without pay, beginning five months before the expected birth of her child. Application for such leave must be made no later than two weeks prior to the date of departure. A teacher on maternity leave is not allowed to return to work until the beginning of the next regular school semester which follows the date when her child attains the age of three months. Because of the mandatory maternity leave rule, each was required to leave her job in March 1971. The District Court held that the regulation violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, and granted appropriate relief. The Court of Appeals upheld the constitutionality of the challenged regulation in a 4-3 decision. Held: 1. The mandatory termination provisions of the Cleveland and Chesterfield County School Boards violate the Due Process Clause. Pp. 541-542. (a) The necessity for continuity of instruction and the state interest in keeping physically unfit teachers out of the classroom can not justify the sweeping mandatory leave regulations that the two school boards have adopted. P. 542. 2. The provisions amount to an irrebuttable presumption of physical incompetency, and that presumption applies even when the medical evidence as to an individual woman's physical status might be wholly to the contrary. The rule does not simply contain reasonable medical and next-semester eligibility provisions, but also requires the mother to wait until her child reaches the appropriate age before the return rules begin to operate. The absolute requirements of termination at the end of the fourth or fifth month of pregnancy are not. Were continuity the only goal, cutoff dates much later during pregnancy would serve as well as or better than the challenged rules, providing that ample advance notice requirements were retained. Moreover, continuity would seem just as well attained if the teacher herself were allowed to choose the date upon which to commence her leave, at least so long as the decision were required to be made and notice given of it well in advance of the date selected. The presumption, moreover, is patently unnecessary, since the requirement of a physician's certificate or a medical examination fully protects the school's interests in this regard. And finally, the three-month provision simply has nothing to do with continuity of teaching and thus serves to hinder attainment of the very continuity objectives that they are purportedly designed to promote, such as ensuring that students have a physically capable instructor in the classroom at all times. Thus, while the advance-notice provisions are wholly rational and may well be necessary to serve the objective of continuity, they cannot pass muster under the Due process Clause because they employ irrebutttable presumptions that unduly penalize a female teacher for deciding to bear a child. The two-month provisions in both cases amount to a conclusive presumption that all pregnant teachers who reach the fifth or sixth month of pregnant are physically incapable of continuing, and there is no individualized determination as to any particular teacher's ability to continue at her job, because they are said to protect the health of the teacher and her unborn child, while at the same time assuring that students are having a physically competent instructor in their classroom. The fact that the rule is wholly rational does not mean that it is arbitrary to impose arbitrary restrictions on the exercise of protected constitutional liberty, since it serves to serve both the school and the teacher's interest in maintaining continuity. The exception to the rule, however, is a precisely drawn means of serving the School Board's interest of avoiding unnecessary changes in classroom personnel during any one school term, and it suffers from the same constitutional deficiencies that plague the irrebutte presumption in the termination rules. P p. 543. 474 F. 2d 395, affirmed.

The Supreme Court held that Individual Retirement Accounts (IRAs) can be exempted from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(10)(E). The case involved Richard and Betty Jo Rousey, who sought to protect their IRAs from creditors after filing for Chapter 7 bankruptcy. The Bankruptcy Court and the Court of Appeals had previously ruled against the Rouseys, stating that IRAs did not qualify for exemption because they were not similar to other plans listed in the statute and did not provide a right to payment "on account of" age.

The Supreme Court disagreed, stating that IRAs are similar to the specified plans because they provide income that substitutes for wages, which is the common characteristic of the listed plans. The Court also found that the right to payment from IRAs is causally connected to age, as evidenced by the tax penalties for early withdrawal and the requirements for minimum distributions at a certain age. These features indicate that IRAs are intended to be used for retirement income, distinguishing them from typical savings accounts.

The Court's decision means that debtors can exempt their IRAs from the bankruptcy estate, allowing them to retain these assets for retirement purposes rather than having them liquidated to pay creditors. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

Opinion Title: Bates v. Arizona Bar
Opinion Date: July 2, 1975
Judge: Warren E. Burger
Summary:
This case involves a challenge to the constitutionality of a rule prohibiting lawyers from soliciting clients in person. The Court holds that the rule is constitutional and applies to the facts of the case. The Court finds that the rule serves a compelling state interest in preventing harm to clients and that the burden placed on lawyers to comply with the rule is minimal.

This case involves a dispute between a black man named Mendez and a white woman named Angulo over ownership of a piece of land in California. The parties reached an oral agreement to sell the land to Mendez for $1,000, but Angulo later reneged on the deal and sold the land to someone else for $1,200. Mendez sued Angulo for breach of contract, arguing that the oral agreement was legally enforceable and that Angulo had violated her promise to sell him the land.

The Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether the 2-year statute of limitations for filing a lawsuit against corporate insiders under Section 16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 begins only upon the insider's filing of a required disclosure statement under Section 16(a). The case arose from actions filed by Vanessa Simmonds against financial institutions involved in IPOs in the late 1990s and 2000, alleging they profited from inflated stock prices and failed to file required disclosures, thus tolling the 2-year limitations period.

The Ninth Circuit had previously ruled that the limitations period is tolled until the insider files the Section 16(a) disclosure, regardless of whether the plaintiff knew or should have known of the conduct at issue. However, the Supreme Court disagreed, stating that the text of Section 16 does not support this rule and that the limitations period begins from the date the profit was realized, not the filing date of the disclosure statement.

The Court also clarified that the usual principles of equitable tolling apply, which require a plaintiff to demonstrate diligent pursuit of their rights and that extraordinary circumstances prevented timely filing. Equitable tolling ceases when the plaintiff becomes aware, or should have become aware, of the facts underlying the claim. The Court emphasized that allowing tolling to continue indefinitely would be inconsistent with the purpose of statutes of limitations, which is to protect defendants from stale claims.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, to consider how the usual rules of equitable tolling apply to the facts of the case. The Court was divided 4 to 4 on whether Section 16(b) establishes a period of repose not subject to tolling, thus affirming without precedential effect the Court of Appeals' rejection of the petitioners' contention on this point. The Chief Justice did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant who was charged with defrauding the public in connection with an investigation into the activities of Soviet spies in the United States.  According to the court's order, filed on June 15, 1976, Ilya Wolston, an attorney who was convicted of espionage in the 1940's and 1950's, was a "public figure" for purposes of comment on the investigation of Soviet espionage.  The court found that, by failing to appear before the grand jury and receiving a contempt citation for contempt, Wolston was a public figure for the purposes of commenting on the case.  In addition, the court held that petitioner was not entitled to the same level of protection afforded to public figures, and that he was not required by the First and Fourteenth Amendments to be a publicly-traded person.  As a result of this conduct, the government pursued him in its investigation, resulting in further arrests, convictions, and guilty pleas.  Wolston also failed to respond to a subpoena for his testimony, which he received in exchange for a 1-year suspended sentence and a 3-year penalty.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court order, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against him from appearing or practicing before the court as an attorney.   The judgment also imposes a $10,000 civil penalty against Wolston.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-17 (January 5, 2019). The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York dismissed a case brought by the Hasidic community alleging that the New York State Senate Reapportionment Act of 1974 violated the Fourteenth Amendment right to vote by reason of race or color. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the lower court's decision, holding that the State's 1974 reapportionment plan did not violate the Fourteent Amendment. The court held that the use of racial criteria by the State in attempting to comply with  5 of the Act was not a violation of the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law. The Second Circuit also found that the state had not violated the provisions of  4 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 by failing to demonstrate that it had met its burden of demonstrating that the plan had abridging the right to the vote. The appeals court concluded that the Act's provisions did not prevent the State from using racial criteria to ensure that its districts would not underrepresent the white population. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate opinion, held that it was not necessary for the Court to determine whether the 1974 plan violated the 14th Amendment because it did not provide for a racial quota. The Appeals Court concluded that, in the absence of a ruling by the Attorney General, the State could use racial criteria in its attempt to secure the approval of the AG under the Act.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Maryland Circuit Court for the Circuit Court of Montgomery County held that a group of young Negroes convicted of criminal trespass for refusing to leave a privately owned and operated amusement park at the command of an employee acting under color of his authority as a deputy sheriff violated the Fourteenth Amendment. The court held that the park's policy of segregation was not to have colored people on the rides, or in the park. The park had employed a special police officer, Francis J. Collins, as a special policeman by arrangement with the National Detective Agency. He was subject to the control and direction of the park management. He reported the petitioners' presence to the park manager. The manager told Collins that petitioners were to be arrested for trespassing if they would not leave. Collins ordered petitioners to leave within five minutes. They declined to do so, pointing out that they had tickets for the carousel. There was no evidence that any of the petitioners were disorderly. At the end of the five-minute period Collins told them that the time was up and that they were under arrest for trespassing. The trial court found that Collins had violated the terms of his contract with the park operator, Kebar Inc.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit ruled that the Export Clause does not apply to a federal tax on insurance premiums paid to foreign insurers that are not subject to the federal income tax. The court held that the Internal Revenue Code's Section 4371 imposes a tax on the premiums paid by IBM to foreign insurance companies that are listed as beneficiaries in the insurance policies. The Court of Federal Claims had previously ruled that a federal stamp tax on policies insuring marine risks could not be constitutionally applied to policies covering export shipments. The Supreme Court held in a similar case in 1915 that the export clause does not extend to policies that cover shipments in the course of exportation and might never be exported. The lower courts have held that, in certain cases, the Export clause does apply to pre-export goods and services, but not to those that are ultimately intended for export. In this case, the Court held that this provision of the Code applies to insurance policies that are insured in export transit. We conclude that the Constitution does not permit the imposition of a generally applicable, nondiscriminatory federal tax.

Petitioner was convicted of capital murder. A separate sentencing hearing before the same jury was then held to determine whether the death penalty should be imposed. Under Tex.Code Crim.Proc.Ann. § 37.071, two special questions were to be submitted to the jury: whether the conduct causing death was "committed deliberately and with reasonable expectation that the death of the deceased or another would result"; and whether "there is a probability that the defendant would commit criminal acts of violence that would constitute a continuing threat to society." The jury answered both of the questions in the affirmative, a result which required the imposition of the death sentence. On appeal to the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals, petitioner urged, among other submissions, that the use of psychiatrists at the punishment hearing to make predictions about petitioner's future conduct was unconstitutional because psychiatrists, individually and as a class, are not competent to predict future dangerousness and hence their predictions are so likely to produce erroneous sentences that their use violated the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments. The court rejected all of these contentions and affirmed the conviction and sentence on March 12, 1980. The Court of Appeals granted petitioner's motion to proceed in forma pauperis and issued a certificate of probable cause pursuant to 28 U. S. C. § 2253, which provides that an appeal may not be taken to the court of appeals from the final order in a habeas corpus proceeding where the detention complained of arises out of process issued by a state court. The Texas courts set January 25, 1983, as the new execution date, and the District Court stayed petitioner's execution pending action on the petition. An evidentiary hearing was held on July 28, 1982, at which petitioner was represented by competent counsel. The District Court granted petitioner a stay of execution pending the filing and disposition of a petition for certiorari, which was filed and then denied on June 29, 1981. The parties were directed to brief and argue "the question presented by the application, namely, the appropriate standard for granting or denying a stay ... pending disposition of an appeal by a federal court of the appeals by a death-sentenced federal habas corpus petitioner, and also the issues on appeal before the United States Court of appeals for the Fifth Circuit." Held: 1. In this case, there is no doubt that petitioner's psychiatric testimony increased the likelihood that petitioner would be sentenced to death, but this fact does not make that evidence inadmissible, any more than it would with respect to other relevant evidence against any defendant in a criminal case. Pp. 5-11. (a) The Court's handling of this case was tolerable under the precedents of the Federal Rules of Evidence, which provide for the testimony of experts. P. 5. (b) The use of psychiatric testimony, when possible, together with the application for a stay, is not inconsistent with the cases in this case. The primary means of separating meritorious from frivolous appeals should be the decision to grant or withhold a certificate. The procedures adopted to facilitate the orderly consideration and disposition are not legal entitlements that a defendant has a right to pursue irrespective of the contribution these procedures make toward uncovering constitutional error. The courts of appeals have a duty to sort out the true testimony from the false, the important matters from the unimportant matters, and, when called upon to do so, to give greater credence to one party's expert witnesses than another's. Such matters occur routinely in the American judicial system, both civil and criminal. The development of these procedures is primarily a function of the courts' courts and the rulemaking processes of the federal courts, but the following general guidelines can be set forth. 1. A prisoner must be afforded an opportunity to make a "substantial showing of the denial of [a] federal right." Stewart v. Beto, 454 F. 2d 268, 270, n. 2 (CA5 1971); Brooks v. Estelle v. Smith, 451 U.S. 454, 473.
