The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's approach, which paid particular attention to the broad purpose of the ADA and accords that factor overriding significance, is consistent with the statutory purpose of ridding the Nation of the evil of discrimination. See, e., § 12111(b). P. 6. (c) The determination whether shareholder-directors are partners-rather than asking whether they are employees-does not affect whether Clackam's physicians are covered under the Act or whether its doctors are employees. Nor does the E. R. Darden approach fare any better. The E. O. C.'s approach, in which the Court selects one of the commonlaw indicia of a master-servant relationship-control over the work of others engaged in the business of the enterprise-and accords those factors overriding significance-is consistent with Congress' statutory purpose. The commonlaw element is the primary guidepost, and the Court's approach adopted by this Court does not fare any worse. The court's focus on the Common-law touchstone of control, see Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U.S. 134, 140 (1944), and specifically by its submission that each of the following six factors is relevant to the inquiry whether the doctor-director appears to be the functional equivalent of a "partner." P. 7. (d) The question whether the patient-shareholder qualification as an employee cannot be answered by asking whether the shareholder-Director appears to appear to be a partner, officer, member of a board of directors, or major shareholder, since Clackams' physicians are not employees for purposes of the federal antidiscrimination laws, and thus the question whether a patient-director's qualification as employees is simply begs the question. Moreover, the fact that the physicians' physicians' medical practice is conducted on behalf of the corporation and the doctors provide services for the corporation does not necessarily mean that they are an employee, but rather that the corporation would have had at least 18 people on site doing the day-to-day work of the clinic for the requisite number of weeks. The question, as here, is whether they "ac[t] independently and participat[e] in managing the organization, or ... [are] subject to [the organization's] control." Id. 271 F. 3d 903, 905, affirmed.

Appellant, a restaurant located within an off-street automobile parking building in Wilmington, Delaware, has refused to serve appellant food or drink solely because he is a Negro. The parking building is owned and operated by the Wilmington Parking Authority, an agency of the State of Delaware, and the restaurant is the Authority's lessee. Appellant claims that such refusal abridges his rights under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The Delaware Supreme Court reversed, holding that Eagle was acting in a purely private capacity under its lease; that its action was not that of the Authority and was not, therefore, state action within the contemplation of the prohibitions contained in that Amendment; and that under 24 Del.Code s 1501, Eagle was a restaurant, not an inn, and that as such it "is not required (under Delaware law) to serve any and all persons entering its place of business." Held: 1. When a State leases public property in the manner and for the purpose shown to have been the case here, the proscriptions of the Amendment must be complied with by the lessee as certainly as though they were binding covenants written into the agreement itself. Pp. 542-543. 2. The action of Eagle in excluding appellant under the circumstances shown to be present here was discriminatory state action in violation of the Equal protection Clause. P. 543. 157 A. 2d 894, reversed and remanded.

An Massachusetts statute makes it a felony "for any person" to give away or possess with intent to give away any drug or device "intended to be used as a contraceptive," including condoms, diaphragms, and sponges. Married couples are permitted to purchase such items legally, while unmarried persons are not. Petitioner, who gave away a packet of condoms during a speech at a university campus, was convicted of violating the statute. He challenged the statute's constitutionality on the grounds that it denies equal protection of the laws to unmarried persons, who are otherwise able to procure contraceptives, and that it is invalid as being directed against freedom of expression. His convictions were upheld by the Massachusetts courts. The Court of Appeals ultimately affirmed, holding that the statute was aimed at preventing premarital sexual intercourse rather than at promoting health, and that the statute was constitutionally valid as applied to married persons. Held: By providing dissimilar treatment for married and unmarried persons who are similarly situated, the Massachusetts statute violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 108-118. (a) No legitimate reason exists for treating differently married and unmarried persons in order to achieve the objectives of the statute, namely, to discourage premarital sexual intercourse and to promote health. Pp. 110-114. (b) Health, on the face of the statute, may no more reasonably be regarded as its purpose than the deterrence of premarital sexual relations. Pp. 114-116. (c) Whatever the rights of the individual to access to contraceptives may be, the rights must be the same for the unmarried and the married alike. Pp. 116-118. Affirmed.

The Supreme Court addressed the interpretation of a federal statute on aggravated identity theft, which mandates a 2-year consecutive prison term for individuals convicted of certain crimes if they "knowingly" use someone else's identification during the commission of those crimes. The central question was whether the statute requires the government to prove that the defendant knew the identification belonged to another person.

The Court concluded that the statute does indeed require this knowledge. The case involved Ignacio Flores-Figueroa, who used false identification documents that turned out to be assigned to real individuals. He was charged with aggravated identity theft, but argued that the government could not prove he knew the numbers on the documents were assigned to others.

The Court's reasoning was grounded in the interpretation of the word "knowingly" as it is used in the statute. The Court determined that "knowingly" applies to all elements of the crime, including the fact that the identification belongs to another person. The Court rejected the government's argument that "knowingly" only applies to the use of the identification, not to the knowledge of whose identification it is.

The Court also addressed the government's argument based on a related provision of the statute concerning terrorism, which the government claimed would render the phrase "of another person" superfluous. The Court found this reasoning flawed, as there are circumstances where a defendant could use a "means of identification" that is neither belonging to another person nor a false document.

The Court's decision emphasizes the importance of the defendant's intent and knowledge in the commission of identity theft. The ruling implies that the government must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant knew the identification used belonged to another person. The Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. This decision clarifies the scope of the aggravated identity theft statute and the government's burden of proof in such cases.

Respondent Sarah Greene, S. G.’s mother, sued the Oregon Department of Human Services (DHS) for damages under 42 U. S. C. §1983, which authorizes suits against state officials for violations of constitutional rights. The District Court granted summary judgment to Camreta and Alford, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed. The Court of Appeals first ruled that the interview violated S.G.s rights, but the court further held that the officials were entitled to qualified immunity from damages liability because no clearly established law had warned them of the illegality of their conduct. The Ninth Circuit agreed, ruling that both officials had violated the Fourth Amendment by failing to obtain a warrant to conduct the interview. The court also held that qualified immunity shielded the officials from monetary liability because the constitutional right at issue was not clearly established under existing law. The two officials sought this Court‘s review of the Ninth’’ ruling. The case has become moot because the child has grown up and moved across the country, and so will never again be subject to the Oregon in-school interviewing practices whose constitutionality is at issue. See, e.g., Arave v. Hoffman, 552 U.S. 277, 287–289, and Mootness has frustrated his ability to challenge that ruling. So whatever else follows, they will not have to pay the damages she sought. Certiorari granted; 588 F. 3d 1011, vacated and remanded.

Respondent was arrested by police officers and advised of his Miranda rights. Subsequently, while being transported to the police station, two police officers engaged in a conversation concerning a missing shotgun. During the conversation, respondent requested that the car be turned around so he could direct the officers to the location of the gun. Upon arriving at the scene of the shooting, the officers again advised respondent of his Miranda rights, and he stated that he understood those rights and wanted to speak with a lawyer. One of the officers then directed that respondent be placed in a caged wagon and that he not be questioned or intimidated in any way. However, during the drive to the police station, another officer joined the two officers already in the car, and the three officers conversed among themselves concerning the possibility that the gun might be dangerous to children playing in the vicinity. Respondent then volunteered information leading the officers to the location of the gun. He was subsequently convicted of various crimes arising out of the shooting, and the Rhode Island Supreme Court reversed, concluding that respondent had invoked his Miranda right to counsel and that the officers had "interrogated" him without a valid waiver of that right. Held: Respondent was not "interrogated" within the meaning of Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U. S. 436, and hence the Rhode Island Supreme Court erred in equating "subtle compulsion" with interrogation. Pp. 449-456. (a) Under Miranda, the special procedural safeguards prescribed therein are required not where a suspect is merely taken into custody, but rather where a suspect in custody is subjected to interrogation. Interrogation means not only express questioning, but also any words or actions on the part of the police (other than those normally attendant to arrest and custody) that the police should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response from the suspect. Pp. 450-453. (b) Here, the first prong of the definition of interrogation was not satisfied, for the conversation between the two officers included no express questioning of respondent. And although the second prong of the definition was satisfied, i. e., the officers should have known that their conversation was reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response from respondent, nevertheless, given the fact that the entire conversation appeared to consist of no more than a few offhand remarks, it cannot be said that the officers should have known that it was reasonably likely that respondent would make a self-incriminating response. Pp. 453-456. Vacated and remanded.

The Freedom of Information Act requires federal agencies to make records and documents publicly available upon request, unless they fall within one of several statutory exemptions. One of those exemptions covers law enforcement records, the disclosure of which “could reasonably be expected to constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.” 5 U. S. C. §552(b)(7)(C). The question presented here is whether corporations have “personal privacy” for the purposes of this exemption. Respondent AT&T Inc., which participated in an FCC-administered program that was created to enhance access for schools and libraries to advanced telecommunications and information services, voluntarily reported to the FCC that it might have overcharged the Government for services it provided as part of the program. The FCC and the Enforcement Bureau launched an investigation. As part of that investigation, AT&t provided the Bureau various documents, including responses to interrogatories, invoices, emails with pricing and billing information, names and job descriptions of employees involved, and AT&&T’s assessment of whether those employees had violated its code of conduct. The Bureau concluded that “individuals identified in [AT&T] submissions” had “privacy rights” that warrant protection under Exemption 7(C), which exempts “records or information compiled for law enforcement purposes,” §552 (b) (7). The Bureau did not apply that exemption to the corporation itself, reasoning that businesses do not possess personal privacy interests as required by the exemption. On review, the FCC agreed with the Bureau. The Commission concluded that some of the information provided (including cost and pricing data, billing-related information, and identifying information about staff, contractors, and customer representatives) should be protected from disclosure under FOIA Exemption 4, which relates to “trade secrets and commercial or financial information” and “specialty information.’” The FCC also decided to withhold other information under FOIA, concluding that the individual identified in the submissions had a personal privacy right to warrant protection. The Court of Appeals reversed. Held: 1. The word “Personal” in Exemption7(C) incorporates the statutory definition of “person” to include “an individual, partnership, corporation, association, or public or private organization other than an agency” (5 U.S. C., §551(2). Because that definition applies here, the argument goes, “[personal’] must mean relating to those ‘person[s]”: namely, corporations and other entities as well as individuals. This reading is dictated by a “basic principle of grammar and usage” of the statute, and the language itself, the specific context in which that language is used, and a broader context of the law as a whole. The ‘personal” phrase is relevant here, because it suggests a type of privacy evocative of human concerns—not the sort usually associated with an entity like, say, AT.T. Pp. 4–6. 2. “Person” is a defined term in the statute; “ personal” does not. When a statute does not define a term, we typically “give the phrase its ordinary meaning.“” Johnson v. United States, 559 U. . S. ___, ___, ___. The phrase “‘person’ in common legal usage’ is understood to include a corporation. See, e.g., Johnson v., at 8–9, 16. In ordinary usage, a noun and its adjective form may have meanings as disparate as any two unrelated words. The Government has long interpreted the phrase as a matter of constitutional or common law. The language of the phrase in the Dictionary Act makes that clear. The term “ ‘Personal’ often refers to artificial entities,’ and when it comes to the phrase, the phrase is pertinent in construing Exemption 8. The phrase, however, elides the difference between the noun and the adjective. See id., at 31–32 (emphasis added). The significance of the pertinent phrase—“[o]f or pertaining to a particular person”—cannot be so readily dismissed. In the same context therefore can and should have the same scope, especially here in light of the statutory definitions. See Id., at 4–9. Memphis, 161 U. s. 161, 171); and while “crank” can mean “given to fretful fussiness” if “corny” has no personal right of privacy. See Washington Post Co., supra, at 599. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in a defamation action brought by a private company and its principal stockholder against a public figure for defaming them.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Philadelphia, alleges that, in 1975 and 1976, General Programming, Inc. ("GPI"), a Pennsylvania-based corporation that franchises a chain of stores selling beer, soft drinks, and snacks, published five articles that alleged that a state legislator had links to organized crime and used some of those links to influence the state's governmental processes, both legislative and administrative. The complaint further alleges that the defendants' statements were false, and that GPI was liable for civil injunctive relief.  According to the complaint, GPI and Gertz agreed to settle the case without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint. The SEC also agreed to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and to pay civil penalties.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania today announced criminal charges against GPI.  On May 24, 2018, the U. S. District Judge for the Western District of North Carolina entered a judgment that permanently enjoins GPI from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders GPI to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The court also ordered GPI not to violate the reporting provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) of its books, and ordered GGI to comply with the reporting requirements of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of their books, including the reporting and reporting requirements.  GGI has agreed to a settlement where it will pay a $2,500 civil penalty. The settlement is subject to court approval.

What is the main idea behind the decision in Burger King Corporation v. Hernandez?

The main idea behind the decision in Burger King Corporation v. Hernandez is that a state court cannot exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident defendant based solely on the fact that the defendant's products have been sold in the state. Instead, the court must look for other connections or contacts between the defendant and the state before exercising jurisdiction.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Minnesota on May 28, 1974, entered a final judgment in favor of a Minnesota-based insurance company in a civil action brought by a Minnesota resident who was injured in an automobile accident.  The court held that the obligation of an insurance company to defend and indemnify a nonresident insured under an automobile liability insurance policy is a contractual obligation under the federal securities laws.  According to the court's order, filed in federal court in Minnesota, Appellee Savchuk, who was a passenger in the car driven by appellant Rush, was injured and required to pay a civil penalty of $125,000.  As alleged in the complaint, the insurance policy was taken out in anticipation of litigation, and the insurer did business in the state.  In a parallel action, the Minnesota state court issued a temporary restraining order, freezing the insurance company's assets, and barring the insurer from participating in any civil action.  On May 29, 1974 the Minnesota court granted the SEC's request for an emergency court order halting the action against Rush.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted in the Chicago Regional Office and the case is being supervised by Joseph G. Sansone, Chief of the Division of Insurance. Â The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Minnesota Department of Insurance in this matter.

Section 12(f) of the Military Draft Act of 1971 (Act) denies federal educational assistance to any student who is required to register for military service under the Military Selective Service Act of 1967 (Selective Service Act) but who fails to do so. Section 12(f) applies to students who became 18 years old prior to October 1, 1971, and who were required to register pursuant to the Selective Service Act. Section 12(f) was added to the Act by the Departmient of Defense Authorization Act of 1982. Appellees, who were required to register for military service but who had not done so, brought suits challenging the validity of § 12(f) under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and the Bill of Attainder Clause of Article I of the Constitution. They claimed that § 12(f) violated due process because it left open perpetually the possibility of obtaining federal educational assistance while conditioning receipt of such assistance on registration for military service, thereby placing an unfair burden on students who had already graduated or who would graduate soon. They also claimed that § 12(f) violated the Bill of Attainder Clause because it singled out an identifiable group that would be ineligible for federal educational assistance and because it inflicted punishment within the meaning of the clause. Finally, appellees claimed that § 12(f) violated the Fifth Amendment because it forced them to acknowledge during the registration process that they had registered late. The District Court upheld the challenges to § 12(f) and enjoined its enforcement. Held: 1. Section 12(f) does not violate the Bill of Attainder Clause. Pp. 20-26. (a) Because § 12(f) allows late registration, it is clearly distinguishable from the provisions of the Selective Service Act that were invalidated in Cummings v. Missouri ex rel. Moore, 367 U. S. 481, and Garland v. Teamsters Union, 367 U. S. 340. Those cases involved provisions of the Selective Service Act that absolutely barred individuals from participating in certain occupations for reasons that were irreversible. Here, however, § 12(f)'s requirements, far from being irreversible, can be met readily by either timely or late filing. Pp. 20-22. (b) Even assuming that § 12(f) satisfies the first criterion for an attainder-that it falls within the historical meaning of legislative punishment-it nevertheless does not inflict punishment within the meaning of the Bill of Attainder Clause. Such punishment involves depriving an individual of life, liberty, or property. While § 12(f) imposes none of the burdens historically associated with punishment, it nonetheless leaves open perpetually the possibility of obtaining federal educational assistance while conditioning receipt of such assistance on registration for military service. But a statute that leaves open perpetually the possibility of qualifying for aid does not fall within the historical meaning of forbidden legislative punishment. Moreover, to ensure that the Legislature has not created an impermissible penalty not previously held to be within the proscription against bills of attainder, it must be determined whether the challenged statute can be reasonably said to further nonpunitive goals. Pp. 22-26. 2. Section 12(f) does not violate the Fifth Amendment by compelling nonregistrants to acknowledge that they have failed to register timely when confronted with certifying to their schools that they have complied with the registration law. Nonregistrants such as appellees are not in the same position as potential public contractors in Lefkowitz v. Turley, 414 U. S. 70, where it was held that the plaintiff architects' disqualification from public contracting for five years as a penalty for asserting a constitutional privilege was violative of their Fifth Amendment rights. Unlike the architects in Turley, appellees have not been denied the opportunity to register and in no sense have they been disqualified for financial aid "for asserting a constitutional privilege." Pp. 26-27. 574 F. Supp. 131, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri today entered final judgments in favor of the University of Missouri at Kansas City in a civil injunctive action.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Kansas City, Missouri, alleges that the University violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17(b) thereunder, and that, in violation of Section 10(b)(5) of Exchange Act Rule 10b-5, the University's right to exclude certain religious groups and speakers from using its facilities for purposes of religious worship and discussion.  According to the complaint, from 1973 until 1977, the U.M. had provided University facilities for the purpose of accommodating religious groups.  In 1977, however, the university informed the group that it could no longer meet in University buildings.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the college consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins the University from violating the federal securities laws, and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $41 per semester, $5,000 in disgorgement, and a $10,000 civil penalty.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

The Interstate Commerce Act, as amended by the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994, and the ICC Termination Act of 1995, generally preempts state and local regulation "related to a price, route, or service of any motor carrier ... with respect to the transportation of property." 49 U. S. C. § 14501(c)(1), which provides that "the federal legislation preempts provisions by [or] political subdivision of a State ... related to ... [the safety regulatory authority of [a State]" and "political subdivision[s]" of "a State"), specifically excludes "safety regulatory authority" (and "authority of [the State] to enact or enforce a law, regulation, or other provision, with respect ... [inter alia] uniform cargo liability rules ... if such law or regulation meets [various enumerated] requirements." The District Court ruled for the plaintiffs; the court declared the tow-truck regulations preempted and enjoined their enforcement. Columbus and its officials appealed to the Sixth Circuit, which affirmed the District Court's injunction against enforcement. Held: 1. The safety regulation exception to preemption does not encompass the preemption provision. The statute does not bar a State from delegating to municipalities and other local units the State's authority to establish safety regulations governing motor carriers of property, including tow trucks. Pp. 5-11. (a) The statute's reference to the "regulatory authority" of a "State" does not exclude political subdivisions from preemption local as well as state regulation. P. 5. (b) The phrase "the authority of ... a State or a political subdivision ... to enact ... [a] law ... or any other provision" refers only to the "[authority ... or a ... political subdivision [of a State]," and the exception for safety regulations, § 14500(c),2)(A), refers to the authority of the State or political subdivision "to enact ... or enforce ... [an] other provision ... [in a State's] ... jurisdiction." The phrase is not used in the statute's language, but rather in the language and structure of the statute, which indicates that Congress meant to limit the safety exception to States alone. The provision's single exception, preserving the "safety" authority of a state, preserves the authority to delegate the state police power over safety to localities, and does not apply to motor carriers "with respect to ... commercial motor vehicle transportation by a tow truck, if such transportation is performed without the prior consent or authorization of the owner or operator of the motor vehicle." P. 6. (c) The statutory construction is surely resistible here, since the statute contains no reference at all to "political subdivisions" or to any "authorities ... to regulate ... motor carriers ... [with respect] to the intrastate transportation ... of property by motor carriers," and the provision's exceptions are unambiguously imposed by the statute. Moreover, reading the statute in combination with the exceptions in combination, and with a view to the basic tenets of our federal system pivotal in Mortier, does not provide the requisite "clear and manifest indication that Congress sought to supplant local authority." 501 U., S. 1073, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit recently ruled that the Federal Arbitration Act of 1996 (FAA) does not apply to state laws that refer certain disputes to an administrative agency. The FAA provides that when parties agree to arbitration, questions concerning the validity of the entire contract are to be resolved by the arbitrator in the first instance, not by a federal or state court. The Court held that the FAA does not override state law that refers certain state-law controversies initially to a judicial forum, but also state laws referring certain disputes initially to the Labor Commissioner. The court held that, in this case, the issue of whether the contract's validity was valid was a matter of public interest, and therefore not subject to the FAA's jurisdiction. The opinion concludes that the Court's decision is consistent with the decisions of the United States District Court for the Central District of California and the U.N. Supreme Court.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana yesterday ruled that Falls City Industries, Inc., a Kentucky-based manufacturer of beer, violated the antifraud provisions of Section 2(b) of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Evansville, Indiana, Falls City violated the "meeting-competition" provision of the anti-discriminatory provisions of Sections 2(a) and 3(b)(2)(B).  The complaint alleges that, in violation of these provisions, Falls city failed to show that it had made a reasonable effort to meet a competitor's low price, and that its lower price was not a good faith response to the competitor's lower price.  The SEC further alleges that the defendants failed to demonstrate that they had acted in good faith to meet or exceed the price offered by their competitors.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Kentucky today announced criminal charges against Falls City.  On May 24, 2018, the Honorable Paul G. Gershfeld of the U. S. District court for the Northern District of Illinois entered a final judgment that permanently enjoins Falls City from violating these provisions and orders it to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000,000.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from future violations of the charged provisions, ordering them to pay civil penalties of $2,500, and ordering Falls City to disgorge its ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and to pay disgorgement of $3,500.  Vanco also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years and ordered to pay an $80,000 civil penalty.   The settlement is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by Michael J. Karpel and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal District Court for the Western District of Kentucky has ruled that a Kentucky couple's use of the name "Victor's Little Secret" for a store selling lingerie violated the Federal Trademark Dilution Act of 1995 (FTDA). The FTDA provides a remedy for the "dilution of famous marks" when a mark is likely to cause confusion or dilute the distinctiveness of a famous mark. The court ruled that the court's earlier decision in favor of the defendants did not adequately consider the impact of their use of "Victor" on the reputation of the well-known Victoria's Secret trademark. The Court's decision was based on the testimony of a marketing expert who explained the enormous value of the VICTORIA'S SECRET mark to the court. The opinion concludes that the lower court was wrong to conclude that the defendants' conduct was likely to blur and erode the distinctiveity and "tarnish the reputation" of the mark. In a separate ruling, the court ruled against the defendants, finding that they had not violated the FTDA's provisions for trademark infringement and unfair competition in violation of the common law of Kentucky. The high court concluded that there was no evidence of actual confusion between the parties' marks. The decision is subject to further review by the U.N. Supreme Court.

What is the main argument made by the majority?

The main argument made by the majority is that the EEOC is not barred from seeking victim-specific relief in court when it has signed an arbitration agreement with the employer. The majority believes that the EEOC's statutory authority to vindicate the public interest allows it to pursue legal action beyond just arbitration, even if the employee has previously signed an arbitration agreement.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has ruled that the preclearance requirements of Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 are constitutional. The case involves a small utility district that has never had any evidence of racial discrimination in voting. The district sought relief from these preclearance obligations under the Act's "bailout" provision, which allows the release of a "political subdivision" from preclearance if certain rigorous conditions are met. The court ruled that bailout was unavailable to a political subdivision like the district that did not register its own voters. We therefore reverse, and do not reach the constitutionality of 5.

This case involves a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the mother of a man who drowned in state territorial waters while working on a vessel owned by Norfolk Shipyard Corporation. The plaintiff alleges that the decedent's death was due to the negligence of several individuals, including Norfolk Shipyard Corporation. The court discusses the history of maritime law regarding wrongful death and holds that a negligent breach of a maritime duty of care causing death can be recovered under general maritime law.

After respondent Simmonds filed numerous suits alleging violations of §16(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, petitioners moved to dismiss the complaints on the ground that the 2-year limitations period set forth in §16(b) had expired. The Federal District Court agreed, finding that §16(b)’s limitations period is tolled until the insider files a report under §16(a)(2)(C), which requires insiders to disclose any changes to their ownership interests on a document known as a Form 4. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit reversed in relevant part, ruling that §16(b)’s limitations period is tolled until the insider discloses his transactions in a §16(a) filing, regardless of whether the plaintiff knew or should have known about the conduct at issue. Held: Section 16(b)’s 2-year limitations period is not tolled until the filing of a §16(a) statement. Pp. 4−11. (a) These suits were properly dismissed because they were filed more than two years after the alleged profits were realized. While petitioners make a valid point in urging that §16(b)’s limitations period is a period of repose, which is not to be “extended to account for a plaintiff’s discovery of the facts underlying a claim,” Lampf, Pleva, Lipkind, Prupis & Petigrow v. Gilbertson, 501 U.S. 350, 360, n. 5, this Court does not reach that question, because it concludes that, even assuming that the 2-year period can be extended, the Ninth Circuit erred in determining that it is tolled until the filing of a §16(a) statement. Pp. 4−6. (b) When a limitations period is tolled because of fraudulent concealment of facts, the tolling ceases when those facts are, or should have been, discovered by the plaintiff. Here, the limitations period does not start running until discovery of the fraud. Because the theory of §16(b) liability of underwriters is so novel that petitioners can plausibly claim that they were not aware they were required to file a §16(a) statement, the Whittaker rule would quite certainly be inequitable and inconsistent with the general purpose of statutes of limitations. That rule is also contrary to the most glaring indication that Congress did not intend that the limitations period be categorically tolled until the statement is filed: The limitations provision does not say so. Moreover, §16’s purpose is fully served by the rules outlined above, under which the limitations period would not expire until two years after a reasonably diligent plaintiff would have learned the facts underlying a §16(b) action. The usual equitable-tolling inquiry will thus take account of the unavailability of sources of information other than the §16(a) filing. Pp. 6−10. (c) There is no merit to petitioners’ contention that applying established equitable-tolling doctrine in this context would be inconsistent with Congress’ intent to establish in §16 a clear rule that is capable of mechanical application. Nor is there any merit to Simmonds’ countercontention that application of established equitable-tolling doctrine in this context would be inconsistent with Congress’ intent to establish in §16 a clear rule that is capable of being applied judicially. Both arguments counsel just as much in favor of the “statute of repose” rule that petitioners urge (that is, no tolling whatever) as in favor of the Whittaker rule. Pp. 10−11. Vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Sotomayor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

In 1977, the Minnesota Legislature enacted a statute banning the retail sale of milk in plastic nonreturnable nonrefillable containers, but permitting such sale in other nonreturnables, such as paperboard milk cartons. The statute was introduced with the support of the state Pollution Control Agency, Department of Natural Resources, and Department of Agriculture, Consumer Services Division, and Energy Agency. Proponents of the legislation argued that it would promote resource conservation, ease solid waste disposal problems, and conserve energy, and that the use of returnable and reusable packaging for these products is preferred and should be encouraged. After the Act was passed, respondents filed suit in Minnesota District Court, seeking to enjoin its enforcement. The court resolved the evidentiary conflicts in favor of respondents, and concluded that the Act will not succeed in effecting the Legislature's published policy goals. The State Supreme Court, however, did not reverse on the basis of this patent violation of the principles governing rationality analysis under the Equal Protection Clause. Held: 1. The Act is rationally related to the articulated statutory purposes. Pp. 463-464. (a) The Act does not effect "simple protectionism," but "regulates evenhandedly" by prohibiting all milk retailers from selling their products in plastic, nonreturnible milk containers, without regard to whether the milk, the containers, or the sellers are from outside the State. Thus, the State's approach is fully supportable under its precedents. P. 464. (b) The State's argument that the ban on plastic non returnable milk containers will help to conserve energy is not invalid simply because it causes some business to shift from a predominantly out-of-state industry to a predominantly in-state one, and only if the burden on interstate commerce clearly outweighs that State's legitimate purposes does such a regulation violate the Commerce Clause. This Court has held that a legislature need not "strike at all evils at the same time or in the same way," Semler v. Oregon State Board of Dental Examiners, 294 U. S. 608, 610, but "may implement [its] program step by step, . . . adopting regulations that only partially ameliorate a perceived evil and deferring complete elimination of the evil to future regulations." New Orleans v. Dukes, 427 U.S. 106, 110. Moreover, "the extent of the burden that will be tolerated will of course depend on the nature of the local interest involved, and on whether it could be promoted as well with a lesser impact on interstate activities." Ibid. The fact that the statute does not discriminate between interstate and intrastate commerce does not deny the State the authority to ban one type of milk container conceded to cause environmental problems, merely because another type, already established in the market, is permitted to continue in use. Whether in fact the act will promote more environmentally desirable milk packaging is not the question: the equal protection Clause is satisfied by the conclusion that the Legislature could rationally have decided that its ban would foster greater use of environmentally desirable alternatives. Id., at 127-128, 98 S.Ct. 778, 784, and it cannot prevail so long as "it is evident from all the considerations presented to [the legislature], and those of which we may take judicial notice, that the question is at least debatable." Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc., supra, at 142, 90 S. Ct., at 847. Where there was evidence before the legislature reasonably supporting the classification, litigants may not procure invalidation of the Act merely by tendering evidence in court that the legislature was mistaken, but the State was able to prevent the industry from becoming reliant on the new container, while avoiding severe economic dislocation. The District Court also held that, contrary to the statement of purpose in § 1, the "actual basis" for the Act "was to promote the economic interests of certain segments of [the] local dairy and pulpwood industries at the expense of other segments of the dairy industry and the plastics industry," and acknowledged the legitimacy of this purpose. The Court therefore declared the Act null, void, and unenforceable and enjoined its enforcement, basing the judgment on substantive due process under the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution and Art. 1, § 7, of the Minnesota Constitution; equal protection under the First Amendment; and prohibition of unreasonable burdens on interstate Commerce under Art. I, § 8, of that Clause. P p. 466. (c) The burden imposed on interstate business by the Act is relatively minor. Milk products may continue to move freely across the Minnesota border, and since most dairies package their products into more than one type, plastic pouches, plastic returnable bottles, and paperboard itself, the inconvenience of having to conform to different packaging requirements in Minnesota and the surrounding States should be slight. Moreover the State argues that the act is designed to prevent a new container from becoming entrenched in the solid waste stream. This was one of the State

The Florida felony offense of battery by “[a]ctually and intentionally touch[ing] another person against the will of the other,” 18 U. S. C. §924(e)(2)(B)(i), is defined as “any crime punishable by imprisonment for a term exceeding one year” that: “(i) has as an element the use … of physical force against the person of another; or (ii) is burglary, arson, or extortion, involves use of explosives, or otherwise involves conduct that presents a serious potential risk of physical injury to another person.” The Florida Supreme Court has held that the element of “actually and intentionally touching” under Florida’s battery law is satisfied by any intentional physical contact, “no matter how slight” and thus constitutes a “violent felony” for a defendant who has been convicted of battery (even simple battery) before, §784.03(1)(a). The District Court concluded that it does, and accordingly sentenced Johnson to a prison term of 15 years and a maximum of life. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed. Held: The phrase “physical force” as used in defining not the crime of battery, but rather the statutory category of violent felon[ies], is not a forcible felony. Pp. 5–7. (a) The phrase is not “force” in the context of a statutory definition of battery. See, e.g., Jackson v. Virginia, 443 U.S. 307, 324, n. 16. The “ ‘modified categorical approach’ ” that Nijhawan v. Holder, 557 U. . S. ___, ___ (2009) permits a court to determine which statutory phrase was the basis for the conviction by consulting the trial record—including charging documents, plea agreements, transcripts of plea colloquies, findings of fact and conclusions of law from a bench trial, and jury instructions and verdict forms. The absence of such language in §922(g)(8)(C)(ii), the Government contends, proves that the merest touch suffices. Even as a matter of logic that does not follow, Specifying that “Physical Force” must rise to the level of bodily injury does not suggest that without the qualification it would consist of only that degree of force necessary to inflict pain—a slap in the face, for example. Moreover, the meaning of the “bodily injury” specification added to the phrase is even clearer. When the adjective “felony” is attached to the noun “power to affect strongly in physical relations,’” its connotation of strong physical force is even more clear. See id., at 1188. Black’S Law Dictionary 717 (9th ed. 2009) (hereinafter Black's) defines ““[p]ower, violence, or pressure directed against a person or thing” (emphasis added) and defines physical force as a force capable of causing physical pain or injury to one person. Even if the word “physio” were to be attached to that noun, it would often frustrate application of the modified categorical method—not just to battery but to many other crimes as well. It is implausible that avoiding that common-enough consequence with respect to the single battery, under the single statute that is the Armed Career Criminal Act, caused Congress to import a term of art that is a comical misfit with the defined term “Viol felony. ” The Government asks to remand to the Eleventh for its consideration of whether Johnson’d 2003 battery conviction is a violent felony. That question is not before us, so we do not decide it. The Government contends that in deciding whether any unwanted physical touching constitutes “peculiar” battery, the phrase has the same meaning in its context of defining a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. But it has no bearing upon whether the substantive element of those offenses—making unwanted physical contact with certain special categories of individuals—involves the use of force, because Congress specifically named “burglary” or “extortion” to be “violence felon[ie],” §16(a), notwithstanding that those offenses can be committed without violence. The dissent likewise anticipates that in the States it has identified, post, at 6–7, and n. 3, as having generic felony-battery statutes that cover both violent force and unwanted physicalcontact, our decision will render convictions under those statutes “outside the scope of [the ArmedCare Criminal Act]” post. This exaggerates the practical effect of the decision. P. 7. 528 F. 3d 1318, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled that a federal court should not have granted an employer's request to recognize a cause of action under the Labor Management Relations Act of 1947 (LMRA) for an international union's alleged interference with a collective-bargaining agreement (CBA) during a 2004 strike. The court ruled that the parties' dispute over the CBA's ratification date was a matter for the District Court or an arbitrator to resolve. The Court also ruled that, because the CBA contained a no-strike provision, it was not a matter of federal jurisdiction. The 9th Court held that the Court should have granted Granite Rock Company's motion for an injunction against the ongoing strike and strike-related damages because the parties had not agreed to a back-to-work or hold-harmless agreement during the strike period. The 8th Circuit agreed with the lower court's decision, and the Court ruled that Granite Rock had not shown that the International Brotherhood of Teamsters' (IBT) interference with the CBA violated the CBA. The 10th Circuit held that, as a result, the Court had erred in declining to grant the request for a temporary restraining order and an injunction. The appeals court concluded that the issue of whether the CBA was validly ratified should be resolved by an arbitrator rather than a district court. The case is now subject to judicial resolution.

Section 102 of the Comprehensive Environmental Resource Cleanup, Limititation, and Recovery Authority (CERCLA) makes producers primarily and financially responsible for properly managing hazardous substances, except for any contributions made by, inter alios, government units that carry out programs dealing with the preservation, enhancement, or exclusive official uses of federal lands, outdoor recreation areas thereunder, historic properties, cultural heritage sites, religious studies, wilderness studies, wildlife sanctuaries …, fish and wildlife reserves …, migratory bird sanctuaries … , animal parks …, aquaculture centers or research components, watershed restoration projects focused entirely on military environmental protection and other defense environment functions, mineral mineral mines which accept private individuals under outreach training incentives related to historic engine criteria and open pit mining facilities pertaining thereto, museum or school sites administered and serving institutional schools, nuclear testing license agreements with additional options with regard to decommissioning payments or contributing consideration received pursuant to Defense Logistics Distribution Centers Decision –II, wetlands enhanced transportation system mitigation contracts, and storage production reservoirs created under intergovernment service compacts relating solely to flood control development needs but excludes Federal agencies performing planning, administration, oversight assistance, or public interest safeguards of such grants. Unless induced otherwise to act therein individually with respect to …trade disputes. Except where and in accordance with jurisdictional amounts to be prescribed by the President over which consensus or conformance can be developed pursuant to memoranda implementing a performance security agreement negotiated April 3, 1966: Uehling [Informational material omitted].

The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled that a Georgia county cannot be held liable for a boat collision caused by a malfunctioning bridge. The Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit had previously ruled that the county did not qualify as an "arm of the State" under the "universal rule of state immunity from suit without the state's consent"<n>The Supreme Court's decision is the latest in a series of high-profile cases that have examined the issue of sovereign immunity. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the county, saying that the lower court had correctly concluded that sovereign immunity does not extend to counties. The high court's ruling is consistent with the decisions of the United States District Court for the Southern District of Georgia, the U.N. Court of Justices, and the Supreme Court of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. The court also noted that the high court had previously held that a state cannot be liable for an individual's actions in the course of business.

Respondents, a not-for-profit corporation and self-described "citizens' lobby," sued for summary judgment pursuant to Rule 56 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, alleging that some 28 statements and 2 illustrations in three articles were false and derogatory. Petitioners asserted that because respondents are public figures they were required to prove their case under the standards set forth in New York Times, and also asserted that summary judgment was proper because actual malice was absent as a matter of law. In support of this assertion, petitioners submitted the affidavit of Charles Bermant, an employee of petitioners and the author of the two longer articles, in which Bermant stated that he had spent a substantial amount of time researching and writing the articles and that his facts were obtained from a wide variety of sources. Bermant detailed the sources for each of the statements alleged by respondents to be libelous. The District Court granted summary judgment for the defendants, holding that for the purposes of summary judgment the requirement that actual malice be proved by clear and convincing evidence, rather than by a preponderance of the evidence, was irrelevant: To defeat summary judgment respondents did not have to show that a jury could find actual malice with "convincing clarity." The Court of Appeals reversed, holding, with respect to nine of respondent's statements, that the summary judgment had been improperly granted because "a jury could reasonably conclude that the . . . allegations were defamatory, false, and made with actual malice." Held: 1. A court ruling on a motion for a summary judgment or for a directed verdict necessarily implicates the substantive evidentiary standard of proof that would apply at the trial on the merits. Rule 56 (c) provides that the mere existence of some alleged factual dispute between the parties will not defeat an otherwise properly supported motion for summary- judgment; the requirement is that there be no genuine issue of material fact. The substantive law will identify which facts are material. Only disputes over facts that might affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law will properly preclude the entry of summary-judgment judgment. This materiality inquiry is independent of and separate from the question of the incorporation of the evidentiary standards into the summary-guidance determination. The evidence of the non-movant is to be believed, and all justifiable inferences are drawn in his favor. Any proof or evidentiary requirements imposed by the substantive law are not germane to this inquiry, since materiality is only a criterion for categorizing factual disputes in their relation to the legal elements of the claim and not a criteria for evaluating the evidentiaries underpinnings of those disputes. Pp. 5-7. 2. The determination of whether a given factual dispute requires submission to a jury must be guided by the "clear and convincing" standard. This is true at both the directed verdict and summary judgment stages, where the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard applies and where the trial judge asks whether a reasonable jury can find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. P. 5. 3. The inquiry involved in a ruling on the motion for the "directed verdict" requires a "clearly convincing" evidentiary requirement, which is that the defendant must present affirmative evidence in order to defeat a properly supported summary judgment motion. If the evidence presented is sufficiently colorable, Dombrowski v. Eastland, 387 U. S. 82, or is not significantly probative, Cities Service, Inc. v. NLRB, 461 U.S. 731, 745, there is a genuine issue for trial. The "genuine issue" summary judgment standard is "very close" to the "reasonable jury" directed verdict standard, and Rule 56(e) itself provides that a party opposing a proper supported motion to summary judgment may not rest upon mere allegation or denials of his pleading, but must set forth specific facts showing that there is "a genuine issue" for trial, and that such actual malice must be shown with convincing clarity. In order for a jury to return a verdict for the nonmoving party, there must be sufficient evidence to support a jury verdict. The defendant, to survive the defendant's motion, need only present evidence from which a jury might return a guilty verdict in that party's favor. If he does so, the genuine issue requires a trial. This conclusion is mandated by the nature of the inquiry. The question here is whether a defendant could reasonably find either that the plaintiff proved his case by the quality and quantity of evidence required by the governing statute or that he did not. If there are no genuine factual issues as to actual malice exists in a libel suit brought by a public figure, a trial judge must bear in mind the actual quantum and quality of proof necessary to support liability. If this is true even where the evidence is likely to be within the possession of the defendant, as long as the plaintiff has had a full opportunity to conduct discovery, the judge's inquiry, therefore, unavoidably asks whether the evidence would enable the jury to find for either the plaintiff or the defendant

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California today entered a final judgment in a civil injunctive action action against Richard Ceballos, a former deputy district attorney for the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office.  The court found that, as a public employee, the First Amendment protects the rights of citizens to express their views in the course of performing their official duties.  According to the court, in February 2000, a Los Angeles county district attorney wrote a memo in which he questioned the accuracy of an affidavit obtained pursuant to a critical search warrant. The memo allegedly contained serious misrepresentations concerning the location of a long driveway, and the manner in which the driveway led from a stripped-down truck to the premises covered by the warrant. Ceballo allegedly replied that, in any event, he did not receive a satisfactory explanation for the perceived inaccuracies in the affidavit. The court also ruled that, when confronted by a supervisor or a supervisor about whether to proceed with a criminal case, Ceballi consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000. The settlement is subject to court approval.  In a separate administrative proceeding, the court issued a temporary restraining order and issued an order suspending the issuance of the order. The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Pickering and Carol A. Connick of the SEC's Public Finance Abuse Unit. The litigation will be led by Mr. and Ms. Pickling.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Washington State Apple Commission in its dispute with the state of North Carolina over the legality of a North Carolina law that banned the display of Washington State grades on closed containers of apples shipped into the state. The Court held that the law violated the Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits states from placing undue burdens on interstate commerce. The Court found that the law had a discriminatory effect on Washington apple growers and dealers, who were forced to change their marketing practices and pay higher fees to comply with the law, while North Carolina apple producers were not similarly affected. The Court also found that the law did not provide a rational basis for protecting consumers from fraud and deception in the marketplace, as claimed by North Carolina.

In the case of Miranda v. Arizona, the United States Supreme Court ruled that once a defendant in custody requests legal representation, all interrogation must stop until a lawyer is present. The ruling applies to custodial interrogations, which include questioning initiated by law enforcement officers after a person has been taken into custody or otherwise deprived of their freedom of action in any significant way. However, the Court clarifies that not all statements obtained by the police after a person has been taken into custody are considered products of interrogation. Instead, the term "interrogation" refers to any words or actions on the part of the police that they should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response from the suspect.

Petitioner Krupski tripped over a cable and fractured her femur while on board the cruise ship Costa Magica. Upon her return home, she acquired counsel and began the process of seeking compensation for her injuries. Her passenger ticket, which explained that it was the sole contract between each passenger and the carrier, included a variety of requirements for obtaining damages for an injury suffered on one of the carrier’s ships. The ticket identified the carrier as “Costa Crociere S. p. A., an Italian corporation, and all Vessels and other ships owned, chartered, operated, marketed, and provided by Costa Crocier, S. P. A. and all officers, staff members, crew members, independent contractors, medical providers, concessionaires, pilots, suppliers, agents, and assigns onboard said vessels and all their component parts.” The ticket required an injured party to submit “written notice of the claim with full particulars … to the carrier or its duly authorized agent within 185 days after the date of injury,” Fed. Rules Civ. Proc. 15(c)(1)(B), (C). Second, “within the period provided by Rule 4 (m) for serving the summons and complaint” (which is ordinarily 120 days from when the complaint is filed, see Rule 4(m), the newly named defendant must have “received such notice [of the action that it will not be prejudiced in defending on the merits].” Rule 15(1)(C)(i). The court also held that relation back under Rule 15 (c) was not appropriate because the plaintiff had unduly delayed in seeking to amend the pleading. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed. Held: The Court of Appeals did not abuse its discretion in denying relation back. Pp. 5–7. (a) Under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, an amendment to a pleading relates back to the original pleading when: “(A) the law that provides the applicable statute of limitations allows relation back; (B) the amendment asserts a claim or defense that arose out of the conduct, transaction, or occurrence set out—or attempted to be set out-in the original complaint; or (C) the amendments changes the party or the naming of the party against whom a claim is asserted, if Rule 15’c (1)()(B) is satisfied and if, within the period providing by Rule4(m)(2), the party to be brought in by amendment: (i) received such notice of an action that the action would have been brought against it, but for a mistake concerning the proper party‘s identity; and (ii) knew or should have known that [it] would be brought against [it], but for [a] mistake concerning [it’”] the proper parties’ identity. The Rule does permit a court to examine a plaintiff “in the way or for the purpose” of the Rule, see, e.g., Leonard v. Parry, 219 F. 3d 25, 29, and nn. 49–50, but not on the amending party’S knowledge or timeliness of the amended complaint. The reasonableness of the mistake is not itself at issue. A plaintiff might know that the prospective defendant exists but nonetheless harbor a misunderstanding about his status or role in the events giving rise to the claim at issue, and she may mistakenly choose to sue a different defendant based on that misimpression. That kind of deliberate but mistaken choice does not foreclose a finding that Rule 15 has been satisfied. The rule mandates relation back once the Rule is satisfied; it does not leave the decision whether to grant a motion to amend a pleading back to a district court’d equitable discretion. See Rule 15.

The U.S. Supreme Court has granted certiorari in two cases challenging the constitutionality of mandatory maternity leave rules for public school teachers. The cases involve two female teachers who were forced to quit their jobs after informing their local school boards that they were pregnant. The court held that the Cleveland Board of Education's maternity leave rule violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled that the Ohio rule was constitutional. The Supreme Court's decision in the case of Susan Cohen v. Chesterfield County, Virginia, found that the Virginia rule was not in violation of the Constitution's equal protection clause. The high court's ruling will determine whether there is a reasonable basis for the lower court to conclude that there is no basis for a district court order requiring the school board to comply with the maternity leave provisions of the Ohio law. The justices also ruled that there was no reason to believe that there would be a significant impact on the school boards' ability to determine whether or not to implement such a rule. The case is being handled by the same lawyer who successfully argued the case before the Supreme Court.

Respondent was tried in a Nebraska court for the capital offense of felony murder, which includes the commission of specified enumerated felonies. At the time of his arrest, Nebraska law provided that the use of force causing death in committing one of those felonies was a separate offense punishable by up to five years' imprisonment. The jury was instructed that it could return verdicts of guilty of either felony murder or the lesser included offense of using force causing death in committing a felony. Respondent was convicted of felony murder and sentenced to death. His Federal District Court habeas petition was ultimately dismissed after the Nebraska Supreme Court affirmed his conviction and sentence. While his Federal appeals were pending, the Federal Courts of Appeals issued conflicting opinions regarding the availability of lesser included offense instructions in felony murder trials. Ultimately, the Eighth Circuit held that the constitutional error in Beck v. Alabama, 447 U. S. 638, occurred here because Nebraska's refusal to give lesser included offense instructions violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Held: Instructions on offenses that have been determined to be lesser included offenses of the charged crime are available to defendants when the evidence supports them, in capital and noncapital cases alike. However, the Nebraska trial court did not deny respondent instructions on any existing lesser included offense of felony murder; it merely declined to give instructions on crimes that are not lesser included offenses. By ignoring these distinctions, the Eighth Circuit limited state sovereignty in a manner more severe than the rule in Beck. Pp. 359-365. (a) The Alabama statute prohibited instructions on offenses that state law clearly recognized as lesser included offenses of the charged crime, and it did so only in capital cases. By contrast, the Nebraska trial court did not erect an "artificial barrier" for the jury; instead, it followed the Nebraska Supreme Court's interpretation of the relevant offenses under state law. Pp. 359-361. (b) The Eighth Circuit's holding ignores significant distinctions between this case and Beck. Unlike the situation in Beck, respondent's jury did not have the burden of imposing a sentence, and the three-judge panel that imposed the death penalty did not have to consider the dilemma faced by Beck's jury. Moreover, allowing respondent to be convicted of homicide offenses that are not lesser included offenses of felony murder would introduce another kind of distortion at trial. Where no lesser included offense exists, a lesser included offense instruction detracts from, rather than enhances, the rationality of the process. Finally, the Eighth Circuit misread Tison v. Arizona, 481 U. S. 137, and Enmund v. Florida, 458 U. S. 782, to support its holding. Those cases establish no new elements of the crime of murder that must be found by the jury, and do not affect the State's definition of any substantive offense. Nor does the Nebraska Supreme Court's longstanding interpretation that felony murder has no lesser included homicide offenses appear arbitrary. That interpretation was not challenged on respondent's direct appeal, and this Court will not secondguess the Nebraska Supreme Court's 100-yearold interpretation of state law when respondent failed to present his challenge to that Court in the first instance. Pp. 361-365. 102 F. 3d 979, reversed.

Title 8 U. S. C. §1252(f)(2) provides that no court may enjoin the removal of an alien whose removal has been upheld by the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) unless the court determines that the removal would violate the Constitution or laws of the United States. Petitioner Nken, an immigrant from Nigeria, was ordered removed by an Immigration Judge (Judge) after he failed to establish eligibility for asylum. He filed a timely motion to reopen, but the BIA dismissed the motion. While his appeal was pending, he filed a motion to stay removal pending judicial review. The Fifth Circuit rejected his motion, rejecting his arguments that the stay standard articulated in Hilton v.braunfelser, 481 U. S. 774, 777, governed. Instead, the court found that §1252(f)(2) controlled. Held: The stay standard articulated in Hilton, supra, at 776, governs a request for a stay of removal pending judicial review. Pp. 4–12. (a) The traditional stay standard articulated in Hilton, supra, at 776, is controlling here. The Court agrees with petitioner that an alien need not satisfy the demanding standard of §1252(f)(2) when asking a court of appeals to stay removal pending judicial review. Rather, the stay standard is an exercise of judicial discretion, and the party requesting a stay bears the burden of showing that the circumstances justify an exercise of that discretion. The fact that the issuance of a stay is left to the court’s discretion does not mean that no legal standard governs that discretion. Here, the relevant legal principle is contained in the four-factor test derived from Hilton, supra, at 776. Those factors are: (1) whether the stay applicant has made a strong showing that he is likely to succeed on the merits; (2) whether the applicant will be irreparably injured absent a stay; (3) whether issuance of the stay will substantially injure the other parties interested in the proceeding; and (4) where the public interest lies. Pp. 4–7. (b) The first two factors of the traditional stay standard are the most critical. Simply showing some “possibility of irreparable injury,” Abbassi v. INS, 143 F. 3d 513, 514, fails to satisfy the second factor. And although removal is a serious burden for many aliens, it is not categorically irreparable, as some courts have said. Thus, the burden of removal alone cannot constitute the requisite irreparable injury. Once an applicant satisfies the first two factors, the traditional stay inquiry calls for assessing the harm to the opposing party and weighing the public interest. These factors merge when the Government is the opposing party. In considering them, courts must be mindful that the Government’s role as the respondent in every removal proceeding does not make the public interest in each individual one negligible, as some courts have concluded. However, there is always a public interest in prompt execution of removal orders, and that interest may be heightened by the circumstances as well. A court asked to stay removal cannot simply assume that “[o]rdinarily, the balance of hardships will weigh heavily in the applicant’s favor.” Andreiu v. INS, 253 F. 3d 477, 484. Pp. 7–10. 507 F. 3d 407, vacated and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

Following respondent's conviction for rape in a Tennessee state court, the Tennessee Supreme Court, sitting en banc, affirmed the conviction by an equally divided vote. Subsequently, while confined in prison awaiting execution of sentence, respondent filed a habeas corpus petition in Federal District Court challenging the constitutionality of his conviction. The District Court concluded that the "totality of the circumstances" required reversal of the conviction, holding that the identification of respondent by the victim was unreliable because the confrontation procedure employed was suggestive. Held: 1. An affirmance by an equally divided Court does not preclude relief on habeas corpus. Pp. 108-111. 2. Under the "totality of the circumstances," the identification of respondent by the victim was sufficiently reliable to warrant submission of the case to the jury. Pp. 111-116. Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded.

In the case presented, the Supreme Court addressed whether an arrest is lawful under the Fourth Amendment if the offense for which there is probable cause is not the same as the offense stated by the arresting officer at the time of arrest.

The case originated when Jerome Alford was stopped and arrested by Washington State Patrol officers on suspicion of violating the Washington Privacy Act by recording his interactions with the police without consent. The officers initially suspected Alford of impersonating a police officer, but he was ultimately arrested for the recording, which he claimed was legal based on a state court decision.

Alford sued the officers, claiming his arrest was without probable cause and thus violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. The District Court ruled in favor of the officers, but the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the decision, stating that the officers could not have had probable cause for the Privacy Act violation and that the other potential charges were not "closely related" to the stated reason for the arrest.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the Ninth Circuit's ruling, stating that the Fourth Amendment does not require the offense establishing probable cause to be closely related to the offense cited by the arresting officer. The Court emphasized that an officer's subjective intent is irrelevant to the existence of probable cause, which should be determined objectively based on the facts known to the officer at the time of the arrest.

The Court found that the "closely related offense" rule proposed by the Ninth Circuit would lead to arbitrary and variable protection under the Fourth Amendment, which is not the intention of the law. The Court also noted that such a rule could discourage officers from providing reasons for arrest or encourage them to list all possible reasons, leading to further complications.

The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, without addressing whether there was probable cause for the other potential charges of impersonating an officer or obstructing an officer. The Chief Justice did not participate in the decision.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced today that it filed a civil injunctive action against the Department of Labor for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York City, alleges that, in 1974, Congress amended the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA) to include certain third-party-employed companionship workers, including babysitters, housekeepers, and chauffeurs.  According to the complaint, these workers were previously exempt from the federal minimum wage and maximum hour requirements.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the federal government initially proposed a rule that exempts certain third parties from certain of the federal requirements, including those paid directly by a family member of an elderly or infirm person receiving such services whenever the family member resided in the same household as the person receiving the services.  For example, the SEC previously ruled that certain third party workers should be included within the scope of the statutory exemption.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the Department has agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the federal securities laws, orders it to pay a civil penalty of $1,000, and orders the SEC to conduct an independent examination of the relevant provisions of the 1934 Rules. The SEC is continuing its investigation into the matter.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Ohio's Secretary of State's Office for the Promotion of a Two-Party System.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Columbus, Ohio, alleges that Ohio violated the antifraud provisions of the federal election laws.  According to the complaint, Ohio's laws impose a significant burden on the right of individual citizens to associate for the advancement of political beliefs, the right to form a political party, and the right for qualified voters to cast their votes.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the state laws impose significant restrictions on the number of registered voters who can participate in the primary, and on the ability of qualified voters, regardless of their political persuasion, to cast a ballot.  As the complaint further alleges, the state's statutes impose significant burdens on the rights of minority groups, including those who have proved both unwilling and unable to vote.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Ohio has agreed to the entry of an order that permanently enjoins the state from violating these provisions, and orders the imposition of a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and a temporary restraining order from further violations of the First and Second Amendments of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rules 10b-5, 13a-1, 13b2-2, and 14a-11 thereunder.  It has also agreed to pay a civil penalty of $100,000, which is equal to the amount of disgorgement and prejudgment interest paid to the parties in the case by the court.    In a parallel action, the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Ohio today announced criminal charges against Ohio Attorney General Patrick J. McCluskey. Â McCluskey agreed to settle the matter by consenting to a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the federal securities laws, ordering him to disgorge $10,000 in ill-gotten gains plus interest, and to pay civil penalties of $150,000 and $100 million, respectively.  McCloskey agreed with the judgment and agreed to be barred from the federal district court system for the rest of his life.

Petitioners, two Drug Enforcement Administration agents, were awarded qualified immunity from respondent’s 42 U. S. C. §1983 damages claim arising from a consensual entry into a suspected marijuana growhouse. They had obtained a warrant authorizing a search of the house, but the owner refused to admit them. One agent called the owner’s neighbor, who allowed the agents to enter the house. While searching the basement, the agents discovered cocaine and arrested the owner. Respondent filed suit, claiming that the agents’ entry constituted a Fourth Amendment violation. The District Court dismissed the complaint, finding that the agents were entitled to qualified immunity. The Tenth Circuit reversed, holding that the agents’ conduct was objectively unreasonable and that the “consent-once-removed” doctrine did not provide immunity. Held: The agents are entitled to qualified immunity because the entry did not violate clearly established law. Pp. 4−12. (a) The doctrine of qualified immunity governs liability for damages awards in §1983 actions. Its central aim is to balance competing values: protecting society’s interest in ensuring that government employees act within the bounds of the law, and protecting the employee’s interest in avoiding personal financial loss. Harrop v. Bell Atlantic Corp., 529 U. S. 224, 234.
