To qualify for immunity, an officer must prove that his or her conduct was objectively reasonable in light of the legal rules that existed at the time it was taken. Anderson v. New York City, 483 U. S. 638, 641. Pp. 4−5. (b) The Saucier Protocol, which governed the lower courts until this term’s decision in Hinton v. Ohio Public Participation Network, Inc., ante, p. 2, sets forth a two-step procedure for determining whether a government official is immune from liability. First, the court determines whether the facts alleged establish a violation of clearly established law. If so, the court proceeds to the second step and asks whether the relevant facts make out a constitutionally protected behavior. Saucier v. Gonzales, 546 U. S. __, ___. Pp. 5−6. (c) The Saucier Protocol is often, but not always, advantageous. The lower courts can choose between the two steps depending on the circumstances of the case. Here, the officers are entitled to rely on the “consent-once-removed” doctrine, which had been accepted by every circuit that had considered it since the late 1980s. Even though the officers’ own Circuit had not yet ruled on “consent-once-removed” entries, they were entitled to rely on existing lower court cases without facing personal liability for their actions. Pp. 6−12. 527 F. 3d 1178, reversed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, Breyer, and Kagan, JJ., joined.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the authors of articles published online, stating that copyright registration is not a requirement for bringing a civil infringement claim. The court found that the registration requirement in 17 U.S. Code A §411(a) is nonjurisdictional, meaning it does not affect the subject-matter jurisdiction of federal courts. The court cited previous cases where similar conditions were found to be nonjurisdictional, and noted that the registration requirement is more akin to a claim processing rule than a jurisdictional prerequisite.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Louisiana today entered a final judgment against a public official for defaming a member of a Teamsters Union local.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, alleges that, on June 27, 1962, J. D. Albin read a series of questions which he had put to an East Baton Rouge Parish deputy sheriff and respondent, Herman A. Thompson, who made recent visits to the Hall to see Ed. Partin.  According to the complaint, Albin's answers concerned his efforts to prevent Partin from secreting union records; in this answer Albin referred to Herman Thompson, a state trooper who was involved in the Sheriff's Office or the State Police office through that jurisdiction.  Albin also allegedly made an unverified telephone call to Thompson.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Albin.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering them to pay disgorgement of $5,000, prejudgment interest of $2,500, and a civil penalty of $1,500.  St. Amant also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company and to pay a $20,000 civil penalty.

Respondents filed claims against respondent Sisson for damages to the marina and other vessels in the wake of a fire on his vessel. Invoking the Limited Liability Act that limits the liability of an owner of a vessel for any damage done "without the privity or knowledge of such owner" to the value of the vessel and its freight, Sisson argued that the federal court had maritime jurisdiction over his limitation of liability action pursuant to 28 U. S. C. § 1333 (1). The District Court disagreed, dismissing the petition for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. In re Complaint of Sisson, 867 F. 2d 341, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York on March 2, 1977, entered a final judgment in favor of the Equal Protection Clause of the federal Social Security Act of 1940.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, from 1940 to 1940, widows and widowers were entitled to Social Security benefits based on the earnings of a deceased husband covered by the federal insurance program.  The complaint alleges that, under the federal law, widowers and widows are not entitled to equal protection under the law.  As alleged in the complaint, the difference in treatment of widows is not entirely without merit.  For example, in 1940, the federal government provided widow and widower benefits to widows in the form of "mother's benefits," which were paid to the widower by the widows' widowers.  In contrast, the SEC alleges that widows receive benefits only to their widowers when they are dependent on their widows.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Wiesenfeld agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 402(f)(1)(D) and orders him to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount of his benefit.  On March 5, 2020, the Honorable Judge Paul G. Bentsen of the U.N. Division of Economic and Risk Analysis issued an order imposing an injunction against the alleged violations of the Due Process Clause.   The SEC's investigation was conducted by Marc Blau and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Chicago Regional Office. Â The litigation will be led by Joseph A. Califano.

The Supreme Court affirmed the decisions of three District Courts that found state and District of Columbia statutes unconstitutional. These statutes denied welfare assistance to residents who had not lived within the jurisdiction for at least one year prior to applying for aid. The cases involved appellants from Connecticut, the District of Columbia, and Pennsylvania who were denied welfare benefits due to these residency requirements.

The Court held that the one-year residency requirement created an unconstitutional classification that discriminated against new residents, violating the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The Court rejected the states' arguments that the requirement protected fiscal integrity, facilitated budget planning, provided an objective residency test, minimized fraud, and encouraged employment. The Court found these justifications either constitutionally impermissible or not compelling enough to justify the discrimination against new residents.

The Court emphasized the fundamental right to interstate travel and the unconstitutionality of penalizing individuals for exercising this right. It stated that saving welfare costs could not justify an invidious classification and that a state could not deny services based on past tax contributions.

The Court also addressed the argument that Congress had approved the one-year waiting period in the Social Security Act. It clarified that the Act did not prescribe such a requirement but merely prevented the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare from disapproving state plans that included it. The legislative history showed that Congress intended to reduce hardships from lengthy residence requirements, not to encourage them.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court found that the one-year residency requirements for welfare assistance were unconstitutional, affirming the lower courts' judgments and invalidating the statutes in question.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit has declined to rule on the constitutionality of two Pennsylvania statutes that impose lump-sum annual taxes on the operation of trucks and truck tractors. The laws were upheld by the Pennsylvania State Supreme Court, which ruled that the taxes provide a competitive advantage to local businesses. The appeals court found that the laws violate the principle that no State may discriminate against interstate commerce by enacting a tax which provides a competitive edge to local business. The court concluded that "the laws are facially neutral" and therefore the laws' constitutional validity is not in question. The three-judge panel of the appeals court agreed, however, that the lower court's decision to uphold the laws should be reversed.

The Supreme Court had to determine whether evidence obtained after an allegedly unlawful arrest by Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) officials should be excluded from civil deportation hearings. The case involved two respondents, Adan Lopez-Mendoza and Elias Sandoval-Sanchez, who were ordered deported and challenged the legality of their arrests.

The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit had ruled in favor of Sandoval-Sanchez, stating that his admission of illegal presence was the result of an unlawful arrest and thus should be excluded from the deportation proceeding. It also vacated Lopez-Mendoza's deportation order for further investigation into the legality of his arrest.

The Supreme Court, however, held that the exclusionary rule, which typically prevents the use of evidence obtained through violations of the Fourth Amendment in criminal trials, need not be applied in civil deportation proceedings. The Court reasoned that deportation proceedings are not punitive but rather aim to determine an individual's eligibility to remain in the United States. The Court emphasized that the identity of a person is not suppressible, even if obtained through an unlawful arrest, and that the INS often has sufficient evidence to establish alienage without relying on evidence from an unlawful arrest.

The Court also considered the practical implications and costs of applying the exclusionary rule in deportation proceedings, noting that it would complicate and delay proceedings, burden the immigration system, and potentially lead to the suppression of lawfully obtained evidence. The Court acknowledged that the INS has its own mechanisms to deter Fourth Amendment violations, such as internal regulations and training for officers.

The Court concluded that the social costs of applying the exclusionary rule in deportation proceedings outweigh the potential benefits and that the rule's application would not significantly enhance Fourth Amendment protections. The Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, ruling that evidence obtained after an unlawful arrest by INS officials could be used in civil deportation hearings. The Court clarified that this decision does not condone Fourth Amendment violations and that its stance could change if evidence of widespread violations by INS officers emerged.

In the case of A.L. Dutton, Warden v. Alex S. Evans, the Supreme Court reversed a decision by the Court of Appeals that had found a Georgia statute unconstitutional under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments' right to confrontation. The statute in question allowed the admission of a co-conspirator's out-of-court statement made during the concealment phase of the conspiracy.

Alex S. Evans was convicted of first-degree murder, and during his trial, a witness named Shaw testified about a statement made by an alleged accomplice, Williams, which implicated Evans in the crime. The Georgia Supreme Court had upheld the conviction, stating that the statement was admissible under Georgia law because the conspiracy to conceal the crime was ongoing.

The federal Court of Appeals, however, reversed the conviction, arguing that the Georgia statute violated Evans' right to confrontation because it was broader than the federal hearsay exception for conspiracy trials, which only allows statements made during the conspiracy and in furtherance of it, not during the concealment phase.

The Supreme Court, in a decision written by Justice Stewart and joined by Chief Justice Burger, Justice White, and Justice Blackmun, disagreed with the Court of Appeals. The Court held that the Georgia statute was not invalid under the Confrontation Clause simply because it did not match the federal hearsay exception. The Court emphasized that the federal rule was not a product of the Sixth Amendment but rather the Court's rule-making power regarding federal evidence law.

The Court also found that in the specific circumstances of this case, the admission of Williams' statement did not result in a denial of Evans' confrontation right. The statement bore sufficient indicia of reliability to be presented to the jury. Justice Harlan, in a separate opinion, argued that hearsay exceptions should be evaluated under due process standards, not the Confrontation Clause, and found the Georgia statute constitutional as applied in this case.

The Supreme Court's decision implies that states have some leeway in defining their own hearsay exceptions, and these do not have to align perfectly with federal rules to be constitutional. The ruling also suggests that the right to confrontation is not absolute and can be satisfied if the out-of-court statement has sufficient indications of trustworthiness. The case was remanded to the Court of Appeals for consideration of other issues in the habeas corpus proceeding.

In the case of Harris County Commissioners Court et al. v. Richard E. Moore et al., the Supreme Court reversed a lower court's decision that had declared a Texas statute unconstitutional. The statute in question allowed for the removal of justices of the peace and constables when precinct boundaries were redrawn, potentially leaving more officials than positions available in a precinct.

The appellees, who were justices of the peace and constables, argued that their removal from office due to redistricting violated the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court agreed, finding the statute unconstitutional and ordering their reinstatement.

However, the Supreme Court held that the District Court should have abstained from deciding the federal constitutional issue because the interpretation of Texas law was not clear. Specifically, there was uncertainty about whether the Texas Constitution guaranteed these officials tenure until the end of their elected terms, even if redistricting affected their positions.

The Supreme Court cited the "Pullman doctrine," which suggests that federal courts should avoid deciding constitutional questions when an underlying state law question might resolve the issue. The Court noted that Texas law was unsettled on whether the officials in question were entitled to serve their full terms or could be removed due to redistricting.

The Supreme Court directed the District Court to dismiss the complaint without prejudice, allowing the state courts to address the state-law questions first. This would enable any remaining federal claims to be raised in a federal forum after the state courts had an opportunity to interpret the relevant Texas law.

The Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals affirmed the constitutionality of Chapter 33 of the Virginia Acts of Assembly, 1956 Extra Session, on the ground that the statutes, as applied to the activities of the NAACP and its members and lawyers, violated the Fourteenth Amendment. Held: Chapter 33 as construed and applied abridges the freedoms of the First Amendment protected against state action. Pp. 531-532. (a) The activities of NAACP, its affiliates and legal staff shown on this record are modes of expression and association protected by the First and Fourteenth Amendments which Virginia may not prohibit, under its power to regulate the legal profession, as improper solicitation of legal business violative of the Chapter 33 and the Canons of Professional Ethics. P. 533. (b) Petitioner, as a corporation, is directly engaged in activities of expressive and association on behalf of the rights of Negro citizens to equal opportunity, and its activities are not limited to those activities which Virginia has not prohibited, under the power of the State Supreme Court to regulate law, as well as those which would constitutionally be proscribed by the chapter's expanded definition of improper solicitation, and also violate Canons 35 and 47 of the American Bar Association's Canons. Pc. 534-535. (c) Although the NAACP's activities fall within the First amendment's protections, the State has failed to advance any substantial regulatory interest, in the form of substantive evils flowing from petitioner's activities, which can justify the broad prohibitions which it has imposed. P p. 535. 202 Va. 842, 81 S. C. 2d 807, reversed.

The Supreme Court addressed the constitutionality of 23 U.S.C. § 409, which protects certain highway safety information from being used in court. This statute was enacted to encourage states to identify and improve hazardous road conditions without fear of increased liability. The law was amended to clarify that it applied to pretrial discovery and to include information "compiled or collected" for federal highway safety programs.

The case arose from a fatal accident at a Washington intersection. The local government had sought federal funds for safety improvements but was denied. After the accident, the government refused to provide accident information, citing § 409. The Washington courts ruled that § 409 did not protect all requested documents and questioned the constitutionality of the statute.

The Supreme Court held that § 409 protects documents created or collected for federal highway safety purposes but does not protect information collected for unrelated purposes by agencies not involved in federal safety programs. The Court found that § 409, as a measure to improve safety in interstate commerce, falls within Congress' Commerce Clause power. Therefore, the Court reversed the Washington Supreme Court's decision and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The U.S. Court of Criminal Appeals for the Western District of Texas granted a new trial to Raymond Levi Cobb, who was convicted of capital murder for killing his neighbor's wife and their 16-month-old daughter. The court held that Cobb's Sixth Amendment right to counsel attaches not only to the offense with which he is charged, but to other offenses "closely related factually" to the charged offense. Cobb argued that his confession should have been suppressed because it was obtained in violation of his Sixth Amendment rights to counsel. But the court found that the confession had not been a harmless error and that it was not a violation of respondent's rights. The appeals court agreed with the lower court's finding that the admission of the confession was "factually interwoven with the burglary" and that Cobb had waived his rights. In a separate appeal, the Texas Supreme Court ruled that the trial court should have allowed the jury to consider a confession that was not related to the burglary. The Supreme Court held that the court had erred in denying the defense's motion for a retrial. The high court also ruled that it would have granted clemency if the jury had been allowed to consider the confession.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around a dispute between Granite Rock Company and the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, Local 287 (Local), and the International Brotherhood of Teamsters (IBT), concerning economic damages resulting from a 2004 strike. The central issues are whether a collective-bargaining agreement (CBA) with a no-strike provision was validly formed during the strike and whether Granite Rock could establish a new federal cause of action for tortious interference with the CBA against the IBT.

The Supreme Court concluded that the question of the CBA's ratification date was a matter for judicial resolution, not arbitration, despite the CBA containing an arbitration clause. The Court determined that the formation date of the CBA was crucial to deciding whether the parties consented to arbitrate the dispute, as the strike and subsequent claims occurred during a period when the validity of the CBA was contested.

Furthermore, the Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals to reject Granite Rock's request to recognize a new federal cause of action under §301(a) of the Labor Management Relations Act for tortious interference with the CBA by the IBT. The Court reasoned that creating such a federal tort claim would require policy choices that could disrupt the balance between employer and union relations established by federal statutes. The Court also noted that other potential remedies, such as state law claims or administrative claims, had not been fully explored in this case.

The Supreme Court's decision emphasizes the principle that arbitration is a matter of consent and that courts should only order arbitration of disputes that the parties have agreed to submit to arbitration. The decision also underscores the Court's reluctance to expand federal common law to include new causes of action that could upset the delicate balance of labor relations without clear evidence that existing remedies are inadequate.

In summary, the Supreme Court ruled that the dispute over the CBA's ratification date should be resolved by the courts, not through arbitration, and declined to create a new federal tort cause of action for interference with a CBA, affirming the lower court's dismissal of Granite Rock's tortious interference claims against the IBT. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion.

In the case under review, the Supreme Court addressed the definition of "interrogation" under Miranda v. Arizona, which established that a defendant must be informed of their rights (Miranda rights) and that interrogation must cease if the defendant requests an attorney until one is present. The case involved a respondent who, after being arrested and informed of his Miranda rights, indicated he wanted a lawyer. While being transported to the police station, the respondent was not directly questioned, but overheard officers discussing the potential danger of a missing shotgun to nearby children. The respondent then volunteered the location of the shotgun.

The trial court admitted the shotgun and related statements as evidence, considering the respondent's actions a waiver of his Miranda rights. However, the Rhode Island Supreme Court overturned the conviction, ruling that the respondent had been "interrogated" without a valid waiver of his right to counsel, as the officers' conversation constituted "subtle coercion."

The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to clarify the meaning of "interrogation" under Miranda. The Court held that "interrogation" includes both express questioning and any actions or words by police (other than those normally attendant to arrest and custody) that they should know are likely to elicit an incriminating response. However, the Court found that in this case, the police officers' conversation did not constitute interrogation as they could not have known it would likely elicit an incriminating response from the respondent.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Rhode Island Supreme Court, concluding that the respondent was not subjected to interrogation as defined by Miranda, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. The decision implies that not all police statements or actions that lead to a suspect's incriminating response are considered interrogation if the police could not reasonably expect such a response.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of New Mexico recently ruled that a sentencing court that missed a deadline for ordering restitution in a criminal case still retains the power to order restitution. The court held that the court's failure to comply with the mandatory restitution deadline did not amount to a violation of the law. The Court held that, in this case, the court had made clear prior to the deadline's expiration that it would order restitution, leaving open (for more than 90 days) only the amount of restitution that was owed. The case involves Brian Dolan, who pleaded guilty in 2007 to a federal charge of assault resulting in serious bodily injury. Dolan was sentenced to 21 months imprisonment along with 3 years of supervised release. The sentencing court ordered restitution for the victim's medical expenses, lost wages, and other costs associated with the assault. The deadline for the final determination of the victim’s losses was 90 days after Dolan's sentencing. The trial court set a restitution hearing for February 4, 2008—about three months after the 90-day deadline expired. Dolan argued that the law did not authorize the court to enter restitution orders past 90 days. The Appeals Court ruled that the trial court had not violated the law, and that the restitution order was upheld.

This document contains the text of the dissenting opinions of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Justice Stephen Breyer in the case of Ashcroft v. Iqbal. Both justices disagree with the majority's ruling that a plaintiff must prove actual damages in order to recover under Section 552a(g)(4) of the Privacy Act of 1974. Justice Ginsburg believes that the plain language of the statute supports the conclusion that a plaintiff may recover for emotional distress caused by an intentional or willful violation of the Act, regardless of whether actual damages can be proven. She cites numerous decisions from lower federal courts that have reached this conclusion. Justice Breyer, while acknowledging that the majority's interpretation of the statute is possible, joins Justice Ginsburg's dissent and argues that the prevailing interpretation of the phrase "intentional or willful" in the context of the Privacy Act is narrower than the majority suggests. He notes that the phrase has been construed as essentially a term of art, and that the prevailing test for determining whether an action is intentional or willful is whether a reasonable officer in the defendant's position could have believed the action to be legal.
