The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment against the agency that issued a temporary restraining order and temporarily suspended the issuance of a new mandatory safety standard.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Atlanta, Georgia, alleges that the agency violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, the agency failed to adequately consider the safety benefits of mandatory passive restraint systems when it issued its original guidance on the subject.  For example, the complaint alleges that, as a result of the agency's actions, approximately half of all cars in the United States were not equipped with passive restraints.  In addition, the SEC alleges that most of the cars in which the agency issued its guidance did not have enough safety features to support the mandatory safety standards.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the Commission issued its final judgment, which permanently enjoins the agency from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders it to conduct an independent review of the safety requirements of all mandatory safety products. The Commission's final judgment also orders the agency to provide a reasoned analysis for why it should not revoke the mandatory airbag safety standard, which it did not do in the first instance.  It also orders that the Commission consider the pros and cons of any action that may be taken in the future, including whether to impose a "reasonable" or "capricious" response to the Commission's findings.  Finally, it orders the Commission to consider whether to suspend the mandatory suspension of the mandatory seatbelt requirement until it has determined that it is reasonable and capricious to do so.  On August 4, 2017, the Court of Appeals in Atlanta issued an order suspending the mandatory mandatory airbelt requirement for new cars produced after September 1982, and ordering the Commission of Inspections and Examinations to conduct a preliminary examination of the issue.  Among other things, the court granted the Commission the right to request an asset freeze and other emergency relief.

Under Kentucky’s current lethal injection protocol, a prisoner is first sedated with sodium thiopental, followed by paralyzing agents, and finally potassium chloride to stop the heart. Before being administered the first drug, the prisoner receives a visual inspection of the intravenous site to verify that the line is properly placed. Following the execution, the body is examined to check for signs of movement. Petitioners, two prisoners scheduled for execution, filed suit challenging the constitutionality of Kentucky’s procedure. They claimed that the lack of a visual inspection prior to the first drug increases the risk of administering the wrong dose of the first drug, thereby increasing the risk of maladministration of subsequent doses. They also argued that the absence of a visual inspection makes it impossible to detect whether the first drug has reached the prisoner’s bloodstream. The trial court denied relief, but the Kentucky Supreme Court reversed, holding that the risk of maladministration created by the lack of a visual inspection violated the Eighth Amendment. Held: Kentucky’s lethal injection protocol does not pose a substantial risk of severe pain warranting a stay of execution. Pp. 3−12. (a) To establish that a State’s lethal injection protocol creates a demonstrated risk of severe pain, a prisoner must show that the risk is substantial when compared to the known and available alternatives. Here, petitioners failed to meet this burden. Their proposed alternative—visual inspections before the first drug—has never been tried by a single State and presents practical problems. And although the dissent proposes additional checks, none of those suggestions address the risk of maladministration. Pp. 3−7. (b) The fact that the States using lethal injection adopted the protocol first developed by Oklahoma without significant independent review of the procedure does not render the method constitutionally suspect. Rather, the States were motivated by a desire to find a more humane alternative to then-existing methods. See, e.g., Fordham Brief 2–3. In this regard, Kentucky was no different. Pp. 7−8. (c) Courts lack the authority and expertise to function as boards of inquiry determining best practices for executions. Any concern about the potential impact of the standard announced here on the ability of states to carry out executions efficiently is effectively addressed by the threshold requirement of a “‘substantial risk of serious harm’ ” or an “‘objectively intolerable risk of harm,’ ” see supra, at 11, and by the substantive requirements in the articulated standard. Pp. 8−10. (d) The dissent erroneously claims that the risk addressed by pancuronium bromide is vastly outweighed by the risk of pain at issue here. That risk is insignificant in light of the safeguards Kentucky has adopted. P. 10. (e) Nothing in this opinion undermines or remotely addresses the validity of capital punishment. The fact that society has moved to progressively more humane methods of execution does not suggest that capital punishment itself no longer serves valid purposes. Pp. 10−11. 275 S.W. 3d 65, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and concurring in the judgment, in which Souter, J., joined. Breyer, J., filed a concurrence.

Appellant was indicted by a grand jury for aggravated kidnaping. He moved the trial court to quash the petit jury venire drawn for the special criminal term beginning with his trial the following day. There were no females on the venire. The Louisiana jury-selection system does not disqualify women from jury service, but in operation its conceded systematic impact is that only a very few women, grossly disproportionate to the number of eligible women in the community, are called for jury service. In this case, no women were on the jury. Held: The Louisiana trial court's operation of the jury selection system deprived appellant of his Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment right to an impartial jury trial. Pp. 531-532. 282 So. 2d 491, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit granted certiorari to address the relationship between 2254(d)(2) and (e)(1) of the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 and the Alabama state court's finding that a capital defendant's attorneys' failure to pursue and present mitigating evidence of his borderline mental retardation was a strategic decision rather than a negligent omission. We conclude, however, that the state court’s factual determination was reasonable even under petitioner’s reading of that provision and therefore we need not address that provision's relationship to  2254(e) (1) .<n>The court also found that counsel appeared to have made the strategic decision not to present to the jury the limited evidence of Wood's mental retardation, and that his trial counsel were ineffective under the Alabama Rule of Criminal Procedure 32. The court also rejected Wood’s factually related claim of ineffective assistance of counsel, concluding that Wood had failed to establish that his counsel’s performance was deficient or that any deficiency prejudiced his defense. Wood was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1993 murder of his ex-girlfriend. The jury recommended a death sentence at the penalty phase, and the trial judge imposed the death penalty. After a separate sentencing hearing, Wood was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed his conviction and sentence, and denied his request for postconviction relief. The Court of appeals remanded the case for further consideration in light of Atkins v. Virginia, which held that the Eighth Amendment prohibits the execution of the mentally retarded. The Eleventh Circuit's decision in Wood v. State was consistent with that decision, and we affirm.

Petitioner Morales was born in 1969 in McAllen, Texas, and is thus a United States citizen by birth. His parents are Mexican citizens who reside in Reynosa, Mexico. He left Reynosa in 1977 and returned to McAllen to live with his sister, petitioner Oralia Martinez, for the primary purpose of attending school in the McAllen Independent School District. Although Martinez is now Morales's custodian, she is not-and does not desire to become-his guardian. As a result, Morales is not entitled to tuition-free admission to the schools. The Texas Education Agency (Texas Education Agency) and various local school officials denied Morales's application for admission in the fall of 1977. The District Court denied a preliminary injunction in August 1978, finding that the school boards had been more than liberal in finding that certain children were not living away from parents and residing in the district indefinitely. The Court of Appeals affirmed. In an appeal by two plaintiffs, the Fifth Circuit affirmed. Held: 1. A bona fide residence requirement, appropriately defined and uniformly applied, furthers the substantial state interest in assuring that services provided for its residents are enjoyed only by residents. Pp. 5-7. (a) A bona-fide residence requirement is a requirement of the State's "legitimate interest in protecting and preserving . . . the right of its own bona fide residents to attend [its colleges and universities] on a preferential tuition basis." Vlandis v. Kline, 412 U. S. 441, and Plyler v. Doe, 457 U.S. ----, 102 S. C. 2382, distinguished. P. 5. (b) The State has a substantial interest in imposing bona fide residences requirements to maintain the quality of local public schools, and the State thus has an interest in establishing a bona fide residency requirement to maintain that quality. The State's substantial interest is rooted in the history of the United States, which has a long tradition of preserving the quality and autonomy of public education, and in the tradition of the American tradition of "preserving and preserving" that quality of education, which affords citizens the opportunity to travel and participate in the local community, is deeply rooted in this tradition, and it affords the State the power to require that voters be bona fide citizens of the relevant political subdivision, and thus the State has an important interest in implementing bona fide requirements to preserve that quality in the schools' planning and operation. The fact that the State is not restricted by the fact that it does not want to penalize residents is not an empty distinction, since the State does not restrict its constitutional right to a single-part residence requirement. The state's interest in ensuring that services are provided for residents are not restricted to those who are not bona fide, but who have come there solely for educational purposes, cannot be restricted to residents, since it has a significant interest in maintaining the quality in local public education. In view of the importance of the issue, this Court granted Martinez's petition for certiorari, which is granted to him. 457 F. 2d 425, affirmed.

Title to federally funded inventions is governed by the University and Small Business Enabling Act of 1980 (Bayh-Dole Act), which seeks to encourage innovation by promoting the commercialization of federally funded research. Section 202(a) permits contractors to “elect to retain title” to “subject inventions,” which are defined as “any invention of the contractor conceived or first actually reduced to practice in the performance of work under a funding agreement.” 35 U. S. C. §201(e). Here, respondent Roche sued petitioner Stanford University for patent infringement, alleging that its patents covered processes for testing antiretroviral therapies for treating HIV infection. Stanford counterclaimed that Roche’s products infringe its patents covering similar processes. The District Court dismissed the counterclaim, holding that the Bayh-Dole Act displaced Stanford’s rights in the patents. On appeal, the Federal Circuit reversed, concluding that the Act did not automatically vest title to federally funded inventions in federal contractors. Held: The Bayh-Dole Act does not automatically vest title to federally funded inventions in federal contractors. Pp. 4−11. (a) This Court construes the term “invention of the contractor” in §202(a) to refer to a particular category of inventions conceived or reduced to practice under a funding agreement—those owned by or belonging to the contractor. Read in this way, the phrase “of the contractor” gives meaning to the otherwise superfluous term “contractor.” Moreover, the Act’s disposition of rights serves to clarify the order of priority of rights between the Federal Government and a federal contractor in a federally funded invention that already belongs to the contractor. Pp. 4−7. (b) The isolated provisions of the Bayh-Dole Act dealing with inventors’ rights in subject inventions are consistent with this construction. Under the Act, a federal agency may “grant requests for retention of rights by the inventor…if a contractor does not elect to retain title to a subject invention.” §202(d). If an employee inventor never had title to his invention because title vested in the contractor by operation of law, it would be odd to allow the Government to grant “requests for retention of rights by the inventor.” By using the word “retention,” §202(d) assumes that the inventor had rights in the subject invention at some point, undermining the notion that the Act automatically vests title to federally funded inventions in federal contractors. Also, the limited scope of the Act’s procedural protections bolsters this conclusion. The Act expressly confers on contractors the right to challenge a Government-imposed impediment to retaining title to a subject invention, §202(b)(4), and it contains no procedural protections for third parties that have neither sought nor received federal funds, such as cooperating private research institutions. These limitations make perfect sense if the Act applies only when a federal contractor has already acquired title to an inventor’s interest. Pp. 7−10. (c) Contrary to Stanford’s contention, the Court’s construction of the Bayh-Dole Act does not fundamentally undermine the Act’s framework or severly threaten its continued successful application. Universities typically enter into agreements with their employees requiring the assignment to the university of rights in inventions. With an effective assignment, those inventions—if federally funded—become “subject inventions” under the Act, and the Act as a practical matter works pretty much the way Stanford says it should. The only significant difference is that it does so without violating the basic principle of patent law that inventors own their inventions. Pp. 10−11. 583 F. 3d 832, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Sotomayor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Stevens, J., joined.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central issue was whether a judge, specifically Judge Harold D. Stump, was immune from damages liability when sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for approving a mother's petition for her minor daughter's sterilization without the daughter's knowledge or consent. The daughter, Linda Spitler, later discovered the sterilization after being unable to conceive, leading to a lawsuit against various parties, including the judge.

The District Court initially ruled that Judge Stump was immune from suit under the doctrine of judicial immunity, even if his approval of the petition was based on an erroneous view of the law. However, the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit reversed this decision, stating that Judge Stump was not immune because he acted outside his jurisdiction and failed to comply with procedural due process.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the case and reversed the Court of Appeals' decision. The Supreme Court held that judges are immune from civil actions for their judicial acts, even if such acts are in excess of their jurisdiction or alleged to have been done maliciously or corruptly, as long as there is not a "clear absence of all jurisdiction." The Court found that Judge Stump, as an Indiana Circuit Court Judge, had broad jurisdiction and there was no statute or case law in 1971 that prohibited a circuit court from considering a sterilization petition for a minor in the custody of her parents.

The Court also determined that the approval of the sterilization petition was a judicial act, despite the lack of formality in the process, because it was a function normally performed by a judge and the parties dealt with Judge Stump in his judicial capacity. The Court emphasized that judicial immunity is essential for judges to act upon their convictions without fear of personal consequences, even in controversial cases.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court ruled that Judge Stump was entitled to judicial immunity and reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with their opinion. Justice Brennan did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

This case involves a dispute over the legality of certain hiring practices implemented by a cigarette manufacturing company in Virginia. The company had separate seniority lists for African Americans and whites, with blacks being placed primarily in low-skilled positions while whites dominated higher-skilled roles. The parties involved in the lawsuit include the company, several unions representing the employees, and individual workers who claimed to have been unfairly treated.

The main issues raised in the case revolve around the applicability of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 to the seniority system in question, as well as the constitutionality of the state law prohibiting affirmative action in public employment. The court examines various aspects of the seniority system, including its historical origins, its effects on minority workers, and its relationship to the broader principles of equal opportunity and non-discrimination.

Throughout the decision, the court draws heavily on precedential authority, including landmark cases like Brown v. Board of Education and Griggs v. Duke Power Company. The court ultimately holds that the seniority system in question violates Title VII, as it creates a disparate impact on minority workers despite having originally been designed to promote fairness and equality. Additionally, the court finds that the state law prohibiting affirmative action in public employment is unconstitutional, as it conflicts with the federal interest in promoting equal opportunity and preventing discrimination.

Overall, the decision highlights the ongoing struggle to achieve true equality and justice in the workplace, and underscores the critical role played by laws and regulations in protecting the rights of marginalized groups.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has reversed a lower court's ruling that a qualifying test administered to applicants for positions as police officers in the District was not racially discriminatory. The lower court had found that the test was not designed to discriminate against otherwise qualified blacks. The appeals court agreed with the lower court, and held that the District Court's decision to dismiss the defendants' motion for summary judgment on the issue of the test's validity was not supported by the evidence. The court also found that there was no basis for a finding of racial discrimination in the recruiting process. The Court concluded that the defendants were not entitled to relief on any of the issues raised in the case. The Appeals Court held that, in the absence of any basis for racial discrimination, there was sufficient evidence to conclude that the testing was not "designed to discriminate" and that it had no impact on job performance. The decision is consistent with the findings of the lower courts and with the decisions of the United States Supreme Court and the Federal Court of Justices.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit held that the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) provides the exclusive avenue to judicial review when a qualifying employee challenges an adverse employment action by arguing that a federal sta- tute is unconstitutional. The CSRA provides for review of major adverse actions taken against federal employees for such cause as will promote the efficiency of the service. An employee who is dissatisfied with an agency's decision is entitled to a hearing before the Merit Systems Pro-tection Board (MSPB). The MSPB is authorized to order relief to prevailing employees, including reinstatement, backpay, and attorney's fees. The Federal Circuit has "exclusive jurisdiction" over appeals from a final decision of the MSPB. The court held that it has jurisdiction because it "lacks authority to determine the constitutionality of a statute." The court also held that an employee is not entitled to MSPB review of agency action that is based on an absolute bar to employment. The Court held that "the court of appeals has the right to review the record and set aside any agency action, findings, or conclusions" that are "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law" or "unsupported by substantial evidence"

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York today entered a final judgment against nine manufacturers of Agent Orange, agreeing to pay $192 million in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  The court's order, which was entered on May 24, 2018, permanently enjoins the defendants from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay disgorge interest, interest, penalties, and injunctive relief in amounts to be determined by the court at a later date.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Manhattan, the defendants agreed to settle the litigation without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint.  As alleged in the Complaint, however, the settlement did not provide for indemnification for the purpose of recovering the alleged ill-gotten gains.  Instead, the complaint alleges that the defendants consented to the entry of judgments that permanently enjoin them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and order the companies to pay civil penalties in the amount of $192,575.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Basinger and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter. The litigation will be led by Jennifer C. Barry. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The Supreme Court ruled in Miller v. Alabama (1982) that the Eighth Amendment's prohibition of cruel and unusual punishment includes the death penalty for children under the age of 15. However, the Court did not explicitly rule on the constitutionality of life without parole sentences for juvenile offenders.

The Supreme Court of the United States holds that a blood-alcohol report generated by a state laboratory pursuant to a legal requirement is not a "non-testimonial" document that can be introduced into evidence without the witness who authored the report appearing in court to testify. Rather, the report constitutes "testimony," and the witness who wrote the report must appear in court to provide live testimony. The Court's decision applies retroactively to cases currently pending in lower federal courts.

After Pennsylvania enacted the Subsidence Act of 1980, which subjects coalmining companies to liability for subsidence damage resulting from the withdrawal of coal underlying surface structures, petitioners brought suit challenging the Act's constitutionality. The District Court ultimately dismissed the suit, ruling that the Act did not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Act violated the Takings Clause of the same Amendment. Held: 1. The Act does not violate the Takings Clause. Pp. 28-36. (a) The Act does not take private property for public use. Rather, it regulates the use of privately owned property. The Act does not affect the value of the coal that petitioners own, but instead affects the value of the support estate, i.e., the right to remove the strata of coal and earth that undergird the surface or to leave those layers intact to support the surface and prevent subsidence. The support estate is valued only insofar as it protects or enhances the value of the estate with which it is associated. Because petitioners retain the right to mine virtually all of the coal in their mineral estates, the burden the Act places on the support estate does not constitute a taking. Even assuming that the support estate is a distinct segment of property for takings purposes, petitioners have not sustained a facial challenge to the Act. Their argument that the Act takes their support estate because it renders the estate unusable for its original purpose ignores the fact that the estate is valuable only insofar as it protects or enhances the value of the estate with which it is associated. Pp. 28-33. (b) The Act does not deny petitioners the economically viable use of their property. Only about 75% of their underground coal can be profitably mined in any event, and there is no showing that the Act's requirements to retain the small percentage that must be used to support the structures protected by the Act materially affect petitioners' reasonable "investment-backed expectations." Pp. 33-34. (c) The Act does not take petitioners' separate interest in the support estate. Such an estate is not a separate segment of property for takings clause purposes. The Court of Appeals correctly concluded that as a practical matter the support estate is always owned by either the owner of the surface or the owner of the minerals. Pp. 34-35. (d) Even assuming that the support estate is a distinct segment of property for takings clause purposes, petitioners have not satisfied their heavy burden of sustaining a facial challenge to the Act. They have acquired or retained the support estate for a great deal of land, only part of which is protected under the Act. The record is devoid of any evidence on what percentage of the purchased support estates, either in the aggregate or with respect to any individual estate, has been affected by the Act. Under these circumstances, petitioners' facial attack under the Takings Clause must surely fail. Pp. 35-36. 2. The Act does not violate the Contracts Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by not allowing petitioners to hold surface owners to their contractual waivers of liability for surface damage. The Act operates as a substantial impairment of a contractual relationship, and the impairment is amply justified by the public purposes served by the Act. The Commonwealth has a strong public interest in preventing the type of harm that the Act prevents, and the Act is the most appropriate way of dealing with the problem. Pp. 36-39. 771 F. 2d 709, affirmed.

Title: Exclusionary Rule in Civil Deportation Proceedings

Summary:

In this case, the Supreme Court considers whether the exclusionary rule should be applied in civil deportation proceedings involving illegal immigrants. The Court holds that the exclusionary rule is not applicable in these situations because the potential deterrence provided by the rule is outweighed by the social costs associated with its implementation. Specifically, the Court finds that the likelihood of Fourth Amendment violations by INS officers is low, and that the costs of implementing the exclusionary rule, such as increased delays and confusion in deportation proceedings, would be significant. Additionally, the Court notes that the INS has implemented its own measures to ensure compliance with Fourth Amendment standards, making the need for judicial intervention unnecessary.
What is the main idea behind this article?

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit granted certiorari in a case involving an officer's search of a backyard for marijuana plants. The officer obtained a search warrant based on an anonymous telephone tip that marijuana was growing in the backyard of a Santa Clara, California home. The trial court denied the defendant's motion to suppress the evidence of the search. The California Court of Appeal reversed, however, on the ground that the overflight violated the Fourth Amendment. The court held that the officer had not obtained a warrant, and that the flight was not the result of any routine patrol overflight. We reverse. We conclude that the trial court's finding that the search violated respondent's reasonable expectation of privacy was not supported by the evidence. We also conclude that there is no basis for the appeal's contention that the officers violated the search warrant. The Court concludes that the warrantless observation of the backyard was not a legitimate law enforcement or public safety objective, but was undertaken for the specific purpose of observing this particular enclosure within the curtilage of the home.

Petitioner was indicted in a Georgia state court for misdemeanor violations of state laws relating to exhibition of obscene material. His pretrial motions for a jury trial by 12 men were denied, and he was tried by a five-man jury, which found him guilty. The Georgia appellate court affirmed, rejecting petitioner's claims that the five-man jury violated the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. Held: Reduction of the number of jurymembers from six to five creates a substantial threat to Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment guarantees, and hence petitioner's trial by a five-man jury deprived him of the right to trial by jury guaranteed by those Amendments. Pp. 389-402. (a) While the Sixth Amendment applies only to federal cases, the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment makes the right to a jury trial available in state criminal cases involving deprivation of liberty. Pp. 389-390. (b) Empirical studies show that the purpose and functioning of the jury in a criminal trial are seriously impaired, and to a constitutional degree, by a reduction in size to below six members. Such a reduction impairs the jury's ability to apply the sense of the community, to engage in meaningful deliberation, to remember all the important facts and arguments, and to represent fairly the whole community. Pp. 390-399. (c) Georgia's retention of the unanimity requirement does not solve the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment problem, since the ability of the smaller group to perform the functions mandated by the Amendments cannot be determined solely by the possibility of returning a unanimous decision. Pp. 399-400. (d) Georgia's empirical data do not relieve the doubts created by the other studies, especially since the Saks study supports the conclusion that further reduction in jury size threatens Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment interests. Pp. 400-401. (e) With the reduction in the number of jurymembers below six creating a substantial threat to Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment guarantees, Georgia has offered little or no justification for its reduction to five members. Pp. 401-402. Reversed and remanded.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) defines the term “aggravated felony” by a list that mentions “illicit trafficking in a controlled substance … including a drug trafficking crime (as defined in section 924(c) of title 18).” §101(a)(43)(B), as added by §7342, 102 Stat. 4469, and as amended by §222(a), 108 Stat. 4320. The Attorney General’s discretion to cancel the removal of a person otherwise deportable does not reach a convict of an aggravated felony. Under the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS), the Immigration Judge agreed with Lopez that his state offense was not an aggravated misdemeanor because the conduct it proscribed was no felony under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA). But after the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) switched its position on the issue, the same judge ruled that Lopez was drug crime after all, owing to its being a felony under state law. After Lopez was released for good conduct after 15 months, the INS began removal proceedings against Lopez, on two grounds: that his State conviction was a controlled substances violation, see 8 U. S. C. §1227 (a)(2)(B)(i), and that his aggravated felony conviction was also for a prior aggravated felony, see §1229b(a) (3). Lopez conceded the controlled substance violation but contested the aggravated felony determination, which would disqualify him from discretionary cancellation of removal. At first, the immigration Judge agreed that Lopez’ state offense should be dismissed, but after the BBIA switched it on the other side, he ruled that the drug crime was a felony after all. The BIA affirmed. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Lopez is ineligible for removal. Held: 1. Section 924 (c) (2) of the INA defines “drug trafficking crime” as “any felony punishable under the [Federal or State] Act” or, under either of two other federal statutes having no bearing on this case. Pp. 5–11. (a) The INA’S definition of “ ‘drug trafficking’” includes a drug-trafficking crime as defined in federal Title 18. Title 18 defines the word “‘‘[T]he term [‘drug]’ applies to an offense described in this paragraph whether in violation of Federal or State law’ or, in certain circumstances, “the law of a foreign country.’ ” §§1158(b)( 2)(A)(ii), 1158 (b)(2) (B) (i). And under the sentencing law, the Federal Guidelines attach special significance to the term, see, e. g., S. D. Codified Laws §§22–42–5 (2004), 22–6–1 (2005 Supp.); Tex. Health & Safety Code Ann. §481.115 (West 2003). But the term ultimately being defined is “felony punishable as such under the Act,” id., comment., n. 3. The everyday understanding of the term should count for a lot here, for the statutes in play do not define the term and so remit us to regular usage to see what Congress probably meant. FDIC v. Meyer, 510 U.S. 471, 476. But this coerced inclusion of a few possession offenses in the definition does not call for reading the statute to cover others for which there is no clear statutory command to override ordinary meaning. The Government thinks it has a good enough reason for doing just that, in the InA provision already mentioned, that §924(C) (43) “applies” “to … an offense … in this … paragraph … .” 8U.S.-C. §1101(a(43). But before this provision is given the Government's expansive treatment, it makes sense to ask whether it would have some use short of wrenching the expectations raised by normal English usage, and in fact it has two perfectly straightforward jobs to do. First, it provides that a generic description of an offense “in this paragraph” one not specifically couched as a state offense or a federal one, covers either one, and it confirms that a State offense whose elements include the elements of a felony punishable by the CSA is an aggravated. Second, the phrase confirms that the offense is a crime punishable as a CSA felony, as opposed to a federal felony. See §925(c)(1)(A). Third, the Government stresses that the text does not read “punishable as a felony.” See §844(a). Fourth, it would render the law of alien removal and sentencing for illegal entry into the country, see USSG §2L1.2, dependent on varying state criminal classifications even when Congress has apparently pegged the immigration statutes to the immigration

After respondents, a limited partnership and its general partner, sued petitioners, publishers of magazines containing articles about them, for damages arising from the publications, petitioners filed a motion for summary judgment, contending that they were protected by the qualified privilege against recovery for defamatory statements concerning matters of public concern. The District Court granted the motion, relying on New York Times Co. v. United States, 403 U. S. 713, which held that in a libel suit brought by a public figure, the plaintiff must prove actual malice with convincing clarity. On respondents' crossappeal, the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that although the plaintiffs had met the prima facie burden of proving actual malice, they had not satisfied the heightened burden of proving actual malice with convincing clarity. Held: Where the New York Times "clear and convincing" evidence requirement applies, the trial judge's summary judgment inquiry as to whether a genuine issue exists will be whether the evidence presented is such that a jury applying that evidentiary standard could reasonably find for either the plaintiff or the defendant. Pp. 355-363. (a) Summary judgment should be granted where the evidence is such that it "would require a directed verdict for the moving party." Sartor v. Arkansas Gas Corp., 321 U. S. 620, 624. Here, the inquiry involves the substantive evidentiary standard of proof that would apply at the trial on the merits. If the defendant moves for summary judgment or for a directed verdict based on the lack of proof of a material fact, the judge must ask himself not whether he thinks the evidence unmistakably favors one side or the other but whether a fair-minded jury could return a verdict for the plaintiff on the evidence presented. The mere existence of a scilila of evidence in support of the plaintiff's position will be insufficient; there must be evidence on which the jury could reasonably find for the plaintiff. Pp. 355-359. (b) Since the determination of whether a given factual dispute requires submission to a jury must be guided by the substantive evidentiary standards that apply to the case, the appropriate summary judgment question will be whether the evidence in the record could support a reasonable jury finding either that the plaintiff has shown actual malice by clear and convincing evidence or that the plaintiff has not. Pp. 359-361. (c) While the plaintiff, to survive the defendant's motion, need only present evidence from which a jury might return a verdict in his favor, if he does so, there is a genuine issue of fact that requires a trial. Pp. 361-363. 242 U. S. App. D. C.-215, 741 F. 2d 1277, vacated and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed a lower court's decision that the Navajo Nation's occupancy tax on a Grand Canyon-area hotel violated Montana's general rule that Indian tribes lack civil authority over nonmember activity on non-Indian fee land within a reservation. The court held that, with limited exceptions, the general rule does not apply to tribal attempts to tax nonmember activities on the land. The Navajo Nation enacted a hotel occupancy tax in 1992, which imposes an 8 percent tax upon any hotel room located within the exterior boundaries of the Navajo Reservation. The lower courts rejected the tribe's efforts to impose the tax on the Cameron Trading Post, which is located near the intersection of Arizona Highway 64 and United States Highway 89, which connects Flagstaff on the south with Glen Canyon Dam to the north. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate opinion, held that the tax did not violate the general general rule because the tax was imposed on a "consensual relationship" between the tribe and the nonmember guests. The Court's majority opinion, however, found that the "consensual" relationship did not exist. The majority also found that, in the absence of a general rule of law, the tax is not subject to civil jurisdiction under Montana law. The opinion concludes that, for the purposes of this case, "the general rule" does apply to the tax. We hold that it does and that neither of the Montana exceptions obtains here.

A Washington deputy prosecuting attorney prepared and filed an "Information," which charged respondent with misconduct in office, and a Motion for Arrest Warrant, which sought a warrant to arrest respondent. Both documents were unsworn. Under Washington law, an arrest warrant must be supported by either an affidavit or sworn testimony establishing the grounds for issuing the warrant. To comply with this requirement, the Information was accompanied by a Certification for Determination of Probable Cause ("certificate"), which the prosecuting attorney personally vouched for under oath. Ultimately, the charges were dropped, and the prosecuting attorney resigned. Respondent sued her under 42 U. S. C. § 1983, alleging that the certificate violated his Fourteenth Amendment due process rights. He claimed that the prosecuting attorney was not immune from liability because she acted as a complaining witness rather than a lawyer when she executed the certificate. The Federal District Court entered summary judgment for the prosecuting attorney, concluding that she was absolutely immune from liability under Imbler v. Pachtman, 424 U. S. 409. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit reversed, ruling that the prosecuting attorney was not immune from liability because she acted as a complaining witness rather than a lawyer when she executed the certificate. Held: Section 1983 provides a remedy for respondent insofar as the prosecuting attorney performed the function of a complaining witness. Pp. 12-18. (a) Absolute immunity is not grounded in any special esteem for those who perform certain functions, but because any lesser degree of immunity could impair the judicial process itself. Here, the prosecuting attorney's activities in connection with the preparation and filing of the Information and the Motion for Arrest Warrant are protected by absolute immunity. Although the prosecuting attorney's act in personally attesting to the truth of the averments in the certificate is not similarly protected, the critical question is whether she was acting as a complaining witness rather than a lawyer when she executed the certificate. Pp. 12-15. (b) Since most prosecutions in Washington begin with an unsworn Information, Washington law requires that an arrest warrant be supported by either an affidavit or sworn testimony establishing the grounds for issuing the warrant. The certificate was designed to satisfy those requirements. However, neither federal nor state law made it necessary for the prosecuting attorney to make that certification. In doing so, she performed an act that any competent witness might have performed. While the prosecuting attorney's drafting of the certificate, her determination that the evidence was sufficient to justify a probable-cause finding, her decision to file charges, and her presentation of the Information and the Motion to the court each involved the exercise of professional judgment, none of those judgments could affect the truth or falsity of the factual statements themselves. Testifying about facts is the function of the witness, not of the lawyer. Denying the prosecuting attorney absolute immunity will not harm the administration of justice. It may well be true that prosecutors in King County may abandon the practice of routinely attesting to the facts recited in a certificate and pattern their procedures after those employed in other parts of the Nation. However, there is no evidence that the administration of justice is harmed where the King County practice is not followed. Pp. 15-18. 149 F. 3d 1159, affirmed.

On March 1, 1977, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York entered a final judgment against the New York State Attorney General's Office for the District of Columbia for its alleged violations of the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, alleges that New York violated the antifraud provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 5(d) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 5b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, the Attorney General improperly used racial criteria in drafting the 1974 plan in order to justify reapportionment plans for Kings County, N.Y., and Bronx Counties.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the 1974 redistricting plan substantially increased the number of nonwhite majority districts in Kings County.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, however, this was not a sufficient basis for granting the court's order to halt the litigation.  Instead, the court found that the state violated the federal districting laws and that it had failed to adequately consider the impact of the 1974 changes on the voting strength of the Hasidic Jewish community.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the SEC in its Complaint and the Court's Order to Restart, the SEC consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins New York from violating the federal securities laws and orders it to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000,000 and a $100,000 civil penalty, and orders the state to comply with the federal court's orders.  On March 2, 2017, the United States District Court in Brooklyn entered a judgment against New York for the purpose of finding that the districting plan violated the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments.  It also ordered New York to pay civil penalties in the amounts of $2,500, $1 million in disgorgement, and $250,000 in prejudgment interest in the matter.   The court also issued an order suspending the issuance of a civil injunctive relief order against the defendants.

The United States and the Republic of Haiti entered into an agreement authorizing the Coast Guard to intercept vessels engaged in the illegal transportation of undocumented aliens to our shores. While the parties agreed to prosecute "illegal traffickers," the United States Government also guaranteed that its repatriated citizens would not be punished for their illegal departure. After interviews conducted on Coast Guard cutters, aliens who were identified as economic migrants were "screened out" and promptly repatriated. Those who made a credible showing of political refugee status were then transported to the U. S. to file formal applications for asylum. The District Court denied an application for a temporary restraining order to enjoin implementation of the Executive Order. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that § 243 (h) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 (INA) does not apply to actions taken by the President or Coast Guard on the high seas. Held: The Executive Order does not violate § 243(h)(1). Pp. 531-532. (a) The text and negotiating history of the Convention do not indicate that Congress intended to impose extraterritorial obligations on the contracting parties that are broader than the text commands. P. 533. (b) The fact that the text and the negotiating history are both completely silent with respect to the Article 33 of the United Nations Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees does not support an interpretation of the statute as applying only within United States territory. The text of the INA does not indicate any limit on the President's authority to repatriate aliens interdicted beyond the territorial seas of the States, and the language of the Act indicates that it was not intended to have any extraterritororial effect. Pp 533-534. (c) The history of Article 33 indicates that Congress used the two words "deport or return" only to make § 243's protection available in both deportation and exclusion proceedings, and that the legislative history of both the Act and the Convention indicate that it did not intend to have an extraterritual effect. Moreover, the fact that Article 33 does not include the word "return" in the Act does not mean that the statute was intended to apply only to aliens within the United S. Although the Act's text and its negotiating history do not support the interpretation of § 243, it is clear that Congress was not intending to impose an extraterriterorial obligation on those who ratify it through no more than its general humanitarian intent, and it is not persuaded that either of the provisions of the treaty or the Convention's text or the statute clearly prohibits such an intent. The legislative history supports their reading; and both the text's and the negotiation history indicate that the Act was not designed to have extraterritory effect. Thus, even if the text were not limited to strictly domestic procedures, the presumption that Acts of Congress do not ordinarily apply outside our borders would support an interpretive interpretation of Article33 to limit the Attorney General's actions in geographic areas where she has not been authorized to conduct such proceedings. P p. 534. 969 F. 2d 1350, reversed and remanded.

Respondent Mirzayance was charged with first-degree murder. His pretrial motion to compel the prosecution to comply with California’s requirement that expert testimony used to prove insanity at trial be admitted at the penalty phase of sentencing was denied. Mirzayange subsequently pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 25 years to life in prison. He later moved for postconviction relief, claiming that his counsel’s recommendation that he withdraw his insanity defense was constitutionally defective under Strickland v. Washington, 466 U. S. 668. That recommendation resulted in Mirzayange being tried twice, each time resulting in a conviction. Ultimately, the California Court of Appeal denied relief. The Federal District Court dismissed Mirzayange’s subsequent habeas petition, but the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded for an evidentiary hearing. The Magistrate Judge conducted that hearing and issued a report concluding that counsel’s performance was not deficient. However, the Magistrate Judge found that counsel’s performance was deficient under the “nothing to lose” standard, i.e., that counsel’s recommendation to drop the insanity defense was justified because there was little chance that the defense would succeed. The Ninth Circuit disagreed, reasoning that counsel’s decision was careless and impulsive. The court ultimately agreed with the Magistrate Judge that counsel’s performance was deficient, but found that the state court erred in applying the “nothing to lose” standard. Held: Mirzayange has not met his burden to show that the state court’s conclusion that there was no ineffective assistance of counsel “was contrary to, or involved an unreasonable application of, clearly established Federal law” under 28 U. S. C. §2241(d)(1). Pp. 10–18. (a) Section 2241(d)(1) bars a federal court from issuing a writ of habeas corpus “with respect to any person detained in custody pursuant to … any … State statute … unless the person to whom the writ is directed is released from such custody, or the Attorney General … files a certificate of probable cause.” The provision allows a federal court to issue a writ of habeas corpus “only if the person to whom the writ is directed is released from custody, or the Attorney General … files a certificate of probable cause.” 28 U. S. C. §§2241(d)(1), (2). Thus, a federal court may issue a writ of habeas corpus only if the state court’s ruling is either contrary to, or involves an unreasonable application of, clearly established federal law. Pp. 10–11. (b) Mirzayange has not met his burden to show that the state court’s conclusion that there was no ineffective assistance of counsel “was contrary to, or involved an unreasonable application of, clearly established Federal law.” Pp. 11–18. (1) There is no “nothing to lose” standard for determining whether counsel’s performance is deficient. Courts of appeals may not set aside a district court’s factual findings unless those findings are clearly erroneous. Here, the Ninth Circuit failed even to mention the clearly-erroneous standard, let alone apply it, before effectively overturning the lower court’s factual findings related to counsel’s behavior. In light of the Magistrate Judge’s factual findings, the state court’s rejection of Mirzayange’s ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claim was consistent with Strickland. Pp. 11–15. (2) Mirzayange has not met his burden to show that he suffered prejudice from his counsel’s performance. To prevail on his ineffective-assistance claim, he must show that there is a “reasonable probability” that he would have prevailed on his insanity defense had he pursued it. It was highly improbable that a jury, which had just rejected testimony about Mirzayange’s mental condition when the State bore the burden of proof, would have reached a different result when Mirzayange presented similar evidence at the NGI phase. Pp. 15–16. (3) Mirzayange has not met his burden to show that the state court’s conclusion that there was no ineffective assistance of counsel “was contrary to, or involved an unreasonable application of, clearly established Federal law.” In fact, he has not shown ineffective assistance at all. Pp. 16–18. 175 Fed. Appx. 142, reversed and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Alito, JJ., joined, except as to Part II. Scalia, J., filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part, in which Ginsburg, J., joined. Breyer, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter and Alito, JJ., joined.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) obtained a subpoena duces tecum upon respondent's former counsel, respondent's then-interim trustee, to compel respondent's testimony about various matters, including suspected misappropriation of customer funds by respondent's officers and employees, and other fraudulent activities. Respondent then filed a voluntary petition in bankruptcy under Subchapter IV of the Bankruptcy Code, which provides for the appointment of a receiver and for the receiver to file a petition for liquidation under Chapter 7. The District Court appointed respondent as receiver and, later, as permanent trustee. The CFTC then sought respondent's consent decree with the Commission, which provided for appointment of an interim trustee and a receiver, and for respondent's receivership. The Commission then appointed respondent, respondent Notz, Jr., as interim trustee, and the receiver filed a petition in the bankruptcy court. Respondents then sought relief from the CFTC by filing a petition to liquidate respondent's bankrupt commodity brokerage house, which was then registered with the FTC. The FTC then served the subpoena duce tecum on respondent, which sought respondent Weintraub's testimony, including allegations that respondent had misappropriated customer funds, and that he had waived "any interest I have in the attorney/client privilege possessed by that debtor for any communications or information occurring or arising on or before October 27, 1980"—the date of Notz' appointment as receiver. The Federal District Court upheld the Magistrate's order, but the District Court entered a new order requiring respondent to testify without asserting an attorney-client privilege on behalf of respondent. The Court of Appeals reversed. Held: The trustee of a corporation in bankruptcy has the power to waive the corporation's attorneyclient privilege with respect to communications that took place before the filing of the petition. Pp. 7-11. (a) The power of the trustee to assert and waive the corporations' attorney-privilege is controlled, outside of bankruptcy, by a corporation's management. The actor whose duties most closely resemble those of management should control the privilege in bankruptcy, unless such a result interferes with policies underlying the bankruptcy laws. P. 11. (b) The trustee's power to exercise the corporation-privileged privilege most closely comports with the allocation of the waiver power to management outside of the bankruptcy system without in any way obstructing the careful design of the Code. In light of the lack of direct guidance from the Code, it is clear that the trustee plays the role most closely analogous to that of a solvent corporation. Given that the debtor's directors retain virtually no management powers, it could use the privilege as a shield against the trustee's efforts to identify those assets. The Code's goal of uncovering insider fraud would be substantially defeated if the creditor's directors were to retain the one management power that might effectively thwart an investigation into their own conduct. See generally In re Browy, 527 F. 2d 799, 802 (CA7 1976) (per curiam). Respondents' other arguments are similarly unpersuasive. First, respondents' argument that giving the trustee control over the corporation privilege will have an undesirable chilling effect on the disclosure of communications relating to the planning or commission of ongoing fraud, crimes, and ordinary torts, see, e.g., Clark v. United States, 289 U. S. 1, 15, 53 S.Ct. 465, 469, and even normal succession, would be unpalatable. Second, the rule suggested by respondents-that they have no management functions at all-would frustrate an important goal of the Chapter 7 bankruptcy laws, since the Code creates numerous incentives, both for and against filing of bankruptcy petitions. Third, the legislative history establishes that Congress did not intend to give the debtor’s directors the right to assert the corporations’ attorney-pond privilege against the trustees, and thus that Congress intended that the courts deal with this problem. The legislative history also makes clear that Congress never intended to give them the right, as privileges of parties other than the corporation would still be “applicable” as to the trustee. Finally, respondents’ argument ignores the fact that if a debtor remains in possession—that is, if a trustee is not appointed—the debtor‘s directors bear essentially the same fiduciary obligation to creditors and shareholders as would the trustee for a debtor out of possession. Finally: the rule suggests by respondents—that the debtor-in-possession would have to exercise control of the corporate privilege consistently with this obligation to treat all parties, not merely the shareholders, fairly. The "subject to any applicable privilege" language is thus merely an invitation for judicial determination of privilege questions. Finally and most importantly, respondents maintain that the bankruptcy trustee can adequately investigate fraud without controlling the corporation’e privilege, since it is not shielded from disclosure by former officers and directors, whereas the debtor, in contrast, exercise virtually no such management functions. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is responsible for protecting consumers from fraudulent schemes and deceptive advertising. One common tactic used by scammers is to send unsolicited emails or text messages containing links to fake websites that purportedly offer discounts or deals on products or services. When consumers click on these links, they may be directed to a website that looks legitimate but is actually controlled by the scammer. Once on the site, consumers may be asked to enter personal information, such as credit card details, in exchange for a supposed discount or deal. However, the scammer uses this information to steal the victim's identity and commit financial crimes.

When petitioner city began filling positions in its fire department in 1996, it decided to select only those who had scored 89 or higher on a 1995 written examination. No one disputes that the conduct petitioners challenge—excluding passing applicants who scored below 89 when choosing those who would advance—occurred within the 300-day charging period prescribed by Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. However, petitioners did not file a timely EEOC charge. They sued in 2006, claiming that the city’s practice caused a disparate impact on African Americans. The District Court rejected the city’s arguments that the practice was too old to support a claim and that petitioners should have raised the issue in a previous suit. Instead, it applied the “continuing violation” doctrine, finding that the city’s ongoing use of the practice created a continuing violation of Title VII. The Seventh Circuit affirmed. Held: 1. A plaintiff establishing a prima facie disparate-impact claim under Title VII need only show that the employer “us[es] a particular employment practice that causes a disparate impact” on one of the prohibited bases, 42 U.S.C. §2000e–2(k)(1)(A)(i). Here, petitioners satisfied that requirement. Their claim challenges the city’s practice of picking only those who had scored 89 or above on the 1995 examination when it later chose applicants to advance. This exclusion caused a disparate impact. Even though the city had adopted the eligibility list embodied in the 1995 scores earlier and announced its intention to draw from that list, it made use of the practice of excluding those who scored 88 or below each time it filled a new class of firefighters. Pp. 4–6. 2. The city erroneously contends that the unlawful employment practice here was the initial decision to adopt the cutoff score and create the eligibility list, and that since no timely charge attacked that decision, it cannot be the basis for liability. While it may be true that the city’s January 1996 decision to adopt the cutoff score gave rise to a freestanding disparate-impact claim, cf. Connecticut v. Teal, 457 U. S. 440, 445–451, it does not follow that no new violation occurred—and no new claims could arise—when the city implemented that decision down the road. If petitioners could prove that the city “use[d]” the “practice” that “causes a disparate impact,” they could prevail. The city misreads United Air Lines, Inc. v. Evans, 431 U. S. 553, 558, and a line of cases following it, which hold that present effects of prior actions cannot lead to Title VII liability. These cases establish only that a Title VII plaintiff must show a “present violation” within the limitations period. Evans, supra, at 558 (emphasis deleted). What that requires depends on the claim asserted. For disparate-treatment claims—and others requiring discriminatory intent—plaintiffs must demonstrate deliberate discrimination within the limitations period. But for disparate-impact claims, no such demonstration is needed. The city also argues that, even if petitioners could have proven a present disparate-impact violation, they never did so under the proper test. Since the theory petitioners initially advanced treated the adoption and application of the cutoff score as a single, ongoing wrong, the city says, “petitioners never proved, or even attempted to prove, that use of the [eligibility] list had disparate impact,” since the theory they advanced did not require them to do so. If the Seventh Circuit determines that the argument has been preserved, it may be available on remand. But it has no bearing here. The only question presented to this Court is whether the claim petitioners brought is cognizable. Because it is, this Court’s inquiry is at an end. Pp. 6–10. 3. The city urges this Court to change the District Court’s judgment by holding that the first round of hiring firefighters occurred outside the charging period even for the earliest EEOC charge. Petitioners do not disagree, and they do not oppose the city’s request for a remand to resolve this issue. Therefore, the Seventh Circuit is left to decide, to the extent that point was properly preserved, whether the judgment must be modified in light of this Court’s decision. P. 10. 528 F. 3d 481, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New Mexico today entered final judgments against Blaze Construction Company, a Montana-based construction company, for its failure to pay Arizona's transaction privilege tax on the proceeds from contracts with the Federal Government.  The court also issued a final judgment that permanently enjoins the company from violating Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders the company to pay a civil penalty equal to the amount of its revenue.  In a parallel action, the Arizona Department of Revenue (DOR) issued a tax deficiency assessment against Blaze for failing to pay the tax.  According to the court's order, Blaze was the equivalent of a non-Indian for purposes of this case because none of its work occurred on the Blackfeet Reservation.  As a result of this finding, the federal government has retained contracting responsibility for Blaze's work.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Arizona case, Blaze agreed to settle the matter by consenting to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining it from future violations of the federal securities laws, ordering it to pay civil penalties equal to its revenue, and imposing a $10,000 civil penalty.  Blaze also agreed to be permanently enjoined from participating in any federal program that is not subject to federal law, including school construction and school construction.   The settlement is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Michael J. Burt of the Denver Regional Office, and the litigation will be led by Jennifer C. Barry.

The Supreme Court addressed whether state common-law tort actions seeking damages from a boat motor manufacturer for not including a propeller guard are pre-empted by the Federal Boat Safety Act of 1971 (FBSA) or by the Coast Guard's decision not to mandate propeller guards. The case arose from a fatal boating accident involving a motor manufactured by Mercury Marine, a division of Brunswick Corporation.

The Illinois trial court dismissed the case, and the appellate court affirmed, citing express pre-emption by the FBSA. The Illinois Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal but based it on implied pre-emption grounds. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the pre-emption issue.

The Supreme Court held that the FBSA does not expressly pre-empt state common-law claims. The Court reasoned that the language of the FBSA's pre-emption clause, which refers to "a law or regulation," does not naturally include common-law claims. The Court also pointed to the Act's saving clause, which states that compliance with the Act does not relieve a person from liability at common law or under state law, suggesting that Congress did not intend to pre-empt common-law claims.

The Court rejected the argument that the Coast Guard's decision not to regulate propeller guards implicitly pre-empts state common-law claims. The Court found that the Coast Guard's decision not to require propeller guards did not convey a policy against such guards and did not conflict with state common-law claims.

Finally, the Court concluded that the FBSA's statutory scheme does not occupy the field of recreational boat safety so completely as to preclude state common-law remedies. The Court emphasized that the Act does not require the Coast Guard to regulate every aspect of boat safety and design and that the Act's structure does not show a clear intent to pre-empt state common law.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Illinois Supreme Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, allowing the state common-law tort claims to proceed.

The Supreme Court considered whether an accused person could invoke the privilege against adverse spousal testimony to prevent their spouse from voluntarily testifying against them. This issue required revisiting the precedent set in Hawkins v. United States (1958), which allowed an accused to bar adverse testimony from their spouse unless both consented.

The case in question involved Otis Trammel, who was indicted for drug-related charges and whose wife, Elizabeth Trammel, was prepared to testify against him under a grant of immunity. Otis Trammel sought to prevent her testimony, claiming spousal privilege. The District Court allowed her to testify about acts she observed and communications made in the presence of a third person, but not confidential communications. Otis Trammel was convicted, and the Court of Appeals upheld the decision, rejecting his claim of privilege.

The Supreme Court acknowledged the historical roots of the privilege against adverse spousal testimony, which originated from the idea that a wife could not testify against her husband due to their legal unity and the husband's interest in the proceeding. However, the Court noted that the rationale for this rule has long been abandoned, and the modern justification for the privilege is to foster marital harmony.

The Court recognized that the Federal Rules of Evidence allow for the evolution of testimonial privileges based on "reason and experience." It observed that many jurisdictions have moved away from the privilege that allows an accused to prevent adverse spousal testimony, and scholarly criticism has continued.

The Court emphasized that testimonial privileges must be strictly construed and that the privilege against adverse spousal testimony must be weighed against the need for evidence in criminal justice. The Court found that the privilege is not necessary to protect private marital communications, which are already protected under a separate privilege.

The Court concluded that the privilege against adverse spousal testimony is outdated and does not serve its intended purpose of preserving marital harmony when one spouse is willing to testify against the other. The Court decided to modify the rule, granting the privilege to the witness-spouse alone, who may choose to testify or not, without being compelled or prevented by the accused.

The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' decisions, allowing Elizabeth Trammel's testimony against her husband, Otis Trammel, as she chose to testify voluntarily after receiving immunity and assurances of lenient treatment.

The Supreme Court addressed the issue of when the one-year limitation period for a federal prisoner to seek postconviction relief under 28 U.S.C. § 2255 begins. Specifically, the Court considered whether the period starts when the appellate court issues its mandate affirming the conviction or when the time to file a petition for certiorari to the Supreme Court expires.

The Court held that the one-year limitation period begins when the time for filing a petition for certiorari expires, not when the appellate court's mandate is issued. This decision is in line with the Court's consistent interpretation of finality in the context of collateral review and resolves a split among lower courts.

The case involved Erick Cornell Clay, who was convicted in 1997 and whose conviction was affirmed by the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals in 1998. Clay did not seek certiorari, and the time to do so expired in February 1999. He filed his § 2255 motion exactly one year after the certiorari petition deadline, which the District Court and the Seventh Circuit deemed untimely based on their interpretation that finality occurred upon the issuance of the appellate court's mandate.

The Supreme Court reversed the Seventh Circuit's judgment, stating that the relevant context is postconviction relief, where finality is understood to occur when the Supreme Court affirms a conviction on direct review, denies a writ of certiorari, or when the time for filing a certiorari petition expires. The Court rejected the argument that the wording differences between § 2255 and a parallel provision for state prisoners (§ 2244(d)(1)) required a different interpretation of finality.

The Court's decision ensures that federal prisoners have a clear and uniform starting point for the one-year limitation period for seeking postconviction relief, which is when the time for seeking review by the Supreme Court expires if no certiorari petition is filed. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

After the Indian Land Consolidation Act of 1983 (Act) was enacted, respondents' father, an enrolled member of two Indian tribes, died testate, leaving several undivided interests in allotted trust lands to respondents, each interest being devised to a single descendant. Under the Act's "escheat" provision, such interests would escheat to the tribes unless inherited pursuant to a valid will. When respondents challenged the constitutionality of the escheat provision after their father's death, an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) ruled that the interests devised to each respondent fell within the scope of the provision and should escheat to the tribes. The Board of Indian Appeals dismissed respondents' appeal, finding itself without jurisdiction to consider their constitutional claim. They then sued the Secretary of the Interior in Federal District Court, claiming that the escheat provision violated the Just Compensation Clause of the Fifth Amendment. The District Court agreed and entered declaratory and injunctive relief. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, concluding that the escheat provision did not cure the defects that rendered its predecessor unconstitutional in Hodel v. Irving, 481 U. S. 404. It reasoned that the escheat provision remains an extraordinary and impermissible regulation of Indian lands and effects an uncompensated taking. Held: The escheat provision remains constitutionally flawed despite the changes wrought by the 1984 amendments. Although the amendments look back five years instead of one to determine the income produced from a small interest, create a rebuttable presumption that this income stream will continue, permit devise of otherwise escheatable interests to persons who already own an interest in the same parcel, and authorize tribes to develop their own codes governing the disposition of fractional interests, none of these modifications warrants a disposition different from the one this Court announced and explained in Irving. Even if the economic impact of the amended provision is not significantly less than that of the original, the "extraordinary" character of the governmental regulation rests primarily on the fact that the original provision virtually abolished the right to pass on a certain type of property-small undivided interests-to one's heirs. Creation of an ever-so-slight class of individuals equipped to receive fractional interests by devise does not suffice to rehabilitate the measure. More importantly, although giving effect to the father's directives would not further fractionate Indian landholdings, allowing a decedent to leave an interest only to a current owner in the same parcel shrinks drastically the universe of possible successors. Furthermore, the very limited group of permissible devisees is unlikely to contain any lineal descendants. Also unpersuasive are the Government's contentions that the amended provision satisfies the Constitution's demands because it does not diminish the owner's right to use or enjoy property during his lifetime, and does not affect the right to transfer property at death through nonprobate means. Nor does the new provision permitting tribes to adopt their own codes satisfy the Constitution since tribal codes governing disposition of escheatable interests have apparently not yet been developed. Pp. 108-112. 67 F. 3d 194, affirmed.

After petitioners opened a new store called "Victor's Little Secret," respondents, owners of the famous trademark Victoria's Secret, sued them for dilution of their mark under the Federal Trade Commission Act's amendment in 1995, now codified in 15 U. S. C. § 1125(c)(1), which allows recovery against a party whose commercial use of a mark or trade name causes dilution of a famous mark's distinctive quality. Section 1125(c)(1)'s text unambiguously requires a showing of actual dilution, rather than a likelihood of dilution. However, the District Court enjoined petitioners from using the name "Victor's Little Secret" on the basis that it caused dilution of the Victoria's Secret mark because of its tarnishing effect upon the mark. The Sixth Circuit affirmed, relying on a distinction suggested by the House Report accompanying the 1995 amendment, and rejecting the Fourth Circuit's contrary ruling in Ringling Bros.-Barnum & Bailey Combined Shows, Inc. v. Utah Div. of Travel Dev., 170 F. 3d 449, 461. Held: Objective proof of actual dilution of a famous mark's economic value is required for relief under § 1125(c)(1). Pp. 3-11. (a) Unlike traditional trademark infringement law, which protects consumers from being misled by the use of infringing marks and also protects producers from imitating competitors, the prohibitions against trademark dilution are not the product of common-law development, and are not motivated by an interest in protecting consumers. Rather, the seminal discussion of dilution is found in Frank Schechter's 1927 law review article concluding that the preservation of a trademark's uniqueness should constitute the only rational basis for its protection. Some 20 years later, Massachusetts became the first State to adopt a statute prohibiting both the likelihood of "injury to business reputation" and "dilution" of a trademark. Notably, that statute, unlike the "Odol" case cited in Schechter, prohibited both the likelihood of "injury to business reputation" and "dilution." Thus, at least 25 States passed similar laws in the decades before the 1995 amendment was enacted. Pp. 3-5. (b) Although the legislative history indicates that Congress considered an exception permitting fair use of a registered mark in comparative advertising or promotion, and providing that noncommercial use of a mark shall not constitute dilution, these exceptions cannot be read into the statute here. Nor is there any merit to petitioners' contention that the statutory protection is limited to identical uses of famous marks, since the statutory text clearly applies to dilution of the distinctive quality of a mark, and the legislative history does not indicate that Congress meant to limit the scope of the statute to identical uses. Pp. 5-7. (c) While the contrast between the state statutes, which expressly refer to both "injury to business reputation" and to "dilution of the distinctive quality of a trade name or trademark," and the federal statute, which refers only to the latter, argues for a narrower reading of the FTDA, the contrast between the initial reference to an actual "lessening of the capacity" of a mark, and the later reference to a "likelihood of confusion, mistake, or deception" in the second caveat confirms the conclusion that actual dilution must be established. The mere fact that consumers mentally associate the junior user's mark with a famous mark is not sufficient to establish actionable dilution. Here, although the record establishes that an army officer who saw the advertisement of the opening of a store named "Victor's Secret" did make the mental association with "Victoria's Secret," it also shows that he did not therefore form any different impression of the store that his wife and daughter had patronized.
