According to the SEC's order, filed in the District Court in Wyoming, Wyoming violated a federal law requiring that each county have at least one representative, and that the allocation of a representative to each of those counties should be based on the principle of population equality.  In addition, the court held that Wyoming's policy of preserving county boundaries was reasonable and reasonable.  For example, under the Wyoming statute, one representative is required to be allocated to a county the population of which is less than half of the ideal district of 7,337.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Wyoming consented to the entry of a final judgement that permanently enjoins Wyoming from violating the federal law and orders the state to provide for a separate representative to Niobrara County, Wyoming, for the purpose of providing for a fair and effective representation of the people of Wyoming.   The court also granted Wyoming's request for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an accounting of the amount of money spent on the settlement. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Reynolds and supervised by Scott A. Thompson of the Denver Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Carl Edwin Wiggins, Jr., a recidivist convicted of a felony and sentenced to life imprisonment as a "standby counsel."  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, Wiggins, who was previously convicted of robbery and sentenced in a parallel criminal case, requested that counsel be present to assist him in his defense.  The complaint alleges that, in the course of the trial, Wiggins raised the issue of whether counsel should be allowed to participate in the presentation of a defense, and whether he should be permitted to do so in the presence of the jury.  As alleged in the complaint, Wiggins' request for counsel was met with a barrage of unsolicited, aggressive, and unsolicited comments from counsel.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against Wiggins, charging him with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations, Wiggins consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  Wiggins also agreed to be barred from appearing before the court as a defendant in the status of a pro se defendant, and to be restrained from participating in the prosecution's defense.

Appellee was convicted of murder in a Georgia state court and his conviction was sustained by the Georgia Supreme Court. Subsequently, he sought relief in Federal District Court under 28 U. S. C. § 2254, claiming that his conviction violated his right of confrontation under the Sixth Amendment as made applicable to the states by the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court denied relief, but the Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the Georgia rule allowing the introduction of a coconspirator's out-of-court statement during the "concealment phase" of the conspiracy violated the Confrontation Clause. Held: 1. The Georgia rule does not contravene the Confrontation Clause. Pp. 408-416. (a) Though the federal hearsay exception applicable to conspiracy trials in the federal courts permits the introduction of an out-of-court statement of a coconspirator only if the statement was made in the course of and in furtherance of the conspiracy, the Georgia rule permitting such introduction applies regardless of when the statement was made. Pp. 408-411. (b) Merely because the Georgia rule does not precisely track the federal hearsay exception does not mean that it violates the Confrontation Clause. Pp. 411-413. (c) Nor does the Georgia rule violate the Confrontation Clause as made applicable to the states by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 413-414. 2. On the record in this case, the Georgia rule did not deny appellee the right of confrontation. Pp. 414-416. 409 F. 2d 117, reversed and remanded.

In 1995, the City of Chicago administered a written examination to over 26,000 applicants seeking to serve in the Chicago Fire Department. After scoring the examinations, the city announced that it would begin drawing randomly from the top tier of scorers, i. e., those who scored 89 or above on the 1995 examination. Those who scored between 65 and 88 were notified that they had passed the examination but that, based on the City’s projected hiring needs and the number of “well qualified” applicants, it was not likely they would be called for further processing. Five others followed suit, and the EEOC issued all six of them right-to-sue letters. Two months later, they filed this civil action against the City, alleging (as relevant here) that its practice of selecting for advancement only applicants who scored 90 or above caused a disparate impact on African-Americans in violation of Title VII. The District Court certified a class-petitioners here-consisting of the more than 6,000 African-American applicants who had not been hired. The City sought summary judgment on the ground that petitioners had failed to file EEOC charges within 300 days after their claims accrued. The Court of Appeals denied the motion, concluding that the City had “ongoing reliance” on the test results constituted a “continuing violation of” Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The Seventh Circuit reversed, holding that the city had violated §2000e–5(e)(1). Held: 1. A plaintiff who does not file a timely charge challenging the adoption of a practice—here, an employer's decision to exclude employment applicants who did not achieve a certain score on an examination—may assert a disparate-impact claim in a timely charging challenging the employer’’re later application of that practice. Pp. 5–11. (a) The District Courts’ determination that the practice was “unlawful employment practice based on disparate impact” does not require a determination of whether a claim predicated on that conduct is timely, but whether the practice thus defined can be the basis for a disparateimpact claim at all. The real question, then, is not whether such a claim is timely but whether it is coextensive. If the effect of applying Title VII is that some claims that would be doomed under one theory will survive under the other, that is the product of the law Congress has written. It is not for us to rewrite the statute so that it covers only what we think is necessary to achieve what Congress really intended. See Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services, Inc., 523 U. S. 75, 79–80. The only actionable discrimination, it argues, occurred in 1996 when it “used the examination results to create the hiring eligibility list, limited hiring to the ‘well qualified,’ classification, and notified petitioners.” Brief for Respondent 23. That initial decision, it concedes, was unlawful. But because no timely charge challenged the decision, that cannot now be a basis for liability. And because, the District Court claims, the exclusion of petitioners when selecting classes of firefighters followed inevitably from the earlier decision to adopt the cutoff score, no new violations could have occurred. The Sixth Circuit adopted the same analysis. See 528 F. 3d, at 490–491. Petitioners’ claim satisfies that requirement. Title VII does not define “employment practice,” but it is clear that the term encompasses the conduct of which petitioners complain. The exclusion of passing applicants who score below 89 (until the date of the first round of selection in May 1996) gave rise to a freestanding disparate impact claim, United Air Lines, Inc. v. Evans, 431 U.S. 553, 558. But it does not follow that no new violation occurred-and no new claims could arise-when the City implemented that decision down the road. If petitioners could prove that the “practice” that “causes a disparate Impact” is a single, ongoing wrong, they could prevail. The case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Respondent International Brotherhood of Teamsters (IBT), which had advised Local throughout the CBA negotiations and whose leadership and members supported the June 2004 strike, opposed Local’s decision to return to work without a back-to-work agreement shielding both Local and IBT members from liability for strike-related damages. In an effort to secure such an agreement, IBT instructed Local to continue the work stoppage until Granite Rock agreed to hold Local and iBT members harmless for damages incurred during the strike. Local responded by announcing a companywide strike that involved numerous facilities and hundreds of workers, including members of IBT locals besides Local 287. The District Court entered the verdict and ordered the parties to proceed with arbitration on the breach-of-contract claims. The Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part, concluding that the date of the ratification was a matter for judicial resolution. Held: 1. The parties’ dispute over the ratification date was for the District Court, not an arbitrator, to decide. Pp. 5–7. (a) The Court has applied the presumption favoring arbitration, in FAA and labor cases, only where it reflects, and derives its legitimacy from, a judicial conclusion that arbitration of a particular dispute is what the parties intended because their express agreement to arbitrate was validly formed and (absent a provision clearly and validly committing such issues to arbitrator) is legally enforceable and best construed to encompass the dispute. See First Options, 514 U. S. 943; AT&T Technologies, Inc. v. Communications Workers, Inc., 473 U.S. 614, 626. This Court has recognized a federal common-law claim for breach of a CBA under LMRA §301(a), because at least in cases governed by the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) §1 et seq., courts must treat the arbitration clause as severable from the contract in which it appears, and thus apply the clause to all disputes within its scope “ ‘[u]nless the [validity] challenge is to the arbitration clauses itself’ ” or the party “disputes the formation of [the] contract,” 546 F. 3d 1169, and “any doubts concerning the scope of arbitral issues should be resolved in favor of arbitration.” Howsam v. Dean Witter Reynolds, II., 537 U. s. 79, 83. The question before this Court is a narrow one. It is not whether the conduct here is remediable, but whether the parties should augment the claims already available to GraniteRock by creating a new federal commonlaw cause of action under §301 (a). This simple framework compels reversal of the Court of appeals’ judgment because it requires judicial resolution of two questions central to the Local arbitration demand. First, the parties agree that their arbitration clause pertains only to disputes that “arise under” the agreement. Second, the fact that Local raised the formation date dispute as a defense to the claim does not make that dispute attributable to the parties in the waiver or estoppel sense the Court suggested. See, e.g., id., at 434–437. Local contends that the District court erred in holding that it was not necessary for the district court to determine whether the arbitration date was an issue for the court to decide, and that the parties consented to arbitration by suing under the contract. The court did not rule on the merits of this claim, and the parties need not do so either. See Brief for Respondent IBT, supra, at 14–19. The second principle the Court invoked is that this presumption of arbitrability applies even to disputes about the enforceability of the entire contract containing the Arbitration Clause, because it relates to Local‘s arbitration demand in such a way that it is not the only possible remedy for this conduct. See: 1–3. The dispute here, whether labeled a formation dispute or not, falls outside the scope and scope of the parties‘ arbitration clause on grounds the presumption of arbitration cannot cure. The CBA contains the parties' arbitration clause, and therefore “is a way to resolve those disputes-but only those disputes—that the parties have agreed to submit to arbitration,’” First Options and the “Federal Policy favoring Arbitration” (“Policy favoring arbitration”) reflect its foundation in “the federal policy favoring arbitration . . .” Lewis v. Benedict Coal Corp., 361 U . S. 459, 470. This rule is the foundation for the arbitrarability framework this Court announced in the Steelworkers Trilogy for deciding arbitrable disputes in LMRA cases. See also Mastrobuono v. Shearson Lehman Hutton, Inc.'s Cardegna, 546 U. .S. 440, 444, n. 1. Where a party contests either or both matters, the court must resolve the disagreement.

Petitioner, a "statutory producer" of gasoline, had a license to distribute gasoline in Mississippi, which he obtained from out-ofstate suppliers. Under Mississippi law, the supplier pays the federal excise tax on the gasoline, and the distributor pays the state excise tax. Both taxes attach to the first sale of the gasoline in the State. Petitioner adds the federal and state excise taxes to the purchase price of the gasoline, thus shifting the economic burden of the taxes to consumers. Petitioner challenged the validity of the state statute requiring the inclusion of the federal and state excise taxes in the calculation of his "gross proceeds of retail sales," claiming that the taxes were levied on the ultimate consumer and hence were not applicable to him. The Mississippi Supreme Court upheld the statute, ruling that the federal excise tax is imposed solely on producers such as petitioner and not on the purchaser. Held: 1. The legal incidence of the federal excise tax is on petitioner, not on the purchaser. Pp. 408-413. (a) Since the purchaser-consumer who buys gasoline for use on his farm, 26 U. S. C. §§ 6420 (a), 6421 (a), or for a local transit system, § 6421 (b), can recover payment of all or part of the amount of the federal excise tax passed on by the "producer," the tax is not imposed on the purchaser-consumer. Pp. 409-410. (b) References by President Johnson to the tax as a "user tax" do not prove that it was not intended to be imposed on the "producer." Such references were rejected by the Illinois Supreme Court as irrelevant to the question whether the tax must be considered as one whose incidence rests on the purchaser-consumer. Martin Oil Service, Inc. v. Dept. of Revenue, 49 Ill. 2d 260, 273 N. E. 2d 823, followed. Pp. 410-411. (c) When a state court has made its own definitive determination as to the operating incidence of a state excise tax, this Court gives that finding great weight in determining the natural effect of the statute, and if it is consistent with the statute's reasonable interpretation it will be deemed conclusive. Here, the Mississippi Supreme Court's holding that the legal incidence of the state excise tax fell on petitioner should be deemed conclusive. Pp. 411-412. (d) Panhandle Oil Co. v. Mississippi, 277 U. S. 218, distinguished. Pp. 412-413. 2. Even assuming that the legal incidence of the federal excise tax is on petitioner, the provision of the Mississippi statute denying the deduction of the taxes in the computation of petitioner's "gross proceeds of retail sales" is not invalid. Pp. 413-415. (a) Assuming that the liability for the federal excise tax and the liability for the state sales tax arise simultaneously, they are not mutually exclusive. There is no legal distinction, constitutional or otherwise, resulting from that circumstance. Pp. 413-414. (b) The prohibition of the Equal Protection Clause is against denial by the State, here Mississippi, as between taxpayers subject to its laws. Petitioner makes no claim of unconstitutional discrimination by Mississippi in the application of its sales tax act to taxpayers subject to that tax. P. 415. Affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Alabama today entered a final judgment in favor of the six maritime unions in an action brought by the United States Attorney's Office for the Central District of Florida.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Mobile, Alabama, alleges that, in 1971, American shipowners and longshoremen participated in a nationwide picketing to publicize the adverse impact on American seamen of the operations of foreign-flag carriers that employ American crewmen at wages substantially below those paid to them.  According to the complaint, the picketing took place on the dock adjacent to the Aqua Glory, a ship of Liberian origin, and was conducted in the manner of a secondary boycott. The complaint alleges that the pickets were for all practical purposes identical, that they were for purposes of preventing secondary boycotts, and that the Board had jurisdiction over the matter.  In its judgment, the court held that the actions in Mobile violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the SEC's action, the defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, orders them to pay disgorgement of $1,078, and orders them each to pay a civil penalty of $100,000, and bars them from serving as officers or directors of a public company.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York ruled in 1983 that Hercules Inc. and Wm. T. Thompson Co. were not liable for the health effects of exposure to dioxin caused by the herbicide Agent Orange used by the United States military during the Vietnam War. The case was transferred to the Claims Court, which ruled in favor of the Government's motion for summary judgment. The Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit affirmed the decision, holding that the Government was not liable because it did not provide any implied warranty of the manufacturer's performance of the contract. The court also rejected Thompson's claim of contractual indemnification, which the court held would have barred the imposition of liability for which the Government is not responsible. Hercules and Thompson then sued the Government under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) and the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) for the costs of defending and settling the cases. The U,S. Court of Justices held that the UCC provides no protection against liability for the Government. The FTCA provides for the protection of contractors from liability for products manufactured for the government. The Supreme Court has held that there is no such protection. The Federal Circuit held that, in this case, the Government has no obligation to pay the Petitioners' costs.

Appellant, a college student, displayed a United States flag out of his window on private property in Seattle, Washington. The flag was upside down, and attached to both surfaces was a peace symbol (i.e., a circle enclosing a trident) made of removable black tape. The window was above the ground floor. Appellant was convicted under a Washington statute forbidding the exhibition of a flag to which is attached or superimposed figures, symbols, or other extraneous material. The Washington Supreme Court affirmed. Held: The statute impermissibly infringed protected expression under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 788-788. 81 Wash. 2d 788, 506 P.2d 293, reversed.

Respondent, a 15-year veteran of the District of Columbia Metropolitan Police Department, was convicted in Federal District Court of the possession and facilitation of concealment of heroin in violation of 26 U. S. C. § 4704(a) (1964 ed.), and 21 U.S.C. § 174 (1964). He was sentenced to concurrent terms of imprisonment for these offenses. On his appeal to the Court of Appeals, that court first remanded the case to the District Court for an evidentiary hearing concerning the scope of the search of respondent's person which had occurred at the time of his arrest. At that point, respondent informed respondent that he was under arrest for "operating after revocation and obtaining a permit by misrepresentation." Respondent testified that at this point he still did not know what was in the package, and that at that point he knew they were cigarettes. Respondent then opened the cigarette pack and found 14 gelatin capsules of white powder which he thought to be, and which later analysis proved to be heroin. The heroin seized from respondent was admitted into evidence at the trial which resulted in his conviction. Held: 1. The validity of a search incident to a lawful arrest has been regarded as settled from its first enunciation, and has remained virtually unchallenged until the present case. Pp. 531-532. (a) A police officer's determination as to how and where to search the person of a suspect whom he has arrested is necessarily a quick ad hoc judgment which the Fourth Amendment does not require to be broken down in each instance into an analysis of each step in the search. P. 532. 2. In the case of a lawful custodial arrest, a full search of the person is not only an exception to the warrant requirement of the Fourth amendment, but is also a "reasonable" search under that Amendment. Such a search is not a "frisk" incident to an investigative stop based on less than probable cause to arrest, since the search partook of none of the extreme or patently abusive characteristics which were held to violate the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment in Rochin v. California, 342 US. 165, and it is of no moment that Jenks did not indicate any subjective fear of the respondent or that he did not himself suspect that respondent was armed. Terry v. United States, ante, p. 533. The justification or reason for the authority to search in this case rests quite as much on the need to disarm the suspect in order to take him into custody as it does on a need to preserve evidence on his person for later use at trial. P p. 560. (b) The search, while permissible under established Fourth Amendment law, was not limited to that which is necessary for the discovery of weapons which might be used to harm the officer or others nearby, and may realistically be characterized as something less than a "full" search, even though it remains a serious intrusion on the privacy of the arrestee's person, and the interests each is designed to serve are likewise quite different from those of the police officer. The search was lawful when grounds for arrest and accusation have been discovered, and a search for weapons in the absence of probable cause, must, like any other search, be strictly circumscribed by the exigencies which justify its initiation. Warden v. Hayden, 387 U. s. 699, 699. Thus, it must be limited to those which are necessary for discovery of weapon or fruits which might potentially be used in a search upon less-custody arrest, and to seize and hold them until the prisoner should be discharged, or until they could be otherwise properly disposed of. Such searches also meet Fourth Amendment's requirement of reasonableness, and such searches also constitute a valid arrest under that amendment, P. 540. (c) There is no merit to the contention that there must be litigated in each case the issue of whether or not there was present one of the reasons supporting the authority for a search of a person incident to lawful arrest. The fact of the lawful arrest, while based upon the need of disarm and to discover evidence, does not depend on what a court may later decide was the probability in a particular arrest situation that weapons or evidence would in fact be found upon the suspect of the suspect, and this is an adequate basis for treating all custodial arrests alike for purposes of search justification. The Fourth Amendment, as well as the interest of the State in the person charged being brought to trial in due course necessarily extends as well to the preservation of material evidence of his guilt or innocence, as to his custody for the purpose of trial. Under the circumstances surrounding Williams' possession of the gun seized by Sgt. Connolly, the arrest on the weapons charge was supported by probable cause; and the search was reasonably limited in scope by these purposes. Moreover, it was reasonable to search, and officer Lasky did not engage in an unrestrained and thorough-going examination of Peters and his personal effects." Id., at

After the city refused to promote petitioners, two police officers, despite their excellent performance evaluations, petitioners sued respondents, members of the Board of Alderman, alleging that they were nonexempt employees who should receive overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standard Agreement Act (FLSA). Section 3(m) of the FLSA defines bona fide executive, administrative, or professional employees as those who perform duties relating to management functions, including supervision, setting priorities, and appraising performance, and who are compensated on a salary basis, i. e., receive fixed annual payments that are not subject to significant fluctuations based on the number of hours worked. Regulations implementing § 3(m) define the "salary basis" requirement as applying to employees who "regularly ... earn[] a wage equivalent to at least $30 per week." 29 CFR § 541.118(a)(1). To qualify for this "wage equivalent," employees must be paid a certain minimum hourly rate plus additional amounts equal to twice the difference between that rate and the prevailing minimum wage, minus the product of the difference times the average hours worked per year. Thus, an employee earning $30 per hour would need to earn another $6 per hour ($30-$15) plus an additional $12 per month ($6 x 4 weeks) to satisfy the "salary basis" requirement. Petitioners alleged that they received a lump sum bonus instead of regular bonuses and that the Police Department Manual listed various types of disciplinary actions, including a deduction in pay, which could affect their wages. One officer admitted receiving a deduction after violating a residency rule, while the other never received any deduction. Although the District Court ruled in favor of petitioners, the Court of Appeals concluded that neither officer qualified for the "salary basis" requirement because the Manual included a list of potential deductions and allowed for discretionary changes in pay. 

Held: 
1. Neither the salary-basis nor the duty tests used by the Court of Appeals provides a sufficient foundation for concluding that petitioners were not exempt. Pp. 119-122.
	 (a) The salary-basis test is a reasonable way to implement the statutory purpose of providing protection for white collar workers. Pp. 119-120.
	 (b) Whether an employee qualifies for the "salary basis" requirement depends on how closely tied his compensation is to the managerial function of performing duties like those described in § 3(m). He is not required to prove that he performs these duties exclusively, just that he performs them sufficiently often. And although a few minor errors occurred in calculating the amount due petitioners, the evidence supports the conclusion that they were properly classified as exempt. Pp. 120-122. 
2. The Secretary of Labor\'s "salary basis" definition satisfies the standards for reasonable interpretation. Pp. 122-126.
	 (a) The salary-basis test is a creature of the Secretary\'s own regulations, and his interpretation controls absent error. Here, the key words "subject to" comfortably bear the meaning assigned by the Secretary. Even assuming that petitioners\' compensation is potentially susceptible to being reduced through disciplinary deductions, the Manual does not effectively communicate that deductions are an expected form of punishment for employees in petitioners\' category. Moreover, the fact that the Manual covers all employees and mentions disciplinary deductions does not establish a likelihood that such deductions will occur to employees such as petitioners. Pp. 122-125.
	 (b) The Secretary\'s interpretation is supported by his experience and expertise, and it comports with the legislative history of the FLSA. Its adoption by the Courts below is therefore entitled to deference. Pp. 125-126. 
3. The Court of Appeals erred in finding that the initial condition of the Secretary\'s correction provision-that the employer show that the deductiohs were inadvertent-was not satisfied because the deduction to Officer Guzy was not inadvertent. Instead, the relevant conditions are "inadverten[ce]" and "made for reasons other than lack of work," and the Court of Appeals erred again in suggesting that the correction provision is unavailable because Guzy has not been reimbursed for the residency-based deduction. Reimbursement need not be made immediately upon the discovery that an improper deduction was made. Pp. 126-127. Affirmed.

Title: United States Olympic Committee v. Gay Olympic Games, Inc.

Year: 1986

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the Amateur Sports Act of 1978, which granted the United States Olympic Committee (USOC) exclusive rights to use the Olympic brand and related terms. The Court ruled that the USOC's enforcement of these rights was not discriminatory, despite allegations that it targeted LGBTQ+ organizations like the Gay Olympic Games, Inc. The Court based its decision on the idea that the USOC's actions were not those of the government, and that the federal government had not engaged in discrimination.

A Federal Agent who had been informed by another person that a certain individual was importing narcotics into Denver and distributing them there was watching the arrival of trains from Chicago. When he saw a passenger arriving on a train from Chicago whom he believed to be the same individual, he followed him off the train and arrested him. Shortly thereafter, the arrested man was searched and two envelopes containing heroin and a hypodermic syringe were found on his person. Held: In these circumstances, the arrest was lawful, the search and seizure were valid, and the evidence was competent. Pp. 48-53. (a) Information obtained from an informant may be hearsay, but it need not necessarily be excluded from consideration in determining whether there was probable cause for arrest. Brinegar v. United States, 338 U. S. 160. Pp. 50-51. (b) Coming from one employed for that purpose and whose information had always been found accurate and reliable, the information given to the Agent by the informant was clearly not hearsay to the Agent. P. 51. (c) With every other bit of the informant's information being thus personally verified by the Agent, he had "reasonable grounds" to believe that the remaining unverified bit -i. e., that the arrested man had the heroin with him--was also true. Pp. 51-52. (d) Under the facts and circumstances here, the Agent had probable cause and reasonable grounds to believe that the arrested man was committing a violation of the narcotic laws at the time he arrested him. P. 52. (e) Since the arrest was lawful, the subsequent search and seizure, having been made incident to that lawful arrest, were likewise valid. P. 52. (f) Petitioner's motion to suppress was properly denied, and the seized heroin was competent evidence lawfully received at the trial. P. 53. 248 F. 2d 295, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Kentucky has ruled that Kentucky's special retirement plan for state and county employees does not discriminate against those who are disabled and are not yet eligible for normal retirement benefits. The court found that the plan does not apply to those who become seriously disabled but have not otherwise become eligible for retirement and who have worked for five years or more in the line of duty. The EEOC had alleged that, under the plan, the disabled employee would have had to continue working in order to be eligible for a certain minimum amount of retirement benefits, and that the Plan did not impute any additional years of service for purposes of the calculation. The district court held that, based on the facts of the case, the Plan does not violate the federal anti-age discrimination provisions of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) and the Kentucky Constitution's Section 10(b)(1) and (2). The Court also found that, in the absence of a finding of age discrimination, the plan's benefit calculations are not based on a preponderance of the evidence. The District Court's decision is a victory for the state of Kentucky and for the special plan.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Washington sentenced a convicted felon to 10 years in prison for possession of a firearm in violation of the Armed Career Criminal Act of 2000 (ACCA) for three drug-trafficking convictions in Washington state. The district court's decision was based on the fact that the three Washington drug convictions occurred on the same day but were based on deliveries that took place on three separate dates. The District Court agreed with the government's argument that these three convictions were not for serious drug offenses, but the District Court held that the district court should have determined the maximum term of imprisonment based on those three convictions. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that this decision conflicted with its prior precedent in United States v. Corona-Sanchez, which held that a person convicted of a second or subsequent offense could be imprisoned for a term up to twice the term otherwise authorized. The Ninth Circuit also held that there was no need to determine the maximum sentence based on these convictions because they were not "serious drug offenses" for the purposes of the ACCA. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate opinion, held that it was not necessary to determine a maximum sentence for a serious drug offense based on a person's prior convictions, and that the federal sentencing guidelines did not apply. The United States appeals court reversed, holding that the lower court had properly determined the sentence. The appeals court also found that the sentencing guidelines were not in conflict with the federal guidelines. The court concluded that the 10-year sentence imposed on the three drug convictions did not constitute a "serious" drug offense. The case is now remanded for further consideration.

1. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits the application of state laws in a way that would deprive any person of the rights granted under the Act. P. 596. 2. The convictions of petitioners, who are Negroes, for participating in "sit-in" demonstrations in the luncheon facilities of retail stores in their respective States, are abated by the passage of the Act, which prohibits discrimination in places of public accommodation and removes peaceful attempts to be served on an equal basis from the category of punishable activities. Held: The convictions must be vacated and the prosecutions dismissed. Pp. 598-599. 3. The Act does not require that the convictions be vacated or the charges are dismissed, and the judgment in each case is therefore vacated and dismissed.

After respondents brought suit alleging that petitioner company, Hughes, had violated the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) by amending its defined benefit pension plan to permit participation by employees who previously participated in a separate defined contribution plan, the Federal District Court entered summary judgment for Hughes. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit affirmed, concluding that the amendment resulted in the termination of the defined benefit plan and the creation of two separate plans. Held: Hughes did not violate ERISA by amending its defined benefit plan. Pp. 10-18. (a) Respondents' argument that the amendment violated ERISA's vesting requirements by using assets from the surplus attributable to the employees' contributions to fund the noncontributory structure is meritless. An employee's minimum accrued benefit is assumed unless limited to a certain percentage of benefits depending on the employee's years of service. Here, Hughes never deprived respondents of their accrued benefits, and indeed allowed them to switch into the new structure. Moreover, the amendment did not allow Hughes to use assets from the surplus attributable to employer and employee contributions for its own benefit, in violation of ERISA's antienrichment provision. The amendment focused exclusively on adding the noncontributory structure to the plan, and Hughes continued to satisfy its continuing obligation under ERISA to assure that the plan was adequately funded. Pp. 10-13. (b) Each of respondents' fiduciary duty claims must fail because ERISA's fiduciary provisions are inapplicable to the amendments. Amending a plan does not constitute an exercise of fiduciary duty. Without exception, "[pla[n] sponsor[s]...who alter the terms of a plan ...do not fall into the category of fidelity." Lockheed Martin Corp. v. Hawkins, 517 U. S. 216, 289. Hughes acted as the plan's settlor, deciding about the form or structure of the plan, including who is entitled to receive plan benefits and in what amounts, or how such benefits are calculated. Receiving incidental benefits from the amendments, such as attracting and retaining employees, paying deferred compensation, and reducing the likelihood of lawsuits, no more constitutes a breach of fiduciary duties than it would constitute improper inurement or otherwise violate ERISA. Pp. 13-16. (c) Respondents' claim that the amendment works an effective termination of the defined benefit plan based on the common-law theory of a wasting trust also fails. Because ERISA is a comprehensive and reticulated statute, it should not be supplemented by extra-textual remedies, such as the common-law doctrines advocated by respondents. Applying the wasting trust doctrine in this context appears to be inconsistent with ERISA's termination provisions. Even assuming that the doctrine might apply in certain circumstances, it is by its own terms inapplicable here. Thousands of active participants in the noncontributory benefit structure continue to accrue benefits, and the Plan continues to accept new members and pay all promised benefits to eligible participants. Thus, the circumstances cannot be construed to constitute an enfeebled plan whose membership has dwindled to a mere remnant that would no longer benefit from the Plan's administration. Pp. 16-18. 159 F. 3d 1055, reversed.

Case Name: Virginia v. Landmark Communications, Inc.
Year: 1979
Jurisdiction: United States Supreme Court
Issue: Whether the First Amendment bars the states from imposing criminal penalties on third parties who publish truthful information about ongoing judicial proceedings.
Holding: Yes, the First Amendment bars the states from imposing criminal penalties on third parties who publish truthful information about ongoing judicial proceedings.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit ruled that the State of Georgia is immune from suits brought under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA) for violations of the ADA's provisions relating to the confinement of disabled inmates. The court held that the District Court had erred in its dismissal of the state defendants' claims for money damages under the ADA. The Eleventh Circuit held that there was no basis for the district court's dismissal of Goodman's 1983 claims. The district court had previously dismissed Goodman’s claims against individual defendants for violating the ADA, but the court had also granted summary judgment to the State defendants. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate opinion, held that Goodman had not shown that he was deprived of his right to a fair trial. The Court held that, under the circumstances, the State's motion for summary judgment was not supported by the facts of the case, and that the case should be remanded for further consideration.

After petitioner promotional agency applied for the use of a municipal theatre for presentation of a controversial musical, respondents, members of the theatre's governing body, rejected the application without stating why. When petitioner sued in Federal District Court for a preliminary injunction, respondents filed no answer for five months. At the subsequent hearing, the District Court refused to grant the requested injunction, ruling that petitioner had not shown irreparable harm likely to result from denial of the requested relief. More than five months elapsed before the District Court finally reviewed the merits of the dispute and ultimately upheld the rejection of petitioner's application. Meanwhile, petitioner had changed the dates of the performances and had to bear substantial expenses resulting from the change. Held: Under the circumstances, including the absence of any provision for prompt judicial review, the rejection of petitioner's application for use of the theatre constituted a prior restraint of the right of free expression contrary to the First Amendment. Pp. 208-216. (a) Whether the rejection of petitioner's application for use of the theatre constitutes a prior restraint turns not on whether the musical is obscene but on whether the rejection contravenes the First Amendment. Since the theatre is a municipal facility, the Government being the ultimate beneficiary of the property, the rejection of petitioner's application cannot be justified solely on the assertedly obscene character of the musical. Pp. 208-210. (b) Labeling the rejection of petitioner's application a prior restraint does not end the inquiry, since prior restraints are not unconstitutional per se. However, any system of prior restraint comes to this Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity, and the presumption against prior restraints is heavier -and the degree of protection broader- than that against limits on expression imposed by criminal penalties. To be held lawful, respondents' action must both fall within one of the narrowly defined exceptions to the prohibition against prior restraints and must have been accomplished with procedural safeguards that reduce the danger of suppressing constitutionally protected speech. Here, although the standard applied by respondents or the courts below may have been sufficient, the procedures followed were insufficient to assure prompt judicial review with a minimum restriction of First Amendment rights. Pp. 210-216. 464 F. Supp. 1361, reversed.

The Supreme Court case in question revolved around the legality of a written test (Test 21) used by the District of Columbia Metropolitan Police Department to screen applicants for police officer positions. The test was challenged by two African American police officers who claimed it was racially discriminatory because it disproportionately disqualified black candidates. They argued this violated their rights under the Fifth Amendment's due process clause, as well as under federal and local laws.

The District Court had originally upheld the test, finding no intentional discrimination and determining that the test was reasonably related to the requirements of the police training program. However, the Court of Appeals reversed this decision, applying standards from Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (as interpreted in Griggs v. Duke Power Co.) and concluding that the disproportionate impact of the test on black applicants was sufficient to establish a constitutional violation, regardless of intent.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the Court of Appeals, stating that the standards from Title VII cases should not be applied to constitutional claims of racial discrimination. The Supreme Court emphasized that a racially neutral law or test does not violate the Constitution simply because it has a disproportionate impact on a particular racial group. Instead, there must be evidence of a discriminatory purpose.

The Supreme Court found that Test 21 was neutral on its face, served a legitimate purpose, and was related to the police training program. The Court also noted the efforts made by the police department to recruit black officers and the changing racial composition of the force, which argued against any inference of racial discrimination.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, holding that the test did not violate the Fifth Amendment and that the respondents were not entitled to relief on constitutional or statutory grounds. The Court concluded that the District Court's decision to uphold the test was correct and that the Court of Appeals had erred in applying Title VII standards to a constitutional claim. The Supreme Court's decision implies that while discriminatory impact can be considered, it is not the sole basis for proving a constitutional violation of equal protection or due process without evidence of discriminatory intent.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has reversed a lower court's ruling that found that the Freedom From Religion Foundation and others had standing to sue the White House Office of Faith-Based and Community Initiatives for using federal funds to pay for a conference that included speeches by President Bush and former Secretary of Education Paige Paige Paige praising the efficacy of faith-based programs in delivering social services. The plaintiffs contend that they meet the standing requirements of Article III of the Constitution because they pay federal taxes. The court held that, in light of the size of the federal budget, it is a complete fiction to argue that an unconstitutional federal expenditure causes an individual federal taxpayer any measurable economic harm. We therefore reverse the decision of the Appeals Court, which held that the plaintiffs have standing as taxpayers because the conferences were paid for with money appropriated by Congress. The case is now before the United States Supreme Court.

Petitioner Clark filed a support complaint in the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas on behalf of her minor daughter, Tiffany, who was born out of wedlock on June 11, 1973. The court ordered blood tests, which showed a 99.3% probability that Jeter was Tiffany's father. The trial court upheld the statute of limitations on the authority of Astemborski v. Susmarski, 499 Pa. 99, 451 A. 2d 1012, vacated. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court denied Clark's motion for allowance of appeal. Held: The Pennsylvania statute does not withstand heightened scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 518-527. 358 Pa. Super. 550, 518 A.2d 276, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit is considering whether the Constitution permits a juvenile offender to be sentenced to life in prison without parole for a nonhomicide crime. Petitioner Terrance Jamar Graham, who was 16 at the time of the crime, was charged as an adult with armed burglary with assault and attempted armed robbery. The trial court sentenced him to concurrent 3-year terms of probation. The court held hearings on Graham's violations of his probation, and he was arrested less than 6 months later for a second home invasion. Graham was convicted of the home invasion and sentenced to a life sentence without the possibility of parole. The Florida Supreme Court denied his motion for a retrial. The 4th District Court of Appeal ruled that the trial court did not have to impose a sentence because Graham had pleaded guilty to the charges against him. The appeals court found that Graham had violated his probation by failing to disclose that he had been involved in a home invasion that resulted in the death of Meigo Bailey, and that Graham was not present when Bailey was shot. The Appeals Court concluded that Graham should be granted a new trial based on the new evidence. The Court also found that the prosecution had not proved that Graham committed the crime with intent to commit murder. The case is being heard by Justices Barry S. Sullivan, Jennifer A. Gibson, and John G.

In a class action lawsuit, Negro citizens of Greene County, Alabama, challenged the exclusion of Negroes from grand and petit juries. They alleged that despite being qualified, they were never summoned for jury service due to discriminatory practices by the jury commissioners, the local judge, and the Governor of Alabama. The plaintiffs sought a declaration that such exclusions were systematic and unconstitutional, an injunction to prevent future exclusions, and an order to reconstitute the jury commission without racial discrimination.

The Supreme Court reviewed the case after a three-judge District Court found evidence of racial discrimination in the jury selection process. The District Court concluded that the process deviated from Alabama's statutory requirements, with the jury commission and its clerk failing to consider all eligible citizens and relying on a limited and biased pool of potential jurors, which resulted in a disproportionately low number of Negroes on the jury rolls compared to their population in the county.

The Supreme Court held that the plaintiffs had the right to challenge the discriminatory jury selection process, not just as defendants in criminal cases but also as citizens excluded from jury service due to their race. The Court found that the State must ensure jury selection is free from racial bias once it decides to provide juries.

The Court did not agree that the Alabama statute, which required jury commissioners to select jurors reputed to be honest and intelligent, was unconstitutional on its face. The statute did not mention race, and similar provisions exist in many states. The Court believed that the statute could be administered without racial discrimination and that the federal courts could enforce compliance.

The Court also did not find sufficient evidence to conclude that the absence of Negroes from the jury commission was due to discriminatory selection by the Governor. The plaintiffs had not presented a compelling case that the Governor had deliberately appointed a segregated jury commission.

The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's injunction against the systematic exclusion of Negroes from the jury roll and its directive for the jury commission to compile a new jury list in accordance with Alabama law and constitutional principles. The Court noted that the District Court should consider whether the new jury roll complied with its decree and that further relief might be necessary to eliminate past discrimination and prevent future occurrences.

In summary, the Supreme Court upheld the District Court's findings of racial discrimination in the jury selection process in Greene County, Alabama, and affirmed the need for injunctive relief to correct the discriminatory practices, while not invalidating the Alabama statute on jury selection or mandating the appointment of Negroes to the jury commission.

Section 4371 of the Internal Revenue Code imposes a tax on insurance premiums paid to foreign insurers that are not subject to the federal income tax. International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) ships products that it manufactures in the United States to numerous foreign subsidiaries and insures those shipments against loss. When the foreign subsidiary makes the shipping arrangements, the subsidiary often places the insurance with a foreign carrier. When it does, both IBM and the subsidiary are listed as beneficiaries in the policy. When IBM filed federal excise tax returns for the years 1975 through 1984, but reported no liability under Section (s) 4371, the IRS assessed a tax against IBM for each of those years. IBM paid the assessments and filed refund claims, which the IRS denied. IBM then commenced suit in the Court of Federal Claims, contending that application of Section 4371 to policies insuring its export shipments violated the Export Clause. The focus of the suit was this Court's decision in Thames & Mersey Marine Ins. Co. v. United States, 237 U. S. 19 (1915), in which this Court held that a federal stamp tax on policies in export transit could not be constitutionally applied to policies covering export shipments. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The Export Clause of the Constitution permits the imposition of a generally applicable, nondiscriminatory federal tax on goods in export transportation. Pp. 5-11. (a) The Export clause of the Commerce Clause permits the application of generally applicable nondiscrimination taxes, even on goods that are no longer in import transit. The Commerce Clause strictly prohibits any tax or duty, discriminatory or not, that falls on exports during the course of exportation. P. 5. (b) The Import-Export Clause jurisprudence, which is based partly on an outmoded view of the commerce Clause, has become an anachronism in need of modernization. The Government's argument falls short of its goal of showing that the Import-Import-Export-Clause jurisy, which has historically been treated as broad bans on taxation of exports, has shifted dramatically and that our traditional understanding of the export Clause can no longer be justified. Michelin Tire Corp.v. Wages, 423 U.S. 276, and Department of Revenue v. Association of Wash. Stevedoring Cos., 435 U. s. 734, do not require judgment in its favor. The fact that Michelin drew its analysis around the phrase "Imposts or Duties" and expressly excluded the broader term "Tax" that appears in the Export-Export clause does not mean that the tax is, in essence, a "Tax on exports," id., at 294. The text of the Export, on the other hand, expressly prohibits Congress from laying any taxes on imports or exports, and has no direct effect on the way the States treat imports and exports. The principles that animate stare decisis caution against overruling a longstanding precedent on a theory not argued by the parties, and we decline to do so in this case. Cf. Richfield Oil Corp., v. State Bd. of Equalization, 329 U. K. 2d 905, 915. The import-export Clause cases have broadly exempted from federal taxation not only export goods, but also services and activities closely related to the export process. At the same time, the Government has attempted to limit the term "Articles exported" to permit federal taxation of pre-export goods and services. The export Clause, which was intended to protect federal supremacy in international commerce, to preserve federal revenue from import duties and imposts, and to prevent coastal States with ports from taking unfair advantage of inland States, see Michelin, supra, at 285-286, serves none of those goals. The Text of the Ex-Export Clauses, which are based on an unexceptively stricter language of theExport Clause, does quite the opposite. It specifically forbids Congress from regulating international commerce through export taxes, disallows any attempt to raise federal revenues from exports, while an identical federal assessment might properly be called a tax and would be subject to an Export Clause tax on exports. This Court has never upheld a state tax assessed directly on goods sold in import or export transit. In both Michelin and Washington Stevedored, the text did not require that view, and there is substantial evidence from the Debates that proponents of the Clause fully intended the breadth of scope that is evident in the language. In fact, Michelin has been controlling precedent for over 80 years, and the Government does not, indeed could not, argue that the rule established there is "unworkable." This Court's longstanding parallel interpretations of the two Clauses have not, and indeed cannot, govern our interpretation of the Import

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California today entered a final judgment against First English Evangelical Lutheran Church, Inc. ("First English"), a California-based registered representative, and a Los Angeles County district attorney, in a civil injunctive action.  According to the SEC's complaint, First English purchased a 21-acre parcel of land in a canyon along the banks of the Middle Fork of Mill Creek in the Angeles National Forest in January 1979. The complaint alleged that the county's ordinance denied First English all use of its property, and that the city's preliminary ordinance denied it all use. First English's complaint alleges that, in the event of a taking, the city would not be able to collect compensation for the period during which the taking was effective. The SEC also alleges that First English violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 17(a)(1) of Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act"). The complaint further alleges that the defendants were liable under Section 5 of the Exchange Act for the risk of future violations of the securities laws, and the federal district court for the Central Valley of California issued an order requiring First English to pay a civil penalty of $100,000. First English has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining it from violating the federal securities laws. The settlement is subject to court approval. Section 6511(b)(2)(A) imposes a ceiling on the amount of credit or refund to which a taxpayer is entitled as compensation for an overpayment of tax. The plain language of §6513(b) provides that the two remittances at issue were "paid" on the due date of the taxpayer's income tax return. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) assessed the tax liability reported on this belated return. Respondent Baral claimed that he had remitted more with respect to the 1988 taxable year than he actually owed, and requested that the IRS apply the excess as a credit toward his outstanding tax obligations for the 1989 taxable year. The IRS denied the request, and Baral then commenced the instant suit for refund in Federal District Court, which sustained the IRS's position and granted summary judgment in its favor. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Certiorari granted.

When petitioner Baker applied for a job at respondent restaurant chain, he signed an agreement requiring that any employment-related disputes be submitted to arbitration. He subsequently worked there until he was fired. He then filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), claiming that his firing violated the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA). Under § 107 of the ADA, the EEOC has exclusive jurisdiction over the claim for 180 days after the filing of a charge, during which time the employee must obtain a "right-to-sue" letter from the agency before prosecuting the claim. If the EEOC files suit on the employee's behalf, the employee has no independent cause of action, though he may intervene in the lawsuit. Section 107 also specifies that the EEOC may pursue a claim on the employee's behalf even after he has disavowed any desire to seek relief. The EEOC took the position that it could pursue a claim on Baker's behalf even after he had disavowed any desire to seek relief. The EEOC then sued respondent in Federal District Court, seeking injunctive relief and victim-specific relief, including backpay, compensatory and punitive damages, and attorney's fees. The District Court dismissed the suit, ruling that the arbitration agreement barred the EEOC from pursuing victim-specific relief. The Fifth Circuit disagreed, concluding that the EEOC was entitled to pursue victim-specific relief, but that it was barred from doing so because the public interest served when the EEOC pursued make-whole relief was outweighed by the policy goals favoring arbitration. Held: An agreement between private parties to arbitrate employment-related disputes does not bar the EEOC from pursuing victim-specific relief in court. Pp. 3-12. (a) The Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) places arbitration agreements on the same footing as other contracts, see Gilmer v. Interstate/JohnsonLaneCorporation, 500 U. S. 20, 25, and requires courts to stay proceedings when an issue is referrable to arbitration, see 9 U. S. C. §§ 3, 4. However, the FAA does not mention enforcement by public agencies, and it ensures the enforceability of private agreements to arbitrate, but otherwise does not purport to restrict a nonparty's choice of a judicial forum. Nor does the FAA mandate that courts compel arbitration of any issues not already covered in the agreement. The FAA thus favors arbitration agreements, but does not require them. Pp. 3-6. (b) The EEOC here has the authority to pursue victim-specific relief regardless of the forum that Baker and respondent chose to resolve their dispute. Whenever the EEOC chooses from among the many charges filed each year to bring an enforcement action in a particular case, the agency may be seeking to vindicate a public interest, not simply providing make-whole relief for the employee, even when it pursues entirely victim-specific relief. To hold otherwise would undermine the detailed enforcement scheme created by Congress simply to give greater effect to an agreement between private parties that does not even contemplate the EEOC's statutory function. Pp. 6-10. (c) Although the courts can and should preclude double recovery by an individual, no question concerning the validity of Baker's claim or the character of the relief that could be appropriately awarded in either a judicial or an arbitral forum is presented by the record. The only issue before this Court is whether the fact that Baker has signed a mandatory arbitration agreement limits the remedies available to the EEOC. The text of the relevant statutes provides a clear answer to that question. They do not authorize the courts to balance the competing policies of the ADA and the FAA or to second-guess the EEOC's judgment concerning which of the remedies authorized by law that it shall seek in any given case. Moreoever, it simply does not follow from the cases holding that the employee's conduct may affect the EEOC's recovery that the EEOC's claim is merely derivative. Pp. 10-12. 193 F. 3d 808, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Southern District of Florida recently reversed a lower court's dismissal of a negligence action filed against Costa Cruise Lines by a passenger who tripped over a cable and fractured her femur on a cruise ship. The lower court had dismissed the complaint because the passenger had not complied with the terms of her ticket, which required her to file a complaint within one year of the date of her injury and to be served within 120 days of filing. The court held that the passenger's delay in seeking to amend her complaint was not appropriate because she knew or should have known of the proper defendant before filing her original complaint. The appeals court also held that Krupski's amended complaint did not meet the requirements of Rule 15(c)(1)(C) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which requires the party to be brought in by amendment for a mistake concerning the proper party's identity. The Appeals Court held that, in this case, Krupski had not known of Costa Cruise or its officers, staff members, crew members, independent contractors, medical providers, concessionaires, pilots, suppliers, agents, and assigned onboard the cruise ship before filing the amended complaint. We hold that relation back under the Rules depends on what the party is known or should know, not on the amending party''s knowledge or its timeliness. The parties were unable to reach a settlement, however, and Krupski filed her complaint on February 1, 2008 invoking the diversity jurisdiction of the federal court in Florida. The complaint alleged that Costa Cruise breached its duty of care by failing to take steps to prevent Krupski from entering the ship and that it owed Krupski a duty to provide a certain certification of quality, which it failed to do. Krupski also alleged that the cruise line had violated its duty to ensure that the ship was safe. The district court ruled that the complaint was filed within the one-year limitations period of the ticket and that the limitations period had expired.
