The Bar of South Carolina's Board of Commissioners on Grievances and Discipline charged Edna Smith Primus with soliciting a client on behalf of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) in violation of the Bar's Code of Ethics and Rules 2103 and 2103(2). Primus filed a motion to dismiss the charges, claiming that her conduct was protected by the First and Fourteenth Amendments and by the Code of Professional Responsibility of the ACLU. The Commission found that Primus had engaged in solicitation and recommended that she be found guilty of violating the Code. Primus's motion was denied, and the Commission held a hearing on her appeal. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued a decision on the matter.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the issue of racial discrimination in the use of peremptory challenges during jury selection. The petitioner, Larry Joe Powers, a white man, argued that the prosecution's exclusion of black jurors violated his rights under the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments, as well as statutory law, regardless of his own race. The Court of Appeals affirmed Powers' conviction, but the Supreme Court granted certiorari to consider whether a white defendant could object to the exclusion of black jurors based on the Equal Protection Clause.

The Supreme Court held that the Equal Protection Clause prohibits the exclusion of jurors based solely on their race, as it offends the dignity of the excluded individuals and undermines the integrity of the courts. The Court emphasized the importance of jury service as a civic duty and a means to ensure fairness in the judicial process. It rejected the notion that the race of the defendant is a necessary precondition for challenging racial discrimination in jury selection.

The Court also addressed the issue of standing, concluding that a criminal defendant has the right to raise the equal protection claims of excluded jurors. The Court reasoned that the defendant suffers a real injury when the prosecutor excludes jurors on account of race, as it casts doubt on the fairness of the trial. The Court found that the defendant is an effective advocate for the rights of excluded jurors and that practical barriers make it unlikely that excluded jurors would be able to assert their own rights.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the lower court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, establishing that defendants have the right to object to racially discriminatory use of peremptory challenges, regardless of whether they share the same race as the excluded jurors. This decision reinforces the constitutional imperative of race neutrality in jury selection and the broader goal of eliminating racial discrimination from the judicial process.

Title: Arizona v. Marshall (1977)

Summary: In Arizona v. Marshall (1977), the Supreme Court held that the First Amendment protects commercial speech, including advertising by lawyers. The Court struck down a disciplinary rule that prohibited lawyers from placing ads in newspapers announcing the availability of routine legal services at a fixed fee. The Court found that the rule was too broad and chilled protected speech, and that the public had a right to receive accurate information about legal services. The Court also rejected the idea that the rule was necessary to preserve the dignity and prestige of the legal profession.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia granted certiorari in the case of a bankruptcy case involving a student loan debt discharge. The court ruled that the bankruptcy court's order confirming the discharge of the debt was void because it was issued in violation of the Bankruptcy Code and Rules of Court. The Court held that the Bankruptcy Court did not have to hold an adversary proceeding to determine the dischargeability of that debt. In a parallel action, the U.N. Department of Education had commenced efforts to collect the unpaid interest on the debt. The bankruptcy court confirmed the debt discharge plan without holding an adversary hearing or making a finding of undue hardship. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the debtor, concluding that the court did not need to hold such a hearing to determine that the discharge was not in the best interests of the debtors and their dependents. The appeals court also ruled that there was no need for a hearing on the adversary proceeding because the parties had agreed not to proceed with it. The Appeals Court concluded that, in the absence of such a finding, the bankruptcy judge had not violated the Code's provisions for the discharge. In the parallel proceeding, the appeals court found that there had been no undue hardship on the debtors, and that the plan was valid. The case is now before the Supreme Court for further consideration.

Petitioner McNeill was arrested in 2008 while in possession of drugs and a gun. He pleaded guilty to federal charges of being a felon in possession of a firearm and possession with intent to distribute cocaine. Because of his multiple prior drug convictions, he qualifies for enhanced sentencing under the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA). Section 924(e)(1) provides that a person who violates 18 U.S.C. §922(g) and “has three previous convctions…for a violent felony or a serious drug offense” is subject to a mandatory minimum 15-year prison sentence. Section 924(e)(2)(A)(ii) defines a “serious drug offense” as “an offense under State law, involving manufacturing, distributing, or possessing with intent to manufacture or distribute, a controlled substance … , for which a maximum term of imprisonment of ten years or more is prescribed by law.” Before applying ACCA’s sentencing enhancement, the Federal District Court considered whether McNeill’s drug offenses were “serious drug offenses” by examining the maximum sentence under current state law. Ultimately, the court found that McNeill met the criteria for ACCA’s sentencing enhancement and imposed a 300-month sentence. On appeal, the Fourth Circuit agreed with the lower court’s determination that the drug offenses were “serious drug offenses,” although it acknowledged that McNeill might have been subject to shorter sentences had the sentencing scheme in place during the commission of those offenses remained in effect. Held: A federal sentencing court determines whether a “previous conviction” was for a “serious drug offense” by considering the “maximum term of imprisonment” applicable to the defendant’s previous drug offense at the time of that conviction. Pp. 4−8. (a) The plain text of ACCA requires a federal sentencing court to consult the maximum sentence applicable to a defendant’s previous drug offense at the time of that conviction. Here, McNeill argues that the present-tense verb in the phrase “is prescribed by law” requires federal courts to determine the maximum sentence for a potential predicate offense by looking to the state law in effect at the time of the federal sentencing, as if the state offense were committed on the day of federal sentencing. However, ACCA is concerned with convictions that have already occurred. And whether the prior conviction was for an offense “involving manufacturing, distributing, or possessing with intent to manufacture or distribute, a controlled substance” can only be answered by reference to the law under which the defendant was convicted. Pp. 4−5. (b) The broader context of the statute as a whole supports this interpretation. Specifically, the adjacent definition of “violent felony” confirms this interpretation. Even though Congress used present-tense verbs in that definition, when determining whether a defendant was convicted of a “violent felony,” this Court has turned to the version of state law that the defendant was actually convicted of violating. See, e.g., Taylor v. United States, 495 U. S. 575 ; James v. United States, 550 U. S. 192 . There is no reason to interpret “serious drug offenses” in the adjacent section of the same statute any differently. Both definitions require the present tense to refer to past convictions. Moreover, this natural reading of ACCA avoids the absurd result that would follow from consulting current state law to define a previous offense. Had McNeill approached the matter correctly, a prior conviction could disappear altogether for ACCA purposes if a State reformulated the offense between the defendant’s state conviction and federal sentencing. Such a natural reading also ensures consistency across ACCA’s various sections. Pp. 5−7. (c) Application of this holding to this case shows that the District Court properly applied ACCA’s sentencing enhancement to McNeill. All six of his prior drug convictions qualify as “serious drug offenses” within the meaning of ACCA. His first two convictions were for selling cocaine in 1991 and possessing cocaine with intent to sell in 1992. Those convictions were for “serious drug offenses” because the maximum sentence for selling cocaine in 1991 and the maximum sentence for possessing cocaine with intent to sell in 1992 was 10 years in prison under North Carolina law at the times of those convictions. The fourth conviction involved possessing cocaine with intent to sell in September 1994. By April 1995, North Carolina had changed the sentence applicable to that type of drug offense but still provided that the maximum sentence for possessing cocaine with intent to sell in September 1994 was 10 years in prison. Pp. 7−8. 598 F. 3d 165, affirmed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court.

In the Supreme Court case of Brecht v. Abrahamson, the Court addressed whether the standard for determining harmless error established in Chapman v. California should apply when reviewing a habeas corpus petition. The petitioner, Todd A. Brecht, had been convicted of first-degree murder, and during his trial, the prosecution had used his post-Miranda silence for impeachment purposes. This use of silence was deemed a violation of due process under Doyle v. Ohio.

The Court held that the Chapman standard, which requires an error to be harmless beyond a reasonable doubt to uphold a conviction, does not apply in the habeas corpus context. Instead, the Court adopted the standard from Kotteakos v. United States, which asks whether the error had a "substantial and injurious effect or influence in determining the jury's verdict." This standard is considered more appropriate for the nature of collateral review in habeas cases.

The Court reasoned that applying a less stringent standard on habeas review aligns with the limited role of federal habeas proceedings, respects the finality of state court convictions, and acknowledges the sovereignty of states over criminal matters. The Court also noted that the federal habeas corpus statute does not specify a standard for harmless-error review, leaving it to the Court to determine the appropriate standard.

Applying the Kotteakos standard to Brecht's case, the Court concluded that the references to his post-Miranda silence were infrequent and largely cumulative given other permissible references to his pre-Miranda silence. Additionally, the evidence against Brecht was strong, including inconsistencies in his account of the shooting and other circumstantial evidence. Therefore, the Court determined that the Doyle error did not substantially influence the jury's verdict, and Brecht was not entitled to habeas relief. The judgment of the Court of Appeals was affirmed.

Under agreements with periodicals' publishers, two computer database companies placed copies of the freelancers' articles along with all other articles from the periodicals in which the articles appeared into three databases. The publishers, in response, relied on the privilege of reproduction and distribution accorded them by 17 U. S. C. § 201(c), which provides: "Copyright in each separate contribution to a collective work is distinct from copyright in the collective work as a whole, and vests initially in the author of the contribution. In the absence of an express transfer of the copyright or of any rights under it, the owner of copyright in [the collective work] is presumed to have acquired only the privilege" §201(c) accords them to "reproduc[e] and distribut[e]" the author's discretely copyrighted contribution. To qualify as "revisions," according to the court, works need only "preserve some significant original aspect of [collective works]" whether an original selection of the articles originally appeared, or "as part of any later collective work in the same series." Both the print publishers and the electronic publishers infringed the Authors' copyrights by reproducing and distributing the articles in a manner not authorized by the Authors and not privileged by §201 (c). The court determined that the Databases reproduced and distributed the articles as part of a revision of that collective work to which the Authors had first contributed. The Court of Appeals ruled that Newsday and Time had entered into agreements authorizing reproduction of the Articles in the databases. After discovery, both sides moved for summary judgment. The District Court granted summary judgment for the Publishers, holding that § 201 (c) shielded the Database reproductions. Held: 1. The Copyright Act, as amended in 1976, "opyright protection subsists in original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated." 17 U., S.C. § 102(a). When, as in this case, a freelance author has contributed an article to a "collective work" such as a newspaper or magazine, see §101 (defining "collectively work"), the statute recognizes two distinct copyrighted works: Copyright in the separate contribution "vests initiallyin the author" (here, the freelancer), and extends only to the creative material contributed by that author, not to "the preexisting material employed in the work," §103(b). The Databases, like the hypothetical library, store and retrieve articles separately within a vast domain of diverse texts. Such a storage and retrieval system effectively overrides the Copyright Act's exclusive right to control the individual reproduction, distribution, and reproduction of each Article. Pp. 5-11. 2. The copyright laws, as construed by the courts below, are designed to provide the author with the power to negotiate for the realized value of the work. P. 5. The fact that a third party can manipulate a database to produce a noninfringing document does not mean the database is not infringing. Under §201, the question is not whether a user can generate a "revision" of that work, but whether a copyright in "compilation" a term that includes the compiler's original "selection, coordination, and arrangement." P. 6. 3. In determining whether the articles have been reproduced, as presented to, and perceptible by, the user of the databases, it is unnecessary to determine whether the copyright is transferable. The Publishers' encompassing construction of the §201-c privilege is unacceptable, for it would diminish the Authors’ exclusive rights in the Articles. The court did not reach the question whether the § 201-c-privilege is transferredable, for theDatabases do not reproduce and distribute the Articles as part-a “revision” of the collective works in issue. Accordingly, the judgment is vacated and the case is remanded.

This case concerns the legality of a decision by the Secretary of Commerce not to implement a proposed statistical adjustment to the results of the 1990 census. The proposed adjustment, known as the Post-Enumerate Survey (PES), was intended to account for potential undercounts identified during the initial enumeration process. However, the Secretary determined that the PES adjustment would not significantly improve the accuracy of the census and could lead to confusion and mistrust of the final results. The Court of Appeals held that the Secretary's decision was arbitrary and capricious, and that it violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. On appeal, the Supreme Court upheld the Secretary's decision, finding that it was well within the constitutional bounds of discretion afforded to Congress in conducting the census.

A joint trial of petitioner and one Evans resulted in the conviction of both by a jury on a federal charge of armed postal robbery. A postal inspector testified that Evans orally confessed to him that Evans and petitioner committed the armed robbery. The postal inspector obtained the oral confession, and another in which Evans admitted he had an accomplice whom he would not name, in the course of two interrogations of Evans at the city jail where Evans was held in custody on state criminal charges. Both petitioner and Evans appealed their convictions to the Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, which set aside Evans' conviction on the ground that his oral confessions to the postal inspector should not have been received in evidence against him. However, the court, relying upon Delli Paoli v. United States, 352 U. S. 232, affirmed petitioner's conviction because the trial judge instructed the jury that although Evans' confession was competent evidence against Evans it was inadmissible hearsay against petitioner and therefore had to be disregarded in determining petitioner's guilt or innocence. Held: 1. The conviction of a defendant at a joint trial should be set aside although the jury was instructed that a codefendant's confession inculpating the defendant had to have been disregarded. Pp. 431-464. 2. The jury, despite instructions to the contrary, looked to Evans' incriminating extrajudicial statements in determining the defendant's guilt. P. 434. 375 F. 2d 355, reversed and cause remanded.

Under the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA), a state drug-trafficking conviction qualifies as a serious drug offense if “a maximum term of imprisonment of ten years or more is prescribed by law” for the “offense,” 18 U. S. C. §924(e)(2)(A). Because the maximum term that respondent faced on at least two of respondent’s drug-delivery charges was 10 years, the District Court sentenced respondent to concurrent sentences of 48 months’ imprisonment on each count. In the federal felon-in-possession case, respondent was convicted under ACCA, which sets a 15-year minimum sentence “[i]n the case of a person who violates section 922(g) of [Title 18] and has three previous convictions . . . for a violent felony or a seriousdrug offense, or both, committed on occasions different from one another … .” §925(e). The District Court agreed, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The maximum term prescribed by ACCA for the state drug convictions at issue in this case was the 10-year maximum set by the applicable recidivist provision. Pp. 5–11. (a) The phrase “maximum term” prescribed by the statute for the drug offenses at issue is not analogous to the ACCA provision that is before this case. The phrase is “not intended to be exclusive” of other potential reasons for departing. P. 5. 464 F. 3d 1072, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia granted a motion by Richard Irizarry, Jr., for a re-sentencing based on a lower-court judge's finding that he had violated a restraining order by sending threatening e-mails to his ex-wife and her new husband. The lower court had recommended a sentence of 41 to 51 months in prison, based on the recommendations of a presentence report (PSR) and a federal sentencing guideline range. The PSR recommended that the sentence be increased based on his criminal history and his intention to carry out the threats. The trial judge agreed with the PSR's recommendation, and the lower court denied the request for an adjustment for acceptance of responsibility. The appeals court ruled that the trial judge had not adequately explained the reasons for her decision. The court held that the sentencing guidelines are not appropriate in this case, and that the judge should have considered the impact on petitioner's family and the community when sentencing him. The Court also ruled that there was no need for the court to determine the amount of credit for time served on the restraining order. The Appeals Court concluded that the court should have determined the appropriate sentence based on all of the evidence presented.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Colorado upheld the conviction of a man convicted of knowingly concealing and transporting narcotic drugs in Denver, Colorado, in violation of the federal narcotics laws. The court found that the arresting officer had probable cause to arrest petitioner without a warrant, and overruled his motion to suppress evidence that the subsequent search and seizure were incident to a lawful arrest. We conclude that the search violated the Fourth Amendment, and therefore the use of the heroin in evidence vitiated the conviction. The trial court's decision to overrule petitioner's motion was correct, and the court also found that there was sufficient evidence to support the arrest.

An Indiana statute authorizes counties to levy special assessments on real estate to finance public improvements, including sewer projects. Pursuant to the statute, respondent City of Indianapolis financed certain sewer projects using a system in which beneficiary property owners paid installation charges and ongoing maintenance fees. Over time, the City abandoned the system and replaced it with another, under which beneficiaries received a credit toward future assessments equal to twice the amount they had paid in connection with the previous system. The City also forgave all outstanding indebtedness accrued during the transitional period. Some property owners who had paid off their assessments in full sought refunds of the amounts they had paid above what they would owe under the new system. The City refused to grant the requested refunds, claiming that to do so would undermine the benefits of the new system. Property owners sued, alleging that the City’s conduct violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Indiana courts agreed, concluding that the City had failed to demonstrate a rational basis for treating differently those who had paid off their assessments in full and those whose assessments remained outstanding. Held: The City did not violate the Equal Protection Clause. Pp. 7–14. (a) Because the City’s classification involves neither a “fundamental right” nor a “suspect” classification, it falls within the scope of this Court’s precedents holding such a law constitutionally valid if “there is a plausible policy reason for the classification, the legislative facts on which the classification is apparently based rationally may have been considered to be true by the governmental decision maker, and the relationship of the classification to its goal is not so attenuated as to render the distinction arbitrary or irrational.” Nordlinger v. Hahn, 505 U. S. 1, 11. There is such a plausible reason here because the City’s decision to stop collecting outstanding debts finds rational support in related administrative concerns. First, continuing to collect would have been complex and expensive, entailing the need to track down defaulting debtors and bring legal action. Second, the City would have had to spread the fixed administrative costs of collection over an ever declining number of debtors, thereby continuously increasing the per-debtor cost of collection. Third, the City could not simply have processed refunds without taking funds from other programs or finding additional revenue. Fourth, the City could not have kept the amount of revenue it lost constant and distributed it evenly among the apparent thousands of homeowners involved in any of the City’s projects without spreading the loss across too many parties. Fifth, the City could not have given refunds to all those involved in all of the City’s projects or in all of the open projects without taking funding from other programs or finding additional revenue. Even if the City had attempted to keep the amount of revenue it lost constant and distribute it evenly among the apparent thousands of homeowners involved in any of the City’s projects, the result would have been yet smaller individual payments, even more likely to have been too small to justify the administrative expense. These administrative considerations are sufficient to show a rational basis for the City’s distinction. Pp. 7–10. (b) Petitioners’ counterarguments are not persuasive. Their contention that the City’s tax distinction would not necessarily favor low-income homeowners is irrelevant, since the administrative considerations discussed above are sufficient to show a rational basis for the City’s distinction. Nor is it necessary to consider the argument that the City’s tax distinction would not necessarily favor low-income homeowners, since the administrative considerations discussed above are sufficient to show a rational basis for the City’s distinction. Petitioners’ proposal that the City adopt a system that includes refunds for at least some of those who had already paid in full is not controlling, since the Constitution does not require the City to draw the perfect line or even to draw a line superior to some other line it might have drawn. It requires only that the line actually drawn be a rational line. And for the reasons stated above, the line the City drew here is rational. Petitioners’ argument that administrative considerations alone should not justify a tax distinction, lest a city arbitrarily allocate taxes among a few citizens while forgiving many similarly situated citizens on the ground that it is cheaper and easier to collect taxes from a few people than from many, is correct, but only because reducing those expenses, in the particular circumstances, provides a rational basis justifying the tax difference in question. Petitioners’ argument that administrative considerations alone should not justify a tax distinction, lest a city arbitrarily allocate taxes among a few citizens while forgiving many similarly situated citizens on the ground that it is cheaper and easier to collect taxes from a few people than from many, is correct, but only because reducing those expenses, in the particular circumstances, provides a rational basis justifying the tax difference in question. However, that is not because administrative considerations can never justify tax differences (any more than they can always do so). The question is whether reducing those expenses, in the particular circumstances, provides a rational basis justifying the tax difference in question. In this case, “in the light of the facts made known or generally assumed,” Carolene Products Co. v. California, 304 U. S. 1, 152, it is reasonable to believe that to graft a refund system onto the City’s forgiveness decision could have (for example) imposed an administrative burden of both collecting and paying out small sums (say, $25 per month) for years. As this Court has said, it is rational for the City to draw a line that avoids that burden. Petitioners, who are the ones “attacking the legislative arrangement,” have the burden of showing that the circumstances are otherwise, i.e., that the administrative burden is too insubstantial to justify the classification. That they have not done. Finally, petitions’ reliance on Allegheny Pittsburgh Coal Co. v. Commission of Westmoreland Cty., 488 U. S. 336, misplaced, since that case involved a clear state law requirement clearly and dramatically violated. Here, the City followed state law by apportioning the cost of its projects equally. State law says nothing about forgiveness, how to design a forgiveness program, or whether or when rational distinctions in doing so are permitted. Pp. 10–14. 282 N. E. 2d 100, affirmed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Alito, J., filed a dissenting opinion.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of William Baird's appeal of his conviction for violating Massachusetts General Laws  272,  21, and  21A, which prohibit the distribution of contraceptives for the prevention of conception. The court found that the laws violate the First Amendment right to free speech and the right of single persons to access contraceptives without regard to their marital status. The lower court had dismissed the appeal on the grounds that Baird was not an authorized distributor of the contraceptives. The appeals court agreed with the lower court, and the court vacated the conviction for giving away the vaginal foam Baird gave to a young woman at the end of a lecture on contraception at Boston University. The high court ruled in favor of the prosecution, saying that the law 'represents the State's interest in protecting the health of its citizens'

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia ruled in 1966 that the New Kent County School Board had violated the federal civil rights law by maintaining a racially segregated school system. The case was brought in 1965 by a group of African-American students who alleged that the school board's use of a "freedom-of-choice" plan to determine which of the two schools their children would attend violated the law. The court ruled in favor of the School Board's motion to dismiss the case, and the case was remanded to the District Court to consider the issue of whether the "freedom of choice" plan is adequate compliance with the law's requirements. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit agreed with the lower court's decision, and sent the case back to the district court for further consideration. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued a decision on the case.

The Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA) provides that internal revenue code provisions regarding the reporting and withholding of taxes with respect to winnings from gaming operations shall apply to Indian gaming operations in the same manner as they apply to state gaming operations. However, the IGRA does not provide specific guidance on whether Indian gaming operations are required to pay income taxes on their profits.

In this case, the Choctaw Nation and the Mississippi Band of Choctaws sought clarification on whether they were required to pay income taxes on their profits from gaming operations. The Tenth Circuit held that the IGRA did not require Indian gaming operations to pay income taxes on their profits, citing several provisions of the IGRA that suggest otherwise.

However, the majority disagreed with the Tenth Circuit's decision, arguing that the plain meaning of the IGRA requires Indian gaming operations to pay income taxes on their profits. The majority cited several provisions of the IGRA that indicate that Indian gaming operations are subject to federal income taxation, including a requirement that Indian gaming operators file annual reports with the Bureau of Indian Affairs and the Internal Revenue Service.

Additionally, the majority noted that the IGRA was passed specifically to address issues related to Indian gaming and taxation, and that Congress intended for Indian gaming operations to be subject to federal income taxation. Finally, the majority pointed to several decisions by the Supreme Court and lower courts that have upheld the requirement for Indian gaming operations to pay income taxes on their profits.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of a Michigan prison inmate who was questioned by two corrections officers about his alleged involvement in a sexual conduct with a 12-year-old boy.  According to the court's order, Randall Fields was not in custody for purposes of Miranda. Rather, the court found that Fields violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17b-5 thereunder. The court also found that, while Fields was in custody, he was subject to custodial interrogation without a Miranda warning. As alleged in the court order, Fields agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of 10 to 15 years.  The court further ordered Fields to comply with the court’s order.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan today announced criminal charges against Fields. The SEC also announced that it was seeking a temporary restraining order against Fields, ordering him to return to his cell, and ordering the release of an officer who questioned Fields about the nature of his alleged misconduct. The Court also issued an order suspending Fields from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in connection with the issuance of the order. The order also prohibits Fields from acting as an unregistered broker or dealer in securities.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's complaint, Fields consented to a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the antiterrorism and effective death penalty provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(b)(5) ofÂ the Securities Act of 1933. The final judgment also ordered that Fields be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company and ordered to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil monetary penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.  On the same day that the court issued its order, the SEC issued a subpoena for Fields to provide a copy of the subpoena. The subpoena was obtained by The New York Times, which obtained the subpoena from the SEC, and the SEC obtained an order appointing a receiver to oversee the issuance and sale of the subpoenaed documents. In its order granting the subpoena, the Court also ordered the receiver to provide an accounting of the amount of time and amount of money spent on the investigation.  To learn more about the investigation, see Litigation Release Release Order No. 562 U. S.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Utah today entered a final judgment in favor of the Central Utah Narcotics Task Force against two officers who conducted a warrantless search of a home without a warrant.  The court found that the officers violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In its judgment, the court held that the defendants were entitled to qualified immunity because they had not violated the federal securities laws, and the officers had not engaged in any unlawful conduct.  According to the court's order, however, the officers were not entitled to qualify immunity because, as a result of their conduct, the defendants could not reasonably have believed that their conduct was lawful.  As a result, the Court found that, in many instances, defendants had to resort to unreasonable searches and seizures in order to obtain a judgment that would impose a permanent injunction.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Defendants consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining them from future violations of the securities laws and ordering the officers to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.   The judgment also ordered the defendants to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest of $2,038, and ordered them to pay civil penalties of $100,000 and $50,000, respectively, for their conduct in connection with the alleged unlawful entry of illegal drugs into the home of a third party.  To learn more about qualified immunity, see Litigation Release No. 5, No. 13, and No. 17, and See Litigation Alert No. 24, Jan. 31, 2013.  For further information, see Judgment No. 1278, 1382, 1383, 1384, 1385, 1387, 1386, 1388, 1396, 1398, 1397, 1393, 1376, 1378, and 1387.  On the other hand, the judgment against the officers found that they had violated the "consent-once-removed" provision of the federal law, which requires courts to determine whether a defendant has a right to a certain amount of immunity, and that the court should determine whether the appropriate amount of compensation should be paid based on the reasonable basis for the defendant’s conduct.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against an alien who was unlawfully removed from the United States.  The court entered the final judgment in favor of the alien, finding that a court of appeals had the authority to grant a stay of removal pending the outcome of an appeal.  According to the court's order, filed in federal court in New York, Jean Marc Nken, a Cameroonian citizen, entered the U. S. on a transit visa in April 2001 and entered the country on a temporary basis in December 2001. The court found that a temporary restraining order, or a stay, was necessary to grant Nken the right to remain in the country pending a court’s decision on the merits of his case.  In its judgment, the court held that there was no reasonable basis for a temporary injunction, and that the court had the power to issue a stay.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Nken consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and to the issuance of a permanent injunction against future violations of Section 1252(f)(2). The court also granted Nken a partial right to reapply as an American citizen in the future, without requiring a court to determine whether to grant him a stay or a penalty.  On May 4, 2008, the U-S. Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against Nken. The SEC's complaint charges Nken with violations of the anti-fraud provisions and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. The case is being handled by Douglas F. Basinger of the New York Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Mr. Fagenson and Ms. Fischer of the SEC's New York office.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland today entered a final judgment against Maryland resident George Calvert, who was refused a commission to serve as a public representative because he would not declare his belief in God.  According to the SEC's complaint, Calvert was one of the first people to escape religious test oaths and declare his "belief in the existence of God."  The SEC alleges that Calvert took a religious test in England at the cost of resigning from high governmental office.  Calvert's religious test, which he refused to take, was deemed "unconstitutional" and required him to declare a belief in "the existence" of God in accordance with that faith.  The complaint further alleges that, when Calvert refused to do so, he was forced to resign from high government office at the expense of his religious beliefs.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Maryland today announced criminal charges against Calvert.

The Supreme Court held that non-citizen detainees held as enemy combatants at Guantanamo Bay have the constitutional privilege of habeas corpus, which cannot be suspended except in accordance with the Suspension Clause of the Constitution. The Court found that the procedures provided by the Detainee Treatment Act of 2005 (DTA) and the Military Commissions Act of 2006 (MCA) were not adequate substitutes for habeas corpus. The Court did not address the President's authority to detain these individuals nor did it order that the writ must issue, leaving these questions to be resolved by the District Court.

The Court's decision was based on several factors:

1. The Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) authorized the President to use force against those responsible for the September 11 attacks, but the Court did not resolve whether this extended to the indefinite detention of individuals at Guantanamo.

2. The Combatant Status Review Tribunals (CSRTs) established to determine if detainees were enemy combatants were found to be insufficient to replace habeas corpus rights.

3. The Court rejected the government's argument that the Constitution does not extend to non-citizens detained outside sovereign U.S. territory, emphasizing that the U.S. exercises complete control over Guantanamo Bay.

4. The Court found that the MCA's provision stripping federal courts of jurisdiction to hear habeas corpus applications from Guantanamo detainees was an unconstitutional suspension of the writ.

5. The Court emphasized the importance of habeas corpus as a check on executive power and a fundamental safeguard of individual liberty, particularly when detentions are not the result of a judicial process.

6. The Court noted that practical considerations, such as the government's interest in national security, do not eliminate the need for habeas corpus but may shape its application.

7. The Court concluded that the detainees are entitled to a prompt habeas corpus hearing to challenge the legality of their detention.

The Supreme Court's decision reaffirmed the role of the judiciary in ensuring that the executive's power to detain individuals is exercised within the bounds of the law and the Constitution.

On November 9, 2005, the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland entered a final judgment against a Maryland-based entity that administers the provision of special education services to nearly 7 million disabled children.  The court found that the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) is a federal law that requires school districts to provide assistance to school districts in developing and executing educational programs for handicapped children. According to the court's order, IDEA requires that school districts identify and evaluate disabled children, and that parents and guardians bear the burden of proof. The court also found that, in 1997, the Department of Education and Montgomery County Public Schools System (MCPS) evaluated Brian and convened an IEP team that generated an initial IEP offering for Brian. The IEP ultimately failed, and the Schaffers were forced to send their child to a private school with a special learning center.  In 2004, the court ruled that the IEP should be placed on school districts, not the school district.  As a result of the court’s order, the district has been unable to obtain an injunction preventing it from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4)-8 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court order, MCPS and MCPS consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating these provisions. MCPS also agreed to pay $1.2 million in disgorgement and prejudgment interest, and to pay a civil penalty of $100,000.  MCPS agreed to settle the case against it by consenting to an injunction and to the issuance of an order permanently enjoining it from future violations of the federal securities laws. The settlement is subject to court approval. The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by J. D. Mauney, J. Graham, and C.J. Kerstetter of the SEC Enforcement Division's Cyber Unit. The litigation will be led by Mr. Strong and Ms. Karpel. The case is being supervised by Jennifer C. Barry.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit recently ruled that a North Carolina state court lacked jurisdiction to hear a wrongful death suit brought by the parents of two 13-year-old boys who died in a bus accident involving a defective tire manufactured in Turkey at the plant of a foreign subsidiary of The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company (Goodyear USA). The court held that the North Carolina court lacked the authority to hear the suit because the tire was manufactured and sold abroad and the controversy surrounding it was unrelated to any activity of the foreign subsidiary in the state. The court concluded that the case should be dismissed because the court had not established a sufficient connection between the controversy and the defendants' activities in North Carolina. The Court also found that the defendants had not shown that they were amenable to the jurisdiction of the state court. In a related case, the U.N. Supreme Court ruled in favor of a defense motion to dismiss the case on the basis that the court did not have jurisdiction over the defendants. The Supreme Court's decision was consistent with the decision of the U,S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina, which held that it had jurisdiction over Goodyear USA. The 4th Justices concluded that there was no basis for the court's dismissal of the suit. The case is now subject to review for compatibility with the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota ruled that Somalia could not be removed from the United States without the explicit, advance consent of that country's government. The Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed, holding that the law does not require the government of the destination country to consent to the removal of an alien. The Supreme Court ruled that the Constitution does not prohibit the government from removing an alien without the consent of the country it is removing. The high court held that the government's request for a temporary restraining order to prevent the removal would be granted if the government could show that the removal was necessary to protect the safety and welfare of the public. The court also held that it was not necessary for the government to show that removing the alien would be prejudicial to the safety or welfare of any of the other countries in which the alien was to be removed.

Title 36 U. S. C. § 110(a) grants the United States Olympic Committee (USOC) the exclusive right to prevent any person from using, without permission, the word "Olympic" in connection with any commercial enterprise relating to the Olympic Games, except where the use is in connection with an official Olympic Games program or is otherwise approved by the USOC. Respondents filed suit in Federal District Court seeking injunctions against petitioners for allegedly infringing § 110(a)'s exclusivity provisions by selling T-shirts, buttons, bumper stickers, and other items bearing the titles "Gay Olympic Games" and "San Francisco Gay Olympics." The District Court entered summary judgments for petitioners, holding that § 110(a) did not violate the free speech rights of respondents under the First Amendment. The Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that § 110(a) gave the USOC exclusive use of the word "Olympic" regardless of whether the use was likely to create confusion among consumers, and that the USOC's enforcement of its rights was discriminatory in violation of the Fifth Amendment. Held: 1. Section 110(a) does not violate the First Amendment. Pp. 10-18. (a) The language of § 110(a)-particularly the phrase "without permission"-indicates that the section is aimed at preventing commercial speech. However, the section's application to commercial speech is not broader than necessary to further a substantial governmental interest. Here, the restriction of § 110(a) on respondents' ability to market their products is justified by the USOC's goals of promoting the participation of American athletes in the Olympic Games and of fostering the Olympic ideal. Pp. 10-15. (b) While the USOC's right to prohibit use of the word "Olympic" in the promotion of athletic events is at the core of its legitimate property right, the fact that respondents claimed an expressive, rather than a purely commercial, purpose does not entitle them to assert a First Amendment defense. Pp. 15-16. (c) The USOC's enforcement of its rights is not discriminatory in violation of the Fifth Amendment. The USOC is not a governmental actor to whom the prohibitions of the Constitution apply. Its exclusive use of the word "Olympic" is not dispositive of this conclusion, since all enforceable trademark rights are created by some governmental act. And although the USOC received federal funds, the Government assumes no constitutional responsibility for the USOC's actions. Furthermore, the USOC's choice of how to enforce its exclusive right to use the word "Olympic" is not a governmental decision. Pp. 16-18. 2. Accordingly, the judgment below is affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was convicted of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 1425(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 14b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, alleges that, on June 6, 1966, James Meredith was shot and killed by a sniper in Mississippi.  According to the complaint, Meredith was among the victims of the sniper's actions.  As alleged, Meredith's death was the subject of an emergency action by the New York State Attorney General's Office, which obtained a temporary restraining order against the defendant and issued an order suspending him from appearing before the court.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against him.  On August 2, 2018, the U. S. District Judge in Manhattan issued a temporary injunction against further violations of the federal securities laws, ordering a preliminary injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and an officer-and-director bar.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of these provisions, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.   The judgment also prohibits him from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in connection with any offering of a security deposit or offering of any security deposit in the name of the security deposit company or any other security deposit that may be required to be obtained by the SEC.

The Supreme Court held that the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA) provides the exclusive avenue for judicial review when a federal employee challenges an adverse employment action by arguing that a federal statute is unconstitutional. The Court affirmed that the CSRA's comprehensive system for reviewing personnel actions against federal employees means that employees must follow the CSRA's procedures, which include administrative hearings and potential appeals to the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) and then to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.

The case involved former federal employees who were discharged for failing to comply with the Military Selective Service Act's registration requirement. They argued that the statute mandating their removal was unconstitutional. The MSPB administrative law judge dismissed their appeal for lack of jurisdiction, stating that the MSPB could not determine the constitutionality of statutes. The employees then filed suit in a district court, which the First Circuit Court of Appeals vacated, instructing the district court to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court reasoned that the CSRA's detailed framework indicates Congress's intent to preclude alternative judicial review outside of the CSRA scheme. The Court rejected the argument that district courts have jurisdiction over constitutional claims, noting that the CSRA does not exempt such claims from its exclusive review scheme. The Court also emphasized that allowing district court review would undermine the CSRA's goal of creating a uniform and efficient review process.

The Court concluded that the Federal Circuit, as an Article III court, is fully competent to adjudicate constitutional claims and that the CSRA provides mechanisms for developing the necessary factual record for such claims. The decision affirms that federal employees must use the CSRA's review process, even for constitutional challenges, and cannot seek review in district courts.

Respondent union, whose members worked exclusively in the plumbing and pipe fitting trades, entered into an agreement with petitioner builder requiring petitioner to subcontract work only to firms that had a contract with respondent. Petitioner sued in Federal District Court seeking declaratory relief and injunctive relief to prevent enforcement of the agreement, claiming that it violated §§ 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act. The District Court upheld the validity of the agreement under the "construction-industry" proviso to § 8 (e) of the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), which permits "agreements . ..between a labor organization and an employer in the construction industry relating to the contracting or subcontracting of work to be done at the site of the construction, alteration, painting, or repair of a building, structure or other work." The Court of Appeals reversed, finding that the provision came within the "exclusive jurisdiction" of the National Labor Relations Board. Held: 1. The agreement between respondent and petitioner is subject to the federal antitrust laws. Pp. 108-116. (a) Though respondent's goal was to organize as many subcontractors as possible, the methods chosen are not immune from antitrust sanctions merely because the goal is legal. Here, where the union directly restrained the business market by making nonunion subcontractors ineligible to compete for a portion of the available work, the restraint contravened antitrust policies to a degree not justified by congressional labor policy. Pp. 108-112. (b) The construction-industry proviso does not allow this type of agreement. Its authorization extends only to agreements in the context of collective-bargaining relationships and in light of congressional references to the Denver Building Trades problem, possibly to common-situs relationships on particular jobsites as well. Pp. 112-116. (c) Whatever significance the legislative history of the 1947 Taft-Hartley Amendments has for antitrust suits based on "hot cargo" agreements outlawed in 1959, it has no relevance to the question whether Congress meant to preclude antitrust suits based on such agreements. Pp. 116-117. 2. However, the fact that the agreement is subject to the federal antitrust laws does not mean that state antitrust laws may apply as well. Because the use of state antitrust laws to regulate union activities in aid of organization creates a substantial risk of conflict with policies central to federal labor law, federal law does not admit the use of state antitrust laws to regulate union activity that is closely related to organizational goals. Pp. 117-119. 3. Since the issue whether the agreement violated the Sherman Act was not briefed and argued fully in this Court, the case is remanded for consideration of that issue. P. 119. 483 F. 2d 1158, affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded.

Petitioners, Negro employees of respondent company, filed suit challenging the validity of certain employment requirements imposed by the company after passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. They alleged that the requirements resulted in substantial disparate impact on Negroes and violated Title VII of the Act. A threejudge District Court upheld the constitutionality of the requirements. The Court of Appeals reversed in pertinent part, concluding that since there was no showing of a racially discriminatory purpose in adopting the requirements, they were permissible absent proof that they were "job related." Held: An employer is prohibited by Title VII of the Act from imposing educational or intellectual ability requirements as conditions of employment in or transfer to jobs when (a) neither requirement is shown to be significantly related to successful job performance, (b) both requirements operate to disqualify Negroes at a substantially higher rate than white applicants, and (c) the jobs in question formerly had been filled only by white employees as part of a longstanding practice of giving preference to whites. Pp. 108-116. (a) While the Act requires that the posture and condition of the job-seeker be taken into account, it does not command that any person be hired simply because he was formerly the subject of discrimination, or because he is a member of a minority group. Pp. 110-111. (b) Here, neither the high school completion requirement nor the general intelligence test is shown to bear a demonstrable relationship to successful performance of the jobs for which it was used. Pp. 111-112. (c) Good faith or absence of discriminatory intent does not redeem employment procedures or testing mechanisms that operate as built-in headwinds for minority groups and are unrelated to measuring job capability. P. 112. (d) Section 703 (h), providing that nothing in Title VII shall invalidate any employment practice that is based on "ability," applies only to those abilities that are genuinely related to job performance. Pp. 112-115. 420 F. 2d 1225, reversed in part.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Kentucky today announced that it has filed a civil injunctive action against Jose Padilla, a convicted felon who was sentenced to prison for a drug-related felony.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Kentucky, alleges that, from 1917 forward, Padilla relied on his counsel’s erroneous advice when he pleaded guilty to the transportation of a large amount of marijuana in his tractor-trailer in the Commonwealth of Kentucky.  According to the complaint, the counsel failed to advise Padilla about the potential consequences of his guilty plea, and instead provided him false assurance that his conviction would not result in his removal from the country.  In addition, the complaint alleges that Padilla failed to inform Padilla of the risks of his impending deportation.  Padilla has agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, the Honorable Joseph G. Sansone of the United States District Court for the Northern District of New York has issued a temporary restraining order and issued an order temporarily suspending the issuance of the order.  On May 2, 2019, the U. S. District Court entered a final order permanently enjoining Padilla from future violations of the federal securities laws, ordering him to comply with the court order, and imposing a $2,000 civil penalty against him.  Separately, on May 9, 2018, the Court issued an Order suspending the issuing of the Order, ordering Padilla to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil monetary penalty.  It also ordered Padilla and Sansone to pay civil penalties in the amount of $3,000 each.

The Supreme Court case involves Robert Sindermann, a former professor at Odessa Junior College in Texas, who claimed his contract was not renewed in retaliation for his public criticism of the college administration, violating his First and Fourteenth Amendment rights. Sindermann also argued that the college's failure to provide a hearing on the nonrenewal violated his right to procedural due process.

The Supreme Court held that the lack of a formal tenure or contractual right to re-employment does not defeat Sindermann's free speech claim. The Court emphasized that the government cannot deny a benefit, such as employment, on grounds that infringe upon constitutionally protected interests, particularly freedom of speech. The Court found that Sindermann presented a bona fide constitutional claim, as public criticism by a teacher on matters of public concern may be protected speech.

Regarding the procedural due process claim, the Court stated that while Sindermann's lack of formal tenure is relevant, it is not necessarily dispositive. The Court referenced its decision in Board of Regents v. Roth, which established that a hearing is not required for nonrenewal of a nontenured teacher's contract unless there is a deprivation of a liberty or property interest. Sindermann alleged that there was an implied tenure system at the college, based on policies and understandings, which could constitute a property interest deserving of due process protection.

The Supreme Court agreed with the Court of Appeals that Sindermann should have the opportunity to prove his entitlement to continued employment and, if successful, to a hearing on the nonrenewal of his contract. The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, remanding the case to the District Court for further proceedings. Justice Powell did not participate in the decision.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California today entered a final judgment in favor of a California-based three-strike sentencing law that imposes a 25-year prison sentence on repeat offenders.  The court's order, which was entered on March 5, 2003, finds that California's three strikes sentencing law is grossly disproportionate to the amount of time a recidivist offender has already served in prison.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Los Angeles, California, Richard Ewing was convicted of felony grand theft and sentenced to 25 years to life. The SEC alleges that Ewing's sentence was disproportionate because he had been previously convicted of two serious or violent felonies and had served only half of his most recent sentence. Ewing also had a prior felony conviction for felony burglary.  As alleged in the complaint, Ewing had a long criminal history that included at least two prior felony convictions, and had been on probation for at least 16 years.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Ewing, charging him with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and the mandatory minimum sentencing provisions of Sections 5(a) and 5(c).  The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by David M. Porter, Karyn H. Bucur, and Mark E. KENNEDY of the Los Angeles Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Kelly L. Gibson and supervised by Amy C. Welshhans. The case is being supervised by Sanjay Wadhwa.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

In this Supreme Court case, a group of African American residents from Chicago, Illinois, filed a lawsuit in federal court against various city and county officials. They sought a judgment to prevent the enforcement of certain Illinois statutes and Chicago ordinances, arguing that these laws violated the Federal Constitution. Specifically, they claimed that the laws in question were being used to intimidate and harass members of the African American community, infringing upon their First Amendment rights.

The plaintiffs challenged the constitutionality of statutes related to mob action, resisting arrest, aggravated assault, aggravated battery, and intimidation. They also alleged that some plaintiffs had been arrested under these statutes and were facing ongoing prosecutions in state courts. They requested the establishment of a three-judge federal court to declare the statutes unconstitutional and to issue injunctions against their enforcement.

The defendants, which included city and county officials, opposed the formation of a three-judge court and the issuance of an injunction. They argued that the plaintiffs already had an adequate legal remedy through the state court system where they could challenge the constitutionality of the statutes. Additionally, they contended that the federal court was barred from interfering with state court proceedings and that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated a credible threat of prosecution or irreparable harm.

A single federal district judge rejected the defendants' motion to dismiss and convened a three-judge court, which upheld most of the challenged statutes. However, it found two subsections—one from the mob-action statute and one from the intimidation statute—to be overly broad and unconstitutional. The court issued an injunction against the enforcement of these two subsections.

The Supreme Court, in reviewing the case, found that the plaintiffs' allegations did not demonstrate any irreparable injury from the enforcement of the intimidation statute or from other actions by state or city officials. The Court noted that none of the plaintiffs had been prosecuted or arrested under the specific intimidation statute that was declared unconstitutional. The complaint was seen as speculative about potential future prosecutions rather than based on concrete threats or actions.

The Supreme Court's decision was influenced by its rulings in Younger v. Harris and Samuels v. Mackell, which emphasized the principle of non-interference by federal courts in state law enforcement unless there is a clear and immediate constitutional issue at stake. The Court reversed the lower court's decision and remanded the case, effectively upholding the enforcement of the intimidation statute and reinforcing the longstanding policy against federal court intervention in state criminal proceedings. Justice Brennan, Justice White, and Justice Marshall concurred with the result.

In this case, the United States sought to condemn certain property owned by respondents for the construction of a dam and reservoir. The parties reached an agreement allowing the United States to have temporary possession of the property while the validity of the respondents' mining claims was determined through administrative proceedings. However, the United States later filed a lawsuit challenging the validity of the mining claims. The lower courts held that the United States could only challenge the mining claims through the administrative process established by Congress. The Supreme Court disagreed, ruling that the United States was entitled to pursue both the administrative and judicial processes simultaneously.

These two actions were brought by petitioners claiming the property-tax exemption provided by Art. XIII, § 11/2, of the California Constitution for realty and buildings used solely and exclusively for religious worship. In both instances, the assessors had denied such exemptions on the ground that the applicants had failed to comply with an oath required by § 19 of Art. XX of the State Constitution and § 32 of the Revenue and Taxation Code that they would not advocate the overthrow of the Governments of the United States and of California by force or violence or other unlawful means nor advocate the support of a foreign government against the United States in the event of hostilities. Held: Enforcement of § 19 of Art. XX of the State Constitution through procedures which place the burden of proof and persuasion upon the taxpayers is repugnant to due process; and the judgment sustaining its validity must be reversed. Speiser v. Randall, ante, p. 513. Pp. 530-531. Reversed and cause remanded.

This case involves a challenge to a guilty plea entered by a prisoner named Alford in a North Carolina court. The plaintiff alleges that the plea was obtained through coercion and fraud, specifically due to threats of the death penalty. The defendant argues that the plea was voluntary and well-advised given the strength of the evidence against him. The Supreme Court ultimately rules in favor of the defendant, holding that the plea was not obtained through coercion or fraud and was thus valid.

The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals in the case concerning Richard Irizarry, who was sentenced to a term of imprisonment longer than the range recommended by the Federal Sentencing Guidelines. The central issue was whether Rule 32(h) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which requires notice before a court can depart from the sentencing range on a ground not identified in the presentence report or prehearing submission, applies to sentences that are variances rather than departures as originally understood.

The Court held that Rule 32(h) does not apply to variances from the Guidelines range. This decision is based on the fact that the Guidelines are now advisory, not mandatory, following the Supreme Court's decision in United States v. Booker. As a result, the expectation that a sentence will fall within the Guidelines range no longer exists, and the due process concerns that motivated the notice requirement in Burns v. United States are no longer applicable.

The Court reasoned that sentencing is a dynamic process, and requiring notice for variances could lead to unnecessary delays. It was noted that competent lawyers should generally anticipate the factors that might influence a sentence. The Court suggested that if a party is surprised in a way that is prejudicial, the appropriate response is for the judge to consider granting a continuance, rather than extending the notice requirement to all variances.

The opinion emphasizes that district judges and counsel should ensure that all relevant matters are considered before making a final sentencing decision, and that Rule 32's other procedural protections are sufficient to ensure a fair sentencing process.

The implications of this decision are that courts are not required to give notice of variances from the Guidelines range, and that the parties should be prepared to address a wide range of issues at the sentencing hearing. This ruling aims to streamline the sentencing process while still allowing for adequate opportunity to debate relevant sentencing issues.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California today entered a final judgment against a group of individuals and companies charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 5(b) of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed on March 10, 1964, a federal district court in the District of Utah issued an order suspending the running of a federal class action.  The complaint alleges that the defendants combined and conspired together in restraint of trade in steel and concrete pipe by submitting collusive and rigged bids for the sale of such pipe and by dividing and allocating business among themselves.  As alleged in the complaint, the defendants failed to meet the prerequisites to a class action and instead engaged in a "one-way intervention" to prevent the class action from arising.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  On March 24, 2016, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against a number of defendants, including the defendants in Utah, alleging that they had conspired to rig prices for concrete and steel pipe in violation of § 1 of the Sherman Act.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Defendants consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from participating in any class action that is not subject to the federal statute of limitations, and orders Defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $100,000.  Defendants have also agreed to be permanently enjoined from future securities law violations.

This case involves a challenge to the validity of a "less-than-unanimous" jury verdict in a criminal case in Oregon. The petitioners, who were found guilty of various felonies, claimed that their convictions violated their right to trial by jury under the Sixth and Fourth Amendments. The court ruled in favor of the state, holding that the Sixth Amendment does not require unanimous jury verdicts and that the requirement of unanimity is not mandated by the Fourteenth Amendment's provisions regarding equal protection and fairness.

Title IV of the Social Security Act authorizes a parent to sue for child support and visitation rights, and requires the nonparent to bear the burden of proof. Here, petitioner EJ sued respondent AL for child support and visitation rights, claiming he was the father of her minor son. At the trial, AL used nine of his 10 peremptory challenges to strike virtually all the males from the jury pool, leaving only four men and eight women. He won the case, and the judge entered judgment against EJ. His appeal was dismissed by the trial court, but the appellate court reversed, holding that AL's peremptory challenges violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. That court concluded that gender-based peremptory challenges are constitutionally permissible unless they are intended to eliminate jurors because of their gender. Held: Litigants may not strike potential jurors solely on the basis of gender. Pp. 48-58. (a) While gender-based classifications receive heightened scrutiny under equal protection principles, the only question here is whether discrimination on the basis of gender in jury selection substantially furthers the State's legitimate interest in securing a fair and impartial trial. In making this assessment, the Court considers whether peremptory challenges based on gender stereotypes provide substantial aid to a litigant's effort to secure a fair and impartial jury. Far from providing an exceptional justification for its gender-based peremptory challenges, AL offered virtually no support for the conclusion that gender alone is an accurate predictor of juror's attitudes. Its rationale, not unlike those regularly expressed for gender-based strikes, assumes that gross generalizations that would be deemed impermissible if made on the basis of race are somehow permissible when made on the basis of gender. Moreover, striking individual jurors on the assumption that they hold particular views simply because of their gender is practically a brand upon them, affixed by law, an assertion of their inferiority. Such discrimination denigrates the dignity of the excluded juror, and, for a woman, reinvokes a history of exclusion from political participation. Finally, the message sent to all those in the courtroom and all those who may later learn of the discriminatory act is that certain individuals, for no reason other than gender, are presumed unqualified by state actors to decide important questions upon which reasonable people could disagree. Pp. 48-54. (b) Although the Court's conclusion does not imply the elimination of all peremptory challenges, it conflicts with nothing in Batson v. Kentucky, 476 U. S. 98, which established that peremptory challenges may not be used to exclude prospective jurors because of their race. Nor does it conflict with a State's legitimate interest in using such challenges in its efforts to secure a fair and impartial jury. If conducted properly, voir dire can inform litigants about potential jurors, making reliance upon stereotypical and pejorative notions about a particular gender or race both unnecessary and unwise. Voir dire provides a means of discovering actual or implied bias and a firmer basis upon which the parties may exercise their peremptory challenges intelligently. The experience in the many jurisdictions that have barred gender-based challenges belies the claim that litigants and trial courts are incapable of complying with a rule barring strikes based on gender. As with race-based Batson claims, a party alleging gender discrimination must make a prima facie showing of intentional discrimination before the party exercising the challenge is required to explain the basis for the strike. When an explanation is required, it need not rise to the level of a "for cause" challenge; rather, it merely must be based on a juror characteristic other than gender, and the proffered explanation may not be pretextual. Failure to provide jurors the same protection against gender discrimination as race discrimination could frustrate the purpose of Batson itself. Because gender and race are overlapping categories, gender can be used as a pretext for racial discrimination. Allowing parties to remove racial minorities from the jury not because of their race, but because of their gender, contravene well-established equal protection principles and could insulate effectively racial discrimination from judicial scrutiny. Pp. 54-58. Reversed and remanded.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit granted certiorari to re-examine the constitutionality of certain provisions of the federal wagering tax statutes. The issues in this case involve the registration and payment of a tax imposed by the federal government on those engaged in the business of accepting wagers. Section 4401 of Title 26 imposes a 10% excise tax on the gross amount of all wagers accepted, including the value of bets purchased in lotteries conducted for profit. Section 4412 requires those liable for the occupational tax to register each year with the director of their local internal revenue district. The registrants must submit Internal Revenue Service Form 11—C,2 and upon it must indicate whether they are engaged in a business of taking wagers, and must list the names and addresses of their agents and employees. The registration process is essentially inseparable from the payment of the tax. The court held that the registration provisions violate the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination. The Second Circuit's decision in Kahriger v. United States was consistent with that finding, and the court granted a rehearing on the issue of whether these provisions should be employed to punish those who have defended a failure to comply with their requirements with a proper assertion of the privilege. We conclude that these provisions are not necessary to punish persons who have not complied with their obligations. The issue is not whether the United States may tax activities which a State or Congress has declared unlawful. The Court has repeatedly indicated that the unlawfulness of an acivity does not prevent its taxation, and nothing that follows is intended to limit or diminish the vitality of those cases.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Georgia today entered a final judgment against a former Georgia prison inmate who, at all relevant times, was housed at the Georgia State Prison in Reidsville, Ga.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against a previously convicted felon for his alleged violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the SEC's complaint, Tony Goodman, a paraplegic inmate in the state prison system, was incarcerated for 23-to-24 hours per day in a 12-by-3-foot cell in which he could not turn his wheelchair around.  As alleged in the complaint, Goodman alleges that the lack of accessible facilities rendered him unable to transfer from his wheelchair to the shower or toilet on his own, and, on several occasions, he had been forced to sit in his own feces and urine while prison officials refused to assist him in cleaning up the waste.  In addition, the complaint alleges that Goodman had been denied physical therapy and medical treatment, and denied access to the toilet and toilet.
