The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) charged respondent O'Hagan with violating §10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 by using for his own trading purposes material, nonpublic information regarding a potential tender offer for the common stock of petitioner Pillsbury Co. (Pillsbury), a Minneapolis, Minn.-based corporation. The SEC alleged that, in violation of §10 (b) of the Exchange Act, he defrauded his law firm and its client, Grand Met, by using nonpublic, non-public information about the tender offer to conceal his previous embezzlement and conversion of unrelated client trust funds. The court held that the misappropriation theory was not moored to Rule 10 (b)'s requirement that "the fraud be "in connection with the purchase or sale of any security." Held: 1. Under §10'b, a person who trades in securities for personal profit, using confidential information misappropriated in breach of a fiduciary duty to the source of the information, must be convicted of violating Rule 14e-3(a). Pp. 5-11. (a) The misappropriations theory is not mooved to §10's requirement that the fraud be in connection with a tender offer, since the fraud is "in relation with" a securities transaction, and the rule does not require a showing that the trading at issue entailed a breach of fiduciar duty. P. 5. 2. In determining whether §10"b"s "disclose or abstain from trading" requirement is reasonably designed to prevent fraudulent acts, the court must accord the Commission's assessment "controlling weight unless [it is] arbitrary, capricious, or manifestly contrary to the statute." Batterton v. Francis, 432 U. S. 416, 424-426, distinguished. Id., at 627-628. The Eighth Circuit erred in holding that the "misappropriation" theory is a proper exercise of §14(e)'s rulemaking authority because the rule contains no breach of duty requirement, and that the SEC did not exceed its Rulemaking authority when it adopted Rule 14(e) without requiring proof of a breach-of-federal-fiduciary-duty requirement. Id. At 627, the Eighth Circuit held that §10 "was not a general duty between the shareholders of a corporation and those insiders who have obtained confidential information by reason of their position with that corporation," and that, by covering pre-offer conduct, the rule would be a virtual nullity were the SEC not permitted to go beyond common law fraud. Held: (1) That §10’b’s “disclose and abstain” requirement is not inconsistent with §10, since it requires neither misrepresentation nor nondisclosure, and thus could not stand once the securities fraud convictions were reversed. The rule “does not require” a showing of a violation of the securities laws, see, e. g., §14e3(b), and thus cannot be read to foreclose that theory. Pb. 527-627. (2) That the rule is not "inapplicable” to indictments for violations of §§10“b” and Rule “10” does not mean that the regulation is a “deceptive device or contrivance” used “in connection . . . with” securities trading, see id., at 739-747, or that it is a "means reasonably designed” violation of Rule 10 “b.” P. 627. (3) The rule is also well-tuned to an animating purpose of the Act: to insure honest securities markets and thereby promote investor confidence. See, for example, that misappropriators, as the Government describes them, deal in deception. A misappropriator who trades on the basis of material,nonpublic information gains his advantageous market position through deception; he deceives the source and simultaneously harms members of the investing public. See Aldave, 13 Hofstra L. Rev. 101, 119. The misequation theory, as applied to cases of this genre, qualifies under §10 “as a ‘means reasonable designed’ to prevent’ fraudulent trading on material,Nonpublic information in the tender-offer context. P p. 629. 92 F. 3d 933, reversed and remanded.

Respondent Southern Railway challenged the validity of the Interstate Commerce Commission's order allocating to respondents a smaller percentage of the revenues from joint rates than would be justified by their respective shares of the expenditures made in providing the joint service. Both parties used Rail Form A, a rail freight formula for determining freight service costs, which utilizes the expenses and statistics for a given year as reported to the Commission by the carriers and supplemented by special studies of the carriers. The Commission found that the existing divisions violated § 15 (6) of the Interstate Commerce Act because they allocated to Northern lines a lesser share of the revenues from the joint rates than would be warranted by their share of the expenditures made in providing the joint service. To correct this, the Commission shifted the revenues resulting from the new divisions so as to give the Northern lines an overall increase in revenues from the traffic involved of 3.5%, and reduce the revenues of the Southern lines by about 3%. When petitioner Northern Railway intervened as a defendant, the District Court set aside the Commission's order, holding that it was not supported by substantial evidence and reasoned findings within the meaning of §§ 8 (b) and 10 (e) of the Administrative Procedure Act. Held: 1. Where the costs of North-South traffic are not isolated in the Commission's findings, the use of "unsifted" averages of costs does not necessarily establish greater costs either in rate cases or in divisioh cases. Pp. 356-357. 2. Territorial average costs do not necessarily represent the costs of North-South traffic. Pp. 357-358. 3. Mathematical exactness in dividing each rate of each carrier is not necessary, because practical necessities demand otherwise. P. 358. 4. Though precision and exactitude in the mathematical sense are not possible, the nature and volume of the traffic in question must be known and exposed if the costs of other traffic are to govern a division of rates. P. 358. 5. Where Rail Form A costs are shown to be a distortion when applied to the particular traffic over which the disputes arise, some effort must be exerted to make an adjustment which fairly reflects the differences in costs or to make clear that there is in fact no basic, material difference. P. 358. 6. Specific findings must be made on the several items of so-called "adjustment" of average territorial costs here involved. Pp. 358-360. 7. Costs related solely to commuter service in the North can be determined. P. 359. 8. Since the Commission allowed the Northern line a border interchange cost that is 58% higher than the one allowed the Southern line, despite evidence that the interchange operations performed by the Northern line were no more costly than those performed by the Southern line, the Commission erred in relying solely on its expertise to conclude that no difference meant a substantial difference. P. 359. 9. Higher costs of Northern lines result from the Commission's use of higher northern territorial average empty return ratios, which were not shown to be applicable to North-South traffic. P. 360. 270 F. Supp. 695, affirmed as modified.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland has ruled that members of Westboro Baptist Church can't be held liable for picketing at a soldier's funeral. The church's members picketed the funeral of a Marine who was killed in Iraq in the line of duty. The court found that the church members' actions caused the Marine's father, Matthew Snyder, to suffer severe emotional distress and exacerbated pre-existing health conditions. Snyder sued the church and its members, claiming that the picketing violated his son's civil rights and caused him to suffer emotional distress. The jury found in favor of Snyder, awarding him $2.9 million in compensatory damages and $8 million in punitive damages. The Court ruled that the First Amendment protects the church from liability for its speech. The ruling could have a significant impact on the protection of religious freedom in the United States.

Petitioner was convicted of violating a Pennsylvania statute prohibiting the operation of a hazardous waste facility without a permit. After his conviction became final, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court interpreted the statute for the first time, and made clear that Fiore's conduct was not within its scope. The Pennsylvania courts refused to grant Fiore collateral relief. The Federal District Court granted certiorari in part to decide when, or whether, the Federal Due Process Clause requires a State to apply a new interpretation of a state criminal statute retroactively to cases on collateral review. In order to determine if that question was in fact presented, this case asked the Pennsylvania State Supreme Court whether its decision interpreting the statute not to apply to conduct like Fiore did not apply to Fiore, and whether it was, instead, a correct statement of the law when Fiore was convicted. The court's reply specifies that the interpretation of §6018.401(a) set out in Scarpone "merely clarified" the statute and was the law of Pennsylvania-as properly interpreted-at the time of Fiore’s conviction. Respondent, who was unsuccessful in his subsequent state-court attempts to have his own conviction set aside, agreed that the Commonwealth presented no evidence whatsoever to prove that basic element. To the contrary, the Commonwealth concedes that it did not prove Fiore failed to possess one. The Court also concedes that the statute made it unlawful to operate a facility with a permit; one who deviated from his permit's terms was not a person without permit; hence, a person who deviate from his permits did not violate the statute. Reversing the contrary judgment of the Third Circuit and remanding the case for proceedings consistent with this opinion.

In March 1999, a federal grand jury returned a 20-count indictment charging petitioners and five codefendants with conspiracy to launder money, in violation of 18 U. S. C. § 1956 (h). The indictment described, in general terms, the "manner and means" used to accomplish the objects of the money laundering conspiracy, but did not charge the defendants with the commission of any overt act in furtherance thereof. At trial, the Government presented evidence that petitioners were members of the executive board of an entity known as Greater Ministries International Church (GMIC), which operated a "gifting" program that took in more than $400 million between 1996 and 1999. Most of these claims were false. GMIC made none of the promised investments, had no assets, and gave virtually nothing to charity. Many participants in GMIC's program received little or no return on their money, and their investments indeed largely turned out to be "gifts" to GMIC representatives. Petitioners then asked the District Court to instruct the jury that the Government was required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that at least one of the co-conspirators had committed an overt act. The court denied that request, and the jury returned the verdict of guilty. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed petitioners' convictions, holding, in relevant part, that the jury instructions approved by the district court were proper because § 1956(h) does not require proof of a overt act to obtain a conviction. The Court of Appeals noted that some of its sister Circuits had taken the opposite position, and concluded that those decisions were erroneously based on case law interpreting the general conspiracy statute, which expressly includes an overt-act requirement. Held: 1. The drug conspiracy statute in § 1956 does not need proof of an overt acts to obtain conviction. Pp. 5-11. (a) The drug-conspiracy statute in Shabani, which, unlike § 1956-h), supersedes the common-law rule by expressly including an overtact requirement, is "nearly identical," and the language of § 1956--which, in light of this longstanding rule--does not establish a new conspiracy offense; rather, they say, it merely increases the penalty for conviction of a money-laundering conspiracy under § 371. P. 5. (b) Petitioners' legislative history argument is particularly inapt here, since Congress is presumed to have knowledge of the governing rule described in Shabbani. While Shaban was decided two years after § 1956 was enacted, the rule it articulated was established decades earlier in Nash and Singer. These decisions establish a "formulary" that provides clear and predictable guidance to Congress. As the Government points out, Congress has included an express overt-Act requirement in at least 22 other current conspiracy statutes, clearly demonstrating that it knows how to impose such a requirement when it wishes to do so. Where Congress has chosen not to do, we will not override that choice based on vague and ambiguous signals from legislative history. P p. 5-'11. 2. The rule that governed shabani is inapplicable here, because the text of §56(h)'s authorization of venue in a district where the overt act took place cannot be taken to indicate that Congress deemed such an act necessary for conviction under § 1956. Instead, Congress appears merely to have confirmed the availability of this alternative venue option in money laundering conspiracies. The fact that the statute's text makes clear that Congress did so precisely by establishing a new offense does not make it untenable for two principal reasons. First, petitioners concede that the text does not expressly make the Commission of an " overt act" an element of the conspiracy offense, but that Congress need not prove such a act. Second, they argue that the provision serves to supplement, rather than supplant, the default venue rule: "Unless a statute or these rules permit otherwise, the government must prosecute an offense in a District where the offense was committed." Fed. Rule Crim. Proc. 18. Nor do they find it significant that Congress chose to label § 1956 a "penalty" rather than an "offense" provision. See, e. g., United States v. Wells, 519 U.S. 482, 496-497. Finally, the legislative history argues that Congress' decision to place a qualitatively different conspiracy offense provision in a separate subsection is untenable because it fails to support the contention that § 1956's language is plain and unambiguous, and that, if Congress had wanted to enact an additional overt act provision, it would have titled it accordingly. The legislative history also shows that Congress intended § 1956 to increase the penalties for money laundering conspiracies, but it did so only by establishing the new offense. Moreover, the history does not show that Congress would have placed it with the other offenses in its own separate subsection. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed a lower court's decision that Texaco Inc. and Shell Oil Co. had violated the Sherman Act by agreeing to a single price for both Texaco and Shell oil brand gasoline. The court found that the agreement did not violate the law's antitrust provisions because the parties did not engage in unlawful price fixing. The Court also found that there was no evidence that the price fixing was anticompetitive. The lower court had previously found that, by pooling their resources and sharing profits, the companies had violated Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The appeals court held that the lower court misapplied the law by failing to apply the rule of reason, which requires plaintiffs to show that a particular contract or combination is in fact unreasonable and anticompetitive before it will be found unlawful. Without a finding that price fixing is unlawful, the appeals court concluded that the parties had not violated the law. The Supreme Court of the United States has not yet issued a decision on the issue of whether price fixing in a joint venture is per se illegal. The case will be decided by the full appeals court at a later date.

In a petitory action in a Louisiana state court against respondent-mineral-lessees of the United States, a suit by one out of possession claiming title to, and possession of, immovables, petitioner sought to have itself declared owner of the mineral rights under land owned by the Government, and it also sought an accounting for oil and other minerals removed by respondent lessees under their lease from the Government. The United States brought an action in the District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, seeking a preliminary injunction to restrain petitioner from prosecuting its action in that court. The state trial court found that a cause of action had been stated, and overruled the exceptions. Held: The District Court properly exercised its jurisdiction to entertain the suit in the federal court and to prevent the effectuation of state court proceedings that might conflict with the ultimate federal court judgment. Pp. 531-532. (a) Where questions of constitutionality are involved-and the Government contends that an application of the state statute adverse to its interests would be unconstitutional-our rule has been precisely the opposite: "as questions of federal constitutional power have become more and more intertwined with preliminary doubts about local law, we have insisted that federal courts do not decide such questions on the basis of preliminary guesses regarding local law." Spector Motor Service v. McLaughlin, 323 U. S. 101, 105; Stainback v. Mo Hock Ke Lok Po, 336 U.S. 368, 383, 383; Railroad Commission of Texas v. Pullman Co., 312 US. 496, 498-502, 644-502. P. 532. 224 F. 2d 381, affirmed.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the case of a respondent convicted of murdering his wife, where a key piece of evidence was a recorded conversation between the respondent and an insurance agent, Ray Travers. The respondent argued that the recording was an involuntary confession and should not have been admitted as evidence. The California Supreme Court rejected this argument, finding no coercion or inducement in the conversation, and affirmed the conviction.

Years later, the respondent sought habeas corpus relief, claiming that subsequent Supreme Court decisions established the recording's introduction as unconstitutional. The District Court agreed that the state trial court had not reliably determined the voluntariness of the confession due to excluded evidence and granted relief. The Court of Appeals affirmed this decision.

The Supreme Court, however, reversed the lower courts' decisions. It emphasized that the respondent's trial predated the Escobedo and Miranda decisions, which were not retroactively applied, and that the due process standard of voluntariness governed the admissibility of the statement. The Court found that the California courts had applied the correct constitutional criteria and had assumed the truth of the respondent's version of the facts. The Court concluded that the respondent's allegations, even if true, would not establish that the confession was involuntary.

The Supreme Court's opinion clarified that the respondent was not entitled to a new hearing on the voluntariness issue merely because of procedural shortcomings in the state court. The Court held that the California courts had given full consideration to the issue and had correctly determined the admissibility of the respondent's statement. Therefore, the judgment of the lower federal courts was reversed, upholding the original conviction.

The Supreme Court ruled that the Federal Boating Safety Act (FBSA) does not preempt state common-law tort claims related to defectively designed motorboats. The majority opinion focused on the text of the FBSA, including the express pre-emption clause and the savings clause, as well as historical precedents and congressional intent. The majority determined that the express pre-emption clause applied only to state or local laws or regulations, while the savings clause preserved liability at common law or under state law. The majority also noted that the Coast Guard's decision not to regulate propeller guards did not constitute an explicit pre-emption of state common-law claims. Finally, the majority distinguished the situation in this case from previous decisions upholding pre-emption in similar situations due to differences in the nature of the regulations being challenged and the interests served by the FBSA.

Appellee, a Minnesota corporation, had a written pension plan covering its employees, including a provision that the plan should be funded through contributions by the employer. When appellee decided to close its Minnesota office, it paid off its pension obligations to those employees who had received pensions under the plan. However, pursuant to the Minnesota Private Pension Benefits Protection Act, which requires private employers having at least 100 employees, at least one of whom works in Minnesota, and who have established voluntary private pension plans, qualified under § 401 of the Internal Revenue Code, to purchase deferred annuity contracts to fund future pension benefits whenever the employer terminates his pension plan or closes his office in Minnesota, appellee was assessed a penalty of over $185,000. Held: Application of the Act to appellee constituted a violation of the Contract Clause of the Federal Constitution. Pp. 408-416. (a) If the Contract Clause is to retain any meaning at all, it must be understood to impose some limits upon the power of a State to abrogate existing contractual relationships, even in the exercise of its otherwise legitimate police power. Pp. 408-411. (b) Here, the Act nullifies express terms of appellee's contractual obligations and imposes a completely unexpected liability in potentially disabling amounts. Moreover, there is no showing in the record that this severe disruption of contractual expectations was necessary to meet an important general social problem. Pp. 411-414. (c) Whether or not the Act was aimed largely at appellee, it clearly has an extremely narrow focus, applying only to certain private employers who have established voluntary private pension plans, qualified under § 401 of the Internal Revenue Code, and who close their Minnesota office or terminate their pension plan. Pp. 414-415. (d) Entering a field it had never before sought to regulate, the Minnesota Legislature grossly distorted appellee's existing contractual relationships with its employees by superimposing retroactive obligations upon the company substantially beyond the terms of its employment contracts. Pp. 415-416. Reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit granted clemency to Leonel Torres Herrera, who was sentenced to death for the 1982 murder of a Texas police officer. The court ruled that Herrera's "actual innocence" in the murder of Officer Enrique Carrisalez was not sufficient to grant a new trial. The Court also ruled that the trial judge should not have allowed the testimony of two men who identified Herrera as the shooter. The 5th Court's decision is consistent with the decisions of the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals and the Texas District Court for the Western District of Texas.

The Supreme Court was tasked with evaluating the constitutionality of mandatory maternity leave rules for public school teachers in Cleveland, Ohio, and Chesterfield County, Virginia. The rules required pregnant teachers to take unpaid leave starting several months before their expected delivery date and placed restrictions on when they could return to work postpartum.

The Court recognized that personal choice in matters of family life is protected by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. It found that the mandatory leave rules imposed an undue burden on the teachers' constitutional liberties by using arbitrary cutoff dates for when leave must begin, without considering individual circumstances or the actual ability of the teachers to continue working.

The Court determined that while continuity of instruction and ensuring physically capable teachers are legitimate goals, the rules in question did not have a rational relationship to these objectives. The rules were deemed to be based on irrebuttable presumptions of physical incapacity due to pregnancy, which violated due process because they did not allow for individualized assessments of the teachers' fitness to work.

The Court also examined the rules regarding eligibility to return to work after childbirth. It found that the Cleveland rule, which required a teacher to wait until her child was three months old before returning, was arbitrary and unconstitutional. However, the Chesterfield County rule, which allowed teachers to return upon providing a medical certificate and guaranteed re-employment no later than the start of the next school year, was found to be constitutionally sound.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment in the Cleveland case (No. 72—777), finding the mandatory termination provisions and the three-month return rule unconstitutional. In the Chesterfield County case (No. 72—1129), the judgment was reversed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion, as the return rule was found to be constitutional.

In the case of Wanda Krupski vs. Costa Crociere S.p.A., the Supreme Court addressed the issue of when an amended complaint "relates back" to the date of the original complaint under Rule 15(c) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. This is significant when the amended complaint is filed after the statute of limitations has expired but seeks to correct a mistake concerning the identity of the proper party to be sued.

Krupski had initially filed a negligence lawsuit against Costa Cruise, believing it to be the operator of the cruise ship where she was injured. However, the actual operator was Costa Crociere, a related but distinct entity. After learning of her mistake, Krupski sought to amend her complaint to include Costa Crociere, but by this time, the statute of limitations had expired.

The Court of Appeals had denied the relation back of the amended complaint, arguing that Krupski should have known the correct party to sue based on the information in her possession, and that she had unduly delayed in seeking to amend her complaint.

The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the relation back under Rule 15(c)(1)(C) depends on what the party to be added (Costa Crociere) knew or should have known, not on the plaintiff's knowledge or timeliness in seeking to amend. The Court clarified that a plaintiff's knowledge of a party's existence does not prevent a mistake concerning the party's identity from being made. The Court also stated that the plaintiff's delay in seeking to amend the complaint is not a factor in determining whether the amended complaint relates back under Rule 15(c).

The Supreme Court's decision allows Krupski's amended complaint to relate back to the date of the original filing, meaning that it can proceed despite the expiration of the statute of limitations. This decision emphasizes the importance of focusing on the defendant's knowledge and potential confusion about identity, rather than the plaintiff's knowledge or actions, in relation back cases under Rule 15(c).

Section 29-3812 of the Indiana Ann. Stat. provides that "[n]o existing or newly-organized political party or organization shall be permitted on or to have the names of its candidates printed on the ballot used at any election" unless "such political party or organization shall file an affidavit ... that it does not advocate the overthrow of local, state or national government by force or violence . . ." Appellant Communist Party of Indiana, a new political party, certain of its officers and potential voters, and its presidential and vice presidential candidates brought suit challenging the validity of the above section. After the trial court upheld the statute, appellants withdrew their notice of appeal pending resolution of a related issue concerning the printing of their names on the ballots; but when the trial court later refused to consider that issue, appellants again gave notice of appeal. Held: 1. Since appellants' withdrawal of their notice of appeal did not suspend the time for taking an appeal, the appeal was timely. Pp. 108-109. 2. The loyalty oath requirement of the Indiana statute violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments since it burdens access to the ballot, rights of association in the political party of one's choice, interests in casting an effective vote and in running for office, not because the party urges others "to do something," now or in the future, but merely to believe in something. Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U. S. 444. Pp. 109-112. Reversed.

On January 11, 2000, the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota entered a final judgment against the University of Minnesota for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Minneapolis, Minnesota, alleges that the university violated the federal securities laws by failing to file an amended complaint with the SEC.  According to the complaint, the university's amended complaint alleges that, in violation of Section 13(b)(1), the university was not entitled to equitable tolling of its claims under the Exchange Act.  In addition, the complaint alleges the university waited nine months before filing its amended complaint in state district court to determine whether it had sufficient jurisdiction to respond to the SEC's request for a hearing on the matter.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Defendants agreed to settle the case by agreeing to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the securities laws and orders them to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest in the amount of $10,000 and a civil penalty of $100,000.  Defendants also agreed to pay a $75,000 civil penalty and a $50,000 penalty.  Finally, Defendants consented to a judgment permanently enjoining them from violating Sections 13(a), 13(c), and 13(d) ofÂ the Exchange Act and Rule 13b2-1 thereunder, and ordering Defendants to pay $25,000 in civil penalties.   The settlement is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's Office of Investor Education and Advocacy has issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the background of anyone selling or offering them investments using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Bail Reform Act of 1984, which provides for the right to bail in the federal courts.  According to the court's order, filed on March 21, 1986, Anthony Salerno and Vincent Cafaro were arrested and held without bail pending trial in connection with various Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) violations, mail and wire fraud offenses, extortion, and conspiracy to commit murder.  The court found that, consistent with the First Amendment, defendants were entitled to pretrial detention on the basis of reasonable and convincing evidence, without which they would not be entitled to bail.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Salerno, Cafaro, and others for their roles in the RICO violations.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Court's judgment, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of Investment Advisers, LLC, and Rule 206(3)-8 thereunder. The court granted the defendants' requests for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an accounting of the amount of money that has been collected from the defendants so far, and ordered the release of the remaining defendants.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York recently ruled that the Securities and Exchange Commission's enforcement action against E. L. Aaron & Co., a New York-based registered broker-dealer, should be dismissed because the SEC's complaint alleged that the firm's registered representatives made false and misleading statements in an effort to solicit orders for the purchase of Lawn-A-Mat common stock. The SEC alleged that Norman Schreiber and Donald Jacobson made projections of substantial increases in the price and optimistic statements concerning the company's financial condition without basis in fact. The District Court found that the petitioner had violated and aided and abetted violations of  17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and  10(b) and Rule 10b-5 promulgated under that section of the 1934 Act. The court concluded that the fact that he knew or had reason to know that the employees under his supervision were engaged in fraudulent practices, but failed to take adequate steps to prevent those practices from continuing, is sufficient to establish his scienter under the securities laws. The Court concluded that, because the firm had since gone bankrupt and the petitioner was no longer employed by the firm, the court's decision should be upheld. The case involves whether the SEC is required to establish scienter as an element of a civil enforcement action to enjoin violations of the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws, and whether the District Court's finding of past violations of these provisions was sufficient to do so.

In 2004, voters in Washington, D. C., passed an initiative changing the State’s primary election system. In 2004, the People’S Choice Initiative of 2004, or Initiative 872 (I–872), provides that candidates for office shall be identified on the ballot by their self-designated “party preference”; that voters may vote for any candidate; and that the top two votegetters for each office, regardless of party preference, advance to the general election. The State used a nearly identical primary in its own elections until California Democratic Party v. Jones, 530 U. S. 567, which held that the blanket primary severely burdened the parties’ associational rights because it forced them to allow nonmembers to participate in selecting the party nominees. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The primary does not impose a severe burden on political parties, and because respondents’ arguments to the contrary rest on factual assumptions about voter confusion that can be evaluated only in the context of an as-applied challenge, the First Amendment does not require this extraordinary and precipitous nullification of the will of the people. Pp. 5–7. (a) The First Amendment is not required to construe a “plainly legitimate sweep.” Washington v. Glucksberg, 521 U.S. 702, 739–740, and n. 7 (b) The State has the “ ‘ ‘responsibility to observe the limits established by First Amendment rights of the State,’ ” including the freedom of political association. P. 5. (c) The States possess a ‘broad power to prescribe the ‘Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives,” Art. I, §4, cl. 1, which power is matched by state control over the election process for state offices. That power is not absolute, but is “subject to the limitation that [it] may not be exercised in a way that violates … specific provisions of the Constitution.’ .” Williams v. Rhodes, 393 U. .S. 23, 29. In particular, the State has “the ‘Respondents object to I-872 not in an actual election, but in a facial challenge.“ The remaining interests—promoting fairness, affording voters greater choice, increasing voter participation, and protecting privacy—were not compelling on the facts of the case. Even if they were, the partisan California primary was not narrowly tailored to further those interests because a nonpartisan blanket primary, in which the top 2 votegetter advance to a general election regardless of their party affiliation, would accomplish each of those interests without burdening the parties' associational right. P p. 581. (d) Respondents’ argument that voters can be “misled” by candidates’ party-preference designations does not amount to forcing the political party to speak. See, e.g., “[a] ruling of unconstitutionality frustrates the intent of the elected representatives of the [state]’ …” Ayotte v. Planned Parenthood of Northern New Eng., 546 US. 320, 329, 329. The fact that respondents brought their suit as a facial challenged does not mean that they will be confused by the party designations, but rather that the State need not assert a compelling interest. Because the State affords candidates the opportunity to indicate their party preference on the ballots, it has the same “constitutionally crucial” infirmity that doomed a blanket primary: it allows primary voters who are unaffiliated with a party to choose the party’�s nominee. The Constitution does not give political parties a right to have their nominees designated as such on ballots, and that factual determination must await an “asapplied” challenge. The First and Judicial Courts should neither ‘anticipate a question of constitutional law in advance of the necessity of deciding it’ nor ‘formulate a rule of constitutional-law broader than is required by the precise facts to which it is to be applied. ” Sabri v. United States, 541 U.

Appellant Philadelphia Newspapers, Inc., owns the Philadelphia Inquirer (Inquirer), which published a series of articles containing the statements at issue here. The articles discussed a state legislator, described as "a Pittsburgh Democrat and convicted felon," whose actions displayed a clear pattern of interference in state government by the legislator on behalf of Hepps and Thrifty stores. Appellees brought suit for defamation against appellants in a Pennsylvania state court, alleging that the articles tended to injure the plaintiff's reputation or bring him into public contempt, and were therefore libelous per se. The trial court instructed the jury that it could presume falsity, malice, and some damage to reputation, as long as it found that the defendant had published the statements and that the statements concerned the plaintiff. The jury found for the plaintiff and made an award of damages that did not distinguish between compensatory and punitive damages. The Alabama Supreme Court upheld the judgment of the trial court in all respects, holding that "libel can claim no talismanic immunity from constitutional limitations." Held: 1. The common-law presumption that defamatory speech is false cannot stand when a plaintiff seeks damages against a media defendant for speech of public concern. Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. 418 U. S. 323, 325. Pp. 531-532. 2. A private figure who brings a defamation suit cannot recover damages without also showing that the media defendant was at fault in publishing the statements. The State's "shield" law allows employees of the media to refuse to divulge their sources, and that showing must be made with "convincing clarity," id., at 285-286, or, in a later formulation, by "clear and convincing proof." Pp532-534. 3. The public figure plaintiff must bear the burden of showing falsity before recovering damages for defamation. P. 534. (a) The common law's rule on falsity must similarly fall here to a constitutional requirement that the plaintiff bear that burden of proving falsity and fault, before recovering damages. Here the speech concerns the legitimacy of the political process, and therefore clearly "matters," and the burden must also take into account the "legitimate state interest underlying the law of libel [in] the compensation of individuals for the harm inflicted on them by defamation falsehood." P. 529. (b) The fact that the speech is of public interest and the newspaper articles are of public concerns does not necessarily mean that a private figure plaintiff has the burden to show falsity in order to prevail in a libel action for defamation, but rather that a public-figure plaintiff must show that falsity as well as fault before recovery damages. In light of that interest, and in light of the fact that private figures have lesser access to media channels useful for counteracting false statements and have not voluntarily placed themselves in the public eye, the common law rule must similarly be superseded by a constitutional rule. The Court's previous decisions on the restrictions that the First Amendment places upon the common- law of defamation firmly support this conclusion. In attempting to resolve related issues in the defamation context, the Court has affirmed that "[t]he First Amendment requires that we protect some falsehood in order ... to protect speech that matters." GertZ, supra, at 344-345, 94 S.Ct., at 3007. Here, even when private figures are involved, the constitutional requirement of fault supersedes the common laws' presumptions as to fault and damages. Pc. 533-536. (c) In the context of governmental restriction of speech, it has long been established that the government cannot limit speech protected by the First First Amendment without bearing the burden that its restriction is justified. The state interest [in preserving private reputation] adequately supports awards of presumed, punitive damages-even absent a showing of "actual malice.' " P. 550. (d) The Court has been willing to insulate from liability some speech that is false, but unprovably so. In order to avoid self-censorship by the news media, the Constitution still supplants the standards of the Common Law, but the constitutional requirements are, in at least some of their range, less forbidding than when the plaintiff is a public figure and the Speech is of Public concern. When that speech is exclusively private concern and the plaintiff-is a "public figure," the Constitution clearly requires the plaintiff to surmount a much higher barrier before recover damages from a newspaper defendant than is raised by the commonlaw. When the speech-of public concern but the plaintiff--is a public official or figure, it clearly requires that plaintiff to be able to surmise the truthfulness of some of the sources. The court's precedents on such restrictions support the conclusion here with respect to the allocation of the burden-of-proof. The First Amendment's common law presumption, which the defendant must show the falsity of the statements, is not a valid, but not the exclusive, concern in suits for defamation

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered final judgments against Xerox Corporation and its former plan administrator in a civil injunctive action brought by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in San Diego, California, alleges that the Plan Administrator violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The complaint further alleges that, in violation of the federal securities laws, the plan administrator failed to apply a deferential standard of review to his or her interpretation of the Plan.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the administrator.  According to the complaint, the SEC's order against the Plan administrator violated Section 13(b)(2)(A) and (c) of Exchange Act Rule 13b2-3.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Xerox agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins it from future violations of the Exchange Act and Rules 12b-20, 13a-1, and 13b-11 thereunder, and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $150,000.  Xerox also agreed to a $50,000 civil penalty.

The Supreme Court ruled in Beal v. Doe (1978) that the Connecticut regulation placing no obstacles in the path of an indigent woman seeking an abortion, but which encouraged childbirth by funding it, did not impinge upon the fundamental right recognized in Roe v. Wade. The Court distinguished direct state interference with a protected activity from state encouragement of an alternative activity consonant with legislative policy. The Court held that the Connecticut regulation placed no obstacles absolute or otherwise in the pregnant woman's path to an abortion and that an indigent woman who desires an abortion continued as before to be dependent on private sources for the service she desired. The Court also held that the regulation did not place an undue burden on the right to seek an abortion.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the respondent, Deputy District Attorney Richard Ceballos, in a case concerning his disciplinary action for making a disposition memo regarding a pending criminal case. The Court held that when public employees make statements pursuant to their official duties, they are not speaking as citizens for First Amendment purposes, and the Constitution does not insulate their communications from employer discipline. The Court distinguished Ceballos' case from previous cases where the First Amendment provided protection against discipline, citing the fact that his memo was written as part of his job responsibilities. The Court also emphasized the importance of allowing government employers to maintain control over their operations and ensuring that their employees' official communications are accurate and reflect sound judgment.

Petitioner, a resident of Louisiana, was charged with aggravated kidnapping and brought to trial in a state court. He moved to strike from the jury list women whose percentage of the entire potential jury pool exceeded 53%. That motion was denied, and after petitioner's conviction was sustained on appeal, he applied to the Louisiana Supreme Court for postconviction relief, claiming that the exclusion of women from the jury violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. That court found that the exclusion of women from the jury pool was constitutional, and the Louisiana Supreme Court subsequently affirmed petitioner's conviction. Held: 1. The selection of a petit jury from a representative cross section of the community is an essential component of the Sixth Amendment right to a jury trial, and the requirement has a solid foundation. Pp. 380-384. 2. The fair-cross-section requirement is violated by the systematic exclusion of women, who in the judicial district involved here amounted to 53% of the citizens eligible for jury service. Pp. 384-386. 3. Women as a class cannot be excluded from jury service without denying the defendant his Sixth Amendment right to trial by an impartial jury drawn from a fair cross section of the community. Pp. 386-388. 4. The fair-cross-section principle must have much leeway in application, and nothing requires that petit juries actually chosen must mirror the community and reflect the various distinctive groups in the population. However, the jury wheels, pools of names, panels, or venires from which juries are drawn must not systematically exclude distinctive groups in the community and thereby fail to be reasonably representative thereof. Pp. 388-389. 254 La. 101, 223 So. 2d 108, reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Connecticut today entered a final judgment in favor of the right of a pregnant woman to have an abortion.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Boston, Connecticut, the state's Department of Social Services issued a temporary restraining order on March 5, 2019, freezing the assets of two indigent women who were unable to obtain a physician's certificate of medical necessity.  The SEC alleges that the Connecticut regulation violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In its judgment, the court held that the federal government has the right to determine whether to fund a certain type of abortion when it pays for childbirth.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the Connecticut Department of Health and Human Services has agreed to the entry of an order permanently enjoining it from violating the federal securities laws, and ordering the payment of a civil penalty in the amount of $10,000. The settlement is subject to court approval.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the plaintiff in this case, finding that the defendant's use of a "county unit" system to allocate seats in the state legislature based on the size of each county's population was unconstitutional. The Court found that the system resulted in unequal representation of citizens and violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court also rejected the argument that the system was intended to reflect the relative importance of rural versus urban areas and thus promote fairness in representation.

The Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (Gaming Act) subsection, as codified in 25 U. S. C. 2719(d)(i), reads as follows: "The provisions of [the Internal Revenue Code of 1986] (including sections 1441, 3402(q), 6041, and 6050I, and chapter 35 of such Code) concerning the reporting and withholding of taxes with respect to the winnings from gaming or wagering operations shall apply to Indian gaming operations conducted pursuant to this chapter, or under a Tribal-State compact entered into under section 2710 (d)(3) of this title that is in effect, in the same manner as such provisions apply to State gaming and wagers operations." Section 35, however, says nothing about the reporting or the withholding of tax. Rather, that chapter simply imposes taxes-excise taxes and occupational taxes related to gambling-from which it exempts certain state-controlled gambling activities. Section 35 also says that those provisions "includ[e]" Internal RevenueCode "chapter 35." Chapter 35's parenthetical also says "provisions of the ... Code including chapter 35 and also provisions ... concerning the taxation and the reporting of taxes ... ." Section 35's language is unambiguous. It says without qualification that the subsection applies to "gambling operations" and says in its parenthetical that "concer[n] the reporting ... of taxes" with respect thereto "in the same way as they apply to States." The subsection also says in the parenthetical, prefaced with the word "including," that "including ... and," "include" is to "contain" or "comprise as part of a whole." See, e. g., 26 U.S.C. 4401(a) (1994 ed.) (imposing 0.25% excise tax on each wager); 4411 (impose $50 occupational tax oneach individual engaged in waging business); 4402(3) (exempting state-operated gambling operations, such as lotteries). Section 35 does not include the reporting "taxation" section of the Code, but merely imposes taxes excise taxes, occupational taxes, and other taxes related thereto. The section's language outside the parenthesis says that it applies to those provisions, but the other four parenthetical references are to provisions that concern, or at least arguably concern, reporting and withhold. Section 34's language does not contain the section's explicit parenthetical reference to chapter 35, but it expresses the views of only one member of the committee, and it makes no effort to explain the critical legislative circumstance, namely, the elimination of the word taxation from the bill. The letter may express the Senator's interpretive preference, but that preference cannot overcome the language of the statute and the related considerations. Cf. Little Six, Inc. v. United States, 210 F. 3d 1361, 1366. Pp. 6-8. (a) To adopt the Tribes' interpretation would read back into the Act the very word "Taxation" that the Senate committee deleted. It is far too convoluted to believe Congress intended to enact statutory language that it has earlier discarded in favor of other language. Common sense suggests that the cross-reference is simply a drafting mistake, a failure to delete an inappropriate crossreference in the bill that Congress later enacted into law. See Heintz v. Jenkins, supra, at 3. The more plausible role for a parenthetical to play in this subsection is that of providing an illustrative list of examples. The presence of a bad example in a statute does not warrant rewriting the statute's language. Nor does it necessarily mean that the statute is ambiguous, i.e., "capable of being understood in two or more possible senses or ways." Webster's Ninth New Collegiate Dictionary 77 (1985). Moreover, the canon that assumes Congress intends its statutes to benefit the tribes is offset by a canon that warns us against interpreting federal statutes as providing tax exemptions unless those exemptions are clearly expressed. See United States v. Wells Fargo Bank, 485 U. . . 351, 354 (1988). The canon requiring a court to give effect to each word "if possible" is sometimes offset by an canon that permits a court-to reject words "as surplusage" if "inadvertently inserted or if repugnant to the rest of the Act ... ." K. Llewellyn, The Common Law Tradition 525 (1960). Nor can one say that the pro-Indian canon is inevitably stronger-particularly where the interpretation of a congressional statute rather than an Indian treaty is at issue. Nor can it say that Congress intended the statute to be interpreted liberally in favor the Indians with ambiguous provisions interpreted to their benefit. P. 8-10. Respondents, alleged former Cold War spies, brought suit against the United States and the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), asserting estoppel and due process claims for the CIA's alleged failure to provide respondents with the assistance it had promised in return for their espionage services. The District Court dismissed some of respondents' claims but denied the Government's objection, ruling that the due process claim could proceed. After minimal discovery, the Government renewed its motion to dismiss based on Totten v. United States, 345 U. S. 1, and moved for summary judgment. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The Government was entitled to the privilege in this case. Totten does not require dismissal of the claims. Pp. 488-481. (a) The State Secrets privilege and the more frequent use of in camera judicial proceedings simply cannot provide the absolute protection necessary in enunciating the Totten rule. The possibility that a suit may proceed and an espionage relationship may be revealed, if the state secrets privilege is found not to apply, is unacceptable: "Even a small chance that some court will order disclosure of a source's identity could well impair intelligence gathering and cause sources to "close up like a clam." CIA v. Sims, 471 U.S. 159, 175. Forcing the Government to litigate these claims would also make it vulnerable to "graymail," i. e., individual lawsuits brought to induce the CIA to settle a case (or prevent its filing) out of fear that it would reveal classified information that may undermine ongoing covert operations. P. 489. 99 F. Supp. 2d 1284, reversed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the state of Wisconsin in a case involving a hate crime. The court held that the state's penalty-enhancement statute, which increases the maximum punishment for a crime based on the defendant's intentional selection of the victim due to the victim's race or other protected characteristic, does not violate the First Amendment. The court noted that while the statute punishes the defendant's discriminatory motive, it does not punish the defendant's belief system or association with a particular ideology.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of allowing a tax deduction for educational expenses incurred by parents for their children, regardless of whether the child attends public or private school. The court found that the deduction satisfied the three-part test set forth in Lemon v. Kurtzman, which requires that the statute have a secular legislative purpose, its primary effect must be one that neither advances nor inhibits religion, and the statute must not foster an excessive government entanglement with religion. The court determined that the deduction served a secular purpose, had no primary effect on advancing religion, and did not excessively entangle the government in religion.

Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 prohibits sex discrimination in "any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance," and § 902 directs agencies awarding most types of assistance to promulgate regulations to ensure that recipients adhere to that prohibition. Compliance with departmental regulations may be secured by termination of assistance "to the particular program, or part thereof, in which . . . noncompliance has been found" or by "any other means authorized by law." Section 902, 20 U. S. C. § 1681(a), provides that "[c]omply, to the extent applicable to it, with Title IX and all applicable requirements imposed by or pursuant to the Department's regulation ... to the end that no person shall, on the basis of sex, be ... subjected to discrimination under any education program ... for which [it] receives or benefits from federal financial assistance from the Department." Petitioner Grove City College accepts no direct assistance but enrolls students who receive federal grants that must be used for educational purposes. The Department concluded that Grove City was a "recipient" of "Federal financial assistance" as those terms are defined in the regulations implementing Title IX, 34 CFR §§ 106.2(g)(1), (h) (1982), and requested that the College execute the Assurance of Compliance required by 34 CFR § 106.4 (1982). If Grove City had signed the Assurances, it would have agreed to comply with Title VIII's prohibition of discrimination as a condition for its continued eligibility to participate in the BEOG program. If GroveCity had complied with the regulations, the Department could not terminate the students' aid because of the College's refusal to execute an Assurance. The Court of Appeals reversed. Held: The Department may properly condition federal assistance on the recipient's assurance that it will conduct the aided programs or activity in accordance with Title X and the applicable regulations. Pp. 687-692. (a) The language of § 901(a) contains no hint that Congress perceived a substantive difference between direct institutional assistance and aid received by a school through its students. Nor does the Court's holding that BEOGs received by Grove City's students constitute aid to the entire institution's student financial aid program infringes no First Amendment rights of the college or its students, and the judgment of the Court is affirmed. P. 691. (b) The Court is reluctant to read into § 903(a)'s limitation that only institutions that themselves apply for federal aid or receive checks directly from the federal government are subject to regulation. The economic effect of direct and indirect assistance often is indistinguishable from the effect of nonearmarked direct grants to institutions themselves since the former, unlike the latter, increases both the total resources available to educational institutions and the costs of higher education. Nor is there any persuasive evidence suggesting that Congress intended that Title IX's regulatory authority follow federally aided students from classroom to classroom, building to building, or activity to activity. Nor can the Court conclude that a decision treating a BEOg as "Federal Financial Assistance" cannot be reconciled with the program-specific language of Title IX. Nor do the Department now claim that its regulations reach beyond the college's student aid program, since the fact that federal funds eventually reach the College and pay back to the school when tuition comes due cannot subject Grove City to institutionwide coverage. Respondent Buckley, an insulation worker, filed suit under the Federal Employers' Liability Act (FELA), alleging that petitioner asbestos manufacturer had negligently exposed him to asbestos-laden insulation dust, causing him to suffer emotional distress and to incur medical monitoring costs. The District Court dismissed the action, but the Second Circuit reversed, holding that a reasonable jury could award Buckley the costs of medical monitoring. 

Held: 
1. The Second Circuit erred in holding that the FELA permitted Buckley to recover the costs of medical monitoring. Pp. 29-39.
	 (a) The FELA does not permit a plaintiff without symptoms or disease to recover for emotional distress. The emotional distress at issue here is not a compensable "injury" within the meaning of the FELA, which defines "injury" as "any disease, disorder, or other damage resulting from exposure to asbestos." The emotional distress at issue is not a compensable "injury" because it is not a disease, disorder, or other damage resulting from exposure to asbestos. Pp. 29-32.
	 (b) Nor does the FELA permit a plaintiff without symptoms or disease to recover the costs of medical monitoring. The Second Circuit's holding, insofar as it suggests the existence of a traditional, full-blown tort law cause of action permitting (as tort law ordinarily permits) the recovery of medical cost damages in the form of a lump sum, irrespective of insurance, is beyond the bounds of currently "evolving common law." The cases authorizing recovery for medical monitoring in the absence of physical injury do not endorse a full-blown, traditional tort law cause of action of the sort that the Second Circuit seems to have endorsed here. Rather, those courts, while recognizing that medical monitoring costs can amount to a harm that justifies a tort remedy, have suggested, or imposed, special limitations on that remedy. The particular, say cancer-related, costs at issue here are the extra monitoring costs, over and above those otherwise recommended, and their identification will sometimes pose special difficulties for judges and juries. Moreover, tens of millions of individuals may have suffered exposure to substances that might justify some form of substance-exposure-related medical monitoring. And that fact, along with uncertainty as to the amount of liability, could threaten both a "flood" of less important cases and the systemic harms that can accompany "unlimited and unpredictable liability." A traditional, full-blown ordinary tort liability rule would ignore the presence of existing alternative sources of payment, thereby leaving a court uncertain about how much of the potentially large recoveries would pay for otherwise unavailable medical testing and how much would accrue to plaintiffs for whom employers or other sources (say, insurance now or in the future) might provide monitoring in any event. Nor could an employer necessarily protect itself by offering monitoring, for that is not part of the rule of law that the Second Circuit would endorse-a rule that, if traditional, would, as this Court has noted, allow recovery irrespective of the presence of a "collateral source" of payment. Pp. 32-39. 
2. Buckley's policy-based arguments do not convince this Court that the FELA contains a tort liability rule of the unqualified kind at issue here. Pp. 39-40. 79 F. 3d 1257, reversed and remanded.

This case involves a federal district court's decision to hold a railroad company liable for the costs of remedying environmental contamination at a chemical plant in California. The contamination was caused by the release of hazardous chemicals from the plant, which had been owned and operated by a different company for many years. The railroad company had delivered chemicals to the plant and had taken possession of a small portion of the plant's land for several years. The district court found that the railroad company was liable under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA) for "arranging" the delivery of hazardous chemicals to the plant, even though the railroad company had not acted with the intent to create a hazardous condition. The court also found that the railroad company was liable for 9% of the total costs of remediation, based on the size of the portion of the plant that the railroad company had controlled and the duration of its control. The case raises important issues about the scope of CERCLA liability and the criteria for determining when a defendant can be held liable for arranging the delivery of hazardous materials.

In the case of Jeffrey Skilling, a former executive of Enron Corporation, the Supreme Court considered two key questions: whether pretrial publicity and community prejudice prevented Skilling from obtaining a fair trial, and whether his conviction for conspiracy to commit "honest-services" wire fraud was proper.

The Court affirmed the Fifth Circuit's decision that Skilling did not establish juror prejudice and thus received a fair trial. The Court held that Skilling did not demonstrate that the jury was biased against him, despite the extensive media coverage of Enron's collapse.

However, the Court disagreed with the Fifth Circuit's interpretation of the "honest-services" statute. The Court clarified that the statute, 18 U.S.C. §§ 371, 1343, 1346, was intended to cover schemes involving bribes and kickbacks. The Court concluded that extending the statute beyond bribery and kickback schemes would be unconstitutionally vague. Since Skilling's alleged misconduct did not involve bribes or kickbacks, his actions did not fall within the scope of the statute.

As a result, the Supreme Court affirmed in part and vacated in part the Fifth Circuit's decision. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion. The Court's decision narrowed the application of the "honest-services" statute to bribery and kickback schemes, excluding other types of misconduct that could be considered honest-services fraud. This interpretation aimed to provide clearer legal standards and avoid due process concerns related to vagueness in the law.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding the provision in the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1988 that allows public housing authorities to evict tenants for drug-related criminal activity committed by a member of the tenant's household or a guest, regardless of the tenant's knowledge or involvement in the activity. The Court found that the statute's language is clear and unambiguous in granting housing authorities the discretion to terminate tenancy for any drug-related criminal activity, without a requirement for the tenant to have knowledge of such activity.

The case involved four tenants from the Oakland Housing Authority who faced eviction after their household members or guests engaged in drug-related crimes. The tenants argued that they were "innocent" because they were unaware of the criminal activities. However, the Supreme Court determined that the statute does not require proof of the tenant's knowledge or fault for eviction to proceed.

The Court emphasized that the statute's use of the term "any" to describe the drug-related criminal activity that could lead to eviction indicates Congress's intent not to impose a knowledge requirement. The Court also rejected the argument that the statute's language implied a need for the tenant to have control over the household member or guest involved in the criminal activity.

The Court further noted that the statute provides discretion to housing authorities to consider all circumstances before deciding on eviction, which could include the seriousness of the offense and the tenant's efforts to prevent such activities. The Court concluded that strict liability for drug-related criminal activity on the premises is consistent with landlord-tenant law and serves as a deterrent.

The Court dismissed the constitutional concerns raised by the Court of Appeals, stating that the government, acting as a landlord, is entitled to enforce lease terms agreed upon by tenants. The Court also clarified that due process is preserved through the state court proceedings where eviction actions are brought.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision confirms that public housing authorities have the authority to evict tenants for drug-related criminal activity by household members or guests without the need to establish the tenant's knowledge or culpability, as mandated by the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1988. The cases were remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Court's opinion. Justice Breyer did not participate in the consideration or decision of the cases.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia granted certiorari and affirmed the conviction of a former member of the Communist Party for refusing to answer questions at a hearing before a House Committee on Un-American Activities subcommittee in 1958. The Committee's purpose was to determine the necessity for, and advisability of, amendments to the Foreign Agents Registration Act designed more effectively to counteract the Communist schemes and devices now used in avoiding the prohibitions of the Act. The petitioner, Amendo Penha, was convicted for having unlawfully refused to answer a question pertinent to a matter under inquiry before the subcommittee. The Court of appeals held that our decision in Barenblatt v. United States, 360 U. S. 109, 79 S.Ct. 1081, 3 L.Ed.2d 1115, was 'controlling' 272 F.2t.783. The Supreme Court of the United States later ruled that the Court of Appeal had misconceived the meaning of the Baranblatt decision, and that the lower court's decision in favor of the Committee was correct. In this case, the Supreme Court held that the Committee had not violated the Constitution's guarantees of due process and the right to a fair trial. We conclude that, in the light of the foregoing, the Court is correct to affirm the conviction.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Appeals for the Louisiana Fifth Circuit reversed a lower court's judgment in favor of a former East Baton Rouge Parish deputy sheriff in a defamation action brought by a candidate for public office against him. The court held that the lower court had erred by failing to apply the rule of New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, which requires a defamation plaintiff to prove that the publication was made with 'actual malice' or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not. The Court held that there was sufficient evidence that St. Amant recklessly disregarded whether the statements about Deputy Sheriff Herman A. Thompson were true or false, and that he had no responsibility for the broadcast because he was merely quoting a union member's words. The high court held, however, that Thompson had sustained the burden of proving that the false statements about Thompson were made with actual malice as defined in New YorkTimes and later cases. The Fifth Circuit held that this burden did not apply to Thompson's actions, since he had not proven that the statements were false or false. The justices held that, in the absence of a finding of actual malice, Thompson had not shown that the broadcast was reckless. The case is now back before the Fifth Circuit for further consideration.

The U.S. Supreme Court for the District of Georgia ruled that a police search of a shared home in Americus, Georgia, was unlawful because a co-occupant's refusal to consent to the search was unreasonable and invalid. The court held that Scott Randolph's wife, Janet, who was present at the time of the search, had consented to it. The Court of Appeals of Georgia had previously ruled that Janet Randolph had common authority to consent. The Supreme Court of Georgia held that the lower court had erred in holding that the officers had not been "faced with the physical presence of joint occupants, with one consenting to conduct a warrantless search and the other objecting"

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the town of Hempstead in its attempt to regulate mining activities within its limits. The court determined that the ordinance prohibiting any excavation below the water table and requiring the refilling of any existing excavation was a valid exercise of the town's police power, despite the fact that it prevented the appellants from continuing their business and potentially confiscated their property without due process of law. The court based its decision on the principle that every regulation necessarily speaks as a prohibition, and that the fact that the ordinance deprived the property of its most beneficial use did not make it unconstitutional.

Respondent sued petitioner for damages for alleged infringement of a patent relating to a "shipper-sprayer" for automatic installation on a container of a liquid substance. The shipper-sprayer consists of a pump unit fitted with a detachable overcap containing a flexible seal which holds the pump unit firmly to the container and forms a seal between the pump unit and the container. The District Court found the subject matter of the patent new, useful, and nonobvious and awarded damages. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The claims in issue in the patent must fall as not meeting the test of 35 U. S. C. § 103 since the differences between them and the pertinent prior art would have been obvious to a person reasonably skilled in that art. Pp. 138-146. 2. The patentee obtained his patent only by accepting the limitations imposed by the Patent Office. The claims were carefully drafted to reflect these limitations and petitioner is not now free to assert a broader view of the patent. P. 142. 3. The limited claims of the patent are clearly evident from the prior art as it stood at the time of the invention. Pp. 143-146. 336 F. 2d 109, 114, affirmed.

Petitioners brought a tort suit against the maker of a product that caused Betty O'Gilvie's death. They received the net proceeds of a jury award of $1,525,000 actual damages and $10 million punitive damages. Insofar as the proceeds represented punitive damages, petitioners paid income tax on the proceeds but immediately sought a refund. The Federal District Court held that the statutory phrase "damages . . . on account of personal injury or sickness," as it read in 1988, excluded punitive damages from gross income and entitling them to obtain, and the children to keep, their refund. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the exclusionary provision does not cover punitive damages and that the statute does not apply and the damages are taxable. Held: 1. The punitive damages received here were not received "on account of" personal injuries; hence the provision did not apply. Pp. 531-532. (a) The language of § 104 (a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code (which provides that "[a]civil action brought in the name of the United States'' to recover any "portion of a tax . ... which has been erroneously refunded") does not extend to compensatory damages, since they are "punitive in nature," and the statute's language does not require, or strongly suggest, their exclusion from income. P. 532. 2. The Government's interpretation of the statute is more faithful to the history of the statutory provision as well as the basic tax-related purpose that the history reveals. The fact that Congress might have wanted the exclusion to have covered punitive damages does not change its original focus upon damages that restore a loss, that seek to make a victim whole, with a tax-equality objective providing an important part of, even if not the entirety of, the statutory rationale. Schleier, 515 U. S. 229, distinguished. The statute's history and the approach it reflects suggest there is no strong reason for trying to interpret the statute to reach beyond those damages that, making up for a loss or seek to return the victim's personal or financial capital. The legislative history and approach suggest that Congress sought to codify the Treasury's basic approach in enacting the statute, and this Court's normal practice of construing ambiguous statutes of limitations in Government action in the Government's favor. P p. 533. (b) Petitioners' argument that to some extent the purposes that might have led Congress to exclude, say, lost wages, which would have been taxed had the victim earned them, would also have led the Government to exclude punitive damages for doing so is both generous to victims and avoids such administrative problems as separating punitive from compensatory portions of a global settlement or determining the extent to which a punitive damages award is itself intended to compensate. The problem of identifying the elements of an ostensibly punitive award does not exist where, as here, relevant state law makes clear that the damages at issue are not at all compensatory, but entirely punitive. This circumstance alone, however, does not argue strongly for an interpretation that covers punitive damages because coverage of compensatory punitive damages has both language and history in its favor. Moreover, this policy argument assumes that coverage of lost wages is something of an anomaly; if so, that circumstance would not justify the extension of the anomaly or the creation of another. Pm. 534-535. (c) The Government is correct in its claim that its lawsuit was timely. The language here admits of both interpretations. But the law ordinarily provides that an action to recover mistaken payments of money "accrues upon the receipt of payment," New Bedford v. Lloyd Investment Associates, Inc., 363 Mass. 112, 119, 292 N. E. 2d 688, 692 (1973); accord Sizemore v. Barwick Industries, Inc. v. Thurston, 469 U.S. 111, 125. The history of § 1605 of the Small Business Job Protection Act of 1996, Pub. L. 104-188, explicitly excepts most punitive damages of the exclusion provided by § 104(a) (2). Because it is of prospective application, the section does notapply here. The provision is similar to the cited materials from the Attorney General and the Secretary of the Treasury in language and structure, all of which suggests thatCongress sought, in enactmenting the statutory statute, to codifying the Treasury-basic approach in the case of money paid erroneously made.
