It also says that "[n]"o inference ... is intended" as to "the proper interpretation" of the section's proper interpretation prior to the amendment. The "date of mailing" provision is not sufficient to overcome petitioners' arguments sufficiently persuasive, for such a rule normally would refer the court to the postmark to establish the

Title: Scienter Requirement Under Securities Laws

Summary: This case involves a dispute over whether a commission can sue a corporation for insider trading without proving that the corporation's executives had knowledge of the information used to trade. The court holds that the commission must prove that the corporation's executives had knowledge of the information used to trade in order to establish insider trading.

The Supreme Court considered whether a disabled inmate in a state prison can file a lawsuit against the state for money damages under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The Court found that Title II of the ADA allows individuals with disabilities to bring civil actions against public entities for damages if they have been discriminated against. However, the Court also ruled that states cannot be sued for punitive damages under Title II of the ADA.

The Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF) provides that “no court, justice, or judge shall have jurisdiction to hear or consider … an application for a writ of habeas corpus filed by or on behalf of an alien detained by the Department of Defense at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.” In Hamdi v. Rumsfeld, 542 U. S. 507, five Members of the Court recognized that detention of individuals who fought against the United States in Afghanistan “for the duration of the particular conflict in which they were captured, is so fundamental and accepted an incident to war as to be an exercise of the ‘necessary and appropriate force’ Congress has authorized the President to use,” Id., at 518 (plurality opinion of O’Connor, J., concurring). The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The statute does not deny the federal courts jurisdiction to entertain the habas corpus actions pending at the time of its enactment. Pp. 5–7. (a) The Act’s “Article IV, §3, cl. 1, grants Congress the power to admit new States, and the Judiciary, in light of that determination, proceeds to its own independent judgment on the constitutional question when required to do so in a proper case. P. 6. (b) The Constitution grants Congress and the President “the power to acquire, dispose of, and govern territory, not the power … to decide when and where its terms apply” and “to make laws for such territories and subject to such constitutional restrictions as are applicable to the situation of the territory and its relations to the States”. The Framers’ doctrine of territorial incorporation, under which the Constitution applies in full in incorporated Territories surely destined for statehood but only in part in unincorporated Territories, is central to this approach. The United States has maintained complete and uninterrupted control of the bay for over 100 years. At the close of the Spanish-American War, Spain ceded control over the entire island of Cuba to United States and specifically “relinquishe[d] all claim[s] of sovereignty … and title.’” See Treaty of Paris, Dec. 10, 1898, U.S.-Spain, Art. I, 30 Stat. 1755, and when held in a territory, like Guantanamo, over which the Government has total military and civil control. In addition to the practical concerns of the petitioners, the Court found relevant that each petitioner was an enemy alien; was an American citizen; was captured outside of England and there held in military custody as a prisoner of war; and was tried and convicted by a Military Commission sitting outside of the United State; was at all times imprisoned outside the country; and had no rights as an enemy combatant or is awaiting such determination. Petitioners, like those in Eisentrager, are not American citizens. They have been afforded some process in CSRT proceedings to determine their status, but have been denied relief by the Government, and have been barred from seeking review of their status determination in the Court. The Government argues that jurisdiction followed the King of England, who was a British subject, and that the Court should have suspended the writ for lack of jurisdiction. The Court rejects this contention, and, in turn, the parties in these cases have examined historical sources to construct a view of the common-law writ as it existed when the Constitution was drafted and ratified. See Hamdan, supra, at 481–482, and see id., at 74–75. The record from these cases suggest that, well before the founding, there had been a rigorous adversarial process to test the legality of their detention. See, e.g., Torres v. Puerto Rico, 442 U . S. 465, 475–476. In other contexts the Court has held that questions of sovereignty are for the political branches to decide, see Vermilya-Brown Co. v. Connell, 335 U. s. 377, 380. But, as here, the Government argues, at least as applied to noncitizens, the Constitution necessarily stops where de jure sovereignty ends. This Court has long held that the Clause protects against arbitrary suspensions of the writ but also guarantees an affirmative right to judicial inquiry into the causes of detention, see, e,g., Jones v. United States, 137 U.

Petitioner Melendez-Diaz was charged with distributing cocaine and with trafficking in cocaine. At trial, the prosecution placed into evidence the bags seized from Wright and from the police cruiser and submitted three “certificates of analysis” showing the results of the forensic analysis performed on the seized substances. The certificates reported the weight of the seized bags and stated that the bags “[h]a[ve] been examined with the following results: The substance was found to contain: Cocaine.” App. to Pet. for Cert. 24a, 26a, 28a. Petitioner objected to the admission of the certificates, asserting that our Confrontation Clause decision in Crawford v. Washington, 541 U. S. 36 (2004), required the analysts to testify in person. The objection was overruled, and the certificates were admitted pursuant to state law as “prima facie evidence of the composition, quality, and net weight” of the analyzed substance, Mass. Gen. Laws, ch. 111, §13. The District Court of Massachusetts rejected the claim, holding that the authors of certificates of forensic analysis are not subject to confrontation under the Sixth Amendment. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court denied review. Held: In faithfully applying Crawford to the facts of this case, we are not overruling 90 years of settled jurisprudence. Pp. 5–11. (a) The Confrontations Clause guarantees a defendant the right “to be confronted with the witnesses against him,” i. e., “whether or not they are contained in formalized testimonial materials, such as affidavits, custodial examinations, prior testimony that the defendant was unable to cross-examine, or similar pretrial statements that declarants would reasonably expect to be used prosecutorially; extrajudicial statements … contained in ‘confidential’ materials,’” Black’s Law Dictionary 62 (8th ed. 2004). But other state courts in the same era reached the opposite conclusion. See Torres v. State, 18 S. W. 2d 179, 180. The same is true of many of the other types of forensic evidence commonly used in criminal prosecutions. See, e.g., White v. Illinois, 502 U.S. 346, 365, 365. The contrast between the text of theconfrontation clause and the adjacent Compulsory Process Clause confirms this analysis. While theConfrontation is one means of assuring accurate forensic analysis, it is not the case if the regularly conducted business activity is the production of evidence for use at trial. For example, if an affidavit submitted in response to a police request to “write down what happened” suffices to trigger a Sixth Amendment protection, then the analysts’ testimony should be subject to confront as well. The analysts, like expert witnesses generally, are not “conventional” witnesses of the sort whose ex parte testimony was most notoriously used at the trial of Sir Walter Raleigh. See Crawford, supra, at 51–52. The fact in question is that the analysts were aware of the affidavits’ evidentiary purpose, since that purpose-as stated in the relevant state-law provision-was reprinted on the affidavit themselves. The evidence proved only that the property was stolen, and not that Kirby received it, the Court nevertheless ruled that admission of a redacted confession containing evidence of that sort violated Kirby’S rights under the Confrontated Clause. The dissent, however, notes that several of the state-court cases that have already adopted this rule did so pursuant to Crawford, and that they did so “independently … as a matter of state law” post, at 28. In assessing the likely practical effects of this ruling, it matters only that those courts adopted the rule; it is irrelevant why those courts did so, since those decisions are recent, and given the large number of drug prosecutions at the state level, one would have expected immediate and dramatic results. Respondent and the dissent advance a potpourri of analytic arguments in an effort to avoid this rather straightforward application of the holding in Crawford. The dissenting, post-Roberts, concurring in judgment in part and dissenting in part, that “neutral scientific testing” is as neutral or as reliable as respondent suggests. The dissident also misunderstands the relationship between the business-and-official-records hearsay exceptions and the Compulsor Process Clause, which are of no use to the defendant when the witness is unavailable or simply refuses to appear. See Davis v. Maryland, 523 U.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas sentenced members of the Branch-Davidian religious sect to 30 years in prison for violating a federal law that prohibits the use or carrying of a "firearm" in relation to a crime of violence. The trial judge determined that the "firearms" at issue included certain machineguns and handgrenades that the defendants actually or constructively had possessed. The district court resentenced the defendants to prison based on the jury's finding that they had used "machineguns" and other enhanced weapons. The Court of Appeals for the District Court granted the defendants' motion for a retrial, finding that the jury was not required to determine whether the defendants had used or carried "machine guns" or other weapons. In a similar case, the U.N. Court of Justice ruled that the word "machine gun" in the law creates a sentencing factor that enhances a sentence, not elements of a separate crime. The District Court agreed, and the trial judge imposed a sentence that was longer than the 30-year mandatory sentence. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a concurring opinion, agreed with the lower court's decision, and sent the case back to the trial court for further proceedings. The court held that the trial Judge's instructions to the jury were not sufficient to determine the nature of the weapons at issue and that the sentencing factor should be determined by the jury, not the judge. The high court concluded that "machineGuns" in  924(c)(1) created a new substantive crime that was not determined by a jury or by a judge.

Title: United States v. Garcia
Year: 1985
Decided: June 25, 1985
Supreme Court Justice: John Paul Stevens
Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that the Bail Reform Act of 1984, which authorized judges to deny bail to certain individuals charged with serious crimes, did not violate the Constitution's Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, or Seventh Amendments. The Court found that the act provided adequate procedural protections and served a compelling government interest in ensuring public safety.

In this Supreme Court case, the Bishop Paiute Tribe, a federally recognized Native American tribe, sued Inyo County, California, and its officials, claiming sovereign immunity from state-court processes after county law enforcement executed a search warrant on the tribe's reservation for casino employment records related to a welfare fraud investigation.

The central legal question was whether the Tribe could sue under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which allows individuals to seek relief against those who, under state law, violate federally protected rights. The Supreme Court held that the Tribe does not qualify as a "person" who may sue under § 1983, aligning with the parties' agreement and the Court's precedent that states and Native American tribes are not "persons" subject to suit under this statute.

The Court did not address whether the Tribe's suit could proceed under federal law other than § 1983, as the parties had not clearly presented this issue, and the lower courts had not decided on it. Therefore, the Supreme Court remanded the case for further consideration of whether there is another federal law that could provide jurisdiction for the Tribe's claims.

The implications of this decision are that the Tribe cannot use § 1983 to assert sovereign immunity and block the state's investigation. However, the case leaves open the possibility that there may be other federal legal grounds for the Tribe to assert its claims, which the lower courts will need to examine. The decision maintains the principle that Native American tribes, like states, are not "persons" who can sue or be sued under § 1983, but it does not preclude tribes from seeking relief through other federal laws.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the widow and two daughters of a former Army Medical Corps doctor who were brutally murdered in their home on the Fort Bragg, N.C., military reservation.  According to the court's order, filed in federal district court in New York, on February 17, 1970, a physician who was assigned to the unit that investigated the deaths of his wife, his two daughters, aged 2 and 5, told of a bizarre and ritualistic murder. He also told of three men standing near the couch who attacked him, tore his pajama top, and clubbed him into unconsciousness. The court found that the delay in bringing the charges and specifications against MacDonald violated his Sixth Amendment right to a speedy trial.  The court also ruled that, once charges were dismissed, MacDonald could not appeal the denial of a motion to dismiss on Speedy Trial Clause grounds until after the trial had been completed.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against MacDonald. The SEC's complaint charges MacDonald with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty. The complaint also seeks an officer-and-director bar against MacDonald and a bar against him from serving as an officer or director of a public company.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 531 F.2d 206 (January 24, 1975).

Washington’s People’s Choice Initiative (Initiative 980) replaced the State’s former blanket primary system with a two-stage voting process. In the first stage, registered voters cast ballots listing all eligible candidates for governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary of state, treasurer, commissioner of lands, superintendent of public instruction, insurance commissioner, labor and industries commissioner, and auditor. Only the top two candidates from each race move on to the second stage, where they compete for the governorship. The State’s Secretary of State certified the initiative measure for inclusion on the November 2004 ballot. Shortly afterward, respondent Washington State Republican Committee sued, claiming that Initiative 980 violated its free-speech rights by forcing it to present candidates whom it did not want to endorse. The Federal District Court entered a preliminary injunction, but the Ninth Circuit vacated it, concluding that Initiative 980 imposed a severe burden on the First Amendment rights of both respondent committees. Held: Initiative 980 is facially constitutional. Pp. 4−13. (a) Initiative 980 does not on its face impose a severe burden on respondents’ associational rights. Such a burden occurs when a governmental restriction on protected speech is not reasonably related to the achievement of a compelling state interest. See, e.g., Elk Grocery Ltd. v. Board of Trustees of Paterson, 325 U.S. 161, 167. Here, Initiative 980 does not severely burden respondents’ associational rights because it does not on its face provide for the nomination of candidates or compel political parties to associate with or endorse candidates. Nor is there any basis in this facial challenge for assuming that candidates’ party-preference designations will confuse voters. Without the specter of widespread voter confusion, respondents’ arguments about forced association and compelled speech fall flat. Pp. 4−8. (b) Because Initiative 980 does not on its face provide for the nomination of candidates or compel political parties to associate with or endorse candidates, and because there is no basis in this facial challenge for presuming that candidates’ party-preference designations will confuse voters, Initiative 980 does not on its face severely burden respondents’ associational rights. Pp. 8−10. (c) The First Amendment does not require this Court to invalidate a popularly enacted election process that has never been carried out. P. 10. 460 F.3d 1108, reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Breyer, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan issued a writ of habeas corpus to Reginald Lett on the ground that his Michigan murder conviction violated the Double Jeopardy Clause of the Constitution. Lett was convicted of shooting a taxi driver to death after an argument broke out in a Detroit liquor store. The jury in Lett's first trial was unable to reach a unanimous verdict, and the trial judge declared a mistrial and dismissed the jury. The trial judge then called the jury back into the courtroom, along with the prosecutor and defense counsel, and asked them what if they could not agree on a verdict? The jury sent out another note, asking "What if we can't agree? [M]istrial? [W]hat? "I'd like to ask you what if you're going to say, or how the split is, or any of that. So, I'm sorry. I don't want to know what your verdict might be," and the judge called Lett back into court. The next day, the jury was able to find him guilty of second-degree murder after deliberating for only 3 hours and 15 minutes. The court granted Lett a new trial, and he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the lower court's decision. The Supreme Court of Michigan reversed, holding that Lett had not shown that his conviction violated his right to a fair trial under the Constitution's "deferential standard of review"

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit reversed a lower court's ruling that barred a Kansas inmate from participating in a sex offender treatment program. The court ruled that the program's requirements for inmates to sign an "Admission of Responsibility" form violated his Fifth Amendment rights against compelled self-incrimination. The Supreme Court held that the "Admission" form is not privileged, and the program is not a subterfuge for the conduct of a criminal investigation. The justices held that there was no evidence that the information obtained from the program would be used against the inmate in future criminal proceedings. The high court held that "the admission of culpability regarding his crime of conviction would create a risk of a perjury prosecution"

Appellee, who is qualified to vote in primary and general elections in Georgia, filed suit in Federal District Court to restrain appellants from using Georgia's county unit system as a basis for counting votes in a Democratic primary for the nomination of a United States Senator and statewide officers, and for declaratory relief. Appellee alleged that the use of the County unit system in counting, tabulating, consolidating, and certifying votes cast in primary elections violates the Equal Protection Clause and the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and the Seventeenth Amendment. As the constitutionality of a state statute was involved and the question was a substantial one, a three-judge court was properly convened. Held: 1. The action of appellee in the conduct of its primary constitutes state action within the meaning of the Amendment. Pp. 463-464. (a) The fact that the Democratic Committee voted to hold the primary on a popular vote basis does not relieve a court of adjudicating its legality, particularly where the practice is deeply rooted and long standing. P. 464. (b) The District Court did not proceed on the basis that in a statewide election every qualified person was entitled to one vote and that all weighted voting was outlawed. Rather it allowed a county unit-based system to be used in weighting the votes if the system showed no greater disparity against a county than exists against any State in the conducting of national elections. Baker v. Carr, 369 U. S. 186, distinguished. The concept of political equality in the voting booth contained in the Fifteenth Amendment extends to all phases of state elections and, as previously noted, there is no indication in the Constitution that homesite or occupation affords a permissible basis for distinguishing between qualified voters within the State. And these rights must be recognized in any preliminary election that in fact determines the true weight a vote will have. Cf. Nixon v. Herndon, 273 U.S. 536, and the Nineteenth Amendment does the same for women, and if the case were dismissed as moot appellants would be "free to return to their old ways." United States v. W. T. Grant Co., 345 U. s. 629, 632, 73 S. C. 894, 897, 97 L. Ed. 987, 98 F. Supp. 158, vacated and remanded.

The Supreme Court of the United States issued a landmark ruling in the case of Blumblau v. Mead Data Central, Inc., 496 U. S. 581 (1990), regarding the interpretation of Section 505 of the Copyright Act of 1976. The Court held that prevailing plaintiffs and defendants in copyright disputes should be treated equally, and attorney's fees should be awarded to prevailing parties only as a matter of the court's discretion. The Court overturned a previous decision by the Federal Circuit Court of Appeals, which had upheld a "dual standard" for awarding attorney's fees in copyright cases, providing that prevailing plaintiffs were entitled to receive fees automatically, while prevailing defendants needed to demonstrate bad faith or frivolousness in order to qualify for fees.

The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA) exempts from the statute’s minimum wage and maximum hours rules “any employee employed in domestic service employment to provide companionship services for individuals who (because of age or infirmity) are unable to care for themselves (as such terms are defined and delimited by regulations of the Secretary [of Labor]).” 29 U. S. C. §213(a)(15). A Department of Labor regulation (labeled an “interpretation”) defines “domestic service employment” as “services of a household nature performed by an employee in or about a private home … of the person by whom he or she is employed … such as cooks, waiters, butlers, valets, maids, housekeepers, governesses, nurses, janitors, laundresses, caretakers, handymen, gardeners, footmen, grooms, and chauffeurs of automobiles for family use [as well as] babysitters employed on other than a casual basis.” Respondent argues that the 1974 agency notice-and-comment procedure, leading to the promulgation of the third-party regulation, was legally “defective” because it is inconsistent with another, legally governing regulation. The Court of Appeals concluded that the regulation did not fill a statutory gap and hence was not legally binding. Held: 1. The 1974 regulation is legally binding under the Administrative Procedure Act, which requires an agency conducting notice of proposed rulemaking to publish in its notice “either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved,” and that Congress intended its broad grant of definitional authority to the Department to include the authority to answer these kinds of questions. Pp. 5–11. (a) When an agency fills such a “gap” reasonably, and in accordance with other applicable (e.g., procedural) requirements, the courts accept the result as legally binding, and this Court has accepted that interpretation. P. 5. (b) The 1974 rule-making procedure is not binding because notice was inadequate and the Department‘s explanation also inadequate. Respondent refers to the Social Security statute and the legislative history as well as to the relevant sections of the statute, which govern the scope and definition of statutory terms, and the relevant section of the regulation, 29 CFR §552.109(a), which provides the Department with the power to fill these gaps through rules and regulations. The sole purpose of the Third-Party Regulation is to explain how the companionhip services exemption applies to persons employed by third-part-party entities, whereas the primary (if not sole) purpose of that regulation is to describe the kind of work that must be performed by someone to qualify as a domestic service employee. The Department focused fully upon the matter in question. It gave notice, it proposed regulations, it received public comment, and it issued final regulations in light of that comment. The resulting regulation says that employees who provide “companionship services” fall within the terms of the statutory exemption irrespective of who pays them. Since on its face the regulation seems to fill a statute gap, one might ask what precisely is it about the regulation that might make it unreasonable or otherwise unlawful? Respondent contends that a thorough examination of the regulations’ content, its method of promulgation, and its context reveals serious legal problems-problems that led the Second Circuit to conclude that the Regulation was unenforceable. The statutory language refers broadly to “Domestic service” employment and to the categories of companionship workers paid by large institutions, but also to those paid directly by a family member of an elderly or inirm person receiving such services whenever the family member lived in a different household than the invalid. In this case, the parties to a multinational business transaction agreed to submit any disputes arising out of the transaction to binding arbitration in London. However, one of the parties later sued in a US district court, claiming that the arbitration clause was void and unenforceable. The lower court dismissed the lawsuit, ruling that the parties had waived their right to sue in court by agreeing to arbitration. The appeals court upheld the lower court's decision, stating that the parties had explicitly agreed to submit any disputes to arbitration and that the court should not interfere with that agreement.

Respondent, a new institution, applied to the Federal Home Loan Bank Board (FHLBB) for the approval necessary to obtain account insurance from the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation (FSLIC). Under FHLBB regulations, approval of new institutions was withheld if their "financial policies or management" were found to be "unsafe" for any of various reasons, including "character of the management." Respondent filed a notice of appeal, which, on respondent's motion, the District Court certified as frivolous. The Ninth Circuit dismissed the appeal "for lack of jurisdiction." Held: A district court's rejection of a defendant's qualified-immunity defense is a "final decision" subject to immediate appeal under the general appellate jurisdiction statute, 28 U. S. C. § 1291. Pp. 6-8. (a) A district-court order denying qualified immunity, to the extent it turns on an issue of law, is an appealable "final" decision within the meaning of the Cohen v. Beneficial Indust. Loan Corp., 337 U.S. 541, regardless of whether that denial takes the form of a refusal to grant a defendant’s motion to dismiss or a denial of summary judgment. P. 6. (b) The Harlow right to immunity is a right that immunity with respect to those claims has been finally denied, not from litigation in general, and when immunity has been denied, appeal must be available, and cannot be foreclosed by the mere addition of other claims to the suit. Thus, an order rejecting the defense of qualified immunity at either the dismissal stage or the summary-judgment stage is a “final decision” subject to instant appeal under Cohen and Mitchell, supra, at 526. The Court of Appeals in the present case, in the first of its two decisions, rested its "one-appeal" pronouncement upon the proposition that resolving the question of entitlement to qualified immunity “should not require more than one judiciously timed appeal.” Pelletier v. Federal Loan Bank of San Francisco, No. 94-56507, reprinted in App. to Pet. for Cert. 1a, reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court of the United States holds that a prisoner's confession obtained during an interrogation in violation of Miranda's constitutional protection against self-incrimination cannot be used as evidence in a criminal prosecution. The Court rules that the "categorical" rule set forth by the Michigan Court of Appeals, which states that a prisoner is in custody for Miranda purposes if he is taken from his cell for questioning and if the questioning involves events that took place outside the prison, is incorrect. The Court finds that the rule fails to adequately consider the specific circumstances of the interrogation and ignores the fact that a prisoner is not in custody for Miranda purposes unless he is being questioned about crimes committed inside the prison.

United States v. Kelly O'Gilvie, et al.
No.: 95-1101

Argued: March 1, 1996
Decided: June 25, 1996

ON APPEAL FROM THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK, JOHN V. LEBLANCHER, Judge

---

Before: Breyer, Stevens, and Thomas
Opinion by: Breyer

---

COUNTRY OF ORIGIN: United States

DATE OF ARGUMENT: February 28, 1996

---

OPINION OF THE COURT

JOHN PAUL STEVENS, Justice

I concur in the majority opinion. I write separately to express my belief that the Internal Revenue Code's exclusion of punitive damages from gross income under Section 104(a)(2) applies to punitive damages awarded in cases of personal injury.

PUNITIVE DAMAGES AND PERSONAL INJURIES

The Internal Revenue Code defines "personal injuries" as "any damage arising from bodily harm." 26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(1). Punitive damages are defined as "any damages received (whether by suit or agreement)" on account of personal injuries. § 104(a)(2). Thus, punitive damages are clearly designed to compensate for personal injuries.

It is true that punitive damages may serve additional purposes, including deterring wrongdoing and punishing the wrongdoer. However, these purposes do not alter the fundamental character of punitive damages as compensation for personal injuries. As the Supreme Court of California observed in People v. Escola, "[w]hen punitive damages are awarded, they are usually accompanied by an award of compensatory damages." 1 Cal.4th 480, 491, 6 Cal.Rptr.2d 581, 588 (1992). Indeed, punitive damages often represent a significant percentage of the total damages awarded in a case involving personal injury.

Furthermore, punitive damages are typically awarded in conjunction with compensatory damages. In many cases, punitive damages are viewed as necessary to ensure that the injured person receives adequate compensation. As the Supreme Court of Illinois noted in People ex rel. Harris v. City of Chicago, "Without punitive damages, the injured party will receive little or nothing for his losses." 122 Ill.2d 137, 146, 521 N.E.2d 112, 116 (1988).

Despite these facts, the government contends that punitive damages are not "on account of personal injuries," and thus are not subject to the exclusion under Section 104(a)(2). The government bases its position on the distinction between compensatory and punitive damages, arguing that punitive damages are not truly compensatory. While it is true that punitive damages serve additional purposes beyond mere compensation, it is equally true that they are closely related to compensatory damages.

Indeed, punitive damages are often awarded in response to the perceived inadequacy of compensatory damages. As the Supreme Court of Texas observed in Johnson v. Dallas Independent School Dist., "When compensatory damages fail adequately to compensate the injured party, punitive damages may be awarded to provide additional relief." 805 S.W.2d 532, 536 (Tex.1991). Similarly, in People v. Escola, the California Supreme Court recognized that punitive damages are often awarded "to supplement compensatory damages when they prove insufficient." 1 Cal.4th 480, 491, 6 Cal.Rptr.2d 581, 588 (1992).

In light of these considerations, it seems reasonable to treat punitive damages as falling within the category of "damages received (whether by suit or agreement)" on account of personal injuries. Such a treatment is consistent with the plain language of Section 104(a)(2), which uses the broadest possible terms to describe the types of damages that must be excluded from gross income. Furthermore, treating punitive damages as compensatory damages serves the practical purpose of ensuring that individuals who suffer personal injuries receive adequate compensation.

CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, I believe that the Internal Revenue Code's exclusion of punitive damages from gross income under Section 104(a)(2) applies to punitive damages awarded in cases of personal injury.

The Supreme Court of the United States has reversed the decision of the Arkansas Supreme Court, holding that the common-law "knock and announce" principle is indeed part of the reasonableness inquiry under the Fourth Amendment. The case involved Sharlene Wilson, who was convicted on various narcotics charges after police entered her home without knocking or announcing their presence, despite the main door being open.

The Court's opinion emphasizes that at the time the Fourth Amendment was framed, the common law recognized the authority of law enforcement to enter a dwelling but generally required officers to announce their presence and authority before doing so. This principle was seen as part of the reasonableness of a search, which is the central requirement of the Fourth Amendment.

The Court acknowledged that there are exceptions to the knock-and-announce requirement, such as when there is a threat of physical violence, when a suspect has just escaped custody, or when there is a risk that evidence might be destroyed if notice is given. However, the Court did not provide a comprehensive list of exceptions, leaving it to lower courts to determine the specific circumstances under which an unannounced entry might be reasonable.

In Wilson's case, the Arkansas Supreme Court had rejected the argument that the Fourth Amendment requires officers to knock and announce before entering a residence, leading to the affirmation of her conviction. The U.S. Supreme Court disagreed with this conclusion, stating that the knock-and-announce principle is embedded in the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures.

The Supreme Court remanded the case to the state courts to make the necessary factual findings and to assess the reasonableness of the unannounced entry in the first instance, taking into account the specific circumstances of the case, such as the potential threat to officer safety and the risk of evidence destruction. The decision implies that evidence obtained in violation of the knock-and-announce principle could potentially be suppressed under the Fourth Amendment.

Appellee MITE Corp. and its wholly owned subsidiary, MITE Holdings, Inc., are corporations organized under the laws of Delaware with their principal executive offices in Connecticut. Under the Illinois Business Takeover Disclosure Act, any takeover offer for the shares of a target company must be registered with the Secretary of State unless the Secretary calls a hearing. MITE filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission a Schedule 14D-1 indicating that MITE was willing to pay $28 per share for any and all outstanding shares of Chicago Rivet & Machine Co., a publicly held Illinois corporation, a premium of approximately $4 over the then-prevailing market price. On February 2, 1979, Chicago-Rivet notified MITE that it would file suit in Illinois state court to enjoin MITE from enforcing the Illinois Act. The complaint asked for a declaratory judgment that the Act was pre-empted by the Williams Act and violated the Commerce Clause, and MITE sought a temporary restraining order and permanent injunctions prohibiting the Secretary from enforcing Illinois Act enforcement. The District Court entered a final judgment against MITE, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The Illinois Act is unconstitutional under the Supremacy Clause. Pp. 633-636. (a) Section 28(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which provides that "nothing in this title shall affect the jurisdiction of the securities commission (or any agency or officer performing like functions) of any State over any security or any person insofar as it does not conflict with the provisions of this title or the rules and regulations thereunder," provides that nothing in this Act shall affect a corporation's jurisdiction over its stockholders living in Illinois, but also with those living in other States and having no connection with Illinois. Thus, a state statute is void to the extent that it actually conflicts with a valid federal statute; and "[a] conflict will be found "where compliance with both federal and state regulations is a physical impossibility . . .," Florida Lime & Avocado Growers, Inc. v. Paul, 373 U. S. 132, 142-143. P. 634. (b) The Illinois act does not violate these principles for two reasons. First, it directly regulates and prevents, unless its terms are satisfied, interstate tender offers which in turn would generate interstate transactions. Second, the burden the Act imposes on interstate commerce must not be excessive in relation to the local interests served by the statute. See, e. g., Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc.'s § 302, Comment b, pp. 307-308. The Act purports to regulate directly and to interdict interstate commerce, including commerce wholly outside the State, it must be held invalid as were the laws at issue in Shaffer v. Heitner, 433 U.S. 186, 197. The Commerce Clause also precludes the application of a State statute to commerce that takes place wholly outside of the State's borders, whether or not the commerce has effects within the State. The most obvious burden is the Illinois statute's previously described nationwide reach, purporting to give Illinois the power to determine whether a tender offer may proceed anywhere. The effects of allowing the Illinois Secretary to block a nationwide tender offer are substantial. Shareholders are deprived of the opportunity to sell their shares at a premium. The reallocation of economic resources to their highest valued use, a process which can improve efficiency and competition, is hindered. The incentive the tender offer mechanism provides incumbent management to perform well so that stock prices remain high is reduced. The potential for delay provided by the hearing provisions upset the balance struck by Congress by favoring management at the expense of stockholders. The Illinois law, unless complied with, sought to prevent MITE's competitor from making a competing tender offer for its own stock without complying with the Act, leaving Chicago R.ivet's shareholders to depend only on the protections afforded them by federal securities law, protections which Illinois views as inadequate to protect investors in other contexts. This distinction is at variance with Illinois' asserted legislative purpose, and tends to undermine appellant's justification for the burdens the statute imposes on the interstate commerce. The State has no legitimate interest in protecting nonresident shareholders. While protecting local investors is plainly a legitimate state objective, the State has, insofar as the Illinois law burdens out-of-state transactions, there is nothing to be weighed in the balance to sustain the law. Moreover, the Act completely exempts from coverage a corporation’s acquisition of its own shares. Thus Chicago Rivedt was able to make a competing offer for it own stock, leaving the shareholders to rely only on protections which the Illinois Court views as insufficient to protect them in other circumstances. This decision is not a frivolous question by any means; it is an issue to be decided when and if the Secretary initiates an action. The case is not moot in these respects, and therefore, the case is inapplicable to this Court in all essential respects.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Nevada has ruled that a bankruptcy judge erred in denying a debtor's motion to dismiss a claim for a tax-free allowance under the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005 (BAPCPA). The BAPCPA was passed by Congress in 2005 to address perceived abuses of the bankruptcy system. The court held that the text, context, and purpose of the law precluded the court's finding that a debtor who owns his car outright and does not make loan or lease payments may not claim an allowance for vehicle-ownership costs. The B APCPA provides a means test to determine how much income a debtor is capable of paying. The test requires a debtor to deduct specified expenses from his current monthly income. The result is his "disposable income," the amount he has available to reimburse creditors. The bankruptcy judge's decision found that the means test does not apply to the "reasonable living expenses" that the debtor can claim as his reasonable living expenses and thereby shield from creditors. Without a ruling on the issue, the bankruptcy court will have to determine whether the bankruptcy judge should have granted the motion to discharge the debt.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Dura Pharmaceuticals, Inc., a now-defunct microcap company, for defrauding investors by making false statements concerning both the company's drug profits and future FDA approval of an asthmatic spray device.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed on April 15, 1997, and unsealed on February 24, 1998, Dura falsely claimed that its drug profits would be lower than expected, principally due to slow drug sales.  The complaint also alleges that the defendants' sales of its securities were inflated because of the misrepresentations.  As alleged in the complaint, however, the defendants had no intention of causing any loss.  Dura's share price fell significantly after the truth became known, and the price on the date of purchase was inflated.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, the Defendants have consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering Dura to pay a civil penalty of $1,000,000.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  To learn more about this matter, see Investor.gov/Investor.gov.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida today entered a final judgment in favor of the Florida government in a related case.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Miami, Florida, alleges that an anonymous tip provided the basis for a stop and frisk of a person suspected of carrying a concealed firearm.  According to the complaint, on October 13, 1995, an anonymous caller reported to the Miami-Dade Police that a young black male standing at a particular bus stop and wearing a plaid shirt was carrying a gun. The tip, which the tipster provided to the officers, was not reliable because it was not accompanied by specific indicia of reliability, for example, the correct forecast of a subject's "not easily predicted" movements. The complaint further alleges that the tip led the officers to believe that the individual was armed and presently dangerous, and that the officer had no basis for believing he had inside information about the person.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Florida today announced criminal charges against J. L. Gibson, who was charged under state law with carrying a firearm without a license and possessing a firearm while under the age of 18. Gibson consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar. Gibson also agreed to be enjoined from associating with any third party that may have provided material assistance in this matter. Gibson agreed to settle the SEC's case by consenting to a permanent injunction against future violations. The court's order also ordered Gibson to disgorge $1,078 in prejudgment interests and pay a $20,000 civil penalty. Gibson will be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Respondents were arrested on March 21, 1986, after being charged in a 29-count indictment alleging various Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) violations, mail and wire fraud offenses, extortion, and various criminal gambling violations. At respondents' arraignment, the Government moved to have Salerno and Cafaro detained pursuant to § 3142(e), on the ground that no condition or combination of conditions of release would assure the safety of the community or any person. The District Court held a hearing at which the Court of Appeals affirmed, concluding that the Government had established by clear and convincing evidence that no conditions of pretrial release would ensure the community's safety. Held: The Bail Reform Act of 1984 (Act) does not violate substantive due process because the pretrial detention it authorizes violates "substantive due process." Pp. 531-532. (a) The Act provides that, after a hearing pursuant to subsection (f) of the Act, the judicial officer shall order the detention of the arrestee prior to trial if the Government demonstrates that no such conditions "will reasonably assure the ... safety of any other person and the community." Schall v. Martin, 467 U. S. 253, distinguished. Section 3143(f) provides that "the judicial officer ... shall order [the] detention of [the arrestee] before trial." If the Government finds that no pre-trial conditions can reasonably assure a person's safety, he must state his findings of fact in writing and support his conclusion with "clear and convincing [evidence]," §3142(i)(2). If the judge finds that such conditions cannot reasonably assure his detention, the detention must be subject to immediate appellate review. The Act's review provisions provide for immediate review of the detention decision. Schall, supra, at 269, n. 18, and the Act review provisions, § 3145(c), provide for instant appellate review of detention decisions. The Bails Reform Act is valid, since the Act's legislative history clearly indicates that Congress did not formulate the pretririal detention provisions as punishment for dangerous individuals, see S. Rep. No. 98-225, at 4-7. There is no doubt that preventing danger to the community is a legitimate regulatory goal, but there is no evidence that the Act imposes some substantive limitations on the National Legislature's powers in this area. Nor are the incidents of pretri-detrial detention excessive in relation to the regulatory goal Congress sought to achieve. The fact that the Bail Act might operate unconstitutionally under some conceivable set of circumstances is insufficient to render it wholly invalid, since this Court has not recognized an "overbreadth" doctrine outside the limited context of the First Amendment. P. 527. 794 F. 2d 64, reversed.

After the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (HEW) transferred a parcel of federal property to a private corporation pursuant to the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949, which was an evident exercise of Congress' power under the Property Clause of the Constitution, respondents, a group of organizations representing evangelicals and fundamentalists, filed suit against HEW and others in Federal District Court, alleging that the transfer violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. The District Court upheld the transfer, and the Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Respondents failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted, since they lacked standing to sue. Pp. 108-118. (a) Standing to sue is a jurisdictional requirement that arises from the limitations imposed by Art. III of the Constitution on the exercise of the judicial power of the United States. Pp. 108-110. (b) Under the rule announced in Flast v. Cohen, 392 U. S. 83, taxpayers have no standing to challenge the validity of federal expenditures except as they relate to the exercise of congressional power under the Taxing and Spending Clause of Art. I, § 8. Since the transfer here involved was not an exercise of authority conferred by that Clause, respondents lacked standing to sue as taxpayers. Pp. 110-112. (c) Neither do respondents have standing to sue as citizens. Assertion of a right to a particular kind of Government conduct, which the Government has violated by acting differently, cannot alone satisfy the Art. III requirements of standing without draining those requirements of meaning. And although respondents claimed that the Constitution had been violated, they identified no personal injury suffered by them as a consequence of the alleged constitutional error, other than the psychological consequence presumably produced by observation of conduct with which one disagrees. Pp. 112-115. (d) Enforcement of the Establishment Clause does not demand special exceptions from the Art. III requirement that a plaintiff allege "distinct and palpable injury to himself" that is likely to be redressed if the requested relief is granted. Implicit in the Court of Appeals' ruling below was the philosophy that the business of the federal courts is correcting constitutional errors, and that "cases and controversies" are at best merely convenient vehicles for doing so and at worst nuisances that may be dispensed with when they become obstacles to that transcendent endeavor. This philosophy has no place in our constitutional scheme. Pp. 115-118. 619 F. 2d 258, reversed.

Petitioner Davis was convicted of capital murder in a Texas state court and sentenced to death. His conviction became final when the Texas Court of Appeals rejected his contention that the trial court erred in admitting into evidence a statement he gave to police shortly after the murders. While awaiting execution, Davis moved for postconviction relief in the trial court, claiming that the admission of the statement violated his Sixth Amendment right to confront the witnesses against him. The trial court denied relief, rejecting Davis' contention that the statement was coerced. On interlocutory appeal, the Texas Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the statement was involuntary and that its introduction constituted a denial of due process. The State Supreme Court affirmed, agreeing that the statement was involuntary, but ruling that the admission of the statement did not deny due process because the victim's widow had been permitted to give a tearful recital of the events leading to her husband's murder. Subsequently, the Texas Court of Appeals denied Davis' petition for rehearing, and the State Supreme Court declined to review. Meanwhile, Davis learned that another man had confessed to the murders and that the real killer had been released on bail pending retrial. Davis then filed suit in Federal District Court seeking habeas corpus relief, claiming that the true killer's confession proved his own innocence. The District Court denied relief, but the Fifth Circuit reversed, holding that the true killer's confession created a constitutional right to habeas corpus relief. Held: The Fifth Circuit correctly ruled that the true killer's confession created a constitutional right to habeas corpus relief. Pp. 10-18. (a) The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees a meaningful opportunity to establish innocence. If the true killer's confession establishes Davis' innocence, then the Due Process Clause creates a constitutional right to habeas corpus relief. Pp. 10-12. (b) The Fifth Circuit correctly applied the rule that a constitutional right to habeas corpus relief arises whenever a defendant presents a prima facie showing of innocence. The true killer's confession provides a strong indication that Davis is actually innocent. Pp. 12-15. (c) The Fifth Circuit correctly refused to recognize a constitutional right to habeas corpus relief based on Davis' affidavits alone. Those affidavits were given long after the murders, and the lack of explanation for their tardiness raises doubts about their credibility. They also contained conflicting information regarding key aspects of the murders, and must be considered in light of the overwhelming evidence of Davis' guilt at trial. Pp. 15-18. Affirmed.

The ADA requires employers to include at least 15 employees in their work force for each working day in each of 20 or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Nebraska reversed the death sentence of a man convicted of two counts of felony murder for the 1980 stabbing deaths of two women. The court held that the trial court did not have to instruct the jury on the lesser included offenses of second-degree murder and manslaughter. The trial court refused to do so, and the Nebraska Supreme Court overturned the conviction on the grounds that the jury had not been properly instructed. We conclude that such instructions are not constitutionally required.

This case involved a group of individuals who were arrested for "disturbing the peace" while protesting the US involvement in the Vietnam War. They challenged the constitutional validity of Texas House Bill 1274, which criminalizes disruptive behavior in public places. The Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the bill is unconstitutional due to its broadness and lack of clarity regarding what constitutes "disruptive behavior."

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around a will executed by Senator Augustus O. Bacon in 1911, which bequeathed land to the City of Macon, Georgia, to be used as a park exclusively for white people. Over time, the city allowed access to all races, leading to a lawsuit by the park's Board of Managers to appoint new trustees who would enforce the racial segregation stipulated in the will. The Georgia courts affirmed the appointment of new trustees without addressing the racial segregation issue.

The Supreme Court had to reconcile two principles: the right of an individual to associate with whomever they choose and the constitutional prohibition of state-sponsored racial inequality under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court determined that while private entities can restrict membership based on race, a city cannot manage a public facility on a segregated basis. The Court found that the park had been maintained as a public facility for white people only and that the mere appointment of private trustees did not change its public character. The Court held that the park's public nature and the city's historical involvement meant that it remained subject to the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection requirements.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Georgia courts, concluding that the park must be treated as a public institution and could not be operated on a segregated basis, regardless of the change in trustees. The Court implied that the Georgia courts' decision was influenced by an incorrect assumption that private trustees could enforce the racial restriction without violating the Constitution.

Justice White concurred with the majority's decision but for different reasons, focusing on state legislation that validated racial restrictions in charitable trusts. He argued that this legislation involved the state in private discrimination, converting it into state action that violates the Fourteenth Amendment. He suggested that the judgment be vacated and the case remanded for further proceedings free from the influence of an erroneous view of federal law.

This Supreme Court decision involves a man named Ahmed Ressam, who tried to enter the US through a port in Washington state with explosives in his car. He was caught and charged with several crimes, including lying to a customs officer about being a Canadian citizen. The Court of Appeals overturned his conviction on one count because it believed the law required that the explosive be carried "in relation to" the underlying felony. However, the Supreme Court disagreed and ruled that the most natural reading of the statutory text showed that the man's actions constituted a violation of the law.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against two New York City officers who were convicted of felony drug possession.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the officers.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, on March 9, 1965, Officer Samuel Lasky of the New York Police Department observed Sibron in the hallway of an apartment building where he had just finished taking a shower and was about to go to dinner when he saw two men tiptoeing about the hallway. The complaint alleges that the officers' search was conducted in self-protection and did not result in any collateral legal consequences. The court further ruled that the search was not justified because the officers had probable cause to believe that the individual was in possession of a dangerous weapon.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against the two officers, charging them with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 15(a) of Exchange Act Rule 15a-1 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the officers consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, civil penalties, and officer-related injunctive relief.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin today entered a final judgment in favor of the school district and its school board in a teachers' strike case.  The court held that the school board had a duty to determine whether to employ and dismiss teachers engaged in a strike prohibited by state law.  According to the court's order, filed on March 18, 1974, the teachers' union went on strike, in direct violation of the federal due process provisions of Wisconsin law. The court found that the teachers were entitled to the right to return to work after a three-day strike, and that the Board had the power to make a reasonable decision about whether to fire them.  In a parallel action, the Wisconsin Attorney General's Office today announced criminal charges against one of the teachers.  On March 23, the Board voted to terminate the teachers, and the same letter invited all teachers on strike to reapply for teaching positions. None of these teachers returned to work.  After conducting classes with substitute teachers on March 26 and 27, the board decided to suspend the teachers for cause.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the district and school board agreed to the suspension.  As set forth in the court order, the suspension order is not ideal because it leaves the balance of power in labor relations where the state legislature struck it, and requires the Board to make the decision whether to suspend or fire the teachers at a time when it has no reasonable basis for making such a decision.  Additionally, the court ruled that the district's prior involvement in negotiating with the teachers was not sufficient to overcome the presumption of honesty and integrity in policymakers with decisionmaking power.  For example, the Court found that a school board member had some personal or official stake in the decision to dismiss teachers, but preferred to be treated as a group rather than as an individual.   The Court also ruled that a district attorney could not determine whether a school district employee had a right to terminate a teacher without due process.  To learn more about the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, see, for example, Wisconsin Public Finance Abuse Task Force v. Miller, Inc. (1962); Wisconsin Department of Education v. Kelly, (1961); Wisconsin Secretary of State's Office v. Schlegelmilch, (1972); and for further information on the subject of school district disciplinary actions, see: Wisconsin Secretary Of State's Complaint, v. Board of Education, (Sept. 24, 1974); Wisconsin Auditor General, (Nov. 26, 1974), and Board of Regents v.

The U.S. Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Oklahoma Court of Appeals, upholding the doctrine of sovereign immunity for the Kiowa Tribe of Oklahoma in a commercial suit. The Court confirmed that an Indian tribe is immune from suit unless Congress has explicitly authorized the suit or the tribe has waived its immunity. This immunity applies regardless of whether the tribe's activities are commercial or governmental, and whether they occur on or off the reservation.

The case involved the Kiowa Tribe defaulting on a promissory note for $285,000 plus interest, which was part of a commercial transaction with Manufacturing Technologies. The Oklahoma Court of Appeals had ruled that Indian tribes could be sued in state court for off-reservation commercial activities, but the Supreme Court disagreed, stating that tribal immunity is a matter of federal law and cannot be diminished by the states.

The Court acknowledged that the doctrine of tribal immunity has developed over time, often without extensive reasoning, and that there are arguments against its modern application, especially in the context of commercial activities that extend beyond traditional tribal customs. However, the Court chose not to make any changes to the doctrine in this case, deferring to Congress's authority to legislate on the matter. The Court noted that Congress has occasionally limited tribal immunity in specific instances but has not chosen to abrogate it generally.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court held that the Kiowa Tribe is immune from the lawsuit filed by Manufacturing Technologies, and the judgment of the Oklahoma Court of Appeals was reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California today entered a final judgment against the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) in an emergency action brought by a group of railroad safety professionals.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, alleges that the FRA violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, the federal government's interest in regulating the conduct of railroad employees is at the core of the agency's business.  For example, the complaint alleges that train employees are required to submit to breath and urine tests in the event of a serious train accident, and that these tests can be performed safely outside a hospital environment and with minimal risk to the safety of the train.  In addition, as the complaint further alleges, train employees may be required to provide blood and urine samples to certain train crew members.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has issued an order requiring train employees to provide samples of their blood, urine, or breath to the FBI for testing purposes. The order also requires train workers to submit written consent to the entry of a subpoena, which is required by the federal law. The court's order also provides for the issuance of an officer-and-director bar and a temporary restraining order.  On May 2, 2020, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against the defendants, charging them with violations of Section 5 of the federal securities laws. The complaint seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  A hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2020.  An SEC examination that led to the investigation was conducted in the Office of Inspector General's Analysis and Detection Center in the Philadelphia Regional Office. The case was supervised by Kelly L. Gibson, Chief of the Enforcement Division's Market Abuse Unit. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the FBI.

The U.S. District Court for the Central District of California today entered a final judgment in favor of San Jose, California residents who are seeking to have their rent increased by as much as eight percent in violation of the antifraud provisions of the city's rent control ordinance.  According to the court's order, filed on May 24, 2019, San Jose residents Richard Pennell and Carol Willingham filed a civil injunctive action against the city in 1979, alleging that the city violated the federal securities laws when it imposed rent control provisions on tenants.  The court found that the rent control provision, in particular the "tenant hardship" provisions, are "facially unconstitutional and therefore . . . illegal and void."  The Court also ruled that the tenant hardship provisions are "unreasonable" and "unnecessary" and that a hearing officer may order the excess of the increase to be disallowed.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Pennell.  On May 26, 2018, the Honorable Joseph G. Sansone of the Court of Appeal granted the defendants' request for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an accounting of the amount of the rent increase that would be required to determine the standing of the tenants in the case.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Pennell, Willingham, and Sansone agreed to the entry of judgments that permanently enjoin them from future violations of Section 5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The court also ordered Pennell to pay a civil penalty of $1,000. The settlement is subject to court approval.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 5703.28(c)(7).  The SEC's Office of Investor Education and Advocacy has issued an Investor Alert warning investors to be aware of the dangers of excessive rent increases.

The Supreme Court held that 42 U.S.C. §1981, a civil rights law originating from the post-Civil War era, includes protection against retaliation for individuals who complain about violations of another person's contract-related rights due to racial discrimination. The case involved Hedrick G. Humphries, a black man and former assistant manager at a Cracker Barrel restaurant, who claimed he was fired both due to racial bias and for complaining about the racially motivated dismissal of another black employee.

The Court's decision was influenced by the principle of stare decisis, which emphasizes the importance of adhering to established legal precedents. The Court examined the interpretive history of §1981 and its sister statute, §1982, which similarly protects the rights related to property ownership. The Court noted that past decisions, such as Sullivan v. Little Hunting Park, Inc. (1969), have interpreted these statutes to include protection against retaliation.

The Court also considered the impact of the Civil Rights Act of 1991, which amended §1981 to clarify the scope of the right "to make and enforce contracts" to include post-contract-formation conduct, effectively superseding the narrower interpretation from Patterson v. McLean Credit Union (1989). The legislative history indicated that Congress intended to restore the broader interpretation of §1981 that included retaliation claims.

CBOCS West, Inc., the petitioner, argued that §1981's text does not explicitly cover retaliation, that Congress did not intend to include retaliation in the 1991 amendments, and that allowing §1981 to cover retaliation would create an unnecessary overlap with Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which has its own procedural requirements. The Court rejected these arguments, noting that the overlap was by congressional design and that the principle of stare decisis supports the inclusion of retaliation claims under §1981.

The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had ruled in favor of Humphries on his §1981 retaliation claim, allowing the case to proceed to trial. This decision confirms that §1981 protects against retaliation for advocating the rights of individuals facing racial discrimination in contract-related matters.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against AT&T Inc. and BellSouth Corp., agreeing to settle charges that they violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Los Angeles, alleges that AT&&T violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by failing to deal with its competitors at the wholesale and retail levels.  According to the complaint, the defendants failed to adequately assess the impact of price squeezes on the profitability of their competitors, and instead engaged in a price squeeze.  In its judgment, the court held that a firm with no antitrust duty to deal directly with its rivals has no duty to deals with its competitor at the retail level.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's action, the Defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, ordering them to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty equal to the amount of their profits.  On May 24, 2018, the Honorable Judge David J. Trinko of the U. S. District court for the Northern District of California granted the defendants a temporary restraining order and ordered the defendants to pay a $1,000 civil penalty, which is subject to court approval.  At a hearing on May 26, 2019, the Court of Appeals for the Central District of Florida issued a preliminary injunction against the defendants from violating these provisions.  It also issued an order temporarily suspending the Defendants from participating in any future price-squeeze litigation.   The court's order temporarily halted the Defendants’ motion for an injunction against further violations of these provisions, and the defendants agreed to settle the case by consenting to a judgment that permanently enjoins them from future violations of the anti-price squeeze provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(b)(5) ofÂ the Securities Act. Â The court also ordered the Defendants to pay civil penalties of $1.5 million each, which would be offset by a $500 civil penalty.

Case Name: Smith v. Johnson
Case Number: 12345
Issue: Whether John Smith's claim for wrongful termination is based on a breach of contract or tortious behavior.
Background Information: John Smith was employed by ABC Company as a sales representative. He was fired from his job due to poor performance. Smith believes that he was unfairly dismissed and wants to pursue legal action against the company.
Legal Analysis: The legal analysis begins by examining the terms of Smith's employment contract. The contract specifies that either party can terminate the agreement with notice. However, the contract does not specify the amount of notice required or the circumstances under which termination can occur. Therefore, it is unclear whether Smith's firing was based on a breach of contract.
Next, the analysis considers whether Smith's firing was based on tortious behavior. Tortious behavior occurs when someone engages in harmful or illegal activity that causes harm to another person. In this case, there is no evidence that Smith engaged in any tortious behavior prior to being fired.
Finally, the analysis looks at whether Smith's firing was based on discrimination. Discrimination occurs when someone treats someone else differently based on their race, gender, religion, or other protected characteristic. In this case, there is no evidence that Smith was treated differently based on any of these characteristics.
Based on the above analysis, it is concluded that John Smith's claim for wrongful termination is not based on a breach of contract or tortious behavior.

The Supreme Court held that the traditional four-factor test used by courts of equity applies to disputes arising under the Patent Act. The Court agreed with petitioners' argument that the Patent Act does not indicate that Congress intended a departure from the long tradition of equity practice. The Court also noted that the Patent Act expressly provides that injunctions "may" issue "in accordance with the principles of equity." The Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The Supreme Court of the United States reversed the decision of the Minnesota Supreme Court, holding that respondents Carter and Johns did not have a legitimate expectation of privacy in the apartment where they were observed bagging cocaine by a police officer. The respondents were not overnight guests but were there for a short-term business purpose, and they had no previous relationship with the lessee of the apartment, nor any significant connection to the apartment itself.

The Court clarified that the Fourth Amendment protects individuals against unreasonable searches of their persons, houses, papers, and effects. However, to invoke this protection, an individual must demonstrate a reasonable expectation of privacy in the place searched. The Court referenced past decisions, including Minnesota v. Olson, which recognized that overnight guests in a home have a legitimate expectation of privacy, but distinguished this from the respondents' situation.

The Court emphasized that property used for commercial purposes is treated differently under the Fourth Amendment than residential property. Since the respondents were in the apartment for a purely commercial transaction and only for a few hours, they did not have the same expectation of privacy as someone who lives in or is an overnight guest in the home.

As a result, the Court did not need to decide whether the police officer's observation through the window constituted a "search" under the Fourth Amendment because the respondents did not have a legitimate expectation of privacy in the first place. The judgment of the Minnesota Supreme Court was reversed, and the case was remanded for proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

Respondents sued petitioners, members of Operation Rescue, claiming that they had violated various state and federal statutes by engaging in a series of tactics aimed at preventing women from obtaining abortions at respondents' clinics. Among other things, petitioners demonstrated near the clinics, followed and crowded individuals trying to enter or exit the clinics, and refused to move when told to do so by police. The Federal District Court ultimately entered a permanent injunction against petitioners' demonstrations, striking down the floating buffer zones around people entering and leaving the clinics, but upholding the fixed buffer zones around the clinics' doorways, driveways, and driveway entrances. It also rejected petitioners' claim that the injunction violated their First Amendment rights. The Court of Appeals affirmed the injunction's facial validity, but ruled that it should not be enforced against petitioners because they had committed new crimes after entry of the original suit. Held: 1. The Government Has Interests Significant Enough to Justify Appropriately Tailored Injunctions Securing Unimpeded Physical Access to Abortion Clinics. Pp. 10-16. (a) Given the factual similarity between this case and Madsen v. Watkins, 512 U. S. 741, the governmental interests underlying the injunction in Madsen-ensuring public safety and order, promoting the free flow of traffic on streets and sidewalks, protecting property rights, and protecting a woman's freedom to seek pregnancy-related services-also underlie the injunction here, and in combination are certainly significant enough to justify an appropriately tailored injunction to secure unimpeded physical access to the clinics. Pp. 10-12. (b) However, the floating buffer zones around people entering and leaving the clinics burden more speech than is necessary to serve the relevant governmental interests. Such zones prevent defendants-except for two sidewalk counselors, while they are tolerated by the targeted individual-from communicating a message from a normal conversational distance or handing leaflets to people entering or leaving the clinics who are walking on the public sidewalks. This is a broad prohibition, both because of the type of speech that is restricted and the nature of the location. Speech in public areas is at its most protected on public sidewalks, a prototypical example of a traditional public forum. On the other hand, the record shows that physically abusive conduct, harassment of the police that hampered law enforcement, and the tendency of even peaceful conversations to devolve into aggressive and sometimes violent conduct rendered a prohibition on classic speech in limited parts of a public sidewalk permissible. Pp. 12-14. (c) Likewise, the floating buffer zones around vehicles burden more speech than necessary to serve the relevant governmental interests.
