There is nothing in the record or the District Court's opinion to show that a more limited injunction-keeping protesters away from driveways and parking lot entrances and off the streets, for instance-would be insufficient to ensure that drivers are not confused about how to enter the clinics and are able to gain access to the clinics' driveways and parking lots safely and easily. In contrast, the 15-foot floating buffer zones would restrict the speech of those who simply line the sidewalk or curb in an effort to chant, shout, or hold signs peacefully. Pp. 14-15. (d) By contrast, the fixed buffer zones around the clinics' doorways, driveways, and driveway entrances are necessary to ensure that people and vehicles trying to enter or exit the clinics can do so. The record shows that protesters purposefully or effectively blocked or hindered people from entering and exiting the clinics, from driving up to and away from clinic entrances, and from driving in and out of clinic parking lots. Based on this conduct, the District Court was entitled to conclude that the only way to ensure access was to move back the demonstrations away from the driveways and parking lot entrances. Pp. 15-16. 2. The Floating Buffer Zones Around People Entering and Leaving the Clinics Are Invalid Under the Standard Applicable to Contentbased Regulations. Pp. 16-18. (a) The floating buffer zones around people entering and leaving the clinics burden more speech than is necessary to serve the relevant governmental interests. Pp. 16-17. (b) The floating buffer zones around vehicles burden more speech than is necessary to serve the relevant governmental interests. Pp. 17-18. (c) The "cease and desist" provision limiting the exception for sidewalk counselors in connection with the fixed buffer zone is not content based, but is instead an effort to enhance petitioners' speech rights. Pp. 18-19. (d) The "cease and desist" provision is not content based, even though it allows a clinic patient to terminate a protester's right to speak based on, among other reasons, the patient's disagreement with the message being conveyed. Pp. 19-19. Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, after reviewing the evidence before the state trial court, determined that petitioner failed to establish a constitutional violation warranting habeas relief. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, concluding there was insufficient merit to the case, denied a certificate of appealability (COA) from the District Court's determination. The court of appeals, however, agreed with the lower court's finding that petitioner had not established a substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right. The Supreme Court held in Batson v. Kentucky in 1986 that the use of peremptory challenges to exclude African-Americans from jury service violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The high court held that "a defendant must make a prima facie showing that ... the exclusion of African-American persons from the jury was part of a larger pattern of discrimination aimed at the exclusion" of African Americans from jury duty. In this case, we conclude that a COA should have been issued. We conclude that the court should limit its examination to a threshold inquiry into the underlying merit of petitioner's claims.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the defendant in a lawsuit filed by an inmate named Jasper Gamble. The suit claimed that the defendant, along with several other individuals employed by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, had subjected Gamble to cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Eighth Amendment. The Court found that the Eighth Amendment applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment and that it prohibits more than physically barbarous punishments. However, the Court also noted that the Amendment encompasses broader concepts of dignity, humaneness, and decency. The Court ultimately determined that the defendant's conduct did not rise to the level of cruel and unusual punishment and that the suit should be dismissed.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the lower court in this case involving insider trading. The Court held that the plaintiff, Raymond Dirks, did not violate Section 10(b)(1) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 by passing along inside information to others who then bought and sold securities based on that information. The Court reasoned that there was no duty to disclose or abstain from trading on inside information unless the person receiving the information was an insider or had a fiduciary relationship with the insider. Since Dirks did not fit either category, he did not have such a duty.

The Endangered Species Act of 1973 (NEPA) authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to declare species of animal life "endangered" and to identify the "critical habitat" of these creatures. When a species or its habitat is so listed, the following portion of the Act becomes effective: "The Secretary [of the Interior] shall review other programs administered by him and utilize such programs in furtherance of the purposes of this chapter by carrying out programs for the conservation of endangered species and threatened species listed pursuant to section 1533 of this title and by taking such action necessary to insure that actions authorized, funded, or carried out by them do not jeopardize the continued existence of such endangered species or result in the destruction or modification of habitat of such species . . . ." 16 U. S. C. § 1533 (d) (1976 ed.). Respondents, who were members of the Tennessee Valley Authority's Board of Directors, filed suit in Federal District Court, seeking to enjoin completion of the dam and impoundment of the reservoir on the ground that those actions would violate the Act by directly causing the extinction of the snail darter's habitat. The District Court denied respondents' request for a preliminary injunction and set the matter for trial. The Court of Appeals agreed, and on January 31, 1977, it reversed, remanding with instructions that a permanent injunction issue halting all activities incident to the Tellico Dam, which may destroy or modify the critical habitat of the snails darter. After finding TVA to be in violation of the NEPA, the District Court enjoined the dam's completion pending the filing of an appropriate environmental impact statement. The court entered its memorandum opinion and order denying respondents' requested relief and dismissing the complaint. Held: 1. The Act is not in any respect amended or repealed. Pp. 5-7. (a) The Act's explicit provisions require precisely that result. P. 5. (b) The Endangered Act does not apply to a federal project which was well under way when Congress passed the Act of 1972, and it is not the exclusive province of the Congress not only to formulate legislative policies and mandate programs and projects, but also to establish their relative priority for the Nation. This Court's function is to view the Act "reasonably," and hence shape a remedy "that accords with some modicum of common sense and the public weal." P. 6. (c) Congress has spoken in the plainest of words, making it abundantly clear that the balance has been struck in favor of affording endangered species the highest of priorities, thereby adopting a policy which it described as "institutionalized caution." Committee for Nuclear Responsibility v. Seaborg, 149 U.S. App. D.C. 380, 382, 463 F. 2d 783, 785, reversed and remanded.

While working in Alabama, petitioners, who are private employees, challenged the constitutionality of a county occupational tax levied upon them. Their action was dismissed as barred by the Tax Injunction Act, but they later obtained relief in state circuit court. However, the Alabama Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal, ruling that the county's previous successful defense of the tax in a related state court action barred petitioners' action. Held: Under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, the state court's holding that petitioners were bound by the prior action's outcome deprived them of the procedural safeguard necessary to secure their constitutional rights. Pp. 108-116. (a) Although state courts are generally free to develop their own rules for protecting against the relitigation of common issues or the piecemeal resolution of disputes, see, e. g., Martin v. Wilks, 490 U. S. 755, 762, extreme applications of the doctrine of res judicata may be inconsistent with a federal right that is fundamental in character. Here, the parties to the prior action failed to give petitioners notice that a suit was pending which would conclusively resolve their legal rights. Such a failure is troubling because the right to be heard secured by due process has little value if one is not informed that the matter is pending and can choose for himself whether to appear or default, acquire or contest. Assuming that Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U. S. 32, leaves open the possibility that in some class suits adequate representation might cure a lack of notice, that opinion may not be read to permit the application of res judicata here. Unlike the situation in Hansberry, the Bedingfield action does not meet the requirement that a prior proceeding have binding effect on absent parties. The individuals who were parties to the Bedingfield action did not sue on behalf of a class; their pleadings did not purport to assert any claim against or on behalf of any nonparty; and the judgment they received did not purport to bind any county taxpayers who were nonparties. Since petitioners and the Bedingfield litigants are best described as mere "strangers" to each other, it is impossible to conclude that the Bedingfield plaintiffs provided representation sufficient to make up for the fact that petitioners neither participated in, nor had the opportunity to participate in, the Bedingfield action. Pp. 108-113. (b) The nature of petitioners' action does not render the usual constitutional protections inapplicable. Governmental and private entities have substantial interests in the prompt and determinative resolution of challenges to important legislation, but a state court's freedom to rely on prior precedent in rejecting a litigant's claims does not afford it similar freedom to bind a litigant to a prior judgment to which he was not a party. Given the amount of money at stake, respondents were not entitled to rely on the assumption that the Bedingfield action established the tax's constitutionality. Pp. 113-116. 662 So. 2d 1098, reversed and remanded.

Dissenting Opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia

I dissent from the majority's decision to reinstate the appeal in this case and to reconsider the judgment below. The majority holds that the customs service's classification of certain products as exempt from import taxes cannot be sustained under the Harmonized System of Tariffs and Related Matters (HSTSM), and that the customs service's actions constituted an improper exercise of its authority. However, the majority's analysis ignores important facts and misinterprets key provisions of the HSTSM. Moreover, the majority's decision conflicts with previous cases interpreting the HSTSM and undermines the stability of international trade relations. For these reasons, I dissent.

Background

This case involves the classification of certain products as exempt from import taxes under the HSTSM. The HSTSM is a comprehensive system of tariffs and related measures designed to promote international trade and facilitate the exchange of goods among nations. Under the HSTSM, countries agree to apply standardized codes to identify goods for purposes of tariff classification and valuation. These codes are based on a hierarchical structure that groups goods into categories and subcategories, allowing for easy identification and categorization.

The dispute in this case arises from the classification of certain products as exempt from import taxes under Chapter 99 of the HSTSM. Specifically, the products in question are daily planners that meet certain criteria, such as containing space for brief daily entries and being bound with rings rather than loose covers. The customs service has determined that these products fall under the exemption provided for "diaries" in Chapter 99, Section 4820.10.20. However, the appellant argues that the products do not meet the criteria for "diaries" under the HSTSM and should instead be classified under another section of the chapter.

Analysis

The majority's decision rests on several errors of fact and interpretation. First, the majority incorrectly assumes that the HSTSM defines "diaries" as consisting solely of printed calendars and almanacs. However, the HSTSM specifically excludes "memoirs, chronicles, autobiographies, biographical sketches, historical accounts, scientific treatises, technical reports, literary works, newspapers, periodicals, photographs, films, sound recordings, magnetic tapes, computer programs, databases, CD-ROMs, DVDs, video games, software, and electronic publications" from the scope of the "diaries" exemption. Therefore, the majority's assumption that the products in question are excluded from the exemption because they do not consist solely of printed calendars and almanacs is unwarranted.

Second, the majority misunderstands the purpose of the HSTSM's exemptions for "diaries" and "notebooks and address books, bound." The exemptions are intended to exclude from import taxes certain types of personal use items that are widely used and often consumed in large quantities. Daily planners, which serve a similar purpose as diaries and are commonly used for organizing appointments and tasks, clearly fall within the spirit of the exemptions provided for "diaries" and "notebooks and address books, bound." To exclude daily planners from the exemption would effectively negate the purpose of the exemptions and create unnecessary barriers to international trade.

Third, the majority's decision contradicts previous cases interpreting the HSTSM. In United States v. Haggar Apparel Company, Ltd., the Court held that the customs service's classification of certain clothing items as exempt from import taxes under Chapter 99 of the HSTSM was supported by substantial evidence and was entitled to Chevron deference. Similarly, in Christensen v. Department of Commerce, the Court held that the customs service's classification of certain products as exempt from import taxes under Chapter 99 of the HSTSM was reasonable and entitled to Skidmore deference. These cases demonstrate that the customs service's classifications under the HSTSM are generally accepted and respected by the courts.

Finally, the majority's decision threatens the stability of international trade relationships. The HSTSM is a critical component of the global trading system, and its effectiveness depends on the ability of countries to accurately classify goods for tariff purposes. By challenging the customs service's classifications under the HSTSM, the majority risks creating confusion and uncertainty in the international trade community. Furthermore, the majority's decision could lead to retaliatory actions by other countries, who may seek to restrict or impose higher tariffs on goods exported from the United States.

Conclusion

For the foregoing reasons, I dissent from the majority's decision to reinstate the appeal in this case and to reconsider the judgment below. The majority's analysis overlooks crucial facts and misinterprets key provisions of the HSTSM. Moreover, the majority's decision conflicts with

Respondent Marley Co. brought a diversity action in Federal District Court, alleging that a defect in an electric baseboard heater caused both the fire and his mother's death. At trial, Marley introduced the testimony of three witnesses, proffered as experts, in an endeavor to prove the alleged defect in the heater and its causal connection to the fire. The District Court overruled defendant Marley's objections, lodged both before and during the trial, that this testimony was unreliable and therefore inadmissible under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 as elucidated by Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 509 U. S. 579. At the close of Weisgram's evidence, and again at the closing of all the evidence, the jury returned a verdict for Marley. Marley again requested judgment as a matter of law, and additionally requested, in the alternative, a new trial, pursuant to Rules 50 and 59. The court of appeals then ordered that the expert testimony essential to prove Weisggram's case be admitted and that Marley should appeal to the District Court for a judgment against the jury-verdict winner. The district court denied the motion, and the jury found that the evidence was insufficient to support the verdict. The Eighth Circuit affirmed. Held: 1. The Court of Appeals has authority to direct the entry of judgment for a verdict loser. Pp. 521-522. (a) Federal Rule, §2521, governs motions for judgment, and Subdivision (d) controls when, as here, the verdict loser appeals from the trial court's denial of a motion for judgment. P. 522. 2. In this case, the appellate tribunal's decision that the jury verdict was erroneously admitted at trial and that the remaining, properly admitted evidence is insufficient to constitute a submissible case, is not inadvertent, since the appellate court's discretion to do so is the appropriate exercise of the appellate courts' discretion when it reverses a defendant's Rule 50(b) motion for a trial, not judgment, as in the instant case, since it is implausible to suggest, post-Daubert, that parties will initially present less than their best expert evidence in the expectation of a second chance should their first try fail. Nor is it implausible for an appellee, who is wholeheartedly urging the correctness of the verdict, to point out that the court's proof introduced becomes insufficient because the court determines that the trial judge erred in denying the motion. In these circumstances, the Eighth Circuit did not abuse its discretion by directing entry of the judgment for the verdict winner, instead of returning the case to the district court for further proceedings, without excising evidence inadmissible under Federal rule of evidence 702. Id., at 325 326. The parties before this Court diverge regarding Neely's scope. In a series of pre-1967 decisions, this Court refrained from deciding the question, while emphasizing the importance of giving the party deprived of a verdict the opportunity to invoke the discretion of a trial judge. See, e.g., Kinser v. West Virginia Pulp & Paper Co., 330 U.S. 212, 216 218. In Neely, moreover, parties relying on expert evidence have had notice of the exacting standards of reliability such evidence must meet. And the Court of appeals' decision that if a trial court erroneously denied a motion to judgment in the case, it may remand the case for consideration whether the new trial is warranted, or (3) direct that the moving party is entitled to the judgment. This Court's decision in Neely is consistent with Eighth Circuit precedent existing at the time of trial in the WeisGgram case. See also Louis, Post-Verdict Rulings on the Sufficiency of the Evidence: Neely v. Martin K. Eby Construction Co. Revisited.

The U.S. Supreme Court of Alabama ruled that a group of private-sector workers who challenged the validity of an occupational tax in Jefferson County, Alabama, were not entitled to summary judgment because they had not been adequately represented in an earlier case involving the same issue. The court held that the earlier case, in which the county was found to have violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses, had been decided by the Alabama Supreme Court in Bedingfield, 527 So. 2d 1270 (1988). The majority opinion noted that in Alabama, as in most States, a prior judgment on the merits rendered by a court of competent jurisdiction precludes the relitigation of a claim if there is a "substantial identity of the parties" and if the "same cause of action" is presented in both suits. The opinion also noted that the prior judgment is generally "res judicata not only as to all matters which could have been but were not raised and in the suit" and "as to all relevant issues which could be but not raised" and in which they were not adequately represented. The Court concluded that the petitioners' respective interests were "essentially identical" and deprived them of the due process of law guaranteed by the 14th Amendment.

Respondent was sentenced to death for aggravated murder committed in the course of a carjacking. The Ohio General Assembly has delegated in large part the conduct of clemency review to petitioner Ohio Adult Parole Authority. In the case of an inmate under death sentence, the Authority must conduct a clemeency hearing within 45 days of the scheduled date of execution. Prior to the hearing, the inmate may request an interview with one or more parole board members. Counsel is not allowed at that interview. Respondent objected to the short notice of the interview and requested assurances that counsel could attend and participate in the interview. When the Authority failed to respond to these requests, respondent filed suit in Federal District Court, alleging under Rev. Stat. §1979, 42 U. S. C. §1983, that Ohio's Clemency process violated his Fourteenth Amendment right to due process and his Fifth Amendment right not to remain silent. The District Court granted the State's motion for judgment on the pleadings. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that a voluntary inmate interview does not violate an inmate's Fifth Amendment rights. Held: The Ohio parole board interview, even on assumptions most favorable to respondent's claim, did not violate the Fifth Amendment privilege against compelled self-incrimination. Pp. 463-64. (a) The Due Process Clause is not violated where, as here, the procedures in question do no more than confirm that the clememency and pardon power is committed, as is our tradition, to the authority of the executive. P. 464. 107 F. 3d at 1186, reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around a defamation lawsuit brought by Herman A. Thompson, a public official, against petitioner St. Amant, who made potentially defamatory statements during a televised speech. The central legal issue is whether St. Amant's actions met the "actual malice" standard established by the landmark New York Times Co. v. Sullivan case, which requires a public official to prove that false statements were made with knowledge of their falsity or with reckless disregard for the truth.

The Louisiana Supreme Court had previously ruled in favor of Thompson, finding that St. Amant had acted recklessly by not verifying the information he broadcasted, which was based on an affidavit from J. D. Albin. However, the U.S. Supreme Court disagreed with this conclusion, stating that the Louisiana courts did not correctly apply the actual malice standard.

The U.S. Supreme Court clarified that "reckless disregard" for the truth requires more than just a failure to investigate; there must be sufficient evidence that the defendant actually doubted the veracity of the publication. The Court emphasized that the First Amendment protects some erroneous statements about public officials to ensure robust debate on public issues, and that the actual malice standard is a safeguard against self-censorship.

In St. Amant's case, the Court found no indication that he was aware of the probable falsity of the statements he made. The mere absence of evidence regarding Albin's reputation for truthfulness did not suffice to prove actual malice. Additionally, the Court noted that St. Amant had some reasons to believe Albin, as he had verified other aspects of Albin's information, and Albin had sworn to his statements.

Consequently, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Louisiana Supreme Court and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the correct application of the actual malice standard. This decision reinforces the high burden of proof required for public officials to win defamation suits and underscores the importance of free speech protections in public discourse.

Respondent Central Gulf Lines, Inc., assumed personal liability for petitioner Exxon Corporation's unpaid bill for supplying waterfront marine fuels to the vessel operated by another corporation, which had entered into a marine fuel requirements contract with Exxon. When the latter company procured bunker fuel for the vessel in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, from a third party, the vendor delivered the fuel to the vessel and billed Exxon. After Exxon paid the bill, it filed suit in the District Court against Central Gulf in personam and against the vessel in rem, claiming to have a maritime lien under the Federal Maritime Lien Act. The court ruled that it lacked admiralty jurisdiction over the claim, rejecting Exxon's contention that it should be excepted from the holding of Minturn v. Maynard, 17 How. 477, 481, that an agent cannot maintain a maritime claim on behalf of his principal. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Admiralty jurisdiction extends to Exxon's claim. Pp. 108-115. (a) Admiralty jurisdiction is governed by the fundamental interest of protecting maritime commerce. Although Minturn rests on two rationales -that the agent's claim was merely a "demand for a balance of accounts" that could be remedied at common law through an action of assumpti; and that the agent had no contractual or legal right to advance monies on the vessel's credit-both of those rationales have since been discredited. Moreover, Minturn's approach to determining admiralty jurisdiction is inconsistent with the principle that the nature and subject-matter of the contract at issue should be the crucial consideration in assessing admiralty jurisdiction. And the proposition for which Minturn stands-a per se bar of agency contracts from admiralty-is incompatible with current principles of admiralty jurisdiction over contracts and should be overruled. Lower courts should instead look to the subject matter of the agency contract and determine whether the services performed under the contract are maritime in nature. Pp. 108-112. (b) Here, the arrangements for delivering fuel in Jeddah and New York were essentially the same as they related to maritime commerce. If admiralty jurisdiction extended to the former, it must extend to the latter. Pp. 112-115. Reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the government officials accused of discrimination against a Muslim prisoner named Mohammed Ibrahim Makkawi. The court held that the plaintiff's complaint failed to meet the "well-pleaded" requirements of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a)(2), which means that it did not include enough concrete details about the alleged discrimination to justify a lawsuit. The court also rejected the plaintiff's argument that the government officials could be held liable for discrimination under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

Under § 701 of the New York Education Law, local school boards are required to purchase textbooks and lend them without charge "to all children residing in such district who are enrolled in grades seven to twelve of a public or private school." Held: 1. There is no violation of the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment since the section does not establish a religion or constitute the use of public funds to aid religious schools. Pp. 174-176. 2. Nor is there a violation of the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment since the section does not coerce anyone in the practice of his religion. P. 176. 20 N. Y. 2d 109, 228 N. E. 2d 791, affirmed.

When respondent’s car broke down on a Washington State highway, Officers Haner and Devenpeck stopped to help. Suspicious that respondent was impersonating a police officer, Haner radioed his superior, who sent Devenpeck to investigate. During the ensuing conversation, Devenpeck discovered that respondent had been recording the encounter. Based on this discovery, he placed respondent under arrest for violating the Washington Privacy Act. At booking, Haner charged respondent with violating the Act and issued a ticket for using flashing headlights. Both charges were ultimately dismissed. Respondent then brought suit in Federal District Court, claiming that petitioners had arrested him without probable cause in violation of the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. The jury returned a verdict in petitioners’ favor, but the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that petitioners could not have had probable cause to arrest because they cited only the Privacy Act charge and that the offenses of impersonating a law-enforcement officer and obstructing a law-enforcement officer were not “closely related” to the offense invoked by Devenpeck at the time of respondent’s arrest. Held: There is no merit to the “closely related offense” rule adopted by the Ninth Circuit. Pp. 4–10. (a) Probable cause to make a warrantless arrest exists if the arresting officer’s knowledge warrants a prudent person to conclude that the suspect has committed, is committing, or is about to commit a crime. Here, the Court of Appeals erred in concluding that the probable-cause inquiry is limited to the known facts bearing upon the offense actually invoked at the time of arrest and that the offense supported by those facts must be “closely related” to the offense that the officer invoked. It is irrelevant what the arresting officer knew or believed at the time of arrest. His subjective reason for making the arrest need not be the criminal offense as to which the known facts provide probable cause. Evenhanded law enforcement is best achieved by applying objective standards of conduct, rather than standards dependent on the subjective state of mind of the officer. To hold otherwise would mean that the constitutionality of an arrest turns upon the motivation of the arresting officer, eliminating, as validating probable cause, facts that played no part in the officer’s expressed subjective reason for making the arrest, and offenses that are not “closely related” to that subjective reason. Pp. 4–7. (b) The “closely related offense” rule is condemned by its perverse consequences. Although it may be good police practice to inform a person of the reason for his arrest at the time he is taken into custody, this Court has never held that to be constitutionally required. Thus, the predictable consequence of the “closely related offense” rule is not that officers will cease making sham arrests on the hope that such arrests will later be validated, but rather that officers will cease giving reasons for arrest. If this option were foreclosed by adoption of a statutory or constitutional requirement, officers would simply give every reason for which probable cause could possibly exist. The facts of this case exemplify the arbitrary consequences of the “closely related offense” rule. Had Haner made the arrest, on the stated basis of his suspicions, rather than Devenpeck, the outcome might well have been different. Similarly, had Devenpeck abided the county’s policy against stacking charges or had either officer made the arrest without stating the grounds, the outcome might have differed as well. Consistent with this Court’s rejection of a conception of the Fourth Amendment producing such haphazard results, the Court declines to address the question whether petitioners lacked probable cause to arrest respondent for obstructing a law-enforcement officer or for impersonating a law-enforcement officer. Pp. 7–10. 333 F. 3d 975, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which O’Connor, J., joined.

Under Iowa law, adjusted revenues from slot machines operated aboard riverboats are taxed at a higher rate than adjusted revenues from slot machines operated at racetracks. Respondent racetracks and an association of dog owners challenged the statute on the ground that the 20 percent/36 percent tax rate difference violated the Federal Equal Protection Clause, Amdt. 14, § 1. The Iowa Supreme Court agreed, concluding that the differential tax defeated the statute's purpose of helping racetracks recover from economic distress. Held: There is a plausible policy reason for the classification, the legislature rationally may have considered the related justifying facts, and the relationship of the classification to its goal is not so attenuated as to make the distinction arbitrary or irrational. Pp. 2-6. (a) This Court has jurisdiction to review the Iowa Supreme Court's determination, since the latter said that state and federal constitutional protections are identical. See Pennsylvania v. Muniz, 496 U.S. 582, 588, n. 4. Pp. 2-3. (b) Because the statute distinguishes for tax purposes among revenues obtained within the State by two enterprises doing business there, it is subject to rational-basis review. Rational-basis review is especially deferential in the context of classifications made by complex tax laws. Allied Stores of Ohio, Inc. v. Bowers, 358 U. S. 522, 527. The Iowa Supreme Court erred in denying that the statute might balance objectives while serving its general objective of advancing the racetracks' economic interests. Once one recognizes that not every provision in a law need share a single objective, he finds the necessary rational support for the 20 percent/36 percent differential here at issue. Both the racetracks and riverboats faced financial difficulties, and the legislature could reasonably want to aid the riverboats, encourage river community economic development, promote riverboat history, or protect riverboat operator reliance interests. Thus, the legislature could rationally choose to help the riverboats while harming the racetracks. Allegheny Pittsburgh Coal Co. v. Comm'n of Webster Cty., 488 U. S. 336, distinguished. Pp. 3-6. Reversed and remanded.

Title: Occupational Safety and Health Act

Case Name: Occupational Safety and Health Administration v. Injured Workmen's Insurance Corporation et al.

Issued Date: July 1, 1980

Decision Type: Affirmation

Background Information:

Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) is a government agency created by the Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA Act) in 1970. Its mission is to ensure safe and healthy working conditions for employees.

The Cotton Dust Standard is a regulation developed by OSHA to protect workers exposed to cotton dust in the textile industry. The standard sets various requirements for employers to follow in order to protect their employees from exposure to cotton dust.

Facts:

Injured Workmen's Insurance Corporation (IWIC) filed a lawsuit challenging the Cotton Dust Standard. IWIC argued that the standard imposed excessive burdens on employers and would harm the textile industry.

The trial court ruled in favor of IWIC, holding that the Cotton Dust Standard was invalid. The trial court found that the standard exceeded the authority delegated to OSHA by Congress and that the standard was not supported by substantial evidence.

The appellate court reversed the trial court's decision, ruling that the Cotton Dust Standard was valid and supported by substantial evidence. The appellate court also found that the standard was reasonably related to ensuring safe and healthful working conditions for employees.

Analysis:

The Supreme Court reviewed the Cotton Dust Standard and the supporting evidence provided by OSHA. The Court found that the standard was supported by substantial evidence and that it was reasonably related to ensuring safe and healthful working conditions for employees.

The Court also addressed the constitutional challenges raised by IWIC. The Court found that the Cotton Dust Standard did not violate due process or equal protection clauses of the Constitution. The Court reasoned that the standard was narrowly tailored to achieve a compelling government interest in protecting workers from exposure to cotton dust.

Finally, the Court examined the delegation of authority to OSHA by Congress. The Court found that Congress had delegated broad authority to OSHA to regulate workplace safety and health, and that the Cotton Dust Standard fell within the scope of that authority.

Conclusion:

The Supreme Court affirmed the Cotton Dust Standard and the authority of OSHA to enforce it. The Court held that the standard was supported by substantial evidence and was reasonably related to ensuring safe and healthful working conditions for employees.

On June 9, 2008, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York entered a final judgment against a former administrator of a long-term employee benefit plan who was found to have a conflict of interest in denying benefits.  According to the court's order, MetLife Insurance Company (MetLife) was the administrator of Sears, Roebuck & Company (SRIC) Long-Term Disability Insurance Plan, an ERISA-governed benefit plan. The ERISA provision provides for the administrator to determine whether an employee is eligible for benefits and pays benefits out of its own pocket. The court found that MetLife had a much greater incentive than a self-insuring employer to provide accurate claims processing, and MetLife failed to provide its independent vocational and medical experts with all of the relevant evidence.  The court also found that, in the circumstances where a trustee is conflicted, the amount of money spent on a claim for benefits does not change the legal need for a judge later to take account of that conflict in reviewing the trustee’s discretionary decisionmaking.  MetLife agreed to settle the case without admitting or denying the allegations of the court. The settlement is subject to court approval.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York today announced criminal charges against MetLife. The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Manhattan, charges MetLife with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The complaint seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty. The case is being handled by David J. Scott, W. Fratcher, & M. Scott. The litigation will be led by Mr. Scott and Ms. Frattan. The Commission appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in this matter.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Iowa granted a motion by the State of Iowa to use a screen in the trial of a man charged with sexually assaulting two 13-year-old girls. The trial court approved the use of the screen, which would enable appellant dimly to perceive the witnesses, but the witnesses to see him not at all. Appellant objected strenuously to the screen based on his Sixth Amendment right to face-to-face confrontation. He also argued that his right to due process was violated, since the procedure would make him appear guilty and thus erode the presumption of innocence. The Iowa Supreme Court affirmed his conviction, 397 N.W.2d 730 (1986), on the ground that there was no violation of the Confrontation Clause. The Court also rejected appellant's due process argument on the grounds that the screening procedure was not inherently prejudicial. The District Court granted the State's motion for a new trial, and the Court of Appeals granted a new hearing on the matter. The Appeals Court agreed with the trial court's decision, and sent the case back for further proceedings.

Respondents, four environmental groups, brought suit seeking to block enforcement of two regulations promulgated by petitioner Department of Agriculture’s Forest Service. One prohibited the agency from requiring public comment on certain types of forestry projects, while the other allowed the agency to exclude from the scope of its notice requirements smaller projects that would otherwise trigger a full analysis. Because the regulations did not require any action on respondents’ parts, they can establish standing only if application of the regulations by the Government will affect them in the manner described above. Respondents can demonstrate standing only if application of the regulations by the Government will affect them in the manner described above. To establish the concrete and particularized injury that standing requires, respondents point to their members’ recreational interests in the National Forests. When a plaintiff has sued to challenge the lawfulness of certain action or threatened action but has settled that suit, he retains standing to challenge the basis for that action (here, the regulations in the abstract), apart from any concrete application that threatens imminent harm to his interests. However, respondents have identified no other application of the invalidated regulations that threatens imminent and concrete harm to the interests of their members. Nor do they have standing to bring their challenge based on procedural injury. Deprivation of a procedural right without some concrete interest that is affected by the deprivation—a procedural right in vacuo—is insufficient to create Article III standing. Pp. 3−10. 492 F. 3d 1059, reversed in part and affirmed in part. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado dismissed a complaint filed by two twin sisters who were denied employment as commercial airline pilots because they did not meet a minimum vision requirement. The complaint alleged that the denial violated the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA), which prohibits certain employers from discriminating against individuals on the basis of their disabilities. The District Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. The Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed the District Court's judgment, holding that petitioners had not alleged that they were "regarded" by the employer as having an impairment that substantially limits a major life activity. We conclude that the complaint was properly dismissed. In reaching that result, we hold that the determination of whether an individual is disabled should be made with reference to measures that the individual's impairment, including, in this instance, eyeglasses and contact lenses. We also hold that petitioners failed to allege properly that the employer regarded them as having a disability within the meaning of the ADA. The Tenth Circuit's decision is in tension with the decisions of other courts that have held that such a disability cannot be considered when determining a disability. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a separate decision, held that the ADA does not require employers to consider a person's ability to work when determining whether a person is disabled. In a similar case, the Court of Justices ruled that a person can be considered disabled if he or she has a "substantially limited" ability to perform a job. In this case, we find that the district court properly dismissed petitioners' complaint for failing to allege that they are disabled.

An anonymous tip that a young black male standing at a particular bus stop and wearing a plaid shirt was carrying a gun was reported to the Miami-Dade Police, who had no reason to suspect any of the three of illegal conduct. Respondent J. L., who was at the time of the frisk "10 days shy of his 16th birth[day]," was charged under state law with carrying a concealed firearm without a license and possessing a firearm while under the age of 18. The trial court granted his motion to suppress the gun as the fruit of an unlawful search, but the Supreme Court of Florida quashed that decision and held the search invalid under the Fourth Amendment. Held: An anonymous tip lacking indicia of reliability of the kind contemplated in Terry v. Ohio, 392 U. S. 1, does not justify a stop and frisk whenever and however it alleges the illegal possession of a firearm. Pp. 488-478. (a) An anonymous "tip" that a person is carrying a firearm is, without more, sufficient to justify a police officer's stop-and-frisk of that person. The tip in the instant case lacked the moderate indicia present in White and essential to the Court's decision in that case. The anonymous call concerning J. provided no predictive information and therefore left the police without means to test the informant's knowledge or credibility. That the allegation about the gun turned out to be correct does not suggest that the officers, prior to the frisks, had a reasonable basis for suspecting J. J. of engaging in unlawful conduct: The reasonableness of official suspicion must be measured by what the officers knew before they conducted their search. All the police had to go on in this case was the bare report of an unknown, unaccountable informant who neither explained how he knew about the weapon nor supplied any basis for believing he had inside information about J. . If White was a close case on the reliability of anonymous tips, this one surely falls on the other side of the line. Florida contends that the tip was reliable because its description of the suspect's visible attributes proved accurate: There really was a young Black male wearing a t-shirt at the bus stop. The Florida Supreme Court observed, provided no such predictions, nor did it contain any other qualifying indicia. The court dissented. The safety of the police and the public, they maintained, justifies a "firearm exception" to the general rule barring investigatory stops and frisks on the basis of bare-boned anonymous tips. The State of Florida noted that the decision of the State's Supreme Court conflicts with decisions of other courts declaring similar searches compatible with the Amendment. The Court granted certiorari and affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Kansas granted certiorari in the case of Leroy Hendricks, an inmate who was committed for the first time under Kansas's Sexually Violent Predator Act of 1994 because he had a history of sexually molesting children. The Court held that the Act's pre-commitment condition of a "mental abnormality" did not satisfy the "substantive'' due process requirement that involuntary civil commitment must be predicated on a finding of "mental illness"<n>The Court also held that Hendricks's right to a trial by jury was violated because the trial court did not have the authority to determine whether or not Hendricks had a mental illness. Hendricks was committed shortly after the Act became law, and the Court granted the State's motion for a preliminary injunction. Hendricks then filed a cross-petition, challenging the state's use of the Act on the basis of the due process, double jeopardy, and ex post facto grounds. The Supreme Court ruled that Hendricks had not shown that his due process rights were violated, and that the act did not require a finding that he had "a mental abnormality" or "personality disorder" that would make him eligible for civil commitment. Hendricks also challenged the state on the issue of whether he was entitled to a jury trial. The court held that he was not eligible for a trial because the court had not found that he "argued that he has a mental abnormality or personality disorder which makes him likely to engage in the predatory acts of sexual violence"

Petitioners, who were charged with price fixing in a federal criminal prosecution, were convicted and fined $1 million. After the conviction became final, the Government brought a civil antitrust suit against petitioners and others, alleging price fixing and obtaining injunctive relief. Later, the Government brought another civil antitrust suit against petitioners and others, alleging price fixing and obtaining injunctive relief. Both suits were consolidated and the District Court entered a "consent" judgment, wherein petitioners agreed to cease and desist from engaging in price fixing activities. About two years later, the State of Utah, acting for itself and on behalf of public entities and others, brought a class action in the District Court against petitioners and others, alleging price fixing and seeking injunctive relief. Respondents, who were residents of various states, sought to intervene in the class action as representatives of classes of persons similarly situated to those involved in the class action. The District Court ruled that the suit could not go forward as a class action, finding that the named plaintiffs failed to show that the class was sufficiently numerous to warrant permitting joinder of all members. The District Court accordingly denied respondents' motions to intervene. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the District Court erred in refusing to permit intervention. Held: 1. Where the District Court found that the suit could not go forward as a class action solely because of failure to demonstrate that "the class is so numerous that joinder of all members is impracticable," the commencement of the original class suit tolled the running of the statute of limitations as to all purported members of the class who made timely motions to intervene after the court had found the suit inappropriate for class action status. Pp. 308-312. 2. The federal courts are empowered to extend the limitation period beyond the period set by Congress, and hence the statute of limitations was properly tolled in this instance. Pp. 312-315. 3. Denial of permission to intervene in this case was not an exercise of discretion but rather a conclusion of law, and the Court of Appeals correctly found the error in the District Court's determination. Pp. 315-316. 4. The precise effect of the commencement of the class action on the relevant limitation period is that the running of the limitation period was suspended only during the pendency of the motion to strip the suit of its class action character. Pp. 316-317. 473 F. 2d 584, affirmed.

Petitioners, the six maritime unions which appeared before this Court as respondents in Windward Shipping (London) Ltd. v. American Radio Assn., AFL-CIO, 415 U. S. 104, contend that their picketing was at least arguably a secondary boycott prohibited by § 8 (b) (4) (B) of the National Labor Relations Act, and that their Mobile picketing, although neither obstructive nor violent, brought about an immediate refusal by stevedore workers of the locals of International Longshoremen's Association to cross picket lines to load and unload petitioners' vessels. Held: 1. The Alabama courts were competent to apply their own law in resolving the dispute between petitioners and respondents unless, as petitioners claim, such a resolution violated them' rights under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Pp. 563-564. 2. The state courts in this case did nothing more than establish that the maritime operations of foreign ships are not "in commerce," and that the question of pre-emption of state-court jurisdiction by the NLRA should be answered differently than it was in the Windward litigation. P. 564. 3. Since petitioners were not the foreign owners of a picketed ship, but are instead stevedoring companies which seek to service the ship and a shipper who wishes to have his crops loaded on it, the question whether the picketing activities were "affecting commerce" within the meaning of the Act is not a question whether petitioners are "employers" or "persons" engaged in "commerce," and since petitioners have not been charged with an unfair labor practice under § 8(b)(4) of that Act, the state courts were not in fact ceded their jurisdiction over the particular dispute that had been presented to the Mississippi courts. P p. 565. 4. The judgment of the Alabama Supreme Court of Alabama, in affirming a temporary injunction issued by the Alabama Circuit Court, is affirmed.

Property and casualty insurers maintain accounting reserves for "unpaid losses." Before enactment of the Tax Reform Act of 1986, these insurers received a full deduction for those reserves as "losses incurred," allowing them to treat their reserves as a current deduction for future loss payments without adjusting for the time value of money. After passage of the 1986 Act, which requires insurers to discount unpaid losses to present value when claiming them as a deduction, respondents Atltic Mutual Insurance Co. and its affiliate Centennial Ins. Co. (collectively Atlantic) continued to maintain loss reserves. They also took advantage of a special rule in the 1986 Act that allowed them to exclude from taxable income the difference between undiscounted and discounted year-end 1986 loss reserves. Because they recognized as income the difference between undiscounted and discounted year-end 1986 reserves, they were subject to a penalty imposed by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) for failing to make timely elections to defer recognition of such differences until the next taxyear. When the IRS determined that Atlantic had made net additions to its reserves during 1986, reducing the "fresh start" entitlement by an amount resulting in a tax deficiency, the company sought review in the Tax Court. Ultimately, the Court of Appeals concluded that the Treasury Regulation defining "reserve strengthening" to include any net addition to reserves is based on a permissible construction of the statute. Held: The Treasury Regulation represents a reasonable interpretation of the term "reserve strengthening." Pp. 42-48. (a) Neither prior legislation nor industry use establishes the plain meaning Atlantic ascribes to "reserve strengthening": that the term includes only increases in reserves that result from a change in methods or assumptions. Prior legislation suggests, if anything, that a change in basis is a sufficient, but not a necessary, condition for "reserve strengthening." Nor does industry use indicate that the term has a well-defined meaning. Pp. 42-45. (b) Since the term "reserve strengthening" is ambiguous, the task that confronts this Court is to decide whether the Treasury Regulation represents a reasonable interpretation of the statute. As a purely linguistic matter, the phrase is broad enough to embrace all increases in (all "strengthening of") the amount of the reserve, for whatever reason and from whatever source. Although Atlantic contends that this interpretation is unreasonable because, in theory, it produces absurd results, the Court agrees with the IRS that Atlantic's hypothetical example is unrealistic. Moreover, the provision at issue here is a limitation upon an extraordinary deduction accorded to property and casualty insurers, and the interpretation adopted by the Treasury Regulation seems to be a reasonable accommodation-and one that the statute very likely intended-of the competing interests of fairness, administrability, and avoidance of abuse. Pp. 45-48. 111 F. 3d 1056, affirmed.

The Supreme Court reviewed the Support Our Law Enforcement and Safe Neighborhoods Act (S.B. 1070), enacted by Arizona in 2010, which aimed to discourage and deter unlawful entry and presence of aliens in the United States. The United States government challenged four provisions of the Arizona law, arguing that they were preempted by federal law.

The Court held that the federal government has broad and exclusive power over immigration and the status of aliens, which includes the power to establish a uniform rule of naturalization and to conduct foreign relations. The Court recognized that while states have significant interests in managing the consequences of illegal immigration, the federal government has established a comprehensive framework for immigration enforcement that must be respected.

The Court found three of the challenged provisions of S.B. 1070 to be preempted by federal law:

1. Section 3, which made failure to comply with federal alien-registration requirements a state misdemeanor, was preempted because the federal government has occupied the field of alien registration, leaving no room for state regulation.

2. Section 5(C), which criminalized unauthorized aliens seeking or engaging in work in Arizona, was preempted because it conflicted with the federal Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 (IRCA), which deliberately refrained from imposing criminal penalties on unauthorized workers.

3. Section 6, which authorized state officers to arrest without a warrant any person believed to have committed a public offense making them removable from the United States, was preempted because it interfered with the federal government's discretion in the enforcement of immigration laws and could lead to the harassment of aliens whom federal officials have chosen not to remove.

However, the Court did not strike down Section 2(B), which required state law enforcement officers to verify the immigration status of any person stopped, detained, or arrested if there was reasonable suspicion they were unlawfully present in the United States. The Court held that it was premature to enjoin this provision before the state courts had a chance to interpret it and without evidence that its enforcement would conflict with federal immigration law and its objectives.

The Court's decision affirmed in part and reversed in part the judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. Justice Kagan did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

The Supreme Court affirmed the regulations of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) that limit the ability of Title X fund recipients to engage in abortion-related activities. Title X is a federal program that provides funding for family planning services but explicitly excludes abortion as a method of family planning. The regulations in question prohibit Title X projects from providing counseling or referrals for abortion and require physical and financial separation between Title X funded activities and abortion services.

The Court held that the regulations are a permissible interpretation of Title X and do not conflict with the First or Fifth Amendments of the Constitution. The Court reasoned that the government may choose to fund childbirth over abortion and that the regulations do not create an unconstitutional condition by requiring the separation of Title X activities from abortion-related services. The Court also found that the regulations do not infringe on the doctor-patient relationship within the context of Title X, as they do not prevent doctors from providing information about abortion outside of the Title X program.

The Court concluded that the regulations do not impose an unconstitutional burden on a woman's right to choose an abortion, as they do not prevent access to abortion but merely do not subsidize it with federal funds. The decision to fund childbirth but not abortion was seen as a valid exercise of Congress's power to allocate funds for public interest without funding alternative activities.

The implications of the decision are that Title X grantees must comply with the regulations that separate their family planning services from abortion services, and the government is not required to provide funding for abortion counseling or referrals as part of the Title X program.

Respondent, who had suffered from asthma and was sensitive to secondhand smoke, learned for the first time that petitioner allowed its passengers to smoke on international flights. Because Dr. Hanson's asthma had caused him to suffer from asthma, respondent requested and obtained seats away from the smoking section of the aircraft's economy-class smoking section. Respondent advised Maria Leptourgou, a flight attendant for petitioner, that the flight attendant could not sit in a smoking area because the plane was full. After all the passengers had boarded but prior to takeoff, respondent again asked Ms. Leptougou to move the passenger, explaining that he was "allergic to smoke." While she was leaning against a chair near the galley area, she was soon surrounded by ambient cigarette smoke, and she refused, stating that the plane had been full. The flight attendant then told her that she could switch seats with another passenger, but that respondent would have to ask other passengers herself, without the flight crew's assistance. The attendant refused to move, and the attendant died shortly thereafter. Petitioner then filed an emergency action in Federal District Court, alleging wrongful death. The District Court affirmed. Held: 1. The conduct here constitutes an "accident" under Article 17 of the Warsaw Convention. Pp. 431-464. (a) The conduct of petitioner's flight attendant in three times refusing to reseat the passenger was "unexpected and unusual," ibid., which is the operative language under Saks and the correct Article 17 analysis. P. 434. (b) The "accidents" inquiry under Article 18 of the Convention does not define the term "Accident" and the context in which it is used is not "illuminating." 470 U. S., at 399. The Court nevertheless discerned the meaning of the term's meaning from the Convention's text, structure, and history as well as from the subsequent conduct of the parties to the Convention. Moreover, other provisions of Saks suggest that there is often no distinction between action and inaction on the issue of ultimate liability. For example, Article 25 provides that Article 22's liability cap does not apply in the event of "wilful misconduct or . . . such default on [the carrier's] part as, in accordance with the law of the court to which the case is submitted, is considered to be equivalent to wilful misconduct." 49 Stat. 3020 (emphasis added). Moreover, Article 20 (1) makes clear that the "due care" defense is unavailable when a carrier has failed to take "all necessary measures to avoid the damage." Id., at 3019. These provisions suggest that an air carrier's inaction can be the basis for liability. Petitioners' focus on the ambient cigarette-smoke as the injury producing event is misplaced. The difference in these provisions implies that the meaning is different from that of "occurrence." Ibid. Second, the Court found significant the fact that Article 17 focuses on the "accid which caused" the passenger's injury and not an accident that is the passenger’s injury, and that the District Court correctly found to be a "link in the chain" of causes that led to Dr Hanson's death, 116 F. 3d 829, at 837. The very fact that multiple events will necessarily combine and interrelate to cause any particular injury makes it difficult to define, in any coherent or non-question-begging way, any single event as the "injury producing event." Moreover, these provisions suggest, inter alia, that a air carrier”s inaction is the basis of liability. Finally, petitioner contends that the Ninth Circuit improperly created a negligence-based standard under § 17 by focusing on the flight attendants’ negligence as the “accident.” The Ninth Circuit stated that “The failure to act in the face of a known, serious risk satisfies § 17 so long as reasonable alternatives exist that would substantially minimize the risk and implementing these alternatives would not unreasonably interfere with the normal, expected operation of the airplane,” 316 F.3d 837, and it explained that it is the cause of the injury-rather than the occurrence of it-that must satisfy the definition of “Accident." Id. Ibid. The court also looked to the French legal meaning of "accaccident," which when used to describe an injury, is usually defined as a “fortuitous, unexpected, unusual, or unintended event. . . ." The Court noted that the Convention distinguishes between liability and liability for death or injuries to passengers caused by an ‘accident’ and liability under § 18 for destruction or loss of baggage caused by a ‘occurrence,’ id., at 398, and also emphasized that the definition “should be flexibly applied after assessment of all the circumstances surrounding a passenger's injuries.’ ” Brief for Petitioner 24, and explained that intentional conduct could fall within the definition under §17, id., id.,

IN THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA CIRCUIT
No. 10-CV-0001
IN RE: EDWARD DOE AND JOHN SMITH, Plaintiffs,
V.
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, Defendant.
ON PETITION FOR WRITE OF CERTIORARI
FROM THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA
No. CV-0001
THE MEMORY OF ARGUMENT
INTRODUCTION
This appeal presents a timely challenge to the constitutional validity of Section 109 of the Act of February 25, 1871, 16 Stat. 432, codified as 1 U.S.C. § 109, which states that "the repeal of any statute shall not have the effect to release or extinguish any penalty, forfeiture, or liability incurred under such statute." Petitioners contend that this provision violates due process and equal protection guarantees under the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution. Specifically, they assert that the provision impermissibly limits judicial review of the constitutionality of laws passed during the Civil War era and prevents future challenges to the constitutionality of such laws based on newly discovered evidence or historical understanding.
Petitioners' argument relies on several premises. First, they claim that the Act of February 25, 1871, was enacted in response to the end of the American Civil War and the desire to restore the Union. According to petitioners, the act was intended to ensure that the South would comply with the terms of the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery, and to protect the rights of African Americans living in the former Confederacy. Second, they maintain that the provision at issue in this case was included in the act as a safeguard against attempts to overturn the Thirteenth Amendment and to protect the rights of African Americans. Third, they contend that the provision violates due process and equal protection guarantees because it effectively bars judicial review of the constitutionality of laws passed during the Civil War era and prevents future challenges to the constitutionality of such laws based on newly discovered evidence or historical understanding.
In support of their argument, petitioners cite several sources, including the legislative history of the Act of February 25, 1871, and decisions of the Supreme Court of the United States. While these sources provide some insight into the motivations behind the act and the intentions of its framers, they do not establish that the provision at issue in this case violates due process or equal protection guarantees. Rather, they suggest that the provision was intended to promote stability and certainty in the administration of justice and to prevent political interference with judicial decisionmaking.
CONSTITUTIONAL AUTHORITY TO REPEAL LAWS
Article V, Section 2 of the United States Constitution grants Congress the power to repeal laws. This power is limited, however, by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, which requires that no state shall deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law. The Supreme Court has recognized that the right to due process includes the right to judicial review of the constitutionality of laws. See, e.g., Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. (6 Wheat.) 137 (1803); Baker v. Carr, 96 U.S. 684 (1877); Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 477 (1964); Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 435 (1966); Furman v. Georgia, 408 U.S. 232 (1972); Moore v. Sims, 442 U.S. 775 (1981); Planned Parenthood v. Casey, 502 U.S. 929 (1992); Obergefell v. Hodges, 579 U.S. __ (2015).
Under this doctrine, a law may be challenged as unconstitutional if it violates due process or equal protection guarantees. Such challenges may be raised in federal or state court, and the burden of proof falls on the party challenging the constitutionality of the law. If the challenger establishes that the law is unconstitutional, the law is void and may not be enforced.
However, the Supreme Court has also recognized that the power to repeal laws extends to laws that are deemed unconstitutional. In Marbury v. Madison, the Court held that the power to repeal laws includes the power to declare laws void. The Court observed that "[t]he power to annihilate a government, to control the exercise of jurisdiction, and to render the laws null, is a power exercised by every independent nation," and that "[t]his power is coextensive with sovereignty itself." 5 U.S. (6 Wheat.) 137, 141. The Court further held that "[t]he power to repel invasion, and to suppress rebellion, is complete in itself, and distinct from the power of declaring war." Id. at 142.
Similarly, in Baker v. Carr, the Court held that the power to repeal laws includes the power to declare laws void. The Court observed that "[t]he power to annihilate a government, to control the exercise of jurisdiction, and to render the laws null, is a power exercised by every independent nation," and that "[t]his power is coextensive with sovereignty itself." 96 U.S. 684, 691. The Court further held that "[t]he power to repel invasion, and to suppress rebellion, is complete in itself, and distinct from the power of declaring war." Id. at 692.
In both cases, the Court upheld the power of Congress to repeal laws that were deemed unconstitutional. The Court recognized that the power to repeal laws includes the power to declare laws void, and that this power is essential to maintaining the integrity of the rule of law and protecting individual liberties.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reversed a lower court's judgment of acquittal in the case of a company and two of its employees charged with a conspiracy and the substantive offense of concealing material facts in a matter within the jurisdiction of an agency of the United States. The court held that the district judge had no power to direct acquittals based solely on the alleged improper conduct of the prosecutor and a lack of credibility in the testimony of the witnesses for the prosecution who had testified up to that point. The government filed a petition for a writ of mandamus, praying that the judgments of acquittal be vacated and the case reassigned for trial. The trial did not terminate prior to the entry of judgment, as in Gori v. United States 367, 81 S.C.t. 1523, 6 L.Ed.2d 901, and the court of appeals thought, not without reason, that the acquittal was based upon an egregiously erroneous foundation. Nevertheless, '(t)he verdict of acquittal was final, and could not be reviewed without putting (the petitioners) twice in jeopardy, and thereby violating the constitution'

The 1965 Amendment to the Universal Military Training and Service Act (Act) prohibits the knowing destruction or mutilation of certificates issued by the Selective Service System. The 1965 Amendment, which was amended by Congress in 1965, provides that a person who forges, alters, or changes a registration certificate is subject to a fine of not more than $10,000 or imprisonment of not less than 5 years, and that the resulting statute must be directed at public as distinguished from private destruction. The District Court rejected O'Brien's argument that the 1965 Amendment ran afoul of the First Amendment by singling out persons engaged in protests for special treatment. On appeal, the Court of Appeals held the 1965 amendment unconstitutional as a law abridging freedom of speech on its face, because it regarded such violation to be a lesser included offense of the crime defined by § 12 (b) (3) of the Act. Held: 1. Since the 1964 Amendment is constitutional as enacted and as applied, it should have affirmed the conviction entered by the District Court. Pp. 531-532. (a) A government regulation is sufficiently justified if it is within the constitutional power of the Government; if it furthers an important or substantial governmental interest; if the governmental interest is unrelated to the suppression of free expression; and if the incidental restriction on alleged First Amendment freedoms is no greater than is essential to the furtherance of that interest. P. 532. 2. A Government regulation is not a basis for declaring a statute unconstitutional on the basis of an alleged illicit legislative motive. The 1964 Amendment does not abridge free speech on the face of the fact that it is unwise legislation which Congress had the undoubted power to enact and which could be reenacted in its exact form if the same or another legislator made a "wiser" speech about it. Id. 3. Inquiries into congressional motives or purposes are a hazardous matter. In the Supreme Court case of Lindh v. Murphy, the Court determined that the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) does not apply to cases that were pending in federal court as of its effective date, April 24, 1996. The question before the Court in this case was when a capital habeas case becomes "pending" for the purposes of this rule.

The respondent, Robert Garceau, was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death. His conviction and sentence were affirmed by the California Supreme Court, and his petition for state postconviction relief was denied. Garceau then sought federal habeas relief, filing various preliminary motions in federal court before AEDPA's effective date, but he did not file his actual habeas application until after that date.

The District Court and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that AEDPA did not apply to Garceau's application because he had initiated related proceedings before the effective date. However, the Supreme Court disagreed, holding that a case becomes "pending" only when an actual application for habeas corpus relief is filed in federal court. Since Garceau's application was filed after AEDPA's effective date, it was subject to AEDPA's amendments.

The Court's reasoning emphasized that AEDPA was enacted to reduce delays in the execution of sentences and to revise the standards used for evaluating the merits of a habeas application. The Court concluded that preliminary filings, such as requests for the appointment of counsel or motions for a stay of execution, do not make a case "pending" for the purposes of the Lindh rule. The Court reversed the judgment of the Ninth Circuit and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Justice O'Connor concurred in the judgment but disagreed with the breadth of the Court's reasoning, while Justice Souter, joined by Justices Ginsburg and Breyer, dissented, arguing that the case should be considered filed for purposes of the Lindh rule when the habeas court first considers standards for federal relief, which in this case occurred before AEDPA's effective date.
