After reviewing several "Detroit-only" desegregation plans, the District Court concluded that an interdistrict plan was required to "achieve the greatest degree of actual desegregregation . . . (so that) no school, grade or classroom (would be) substantially disproportionate to the overall pupil racial composition." The court also ordered the Detroit Board and the state defendants to institute comprehensive programs as to the four educational components by the start of the September 1976 school term. The cost of these programs was to be equally borne by the Detroit school board and the State. The State Board of Education submitted a critique of the plan, in which it concluded that, although "[i]t is possible that none of the thirteen "quality education" components is essential ... to correct the constitutional violation," 8 of the 13 proposed programs nonetheless deserved special consideration in the desegregate setting. The District Court then issued a final order, concluding that, as a matter of substantive constitutional right, (a) particular degree of racial balance is required, and by subjecting other school districts, uninvolved with and unaffected by any constitutional violations, to the court's remedial powers. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that the order exceeded appropriate limits of federal equitable authority as defined in Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Ed, 402 U. S. 1, 24. Held: The order exceeds the scope of the constitutional violations found in this case. Pp. 4-6. (a)(1) The order does not violate the Tenth Amendment and general principles of federalism. P. 4. (b) The District's order, even if otherwise proper, violates the Eleventh Amendment, since the order is directed toward the State defendants as a part of a prospective plan to comply with a constitutional requirement to eradicate all vestiges of de jure segregation, and the remedy does not "exceed" the violation if the remedy is tailored to cure the "condition that offends the Constitution." P. 5. (2) In light of the mandate of Brown I and Brown II, federal courts have, over the years, often required the inclusion of remedial programs to overcome the inequalities inherent in dual school systems, see Pasadena City Board of Public Education v. Spangler, 427 U.S. 424, or if they are imposed upon governmental units that were neither involved in nor affected by the constitutional constitutional violation, as in Milliken I, supra. The court has neither attempted to restructure local governmental entities nor to mandate a particular method or structure of state of local financing. The Tenth Amendment's reservation of nondelegated powers to the States is not implicated by a federal-court judgment enforcing the express prohibitions of unlawful state conduct enacted by the Fourteenth Amendment. Nor are principles of Federalism abrogated by the decree. The district court, in short, was true to the principle laid down in Brown II: "In fashioning and effectuating the decrees, the courts will be guided by equitable principles." Brown v. Co. Education, 349 U. . 294, 300, and in a manner that does not jeopardize the integrity of the structure or functions of state and local government, see, e. g., Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U. s. 651. The order is not barred by this Court's holding in Edelman, supra, that the nature and scope of a remedy are to be determined by the violation itself, and that federal courts need not, and cannot, close their eyes to inequalities, shown by the record, which flow from a longstanding segregated system. Moreover, the order did not punish anyone, nor does it impair or jeopardize Detroit's educational system in the way that it was designed to do so. In addition to other remedial program, which could, if circumstances warranted, include programs to remedy deficiencies, particularly in reading and communications skills, federal court has expressly ordered special in-service training for teachers, see United States v. Montgomery County School Board, 380 F. 2d 385, 394, and have altered or suspended testing programs employed by school systems undergoing des-egregation. The decree to share the future costs of educational components here fits squarely within the prospective-compliance exception reaffirmed by Edelman. The fact that the district court's order is designed to restore the schoolchildren of Detroit to a position they would have enjoyed absent constitutional violations by state officials does not change the fact that they are part of an integrated plan that operates prospectively to bring about the delayed benefits of a unitary school system, consistent with the Federal Constitution. The remedy is also remedial in nature, that is, it must be designed as nearly as possible "to restore the victims of discriminatory conduct to the position they will have occupied in the absence of such conduct," and the federal courts in devising a remedy must take into account the interests of state, local authorities in managing their own affairs. This case involves a dispute over the right to privacy in the United States. The plaintiff claims that her personal life has been invaded by the defendant's publication of intimate details about her. The defendant argues that the publication was part of a legitimate journalistic effort to expose corruption in government. The Supreme Court ultimately rules in favor of the defendant, finding that the publication was protected by the First Amendment's freedom of speech clause.

Petitioner O'Connor, then 56, was fired by respondent catering company while working at its restaurant. Claiming that he had been dismissed because of his age in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), O'Connor filed suit in Federal District Court. After discovery, the court granted respondents motion for summary judgment, finding that O'Connors claim could not survive without benefit of the McDonnellDouglas Corp.v . Green, 411 U.S. 792, presumption. In affirming, the Fourth Circuit found that O'Connor had failed to meet the fourth prong of the McDonnellDouglas test, i. e., that he was replaced by someone of comparablequalifications outside the protected class. Since his replacement was only 40 years old, the courtconcluded that the last element of the prima facie case had not been made out. Held: An ADEA plaintiff need not show that he was replaced by someone outside the protected class to make out a prima facie case. Because the ADEA prohibits employment decisions based on age and not class membership, see, e. g., Teamsters v. United States, 431 U. S. 324, 358, the fact that a replacement is significantly younger than the plaintiff is a far more reliable indicator of age discrimination than is the fact that the plaintiff was replaced by someone outside the protected class. Pp. 154-156. Reversed and remanded.

In this Supreme Court opinion, the Court examined whether Section 954(d)(1) of the National Foundation on the Arts and Humanities Act, as amended in 1990, was unconstitutional on the grounds of viewpoint discrimination and vagueness under the First and Fifth Amendments. The provision in question requires the Chairperson of the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) to consider "artistic excellence and artistic merit" as well as "general standards of decency and respect for the diverse beliefs and values of the American public" when awarding grants.

The Court concluded that Section 954(d)(1) is facially valid and does not inherently interfere with First Amendment rights or violate constitutional vagueness principles. The Court reasoned that the provision does not categorically restrict funding based on content or viewpoint but rather adds considerations to the grant-making process. It does not prevent awards to projects that might be considered "indecent" or "disrespectful," nor does it specify how these factors should be weighed.

The Court also noted that the NEA has discretion in awarding grants and that the criteria for "decency" and "respect" are not so precise as to lead to the suppression of protected expression. The Court emphasized that the NEA's mandate is to make aesthetic judgments, and the inherently content-based "excellence" threshold for NEA support is distinct from the subsidy at issue in previous cases where viewpoint discrimination was found.

The Court rejected the argument that Section 954(d)(1) is unconstitutionally vague, stating that in the context of selective subsidies, precision in legislation is not always feasible. The Court pointed out that if this provision were unconstitutionally vague, it would call into question the constitutionality of many government programs that award grants and scholarships based on subjective criteria.

In summary, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, upholding the constitutionality of Section 954(d)(1) and remanding the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The decision implies that while the government has broad discretion in funding the arts, it must not use this power to suppress specific viewpoints or ideas.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the distinction between direct condemnation (eminent domain) proceedings and inverse condemnation actions, particularly in the context of a § 1983 claim. The Court concludes that inverse condemnation actions, where the government takes property without providing just compensation or an adequate forum for seeking it, sound in tort and are analogous to common-law actions for damages due to interference with property interests. This conclusion is consistent with historical practice and the original understanding of the Takings Clause.

The Court rejects the argument that because the Constitution allows the government to take property for public use, such a taking cannot be tortious or unlawful. It clarifies that the government acts lawfully only when it provides just compensation for the property taken. If the government fails to provide just compensation or a means to obtain it, its actions are unconstitutional, unlawful, and tortious.

The Court also determines that issues of liability in inverse condemnation cases are predominantly factual questions appropriate for jury determination. This is in line with historical practice where juries decided questions of liability in tort suits for money damages. The Court notes that whether a land-use decision substantially advances legitimate public interests is a mixed question of fact and law, which was properly submitted to the jury in this case.

The Court's decision is limited and does not address the jury's role in ordinary inverse condemnation suits or define the precise elements of a temporary regulatory takings claim. It also does not extend to broad challenges against general land-use ordinances or policies. The decision affirms the judgment of the Court of Appeals, recognizing the right to a jury trial in the specific context of a § 1983 suit for inverse condemnation.

Justice Scalia concurs in part and in the judgment, emphasizing that all § 1983 actions seeking monetary damages must be treated alike concerning the Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial.

Justice Souter, joined by Justices O'Connor, Ginsburg, and Breyer, concurs in part and dissents in part. They argue that there is no constitutional right to a jury trial in eminent domain proceedings and that inverse condemnation actions should not be treated differently. They also criticize the majority's analogy to tort actions and express concern about the implications of extending the right to a jury trial to inverse condemnation cases.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the defendant in this case, holding that the warrantless search of his luggage was unconstitutional. The Court based its decision on the principle that individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their homes and belongings, and that this expectation extends to luggage taken from an automobile during a traffic stop. The Court also cited previous precedents establishing that warrants are typically required for searches of private property, except in certain limited circumstances such as border stops and searches incident to arrest.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against the Department of Labor in a civil injunctive action brought by Buck Doe.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that the U. S. Attorney's Office for New York and the Federal Bureau of Investigation violated the antifraud provisions of Section 5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 5b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, the federal agency violated the reporting provisions of Sections 552a(g)(4) and 552b(c) of the Privacy Act of 1974.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Doe consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Department of New Jersey today announced criminal charges against Doe arising from the same conduct alleged in the complaint.  To learn more about civil injunctions, see Litigation Release No. 551a-4 (1974).

In the case of J. W. Gamble, an inmate who was injured while working in a Texas prison, the Supreme Court considered whether his treatment by prison officials constituted cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Eighth Amendment. Gamble filed a civil rights action under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging that the medical care he received after his injury was inadequate.

The Supreme Court held that "deliberate indifference to serious medical needs of prisoners" does indeed constitute cruel and unusual punishment. However, the Court clarified that not every complaint about inadequate medical treatment rises to the level of an Eighth Amendment violation. To do so, the prisoner must show that the indifference was deliberate and the medical needs were serious.

In Gamble's case, the Court found that the medical staff had seen him multiple times and provided treatment for his back injury, high blood pressure, and heart problems. The Court determined that the decisions made by the medical staff, such as not ordering an X-ray, were matters of medical judgment and not necessarily indicative of deliberate indifference.

As a result, the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision that had reinstated Gamble's complaint, stating that the alleged insufficiency of the medical treatment did not constitute cruel and unusual punishment. The Court remanded the case for further consideration of whether a cause of action was stated against other prison officials, separate from the medical staff.

The implication of this decision is that while prisoners are entitled to medical care, and deliberate indifference to their serious medical needs can violate the Eighth Amendment, not all inadequate medical care meets this standard. Claims of medical malpractice without evidence of deliberate indifference do not constitute constitutional violations and are more appropriately addressed in state courts.

The Supreme Court reversed a decision by the Court of Appeals that had set aside a judgment of acquittal for a corporation and two of its employees who were charged with conspiracy and concealing material facts from a U.S. agency. The district judge had directed the jury to acquit the defendants based on perceived prosecutorial misconduct and questions about witness credibility. The government sought a writ of mandamus to vacate the acquittal and retry the case, which the Court of Appeals granted.

The Supreme Court, however, found that the Fifth Amendment's protection against double jeopardy was central to the case. The Court emphasized that the defendants had been tried under a valid indictment and that the trial concluded with a final judgment of acquittal. Despite the Court of Appeals' belief that the acquittal was based on an erroneous foundation, the Supreme Court held that the acquittal was final and could not be reviewed without violating the constitutional protection against double jeopardy. Therefore, the defendants could not be retried for the same offense, and the Court of Appeals' decision was reversed. Justice Whittaker did not participate in the decision.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of Arizona taxpayers who are seeking to challenge the STO tax credit.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Phoenix, Arizona, Arizona taxpayers were entitled to a tax credit for contributions to school tuition organizations, or STOs.  The complaint alleges that, in violation of the federal tax law, some Arizona taxpayers failed to show that they had a legitimate interest in ensuring that the funds were used to support religious education.  In addition, the complaint alleged that Arizona taxpayers lacked standing to challenge an exemption for religious education, because they are state taxpayers.  As alleged in the complaint, however, the exemption was based on the fact that the taxpayer was a member of a religious organization, not the government.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, the Arizona Department of Revenue and the Arizona Secretary of State's Office have issued an order suspending the exemption.  To determine whether or how to proceed with the litigation, the SEC requested an emergency court order halting the suspension of the exemption, and the issuance of an order requiring Arizona taxpayers to pay a civil penalty of $1,000, and a $100,000 civil penalty for each of the Arizona taxpayers.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida today entered a final judgment against Florida's denial of unemployment compensation benefits to a former trainee and assistant manager of a retail jewelry store.  The SEC's complaint alleges that, in 1981, Lawton and Company (Lawton) hired Paula Hobbie as an assistant manager at a jeweler. According to the complaint, Hobbie told her immediate supervisor that she was going to be baptized into the Seventh-day Adventist Church and that, for religious reasons, she would no longer be able to work on her Sabbath. Hobbie agreed to work evenings and Sundays, and he agreed to substitute for her whenever she was scheduled to work. The SEC alleges that Hobbie refused to work scheduled shifts because she had been discharged for "misconduct connected with [her] work." Hobbie also agreed to be on an equal footing with all other workers, provided she avoids employment that conflicts with her religious beliefs.  In a parallel action, on September 10, 1985, the Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal issued a judgment that permanently enjoins the state from denying Hobbie unemployment compensation. The court also ordered the state to pay a civil penalty of $1,000, which Hobbie consented to.  Hobbie's conversion was the subject of an administrative proceeding by the Florida Department of Labor and Employment Security, which issued an order suspending her from receipt of unemployment benefits. The Court's order also prohibits the payment of benefits to Hobbie, unless she has already agreed to participate in a religious program.  On September 11, 2018, the Court issued a temporary restraining order against Hobbie and ordered her to surrender her passport and other documents related to her religious convictions.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's action, Hobbs consented, without admitting or denied the Commission's findings, to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining her from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering her to disgorge her ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest and pay civil penalties in the amount of $2,500. The judgment also orders Hobbie to pay disgorgement of $3,500, which is equal to the civil penalty in Sherbert and Thomas. The Commission's investigation was conducted by John R. Rymas and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry. The litigation will be led by Gregory A. Kasper. The case is being supervised by Kelly L. Gibson.

Petitioner Atlantic Tel. & Tel. Co. of the Carolinas (ATT) offers wireless phone services and sells devices for those services. Its standard form contract gives customers the option to return unused equipment after thirty days, refunding up to half the purchase price minus restocking charges. Customers signing the contract consent to binding arbitration of any resulting disputes. In 2007, respondents Timothy and Karen Conception bought new iPhones directly from Apple, paying cash on delivery. Their account statement indicated that they had paid a deposit toward the purchase price. On learning that they had received defective products, they returned them to Apple stores, claiming that they had discovered damage during unpackaging. Both stores told them that Apple accepted returns only for items sold by Apple, and gave them forms stating that they needed to contact ATT for a refund. They contacted ATT, which refused to refund the money, telling them instead that they needed to wait until the expiration date of their warranty period. Respondents sued ATT in California state court, seeking to recover the entirety of the payments they had made to Apple. The trial court ruled in ATT’s favor, rejecting respondents’ arguments that the arbitration clause violated California law. The California Supreme Court disagreed, ruling that the clause contravenes the state’s Discovery Bank rule, which renders void any collective-action arbitration clause unless it is narrowly confined to the specific facts underlying the dispute. Rejecting ATT’s argument that the rule was superseded by the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), the court relied on the presumptively exclusive jurisdiction of the FAA to control the outcome of the case. Ultimately, the Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that the Discovery Bank rule survived preemption under the FAA. Held: The FAA preempts California’s Discovery Bank rule. Pp. 4−14. (a) The FAA saves an arbitration agreement from being rendered void by a general contract defense unless the defense goes to the heart of the agreement. Perkins Trading Co. v. Levi Strauss & Co., 290 U.S. 438, 444. Here, the Conceptions argued that the arbitration clause violated California law, specifically the Discovery Bank rule. However, they failed to show that the clause contradicted any essential feature of the contract. Rather, the arbitration clause served as a fallback mechanism for resolving disputes, providing an alternate forum for dealing with problems related to the iPhone purchases. The Conceptions’ argument is similar to the argument advanced in Alexander v. Gardner Greene Hubbard Jr., Ltd., 463 U.S. 136, 149, wherein petitioners challenged the validity of a contract containing an arbitration clause. The Court held that the arbitration clause did not defeat the contract, explaining that “if the contract contained a clause calling for submission of disputes to arbitration, it remains intact regardless of whether or not it survives the test of severance.” Id., at 149. Likewise, here, the arbitration clause does not defeat the contract, and the FAA controls. Pp. 4−6. (b) Even assuming that the FAA saved the arbitration clause from being struck down as violative of California law, the Discovery Bank rule nonetheless remains preempted. The rule stands as an obstacle to the FAA’s achievement of its purposes. See Hines v. Davidowitz, 312 U.S. 52, 67. Because the rule prevents arbitration of collectively asserted claims, it conflicts with the FAA’s core purpose of facilitating the enforcement of arbitration agreements. To the extent that the rule impedes the fulfillment of the FAA’s aims, it is preempted. See Hall Street Assn. v. Mathews, 559 U.S. ___, ___. The Court agrees with the Ninth Circuit that the FAA does not permit States to impose conditions on arbitration agreements that render them incapable of functioning effectively. However, unlike the Ninth Circuit, the Court finds that the rule does precisely that. Pp. 6−11. (c) The Ninth Circuit erred in viewing the rule as having a close relationship to traditional class litigation. While it is true that the rule’s aim is to prevent classwide arbitration, it achieves that end by eliminating the possibility of aggregate liability, not by creating a parallel regime for class litigation. There is no analogy between class arbitration and class litigation. Unlike class litigation, class arbitration involves numerous parties whose interests are not aligned, making it impossible to create fair procedures. Furthermore, like other forms of alternative dispute resolution, class arbitration presents special challenges to the integrity of the arbitration process. Finally, there is no indication that the FAA intends to govern class arbitration differently from ordinary arbitration. Any differences lie in the distinct characteristics of each procedure. The Court rejects the notion that the FAA leaves room for States to establish procedures that depart significantly from the norms of arbitration. See, e.g., Hall Street Assn, supra, at __. Instead, the FAA establishes a uniform body of standards that guide the administration of arbitration agreements. These standards ensure that the parties receive the benefits of arbitration, namely, reduced delay, lower costs, and quicker justice. Pp. 11−14. 584 F.3d 849, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Sotomayor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Stevens, J., joined.

After petitioner Oakland Housing Authority (OHA) instituted eviction proceedings in California state court against respondents, four public housing tenants, based on alleged violations of a lease provision requiring assurance that the tenant, his household, a guest, or another person under the tenant's control would not engage in drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises, they filed suit in Federal District Court challenging the validity of the provision under the Administrative Procedure Act. The District Court entered a preliminary injunction, and the Ninth Circuit ultimately affirmed. Held: Title 42 U. S. C. § 1437d(l)(6)-which requires that public housing agencies utilize leases providing that any drug-related criminal activity on or off the premises, engaged in by a public housing tenant, any member of the tenant's household, or any guest or other person under the tenant's control, shall be cause for termination of tenancy--unambiguously requires lease terms giving local public housing authorities the discretion to evict tenants for the drug-related activity of household members and guests whether or not the tenant knew, or should have known, about the activity. Pp. 129-137. (a) The plain language of § 1437d(l)(6)'s disjunctive phrase "any... drug-related criminal activity" indicates that any drug-related activity engaged in by the specified persons is grounds for terminating the lease, not just drug-related activity that the tenant knew, or should have known, about. Moreover, since the section uses the term "any" to modify "drug-related criminal activity," it precludes any knowledge requirement. Nor does the phrase "under the tenant's control" modify anything except "other person." To interpret otherwise would mean that the statute applies to "a public housing tenant ... under the tenant's control," a nonsensical reading. The Housing and Urban Development Department's administrative regulation tracks the statutory language and confirms that the statute allows local housing authorities to evict tenants whose household members or guests engage in drug-related activity even though the tenant did not know, could not foresee, or could not control the behavior. Pp. 129-132. (b) Comparing § 1437d(l)(6) to a related statutory provision showing that Congress knows how to provide an innocent landowner defense strengthens the plain reading of the former. The latter statute, which deals with drug forfeiture, explicitly excludes from forfeiture tenants who had no knowledge of the activity. Here, however, Congress provided no similar protection for tenants who do not know of the drug-related activity. The en banc court erred in resorting to legislative history, since the finding of textual ambiguity is incorrect. Its attempt to invoke the canon of constitutional avoidance is also misplaced, since that doctrine has no application in the absence of statutory ambiguity. Finally, the court's assertions that allowing local housing authorities to make no-fault evictions raises due process concerns are refuted by the facts that the government is not attempting to criminally punish or civilly regulate respondents as members of the general populace, but is instead acting as a landlord of property that it owns, invoking a clause in a lease to which respondents have agreed and which Congress has expressly required. Pp. 133-137. Reversed and remanded.

Respondent, a Nevada man, entered the Red Pearl Saloon bar and shot the bartender and a patron four times each with an automatic pistol. He then walked behind the bar and removed the cash register. Nine days later, he arrived at the apartment of his former wife and opened fire on her; five of his seven shots hit their target. Respondent then shot himself in the abdomen and attempted, without success, to slit his wrists. The Nevada Supreme Court affirmed his sentences for the murders, but reversed his sentence for the murder of his ex-wife and remanded for imposition of a life sentence without the possibility of parole. On July 30, 1987, respondent filed a petition for post-conviction relief in state court. Following an evidentiary hearing, the trial court rejected respondent's claim that he was "mentally incompetent to represent himself," concluding that "the record clearly shows that respondent was examined by two psychiatrists both of whom declared [him] competent." The Supreme Court dismissed respondent's appeal, Moran v. Warden, 105 Nev. 1041, 810 P. 2d 335, and denied certiorari, 493 U. S. 874. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the state court's postconviction ruling was premised on the wrong legal standard of competency. Held: The competency standard for pleading guilty or waiving the right to counsel is higher than that of the Dusky standard for standing trial. Pp. 5-18. (a) The competencies standard for plead guilty or to waive the right of counsel is not higher than the competency standards for standing trials. P. 5. (b) The competence that is required of a defendant seeking to waive his right to the assistance of counsel, whether the defendant has a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings and is capable of assisting his counsel, is not a heightened standard of competence. P p. 5–6. (c) A finding that a defendant is competent to stand trial is not all that is necessary before he may be permitted to plead guilty. In addition to determining whether a defendant has the capacity for "reasoned choice" among the alternatives available to him, a trial court must satisfy itself that the waiver of his constitutional rights is knowing and voluntary. Johnson v. Zerbst, 304 U.S. 458, 468. While psychiatrists and scholars may find it useful to classify the various kinds and degrees of competence, and while States are free to adopt competencies standards that are more elaborate than Dusky's formulation, the Due Process Clause does not impose these additional requirements. Cf. Medina v. California, supra, at 874, distinguished between "competence to plead" and "compete to waive" as a shorthand for the "intelligent and competent waiver" requirement of Johnson. The standard adopted by the Ninth Circuit is whether a criminal defendant has "sufficient present ability to consult with his lawyer with a reasonable degree of rational understanding" and has "a rational as well as factual understanding," id., at 402, and, in consultation with counsel, he may have to decide whether (and how) to put on a defense and whether to raise one or more affirmative defenses. While the decision to plead is undeniably a profound one, it is no more complicated than the sum total of decisions a defendant may be called upon to make during the course of a trial. Moreover, a defendant who chooses to plead does not waive his rights to counsel, since there is no reason to believe that the decision requires an appreciably higher level of mental functioning than the one that waives other constitutional rights. Nor does a defendant waives his right "to stand trial" because there is a "heightened" standard for the pleading guilty and waiving of the right-to- counsel requirement, since the waiver must also be intelligent and voluntary before it can be accepted. The same standard is applicable for those who plead not guilty, but it is not "a heightened" standard. The competence to plead, however, is the competence to waive, not the competence of represent himself. In this sense, the standard is different from (much less higher than) the "Dusky" standard-whether the defendant had a "rational understanding" of proceedings-is not a "higher standard," since the defendant's "rational choice" has no bearing upon his competence to choose self-representation. Pc. 214-215. (d) Respondent's contention that the difference between the two standards is merely one of "terminology," Brief in Opposition 4, and he devotes little space in his brief on the merits to a defense of that standard, see, e.g., Brief for Respondent 17-18, 27, 32; see also Tr. of Oral Arg. 33, "Due process does not require [a] higher standard, [it] requires a separate inquiry." P. 215. (e) The question whether the standard of pleading guilty is higher is a question that has divided the federal courts of appeals and state courts of last resort

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Virginia today entered a final judgment against a private party for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the private party and ordered it to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $10,000.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia, in 1977, Edmondson Oil Co., Inc. ("Edmondson"), a Virginia-based oil company, was indebted to a state-appointed receiver, and the receiver had acted jointly with the state to deprive him of his property without due process of law.  In addition, the complaint alleged that in attaching his property to the receiver, the receiver violated the federal securities laws.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating the above-mentioned provisions of the Exchange Act, and ordered them to pay civil penalties in the amounts of $15,000 and $20,000, respectively, in amounts to be determined by the court at a later date.    The final judgment, which permanently enjoins the defendants from violating these provisions, also orders the receiver to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil money penalties in a parallel action. Â The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by John R. Rymas and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Virginia Attorney General's Office and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

These suits challenging the constitutionality of state statutes requiring a one-year waiting period before an indigent alien may receive welfare benefits were heard together with a suit attacking the constitutionality of a regulation of the District of Columbia requiring the same waiting period. The Connecticut statute was upheld by the District Court and the Court of Appeals, while the Pennsylvania statute was struck down by the District Court and the Court of Appeals affirmed. The District of Columbia statute was upheld by the District Court and the Court of Appeals reversed. Held: 1. The Connecticut and Pennsylvania statutes violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 108-116. (a) Neither deterrence of indigents from migrating to the State nor limitation of welfare benefits to those regarded as contributing to the community is a constitutionally permissible state objective. Pp. 110-112. (b) The waiting-period requirement does not facilitate the planning of the welfare budget, provide an objective test of residency, minimize the opportunity for recipients fraudulently to receive payments from more than one jurisdiction, or encourage early entry of new residents into the labor force. Pp. 112-115. (c) Even assuming that Congress intended to encourage state participation in the AFDC program by the Social Security Act, the Connecticut and Pennsylvania statutes still violate the Equal Protection Clause. Section 402 (b) of the Act merely requires the Secretary of HEW not to disapprove state plans containing a one-year waiting period requirement, and its legislative history shows that it was enacted to curb restrictions on residence requirements rather than to encourage state participation in the AFDC program. Pp. 115-116. 2. The District of Columbia statute violates the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. Pp. 116-117. Affirmed.

Petitioners, consisting of more than 60 towns, municipalities, and water districts in the State of Utah, brought a civil action for treble damages against petitioners, alleging that they had conspired together in restraint of trade in steel and concrete pipe by submitting collusive and rigged bids for the sale of such pipe and by dividing and allocating business among themselves. Shortly thereafter, pleas of nolo contendere were accepted and judgments of guilt were entered. Four days later, on June 23, 1964, the United States filed civil complaints in the Federal District Court for the Central District of California against the same defendants, which complaints, as subsequently amended, sought to restrain further violations of the Sherman and False Claims Acts. The District Court denied the respondents' motion in all respects concluding that the limitations period imposed by § 4B of the Clayton Act, as tolled by § 5(b), had run as to all these respondents and had not been tolled in their behalf. The Court of Appeals affirmed as to the denial of leave to intervene as of right under Rule 24(a)(2), but reversed as to permission to intervene under Rule24(b)(2). Held: 1. A federal class action is no longer "an invitation to joinder" but a truly representative suit designed to avoid, rather than encourage, unnecessary filing of repetitious papers and motions. The mere fact that a federal statute providing for substantive liability also sets a time limitation upon the institution of suit does not restrict the power of the federal courts to hold that the statute of limitations is tolled under certain circumstances not inconsistent with the legislative purpose. Pp. 5-7. 2. The commencement of a class action suspends the applicable statute-of limitations as to those who might subsequently participate in the suit as well as those who would have been parties had the suit been permitted to continue as a class. P. 6. 473 F. 2d 580, affirmed.

After respondent Mendelsohn was fired during a company-wide reduction in force, she filed suit under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) alleging disparate treatment based on her age. Seeking to introduce testimony by several other former Sprint employees claiming that their supervisors had discriminated against them because of age, Mendelsohn moved to admit the evidence pursuant to Federal Rules of Evidence 401 and 403. The District Court granted Sprint’s in limine motion to exclude the testimony, defining “similarly situated employees” as requiring proof that the decisionmaker in any adverse employment action was the person who made the discriminatory comments. On appeal, the Tenth Circuit treated the minute order as applying a per se rule that evidence from employees with other supervisors is irrelevant to proving discrimination in an ADEA case. Held: The Federal Rules of Evidence do not require admission of testimony by nonparties alleging discrimination at the hands of persons who played no role in the adverse employment decision challenged by the plaintiff. Pp. 4−8. (a) Courts of appeals afford broad discretion to a district court’s evidentiary rulings. They uphold Rule 403 rulings unless the district court has abused its discretion. However, the Tenth Circuit did not accord the District Court the deference due under this standard. Instead, it reasoned that the District Court had erroneously concluded that Aramburu v. Boeing Co., 112 F. 3d 1398, controlled the fate of the evidence. While Aramburu does define “similarly situated employees” in the context of a plaintiff’s allegation that nonminority employees were treated more favorably than minority employees, absent reason to do so, this Court will not assume the District Court adopted that definition when addressing a very different kind of evidence. Nor can the Tenth Circuit presume that the District Court intended an incorrect legal result where the order is equally susceptible of a correct reading, particularly when the applicable standard of review is deferential. And although the in limine motion did argue that the evidence was irrelevant, it did not suggest that it was never admissible. Pp. 4−6. (b) Questions of relevance and prejudice are for the District Court to determine in the first instance. Had the District Court applied a per se rule excluding the evidence, the Tenth Circuit would have been correct to conclude that it had abused its discretion. But there is no basis in the record for concluding that the District Court applied a blanket rule. Thus, the Tenth Circuit should have allowed the District Court to make these determinations in the first instance, explicitly and on the record. Pp. 6−7. (c) Whether evidence of discrimination by other supervisors is relevant in an individual ADEA case is fact based and depends on many factors, including how closely related the evidence is to the plaintiff’s circumstances and theory of the case. Applying Rule 403 to determine if evidence is prejudicial also requires a fact-intensive, context-specific inquiry. Because Rules 401 and 403 do not make such evidence per se admissible or per se inadmissible, and because the inquiry required by those Rules is within the province of the District Court in the first instance, this Court vacates the Tenth Circuit’s judgment and remands the case with instructions to have the District Court clarify the basis for its evidentiary ruling under the applicable Rules. Pp. 7−8. 466 F. 3d 1223, vacated and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Alito, and Ginsburg, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

This case involves a defamation lawsuit filed by a public official named Thompson against a politician named St. Amant. The claim is that St. Amant made false statements about Thompson during a television speech, accusing him of engaging in illegal activities. The key issue in the case is whether St. Amant acted with "actual malice" when making these statements, as required by the landmark case of New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. The Supreme Court ultimately rules that St. Amant did not meet this requirement and that the lower courts erred in applying the New York Times malice standard.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, which had upheld a state statute restricting corporate expenditures aimed at influencing voter decisions on referendum proposals. The Massachusetts court had ruled that corporations' First Amendment rights were limited to matters materially affecting their business, property, or assets, and that the statute did not violate the First or Fourteenth Amendments.

The Supreme Court disagreed, stating that the proper question was not whether corporations have First Amendment rights, but whether the statute abridged expression that the First Amendment was meant to protect. The Court held that the speech in question—corporate speech on referendum issues—was at the heart of First Amendment protection. It emphasized that the freedom to discuss matters of public concern is fundamental to democracy and that this freedom is not diminished because the speaker is a corporation.

The Court found no support for the notion that corporate speech loses First Amendment protection simply because it comes from a corporation. It also rejected the state's justifications for the statute, which included preserving the integrity of the electoral process and protecting shareholders from corporate speech with which they might disagree. The Court concluded that the statute was both underinclusive and overinclusive and did not serve a compelling state interest in a closely drawn manner.

The implications of the decision are that corporations cannot be barred from engaging in speech about public referendum issues and that restrictions on such speech must meet strict scrutiny—meaning they must serve a compelling state interest and be narrowly tailored to achieve that interest. The ruling protects corporate speech on public issues, recognizing it as an important part of the democratic process.

Respondent was convicted of possessing nontaxpaid liquor in violation of 26 U. S. C. § 5205(a)(2). The Court of Appeals reversed on the ground that the federal tax investigator's affidavit supporting the search warrant, the execution of which resulted in the discovery of illicit liquor, was insufficient to establish probable cause. Held: The affidavit, considered as a whole, was sufficient to support issuance of the warrant. Pp. 577-585. 412 F. 2d 796, reversed.

Petitioners are members of the Branch-Davidian religious sect and are among those who were involved in a violent confrontation with federal agents from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms near Waco, Texas, in 1993. Petitioners' indictment alleges that, among other things, petitioners conspired to murder federal officers. At the time of petitioners' trial, the criminal statute at issue (reprinted in its entirety in the Appendix, infra) read in relevant part: (1) Whoever, during and in relation to any crime of violence . . . uses or carries a firearm, shall, in addition to the punishment provided for such crime, be sentenced to imprisonment for five years, and if the firearm is a machinegun, or a destructive device, or is equipped with a firearm silencer or firearm muffler, to imprisonment." The District Court found that petitioners had violated this section by, in the words of the trial judge's instruction, "knowingly using or carrying a firearm during and . . .." the commission of a crime. At sentencing, the judge found that the "firearms" at issue included certain machineguns (many equipped with silencers) and handgrenades that the defendants actually or constructively had possessed. The judge then imposed the statute's mandatory 30-year prison sentence, which petitioners appealed. The Court of Appeals subsequently held that Bailey v. United States, 516 U. S. 137, 143, 133 L. Ed. 2d 472, reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court addressed whether a government motion under Section 5K1.1 of the Sentencing Guidelines, which acknowledges a defendant's substantial assistance in a criminal investigation, also allows a district court to impose a sentence below the statutory minimum. The Court held that it does not.

The petitioner was involved in a drug conspiracy and faced a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years. After cooperating with the government, the government filed a motion for a reduced sentence under the Guidelines, but did not move for a sentence below the statutory minimum. The district court ruled it could not impose a sentence below the statutory minimum without such a motion from the government.

The Court of Appeals affirmed the district court's decision, leading to the Supreme Court's review. The Supreme Court concluded that a government motion under Section 5K1.1 alone does not authorize a district court to impose a sentence below the statutory minimum. The Court reasoned that the statutes and the Guidelines require a specific government motion requesting or authorizing a sentence below the statutory minimum before a court can impose such a sentence.

The Court's decision clarifies that while the government can move for a sentence reduction based on a defendant's substantial assistance, this does not automatically grant the court the authority to go below the statutory minimum unless the government explicitly authorizes it. The judgment of the lower court was affirmed, meaning the petitioner was not eligible for a sentence below the 10-year statutory minimum.

The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled that an anonymous tip that a person was carrying a gun does not justify a police officer's stop and frisk of that person. The case involves a Florida man who was stopped and frisked by a Miami-Dade Police Department officer in 1995 after an anonymous caller reported that a young black male stood at a bus stop and was wearing a plaid shirt with a gun. The court ruled that the officer had probable cause to search the man's pocket and found no evidence that the caller's tip had any bearing on the search. The Florida Supreme Court overturned the lower court's ruling and held that the search was unlawful under the Fourth Amendment. The Supreme Court of Florida, however, held that there was no reasonable cause to suspect that J. L. was armed. In the case before the Supreme Court, Humberto Fidel Regalado Cuellar was convicted under the federal money laundering statute for attempting to transport proceeds of unlawful activity across the Mexican border. The statute in question, 18 U.S.C. §1956(a)(2)(B)(i), requires the government to prove that the transportation was designed to conceal or disguise the nature, location, source, ownership, or control of the money.

Cuellar argued that his conviction should be overturned because the evidence only showed that he took steps to hide the money during transport, not that the transport itself was intended to create the appearance of legitimate wealth. The Supreme Court agreed with Cuellar, stating that while the statute does not require proof of an attempt to "legitimize" illicit funds, it does require more than evidence of mere concealment during transport.

The Court emphasized that the term "design" in the statute refers to the purpose or plan of the transportation, not just the method of concealment. Therefore, the government must prove that the defendant knew the transportation was intended, at least in part, to conceal or disguise one of the specified attributes of the funds.

The Court found that the evidence presented by the government was insufficient to prove that Cuellar's purpose in transporting the money was to conceal or disguise its illicit nature. The evidence showed extensive efforts to hide the money en route to Mexico, but there was no evidence that the purpose of the transportation was to conceal or disguise the money's attributes.

As a result, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Fifth Circuit, which had upheld Cuellar's conviction. The decision clarifies that under the money laundering statute, the government must prove that the transportation of illicit funds was designed with the intent to conceal or disguise the funds' illegal attributes, not just that the funds were hidden during transport.

Title: Chevron Corporation v. Hawaiian Electric Company, Inc.

Citation: 537 U. S. __ (2003)

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether a rent control law passed by the state of Hawaii constituted a taking of private property for public use under the Fifth Amendment. The Court held that the law did not take private property for public use, and therefore did not require just compensation. The Court also rejected the idea that the "substantially advances" formula from Agins v. Tiburon, Calif., 447 U. S. 260 (1980), could be used as a takings test. Instead, the Court looked to four traditional takings tests: physical takings, total regulatory takings, Penn Central Transportation Co. v. New York City Transit Authority, 448 U. S. 154 (1980), and Lucas v. South Dakota Department of Environmental Protection, 505 U. S. 1028 (1992).

Petitioner, his wife Dorothy Miller-El, and one Kenneth Flowers robbed a Holiday Inn in Dallas, Texas, and ordered two employees, Walker and Hall, to lie on the floor. When Flowers hesitated or refused, petitioner shot Walker twice in the back and shot Hall in the side. Walker died from his wounds. The State indicted petitioner for capital murder. When voir dire had been concluded, petitioner moved to strike the jury on the grounds that the prosecution had violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by excluding African-Americans through the use of peremptory challenges. The District Court, after reviewing the evidence before the state trial court, determined that petitioner failed to establish a constitutional violation warranting habeas relief. The Court of Appeals denied a certificate of appealability (COA) from the District Court's determination. Held: A prisoner seeking postconviction relief under 28 U. S. C. § 2254 has no automatic right to appeal a district court's denial or dismissal of the petition. Instead, petitioner must first seek and obtain a COA. The COA determination under § 2253(c) requires an overview of the claims in the habeaas petition and a general assessment of their merits. Pp. 479-478. (a) When a court of appeals seeks permission to initiate appellate review of the dismissal of a petition, the court of the appeals should limit its examination to a threshold inquiry into the underlying merit of the claim. The statute does not require a showing that a decision is objectively unreasonable by clear and convincing evidence. P. 478. (b) In resolving the equal protection claim against petitioner, the state courts made no mention of either the jury shuffle or the historical record of purposeful discrimination. The evidence alone raises some debate as to whether the prosecution acted with a race-based reason when striking prospective jurors, and it reveals that the culture of the District Attorney's Office in the past was suffused with bias against African-American veniremen in jury selection. This finding established that petitioner had failed to carry his burden at step three of the inquiry set out in Batson v. Kentucky, 476 U.S. 79 (1986), which required that a state court "presum[e]" the state court's findings of fact "to be correct" unless petitioner can rebut the presumption "by clearand convincing evidence." The Court's rejection of this conclusion also conflicts with pre-AEDPA practice. Prior to AEDPA, access to a merits appeal in federal habas corpus proceedings was governed by a mechanism similar to the COA's, known as a "Certificate of probable cause, or CPC." See Slack v. McDaniel, 529 U. s. 473, 481. The concept of a threshold, or gateway, test was not the innovation of the statute. Congress established a threshold prerequisite to appealability in 1908, in large part because it was "concerned with the increasing number of frivolous petitions challenging capital sentences which delayed execution pending completion of the appellate process. . . ." Barefoot, supra, at 892, n. 3. A federal court's collateral review of a state-court decision must be consistent with the respect due state courts in our federal system. Here, a reviewing court, which analyzes only the transcripts from voir- dire, is not as well positioned as the trial court is to make credibility determinations, and the Court should have inquired whether a "substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right" had been proved. The record demonstrates that petitioner has not presented anything remotely resembling a "clear and convincing" evidence of the existence of a "creditor" in the manner the prosecutors questioned members of the venire. The court also errs, albeit in dicta, when it implies that delayed state factfinding-here the two years between voir' dire and the post-trial Batson hearing-is an excuse for weakened factual deference. Moreover, because the State court entered a finding of fact that the prosecutor's purported reasons for exercising its peremotory challenges were not pretexts for discrimination, the Court's use of the practice here tends to erode the credibility of the prosecution's assertion that race was not a motivating factor in the jury selection process. The failure of this approach to resolve the merits of petitioner's constitutional claims is further evidenced by the fact that, when presented with this evidence, the State trial court somehow reasoned that there was not even the inference of discrimination to support a prima facie case. The lack of such evidence in the case of the two white venire men who were not struck by the prosecution is debatable, since the State's proffered race-neutral rationales for striking them appear to have been selective and based on racial considerations. The state court also had before it, and apparently ignored, testimony demonstrating that the Dallas County District Attorney had, by its own admission, used this process to manipulate the racial composition of the jury in the present case.

In 1981, the General Assembly initiated the process of reapportioning the State's legislative districts pursuant to the 1980 census. At this time, there were Republican majorities in both Houses and the Senate, and the Governor was Republican. The division of the State into districts is accomplished by legislative enactment. Reapportionment is required every 10 years and is based on the federal decennial census. In 1982, elections were held under the new districting plan. All of the House seats and half of the Senate seats were up for election. Only 43 Democrats, however, were elected to the House. Over all the Senate races statewide, Democratic candidates received 53.1% of the vote. Thirteen (of twenty appellees) filed suit in Federal District Court, alleging that the 1981 reapportionment plans constituted a political gerrymander intended to disadvantage Democrats. The District Court invalidated the statute. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that the case was justiciable and that an equal protection violation had occurred. Held: 1. A threshold showing of discriminatory vote dilution is required for a prima facie case of an Equal Protection Clause violation. Baker v. Carr, 369 U. S. 186; Whitcomb v. Chavis, 403 U.S. 124. Pp. 531-532. (a) The fact that there are multimember districts in the State and that those districts are constructed so as to be safely Republican or Democratic in no way bolsters the contention that there has been statewide discrimination against Democratic voters, and that adjudication of such claims requires an initial policy decision that the judiciary should not make. P. 533. (b) A mere lack of proportionate election results in one election cannot support a finding of an unconstitutional gerrymandering violation. In the multimember district context, the question is whether a particular group has been unconstitutionally denied its chance to effectively influence the political process. The question here is the consistency of state action with the Federal Constitution, and this Court has consistently adjudicated equal protection claims in the legislative districting context regarding inequalities in population between districts. The very essence of districting is to produce a different-a more "politically fair" result than would be reached with elections at large, in which the winning party would take 100% of legislative seats. In both contexts, this inquiry focuses on the opportunity of members of the group to participate in party deliberations in the slating and nomination of candidates, their opportunity to register and vote, and hence their chance to directly influence the election returns and to secure the attention of the winning candidate. The inquiry centers on the voters' direct or indirect influence on the elections of the state legislature as a whole, and as in individual district cases, an equal-protection violation may be found only where the electoral system substantially disadvantages certain voters in their opportunity of influence. In this context, such a finding must be supported by evidence of continued frustration of the will of a majority of the voters or effective denial to a minority of voters of a fair chance to influence the electoral process. In addition to being contrary to the above-described conception of a "political fairness" approach in Gaffney v. Cummings, supra, at 729-732, such an approach would invite attack on all or almost all reapportionments statutes, since there is no risk of foreign or domestic disturbance, and in light of this Court's cases since Baker, the "one person, one vote" principle is at the same time consistent with the prior cases regarding individual multimember Districts, which have formulated a parallel standard. In these cases, a substantially greater showing of adverse effects than a mere loss of proportional representation is required to support a determination of an equal protected violation. The factors other than disproportionate election results do not contribute to a finding that Democratic voters have been disadvantaged in fact. The mere fact that the districts were drawn in accordance with that intention does not compel a conclusion that the claims presented here are nonjusticiable. Moreover, there are other cases in which federal or state courts adjudicated political-gerrymandered claims and summarily affirmed or dismissed for want of a substantial federal question. See, e.g., White v. Regester, 446 U.

The Long Family Land and Cattle Company (Long Company), a South Dakota corporation, is a respondent here, along with Ronnie and Lila Long, husband and wife, who together own at least 51 percent of the Long Company’s shares. The Long Company and their company have been customers for many years at Plains Commerce Bank (Bank), located some 25 miles off the reservation as the crow flies in South Dakota. Following the sale of fee land on the reservation, an Indian couple, customers of the Bank, claimed the bank discriminated against them by offering the land to non-Indians on terms more favorable than those the bank offered to them. After the Longs sued on that claim in tribal court, the Tribal Court concluded that it had jurisdiction and proceeded to hear the case. The jury found against the Bank on three of the four causes, including the discrimination claim, and awarded a $750,000 general verdict. The Tribe appealed to the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribal Court of Appeals, which affirmed the judgment of the trial court. The Bank then filed the instant action in the District Court for the District of South Dakota, seeking a declaration that the tribal judgment was null and void because, as relevant here, the tribal court lacked jurisdiction over the Longsell’ discrimination claim. The court found tribal court jurisdiction proper because the Bank had entered into a consensual relationship with Longs and Long Company. The Tribes have, by virtue of their incorporation into the American republic, lost “the right of governing . . . person[s] within their limits except themselves,” United States v. Lara, 523 U. S. 83, 94–95, and efforts by a tribe to regulate nonmembers, especially on non-Indian fee land, are “presumptively invalid.” Id., at 659. The burden rests on the Tribes to establish one of the exceptions to Montana’“general rule that would allow an extension of tribal authority to regulate the business conduct of persons who ‘voluntarily deal with tribal members,’ ” Montana, 450 U.S. 544, 565. These exceptions are limited” ones at 647, and cannot be construed in a manner that would “swallow the rule, id., at 655, or “severely shrink” it, Strate, 520 U., at 458. Those injuries can be remedied by a ruling in favor of the Tribe that it lacked jurisdiction and that its judgment on the Discrimination claim is null andvoid. The ultimate collateral consequence of such a determination is that the Tribe lacks jurisdiction to exercise jurisdiction. Pp. 5–7. 491 F. 3d 878, reversed.

Respondents, a private corporation and its owner and principal officer, sued in Federal District Court alleging that the Postal Service had sought to suppress competition and create a monopoly in mail sack production. The District Court dismissed the antitrust claims, concluding that the USPS is not subject to liability under the controlling antitrust statute. The Court of Appeals reversed. Held: 1. The Postal Service is not a "person" amenable to suit under the federal antitrust laws. United States v. Cooper Corp., 312 U. S. 600, 614. Pp. 561-564. 2. When Congress passes enabling legislation allowing an agency or other entity of the Federal Government to be sued the waiver should be given a liberal construction. Federal Housing Administration v. Burr, 309 U.S. 242, distinguished. P. 562. 3. Under the Sherman Act, as amended, the United States Postal Service, as an "independent establishment of the executive branch of the Government of the United United States," is part of the Executive Branch and that status indicates immunity unless there is a waiver. The sue-and-be-sued clause waives immunity, and makes the Postal service amenable, as well as to the incidents of judicial process. § 401. The PRA waives the immunity of the USPS from suit by giving it the power "to sue and be sued in its official name." § 401-410. The waiver does not result in liability if the substantive law in question is not intended to reach the federal entity. The choice of words likely was more informed than unconsidered, because Congress debated proposals to make the postal service a Government corporation before it enacted the PRA. The silence leads to no helpful inference one way or the other on the issue before us; but the other considerations lead us to say that absent an express statement from Congress that the postal Service can be sued for antitrust violations despite its status as an independent establishment of a Government, that agency is not less amenable-to judicial process than a private enterprise under like circumstances would be. See, e. g., United States, Cooper Corp. v. Frank, 486 U. s. 549, 659 F. 2d 243, 245. The two-step analysis applies here. The first question, which is whether there is any waiver of sovereign immunity for actions against the USPS, is whether the substantive prohibitions of the Sherman-Act apply to an independent "institution" of the Constitution. The second question is whether, for purposes of the antitrust laws, the Postal Services is a person separate from the Government. It is not. The statutory designation of the PostalService as an establishment "of the Executive branch of [the Government] of the [United States]" is not consistent with the idea that it is an entity existing outside the Government, and Congress did not strip it of its governmental status. While Congress waived the immunity, Congress did, in fact, strip it, of its power to provide universal mail delivery, the provision of free mail delivery to certain classes of persons, §§ 3201-3405, and, most recently, increased public responsibilities related to national security. The distinction is important. An absence of immunity does not end in liability, since the substantive laws in question are not intended only to reach a federal entity, but to the non-applicability of antitrust laws to the Postal. The federal prohibition, for instance, binds state governmental bodies. See Georgia v. Evans, 316 U. .S. 159 (1942); see also Pfizer Inc.' v. Government of India, 434 U. G. 308 (1978). P. 525. The fact that the Government has different goals, obligations, and powers from private corporations indicates that it should be treated under the antitrust law as part of its Government, not a market participant separate from it. The Government's public characteristics and responsibilities indicate it should not be treated as a person who could bring a treble-damages claim for its own alleged antitrust injury. The postal service does operate nonpostal lines of business, for which it is free to set prices independent of the Commission, and in which it may seek profits to be offset by the cost of its services. The regulatory prohibition, however, does not allow the Government to seek profits, but only to break even, and it has many powers more characteristic of Government than of private enterprise, including its state-conferred monopoly on mail delivery and power of eminent domain, and the power to conclude international postal agreements. On the other hand, it lacks the prototypical means of engaging in anti-competitive behavior: the power of setting prices. This is true both as a matter of mechanics, because pricing decisions are made with the participation of the separate Postal Rate Commission, because price decisions are governed by principles other than profitability. Similarly, before it can close a post office, it must provide written reasons, and its decision is subject to reversal by the Commission for arbitrariness, abuse of discretion, failure to follow procedures, or lack of evidence. Respondents were convicted of illegally possessing M16 rifles after the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives traced the rifles back to earlier sales that violated federal export control regulations governing shipment overseas of goods subject to a Duval County ordinance requiring reporting to local officials before leaving the county or entering the shipment inside another ordinance area during specified hours or in vehicles larger than pickups. After hearings resulting in administrative revocation of the sale transactions, including, as to “firearms containin[gs]. The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania today entered a final judgment in favor of a flat tax on the operation of trucks and truck tractors.  The court held that the flat tax violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In its judgment, the court found that Pennsylvania's flat taxes were not discriminatory because they did not impose a significant burden on interstate commerce.  According to the court's order, however, the flat taxes violated the federal securities laws because they disproportionately burdened out-of-state and in-state trucking and trucking companies.  As a result of the Court's ruling, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  To learn more about flat taxes, see http://www.securities.gov/flat-tax.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has ruled that the President cannot remove an officer of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) who disagrees with his decision. The court held that the Board's members and employees are not considered Government "officers" or "employees" for statutory purposes. The Board is a Government-created, Government-appointed entity with expansive powers to govern an entire industry. The Court held that such multilevel protection from removal is contrary to Article II of the United States Constitution, which vests executive power in a President who must "take care that the laws be faithfully executed"<n>The Court also held that, in the case of the PCAOB, the President could not remove a member of the Board, even if he determines that the officer is neglecting his duties or discharging them improperly. The decision is the latest in a series of cases that have held that President's power to remove officers is limited. The case is being brought by the Office of the Chief Justice of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Federal Taxpayer's Office.

In the Supreme Court case concerning the Tellico Dam and the endangered snail darter fish, the Court was presented with two main questions: (1) whether the Endangered Species Act of 1973 (ESA) requires the halting of a nearly completed dam that would eradicate an endangered species, and (2) whether continued congressional appropriations for the dam after the ESA's enactment implied a repeal of the Act's application to the dam.

The Tellico Dam, part of a project started by the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) in 1967, was nearly complete when the snail darter, a previously unknown species of fish, was discovered in the Little Tennessee River. The Secretary of the Interior listed the snail darter as an endangered species and identified the area to be flooded by the dam as its critical habitat. Despite this, Congress continued to appropriate funds for the dam's completion.

The Supreme Court held that the ESA's clear and unambiguous language required federal agencies to ensure that their actions do not jeopardize endangered species or their habitats. The Court found that the ESA's provisions applied to the Tellico Dam, regardless of the project's advanced stage, and that the Act mandated the protection of endangered species as a priority above the completion of federal projects.

The Court also addressed the argument that congressional appropriations for the dam after the ESA's passage implied a repeal of the Act's application to the dam. The Court rejected this argument, stating that repeals by implication are not favored and that there was no clear and manifest intention by Congress to repeal the ESA with respect to the Tellico Dam.

As a result, the Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals, which had reversed the District Court's decision and instructed that a permanent injunction be issued to halt activities related to the Tellico Project that could destroy or modify the critical habitat of the snail darter.

The Supreme Court's decision underscored the importance of adhering to the explicit provisions of environmental legislation and the principle of separation of powers, emphasizing that it is not the role of the judiciary to second-guess the policy choices made by Congress.
