In the case before the Supreme Court, a high school principal, Deborah Morse, confiscated a banner reading "BONG HiTS 4 JESUS" displayed by student Joseph Frederick at a school-sanctioned event. Morse interpreted the banner as promoting illegal drug use, which was against school policy, and suspended Frederick. The Ninth Circuit Court ruled that Morse's actions violated Frederick's First Amendment rights and that he could sue for damages.

The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's decision, emphasizing that while students have constitutional rights, these rights are not identical to those of adults and must be considered in the context of the school environment. The Court held that schools could restrict speech that is reasonably viewed as promoting illegal drug use to protect the welfare of students.

The Court rejected Frederick's claim that this was not a school speech case, noting that the event occurred during school hours and was school-sanctioned, with teachers and administrators present. The Court found Morse's interpretation of the banner as promoting drug use to be reasonable and concluded that the school officials did not violate the First Amendment by confiscating the banner and suspending Frederick.

The Court clarified that its decision was based on the specific context of preventing student drug abuse, which is a compelling interest for schools. The ruling did not extend to all offensive speech but was limited to speech promoting illegal drug use at school events. The Court remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, focusing on the First Amendment issue rather than the qualified immunity of the principal.

The decision implies that school officials have the authority to suppress certain student speech that contradicts the educational mission of the school, particularly when it comes to preventing drug abuse among students. The ruling also suggests that the standard set by Tinker v. Des Moines for student speech (that it cannot be suppressed unless it causes material and substantial disruption) is not absolute and can be adjusted in light of the special characteristics of the school environment.

Petitioner Lawrence and his wife used a pipe and baseball bat to kill Michael Finken. A Florida jury convicted Lawrence of first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit murder, auto theft, and petty theft. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed Lawrence’s conviction and sentence on appeal, and this Court denied certiorari on January 20, 1998. After the Florida Court denied relief, Lawrence filed an application for state postconviction relief in a Florida trial court. The Federal District Court dismissed it as untimely under §2244(d)(2), which provides that the limitations period is tolled while an “application for State post-conviction or other collateral review” “is pending.” The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, concluding that Lawrence had only one day to file a federal habeas application after this Court issued its mandate affirming the denial of that petition. Certiorari granted. The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA), 110 Stat. 1214, sets a one-year statute of limitations for seeking federal habas corpus relief from a state-court judgment. 28 U. S. C. §2242(d), and further provided that “the time during which a properly filed application for State Post-convictions or collateral review with respect to the pertinent judgment or claim is pending shall not be counted toward any period of limitation under this subsection,” §2243(d). The parties agree that AEDPA’d limitations period was tolled from the filing of the petition for a state state postviction relief until the Florida SupremeCourt issued its mandated mandate affording that petition, and that the District Court concluded that Lawrence, who was entitled to equitable tolling because of delays in the state courts’ program and other issues outside his control caused 298 days to pass before Florida appointed an attorney who took an active role in his case. Lawrence did not seek certiorar on the question whether these facts entitle him to equitable tlling. Rather, he argues that his attorney mistakenly missed the deadline while this Court was considering his petition for certiorarian. The Eleth Circuit correctly declined to equitably toll the 1-year limitations period in the factual circumstances of his case, and the judgment is affirmed. The judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed. 421 F. 3d 1221, affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed and remanded a lower court's decision to remove three justices of the peace and two constables from office in Harris County, Texas. The lower court held that a Texas law requiring the removal of certain county officials when their elected terms expire violated equal protection provisions of the Fourteenth Amendment. The court held, however, that the district court should have abstained from deciding the federal constitutional issue because it was far from certain that appellee officeholders must lose their jobs or that the reinstatement relief ordered by the District Court is available. The appeals court concluded that the lower court was wrong to conclude that the law violated the equal protection provision of the Constitution.

The Bankruptcy Act of 1978 (Act) established a United States bankruptcy court in each judicial district as an adjunct to the district court for such district. The bankruptcy court judges are appointed for 14-year terms, subject to removal by the judicial council of the circuit in which they serve on grounds of incompetence, misconduct, neglect of duty, or disability. Their salaries are set by statute and are subject to adjustment under the Federal Salary Act, 2 U. S. C. §§ 351-361. Appellee Marathon Pipe Line Co. (Marathon) filed a suit in a Bankrupty Court, alleging breach of contract and warranty, as well as for misrepresentation, coercion, and duress. Marathon sought dismissal of the suit on the ground that the Act unconstitutionally conferred Art. III judicial power upon judges who lacked life tenure and protection against salary diminution. The District Court denied the motion to dismiss, but on appeal the District Court granted the motion. Held: The judgment is affirmed. Pp. 87-88. (a) Section 1471's broad grant of jurisdiction to bankruptcy judges violates Art. I of the Constitution, since the bankruptcy courts do not lie exclusively outside the States, like the courts of the Territories or of the District of Columbia, or bear any resemblance to courts-martial, nor can the substantive legal rights at issue in the present action be deemed "public rights." There is no persuasive reason in logic, history, or the Constitution why bankruptcy courts lie beyond the reach of Art. II, since there is no merit to the argument that the bankruptcy judges created by the Act are not Art. IV judges. P. 88-89. (b) The bankruptcy courts in question do not fall within any of the historically recognized situations-non-Art. III courts, courtsmartial and resolution of "public" issues-in which the principle of independent adjudication commanded by Art.III does not apply. The Court has sustained the use of adjunct factfinders even in the adjudication of constitutional rights- so long as those adjuncts were subject to sufficient control by an Art. i district court. Pc. 63-76. (c) The Act's conferral of broad adjudicative powers upon judges unprotected by Art III does not impermissibly remove most, if not all, of the essential attributes of the judicial power from the Art. iii district court and vested those attributes in a non-Art III adjunct. Crowell v. Benson, 285 U.S. 22, at 408. The Act does not create a "specialized area" where the law of bankruptcy is a specialized area, and Congress has found a "particularized need" that warrants "distinctive treatment." See, e. g., Murray's Lessee v. Hoboken Land & Improvement Co., 18 How., at 280-282. The distinction between public rights and private rights has not been definitively explained in this Court's precedents, for it suffices to observe that a matter of public rights must at a minimum arise "between the government and others," and that the ultimate decision was made by the District court. In contrast, "the liability ofone individual to another under the law as defined," Crowell, supra, at 51, is a matter "of private rights." P. 89-92. (d) Appellants' contention that Congress' power to create "adjuncts" to consider all cases related to those arising under Title 11 is as great as it was in the circumstances of Crowell and Raddatz, is grounded in a historically recognized distinction between matters that could be conclusively determined by the Executive and Legislative Branches and matters that are "inherently . . . judicial." The "plenary authority" under the District Of Columbia Clause, Art.I, § 8, cl. 17, provides that "the President shall be Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States, and the exercise of that jurisdiction by the adjunct bankruptcy court was made subject to appeal as of right to an Article III court." The Court's scrutiny of the adjunct scheme was far stricter than it had been in either Crowell orRaddatz. After respondent Nussle, a Connecticut state prisoner, was beaten by corrections officers, he filed suit in the District Court under 42 U. S. C. §1983, alleging that the officers had violated his Eighth Amendment right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. He bypassed the Connecticut grievance procedure prescribed by the Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (PLRA), which provides that no action may be brought under §1983 by a prisoner unless the prisoner has first exhausted available administrative remedies. The District Court dismissed the suit, holding that the PLRA's exhaustion requirement applied to Nussle's case. The Second Circuit reversed, concluding that the requirement does not apply to suits involving a single act of violence committed by corrections officers. Held: The PLRA's exhaustion requirement applies to all inmate suits about prison life, regardless of whether they involve general circumstances or particular episodes, and whether they allege excessive force or some other wrong. Pp. 3-11. (a) When Congress passed the PLRA, it replaced the limited exhaustion requirement of the earlier version of the PLRA with a new mandate requiring exhaustion of all "available" remedies. Unlike the predecessor provision, which encompassed only §1983 suits, the new requirement applies to all "actions... brought with respect to prison conditions." Because Congress did not define the term "prison conditions," this Court looks to the PLRA's text and context, and to its prior decisions relating to "[s]uits by prisoners," 42 U. S. C. §1997e. Pp. 3-5. (b) Read in its proper context, the term "prison conditions" includes suits about prison guards' use of excessive force, one or many times. To conclude otherwise would require ignoring the plain meaning of the word "conditions," which refers to facts or circumstances surrounding something, and would create an anomaly whereby a prisoner could sue about a single violent act without having to go through the grievance process, but could not sue about multiple violent acts without doing so. Although Hudson v. McMillian, 503 U. S. 1, and Farmer v. Brennan, 511 U. S. 825, distinguished excessive force claims from "conditions of confinement" claims, those decisions focused on proof requirements, whereas the present inquiry involves the threshold question whether resort to a prison grievance process must precede resort to a court. There is nothing to indicate that Congress meant to release the evidentiary distinctions drawn in Hudson and Farmer from their moorings and extend their application to the otherwise invigorated exhaustion requirement. Moreover, it is at least equally plausible that Congress inserted "prison conditions" into the exhaustion provision simply to make it clear that preincarceration claims fall outside the provision, for example, a Title VII claim against the prisoner's preincarceration employer, or, for that matter, a §1983 claim against his arresting officer. Furthermore, the asserted distinction between excessive force claims that need not be exhausted, on the one hand, and exhaustion-mandatory "frivolous" claims on the other, is untenable, since excessive force claims can be frivolous, and exhaustion serves purposes beyond weeding out frivolous allegations. Other infirmities inherent in the Second Circuit's disposition include the likelihood that Congress, when it included in the PLRA a firm exhaustion requirement, meant to leave the need to exhaust to the pleader's option, and scant sense supporting the single occurrence, prevailing circumstance dichotomy. Pp. 5-11. 224 F. 3d 105, reversed and remanded.

In the case before the Supreme Court, the central question was whether a plaintiff must present direct evidence of discrimination to receive a mixed-motive instruction under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended by the Civil Rights Act of 1991. The Court ruled that direct evidence is not required for such an instruction.

Title VII prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. The Court referenced the Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins case, which dealt with mixed-motive discrimination (where both legitimate and illegitimate reasons motivated an employment decision). The Court noted that the 1991 Act was partly a response to Price Waterhouse and aimed to clarify the standards for mixed-motive cases.

The Court examined the statutory text of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(m), which states that an unlawful employment practice is established when a plaintiff demonstrates that a protected characteristic was a motivating factor for any employment practice, even if other factors also played a role. The Court emphasized that the statute's language does not require direct evidence and that the term "demonstrates" is defined in Title VII as meeting the burdens of production and persuasion, without specifying the need for direct evidence.

The Court also highlighted the conventional rule in civil litigation that requires a plaintiff to prove their case by a preponderance of the evidence, which can include both direct and circumstantial evidence. The Court noted that circumstantial evidence is often used in discrimination cases and is considered equally persuasive as direct evidence.

The Court concluded that the plaintiff in this case only needed to present sufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to conclude that sex was a motivating factor for any employment practice. Since direct evidence is not required in mixed-motive cases, the Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had concluded that the District Court did not abuse its discretion in giving a mixed-motive instruction to the jury.

Justice O'Connor concurred with the Court's opinion, noting that the Civil Rights Act of 1991 codified a new evidentiary rule for mixed-motive cases under Title VII, which no longer requires direct evidence to shift the burden of persuasion.

Respondent Lett was convicted of murdering a taxi driver. At his trial, the jury deliberated for only four hours before sending the trial judge a note stating that it was having difficulty coming to a verdict. The judge then excused the jury and declared a mistrial. The Michigan Supreme Court ultimately upheld the trial judge’s exercise of discretion in declaring a mistrial, rejecting Lett’s claims that the trial court had committed reversible errors. The Sixth Circuit reversed, holding that the Michigan Supreme Court’s decision was both procedurally flawed and objectively unreasonable under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA). Held: The Sixth Circuit erred in applying AEDPA’s deference requirement to the Michigan Supreme Court’s decision. Pp. 4−12. (a) Under AEDPA, a federal district court may grant relief only where a state court has acted unreasonably. To determine whether a state court’s application of federal law is unreasonable, “the range of reasonable judgment can depend in part on the nature of the relevant rule” that the state court must apply. Yarborough v. Alvarado, 541 U.S. 652, 664. Here, the relevant rule involves the scope of a trial judge’s authority to declare a mistrial. Such declarations are subject to a high level of judicial deference, and the more general the rule at issue, the more leeway state courts have in reaching outcomes in case-by-case determinations. Pp. 4−6. (b) The Michigan Supreme Court’s decision here was not unreasonable. Its adjudication involved a straightforward application of this Court’s longstanding precedents to the facts of Lett’s case. The court cited those precedents, including United States v. Perez, 9 Wheat. 579, and Arizona v. Washington, 434 U.S. 592, which establish that a trial judge may declare a mistrial whenever, in the judge’s opinion, taking all the circumstances into account, there is a “manifest necessity” for doing so. The court then applied those precedents to the particular facts before it and found no abuse of discretion, especially in light of the length of deliberations after a short and uncomplicated trial, the jury notes suggesting heated discussions and asking what would happen “if we can’t agree,” and—most importantly—the fact that the jury foreperson expressly stated that the jury was not going to reach a verdict. In these circumstances, it was reasonable for the Michigan Supreme Court to determine that the trial judge had exercised sound discretion in declaring a mistrial. The Sixth Circuit disagreed, reasoning that the trial judge’s mistakes were so egregious that the Michigan Supreme Court’s opinion finding no abuse of discretion was not only wrong but objectively unreasonable. While the Sixth Circuit’s interpretation of the trial record is not implausible, other reasonable interpretations are also possible. Moreover, the standard applied by the Michigan Supreme Court—whether the judge exercised sound discretion—is a general one, to which there is no “plainly correct or incorrect” answer in this case. Finally, the Sixth Circuit erred in relying on its own decision in Fulton v. Moore, 520 F.3d 522, for the proposition that Arizona v. Washington establishes three factors determining whether a judge has exercised sound discretion in declaring a mistrial. First, the Fulton decision does not constitute “clearly established Federal law, as determined by the Supreme Court,” §2254(d)(1), so any failure to apply that decision cannot independently authorize habeas relief under AEDPA. Second, Washington nowhere established those three factors as a constitutional test that determines whether a trial judge has exercised sound discretion in declaring a mistrial. Pp. 6−12. 316 Fed.Appxs. 421, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

This case deals with the question of whether a Native American tribe has the authority to hear a car accident lawsuit brought by a non-Native American woman against two men working on a construction site on the tribe's land. The Supreme Court held that the tribe's authority to hear the case is limited to situations where the defendant entered into a consensual relationship with the tribe or its members, or where the defendant's conduct threatened or had a direct impact on the tribe's political integrity, economic security, or health and welfare. Since none of these conditions were met in this case, the Supreme Court upheld the lower court's decision to dismiss the case.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Tennessee today announced criminal charges against a Tennessee man accused of orchestrating a series of state executions.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Memphis, Tennessee, alleges that former federal prison officer Edward Jerome Harbison was falsely convicted and sentenced to death in 1983. According to the complaint, Harbhison's federally appointed counsel developed extensive information about his life history and cognitive impairments that was not presented during his trial or appeals. In addition, the complaint alleges that the federal district court that appointed him to represent him in state clemency proceedings found that he was not entitled to the same level of representation as federal defendants. The complaint further alleges that, as a result of the federal court's decision, Harhison was not eligible to represent his client in state court proceedings. In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney’s Office for Eastern Tennessee today filed criminal charges in connection with the same conduct alleged in the SEC complaint. The SEC complaint charges that HarbISON violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks a permanent injunction, a conduct-based injunction, and a penny stock bar.  In its complaint, the SEC alleges that federal law does not authorize the appointment of federal counsel to represent state defendants in state criminal proceedings, and that the SEC is not required to do so. The court also ruled that the amount of federal funds available to the SEC was insufficient to adequately represent the needs of state defendants.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants agreed to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins them from violating the federal securities laws, orders them to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and requires the defendants to pay civil penalties. IN RE GRAHAM AND OTHERS
No. 37
On Appeal from the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York

Before MR. CHIEF JUSTICE WARREN Burger, MR. JUSTICE WHITE, MR. JUSTICE BLACKMUN, MR. JUSTICE POWELL, MR. JUSTICE REHNQUIST, and MR. JUSTICE CLARK.
Argued April 15, 1974
Decided June 24, 1974

---

APPEAL FROM DISTRICT COURT FOR SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK

No. 43
On Appeal from the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York

Before MR. CHIEF JUSTICE WARREN Burger, MR. JUSTICE WHITE, MR. JUSTICE BLACKMUN, MR. JUSTICE POWELL, MR. JUSTICE REHNQUIST, and MR. JUSTICE CLARK.
Argued May 13, 1974
Decided July 2, 1974

---

OPINION OF THE COURT

MR. JUSTICE WHITE delivered the opinion of the Court.

---

I. Introduction

These appeals raise questions concerning the proper interpretation of the doctrine of equivalency in patent law. Specifically, they involve disputes over whether certain modifications of a machine or chemical composition amount to "equivalent" changes that render a subsequent invention nonobvious and therefore eligible for protection.

In Graham v. Johnson, No. 37, post, p. ____, we consider the validity of a patent for a flexible coupling device that replaces a rigid coupling in a steam turbine generator. The flexible coupling consists of a rubber sleeve encircling the shaft of the turbine and secured to the housing of the generator by a pair of compression bands. The defendant, Johnson Manufacturing Corporation, challenges the validity of the Graham patent on the grounds that the flexible coupling is not truly equivalent to the rigid coupling it replaced. Instead, Johnson argues that the flexible coupling represents a fundamentally different design that lacks the reliability and durability of the rigid coupling.

In Fleischmann v. Crocker Brewing Company, No. 43, post, p. ____, we examine the validity of a patent for a continuous brewing process using a heat exchanger. The patent covers a method of heating water in a heat exchanger and mixing it with a sugar syrup to create beer. The defendant, Crocker Brewing Company, challenges the validity of the Fleischmann patent on the grounds that the continuous brewing process is not equivalent to batch brewing methods traditionally used in the brewery industry.

In both cases, the central question concerns the extent to which the doctrine of equivalency allows for the expansion of the scope of a patent beyond the literal language of the claims. Our answer depends on the nature of the modifications at issue and the impact they have on the functionality of the invention.

II. The Doctrine of Equivalency

The doctrine of equivalency in patent law holds that a substitute or alternative component or process that performs the same function as the patented component or process is equally entitled to protection. The origins of this doctrine can be traced back to the famous case of Parker v. Sabra Laboratories Ltd., 105 U.S. 383, 25 L.Ed. 711 (1882), where the Supreme Court held that a patent for a compound containing sulphur trioxide and hydrogen peroxide covered a similar compound containing potassium nitrate instead of sulphur trioxide.

Since Parker v. Sabra, the doctrine of equivalency has been expanded to include a range of situations involving substitutions or alternatives that affect the performance of an invention. For example, in Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Thompson Chemical Company, Inc., 377 U.S. 137, 84 S.Ct. 1178, 12 L.Ed. 2d 149 (1964), the Supreme Court held that a patent for a drug containing a specific ester moiety covered a similar drug containing a different ester moiety. Similarly, in Warner Communications, Inc. v. CBS Broadcasting System, Inc., 417 U.S. 849, 94 S.Ct. 2580, 41 L.Ed. 2d 628 (1974), the Supreme Court held that a patent for a television broadcasting system covered a similar system using a different frequency band.

Despite these expansions, the doctrine of equivalency remains a somewhat murky area of patent law. Some commentators have criticized the doctrine as being too broad and potentially leading to unnecessary confusion in the field of patent law. See, e.g., Note, The Doctrine of Equivalency in American Patent Law, 59 Geo. L.Rev. 1171 (1971). Others have attempted to establish guidelines for determining when a modification amounts to an equivalent change. See, e.g., id.; Comment, The Doctrine of Equivalency in Patent Law, 1964 Duke L.J. 1011.

III. The Nature of Modifications

In evaluating whether a modification amounts to an equivalent change, it is helpful to distinguish between two types of modifications: structural modifications and functional modifications. Structural modifications alter the physical makeup of an invention, while functional modifications affect the way an invention operates.

Structural modifications typically involve changing the shape, size, or location of components within an invention. Examples of structural modifications include replacing a wooden handle with a plastic handle or adding a protective coating to a metallic component. Functional modifications, on the other hand, involve changing the way an invention works. Examples of functional modifications include replacing a manual transmission with an automatic transmission or adjusting the temperature control settings on a refrigerator.

In determining whether a modification is equivalent, it is generally easier to apply the doctrine of equivalency to functional modifications than to structural modifications. This is because functional modifications tend to be more easily understood and evaluated based on their impact on the performance of the invention. In contrast, structural modifications may involve complex interactions between components that are more difficult to analyze and evaluate.

IV. Impact on Performance

Regardless of whether a modification is structural or functional, the key factor in determining whether it amounts to an equivalent change is the impact it has on the performance of the invention. If a modification significantly alters the way an invention operates or affects its ability to perform its intended function, it is unlikely to qualify as an equivalent change.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit reversed a lower court's judgment that dismissed a suit brought by an Oklahoma company against a Native American tribe for breach of contract. The court held that the tribe's sovereign immunity from suit was "well founded" and that it had waived its immunity by signing a promissory note in the name of the tribe. The lower court had found that the note did not limit the sovereign rights of the Kiowa Indian Tribe of Oklahoma. The Tribe moved to dismiss the suit for lack of jurisdiction, relying in part on its sovereign immunity. The Oklahoma Supreme Court declined to review the ruling, and we granted certiorari. We conclude that the lower court misapplied the rule of tribal immunity and that the ruling should be reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has ruled that a provision of the Indian Land Consolidation Act (ILCA) is unconstitutional. The ILCA was enacted in 1983 to address the extreme fractionation problem associated with a century-old allotment policy that yielded multiple ownership of single parcels of Indian land. In Hodel v. Irving, the Court ruled that the original version of  207 of the ILCA, as amended in 1984, violated the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution by taking private property without just compensation. The Court held that the amended version does not cure the constitutional deficiency identified in Hodel. We now hold that the amendment does not remedy the problem. In the 1980s, Congress passed a law that provided that certain small interests in Indian lands would transfer-or ''escheat''-to the tribe upon the death of the owner of the interest. The court held that this provision was unconstitutional because it did not provide compensation for the loss of the small interests. The majority of the Court agreed, and the Court concluded that the amendments did not address the constitutional deficiencies identified in the Hodel decision. The decision is available on the Internet at http://www.courts.gov/news/opinions/cboe/c/v/vv/h/hv-v-iv/v.

Summary:
This case involves police officers in St. Louis, Missouri who sued their city for back wages after being classified as non-exempt employees under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). The FLSA provides certain workers with an exemption from minimum wage and overtime laws based on various factors, including job duties and salary levels. The plaintiffs in this case alleged that they performed executive, administrative, and professional duties and earned above the required salary level, therefore qualifying for the exemption. However, the district court ruled against them, finding that the FLSA did not apply to public sector employees like those in St. Louis. On appeal, the case went through several rounds of review before reaching the United States Supreme Court.

Summary:
Title: Refund Claims Against the United States
Author: Justice Ruth Ginsburg
Date: June 25, 2007
Summary:
This opinion holds that a taxpayer who seeks to challenge a tax assessed in violation of the Export Clause of the Constitution must first comply with the refund scheme set forth in Title 26 of the United States Code. Specifically, the opinion holds that the taxpayer must file a timely administrative refund claim before bringing suit against the government. The opinion rejects the argument that the Export Clause creates a separate cause of action that allows the taxpayer to sue directly against the government without complying with the refund scheme.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the defendant, AT&T Corporation, in a lawsuit brought by four women who claimed that AT&T's pension plan discriminated against them because it awarded fewer credits for time off taken during pregnancy compared to other types of absences. The court held that the plaintiffs had not shown that the difference in treatment was "facially" discriminatory, and that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated that the difference was caused by an intent to discriminate. The court also pointed out that the plaintiffs had waited too long to bring their lawsuit, as the relevant laws had changed since the time when the plaintiffs took their vacations.

The Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976 (FSIA) establishes the conditions under which a foreign state can assert immunity from being sued in US courts. Under the FSIA, a foreign state is considered an agency or instrumentality of the United States if it meets certain criteria, including having a significant degree of autonomy and performing essential governmental functions. However, the FSIA does not define what constitutes an "agency or instrumentality of the United States".

Section 101 (a) (27) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (Act) defines as one variety of "special immigrant" an immigrant "lawfully admitted for permanent residence, who is returning from a temporary visit abroad." Section 1101(a)(27)(B) provides that "an alien having a residence in a foreign country which he has no intention of abandoning . . . (ii) who is coming temporarily to the United States to perform temporary services or labor, if unemployed persons capable of performing such service or labor cannot be found in this country." The Act authorizes the Attorney General to re-admit such an alien without a visa or other formal documentation. He has exercised that authority, allowing such an immigrant to return with what was called in the briefs and oral argument as the "green card." This suit was brought by the United Farm Workers Organizing Committee against the practice of giving alien commuters the documentation and labor certification benefits of classification as immigrants "lawsfully admitted" who are "returning to an unrelinquished lawful permanent residence." The District Court dismissed the action without opinion. The Court of Appeals held that the admission of daily commuters was proper but that the seasonal commuters were not. Held: 1. An alien commuter who has not shown he must be classified as a nonimmigrant must be classed as an immigrant. Pp. 479-481. 2. The practice on the facts of these cases does not conform with the Act's meaning, since it does not cover an alien, like the commuter, who has a "permanent residence" here and who comes to perform a job of a permanent character, even though the period of his service is limited. The administrative construction of this subsection (15)(H)(ii) by the Immigration Service has been that it covers an alien who has "a permanent residence," who has an "immediate relatives" of a United States citizen or "special immigrants," who comes temporarily to this country to perform "temporary services" or "labor," if unemployed people capable of doing such service cannot find in this Nation. P. 478. 3. The Act's administrative construction is entitled to great weight, particularly when Congress has revisited the Act and left the practice untouched. Such a history of administrative construction and congressional acquiescence may add a gloss or gualification to what is on its face unqualified statutory language. Massachusetts Trustees v. United States, 377 U. S. 235; United States v. Midwest Oil Co., 236 U.S. 459, 35 S.Ct. 309, 59 L. Ed. 673, and United Statesv. Midwest Petroleum Co., 235 U. C. 236, all of which affirm that an alien is an immigrant until he establishes to the satisfaction of the consular officer and the immigration officers that he is entitled, under § 1101 (a)(15), that his status is acquired when an alien satisfies (1) any numerical limitations on the entry of immigrants, (2) requirements as to qualitative matters such as health, morals, and economic status, and (3) the need for an immigrant visa. The legislative history of the Act shows that Congress has not reached a consensus that the administrative policy reaching back at least to General Order No. 86 is wrong, and that Congress' administrative approach has been inconsistent with the meaning of the same language in other sections of the statute where the same history is not present, and Congress' acquiescence to the practice may add to the unqualified language in the Act where the very same history of legislative language is not presented. P p. 477. 433 F. 2d 479, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia recently ruled that a group of coal companies could not sue the United States for a refund of taxes they paid in violation of the Export Clause of the Constitution. The court held that the companies had not complied with the Internal Revenue Code's time limits for filing a tax refund claim. The Court ruled that the time limits set by the Code did not apply to the case because the companies did not file a claim with the IRS within the required time limits. The companies also did not comply with the provisions of the Federal Tax Act, which allows for the filing of tax refund claims within six years of the date the tax was paid. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the companies, and the case will be appealed. The case is being closely watched by tax attorneys who are concerned that the Court's decision will open the door to other potential tax refund cases.

Petitioner, a candidate for public office, made a televised speech during which he read a series of questions asked by a union leader concerning the alleged nefarious activities of the union president and the alleged relationship between the president and petitioner's political opponent. Respondent, a deputy sheriff, sued petitioner for defamation after petitioner quoted the union leader's assertion that respondent had been paid money by the union president "from Ed to Herman." After petitioner's conviction for defamation was upheld by both the trial court and the intermediate appellate court, the latter court reversed on the ground that petitioner had not satisfied the requirement of New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U. S. 254, that the plaintiff in a public official's defamation action must prove that the defamatory publication was made with "actual malice" -i. e., with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not. The Louisiana Supreme Court reinstated the lower court's judgment. It concluded that while petitioner had no personal knowledge of respondent's activities, he should have realized that his source was unreliable and therefore should have exercised greater caution in repeating the accusation. Held: By no proper test of reckless disregard was petitioner's broadcast a reckless publication about a public official. Pp. 208-214. Reversed and remanded.

In the case before the Supreme Court, Time magazine was sued for libel by Deputy Chief of Detectives Pape of the Chicago Police Department. The lawsuit stemmed from a Time article that reported on a U.S. Commission on Civil Rights document, which included a description of a complaint alleging police brutality by Pape and other officers. The Time article did not explicitly state that the events were allegations rather than confirmed facts.

The legal issue centered on whether Time's omission of the word "alleged" constituted "actual malice," as defined by the precedent set in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. "Actual malice" requires proof that a statement was made with knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for its truth.

The Supreme Court held that Time's omission of the word "alleged" was not sufficient to establish actual malice. The Court reasoned that the Civil Rights Commission's report was ambiguous and that Time's interpretation, although possibly incorrect, did not amount to reckless disregard for the truth. The Court emphasized that the First and Fourteenth Amendments protect not only accurate reports but also some erroneous interpretations to ensure freedom of expression and the press.

The Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had previously ruled that the issue of malice should be decided by a jury. The Supreme Court remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, effectively protecting Time from liability based on the specific facts of this case and the constitutional protections afforded to the press.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has ruled that a federal law prohibiting the disclosure of information collected in connection with certain federal highway safety programs is valid under the Constitution's First Amendment protection. The case involves the Hazard Elimination Program (Program), which provides state and local governments with funding to improve the most dangerous sections of their roads. To be eligible for funds under the Program, a state or local government must undertake a thorough evaluation of its public roads. Specifically,  152(a)(1) requires them to "conduct and systematically maintain an engineering survey of all public roads to identify hazardous locations, sections, and elements, including roadside obstacles and unmarked or poorly marked roads, which may constitute a danger to motorists, bicyclists, and pedestrians"

The Supreme Court of the United States reviewed a case involving the constitutionality of an Indiana statute requiring political parties to file an affidavit affirming they do not advocate the overthrow of government by force or violence before their candidates can appear on the ballot. The appellants, the Communist Party of Indiana and associated individuals, challenged the statute after their refusal to submit the required oath led to their exclusion from the ballot.

The Court held that the loyalty oath requirement violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments, which protect freedom of speech and association. The Court emphasized that the Constitution does not allow states to prohibit advocacy of the use of force or law violation unless such advocacy is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and is likely to incite or produce such action. This principle, established in Brandenburg v. Ohio, requires precision in regulation to avoid infringing upon fundamental freedoms.

The Court rejected the argument that the statute was justified as a means to prevent groups that advocate violent overthrow in abstract terms from gaining political support through the democratic process. The Court found that this rationale would effectively reinstate the discredited legal regime of Whitney v. California, which had been overruled in Brandenburg.

The Court concluded that the Indiana statute was overly broad and impermissibly infringed upon the appellants' constitutional rights to political association and participation in the electoral process. As such, the Court reversed the judgment of the District Court, which had upheld the constitutionality of the loyalty oath requirement.

This case involved a challenge to the constitutionality of a Texas residency requirement for minors seeking to attend public schools in the state. The plaintiff, Roberto Morales, was born in the US but raised in Mexico by his parents who were not US citizens. He moved to Texas to live with his sister and attend school in the McAllen Independent School District. However, the district refused to admit him due to section 21.031(d) of the Texas Education Code, which denied tuition-free admission to anyone who lived apart from a "parent, guardian, or other person having lawful control of him under an order of a court" if their presence in the school district was primarily for the purpose of attending school.
The Supreme Court held that section 21.031(d) was a bona fide residence requirement that satisfied constitutional standards. The Court noted that the residency requirement was intended to ensure that services provided for residents were enjoyed only by residents, and did not burden or penalize the constitutional right of interstate travel. Additionally, the Court pointed out that local residence requirements in the public-school context allowed for community involvement and participation in decision making, and helped maintain the quality of local public schools.

Appellants are merchants in Philadelphia who engage in the retail sale of clothing and home furnishings within the proscription of the statute in issue. Each of the appellants is a member of the Orthodox Jewish faith, which requires the closing of their places of business and a total abstention from all manner of work from nightfall each Friday until nightfall. They instituted a suit in the court below seeking a permanent injunction against the enforcement of the 1959 statute. Their complaint alleged that appellants had previously kept their place of business open on Sunday, compensating somewhat for their closing on Saturday; that Sunday closing will result in impairing the ability of all appellants to earn a livelihood and will render appellant Braunfeld unable to continue in his business, thereby losing his capital investment; that the statute is unconstitutional for the reasons stated above. A three-judge court dismissed the complaint on the authority of the Two Guys from Harrison-Allentown, Inc., v. McGinley, 366 U. S. 582, and the Court noted probable jurisdiction. Held: 1. The statute does not violate the freedom of religion protected by the First Amendment. Pp. 437-440. (a) The freedom to act, even when the action is in accord with one's religious convictions, is not totally free from legislative restrictions. P. 438. (b) The fact that the State regulates conduct by enacting a general law within its power, the purpose and effect of which is to advance the State's secular goals, is valid despite its indirect burden on religious observance unless the State may accomplish its purpose by means which do not impose such a burden. McGowan v. Maryland, ante, p. 158. 2. The freedom of the State to regulate conduct that may in some way result in an economic disadvantage to some religious sects and not to others because of the special practices of the various religions is not an absolute test for determining whether the legislation violates the Freedom of Religion protected by that Amendment. McGowen v. United States, ante. p. 439. 3. In view of the particular protection that the Constitution has accorded it, it cannot be expected, much less required, that legislators enact no law regulating conduct that is in any way in violation of important social duties or subversive of good order, even though the burden may be characterized as being only indirect. Pc. 441-467. 184 F. Supp. 352, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant in a civil action brought under the federal securities laws against him.  The court's order, which entered a temporary restraining order against the defendant, permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty equal to the amount of his ill-gotten gains.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, the defendants sought a court-ordered injunction against the destruction of their property, and the court granted the defendants' requests for a temporary injunction.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, defendants consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from future violations of the securities laws, and from participating in any future conduct that constitutes a civil injunctive action.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 17-cv-01-17 (1911).  The SEC's order also prohibits defendants from imposing civil injunctions, imposing a $25,000 civil penalty, and imposing an officer-and-director bar against defendants who violate the securities law.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eastern District of Louisiana granted a preliminary injunction against prosecution of a state court action that seeks to determine the ownership of oil and other mineral rights under land owned by the United States. The court held that the federal district court had jurisdiction to grant the injunction because the state court had already assumed jurisdiction over the property in question and that the injunction was proper because the federal court had the exclusive jurisdiction to determine ownership of the property. The Court also held that, in the absence of a federal court ruling, the injunction would not be in effect until the case was decided in state court. The case presents for decision important questions regarding the applicability of the restrictions against stay of state court proceedings contained in the provisions of 28 U. S.C.  2283, 28 US. C.A. 1345, and 29 U.N.C  101. The United States's position is that the case should be dismissed on the ground that it is not a party to the state action and that it has no cause of action to be sued. The decision also questions the propriety of the injunction granted by the District Court and the injunction sustained by the Court of appeals. The U

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has ruled that the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 does not apply to those sentenced before the Act took effect. The Court held that the Act's more lenient penalty provisions do apply to pre-Act offenders sentenced after August 3, 2010 .<n>The Court's decision was based on an analysis of the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984 and its Sentencing Guidelines Manual. The Guidelines determine most drug-crime offenses in a special way, based on specific characteristics of the offender's behavior and the amount of the drug involved. The guidelines determine the applicable offense level and offender category and then determine a sentencing range based on that range. For example, a first-time offender with a base offense level of 24 would receive a sentence of 51 to 63 months in prison. The Sentencing Act, however, imposes a mandatory minimum term of five years for those who deal in one hundredth or more of the total amount of crack cocaine. The minimum term for those dealing in powder cocaine is five years, and the minimum sentence for dealing in five hundredths or more is one year. In 2010, Congress enacted a new statute reducing the disparity between the crack-to-powder cocaine disparity from 100-to-1 to 18-to-1. The new statute took effect on August 3. 2010 and became effective on January 1, 2011 . The court held that, because the Act did not clearly indicate to the contrary, it does apply to offenders sentenced before that date.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a federal tax lien on a deceased Pennsylvania businessman's real property was not valid because the IRS had not issued a notice of default. The court held that the Federal Tax Lien Act of 1966 does not provide for a preference over a judgment creditor's perfected lien on real property. The Court of Common Pleas of Cambria County, Pennsylvania, entered a judgment for $400,000 in favor of Romani Industries, Inc. and against Francis J. Romani. The judgment was recorded in the clerk's office and therefore, as a matter of Pennsylvania law, it became a lien on all of the defendant's actual property in Cambria County. The IRS filed a series of notices of tax liens on Mr.Romani's property, and the IRS claimed that the tax liens were not valid as against the earlier judgment lien. The estate's administrator sought permission from the court to transfer the property to the judgment creditor in lieu of execution. The government opposed the transfer on the ground that the priority statute gave it the right to "be paid first"

The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania today entered a final judgment against Carol Anne Bond, a Pennsylvania resident charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against Bond, ordering her to surrender her passport, and ordered her to pay a $1,000 civil penalty.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Philadelphia on December 3, 2010, Bond was charged with two counts of violating the federal securities laws. The SEC alleges that, in violation of the federal law, Bond sought to obstruct the federal government's enforcement of the securities laws and, in a parallel action, entered a conditional plea of guilty, and was sentenced to six years in prison.  Bond has agreed to the settlement without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint.  In its judgment, the court also ordered Bond to disgorge her ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and to pay civil penalties of $2,500 and $3,500, respectively.  On December 4, 2011, the Court granted Bond's motion for a preliminary injunction against further violations of the anti-fraud provisions and ordered a hearing on the matter on January 5, 2013, to determine whether to proceed with a permanent injunction. The court's order, which is subject to court approval, orders Bond to comply with the SEC’s order, pay a civil penalty of $500,000, and appoint an amicus curiae to represent her at the hearing.  A hearing scheduled for January 6, 2013 is scheduled for 7:30 p.m. Eastern.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 562 (2010).

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit ruled that police officers did not violate the Fourth Amendment when they prevented a man from entering his home while they obtained a search warrant. The court held that the officers acted reasonably in their search of the trailer where the man lived with his wife. We reverse a lower court's ruling that the search warrant violated the man's Fourth Amendment rights. The lower court had granted the police officers' motion to suppress the evidence they found under the sofa, a marijuana pipe, a box for marijuana, and a small amount of marijuana. The Supreme Court held that there was no violation of the warrant's requirements because the officers had reasonable cause to believe that the man had hidden marijuana in the trailer. The high court also ruled that the lower court erred in denying the officers' request for leave to appeal.

The State of Kansas imposes a tax on the receipt of motor fuel by fuel distributors within its boundaries. Kansas applies that tax to motor fuel received by non-Indian fuel distributors who subsequently deliver that fuel to a gas station owned by, and located on, the Reservation of the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation (Nation). The Nation owns and operates a casino on its reservation. In order to accommodate casino patrons and other reservation-related traffic, the Nation constructed, and now owns, a gas-station next to the casino. Seventy-three percent of the station’s fuel sales are made to casino patrons, while 11 percent are to persons who live or work on the reservation. The Nation purchases fuel for its gas station from nonIndian distributors located off its reservation, who pay a state fuel tax on their initial receipt of the motor fuel, Kan. Stat. Ann. §79–3408(c), and pass along the cost of the tax to their customers, including the Nation, which purchases fuel from the distributors. The station owners have standing to challenge the tax because it is the distributor, rather than the retailer, that is liable to pay the tax, and because the ultimate purchasers of the fuel receive the bulk of their governmental services from the State. The court determined that the station owners were not entitled to an injunction, however, because they were not members of a Kansas Tribe and thus there had been no showing by Retailers that payment of fuel tax to Kansas interferes with the self-government of the tribe or a Kansas tribal member. The Tenth Circuit reversed, holding that the tax was invalid under the interest-balancing test set forth in White Mountain Apache Tribe v. Bracker, 448 U. S. 136. Held: Kansas’ motor fuel tax is not impermissibly discriminatory. Pp. 5–11. (a) The “who” and the “where” of the challenged tax have significant consequences. Kansas law makes clear that the distributor is the source of the state tax, not the retailer. And, as here, the tax is imposed not on the off-reservation receipt of fuel, but on its receipt of that fuel. The Court of Appeals’ decision in Kaul v. Kansas Dept. of Revenue, 266 Kan. 464, 970 P. 2d 60, confirms that the Bracker test applies only where “a State asserts authority over the conduct of non-Indians engaging in activity on the reservations.” Oklahoma Tax Comm’n v. Chickasaw Nation, 515 U.S. 450, 458. It does not apply where a State asserts its taxing authority over nonIndians off the reservation, see, e.g., Kansas Tax Comm'n v., Sac and Fox Nation of Missouri v. LaFaver, 31 F. Supp.2d 1298, 1307. Nor is the Nation entitled to interest balancing by virtue of its claim that the Kansas Motor Fuel Tax is owed only on a distributor’’ postreceipt delivery of fuel to retailers such as the Nation. Moreover, the fact that the Nation sells gas at prevailing market rates does not change the nature of the taxable event, here the distributor receives the fuel, and the distributor must pay tax on that fuel even if it is not subsequently delivered or sold. Thus, even when a State imposes the legal incidence of its tax on a nonIndian seller, it may nonetheless be pre-empted if the transaction giving rise to tax liability is on the Tribe or one of its members, and that imposition fails to satisfy that test. Finally, the availability of tax deductions does not alter the nature and nature of a taxable event here. See, e., at 461. Kansas also has a “significant geographical component,” Bracker v. Kaul, supra, at 151, which provides that “[a] tax . . . is hereby imposed on the use, sale or delivery of all motor vehicle fuels or special fuels which are used, sold or delivered in this state for any purpose whatsoever.’ ” Sac andFox Nation v.LaFaver. The tax is therefore “exempts from taxation fuel sold or delivery to all other sovereigns,“ id.,” id., at 66. The Tax is therefore impermissible, since Kansas uses the proceeds from its fuel tax only to pay for a significant portion of the costs of maintaining the roads and bridges on the Nation‘s reservation, including a main highway used by the Nation's casino patrons. Kansas offers no such services to the several States or the Federal Government, and to the extent Kansas fuel retailers bear the cost, that burden falls equally upon all retailers within the State regardless of whether those retailers are located on an Indian reservation. Accordingly, the Kansas motor fuel taxes are not impermissible. The United States, as amicus, contends that this conclusion is foreclosed by the Kansas Supreme Court decision, which held that the State is categorically barred from placing the

After respondent pleaded guilty to possession of 672 grams of cocaine, a Michigan trial court entered a judgment imposing a mandatory minimum sentence of life imprisonment without possibility of parole. The Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed, rejecting respondent's contention that the sentence violated the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause. Held: Respondent's sentence does not violate the Eighth Amendment. Pp. 10-18. (a) Although the Eighth Amendment includes a Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause, it does not establish a proportionality requirement. Rather, the Clause reflects the Framers' belief that some punishments are so severe that they are morally repugnant regardless of their relationship to the crime committed. See, e. g., Weems v. United States, 217 U. S. 349. Since the Clause does not establish a proportionality requirement, the Court need not address the validity of the proportionality test set forth in Solem v. Hohenberg, 463 U. S. 641. Nor is the Court bound by the Court's subsequent decision in Rummel v. Estelle, 445 U. S. 263, which extended the Clause's reach to cover noncapital punishments. Such extension was unwarranted, since the Clause's text and history demonstrate that it was intended to apply only to capital punishment. Pp. 10-14. (b) Respondent's alternative argument-that his sentence is "cruel and unusual" because it is mandatory without regard to so-called mitigating factors such as the lack of prior felony convictions-has no support in the text and history of the Eighth Amendment. Mandatory death sentences abounded in the nation's early history, and mandatory life sentences without possibility of parole are still commonly imposed in various states. There is thus no basis for requiring that a mandatory sentence be accompanied by an individualized determination that it is appropriate. See, e. g., Woodson v. North Carolina, 428 U. S. 282. Pp. 14-18. 219 Mich. App. 417, 61 N. W. 2d 108, affirmed.

The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced that it has agreed to settle a civil action brought by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New York against Janus Capital Group, Inc., a Massachusetts business trust that created the Janus family of mutual funds.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Denver, N.Y. on June 10, 2010, alleges that Janus Investment Fund and its wholly owned subsidiary, JCM, made materially false and misleading statements in their securities prospectuses.  According to the complaint, the defendants knew or should have known that JCM would implement policies to curb the practice of market timing in certain funds run by JCM.  In fact, the complaint alleges, the Defendants made the false statements in the prospectuses because they knew or were aware of the material misstatements in the defendants’ prospectuses, and because JCM had agreed to arrangements that allowed the defendants to mislead its auditor and issue a misleading financial statement.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, First Derivative Traders, a registered broker-dealer based in Atlanta, Georgia, has consented to the entry of a final judgment permanently enjoining it from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The final judgment also prohibits FirstDerivative from participating in the drafting or dissemination of any false statement, and requires it to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and injunctive relief.  On June 11, 2011, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. McCole granted the SEC's request for a temporary restraining order and a preliminary injunction against further violations of the federal securities laws, ordering the SEC to conduct an examination of the securities registration provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) ofÂ the Securities Act of 1933. The SEC is seeking a permanent injunction against future violations of Section 5 of the Exchange Act, as well as a civil penalty.  A hearing on June 13, 2011 was scheduled for 7:30 p.m. Eastern.  An SEC examination that led to the investigation was conducted by John R. Rymas and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Atlanta Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Timothy R. Welshhans. The Commission appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Internal Revenue Service, and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Middle District of Tennessee granted a new trial for a Tennessee man convicted of second-degree murder for stabbing his victim in the heart. The trial court had previously upheld the conviction on the basis of a common law "year and a day rule" that barred a defendant from being convicted of murder unless his victim had died within a year and aday of the act. The court's decision to abolish the rule was based on the fact that it had been legislatively or judicially abolished by the "vast majority" of jurisdictions recently to have considered the issue. The Court of Criminal Appeals, however, held that the 1989 Act had not abolished the rule. The Supreme Court of Tennessee applied its decision to Petitioner's case and granted his motion for a retrial, finding that the trial court was not entitled to have relied on the year-and-a-day rule because it had not been established by the legislature or by the court of common law. The appeals court also found that the Supreme Court had not violated the Fourteenth Amendment by applying its decision in the case. The case involves the question of whether the court denied Petitioner due process of law in violation of the 14th Amendment.
