Section 290.09(22) of the Minnesota Statutes authorizes state tax deductions for educational expenses incurred by parents in connection with the education of their children in elementary and high schools. Although the section applies to all parents regardless of the type of schools their children attend, it is only one of many deductions available under the Minnesota tax laws. Held: Section 290.09(22) does not violate the Establishment Clause of the Federal Constitution. Pp. 20-28. (a) The fact that the section is only one of many deductions available under the Minnesota tax laws supports the conclusion that it has a secular purpose. Its availability to parents of children in public schools as well as those in private schools demonstrates that it is intended to further the secular purpose of ensuring that the state's citizenry is well-educated. And although private schools may serve as a benchmark for public schools, the State has a legitimate interest in facilitating education of the highest quality for all children within its borders, regardless of the school they attend. All these justifications are sufficient to satisfy the secular purpose inquiry of the three-part test set forth in Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U. S. 612, 612-613. Pp. 20-22. (b) Since the section has a secular purpose, it cannot be said to have the primary effect of advancing the sectarian aims of the nonpublic schools. That the section is only one of many deductions available under the Minnesota tax laws gives substance to the legislature's judgment that a deduction for educational expenses fairly equalizes the tax burden of its citizens and encourages desirable expenditures for educational purposes. Furthermore, the fact that the deduction is available for educational expenses incurred by all parents, including those whose children attend public schools and those whose children attend nonsectarian private schools or sectarian private schools, argues strongly for the provision's constitutionality. Cf. Widmar v. Vincent, 454 U. S. 263. Pp. 22-25. (c) By channeling whatever assistance it may provide to parochial schools through individual parents, Minnesota has reduced the Establishment Clause objections to which its action is subject. Here, aid to parochial schools is available only as a result of decisions of individual parents, thus reducing the risk of significant religious or denominational control over the democratic process. Pp. 25-26. (d) The fact that private educational institutions, and parents paying for their children to attend these schools, make special contributions to the areas in which they operate should be taken into account in evaluating the constitutionality of the statute. But if parents of children in private schools choose to take special advantage of the relief provided by the statute, it is no doubt due to the fact that they bear a particularly great financial burden in educating their children. Whatever unequal effect may be attributed to the statutory classification can fairly be regarded as a rough return for the benefits provided to the State and all taxpayers by parents sending their children to parochial schools. Thus, it is wise to decline to engage in the type of empirical inquiry into those persons benefited by state law urged by petitioners. Pp. 26-28. 669 F. 2d 1036, affirmed.

Respondent, who is not an Indian, operates a general store in Arizona on the Navajo Indian Reservation under a license required by federal statute. He brought this action in the Arizona Superior Court against petitioners, a Navajo Indian and his wife who live on the Reservation, to collect for goods sold there on credit. Over petitioners' motion to dismiss on the ground that jurisdiction lay in the tribal court rather than in the state court, judgment was entered in favor of respondent. The Arizona Supreme Court affirmed, holding that since no Act of Congress expressly forbids their doing so Arizona courts are free to exercise jurisdiction over civil suits by non-Indians against Indians though the action arises on an Indian reservation. Held: 1. To allow the exercise of state jurisdiction here would undermine the authority of the tribal courts over Reservation affairs and hence infringe on the right of the Indians to govern themselves. Pp. 564-566. 2. If this power is to be taken away from them, it is for Congress to do it. Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U. S. 553. P. 566. 3. The basic policy of Worcester v. Georgia, 6 Pet. 515, which held that the internal affairs of Indians remained exclusively within the jurisdiction of whatever tribal government existed, has remained as law. The Court has modified these principles in cases where essential tribal relations were not involved and where the rights of Indians would not be jeopardized, but the basic policy has remained. Thus, suits by Indians against outsiders in state courts have been sanctioned. Cf. Donnelly v. United States, 228 U.S. 243, 269-272, and Williams v., United States 327, 327, 328-329. P p. 567. 84 Ariz. 241, 319 P. 2d 998, reversed.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power's practice of requiring female employees to make larger contributions to its pension fund than its male employees violated the Equal Pay Act of 1963 and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 .<n>The court held that the practice was based on a "stereotyped" assumption that women live longer than men. The court concluded that the department's policy was not discriminatory because it was offset by a difference in the value of the pension benefits provided to the two classes of employees. The justices also held that there was no evidence that the difference in take-home pay was a factor "other than sex" within the meaning of  703(a)(1). The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit agreed with the lower court's summary judgment finding that the policy violated the law and ordered the department to pay back all excess contributions. The Supreme Court held that this case involves a generalization that the parties accept as true: Women, as a class, do live longer. The case is not about whether there is a real or fictional difference between men and women, it is about whether the department treated its women employees differently from its men employees because the two groups are in fact different. We conclude that the issue of whether there was a real and fictional difference is not relevant to this case and that there is no basis for the court to determine whether the policy is a violation of the law.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Michigan today entered a final judgment against Michigan prison authorities for violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Michigan, alleges that the Michigan Department of Corrections (MDOC) issued prison visitation restrictions in 1995.  According to the complaint, the restrictions on visitation for inmates with substance-abuse or drug-related violations were designed to reduce the number of visitors to the prison.  In addition, the complaint alleges that, as a result of these restrictions, prison officials found it difficult to maintain order during visitation and to prevent smuggling or trafficking in drugs and alcohol.  As a result, many of the visitors were children, who are at risk of seeing or hearing harmful conduct during visits and must be supervised with special care in prison visitation facilities.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's complaints, MDOC consented to the entry of the final judgment, which permanently enjoins MDOC from violating these provisions and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $1,000,000. The final judgment orders MDOC to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, penalties, and injunctive relief.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit recently ruled that the Virginia Supreme Court and its chief justice are immune from a civil action brought by a consumer group against them for failing to pay attorney's fees under the Civil Rights Attorney's Fees Awards Act of 1976 .<n>The court's own disciplinary rules for attorneys were found to be inconsistent with the Bar Association's Code of Professional Responsibility. The court found that the Bar Code's prohibition against advertising in legal directories violated the Bar's strict prohibition against attorney advertising, and that the court had no authority to impose sanctions on attorneys who had not complied with its rules. The 4th Court found that, as a result, the court was not immune from the action brought against it by the Consumer Union of the United States, Inc. and the Virginia Citizens Consumer Council. The Court's decision is a significant victory for the consumer group and for the rule of professional conduct in the legal profession.

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (or Act), which provides that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) shall “assist the supreme Magistrate in discharging the duties of his trust,” provides for a Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB), composed of five members, appointed to staggered 5-year terms by the SEC. The Board is modeled on private self-regulatory organizations in the securities industry-such as the New York Stock Exchange—that investigate and discipline their own members subject to Commission oversight. The Commission can thus recruit its members and employees from the private sector by paying salaries far above the standard Government pay scale, see §§7211(f)(4), 7219. The Act places the Board under the SEC’s oversight, particularly with respect to the issuance of rules or the imposition of sanctions (both of which are subject to SEC approval and alteration). But the individual members of the Board are substantially insulated from the Commission, and the President cannot “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed” if he cannot oversee the faithfulness of the officers who execute them. Pp. 5–7. (a) The Act does not restrict judicial review unless the “statutory scheme” displays a “fairly discernible” intent to limit it. P. 7. (b) Section 78y provides only for judicial review of Commission action, and not every Board action is encapsulated in a final Commission order or rule. See, e.g., United States v. Perkins, 116 U. S. 483, 662–663. The Court has previously upheld limited restrictions on the removal power of principal officers appointed by the President, whom the President may not remove at will but only for good cause. The Constitution vests “[t]he executive Power … in a President of the United States” who “exercis[e] significant authority pursuant to the laws.” Buckley v. Valeo, 424 U.S. 1, 125–126. The Appointments Clause necessarily contemplates collective appointments by the Courts of Law, Art. II, §2, cl. 2, and each House of Congress, too, appoints its officers collectively, see Art. I, §§2, 4, 5, and §3. In this case, however, the Board members are not “inferior officers” but are “officially responsible to the President.’ ” Id., at 682–683. The President cannot remove an officer who enjoys more than one level of good-cause protection, even if the President determines that the officer is neglecting his duties or discharging them improperly. That judgment is instead committed to another officer, who may or may not agree with him, and whom he cannot remove simply because that officer disagrees with him. This contravenes the President’S “constitutional obligation to ensure the faithful execution of the laws” in the Executive Branch, id., at 915. The Government‘s argument from bureaucratic expertise limited only to the field of accounting is not supported by the fact that the Commission has no power to fire Board members for violations of other laws that do not relate to the Act, the securities laws, or the Board’’ authority. The Civil Service Commission is then fully responsible for their actions, which are no less subject to Presidential oversight. This violates the basic principle that the President “cannot delegate ultimate responsibility or the active obligation to supervise that goes with it” because Article II “makes a single President responsible for the actions of the executive Branch.“ Bowsher v. Synar, 478 U. . S. 714, 723–724. This Court has upheld for-cause limitations on that power as well. See: 1. In Perkins, a naval cadet-engineer was honorably discharged from the Navy because his services were no longer required, and he brought a claim for his salary under statutes barring his peacetime discharge except by a court-martial or by the Secretary of the Navy “for misconduct” and similar procedures govern the removal of officers and directors of public companies. The parties agree that the Commissioner cannot remove a Board member at will, and that he cannot be removed except for willful violations of the Act or Board rules. The Commissioner is not responsible for his own determination of whether the Act is met, and even if he disagrees with their determination, he is powerless to intervene-unless that determination is so unreasonable as to constitute “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office.�” Bowsher, supra, at 727. The District Court did not exercise jurisdiction over petitioners’ claims, which were properly presented for this review. The judgment of the Court is affirmed in part and reversed in part, and this case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

The Supreme Court had to determine whether certain terms in a federal criminal statute, specifically the type of firearm used in a crime, should be considered elements of a separate offense (to be decided by a jury) or merely sentencing factors (to be decided by a judge). The case involved members of the Branch-Davidian sect who were involved in a violent confrontation with federal agents in Waco, Texas, and were charged with using or carrying firearms, including machineguns, during a crime of violence.

The Court concluded that terms like "machinegun" in 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1) define elements of a separate offense, not just sentencing factors. This decision was based on an analysis of the statute's language, structure, context, and history, as well as the traditional role of juries in determining elements of a crime.

The Court reasoned that the structure of the statute suggests that the first sentence defines the crime, while subsequent sentences pertain to sentencing factors. It also noted that traditionally, the type of firearm has not been used as a sentencing factor in similar crimes. Furthermore, the Court argued that asking a jury to determine the type of firearm used would not complicate trials or risk unfairness.

The Court also addressed the legislative history of the statute, which the government argued favored a sentencing factor interpretation. However, the Court found that the history did not significantly support the government's position.

Finally, the Court emphasized that the significant increase in mandatory sentencing based on the type of firearm used supports treating such terms as elements of a separate offense. The Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, which had held that these terms were sentencing factors, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

The Supreme Court held that the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) preempts a Washington state statute that automatically revokes a spouse as the beneficiary of nonprobate assets, including ERISA plans, upon divorce. The case involved Donna Rae Egelhoff, who was designated as the beneficiary of her husband's life insurance policy and pension plan, both governed by ERISA. After their divorce and Mr. Egelhoff's death, his children from a previous marriage sued to claim the benefits, citing the Washington statute.

The Court reasoned that ERISA's preemption clause is broad and is meant to supersede any state laws that relate to employee benefit plans. The Washington statute was found to have an impermissible connection with ERISA plans because it required plan administrators to follow state law rather than the plan documents to determine beneficiary status. This interferes with ERISA's goal of uniform plan administration across states and imposes administrative burdens on plan administrators, which ERISA aims to minimize.

The Court rejected arguments that the Washington statute's opt-out provision or its relation to areas of traditional state regulation, such as family law, would save it from preemption. The Court emphasized that ERISA's preemption is intended to avoid the complexity and inconsistency that would result from plans being subject to different state laws.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Supreme Court of Washington and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, thereby confirming that ERISA plans must be administered and benefits paid according to the plan documents, not state law.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant who was convicted of rape and was sentenced to 20 years' imprisonment.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed on January 22, 1965, a Tennessee man with a butcher knife confronted a woman in her home and confronted her there.  The complaint alleges that the woman confronted the man and told him that she had "no doubt" that he was the person who had raped her.  She also allegedly told the man that she "saw him in the headlights of a passing car" and that he had a "real good look" at his assailant.  As alleged in the complaint, however, the woman had no doubt that the man had been the victim of a previous rape.  In fact, the complaint alleges, the victim had no evidence to support a finding that the in-court identification was reasonable and reasonable.   The SEC alleges that, in a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for New York announced criminal charges against the defendant. Â The SEC's Complaint, filed in federal district court in Manhattan, charges the defendant with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4)-8 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, orders him to pay a civil penalty of $1,000, and bars him from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney.  He also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company and to be restrained from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in connection with the alleged conduct of the alleged crime.  It also ordered him to comply with the bar set forth in the Complaint.

Petitioners, three former Hazelwood East students who were staff members of a high school newspaper produced as part of the school's journalism curriculum, filed a First Amendment action in Federal District Court, seeking a declaration that their First Amendment rights had been violated, injunctive relief, and monetary damages. The District Court denied an injunction, holding that no First Amendment violation had occurred. The Court of Appeals reversed. Held: 1. The First Amendment does not require a school to tolerate particular student speech. The public schools do not possess all of the attributes of streets, parks, and other traditional public forums that "time out of mind, have been used for purposes of assembly, communicating thoughts between citizens, and discussing public questions." Hague v. CIO, 307 U. S. 496, 515, and must be "applied in light of the special characteristics of the School environment." Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District No. 403 v. Fraser, 478 U.S. 675, 682. Pp. 598-599. 2. School officials were entitled to censor the articles on the ground that they invaded the rights of others, only if publication of the articles could have resulted in tort liability to the school. The court concluded that no tort action for libel or invasion of privacy could have been maintained against the school by the subjects of the two articles or by their families. Accordingly, the court held that school officials had violated respondents' First Amendment right by deleting the two pages of the newspaper. Certiorari granted; 795 F. 2d 1368, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Georgia today entered a final judgment against Georgia's use of the county unit system in determining the results of a statewide election to determine the number of representatives in the lower house of the legislature.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Atlanta, Georgia, alleges that Georgia violated the antifraud provisions of the federal election laws.  According to the complaint, from 1960 through the mid-1970s, Georgia used the county-unit system to count the votes of eligible candidates for statewide office.  As alleged, the county units system was designed to achieve a reasonable balance as between urban and rural electoral power.  For example, the complaint alleges that in 1960, the majority of the counties in which a candidate was nominated were allocated two units; one unit for each of the next five,000 persons; and, thereafter, two units for each increase of 30,000 person.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Georgia announced criminal charges against one of the defendants.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the federal securities laws and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.   The judgment also prohibits him from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in connection with the issuance of any security deposit or other security deposit, and from participating as an officer or director of a public company in any future state or federal election.

Petitioner was found guilty by a jury of capital murder and sentenced to death. Following two resentencings, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the District Court's denial of petitioner's first federal habeas petition challenging the most recent death sentence. Because he failed to make a timely request, petitioner waived his option to be executed by electrocution. Petitioner filed a civil rights action in Federal District Court, alleging that the use of a "cut-down" procedure to access his veins would violate the Eighth Amendment. The District Court dismissed the complaint on the ground that petitioner's § 1983 claim and stay request were the "functional equivalent" of a second or successive application subject to the gatekeeping provisions of 28 U. S. C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii), which authorizes a "suit in equity, or other proper proceeding for redress," against any person who, under color of state law, "subjects, or causes to be subjected, any citizen of the United States . . . to the deprivation of any rights, privileges, or immunities secured by the Constitution." Petitioner's complaint states such a claim. Despite its literal applicability, § 1983 requires that a district court dismiss "any action brought with respect to prison conditions under section 1983 of this title," if the court is satisfied that the action is frivolous, malicious, fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted, or seeks monetary relief from a defendant who is immune from such relief." The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that petitioner was without recourse to challenge the constitutionality of the cut-down procedure in federal District Court. Held: 1. The mere fact that an inmate states a cognizable §1983 claim does not warrant the entry of a stay as a matter of right. Pp. 5-11. (a) The merefact that an individual states a "cognizable § 1983" claim does, in fact, not warrant an entry of the stay, is not cognizable under § 1983 unless and until the inmate obtains favorable termination of a state, or federal, challenge to his conviction or sentence. P. 5. (b) The ability to bring a § 1983 challenge, rather than a habas application, does not entirely free inmates from substantive or procedural limitations. The Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (Act) imposes limits on the scope and duration of preliminary and permanent injunctive relief, including a requirement that, before issuing such relief, "[a] court shall give substantial weight to any adverse impact on . . .. the operation of a criminal justice system caused by the relief." 18 U.S. C.'§ 3626(a)(1); accord, § 3626 (a)(2). It requires that inmates exhaust available state administrative remedies before bringing § 1983 action challenging the conditions of their confinement. The Act mandates that a District court "shall," on its own motion, dismiss any action brought under §1983, if the "conditions" nor the "fact or duration" label is required. Such claims fall within the "core" of habbeas corpus and are thus not " cognizable" when brought pursuant to § 1983. By asking for broader relief than necessary, petitioner undermines his assertions that: (1) his § 1983 suit is not a tactic for delay, and (2) he is not challenging the fact of his execution, but merely a dispensable preliminary procedure. Moreover, he undermines his assertion that, as a legal matter the cutdown were a statutorily mandated part of the lethal injection protocol, or if as a factual matter petitioner were unable or unwilling to concede acceptable alternatives for gaining venous access, respondents might have a stronger argument that success on the merits would call into question the death sentence itself. The fact that the State has maintained, from the outset of this litigation, that it would attempt other methods of venous-access prior to engaging in the cutting-down does not necessarily mean that a particular means of gaining such access is likewise necessary. The "favorable termination" requirement is necessary to prevent inmates from doing indirectly through damages actions what they could not do directly by seeking injuncctive relief-challenge the fact or duration of their imprisonment without complying with the procedural limitations of the federal statute. And while it makes little sense to talk of the "duration" of an inmate's sentence, a State retains a significant interest in meting out a sentence of death in a timely fashion. See, e.g., Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.. 538, 538. P p. 511. 2. The ability of an individual to bring § 1983 claims rather than an application does not fully free him from substantive limitations. Under 28 U. S. C. §2254(d)(2), a federal court may not grant a state prisoner’s application for a writ of habeas corpus based on a claim already adjudicated on the merits in state court unless that adjudication “resulted in a decision that was based on an unreasonable determination of the facts in light of the evidence presented in the State court proceeding.” Under 28 F. Supp. 2d (2), “a determination of a factual issue made by a State court shall be presumed to be correct,” and the petitioner “shall have the burden of rebutting the presumption of correctness by clear and convincing evidence.’ ” In this case, petitioner Holly Wood, a capital defendant, challenges the key factual finding made by the Alabama state court that denied his application for postconviction relief: that his attorneys’ failure to pursue and present mitigating evidence of his borderline mental retardation was a strategic decision rather than a negligent omission. The Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed, but the Alabama Supreme Court denied certiorari. Wood v. Alabama, 525 U.S. 1042, reversed. (a) The state-court decision involved an unreasonable application of federal law under Strickland v. Washington, 466 U. s. 668 (1984), which held that the Eighth Amendment prohibits the execution of the mentally retarded. Wood argues that this standard applies only when a state court makes a strategic- decision not to pursue or present evidence of a mental deficiency. The court also accepted as not “objectively unreasonable” the state’tional determination that Wood had failed to show prejudice from counsel’re failure to present the evidence. Id., at 1304–1306. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that, even under the State Court’m conclusion that counsel made a strategic choice to not pursue evidence of mental deficiencies was not an unreasonable determination of facts, and that, in the absence of a reasonable investigation, these decisions were an unreasonable exercise of professional judgment and constituted deficient performance under Strrickland. Respondents’ amici offer still variations on the question whether a decision was strategic, but they are “not fairly included therein” Yee v. Escondido, 503 U. . S. 519, 537. The fact that respondent Trotter discussed this issue in the text of his petition for certiorar does not bring it before the Court. Under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996, a federal district court must order a convicted felony defendant to pay restitution to the victim of the crime, absent extraordinary circumstances. 18 U. S. C. §1696a(a)(1). Section 1696a(b)(1) establishes a procedure for calculating the total amount of restitution. If the loss suffered by the victim is not readily ascertainable, the court must set a date for the final determination of the victim’s losses, not later than 90 days after the date of the defendant’s conviction. §1696a(d)(5). When petitioner Dolan pled guilty to violating the Arson Prevention Act, the Federal District Court issued a judgment ordering him to pay restitution to the victim of the arson attack that killed his wife. Because the victim’s estate had already filed suit against Dolan, the court used the figure of $1 million as the total amount of restitution. The court also set a date for the final determination of the victim’s losses, 90 days hence. Three months later, the court heard oral argument on Dolan’s request to vacate the restitution order because the victim’s estate had submitted a revised estimate of the damages, increasing the total amount of restitution to $1.5 million. The court denied the request, finding that the increase was insubstantial. The Tenth Circuit reversed, concluding that the court erred in refusing to correct the error in the restitution calculation. Held: A sentencing court that fails to meet the 90-day deadline established by §1696a(d)(5) nevertheless retains the power to order restitution. Pp. 3−12. (a) The 90-day deadline was clearly missed here. Neither the Government nor Dolan explained why the deadline was missed, and the Government did not argue that the deadline was tolled. Pp. 3−4. (b) Where a statute does not address the effect of a missed deadline, federal courts generally decline to impose their own coercive sanctions. See, e.g., United States v. Montuflores-Rodriguez, 497 U.S. 426, 431. However, there are exceptions. One exception is created by statutes that expressly give the sentencing court the power to proceed despite a missed deadline. Another exception exists where the statute is silent on the effect of a missed deadline, yet the sentencing court’s actions are subject to meaningful judicial oversight. See, e.g., United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41. Both exceptions exist here. Although the statute is silent on the effect of a missed deadline, the sentencing court’s actions are subject to meaningful judicial oversight. The court’s decision to deny Dolan’s request to vacate the restitution order was reviewed by the Tenth Circuit, and the court’s ruling was ultimately reversed. Had the court acted outside the bounds of its authority, the Tenth Circuit would have corrected the error. Pp. 4−6. (c) Reading the statute as requiring the sentencing court to await completion of the restitution calculation before issuing the restitution order would produce absurd results. Such a requirement would allow a defendant to manipulate whether restitution could be awarded at all. By contrast, the sentencing court’s actions here fall within the scope of its authority. The court’s decision to deny Dolan’s request to vacate the restitution order was supported by the record below, and the Tenth Circuit’s ultimate reversal demonstrates that the court’s actions were subject to meaningful judicial oversight. Pp. 6−10. (d) The Tenth Circuit correctly rejected Dolan’s contention that the “rule of lenity” favors his interpretation of the statute. Assuming for argument’s sake that the rule might be so applied, and after considering the statute’s text, structure, and purpose, this Court finds no statutory ambiguity sufficiently grievous to warrant applying the rule in this case. Pp. 10−12. 555 F.3d 1170, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Roberts, C. J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

Respondent, a citizen of Pakistan and a Muslim, was arrested in the United States on criminal charges and detained by federal officials. In the District Court, respondent raised the defense of qualified immunity and moved to dismiss the suit, contending that the complaint was not sufficient to state a claim against them. The District Court denied the motion to dismiss, concluding that respondent’s complaint was sufficient to show his own involvement in clearly established unconstitutional conduct. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Respondent, as the plaintiff in this case, has not “nudged [his] claims” of invidious discrimination “across the line from conceivable to plausible.” Mitchell v. Forsyth, 472 U. S. 511, 530. Pp. 4–6. (a) Respondent’d complaint does not plead sufficient facts to show a claim for purposeful and unlawful discrimination against petitioners. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a)(2), a pleading must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to “state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face,” id., at 570. A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable for the misconduct alleged. Id., at 556. A pleading that offers “labels and conclusions” or “a formulaic recitation of the elements of a cause of action” will not do. Nor does a complaint suffice if it tenders “Naked assertion[s]” devoid of “further factual enhancement.’ ” Id. At 555. The complaint also alleges that petitioners purposefully adopted a policy of classifying post-September-11 detainees as “of high interest” because of their race, religion, or national origin. Respondent contends that, under the collateral-order doctrine, petitioners can be liable for “knowledge and acquiescence in their subordinates’ use of discriminatory criteria to make classification decisions among detainees” in violation of the Sherman Act, 15 U.S. C. §1. The Federal Rules do not require courts to credit such pleadings without reference to its factual context. Rather, the Court should assume their veracity and then determine whether they plausibly give rise to an entitlement to relief. P. 5–7. (b) In the context of determining whether there is a violation of clearly established right to overcome qualified immunity, purpose rather than knowledge is required to impose Bivens liability on the subordinate for unconstitutional discrimination; the same holds true for an official charged with violations arising from his or her superintendent responsibilities. See 5A C. Wright & A. Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure §1301, p. 291. The term “supervisory liability” is a misnomer. Absent vicarious liability, each Government official, his title notwithstanding, is only liable for his own misconduct. In order to survive a motion to dismissal, a plaintiff must plead that each Government-official defendant, through his own individual actions, has violated the Constitution. The concerns that animated the decision in Johnson v. Jones, supra, at 557, are absent when an appellate court uses the “fact-related” question of law to determine whether a complaint avers a clearly established constitutional violation. The costs of diversion are only magnified when Government officials are charged with responding to, as Judge Cabranes aptly put it, a national and international security emergency unprecedented in the history of the American Republic. The Costs of diversion, though necessary to ensure that officials comply with the law, exacts heavy costs in terms of efficiency and expenditure of valuable time and resources that might otherwise be directed to the proper execution of the work of the Government. Respondents’ constitutional claims against petitioner, however, rest solely on their ostensible “policy of holding post- September-11th detainees in highly restrictive conditions of confinement until they were ‘cleared’ by the FBI” and “directly implicated by” Hartman v. Moore, 547 U.

Respondent was arrested and convicted of possession of marihuana with intent to deliver in violation of Ark. Stat. Ann. § 82-2617 (1976). Before trial, respondent moved to suppress the evidence obtained from the suitcase, contending that the search violated his rights under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. The trial court denied the suppression motion without explanation. The Arkansas Supreme Court reversed, ruling that the trial court should have suppressed the evidence because it was obtained through an unlawful search of the suitcase. Relying upon United States v. Chadwick, 433 U. S. 1, and Coolidge v. New Hampshire, 403 U.S. 443, the court concluded that a warrantless search generally must be supported by "probable cause coupled with exigent circumstances." Held: 1. The Fourth Amendment protects the privacy and security of persons in two important ways. First, it guarantees "[t]he right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures." In addition, this Court has interpreted the Amendment to include the requirement that normally searches of private property be performed pursuant to a search warrant issued in compliance with the Warrant Clause. See, e. g., Mincey v. Arizona, 437 US. 385, 390, 98 S.Ct. 2408, 2412, 57 L.Ed. 2d 543. Pp. 531-532. 2. The warrantless searches of luggage properly taken from automobiles are not justified under some exception to the warrant requirement other than that applicable to automobiles stopped on the highway. P. 532. (a) In the ordinary case, a search of a closed suitcase in the trunk of an automobile may be as mobile as the vehicle in which it rides, but the exigency of mobility must be assessed at the point immediately before the search-after the police have seized the object to be searched and have it securely within their control. The mere reasonableness of a search, assessed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, is not a substitute for the judicial warrant required under the Amendment. See United Statesv. Martinez-Fuerte, supra, at 599, 559 S.W.2d 704, supra. The fact that the police, without endangering themselves or risking loss of the evidence, lawfully have detained one suspected of criminal activity and secured his suitcase, should have taken it along with respondent to the police station and there obtained a warrant for the search. Where, as in the present case, the police had seized the luggage and were justified in stopping the vehicle, searching it on the spot, and seizing the suitcase they suspected contained contraband, they should delay the search thereof until after judicial approval has been obtained. Moreover, the few situations in which a search may be conducted in the absence of a warrant have been carefully delineated and "the burden is on those seeking the exemption to show the need for it." United States

In 1983, Congress amended § 207 of the Indian Land Consolidation Act (ILCA) to ameliorate the extreme fractionation problem attending a century-old allotment policy that yielded multiple ownership of single parcels of Indian land. An enrolled member of the Sioux and Assiniboine Tribes of the Fort Peck Reservation in Montana, William Youpee died testate in October 1990. His will devised to respondents, all of them enrolled tribal members, his several undivided interests in allotted trust lands on various reservations in Montana and North Dakota. These interests, as the Ninth Circuit reported, were valued together at $1,239. In 1992, in a proceeding to determine the heirs to and claims against Youpee's estate, an administrative law judge in the Department of the Interior found that interests devised to each of the respondents fell within the compass of amended §§ 207 and should therefore escheat to the tribal governments of Fort Peck, Standing Rock, and Devils Lake Sioux Reservations. The District Court agreed with respondents and granted their request for declaratory and injunctive relief. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: In determining whether the 1984 amendments to § 207 render the provision constitutional, this Court is guided by Irving v. Irving, 481 U. S. 704, which held that the original version of § 207 effected a taking of private property without just compensation, in violation of the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. Pp. 5-11. (a) The 1984 amendments, though enacted three years prior to the Irving decision, effectively anticipated the concerns expressed in this Court's opinion. The amendments, however, did not cure the deficiencies that rendered the original provision unconstitutional. The United States does not rely on the new provision to defend the statute. Nor does it appear that it could do so at this time: Tribal codes governing disposition of escheatable interests have apparently not been developed. P. 5. (b) The Government's regulation of fractional interests in allotments, which the Government contends is an extraordinary and impermissible regulation of Indian lands and effect[ed] an unconstitutional taking of property at death through non-probate means, does not meet the Constitution's demand because it does not diminish the owner's right to use or enjoy property during his lifetime, and does not affect the right to transfer property at the death of the decedent. The Government contends that the revisions moderate the economic impact of the provision and temper the character of the Government regulation, and that the latter factor weighed most heavily against the constitutionality of the original § 207. The Federal Government's arguments did not persuade this Court in Irving and they are no more persuasive today. See, e. g., Irving, supra, at 716-717, 717-718. The fact that the amendments did not repeal Irving's deficiencies does not mean that the Government's regulations did not interfere with investment-backed expectations. The Bureau of Land Management's (Bureau of Land Survey) analysis of the allotment program showed that the Bureau's regulations would not conflict with the further descent of the property, and the value of the disputed parcels in this case is not of a different order; as the District Court reported, the value was $1239. The value of decedents' fractional interest was $2,700 and $1816, amounts that were found "not trivial." The Bureau's analysis indicated that § 207 likely would not interfere, under a fair reading of Irving, with the Bureau finding that it likely did interfere with interest-backed interests to persons who already own an interest in the same parcel; and that it would not further fractionate Indian land holdings. In addition, the Bureau found that the "extraordinary" character of its regulation did not preclude the Bureau from developing its own codes governing the disposition of interest in allotment land. This Court tested the legitimacy of the regulation by considering its economic impact, its effect on investment-bargaining expectations, and its essential character, and concluded that it did not require the Bureau to develop its own code governing disposition. The Ninth Circuit affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Southern District of Ohio recently ruled that the False Claims Act does not apply to a person who uses a false record or statement to get a false or fraudulent claim approved by the government. The court held that it is insufficient for a plaintiff to show that the false record was material to the Government's decision to pay or approve the false claim. The Court of Appeal ruled that it would be difficult for a person to prove that they intended to defraud the Government by making the false statement. The lower court previously found that there was insufficient evidence to support the government's claims against two shipbuilders that they fraudulently sought payment for work that had not been done in accordance with contract specifications. The trial court found that the shipyards' invoices for the construction of three generator sets (Gen-Sets) were false and misleading. The jury found that Gen-Sets were defective and leaked oil, that the welders who worked on the first 67 Gen-Set did not meet military standards, and that the gearboxes installed by Allison Engine in the first 52 Gen- Sets were defective. The Navy's contract specified that every part of each destroyer be built to the contractually required specifications, and each Gen-set was required to be accompanied by a certificate of conformity (COC) certifying that the unit was manufactured in compliance with the Navy’s requirements. The COCs were not required, however, to be submitted to the Navy for payment. The complaint alleged that the three shipyards fraudulently sought payments from the Navy by submitting invoices that falsely claimed that they had completed the required work. The contract also required that the Gen-sets be certified by the Navy as being in compliance, but the Navy did not require that the COC be submitted. The case was brought by two former employees of General Tool Company (GTC) and Southern Ohio Fabricators, Inc. (SOFCO), who were paid over $100,000 each for the three generators. The defendants, Allison Engine, GTC, and SOFCO were found guilty of violating the antifraud provisions of the FCA and paid millions of dollars in disgorgement and civil penalties.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York has ruled that the Federal Communications Commission has no power to regulate a radio broadcast that is indecent but not obscene. The case involves a 1973 broadcast of a monologue by comedian George Carlin in which he enumerates words that he would never say on the public airwaves. The complaint against Pacifica Foundation, the radio station that broadcast the broadcast, was filed by a man who heard the broadcast while driving with his young son. The Commission concluded that certain words depicted sexual and excretory activities in a patently offensive manner, and that the prerecorded language was "deliberately broadcast"

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed the Federal Reserve Board's approval of three bank holding companies' applications to acquire banks in New England states other than the ones in which they are principally located. The Court of Justice granted certiorari because of the importance of the issues raised by the petition filed by Northeast Bancorp, Inc., Union Trust Company, and Citicorp. The Petitioners claimed that the acquisitions were not authorized by the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, 70 Stat. 133, as amended, 12 U.N.C.  1841(c)(5). The Act regulates the acquisition of state and national banks by the bank holding company. In addition, the Act prohibits the Board from approving an application of a bank holding firm or bank located in one State to acquire a bank in another State, or substantially all of its assets, unless the acquisition "is specifically authorized" by the statute laws of the State in which such bank is located, by language to that effect and not merely by implication. The Second Circuit found that the laws of each state violated the Constitution's Commerce Clause and the Compact Clause of the United States, and that the Board had not adequately explained its reasons for its approval of the acquisitions. The court held that the acquisition approval was not required under the Act, and the Board did not adequately explain why it did not approve the acquisition. In a separate opinion, the court found that there was no reason why the Board should not have approved the acquisition because the acquisition was not specifically authorized by state law. The Supreme Court held that there is no basis for the Court's finding that the Act violated the Commerce Clause.

In 1996, respondents, a group of Ohio taxpayers, challenged the Ohio program in state court on state and federal grounds. The Ohio Supreme Court rejected respondents' federal claims, but held that the enactment of the program violated certain procedural requirements of the Ohio Constitution. In July 1999, respondents filed this action in Federal District Court, seeking to enjoin the reenacted program on the ground that it violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. In December 1999, the District Court granted summary judgment for respondents. The Court of Appeals affirmed, finding that the program had the "primary effect" of advancing religion in violation of the Constitution. Held: 1. The program is neutral with respect to religion. It provides benefits directly to a broad class of citizens, defined only by financial need and residence in a particular school district, and permits such individuals to exercise genuine choice among options public and private, secular and religious. Pp. 4-7. (a) The program's practical application is to provide educational choices directly to children in a school district that is or has been "under federal court order requiring supervision and operational management of the district by the state superintendent." Simmons-Harris v. Goff, 86 Ohio St. 3d 1, 8-9, 711 N. E. 2d 203, 211. P. 4. (b) There is no merit to respondent's argument that, because the program is one of true private choice, the program does not offend the Constitution, since it is one that is neutral in all respects toward religion, and the program's incidental advancement of a religious mission is reasonably attributable to the individual recipient, not to the government, whose role ends with the disbursement of benefits. Moreover, there is no evidence that any voucher-eligible student was turned away from a nonreligious private school in the voucher program in the 1999-2000 school year, when the program provided relief to less than five percent of the students enrolled in the school's schools, and that the vast majority of the voucher recipients were parents of children in religious schools. The record indicates that the schools are failing to serve their objective, whereas the vouchers in issue here are said to be needed to provide adequate alternatives to them. The fact that the school district has a large proportion of voucher recipients is irrelevant to the constitutional inquiry that they are parents of religious schools, since the program provides no religious affiliation and no proof that the State deliberately skewed incentives toward religious schools in the program. P p. 4–7. 2. In view of the record in these cases, respondent's contention that, after the program was enacted, parents were free to direct state educational aid to religious schools solely as a result of the numerous independent decisions of private individuals, carries with it the imprimatur of government endorsement. This conclusion is not supported by the fact that, in the absence of a financial incentive for parents to choose a religious school, they need only be adequate substitutes for religious schools; and the mere fact that a family that cannot afford a private education wants its children educated in a parochial school is a sufficient justification for the use of public funds to support private school education over and above its traditional obligation that is at issue here. The conclusion that, even if the program challenged in Nyquist is far removed from that program, it is consistent and unbroken with the prior Establishment Clause jurisprudence, and it is the goal of the Court's Establishment Clause to determine whether the program should constrain state action under the Fourteenth Amendment. This Court has repeatedly recognized that no reasonable observer would think that state action should be evaluated on different terms than similar action by the Federal Government, and this Court has never found a neutral program of private choice that, like the program here, offer aid directly to an individual recipients defined without regard to religion, see, e. g., Mitchell v. Helms, 530 U. S. 793, 810-814. Nor does this Court's decision signal a major departure from this Court, which has long considered that neutral programs of school choice are not readily subject to challenge under the Establishment

The Supreme Court opinion addresses whether taxpayers can seek a refund for taxes collected in violation of the Export Clause of the Constitution under the Tucker Act, when they do not meet the time limits for refund actions in the Internal Revenue Code. The Court concludes that taxpayers must adhere to the specific tax refund procedures set forth in the Internal Revenue Code, which require filing an administrative claim with the IRS within strict timeframes, before they can file a lawsuit against the Government.

The case involves coal companies that paid taxes on coal exports and sought refunds for taxes paid between 1994 and 1996, arguing that the tax was unconstitutional under the Export Clause. However, they did not file timely administrative claims with the IRS for those years. The Court of Federal Claims allowed the companies to pursue their suit under the Tucker Act, which has a more lenient 6-year statute of limitations, but the Supreme Court reverses this decision.

The Supreme Court's reasoning is based on the clear language of the Internal Revenue Code, which states that no suit for a tax refund can be maintained without first filing a claim with the IRS within the prescribed time limits. The Court rejects the companies' arguments that the refund scheme should not apply to Export Clause cases or to taxes that are facially unconstitutional. The Court emphasizes that Congress has the authority to require administrative exhaustion and to establish reasonable time limits for tax refund claims, even when the constitutionality of a tax is challenged.

The Court also notes that the unconstitutionality of the coal export tax was not so obvious that it would have been impossible for the Government to prevail at the time the tax was assessed. Therefore, the companies' claims do not fall under the "under no circumstances" exception that might apply to the Anti-Injunction Act.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court holds that taxpayers seeking a refund for taxes assessed in violation of the Export Clause must comply with the tax refund procedures in the Internal Revenue Code, including filing a timely administrative claim, before suing the Government. The judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed, and the companies are not allowed to bring suit for the 1994–1996 tax refunds. The question of whether the companies are entitled to interest on those amounts is not addressed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the appellants who were challenging a San Diego ordinance that prohibited the installation of new billboards and required the removal of old ones. The Court found that the ordinance went beyond what was necessary to achieve the city's claimed goals of improving traffic flow and enhancing the aesthetic quality of the city. Specifically, the Court determined that the ordinance was overly burdensome and discriminated against certain types of speech, namely commercial speech. The Court also found that the ordinance was inconsistent with the First Amendment's protection of freedom of speech.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Michigan today entered a final judgment in favor of Reginald Lett, a Michigan man convicted of second-degree murder in 1997.  The court also issued a temporary restraining order halting Lett from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17b-5 thereunder, and ordered Lett to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Detroit on June 12, 1997, Lett pleaded guilty to second- and third-degree felony murder and was sentenced to a one-and-a-half-year prison term. The court ruled that Lett was not entitled to a writ of habeas corpus because he had not exercised sound discretion in declaring a mistrial.  In its judgment, the court held that the jury was deadlocked and therefore could not have reached a unanimous verdict.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay $9,500 in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil monetary penalty equal to the amount of his penalty.  Lett also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company, and to be restrained from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any securities in connection with the sale or issuance of any security deposit in the company's securities.  Finally, the Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit today issued a final order halting the imposition of a permanent injunction against Lett and ordering him to comply with the court's order.  On June 13, 2017, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced that it had obtained an emergency court order temporarily halting the execution of Lett's criminal conviction.  It also issued an order suspending Lett for a period of two years, and appointing a receiver to monitor the progress of the case.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Daniel A. Welshhans and supervised by Eric R. Werner. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Michigan Attorney General's Office, and the Michigan Department of Justice.

After petitioner Alford was indicted for first-degree murder, the court appointed an attorney to represent him, and this attorney questioned all but one of the various witnesses who appellee said would substantiate his claim of innocence. The witnesses, however, did not support Alford's story but gave statements that strongly indicated his guilt. Faced with strong evidence of guilt and no substantial evidentiary support for the claim, the trial court sentenced him to 30 years' imprisonment, the maximum penalty for second-degree homicide. After a hearing, the state court found that the plea was "willingly, knowingly, and understandingly" made on the advice of competent counsel and in the face of a strong prosecution case. Subsequently, Alford petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in the Federal District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, which denied relief on the grounds that the guilty plea was voluntary and waived all defenses and nonjurisdictional defects in any prior stage of the proceedings and that the findings of the state trial court in 1965 clearly required rejection of his claim that he was denied effective assistance of counsel prior to pleading guilty. The Court of Appeals reversed on the ground that Alford had an absolute right to have his guilty plea accepted, but implied that there would have been no constitutional error had his plea been accepted even though evidence before the judge indicated that there was a valid defense. Conceding that Jackson did not require the automatic invalidation of pleas of guilty entered under the North Carolina statutes, the Court held that the conviction entered on his guilty pleas was invalid, since his assertion of innocence negatived any admission of guilt, which, as in Brady v. United States, 397 U. S. 748, was normally "c) entral to the plea and the foundation for entering judgment against the defendant." Held: 1. A judgment of conviction resting on a plea of guilty is justified by the defendant's admission that he committed the crime charged against him and his consent that judgment be entered without a trial of any kind. The plea usually subsumes both elements, and justifiably so, even though there is no separate, express admission of the defendant that he participated in the acts claimed to constitute the crime. When his plea is viewed in light of the evidence against him, which substantially negated his innocence and further provided a means by which the judge could test whether the plea is being intelligently entered, its validity cannot be seriously questioned. In view of the strong factual basis for the plea demonstrated by the State and the State's clearly expressed desire to enter it despite his professed belief in his innocence, there obviously existed a factual and legal dispute between him and the state. Without more, it might be argued that the convictions entered on the guilty pleas were invalid since the conviction was invalid because his assertion was invalid. Pp. 531-532. 2. The fact that his plea was denominated a guilty rather than a nolo contendere is of no constitutional significance with respect to the issue now before us, since the Constitution does not bar imposition of a prison sentence upon an accused who is unwilling expressly to admit his guilt but who, faced with grim alternatives, is willing to waive his trial and accept the sentence. P. 532. 405 F. 2d 340, vacated and remanded.

The Supreme Court held that the Bayh-Dole Act does not automatically vest title to federally funded inventions in federal contractors, such as universities or businesses. The case involved a dispute between Stanford University and Roche Molecular Systems over the ownership of patents related to HIV testing technology. The technology was developed by a Stanford researcher who had also signed an agreement with Cetus (later acquired by Roche) to assign inventions resulting from his access to Cetus.

The Court explained that historically, patent rights belong to the inventor, and an inventor can assign those rights to another party. The Bayh-Dole Act allows federal contractors to elect to retain title to inventions conceived or first reduced to practice under a federal funding agreement, but it does not automatically assign ownership to the contractor. The Act's use of the term "retain" implies that the contractor must already have title to the invention to keep it, rather than the Act granting title.

The Court also noted that the Act does not contain language that explicitly vests title in contractors or deprives inventors of their rights, unlike other statutes that clearly assign ownership to the government for inventions arising under specific federal contracts. The Court found that the Bayh-Dole Act operates only when a contractor has already acquired title to an invention, and it does not displace the inventor's antecedent title.

The Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which had held that Roche possessed an ownership interest in the patents that was not extinguished by the Bayh-Dole Act, thus depriving Stanford of standing to sue for patent infringement.

The decision reinforces the principle that inventors initially own their inventions and that any transfer of rights must be clearly established through assignment or other legal mechanisms. The ruling also clarifies that the Bayh-Dole Act does not disrupt the traditional patent ownership norms but rather provides a framework for managing rights between federal contractors and the government when the contractor has already obtained title to an invention.

Petitioner Coolidge, a New Hampshire man, was arrested on a charge of murder in connection with the disappearance of a 14-year-old girl from her home. The police, having learned from a neighbor that Coolidge had been away from home on the evening of the disappearance, went to his house to question him. They asked him, among other things, if he owned any guns, and he produced three, two shotguns and a rifle. They also asked him whether he would take a lie-detector test concerning his account of his activities on the night of the murder. He agreed to do so on the following Sunday, his day off, and attempted to show through microscopic analysis that there was a high probability that the clothes had been in contact with Pamela Mason's body. After the police returned from Concord, New Hampshire, they arrested Coolidge in his house on the day the warrant was issued. He confessed to the murder and was sentenced to life imprisonment. The New Hampshire Supreme Court affirmed the conviction. Held: 1. The warrant authorizing the seizure and subsequent search of the Pontiac automobile was invalid because not issued by a neutral and detached magistrate. Pp. 531-532. (a) The rule that "searches conducted outside the judicial process, without prior approval by judge or magistrate, are per se unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment subject only to a few specifically established and well-delineated exceptions," is not so frail that its continuing vitality depends on the fate of a supposed doctrine of warrantless arrest. P. 533. (b) The "plain view" exception to the warrant requirement is inapplicable to this case. It is not an inconvenience to be somehow "weighed" against the claims of police efficiency, since it is an important working part of the machinery of government, operating as a matter of course to check the "well-intentioned but mistakenly overzealous, executive officers" who are a part of any system of law enforcement. The Fourth Amendment's fundamental guarantee is not to be reduced to complete order and harmony, since there is nothing constitutionally suspect in the existence, without more, of these incentives to full disclosure or active cooperation with the police, unless the police can show that it falls within one of a number of well defined exceptions based on the presence of "exigent circumstances." Id., at 534-535. P p. 535. 2. The "plaintiff" exception cannot justify the police seizure of a Pontiac car in this case, since the car itself was an "instrumentality of the crime," and as such might be seized by the police on Coolidge's property because it was in plain view, and the subsequent search at the station house was not justified on some other theory. The doctrine of the exception, as just stated, is that a plain-view seizure will not turn an initially valid (and therefore limited) search into a "general" one, while the inconvenience of procuring a warrant to cover an inadvertent discovery is great, and no exigent circumstances justified the police in proceeding without a warrant. Thus, the requirement of the warrant to seize imposes no inconvenience whatever, or at least none which is constitutionally cognizable in a legal system that regards warrantless searches as "per se unreasonable" in the absence of such circumstances. The application of the basic rule of Fourth Amendment law therefore requires that the fruits of this warrantless seizure be suppressed. This Court has chosen to assume the validity of an arrest and decide the case before it on the issue of the scope of permissible warrantless search, and, consequently, it implied no total obliteration of state laws relating to arrests and searches in favor of federal law. Pd. 536-537. (c) The doctrine that a search "incident" to a lawful arrest may encompass all of the premises where the arrest occurred, however spacious those premises might be, does not require that the police obtain a warrant if they anticipate that they will find specific evidence during the course of such a search. Nor does it require that an object that comes into view during a search incident to arrest, under circumstances where no reason appears why an arrest warrant could not have been sought, is inconsistent with the rule of Carroll v. United States, 267 U. S. 132, which held that "no amount of probable cause can justify a search of a person's house without a search." Pp 537-538. 109 N. H. 403, 260 A. 2d 547, reversed and remanded.

Title 18 U. S. C. §641 prohibits the knowing transfer of national security information to foreign governments. Section 641’s implementing regulation bars the export of “dualuse” goods, which are products that have both civilian and military applications. Petitioner, a special agent of the Department of Justice’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), investigated reports that respondents, residents of Nevada, had purchased dual-use goods from China. OFAC regulations require that an investigator submit a report to the agency’s Director before initiating an investigation. Pursuant to those regulations, petitioner submitted a report stating that he planned to investigate the purchases. The Director approved the report and assigned petitioner to lead the investigation. Petitioner traveled to Nevada and met with respondents, who admitted purchasing the goods. They consented to a search of their ranch, and petitioner obtained a warrant from a Magistrate to search the ranch for the goods. Before executing the warrant, petitioner briefed the search team and provided copies of the warrant application, affidavit, and warrant to the officers to review. Petitioner orally reviewed the terms of the warrant with the officers, including the specific items for which they were authorized to search. During the search, the officers seized nothing. Following the search, petitioner gave respondents a copy of the warrant. The next day, petitioner faxed respondents a copy of the more detailed warrant application. Subsequent to learning of the warrant’s defects, petitioner contacted the Magistrate, who confirmed that she had signed off on the warrant application and made no corrections to the warrant itself. Thereafter, the Government brought suit against respondents, seeking damages for their alleged violations of §641. The District Court dismissed the indictment, ruling that the warrant was fatally flawed because it did not specifically mention the items to be seized. The Ninth Circuit reversed, concluding that the warrant was not fatally flawed because the items to be seized were clearly specified in the warrant application and affidavit, both of which were given to the Magistrate. Held: 1. The warrant was not fatally flawed. The warrant was not so obviously deficient that the ensuing search must be regarded as a warrantless search and thus presumptively unreasonable. The warrant was facially defective because it did not specifically mention the items to be seized. Nonetheless, the warrant was not fatally flawed because the items to be seized were clearly specified in the warrant application and affidavit, both of which were given to the Magistrate. The Magistrate reviewed all of the documents and signed the warrant application and made no adjustment or correction to the application or the warrant itself. Putting aside the technical defect in the warrant, it is hard to imagine how the actual search could have been carried out any more reasonably. Assuming a constitutional violation, petitioner is entitled to qualified immunity. Pp. 558–565. 2. Qualified immunity is not available. The qualified immunity inquiry rests on “the ‘objective legal reasonableness’ of the action … , assessed in light of the legal rules that were ‘clearly established’ at the time it was taken.” Anderson v. Creighton, 483 U. S. 635, 639. Here, the Court errs not only by defining the question at too high a level of generality but also by assessing the question without regard to the relevant circumstances. Depending on the circumstances of the particular case, a warrant may be so facially deficient that the executing officers cannot reasonably presume it to be valid. United States v. Leon, 468 U. S. 897, 923. This language makes clear that this exception to Leon’s good-faith exception does not apply in every circumstance. The Court does not explain why it should apply here. Nor does the Court point to any cases directing an officer to proofread a warrant after it has been passed on by a neutral magistrate, where the officer is already fully aware of the scope of the intended search and the magistrate gives no reason to believe that he has authorized anything other than the requested search. Nor does the Court point to any case suggesting that where the same officer both prepares and executes the invalid warrant, he can never rely on the magistrate’s assurance that the warrant is proper. Petitioner’s actions were objectively reasonable, and thus he should be entitled to qualified immunity. Pp. 565–566. 298 F. 3d 1022, reversed.

The Supreme Court of the United States, in this opinion, addresses the constitutionality of a Georgia statute that criminalizes the mere private possession of obscene material. The appellant was convicted under this statute for possessing obscene films in his home, and the conviction was affirmed by the Supreme Court of Georgia. The appellant appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing that the statute violated the First Amendment as applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court acknowledges that previous decisions, such as Roth v. United States, have held that obscenity is not protected by the First Amendment. However, the Court distinguishes this case by noting that those decisions did not address the issue of private possession of obscene materials, but rather dealt with public distribution or dissemination.

The Court emphasizes the constitutional protection of the right to receive information and ideas, which is fundamental to a free society. It also underscores the right to privacy, including the right to be free from unwarranted governmental intrusions into one's home.

The Court rejects Georgia's argument that the state can regulate private possession of obscene materials to protect the individual's mind, stating that this is inconsistent with the philosophy of the First Amendment. The Court also dismisses the state's concern that exposure to obscene materials may lead to antisocial behavior, noting a lack of empirical evidence and the principle that education and legal punishment are the appropriate means to prevent crime.

The Court concludes that the First and Fourteenth Amendments prohibit the criminalization of mere private possession of obscene material. The decision reaffirms the states' broad power to regulate obscenity but clarifies that this power does not extend to the private possession of such material in one's home.

The judgment of the Supreme Court of Georgia is reversed, and the case is remanded for proceedings consistent with this opinion. The Supreme Court's decision thus protects the individual's right to possess obscene material in the privacy of their own home from state interference.

In 1999, an Ohio jury convicted petitioner Bowles of murder for his involvement in the beating death of Ollie Gipson. Bowles unsuccessfully challenged his conviction and sentence on direct appeal. On September 9, 2003, the District Court denied Bowles habeas relief. After the entry of final judgment, Bowles moved to reopen the period during which he could file his notice of appeal pursuant to Rule 4(a)(6), which allows district courts to extend the filing period for 14 days from the day the district court grants the order to reopen, provided certain conditions are met. On February 10, 2004, the court granted Bowles’ motion. But rather than extending the time period by 14 days, as Rule 4’s 180-day period allow, the Court inexplicably gave Bowles 17 days—until February 27—to file. On appeal, respondent Russell argued that Bowles was untimely and that the Court of Appeals therefore lacked jurisdiction to hear the case. The court of appeals agreed, and Bowles agreed. Held: The taking of an appeal within the prescribed time is “mandatory and jurisdictional,” Griggs v. Provident Consumer Discount Co., 459 U. S. 56, 61. Pp. 5–7. (a) The time limits for filing an appeal are jurisdictional in nature. P. 5—6. (b) The Court has long held that the time limit for filing a notice of appeals is jurisdictional. See, e.g., Federal Election Comm’n v. NRA Political Victory Fund, 513 U.S. 88, 90. But the Court has consistently held that this Court has no authority to create equitable exceptions to jurisdictional requirements, use of the “unique circumstances” doctrine is illegitimate. This Court has also treated the rule-based time period for civil and criminal cases differently, stating that it may be waived because “[t]he procedural rules adopted by the Court for the orderly transaction of its business are not jurisdictional and can be relaxed in the exercise of its discretion … .” Schacht, supra, at 64.[Footnote 4] P. 6. (c) Because Congress specifically limited the amount of time by which district courts can extend the notice-of-appeal period in §2107(c), that limitation is more than a simple “claim-processing rule.” As we have long held, when an “appeal has not been prosecuted in the manner directed, within the time limited by the acts of Congress, it must be dismissed for want of jurisdiction” Curry, 6 How., at 113. The notion of “subject-matter” jurisdiction obviously extends to “ ‘classes of cases … falling within a court’’ adjudicatory authority,’ ” Eberhart, supra. But it is no less “jurisdictional” when Congress forbids federal courts from adjudicating an otherwise legitimate “class of cases” after a certain period has elapsed from final judgment. Thus, the resolution of this case follows naturally from this reasoning. Like the initial 30-dayperiod for filing, the limit on how long a district court may reopen that period is set forth in a statute, 28 U. . S. C. §2108(c). Because Congress has limited authority to extend that period, it can also determine when, and under what conditions, federal courts can hear them. Kontrick v. Ryan, 540 U. s. 443 (2004), which held that failure to comply with the time requirement in Federal Rule of Bankruptcy Procedure 4004 did not affect a Court of appeals’ subject-matter jurisdiction, deprived the court of jurisdiction, and because Bowles is one of jurisdictional magnitude, he cannot rely on forfeiture or waiver to excuse his lack of compliance with the statute’tional time limitations. Arbaugh, J., and Breyer, JJ., inter alios, reversed.

Title: United States v. Carlton Deck

Case Number: 05-10295

Date Decided: June 27, 2006

Opinion Author(s): John Paul Stevens

Summary:

United States v. Carlton Deck is a landmark United States Supreme Court case concerning the constitutionality of using physical restraints, such as handcuffs and shackles, during criminal trials. The case involves a man named Carlton Deck, who was convicted of two counts of murder and attempted armed robbery in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. Prior to his trial, Deck had escaped from jail several times, leading authorities to believe that he posed a significant flight risk.

During Deck's trial, he was repeatedly shackled and restrained, despite protests from his lawyers and requests from the trial judge to remove the restraints.
