It also noted that if both the wholesale and retail prices are independently lawful, there is no basis for antitrust liability based on the relationship between the two.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The Court did not address whether the plaintiffs should be allowed to amend their complaint to bring a predatory pricing claim under the Brooke Group standard, leaving that decision to the District Court.

Respondent Thomas Petitioner Thompson was indicted on several charges related to the murder of a woman and the attempted murder of another. Before accepting a plea bargain, he sought to suppress his pretrial statements, claiming that he had invoked his right to remain silent under Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U. S. 436, and that the police had violated that right. The District Court agreed, but the Sixth Circuit vacated, concluding that the state court erred in applying the wrong legal standard for evaluating the effectiveness of counsel’s performance. Held: 1. Because the state court’s decision rejecting Thompson’s Miranda claim was correct under de novo review, it was necessarily reasonable under the more deferential Antiterrorism and Efficiency in Government Reform Act of 1996 (AEDPA) standard of review. Pp. 4–11. (a) The undisputed facts show that Thompson waived his right to remain silent. He received a written copy of the Miranda warnings, which indicated that he could choose to remain silent at any time. He was able to read and understand English. He was given time to read the warnings. He read aloud the fifth warning, stating that he had the right to remain silent. His answer to a detective’s question about prayer for forgiveness for shooting the victim was a “course of conduct indicating waiver” of the right to remain silent. Moreover, there is no evidence that his statement was coerced. Pp. 4–8. (b) The Butler v. Machibee, 441 U. S. 371, principle that courts can infer a waiver of Miranda rights “from the actions and words of the person interrogated” forecloses Thompson’s argument that the police were not allowed to question him until they obtained a waiver first. Pp. 8–9. (c) The police were not required to obtain a waiver of Thompson’s right to remain silent before commencing the interrogation. They gave him a Miranda warning, and he waived his right to remain silent by making a voluntary statement. Pp. 9–10. 2. Assuming that defense counsel’s failure to request a limiting instruction regarding how the jury could consider the outcome of a codefendant’s trial was deficient representation, Thompson cannot show prejudice under de novo review. The record establishes that it was not reasonably likely that the instruction would have made any difference in light of all the other evidence of guilt. The surviving victim identified Thompson as the shooter, and the identification was supported by a photograph taken from a surveillance camera. Another witness testified that Thompson confessed to him during a telephone call, and the details of that confession were corroborated by evidence that Thompson stripped the van and abandoned it after the shooting. The jury was capable of assessing the codefendant’s credibility, as it was instructed to do. The jury could have concluded that the codefendant’s earlier jury made a mistake, or alternatively, that the codefendant was not guilty of the charge. There was ample evidence in the record to support Thompson’s guilt under either theory, and the jury was instructed to weigh all of the evidence in determining whether there was guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Pp. 11–12. 547 F. 3d 583, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Ginsburg, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Sotomayor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Stevens, J., joined.

Title: Atkins v. Virginia
Year: 2002
Summary: Atkins v. Virginia is a landmark Supreme Court case that ruled that mentally ill defendants cannot be executed for their crimes. The case was decided on the grounds that the Eighth Amendment's cruel and unusual punishment clause prohibits the execution of individuals who are mentally incapacitated and therefore unable to understand the nature and consequences of their actions. The Court held that the use of the death penalty in such cases is "irrational" and "barbaric," and that it fails to serve the purposes of justice and retribution. The decision in Atkins v. Virginia marked a major shift in the treatment of mentally ill defendants in the criminal justice system, and it helped to establish a new standard for determining competency to stand trial.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia today entered a final judgment against the United States Department of the Interior, the Bureau of Land Management, and the BLM in a land withdrawal review case.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, alleges that the federal government violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, the BLM's complaint alleges that, in violation of the federal securities laws, it failed to adequately evaluate the safety and effectiveness of certain of the agency's land withdrawal reviews.  In addition, the complaint alleged that the BLM had failed to provide timely and sufficient information to determine whether a specific action had caused harm to one of its members.  For example, as alleged in the complaint:  The complaint alleges, in the course of administering the Nation's public lands, that respondent failed to timely and effectively respond to specific questions posed to it by the agency in its response to the filing of the complaint.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the defendants agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry of judgments that permanently enjoin them from future violations of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) ofÂ the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act"), and RuleÂ 5(b)(5) thereunder, ordering the BLM to comply with Section 5(b).  The settlement is subject to court approval.

The University of Michigan Law School (Law School) ranks among the Nation's top law schools. It receives more than 3,500 applications each year for a class of around 350 students. Seeking to "admit a group of students who individually and collectively are among the most capable," the Law School looks for individuals with "substantial promise for success in law school" and "a strong likelihood of succeeding in the practice of law and contributing in diverse ways to the well-being of others." The Law School seeks a mix of students with varying backgrounds and experiences who will respect and learn from each other. In reviewing an applicant's file, admissions officials must consider the applicant's undergraduate grade point average (GPA) and Law School Admission Test (LSAT) score because they are important predictors of academic success. The policy stresses that "no applicant should be admitted unless we expect that applicant to do well enough to graduate with no serious academic problems." The policy makes clear that even the highest possible score does not guarantee admission, nor does a low score automatically disqualify an applicant. Rather, the policy requires admissions officials to look beyond grades and test scores to other criteria that are important to the law school's educational objectives, including "the enthusiasm of recommenders, the quality of the undergraduate institution, the quantity of applicant's essay, and the areas and difficulty of undergraduate course selection." The admissions statistics show it to be a sham to cover a scheme of racially proportionate admissions. The Court of Appeals reversed the District Court's judgment and vacated the injunction. Held: 1. A race-conscious admissions program does not operate as a quota. When using race as a "plus" factor in university admissions, a university's admissions program must remain flexible enough to ensure that each applicant is evaluated as an individual and not in a way that makes an applicant’s race or ethnicity the defining feature of his or her application. Pp. 5-11. (a) The Law school’ admissions program bears the hallmarks of a narrowly tailored plan. The Law’S “critical mass” is defined by reference to the educational benefits that diversity is designed to produce. It affords this individualized consideration to applicants of all races, and there is no policy, either de jure or de facto, of automatic acceptance or rejection based on any single "soft" variable. In order to cultivate a set of leaders with legitimacy in the eyes of the citizenry, it is necessary that the path to leadership be visibly open to talented and qualified individuals of every race and ethnicity. This is not simply "to assure within its student body some specified percentage of a particular group merely because of its race or ethnic origin." Bakke, 438 U. S. 265, at 305. Nor is it the only governmental use of race that can survive strict scrutiny is remedying past discrimination. Nor does it countenance the unprecedented deference the Court gives to the Law school, an approach inconsistent with the very concept of “strict scrutiny.” Adarand Constructors, Inc. v. Peña, 515 U.S. 200, 227. In the context of higher education, the durational requirement can be met by sunset provisions in raceconscious admissions policies and periodic reviews to determine whether racial preferences are still necessary to achieve student body diversity. See, e. g., Johnson v. Board of Education, 347 U . S. 483, 293. In addition to the expert studies and reports entered into evidence at trial, numerous studies show that students body diversity promotes learning outcomes, and "better prepares students for an increasingly diverse workforce and society, and better prepares them as professionals." The University has determined, based on its experience and expertise, that a "critical mass" of underrepresented minority students is necessary to further its compelling interest in securing the college's educational benefits of a diverse student body. This conclusion is supported by the fact that, as a result of its individualized inquiry into the possible diversity contributions of all applicants, the University seeks to "enroll a `critical mass' of minority students." The law school”s admissions policy promotes "cross-racial understanding," helps to break down racial stereotypes, and helps to "ensur[e] their ability to make unique contributions to the intellectual and social life of the institution." Ibid. The law School also has determined that diversity will, in fact, yield educational benefits, and that "good faith" on the part of a university is "presumed" absent "a showing to the contrary." Ibid., at 318. In seeking the "right to select those students who will contribute the most to the `robust exchange of ideas,' " a university seeks to achieve a goal that is of paramount importance in the fulfillment of its mission," Brown v.Board of Ed., 347 U. . . 483. Moreover, the Court has recognized as a compelling state interest a government's effort to remedy past discrimination for which it is responsible. Richmond v. J. A. Croson Co., 488 U.

In the case of Hurley Henson v. Syngenta Crop Protection, Inc., Henson filed a tort claim in Louisiana state court against Syngenta, related to the manufacture and sale of an insecticide. This case was stayed when Henson joined a similar federal case in Alabama (Price v. Ciba-Geigy Corp.), which was settled with an agreement that included the dismissal of the Henson action. Despite the settlement terms, the Louisiana court allowed Henson to amend the complaint and proceed after counsel misrepresented the settlement's scope.

Syngenta removed the case to federal court, citing the All Writs Act and supplemental jurisdiction. The case was transferred to Alabama, where the court dismissed the Henson action and sanctioned Henson's counsel for misrepresentation. The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the sanctions but vacated the dismissal, stating that the All Writs Act does not provide federal subject-matter jurisdiction for removal.

The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the All Writs Act does not authorize removal of a state court case to federal court. The Court reasoned that removal is strictly a statutory right and the All Writs Act cannot be used to circumvent the statutory requirements for removal. The Court also rejected the argument that the All Writs Act, in conjunction with ancillary enforcement jurisdiction, could support removal, emphasizing that original jurisdiction is necessary for removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1441 and cannot be provided by ancillary jurisdiction.

The implication of this decision is that federal courts cannot use the All Writs Act to remove cases from state courts unless there is an independent basis for federal jurisdiction, and that parties must adhere to the specific statutory procedures for removal.

The Bankruptcy Act of 1978 amended the Bankruptcy Act of 1966 to add a new subsection (a) to 28 U. S. C. § 1471, providing that "[i]n any case under chapter 11 of title 11, United States Code, wherein the trustee has assumed the duties of collecting, paying, and accounting for taxes, the court shall have jurisdiction to enter a judgment against any person liable for such taxes, whether or not such person has appeared in the proceeding." Subsequently, respondent Northern filed a complaint in the District Court alleging that appellant insurance company had breached a contract of insurance covering Northern's automobile and seeking damages for personal injury resulting from the accident. Northern moved to transfer the case to the newly created bankruptcy court, claiming that the insurance company had failed to pay the premiums on the policy. The District Court transferred the case to the bankruptcy court, which dismissed the complaint on the ground that Northern's claim fell within the exclusive jurisdiction of the bankruptcy court under § 1471 (a). The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the bankruptcy court lacked jurisdiction over the case. Held: 1. The Bankruptcy Act of 1978 carried the possibility of an unwarranted encroachment upon the judicial power of the United States, which Art. III of the Constitution reserves for Art. III courts. While Congress possesses substantial discretion to prescribe the manner in which a congressionally created right may be adjudicated, including the assignment to an adjunct of some functions historically performed by judges, the functions of the adjunct must be limited in such a way that "the essential attributes" of judicial power are retained in the Art. III court. Here, although the Act's creation of a statutory right to sue for breach of contract and misrepresentation is not unlike the creation of a right to sue for maritime torts, which was upheld in Crowell v. Berg, 285 U. S. 462, the Act vests all "essential attributes" of the judicial power of the United States in the "adjunct" bankruptcy court, whereas in Crowell the agency assigned to make specialized, narrowly confined factual determinations regarding a particularized area of law had only a limited power to issue compensation orders pursuant to specialized procedures, and its orders could be enforced only by order of the district court. Unlike the administrative scheme in Crowell, the Act's "adjunct" bankruptcy courts exercise jurisdiction behind the facade of a grant to the district courts, and are exercising powers far greater than those lodged in the adjuncts approved in either Crowell or Raddatz v. United States, 447 U. S. 603. Pp. 108-116. 2. Since the Act's grant of jurisdiction to the bankruptcy courts presents an unprecedented question of interpretation of Art. III, and since retroactive application of this decision would not further the operation of the holding, and would surely visit substantial injustice and hardship upon those litigants who relied upon the Act's vesting of jurisdiction in the bankruptcy courts, the decision below shall apply only prospectively. Pp. 116-117. Affirmed.

In the case of United States v. Robinson, the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals, which had held that the heroin seized from Robinson was obtained through a search that violated the Fourth Amendment. The Supreme Court concluded that the search conducted by Officer Jenks, which led to the discovery of heroin on Robinson's person, did not violate the Fourth Amendment.

The Court reaffirmed the principle that a search incident to a lawful arrest is a traditional exception to the warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment. The Court distinguished between the search of the person of the arrestee and the search of the area within the control of the arrestee, noting that the former has been regarded as settled law and virtually unchallenged.

The Court of Appeals had limited the search of an arrestee to a frisk for weapons unless there was a reason to believe that further evidence of the crime for which the arrest was made could be found. However, the Supreme Court rejected this limitation, emphasizing that the authority to search an arrestee is not only based on the need to disarm and to discover evidence but also does not require additional justification beyond the fact of a lawful arrest.

The Court noted that the danger to an officer is greater after taking a suspect into custody, which justifies treating all custodial arrests alike for search purposes. The Court also rejected the idea that the justification for a search must be litigated in each case, stating that the authority to search incident to a lawful arrest does not depend on the probability that weapons or evidence would be found.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court held that a full search of the person is a reasonable search under the Fourth Amendment when it is incident to a lawful custodial arrest, and that no additional justification is required. The heroin seized from Robinson was therefore admissible evidence, and the judgment of the Court of Appeals was reversed.

In the case of Behrens v. Pelletier, the Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether a government official can appeal a denial of qualified immunity more than once before a case goes to trial. Qualified immunity protects government officials from civil liability as long as their actions do not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights.

The Court held that a defendant can appeal a denial of qualified immunity at both the motion to dismiss stage and the summary judgment stage. The Court reasoned that the qualified immunity defense is meant to protect officials not just from trial, but also from the burdens of pretrial matters such as discovery. Therefore, an order denying qualified immunity is considered a "final" decision that can be appealed immediately, even if other claims in the case are still pending.

The Court rejected the argument that an appeal is not available when factual disputes exist, clarifying that while determinations of evidentiary sufficiency are not appealable, legal questions about whether the conduct violated clearly established law are appealable.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. This decision confirms that government officials have the right to multiple appeals on qualified immunity before trial, which can potentially reduce the likelihood of unnecessary trials and pretrial proceedings.

In Montana v. United States, the Supreme Court ruled that Indian tribes have limited civil authority over non-Indians on non-Indian fee land within their reservations. The Court held that the inherent sovereign powers of an Indian tribe do not extend to the activities of nonmembers of the tribe, unless those activities fall under one of two exceptions: either they involve a consensual relationship between the tribe and the nonmember, or they pose a direct threat to the tribe's political integrity, economic security, or health or welfare.

In this case, the Navajo Nation attempted to impose a hotel occupancy tax on non-Navajo individuals staying at hotels located on non-Navajo fee land within the Navajo reservation. However, the Supreme Court determined that the tax violates Montana's general rule limiting the civil authority of Indian tribes over non-Indians on non-Indian fee land. The Court found that the Navajo Nation had not shown that the tax was connected to a consensual relationship between the tribe and the nonmembers, nor that it posed a direct threat to the tribe's political integrity, economic security, or health or welfare.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California today entered final judgments in a case brought by the United States Attorney's Office for the Central District of New York against California.  The court's order, which entered a final judgment on the merits of the case, permanently enjoins California from imposing a nationwide corporate franchise tax on foreign corporations.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Los Angeles, California, California and Washington, D.C., imposed a nationwide combined reporting obligation on foreign companies and foreign subsidiaries of domestic corporations. The SEC alleges that California's combined reporting obligations violated the Due Process and Due Process provisions of the federal tax laws. The court also ruled that California had a duty to determine whether to impose a worldwide combined reporting duty on foreign businesses.  In its final judgment, the court found that California violated the federal reporting obligations and imposed a "permanent injunction" against the imposition of the combined reporting requirement.  Without admitting or denying the Court's findings, the Court also ordered California to comply with its obligations under the federal securities laws, including Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordered the company to pay a civil penalty of $1,678, which is equal to the amount of income earned by each of its foreign subsidiaries. The company agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining it from future violations of the charged provisions. The settlement is subject to court approval.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 5444 (Aug. 20, 2018).  The SEC's Office of Investor Education and Advocacy has issued an Investor Alert on the dangers of multi-level tax reporting, including the potential for fraud. The Office of Regulatory Affairs has issued aÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the background of anyone selling or offering them an investment using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

In the case of Tilton v. Richardson, the Supreme Court addressed the constitutionality of the Higher Education Facilities Act of 1963, which provided federal construction grants for college and university facilities, with the stipulation that these facilities could not be used for sectarian instruction or religious worship. The Act also included a 20-year limitation on the government's interest in the facilities, after which the institutions could use them without restriction.

The Court found that the Act was intended to include colleges and universities with religious affiliations and that the primary objective of providing more opportunities for college education was a legitimate secular goal. The Court determined that the record supported the conclusion that the colleges involved had not violated the statutory restrictions and that their religious affiliations did not interfere with their secular educational functions.

However, the Court held that the 20-year limitation on the religious use of the facilities was unconstitutional. The Court reasoned that allowing unrestricted use of the facilities after 20 years effectively amounted to a contribution to a religious body, which violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

The Court distinguished this case from Lemon v. Kurtzman, noting that there was less danger of religious indoctrination in higher education compared to primary and secondary schools, the facilities provided were religiously neutral, and the aid was a one-time construction grant with minimal need for ongoing government surveillance.

The Court concluded that the Act did not foster an excessive government entanglement with religion and did not inhibit the free exercise of religion. The Court vacated the lower court's decision and remanded the case with directions to enter a judgment consistent with the opinion, except for the unconstitutional 20-year limitation.

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Ohio today filed a brief in support of the Ohio Department of Education's program that provides tuition assistance to parents of children living in the Cleveland City School District. The brief argues that the program does not violate the Constitution's guarantees of equal protection under the law and the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. In 1995, a Federal District Court placed the entire Cleveland school district under state control. The state auditor found that Cleveland's public schools were in the midst of a "crisis that is perhaps unprecedented in the history of American education." The state audit also found that only 1 in 10 ninth graders could pass a basic proficiency examination, and students at all levels performed at a dismal rate compared with students in other Ohio public schools. The program provides tuition aid for students in kindergarten through third grade, expanding each year through eighth grade, to attend a participating public or private school of their parent's choosing. The tuition aid portion of the program is designed to provide educational choices to parents who reside in a covered district. Any private school, whether religious or nonreligious, may participate in the program and accept program students so long as the school is located within the boundaries of a covered school and meets statewide educational standards. The test of the tuition aid program is whether the school has a policy of nondiscrimination. The court held that there is no policy of discrimination against non-religious private schools.

The Washington Promise Scholarship Program offers qualified students a grant to help cover tuition costs at participating colleges, including private, religiously affiliated institutions like respondent’s Northwest College. Eligible students must apply for admission to an “eligible” institution, which includes institutions accredited by a nationally recognized accrediting agency. An “eligible” institution must agree to certify that the student is enrolled at least half time and is not pursuing a degree in devotional theology. When petitioner Davey received a Promise Scholarship, he planned to study for a career as a pastor. However, once he learned that he could not use the scholarship to pursue a devotional theology degree, he declined to sign the certification form and did not receive any scholarship money. He then sued various state officials, alleging, inter alia, that the State’s exclusion of theology majors violated the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, as incorporated by the Fourteenth Amendment. The District Court rejected his claims, and the Ninth Circuit reversed. Held: The Promise Scholarship Program does not violate the Free Exercise Clause. This case presents the “room for play in the joints” between the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses. While the State could, consistent with the Federal Constitution, allow Promise Scholarships to be used to pursue a devotional theology degree, the State does not contend otherwise. Rather, the question here is whether the State, pursuant to its own constitution, can deny such funding without violating the Free Exercise Clause. The State’s disfavor of religion—which is of a much milder sort than the suppression of animal sacrifice held impermissible in Church of Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. Hialeah, 508 U. S. 520—imposes neither criminal nor civil sanctions on any type of religious service or rite, and does not require students to choose between their religious beliefs and receiving a government benefit. Thus, the State has merely chosen not to fund a particular category of instruction. Even though the Washington Constitution draws a more stringent line than the Federal Constitution, the interest it seeks to further is hardly novel. Most States that sought to avoid an establishment of religion around the time of the founding placed in their constitutions formal prohibitions against using tax funds to support the ministry. Nothing indicates that these provisions would not have applied so long as the State equally supported other professions or if the amount at stake was de minimis. Far from evincing hostility toward religion, the entirety of the Promise Scholarship Program goes a long way toward including religion in its benefits. The program allows students to attend pervasively religious schools, so long as they are accredited, and under its current guidelines, students remain eligible to take devotional theology courses. Certification forms show that most Northwest students are required to take several devotional courses, and some may have additional religious requirements as part of their majors. Pp. 718–726. 299 F. 3d 748, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of California granted summary judgment in favor of the Inyo County District Attorney's Office and the Sheriff, finding that the defendants violated the Tribe's right to self-government by executing a search warrant without authorization. The court also granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment, concluding that the Tribe did not have standing to sue in federal court because it was not a "person" subject to suit under the federal Indian Gaming Regulatory Act of 1934 (IGRA) and the federal common law of Indian affairs. The Tribe also argued that the search warrant violated its Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights, and that the District Attorney and Sheriff violated their authority to search tribal records. The Court agreed with the parties that, as a sovereign tribe, the Tribe does not qualify for federal court jurisdiction under IGRA. The trial and appellate courts have not clearly decided whether the case qualifies for federal-court jurisdiction because it arises under some federal law other than  1983. We therefore remand the case for close consideration and specific resolution of the threshold question.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Federal Express Corporation (FedEx) in a civil injunctive action brought by 14 former and current and former couriers over the age of 40 who sought to represent a class of retirees who were subject to alleged acts of age discrimination by FedEx.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed on April 30, 2002, Federal Express initiated two programs, designed to make its 45,000-strong courier network more productive. The programs tied the couriers’ compensation and continued employment to certain performance benchmarks, for instance the number of stops a courier makes per day. The complaint alleges that the programs were veiled attempts to force older couriers out of the company before they would be entitled to receive retirement benefits.  The complaint further alleges that, in 2001, the agency filed a Form 5 (a charge) with the Commission, which required the agency to respond to the complaint at least 60 days before filing a charge. The SEC alleges that this filing violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 17a-3 thereunder, and the reporting provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4), of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and Rule 206(3)-8 thereunder. Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the complaint seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  Federal Express has agreed to settle the case against it by consenting to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, orders it to pay a civil penalty of $1.5 million, and orders the company to pay an $80,000 civil penalty. The settlement is subject to court approval.

Title: United States v. Alvin A. Miklowitz

Case Number: 91-1021

Date Decided: June 29, 1992

Supreme Court Justices: William J. Brennan Jr., Byron White, John Paul Stevens, Antonin Scalia, Ruth Ginsburg

Summary: In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that the Second Amendment did not protect the rights of individuals to carry weapons openly in public places. The court held that the right to bear arms was protected only in the context of hunting or sport shooting, and that the ability to carry weapons openly in public places was a privilege rather than a right. The court also noted that the majority of states had banned open carry of weapons, and that the right to bear arms was not absolute.

The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of a man who refused to testify before a federal grand jury investigating allegations of violations of the Motor Carrier Act. The Court found that Section 205(e) of the Interstate Commerce Act grants a witness testifying in a grand jury investigation the same immunity as if they were testifying in a court trial, including immunity from prosecution based on their testimony. The Court rejected arguments that the immunity provided by Section 205(e) is not fully importable into Part II of the Interstate Commerce Act, or that the immunity is not commensurate with that of Part I. The Court also found that the procedures used by the district court in adjudicating the man in contempt were constitutional and proper.

This case involves a lawsuit brought by a man named Matthew Snyder against a religious organization called the Westboro Baptist Church. The dispute arose after the church organized a protest outside of Snyder's home, which included pickets bearing signs with inflammatory language directed towards Snyder and his family. Snyder alleges that the protests caused him significant emotional distress and seeks compensation for various torts, including intentional infliction of emotional distress, invasion of privacy, and civil conspiracy. The case raises important questions about the limits of free speech under the First Amendment and the role of religion in public life.

Title: Preemption Clause Exclusion of Self-Insured Benefit Plans from Insurance Regulation

Summary: This case involves a challenge to the constitutionality of a provision in the Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA) that excludes self-insured employee benefit plans from the requirement to provide notice to employees regarding the availability of family leave. The plaintiff argues that the provision violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment by treating self-insured plans unfairly compared to fully insured plans. The defendant contends that the provision is necessary to prevent confusion among employers about their compliance obligations under the FMLA. The Supreme Court holds that the provision is constitutional and serves a legitimate government interest in avoiding confusion among employers.

Respondents, an Indian organization, individual Indians, nature organizations and individual members of those organizations, and the State of California, challenged both the road-building and timber-harvesting decisions in the Federal District Court, claiming that the decisions violated the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause, the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (FWPCA), the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), several other federal statutes, and governmental trust responsibilities to Indians living on the Hoopa Valley Reservation. The District Court issued a permanent injunction prohibiting the Government from constructing the Chimney Rock section of the G-O road or putting the Timber-Harvesting management plan into effect. The court found that both actions would violate the Free exercise Clause because they would seriously damage the salient visual features of the area, and that the Government could have abandoned the road without thereby creating a religious preserve for a single group in violation of the establishment clause. The Ninth Circuit affirmed in part, rejecting the District Court's conclusion that the proposed actions would breach its trust responsibilities. The panel also vacated the injunction to the extent that it had been rendered moot by the California Wilderness Act, which now prevents timber harvesting in certain areas covered by the district court's order. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The First Amendment does not prohibit the Government's construction of a road through a portion of a National Forest that has traditionally been used for religious purposes by members of three American Indian tribes in northwestern California. Pp. 4-18. (a) The First and First Amendments do not prohibit direct coercion or penalties on the free exercise of religion, not just outright prohibitions, are subject to scrutiny under the First and the First Amendments. The Constitution does not permit government to discriminate against religions that treat particular physical sites as sacred, and a law prohibiting the Indian respondents from visiting the area would raise a different set of constitutional questions. Nor does it permit the Government to dictate the conduct of its internal procedures. Nor can the Government be more solicitous, since the Government is not required to show a compelling need to complete the road or to engage in timber harvesting. Nor is the Government required to bring forward a compelling justification for its otherwise lawful actions. P. 5. (b) In order that the injunction may be reconsidered in light of this holding, and in the light of any other relevant events that may have intervened since the injunction issued, the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion of this Court. The Government, which petitioned for certiorari on the constitutional issue alone, has informed the Court that it believes it can cure the statutory defects identified below, intends to do so, and will not challenge the adverse statutory rulings. Moreover, the silence of the Ninth Circuit as to the necessity of reaching that issue may have reflected its understanding that the District-Court's injunction necessarily rested in part on constitutional grounds. The conclusion is strengthened by considerations of judicial economy, and this Court cannot determine the truth of the underlying beliefs that led to the religious objections here or in Roy, see Hobbie v. Yoder, 406 U. S. 205, and accordingly cannot say that the "impact" on the Amish religion would have been constitutionally problematic if the statute at issue had not been coercive in nature. Cf. Hobbie, supra, at 692-693. The courts below properly relied on a factual inquiry into the degree to which the Indians' spiritual practices would become ineffectual if the road were built. They rely on several cases in which this Court has sustained free exercise challenges to government programs that interfered with individuals' ability to practice their religion. See, e. g., Bowen v. Roy, 476 U.S. 693, where ineligibility for unemployment benefits, based solely on a refusal to violate the Sabbath, has been analogized to a fine imposed on Sabbath worship. This does not and cannot imply that incidental effects of government programs, which may make it more difficult to practice certain religions but which have no tendency to coerce individuals into acting contrary to their religious beliefs, require government to bring forth a compelling rationale for its actions. The crucial word in the constitutional text is "prohibit," which means "to the individual, not in terms of what the individual can exact from the government." Sherbert v. Verner, 374 U.

In this case, the Supreme Court of the United States decided that the Kake and Angoon Indians did not have the right to use fish traps in the rivers and lakes near their villages in Alaska. The Court held that the use of fish traps was harmful to the salmon population and that the Indians had no legal right to use them. The Court also held that the Alaska Statehood Act did not reserve the right to use fish traps for the Indians.

Petitioner Bowles was convicted of murder and sentenced to prison. While incarcerated, he filed a habeas action challenging his conviction. When the District Court denied him relief, he filed an appeal. Under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(6), the District Court extended the time to file the appeal for 14 days, but Bowles filed his notice of appeal outside that window. Respondents argue that the Court of Appeals lacked jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. Held: The Court of Appeals properly concluded that it lacked jurisdiction. Statutes setting time limits for appealing judgments are jurisdictional. See, e.g., Kontrick v. Ryan, 540 U. S. 443. Here, the relevant statute, 28 U. S. C. §2107(c), sets a maximum duration for extensions of the time to file a notice of appeal. By failing to file his notice of appeal within the statutorily mandated time frame, Bowles deprived the Court of Appeals of jurisdiction. His untimely filing does not fall within the “unique circumstances” exception created by Harris Truck Lines, Inc. v. Cherry Meat Packers, Inc., 371 U. S. 215, which has been rarely invoked since it was decided. Overruling Harris Truck Lines and Thompson v. INS, 375 U. S. 384, to the extent they purport to authorize an exception to a jurisdictional rule, this Court declares that the timely filing of a notice of appeal in a civil case is a jurisdictional requirement. Pp. 3−8. 455 F. 3d 337, affirmed. Roberts, C. J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Roberts, JJ., joined. Souter, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Stevens, Ginsburg, and Breyer, JJ., joined.

The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the jurisdiction of a tribal court to adjudicate a discrimination claim related to the sale of fee land on a tribal reservation by a non-Indian bank to non-Indian individuals. An Indian couple, who were customers of the bank and had defaulted on their loans, claimed that the bank discriminated against them by offering the land to non-Indians on more favorable terms. The tribal court ruled in favor of the Indian couple, awarding them damages and the right to purchase a portion of the land.

The Supreme Court held that the tribal court did not have jurisdiction to adjudicate the discrimination claim concerning the sale of fee land owned by the non-Indian bank. The Court reasoned that tribes generally do not have authority over non-Indians who come within their borders, especially when the nonmember's activity occurs on land owned in fee simple by non-Indians. The Court recognized two exceptions to this principle, which allow tribes to regulate the activities of nonmembers who enter consensual relationships with the tribe or its members, or when nonmember conduct threatens the political integrity, economic security, or health or welfare of the tribe. However, the Court found that neither exception applied in this case.

The Court also addressed the argument that the bank consented to tribal court jurisdiction by seeking the tribal court's assistance in serving a notice to quit. The Court concluded that seeking assistance for a state-court action did not constitute consent to future litigation in the tribal court.

The implications of the decision are that tribal courts do not have the authority to regulate the sale of non-Indian fee land, even if the land is located within the reservation, and that tribal jurisdiction over nonmembers is limited. The decision reinforces the principle that tribal sovereignty is confined to managing tribal land and internal matters, and does not extend to the regulation of non-Indian land sales. The ruling clarifies the scope of tribal jurisdiction and the rights of non-Indians with respect to land transactions on reservations.

Petitioner, a member of the Jehovah's Witnesses, resigned from his job at a manufacturing company because of his religious convictions that prohibited him from participating in the production of armaments. After exhausting his remedies in the state courts, he sought unemployment compensation benefits pursuant to an Indiana statute providing such benefits to individuals whose separation from employment was "not caused by misconduct" and who "left work for good cause connected with the work." The Referee found that petitioner had separated from his job because of his religious convictions, but that his separation was not based upon a "good cause" objectively related to the work. Concluding that petitioner had separated from his job for personal reasons, the Referee denied him benefits. The Indiana Review Board affirmed. The Indiana Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the Indiana statute improperly burdened petitioner's rights under the Federal Constitution. Held: Petitioner is entitled to unemployment compensation benefits. Pp. 108-116. (a) Based upon the record, it is clear that petitioner terminated his employment for religious reasons. Although the Indiana Supreme Court concluded that it was uncertain what petitioner's belief was and what the religious basis of his belief was, the record shows that petitioner drew a line, and it is not for this Court to say that the line he drew was an unreasonable one. Moreover, the Indiana Supreme Court gave significant weight to the fact that another Jehovah's Witness had no scruple about working on tank turrets, thus appearing to assume that intrafaith differences of that sort are uncommon among followers of a particular creed and that the judicial process is singularly ill equipped to resolve such differences in relation to the Religion Clauses. Pp. 108-111. (b) Where the state conditions receipt of an important benefit upon conduct proscribed by a religious faith, or where it denies such a benefit because of conduct mandated by religious belief, thereby putting substantial pressure on an adherent to modify his behavior and to violate his beliefs, a burden upon religion exists. Here, as in Sherbert v. Verner, 374 U. S. 398, the employee was put to a choice between fidelity to religious belief or cessation of work. The coercive impact on petitioner is indistinguishable from Sherbert, where the Court held that the pressure upon the employee to cease practicing her religion was unmistakable. Pp. 111-113. (c) The mere fact that petitioner's religious practice is burdened by a governmental program does not mean that an accommodation must be granted. The State may justify an inroad on religious liberty by showing that it is the least restrictive means of achieving some compelling state interest. Neither of the interests urged to sustain the Indiana statute-avoidance of widespread unemployment and the consequent burden on the unemployment compensation fund, and avoiding detailed probing by employers into job applicants' religious beliefs--is sufficiently compelling to justify the burden upon petitioner's religious liberty. Pp. 113-115. (d) To compel benefit payments to petitioner does not involve the State in fostering a religious faith. See Sherbert, supra, at 409. Unless this Court is prepared to overrule Sherbert, supra, petitioner cannot be denied the benefits due him on the basis of the findings of the Refere, the Review Board, and the Indiana Court of Appeals that he terminated his employment because of his religious convictions. Pp. 115-116. Reversed.
*Note: The text above is the majority opinion written by Justice John Marshall Harlan II.

The Racketeering Influence Organization (RIO) is a group of individuals involved in organized crime. The term "organized" refers to the structure and hierarchy of the criminal organization, as well as the level of coordination among members. The RIO typically consists of leaders, middle managers, and foot soldiers, each responsible for carrying out specific tasks within the organization. Members of the RIO often engage in illegal activities such as drug trafficking, extortion, gambling, prostitution, and protection rackets.

The Supreme Court of the United States holds that the anti-injunction act's relitigation exception does not permit a federal court to enter an injunction preventing a state court from deciding a class certification question. The Court finds that the issues in the federal and state lawsuits differed because the relevant legal standards differed. Additionally, the Court finds that the mere proposal of a class in the federal action could not bind individuals who were not parties there. Therefore, the judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed.

Under the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA), certain federal employees may obtain administrative and judicial review of specified ad- verse employment actions. Section 3328 (hereinafter §3328) bars from employment by an Executive agency anyone who has knowingly and willfully failed to register. Petitioners are former federal competitive service employees who failed to comply with the Military Selective Service Act, 50 U. S. C. App. §453. That Act requires male citizens and permanent-resident aliens of the United States between the ages of 18 and 26 to register for the Selective Services. Pursuant to Section 33 28, petitioners were discharged (or allegedly constructively discharged) by respondents, their employing agencies. Among petitioners, only Michael Elgin appealed his removal to the MSPB. Elgin argued that Section 3329 is an unconstitutional bill of attainder and unconstitutionally discriminates on the basis of sex when combined with the registration requirement of the MilitarySelective Service. The MSP Board referred Elgin’s appeal to an ad- ministrative law judge for an initial decision. The ALJ dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction. The District Court concluded that it retained jurisdiction under the general grant of federal-question jurisdiction in 28 U.S. C §1331, which gives district courts authority over constitutional claims, even though they are constitutional claims for equitable relief. The Court of Appeals vacated the judgment and remanded with instructions to dismiss. Held: The CSRA does not pre-cline district court jurisdiction over petitioners’ claims. Pp. 5–11. (a) The CSR’re “integrated scheme” for aggrieved federal employees is designed to replace an “outdated patchwork of statutes and rules” that afforded employees the right to challenge employing agency actions in district courts across the country. Fausto Co. v. Reich, 510 U. s. 200, distinguished. The CSRB’ “clear intent” is to provide alternative forums for judicial review based on the nature of an employees’ claim. See, e.g., id., at 441–441, 448. Moreover, the CSRA provides review in the Federal Circuit, an Article III court fully competent to adjudicate petitions’ constitutional claims. Cf. Thunder Basin Coal Co., Inc., 498 U . S. 439, at 214–215. P. 5. (b) Although petitioners argue that their claims are not the type that Congress intended to be reviewed within the CSR scheme, they are the vehicle by which they seek to reverse removal decisions, return to federal employment, and receive the compensation they would have earned but for the adverse employment action. See Id., at 44–45, and petitioners are correct that the CSB routinely adjudicates some constitutional claims and that the case therefore did not present the ‘serious constitutional question’ that would arise if an agency statute were construed to preclude all judicial review. See Schmittling v. Department of Army, 219 F. 3d 1332, 1336. The case before this Court is a challenge to CSRA covered employment action brought by CSRA-covered employees requesting relief that the CCSRA routinely affords. The purpose of CSRA also supports the conclusion that the statutory review scheme is exclusive, even for employees who bring constitutional challenges to federal statutes. See §7703(b)(2). Petitioners contend that their claim is not “fairly discernible” because it does not expressly bar suits in district court, since it is fairly discernible that Congress did not intend to exclude such claims from exclusive review before the Federal District Court and the Circuit. The fact that petitioners overlook the many threshold questions that may accompany a constitutional claim may obviate the need to address the constitutional challenge, and the case could be “meaningfully addressed” in the Court of appeals, could be remedied in the court of Appeals, and could be considered “by the Court.” Thunder Basin, supra, at 215–215 (internal quotation marks omitted). Moreover, since petitioners do not dispute that they are employees who suffered adverse actions covered by the foregoing provisions, they see no reason to conclude that this Court intended to exempt such claims. Nor do petitioners contest that, absent another infirmity in the adverse action, the MSCB will affirm the MSAB decision rather than dismiss the appeal. See Thunder Basin. At 216–215, the court expressly found that the statute precluded district court authority over petitioner Tucker, who contends that his resignation amounted to a constructive discharge, and that these claims must be brought within CSRA review. The court did not decide the merits of the petitioner Elgin case on the threshold jurisdictional question, but merely dismissed the claim. The judgment of the court, however, was reversed for lack-of- jurisdiction. See Tr. of Oral Arguments 32, 33–44, n. 1. Petitionerai’

After being hired as an associate attorney by respondent law partnership, petitioner, a woman, alleges that respondent promised to consider her for partnership on a "fair and equal basis"; that she relied on this representation when accepting employment; and that ultimately she was passed over for partnership. Subsequently, petitioner filed a charge with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, claiming that respondent had violated Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 by discriminating against her on the basis of her sex in violation of that title. Respondentsuite was dismissed by the Federal District Court on the ground that Title VII was inapplicable to the selection of partners by a partnership. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Petitioner's complaint stated a claim cognizable under Title VII, and thus she is entitled to her day in court to prove her allegations. Pp. 108-113. (a) Acceptance of petitioner's allegations as true is required at this stage of the litigation. A court may dismiss a complaint only if it is clear that no relief could be granted under any set of facts that could be proved consistent with the allegations. P. 108. (b) Because the underlying employment relationship here involved is contractual, it follows that the "terms, conditions, or privileges of employment" clearly include benefits that are part of an employment contract. And since petitioner alleges that respondent made a contract to consider her for partnership, that promise clearly was a term, condition, or privilege of her employment. Alternatively, several allegations in petitioner's complaint would support the conclusion that the opportunity to become a partner was part and parcel of an associate's status as an employee at respondent's firm, independent of any allegation that such an opportunity was included in associates' employment contracts. Pp. 108-111. (c) Nothing in the change in status that advancement to partnership might entail means that partnership consideration falls outside the terms of the statute. Even if respondent is correct that a partnership invitation is not itself an offer of employment, Title VII would nonetheless apply and preclude discrimination on the basis of sex. The benefit a plaintiff is denied need not be employment to fall within Title VII's protection; it need only be a term, condition, or privilege of employment. Furthermore, there is nothing in the statutory language or legislative history that supports respondent's argument that Title VII categorically exempts partnership decisions from scrutiny. Finally, respondent has not shown how its ability to fulfill a distinctive role in society would be inhibited by a requirement that it consider petitioner for partnership on her merits. Pp. 111-113. 678 F. 2d 1022, reversed and remanded.

Respondent was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death. The Arizona death penalty statute, Ariz. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 13-703(F)(6), requires a State to "channel the sentencer's discretion by "clear and objective standards" that provide "specific and detailed guidance," and that "make rationally reviewable the process for imposing a sentence of death." Respondent then petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus in Federal District Court, alleging that Arizona's interpretation of its "especially heinous ... or depraved" aggravating circumstance was unconstitutionally overbroad and vague. The court rejected respondent's vagueness and overbreadth challenge to the aggravating circumstances. The Court of Appeals vacated the death sentence on the ground that, under Arizona law, "this court independently reviews the facts that the trial court found established the presence or absence of aggravating and mitigating circumstances, and we determine for ourselves if the latter outweigh the former when we find both to be present." Held: 1. Arizona's construction of the subsection (F) (6) aggravating condition in this case contravened this Court's decisions in Godfrey v. Georgia, 446 U. S. 420, 428, and Maynard v. Cartwright, 486 U.S. 356. Pp. 531-532. (a) In determining whether a State has adopted a constitutionally narrow construction of a facially vague aggravation circumstance, the "fundamental constitutional requirement" of "channeling and limiting . . . the sentencers' discretion in imposing the death penalty," Cartwright's rule of Jackson v. Virginia, supra, and the "rational factfinder" standard established in Arkansas v. Jeffers, supra. P. 534. (b) The Arizona Supreme Court's narrowing construction to the facts of respondent's case does not render the state court's finding arbitrary or capricious, and is therefore an unconstitutional application of the standard. In light of the Arizona Court's holding that a State's application of its narrowing construction is constitutionally sufficient because it gives meaningful guidance to its sentencer, and in light of that Court's narrow construction, the Arizona court could reasonably have concluded that respondent committed the murder in an especially heinous, cruel, and depraved manner, the court's decision in Walton v. Arizona, which held that, even if Arizona had adopted such a narrowing construction, and even if it applied that narrowing construction in a manner sufficient "to cure the unfettered discretion of the jury and to satisfy the commands of the Eighth Amendment," is equally applicable in safeguarding that Eighth Amendment's bedrock guarantee against the arbitrary orcapricious imposition of death penalty. In making such a determination, respect for a State court's findings of fact and application of itself's own law counsels against the sort of de novo review undertaken by the court of Appeals in this instance. P p. 535. (c) Where the issue is solely whether a state court has properly found the existence of a constitutionally narrowed aggravating situation, we have never required federal courts "to peer majestically over the [state] court's shoulder so that [they] might second-guess" the state courts' construction of that circumstance, see, e.g., Maynard, Cartwright.

Appellees, who were members of a crowd protesting President Johnson's speech in Bell County, Texas, brought this action in Federal District Court against Bell County officials, seeking that enforcement of the disturbing-the-peace statute be temporarily and permanently enjoined, and that the statute be declared unconstitutional on its face, "and/or as applied to the conduct of the Plaintiffs herein." After dismissal of the state charges, appellees filed a motion to dismiss the complaint on the ground that "no useful purpose could now be served by the granting of an injunction to prevent the prosecution of these suits because same no longer exists." The District Court held that the only interlocutory orders that this Court has power to review under § 1253 are those granting or denying preliminary injunctions. Held: 1. Until a three-judge district court issues an opinion expressing the view that a state statute should be enjoined as unconstitutional-and then fails to follow up with an injunction-the result is unfortunate at best. Pp. 463-464. 2. Until the District Court issues an order granting an injunction, or enters an order denying one, it is simply not possible to know with any certainty what the court has decided-a state of affairs that is conspicuously evident here. P. 464. 3. The absence of an injunctive order in this case has, in fact, been fully recognized by the parties. The restraint and tact that evidently motivated the district court in refraining from the entry of such an order are understandable. But when a threejudge court issues such an opinion, and then fails, to follow-up with such a court, the result is bad at best, and the parties are unable to know precisely what the three-junction court intended to enjoin, and unable as well to appeal to this Court. Id. 4. In the absence of any order of any kind, there is no power under the Three-Judge Court Act to "remand to the court below" or deal with the merits of this case in any way at all, and it is precisely because the district Court has issued neither an injunction nor an order granting or denying one that the Court has no power to 'remand' to the courts below' or to deal with this case's merits in any manner at all. Id., 4. When a federal court is asked to nullify a law duly enacted by a sovereign State, it must know with certainty what it has decided, and this Court must be prepared to do so. Id, supra, to prevent confusion and to prevent such confusion. Id . . . Id., supra, supra.

This decision upheld the legality of mandatory blood tests for drivers suspected of driving under the influence of drugs or alcohol. The Court ruled that the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination did not apply to blood tests, as they were not "communicative acts" or "testimony". Additionally, the Court determined that the Fourth Amendment's protection of personal privacy did not extend to blood tests, as they were not invasive enough to justify a warrant.

In a Supreme Court opinion regarding private securities fraud actions, the Court addressed whether plaintiffs must prove "loss causation" to obtain class certification. Loss causation refers to the need to show that the defendant's deceptive actions caused the plaintiff's economic loss. The case involved the Erica P. John Fund, Inc. (EPJ Fund), which filed a class action against Halliburton Co., alleging that Halliburton made false statements that inflated its stock price, leading to investor losses when the truth was revealed.

The District Court initially denied class certification based on circuit precedent requiring proof of loss causation at this stage. The Court of Appeals affirmed this decision. However, the Supreme Court held that plaintiffs do not need to prove loss causation to certify a class. The Court reasoned that loss causation pertains to the actual cause of economic loss, not to the presumption of reliance on a misrepresentation by investors when buying or selling stock.

The Court clarified that reliance and loss causation are distinct concepts. Reliance is about whether investors based their transaction on a misrepresentation, while loss causation is about whether that misrepresentation caused a subsequent economic loss. The Court emphasized that the requirement imposed by the Court of Appeals contradicted the principle that investors are presumed to rely on the integrity of the market price, which reflects all publicly available information, including any misrepresentations.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion. The Court did not address any other questions about the presumption of reliance or its rebuttal, leaving those issues to be potentially considered on remand.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a tax-exempt organization for failing to comply with the federal tax laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that The American College of Physicians (ACOP) violated the antifraud provisions of the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) 1934 Rules of Practice.  According to the complaint, the IRS's 1934 Rules imposed a per se rule of taxation for commercial advertising in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine (Annals) for the purpose of raising revenue.  As alleged, the 1934 Rules expressly prohibited the publication of advertisements that did not directly or indirectly relate to the purposes of the journal's exemption from federal taxation.  For example, as alleged in the Complaint, the 1933 Rules prohibited the dissemination of advertisements without a specific basis for the exemption.  In contrast, the 1940 Rules required the dissemination and dissemination of information about the use of medical products and services, including pharmaceuticals, medical supplies, and equipment useful in the practice of internal medicine, without regard to the source of those advertisements.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint in the Commission Reports, the Court of Appeals held that ASCOP violated Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  ASCOP's complaint charges ASCOP with violations of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4)-8 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus interest, and civil penalties against ASCOP and its associated entities. Â The SEC's investigation was conducted in the SEC's New York Regional Office and supervised by Marc Blau.   The litigation will be led by Mr. Blau and Ms. Sansone.

The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) provides for payment of certain covered medical expenses and requires a beneficiary who “receives benefits” under the plan for such injuries “to ‘reimburse [Mid Atlantic]’ for those benefits from ‘a]ll recoveries from a third party (whether by lawsuit, settlement, or otherwise).’” App. to Pet. for Cert. 38a. Mid Atlantic paid the Sereboffs $74,869.37, plus interest, with a deduction for Mid Atlantic’s share of the attorney’d fees and court costs the defendants had incurred in state court. The Serebofts appealed and Mid Atlantic sought a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction requiring Mid Atlantic to retain and set aside the proceeds. The District Court approved a stipulation by the parties, under which Mid Atlantic agreed to “preserve” a portion of the settlement funds in an investment account, “until the [District] Court rules on the merits of this case and all appeals, if any, are exhausted.” On the merits, the District Court found Mid Atlantic in its favor and ordered Mid Atlantic liable for the damages it had paid on their behalf. On appeal, Mid Atlantic filed suit under §502(a)(3) of ERISA, seeking to collect from Mid Atlantic the medical expenses it paid on the Serebos’ behalf. Since Mid Atlantic had already distributed the settlement proceeds to them, it sought to set aside at least $74.37 from the proceeds, but Mid Atlantic sent similar correspondence to the attorney and to the attorneys, repeating its claim to a lien on a portion, and detailing the medical expense as they accrued and were paid by the plan. The court found in Mid Atlantic its favor, but ordered MidAtlantic to pay Mid Atlantic $74.,869, with an interest deduction of Mid Atlantic's share of its share of attorney fees, court costs, and other court costs. On the ground that Mid Atlantic failed to meet its claimed lien requirement, the court found that it was equitable because it was a subrogation claim. The Court thereafter affirmed Mid Atlantic. Held: Mid Atlantic is a fiduciary under ERISA and that its suit in District Court was “enforce … the terms of ” the “Acts of Third Parties” provision. Pp. 6–11. (a) Mid Atlantic need not characterize its claim as a freestanding action for equitable subrogative. The parcel of equitable defenses the Serebleffs claim accompany any such action are beside the point. P. 11. (b) MidAtlantic’ action in the District court properly sought “equitable relief ” under §501(a) (3). The judgment of the Fourth Circuit is affirmed in relevant part. It is so ordered.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit has ruled that a Texas law prohibiting the 'disturbing the peace' of a public place is impermissibly and unconstitutionally broad. The law was passed in response to a protest at a speech by President Lyndon Johnson in Bell County, Texas, in December 1967 .<n>The court held that the law violated the First Amendment right to free speech. The court ruled that the defendants had failed to show that they would be harmed by enforcement of the law. The ruling is a victory for civil rights groups that have long fought against the laws that criminalize peaceful protest. The case is being closely watched by civil rights activists in other states who are seeking similar relief.

1. A contemplated merger between the G. R. Kinney Company, Inc. (Kinney), a leading manufacturer of men's, women's, and children's shoes, and a retailer with over 1,230 owned, operated or controlled retail outlets, would violate § 7 of the Clayton Act, 15 U. S. C. § 18, which provides that "no corporation engaged in commerce shall acquire, directly or indirectly, the whole or any part of the stock or other share capital . . . of another corporation engaged also in commerce, where in any line of commerce in any section of the country, the effect of such acquisition may be substantially to lessen competition, or to tend to create a monopoly." Pp. 531-532. 2. The District Court properly defined the relevant geographic markets in which to analyze this merger as those cities with a population exceeding 10,000 and their immediate contiguous surrounding territory in which both Kinney and Kinney sold shoes at retail. P. 532. 3. The "area of effective competition" must be determined by reference to a product market (the "line of commerce") and a geographic market (a geographic market), and the supervision of the plan so accepted. In this case, the District Court concluded that the merger would be shown not to endanger competition if the "line(s) of commerce" and the "section(s)" were properly determined. Held: 1. The record supports the conclusion that the relevant lines of commerce are men's and women's shoes in the United States, and that, in the face of the antitrust laws, the most intense and important competition in retail sales will be confined to stores within the particular communities in which the two companies are located. P p. 533. (a) The fact that two merging firms have competed directly on the horizontal level in but a fraction of the geographic markets of which either has operated, does not, in itself, place their merger outside the scope of § 7, and the propriety of divestiture was considered below and is disputed here on an "all or nothing" basis. It is ripe for review now, and will, thereafter, be foreclosed. Repetitive judicial consideration of the same question in a single suit will not occur here, since the trend toward vertical integration in the shoe industry, when combined with Brown's avowed policy of forcing its own shoes upon its retail subsidiaries, may foreclose competition from a substantial share of the markets for men's-women's, children's-and-children's-shoes, without producing any countervailing competitive, economic, or social advantages. Pp 533-534. (b) The record also supports the Court's conclusion that, insofar as the vertical aspect of this merger is concerned, the relevant market is the entire Nation. The relevant geographic market is a "necessary predicate" to an examination of the anticompetitive effects of the merger viewed vertically or of the horizontal merger of Brown's andKinney's manufacturing facilities, and it is necessary to examine the effects of a merger in each such economically significant submarket to determine if there is a reasonable probability that the effect will substantially lessen competition. If such a probability is found to exist, the merger is proscribed. This is not to say, however, that "price/quality" differences, where they exist, are unimportant in analyzing a merger; they may be of importance in determining the likely effect of it, and to recognize competition where, in fact, competition exists. Moreover, the legislative history of the original Clayton Act indicates clearly that the tests for measuring the legality of any particular economic arrangement under the Act are to be less stringent than those used in applying the Sherman Act, which had been interpreted by this Court to require a determination of the extent to which a merger's effect on competition is to be determined. Pc. 534, 541. (c) In the absence of any mitigating factors, such as the business failure or the inadequate resources of one of the parties that may have prevented it from maintaining its competitive position, the percentage of the market foreclosed by the vertical arrangement cannot itself be decisive. The percentage of that market foreclosing by the merger cannot be determined on the basis of the facts available to it, but the fact that Brown manufactures significant, comparable quantities of virtually every type of nonrubber men's shoes and a number of other products, distinct customers, distinct prices, sensitivity to price changes, and specialized vendors, all are aspects, varying in importance with the merger under consideration, which would properly be taken into account. Pct. 535, 537. (d) A review of the sources of the court's jurisdiction is a threshold inquiry appropriate to the disposition of every case that comes before this Court.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant in a civil action brought by the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida against him.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia, alleges that, from at least 1940 through the late 1940s, the defendants violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  According to the complaint, defendants agreed to the entry of judgments that permanently enjoined them from violating the federal securities laws.  In addition, the court found that defendants were entitled to the right to refuse service to any person who was not a member of the same race, regardless of whether he or she was a citizen or not.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's findings, defendants consented to permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties.  Defendants also agreed to pay a $10,000 civil penalty.   The court's final judgment, which permanently enjoins defendants from violating these provisions, orders the defendants to pay disgorgment of $1,000, and orders them to pay civil penalties of $20,000 each.
