The Supreme Court case in question revolves around the constitutionality of Minnesota's Private Pension Benefits Protection Act as it applies to Allied Structural Steel Co. The Act imposed a "pension funding charge" on employers who either terminated their pension plans or closed a Minnesota office, if the pension funds were insufficient to cover full pensions for employees with at least 10 years of service. Allied Structural Steel Co. argued that this Act violated the Contract Clause of the U.S. Constitution by impairing its contractual obligations to its employees.

The Supreme Court acknowledged that while the Contract Clause does not completely eliminate the state's police power to act for the public welfare, it does impose limits on the state's ability to alter existing contractual relationships. The Court examined the severity of the impairment caused by the Act, noting that contracts allow individuals to rely on established rights and obligations.

The Court found that the Act severely impaired the company's contractual obligations by retroactively modifying the terms of the pension plan and imposing a substantial and unanticipated liability. The Act's narrow focus and lack of connection to a broad societal interest distinguished it from other laws that had previously withstood Contract Clause challenges. The Court concluded that the Act did not meet the necessary standards of reasonableness and necessity to justify its interference with private contracts.

Therefore, the Supreme Court reversed the District Court's judgment, holding that the Minnesota law unconstitutionally impaired the company's contractual obligations under the Contract Clause. Justice Blackmun did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

After hearing evidence that petitioner Lassiter had not provided her infant son William with proper medical care, the District Court of N. C. adjudicated him a neglected child and transferred him to the custody of the Durham County Department of Social Services, the respondent here. A year later, after hearing evidence of petitioner's failure to provide her son with adequate medical care and having made no efforts to plan for his future, the Department petitioned the court to terminate her parental rights because she "has not had any contact with the child since December of 1975" and "has willfully left the child in foster care for more than two consecutive years without showing that substantial progress has been made in correcting the conditions which led to the removal of the child, or without showing a positive response to the diligent efforts of the Department to strengthen her relationship to the child or to make and follow through with constructive planning for the future of the Child." The court terminated her status as the Department's parent. The State Supreme Court summarily denied the application for discretionary review. Held: An indigent parent is entitled to the assistance of appointed counsel not only in parental termination proceedings, but also in dependency and neglect proceedings as well. Pp. 531-532. (a) The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires the appointment of counsel when a State seeks to terminate an indigent's parental status. P. 533. (b) The Court's precedents speak with one voice about what "fundamental fairness" has meant when the Court has considered the right to appointed counsel, and they thus draw from them the presumption that an indigant has a right to the appointed counsel only when, if he loses, he may be deprived of his physical liberty. The pre-eminent generalization that emerges from the precedents on an indictigent's right to appoint counsel is that such a right has been recognized to exist only where the litigant may lose his physically liberty if he is unsuccessful. Thus, child-custody litigation must be concluded as rapidly as is consistent with fairness, and the Court must balance these elements against each other, and then set their net weight in the scales against the presumption of there is a right only where indigent, if unsuccessful, may lose their personal freedom. This Court's decisions have by now made plain beyond the need for multiple citation that a parent's desire for and right to "the companionship, care, custody and management of his or her children" is an important interest that "undeniably warrants deference and, absent a powerful countervailing interest, protection." Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U. S. 645, 651, and here, as in that case, "t]he facts and circumstances . . . are susceptible of almost infinite variation. . . ." 411 U.S., at 790, 93 S.Ct. 893, 903, 47 L.Ed. 2d 18, and it is against this presumption that all the other elements in the due process decision must be measured.

The case of "Youngstown Sheet Metal Company Ltd. v. Harris" deals with the legality of President Franklin D. Roosevelt's Executive Order 10340, which established the War Production Board during World War II. The order gave the president broad powers to regulate industry and commerce during the war. The case raises questions about the extent of presidential power under the Constitution and the role of the courts in checking abuses of power.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Washington today entered a final judgment against a defendant in a civil injunctive action brought by the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York.  According to the SEC's complaint, Donna Rae Egelhoff was employed by the Boeing Company, which provided him with a life insurance policy and a pension plan. Both plans were governed by ERISA, and the Egelhoffs were his statutory heirs under state law. The complaint alleges that the Washington statute pre-empts the ERISA pre-emption provisions, and requires that plan administrators pay benefits to the beneficiary of the plan, rather than to those identified in the plan documents.  The complaint further alleges that, in the absence of a qualified named beneficiary, the proceeds would pass to the beneficiaries as their own.  In a parallel action, the U.N. Office of Economic and Risk Analysis (OIEA) today announced that it has issued an order suspending the registration of certain ERISA plans.  OIEA's order suspending registration of ERISA plan beneficiaries would be a violation of the federal securities laws, as well as the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, EIEA has consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating the above-mentioned provisions, orders it to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty of $46,000.  It also imposes a $75,000 civil penalty against the defendant.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted in the Office of Compliance and Assurance, with assistance from John Rymas, Chief of the Enforcement Division's Market Abuse Unit. The litigation will be led by Mr. Dillingham and supervised by Chedly C. Dumornay.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Deschutes County Sheriff Bob Camreta and two state officials for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Oregon, alleges that, in 2003 and 2004, Camretas and two other state officials interviewed a girl at her elementary school about allegations that her father had molested her. The complaint alleges that the officials were entitled to qualified immunity from liability because no clearly established law had warned them of the illegality of their conduct. In addition, the complaint alleged that the government officials conducted an in-school interview that violated the federal securities laws because it was routine and did not require a warrant to conduct the interview. In a parallel action, the United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against the two officials. The SEC also announced that it had obtained a temporary restraining order halting the conduct of the two government officials.  According to the SEC, the court granted the SEC a preliminary injunction against future violations of the securities laws. The court also issued an order requiring the government to comply with a court order requiring it to conduct a background check on any potential violator of the charged provisions. The order also requires the state to provide a copy of the complaint to the court for review.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, the government has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining it from violating the charged sections of the federal law.  In a related action, on January 4, 2011, the U. S. Attorney's Office for Southern New York announced that the SEC had filed a parallel criminal action against the three government officials involved in the alleged misconduct. The case is being handled by Kelly L. Gibson of the SEC Enforcement Division's Chicago Regional Office, and supervised by Chedly C. Dumornay. The litigation will be led by Mr. Gibson and Ms. Gibson.

Petitioner was tried before a Mississippi state court for the capital offense of murder. During the jury selection phase of the trial, the trial judge permitted the prosecutor to use all of the available peremptory challenges to remove venire members who had expressed any degree of hesitation against the death penalty. One of the venire members, Ms. Bounds, was removed for cause after responding to the prosecutor's questioning that she would be unable to give the death penalty if required to do so. She was replaced by another venire member who was eventually chosen to sit on the jury. Ultimately, the jury returned a verdict of guilty and recommended the death sentence, which was imposed by the trial judge. On appeal, the Mississippi Supreme Court vacated the death sentence, holding that the trial judge had erred in removing Ms. Bounds for cause and that the error was harmless because the prosecutor had an unexercised peremptory challenge that he stated he would have used to remove her. However, the court reinstated the death sentence on the ground that the trial judge had corrected his earlier error by granting an invalid for-cause Witherspoon motion as to Ms. Bounds. Held: 1. The judgment of the Mississippi Supreme Court is reversed insofar as it imposes the death sentence, and the case is remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion. Pp. 10-18. (a) There is no merit to the State's argument that the erroneous exclusion of Ms. Bounds was a single technical error that should be considered harmless because it did not have any prejudicial effect. Such an argument ignores the reality that the Witherspoon-Witt standard is rooted in the constitutional right to an impartial jury, and that the impartiality of the adjudicator goes to the very integrity of the legal system. Thus, the Chapman harmless-error analysis cannot apply. Cf. Davis v. Georgia, 236 Ga. 804, 225 S. E. 2d 241. Pp. 16-18. (b) Nor is the erroneous exclusion of Ms. Bounds an isolated incident having no prejudicial effect. While the State argues that the erroneous exclusion of Ms. Bounds was an isolated incident because the record reveals that similar jurors were not excused, the record in this case suggests the opposite -i. e., that the State exercised its peremptory challenges to remove all venire members who expressed any degree of hesitation against the death penalty. Because courts do not generally review the prosecution's reasons for exercising peremptory challenges, and because it appears that prosecutors often use peremptory challenges in this manner, a court cannot say with confidence that an erroneous exclusion for cause of a scrupled, yet eligible, venire member is an isolated incident in that particular case. Pp. 16-18. 472 So. 2d 102, reversed and remanded.

After being convicted of violating a Florida drunk driving statute, petitioner Leocidas Jean Baptiste pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 21/2 years’ imprisonment. During his incarceration, respondents Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) began removing proceedings against him based on his status as an alien “convicted of an aggravated felony,” 8 U. S. C. §§1227(a)(2)(A)(iii)–(iv), and claiming that his conviction constituted a “crime of violence” under 18 U. S. C. § 16. That provision defines the term as “an offense that has as an element the use … of physical force against the person or property of another.” Here, the INS argued that petitioner’s DUI conviction fell within § 16’s purview because it included the use of force against another person. An Immigration Judge agreed, and the Board of Immigration Appeals affirmed. The Eleventh Circuit then dismissed petitioner’s subsequent petition for review, relying on its prior holding in Le v. United States Attorney General, 196 F. 3d 1352, 1354, that a Florida DUI conviction qualified as a crime of violence. Held: Petitioner’s DUI conviction does not fall within § 16’s scope. Pp. 4–10. (a) Whether or not the word “use” alone supplies a mens rea element, the parties’ primary focus on that word is too narrow. Particularly when interpreting a statute featuring as elastic a word as “use,” this Court construes language in its context and in light of the terms surrounding it. See Smith v. United States, 508 U. S. 223, 229. The critical aspect of § 16(a)—that a crime of violence is one involving the “use…of physical force against the person or property of another”—most naturally suggests a higher degree of intent than negligent or merely accidental conduct. Because petitioner’s DUI offense therefore is not a crime of violence under § 16(a), it is not an aggravated felony under the Immigration and Nationality Act (Act). Pp. 4–6. (b) Nor is petitioner’s DUI conviction a crime of violence under § 16(b), which sweeps more broadly than § 16(a) by covering offenses that naturally involve a person acting in disregard of the risk that physical force might be used against another in committing an offense. However, § 16(b) still requires a higher mens rea than the merely accidental or negligent conduct involved in a DUI offense. Moreover, the “risk” in § 16(b) relates not to the general conduct or to the possibility that harm will result from a person’s conduct, but to the risk that the use of physical force against another might be required in committing a crime. The classic example is burglary. A burglary would be covered under § 16(b) not because the offense can be committed in a generally reckless way or because someone may be injured, but because burglary, by its nature, involves a substantial risk that the burglar will use force against a victim in completing the crime. Thus, while § 16(b) is broader than § 16(a) in the sense that physical force need not actually be applied, it contains the same formulation that proved determinative in § 16(a): the use of physical force against the person or property of another. Accordingly, this Court must give the language in § 16(b) an identical construction, requiring a higher mens rea than the merely accidental or negligent conduct involved in a DUI offense. This is particularly true in light of § 16(b)’s requirement that the “substantial risk” be a risk of using physical force against another person “in the course of committing the offense.” No “ordinary or natural” sense can be said to attach to a person’s risking having to “use” physical force against another person in the course of operating a vehicle while intoxicated and causing injury. Pp. 6–8. (c) Interpreting § 16 to encompass accidental or negligent conduct would blur the distinction between the “violent” crimes Congress sought to distinguish for heightened punishment and other crimes. Section 16 therefore cannot be read to include petitioner’s conviction for DUI causing serious bodily injury under Florida law. This construction is reinforced by Congress’ use of the term “crime of violence” in § 101(h) of the Act, which was enacted in 1990. There, Congress separately listed the DUI-causing-injury offense from the definition of “crime of violence” in § 16, indicating that the latter does not itself encompass the former. Pp. 8–10. Reversed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada today entered a final judgment against David Riggins, a convicted felon who was sentenced to prison for his role in a 1987 Las Vegas apartment shooting.  The court also issued an order suspending Riggins from taking any medication that was deemed medically appropriate.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Nevada on July 14, 1988, Riggins told a private psychiatrist that he had been successfully treated with Mellaril, an antipsychotic drug, and that he would offer an insanity defense at trial if he were given the drug.  Riggins allegedly told the psychiatrist that the drug was medically appropriate and, considering less intrusive alternatives, "necessary for the sake of Riggins' own safety or the safety of others."  The complaint alleges that, in reality, the medication was not medically appropriate because Riggins was not competent to stand trial.  In addition, the court found that Riggins had a right to show his true mental condition at the sentencing hearing.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the defendants consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering Riggins to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.  On August 2, 2008, the U. S. District Judge for the Southern District of New York granted the defendants' request for a temporary restraining order and ordered the defendants to surrender their firearms.  A hearing on August 24, 2008 was scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Eastern time.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by Scott A. Thompson and supervised by Jennifer C. Barry of the Chicago Regional Office. The litigation will be led by Mr. Thompson.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia granted summary judgment in favor of the Federal Communications Commission in a case challenging the constitutionality of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002's (BCRA) "candidate request" requirements. The court found that the BCRA's requirements for broadcasters to keep records of political advertising requests are not onerous and do not violate the First Amendment right to freedom of speech. The Court also found that they do not impose an additional administrative burden on broadcasters. The lower court's finding that BCRA  504 is unconstitutional is consistent with the finding that the regulation is not "burdensome and invasive"

Petitioner's father brought this diversity action in Federal District Court against the Sikorsky Division of United Technologies Corporation (Sikorsky), which built the helicopter for the United States. At trial, petitioner presented two theories of liability under Virginia tort law that were submitted to the jury. First, petitioner alleged that Sikorsk had defectively repaired a device called the servo in the helicopter's automatic flight control system, which allegedly malfunctioned and caused the crash, and second, petitioner claimed that the copilot's emergency escape system was ineffective because access to the escape hatch handle was obstructed by other equipment. The jury returned a general verdict in favor of petitioner and awarded him $725,000. The District Court denied the motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict. The Court of Appeals reversed and remanded, finding, as a matter of Virginia law, that petitioner had failed to meet his burden of demonstrating that the repair work performed by Sikorski, as opposed to work that had been done by the Navy, was responsible for the alleged malfunction. Held: The judgment is vacated and the case is remanded.

In the Supreme Court case involving plaintiff-respondent Ronald Nussle, an inmate who alleged that corrections officers in a Connecticut prison beat him in violation of the Eighth Amendment, the Court addressed the issue of whether prisoners must exhaust prison grievance procedures before bringing a lawsuit for denial of federal rights. The Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (PLRA) requires prisoners to exhaust such administrative remedies, but the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit had ruled that this requirement did not apply to specific incidents like the use of excessive force.

The Supreme Court rejected the Second Circuit's interpretation, holding that the PLRA's exhaustion requirement applies to all prisoner lawsuits regarding prison conditions, including claims of excessive force. The Court emphasized that Congress intended the PLRA to reduce the number of prisoner lawsuits and improve their quality by allowing prison officials to address complaints internally before litigation. The Court also noted that the term "prison conditions" should be read broadly to include all aspects of prison life, not just general circumstances.

The Court's decision means that prisoners must use available prison grievance processes for all types of claims related to prison life before they can file a lawsuit in federal court. This includes incidents of alleged excessive force by corrections officers. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The Supreme Court held that neither § 243(h) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 (INA) nor Article 33 of the United Nations Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees applies to actions taken by the U.S. Coast Guard on the high seas. The case involved the U.S. government's policy of intercepting Haitian migrants at sea and returning them to Haiti without determining if they qualified as refugees.

The Court reasoned that the INA's protections apply only to aliens who are in or have arrived at the U.S. border, not to those intercepted on the high seas. The Court also noted that the President has the authority to enforce immigration laws and to suspend the entry of certain classes of aliens, which includes the power to direct the Coast Guard to intercept and return migrants at sea.

The Court examined the text and structure of the INA, the legislative history of the 1980 amendment to § 243(h), and the text and negotiating history of the United Nations Convention. It concluded that the language of § 243(h) and the Convention's Article 33 do not suggest any extraterritorial application, meaning they do not apply to actions taken outside U.S. borders.

The Court also addressed the presumption against extraterritoriality, which holds that unless Congress clearly states otherwise, laws are presumed not to apply outside the U.S. The Court found no evidence that Congress intended § 243(h) to have extraterritorial effect.

The Court's decision effectively upheld the government's policy of repatriating Haitian migrants intercepted at sea, stating that the policy did not violate U.S. law or international treaty obligations as they pertain to refugees. The Court emphasized that its role was not to judge the wisdom of the policy but to determine its legality. The judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had found in favor of the migrants, was reversed.

Respondent petitioner was fired after taking leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA), which allows eligible employees to take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave annually for various qualifying reasons, including family care and self-care. He filed suit in Federal District Court, claiming that the Court of Appeals of Maryland had erred in dismissing his prior appeal challenging the legality of his firing. The District Court entered judgment for petitioner, rejecting the State’s claim of sovereign immunity from suit. The Third Circuit reversed, concluding that the FMLA’s self-care provision, which permits employees to take leave for pregnancy-related illnesses, was not a proper ground for imposing damages liability on the State. Held: The FMLA’s self-care provision does not allow employees to recover damages from States for violations of the provision. Pp. 4–11. (a) Enacting the FMLA, Congress relied upon evidence of a well-documented pattern of sex-based discrimination in family-leave policies. States had facially discriminatory leave policies granting longer periods of leave to women than to men, and States also administered facially neutral leave policies in gender-biased ways. These practices reflected what Congress found to be a “pervasive sex role stereotype that caring for family members is women’s work,” Nevada Div. of Women v. Hibbs, 538 U. S. 721 , 731, a stereotype to which even this Court had succumbed in earlier times, id., at 729. Faced with “the States’ record of unconstitutional participation in, and fostering of, gender-based discrimination in the administration of leave benefits,” Hibbs concluded that requiring state employers to give all employees the opportunity to take family-care leave was “narrowly targeted at the faultline between work and family—precisely where sex-based overgeneralization has been and remains strong.” Id., at 735, 738. By contrast, the self-care provision stands alone and addresses neither sex discrimination nor sex stereotyping. Although the provision offered some women a benefit by allowing them to take leave for pregnancy-related illnesses, it is not congruent and proportional to any identified constitutional violations. Moreover, the provision is not a necessary adjunct to the family-care provision. While the self-care provision might help reduce the difference in the expected number of weeks of FMLA leave that different employees will take for different reasons, the provision does not necessarily accomplish this goal. Nor does the provision offer an incentive to hire women that will counteract the incentives created by the family-care provisions. Finally, although the provision may help single parents retain their jobs when they become ill, it does not explain how it remedies or prevents constitutional violations. Pp. 4–9. (b) Abrogating the States’ immunity from suits for damages for failure to give self-care leave is not a congruent and proportional remedy if the existing state leave policies would have sufficed. More is required to subject unconsenting States to suits for damages, especially where, as here, it is for violations of a provision (the self-care provision) that is a supposedly preventive step in aid of already preventive provisions (the family-care provisions). Here, Congress made no findings and cited no specific or detailed evidence to show how the self-care provision is necessary to the family-care provisions or how it reduces an employer’s incentives to discriminate against women. And Congress said nothing about the existence or adequacy of state sick-leave policies. Pp. 9–10. 626 F. 3d 117, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Kagan, JJ., joined. Sotomayor, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

The U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico today entered a final judgment in favor of the SEC's motion for a temporary restraining order and an asset freeze.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Albuquerque, New Mexico on April 19, 2010, alleges that a forensic analyst with the New Mexico Department of Health, Scientific Laboratory Division (SDLD) failed to disclose that the analyst had used improper amounts of the internal standard to determine whether a blood sample contained cocaine.  According to the complaint, the analyst also failed to corroborate the analyst’s findings, and was subsequently arrested for driving while intoxicated.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney for the district of New Mexican today announced that it would not be calling the analyst as a witness in connection with a criminal case.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, D. Bartell, M. McMurray, & A. ImObersteg, Attacking and Defending Drunk Driving Tests §16:80 (2004), the court ruled that Caylor had the right to present his own testimony in a court-ordered criminal case, and that he had the duty to provide corroborating evidence.   The court also ruled that the independent analyst who signed the SDLD report, Gerasimos Razatos, was not qualified to provide testimony under the court-issued subpoena provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordered the analyst to provide a copy of the report to the court as part of an order appointing a receiver for the receiver of the receiver. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by John Rymas and supervised by Marc Blau. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

After respondents filed a securities fraud class action under 15 U.S.C. §10(b) and SEC Rule 10b–5, appellees moved to dismiss the complaint. The District Court agreed, concluding that the complaint did not meet the heightened pleading standard applicable when “a plaintiff’s allegations … relate[] to matters commonly known,” Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555, and that the complaint failed to identify the specific acts of fraud or misconduct underlying the securities fraud claim. The Ninth Circuit reversed, ruling that the complaint met the heightened pleading standard because it contained enough detail to enable the reader to infer that the company’s management knew that the product it touted would never receive regulatory approval. However, the court concluded that the complaint could still be dismissed because it failed to allege that the company’s misstatements proximately caused any economic loss. The court found that the complaint satisfied this element if the plaintiffs proved that the price of the stock they bought was inflated because of the misstatements. Because the complaint included no allegation that the stock’s price dropped after the truth came out, the court ruled that the plaintiffs could not recover. Held: 1. An inflated purchase price will not itself constitute or proximately cause the relevant economic loss. Pp. 4–8. (a) This conclusion follows directly from the nature of the transaction. As a matter of pure logic, at the moment the transaction takes place, the plaintiff suffers no loss, since the inflated purchase payment is offset by ownership of a share that at that instant possesses equivalent value. Nor is there any inherent link between the inflated share purchase price and any subsequent economic loss. While the higher price may suggest that the misrepresentation touched upon a later loss, it is not sufficient to cause a loss. Pp. 4–6. (b) The Ninth Circuit’s holding lacks support in precedent. Its approach contradicts the common-law roots of the securities fraud action—which subjects a person who “fraudulently” makes a “misrepresentation” to liability “for pecuniary loss caused” to one who justifiably relies upon that misrepresentation, Restatement (Second) of Torts §525—and the common-law requirement that a plaintiff show actual damages. Given the uniqueness of the Ninth Circuit’s perspective, its approach is unlikely to be correct. Finally, the Ninth Circuit’s approach overlooks an important securities law objective: maintaining public confidence in the marketplace by deterring fraud, in part, through the availability of private securities fraud actions. The statutory provisions at issue here and the paragraphs that precede them emphasize this objective. Pp. 6–8. 2. The complaint also failed adequately to allege the second element of causation and economic loss. Even assuming that neither the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure nor the securities laws impose any special further requirement in respect to the pleading of proximate causation or economic loss, the complaint nevertheless fails the simple test that the “short and plain statement” must provide the defendant with fair notice of what the plaintiff’s claim is and the grounds upon which it rests. Although the complaint contains only one statement suggesting that the plaintiffs’ loss consisted of the “artificially inflated” purchase prices, the statement implies that the plaintiffs’ loss consisted of the “artificially inflated” purchase prices alone. The complaint nowhere else provides the defendants with notice of what the relevant economic loss might be or of what the causal connection might be between that loss and the misrepresentation concerning the product. Allowing a plaintiff to forgo providing any indication of the economic loss and proximate cause that the plaintiff has in mind would transform a private securities action into a partial downside insurance policy. Pp. 8–10. 339 F.3d 926, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit ruled that Arizona courts are free to exercise jurisdiction over civil suits by non-Indians against Indians on the Navajo Indian Reservation. The court held that the state's laws prohibiting outsiders from being on the reservation and holding courts violated the Constitution's guarantees of due process and equal protection under the law. The case is the latest in a long line of appeals challenging the constitutionality of state laws over Indian affairs. In the past, the courts have held that state laws violated the rights of Indians to make their own laws and be ruled by them. In this case, the court ruled that the laws of Georgia violated the right of the Cherokees to rule by their own people. The Court held that Georgia's assertion of power was invalid and that the citizens of Georgia had no right to enter, but with the consent of Cherokees themselves, or in conformity with treaties, and with the acts of Congress. The ruling is a victory for tribal governments and courts that have tried to impose their laws and courts on the Indians. The Cherokees have long held that they have the right to decide their own affairs. The 8th Court's decision will have a significant impact on the future of state law over Indian matters. The issue of whether state laws violate the Constitution will be addressed in future appeals.

The Supreme Court case in question dealt with the constitutionality of a Minnesota Supreme Court rule that prohibited judicial candidates from announcing their views on disputed legal and political issues. This rule, known as the "announce clause," was challenged by Gregory Wersal, a candidate for associate justice of the Minnesota Supreme Court, who argued that it violated his First Amendment rights.

The Supreme Court held that the announce clause did indeed violate the First Amendment. The Court reasoned that the clause was not narrowly tailored to serve the state's interest in preserving the impartiality of the judiciary or the appearance of impartiality. The Court found that the clause restricted speech based on its content and burdened a category of speech at the core of First Amendment freedoms—speech about the qualifications of candidates for public office.

The Court also noted that the announce clause was underinclusive, as it only prohibited certain statements during judicial campaigns, and did not address other ways in which judges or judicial candidates might express their views on legal issues. The Court concluded that the announce clause could not be justified by the state's interest in maintaining an impartial judiciary or the appearance of impartiality, as it left appreciable damage to that interest unprohibited.

The Court's decision emphasized the importance of free speech in the context of judicial elections, stating that if a state chooses to elect judges, it must allow candidates to discuss issues relevant to voters. The Court reversed the grant of summary judgment to the respondents and remanded the case for proceedings consistent with its opinion.

In summary, the Supreme Court's decision struck down the Minnesota Supreme Court's announce clause as unconstitutional, reaffirming the principle that restrictions on speech during judicial elections must be scrutinized under the First Amendment, just as they would be in other types of elections.

The Supreme Court ruled in a 5-4 decision that the Kotteakos harmless-error standard applies in determining whether habeas relief must be granted because of constitutional error of the trial type. The Court held that the Kotteakos standard, which requires proof that the error "had substantial and injurious effect or influence in determining the jury's verdict," is better suited to the nature and purpose of collateral review and more likely to promote the considerations underlying recent habeas cases.

Section 12S of the Massachusetts Abortion Reform Act provides that a pregnant unmarried minor may not have an abortion without the consent of each parent or, if none, of a designated relative or guardian, or of a judge of the Superior Court, who must disregard all parental objections, and other considerations, that are not based exclusively on what would serve the minor's best interests. The section contains exceptions allowing judicial authorization of an abortion without parental consent where the minor is unable to notify or locate a parent, or where the parents have abandoned the minor, or where the minor shows that an abortion would be in her best interests. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, in construing the section, held that it did not allow a minor to obtain judicial consent to an abortion without any parental consultation whatsoever, but that it contained exceptions allowing judicial authorization of an abortion without parental consent where the minor is unable to notify or locate a parent, or where the parents have abandoned the minor, or where the minor shows that an abortion would be in her best interests. The Federal District Court, in certifying questions to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, included the question whether § 12S permits any minors--mature or immature--to obtain judicial consent to an abortion without any parental consultation whatsoever. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, answering that question negatively, construed the section as containing an additional exception allowing judicial authorization of an abortion without parental consent where no parent (or statutory substitute) is available. The court also ruled that an available parent must be given notice of any judicial proceedings brought by a minor to obtain consent for an abortion. Held: 1. Section 12S, as authoritatively construed by the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, satisfies constitutional standards in large part. Pp. 643-645. (a) An abortion decision differs in important ways from other decisions that may be made during minority, and the unique nature and consequences of the abortion decision make it inappropriate to give a third party an absolute, and possibly arbitrary, veto over the decision of the physician and his patient to terminate the patient's pregnancy, regardless of the reason for withholding the consent. Therefore, if the State decides to require a pregnant minor to obtain one or both parents' consent to an abortion, it also must provide an alternative procedure whereby authorization for the abortion can be obtained. Pp. 643-644. (b) Here, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court correctly construed § 12S as providing that if a minor satisfies the court that she is mature enough and well enough informed to make her abortion decision, in consultation with her physician, independently of her parents' wishes, the court must authorize her to act without parental consultation or consent. And if she fails to satisfy the court that she is competent to make this decision independently, she must be permitted to show that an abortion nevertheless would be in her best interests. If the court is satisfied that it is, the court must authorize the abortion. However, if the court is not satisfied that the minor is mature or that the abortion would be in her best interests, it may decline to sanction the operation. Pp. 644-645. 2. Nevertheless, § 12S falls short of constitutional standards in two respects. Pp. 645-648. (a) Section 12S permits judicial authorization for an abortion to be withheld from a minor who is found by the Superior Court to be mature and fully competent to make this decision independently. Since the minor must satisfy the court that she has attained sufficient maturity to make a fully informed decision, she then is entitled to make her abortion decision independently. Pp. 645-646. (b) Section 12S requires parental consultation or notification in every instance, without affording the pregnant minor an opportunity to receive an independent judicial determination that she is mature enough to consent or that an abortion would be in her best interests. Pp. 646-648. Affirmed.

Appellant was convicted in Georgia of the crime of distributing obscene material. His conviction, in March 1972, was for showing the film "Carnal Knowledge" in a movie theater in Albany, Georgia. The jury that found appellant guilty was instructed on obscenity pursuant to the Georgia statute, which defines obscene material in language similar to that of the definition in Miller v. Massachusetts, 383 U. S. 413, 418. Appellant then appealed to the Supreme Court of Georgia, which by a divided vote affirmed the conviction on July 2, 1973. Held: The film is not obscene under the constitutional standards announced in Miller. Pp. 531-532. (a) The film could not, as a matter of constitutional law, be found to depict sexual conduct in a parently offensive way, and that it is therefore not outside the protection of the First and Fourteenth Amendments because it is obscene. P. 533. (b) Miller's implicit approval of the trial court's instructions directing jurors to apply "community standards" without specifying what "community" is is not necessary when the films at issue are themselves placed in evidence. Miller held that it was constitutionally permissible to permit juries to rely on the understanding of the community from which they came as to contemporary community standards, and the States have considerable latitude in framing statutes under this element of Miller's Miller decision. Even though questions of appeal to the "prurient interest" or of patent offensiveness are "essentially questions of fact," it would be a serious misreading of Miller to require that the answer be based on some abstract formulation, and to require a State to structure obscenities proceedings around evidence of a national "community standard" would be an exercise in futility, and no other basis appearing in the record upon which the judgment of conviction can be sustained, and this Court reversed the conviction.

The Supreme Court addressed the standard for granting indigent defendants the right to appeal their criminal convictions in forma pauperis, meaning without the burden of court costs. The Court clarified that the right to appeal is effectively guaranteed in federal criminal cases, and the only procedural requirements are timely filings of necessary documents.

The Court held that the "good faith" requirement for in forma pauperis appeals should be interpreted objectively. An appeal is considered to be in "good faith" if it raises any issue that is not frivolous. The Court emphasized that the burden of proving an appeal is frivolous lies with the government, not the defendant seeking to appeal.

If a district court denies an indigent defendant's application to appeal in forma pauperis due to a lack of "good faith," the defendant can seek the same relief from the Court of Appeals. The Court of Appeals should grant the appeal if the defendant's application raises non-frivolous issues. If the issues are not clear from the application, the Court of Appeals must provide the defendant with counsel and a sufficient record to argue their case.

The Court underscored the importance of equal treatment for all litigants and the need for prompt and fair criminal law procedures. It noted that delays in the appellate process can undermine law enforcement and the administration of justice.

The Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had denied the petitioner's application for leave to appeal in forma pauperis, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. The Court did not take a position on the merits of the petitioner's conviction but held that the petitioner's claims were not so frivolous as to justify a summary dismissal of the case.

Justices Frankfurter and White did not participate in the decision.

The Supreme Court case you provided is "Worcester v. Georgia" (6 Pet. 515, 8 L.Ed. 483), decided in 1832. In this case, the Supreme Court held that Georgia's attempt to extend its laws onto the Cherokee Reservation was unconstitutional. The Court found that the Cherokee Nation was a sovereign entity with its own laws and courts, and that the United States had exclusive control over the intercourse between the two nations.

When petitioners, who owned coal mining operations in Pennsylvania, learned that a federal excise tax on coal mined domestically and shipped abroad was being used to fund military activities in Afghanistan and Iraq, they sought a refund of the portion of the tax attributable to the sale of coal produced in Pennsylvania. Their request for a refund was denied because they had not complied with the Internal Revenue Service’s (IRS) refund scheme, which requires a taxpayer to file an administrative claim before he brings suit against the Government. The IRS regulations implementing the scheme specify that the claim must be filed within five years of the date of the tax liability. Petitioners filed suit in the Court of Federal Claims, claiming that the tax was invalid under the Export Clause of Article I of the Constitution. Although acknowledging that the IRS regulations were controlling, the court ruled that the Tucker Act, which permits suit against the Government where the right to sue has accrued prior to the expiration of the limitations period specified in the IRS regulations, provided an alternative forum for relief. The court awarded petitioners partial relief, rejecting the Government’s argument that the Tucker Act was inapplicable because the tax was void ab initio. The Federal Circuit affirmed, concluding that the Tucker Act was the exclusive remedy for challenging the constitutionality of the tax. Held: The plain language of the Internal Revenue Code requires a taxpayer seeking a refund for a tax assessed in violation of the Export Clause to file a timely administrative refund claim before bringing suit against the Government. Pp. 4–11. (a) The language of 26 U. S. C. §§7422(a) and 6511 makes it abundantly clear that a taxpayer seeking a refund for a tax assessed in violation of the Export Clause must file a timely administrative refund claim before bringing suit against the Government. Section 7422(a) provides that “[n]o suit … shall be maintained in any court for the recovery of any internal revenue tax alleged to have been erroneously or illegally assessed or collected…until a claim for refund or credit has been duly filed with the Commissioner of Internal Revenue.” Employing the same language, §6511(a) sets forth a time limit for bringing suit once the claim-filing requirement has been met. The section’s text leaves little room for doubt that it applies to taxes assessed in violation of the Export Clause. Nor does the legislative history suggest that Congress intended to create a different regime for Export Clause challenges. Any contrary conclusion is undermined by the fact that the Companies’ challenge to the constitutionality of the tax was raised in the context of the refund proceedings. Had the Companies wished to raise the Export Clause defense in the suit against the Government, they could easily have done so. Pp. 4–7. (b) The Companies’ arguments to the contrary are unpersuasive. First, they contend that the Tucker Act’s limitations period is inapplicable because the Export Clause itself creates a cause of action against the Government, which can be brought directly under the Tucker Act. However, the Companies’ claims are subject to the Code provisions regardless of how they came to be asserted. Second, the Companies argue that their claims are exempt from the Code provisions because they arise from a constitutional violation. While a constitutional claim can become time-barred just as any other claim can, Congress has the authority to require administrative exhaustion before allowing a suit against the Government, even for a constitutional violation. Third, the Companies contend that Export Clause claims in particular must be treated differently from constitutional claims in general. They argue that the Clause carves one particular economic activity completely out of Congress’s power. However, the Clause is neither a limitation nor a prohibition on congressional power, depending on whether the pertinent authority is viewed as the power to tax exports or as the “power to lay and collect taxes.” Fourth, the Companies maintain that the Code procedures are themselves excessively burdensome. However, the Companies’ own invocation of those procedures for taxes paid within the Code’s limitations period resulted in full refunds with interest. Fifth, the Companies contend that the Code procedure is inapplicable to taxes that are, on their face, unconstitutional. They rely on Enochs v. Williams Packing & Navigating Co., 370 U. S. 1, which held that the Anti-Injunction Act’s prohibition against suits to restrain the assessment or collection of taxes does not apply to situations in which there are “no circumstances” under which the tax imposed could be held valid. However, the anti-suit covenants contained in both the Anti-Injunction Act and §7422(a) track each other closely, and the latter contains additional language making it applicable to “any sum alleged to have been excessive or in any manner wrongfully collected.” Even assuming that the “under no circumstances” limitation on the Anti-Injunction Act applies to §7422(a), the Companies still would not prevail. The question of whether the Government has a chance of ultimate success is to be determined on the basis of the information available to it at the time of suit. Since the Companies sought refunds for taxes paid between 1994 and 1996, when the scope of the Export Clause was sufficiently debatable that this Court granted certiorari in 1996 and again in 1998 to clear it up, the “under no circumstances” rule would judge the Government’s chances of success as of the time the tax was assessed. Finally, the Companies argue that the Tucker Act is inapplicable because the unconstitutionality of the coal export tax was so obvious that the Government had no chance of prevailing. However, if the unconstitutionality of the tax were so obvious that the Government had no chance of prevailing, someone paying the tax would have successfully challenged it long before 20 years after its enactment. Pp. 7–11. 473 F. 3d 135, reversed. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer, and Alito, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Souter, J., joined.

An ordinance of respondent municipality regulates dredging and pit excavating on realty within its limits. Prior to passage of the ordinance, appellants had been operating a quarry on land owned by one of them, and the operation had long been approved by local authorities. After passage of the ordinance, appellants continued to operate the quarry, but the ordinance prohibited further excavation below the water table and imposed an affirmative duty to refill any excavation then below that level. When appellants refused to comply with the ordinance, respondents sued to enjoin further mining by appellants on the ground that they had not complied with the ordinance nor acquired a mining permit as required by it. Held: 1. Though the ordinance completely prohibits a beneficial use to which the property had been devoted, it is not rendered unconstitutional merely because it deprives the property of its most beneficial use. Pp. 593-594. 2. Nor is it of controlling significance that the "use" prohibited is of the soil itself as opposed to a "use" upon the soil, or that the "use" prohibited is arguably not a common-law nuisance. P. 594. 3. Governmental action in the form of regulation cannot be so onerous as to constitute a taking requiring compensation, though there is no set formula to determine where regulation ends and taking begins. P. 594. 4. On the record in this case, the ordinance is not invalidated as an unconstitutional taking. Pp. 594-596. 5. The ordinance is sustained as a valid exercise of the municipal police power. Pp. 596-598. 6. The ordinance is not invalidated as conflicting with earlier decisions sustaining appellants' rights to mine on the same land. P. 598. n. 7. The ordinance is not invalidated as imposing penalties inconsistent with the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. P. 598. 9 N. Y. 2d 101, 172 N. E. 2d 562, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico today entered a final judgment in favor of the Navajo Nation's hotel occupancy tax, which imposes an 8 percent tax on any hotel room located within the boundaries of the reservation.  According to the court's order, filed on June 14, 1934, the reservation was created by Hubert Richardson, a Navajo trader, to facilitate the purchase and operation of a hotel on non-Indian fee land.  The court held that the reservation had a "collective right-of-way" to the hotel, and that it had the authority to impose the hotel occupancy fee on nonmember hotel guests.  In addition, the court found that Richardson had the right to "collect and remit" the property's taxes to respondents, members of the tribe, and the emergency medical services department.  Without admitting or denying the Court's findings, Richardson consented to the entry of the final judgment, which permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of $84,000, prejudgment interest of $1,038, and a civil penalty of $100,000.   In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Arizona today announced criminal charges against Richardson. Â The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, charges Richardson with violating Section 17(a) ofÂ the Securities Act of 1933 and Exchange Act Rules 10b2-1, and seeks permanent injunctions, civil penalties, and an officer-and-director bar against him from serving as an officer or director of a public company.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 565 (1981).

Petitioner was convicted in a Federal District Court for an offense against the United States. He applied for leave to appeal his conviction to the Court of Appeals in forma pauperis. His application was denied. Held: 1. In view of the circumstances of this case, it is appropriate to indicate in somewhat greater detail than in the past, the approach a Court of appeals must take toward an indigent's application for leave-to-appeal from his criminal conviction. Pp. 674-673. (a) The application, to be made to the District Court in which the defendant was convicted, must conform to the requirements of 28 U. S. C. § 1915 (a), which include, in affidavit form, the defendant's representations of poverty, a statement of the case, and his belief that he is entitled to redress. P. 675. (b) The burden of showing that his appeal has merit is so manifest that they merit no further argument or consideration, and that dismissal of petitioner's case is, therefore, in order. 2. In the context of a criminal appeal, this Court has not yet decided whether such a charge, if proven, would require the reversal of the criminal conviction based upon an indictment returned by a grand jury hearing the perjury. The only requirements a defendant must meet for perfecting his appeal are those expressed as time limitations within which various procedural steps must be completed. First, a timely notice of appeal must be filed in a District Court to confer jurisdiction upon the Court, and then, designations of the transcript, a record on appeal and briefs must be submitted in the appropriate forum. Second, if from the face of the papers he has filed, the applicant will present issues for review not clearly frivolous, the Court must provide the would-be appellant with both the assistance of counsel and a record of sufficient completeness to enable him to attempt to make a showing that the district court's certificate of lack of "good faith" is in error and that leave to proceed informa pausperis should be allowed. P p. 676. (c) The District Court's certificate is not conclusive, although it is, of course, entitled to weight, but it serves to demonstrate that petitioner sought consideration of issues that it would be difficult for an appellate court to consider so patently frivolous as to require a dismissal of his case without full briefing or argument. The preference to be accorded criminal appeals recognizes the need for speedy disposition of such cases, and Delay in the final judgment of conviction, including its appellate review, unquestionably erodes the efficacy of law enforcement. P, 678. (d) The fact that there are many meritorious criminal cases come before that court through applications for leave -to appeal from a district Court's judgment of convictions in a criminal case what is, in effect, a matter of right, is not sufficient cause to bypass the orderly processes of judicial review, and it is the burden of the Government to show that the appeal is lacking in merit, indeed, that it is so lacking that the court would dismiss the case on motion of the government, had the case been docketed and the record been filed by an appellant able to afford the expense of complying with those requirements. P., 679. (e) In the light of this delay, and the fact that this Court's materials before this stage of the proceedings are generally inadequate for passing upon an application addressed to it, the court will have before it what is usually the pro se pleading of a layman and the certificate of a district judge that the applicant lacks 'good faith' in seeking appellate review. The court of appeals should then grant leave to the applicant and appoint counsel to represent the appellant and proceed to consideration of the appeal on the merits in the same manner that it considers paid appeals. If, on the other hand, the claims made or the issues sought to be raised by the applicant are such that their substance cannot adequately be ascertained from the applicant's application, the courts should provide the applicant with both counsel and counsel. If the applicant then presents any issue for the court's consideration, leave to continue with the appeal in formas paupais must be allowed, and if, with such aid the applicant presents any issues for the Court's consideration not "frivolous." Leave to proceed with the case in formam paupauperi should be permitted. P; 679 F. 2d 604, vacated and case remanded.

The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA or Act), as amended, is a Spending Clause statute that seeks to ensure that “all children with disabilities have available to them a free appropriate public education,” §1400(d)(1)(A). Under IDEA, school districts must create an individualized education program (IEP) for each disabled child. If parents believe their child’s IEP is inappropriate, they may request an “impartial due process hearing.” §§1415(b)(3), and “a proposed resolution of the problem to the extent known and available . . . at the time,“ §1415[f).” In Maryland, IEP hearings are conducted by administrative law judges (ALJs). After a 3-day hearing, the ALJ deemed the evidence close, held that the parents bore the burden of persuasion, and ruled in favor of the school district. The parents brought a civil action challenging the result. The District Court reversed and remanded, after concluding that the burden is on the School District. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The burden of proof in an administrative hearing challenging an IEP, properly placed upon the party seeking relief. Pp. 5–11. (a) The burden is properly placed on the party who seeks relief. The plain text of IDEA is silent on the allocation of the burden. See, e.g., Minn. Stat. §125A.091, 412–415. It admits of exceptions. See McCormick on Evidence §342, p. 433. In numerous other areas, IDEA relies heavily upon the expertise of school districts to meet its goals, including a so-called “stay-put” provision, which requires a child to remain in his or her “then-current educational placement” during the pendency of an IDEA hearing. The Act also includes a “resolution session” prior to any due-process hearing, which provides parents with the reasoning behind the disputed action, details about the other options considered and rejected by the IEP team, and a description of all evaluations, reports, and other factors that the school used in coming to its decision. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, 42 U. S. C. §2000e–2 et seq., does not directly state that plaintiffs bear the “ultimate” burden of persuasive, but Congress also expressed its approval of the general rule when it chose to apply it to administrative proceedings under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.-C. §556(d). IDEA requires state authorities to organize hearings in a way that guarantees parents and children the procedural protections of the Act. See §141412(a). Finally, and perhaps most importantly, parents may recover attorney’�s fees if they prevail. These protections ensure that the School bears no unique informational advantage. Petitioners and several States urge us to decide that States may, if they wish, override the default rule and put the burden always on the district. Several States have laws or regulations purporting to do so, at least under some circumstances. See Department of Education, J. Chambers, J., Harr, & A. Dhanani, What Are We Spending on Procedural Safeguards in Special Education 1999–2000, p8 (May 2003). Because no such law or regulation exists in Maryland, we need not decide this issue today. The ordinary default rule, of course, admits exceptions. For example, the burden as to certain elements of a plantiff‘s claim may be shifted to defendants, when such elements can fairly be characterized as affirmative defenses or exemptions. Moreover, there is reason to believe that a great deal is already spent on the administration of the statute. P. 4–6. (b) The ordinary rule admits exceptions, but admits no such exceptions. In addition, the standard default rule that a child bears the risk of failing to prove his claims is also admitted by the plain text. The “burden of pleading and proof with regard to most facts have and should be assigned to the plaintiff who generally seeks to change the present state of affairs and who therefore naturally should be expected to bear the risk or proof or persuasion” 34 CFR §300.502 (b)(1) (hereinafter PARC). Moreover, in numerous other area, the default rules admit of exceptions, see McCormick §337, at 412-415. The default rule also admits of “substantial dollars” that should be allocated to litigation and administrative expenditures or to educational services, and is not required to be given a realistic opportunity to access the necessary evidence, or without an expert with the firepower to match the opposition. In fact, many cases will be in evidentiary equipoise. In some cases, there will be no such cases. Petitioner, however, is urged to take instruction from the lower court opinions of Mills v. Board of Education and Mills, 348 F

The U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada granted summary judgment in favor of the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency, which determined that a property owned by Bernadine Suitum was not eligible for development. The court held that the agency's determinations amounted to a "regulatory taking" of her property. The Court held that Suitum has not attempted to sell the development rights she has or is eligible to receive, and therefore the claim is not ripe for adjudication. The trial court concluded that the issue of whether Suitum's property has been taken by the agency is not relevant to the court's finding that the determinations are a "taking" of property. In a parallel action, the U.N. Attorney's Office for the Western District of California filed an emergency motion on behalf of Suitum, seeking a court order to restrain the agency from further enforcement of its development restrictions. The case is being handled by the same team of attorneys who successfully argued the case before the court.

In the case of Gaines Ted Huson vs. Chevron Oil Co., the Supreme Court had to decide whether Huson's lawsuit for a back injury sustained on an artificial island drilling rig was barred by the statute of limitations, and whether state or federal law determined the timeliness of the action under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (Lands Act). The Lands Act extends federal jurisdiction and applicable federal laws to the Outer Continental Shelf, and also applies the laws of the adjacent state when not inconsistent with federal law.

The District Court had ruled that Louisiana's one-year statute of limitations for personal injury actions applied, making Huson's lawsuit untimely. The Court of Appeals, however, held that the admiralty doctrine of laches, not the state statute of limitations, should apply, and remanded the case for trial.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the interpretation of the Lands Act and its application to the case. The Court held that the Lands Act, as interpreted in the prior case of Rodrigue v. Aetna Casualty & Surety Co., requires the application of the state statute of limitations to personal injury actions. However, the Court also determined that the Louisiana statute of limitations should not be applied retroactively to Huson's case, which was filed before the Rodrigue decision. The Court reasoned that nonretroactive application was appropriate because Rodrigue established a new principle of law by overruling past precedent, and retroactive application would produce inequitable results and undermine the purpose of the Lands Act.

The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeals on the grounds of nonretroactivity, allowing Huson's case to proceed to trial despite being filed after the one-year statute of limitations had expired. The decision emphasized the importance of providing comprehensive and familiar remedies to injured employees under the Lands Act and the need to avoid unjust outcomes when applying new legal principles to ongoing cases.

After a fire aboard his pleasure yacht destroyed the vessel and caused damage to several neighboring vessels and the marina where the yacht was docked, Everett Sisson filed a petition for declaratory and injunctive relief in Federal District Court to limit his liability to $800, the salvage value of the yacht after the fire. He claimed that the federal court had maritime jurisdiction over the action under 28 U. S. C. § 1333(1), which gives federal district courts jurisdiction over "[a]ny civil case of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction." Section 1333(1)'s applicability depends on whether the incident underlying the lawsuit has a sufficiently close relationship to traditional maritime activity. Under the "locality" test previously applied to § 1333(1) jurisdiction, the District Court dismissed the petition for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Affirming, the Court of Appeals concluded that neither § 1333(1) nor the Limited Liability Act-which limits the liability of an owner of a vessel for any damage done without his privity or knowledge to the vessel's value and its freight -conferred jurisdiction. Held: Section 1333(1) confers federal jurisdiction over Sisson's limitation of liability suit. Pp. 108-114. (a) Until recently, § 1333(1) jurisdiction over tort actions was determined largely by the application of the "locality" test. However, Executive Jet Aviation, Inc. v. Cleveland, 409 U. S. 249, and Foremost Insurance Co. v. Richardson, 457 U. S. 668, mark this Court's first clear departures from that test. Both decisions rejected petitioners' arguments that a substantial relationship with commercial maritime activity is necessary to a finding of maritime jurisdiction. Instead, they found that the potential disruptive impact of certain accidents on maritime commerce provides a sufficient basis for federal jurisdiction. They did not specify the minimum level of disruption that supports such jurisdiction. Nevertheless, their reasoning suggests that the potential impact of a given type of incident should be examined by determining whether it plainly satisfies the requirement of potential disruption to commercial maritime activity. That is precisely what this case requires. Fire is one of the most significant hazards facing commercial vessels, and the general features of the incident here-storage and maintenance of a vessel at a marina on navigable waters-plainly satisfy the requirement of potential disruption to commercial maritime activity. Pp. 108-112. (b) Once it is established that the incident has a potential impact on maritime commerce, the party seeking to invoke maritime jurisdiction must show a substantial relationship between the activity giving rise to the incident and traditional maritime activity. The relevant "activity" is defined not by the particular circumstances of the incident, but by the general conduct from which the incident arose. Here, the relevant activity was the storage and maintenance of a vessel at a marina on navigable waters. Such activity is substantially related to traditional maritime activity. Navigation is merely one example of conduct that is substantially related to traditional maritime activity. Had this Court intended to suggest that navigation is the only activity that is sufficient to confer jurisdiction, it could have stated the jurisdictional test much more clearly and economically by stating that maritime jurisdiction over torts is limited to torts in which the vessels are in "navigation." More importantly, a narrow focus on navigation would not serve the federal policies that underlie the jurisdictional test. Those policies include the protection of maritime commerce and the need for uniform rules of maritime conduct and liability. Just as navigation, storing and maintaining a vessel at a marina on navigable waters is substantially related to traditional maritime activity. Pp. 112-114. Reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court addressed whether the legal standard for a defendant's competency to plead guilty or waive the right to counsel should be higher than the standard for competency to stand trial. The Court concluded that the standard should not be higher.

Background: The respondent in the case had committed multiple shootings, survived a self-inflicted gunshot, and later confessed to the crimes. After initially pleading not guilty, he later sought to plead guilty and dismiss his legal counsel to avoid presenting mitigating evidence at sentencing. The trial court found him competent based on psychiatric evaluations and accepted his guilty plea and waiver of counsel after ensuring they were made voluntarily and with understanding of the consequences.

Legal Reasoning: The Court held that the competency standard established in Dusky v. United States, which requires a defendant to have a "rational as well as factual understanding of the proceedings" and be able to consult with a lawyer, applies to both standing trial and waiving the right to counsel or pleading guilty. The Court rejected the Ninth Circuit's adoption of a "reasoned choice" standard, which it deemed higher than the Dusky standard, stating that the distinction was not meaningful or necessary.

Implications: The decision clarifies that the same competency standard applies to various stages of criminal proceedings, whether a defendant is standing trial, pleading guilty, or waiving the right to counsel. The Court emphasized that while a defendant must be competent and the waiver of rights must be knowing and voluntary, the Due Process Clause does not require a heightened standard of competence for waiving rights compared to standing trial.

The Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had held that a higher standard of competency was required for waiving constitutional rights, and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled that a Native American father's religious objection to obtaining a Social Security number for his daughter violated the First Amendment's free exercise clause. The court ruled that Stephen J. Roy's daughter, Little Bird of the Snow, was not robbed of her spirit by having a social security number, but by widespread use of the number in the federal or state government's computer systems. The Court ruled that the government had not violated the Constitution's First Amendment protection against unreasonable searches and seizures by requiring Roy to provide his daughter's number. The ruling also found that Roy had not shown that the number would violate his religious beliefs. The three-judge panel concluded that the "free exercise" clause does not require the government to accommodate religious objections to the statutory requirement that social security numbers be provided as a condition of receiving welfare benefits. The panel also ruled that Roy did not show that the Social Security Administration had violated his right to a free exercise of his First Amendment rights by requiring him to provide the number. In a separate opinion, the court ruled in favor of the government that it did not have to comply with the free exercise provision because Roy had shown that his daughter had not been deprived of her right to receive benefits.

The Federal Power Administration (FPA) regulates the "sale of electric energy at wholesale in interstate commerce." Section 824(a) of the FPA states that all rates must be "just and reasonable," and section 824(d) grants the Commission the authority to examine rates and set aside any rate found "unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential" and replace it with a just and reasonable rate. The Mobile-Sierra doctrine originated in two cases decided in 1956 involving natural gas and electric utility rates respectively. In both cases, the Court rejected the idea that the file-all-new-rates requirement allowed the utility to abrogate a lawful contract with a purchaser simply by filing a new tariff. Instead, the Court held that filing was a precondition to changing a rate, not an authorization to do so in violation of a lawful contract. The Sierra case also dealt with a utility's attempt to change a rate, but this time the Commission had already erroneously concluded that a newly filed tariff superseded a contract rate. The Court corrected this mistake and focused on evaluating whether the contract rate was just and reasonable.

The Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Oklahoma Supreme Court, holding that Oklahoma courts could not exercise personal jurisdiction over nonresident defendants Seaway Volkswagen, Inc. and World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. in a products-liability action. The case involved an Audi automobile purchased in New York that was involved in an accident in Oklahoma. The defendants had no significant contacts with Oklahoma; they did not conduct business, solicit business, or have any other meaningful connection with the state, except for the single incident involving the car accident.

The Court reaffirmed the principle that a state court may only exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident defendant if there are "minimum contacts" between the defendant and the forum state. This requirement ensures that defendants are not subject to litigation in a forum that is unfair or unreasonable and respects the limits of state sovereignty within the federal system.

The Court rejected the argument that the mere foreseeability of a product reaching the forum state was sufficient to establish personal jurisdiction. Instead, the Court emphasized that foreseeability must be tied to the defendant's conduct and connections with the forum state, such that the defendant could reasonably anticipate being sued there.

The Court concluded that the defendants' contacts with Oklahoma were too attenuated to justify the state's exercise of personal jurisdiction. The defendants did not purposefully avail themselves of the privilege of conducting activities within Oklahoma, and their connection to the state was incidental and based on the unilateral activity of the car purchasers. As such, the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment would be violated by allowing Oklahoma to assert jurisdiction in this case. The judgment of the Oklahoma Supreme Court was therefore reversed.

Title: Brown v. Board of Education

Year: 1954

Justice: Earl Warren

Opinion: Unanimous

Keywords: Segregation, Constitutional Law, Equal Protection Clause, 14th Amendment, School Integration

Respondent, who was charged with violating a Georgia statute criminalizing sodomy by committing that act with another adult male in the bedroom of respondent's home, challenged the statute's constitutionality insofar as it criminalizes consensual sodomy. The Federal District Court dismissed the complaint, relying on Doe v. Commonwealth's Attorney for the City of Richmond, 403 F. Supp. 1199, which this Court summarily affirmed, 425 U. S. 901. However, the Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Georgia statute violated respondent's fundamental rights because his homosexual activity is a private and intimate association that is beyond the reach of state regulation by reason of the Ninth Amendment and the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Held: The Court of Appeals erred in holding that the Georgia statute violates the fundamental rights of homosexuals to engage in sodomy. None of the rights announced in Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U. S. 479, and subsequent cases bearing on the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment -which include the right to decide whether or not to beget or bear a child-bears any resemblance to the claimed constitutional right of homosexuals to engage in acts of consensual sodomy. Nor can such a right be properly identified as being deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition or implicit in the concept of ordered liberty.
