To claim that a right to engage in such conduct is deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition or implicit in the concept of ordered liberty is, at best, facetious. Nor is there any merit to respondent's contention that the result should be different where the homosexual conduct occurs in the privacy of the home. Although Stanley v. Georgia, 394 U. S. 557, protected conduct that would not have been protected outside the home, the decision was firmly grounded in the First Amendment. Here, the right pressed upon this Court has no similar support in the text of the Constitution, and it does not qualify for recognition under the prevailing principles for construing the Fourteenth Amendment. If the conduct at issue here is not a fundamental right, there is nothing inappropriate about basing the Georgia statute solely on the notion that homosexual sodomy is immoral and unacceptable to a majority of the electorate. Pp. 108-113. 760 F. 2d 1202, reversed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Western District of Arkansas has ruled that the bankruptcy court erred in denying a bankruptcy trustee's motion to transfer assets from two IRAs to the bankruptcy trustee. The bankruptcy trustee objected to the transfer, saying that the accountholders had "unlimited access" to the funds in their IRAs. The Bankruptcy Court agreed with the trustee, but the Appellate Panel held that the Bankruptcy Court had erred in its decision. The court held that, under the Bankruptcy Code's "right-to-receive" provision, the account holders could not transfer the funds to the trustee until the accountholder turns 7012 years old. The Appellate Court held that this provision did not apply to the account holder's IRAs, which had been established for the benefit of an individual or his beneficiaries, and that the trustee had no authority to transfer the account. The Court held, however, that the "right to receive" provision does apply to IRAs established for certain purposes, such as "stock bonus, pension, profitsharing, annuity, or similar plan or contract" distributions. The Appeals Court ruled that, in this case, the bankruptcy judge's decision did not adequately address the issue of whether the account-holders could transfer the assets to the Bankruptcy Trustee. The appeals court concluded that, based on the court's findings, the Bankruptcy Judge had erred by denying the Trustee's Motion to Transfer the IRAs from the bankruptcy estate. The Appeal Court agreed, and held that "the Bankruptcy Court should have granted the motion"

The majority holds that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) lacks authority to regulate tobacco products under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA). The majority bases its decision on the FDA's longstanding practice of excluding tobacco products from its regulatory authority, as well as on Congress' explicit rejection of the FDA's attempts to regulate tobacco in the past. The majority also notes that Congress has enacted several statutes addressing the subject of tobacco and health, creating a distinct regulatory scheme for cigarettes and smokeless tobacco. Additionally, the majority points to the fact that the FDA's representation of its lack of authority has been consistent since 1914, and that Congress has acted to preclude any meaningful role for any administrative agency in making policy on the subject of tobacco and health.

Title 28 U. S. C. §2244(d) establishes a one-year statute of limitations for seeking federal habeas corpus relief from a state-court judgment. During that period, a state prisoner’s application for postconviction relief in state court is deemed not to count against the limitations period. 28 U. S. C. §2244(d)(2). Here, petitioner Lawrence applied for state postconviction relief in a Florida trial court, but the court denied relief, and the Florida Supreme Court affirmed. He then sought review of the denial in this Court, but while his petition for certiorari was pending, he filed an application for federal habeas relief. His federal application was ultimately dismissed as untimely under §2244(d)’s limitations period. Applying then-applicable Eleventh Circuit precedent, the District Court found that Lawrence had only one day left in the limitations period to file his federal habeas application once the Florida Supreme Court issued its mandate. Held: The filing of a petition for certiorari before this Court does not toll the statute of limitations under §2244(d)(2). Pp. 4–10. (a) An “application for State post-conviction or other [State] collateral review … is pending” only while state courts review the application. That reading means that the statute of limitations is tolled only while state courts review the application. State review ends when the state courts have finally resolved an application for state postconviction relief. Once the State’s highest court has issued its mandate or denied review, no other state avenues for relief remain open. And an application for state postconviction review no longer exists. All that remains is a separate certiorari petition pending before a federal court. The application for state postconviction review is therefore not “pending” after the state court’s postconviction review is complete, and §2244(d)(2) does not toll the 1-year limitations period during the pendency of a petition for certiorari. Pp. 4–6. (b) Lawrence’s contrary construction of §2244(d)(2) is rejected. Although §2244(d)(1)(A) uses language similar to §2244(d)(2), the latter section refers exclusively to “State post-conviction or other collateral review,” whereas the former section speaks to “the time for seeking” direct review. Moreover, §2244(d)(2) seeks to know when an application for “State … review” is pending, whereas §2244(d)(1)(A) refers to the “date on which the first petition for post-conviction review or other collateral relief is filed.” Both sections provide that tolling hinges on the pendency of state review. Lawrence’s suggested interpretation would create awkward situations in which state prisoners have to file federal habeas applications while they have certiorari petitions from state postconviction proceedings pending before this Court. But those situations will also arise under the express terms of §2263, which is part of AEDPA’s “opt-in” provisions for States that comply with certain requirements relating to the provision of postconviction counsel. There is no reason for this Court to construe §2244(d)(2) to avoid them. Nor is there any basis for Lawrence’s argument that equitable tolling applies to his otherwise untimely claims. Assuming equitable tolling is available, Lawrence has failed to meet the standard for obtaining it. Pp. 6–10. 407 Fed. Appx. 100, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court.

Petitioner, a felon incarcerated at the Hocking Correctional Facility (HCF), brought this action under 42 U. S. C. § 1983 against respondents Richard Seiter, then Director of the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction, and Carl Humphreys, then warden of HCF. The complaint alleged overcrowding, excessive noise, insufficient locker storage space, inadequate heating and cooling, improper ventilation, unclean and inadequate restrooms, unsanitary dining facilities and food preparation, and housing with mentally and physically ill inmates. The parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment with supporting affidavits describing the challenged conditions and charged that the authorities, after notification, had failed to take remedial action. Respondents' affidavits denied that some of the alleged conditions existed, and described efforts by prison officials to improve the others. The District Court granted summary judgment for respondents. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: The Sixth Circuit erred in dismissing, before it reached the state-of-mind issue, a number of claims (inadequate cooling, housing with mental ill inmates, and overcrowding) on the ground that, even if proved, they did not involve the serious deprivation required by Rhodes v. Chapman, 452 U.S. 337. The source of the intent requirement is not the predilections of this Court, but the Eighth Amendment itself, which bans only cruel and unusual punishment. A prisoner advancing such a claim must, at a minimum, allege "deliberate indifference" to his "serious" medical needs, for each condition must be "considered as part of the overall conditions challenged," Brief for Petitioner 36. A court cannot dismiss any challenged condition, as long as other conditions remain in dispute, for the each condition to be considered as part the overall condition challenged. Pp. 4-14. 893 F. 2d 861, vacated and remanded.

After being removed from his job as a civilian employee of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) for refusing to participate in military training, petitioners filed suit in the District Court, claiming that the VA’s regulations governing military training violated the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the Establishment Clause of the Constitution. They also claimed that the VA’s regulations were void for vagueness. The District Court entered judgment for petitioners, rejecting the VA’s arguments that the regulations were valid under the Administrative Procedure Act and that petitioners were subject to removal because they had resigned from their jobs. On appeal, the Second Circuit reversed, holding that the regulations were invalid for vagueness. While acknowledging that the regulations were ambiguous, the court determined that the regulations were nevertheless enforceable until clarified by the VA. Because the VA had not yet done so, the court upheld the District Court’s judgment. Held: The Court of Appeals properly ruled that the VA’s regulations were void for vagueness. Pp. 4–7. (a) Under the Administrative Procedure Act, an agency may promulgate a regulation that is ambiguous, but the regulation becomes invalid once the agency issues a clarification. See, e.g., Chevron U. S. A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U. S. 837, 842. Here, the VA has not yet issued a clarification, so the regulations are still invalid. Pp. 4–5. (b) The VA’s regulations are vague because they fail to specify what constitutes participation in military training. The VA has offered conflicting explanations of what it meant by the phrase “participation in military training,” and there is no indication that the VA has resolved the conflict. Without clarity, the regulations are too uncertain to guide behavior. Pp. 5–6. (c) The VA’s regulations are not saved by the doctrine of estoppel. The VA has not acted reasonably in failing to resolve the confusion surrounding the meaning of “participation in military training.” There is no indication that the VA has attempted to clarify the regulations, let alone that it has made good faith efforts to do so. Pp. 6–7. 641 F. 3d 10, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion for a unanimous Court.

Respondent sheriff convicted petitioner of violating §§ 19-42 and 19-44 of the General Statutes of Connecticut by accepting money for illegal bookmaking operations without having a license issued pursuant thereto. After petitioner\'s conviction became final, he was summoned to appear before a referee conducting an inquiry into allegations of various forms of organized crime in Hartford County. When asked a series of questions relating to the circumstances surrounding his arrest and conviction for violation of the above provisions, petitioner declined to answer on the ground that doing so "might tend to incriminate myself," invoking the privilege against self-incrimination. For refusing to answer, he was adjudicated guilty of contempt and remanded to custody pending appeal. His motion for a writ of habeas corpus was denied by the State Supreme Court of Errors, which found that none of the questions put to him tended to incriminate him. Held: 1. The privilege against self-incrimination is guaranteed to a citizen by the Fourteenth Amendment and can not be abolished by a State, though it may be limited in its application. Pp. 528-532. 2. The privilege against self-incrimination protects witnesses in similar federal inquiries. P. 532. 3. Whether an accused\'s silence in either a federal or state proceeding is justified depends solely on whether the claim of privilege is supported by the record. This means that the same standards apply in determining whether the claimed privilege exists regardless of whether the proceeding is federal or state. Here, it was "evident from the implications of the questions, in the setting in which they [were] asked, that a responsive answer to the questions or an explanation of why it [could not] be answered might be dangerous because injurious disclosures could result." Hoffman v. United States, 341 U. S. 479, 486-487. Pp. 532-534. 4. Applying the foregoing principles, the judgment below is reversed. Pp. 534-536. 152 Conn. -, 181 Atl. 2d 708, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia denied an application for leave to appeal his conviction to the Court of Appeals in forma pauperis. The Court's denial of the appeal was based on the fact that the defendant had not filed a timely notice of appeal and had not provided a written statement of his poverty. The court concluded that the application was not in good faith. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a recent decision, held that the district court had no discretion to deny an appeal based on a defendant's failure to file a timely appeal notice. The high court held that a defendant could not be granted leave to file an appeal if he had not shown that he was entitled to a review of his conviction. The appeals court concluded, however, that it had the discretion to grant an appeal without prejudgment interest if the defendant was unable to pay the court's costs. The appeal was denied, and the Supreme Court remanded the case to the lower court for further proceedings.

This case involves two challenges to mandatory maternity leave policies implemented by public schools in Ohio and Virginia. The plaintiffs argue that these policies violate their constitutional rights to privacy and equal protection under the law. They claim that being forced to leave work shortly after becoming pregnant creates a hostile working environment and damages their reputations. Additionally, they argue that the policies unfairly target women and create disparities based on gender.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against four tenants of the Oakland Housing Authority for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 1437d(l)(6) of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Reno, Nevada, the federal government violated the anti-fraud provision of the securities laws by failing to provide tenants with the requisite leasehold interests to be able to evict them for drug-related criminal activity.  The complaint alleges that the tenants were caught in the parking lot smoking marijuana and were later found with cocaine and a crack cocaine pipe.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Nevada today announced criminal charges against the tenants.  As the complaint alleges, the defendants agreed to settle the charges without admitting or denying the allegations of the complaint, and agreed to the entry of judgments that permanently restrains and enjoins them from violating these provisions.  Additionally, the court granted the tenants' requests for a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze, and an officer-and-director bar against them from future violations of these provisions, as well as to pay a civil penalty of $100,000.  On May 2, 2018, the SEC filed a civil injunctive action against the defendants, seeking a permanent injunction, and a preliminary injunction against further violations of the anti–fraud provisions, ordering the defendants to pay disgorgement and prejudgment interest, and to pay civil penalties of $150,000 and $75,000, respectively.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Karpel and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Chicago Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Nevada Department of Housing and Urban Development.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit granted certiorari in the case of American Tobacco Co. v. Patterson Bakery, Confectionery & Tobacco Workers' International Union, Inc., and its affiliate Local 182. The case involves the use of a seniority system in the Richmond, Va., plant. The court found that the company's use of the seniority system violated the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Equal Employment Opportunity Act of 1961 (EEOA). The court held that the EEOA does not apply to seniority systems adopted after the effective date of the Act. The Supreme Court's decision in Griggs v. Duke Power Co. in 1971 held that "the Griggs rationale" is not sufficient to invalidate the system's impact. The appeals court found, however, that actual intent to discriminate must be proved. The lower court found in favor of the company and the union, and the court of appeals granted the motion for a judgment of summary judgment. The high court's ruling is the latest in a series of high-profile cases involving discrimination in the tobacco industry.

The United States Supreme Court has ruled in a 5-4 decision that Texas' redistricting plan violates the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The Court found that the plan diluted the voting power of minorities, particularly African Americans and Hispanics, in several districts. The Court also found that the plan was intended to favor certain political parties and was therefore a form of political gerrymandering. However, the Court did not strike down the entire redistricting plan, and it allowed Texas to continue using the plan until a new plan is approved.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Michael H. and Victoria D. of California, finding that they violated the antifraud provisions of Section 621 of the federal securities laws.  The court also found that Michael H., through his court-appointed guardian, had a right to maintain a relationship with his natural father.  According to the court's order, Michael was entitled to visitation rights based on the presumption of legitimacy of a child born to a husband and a wife.  Michael also had the right to establish his paternity by establishing his own relationship with another man.  As alleged in the court order, however, Michael's right to visitation was violated because, unlike his mother and presumed father, Michael had no opportunity to rebut the presumption.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California today announced criminal charges against Michael.   The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Los Angeles, charges Michael with violating the "irrebuttable presumption" provision of Section 5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, penalties, and injunctive relief.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, Michael and Victoria have consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating the charged provisions, and order Michael to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000,000.  Victoria has also agreed to a settlement in which she will be permanently enjoined from future securities law violations, and to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company.  Separately, the court granted Victoria's request for a temporary restraining order and ordered Michael to surrender his passport.

The Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) prohibits certain conduct involving a “pattern of racketeering activity.” §1962 (c). Petitioner National Steel Supply, Inc. (National), a private corporation with a duty to reimburse customers of registered broker-dealers who became unable to meet their financial obligations, alleged that petitioners engaged in an unlawful racketeering scheme aimed at “gain[ing] sales and market share at Ideal’s expense,” because the fraudulent returns were submitted on an ongoing and regular basis. Petitioners allegedly used funds generated by their fraudulent tax scheme to open a New York location. The New York State Department of Taxation and Finance (Dfff) filed suit in Federal District Court, alleging that Petitioners violated §1964(c), which makes it unlawful for “any person employed by or associated with any enterprise engaged in, or the activities of which affect, interstate or foreign commerce, to conduct or participate, directly or indirectly, in the conduct of such enterprise” through a pattern of racketeer activity or collection of unlawful debt. The District Court dismissed the complaint on the ground that Ideal adequately pleaded its claim because it alleged an injury by reason of petitioners’ use and investment of the racketeering proceeds, “as distinct from injury traceable simply to the predicate acts of racketeering alone or to the conduct the business of the enterprise.’” Id., at 263. The Court of Appeals vacated the District Court’mandated judgment, holding that the complaint did not constitute a RICO violation. Held: Petitioners, by submitting the fraudulent tax returns, committed various acts of mail fraud (when they sent them by mail) and wire fraud, and the complaint adequately pleads proximate cause, and plaintiff has standing to pursue a civil RICO claim. The instant case requires us to apply the principles discussed in Holmes v. Securities Investor Protection Corporation, 503 U. S. 258, 268, to a dispute between two competing businesses. Pp. 5–11. (a) The instant cases arise from a motion to dismiss, and this Court accepts as true the factual allegations in the amended complaint. The proper referent of the proximate-cause analysis is an alleged practice of conducting National‘s affairs through a series of fraudulent communications directed to and relied on by a third party rather than the plaintiff. Respondent Ideal Steel Supply Corporation (Ideal) sells steel mill products along with related supplies and services. It operates two stores in New York, one in Queens and one in the Bronx, and it, too, operates two store locations in Queens. The first case is illustrative. The injury Ideal alleges is its own loss of sales resulting from the fraud, which is a set of actions (offering lower prices) entirely distinct from the alleged RICO violations. The second case is more direct. The attenuated connection between the injury and the Anzas’ injurious conduct thus implicates fundamental concerns expressed in Holmes, and further illustrates the speculative nature of the proceedings that would follow if Ideal were permitted to maintain its claim. In the instant case, the court has no occasion to address the substantial question whether a showing of reliance is required. P. 5. (b) Respondent National Steel, Inc., which offers a similar array of products and services, and which, as Ideal alleges, operates one store in Queens, operates another store in a Bronx location, is one of the two petitioners. The State of New York is being defrauded and the State that lost tax revenue as a result. The state can be expected to pursue appropriate remedies. The adjudication of the State claims, moreover, would be relatively straightforward; while it may be difficult to determine facts such as the number of sales Ideal lost due to National’S tax practices, it is considerably easier to make the initial calculation of how much tax revenue they withheld from the State. There is no need to broaden the universe of actionable harms to permit RICO suits by parties who have been injured only indirectly. The fact that Ideal has not satisfied the requirement of proximate causation does not accord with Holmes, since it is at least debatable whether the RICO violated was the direct result of a Racketeering violation. Moreover, there is no appreciable risk of duplicative recoveries, which are another consideration relevant to this proximate inquiry, see id., at 268. Because §1961(1)(B) and §1960(c) set forth distinct prohibitions, it cannot be concluded that a Rico plaintiff may not assert a claim predicated on mail fraud or wire fraud unless it demonstrates that the alleged violation led directly to the plaintiff's injuries. The proximate case is also illustrative, where Ideal alleges that its own losses resulting from its decreased prices for cash-paying customers resulted from factors other than petitioners' alleged acts of fraud. The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia today entered a final judgment against the companies for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Alexandria, Virginia, alleges that, in 1978, Congress imposed a tax on coal from mines located in the United States sold by the producer, and specifically applied the tax to coal exports.  According to the complaint, the tax was imposed in violation of the Export Clause of the federal tax laws, and the companies sought a temporary restraining order to prevent it from being imposed.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  As set forth in the SEC's Complaint, the companies are seeking a permanent injunction, an order requiring the companies to comply with the refund scheme, and a court order requiring them to pay disgorgement, prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.  Without admitting or denying the companies' allegations, the court agreed to the companies’ motion for an injunction, which is subject to the court’s approval.   The settlement is pending final approval by the court. Â The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California today entered a final judgment against the Bishop Paiute Tribe of California, which alleges that it violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the Tribe, ordering a search warrant and other emergency relief.  According to the court's order, the Tribe's complaint, filed in federal district court in Inyo County, California, alleged that three employees failed to report casino earnings on their applications for state welfare benefits.  In a parallel action, the District Attorney's Office and the Sheriff charged the Tribe with violating Section 1983, and the Tribe and the County consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating the federal securities laws.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Tribe’s complaint, the defendants agreed to settle the case by consenting to a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  On December 2, 2002, the court granted certiorari to the Tribe in its action against the County of Indian Affairs, which issued an order suspending the search warrant pending final approval by the court.   The Court also granted the tribe's request for a preliminary injunction against future searches, and ordered the County to provide a copy of the warrant to the Department of Health and Human Services (DOHS).  The District Attorney and Sheriff have also agreed to be enjoined from future search warrants, and to pay civil penalties in the amount of $100,000. Â The court also ordered the county and the sheriff to comply with the order by issuing an order temporarily restraining the County from conducting any search or seizure of the property of the Tribe.  To learn more about tribal sovereign immunity, see Litigation Release No. 549, 554.

Petitioner, a resident of New York, filed a private antitrust complaint in Federal District Court against seven oil companies, alleging the formation and maintenance by them of a worldwide oil cartel since 1928. The complaint alleged that the defendants, other than Cities Service, agreed at that time to boycott Iranian oil in all world markets until Iran should agree to return Anglo-Iranian's property and concession rights. While the dispute between the parties was still continuing, the defendants allegedly succeeded in obtaining a contract to purchase 15,000,000 metric tons of crude oil or refined products from the National Iranian Oil Co. (NIOC), the company formed to take over Anglo- Iranian's nationalized properties, over a five-year period at a rate substantially less than the then current posted price for Persian Gulf oil, and that a substantially final agreement, although not the actual conclusion of a contract, had been reached on the proposed deal prior to the time petitioner first approached Cities. In response to petitioner's claims that the protracted examination of him by the defendants constituted harassment and an undue burden on him, the District Court held that there was no genuine issue as to material facts between them and that respondent was entitled to judgment as a matter of law. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. The District Court's judgment in favor of petitioner was in conformity with Poller v. Columbia Broadcasting System, Inc., 368 U. S. 464, which provides for comparatively limited discovery for the purpose of showing facts sufficient to withstand a summary judgment motion, rather than Rule 26. Poller and other decisions of this Court were correctly applied and accordingly, accordingly, this Court affirmates. Pp. 5-7. (a) Petitioner's contention that summary judgment against him was improper is one to be decided upon the particular facts of that case, since the evidence so obtained shows both that the defendant is in fact tangential and that the allegations by which he was linked to the other defendants are factually incorrect, and the inference of conspiracy sought to be drawn from Cities' "parallel refusal to deal" does not logically follow. P. 6. (b) The evidence to which petitioner points is significantly probative of conspiracy to entitle him to a full-dress trial notwithstanding the absence of any significant probative evidence tending to support the complaint. The record in this case is in large part a period during which petitioner was no longer having any dealings with Cities. The evidence introduced by petitioner, as a result of their fear that countries in which they held concessions would follow the Iranian lead should the nationalization be successful, also communicated to Cities and other domestic oil companies their intention to support petitioner by refusing to deal with any company that handled Iranian oil. In addition, petitioner had at the time of this motion already obtained discovery of a very substantial number of documents having to do with Cities' dealings in Iranian oil prior to November 1, 1952, the latest point in time ever seriously suggested by petitioner for petitioner to have joined the conspiracy. Petitioner is thus forced to take the position that the one fact that he has produced, Cities' failure to make a deal with him for Iranian oil, is sufficiently probative to entitle petitioner to resist summary judgment. The case at hand presents peculiar difficulties because the issue of fact crucial to the petitioner's case is also an issue of law, namely the existence of a conspiracy, and petitioner cannot justifiably claim that Cities has been given an unfair advantage by the extent of his examination by other defendants. Moreover, petitioner's general objections to the length of time that his case has been pending, since there is absolutely no indication that the interests of the parties whose behavior was "consciously parallel" were substantially divergent and thus is inapplicable here, have little relevance to Waldron's theory of how he has introduced evidence that Cities in fact conspired. P p p p 7. (c) The fact that petitioner's documentary requests, and his complaints about improper limitation of his previous discovery presented in support thereof, are not sufficient to support his contention that he should have been permitted additional discovery before the grant of summary judgment to this point in order that it may be evaluated in the light of what he had succeeded in accomplishing as of the date he made the motion for summary judgment, since petitioner was aware long before late 1964 that Cities was contending that it was not a member of any conspiracy that may have existed between the other alleged co-conspirators and that it resisted being put to the expense of participating in what showed every sign of being an extremely protracted litigation. P pp. 7-8. (d) The absence of testimony from petitioner in this litigation is largely happenstance, since it is clear that petitioner has been the only party to the litigation that has exhibited any consistent desire to expedite the proceedings and that, even where postponements and adjournments have been sought by either Cities or the other defendant, petitioner has always been willing to acquiesce in delay. The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Indiana today entered a final judgment in favor of a judge's immunity from liability for his or her role in the sterilization of a minor.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed on July 9, 1971, Ora Spitler McFarlin, the mother of respondent Linda Kay Spitler Sparkman, presented to Judge Harold D. Stump of the Circuit Court of DeKalb County, Ind., a petition to have a tubal ligation performed on her minor daughter.  The complaint alleges that Judge Stump approved the petition on the same day that she had her appendix removed.  As alleged in the complaint, the petition presented to Stump was not a judicial act because it was not subject to the jurisdiction of a court of general jurisdiction.  Instead, the complaint alleges, JudgeStump was acting as a judge in the capacity of a county circuit court judge, and he had jurisdiction over the matter.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Indiana today announced criminal charges against Stump.   The SEC's Complaint, filed in federal court in Indianapolis, charges Stump with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, civil penalties, and a penny stock bar.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, Stump consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty in the amount of $1,000,000.  He also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company, and to pay $2,500 in disgorgment and prejudgment interests, with a $100,000 civil penalty to be determined by the court upon motion by the SEC. The Supreme Court opinion addresses a challenge by the National Park Hospitality Association (Petitioner), a trade association representing concessioners in national parks, to a National Park Service (NPS) regulation. The regulation states that concession contracts in national parks are not subject to the Contract Disputes Act of 1978 (CDA), which provides procedures for resolving disputes over government contracts.

The Court determined that the case was not ripe for judicial resolution, meaning it was premature for the Court to decide on the matter. The ripeness doctrine prevents courts from getting involved in abstract disagreements over administrative policies before they have been formalized and have had a concrete effect on the parties involved.

The Court's analysis focused on two factors: the fitness of the issues for judicial decision and the hardship to the parties of withholding court consideration. The Court found that the regulation did not create immediate legal effects or obligations, nor did it affect the primary conduct of concessioners. Therefore, there was no immediate hardship demonstrated by the Petitioner.

The Court also noted that the NPS does not have the authority to administer the CDA, and thus its regulation could not be considered a legislative rule with the force of law. Instead, the regulation was seen as a policy statement expressing NPS's view on the application of the CDA to concession contracts.

The Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals, which had affirmed the validity of the NPS regulation, and remanded the case with instructions to dismiss the issue due to lack of ripeness.

Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment, emphasizing that the Petitioner had not demonstrated sufficient injury to have standing to invoke federal-court jurisdiction. Justice Breyer, joined by Justice O'Connor, dissented, arguing that the Petitioner did have standing and that the issue was ripe for judicial review, disagreeing with the majority's decision to postpone review.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant who was found not guilty on all three of the charges.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Boston, Massachusetts, defendant Melvin Smith was charged with violating the double jeopardy provision of the federal securities laws.  The SEC alleges that Smith was the only defendant to be found guilty of the three charges, and that the SEC found that Smith had violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the defendants were falsely told that the barrel of a .32 or a .38 was less than 16 inches when, in fact, the barrel was 16 inches.  As alleged in the complaint, the defendants had shot each other with "a pistol," specifically "a revolver" that "appeared to be a "pistol" or "revolver" with a barrel length "less than16 inches."  The complaint further alleges that, as a matter of law, the defendant could pursue no appeal at any stage of a criminal case, however mistaken the trial court's finding of not guilty was.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Smith consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the securities laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of 10 years and a $10,000 civil penalty.  Smith also agreed to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for five years and to be prohibited from participating in any securities offering or sales of any securities.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

This case involves a dispute between the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and a financial institution named Yankees Financial Services Company ("Yankees") regarding the validity of a Massachusetts law requiring employers to pay their workers for unused vacation time upon termination of employment. The Massachusetts legislature passed the bill in response to concerns about the mistreatment of low-wage workers who often lose their jobs without being able to afford to take time off work. The bill applies to all employers operating in Massachusetts, regardless of where they are based, and provides that employers must pay their workers for any unused vacation time owed to them within thirty days of termination of employment.

The case began when the Commonwealth sued Yankees in the Massachusetts Superior Court, alleging that the company had failed to pay its employees for unused vacation time as required by the new law. Yankees responded by challenging the constitutionality of the law, arguing that it conflicted with federal labor laws governing employee benefit plans. The case eventually reached the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, which ruled in favor of the Commonwealth and upheld the constitutionality of the law.

However, the U.S. Supreme Court ultimately reversed the decision of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, holding that the Massachusetts law fell within the category of "state action" protected by the First Amendment's Establishment Clause. The Court reasoned that the law imposed a requirement on private employers to pay their workers for unused vacation time, effectively creating a state-enforced obligation that could chill free association among businesses. As a result, the Court struck down the law as unconstitutional.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment in favor of the Publishers, who are charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Brooklyn, New York, alleges that, from 1990 to 1993, the Publishers and their affiliated companies, Mead Data Central Corp., Inc. and LEXIS/NEXIS, which stores information in a text-only format, misappropriated and distributed articles from hundreds of periodicals.  According to the complaint, these articles were not part of a collective work, but rather a "revision" of that collective work.  In addition, the complaint alleges that the Defendants violated the right to reproduce and distribute the articles in the Databases, which are intended to facilitate the dissemination of newsprint and other digital media.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Complaint, the Defendants have consented to the entry of judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the above-mentioned provisions of the federal securities laws, ordering the Defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and ordering the defendants to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.  Additionally, the defendants have agreed to be permanently enjoined from future violations of the books, records, and advertising provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4), and to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for the rest of their lives.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a former officer of the Los Angeles Police Department who was charged with violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The court also entered a temporary restraining order against the officer who was convicted of violating the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's order, filed in federal court in the District of Columbia, on August 2, 1981, the court entered a judgment that permanently enjoins the officer from violating the Fourth Amendment and orders him to comply with the court's order.  In a parallel action, the Court of Appeals today issued an order requiring the officer to surrender any evidence obtained pursuant to a search warrant, including a shoebox containing a large amount of cash that belonged to "Armando" and "Patsy."  The order also requires the officer not to obstruct or impede the investigation of the matter.    The SEC's complaint, filed on August 4, 2011, charges the officer with violating Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a) of The Securities Act of 1933, and Section 9(b)(5) of Exchange Act Rules 10b2-1, and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, the officer has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations of Section 5 of the Exchange Act, ordering him to disgorge $1,038,427, and pay $2,065 in prejudgment interests, and ordering him not to participate in the issuance of any search warrant. On August 5, 2011 the court granted the request for an emergency court injunction against further violations of Sections 5, 5, and 17 (a)(3) ofÂ the Securities Act, and entered an order imposing a permanent injunction against the officers from violating Section 5.  It also ordered that the officer comply with court orders barring him from participating in any search or seizure of any kind, including that of a motor vehicle or any other motor vehicle.

Respondent was charged with three counts of having unlawfully manufactured and processed methamphetamine and of unlawfully selling and delivering that drug in violation of 21 U. S. C. §§ 331(q)(1), (2), 360a(a), (b) (1964 ed., Supp. V). After a jury trial in which his sole defense was entrapment, respondent was convicted on all three counts. On appeal, the Court of Appeals reversed the conviction solely for the reason that an undercover agent supplied an essential chemical for manufacturing the methamphetamine which formed the basis of respondent's conviction. Held: 1. As a matter of law, a defense to a criminal charge may be founded upon an intolerable degree of governmental participation in the criminal enterprise. Sorrells v. United States, 287 U.S. 435, distinguished. Pp. 459-481. (a) The principle of entraping, regardless of predisposition, whenever the government supplies contraband to the defendants is premised on fundamental concepts of due process and evince the reluctance of the judiciary to countenance "overzealous law enforcement." P. 461. 2. Since the defense is not of a constitutional dimension, Congress may address itself to the question and adopt any substantive definition of the defense that it may find desirable. P. 470. 4. The fact that the Government's deception actually implants the criminal design in the defendant's mind is fatal to his claim of entrapement, since he was an active participant in an illegal drug manufacturing enterprise which began before the Government agent appeared on the scene, and continued after the Government Agent had left the scene. The evidence in the record amply demonstrate that the propanone used in the illicit manufacture of methamphetamine not only could have been obtained without the intervention of respondent but was in fact obtained by these defendants. P p. 462. 458 F. 2d 671, reversed.

Title 26 U. S. C. § 611 allows individuals holding economic interests in oil and gas deposits to elect to treat the gross income from such deposits as coming into income annually instead of actually being withdrawn. Section 613 permits such individuals to elect to compute the percentage depletion allowance on such gross income according to a formula set forth in § 613(a). Section 613A limits the percentage depletion allowance to income attributable to production over a certain level. Held: 1. Neither the language nor the legislative history of § 613A supports the conclusion that Congress meant to eliminate the percentage depletion allowance on lease bonus or advance royalty income arising from oil and gas properties. Pp. 218-226. (a) So long as the income can, by some allocation method, be attributed to production below the ceilings Congress established, lease bonus and advance royalty income comes within the four corners of the percentage depletion provisions. Pp. 220-221. (b) Nothing in § 613A bars percentage depletion on income received prior to actual production. To the contrary, so long as the income can, by some allocation method, be attributed to production below the ceilings Congress established, lease bonus and advance royalty income comes within the four corners of the percentage depletion provisions. P. 221. 2. The Commissioner's construction of § 613A as barring percentage depletion on lease bonus and advance royalty income is unreasonable and therefore not entitled to deference. Pp. 226-229. (a) Although the Commissioner has broad authority to prescribe all "needful rules and regulations" for the enforcement of the tax laws, he cannot resolve the practical problems created by § 613A's various production requirements and limitations by eliminating the allowance altogether. P. 229. 744 Ct. Cl. 15, 484 F. Supp. 105, affirmed; 744 Ct. Cl. 16, 484 F. Supp. 111, reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court case you provided is "Mastro Plastics Corp. v. National Labor Relations Board." In this case, the Supreme Court considered whether a strike occurring during the term of a collective bargaining agreement violates Section 8(d)(4) of the National Labor Relations Act. The court ultimately ruled that the strike did not violate Section 8(d)(4) because the strike occurred after the notice period required by the statute had ended and before the expiration date of the contract.

The Supreme Court of the United States reviewed a case to determine if a school board, authorized by state law to hire and fire teachers, could dismiss teachers who were engaged in a strike that was prohibited by state law without violating the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The case involved a Wisconsin school district and its school board, who dismissed teachers for striking, which was illegal under state law. The teachers and their collective-bargaining agent, the Hortonville Education Association (HEA), sued, claiming that the board was not impartial and that due process required an independent decisionmaker.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court had ruled in favor of the teachers, stating that due process required an impartial decisionmaker other than the school board to evaluate the teachers' conduct and the board's response. The state court also created a remedy allowing for a de novo hearing in any court of record for a teacher dissatisfied with the board's decision.

The U.S. Supreme Court reversed the Wisconsin Supreme Court's decision. The Court held that the school board's involvement in negotiations preceding the strike did not disqualify it from deciding to dismiss the teachers. The Court emphasized that due process does not require inflexible procedures applicable to every situation and that the nature of the bias attributed to the board and the interests at stake must be considered.

The Court found no evidence of personal or financial conflict of interest or personal animosity from the board members towards the teachers. It also noted that mere familiarity with the facts of a case or taking a position on a policy issue does not disqualify a decisionmaker. The Court concluded that the board's decision was not purely disciplinary but also involved significant governmental and public policy dimensions.

The Court determined that the teachers' admission of striking, the governmental interests at stake, and the state law vesting the school board with the power to employ and dismiss teachers supported the board's authority to make the dismissal decision. The Court held that the Due Process Clause did not guarantee that the decision to terminate employment would be made or reviewed by a body other than the school board.

The judgment of the Wisconsin Supreme Court was reversed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the U.S. Supreme Court's opinion.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit reversed a lower court's decision to uphold a life sentence without the possibility of parole for a Michigan man convicted of possessing 672 grams of cocaine. The court held that the sentence was "cruel and unusual" within the meaning of the Eighth Amendment's Eighth Amendment protection against excessive bail. The appeals court concluded that the sentencing judge was statutorily required to impose the sentence, without taking into account the particularized circumstances of the crime and of the criminal. We conclude that the lower court was correct to uphold the sentence. The Court of Appeal's ruling is consistent with the decisions of other courts that have held that it is not unconstitutional to impose life sentences without the prospect of parole.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that a lower court erred in denying John Fogerty's motion for attorney's fees in a copyright infringement case. The Court held that the lower court's decision was consistent with the "dual" standard for awarding fees under the Copyright Act of 1976 and the so-called "evenhanded" approach favored by the Third Circuit. The Supreme Court's ruling is the latest in a series of decisions that have produced conflicting views on the issue of fees in copyright infringement cases. The case involves a 1970 song written by Fogerty and a 1985 song by Warner Brothers Records, Inc., entitled "The Old Man Down the Road"

Respondents, Native Americans, filed suit challenging the validity of the Government's plans to construct a new road across the "Chimney Rock" area of the Six Rivers National Forest and to log commercially in the vicinity of that area. The District Court entered a permanent injunction against the road construction and against the logging, finding that the plans would result in the destruction of the natural beauty of the area and would harm the religious practices of the Indians. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: 1. Because the issues raised by the parties include the validity of the Government's plans, the lower courts erred in issuing the injunction prior to determining the validity of the plans. Pp. 449-450. 2. Since the Government's plans would have a direct and predictable impact on the religious practices of the Indians, the First Amendment bars the Government from carrying out the plans absent a showing of a compelling governmental interest. Bowen v. Roy, 476 U. S. 693. There is no merit to the claim that the Government's plans would violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment merely because they would benefit the Indians economically. Pp. 450-452. 3. The Government's plans would not violate the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment even assuming that the Indians' religious practices are critical to the success of their tribe and to mankind generally. The Government has taken numerous steps to minimize the impact that the road construction will have on the Indians' religious activities. Moreover, the American Indian Religious Freedom Act, while recognizing the Indians' right to access to sites, use and possession of sacred objects, and the freedom to worship through ceremonies and traditional rites, contains no provision conferring on the Indians any judicially enforceable individual rights. Pp. 452-456. 4. The suggestion that the First Amendment guarantees against any form of government action that frustrates or inhibits religious practice cannot withstand analysis. The First Amendment states: "Congress shall make no law ... prohibiting the free exercise [of religion]." Any attempt to construe the Amendment as applying to any form of government action that frustrates or inhibits religious practice would effectively overrule Bowen v. Roy, supra, and would be incompatible with the text of the Constitution, with the precedents of this Court, and with a responsible sense of this Court's institutional role. Pp. 456-460. Reversed and remanded.

In the case of Schneckloth v. Bustamonte, the Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether evidence obtained from a search, consented to by a third party, was admissible in the criminal trial of the defendant, Matlock. Matlock had been indicted for bank robbery and sought to suppress evidence seized from a home he shared with others, including Mrs. Graff, who had consented to the search.

The District Court had established two requirements for the evidence to be admissible: the searching officers must have reasonably believed that the consenter had authority to consent, and the consenter must have actually had such authority. The District Court found the first requirement met but not the second, as it excluded certain out-of-court statements as hearsay, leading to insufficient evidence of Mrs. Graff's authority to consent.

The Supreme Court reversed the lower courts' decisions, holding that the exclusionary rules of evidence do not fully apply to pretrial hearings on the admissibility of evidence. The Court argued that Mrs. Graff's statements should not have been excluded, as they were made to the searching officers and were consistent with other evidence. Additionally, the Court noted that Mrs. Graff's statements were against her penal interest, which typically carries a presumption of reliability.

The Supreme Court concluded that, with the inclusion of Mrs. Graff's and Matlock's out-of-court statements, the government had met its burden of proving that Mrs. Graff's consent to search was valid. However, the Court remanded the case to the District Court to reassess the sufficiency of the evidence in light of this decision.

The implication of this decision is that third-party consent to a search is valid against a co-occupant if the consenting party has common authority over the premises, and that hearsay evidence can be considered by judges during pretrial hearings on the admissibility of evidence.

Section 127 (a) of the Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act of 1997 (FDAMA) exempts "compounded drugs" from the FDA's standard drug approval requirements as long as the providers of those drugs abide by several restrictions, including that they refrain from advertising or promoting particular compounded drugs. Respondents, a group of licensed pharmacies that specialize in drug compounding, sought to enjoin enforcement of the subsections of the Act dealing with advertising and solicitation, arguing that those provisions violate the First Amendment's free speech guarantee. The District Court agreed with respondents and granted their motion for summary judgment, holding that the provisions do not meet the test for acceptable government regulation of commercial speech set forth in Central Hudson Gas & Elec. Corp. v. Public Serv. Comm'n of N. Y., 447 U. S. 557, 566. The court invalidated the relevant provisions, severing them from the rest of § 127(a). The Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part, agreeing that the FDAMA's provisions regarding advertisement and promotion are unconstitutional but finding them not to be severable from the other compounding requirements. Held: 1. The provisions regarding advertising and promotion amount to unconstitutional restrictions on commercial speech, and the court's severability determination is invalidated. Pp. 566-567. 2. Although commercial speech is protected by the First and First Amendments, not all regulation of such speech is unconstitutional. Central Hudson, supra, articulated a test for determining whether a particular commercial speech regulation is constitutionally permissible, and that test must be answered in the affirmative for the regulation to be found constitutional. The Act's speech-related provisions are unconstitutional because they do not directly advance the Government's interests. The Government's interest in protecting the effectiveness and integrity of the FDCA's new drug approval process and the protection of the public health that it provides is a substantial governmental interest. P. 567. 3. The FDAMA does not violate the Free Speech Clause of the First, since the Act exempts compounded drugs from the FDMA's "new drug" requirements and other requirements provided the drugs satisfy a number of restrictions. First, they must be compounded by a licensed pharmacist or physician in response to a valid prescription for an identified individual patient, or, if prepared before the receipt of such a prescription, "c]ompounding, regularly, or in inordinate amounts, drug products that are commercially available ... and that are essentially generic copies of commercially available, FDA-approved drug products"; using commercial scale manufacturing or testing equipment to compound drugs; offering compounded drugs at wholesale; and "[d]istributing inordinate quantities of compounded products out of state." Central Hudson v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council, Inc., 425 U.S. 748. The statute does not directly forbid such sales. It instead restricts advertising, of course not just to those who do not need compounded drugs, but also to individuals who do need the drugs and their doctors. Although the advertising ban may reduce the demand for compounded drugs in those cases, it does nothing to prevent such individuals from obtaining compounded drugs other than requiring prescriptions. Moreover, the provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938 (FDMA) outside § 127 (A) are not an issue here and so remain unaffected. The parties agree that the advertising and soliciting prohibited by FDAMA constitute commercial speech. Although, for the reasons given by the dissent, the Government had not demonstrated that the speech restrictions would directly advance its interests or that alternatives less restrictive of speech were unavailable, the fact that they could advance its asserted interest indicated that the law's legislative history demonstrated that Congress intended to exempt compounding from theFDCA's requirements only in return for a prohibition on promotion of specific compounded drugs is itself a substantial government interest. The fact that the Government has failed to demonstrate that it had an interest in preventing misleading advertisements is also sufficient to justify a ban on such advertising. The amendments to the Federal Drug, Drug Act of 1937 (FDCA) exempting compounded drugs to be made only in "limited quantities" and "in response to valid prescriptions for an individual patient" must be made "inordinate amounts" before receipt of a valid pharmacy prescription if they could document a history of receiving valid prescriptions "generated solely within an established professional practitioner-patient-pharmacy relationship" and if they maintained the prescription on file as required by state law. The Central Hudson test is significantly stricter than the rational basis test, however, requiring the Government not only to identify specifically "a substantial interest to be achieved by [the] restrictio[n] oncommercial speech," 447U. S., at 564, but to prove that the regulation "directly advances" that interest and is not more extensive than is necessary to serve that interest in a world where advertising was permitted. The Amendment does not require the Government to justify its decision to regulate speech, but rather requires that it identify specifically a substantial interest and prove that it is not sufficient to rely on doctors to refrain from prescribing compounded drugs

The U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania entered a decree declaring invalid the liquor license issued to Moose Lodge, a local branch of the national fraternal organization, as long as it follows a policy of racial discrimination in its membership or operating policies or practices. The court found that a Caucasian member in good standing brought appellee, a Negro, to the Lodge's dining room and bar as his guest and requested service of food and beverages. Moose Lodge through its employees refused service to plaintiff solely because he is a negro. The District Court in this connection found that '(t)he lodges accordingly maintain a policy and practice of restricting membership to the Caucasian race and permitting members to bring only Caucasian guests on lodge premises, particularly to the dining room or bar'

Section 2680(a) of the Federal Tort Claims Act bars a tort action against the United States based upon the "discretionary function or duty" of a government employee, unless the employee acted in bad faith or with malicious intent. Respondents in No. 82-1349 allege that the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) was negligent in issuing a type certificate for the Boeing 707 aircraft in 1958 because the lavatory trash receptacle did not satisfy applicable safety regulations. And respondents in No. 82-1350 claim negligence in the CAB's issuance of a supplemental type certificate in 1965 for the De Havilland Dove aircraft, asserting that the installation of the fuel line leading to the cabin heater violated CAB airworthiness standards. There is no indication that either the Boeing 707 trash receptacle or the De Havilland Dove cabin heater was actually inspected or reviewed by an CAB inspector or representative. Rather, the CAB accomplished its task of ensuring that aircraft conformed to safety regulations by implementing a "spot-check" system involving certification of aircraft design and manufacture at various stages of production. The court below upheld the judgments for respondents, concluding that the CAB's alleged negligence fell outside the discretionary function exception of § 2680(a). Held: The discretionary function exception precludes a tort action based upon the conduct of the CAB in certificating these aircraft for use in commercial aviation. Pp. 809-818. (a) Whatever else the discretionary function exception may include, it plainly was intended to encompass the discretionary acts of the Government acting in its role as a regulator of the conduct of private individuals. Pp. 810-813. (b) Both the CAB's decision to implement the "spot-check" system of compliance review and the application of that system to the particular aircraft involved in these cases are barred by the discretionary function exception. The CAB's implementation of a mechanism for compliance review is plainly discretionary activity of the "nature and quality" protected by § 2680(a). And the acts of CAB employees in executing the "spot-check" program in accordance with agency directives are protected by the discretionary function exception as well. Pp. 813-818. 704 F. 2d 1388, 705 F. 2d 1405, reversed.

The Supreme Court opinion in the case involving eBay Inc., Half.com, and MercExchange L.L.C. addresses the issue of whether the traditional four-factor test for awarding permanent injunctive relief applies to patent infringement cases under the Patent Act. The Court affirms that it does, vacating the judgment of the Court of Appeals.

The case arose when MercExchange, holding a patent for an electronic marketplace, sued eBay and Half.com for patent infringement after licensing negotiations failed. The jury found in favor of MercExchange, but the District Court denied MercExchange's request for a permanent injunction. The Court of Appeals reversed this decision, applying a general rule that permanent injunctions should be granted in patent infringement cases unless there are exceptional circumstances.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the Court of Appeals, emphasizing that the traditional four-factor test for injunctive relief must be applied. This test requires a plaintiff to demonstrate: (1) irreparable injury; (2) inadequacy of other remedies, such as monetary damages; (3) that the balance of hardships favors an injunction; and (4) that the public interest would not be disserved by an injunction.

The Court clarified that the right to exclude others from using a patented invention does not automatically entitle the patent holder to an injunction; rather, the decision to grant an injunction must be made based on equitable principles. The Court also noted that the Patent Act itself specifies that injunctions may be issued in accordance with these principles.

The Supreme Court criticized both the District Court and the Court of Appeals for not properly applying the four-factor test. The District Court was too broad in suggesting that a patent holder's willingness to license or lack of commercial activity could preclude irreparable harm, while the Court of Appeals was too rigid in generally favoring injunctions for patent infringement.

The Supreme Court vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with the traditional principles of equity. The Court did not take a position on whether an injunction should be granted in this specific case or others, but emphasized that such decisions are within the equitable discretion of the district courts.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin today entered a final judgment against a Wisconsin man accused of violating the right to counsel in connection with a criminal case. The court found that McNeil had waived his Miranda rights and requested counsel at an initial appearance on a charged offense, and that he was entitled to counsel at the time of the alleged crime.  McNeil also agreed to be barred from appearing with an attorney at a hearing for a pending criminal case, and to have an attorney present to assist him in the defense of his rights.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Michigan today announced criminal charges against McNeil.  On May 24, 2017, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. Snyder granted the court a temporary injunction against future violations of the federal securities laws and ordered McNeil to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.
