The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Wilbert K. Rogers, Jr., a Tennessee man convicted of second-degree murder, for violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Memphis, Tennessee, Rogers was convicted in Tennessee of second degree murder in 1994.  The SEC alleges that, at the time of Rogers' conviction, the year and a day rule had been abolished by the Tennessee state court in 1989, and that, prior to that court's decision, the state court had not recognized the viability of a particular construction of the state's criminal law.  As alleged in the complaint, Rogers had developed a condition that required proof of the defendant's intent to commit the crime.  In its judgment, the court found that, contrary to the conclusion of the court's finding, Rogers violated due process and the pre-judgment provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act") and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the SEC, Rogers consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(b)(2)(A) and (c) of The Securities Act, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against him from serving as an officer or director of a public company.   The court also ordered Rogers to pay a $1,000 civil penalty.  On August 7, 1995, the SEC issued an order suspending Rogers from appearing before the SEC as an expert witness in a case involving a criminal case.  It also ordered him to sign a civil injunctive proceeding against him, which is subject to court approval. Â The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by John Rymas and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter in the Atlanta Regional Office. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was convicted of violating the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Madison, Wis., alleges that Todd Mitchell, a convicted felon who was sentenced to four years' imprisonment for the same conduct, intentionally selected his victim because of his race or other protected status.  According to the complaint, Mitchell told a group of young black men and boys that he wanted to "fuck somebody up" and "go get him."  The complaint further alleges that Mitchell told the group that the victim was a member of a "white supremacist prison gang."  Mitchell allegedly told the men that the "white boy" was a "man who was going to provoke a "race war" and that he would "go and fuck somebody up."  As the complaint alleges, the group ran towards the boy and Mitchell told them: "There goes a white boy; go get him. I'm going to kick him out of here."  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Mitchell.  Mitchell has agreed to settle the charges against him, and agreed to pay a penalty of seven years and a $10,000 civil penalty.  In its order granting the SEC's motion for a preliminary injunction, the court also ordered Mitchell to surrender his passport and other documents related to the alleged conduct.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the court's order, Mitchell consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, and orders him to pay $7,500 in disgorgement and prejudgment interest, and to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company.   The settlement is subject to court approval.

Respondent Citizens for a Better Environment (CBE) is an Illinois not-for-profit corporation organized for the purpose of promoting "the protection of the environment." CBE is registered with the Illinois Attorney General's Charitable Trust Division pursuant to Illinois law, and has been afforded tax-exempt status by the Internal Revenue Service, and gifts to it are deductible for federal income tax purposes. CBE requested permission to solicit contributions in the Village, but the Village denied CBE a permit because CBE could not demonstrate that 75 percent of its receipts would be used for "charitable purposes" as required by § 22-20 (g) of the Code. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that the 75-percent requirement was a form of censorship prohibited by the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Held: 1. The ordinance does not violate the First Amendment. Pp. 531-532. (a) The Village's legitimate interest in preventing fraud can be better served by measures less intrusive than a direct prohibition on solicitation. P. 533. (b) The ordinance is not unconstitutionally overbroad, since it deals only with solicitation and because any charity is free to propagate its views from door to door in the village without a permit as long as it refrains from soliciting money, and it is not an invalid prior restraint on the free exercise of religion, since there is no substantial relationship between the 75 percent requirement and the protection of public safety or of residential privacy. P p. 534. (c) The District Court's determination that the ordinance violates the First, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments does not conflict with the Court's view of prior cases relevant to canvassing and soliciting by religious and charitable organizations, since prior authorities clearly establish that charitable appeals for funds, on the street or door, involve a variety of speech interests-communication of information, the dissemination and propagation of views and ideas, and the advocacy of causes, and that such activities involve interests protected by First Amendment freedoms, and thus cannot be sustained unless it serves a sufficiently strong, subordinating interest that the Village is entitled to protect from fraud, crime, and undue annoyance, is rejected by the Court, which held that a "general regulation, in the public interest, of solicitation, which does not involve any religious test and does not unreasonably obstruct or delay the collection of funds, is not open to any constitutional objection," id., at 305, 60 S.Ct. at 904-905. The court rejected the Village's argument that summary judgment was inappropriate because material issues of fact were disputed. Because CBE challenged the facial validity of the village ordinance on First Amendment grounds, the court ruled that such regulation "must be done, and [the restriction applied, in such a manner as not to intrude upon the rights of free speech and free assembly." Id., at 540-541, the Court held that even if the 75percent requirement might be valid as applied to other types of charitable solicitation, the village's requirement was unreasonable on its face because it barred solicitation by advocacy-oriented organizations even "where it is made clear that the contributions will be used ... for reasonable salaries of those who will gather and disseminate information relevant to the organization's purpose." Id. At 226, the District Court upheld an ordinance prohibiting canvassing by a substantial category of charities to which the75-percent limitation could not be applied consistently with the First Amendments, even if there was no demonstration that CBE itself was one of these organizations. P, 535. (d) The Court's judgment is affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit recently ruled that Arizona's law requiring employers to use a federal electronic verification system to confirm that the workers they employ are legally authorized is not preempted by federal immigration law. The court held that the law's licensing provisions fall squarely within the federal statute's savings clause and that the Arizona regulation does not otherwise conflict with federal law. In a separate opinion, the court held, however, that the state's enforcement of the law is not subject to the same preemption as the federal law, and that it is subject to both civil and criminal sanctions. The Court's decision is the latest in a series of high-profile immigration cases that have raised the issue of whether state laws that require employers to check the immigration status of their employees are valid. The U,S. Supreme Court, and other federal courts have held that federal immigration laws do not prohibit states from imposing civil or criminal sanctions on employers who knowingly employ unauthorized aliens. The Supreme Court has also held that states can use their own laws to determine whether an employee is legally authorized to work in the U. S.

The Supreme Court addressed the issue of whether an ERISA (Employee Retirement Income Security Act) plan administrator should lose deference in interpreting plan terms after making a single mistake. The case involved Xerox Corporation's pension plan and how to calculate benefits for employees who were rehired after receiving lump-sum distributions upon leaving the company. The plan administrator initially used a "phantom account" method, which was later found unreasonable by the Second Circuit Court of Appeals due to lack of adequate notice to the employees.

Upon remand, the plan administrator proposed a new method, but the District Court did not apply a deferential standard of review and instead adopted an approach proposed by the employees that did not account for the time value of money. The Second Circuit affirmed the District Court's decision.

The Supreme Court held that a single honest mistake by a plan administrator does not justify stripping them of deference for subsequent related interpretations of the plan. The Court emphasized the importance of deference in promoting efficiency, predictability, and uniformity in the administration of ERISA plans. It rejected the "one-strike-and-you’re-out" approach of the Court of Appeals, stating that it had no basis in the Court's precedent or trust law principles.

The Court also noted that trust law does not provide a clear answer to the issue but that the principles underlying ERISA support maintaining deference. The Court argued that removing deference after a single mistake would undermine the goals of ERISA by increasing litigation costs and discouraging employers from offering plans.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, emphasizing that the lower courts should have applied the deferential standard established in previous cases like Firestone Tire & Rubber Co. v. Bruch. Justice Sotomayor did not participate in the decision.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit ruled that a warrantless entry by police into an apartment without a search warrant violated the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. The court held that the entry was valid because it was based on the consent of a third party who possessed common authority over the premises, but who in fact did not do so. The Court held that Edward Rodriguez was not a "usual resident" but rather an "infrequent visitor" at the apartment where he was arrested and charged with possession of a controlled substance with intent to deliver. Rodriguez moved to suppress all evidence seized at the time of his arrest, claiming that Fischer had vacated the apartment several weeks earlier and had no authority to consent to the entry. The Appellate Court of Illinois denied the State's petition for leave to appeal, and the Supreme Court granted the motion, holding that Fischer did not have "common authority" over the apartment. In a separate opinion, the Appellate Justices agreed with the lower court's finding that Fischer was not an "usual" resident but rather "an frequent visitor" and that she did not contribute to the rent, that she was not allowed to invite others to the apartment on her own, and that Fischer moved some of her possessions from the apartment when Rodriguez was away. The Supreme Court ruled that Fischer's consent was sufficient for the entry to be valid. The lower court also found that Rodriguez had violated the prohibition against warrantless searches when he was asleep in the apartment and that the officers had probable cause to believe that Fischer possessed the common authority. The high court ruled that Rodriguez's motion to suppress the evidence was not supported by the evidence. The appeals court agreed that the trial court had erred in denying his motion for a judgment of acquittal. The 7th Court agreed, and sent the case back to the lower courts for further consideration.

Petitioner Ewing’s 1994 California conviction for grand larceny—for taking golf clubs valued at more than $500 from a department store—carried a maximum sentence of 10 years. Because he had two prior felony convictions, he was subject to California’s “three strikes” law, which provides that a third felony conviction carries a mandatory life sentence. Following his arrest for subsequent felonies, Ewing was convicted of violating California’s “three strikes” law. The California trial court sentenced him to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. The State Court of Appeal reversed, finding that the trial court erred in calculating Ewing’s sentence. The State Supreme Court affirmed, reasoning that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to impose a sentence greater than the maximum allowed by the original grand larceny conviction. Held: Ewing’s sentence violates the Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause. Pp. 58–66. (a) Ewing’s sentence is grossly disproportionate to the offense of grand larceny. The Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause prohibits sentences that are grossly disproportionate to the offense committed. See, e.g., Gregg v. Georgia, 428 U. S. 103, 109. Here, Ewing’s sentence is grossly disproportionate to the offense of grand larceny because it is much longer than the maximum sentence that could have been imposed for that offense. Pp. 58–60. (b) The Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause is not rendered inapplicable by the existence of a recidivist enhancement provision. The existence of a recidivist enhancement provision does not render the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause inapplicable. See, e.g., Plata v. New Hampshire, 542 U. S. ___, ___. Instead, the clause serves as a safeguard against the arbitrary application of recidivist provisions. See, e.g., id., at ___. Pp. 60–61. (c) The Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause is not rendered inapplicable by the availability of a remedy other than habeas corpus. The availability of a remedy other than habeas corpus does not render the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause inapplicable. See, e.g., Plata, supra, at ___. Pp. 61–62. (d) The Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause is not rendered inapplicable by the availability of a remedy other than a writ of error correction. The availability of a remedy other than a writ of error correction does not render the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause inapplicable. See, e.g., Plata, supra, at ___. Pp. 62–63. (e) The Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause is not rendered inapplicable by the availability of a remedy other than a writ of prospective relief. The availability of a remedy other than a writ of prospective relief does not render the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause inapplicable. See, e.g., Plata, supra, at ___. Pp. 63–64. (f) The Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause is not rendered inapplicable by the availability of a remedy other than a writ of retroactive relief. The availability of a remedy other than a writ of retroactive relief does not render the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause inapplicable. See, e.g., Plata, supra, at ___. Pp. 64–65. (g) The Eighth Amendment’s Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause is not rendered inapplicable by the availability of a remedy other than a writ of collateral relief. The availability of a remedy other than a writ of collateral relief does not render the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause inapplicable. See, e.g., Plata, supra, at ___. Pp. 65–66. 35 Cal. 4th 1199, 1242 P. 2d 197, reversed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

Respondent Washington State Apple Marketing Commission sued appellee North Carolina Attorney General and others to enjoin enforcement of a North Carolina statute requiring that all apples sold in closed containers in the State be labeled according to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) grades, and prohibiting the display of any other grades, including respondent's Washington State grades. The District Court entered a temporary restraining order pending trial, and later permanently enjoined enforcement of the statute. On crossappeals, the Court of Appeals reversed the District Court's denial of appellants' motion to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted, and upheld the District Court's grant of injunctive relief. Held: 1. Respondent has standing to seek injunctive relief against enforcement of the statute. Pp. 108-111. (a) Respondent, though a state agency, is not a member of the class of organizations that traditionally are viewed as having standing to sue in their own names, Warth v. Parker, ante, p. 493, and hence is not foreclosed from obtaining standing simply because it is a state agency. Pp. 108-109. (b) Standing to sue is not dependent upon whether the plaintiff has a personal stake in the outcome of the litigation. P. 109. (c) Respondent has standing to sue based upon the assertions that the statute causes irreparable harm to its ability to promote the sale of Washington apples in North Carolina, and that the statute conflicts with the Commerce Clause. Pp. 109-111. 2. The District Court did not err in concluding that the statute violated the Commerce Clause insofar as it prohibited the display of Washington State grades on closed containers of apples shipped into the State. Pp. 111-121. (a) Not every exercise of state authority imposing some burden on the free flow of commerce is invalid. But the Commerce Clause limits the states' power to impose burdens on interstate commerce unless the regulations are necessary to protect local concerns. Pp. 111-112. (b) When state legislation comes into conflict with the Commerce Clause's overriding requirement of a national common market, the task is to effect an accommodation of the competing national and local interests. P. 112. (c) The statute has the practical effect of not only burdening interstate sales of Washington apples, but also discriminating against them. First, the statute raises the costs of doing business in the North Carolina market for Washington apple growers and dealers, while leaving those of their North Carolina counterparts unaffected. Second, the statute has the effect of stripping away from the Washington apple industry the competitive and economic advantages it has earned for itself through its expensive inspection and grading system. Third, by prohibiting Washington growers and dealers from marketing apples under their State's grades, the statute has a leveling effect which insidiously operates to the advantage of local apple producers. Despite the statute's facial neutrality, the Commission suggests that its discriminatory impact on interstate commerce was not an unintended byproduct and there are some indications in the record to that effect. Nevertheless, the burden fell on the State to justify the statute's discriminatory impact both in terms of the local benefits flowing from the statute and the unavailability of nondiscriminatory alternatives adequate to preserve the local interests at stake. North Carolina has failed to sustain that burden on both scores. Pp. 112-121. 548 F. 2d 1221, affirmed.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed and remanded for a new trial, holding that the jury had been incorrectly instructed under the standard established in Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins, 490 F. 3d, 358 (2008), in which the Supreme Court held that the burden of persuasion should shift to the employer to show that it would have taken the same action regardless of that impermissible consideration. The Court also held that a plaintiff must present direct evidence of age discrimination in order to obtain a mixed-motives jury instruction in a case brought under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), 81 Stat. 602, as amended, as 621 et seq. In this case, Jack Gross began working for respondent FBL Financial Group, Inc. (FBL) as a claims administration director in 1971 and was reassigned to the position of claims project coordinator in 2003 when he was 54 years old. Gross filed suit in 2004 alleging that his reassignment violated the ADEA, which makes it unlawful for an employer to take adverse action against an employee "because of such individual's age"

Case Name: Amfac Resorts, L.L.C. v. United States Department of the Interior
Case Number: 00-1100
Decided By: Supreme Court of the United States
Date Decided: February 20, 2002

Summary:
Amfac Resorts, L.L.C. v. United States Department of the Interior involves a dispute over the legality of a regulation defining "concession contract" to exclude coverage under the Contract Disputes Act of 1978. The regulation was adopted by the National Park Service, which manages the national parks involved in the concession contracts. The regulation was challenged in two separate suits, each of which reached the Supreme Court. The Court held that the regulation did not conflict with the Contract Disputes Act and that the National Park Service had the authority to adopt the regulation.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the City of Chicago's Park District in their denial of a permit for a rally advocating the legalization of marijuana. The Court held that the Park District's ordinance did not require a strict adherence to the procedures outlined in Freedman v. Maryland, as it was not subject matter censorship but content neutral time, place, and manner regulation of the use of a public forum. The Court also noted that the Park District's ordinance contained reasonable and specific standards to guide the licensor's determination and was enforceable on review first by appeal to the General Superintendent of the Park District and then by writ of common-law certiorari in the Illinois courts.

Section 21.031(d) of the Texas Education Code provides that a minor who lives apart from a "parent, guardian, or other person having lawful control of him under an order of a court" shall not be permitted to enroll in the public schools unless his presence in the school district is "for the primary purpose of attending the public free schools." Petitioner, a United States citizen who lived in Mexico with her parents, came to Texas to live with her sister, who is petitioner's custodian, primarily for the purpose of attending school in the McAllen Independent School District. Because petitioner did not desire to become her sister's guardian, she was not entitled to tuition-free admission to the McAllen schools. She brought suit in Federal District Court challenging the constitutionality of § 21.031(d). The District Court held that the section was justified by the State's legitimate interest in protecting and preserving the quality of its educational system and the right of its own bona fide residents to attend state schools on a preferred tuition basis. The Court of Appeals affirmed. Held: Section 21.031(d) is a bona fide residence requirement that satisfies constitutional standards. Pp. 449-454. (a) While a durational residence requirement conditions receipt of a benefit on a minimum period of residence within a jurisdiction, a bona fide residence requirement furthers the substantial state interest in assuring that services provided for its residents are enjoyed only by residents. Such a requirement with respect to attendance in public free schools does not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. It does not burden or penalize the constitutional right of interstate travel, for any person is free to move to a State and to establish residence there. And there is a further, independent justification for local residence requirements in the public-school context: Local control over the operation of schools is essential both to maintaining community concern and support for public schools and to ensuring the quality of the educational process. Pp. 449-451. (b) Section 21.031(d) is a bona fide residence requirement. Although the meaning may vary according to context, "residence" generally requires both physical presence and an intention to remain. Here, although the statute is far more generous than the traditional two-part definition of residence, it nevertheless grants the benefits of residency to everyone who satisfies the traditional residence definition and to some who legitimately could be classified as nonresidents. There is no indication that this extension of the traditional definition has any impermissible basis. Pp. 451-454. 648 F. 2d 425, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama has ruled that the Alabama statutes governing jury selection in Greene County, Alabama, are unconstitutional on their face and as applied, and that the Greene County jury commission is a deliberately segregated governmental agency. The court found that the commission's clerk, who is charged with the duty of obtaining the name of every citizen of the county over 21 and under 65 years of age, does not obtain the names of all potentially eligible jurors as provided by Alabama law. The commission members also secured some names from the county's Negro deputy sheriff, but on a basis no more regular or formalized than the efforts of the clerk. The trial court concluded that the jury-selection process as it actually operated in the county departed from the statutory mandate in several respects, including the fact that the clerk did not obtain all of the potential jurors' names. The jury commission members, however, did obtain some names, mainly from public officials, and some of them were white. The three-judge panel concluded that there was no evidence that the selection process was racially biased against the citizens of Greene County. The panel ordered the county jury commissioners and the county circuit court judge to vacate their appointments and ordered the governor to select new members of the jury commission without racial discrimination.
