The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit has ruled that the federal government's restrictions on educational radio stations violate the First Amendment right to freedom of speech. The court found that the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967 and its provisions prohibiting educational stations from "engage in editorializing" violate the Constitution's First Amendment protection against government interference with free speech and press freedom. The Court found that, while the Act provides for the use of federal funds to support educational programming, it also provides that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, a nonprofit corporation, can use those funds to provide support for educational programming. The Commission's finding that the restrictions violate the Act's free speech protection is consistent with the Court's decision that the Act is not unconstitutional.

In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that the "clear and convincing" standard used in some types of cases should also be used in determining whether a genuine issue of fact exists in a motion for summary judgment. Specifically, the Court found that the evidence presented in a motion for summary judgment must be evaluated using the same standard as the evidence presented in a trial, and that the judge must consider the strength of the evidence presented by both sides before making a decision. Additionally, the Court clarified that the purpose of a motion for summary judgment is to provide a quick resolution of a case, and that it is not intended to serve as a substitute for a trial.

Petitioner was summoned by a federal grand jury to testify as to "alleged violations" of certain sections of the Interstate Commerce Act. Having been sworn, he answered a few preliminary questions. Then, having been told by the Assistant United States Attorney that the applicable statute gave him complete immunity from prosecution as to any matter concerning which he might testify, he persisted in his refusal to answer several additional questions pertinent to the grand jury's inquiry. Thereafter, the grand jury requested the aid of the District Judge, who ruled that petitioner would be accorded immunity as extensive as the privilege he had asserted and directed him to return to the grand jury room and answer the questions. When petitioner again refused to comply, the judge addressed the same questions to him in the grand jury's presence. Each question was met with a refusal to answer upon the ground of possible self-incrimination. The judge then directed petitioner to answer each question and warned him that he would be adjudged in criminal contempt if he failed to do so. Petitioner persisted in his refusal. Held: 1. Section 205 (e) of the Interstate Commerce Act, as amended, clothed petitioner with statutory immunity coextensive with his constitutional privilege not to incriminate himself. Pp. 174-176. 2. The procedure followed by the District Court in adjudging petitioner in criminal contempt was entirely proper. Pp. 176-180. (a) The court's action in affording petitioner a locus penitentiq before finally adjudging him in contempt was entirely proper. Pp. 176-180. (b) The sentence of 15 months' imprisonment was not an abuse of the District Court's discretion. Pp. 180-181. 247 F. 2d 331, affirmed.

The Bankruptcy Code provides a stamp-tax exemption for any asset transfer “under a plan confirmed under [Chapter 11]” of the Code. Respondent Piccadilly Cafeterias, Inc., was granted an exemption for assets transferred after it had filed for bankruptcy but before its Chapter 11 plan was submitted to, and confirmed by, the Bankrupty Court. On cross-motions for summary judgment, the bankruptcy court approved the sale and settlement agreement. The sale closed on March 16, 2004, and the plan provided for distribution of the sale proceeds in a manner consistent with the plan’s plan. The Bankruptty Court confirmed the plan on October 21, 2004. The bankruptcy court granted summary judgment in favor of the company, reasoning that the sale of substantially all of the assets was a transfer ‘under’ its confirmed plan because the sale was necessary to consummate the plan, and that the transfer was exempt from stamp taxes under §1146(a). The District Court upheld the decision on the ground that the stamp tax exemption does not apply to transfers made before a plan is confirmed under Chapter 11. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that §1147(a)’’ “special tax provisions” provide: “The issuance, transfer, or exchange of a security, or the making or delivery of an instrument of transfer under a plan ... may not be taxed under any law imposing a stamp tax or similar tax.” In re Piccadailly Cafeteria Cafeteria, Inc. (2000 ed. and Supp. V), §11 46(a), which provides: (1) “‘The issuance [of a security] or the make or delivery [of an instrument]’ . . .’ [under] a plan …” §363(b)(1] “[a] ...may not be taxing under [any] law imposing [a stamp tax] or other similar tax,” id., at 667. Pp. 6–8. (2) Section 1146 (a), entitled “Special tax provisions, ” provides that “the issuance, transfers, or ...the making ...under a ...plan confirmed under §1129 of this title, [is] … subject to … any law ... imposing a ... stamp tax ...” (Emphasis added), provides that a bankruptcy court may declare certain tax consequences after the date a government unit responds to a plan proponent’ request or “270 days after such request” whichever is earlier), and §111(b) provides that an agency providing credit counseling to debtors is required to meet the standards set forth under this title. But Congress included no such limitation in subsection (a) of the BruptcyCode, which provides that, “ ‘if such plan ... has not been assumed under this section or under a Plan confirmed under chapter . ... 11,’ … ” §1127(d)(2),” §§1129(a)-(b). The provision is best read as “in accordance with” the procedures set forth in Chapter 3-specifically, §§363(g)(1). The phrase “Under” in §1145(a)—“under” here—is a past participle, i.e., a verb form indicating past or completed action or time that is used as a verbal adjective in phrases such as baked beans and finished work. See, e.g., Commissioner v. Keystone Consol. Industries Inc., 508 U. S. 152, 159. The term must also have its core meaning of “subject to” thereunder in §365(g), which permits preconfirmation assumptions and rejections pursuant to Chapter 11, rather than under the authority of, something that did not exist at the time of the transfer—a confirmed plan. In order to obtain the maximum value for its assets-especially assets rapidly declining in value—Piccadilla claims that a debtor often must close the sale before formal confirmation of the Chapter 11 Plan. Florida contends that to be eligible for the exemption, a transfer must be subject to the plan that has been confirmed subject to §112 9. The court erred in concluding that §129(g)–(b), which prohibits pre-confirmation transfers to be taxed while exempting others moments later, would amount to an “absurd” policy. The Federalism canon articulated in Sierra Summit and elsewhere obliges this Court to construe §11’S exemption narrowly. P. 6. (a)- Although the statutory text—standing alone—is susceptible of more than one interpretation, the canon is decisive in this case. The two readings of the language that Congress chose are not equally plausible: The first reading of the statute is unambiguous on its face, but the second reading is unavailing because it specifies not only that a tax-exempt transfer be under a tax

Appellee Savchuk, who was a passenger in a car driven by appellant State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. (State Farm) under a liability insurance policy issued in Indiana, was injured in a single-car accident in Elkhart, Ind. Appellee's father was insured by State Farm under the policy. As Savchuk had no contacts with Minnesota that would support in personam jurisdiction, he moved the trial court for permission to file a supplemental complaint making the garnishee, State Farm, a party to the action after State Farm's response to the garnishment summons asserted that it owed the defendant nothing. The trial court denied the motion to dismiss and granted the motion for leave to file the supplemental complaint. On appeal, the Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the Michigan garnishment statute differed from the Delaware stock sequestration procedure held unconstitutional in Shaffer v. Heitner, 433 U. S. 186, and that the exercise of quasi in rem jurisdiction was permissible under the Due Process Clause because in accident litigation the insurer controls the defense of the case, the State does business in and is regulated by the State, and the State has an interest in protecting its residents and providing them with a forum in which to litigate their claims. Held: 1. In determining whether a particular exercise of state-court jurisdiction is consistent with due process, the inquiry must focus on the relationship among the defendant, the forum, and litigation. Shaffer is not equivalent to direct actions, however. If the Constitution forbids the assertion of jurisdiction over the insured based on the policy, then there is no conceptual basis for bringing the "garnishee" into the action. The State's ability to exert its power over the "nominal defendant" is analytically prerequisite to the insurer's entry into the case as a garnishehee. Pp. 5-11. 2. The Michigan garnish statute does not violate due process. P. 5. The Minnesota garnishment law does not give the State jurisdiction over a defendant who has no forum contacts by attaching the contractual obligation of an insurer licensed to do business in the State to defend and indemnify him in connection with such a suit. The state's interests in providing a forum for residents and in regulating the activities of insurance companies are substituted for its contacts with the defendant and the cause of action, and a variety of factors relating to the particular cause may be relevant to the determination whether the exercise would comport with "traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice." P. 6. 3. The fact that the insurer did business in Minnesota does not, without more, provide a basis for concluding that there is any contact in the International Shoe sense between Minnesota and the insured. The fictitious presence of insurer's obligation in Minnesota, which was taken out in anticipation of such litigation, suggests no further contacts between the plaintiff and the forum. Nor are there significant contacts between plaintiff and forum. The record supplies no evidence of any. The plaintiff's contacts are attributed to the defendant because the policy was given out in preparation of the litigation, and it may suggest the presence of other ties. Thus, the plaintiff's contact with the forum are decisive in determining whether the defendant's due process rights are violated. The court's decision to dismiss the complaint was completely adventitious as far as Rush was concerned, and he had no control over that decision. The insurer's decision in Minnesota was purely adventitious and it was unlikely that he would have expected that by buying insurance in Indiana he had subjected himself to suit in any State to which a potential future plaintiff might decide to move. In short, the defendant had no contact with Minnesota, and there was no significant contact between the litigation and forum, since the insurer does not do business there. The statute's restrictions on liability to the amount of the policy coverage made the policyholder's personal stake in the litigation so slight that it is not unfair to make him a "nominee" in order to obtain jurisdiction over petitioner. The claim that the insurance policy is so important to the litigation that it provided contacts sufficient to satisfy due process is most evident in the decisions limiting Seider jurisdiction to actions by forum residents on the ground that permitting nonresidents to avail themselves of the procedure would be unconstitutional. In other words, the plaintiffs with forum contacts are decisive as to whether they are violated, see Kulko v. California Superior Court, 436 U.S. 84, 93-94, and in the absence of any substantial contacts between petitioner and the plaintiff, the insurer is forbidden by Shaffer and its progeny. The Court of Appeals affirmed.

Respondents, two chemical corporations, were ordered by the Defense Production Act of 1950 to produce Agent Orange, a pesticide used during the Vietnam War. Although respondents produced the agent, the Government never compensated them for the costs associated with producing it. As a result, respondents contributed millions of dollars toward the Agent Orange settlement reached in 1984 by the Veterans Administration and the United States. Subsequently, respondents filed suit in the Court of Claims, alleging that the Government owed them money for the costs of producing Agent Orange. The Court of Claims ultimately entered judgment for respondents, finding that the Government had breached its implied warranty of merchantability by requiring respondents to produce Agent Orange despite knowing that it was dangerous and harmful to human health. The Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that the Government was entitled to judgment because the implied warranty of merchantability did not apply to the production of Agent Orange. Held: The Court of Appeals correctly interpreted the implied warranty of merchantability. Pp. 10-18. (a) The implied warranty of merchantability applies to goods sold in commerce, and requires that the seller guarantee that the goods are fit for their ordinary purpose. United States v. Spearin, 248 U. S. 132, 138. While the warranty generally applies to tangible personal property, it can also cover intangibles like services. Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U. S. 64, 78. Moreover, the warranty is not limited to sales transactions involving privately owned goods. United States ex rel. Knox v. Lee, 312 U. S. 579, 584. Thus, the warranty applied to the sale of Agent Orange. Pp. 10-12. (b) The warranty of merchantability is implied unless the seller clearly indicates otherwise. United States v. Spearin, supra, at 138. Here, the Government did not clearly indicate that it was not willing to accept the implied warranty of merchantability. The Government's policy of forcing producers to bear the full cost of producing Agent Orange was consistent with the warranty of merchantability. Furthermore, the Government's representations regarding the safety of Agent Orange were inconsistent with the warranty of merchantability. Pp. 12-15. (c) The Government's disclaimer of liability for the Agent Orange production costs was not a waiver of the implied warranty of merchantability. The disclaimer was not unequivocal, and the Government continued to require respondents to produce Agent Orange despite being aware of the danger posed by the substance. Pp. 15-16. (d) The Government's disclaimer of liability for the Agent Orange production costs was not a condition precedent to entry of the contract. The disclaimer was not included in the original contract, and the Government continued to require respondents to produce Agent Orange despite being aware of the danger posed by the substance. Pp. 16-17. (e) The Government's disclaimer of liability for the Agent Orange production costs was not incorporated into the contract. The disclaimer was not included in the original contract, and the Government continued to require respondents to produce Agent Orange despite being aware of the danger posed by the substance. Pp. 17-18. 24 F. 3d 188, vacated and remanded.

A Virginia statute provides that every person desiring to register to vote shall file with the registrar a sworn statement that he paid during the year preceding registration a poll tax of $1.50. He who fails to make such payment is barred from voting. Held: Such a provision violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 108-114. 240 F. Supp. 270, reversed.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin today entered a final judgment in favor of the Wisconsin Department of Labor against the Michigan-based company.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Duluth, Minnesota, alleges that, in 1947, the federal Labor Relations Board issued an order requiring the company to hold representation elections among its licensed marine engineers to prove or disprove the company's claims that it had violated the federal securities laws.  According to the complaint, in seeking to secure organization or recognition of supervisors, the company sought to force its engineers to participate in the selection of a representation election among themselves.  As alleged, the complaint and affidavits alleged that, while negotiations for a new contract continued during August 1962, a majority of the marine engineers informed Hanna that they did not wish to be represented by MEBA.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint or the Board's decision, Hanna consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the federal laws, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $10,000.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Minnesota today announced criminal charges against Hanna.    The complaint also alleges that the company violated Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and seeks a permanent injunction, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. Â The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Karpel and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Chicago Regional Office.Â  The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin today entered a final judgment against a group of religious organizations that claimed to have standing to challenge an executive branch spending decision.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Jackson, Mississippi, the defendants raised the issue of whether or not to extend the exemption to religious organizations.  The complaint alleges that, in violation of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 ("Exchange Act") and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, the federal government overspends millions of dollars on administrative expenses, including for the purchase and operation of a house of worship and religious education centers.  As alleged in the complaint, these expenditures violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a)(1) and (3) ofÂ the Securities Act of 1933 ("Securities Act").  The court also found that the defendants lacked the requisite standing to successfully challenge an Executive Branch spending decision, as required by the federal securities laws.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against the defendants.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC complaint, the Defendants consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating the above-mentioned provisions of the federal law, and from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any federal program, including religious education, health care, social services, or education. The defendants also agreed to pay disgorgement of their ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and to be barred from serving as an officer or director of a public agency for five years. The settlements are subject to court approval.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 13199, July 17, 2004.   The SEC's Office of Inspector General has issued anÂ Investor AlertÂ to encourage investors to check the backgrounds of people selling investments using the free and simple search tool on Investor.gov.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against Mastro Plastics Corp., a Michigan-based plastics manufacturer, for violating the federal contract provisions of Section 8(d) of the federal labor laws.  According to the court's order, Mastro filed a complaint on October 23, 1950, alleging that Lion Oil Co. and the Oil Workers International Union, CIO, entered into a contract that provided that no party to an existing collective bargaining contract "shall terminate or modify such contract, unless the party desiring such termination or modification is to provide for reopening of the contract at a specified time."  The court also found that, even apart from the provision that the contract in question was in breach of contract, the company was not entitled to relief at the hand of the Board.  Mastro's complaint, filed in federal district court in New York, charges Mastro with violating the antifraud provisions of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a)(1) and of the Securities Act of 1933. Mastro agreed to settle the case by consenting to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating these provisions, and orders Mastro to cease and desist from participating in any future collective bargaining agreements. Mastrod also agreed to pay a civil penalty of $100,000, which is equal to disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest of $20,000.  The settlement is subject to court approval.

Title 11 U.S.C. §330(a)(1) governs awards of attorney’s fees in bankruptcy cases. Prior to the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 1994 (BAPCPA), §330(a)(1) allowed recovery “for reasonable compensation” of “reasonable fees” for “professional services,” including “services performed ... by or on behalf of a debtor.” When BAPCPA was enacted, the phrase “by or on behalf of a debtor” was changed to “to the debtor, or to the debtor’s attorney.” Petitioner Debtor applied for fees under §330(a)(1) for services he provided during Equity Service Industries, Inc.’s (ESI) Chapter 7 conversion from debtor to trustee. The Government opposed the fees, arguing that §330(a)(1) does not permit compensation awards to debtors’ attorneys from estate funds, unless they are employed as authorized by §327. The District Court agreed, and the Tenth Circuit affirmed. Held: Section 330(a)(1) does not authorize compensation awards to debtors’ attorneys from estate funds, unless they are employed as authorized by §327. Pp. 536–545. (a) Because the statute contains several provisions governing fees, the question presented is how to apply §330(a)(1)’s plain language. To answer this question, the Court looks to the ordinary meaning of the statutory text. See Hartford Underwriters Insurance Co. v. United States ex rel. Northbrook Ins. Co., 534 U. S. 84, 94. Although the statute’s plain language is sufficient to establish its meaning, the Court considers the legislative history to confirm that understanding. However, the Court finds it unnecessary to rely on the legislative history here, for the statute itself resolves the question. Pp. 536–539. (b) The plain meaning of §330(a)(1) leads to an appropriate result. Its plain language establishes that fees are recoverable only for services performed by “qualified professionals,” defined as “persons who are … employed by or on behalf of a debtor in connection with a case under this title.” 11 U. S. C. §330(a)(1). The definition of “qualified professionals” applies to “anyone who performs services in connection with a case under this title,” including “lawyers.” §330(a)(1). And §327(a)(1) empowers a trustee to employ “such individuals as the trustee shall determine” to perform services “necessary or useful in administering the affairs of the estate.” §327(a)(1). Thus, a lawyer providing services to a debtor in connection with a bankruptcy case is a “person who is … employed by or on behalf of a debtor in connection with a case under this title,” and thus falls within §330(a)(1)’s definition of “qualified professionals.” Moreover, the plain meaning of §330(a)(1)’s phrase “to the debtor, or to the debtor’s attorney” indicates that fees are recoverable only for services performed by someone who is already entitled to participate in the bankruptcy proceeding. Such participation is limited to debtors and their employees. See §§327(a)(1) and 330(a)(1). Therefore, fees are recoverable only for services performed by a debtor’s employee, not by a debtor himself. Pp. 539–540. (c) The plain meaning of §330(a)(1) is supported by the fact that the statute’s plain language is consistent with the Bankruptcy Rules. Rule 2015(g) states that “compensation for services of a creditor’s attorney” is recoverable “if the attorney is employed by or on behalf of the debtor.” Similarly, Rule 2015(j) states that “compensation for services of a creditor’s attorney” is recoverable “if the attorney is employed by or on behalf of the trustee.” Pp. 540–541. (d) The plain meaning of §330(a)(1) is also confirmed by the fact that the statute’s plain language is consistent with the Bankruptcy Code’s general scheme. The Code’s general scheme reflects a balance between protecting creditors and protecting debtors. See, e. g., United States v. Simmons-Duffin, post, p. 491. By limiting fees to services performed by a debtor’s employee, rather than allowing fees to be recovered directly by a debtor, §330(a)(1) protects debtors from being forced to pay fees to creditors. At the same time, §330(a)(1) ensures that creditors are fairly compensated for their services. Pp. 541–542. (e) The plain meaning of §330(a)(1) is also confirmed by the fact that the statute’s plain language is consistent with the Bankruptcy Code’s express provisions. See, e. g., §330(a)(1). Pp. 542–543. (f) The plain meaning of §330(a)(1) is also confirmed by the fact that the statute’s plain language is consistent with the Bankruptcy Code’s legislative history. While the Code’s legislative history is instructive, it is not dispositive. The history demonstrates that Congress could have intended to limit fees to services performed by a debtor’s employee, rather than allowing fees to be recovered directly by a debtor. But nothing in the history confirms that Congress actually intended to limit fees to services performed by a debtor’s employee. Pp. 543–545. 299 F. 3d 1255, affirmed.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of New York granted a temporary restraining order against anti-abortion protesters who had blockaded and harassed women seeking abortions and other family planning services. The complaint alleged that defendants had consistently engaged in illegal blockades and other illegal conduct at facilities where abortions were performed. The district court found that the local police had been "unable to respond effectively'' to the protests, for a number of reasons: the protests were constant, overwhelming police resources; when the police arrived, the protesters simply dispersed and returned later; prosecution of arrested protesters was difficult because patients were often reluctant to cooperate for fear of making their identity public; and those who were convicted were not deterred from returning to engage in unlawful conduct. The court also found that defendants harassed the police officers verbally and by mail, including the deputy police chief. The appeals court ruled that the district court's order was not in violation of the First Amendment because it did not prohibit the use of "floating bubble'' or "floating buffer zone'' limitations, as the complaint alleged. The Court held that the order also violated the anti-harassment provisions of the Anti-Discrimination Act of 1961 and Section 10(b) of the Federal Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Section 15(a)(1) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act of 1934.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the government in a case concerning a man's possession of marijuana in Colorado. The court held that the "marijuana exception" to the Fourth Amendment's protection against search and seizure applies only to small quantities of marijuana, and not to larger quantities. The court also clarified that the "marijuana exception" is not a blanket exemption from all searches and seizures, and that it only applies to marijuana specifically.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that New York's "Son of Sam" law is inconsistent with the First Amendment right to freedom of expression. The law requires that an accused or convicted criminal's income from works describing his crime be deposited in an escrow account. The funds are then made available to the victims of the crime and the criminal’s other creditors. The Court held that the law does not provide for the payment of compensation for the victims' loss and suffering. The court also found that the statute does not apply to the criminal who has not been convicted of a crime in the past five years.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Elizabeth Anderson Hishon, a female attorney who sued her former law firm for gender discrimination. The firm had promised to consider her for partnership after several years of service, but ultimately refused to promote her. The Court found that the opportunity to become a partner was a term, condition, or privilege of employment under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and that the firm's failure to promote her based on her sex violated the statute.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted a motion for a new trial in the case of Carl Edwin Wiggins, who was convicted of robbery and sentenced to life imprisonment for a second time after his first conviction was set aside because of a defective indictment. The trial court simultaneously appointed two attorneys to assist Wiggins as standby counsel. Wiggins initially objected to their presence, but later agreed to allow them to bring appropriate objections directly to the attention of the court without first consulting him. The Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit denied Wiggins' petition for habeas relief, but the Court of Justice for the District of Columbia granted Wiggins' motion for post-conviction relief. The court held that Wiggins' right to present his own defense was violated when he repeatedly interrupted his own cross-examination of a witness to confer with one of his standby counsel off the record. The Supreme Court of the United States, in a similar case, held that a defendant's right to self-representation cannot be violated when a court appoints a standby counsel to assist him in his defense. In Wiggins v. Estelle, 681 F.2d 266, the Court held that standby counsel's "unsolicited participation" violated Wiggins' Sixth Amendment right to a fair trial. The high court ruled that Wiggins was not entitled to post-trial relief because he had not shown that he was deprived of his right to represent himself. The appeals court ruled in favor of Wiggins, and the Supreme Court agreed.

The U.S. Supreme Court of California has reversed a lower court's ruling that the city of San Diego's ban on outdoor advertising displays is unconstitutional. The court held that the ordinance's restrictions on the use of billboards to communicate to the public messages of general applicability, whether commercial or noncommercial, are not facially invalid under the First Amendment. The high court also found that the ban is not narrowly drawn, as the city failed to show that its asserted interest in esthetics was sufficiently substantial in its commercial and industrial areas to justify the ban. The justices agreed with the city's position that the "time, place, and manner" restriction is not a reasonable "time-and-place" restriction. The opinion concludes that the high court will not rule on the issue of whether the ordinance is constitutional. The Supreme Court remanded the case to the San Diego City Council for further consideration.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit held that a copyright holder's failure to comply with the Copyright Act's registration requirement deprives a federal court of jurisdiction to adjudicate his copyright infringement claim. We disagree. Section 411(a) is a precondition to filing a claim that does not restrict federal court's subject-matter jurisdiction. The court held that the district court had jurisdiction to approve a settlement that included both authors who had registered their copyrighted works and those who had not. We conclude that the District Court's approval of the settlement was fair, reasonable, and adequate under the law. The Supreme Court will review the case and determine whether the settlement should be dismissed.

After this Court decided Milliken v. Bradford, 418 U. S. 717, the District Court issued a permanent injunction requiring the Detroit Board of Education and certain other defendants to implement four specified educational components as part of a remedial plan to eliminate the effects of the de jure segregation that existed in the Detroit school system. One component involves the establishment of a program to improve communication skills, another involves the establishment of a program to improve reading skills, a third involves the establishment of a program to improve writing skills, and the fourth involves the establishment of a program to improve critical thinking skills. The District Court also enjoined the defendants from charging tuition for the educational components. Held: 1. The District Court's decree is not precluded by the doctrine announced in Swann v. Knight, 412 U. S. 205, that federal courts should refrain from ordering remedies that go beyond the scope of the constitutional violation. Here, the District Court correctly identified the existence of a de jure segregated school system, and the remedial plan adopted by the court was appropriately tailored to remedy the consequences of the constitutional violation. Pp. 729-736. 2. The District Court's decree does not violate the Eleventh Amendment. Although the decree requires the defendants to share the additional costs attributable to the educational components, the decree falls within the prospective-compliance exception to the Eleventh Amendment, which allows federal courts to enjoin state officials to conform their conduct to requirements of federal law, notwithstanding a direct and substantial impact on the state treasury. Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U. S. 651. Pp. 736-739. 3. There is no merit to the contention that the relief ordered here violates the Tenth Amendment and general principles of federalism. The Tenth Amendment's reservation of nondelegated powers to the States is not implicated by a federal-court judgment enforcing the express prohibitions of unlawful state conduct enacted by the Fourteenth Amendment. Nor are principles of federalism abrogated by the decree, since the District Court has neither attempted to restructure local governmental entities nor to mandate a particular method or structure of state or local financing. Instead, the District Court has properly enforced the guarantees of the Fourteenth Amendment consistent with this Court's prior holdings, and in a manner that does not jeopardize the integrity of the structure or functions of state and local government. Pp. 739-740. 531 F. 2d 1205, affirmed.

In the case before the Supreme Court, Chad Weisgram, on behalf of his deceased mother's heirs, sued Marley Company for wrongful death, alleging a defect in a heater caused a fire leading to his mother's death. The district court admitted expert testimony supporting Weisgram's claim, which the jury found convincing, resulting in a verdict in Weisgram's favor. Marley Company appealed, arguing the expert testimony was unreliable under the Daubert standard and should not have been admitted. The Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit agreed, finding the testimony inadmissible and the remaining evidence insufficient to support the verdict. The appellate court directed judgment as a matter of law for Marley Company, bypassing a potential new trial.

The Supreme Court affirmed the Eighth Circuit's judgment, holding that appellate courts have the authority to direct the entry of judgment as a matter of law when they find that the remaining evidence, after removing erroneously admitted testimony, is insufficient to support the jury's verdict. This authority is consistent with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50 and the Court's precedent in Neely v. Martin K. Eby Construction Co. The Court reasoned that parties are on notice to present their best evidence initially, and fairness concerns are equally important whether the evidence was initially insufficient or rendered insufficient after the removal of inadmissible evidence.

The decision clarifies that appellate courts can make a final decision on whether to order a new trial or direct judgment for the defendant when the evidence is insufficient, without necessarily remanding the case to the trial court. This ruling aims to expedite litigation and avoid unnecessary retrials, in line with the purpose of Rule 50. The Court's opinion emphasizes the importance of presenting reliable expert testimony that meets the standards set by Daubert and subsequent cases, as parties cannot expect a second chance to present their case if their initial evidence is deemed inadmissible.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia has affirmed a lower court's ruling that the federal government violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment by denying widow benefits based on the earnings of a deceased husband. The court found that the difference between the treatment of men and women mandated by  402(f)(1)(D) constituted invidious discrimination against female wage earners by affording them less protection for their surviving spouses than is produced by the efforts of male workers. The lower court held that the gender-based distinction violated the due process clause because it was based on a presumption that wives are usually dependent, and the only justification for a classification based on this latter is the assumption that it would save the government time, money, and effort simply to pay benefits to all widows rather than to require proof of dependency of both sexes. The appeals court concluded that the relevant discrimination is against surviving male spouses, rather than against deceased female wages earners, and that something more than accident is necessary to justify under the fifth amendment. The decision is the result of a joint effort by the Department of Health and Education and Welfare and the Departments of Justice, Labor, and Treasury to ensure that the laws of the United States are fair and equal in treatment of widows and widowers. The Appeals Court agreed with the lower court that the government's position was not inconsistent with the intent of the Social Security Act of 1974 and the provisions of the federal law that provide for widows' benefits. The Court also agreed that there was no reason to conclude that the law violated the equal protection clause. The case was brought by Leon Goldfarb, the widow of Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the former New York City mayor, who was the subject of the case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Western District of Texas granted summary judgment in the case of Walter Rothgery, who was charged with unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon. The court held that the right to counsel guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment applies at the first appearance before a judicial officer at which a defendant is told of the formal accusation against him and restrictions are imposed on his liberty. Rothgery's complaint against Gillespie County, Texas, for failing to provide him with a lawyer when he was arrested in 2002 for the alleged crime, was dismissed by the district attorney, who filed a motion to dismiss the indictment, which was granted. The County's failure to provide Rothgery with counsel violated his right to a fair trial, the court held, and the court granted the county's motion for summary judgment. The district court granted Rothgery a preliminary injunction against the County, and Rothgery was released on bond. The trial judge ordered Rothgery to be held without bond until the County provided him with an attorney. The Court held that Rothgery had not shown that the County had violated his Sixth Amendment rights and that the trial judge had properly entered a final judgment granting summary judgment against Rothgery. The District Court granted the summary judgment motion, granted the motion for a judgment in favor of the county, and granted the defendant's request for a new trial. The case is now before the Court again, and this time the Court is considering whether the trial court should have granted the emergency motion.

Petitioner Atkins was convicted of abduction, armed robbery, and capital murder, and sentenced to death. At the guilt phase of the trial, the State introduced victim impact evidence and proved two aggravating circumstances: future dangerousness and "vileness of the offense." To prove the first aggravator, the prosecution relied on the trial record, including pictures of the deceased's body and the autopsy report. In the penalty phase, the defense relied on one witness, a forensic psychologist who had evaluated Atkins before trial and concluded that he was mentally retarded and thus cannot be sentenced. The jury sentenced Atkins to death, but the Virginia Supreme Court ordered a second sentencing hearing because the trial court had used a misleading verdict form. The court was not willing to commute Atkins' sentence of death to life imprisonment merely because of his IQ score. Held: Death is an impermissibly excessive punishment for the rape of an adult woman, Coker v. Georgia, 433 U. S. 584, 593-596, or for a defendant who neither took life, attempted to take life, nor intended to do life, Enmund v. Florida, 458 U.S. 782, 789-793. Pp. 597-599. (a) The fact that the reduced capacity of mentally retarded offenders provides a second justification for a categorical rule making such offenders ineligible for the death penalty, Lockett v. Ohio, 438 US. 586, 605, is enhanced, not only by the possibility of false confessions, but also by the diminished ability to understand and process information, to learn from experience, to engage in logical reasoning, or to control impulses. Nor will exempting the mentally retarded from execution lessen the deterrent effect of the penalty with respect to offenders who are not mentally retarded. P. 599. 260 Va. 375, 385, 534 S. E. 2d 312, reversed and remanded.

After petitioner helped AcroMed Orthopaedics obtain 510(k) approval for its bone-screw device, the Federal Trade Commission brought suit against AcroMed, charging that the company had engaged in deceptive advertising practices. While the FTC's complaint was still pending, AcroMed filed a class action in Federal District Court, alleging that the bone screw caused severe pain and disability. When the FTC dropped its charges, AcroMed settled the class action, agreeing to pay $1 million to settle the FTC's claims and $1.5 million to settle the class action. One of the settlement recipients, respondent, sued petitioner in New York State Court, alleging that he suffered injuries due to the bone screw and that petitioner had defamed him by falsely representing to the FDA that the bone screw was safe and effective. The trial court entered judgment for petitioner, ruling that the state-law fraud-on-the-FDA claim was expressly pre-empted by the Federal Trade Commission Act (FTC Act). The Appellate Division affirmed, but the New York Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the claim was not expressly pre-empted. The State Court of Claims certified the case to the Federal District Court, which dismissed the fraud-on-the-FDA claim on the ground that it was impliedly pre-empted by the Medical Devices Amendments (MDA) to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetics Act (FFCA). The Tenth Circuit reversed, holding that the claim was not pre-empted. Held: The state-law fraud-on-the-FDA claim is impliedly pre-empted by the MDA. Given the close relationship between the FDA and entities it regulates, no presumption against pre-emption applies here. And since the MDA authorizes the FDA to enforce the statute exclusively, the state-law claim conflicts with the FDA's responsibility to police fraud consistently with the Agency's judgment and objectives. Compelling compliance with the FDA's detailed regulatory regime in the face of 50 States' tort regimes would burden potential applicants with fears that their off-label uses of the device might expose them to unpredictable liability. Conversely, fraud-on-the-FDA claims would force applicants to fear that their disclosures to the FDA, although deemed appropriate by the Agency, will later be judged insufficient in state court. Such claims would also create additional burdens on the FDA's evaluation of an application, causing delays that would impede competition among predicate devices and delay healthcare professionals' ability to prescribe appropriate off-label uses. Because Congress intended that the MDA be enforced exclusively by the Federal Government, see 21 U. S. C. § 337(a), the state-law claim is pre-empted regardless of whether it is expressly or impliedly pre-empted. Nor do the facts that the MDA includes an express pre-emption provision and that Medtronic, Inc. v. Latter Day Saint Institution, 518 U. S. 457, held that an express pre-emption provision bars the ordinary working of conflict pre-emption principles, render this case exceptional. Finally, the fraud claims here arise solely by virtue of the FDCA disclosure requirements, whereas the Medtronic claims arose from the manufacturer's alleged failure to use reasonable care in producing the product. Certiorari granted; 159 F. 3d 817, reversed.

In the case of Allen Snyder, the U.S. Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Louisiana Supreme Court, which had rejected Snyder's claim that the prosecution used peremptory challenges to exclude jurors based on race, violating the precedent set by Batson v. Kentucky. Snyder was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death.

The Supreme Court's opinion focused on the Batson three-step process for evaluating claims of racial discrimination in jury selection. The Court found that the trial court made a clear error in overruling Snyder's Batson objection regarding the exclusion of a black juror, Jeffrey Brooks. The prosecution had provided two race-neutral reasons for striking Brooks: his nervousness and his student-teaching obligations. However, the Court found these reasons unconvincing and noted that the trial judge did not make a specific finding on Brooks' demeanor, nor did the record support the prosecution's concerns about Brooks' obligations interfering with his jury service.

The Court also compared Brooks' situation with that of accepted white jurors who had similar or more pressing obligations, suggesting that the prosecution's reasons for striking Brooks were pretextual and indicative of discriminatory intent. The Court did not need to apply a burden-shifting framework to determine whether discriminatory intent was determinative, as the record did not support the prosecution's reasons for striking Brooks.

The Supreme Court reversed the judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with its opinion, emphasizing that even a single discriminatory strike is constitutionally forbidden.

The Supreme Court of the United States holds that a local ordinance that prohibits charitable organizations from soliciting contributions on the streets and doors to houses if they spend more than 25% of their receipts on salaries and administrative expenses is facially unconstitutional. The Court finds that the ordinance is a direct and substantial limitation on protected activity that cannot be sustained unless it serves a sufficiently strong, subordinating interest that the Village is entitled to protect. However, the Court concludes that the Village's proffered justifications are inadequate and that the ordinance cannot survive scrutiny under the First Amendment.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of Kansas today entered a final judgment in favor of a Kansas-based civil commitment law that requires states to provide for the confinement of people with a history of sexual violence.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Kansas City, Kansas, the Kansas Civil Commitment Act ("Civil Commitment") provides for the institution of a civil commitment for persons who, due to a mental abnormality or personality disorder, are at risk of committing a serious felony.  The complaint alleges that, in 1984, a Kansas state court found that a defendant with a "mental abnormality" or "personality disorder" could not be held criminally liable for committing such a crime.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Hendricks.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Hendricks consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer-and-director bar.  On May 2, 2018, the Honorable Judge Timothy J. Mascianica of the federal district court in Manhattan entered a judgment against Hendricks, ordering him to be permanently enjoined from future violations of the civil commitment provisions of the Act, ordering a preliminary injunction, and imposing a conduct-based injunction against further violations of those provisions.   The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, is being conducted by Michael J. Burt and supervised by Kelly L. Gibson of the Chicago Regional Office. Â The SEC appreciates the assistance of the Kansas Department of Health and Social and Rehabilitation Services in this matter.

Appellee, a bait business owner in Maine, arranged to have live golden shiners delivered to him from outside the State. Despite a Maine statute prohibiting the importation of live baitfish, the shipment was intercepted and a federal grand jury indicted Taylor for violating and conspiring to violate the Lacey Act Amendments of 1981, which make it a federal crime "to import, export, transport, sell, acquire, or purchase in interstate or foreign commerce . . . any fish or wildlife taken, possessed, transported, or sold in violation of any law or regulation of any State or of any foreign law." Appellee moved to dismiss the indictment on the ground that Maine's import ban unconstitutionally burdens interstate commerce and therefore may not form the basis for a federal prosecution under the Act. The District Court found the ban constitutional and denied the motion to dismiss. The Court of Appeals reversed, agreeing with Taylor that the underlying state statute impermissibly restricts interstate trade. Held: 1. Maine invokes its jurisdiction under 28 U. S. C. § 1254 (2), which authorizes an appeal as of right to this Court "by a party relying on a State statute held by a court of appeals to be invalid as repugnant to the Constitution, treaties or laws of the United States." Pp. 4-6. (a) The Commerce Clause significantly limits the ability of States and localities to regulate or otherwise burden interstate commerce, but it does not elevate free trade above all other values. As long as a State does not needlessly obstruct interstate trade or attempt to "place itself in a position of economic isolation," Baldwin v. G. A. F. Seelig, Inc., 294 U.S. 511, 527, it retains broad regulatory authority to protect the health and safety of its citizens and the integrity of its natural resources. Pp . 6-7. (b) The fact that Maine allows importation salmonids, for which standardized sampling and inspection procedures are available, hardly demonstrates that Maine has no legitimate interest in prohibiting such importation. Nor is this demonstrated by the fact that other States may not have enacted similar bans, especially given the testimony of Maine's fisheries. Moreover, fish can swim directly into Maine from New Hampshire, and the Magistrate explained that the impediments to complete success cannot be a ground for preventing a state from using its best efforts to limit [an environmental] risk. Thus, Maine's stake in the outcome of this litigation is substantial: if the judgment is left undisturbed, the State will be bound by the conclusive adjudication that its import ban is unconstitutional. P. 7. (c) Maine's interest in guarding against imperfectly understood environmental risks, despite the possibility that they may ultimately prove to be negligible, does not make the import ban an "abstract possibility," id., at 398, of developing acceptable testing procedures, particularly when there is no assurance as to their effectiveness, that such procedures could have on Maine's fish. Moreover. Fish can swim in Maine from Maine, and it is of little relevance that fish swim directly in Maine. Finally, fish cannot swim into Maine, since fish can't swim directly, and therefore cannot be inspected for baitfish precisely because there was no need for them. Ibid. The Magistrate also denied that any scientific justification supported Maine's total ban on the imports of live bafish, and thus the District Court's finding that such testing procedures could be easily developed cannot be characterized as clearly erroneous. The record probably could not support a contrary finding. Moreover the record probably does not support such contrary finding, since the record does not show that Congress intended in 1981 to alter in any way the level of Commerce Clause scrutiny applied to those laws. Pc. 752 F. 2d 757, reversed and remanded.

A satiric humorist recorded a monologue entitled "Filthy Words" before a live audience in a California theater. He began by referring to his thoughts about "the words you couldn't say on the public, ah, airwaves, um, the ones you definitely wouldn't say, ever." He proceeded to list those words and repeat them over and over again in a variety of colloquialisms. The transcript of the recording, which is appended to this opinion, indicates frequent laughter from the audience. Respondent Pacifica Foundation, a radio station owned by respondent Pacifica, broadcast the monologue. A few weeks later, a man, who stated that he had heard the broadcast while driving with his young son, wrote a letter complaining to the FCC. Pacifica stated that it could have been the subject of administrative sanctions. The FCC issued a declaratory order granting the complaint and holding that Pacifica had correctly condemned the daytime broadcast as indecent. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the FCC's order was a form of censorship forbidden by § 326 of the Communications Act, and that the broadcast was indecent within the meaning of § 1464. Held: The FCC has no power to regulate a radio broadcast that is indecent but not obscene. Pp. 488-481. (a) The FCC's decision rested entirely on a nuisance rationale under which context is all-important. The concept requires consideration of a host of variables. The time of day was emphasized by the FCC, and the content of the program in which the language is used will also affect the composition of the audience, and differences between radio, television, and perhaps closed-circuit transmissions may also be relevant. When the issue is narrowed to the facts of this case, the question is whether the First Amendment denies government any power to restrict the public broadcast of indecent language in any circumstances. For if the government has any such power, this was an appropriate occasion for its exercise. P. 489. (b) The language used in Pacifica's broadcast was unquestionably "speech" within its meaning, and it is equally clear that the Commission's objections to the broadcast were based in part on its content. The order must therefore fall if, as Pacifica argues, the FCC prohibits all governmental regulation of indecent or obscene language. The fact that society may find speech offensive is not a sufficient reason for suppressing it. Moreover, if it is the speaker's opinion that gives offense, that consequence is a reason for according it constitutional protection. The ease with which children may obtain access to broadcast material, coupled with the concerns recognized in Ginsberg, amply justify special treatment of indecent broadcasting. The danger dismissed so summarily in Red Lion, in contrast, was that broadcasters would respond to the vagueness of the regulations by refusing to present programs dealing with important social and political controversies. Such a danger is not justified by the fact that a broadcast of patently offensive words dealing with sex and excretion may be regulated because their content is so offensive to contemporary moral standards. The plain language of the statute does not support Pacifica. The words "obscene, indecent, or profane" are written in the disjunctive, implying that each has a separate mean ng. Prurient appeal is an element of the obscene, but the normal definition of "indecent" merely refers to nonconformance with accepted standards of morality. The Commission's definition of indecency will deter only the broadcasting of patency offensive references to excretory and sexual organs and activities. While some of these references may be protected, they surely lie at the periphery of First Amendment concern. The mere fact that such references may lie in the periphery is not sufficient reason to suppress the broadcast. The Commissioner's characterization of the Carlin monologue as offensive could have enlarged a child's vocabulary in an instant, and other forms of offensive expression may be withheld from the young without restricting the expression at its source. The language of Pacifica was clearly limited to the obscene. The content of this monologue is not the sort of censorship at which the statute was directed, and its history makes it perfectly clear that it was not intended to limit the FCC FCC's authority to regulate the broadcast of obscene, indecent and profane language. Nor does the Commission’s construction of the statutory language broadly encompass so much constitutionally protected speech that reversal is required even if the broadcast is not itself protected by the First

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Nevada today entered a final judgment against a defendant who pleaded guilty or waiving the right to counsel in a Las Vegas-area criminal case.  The court found that the defendant was competent to stand trial.  According to the court's order, on August 2, 1984, in the early hours of the morning, respondent entered the Red Pearl Saloon in Carson City, Nevada and shot the bartender and a patron four times each with an automatic pistol. He then walked behind the bar and removed the cash register. The court also found that he had a "rational and factual understanding" of the proceedings, and that he was able to determine right from wrong among the options available to him.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for Nevada today announced that it would seek the death penalty against respondent.  On August 13, the court granted certiorari to the defendant and ordered that he be examined by a pair of psychiatrists, both of whom concluded that he is competent to represent himself.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's findings, the defendant consented to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins him from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and orders him to pay a civil penalty of $25,000.  A hearing for the defendant is scheduled for November 28, 2018.  For further information, see Litigation Release No. 5, 2017.

A federal criminal information was filed by the United States against Ludenia Howard, trading as Stokes Fish Company, appellee, in the District Court for the Southern District of Florida, charging her with a violation of the Federal Black Bass Act of May 20, 1926, as amended, c. 346, 44 Stat. 576, 46 Stat. 845, and a criminal penalty imposed by the Florida Legislature for violation. Held: 1. Rule 14.01 of the Commission's regulations, as enforced by § 372.83 of the Florida Statutes, F. S.A., is a "law" of the State of Florida as that term is used in the Federal Act. Pp. 531-532. 2. The phrase "law of the state" as used in this Act is sufficiently broad to encompass the type of regulation used in Florida. P. 532. 3. The rule here involved is of such a character that it should not be considered the law of Florida for purposes of a statute such as the Black Bass. Id. 4. The statute provides that no regulation or amendment to a regulation is effective until 30 days after the filing of a certified copy of such provisions with the secretary of state, and that changes must be published in the county judge's office and that any change in the type regulation involved here is to be filed in the office of each county judge and that "changes must be made in the County judge's order." Id. 5. The rules of the commission are so subject to change that they lack sufficient substance and permanence to be the "law," of Florida. Id., 144 U. S., 1st Sess. 2; Id., 351 U.S. 980, 76 S. C. 1046, reversed and remanded.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the Kiowa Tribe of Oklahoma in a dispute over a business deal with Clinton Sherman Aircraft Company. The court upheld the tribe's immunity from being sued in civil court for off-reservation commercial activities, citing previous rulings that established this principle. However, the court acknowledged that the doctrine of tribal immunity is not absolute and can be altered by Congress if deemed necessary.

After respondent Spink returned to petitioner Lockheed Corp.'s employ in 1991, he learned that he was ineligible to participate in the company's pension plan because he was older than the maximum age allowed by the plan. Under § 1104(a)(1)(D) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA), a plan sponsor may not cause a plan to engage in a "prohibited transaction," i. e., a transaction that constitutes a direct or indirect transfer to, or use by or for the benefit of, a "party in interest," such as the employer. Because Lockheed had altered the terms of its plan to exclude employees over a certain age, it argued that it was acting solely as a settlor rather than a fiduciary, and therefore was immune from liability under § 1104(a)(1)(D). The District Court disagreed, ruling that Lockheed and the Board of Directors breached their fiduciary duties when they adopted the amendments establishing the early retirement programs. On appeal, the Court of Appeals affirmed, concluding that the amendments were void under § 1104(a)(1)(D) because they conditioned the release of employment-related claims by participants on the acceptance of reduced benefits. Held: 1. Nothing in ERISA requires plan sponsors to offer pension benefits to employees beyond a certain age. Although ERISA seeks to assure that employees receive promised pension benefits, nothing in the statute obliges plan sponsors to guarantee benefits to employees past a particular age. Rather, ERISA leaves open the question of the content of benefits to the private parties controlling the plan. See Alessi v. Raybestos-Manhattan, Inc., 451 U.S. 454, 511. Pp. 10-11. 2. Neither Lockheed nor the Board of Directors can be held liable under ERISA's fiduciary rules. An employer acts not as a fiduciary but as a settlor when it amends a pension plan. See Curtiss-Wright Corp.v .Schoonejongen, 514 U. S. ___, ___. There is no reason why the rule of Curtiss- Wright should not extend to pension benefit plans. Moreover, since the Court of Appeals erroneously concluded that the members of Lockheed's Retirement Committee who implemented the amended plan violated § 1104(a)(1)(D)-which applies only to fiduciaries-this Court need not decide whether the committee members acted as fiduciaries when they paid out benefits according to the amended plan's terms. Whatever the precise boundaries of the prohibition in § 1104(a)(1)(D), there is one use of plan assets that it cannot logically encompass: a quid pro quo between the employer and plan participants in which the plan pays out benefits to the participants pursuant to its terms. When § 1104(a)(1)(D) is read in the context of the other prohibited transaction provisions, it becomes clear that the payment of benefits in exchange for the performance of some condition by the employee is not a "transaction" within the meaning of § 1104(a)(1). A standard that allows some benefits agreements but not others, as Spink suggests, lacks a basis in § 1104(a)(1)(D); it also would provide little guidance to lower courts and those who must comply with ERISA. Pp. 11-16. 3. Section 9201 of the Older Americans Reinvestment Act of 1994 (OBRA) and § 9202(a) of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1965 (ADEA), which amended ERISA to prohibit age-based benefit accrual rules, do not apply retroactively. Section 9204(a)(1) of OBRA expressly limits the amendments' temporal scope to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 1988, and to employees having one hour of service in such a plan year. Since the temporal effect of a statute is manifest on its face, there is no need to resort to judicial default rules. Notwithstanding the clarity of § 9204(a)(1), the Court of Appeals believed that the text of §§ 9201 and 9202(a) required retroactive application of the benefit accrual rules. However, when Congress includes a provision that specifically addresses the temporal effect of a statute, that provision trumps any general inferences that might be drawn from the substantive provisions of the statute. Here, even if it were proper to disregard § 9204(a)(1)'s express time limitation in favor of more general language, §§ 9201 and 9202(a) cannot bear the weight of the Court of Appeals' construction. A reduction in total benefits due is not the same thing as a reduction in the rate of benefit accrual; the former is the final outcome of the calculation, whereas the latter is one of the factors in the equation. Pp. 16-17. 60 F. 3d 598, reversed and remanded.

After respondents were arrested on multiple federal criminal charges, the District Court denied their pretrial motions to suppress physical evidence seized during searches conducted without a warrant. Subsequently, the court entered judgments against respondents on the merits, finding that the evidence was admissible under Fed. Rule Crim. Proc. 44(a)(1), which permits admission of physical evidence obtained through a search conducted without a warrant if the defendant consented to the search. On appeal, the Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that the Fourth Amendment barred use of the evidence unless the defendant gave explicit consent to the search. Held: The Fourth Amendment does not require explicit consent to the search. Pp. 10-14. (a) The Fourth Amendment generally bars use of physical evidence obtained through a search conducted without a warrant absent the defendant's voluntary consent. However, the Amendment does not apply to nonconsensual searches conducted pursuant to a valid administrative regulation. Here, the regulations governing the collection of biological samples permit such searches without a warrant if the sample collector reasonably believes that the sample contains controlled substances. Because the regulations are valid, the Fourth Amendment does not bar use of the urinalysis results. Pp. 10-12. (b) The Court of Appeals erred in applying the exclusionary rule to the blood tests, since the Fourth Amendment does not apply to nonconsensual searches conducted pursuant to a valid administrative regulation. Pp. 12-13. 779 F. 2d 143, reversed.

The Committee on Un-American Activities, or any subcommittee thereof, is authorized to investigate "the extent, character, and objects of un-American propaganda activities in the United States, (ii) the diffusion within the United S. of subversive and unAmerican propaganda that is instigated from foreign countries or of a domestic origin and attacks the principle of the form of government as guaranteed by our Constitution, and (iii) all other questions in relation thereto that would aid Congress in any necessary remedial legislation." Held: 1. The subcommittee was without authority to interrogate petitioner, because its purpose in doing so was to investigate public opposition to the Committee itself and to expose him to public censure because of his activities against the Committee. Barenblatt v. United States ante, ante, p. 109. Pp. 110-111. (a) The subcommittee's legitimate legislative interest was not the activity in which petitioner might have happened at the time to be engaged, but in the manipulation and infiltration of activities and organizations by persons advocating overthrow of the Government. P. 111. (b) It was the subcommittee's purpose to investigate the extent of Communist colonization and infiltration in the textile and other basic industries located in the South, and Communist Party propaganda activities, and to investigate into precisely those areas of free speech, religion, peaceful association and assembly, and the press, wherein it cannot legislate and therefore it cannot investigate." P. 112. (c) The Subcommittee was not pursuing a valid legislative purpose, and its interrogation of petitioner did not violate his First Amendment rights of free association and free speech. The Subcommittee's investigation of these subjects, through interrogation of the petitioner, was authorized by Congress, and it was the Committee's purpose, not the subcommittee, to inquire into whether petitioner was an active Communist leader engaged primarily in propaganda activities. The Committee had reasonable ground to suppose that the petitioner was a Communist member, and that as such he possessed information that would substantially aid it in its legislative investigation, and was not compelled to answer the single question "Are you now a member of the Communist Party?" P. 113. 272 F. 2d 783, affirmed.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the two plaintiffs in this case, allowing them to receive money damages from the states for their injuries sustained while working. The ruling overturned a lower court's decision that the states were immune from such damages under the Eleventh Amendment. The Court found that the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) allowed for damages to be awarded against the states, and that the ADA was an appropriate exercise of Congress' enforcement power under section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court further held that the ADA provided for damages to be awarded against the states for violating the rights protected by the Fourteenth Amendment, and that the states had failed to provide adequate accommodations for the plaintiffs' disabilities.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA), after having expressly disavowed any such authority since its inception, asserted jurisdiction to regulate tobacco products. Pursuant to this authority, it promulgated regulations intended to reduce tobacco consumption among children and adolescents. The FDA concluded that, because most tobacco consumers begin their use before reaching the age of 18, curbing tobacco use by minors could substantially reduce the prevalence of addiction in future generations and thus the incidence of tobacco-related death and disease. The agency also concluded that cigarettes and smokeless tobacco are "combination products" because, in addition to containing nicotine, they include device components that deliver a controlled amount of nicotine to the body, id., at 45208-45216. In its rulemaking proceeding, the FDA found that tobacco products are "dangerous" and "unsafe" and that the FDA's access and labeling regulations are permissible, but it also found that the agency's advertising and promotion restrictions exceed its authority under 21 U. S. C. § 360j(e). The court stayed implementation of the regulations it found valid (except the prohibition on the sale of tobacco products to minors) and certified its order for immediate interlocutory appeal. The District Court granted respondents' motion in part and denied it in part. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Congress has clearly precluded the FDA from asserting jurisdiction. Such authority is inconsistent with the intent of Congress, which has expressed in the FDCA's overall regulatory scheme and in the tobacco-specific legislation that it has enacted subsequent to theFDCA. In light of this clear intent, Congress has not given the FDA the authority that it seeks to exercise here. Pp. 5-7. (a) The FDA's assertion of jurisdiction is not inconsistent with Congress' intent to preclude any administrative agency from exercising significant policymaking authority in the area. Congress has enacted several statutes addressing the particular subject of tobacco and health, creating a distinct regulatory scheme for tobacco products, and imposing several tobaccospecific statutes fully cognizant of the FDA position. The FDCA also requires the FDA to place all devices that it regulates into one of three classifications, which the agency relies on to determine the degree of control and regulation necessary to ensure that there is a reasonable assurance that the product's therapeutic benefits outweigh the risk of harm. Thus, if tobacco products were "devices," the FDA would be required to remove them from the market entirely. Moreover, the Act's provisions concerning the misbranding of drugs or devices, which are essentially identical to those in force in 1965, require the FDA "to determine that any regulated product is ...safe" before it can be sold or allowed to remain on the market, and require that all products provide "adequate warnings against use in those pathological conditions or by children where its use may be dangerous to health," id., in order to reduce the level of addiction among tobacco users. The Act also requires that all tobacco products bear adequate directions for use, except where such directions are "not necessary for the protection of the public health." Id., at 44617-44618. Congress, however, has not specifically addressed the question at issue and precluded FDA from regulating tobacco products as customarily marketed. P. 5. (b) In determining whether Congress has spoken directly to the FDA, it is clear that Congress intended to exclude tobacco products from its jurisdiction. Congress enacted a statute reserving exclusive control over both subjects to itself. In addition, Congress enacted several other tobaccospecific legislation, including the Comprehensive Smokeless Tobacco Health Education Act of 1986 (CSTHEA), which essentially extended the regulatory provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) to smokeless cigarettes, and which requires that manufacturers disclose on all packaging and in all print advertising "that cigarette smoking is dangerous." The FDA has consistently asserted that it lacks jurisdiction under §360c(b)(1)(A)(i), and that tobacco manufacturers have designed their products to produce those effects. The FCLAA's regulations, as well as its subsequent tobacco legislation, have effectively ratified Congress' previous position that it lacked jurisdiction under the FDA. The fact that Congress did not intend to delegate a decision of such economic and political significance to an agency in so cryptic a fashion is not determinative, since Congress has acted against the backdrop of its consistent and repeated statements that it does not have authority under the Federal Drug Abuse Act to regulate cigarettes and tobacco products and that such regulation is incompatible with its core objective of ensuring that every drug or device is safe and effective. The same is not true for cigarettes, which Congress has repeatedly asserted that they are safe within the meaning of the Act because, for certain patients, the therapeutic benefits outweighed the risks of harm, and thus such drugs cannot properly be described as being dangerous under § 352(j). Moreover, Congress consistently evidenced its intent of preclude any federal agency from exercise significant policy-making authority. P p. 5–6. (c) Congress has effectively ratified the FDA-and remains-incompatible with FDA regulation of cigarettes.

In the case of Michael H. and Victoria D. v. Gerald D., the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the California Court of Appeal, upholding a California statute that presumes a child born to a married woman living with her husband is a child of the marriage. The statute allows only the husband or wife to challenge this presumption, and only under limited circumstances.

Michael H., who had an affair with Carole D. and believed he was the biological father of her child, Victoria, sought to establish paternity and visitation rights. Victoria, through her guardian ad litem, also sought to maintain relationships with both Michael and Gerald D., Carole's husband. The California courts denied Michael's and Victoria's claims, citing the state's interest in preserving the integrity of the family unit and the marital presumption of paternity.

Justice Scalia, writing for the majority, concluded that the statute did not infringe upon Michael's due process rights, as the state's substantive rule of law deemed it generally irrelevant for paternity purposes whether a child born into a marriage was begotten by someone other than the husband. The Court also found no merit in Michael's claim that he had a constitutionally protected "liberty" interest in the parental relationship he had established with Victoria, as such an interest was not deeply embedded within society's traditions to be considered fundamental.

The Court also rejected Victoria's due process and equal protection claims, stating that the state's decision to limit who could challenge the presumption of legitimacy pursued the legitimate end of preventing disruption to the family unit.

Justice Stevens, concurring in the judgment, suggested that while a natural father might have a constitutionally protected interest in his relationship with a child, the California statutory scheme did not deprive Michael of a fair opportunity to prove his interest in the child's welfare.

The decision emphasizes the state's interest in protecting the marital family and the presumption of legitimacy, and it underscores the historical and traditional importance of these principles in American law. The ruling effectively limits the rights of biological fathers and children to challenge the presumption of legitimacy when a child is born into a married couple's household.
