The Supreme Court of the United States issued a landmark decision in the case of Witherspoon v. Illinois, 391 U.S. 520, 88 S.Ct. 1772, 73 L.Ed. 2d 1056 (1967), establishing the principle known as Witherspoon exclusion. This principle allows a defendant to argue that a juror who has expressed reservations about the death penalty should be excluded from serving on the jury in a capital case. The Court held that the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to an impartial jury, including the right to have jurors who will not impose the death penalty on him. Since then, numerous states have adopted laws allowing for Witherspoon exclusion, and the practice continues to be widely used in the United States.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses a legal challenge to a North Carolina statute that required all closed containers of apples sold or shipped into the state to bear only the applicable U.S. grade or standard, effectively prohibiting the display of state-specific apple grades, such as those from Washington State. The Washington State Apple Advertising Commission brought the action, and a three-judge Federal District Court invalidated the North Carolina statute on the grounds that it unconstitutionally discriminated against interstate commerce.

The Supreme Court considered three main issues: whether the Commission had standing to bring the action, whether the jurisdictional-amount requirement was satisfied, and whether the North Carolina statute constituted an unconstitutional burden on interstate commerce.

The Court found that the Commission did have standing to bring the action on behalf of Washington State apple growers and dealers, as it effectively functioned as a trade association representing their interests. The Court also determined that the jurisdictional-amount requirement was met, as the economic impact on individual growers and dealers due to the statute could exceed the required $10,000 threshold.

On the main issue, the Court concluded that the North Carolina statute unconstitutionally discriminated against interstate commerce. The statute increased costs for Washington apple growers and dealers, deprived them of the competitive advantage of their state's grading system, and had a leveling effect that favored local North Carolina apple producers. The Court held that North Carolina failed to justify the discrimination or show that there were no nondiscriminatory alternatives available to achieve its consumer protection goals.

The Supreme Court affirmed the District Court's decision, upholding the invalidation of the North Carolina statute as it related to the prohibition of displaying Washington State apple grades on containers shipped into the state. Justice Rehnquist did not participate in the consideration or decision of the case.

After seeing a car stop near a streetcorner, one of the occupants of a police cruiser parked nearby observed a man get out of the car and begin to run toward respondent Chesternut, who was standing alone on the corner. Upon catching up with respondent, the cruiser drove alongside him for a short time. During this period, the officers observed respondent discard several packets containing pills. One of them got out of the cruiser to inspect the packets and discovered that they contained codeine. Meanwhile, respondent had begun to walk away. Suspecting that the pills might contain codeine, the officer arrested respondent and searched him after he arrived at the police station. In addition to discovering additional packets of pills, including ones containing heroin and a hypodermic needle, the officers found these items in respondent's pockets. They subsequently charged him with various drug offenses. At a pretrial hearing, the sole witness was the arresting officer, who admitted that there was no probable cause for the arrest. Nevertheless, the Magistrate dismissed the complaint on the ground that the police pursuit preceding respondent's disposal of the packets implicated Fourth Amendment protections and could not be justified by the mere fact that respondent ran at the sight of the police. The trial court upheld the dismissal order. On appeal, the Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that any "investigatory pursuit" amounts to a seizure under Terry v. Ohio, 392 U. S. 1, and that respondent's flight from the police was insufficient, by itself, to give rise to the particularized suspicion necessary to justify this type of seizure. Held: The police conduct in question did not amount to a seizure. Under the "reasonable person" standard set forth in United States v. Mendenhall, 446 U. S. 544, 554, the police can be said to have seized an individual "only if, in view of all of the circumstances surrounding the incident, a reasonable person would have believed that he was not free to leave." Here, although the characterization of the police conduct as a "chase" is not enough, standing alone, to implicate Fourth Amendment protections, the record reflects that the police were not required to have a particularized and objective basis for suspecting respondent of criminal activity in order to pursue him. The police's brief acceleration to catch up with respondent, followed by a short drive alongside him, was not so intimidating that respondent could reasonably have believed that he was not free to disregard the police presence and go about his business. Therefore, the charges against respondent were properly dismissed. Pp. 108-112. 157 Mich. App. 181, 403 N. W. 2d 74, reversed and remanded.

Petitioner was arrested during a gambling raid in 1959 by Hartford, Connecticut police. He pleaded guilty to the crime of pool selling, a misdemeanor, and was sentenced to one year in jail and fined $500. The sentence was suspended after 90 days, at which time he was placed on probation for two years. About 16 months after his guilty plea, petitioner was ordered to testify before a referee appointed by the Superior Court of Hartford County to conduct an inquiry into alleged gambling and other criminal activities in the county. He refused to answer any question "on the grounds it may tend to incriminate me." The Superior Court adjudged him in contempt, and committed him to prison until he was willing to answer the questions. The Connecticut Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination was not available to a witness in a state proceeding, that the Fourteenth Amendment extended no privilege to him, and that petitioner had not properly invoked the privilege available under the Connecticut Constitution. Held: 1. The Fifth Amendment protects the privilege against state invasion of rights enumerated in the first eight Amendments. Pp. 531-532. (a) The privilege of refusing to testify through "sympathy falsely aroused," Spano v. New York, ante, 360 U. S. 46, or other like inducement far short of "compulsion by torture," Haynes v. Washington, supra, it follows a fortiori that it also forbids the States to resort to imprisonment, as here, to compel him to answer questions that might incriminate him. P. 532. 2. The Sixth question, concerning whether petitioner knew John Bergoti, yields a similar conclusion. In the context of the inquiry, it should have been apparent to the referee that Bergoti was suspected by the State to be involved in some way in the subject matter of the investigation. An affirmative answer to the question might well have either connected petitioner with a more recent crime, or at least have operated as a waiver of his privilege with reference to his relationship with a possible criminal. The same standards must determine whether an accused's silence in either a federal or state proceeding is justified, and it must be evident from the implications of the question, in the setting in which it is asked, that a responsive answer to a question or an explanation of why it cannot be answered might be dangerous because injurious disclosure could result, and the person must not have been compelled to incriminating himself. P p. 533. (b) The Sixth and Seventh Amendments are not to be enforced against the States under the Fourth Amendment according to the same standards that protect those personal rights against federal encroachment, since they are not "watered-down, subjective version of the individual guarantees of the Bill of Rights," Ohio ex rel. Eaton v. Price, 364 U.S. 263, 275, and Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U. . .

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed a lower court's dismissal of a complaint filed by an inmate against the Texas Department of Corrections, the prison's director, and the prison hospital's chief medical officer. The complaint alleges that J. W. Gamble was injured on November 9, 1973, while performing a prison work assignment. According to the complaint, he was injured when a bale of cotton fell on him while he was unloading a truck. He continued to work but after four hours he became stiff and was granted a pass to the unit hospital. Within two hours the pain became so intense that Gamble returned to the hospital where he was given pain pills and then was examined by a doctor. The following day, Gamble saw a Dr. Astone who diagnosed the injury as a lower back strain, prescribed Zactirin (a pain reliever), Robaxin ( a muscle relaxant), and placed respondent on "cell-pass, cell-feed" status for two days, allowing him to remain in his cell at all times except for showers. On December 3, Gamble was brought before the prison disciplinary committee for his refusal to work. He told the committee that he could not work because of his severe back pain and his high blood pressure. The committee directed that he be seen by another doctor, who prescribed sodium salicylate for seven days and Ser-Ap-Es for 30 days. On January 7, 1974, he requested to go on sick call for his back pain, and on January 17, 1974, he saw Captain Blunt who prescribed the pain reliever. The next week, he saw Dr. Gray who prescribed Tiognolos (a muscle relaxant). The following week, Gamble went to a Major Muddox who prescribed Febridyne. He refused to work and told him that he was in too much pain to do so. On February 11, 1974, Gamble filed a complaint against the prison and the warden. The district court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. The appeals court held that the complaint could be reinstated. The lower court granted the appeal.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi today entered a final judgment in favor of Mississippi's motion for a temporary restraining order and an asset freeze.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Jackson, Mississippi, alleges that Mississippi violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  In its order, the court held that the federal excise tax is a "user tax" that is imposed solely upon the purchaser-consumer.  According to the complaint, the federal tax is on the producer, not the purchaser.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, filed on May 17, 1965, Mississippi imposed a 5% state excise tax on gasoline sold in the form of "gross proceeds of retail sales" of gasoline.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the Complaint or otherwise, Mississippi has consented to the entry of a permanent injunction against Mississippi from imposing the 5% sales tax, now nine cents per gallon, on the purchaser, and a $10,000 civil penalty for each $100,000 penalty imposed by the federal government.  Mississippi has also agreed to pay a $20,000 asset freeze and a civil penalty of $10 million.  On May 24, 2018, the U. S. District Judge in Jackson granted the SEC request for a preliminary injunction against the imposition of the federal gasoline excise tax, which is subject to court approval.   The court's order, which was entered on May 25, 2017, permanently enjoins Mississippi from future violations of the anti-fraud provisions. Â The SEC's continuing investigation is being conducted by Michael J. Pyszka and supervised by C.J. Kerstetter of the Atlanta Regional Office.

The Supreme Court opinion addresses the constitutionality of a North Dakota statute that allows nonreorganized school districts to charge a fee for school bus transportation. The appellants, a student and her mother, argued that this fee structure violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because it allowed some school districts to charge fees while others could not.

The Court's analysis began by rejecting procedural challenges to the case, such as mootness and estoppel, finding that the appellants were not barred from challenging the statute despite having derived some benefit from it and that there remained an ongoing controversy.

On the merits, the Court applied the rational basis test, the standard level of scrutiny for equal protection challenges to social and economic legislation. The Court held that the statute did not interfere with a fundamental right or discriminate against a suspect class, and therefore did not warrant strict or heightened scrutiny. The Court found that the appellants' argument, which suggested that the fee structure created an unconstitutional barrier to education for poorer families, did not meet the criteria for heightened scrutiny established in previous cases.

The Court also distinguished this case from others where the government was found to have unconstitutionally withheld services from those unable to pay, noting that those cases involved access to the judicial process, which is a unique and exclusive remedy, unlike school transportation where alternatives exist.

The Court concluded that the statute was rationally related to legitimate government objectives, such as encouraging local school districts to provide bus service and managing limited resources. The distinction between reorganized and nonreorganized school districts was found to be rational because it reflected historical agreements and served the purpose of fulfilling reasonable expectations regarding transportation arrangements.

Ultimately, the Court affirmed the judgment of the Supreme Court of North Dakota, holding that the statute did not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because the appellants did not demonstrate that the statute was arbitrary or irrational.

Title 18 U. S. C. §1956(h) criminalizes “any person who conspires to commit” certain money laundering offenses. After being convicted of participating in a money laundering conspiracy in violation of §1956(h), petitioners filed motions to vacate their convictions, arguing that the Government failed to meet its burden of proving an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy. Their motions were denied, and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed, ruling that United States v. Shabani, 513 U. S. 10, distinguished precedent requiring proof of an overt act before a conspiracy can be proved. Held: Conviction for conspiracy to commit money laundering, in violation of §1956(h), does not require proof of an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy. Pp. 4–10. (a) Shabana’s rule—that, absent contrary indications, Congress adopts the common law definition of statutory terms—distills the governing rule for conspiracy statutes. That rule applies here. By choosing a text modeled on §371, which supersedes the common law rule by expressly including an overt-act requirement, Congress got an overt-act requirement. By choosing a text modeled on the Sherman Act, which omits any express overt-act requirement, Congress dispensed with such a requirement. Thus, because §1956(h)’s text does not expressly make the commission of an overt act an element of the conspiracy offense, the Government need not prove an overt act to obtain a conviction. Pp. 4–6. (b) Petitioners’ counterargument—that §1956(h) establishes a new conspiracy offense and thus requires proof of an overt act—is untenable. First, §1956(h)’s text is nearly identical to the drug conspiracy statute at issue in Shabana, which indisputably created an offense. Second, petitioners’ argument is supported by nothing in §1956(h)’s legislative history. Even assuming that the history contained an indication that Congress meant to create a new offense or to eliminate the pre-existing overt-act requirement for money laundering conspiracy prosecutions that hitherto had been brought under §371, the history alone could not overcome the plain and unambiguous meaning of §1956(h)’s text. And the fact that Congress labeled §1956(h) a “penalty,” rather than an “offense” provision, is insignificant. Pp. 6–8. (c) Two additional arguments raised by petitioners relating to the text and structure of §1956as a whole are rejected. First, Congress’ decision to place §1956(h) in a separate subsection rather than with the other money laundering offenses in subsection (a) reflects nothing about whether §1956(h) creates a new offense. Second, §1956(i)’s venue provision confirms the availability of the venue option in money laundering conspiracy cases where an overt act occurred, but does not demonstrate that Congress deemed such an act necessary for conviction under §1956(h). Pp. 8–10. 349 F. 3d 1279, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, Alito, and Souter, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which O’Connor, J., joined.

When petitioner Marrama filed a Chapter 7 bankruptcy petition, he falsely reported that he had paid off a mortgage on his home in Maine and failed to report that he had received rent payments from tenants living elsewhere. His Chapter 7 trustee sold the property to satisfy Marrama’s debts. Later, Marrama filed a Chapter 13 petition, claiming that he had acquired the means to pay down those debts. But respondents, the Chapter 7 trustee and the bank holding the mortgage, moved to dismiss the Chapter 13 case, alleging that Marrama’s false reporting violated the requirements of Chapter 7 and that he had engaged in prepetition bad-faith conduct prohibited by Chapter 13. The Bankruptcy Court agreed and dismissed the Chapter 13 case. The First Circuit reversed, finding that Marrama had an absolute right to convert his Chapter 7 case to a Chapter 13 case under 11 U. S. C. §706(a), which permits a debtor to make such a conversion “at any time” if the case has not previously been converted to Chapter 13. The court concluded that Marrama’s bad-faith conduct did not deprive him of that right. Held: Marrama’s bad-faith conduct did deprive him of his right to convert his Chapter 7 case to a Chapter 13 case. Pp. 4–10. (a) Section 706(a) does not create an unqualified right of conversion. Its reference to an “absolute right” of conversion is more equivocal than petitioner suggests. And although the Senate Committee Report accompanying the provision states that the debtor has an “absolute right” to convert, it also recognizes that the right is limited to a one-time conversion and that the debtor must qualify as a “debtor” under Chapter 13. This latter requirement is met only if the debtor meets the debt limits set forth in 11 U. S. C. §109(e), which governs eligibility for Chapter 13 relief. Because Marrama exceeded those limits, he cannot invoke §706(a) to convert his Chapter 7 case to a Chapter 13 case. Pp. 4–6. (b) Even assuming that Marrama qualified as a Chapter 13 debtor, his bad-faith conduct still deprived him of his right to convert. Prepetition bad-faith conduct is generally considered to be “for cause” under §1307(c), which lists various bases for dismissing a Chapter 13 case. Although §1307(c) does not mention prepetition bad-faith conduct, the Bankruptcy Court’s ruling effectively treats such conduct as impliedly authorized by the phrase “for cause.” Such a ruling is tantamount to a ruling that the individual does not qualify as a Chapter 13 debtor. Thus, the text of §706(d) provides adequate authority for the denial of Marrama’s motion to convert. Furthermore, the broad authority granted to bankruptcy judges to take any action that is necessary or appropriate “to prevent an abuse of process” described in §105(a) is surely adequate to authorize an immediate denial of a motion to convert filed under §706 in lieu of a conversion order that merely postpones the allowance of equivalent relief and may provide a debtor with an opportunity to take action prejudicial to creditors. Here, the debtor’s prior misconduct may provide a sufficient justification for a denial of his motion to convert. Pp. 6–10. 430 F. 3d 470, affirmed. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Stevens, JJ., joined. Souter, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg, J., joined.

While serving as a deputy district attorney, respondent Ceballos received information suggesting that a search warrant obtained by a fellow county employee contained material misstatements. Believing the affidavit supporting the warrant contained serious misrepresentations, Ceballos drafted a memorandum recommending that the warrant be quashed. Although the memorandum addressed the subject matter of Ceballos’ employment, it fell within the scope of his duties as a prosecutor advising his supervisor about how best to proceed with a pending case. Following receipt of the memorandum, Ceballos’ supervisors met with representatives from the sheriff’s department to discuss the memorandum’s implications. One of the sheriff’s department officials challenged Ceballos’ conclusions, prompting a heated exchange during which the sheriff’s representative accused Ceballos of being rude and disruptive. Nonetheless, the prosecutor continued to pursue the case, ultimately obtaining a conviction. Subsequently, Ceballos was transferred to another division, promoted to senior status, and eventually demoted back to his original position. Claiming that he suffered retaliation for making the memorandum, Ceballos filed suit in Federal District Court, asserting a violation of his free speech rights under 42 U. S. C. §1983. The jury awarded damages, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed. Held: The First Amendment does not prohibit managerial discipline based on an employee’s expressions made pursuant to official responsibilities. Pp. 3–11. (a) The First Amendment recognizes that public employees possess certain rights, but it does not empower them to “constitutionalize the employee grievance.” Connick v. Myers, 461 U. S. 138, 154. Instead, the amendment seeks to strike a balance between the individual and societal interests served when employees speak as citizens on matters of public concern and to respect the needs of government employers attempting to perform their important public functions. See, e.g., Pickering v. Board of Education, 391 U. S. 563, 572–573. Here, the controlling factor is that Ceballos’ expressions were made pursuant to his duties as a prosecutor fulfilling a responsibility to advise his supervisor about how best to proceed with a pending case. That consideration distinguishes Ceballos’ situation from those in which the First Amendment provides protection against discipline. Pp. 3–6. (b) When public employees make statements pursuant to their official duties, they are not speaking as citizens for First Amendment purposes, and the Constitution does not insulate their communications from employer discipline. Refusing to recognize First Amendment claims based on government employees’ work product does not prevent them from participating in public debate. Their prospect of constitutional protection for their contributions to the civic discourse remains intact, but it does not entitle them to perform their jobs however they choose. Moreover, giving government employers sufficient discretion to manage their operations is crucial to maintaining effective government. Affordable government employers have heightened interests in controlling speech made by an employee in his or her professional capacity. Official communications have official consequences, requiring substantial consistency and clarity. Supervisors must ensure that their employees’ official communications are accurate, demonstrate sound judgment, and advance the employer’s mission. Ceballos’ proposed contrary rule would commit state and federal courts to a new, permanent, and intrusive role, mandating judicial oversight of communications between and among government employees and their superiors in the course of official business. Such displacement of managerial discretion by judicial supervision finds no support in this Court’s precedents. Pp. 6–10. (c) The First Amendment does not prohibit managerial discipline based on an employee’s expressions made pursuant to official responsibilities. The parties in this case do not dispute that Ceballos wrote his memorandum pursuant to his employment duties. No comprehensive framework exists for defining the scope of an employee’s duties in cases where there is room for serious debate. Nor do formal job descriptions necessarily reflect the duties an employee actually is expected to perform. And although academic freedom may raise special concerns, this Court need not determine whether the analysis applied here would apply in the same manner to a case involving speech related to scholarship or teaching. Pp. 10–11. 361 F. 3d 1167, reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Stevens, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Ginsburg and Breyer, JJ., joined.

Respondent Massey Coal Co. and its affiliates (hereinafter Massey) were found liable for fraudulent misrepresentation, concealment, and tortious interference with existing contractual relations. The jury awarded petitioners Harman Development Corp., Harman Mining Corp., and Sovereign Coal Sales the sum of $50 million in compensatory and punitive damages. In June 2004, the state trial court denied Massey’s post-trial motions challenging the verdict and the damages award, finding that Massey “intentionally acted in utter disregard of [Caperton] rights and ultimately destroyed” its businesses because, after conducting cost-benefit analyses, Massey concluded it was in its financial interest to do so. In March 2005, before Massey filed its petition for appeal in the state court, Caperton moved to disqualify now-Justice Benjamin under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. After the verdict but before the appeal, West Virginia held its 2004 judicial elections. Knowing the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia would consider the appeal in this case, Blankenship decided to support an attorney who sought to replace Justice McGraw. In addition to contributing the $1,000 statutory maximum to the Benjamin campaign committee, he donated almost $2.5 million to “And For The Sake Of The Kids,” a political organization formed under 26 U. S. C. §527. The organization opposed McGraw and supported Benjamin. The judge called the two petitioners before him, but the judge found them untruthful and charged them with perjury. The court denied the motion as a matter of law. In April 2008, the trial court again reversed the jury verdict, and again it was a 3-to-2 decision. The Court granted rehearing, and the parties moved for disqualification of three of the five justices who decided the appeal. Caperton sought rehearing. The parties filed a motion for disqualifications, arguing that Justice Benjamin had failed to apply the correct standard under West Virginia law—i. e., whether “a reasonable and prudent person, knowing these objective facts, would harbor doubts about Justice Benjamin”—but Caperton also included the results of a public opinion poll, which indicated that over 67% of West Virginians doubted Justice Benjamin would be fair and impartial. In Mayberry v. Pennsylvania, 400 U.S. 455, 466, the court reversed, but reversed, based on two independent grounds—first, that a forum-selection clause contained in a contract to which Massey was not a party barred the suit in West Virginia, and, second, that res judicata barred the appeal due to an out-of-state judgment to which respondent was not one a party. The lower court also found that the “possible temptation” the mayor might face was not the real one at work, and dismissed the motion. In December 2006, the Court granted certiorari. The case is remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.

Title: Act of State Doctrine

Summary:

The Act of State Doctrine is a legal principle that prevents US courts from hearing cases challenging the actions of a foreign government within its own territorial boundaries. The doctrine originated in the early 20th century and has been used to shield foreign governments from accountability for human rights abuses and other wrongdoing. Critics argue that the doctrine allows dictatorships to continue committing crimes with impunity, while others contend that it protects the sanctity of sovereignty and promotes stability in international relations. Despite ongoing debate about the effectiveness and morality of the Act of State Doctrine, it remains a fundamental aspect of modern international law.

The Supreme Court held that a dredge, specifically the Super Scoop used in Boston's "Big Dig" project, qualifies as a "vessel" under the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act (LHWCA). The case arose from an injury sustained by Willard Stewart, a marine engineer, who sued Dutra Construction Company under the Jones Act, claiming he was a seaman injured due to negligence. Dutra argued that the Super Scoop was not a vessel under the Jones Act, and the lower courts agreed, denying Stewart's claim.

The Supreme Court disagreed with the lower courts, stating that the definition of a "vessel" includes any watercraft practically capable of maritime transportation, regardless of its primary purpose or whether it is in motion at a particular moment. The Court referenced historical interpretations of the term "vessel" and the Revised Statutes of 1873, which had been used to define "vessel" in maritime law. The Court clarified that the Super Scoop's limited self-propulsion and primary function of dredging did not disqualify it from being a vessel, as it was capable of transporting equipment and workers over water.

The Court also rejected the "snapshot" test used by the lower courts, which focused on whether the Super Scoop was in motion at the time of the injury. Instead, the Court emphasized that a watercraft's status as a vessel is not dependent on its activity at any given moment but on its capability for maritime transport.

The Supreme Court's decision means that the Super Scoop is considered a vessel for the purposes of the LHWCA, and workers injured aboard such watercraft may be eligible for seaman status under the Jones Act, provided they meet other criteria. The case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit has upheld a lower court's ruling that a New York state law prohibiting the sale and distribution of pornography is constitutional. The law, passed in 1954, provides for a limited injunction against the sale or distribution of written and printed matter found after a trial to be obscene. The complaint alleged that the booklets annexed to the complaint, under the general title of 'Nights of Horror,' were "dirt for dirt's sake" and were "clearly obscene." The lower court found that they were obscene and ordered their destruction. The appellants appealed, claiming that the law violated their First Amendment right to freedom of thought and speech. The appeals court found no constitutional infirmity, holding that the lower court had correctly concluded that the "limited injunctive remedy" does not impose an unreasonable prior restraint upon freedom of the press. The court also found that the trial judge had properly concluded that "the primary requirements" of the law are that the publication be of a certain size and volume, and that the material be of the same quality and volume as the original publication. The Court concluded that, in this case, the law does not violate the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment of the United States

The United States Supreme Court ruled in favor of a woman named Cheryl Clark who sought to challenge a Pennsylvania statute requiring illegitimate children to wait until they turn six years old before suing their fathers for child support. The Court determined that the statute violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, stating that it imposed an undue burden on women who wished to pursue legal action against their former partners. The Court cited previous rulings where it had established a framework for evaluating equal protection challenges to statutes of limitations that apply to suits to establish paternity, including the requirement that any time limitation placed on the opportunity to assert a claim must be substantially related to the state's interest in avoiding the litigation of stale or fraudulent claims.

Petitioner, a Negro, was convicted in an Alabama court of burglary with intent to commit rape. Two confessions, allegedly voluntarily given by him, were admitted in evidence over his objection. They consisted mainly of "yes" or "no" answers to leading questions asked him by a policeman and others. Held: Under the totality of the circumstances, including the fact that petitioner was an ignorant and uneducated negro, who was being held incommunicado in a distant state prison, both physically isolated from friends and relatives and legally isolated from the normal safeguards of a preliminary hearing, the use of such confessions violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Pp. 448-454. Reversed and remanded.

In the Supreme Court case concerning the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA), the Court addressed whether the federal criminal offense established by SORNA applies to sex offenders who traveled between states before the Act's effective date. The Act, part of the Adam Walsh Child Protection and Safety Act of 2006, mandates that sex offenders register and update their registration when they travel in interstate or foreign commerce.

The petitioner, Thomas Carr, had traveled from Alabama to Indiana before SORNA was enacted and failed to register as a sex offender in Indiana. He was later charged under SORNA for this failure. Carr argued that applying SORNA to his pre-enactment travel would violate the Ex Post Facto Clause of the Constitution, which prohibits laws that retroactively increase the punishment for a crime.

The Supreme Court held that SORNA's federal criminal offense does not apply to sex offenders whose interstate travel occurred before the Act's effective date. The Court's decision was based on the statutory text, which requires the sequence of events—being subject to SORNA's registration requirements, traveling, and then failing to register—to occur after SORNA's enactment. The Court emphasized the use of the present tense in the statute ("travels") to indicate that it does not include past travel.

The Court rejected the government's arguments that including pre-enactment travel would better serve SORNA's purpose of tracking missing sex offenders and would avoid an anomaly in the statute's coverage of federal versus state sex offenders. The Court found that Congress had a reasonable basis for treating federal and state offenders differently and that the broader statutory scheme of SORNA, not just Section 2250, was designed to address the problem of missing sex offenders.

As a result of the Court's interpretation, the federal criminal liability under SORNA is limited to those who travel and fail to register after the Act's effective date. The Court did not address the Ex Post Facto Clause issue because it determined that SORNA does not apply to pre-enactment travel. The judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit was reversed, and the case was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the Supreme Court's opinion.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment ordering the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to conduct an extensive investigation into the use of mandatory minimum sentencing provisions in federal drug sentencing laws.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in New York, alleges that, from at least August 2010 through August 2010, the federal government unlawfully imposed mandatory minimums on pre- and later-time drug offenders. The complaint alleges that the federal agency charged with creating the mandatory minimum, the Fair Sentencing Act of 1986, improperly imposed a 5-year mandatory minimum and a 10-year minimum for those sentenced after August 3, 2010.  According to the complaint, the new federal minimums imposed by the agency did not apply to pre-Act offenders. Rather, the complaint alleges, defendants with prior drug convictions who had been sentenced prior to August 3 were eligible for mandatory minimum penalties.  In addition, defendants who had previously been convicted of a drug-related felony were not subject to mandatory minimum sentences at the time.  For example, a first-time offender convicted of possessing with intent to distribute 500 grams of crack in August 2010 was subject to a mandatory minimum of 5 years, while an otherwise identical pre-act offender received a 5 year mandatory minimum.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, the SEC consented to the entry of a final judgement that permanently enjoins the agency from violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) of Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder. The final judgment also orders the SEC to conduct a conduct-based investigation and to determine whether there is sufficient evidence to support its findings. The SEC appreciates the assistance of the FBI and the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the city of Macon, Georgia could not be removed as trustee of a park that was to be used only by white people under a will executed by a former senator. The court held that the will did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of equal protection under the law. The case involves an issue of whether the city could be removed from its role as trustee under the terms of the will. The city's position that it could not enforce racial segregation in the park was challenged by members of the park's Board of Managers, who claimed that it violated the laws and public policy of the United States. The high court ruled in favor of the city, holding that the purpose of the trust was clear and that the court could not remove the city as trustee. The justices also ruled that there was no need for the court to appoint new trustees because the city had resigned as trustee and agreed to return the park to the Bacon estate. The Supreme Court's ruling is a significant victory for civil rights activists who have long fought for equal treatment under the laws.

The Mississippi State Tax Commission imposed a markup on liquor sales made by out-of-state liquor distillers and suppliers operating on military installations within Mississippi, in the form of a wholesale markup of 17% to 20% on liquor sold to the installations. The United States asserted before the Commission that the markup was unconstitutional as a tax upon federal instrumentalities, and proposed an escrow account for the amount of the tax pending a judicial determination of its legality. The Commission refused to pay the markup, and the United States thereupon paid the markup under protest. A three-judge District Court granted the Commission's motion for summary judgment. Held: 1. Regulation 25 is an unconstitutional tax upon instrumentalities of the United S. The Twenty-first Amendment prohibits state taxation of instrumentalities. Pp. 531-532. 2. The exception in § 107 (a) is plainly a congressional preservation of federal immunity from any state tax that would violate the principle of McCulloch v. Maryland, supra, prohibiting state taxation. P. 532. 3. The markup is not an unconstitutional state tax on instrumentalities and is not a tax imposed upon instrumentalites of the U. S. Here, the markup is on the seller rather than on the instrumentalities; and the tax upon the sales to the two concurrent jurisdiction bases is not unconstitutional on the purchaser's part, since § 107(a) does not require the markup to be collected by the seller and remitted to the State, and since the tax on the sale to the purchaser is a federal tax, it is not invalid in its imposition of the markup upon the sellers rather than upon the instrumentality of the States. P p. 533. 4. Regulation 26, which provides that no person may be relieved of any sales or use tax levied by a State on the ground that the sale or use occurred in whole or part within a federal area, and that § 105(a)(1) "shall not be deemed to authorize the levy or collection of any tax on or from the States or any instrumentality thereof," does not apply to the markup on the sellers, and is therefore outside the coverage of § 105 (a). P. 530. 5. Regulation, which is not subject to any form of state taxation, does not violate McCulloch's principle that possessions, institutions, and activities of the Federal Government itself in the absence of express congressional consent are not subject thereto. United States v. County of Allegheny, 322 U.S. 174, 177, and Kern-Limerick, Inc. v. Scurlock, 347 US., at 117-118, 74 S. C. 2183, 37 L. Ed. 2d 1, reversed.

After being beaten repeatedly by guards at the Metropolitan Detention Center (ADC) in Brooklyn Park, Arizona, respondent Ali Iqbal filed suit in the District Court, claiming that petitioners Ashcroft, Mueller, and others, acting pursuant to a purportedly secret policy, deliberately inflicted severe physical harm on him because of his race, religion, and national origin. At the time of the assaults, Ali was classified as having “high value information” about al Qaeda, Osama bin Laden’s organization, whose membership included many Middle Easterners. In response to Ali’s request for a protective restraining order, the District Court issued a temporary injunction barring the Government from filing any additional complaints against him. Ultimately, the District Court ruled that the Government failed to satisfy the heightened scrutiny afforded by the Plurality Opinion in Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. __, to the extent that the Government offered evidence that Ali belonged to a group associated with al Qaida. The Eighth Circuit vacated the ruling, reasoning that the Government satisfied the heightened scrutiny standard. The court then reversed the District Court’s permanent injunction, explaining that the Government provided enough evidence to warrant the dismissal of Ali’s complaint. Held: Ali’s complaint fails to plead sufficient facts to state a claim for purposeful and unlawful discrimination against petitioners. Pp. 4−12. (a) Before addressing the substantive merits of Ali’s complaint, the Court must resolve whether the complaint satisfies the formal pleading requirements governing civil actions in the federal courts. Those requirements include the “rule of particularity,” which bars the inclusion of legally irrelevant details and calls for concise expression of essential points, and the “rule of notice,” which prohibits a complaint from stating a claim that a defendant did not know existed. Fed. Rule Civ. Proc. 9(b). More pertinent here, the “rule of relevancy,” which commands that a complaint must relate to a plausible legal theory, see Rule 8(a)(2), guides the assessment of whether a complaint contains enough factual detail to sustain the requested relief. This rule recognizes that a complaint must plead enough factual detail to enable the reader to understand why the complained-about outcome occurred. Blumhofer v. Sebelius, 569 U.S. ___, ___. Thus, although the “rule of relevancy” permits a complaint to rely on “a narrative structure,” Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 164, 179, the complaint must articulate the story’s central point. Id., at 181. Moreover, a complaint that meets the “rule of relevancy” “should focus attention on what happened, not on labels attached thereto.” Wagner v. United States ex rel. Quinn, 569 U.S. ___, ___. Pp. 4−6. (b) The complaint does not satisfy the “rule of relevancy.” Its central point is that the Government intentionally targeted Ali for mistreatment because of his race, religion, and national origin. However, the complaint does not explain why the Government treated Ali differently from other prisoners, except to refer to the fact that he was identified as belonging to a group associated with al Qaida. Given that the Government had already offered sufficient evidence to justify Ali’s dismissal, it is unlikely that the addition of this factual allegation would change the outcome. The “rule of relevancy”’s central point remains undefined, leaving the complaint vulnerable to the very thing it seeks to correct. Pp. 6−8. (c) Ali attempts to distinguish Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, supra, arguing that his complaint presents circumstances different from those involved in that case. Specifically, he emphasizes that the “rule of relevancy” differs from the other rules in that it addresses the substance of the allegations, whereas the other rules deal with procedural aspects of the complaint. Although Twombly recognized that the “rules of relevancy” differ from the other rules, it did not mean that the two types of rules are mutually exclusive. Both share the goal of ensuring that the complaint’s allegations are germane to the relief sought. They also recognize that a complaint must be evaluated according to the degree of factual development, i. e., relevance, of the underlying allegations. Twombly, supra, at 179. Thus, even if the “rule of relevancy” is not identical to the other rules, it shares similarities with them. Pp. 8−9. (d) The “rule of relevancy”’s text supports the idea that it is meant to complement the other rules. Rule 8(a)(2) instructs readers to evaluate a complaint’s factual allegations according to the degree of relevance. Rule 9(b) makes clear that the rule of relevancy includes the rule of particularity. Together, these provisions underscore the importance of focusing on what actually happened. Pp. 9−10. (e) Ali’s claim that the “rule of relevancy” authorizes him to plead his case generically ignores the reality that the rule is intended to promote clarity, accuracy, and precision. Generality is not synonymous with relevance. The “rule of relevancy”’s central point is not advanced by a generic description of the complaint’s subject matter. Instead, the central point is developed by the concrete facts that comprise the complaint. Pp. 10−11. (f) Finally, Ali’s claim that the “rule of relevancy” empowers him to plead the bare elements of his cause of action overlooks the fact that the rule is aimed at promoting clarity, accuracy, and precision. Pleaders are expected to articulate the substance of their claims. See, e. g., Corcoran v. Meeks, 529 U.S. 248, 253. To read the “rule of relevancy” as giving rise to a broad pleading exemption would effectively eliminate the rule of relevancy altogether. Pp. 11−12. Reversed and remanded. Thomas, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer, Kagan, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Alito, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Roberts, C. J., joined.

Case Name: Pittsburgh Coal Company v. Mahon
Case Number: 260 U.S. 414 (1922)
Judge(s): Burton, McReynolds, Van Devanter, Holcomb, Clarke
Issues: Whether the Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Corporation's actions in selling its properties to the Pennsylvania Coal Company constituted a taking?
Background: The Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Corporation sold its properties to the Pennsylvania Coal Company, which planned to open new mines on the land. The Pennsylvania Coal Company wanted to build new structures on top of the old ones, but the Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Corporation objected, claiming that doing so would ruin the structures. The Pennsylvania Coal Company sued the Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Corporation for breach of contract, arguing that the corporation had promised to allow the construction of new structures on top of the old ones.
Reference(s):
https://www.law.cornell.edu/cases/paanthracitecoalcorporationvspennsyliacollectivetrustcompany

The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts today entered a final judgment in favor of a defendant who was found guilty of violating the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Boston, Massachusetts, alleges that two analysts were not subject to confrontation because they were not "conventional" witnesses.  According to the complaint, the analysts' affidavits contained only the bare-bones statement that “[t]he substance was found to contain: Cocaine.”  The complaint further alleges that the analysts provided no corroborating evidence for the analyst’s testimony.  In addition, the complaint alleges that neither the analysts nor the analyst had the capacity to corroborate the evidence presented to the court.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the SEC's Complaint, the defendants have consented to the entry of final judgments that permanently enjoin them from future violations of Sections 5(a), 5(c), and 17(a)(1)(A) and 5(b)(3) of The Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 5b2-1 thereunder, and orders the defendants to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest and a civil penalty equal to the amount of their profits.  Finally, the court granted the defendants a temporary restraining order, which prohibits them from participating in the issuance, purchase, offer, or sale of any security deposit in the name of a federal agency, including the SEC, or any state agency that administers or administers the securities laws.

The United States Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Court of Appeals in a case involving the condemnation of property by the United States for the construction of the Trinity River Dam and Reservoir in California. The property in question was subject to unpatented mining claims held by respondents, and the United States sought to determine the validity of these claims through administrative proceedings before the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) of the Department of the Interior, rather than through the courts.

The Supreme Court emphasized that the Department of the Interior has been granted broad authority over the administration of public lands, including the power to determine the validity of mining claims. The Court noted that a mining claim grants possessory rights to the claimant, but these rights are contingent upon the discovery of minerals within the claim and compliance with statutory requirements. The Court also pointed out that the legal title to the lands remains with the United States until a patent is issued, and until then, the Department of the Interior has the power to declare a claim invalid after proper notice and hearing.

The Court of Appeals had concluded that the validity of the mining claims should be determined judicially because the United States had initiated condemnation proceedings in the District Court. However, the Supreme Court disagreed, stating that there is nothing incompatible between using the courts to obtain immediate possession of the property and using administrative proceedings to determine the validity of the mining claims.

The Supreme Court held that the United States is not precluded from insisting on administrative proceedings to resolve the validity of the mining claims and that the District Court acted appropriately by deferring to the agency's expertise in this matter. The Court concluded that the administrative process prescribed by Congress for perfecting claims against the public domain should be followed, and that judicial review of the administrative decision would be available if necessary.

The implication of the decision is that the United States can proceed with the condemnation of property for public purposes while also allowing the Department of the Interior to determine the validity of any mining claims through its administrative processes. This maintains the established procedure for managing public lands and respects the specialized role of the Department of the Interior in overseeing such claims.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York today entered a final judgment against a defendant who was convicted of the murders of three Gwinnett County, Georgia police officers.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Atlanta, Georgia, alleges that Alfred L. Evans, Jr. of Atlanta, Ga., and his co-defendant, a convicted felon who was later sentenced to prison for the same crime, made false statements to a jury during the concealment phase of the conspiracy.  According to the complaint, Evans and Williams told the jury that they had been engaged in switching the license plates on a stolen car when they were accosted by three prison guards.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, Evans' statement, which was admitted under a provision of the federal law, was false because it was an out-of-court statement, made out of court by one of the defendants, and that had it not been for Evans, he would not be in this now.'  The complaint further alleges that Evans' testimony was not corroborated by any corroborating evidence, and the jury was not allowed to cross-examine the other defendants.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Georgia today announced criminal charges against Evans.  On December 15, 2016, the U. S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Florida entered a temporary restraining order against Evans, freezing his assets, and barring him from participating in any future federal conspiracy trial.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the SEC, Evans has consented to the entry of a judgment permanently enjoining him from future violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and ordering him to pay disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and a bar against him from appearing or practicing before the SEC as an attorney.   The court also issued an order suspending Evans from appearing, practicing, or appearing before the Commission on the subject of a criminal case.

The U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island today entered a final judgment against Pawtucket, Rhode Island, permanently enjoining the city from violating the Establishment Clause of the federal securities laws.  According to the SEC's complaint, filed in federal court in Boston, PawTucket's inclusion of a creche in the city's annual Christmas display violated the antifraud provisions of Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Section 17(a) of Securities Act of 1933 and Rule 17(b)(5) thereunder.  The complaint further alleges that Pawtuck's inclusion violated the religious exemption provisions of Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of its federal securities law.  In a parallel action, the United States Attorney's Office for the Middle District of New York today announced criminal charges against the city for its participation in the display.  Without admitting or denying the allegations in the complaint, Pawtack agreed to the entry of a judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating these provisions and orders it to pay a civil penalty of $1365. The settlement is subject to court approval. The SEC's investigation, which is continuing, has been conducted by John R. Rymas of the Boston Regional Office and supervised by Eric R. Werner of the Market Abuse Unit. The litigation will be led by Mr. Werner. Appellants, Negroes living in Greene County, Alabama, filed this action attacking the constitutionality of the Alabama statutory procedures for selecting grand and petit juries. A three-judge District Court held hearings on the issue of systematic racial discrimination in the jury selection process and found that "there is invalid exclusion of Negroes on a racially discriminatory basis." The court enjoined the jury commissioners and their clerk from systematically excluding Negroes from the jury roll, and directed them to file a new jury list showing the information required by Alabama law for each potential juror, together with his race and, if available, his age, and to submit a report setting forth the procedure by which the commission had compiled the list and applied the statutory qualifications and exclusions. Held: 1. An attack upon allegedly racist jury selection practices by way of a civil suit such as this is permissible. Pp. 10-12. 2. While the guarantee of equal protection of the laws can not be secured only by the total invalidation of the challenged provisions of the Alabama statute, nevertheless the evidence shows that the jury commissioners and their clerk have abused the discretion that the statute confers on them in preparing the jury roll, and thus the statute is not necessarily and under all circumstances invalid. Pp. 12-16. 3. On the record in this case, the District Court correctly ruled that the appellants had not proved a prima facie showing of discriminatory exclusion based on the fact that the jury commission had been composed exclusively of whites for many years. Pp. 16-17. 4. Nor is the absence of Negroes from the jury commission sufficient to warrant the District Court's ordering the Governor to appoint Negroes to the commission. Pp. 17-18. 5. Since the District Court has not yet determined whether the newly compiled jury list comports with the terms of its decree, the cause is remanded to allow the court to make that determination. P. 18. 285 F. Supp. 100, affirmed and remanded.

The U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina today entered final judgments in a libel action brought by a former state attorney against a former federal judge for defrauding others.  The SEC's complaint alleges that, while he was being considered for the position of United States Attorney, William E. Nicholls wrote two letters to President Ronald Reagan.  According to the complaint, the letters falsely accused respondent of "violating the civil rights of various individuals while a Superior Court Judge," "fraud and conspiracy to commit fraud," "extortion or blackmail," and "violations of professional ethics."  The complaint further alleges that the defendants knew that these accusations were false, and that petitioner maliciously intended to injure respondent by undermining his prospect of being appointed United States attorney.  In a parallel action, the U. S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York today announced criminal charges against Nicholls.  As alleged in the SEC's Complaint, filed in federal district court in North Carolina, Nicholls violated the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 10(b) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5 thereunder, and Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of The Investment Advisers Act of 1940.  Without admitting or denying the allegations of the SEC complaint, Nicholl consented to the entry of a final judgment that permanently enjoins him from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, and orders him to pay disgorgement of $1 million, prejudgment interest of $500,000, and a civil penalty of $2 million.  Additionally, the judgment orders Nicholls to pay a $1.5 million civil penalty, which will be determined by the court at a later date.  On May 2, 2018, the Honorable Judge Robert E. Currid of the U District Court in the Western Division of New Jersey issued a temporary restraining order and issued an order temporarily restraining the defendants from further violations of the First Amendment.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Illinois today entered a final judgment against the appellees for violating the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933.  The SEC's complaint, filed in federal district court in Chicago, alleges that, from at least 1951 through the early 1980s, the applees each introduced voluminous cost studies in justification of their pricing systems to show that they were still engaged in illegal price discrimination.  According to the complaint, Borden's pricing system produced two classes of customers, A & P and Jewel, with their combined total of 1,322 stores. The complaint alleges that most of these customers were independent, and that a significant portion of them were grocery store customers.  In addition, the complaint alleges, as a result of the alleged price discrimination, most of the independent stores received the "optional customer services" on a daily basis, thereby raising the average volume of the stores of the smaller of the two chains in relation to the larger independents.  As a result, the defendants were unable to satisfy their burden of showing that their respective pricing plans reflected only a "due allowance" for the difference in price reflected in the price differences between the independent and chain stores.  Without admitting or denying the SEC's allegations, the Appellees each consented to the entry of final judgments permanently enjoining them from violating the charged provisions of the federal securities laws, ordering disgorgement of ill-gotten gains plus prejudgment interest, and imposing civil penalties against each of them.

After serving prison time for involuntary manslaughter, petitioner Judulang sought to enter the United States legally. His visa application was rejected because he had been convicted of a crime of moral turpitude, which rendered him inadmissible under federal law. He then filed a motion to reopen his case, arguing that he qualified for discretionary relief under 8 U. S. C. §212(c), which authorizes the Attorney General to permit individuals who have been lawfully admitted for permanent residence to return to the United States despite their exclusion under §212(a). The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) denied his request, concluding that his conviction fell within a ground of exclusion that lacked a corresponding ground of discretionary relief. On de novo review, the District Court disagreed, finding that the BIA’s ruling conflicted with controlling regulations and case law. The Ninth Circuit reversed, agreeing with the BIA that Judulang’s conviction fell within an exclusion ground lacking a corresponding ground of discretionary relief. Held: The BIA’s policy requiring that an alien’s chances of obtaining §212(c) relief turn on whether the deportation ground charged against him correlates with an exclusion ground is arbitrary and capricious. Pp. 5−16. (a) The BIA’s policy fails the test of reasonableness required by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Its method for determining whether an alien qualifies for §212(c) relief turns on whether the deportation ground charged against him correlates with an exclusion ground. But the BIA has not explained why this correlation is necessary or useful in determining whether an alien deserves to live in the United States permanently. Nor has the BIA shown that its chosen method furthers the purposes of the immigration laws. Instead, the BIA appears to rely on the mistaken belief that §212(c) relief is limited to exclusion grounds. Pp. 5−10. (b) The BIA’s policy is inconsistent with the purposes of the immigration laws. It treats aliens differently depending on whether they have recently left and returned to the United States, thereby creating unequal treatment of similarly situated aliens. Moreover, the BIA’s policy ignores the fact that §212(c) relief is not limited to exclusion grounds. Pp. 10−12. (c) The BIA’s policy is also arbitrary and capricious because it is not moored to the purposes and concerns of the immigration laws. It allows an irrelevant comparison between statutory provisions to govern a matter of paramount importance—whether lawful residents with longstanding ties to this country may stay here. And contrary to the Government’s protestations, it is not supported by text or practice or cost considerations. Pp. 12−16. Reversed and remanded. Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Alito, and Sotomayor, JJ., joined. Breyer, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Stevens, J., joined.

Petitioner Cuellar was stopped for driving erratically in Texas. He claimed to be on a business trip, but he had no luggage or extra clothing with him, and he gave conflicting accounts of his itinerary. When a Spanish-speaking officer asked him about a bulge in his shirt pocket, petitioner produced a wad of cash that smelled of marijuana. After a 2-day trial, the jury found petitioner guilty. The District Court denied petitioner’s motion for judgment of acquittal based on insufficient evidence and sentenced petitioner to 78 months in prison, followed by three years of supervised release. On appeal, the Fifth Circuit reversed, holding that the statute does not require proof that the defendant attempted to “legitimize” tainted funds. Held: 1. The evidence introduced by the Government was not sufficient to permit a reasonable jury to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that petitioner attempted to create the appearance of legitimate wealth. Pp. 5–11. (a) The statute’ “designed … to conceal” element is the common meaning of the term “money laundering.” See American Heritage Dictionary 992 (4th ed. 2000) (defining “launder” as “[t]o disguise the source or nature of (illegal funds, for example) by channeling through an intermediate agent”); Black‘s Law Dictionary 1027 (8th Ed. 2004). The statute prohibits, inter alia, engaging in financial transactions “involv[ing] the proceeds of specified unlawful activity . . . knowing that the transaction is designed in whole or in part to conceal or disguise the nature, the location, the source, the ownership, or the control” of the funds. The statute also prohibits “transportation of illicit funds,” 31 U. S. C. §1956(a)(2)(B)(i), which prohibits the transfer of money derived from unlawful activities. The statutory text makes clear, however, that a conviction under this provision requires proof that “such transportation” was designed to conceal and disguise a listed attribute of the illegally obtained funds. Petitioner argues that this element simply has no basis in the operative provisions of the statute, since it is circumstantial evidence that the ultimate purpose of the transportation—i.e., its “design”—is to conceal that listed attribute. The Government also appears to adopt this meaning, since the evidence introduced to prove this element showed that petitioner engaged in extensive efforts to conceal the funds en route to Mexico, and thus his conviction cannot stand. The Fifth Circuit also rejected as inconsistent with the statutory text that the Government must prove that the transportation was designed “conceal or disguise” the specified attributes of the illegal obtained funds, but it held that petitioner sought to conceal their nature, location, source, ownership, and control. The Court of Appeals reversed, concluding that petitioner knew that taking the funds to Mexico was designed, at least in part, to conceal such an attribute and that the purpose was to create legitimate wealth, but that the evidence was insufficient to sustain his conviction because concealing or disguising the listed attribute could not satisfy the purpose element. The court also held that, even if petitioner had concealed the money in a wallet or concealed it in some other conventional or incidental way, the evidence did not demonstrate that such concealment was the purpose of transportation. The judgment is reversed. 478 F. 3d 282, reversed.

The Supreme Court of the United States issued a landmark decision in the case of Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36 (2004), which established new standards for the admissibility of physical evidence in criminal cases. The Court held that the Fourth Amendment's prohibition of unreasonable searches and seizures applies to the collection and preservation of physical evidence, and that the government must obtain a warrant supported by probable cause before conducting a search or seizing physical evidence. The Court also held that the exclusionary rule, which bars the use of illegally obtained evidence in criminal prosecutions, extends to physical evidence collected through a warrantless search or seizure.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of John Marchetti, who argued that he had a constitutional right to refuse to answer questions about his gambling activities during a grand jury investigation into illegal gambling operations. The court held that the "register and pay" provision of the federal wagering tax scheme violates the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination, as it creates real and substantial hazards of incrimination for individuals involved in legal and illegal gambling activities alike. The court also struck down the argument that the "required records" doctrine applies to the wagering tax scheme, stating that the doctrine is limited to situations where the government seeks access to public documents and cannot assert the privilege against self-incrimination.

While under arrest for an unrelated offense, respondent admitted to investigators that he had broken into the home of Lindsay and Margaret Owens and stolen items from their home. Subsequently, he was indicted for burglary. His lawyer represented him on that charge. Under Texas law, burglary and capital murder are separate offenses. When respondent was free on bond in the burglary case, his father called the county sheriff's office to report that respondent had confessed to killing Margaret Owens in the course of the burglary. Police then interviewed respondent's father and obtained a statement implicating respondent in the murder. Based on that statement, police arrested respondent and read him his Mirandaw rights. Although he waived those rights, respondent eventually confessed to the murders. Respondent was tried and convicted of capital murder. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals reversed, ruling that once the right to counsel attaches to the offense charged, it also attaches to any other offense that is factually related to the offense charged. The court found that respondent's Sixth Amendment right to counsel had attached on the capital murder charge even though he had not yet been charged with that offense. Held: The Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies only to the offense formally charged. McNeilv . Wisconsin, 501 U. S. 171, 175. To allow otherwise would permit law enforcement officers to conduct unwanted and uncounseled interrogations without regard to the fact that a suspect must be apprised of his rights against compulsory selfincrimination and to consult with an attorney before authorities may conduct custodial interrogation. See Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U. S. 436, 479. Furthermore, the Constitution does not negate society's interest in the ability of police to talk to witnesses and suspects, even those who have been charged with other offenses. Adopting the Blockburger v. United States, 284 U. S. 299, test to define an "offense" means that when the Sixth Amendment right to counsel attaches, it encompasses offenses that, even if not formally charged, would be considered the same offense under that test. There is no constitutional difference between the meanings of the terms "offense" in the contexts of double jeopardy and of the right to counsel. Application of the Blockburger test here is straightforward. Burglary and capital murder are not the same offense under Blockburger. Pp. 3-10. Reversed.

Respondents, a husband and wife who use the fictitious name John and Jane Doe, allege that they were once citizens of a foreign country that at the time was considered to be an enemy of the United States, and that John Doe was a high-ranking diplomat for that country. After expressing interest in defection, they were recruited by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to become American spies. Under a promise of financial and personal security, they completed several years of purportedly high-risk, valuable espionage work. However, when they decided to leave the service, the CIA refused to continue supporting them. Asserting that the CIA’s actions violated their procedural and substantive due process rights, respondents then filed suit in Federal District Court, claiming, inter alia, that the CIA had breached its promises. The Government moved to dismiss the complaint under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(1) and 12(b)(6), primarily on the ground that Totten v. United States, 92 U.S. 105, 107–108, barred respondents’ suit. The District Court disagreed, finding that the due process claims could proceed. On renewed motion to dismiss, the District Court reaffirmed that position, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed in relevant part. Held: Suits against the Government based on covert espionage agreements are absolutely barred by Totten. Pp. 4–10. (a) Contrary to the views of both respondents and the Ninth Circuit, Totten was not limited to breach-of-contract claims. Rather, it reflects a broad public policy forbidding the maintenance of any suit “whose trial would inevitably lead to the disclosure of matters which the law itself regards as confidential.” Id., at 107. Public policy forbids the maintenance of any suit in a court of justice that would inevitably lead to the disclosure of matters that the law itself regards as confidential. Pp. 4–5. (b) Nor does United States v. Reynolds, 345 U. S. 1, signal a retreat from Totten’s broader holding that lawsuits premised on alleged espionage agreements are altogether forbidden. Although recognizing “the privilege against revealing military secrets,” id., at 6–7, Reynolds nevertheless declared that Totten—which concerned a contract to perform espionage—was to be dismissed on the pleadings without ever reaching the question of evidence, since it was so obvious that the action should never prevail over the privilege. Moreover, the Court’s subsequent decision in Weinberger v. Catholic Action of Haw./Peace Ed. Project, 454 U. S. 139, confirmed Totten’s continued validity. Here, only in the scenario presented by respondents is Totten’s core concern implicated: preventing the existence of the plaintiff’s relationship with the Government from being revealed. Pp. 5–8. (c) Neither the state secrets privilege nor the more frequent use of in camera judicial proceedings can provide the absolute protection needed to sustain Totten. Allowing suits to proceed and espionage relationships to be revealed increases the risk that the Government will be forced to litigate claims, making it vulnerable to “grey mail”—i. e., individual lawsuits brought to induce settlement out of fear that any effort to litigate the action would reveal classified information that may undermine ongoing covert operations. Requiring the Government to invoke the privilege on a case-by-case basis also risks the perception that it confirms or denies relationships with individual plaintiffs. Pp. 8–9. Reversed.
